title: Karthigai Deepam row: The century-old dispute over a hill in Tamil Nadu, explained

content.value: The Supreme Court, as a one-time measure, has allowed the lighting of a ceremonial lamp at a site in Tamil Nadu’s Madurai district that has long been contested by a Hindu temple and an adjoining Muslim dargah. In its interim order Friday (November 20), the court said only persons authorised by the Subramanian Swamy temple and government officials can perform the ceremony at a disputed stone pillar on Thirupparankundram hill during the Karthigai Deepam festival (on November 24).
The hill is also home to the Sulthan Sikkandar Avulia Dargah.

This is the latest legal chapter in the century-old property disagreement tied to the site. Here’s how the dispute originated, shaped decades of worship at the site, and resurfaced in December last year.
Background of the Thirupparankundram case

Thiruparankundram hill rises about 1050 feet on the outskirts of Madurai. At its base stands the Arulmigu Subramanian Swamy Cave Temple, associated with Hindu worship for centuries. Over time, the hill also became home to Jain rock beds and caves carved over many centuries. At the summit lies the burial site of the Sufi saint Sikkandar Badhusha, where a dargah later came up.

These layers gave the hill more than one identity. It has been referred to as “Samanar Hill” for its Jain associations and “Sikkandar Hill” after the Sufi saint. It has also been a site that regularly requires police deployment during festivals, when questions of access and movement tend to surface.
The hill’s legal history dates back to a civil suit filed in 1920, in which the Arulmigu Subramanian Swamy Temple Devasthanam, which administers the temple, claimed title over the entire hill.

In 1923, the trial court ruled that most of the unoccupied hill and the pilgrim path were temple property, while the topmost peak, the area around the mosque, the Nellithope area, and the steps leading to the mosque were Muslim property. This arrangement became the basis for later disputes.
Earlier disputes
Litigation over Thiruparankundram continued over the decades.

In 2021, a dispute arose over replacing a wooden flagstaff at the dargah with an iron one. In early 2025, another controversy followed an attempt to perform animal sacrifice at the hilltop, which a three-judge Bench later prohibited, noting that the hill is a protected monument under rules of the Archaeological Survey of India.

The present dispute centres on the lighting of a festival lamp at a stone pillar near the hilltop. The pillar is said to be a Deepathoon, a ceremonial structure meant for lighting lamps. It is located approximately 50 metres from the dargah.

Records placed before the court showed that attempts to light lamps near the summit were stopped by authorities in the 19th and early 20th centuries, citing the absence of established custom and public order concerns.

The issue returned to court in 1994, when volunteers sought to light a Deepam at the peak. In a 1996 judgment, the High Court directed that the Karthigai Deepam be lit at a different site on the lower slopes, near the Uchipillaiyar Temple. It also allowed the Devasthanam to consider alternative locations, provided the “suitable place [is] at least 15 metres away from the Dargah, the flight of steps and the Nellithope area”.
For decades, therefore, the Deepam was lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple.
How the Thirupparankundram dispute resurfaced
Against this backdrop, a group of worshippers approached the court in late November 2025 seeking permission to light the Karthigai Deepam on December 3 at the “Deepathoon” on the hilltop.
On December 1, a single-judge bench allowed the petitions, viewing the act as a restoration of religious practice and directing the temple management to light the lamp with police assistance.

“Karthigai is also a festival of light. Lamps are lit all over the house and not in the pooja room alone. The Karthigai Deepam shall be lit from this year onwards at Deepathoon also,” the court said. When temple authorities expressed difficulty in implementing the order, citing law-and-order concerns, the judge initiated contempt proceedings and permitted a small team to climb the hill under security cover.
State objections

The state government and the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department challenged the order, arguing that disputes over custom and usage must be decided under the HR&CE Act and not through writ proceedings. They also questioned whether the pillar was religious in nature, suggesting it could be a survey marker or a remnant linked to Jain use.

Citing concerns over crowd control and public peace, the police imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita. The lamp was not lit on the festival day last year, leading to appeals by the State, the HR&CE Department, and representatives of the dargah.
What the Division Bench held
A Division Bench of the Madras High Court then ruled on the matter earlier this year.
It held that the structure was a Deepathoon, noting that it had a carved cavity capable of holding oil and wicks, and rejected the claim that it was merely a survey marker.

On law and order, the court said the administration’s apprehensions were “nothing but an imaginary ghost,” adding that allowing a small team of temple officials to go up the hill once a year could not be considered unmanageable.

At the same time, the court modified the single judge’s order, directing that the Devasthanam may light the lamp at the Deepathoon only through a limited team, with no public access. The District Collector was asked to coordinate the exercise, subject to conditions imposed by the Archaeological Survey of India to protect the monument.
How the matter reached the Supreme Court
In June this year, the Tamil Nadu government challenged the Division Bench’s ruling.
The dargah authorities and other parties also approached the apex court.

The Tamil Nadu government contended on Wednesday that allowing the lamp-lighting at the stone pillar near the dargah could lead to thousands of survey pillars across the country acquiring a religious character.

Hearing the matter ahead of this year’s Karthigai Deepam festival, the Supreme Court on November 20 passed an interim order allowing the lamp to be lit at the disputed pillar on November 24, but only as a one-time measure and subject to safeguards.
The top court, however, stayed the Madras High Court judgment allowing the lighting of the lamp at the “Deepathoon”.

title: Why common infections are becoming harder to treat in India: ICMR scientist explains

content.value: It has long been known that India faces a challenge from antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a condition where microbes evolve to resist drugs, often owing to the overuse of antibiotics.

But a new report from the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) underlines how big that challenge really is, showing that several common bacteria responsible for both routine and serious infections are now no longer responding to antibiotics that doctors have regularly used for years.

The ICMR’s Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance and Research Network (AMRSN) Annual Report 2025 found particularly low effectiveness of several antibiotics against E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, both responsible for pneumonia, urinary tract and bloodstream infections. It also highlighted worrying resistance to powerful antibiotics such as carbapenems, particularly among bacteria associated with hospital-acquired infections.

For the first time, the report included data from 34 secondary-care hospitals, showing that resistance to commonly used antibiotics is also a concern beyond large, specialised hospitals. The findings are particularly worrying for critically ill patients and newborns, while underscoring the need for better diagnosis, responsible antibiotic use and stronger infection prevention measures.

Dr Kamini Walia, Scientist G & Head, Descriptive Research Division, ICMR, discusses the implications of the findings, why routine infections are becoming harder to treat and what India needs to do to contain the growing threat.
The report shows high resistance to commonly used antibiotics among bacteria such as E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. What does this mean for patients who develop these infections?

Infections caused by E. coli and Klebsiella are very common in India, both among patients admitted to hospitals and those who are not hospitalised. The growing resistance of these two bacteria to important antibiotics is a matter of serious concern for the general public. This makes quicker diagnostics and preventive healthcare imperative.
Does this mean routine infections are already becoming significantly harder to treat?

We have already reached that point. It is high time antimicrobial resistance becomes a priority in healthcare discussions. Infections caused by drug-resistant bacteria are difficult to treat because commonly used antibiotics may no longer work. The alternative medicines, often referred to as last-resort antibiotics, are expensive, carry a higher risk of side effects and may not be as effective.
What are the main reasons behind the declining effectiveness of third-generation drugs like cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones?

The main driver of antimicrobial resistance is the misuse of antibiotics, particularly prescribing or taking them for illnesses that do not require these medicines. For instance, antibiotics do not work against viral infections such as most cases of viral fever. Many diarrhoeal illnesses also do not require antibiotic treatment. Other important factors include poor infection prevention practices, such as inadequate handwashing and respiratory hygiene, as well as the use of antibiotics in animal farming.
The 2025 report includes data from 34 secondary-care hospitals for the first time. What do these findings tell us about antimicrobial resistance beyond major hospitals?

The new data show that resistance to third-generation cephalosporins is very high even in secondary-care hospitals. Carbapenem resistance, however, largely remains a problem in larger, specialised hospitals.
Were any findings particularly surprising? What should district hospitals and smaller healthcare facilities do in response?

We expected to find better effectiveness of third-generation cephalosporins, but clearly that is not the case. It is high time district hospitals and smaller healthcare facilities set up hospital infection control committees and antimicrobial stewardship committees. They need to introduce measures to identify infections early and take the necessary steps to control antimicrobial resistance.
Why are hospital-acquired infections proving so difficult to treat?

The first-line and second-line antibiotics commonly used to treat infections often do not work against hospital-acquired infections caused by resistant bacteria. Doctors are then forced to use third-line antibiotics, which are often the last available treatment option. These medicines are expensive, may be less effective and are associated with a higher risk of side effects.
The report identifies Klebsiella pneumoniae as the leading bacterium found in newborns with bloodstream infections, with worrying resistance patterns. How serious is the threat to newborns?

Klebsiella pneumoniae is a common cause of infections in both adult and newborn intensive-care units. It is known to develop resistance to several drugs and can lead to high mortality. We are still analysing nationwide data from neonatal intensive-care units (NICUs) to get a clearer picture of antibiotic resistance patterns in newborns. Current treatment protocols may need to be adjusted according to what these findings reveal.
How can doctors make better antibiotic choices when resistance patterns vary across regions and hospitals?

Doctors need to be aware of local antibiotic resistance patterns, known as antibiograms. These show which antibiotics are working against common bacteria in that particular hospital. Resistance patterns can differ between a district hospital, a large referral hospital and an intensive-care unit. Knowing these local patterns can help doctors make better initial treatment choices.

Hospitals should also invest in diagnostic tests that can provide results quickly, helping doctors choose the right antibiotic. Doctors must distinguish between initial treatment and treatment based on confirmed laboratory results. When a patient is seriously ill, doctors may have to start antibiotics before knowing exactly which bacteria are responsible. This is called initial or empirical treatment. Once laboratory results become available, the treatment should be reviewed and changed if necessary, so that the patient receives the most appropriate antibiotic rather than a broader or stronger medicine without reason.
Beyond surveillance and awareness campaigns, what policy and healthcare interventions should be prioritised?
Antimicrobial stewardship programmes should be made compulsory in all hospitals. There should also be a compulsory certificate course for all doctors who prescribe medicines.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

Adult vaccination against influenza (flu), typhoid and pneumococcal infections should be encouraged. High-quality infection prevention and control practices are equally important. Drugs reserved for serious infections should be prescribed judiciously, based on laboratory results wherever possible, rather than simply because a resistant infection is suspected.

Doctors should not assume that the same antibiotic will work equally well in every hospital or region. Treatment decisions must take into account the type and seriousness of the infection, the bacteria likely to be responsible, local resistance patterns, the patient’s medical history and previous antibiotic use.

Finally, the choice of antibiotic must depend on where the infection is located. A medicine that works for a simple urinary tract infection may not be suitable for a kidney infection, a bloodstream infection or an infection involving the brain. Doctors must consider the site and seriousness of the infection rather than relying on a single antibiotic for different conditions.

Laboratory testing can also help identify the reasons behind antibiotic resistance. Some tests look for specific changes in bacteria that make certain medicines ineffective. These findings, along with routine laboratory tests that check whether an antibiotic can stop the bacteria from growing, help doctors make better treatment decisions.

title: NEET-2027: What reforms could be proposed, what more needs to be done

content.value: Recurring controversies over the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) have exposed persistent vulnerabilities in India’s public examination system. The NEET-2024 examination, which saw paper leaks, exam malpractices, and candidates getting abnormal scores, led to the constitution of the Radhakrishnan Committee — whose 101 recommendations pertained to exam reforms.

Yet, the NEET-2026 examination in May was marked by allegations of paper leaks and cancellations, and the subsequent retest (Re-NEET) in June was followed by widespread student protests. Repeated and incorrect questions as well as answer-key discrepancies have further undermined confidence in competitive examinations.

In July 2026, the government constituted a Nandan Nilekani-led High-Powered Task Force (HPTF) to recommend comprehensive reforms in public examinations, including those conducted by the National Testing Agency (NTA). Its initial deadline of October 2026 for submitting its report has been extended to January 2027 after receiving over 50,000 suggestions and extensive stakeholder consultations.

With no interim report publicly available, NEET-2027 candidates face considerable uncertainty. With computer-based testing (CBT), a secure question vault, last-minute paper assembly, and digital delivery among the reported proposals, we look at what reforms are likely to be considered, their limitations and challenges, and what needs to be done to restore fairness and institutional accountability beyond NEET-2027.
Why have earlier reforms failed to prevent recurring NEET crises?
Following the NEET-2024 controversy, the Dr Radhakrishnan Committee recommended reforms covering examination security, technology, infrastructure and institutional processes.

But the NEET-2026 crisis raises questions about their implementation and oversight. Vulnerabilities exist across the examination chain — from question setting and review to transportation, storage, examination-centre management, and evaluation. Allegations of insider involvement make these particularly serious.
New recommendations will have little value unless earlier failures are investigated, institutional responsibility is established, and proposed reforms are rigorously piloted.
Is CBT feasible for NEET?

CBT reduces dependence on physical printing, packaging, transportation, and storage, while enabling computerised administration, controlled access, and automated evaluation. But it introduces digital vulnerabilities, system failures, and cybersecurity risks.

A nationwide examination requires adequate centres, secure systems, reliable power and connectivity, trained personnel, and contingency arrangements. Uneven infrastructure and varying computer familiarity among candidates also raise concerns about accessibility and fairness.

CBT’s feasibility must be established through infrastructure assessment, large-scale pilots, and independent technical audits. Changing the examination format alone cannot guarantee security or fairness.
Can a question vault and last-minute digital delivery secure the question paper?

Security must begin with question creation and validation, not merely paper transportation. Question setting, review, syllabus alignment, translation, and answer verification are all potential points of compromise, particularly with concentrated access.

A proposed question vault would maintain a large pool of independently vetted questions. The final paper could be assembled shortly before the examination, encrypted and digitally transmitted to centers, thereby reducing advance access and dependence on physical transport.

The question paper repository, selection software, servers, encryption keys, and transmission networks require restricted access, traceable operations, and independent cybersecurity audits. Ultimately, security depends on the entire chain — from question setters and validators to final selection and delivery.
How can fairness be ensured across multiple CBT sessions?
Multiple NEET sessions require different question papers, yet all candidates must compete on a common merit list. Ensuring equivalent difficulty is therefore a major challenge.

Statistical normalisation, potentially using percentile scores, may help compare performance. But its reliability depends on the comparability of the papers and on statistical assumptions. Even small adjustments can affect ranks and admission prospects.

Through rigorous pilots and independent validation, NTA must establish that papers have comparable syllabus coverage, difficulty, and discriminatory power. The methodology and its limitations must be transparent and auditable. Normalisation cannot compensate for fundamentally unequal question papers.

Beyond technical reforms, changes to eligibility, examination schedules, sessions, and format could further reduce vulnerabilities. Such changes require advance notification and phased implementation. In the absence of timely official announcements, major structural changes to NEET-2027 should be ruled out.
Can a two-stage NEET examination address normalisation concerns?

A two-stage examination, on the lines of IIT-JEE (Mains and Advanced), is one possible alternative. All eligible candidates would appear in a screening examination (Mains), followed by a final examination for shortlisted candidates (Advanced) based on predefined cut-offs or a specified number of qualifiers. A single-session final examination does not need normalisation.

This model raises questions about shortlisting, eligibility, syllabus, question paper format and difficulty, scoring, and cut-offs. It would increase examination overheads but improve fairness in rankings for top scorers.
Should Class XII marks carry weightage in NEET? Can NEET be conducted twice a year?

On Tuesday (November 17), The Indian Express reported that providing weightage to Class 12 board exam scores in NEET-UG has emerged as a key proposal from several states during “consultative meetings” held so far with the Nilekani-led task force. Another proposal discussed was offering more than one attempt in a year.

Weightage to Class XII marks could recognise sustained academic performance, but variations in board examinations and marking standards make equitable weightage difficult. Conducting NEET twice a year could offer candidates another opportunity to improve their scores, but would increase logistical costs and raise concerns about normalisation and admission timelines.
A two-stage NEET, along the lines of IIT-JEE, could address both concerns: Class XII marks could be used in determining eligibility for the second-stage single-session examination.
Could the HPTF recommend changes to eligibility, attempts, or age limits?

With over two million candidates competing for limited medical seats, NEET’s unlimited attempts and the absence of an upper age limit raise questions about the examination’s capacity and the size of the candidate pool. Candidates can appear repeatedly, irrespective of age, even beyond 60.
Age limits and attempt restrictions, common in most competitive examinations, could help narrow the candidate pool.
Can GenAI improve question generation and the quality of examinations?

Conventional software can select pre-vetted questions from a secure vault without GenAI. GenAI could assist in question generation, syllabus mapping, translation, preparing answer options, and calibrating difficulty, creating a larger, more diverse question pool.

AI-generated questions, however, may contain factual errors, ambiguities, incorrect answer keys, syllabus errors, or translation defects. Expert validation is essential; AI may assist question development.
What should the HPTF deliver to restore confidence in public examinations?

The Nilekani-led HPTF must provide a time-bound implementation roadmap that defines institutional responsibilities, resources, technical safeguards, independent oversight, and accountability. Major reforms must undergo large-scale pilots before nationwide implementation.

NTA also needs permanent expertise in examination management, cybersecurity, psychometrics, digital forensics, and vigilance. The HPTF’s success must ultimately be measured by whether examinations become secure, transparent, reliable, and fair. India needs not merely new examination technology but also trustworthy examination standard operating procedures and institutions.

The author is a former computer science professor at IIT Kharagpur, IIT Kanpur, BITS Pilani and JNU, and a former scientist at the Defence Research and Development Organisation and the Department of Science & Technology.

title: Why have gold prices fallen by 25% in nine months, and could they dip further?

content.value: Gold prices (quoted here in Rs per 10 grams of 24k gold in the Delhi market) have crashed by around 25% between February 28 and November 20, marking a sharp correction. Gold owners are understandably worried about whether prices will fall further, while prospective buyers are considering whether the current dip is a good opportunity to buy gold.
The answers to both questions lie in understanding not just why the gold price is falling but also why it rose remarkably in the past few years.
Recent trend
As CHART 1 shows, gold prices have fallen from Rs 1,70,305 per 10 gm on February 28 — when the US and Israeli forces attacked Iran — to Rs 1,26,875 on November 20, according to Google Finance.

However, it would be misleading to only look at the fall without the background. The fact is that gold prices had risen from Rs 51,715 on February 26, 2022, to Rs 64,185 on February 24, 2024, to hit all-time highs this February.
By February 2026, gold prices had grown by 165% in the past 2 years and by 230% in the past 4 years.
The spike has been such that even after the fall, gold prices are up 145% since February 2022 and 98% since February 2024. A 100% increase essentially means doubling of prices.

Two things become clear: The fall in 2026 is quite sharp, but it is happening in the context of an even more exceptional run-up in prices. The reasons for the fall and the future outlook cannot be understood without understanding what factors led to this spike in the first place. That, in turn, has to do with understanding why anyone buys gold at all.
Sources of gold demand
According to the World Gold Council, on average, the net annual demand for gold is around 3,200 tonnes, thanks to four main sources (See CHART 2):
*Jewellery (27% of the total demand)
* Use in technology (8%),
* Purchases by central banks (21%)
* Investment demand (43%)

To be sure, “investment” demand for gold is essentially about using gold as a hedge against other actual investments. At a fundamental level, buying gold itself does not give a return — unlike, say, buying a government bond or the shares of a company. Gold’s real worth is in its ability to be a very good store of value.

For instance, a Rs 100 note typically loses value over a year because of inflation. A year later, the thing you could buy for Rs 100 most likely requires you to pay Rs 105. But if you had exchanged Rs 100 for gold worth Rs 100 in the first year, then chances are that in the second year, that bit of gold would be worth at least or more than Rs 105. That is what it means to be a store of value.

According to the World Gold Council, data since 1971 shows that gold prices have outpaced the US and world consumer price indices (read inflation). In fact, higher the inflation, better the returns that gold provides (See CHART 3). It is this unique ability of gold that makes everyone flock to it during periods of high inflation and uncertainty.
Factors for sharp fall
On the face of it, it seems odd that just when the world started spiralling into great geopolitical uncertainty and higher inflation, gold prices started falling.
The central reason, as explained in a research note by Erik Norland (Managing Director and Chief Economist, CME Group), is “the shift in expectations from (interest) rate cuts to rate increases.”

Norland points out that gold prices, as well as prices of other precious metals, started faltering as soon as the news of Kevin Warsh becoming the new head of the US Federal Reserve came to light. Up until that moment, everyone expected inflation to continue to rise, with the Fed not acting to contain inflation.

But Warsh came with a reputation of being a monetary hawk — someone who likes to keep inflation in check. Despite being the choice of US President Donald Trump, who was critical of raising interest rates, Warsh has led the Fed towards higher interest rates to contain inflation.

“Since his taking the helm, the Warsh Fed first ended the central bank’s easing bias in June and then actually raised rates in September while signaling a likelihood of further rate hikes to come,” points out Norland. In fact, the market now expects the Fed to continue raising interest rates for the coming 12 to 24 months (See CHART 4) by as much as an additional percentage point.
Higher interest rates can provide an alternative to investing in gold: higher the interest rates, lower the attractiveness of gold.

Moreover, the shift in expectations about inflation — that inflation will now be curtailed — has dragged back gold prices. It is noteworthy that the US Fed is not the only central bank raising interest rates; central banks of all major economies, from the Bank of Japan to the European Central Bank, have been ahead of the US in raising rates.
Outlook for gold prices
Seen in this context, the question isn’t why gold prices are falling but why they still remain so high. In other words, can they fall further?

There were four factors that spiked gold prices in the past few years. One, massive borrowings by governments of major economies. High borrowings push up inflation. Two, inflation rates — both headline and core (that is, after taking away the effect of fuel and food prices) — have been above the target rates in most countries. Three, geopolitical volatility. Typically, gold prices outperform most other investments during phases of high uncertainty. Four, purchases by central banks. Central banks have been net buyers of gold since the 2008 financial crisis (see CHART 5). With gold prices cooling off, that trend may resume.

Looking ahead, while rising interest rates will weaken gold prices, as they have done in 2026, other factors — reckless borrowings by governments, geopolitical uncertainties, and central bank purchases — are all still in play. It is the interplay of these factors that will decide what happens to gold prices.

title: Power shortage looms: Why states are flocking to spot market as coal stocks dip

content.value: A looming power shortage, triggered by a shortage of baseload thermal capacity and mounting worries over coal stocks, has spurred a flurry of high-level meetings at the Centre.

With the states now being directed to secure electricity at all costs, the worries about an impending electricity shock early next summer have triggered a panic reaction that is reverberating across the country’s electricity ecosystem.

Multiple states are turning to short-term power procurement tenders, mostly at exorbitant prices, to secure additional electricity for the coming months and guard against potential shortages, particularly during evening peak hours.

Data from the Ministry of Power’s DEEP (Discovery of Efficient Electricity Price) portal showed that tenders have been floated for power procurement by at least five states and private distribution utilities for additional power during the months of January, February, March, April, May and June-July next year. The states seeking to procure additional power include Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Rajasthan and Gujarat.
Uttar Pradesh is also learnt to be vying for securing additional power ahead of the state elections early next year.
Here is why power prices are surging in short-term tenders, how sharply coal stocks have depleted at thermal plants, and what past policy missteps left the grid vulnerable.
Why power prices are soaring in short-term tenders

Private distribution companies, including Noida Power Company Ltd and Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd (AEML), have also floated tenders. Prices discovered in some of these tenders have touched Rs 19-20 per unit, significantly higher than the price caps applicable in power exchanges.

While the cap on spot prices is Rs 10 per unit, prices can go up to Rs 20 per unit in the specialised High Price Day-Ahead Market (HP-DAM). Also, amid a decline in coal stocks, the government is also discussing measures to expand coal storage capacity at thermal power plants beyond the prescribed normative requirement, The Indian Express has learnt.

While the normative requirement is around 59 million tonnes (mt), thermal power plants currently have the capacity to store up to 80 mt, equivalent to about 30 days of consumption. Discussions are also underway on doubling this capacity to 160 mt, which would provide up to 60 days of coal stocks. However, such an expansion would require additional storage space at thermal power plants.

While sporadic instances of rains may have helped mitigate the shortage this year, there are concerns about a problem from early next summer. Grid India’s daily frequency profile data is showing even during these somewhat lean demand months real-time frequency is falling to below the mandated lower limit of 49.9 HZ even during solar hours (when solar generation is available). The situation during the non-solar hours (evenings, when solar generation is not available) is even more precipitous.
Coal stocks at thermal plants fall sharply, raising shortage fears

The increased dependence on coal-based generation has put pressure on coal inventories at thermal power plants. Stocks declined by around 66% between April and September this year, compared with a fall of around 23% during the same period last year, when inventories dropped from 55.2 mt at the beginning of April to 42.6 mt by September end.
The corresponding declines during the same period were 31.8% in 2024 and 36.8% in 2023.

As of November 15, coal inventory at domestic coal-based power plants stood at 20.79 mt, down from around 55 mt at the beginning of April. Officials in the Ministry of Power have also maintained that rebuilding coal stocks ahead of next summer is among the key priorities given the current circumstances.
The fresh directive to ramp up coal storage capacity comes in this backdrop.
How past policy decisions left India vulnerable to a power crunch

Internally, the Union Power Ministry’s planning body — the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) — has already given a broader call for a reassessment of planned coal-based capacity additions, even as the country continues to expand its renewable energy capacity.

With India staring at a power shortage, CEA chairperson Ghanshyam Prasad had flagged the need to to add 105-150 gigawatts (GW) of coal-based power capacity by 2035, significantly higher than the 97 GW currently planned, at a meeting on October 13.

India’s focus on rapid expansion of renewables in the absence of energy storage systems is making the electricity grid increasingly unstable. The issue is compounded by a policy decision from around ten years ago to scale down thermal expansion, which provides critical baseload support to the grid during evenings in summer months, when solar generation dips and demand remains high.

The Union Power Ministry’s National Electricity Plan (2017-22) had ruled out fresh thermal capacity additions beyond 2022, apart from the 50 GW of under-construction projects. It mainly focused on scaling up renewables. Additionally, imported coal-based projects were actively discouraged, primarily in the wake of spiralling global coal prices.

Since the planning misstep of 2016-17, some corrective measures have been taken: a renewed push for nuclear generation in fleet mode, a belated drive to add large thermal capacities, importing coal to restart idle plants, and renewed policy pivots such as the CEA’s directive from last year that mandated storage for all new solar projects.

title: How EPFO’s new plan for PF withdrawals will work

content.value: The Central Board of Trustees (CBT) of the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) held its 240th meeting on Thursday (November 19) to discuss the key proposal of allowing a systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) with periodic payouts at the time of retirement instead of lump sum withdrawal of the entire corpus.

The EPFO also eased withdrawal rules by reducing the minimum balance requirement to 10% from 25% — a reversal of its earlier decision that had faced social media backlash and criticism from Opposition parties at the time of its announcement last year. There was also relief provided to those who opt for premature final settlement, especially after being unemployed, with a reduction in the waiting period for final provident fund settlement.

Members will now once again be allowed to claim premature final settlement of their provident fund after remaining unemployed for two months, instead of the 12-month waiting period introduced in October 2025 for full withdrawal. The minimum waiting period for final pension withdrawal will remain 36 months.
Systematic withdrawal plan

The SWP proposes to allow retiring members to retain their savings within the EPF ecosystem, continue earning EPF interest, and receive post-retirement income without surrendering ownership of the residual corpus. Multiple withdrawal options are proposed to be provided to EPF subscribers: full systematic withdrawal, or partial lump-sum withdrawal with SWP for the balance, or interest-only withdrawal models. Under the SWP, the retiring members will be able to withdraw their accumulated PF savings at regular intervals, such as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, based on their preference.

The facility would be “entirely voluntary, with no compulsion on members to opt for withdrawals”, the Ministry of Labour and Employment said in a statement. The option may also be extended to eligible family members and beneficiaries, for greater flexibility and financial security for the family. “This aims to ensure stable post-retirement income, reduce reinvestment risks, strengthen fund sustainability and facilitate the extension of social security coverage to gig and platform workers,” it said.

Also, the SWP proposes to allow the members to make voluntary contributions directly into their EPF accounts through digital channels designated by EPFO independent of employer payroll systems. Such contributions would not require employer matching contributions and would be credited directly into the member’s provident fund account.

The retiree will also be permitted to terminate the SWP and withdraw the remaining balance at any stage. It is also proposed that the spouse or nominee rights will be continued for the SWP for the balance EPF corpus of the member on same terms in the event of death of the member during the SWP tenure.

At present, EPFO members can withdraw 100% of their accumulated provident fund balance on retirement at the age of 58. Members with at least 10 years of eligible service can separately receive a monthly pension under the Employees’ Pension Scheme.

Around 6.32 lakh members above the age of 55 possess provident fund savings exceeding Rs 5 lakh and are expected to benefit from the SWP. The EPFO, which has over 8 crore active contributing members and over 34 crore total members, manages a retirement corpus of nearly Rs 32 lakh crore.

As per internal estimates listed in the SWP proposal, the periodic withdrawals by a member may generate higher monthly payouts when compared with comparable bank fixed deposit and annuity arrangements.
Coverage for gig, informal workers

The proposal will also introduce a framework to allow direct voluntary contributions and third-party micro-contributions (such as customer tips) directly into EPF accounts through Universal Account Number (UAN)-linked digital payment mechanisms, completely independent of traditional employer payroll systems. This would enable informal and incidental income streams to be converted into long-term retirement savings. Such contributions, however, will be subject to limits prescribed in the Income-tax Act and will be governed by rules and procedures specified by the CBT.

“This SWP scheme intends to provide flexible options to the member for enhancing his corpus in PF by means of voluntary contributions through payroll, direct additional contributions other than payroll and third-party micro-contributions. The proposed architecture of the SWP scheme provides for the possibility that the scheme may be extended to facilitate social security coverage and retirement savings mechanisms for gig workers, platform workers, construction workers, domestic workers, street vendors, home-based workers, among others,” an official said.
Investment proposal for AIFs

The EPFO’s Board gave also in-principle approval to allow investment of up to 3% of fresh accretion (annual inflows) in eligible Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), within the existing overall investment ceiling, initially through government-backed entities. Investment in government-anchored funds under National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) and through “Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0” scheme managed by the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) will be in focus.

AIF means any fund incorporated in India in the form of a trust or a company or a limited liability partnership or a body corporate which – (i) is a privately pooled investment vehicle which collects funds from investors, whether Indian or foreign, for investing it in accordance with a defined investment policy for the benefit of its investors; and (ii) is not covered under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, SEBI (Collective Investment Schemes) Regulations, 1999 or any other regulations of the Board.

The Secretary, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) had written to the EPFO in September 2026 inviting EPFO to examine participation in the Fund of Funds for Startups 2.0 through an appropriate co-investment or contribution structure, subject to EPFO’s applicable investment framework and requisite approvals, The Indian Express had learnt.

Also, the EPFO’s Investment Committee had earlier discussed the proposal for investment in AIFs, where the risk-return profile of AIFs versus Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) or Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) as an asset class was highlighted. While InvITs are pooled investment vehicles that own and manage operational infrastructure assets such as highways and power transmission lines, REITs pertain to income-generating commercial real estate such as office parks and warehouses.

The committee members said that AIFs — particularly those investing in start-ups and venture capital — have a significantly different risk-return profile and do not necessarily generate regular income. The committee then gave an in-principle approval for investment in AIFs limited to 3% of fresh accretions during a financial year.

title: Musadik Malik: Pak minister known for ‘will cut hands’ remark arrives in India. Here’s why

content.value: Pakistan’s Climate Change and Environmental Coordination Minister, Musadik Masood Malik, landed in New Delhi on Friday (November 20) for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum this weekend (November 20-22).

As per protocol, India had invited Pakistan’s Culture and National Heritage Minister, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi, for the forum. However, Pakistan decided to send Malik instead after a high-level discussion between Foreign Ministry officials in Islamabad and the High Commission in New Delhi on Saturday (November 14).

So, who is Malik, and why has Pakistan sent him instead of their Culture Minister for a civilisational dialogue? And what have been his recent statements on India in context of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), currently in abeyance? We explain.
Who is Musadik Masood Malik?

A senior member of the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) and a sitting Senator, he assumed the climate portfolio in March 2025 under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. He previously held the positions of Minister of Water and Power in the caretaker cabinet led by Mir Hazar Khan Khoso (March-June 2013) and the Minister for Water Resources and Minister of Energy (2022-23) in the earlier Sharif government. He was also the spokesperson for former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif in 2014.

The invitation to Pakistan’s minister is part of New Delhi’s obligation to invite representatives from all SCO member countries, as it had proposed to host the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum. It is, however, the invited country’s prerogative to decide on its representation, so Islamabad officially put Malik’s name on Saturday — a day after Union Culture Minister Gajendra Shekhawat said he was “hopeful” of Pakistan’s presence at the event.

Announcing the decision to attend the summit, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said, “The event will bring together representatives from SCO member states to exchange views on issues related to civilisational dialogue and cultural understanding.”

While Malik is expected to spend two days in New Delhi, the final itinerary is still being worked out in discussion with the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi. Before this, Malik had just returned after attending the COP31 UN climate conference in Turkey, and the details of his possible meetings with the Indian side — if any — are being discussed.

This is the first such invitation to a senior Pakistan minister since India and Pakistan had a military confrontation in May 2025, where India conducted its response to the Pahalgam terror attack (in April 2025) under Operation Sindoor.
Malik’s presence at the meet will be a first for a Pakistani minister since May 2023, when India had hosted then Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari in Goa for the SCO Foreign Ministers’ meeting.
What did Musadik Malik say about the Indus Waters Treaty?

Pakistan has been repeatedly raising the issue of India putting the IWT in abeyance. While Malik doesn’t handle the issue directly and is handled by the Water Resources ministry, he has been the public face for international advocacy on it.

In June this year, Malik — a technocrat turned minister — said in a press conference that Pakistan would “cut off those hands” that are attempting to control the Indus waters. He recently said that Pakistan is taking the IWT issue beyond bilateral discussions to the United Nations and other international arbitration forums, calling it “a question of justice and downstream rights”.

When asked by Pakistani media whether he would raise India’s decision to place the Treaty in abeyance during his address in New Delhi, Malik said the trip is not a bilateral negotiation. He, however, declined to rule out raising the issue.
How is Pakistan asserting its claim on the Indus?
In recent months, Pakistan has been asserting its claim on the Indus by highlighting the Indus Valley civilisation of Mohenjodaro, Harappa, and other ancient sites in the country.

On World Heritage Day (April 18) this year, Pakistani PM Shehbaz Sharif had referred to the Indus Valley civilisation in his remarks, saying, “Pakistan’s cultural heritage is enriched with a multifaceted civilisation. Our homeland carries the legacy of some of the world’s oldest civilisations, reflecting a vibrant tapestry of human creativity and diversity.”

When asked about this last week, Shekhawat said, “When a country tries to talk about 5,000 years of Indus Valley Civilisation, they should be self-aware that they didn’t exist at the time. Their story is just 80 years old.”

title: Why the world is closely watching the Trump-Xi-Putin meet in Shenzhen

content.value: As US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin prepare to sit across the table for their first-ever trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, the world, and India, will be watching the summit’s outcomes, and potential consequences, closely.

Many have compared the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with the historic Yalta conference of February 1945, when US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Union premier Joseph Stalin struck a deal that effectively divided post-war Europe into spheres of influence (which we have explained here). At that time, World War II was coming to an end. In this case, the two wars in Russia-Ukraine and in West Asia against Iran appear rather intractable.
What happened at the Quad meeting?

Ahead of the trilateral meeting, Trump met the leaders of fellow Quad countries, India, Japan and Australia. All of them have long flagged China’s belligerence in the Indo-Pacific region, and conveyed the concern at their meeting.

This was reflected in the joint document issued after the meeting of all four Quad leaders. It said the members strongly opposed any destabilising or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability.

The grouping flagged economic coercion, arbitrary export restrictions, choking of critical supply chains, freedom of navigation and overflight, deployment of trusted artificial intelligence (AI), resilient maritime transit corridors. Each of these are key challenges posed by Beijing. If that were not enough, the Quad leaders agreed to hold a maritime military exercise next year, double down on AI development and organise a business forum, signalling that they are keen on sticking together — even as Trump sups with Xi and Putin.
So, the worries of countries including India, Japan and Australia have been conveyed to Trump, despite him being soft on China in his second term. The question is, will he be able to hold the line?
China, to be sure, has always rejected the Quad, calling it a bloc that promotes confrontation and likening it to “sea foam”.
The meeting of the strongmen
With Xi and Putin at the table, the temptation for Trump will be to cut a grand bargain with the two strongmen who face little to no challenge domestically.

Trump, however, is a democratically elected leader who has just been delivered a massive setback in the midterm elections. He may not be able to deliver the goods in the same way that both Xi and Putin can in their respective political contexts.

Xi would want his way in the South China Sea and Taiwan. Putin would want his way in Ukraine, where the war has now crossed World War I in duration. The Europeans will be watching Putin’s actions more closely since it affects their security. Those in Southeast Asia, meanwhile, will be monitoring Xi.

Trump, as part of his strategic calculation, would want their help in stopping both the wars in Ukraine and West Asia. But for Xi, this is a golden opportunity. He wouldn’t want to stop a war that has stretched American military, economic and diplomatic bandwidth.
Spectacle or substance

So, for many in the world watching the summit of the “big 3”, or “group of 3”, this would look like another spectacle — high-decibel, high on optics and without substantive outcomes. This playbook has happened before, from Trump’s high-voltage meetings with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and bilateral meetings with both Xi and Putin.

When Trump met Xi last year in October, the US President was able to buy time for the world. He had postponed the problem of the Rare Earth magnets and brought home the point of managing resilient supply chains when it comes to critical sectors.

The world had come to notice the dependencies on China during the Covid-19 pandemic, and the leverage that Beijing had over the world’s supply chain systems. Washington had managed to buy more time for the world to develop their own supply chain, and diversify from China. So, from that perspective, this was an important win for the US and the world.

For China, Trump’s acknowledgement of it as part of a “group of 2” was a recognition of its status as a global power. Under Xi, Beijing has been pursuing the goal of becoming the world’s foremost power.

That will be the bigger question in New Delhi. India stands to be affected if China is emboldened to take more aggressive actions without facing consequences. Trump’s power play with Xi is particularly consequential for India, given its border with China, which has become “more alive”, as External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said last weekend. This has required India to maintain a much larger troop presence along the frontier on a sustained basis.
New Delhi will be hoping that this G-3 moment is short-lived and does not take India back to 2020, when it had to significantly increase its force deployment along the China border in just 10 days.

title: Trump-Putin-Xi Jinping meeting: China pushes Shenzhen system to co-direct global order

content.value: As President Xi Jinping hosts the first-ever meeting of Chinese, Russian and American leaders in Shenzhen Thursday, his strategic experts are promoting the idea that the summit could mark the beginning of a “Shenzhen International System”.

The phrase, coined by Wang Wen, a professor at Renmin University, is a deliberate play on history. Great-power orders have often taken the names of the places where they were born: Westphalia, Vienna, Versailles and Yalta. Wang would like Shenzhen to join that list.

Xi gave the occasion an edge Wednesday by breaking with protocol to greet Donald Trump at the airport, returning the gesture Trump made when Xi landed in Washington in September. Vladimir Putin, who arrived the same day, held talks with Xi ahead of the main event. On Thursday, Xi will receive Trump at Qilin Villa before Putin joins them for the trilateral summit.

Writing in Moscow’s Russia in Global Affairs journal last month, Wang was careful to explain what the Shenzhen system is not. It will not be a “G-3”, which he believes smacks of big powers ganging up on the rest of the world. Nor is the Shenzhen summit about replacing the United Nations Security Council.

Wang argues that the three permanent members of the Security Council could establish a trilateral channel for crisis management that might help unblock a paralysed UNSC. That is unlikely to impress the two other permanent members – Britain and France – left out in the cold.
From ‘spheres of influence’ to ‘sovereignty’

Wang and other Chinese commentators are eager to separate Shenzhen from Yalta, the 1945 meeting between American, British and Soviet leaders that helped shape the post-war European order. If Yalta was about spheres of influence, Shenzhen is supposedly about the sovereignty of all states. Countries in Europe and Asia facing threats to their sovereignty from Russia and China are bound to smirk.

If Yalta helped divide the world into blocs, Shenzhen, Chinese scholars say, accepts great-power rivalry but seeks “braking mechanisms” to limit competition. For the Chinese strategic community, Shenzhen marks the “beginning of an important political process”.

Despite this attempt to distance Shenzhen from Yalta, Beijing’s official framing also reaches back to 1945. Announcing the summit, a Foreign Ministry spokesperson recalled that China, Russia and America were founding members of the UN and permanent members of the Security Council that “fought side by side” in the World Anti-Fascist War. They now share the responsibility for global peace.

The claim will cause some concern in Tokyo. By invoking World War II, China presents itself as America’s partner in managing the global order while reminding the world of the history of Japanese imperialism and militarism. The political purpose is to separate Japan from America and undermine the US alliance with Japan that has been central to the post-war Asian order.

Expectations of the summit itself are modest. Trump has said the three will discuss “denuclearisation”. Chinese scholars add some substance to Trump’s confusing remarks. They suggest the focus is not on reducing the nuclear arsenals of the three powers but on developing a framework for nuclear stability and crisis management.

This could involve a general commitment to avoiding nuclear war and preventing the use of artificial intelligence in managing nuclear weapons. The three leaders could also address nuclear proliferation in the Middle East and the Korean Peninsula, besides conflicts in Europe and Asia undermining international peace and stability.
‘Need for dialogue’

It is uncertain whether Thursday’s meeting will produce a joint statement. Putin’s top adviser, Yuri Ushakov, said Moscow was “proceeding on the assumption” that the three leaders would adopt a joint communiqué. Neither Washington nor Beijing has confirmed this. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has described the meeting as a “strong message to all humanity about the need for dialogue”.

Adding to the intrigue is talk of a fourth guest. Before leaving for Asia, Trump said he might meet the reclusive North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Shenzhen. “He may come; I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi.”

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reiterated Trump’s commitment to engaging Kim. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung strongly supports US and Chinese engagement with North Korea. If Kim does turn up in Shenzhen, it would significantly raise the theatrical quotient of the summit.

Whether Shenzhen ends up having an international order named after it remains to be seen. But the unprecedented summit could mark a turning point in modern international relations. In any event, Wang’s phrase, the “Shenzhen International System”, tells us what Beijing wants: the prestige of convening a historic summit and recognition as a co-manager of the global order.

The author is a contributing editor on international affairs for The Indian Express. He is a professor and director at the Motwani-Jadeja Institute of American Studies, Jindal Global University, Delhi.

title: Knowledge Nugget: Why is the new Covid variant PJ.2.1 drawing attention?

content.value: Take a look at the essential events, concepts, terms, quotes, or phenomena every day and brush up your knowledge. Here’s your UPSC Current Affairs knowledge nugget for today on the new Covid variant PJ.2.1.
Knowledge Nugget: New Covid variant PJ.2.1
Subject: Science, Health and diseases
Why in the news?

A new SARS-CoV-2 variant, PJ.2.1, is drawing attention after being identified in Canada in May 2026 and subsequently detected in several countries, including the US, Singapore, Australia, France and Spain. Let’s know about this new Covid variant and other viral diseases that have been in the news.
Key takeaways:

1. PJ.2.1, described in the Journal of Infection as a “novel saltation variant”, originated from MC.10.1.7, a descendant of the JN.1 lineage that circulated until May 2025, and was first detected in Ontario, Canada, on May 2, 2026, before cases were reported in other Canadian provinces.

2. By June 30, the variant had also been identified in the US, beginning with a case in New York City. Subsequent detections were reported across several states, including California, Florida, Arizona and New Jersey.

3. Based on wastewater surveillance, the researchers described PJ.2.1 as the “fastest-growing variant in the USA” at the time of the study. Beyond North America, sequences of the variant were reported in Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, Israel, France and Spain, suggesting that its spread is not confined to one region.
4. PJ.2.1 is a saltation variant because it has many new mutations in the spike protein, which help it attach better to human cells and escape some old immunity.
5. Its symptoms look just like a common cold or seasonal flu. Patients report fever, severe sore throat, runny or blocked nose, cough, headache, muscle ache and fatigue.
6. Notably, there is no evidence that PJ.2.1 causes more severe disease or hospitalisation than earlier variants.
What is Covid-19, and how does PJ.2.1 differ from earlier variants?

7. Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) is an infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The most common symptoms of COVID-19 are fever, chills, and sore throat. The key difference between PJ.2.1 and Covid-19 variant lies in its genetic changes and interaction with human cells.

8. The PJ.2.1 has a highly mutated spike protein and showed increased ability to interact with the ACE2 receptor, which the virus uses to enter human cells. Laboratory experiments also indicated greater cell-entry efficiency in certain cell lines.
Other viral diseases

1. Hantavirus: Named after the Hantan River in South Korea, hantavirus is a family of rodent-borne viruses that can cause serious illness and death in humans. However, the virus-carrying rats and other rodents do not fall ill to the virus.

— Human infection primarily occurs through contact with the urine, faeces, or saliva of infected rodents or by touching contaminated surfaces. It is also possible to get the infection by breathing air that contains viral particles stirred up from these droppings, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

— Notably, Hantavirus rarely transmits from one person to another, which means in most cases infected persons have individually come in contact with the urine, faeces, or saliva of infected rodents or by touching contaminated surfaces.

2. Mpox: Previously known as monkeypox, Mpox is a self-limiting viral infection caused by mpox virus (MPXV). The most common symptoms of mpox include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, low energy, and swollen lymph nodes, along with pox-like rashes that last for two to three weeks. It is a self-limiting disease but can lead to death, especially among children and those with weak immune systems.
— According to WHO, there are two broad clades of the Mpox virus: clade I and II. Clade I leads to more severe disease and death than clade II in the populations where it is endemic.

— Mpox spreads from person to person mainly through close contact with someone who has mpox. Someone who comes into physical contact with an animal that carries the virus, such as some species of monkeys or a terrestrial rodent (such as the tree squirrel) may also develop mpox.

3. Nipah virus: Nipah is a viral infection that mainly affects animals such as bats, pigs, dogs, and horses. Being zoonotic, it can jump to humans who come in contact with the infected animals and cause serious disease.

— Nipah can spread to humans after close contact with infected animals or secretions containing the virus on fruit trees, fruits, date palm sap, juice or toddy. It can spread from human to human through close contact at home or in hospitals. It can spread from handling dead bodies of those with Nipah.

— According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), its symptoms are fever, headache, cough, sore throat, difficulty in breathing, and vomiting. In severe cases, disorientation, drowsiness, seizures, encephalitis (swelling of the brain) can occur, progressing to coma and death. Notably, there are no antivirals and there is only symptomatic management.
4. Zika: A mosquito-borne disease—Zika virus— mainly occurs in tropical and subtropical areas of Africa, the Americas, Southern Asia, and the Western Pacific.

— It is infected by Aedes species mosquitoes, which are the same ones that spread dengue and chikungunya viruses, and bite during the first week of infection. It is primarily transmitted through mosquito bites, sex, and breastfeeding.

5. Ebola: It is a virus that can spread quickly and can be fatal in up to 90% of cases. Symptoms include fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, muscle pain and at times internal and external bleeding and can start to occur between two and 21 days from infection, according to WHO.
— The virus is most often spread by close contact with bodily fluids of people exhibiting symptoms and with contaminated objects such as sheets.
BEYOND THE NUGGET: What it means to be ‘Varients of Interest’ (VOI) and ‘Varients of Concerns’?
1. ‘Varients of Interest’ are variants that are less effectively neutralised in labs by antibodies from infection or vaccination and have a potential to spread.
2. A variant is designated as VOI by WHO if it shows a growth advantage over other circulating variants — meaning its proportion increases along with any increase in the total number of cases.

3. A variant can be designated as VOI also if it is predicted to or known to change characteristics such as transmissibility, virulence, antibody evasion, or susceptibility to therapies and diagnostics.

4. Once designated as VOI, the WHO monitors and tracks its global spread. The body also keeps assessing its public health risk and facilitate sharing of isolates. Member states have to report cases of VOI, monitor it, and conduct field investigations to study the potential impact of the variant.
5. ‘Varients of Concerns’ are variants that result in increased transmission, severe disease leading to hospitalisation, and reduce effectiveness of vaccines.
Post Read Questions
(1) Consider the following statements: (UPSC CSE 2017)
1. In tropical regions, Zika virus disease is transmitted by the same mosquito that transmits dengue.
2. Sexual transmission of Zika virus disease is possible.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2
(2) With reference to PJ.2.1, recently seen in the news. It is a:
(a) SARS-CoV-2 variant
(b) Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) strain
(c) Mpox virus variant
(d) Ebola virus strain
Answer Key
1. (c)   2. (a)
(Sources: Fast-spreading Covid variant PJ.2.1: What Indians need to know, WHO tags JN.1 strain as ‘variant of interest’ as Covid cases rise)

title: UPSC Essentials daily subject quiz | History : Tribal revolts, Cultural terms, Medieval history, and more

content.value: UPSC Essentials brings to you its initiative of subject-wise quizzes. These quizzes are designed to help you revise some of the most important topics from the static part of the syllabus. Attempt today’s subject quiz on History & Culture to check your progress.
🚨 Click Here to read the UPSC Essentials magazine for October 2026. Share your views and suggestions in the comment box or at manas.srivastava@indianexpress.com🚨
QUESTION 1
‘Jamdani’ and ‘Ajarakh’ refer to:
(a) Indian desserts with GI tags
(b) Traditional kitchen utensils
(c) Medieval sports of India
(d) None of the above

Relevance: India’s traditional crafts and textile heritage reflect the country’s cultural diversity, regional identities and indigenous knowledge systems. Understanding these art forms is important for UPSC, particularly for questions on Indian culture, heritage, and the preservation of traditional practices.
Explanation

— Jamdani, a centuries-old handwoven textile from the Bengal region—now Bangladesh and West Bengal, India—has deep historical roots. Dr Sadhna, associate professor of fashion design, School Arts and Design at Woxsen University, said that while the term appears in literature from the 3rd century BC in Kautilya’s Arthashastra and during the Gupta period (4th–6th century AD), it was under Mughal rule (16th–18th centuries) that Dhaka’s weavers gained royal patronage.

— Evolving from renowned Bengal muslin, jamdani is traditionally crafted from cotton, and is celebrated for its fine, airy texture and elegance. The name “jamdani” derives from the Persian words jam (flower) and dani (vase), describing its floral designs. In 2013, UNESCO recognized Jamdani weaving as an Intangible Cultural Heritage, underscoring its cultural and historical significance.

— Deep in the heart of India’s Kutch region, a tradition of block printing a textile — ajrakh — famous for its intricate patterns and deep indigo hue has been passed down through generations for centuries.

— Ajrakh is more than just a fabric; it is a cultural symbol, deeply entangled with the lives of the Kutch region,” according to Professor John Varghese from the School of Fashion at the World University of Design, Sonipat.

— Whether ajrakh originated in the Egyptian or Indus Valley Civilisation is still being debated. But Gujarat-printed ajrakh was excavated from Al-Fostat, near old Cairo in Egypt, and was showcased at the ‘India and the World’ exhibit at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya, Mumbai, from November 11, 2017, to February 18, 2018. The priest-king of Mohenjodaro is also depicted wearing what is believed to be an early form of ajrakh, explained J Usha Rani, associate professor of fashion and textiles at Pearl Academy, Bengaluru.
Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 2
Arrange the following tribal revolts in chronological order of their occurrence:
1. Munda Rebellion
2. Tana Bhagat Movement
3. Dhal Revolt
Select the correct code:
(a) 1, 2 and 3
(b) 2, 1 and 3
(c) 3, 1 and 2
(d) 3, 2 and 1
Relevance:

Tribal revolts played an important role in shaping resistance against colonial rule and reflected diverse forms of opposition to British policies and exploitation. Understanding their chronology, regional spread and causes is important for UPSC, particularly for Modern Indian History and the freedom struggle.
Explanation

— The first tribal revolt during British rule in Jharkhand was the Dhal Revolt in 1767, led by Jagannath Dhal, the former king of Dhalbhum, a part of West Bengal today. Triggered by the presence of the British East India Company that marginalised the local population, this revolt lasted 10 years. In response to the ongoing unrest, the British reinstated Jagannath Dhal as the ruler of Dhalbhum in 1777.

— However, this was just the beginning. Several other revolts followed, with the two most notable being the Munda Rebellion and the Tana Bhagat Movement, says Hasnain. “Among the tribal movements organised in Bihar-Jharkhand and the adjoining areas, Birsa Movement is the most widespread and the best known. After….Tana Bhagat Movement occupies the most important place because of its multidimensional significance of far reaching socio-political implications,” Hasnain notes.

— The Munda Rebellion, which lasted from 1899 to 1900, was another significant response to the exploitation faced by the Mundas, traditionally agriculturalists suffering under British officials and moneylenders. Led by the young and charismatic Birsa Munda, who claimed divine inspiration, the rebellion saw guerrilla warfare and direct attacks on colonial property and officials.

— The Tana Bhagat Movement, which began in 1914, emerged alongside the Birsa Movement and was founded by Jatra Bhagat, a leader of the Oraon tribe. He called for a return to traditional practices, rejecting colonial rule and Western influences. Bhagat highlighted agrarian issues and initiated a no-rent campaign, urging labourers to refuse forced or low-wage work.
Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 3
With reference to the History of India, consider the following statements.
1. After the death of Emperor Aurangzeb and the decline of the Mughal Empire, the Maratha Confederacy expanded rapidly, posing a threat to Ahmad Shah Durrani’s Afghan Empire.

2. The smaller but unified Ahmad Shah army decisively overwhelmed the Marathas in the third battle of Panipath due to the technological and tactical superiority of Afghans, combined with internal rivalries within the Maratha ranks.
Which of the above given statements is/are true?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2
Relevance:

The decline of the Mughal Empire and the emergence of regional powers transformed the political landscape of 18th-century India. Understanding the shifting alliances, military strategies and power struggles of this period is important for UPSC, particularly for questions on the transition from Mughal rule to British dominance.
Explanation
Marathas, Ahamd Shah Durrani, and the battle for control

— After the death of Emperor Aurangzeb and the decline of the Mughal Empire, the Maratha Confederacy expanded rapidly, posing a threat to Ahmad Shah Durrani’s (also known as Ahmad Shah Abdali) Afghan Empire. To counter this, Ahmad Shah launched a campaign, capturing large parts of Punjab and aiming to starve the Maratha forces. In response, the Marathas assembled a large army under Sadashivrao Bhau, who managed to reclaim Delhi.

— Ahmad Shah sought to trap the Maratha forces in Punjab, cutting off their supplies while moving troops southward. Surrounded by the enemy and starving, Sadashivrao Bhau attempted to break the siege, leading to a confrontation at Panipat in 1761. In part II of his book, Medieval India, historian Satish Chandra observes that “the Bhau would not have been able to prevail over the Abdali, saddled as he was with heavy artillery and womenfolk.” He contends that while the Maratha soldiers primarily relied on lances and swords, the Afghan forces held a significant advantage with skilled musketeers equipped with quick-loading flintlock guns and mounted on “swift, well-trained horses.” This technological and tactical superiority, combined with internal rivalries within the Maratha ranks, ultimately weakened their forces. The smaller but unified Ahmad Shah army decisively overwhelmed the Marathas.

— The third battle of Panipat on January 14, 1761, devastated the Maratha army, ended their ambition to succeed the Mughals, and plunged northwestern India into decades of instability. “The ultimate beneficiaries were not the Maratha sardars and erstwhile Mughal nobles who stood for regionalism, but the English who brought in centralism of a new-kind, the colonial type,” notes Chandra.
Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 4
Which of the following pairs of UNESCO World Heritage sites in India and their locations is correctly matched?
(a) The Nanda Devi National Park: Uttarakhand
(b) Rani-ki-Vav: Rajasthan
(c) Humayun’s Tomb: Uttar Pradesh
(d) Khangchendzonga National Park : Arunachal Pradesh
Relevance:

India’s UNESCO World Heritage Sites reflect the country’s rich natural and cultural heritage. Understanding their geographical locations, historical significance and unique features is important for UPSC, particularly for topics related to Indian heritage, culture, geography and conservation.
Explanation

— Khangchendzonga National Park, also Kanchenjunga Biosphere Reserve, is a national park and a biosphere reserve located in Sikkim, India. It is a sacred mountain in Tibetan Buddhism, where the area is considered a beyul, a sacred hidden land. It is home to ethnically diverse Sikkimese communities.
— Humayun’s Tomb, the tomb of the Mughal Emperor constructed in the 1560s. It was the first example of a garden tomb in the Indian subcontinent. It is situated in Delhi.
— Rani-ki-Vav or the Queen’s Stepwell at Patan, Gujarat has been called one of the finest examples of a step well, constructed in the 11th century by the Chaulukya dynasty.
— The Nanda Devi National Park and Valley of Flowers National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Uttarakhand, India.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 5

He put an end to the institution of the Yogiatirippads — the erstwhile spiritual heads of the Vadakkumnathan and Perumanam temples, who had conspired against the previous Cochin king in his wars against the Calicut Zamorin — and entrusted temple management to the government.
Who is referred to in the above lines?
(a) K. Kelappan
(b) EMS Namboodiripad
(c) Accamma Cherian
(d) Sakthan Thampuran
Relevance:

The history of regional kingdoms and temple administration offers insights into the relationship between political authority, religious institutions and society in pre-colonial India. Such themes are relevant to UPSC, particularly for understanding regional histories, cultural heritage and the socio-religious developments of India.
Explanation

— Minister of State for Tourism and Thrissur MP Suresh Gopi on Saturday (September 7) pledged to replace a statue of Sakthan Thampuran that was knocked over by a state transport bus in June with a new bronze statue if the Kerala government did not do so within 14 days.
Who was Sakthan Thampuran?

— Raja Rama Varma Kunjipillai or Rama Varma IX, better known today as Sakthan Thampuran, ruled over the Cochin kingdom from 1790 to 1805. He was born in 1751 to Ambika Thampuran and Chendose Aniyan Namboodiri of the Cochin royal family, but was raised by an aunt who called him Sakthan, meaning ‘powerful’. The word thampuran is believed to be an appropriation of the Sanskrit samrat, meaning emperor.

— The Cochin kingdom, which was part of the Late Chera Empire, covered the regions between Ponnani in Malappuram and Thottappally in Alappuzha in today’s Kerala. (Ashalatha Thampuran, History of the Cochin Royal Family: Tracing the Journey of Perumpadappu Swarupam, 2019)
Strategist and ruler

— Sakthan Thampuran became heir apparent in 1769 as an 18-year-old. He advised his king to maintain friendly relations with both the Dutch and the English, who were vying for a larger share of trade in the region.

— Sakthan is said to have orchestrated Mysore’s attempt to invade the Travancore kingdom, which had established relations with the English East India Company. This would result in the Powney treaty which freed the Cochin kingdom from its allegiance to Mysore, and helped formalise its relations with the British.

— Sakthan Thampuran put an end to the institution of the Yogiatirippads — the erstwhile spiritual heads of the Vadakkumnathan and Perumanam temples, who had conspired against the previous Cochin king in his wars against the Calicut Zamorin — and entrusted temple management to the government.
— He built a fearsome reputation for himself, and is said to have largely freed his kingdom of crime.
Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.
