title: UPSC Prelims 2027 Polity Quiz (Week 189): MCQs on Eighth Schedule, summoning of Parliament, and more

content.value: UPSC Essentials brings to you its initiative of daily subject-wise quizzes. These quizzes are designed to help you revise some of the most important topics from the static part of the syllabus. Attempt today’s subject quiz on Polity and Governance to check your progress.
🚨 Click Here to read the UPSC Essentials magazine for November 2026. Share your views and suggestions in the comment box or at manas.srivastava@indianexpress.com🚨
QUESTION 1
Which of the following languages are not mentioned in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
1. Bodo
2. Kannada
3. Awadhi
4. Pali
5. English
6. Nepali
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
(a) 5 and 6 only
(b) 3 and 5 only
(c) 1, 2, 4 and 6 only
(d) 3, 4 and 5 only

Relevance: The Eighth Schedule is an important constitutional provision related to the recognition and promotion of languages in India. It is relevant to Articles 344 and 351, official language provisions and the constitutional framework governing linguistic diversity.
Explanation
— The Constitutional provisions relating to the Eighth Schedule occur in article 344(1) and 351 of the Constitution.
— The Eighth Schedule to the Constitution consists of the following 22 languages:-

— (1) Assamese, (2) Bengali, (3) Gujarati, (4) Hindi, (5) Kannada, (6) Kashmiri, (7) Konkani, (8) Malayalam, (9) Manipuri, (10) Marathi, (11) Nepali, (12) Oriya, (13) Punjabi, (14) Sanskrit, (15) Sindhi, (16) Tamil, (17) Telugu, (18) Urdu (19) Bodo, (20) Santhali, (21) Maithili and (22) Dogri.

— Of these languages, 14 were first incorporated into the Constitution. The Sindhi language was added in 1967. Three additional languages, Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali, were added in 1992. Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali were added in 2004.
Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.
(Other Source: http://www.mha.gov.in)
QUESTION 2
With reference to the summoning of Parliament, consider the following statements:
1. It is specified in Article 85 of the Constitution.
2. It is based on a provision of the Government of India Act, 1935.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2
Relevance: The topic is relevant to parliamentary procedures, the powers of the President and the constitutional relationship between the executive and legislature.
Explanation

— The summoning of Parliament is specified in Article 85 of the Constitution. Like many other Articles, it is based on a provision of the Government of India Act, 1935. Hence, statements 1 and 2 are correct.
— This provision specified that the central legislature had to be summoned to meet at least once a year, and that not more than 12 months could elapse between two sessions.
Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 3
With reference to the business advisory committee (BAC), consider the following statements:
1. It is a parliamentary committee that recommends the allocation of time for government bills and other business before a legislature.
2. There are separate BACs for the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha with equal numbers of members.
3. The members of the BAC are nominated by the Prime Minister.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
(a) Only one
(b) Only two
(c) All three
(d) None

Relevance: The Business Advisory Committee is an important parliamentary body associated with the functioning and legislative business of Parliament. It is relevant to understanding parliamentary procedures, the role of the presiding officers and the conduct of legislative business.
Explanation
— A business advisory committee (BAC) is a parliamentary committee that recommends the allocation of time for government bills and other business before a legislature. Hence, statement 1 is correct.
— It functions as a parliamentary standing committee to organise the legislative agenda and ensure the efficient scheduling of debates, with a key role in managing the house’s schedule.
— In India’s parliament, there are separate BACs for the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, each headed by the Speaker/Chairman, respectively.

— The members are nominated by the Speaker or Chairman in proportion to the strength of various political parties in the house, ensuring representation from across the spectrum. Hence, statements 2 and 3 are not correct.
— The committee typically meets at the beginning of each session and then as needed to plan the legislative schedule.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
(Source: sansad.in)
QUESTION 4
Consider the following statements:
1. A Bill pending in Parliament shall lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses.
2. A Bill pending in the Council of States which has not been passed by the House of the People shall not lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2

Relevance: The question tests the constitutional provisions governing the introduction, passage and lapse of Bills in Parliament. It is relevant to Articles 107 and 108, particularly the distinction between prorogation and dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
Explanation

— A Bill shall not be deemed to have been passed by the Houses of Parliament unless it has been agreed to by both Houses, either without amendment or with such amendments only as are agreed to by both Houses.
— A Bill pending in Parliament shall not lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses. Hence, statement 1 is not correct.
— A Bill pending in the Council of States which has not been passed by the House of the People shall not lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People. Hence, statement 2 is correct.

— A Bill which is pending in the House of the People, or which having been passed by the House of the People is pending in the Council of States, shall, subject to the provisions of article 108, lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People.
Therefore, option (b) is the correct answer.
(Source: Constitution of India)
QUESTION 5
Which of the following are the exceptions under which a foreign judgment would not be considered conclusive in India?
1. If the foreign court lacked jurisdiction
2. If the judgment was not granted on the merits.
3. If the foreign court refused to recognise Indian law despite its applicability.
(a) 1, 2 and 3
(b) 1 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 2 only
(d) 2 and 3 only

Relevance: The topic is relevant to judicial jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments and the application of international law in India. It connects with civil procedure, private international law and the principles of natural justice.
Explanation
— The recognition of foreign rulings in India is governed by Sections 13 and 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC).

— Section 13 lays down six exceptions under which a foreign judgment would not be considered conclusive in India. These include cases where the foreign court lacked jurisdiction, the judgment was not granted on merits, or the order was obtained through fraud. Recognition can also be refused where the foreign court refused to recognise Indian law despite its applicability.
— Section 14 provides that a foreign judgment is presumed valid unless the contrary is proved, but this presumption is easily rebutted when one of the exceptions in Section 13 is shown.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.

title: UPSC Mains Answer Practice — GS 2: Quad and China’s growing influence in India’s neighbourhood (Week 181)

content.value: UPSC Essentials brings to you its initiative for the practice of Mains answer writing. It covers essential topics of static and dynamic parts of the UPSC Civil Services syllabus covered under various GS papers. This answer-writing practice is designed to help you as a value addition to your UPSC CSE Mains. Attempt today’s answer writing on questions related to topics of GS-2 to check your progress.

QUESTION 1
How does the Quad contribute to maintaining a free, open and rules-based Indo-Pacific? Examine the challenges facing the grouping.
QUESTION 2
Discuss how China’s military and economic engagement with India’s neighbouring countries challenges India’s traditional regional influence.
QUESTION 1: How does the Quad contribute to maintaining a free, open and rules-based Indo-Pacific? Examine the challenges facing the grouping.

Relevance: The Quad is an important minilateral grouping shaping the geopolitical and security architecture of the Indo-Pacific. Its evolving role is relevant to India’s foreign policy, maritime security and strategic engagement with major powers.
Note: This is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers.
Introduction:

— The Quadrilateral Security Dialog (Quad), which includes India, the United States, Japan, and Australia, has developed as a significant minilateral grouping in the Indo-Pacific. Originally founded to coordinate disaster relief following the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, it was reactivated in 2017 as China’s regional influence grew.
— The Quad aims to foster a free, open, inclusive, and rules-based Indo-Pacific region through strategic coordination, maritime cooperation, and economic resilience.
Body:
You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer:
How does the Quad contribute to a free, open and rules-based Indo-Pacific?

— Encourages freedom of navigation and overflight, adherence to international law, and the peaceful resolution of maritime issues. Joint naval exercises, like as the Malabar exercises, help member countries enhance their maritime interoperability and cooperation. The proposed Indo-Pacific maritime surveillance collaboration seeks to improve maritime domain awareness and regional security.

— The Quad leaders have rejected destabilising acts that threaten regional peace and stability. It raises concerns about China’s expanding military presence and confrontational behaviour in the South and East China Seas.

— Strengthens supply chains for essential minerals, semiconductors, and new technologies. Encourages collaboration in energy security and eliminates vulnerabilities caused by excessive reliance on individual countries. The proposed Quad Business Leaders’ Forum seeks to strengthen economic involvement and private-sector cooperation.

— The projected Quad AI accelerator and greater cybersecurity collaboration aim to increase technology resilience. Such approaches can help to reduce strategic risks while also promoting trusted technological ecosystems.

— Promotes collaboration in crisis management, humanitarian assistance, climate resilience, and health security. Increases regional capacity for responding to natural disasters and developing international concerns. Encourages practical cooperation that benefits countries beyond the four members.
— Supports ASEAN’s centrality and its Indo-Pacific outlook. The proposed Quad Plus framework has the potential to develop collaboration with nations such as South Korea, Vietnam, and New Zealand.
— India values strategic autonomy, whereas Japan sees the Quad as a crucial security mechanism. Australia must strike a balance between security concerns and major economic connections with China.

— The Quad lacks a permanent secretariat, binding treaty responsibilities, and a systematic decision-making process. Its informal nature has the potential to have an impact on policy continuity and initiative implementation.

— Beijing sees the Quad as an attempt to limit its rise and has condemned the creation of exclusive groups. This image exacerbates regional tensions and undermines the Quad’s attempts to promote an inclusive Indo-Pacific.
— The Quad is not a formal military alliance, and it does not have a collective defence commitment like NATO.
Conclusion:
— The Quad has become a key platform for strategic coordination and regional cooperation in the Indo-Pacific.

— However, its effectiveness is dependent on overcoming internal conflicts, maintaining political commitment, and translating common goals into tangible results. For India, the Quad provides an opportunity to boost maritime security and strategic relationships while maintaining strategic autonomy.

(Sources: Quad leaders meet in Manila: Why the grouping matters amid Indo-Pacific tensions, Quad unveils security, business, AI plans; Trump says ‘phone, office open’, Quad foreign ministers reaffirm free, open Indo-Pacific at Manila meeting, Why the Quad has never picked up momentum, Habit, not the China threat, explains why the Quad endures)
Points to Ponder
How does the Quad promote maritime security, freedom of navigation and respect for international law?
How can the Quad strengthen its institutional framework without evolving into a formal military alliance?
Related Previous Year Questions
Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) is transforming itself into a trade bloc from a military alliance, in present times Discuss. (2020)
How will I2U2 (India, Israel, UAE and USA) grouping transform India’s position in global politics? (2022)
QUESTION 2: Discuss how China’s military and economic engagement with India’s neighbouring countries challenges India’s traditional regional influence.

Relevance: The question is relevant for India’s neighbourhood relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India’s interests. The issue is important for understanding India’s neighbourhood-first policy, regional connectivity initiatives and its approach towards maintaining strategic influence.
Note: This is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers.
Introduction:
— China’s growing economic, diplomatic, and military engagement in India’s neighbourhood has shifted the conventional balance of power in South Asia.

— Beijing has emerged as a major regional player, threatening India’s traditional power in its immediate vicinity, thanks to the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), defence agreements, infrastructure investments, and strategic port development.
Body:
You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer:
How China’s engagement challenges India’s regional influence

— China’s military collaboration with Pakistan has expanded beyond arms sales to include joint exercises, defence co-production, intelligence sharing, and operational interoperability. The Karakoram-2026 exercise, which involves regular army formations from both countries in Xinjiang, demonstrates increased military integration and raises concerns about India’s concerted two-front security challenge.

— China has emerged as a major defence supplier to Bangladesh, with military gear accounting for a sizable portion of the country’s defence imports. The growing defence collaboration between China, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, which includes potential fighter aircraft acquisitions and military training arrangements, adds to India’s eastern security concerns. China’s desire to establish a connection to the Bay of Bengal has strategic consequences for India.

— China’s engagement in Sri Lanka’s Hambantota Port, which was leased to a Chinese business for 99 years, exemplifies how economic investments can lead to long-term strategic influence. India’s rising defence and maritime security involvement with the Maldives and Pakistan poses new strategic threats to the country’s position in the Indian Ocean region.

— Chinese finance gives India’s neighbours new sources of capital, lessening their traditional reliance on India. China’s expanding economic presence also gives it more political leverage in regional affairs.

— China’s increased engagement enables neighbouring countries to diversify their foreign relations and deal with India from a more powerful position. Political instability and strained bilateral relations have occasionally provided opportunities for Beijing to expand its regional presence.

— China’s expanding influence calls into question India’s long-held position as South Asia’s primary development and security partner. It also hampers India’s Neighbourhood First Policy and its efforts to improve regional connectivity and collaboration.
Conclusion:

— China’s growing influence in South Asia is not just an economic challenge, but also a geopolitical and security concern for India. India’s response should go beyond resisting Chinese influence and emphasise becoming a dependable, responsive, and development-oriented partner.
— Long-term regional impact will be based on India’s capacity to deliver on common interests rather than geographical proximity alone.

(Sources: Karakoram-2026: How China and Pakistan are deepening military ties — and what it means for India, With its latest statement on CPEC, recalling how India has sought to counter China in South Asia, New China-Pakistan boundary joint commission: What it is, why India has objected, As the Maldives diversifies its foreign policy, India should make red lines clear, Here’s what’s at stake for India, China and the US in the Bangladesh elections)
Points to Ponder
What challenges does China’s expanding maritime presence pose to India’s interests in the Indian Ocean Region?
Related Previous Year Questions

“China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has transformed South Asia from a regional space into a theatre of great power competition.” Analyse the strategic implications of the BRI for India’s security and regional influence in South Asia (2026)

content.value: UPSC Essentials brings to you its initiative of subject-wise quizzes. These quizzes are designed to help you revise some of the most important topics from the static part of the syllabus. Attempt today’s subject quiz on  International Relations to check your progress.
🚨 Click Here to read the UPSC Essentials magazine for October 2026. Share your views and suggestions in the comment box or at manas.srivastava@indianexpress.com🚨
QUESTION 1
With reference to the East Asia Summit (EAS), consider the following statements:
1. The objectives and principles of EAS are outlined in the 2005 Kuala Lumpur Declaration.
2. The 21st East Asia Summit (EAS) will be held in the Philippines.
3. The Chairmanship of the EAS can only be held by an ASEAN member country.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
(a) Only one
(b) Only two
(c) All three
(d) None

Relevance: It is relevant to India’s engagement with ASEAN-led regional institutions and its Act East Policy. It connects with regional cooperation, Indo-Pacific geopolitics and India’s role in the evolving East Asian security architecture.
Explanation
— A summit of the Quad leaders is expected to take place in Manila next week, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be attending the ASEAN-India and East Asia summits.

— The East Asia Summit (EAS) process was initiated in 2005 with the convening of the 1st East Asia Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. The East Asia Summit’s objectives and principles are outlined in its basic documents, including the 2005 Kuala Lumpur Declaration on the East Asia Summit. Hence, statement 1 is correct.
— Under the Kuala Lumpur Declaration, the EAS is hosted and chaired by an ASEAN member country that assumes the ASEAN Chairmanship. Hence, statement 3 is correct.
— The 21st East Asia Summit is scheduled to be held in the Philippines in 2026. The Philippines holds the ASEAN Chairmanship in 2026. Hence, statement 2 is correct.
Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.
(Other Source: eastasiasummit.asean.org)
QUESTION 2
The ‘NUTEC Plastics’ aims to address the global challenge of plastic pollution. It is an initiative of:
(a) Global Environment Facility
(b) Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
(c) United Nations Environment Programme
(d) International Atomic Energy Agency

Relevance: The question connects with topics such as plastic waste management, recycling technologies, marine pollution and sustainable development. It is relevant to the role of international organisations in developing scientific and technological solutions for environmental protection.
Explanation
— NUTEC Plastics is the IAEA’s flagship initiative to address the global challenge of plastic pollution.

— It brings together countries and partners from around the world to fight plastic pollution on two fronts: at point of source, by introducing new technologies to improve plastic recycling; and in the ocean, where the bulk of plastic waste ends up.
Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.
(Source: http://www.iaea.org)
QUESTION 3
Consider the following statements about the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE):
1. It is an international non-governmental, non-profit organisation.
2. It is headquartered in Geneva.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2

Relevance: The question is relevant to international environmental organisations and their role in promoting environmental education and sustainable development. It is useful for understanding the institutional framework supporting environmental conservation and sustainability at the global level.
Explanation

— The Blue Flag is an internationally recognised voluntary eco-label awarded to beaches, marinas and tourism boats that meet prescribed standards of environmental management, water quality, safety, accessibility and environmental education.

— The programme is run by the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE), an international non-governmental, non-profit organisation headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark. It began in France in 1985 and has since grown into a global certification programme. Hence, statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is not correct.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 4

The Disaster Risk Financing Platform aims to secure access to more than $3 billion in risk financing to protect 75 million people and their livelihoods from potential climate shocks and natural hazards by 2030. The Disaster Risk Financing Platform was launched during:
(a) 7th United Nations Environment Assembly
(b) 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference
(c) 56th World Economic Forum Annual Meeting
(d) 14th G20 Leaders’ Summit

Relevance: The question links to international cooperation on climate change, disaster risk reduction and climate resilience. It is relevant to India’s engagement with multilateral climate negotiations and international climate-financing mechanisms.
Explanation
According to http://www.fao.org,

— “The United Nations today launched a new initiative at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, aiming to secure access to more than $3 billion in risk financing to protect 75 million people and their livelihoods from potential climate shocks and natural hazards by 2030.

— Bringing together six UN agencies, the UN Disaster Risk Financing (DRF) Platform aims to make disaster response funding more predictable, increase the availability of funding for early action during major crises, and maximise the impact of every dollar by combining available resources with private sector support.

— The platform will enable agencies to share expertise, pool data, and coordinate joint solutions to expand the UN’s use of pre-arranged financing. Combining robust data and predictive analysis with funds will help governments and agencies help turn early warnings into anticipatory actions. This will strengthen emergency responses before, during, and after disasters.”
Therefore, option (b) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 5
With reference to the Berlin West Africa Conference, consider the following statements:
1. The Conference set rules governing European expansion on the continent.
2. The Conference divided up and partitioned the entire continent of Africa among European powers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2

Relevance: The question is relevant to the study of European imperialism, colonial expansion and the Scramble for Africa during the 19th century. It connects with themes such as colonialism, geopolitical rivalries and the changing political map of Africa.
Explanation

— The Berlin West Africa Conference, held from November 15, 1884, to February 26, 1885, resulted in the adoption of the General Act, which set rules governing European expansion on the continent. Hence, statement 1 is correct.

— Among other things, the Act established conditions under which European powers could acquire territory along the African coast, internationalised navigation on the Congo and Niger rivers, called for a renewed campaign against the overland slave trade, and declared a vast area of Central Africa, designated the ‘conventional basin of the Congo’, neutral.

— The Conference did not legally partition the African continent amongst European nations. Instead, it established laws that allowed and legitimised further European territorial expansion and the Scramble for Africa. Much of the actual dividing occurred through subsequent accords and colonial invasions. Hence, statement 2 is not correct.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.

QUESTION 1
Despite improvements in TB diagnosis and treatment, India continues to face significant challenges in eliminating tuberculosis. Examine the key bottlenecks in India’s fight against TB.
QUESTION 2
Discuss the role of Production-Linked Incentive schemes in strengthening India’s manufacturing capabilities and integrating the country into global value chains.
QUESTION 1: Despite improvements in TB diagnosis and treatment, India continues to face significant challenges in eliminating tuberculosis. Examine the key bottlenecks in India’s fight against TB.

Relevance: The question is relevant for GS Paper 3 – Science and Technology: Developments and their applications in everyday life. It examines challenges in managing public health, including disease surveillance, early diagnosis and access to affordable treatment. It highlights the role of technological interventions and government programmes in strengthening India’s healthcare system.
Note: This is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers.
Introduction:
— India accounts for roughly one-quarter of the worldwide tuberculosis (TB) burden and has set an ambitious aim of eliminating the illness by 2025, five years ahead of the global target.

— Although advances in diagnosis, treatment coverage, and public health measures have lowered tuberculosis mortality, structural, socioeconomic, and healthcare delivery barriers continue to impede elimination.
Body:
You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer:
— Between 2015 and 2025, India’s tuberculosis mortality rate fell by 38%, from 28 to 18 per lakh population.
— Rapid diagnostic tests accounted for 46% of detected cases in 2025, compared to 38% in 2024.
— The TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan examined more over 25 million people, identifying nearly 49 lakh new cases, including approximately 15 lakh asymptomatic cases.
— In response to falling global health funding, India has increased domestic funding for its tuberculosis program.
Key bottlenecks in India’s fight against TB

— Despite increased screening, many people go untreated, especially in rural and impoverished areas. Limited access to rapid molecular testing, sample transportation delays, and insufficient referral networks all have an impact on prompt diagnosis.

— India’s estimated tuberculosis prevalence is currently being reviewed following district-level sentinel surveillance in 2025. The lack of current national incidence estimates, as well as the delay in the issuance of the annual India TB Report, make it impossible to assess the disease burden. Inadequate granular data can have an impact on district-level planning, resource allocation, and monitoring of eradication targets.

— India continues to have a significant burden of drug-resistant tuberculosis, making treatment more complicated and expensive. Incomplete therapy, incorrect prescriptions, and irregular usage of anti-TB medications all lead to antibiotic resistance. The management of drug-resistant diseases is made much more difficult by a lack of affordable drugs and consistent supplies.

— Patients may abandon treatment due to long treatment durations, severe drug effects, or socioeconomic challenges. Failure to follow up raises the likelihood of disease recurrence, ongoing transmission, and treatment resistance.

— Financial difficulty, poor housing conditions, and a lack of access to nutritional food exacerbate vulnerability among economically disadvantaged groups. Undernutrition reduces immunity and increases susceptibility to active tuberculosis.

— A considerable number of tuberculosis patients seek treatment from private healthcare providers. Inadequate standardisation of diagnostic techniques, treatment regimens, and case notification might result in gaps in patient care.
Conclusion:
— India’s accomplishment in reducing tuberculosis mortality and expanding diagnostic coverage indicates the efficacy of long-term public health efforts.

— To eliminate tuberculosis, we must go beyond case detection and focus on comprehensive disease prevention, nutritional security, inexpensive treatment, and improved healthcare delivery. A sustained, community-driven, and sufficiently supported approach through the National TB Elimination Program is critical to achieving TB-free India.

(Sources: India missed its 2025 TB target. How much progress has it made?, India’s TB incidence missing from WHO’s 2026 global report, India’s progress against TB is real, but not rapid enough, Why hasn’t India met its target of eliminating TB by 2025?, Rs 57 crore unspent: Delhi uses less than half of its tuberculosis budget in 2025)
Points to Ponder
What are the major factors contributing to India’s TB burden?
How can public-private partnerships and community participation strengthen TB control?
Related Previous Year Questions

COVID-19 pandemic has caused unprecedented devastation worldwide. However, technological advancements are being availed readily to win over the crisis. Give an account of how technology was sought to aid management of the pandemic. (2020)

Stem cell therapy is gaining popularity in India to treat a wide variety of medical conditions including Leukaemia, Thalassemia, damaged cornea and several burns. Describe briefly what stem cell therapy is and what advantages it has over other treatments? (2017)
QUESTION 2: Discuss the role of Production-Linked Incentive schemes in strengthening India’s manufacturing capabilities and integrating the country into global value chains.

Relevance: The question is relevant to GS Paper 3 under Indian Economy, particularly changes in industrial policy and their impact on industrial growth. It connects manufacturing growth with export promotion, domestic value addition and India’s integration into global value chains.
Note: This is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers.
Introduction:

— The Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, which was started in 2020, is a key component of India’s industrial policy, aimed at increasing domestic production, attracting investment, reducing import dependence, and improving export competitiveness.
— It offers financial incentives to businesses based on increased production and sales of items made in India.
Body:
You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer:
Role of PLI schemes in strengthening manufacturing capabilities

— PLI plans enable businesses to build new manufacturing facilities and increase their existing capacities. As of March 2026, the 14 projects had drawn investments of ₹2.40 lakh crore and produced ₹22.66 lakh crore.
— Incentives have encouraged multinational corporations to set up manufacturing plants in India, particularly in electronics, autos, and medicines.
— The participation of multinational manufacturers helps the implementation of new production technology, modern manufacturing methods, and quality standards.

— PLI schemes in pharmaceuticals, bulk drugs, electronics, and advanced battery manufacturing aim to increase domestic production capacity while decreasing reliance on imported components and critical inputs.
— Large manufacturing investments can spur the expansion of ancillary businesses, component manufacturers, and domestic suppliers, resulting in greater industrial connections.
— Increased manufacturing capacity and economies of scale can boost cost competitiveness and allow Indian enterprises to enter foreign markets.
— The smartphone manufacturing PLI has attracted firms like Apple and their contract manufacturing partners, allowing India to become a significant electronics production and export powerhouse.
— The expansion of mobile phone manufacturing has greatly enhanced India’s electronics exports and strengthened its place in global manufacturing networks.
— Investing in manufacturing infrastructure, technology, and production skills can help Indian businesses reach international quality standards and compete in global markets.
— India’s manufacturing push provides multinational corporations with an alternative production base, especially in the face of geopolitical uncertainty and efforts to diversify supply chains.
Conclusion:
— PLI plans have boosted India’s manufacturing objectives by encouraging investment, expanding production, and recruiting global businesses.

— However, their long-term success will be contingent on shifting beyond assembly-led growth to deeper domestic value addition, indigenous technology skills, and closer integration of Indian firms into global value chains.

(Sources: How the government’s flagship PLI schemes are lagging in job creation, Six years later, mind the lags in government’s flagship PLI scheme, Disbursals remain under 20% in 6 years since PLI scheme launch: NITI report, How India’s new Rs 62,500-crore smartphone manufacturing scheme will work)
Points to Ponder
How do PLI schemes encourage domestic and foreign investment in manufacturing?
How can MSMEs be integrated into the PLI-led manufacturing ecosystem?
Related Previous Year Questions

How are startups in India promoting entrepreneurship, innovation and employment? Discuss the global and domestic challenges in their working and suggest suitable measures to overcome these challenges. (2026)
Discuss the rationale of the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme. What are its achievements? In what way can the functioning and outcomes of the scheme be improved? (2025)

title: Knowledge Nugget | From battery waste to critical minerals: Why India has banned black mass exports

content.value: Take a look at the essential events, concepts, terms, quotes, or phenomena every day and brush up your knowledge. Here’s your UPSC Current Affairs knowledge nugget for today on lithium-ion battery black mass.
Knowledge Nugget: Lithium-ion battery black mass
Subject: Economy
Why in the news?

With an eye on building a resilient domestic ecosystem for battery recycling and refining, the government has banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass and related battery waste with immediate effect. In this context, let’s know about the black mass and the importance of lithium-ion battery-related waste.
Key takeaways:

1. Black mass is a powder-like material that remains after waste lithium-ion batteries and consumer electronics are broken down. Apart from lithium, this powder contains critical minerals such as cobalt, manganese, silicon, tin, nickel, rhenium, and graphite, among others. Recycling of black mass can help recover these crucial materials, which can be reused to make new batteries.

2. There have been concerns within the government over the export of black mass, particularly at a time when several countries have imposed restrictions on its export to retain critical minerals and strengthen their domestic supply chains.

3. India has limited domestic reserves of these minerals that are instrumental to manufacture batteries and remains heavily dependent on imports. Thus, waste streams from electrical and electronic equipment, as well as discarded lithium-ion batteries, are increasingly viewed as an important secondary source of these materials.
4. On the other hand, limited domestic recycling and refining capabilities have been cited as factors behind the export of such waste.

5. The government said export prohibition is intended to ensure that black mass generated in India is recycled and refined within the country. “The measure is expected to assure feedstock availability for domestic recycling and refining units, improve their capacity utilisation and encourage further investment and employment in the sector,” the government said in a statement.
6. “It will increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, thereby reducing import dependence and the associated foreign exchange outgo.” it added.
7. Notably, the ban on these exports comes days after the Union Cabinet approved a new scheme to provide capital expenditure support for critical mineral processing.
What is CAPEX Support Scheme?

8. With an aim of developing domestic critical mineral processing capacity, the Union Cabinet on November 4 approved a new scheme to provide capital expenditure (capex) support for critical mineral processing. With an outlay of Rs 2,814 crore, the scheme will be focused on establishing an ecosystem for lithium and nickel processing.

9. The scheme aims to provide a 30% capital subsidy on eligible investment for setting up four processing plants — two lithium processing plants with a minimum capacity of 30 kilotonnes (kt) each and two nickel processing plants with a minimum capacity of 50 kt each.
10. The maximum capital support is being capped at Rs 500 crore per lithium beneficiary and Rs 900 crore per nickel beneficiary.

11. The scheme is expected to support sectors such as electric mobility, battery energy storage systems (BESS), electronics, defence and speciality steel, while strengthening India’s domestic critical mineral value chain.
12. The development comes as the government has already identified four states — Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Gujarat and Maharashtra — to promote setting up of critical mineral processing plants.

13. The government plans to develop every park as a complete ecosystem for a particular mineral. Accordingly, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh are looking at rare earth processing, while Odisha and Maharashtra are set to focus on nickel and lithium, respectively.
BEYOND THE NUGGET: What is National Critical Minerals Mission?

1. In January 2025, India launched a National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM) to help achieve self-reliance in the critical mineral sector. In 2023, the Centre also identified 30 critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, tin and copper, which are essential for the country’s economic development and national security.

2. The Rs 16,300-crore NCMM aims to intensify the exploration of critical minerals within the country and in its offshore areas. It plans to create a fast-track regulatory approval process for critical mineral mining projects.

3. The mission aims to strengthen India’s critical minerals value chain by building a technological, regulatory, and financial ecosystem to ensure mineral availability from both domestic and foreign sources. The mission is set to boost access to raw materials used across strategic sectors, from clean energy and electronics to defence and agriculture.

4. The National Critical Minerals Mission also proposes to develop a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme for stockpiling critical and strategic minerals. For the development of such a reserve, the government also commits to allocate Rs 500 crore for the mission period of seven years, from 2024- 25 to 2030-31.
Post Read Question
With reference to lithium-ion batteries black mass, consider the following statements:
1. It is a powder-like material that remains after waste lithium-ion batteries and consumer electronics are broken down.
2. It contains critical minerals.
3. The export of black mass is prohibited in India.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
(a) Only one
(b) Only two
(c) All three
(d) None
Answer Key
(Sources: Government bans export of lithium-ion battery waste days after new scheme on critical minerals processing, Critical Mineral push)

title: Top 20 UPSC Current Affairs Pointers of the past week | November 9 to 15, 2026

content.value: Every Monday, we bring you UPSC Current Affairs Pointers—a concise, exam-focused guide to help you stay ahead in your Prelims and Mains preparation.
If you missed the UPSC Current Affairs Pointers of the past week | November 2 to 8, 2026, read it here.
Report
(FYI: The data provided in these reports can be used to substantiate your Mains answer and create a broad understanding of the topic.)
• Global TB report

— Recently, this year’s Global TB report is released by the World Health Organization (WHO). While India has not achieved its target of eliminating tuberculosis (TB) by 2025, five years ahead of the global deadline, it has been making strides. The incidence and mortality due to the bacterial infection has been on the decline.
— India has also seen an improvement in diagnosis — with more people accessing rapid diagnostics and getting tested for resistance to a commonly used antimicrobial.

— The country also saw a massive active case finding exercise over the last two years. Its incidence, however, remained uncalculated in this year’s Global TB report in view of new district-level surveillance data becoming available.

— Reduction in mortality: India reported a 38% reduction in its TB mortality as compared to 2015 — breaching the 2020 End TB milestone of reducing it by 35%, albeit five years later. India’s TB mortality reduced from 28 per lakh population in 2015 to 18 per lakh population in 2025, according to the Global TB report. The 2025 target of reducing mortality by 75% still remains distant.

— Increase in diagnostics: India saw an increase in rapid diagnostic testing in 2025, with 46% of the cases being diagnosed using these. This is up from 38% the previous year. Quick diagnosis ensures timely treatment and prevents the further spread of the infection.
— Increase in national funding: With a decline in global health funding, with TB funding reducing by 14% globally, India saw an increase in domestic funding.
What are the TB targets?

With TB continuing to be the biggest infectious killer in the world, the WHO set End TB targets to bring down the incidence, mortality, and catastrophic costs associated with it. With 2015 as the base year, countries have been trying to meet targets of reducing TB deaths by 35% by 2020, 75% by 2025, 90% by 2030, and 95% by 2035.
The target for TB incidence is reduction of 20% by 2020, 50% by 2025, 80% by 2030, and 90% by 2035. And, zero catastrophic costs across the years.
• Global Carbon Budget

— A new Global Carbon Budget study, released at the COP31 climate meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, projects a 0.4% decline in global fossil fuel-related CO₂ emissions in 2026 to 38.2 billion tonnes, from 38.4 billion tonnes in 2025.  India, however, is the only major emitter projected to record an increase.
— The marginal decline is attributed partly to supply shocks caused by the ongoing US-Iran conflict and the growing contribution of renewable energy sources.

— India is the only major emitter projected to record an increase in fossil fuel-related CO₂ emissions in 2026, rising by 4.4% over 2025 (higher than its preceding decade’s average annual growth of 3.5%).

— In contrast, China, the US, the EU and Japan are expected to record declines. The projected decline in fossil fuel-related CO₂ emissions in 2026 would be the first since 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic caused a 2% drop, the largest year-on-year decline recorded so far.

— Notably, Global Carbon Budget is an annual scientific assessment coordinated by the Global Carbon Project (GCP). First published in 2006, it accounts for CO₂ emissions from fossil fuel combustion, industrial processes such as cement production, and land-use change such as deforestation. It also estimates atmospheric CO₂ accumulation and absorption by natural carbon sinks, mainly land ecosystems and oceans.
What is Global Carbon Project?

It is a Global Research Project of Future Earth and a research partner of the World Climate Research Programme. It studies the global biogeochemical cycles of three major greenhouse gases-carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O)-including their natural and human-induced sources, sinks and drivers.
International Cooperation
• Lame-duck period

— Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in last week’s midterm elections, dealing a major setback to President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. But Republicans still have roughly seven weeks to advance their legislative agenda before the newly elected Congress takes office.
— The final period, known as the ‘lame-duck’ session, gives Republicans one last opportunity to advance their priorities before handing control of Congress to Democrats.

— The ‘lame-duck’ period refers to the period between federal elections and the newly elected members taking office. The term ‘lame-duck’ refers more to the waning political power of the sitting Congress than to any limitation on its constitutional powers.
• China-Pakistan nexus

— The China-Pakistan nexus refers to the longstanding strategic, economic and military partnership between the two countries. It dates to the 1963 Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement under which Pakistan ceded the Shakasgam Valley, part of Gilgit-Baltistan, to China, thus cementing the strategic alignment. The core pillars of China-Pakistan nexus are:

— Military supplies: China is Pakistan’s dominant arms supplier, accounting for roughly 70-80% of its imported military hardware. Major acquisitions include J-10C and JF-17 fighter aircrafts, Type 054 A/P frigates, Hangor-Class Submarines, HQ-9, 16, 17 series air defence systems, and Wing Loom drones.

— Defence co-production: Both nations regularly collaborate on co-producing military equipment including fighter jets (J-10C and JF-17), main battle tanks (Al-Khalid), missiles, naval platforms, electronic and surveillance systems.

— Information: Information and space are other arenas of close cooperation; encompass intelligence sharing, cyber warfare, satellites (Bei Dou for navigation) and information cum narrative alignment, through initiatives like China-Pakistan Information Corridor.
— Infrastructure: The collaboration extends to infrastructure and strategic projects such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and Gwadar Port under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).
Polity
• Special session of Parliament

— The Indian Express reported on November 13 that a special session of Parliament could be convened before the regularly scheduled Winter Session this year. The Centre is planning to do so to secure passage of its legislative agenda on delimitation of electoral constituencies and implementation of women’s reservation.

— India does not have a fixed parliamentary calendar. The Constitution specifies that six months should not elapse between two parliamentary sessions. The framers of the Constitution borrowed it from the Government of India Act of 1935.

— By convention, Parliament meets for three sessions in a year. The longest, the Budget Session, starts towards the end of January and concludes by the end of April or the first week of May. The session has a recess so that Parliamentary Committees can discuss the budgetary proposals.

— The second session is the three-week Monsoon Session, which usually begins in July and finishes in August. The parliamentary year ends with a three-week-long Winter Session, which is held from November to December. This Winter Session is expected to begin in late November or early December.

— The Constitution does not use the term “special session”. The term sometimes refers to sessions the government has convened for specific occasions, like commemorating parliamentary or national milestones.

— For the two Houses to be in session, the presiding officers (the Lok Sabha Speaker and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) should chair their proceedings. The presiding officers can also direct that the proceedings of their respective Houses be limited, and procedural devices like Question Hour would not be available to MPs during the session.

— While Article 85 empowers the President to summon Parliament, the convention is to give around 15 days’ notice for a regular session. A special session, however, can be convened at shorter notice. If a session has been adjourned sine die but not prorogued (meaning formally ending a session), it technically remains alive, and the Lok Sabha can be reconvened at short notice by the Speaker under Rule 15 of the Rules of Procedure.

— However, Article 352 (Proclamation of Emergency) of the Constitution does refer to a “special sitting of the House”. It specifies that if a Proclamation of Emergency is issued and Parliament is not in session, then one-tenth of Lok Sabha MPs can ask the President to convene a special meeting to disapprove the Emergency.
What the Constitution says on Parliament sessions?

The summoning of Parliament is specified in Article 85 of the Constitution. Like many other Articles, it is based on a provision of the Government of India Act, 1935. This provision specified that the central legislature had to be summoned to meet at least once a year, and that not more than 12 months could elapse between two sessions. Dr B R Ambedkar’s drafting of the provision reduced the gap between sessions to six months, and specified that Parliament should meet at least twice a year.
Economy
•  Surcharge

— Can a state impose a tax on a tax that a dealer already owes? The Supreme Court has reiterated that states can levy a surcharge calculated as a percentage of sales tax payable by dealers, holding that such a levy is essentially an additional sales tax and not a separate tax on tax.

— A surcharge is an additional levy imposed over and above an existing tax. The legal question before the Supreme Court was whether states could impose such a surcharge on the sales tax payable by dealers, or whether doing so amounted to an impermissible ‘tax on tax’.
• Lithium-ion battery black mass

— With an eye on building a resilient domestic ecosystem for battery recycling and refining, the government has banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass and related battery waste with immediate effect.

— Black mass is a powder-like material that remains after waste lithium-ion batteries and consumer electronics are broken down. Apart from lithium, this powder contains critical minerals such as cobalt, manganese, silicon, tin, nickel, rhenium, and graphite, among others. Recycling of black mass can help recover these crucial materials, which can be reused to make new batteries.

— In a notification issued on November 10, the Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) under the commerce ministry amended the export policy for “waste and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators; spent primary cells, spent primary batteries and spent electric accumulators – Unsorted and not containing lead, cadmium or mercury (Lithium-lon Battery Black Mass)” from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’.
Science and Technology
• Cloud seeding

— In Diwali’s aftermath, the Delhi government may be planning to carry out cloud seeding trials to induce artificial rain over the region amid high levels of air pollution, The Indian Express had recently reported. Two trial runs are already learnt to have been conducted near the airport.
— Cloud seeding refers to introducing substances such as silver iodide or sodium chloride into a particular class of clouds to artificially trigger rain.

— Generally, water vapour condenses around small particles in the air to form the droplets that make up a cloud. These droplets collide and grow; as they get heavy and the cloud gets saturated, it rains.

— In case of cloud seeding, the seed particles are “cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), a particle on which water vapour condensates” or “ice nuclei particles, a particle on which water freezes”, the 2024 document said. CCNs have an affinity for water vapour to form cloud droplets or ice particles, respectively. Ice crystals grow faster than drops, and they enlarge and fall.

— To induce rain artificially, clouds are usually injected with salts like silver iodide, potassium iodide, or sodium chloride, which is the ‘seed’. These salts are expected to provide additional nuclei around which more cloud droplets can form. They are dispersed into the cloud either using aircraft or through generators on the ground.
• Integrated Catalytic Thermo Cracking

— Greenjoules Private Ltd plans to set up a plant at Khed City, near Pune, to produce up to 2 lakh litres of bio-crude daily from agricultural residues. The company claims to use its proprietary Integrated Catalytic Thermo Cracking (ICTC) technology to convert these residues into bio-crude for further processing into renewable diesel and bio-naphtha.

— Unlike biofuel production based on food crops such as sugarcane and cereal grains, the proposed project uses agricultural residues as feedstock. This can reduce direct competition between food production and fuel production.

— The Integrated Catalytic Thermo Cracking  technology uses multiple catalysts at approximately 600°C to convert agricultural residues, such as paddy straw and husk, groundnut and cashew shells, and sugarcane bagasse, into bio-crude.
— This bio-crude serves as an intermediate that can be further processed in conventional refineries to produce renewable diesel and bio-naphtha.
What is Bio-crude?

Bio-crude is a liquid intermediate produced by thermochemical conversion of biomass. In hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL), biomass is processed in water under high temperature and pressure to produce an organic liquid, which is separated from the aqueous phase. Generally viscous but thermally stable, it is easier to pump, store and process than solid biomass. However, it is not readily miscible with petroleum. Its density is slightly higher than petroleum but considerably lower than bio-oil.
• Pioxaniliprole

— PI Industries Ltd’s Pioxaniliprole, India’s first indigenously discovered insecticide molecule, has received approval from the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIBRC) for use on rice, chilli, tomato and chana (chickpea) crops.
— PI Industries plans to launch the molecule under the trade name ‘Pioxazon’ in the coming Rabi (winter-spring) crop season.

— Pioxaniliprole belongs to the anthranilic diamide class of insecticides, which acts on calcium-releasing channels in insects. The insecticide is effective against yellow stem borer, leaf folder, fall armyworm, tobacco cutworm, fruit borer and pod borer.

— Pioxaniliprole acts by targeting ryanodine receptors (RyRs), specialised protein channels present in insect muscle cells that regulate the release of calcium ions from intracellular storage compartments into the cell cytoplasm.
— Calcium ions play a crucial role in normal muscle contraction and relaxation. Pioxaniliprole binds to and activates these receptors, triggering an uncontrolled release of calcium ions.
— This disrupts normal muscle functioning in insects, leading to feeding cessation, lethargy, muscle paralysis and eventually death.
Defence
• Karakoram-2026 exercise
— Karakoram-2026, held from October 14-22 in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, was the first joint-army level exercise between People’s Liberation Army (PLA) and Pakistan Army.

— It marked a significant milestone as it involved the participation of regular army formations from both countries. It expanded on the earlier naval, air and counterterrorism exercises (Sea Guardian, Warrior and Shaheen series). The focus was on challenging high-altitude operations, relevant to the PLA’s Western Theatre Command which oversees the border with India.

— The equipment used was Chinese, including small arms, armoured assault vehicles, infantry fighting vehicles and support systems, such as artillery, drones and anti-manned systems. The Chinese Ministry of National Defence described Karakoram-2026 as an opportunity to deepen cooperation and tactical integration between the two armies.
Health
• New Covid variant PJ.2.1

— A new SARS-CoV-2 variant, PJ.2.1, is drawing attention after being identified in Canada in May 2026 and subsequently detected in several countries, including the US, Singapore, Australia, France and Spain.

— PJ.2.1, described in the Journal of Infection as a “novel saltation variant”, originated from MC.10.1.7, a descendant of the JN.1 lineage that circulated until May 2025, and was first detected in Ontario, Canada, on May 2, 2026, before cases were reported in other Canadian provinces.

— Based on wastewater surveillance, the researchers described PJ.2.1 as the “fastest-growing variant in the USA” at the time of the study. Beyond North America, sequences of the variant were reported in Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, Israel, France and Spain, suggesting that its spread is not confined to one region.
— PJ.2.1 is a saltation variant because it has many new mutations in the spike protein, which help it attach better to human cells and escape some old immunity.
— Its symptoms look just like a common cold or seasonal flu. Patients report fever, severe sore throat, runny or blocked nose, cough, headache, muscle ache and fatigue.
— Notably, there is no evidence that PJ.2.1 causes more severe disease or hospitalisation than earlier variants.
Environment
• International Blue Flag certification

— In a first for Maharashtra, three of its beaches have been awarded an international certification that recognises beaches meeting stringent standards of environmental protection, water quality, safety and tourist facilities.

— The Ladghar and Guhagar beaches in Ratnagiri district, and the Shrivardhan beach in Raigad district, have earned the international Blue Flag certification. Only 22 beaches in India carry the certification, awarded by a Denmark-based non-governmental organisation.

— The Blue Flag is an internationally recognised voluntary eco-label awarded to beaches, marinas and tourism boats that meet prescribed standards of environmental management, water quality, safety, accessibility and environmental education.

— The programme is run by the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE), an international non-governmental, non-profit organisation headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark. It began in France in 1985 and has since grown into a global certification programme.

— The certification process is overseen by the FEE, which works through national operators in participating countries. India’s Blue Flag programme prescribes 33 criteria, grouped under four broad heads: environmental education and information, water quality, environmental management, and safety and services.
— Notably, the Blue Flag is awarded for a particular season and has to be renewed. Beaches must continue to meet the prescribed criteria throughout the certification period.
• Smog
— Days after Diwali, the Delhi-NCR region remains blanketed in smog, the thick haze that returns every winter as pollutants accumulate in the air.

— Smog, derived from ‘smoke’ and ‘fog’, occurs when pollutants accumulate in the air, often reducing visibility. These include fine particulate matter, such as PM2.5 and PM10, and gases released by vehicles, industries and other sources.

— Some pollutants, including nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, can also react in sunlight to form ground-level ozone. This process produces what is known as photochemical smog, which is more common in sunny conditions.

— Unlike fog, smog contains harmful pollutants that can affect human health. Fog and smog can also occur together. Smog can persist for several days when pollutants continue to accumulate in the atmosphere, even after temporary sources of emissions have subsided.
What is PM10 and PM 2.5?

PM10 refers to particles measuring 10 micrometres or less in diameter, while PM2.5 refers to finer particles measuring 2.5 micrometres or less. These particles can include dust, soot and smoke, as well as substances formed through chemical reactions involving gases in the atmosphere.
• Air Quality Index (AQI)

— Several monitoring stations in Delhi recorded ‘severe’ air quality on November 9, a day after Diwali festivities were marked by widespread use of firecrackers despite Supreme Court-mandated restrictions.

— AQI is a number which measures air quality. The higher the AQI, the worse the air. The AQI used in India was launched in 2014 as part of the government’s Swachh Bharat campaign. The colour-coded index helps explain the condition of the air and the measures necessary to mitigate the situation depending on its severity.

— The index converts measurements of up to eight major air pollutants into a single number, category and colour. These include particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, ozone, carbon monoxide, ammonia and lead.

— Each pollutant’s concentration is converted into a separate sub-index based on established health-related thresholds. The highest sub-index determines the overall AQI, rather than an average of all pollutants.
— There are six categories of AQI, namely ‘Good’ (0-50), ‘Satisfactory’ (51-100), ‘Moderate’ (101-200), ‘Poor’ (201-300), ‘Very Poor’ (301-400), and ‘Severe’ (401-500).

The difference in AQI across different platforms lies partly in how the index is calculated. India’s official AQI uses a scale that stops at 500, while some international platforms use different thresholds for pollutant concentrations and allow readings to exceed 500.
• El Niño

— El Niño will continue to remain ‘strong’ to ‘very strong’ during the first quarter of 2027, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said. The UN organisation further said that the current El Niño event continues to intensify, and would become the “strongest ever since 1950”. It is set to shatter all previously known records with respective to the sea surface temperatures along the equatorial Pacific Ocean.

— El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon associated with warm seas along the equatorial Pacific Oceans. El Niño alters rain patterns, spikes temperatures, increases incidents of wild fires, leads to extreme weather in the form of fluids or droughts across the world.

— It is one of the three phases of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the other two being ENSO neutral and La Nina (cool). The ENSO phase is subject to the Relative Ocean Nino Index (RONI) value — the sea surface temperature measured over the Nino 3.4 region. An El Niño event is declared when the average RONI value surpasses 0.5 degree Celsius, an average considered over three months.
• Panna-Ranipur Tiger Corridor

— The FAC, under the Union Environment Ministry, recommended in-principle approval for the diversion of 511.91 hectares of forest land in Madhya Pradesh for the 1,800 MW Panari Pumped Storage Project.

— The project falls within the Panna–Ranipur Tiger Corridor, which facilitates wildlife movement between the two reserves and supports tigers, leopards, dholes, wolves, sloth bears, gaurs, sambar and chital. Some project components also overlap with Panna Tiger Reserve’s satellite core areas.

— Panna Tiger Reserve: Situated in the Vindhyan ranges of northern Madhya Pradesh, the reserve extends across Panna and Chhatarpur districts. The Ken river enters the reserve from the southern end and passes through it for almost 55 km.

— Panna National Park was established in 1981 and brought under Project Tiger in 1994. It was the fifth tiger reserve in Madhya Pradesh and the 22nd in India. The reserve is mainly characterised by dry deciduous forests, including dry teak and mixed forest types. Important tree species include teak, mahua, tendu and dhaw.

— Ranipur Tiger Reserve: Situated in Chitrakoot district of Uttar Pradesh, in the Vindhyan hill ranges of the Bundelkhand region, the reserve comprises dry deciduous forests. Ranipur is connected to Panna Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh through the Panna-Ranipur Tiger Corridor.

— Notified in October 2022, Ranipur became the fourth tiger reserve in Uttar Pradesh and the 53rd in India. The reserve is home to teak, mahua, bamboo, tendu, palash, khair, salai and amla. Its wildlife includes tigers, leopards, sloth bears, wolves, hyenas, wild dogs, chinkara, sambar and chital.
Sports
• U-19 Asia Cup
— India U-19 team pulled off a thrilling win against Pakistan to clinch the U-19 Asia Cup title in Muscat, Oman.
— India’s victory secured its ninth Men’s Under-19 Asia Cup title.
• Total Chess

— The Total Chess World Championship Tour that starts next year will have four events around the year in different cities, with the first three events having 24 players each and the finale having four players fighting it out to become the FIDE World Combined Champion. The idea is to crown the most complete chess player in the world.

— Chess currently has three formats — classical, rapid and blitz. And each has its own world championship: the Classical World Championship (the most prestigious, and chess’s equivalent of Test cricket), the Rapid World Championship (comparable to ODIs) and the World Blitz Championship (closest to T20s, with players starting with 10 minutes or less on the clock).
— But at Total Chess, players will have to be good at all three formats. It will involve a modified version of classical, called fast classical.

— Fast classical is simply an accelerated form of classical chess, with players starting a game with 45 minutes on their clock and getting a bonus increment of 30 seconds each time they make a move. In classical chess, players usually start a game with 90 to 120 minutes on the clock, with increments for each move made.
Awards
• 10th edition of the Swachh Survekshan Awards
— The 10th edition of the Swachh Survekshan Awards (2025-26) recognised Visakhapatnam as the cleanest city among cities with a population of over one million, followed by Jabalpur and Lucknow.
— The awards were presented by the President and organised under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs’ (MoHUA) Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0.
— Super Swachh League: Previous years’ winners were assessed under a separate category called the ‘Super Swachh League’. Navi Mumbai secured first place, followed by Surat and Vijayawada.
— Cities with 3 lakh-10 lakh population: Ujjain ranked first, followed by Chandigarh and Guntur.
— Cities with 50,000-3 lakh population: Dewas (Madhya Pradesh) secured first place, followed by New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) and Sagar (Madhya Pradesh).
— New award categories: The 2025-26 edition introduced categories for the cleanest riverfront town, coastal town and Himalayan city.
— Rewa was recognised as the cleanest riverfront town, Puri as the cleanest coastal town, and Rudrapur as the cleanest Himalayan city, followed by Jammu and Shopian.

— Swachh Sheher Jodi: The initiative pairs better-performing cities with lower-performing cities as mentors to improve their cleanliness performance. Ahmedabad-Sanand secured the first position, followed by Indore-Depalpur and Tirupati-Kuppam.
— Launched on 27 September 2025, the Swachh Shehar Jodi initiative is an urban waste-management mentorship and peer-learning programme.
What is Swachh Survekshan?

It is an annual national cleanliness survey launched in 2016 by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs under the Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban (SBM-U). It assesses the cleanliness and sanitation performance of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and encourages improvements through competitive rankings.

NATION
In Arunachal’s Siang, a dam divides a community: ‘We will lose land, history’
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies-II: Government policies and interventions for development in various sectors and issues arising out of their design and implementation.

What’s the ongoing story: Seated on the verandah of his chang ghar, a stilt house built entirely from forest materials, Okam seems to belong to another era. His concerns, however, are firmly rooted in the present. The proposed 11,200-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) threatens to submerge his village, along with its farmland and ancestral homes. “We have protected this land for generations. How can I let that happen? We will lose our livelihoods. We will lose our history.”
Key Points to Ponder:
— What is the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP)?
— What is the Yarlung Tsangpo hydropower project?
— Why is the SUMP important in the context of China’s proposed hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo?
— What is a pre-feasibility report (PFR)?
— Who are the Adi people in Arunachal Pradesh?
— Why are the Adi tribes rejecting the project?
— What are the environmental and social concerns associated with the project?
Key Takeaways:

— Opposition to the project is not new. The UPA government declared it a national project in 2008, but it has made little headway against sustained resistance from the Adi community, Arunachal Pradesh’s second-largest tribe. The immediate flashpoint is a pre-feasibility survey by the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC).

— The government maintains that the exercise is preliminary and does not mean the dam has been approved. Three sites have been identified — Parong and Dite Dime in Siang district, and Ugeng/Komkar in Upper Siang district.

— For villagers, however, the distinction offers little reassurance. They fear that survey and drilling work on their ancestral land will bring the project closer to reality.  Residents have blocked roads, stopped NHPC personnel and machinery, and demanded the withdrawal of security forces. The confrontation escalated in October, with the arrest of activists and clashes with security personnel.

— For the Adi community, the stakes extend beyond individual villages. “We have depended on Siang River since the beginning of time. If this project goes ahead, at least 27 Adi villages will be submerged,” said Diji Tamuk, president of Adi Bane Kebang United, the community’s apex organisation in Arunachal Pradesh.

— The BJP-led state government defends the project on strategic grounds, citing China’s massive dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet and the potential risks of sudden water releases downstream. CM Pema Khandu has said no decision has been taken on constructing the dam and that public consultation and local consent will be necessary. However, BJP MP Tapir Gao’s assertion that the dam “will be built” has deepened distrust.

— Speaking to The Indian Express, Upper Siang Deputy Commissioner Ashok Tajo said the project’s primary objective was to address China’s activities across the border. “We need to counter the Chinese dam, which is 50 km upstream from here… as a security measure, this dam is very important right now.”
— He acknowledged that the project had struck an emotional chord. “…Naturally, there will be protests. There have also been shortcomings in the dissemination of information,” he said.
Do You Know:

— At 11,200 MW, the SUMP is touted to be India’s largest hydropower project. Plans to harness the Siang and Subansiri rivers date back to 1982, when the Brahmaputra Board proposed three smaller projects; countering Chinese projects was not a primary concern then. In 2013, however, the central government raised concerns over Chinese projects on the Yarlung Tsangpo — as the Siang is known in upstream Tibet — and expressed interest in being a downstream user.

— In 2017, the proposed Siang Upper Stage-I and Stage-II were merged under one umbrella, which eventually took shape as the SUMP. The project gained further prominence after China approved its 60,000 MW lower Yarlung Tsangpo hydropower project in December 2024.

Delhi SCO forum: Pak confirms participation, sending minister
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: International Relations; International Organisations; Important International Groupings.

Mains Examination: General Studies-II: Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India’s interests; India and its neighbourhood; Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India’s interests.

What’s the ongoing story: Pakistan is sending its Climate Change and Environmental Coordination Minister Musadik Masood Malik to New Delhi for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s Civilisational Dialogue Forum in the city on November 20-22.
Key Points to Ponder:
— What is the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation? How has the SCO evolved?
— How does SCO work and what are the key takeaways from the SCO Summit 2026?
— What does SCO mean for India’s global and regional interests?
— What is the significance of cultural diplomacy in strengthening people-to-people relations and building trust between countries?
— How does India balance bilateral tensions with Pakistan with its obligations and participation in multilateral groupings such as the SCO?
— Identify the member countries of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). Locate them on a world map
Key Takeaways:
— The announcement Saturday by Islamabad came a day after Union Culture Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat said he remained “hopeful” that Pakistan would confirm its participation.

— Announcing the decision to attend the summit, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said, “The government of Pakistan has nominated Dr Musadik Masood Malik, Federal Minister for Climate Change and Environmental Coordination, to represent Pakistan at the SCO Civilisational Dialogue to be held in Delhi from 20-22 November, 2026.”

— India had invited Culture and National Heritage Minister of Pakistan, Aurungzeb Khan Khichi, to the forum. This was the first such invitation to a senior Pakistan minister since the May 2025 hostilities between India and Pakistan in the wake of Operation Sindoor.
— The last time India hosted a Pakistan minister was in May 2023 when the then Foreign Minister, Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, travelled to Goa for a meeting of the SCO Foreign Ministers.

— The invitation to Pakistan is part of Delhi’s obligation, as host of the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, to invite representatives from all SCO member countries. Pakistan will be hosting the summit of SCO leaders next year.

— China, Kazakhstan, Iran, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Belarus, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Bahrain, Nepal, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Sri Lanka are among the countries that have already confirmed their participation in the Forum which will be hosted at the Purana Qila.

— While Prime Minister Narendra Modi will attend the inaugural ceremony on November 20, four key sessions will follow, themed around civilisational and cultural expression, art and architecture, and language, literature and manuscripts.

— Shekhawat said India’s aim was to ensure that the SCO was not merely a geopolitical and economic platform but also a forum for shared civilisational heritage and human values. He said culture has the power to initiate dialogues and build bridges of trust between countries and civilisations.
Do You Know:

— The SCO is a permanent intergovernmental organisation comprising 10 members: India, China, Russia, Pakistan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Belarus. It represents about 25 percent of global GDP and over 15 percent of international trade.

— Its objectives include strengthening mutual trust and good-neighbour relations, maintaining regional peace and security, promoting cooperation in trade, economy, science and technology, culture, energy, transport and education, and combating terrorism, separatism and extremism.

— The SCO provides India with a multilateral platform to deepen engagement with Central Asian countries and major Eurasian powers. It facilitates regional security and counter-terrorism cooperation through the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS), based in Tashkent, and offers opportunities to strengthen trade, investment, energy cooperation and connectivity.

— RATS is one of the SCO’s two permanent bodies, with its Executive Committee based in Tashkent, Uzbekistan. It facilitates cooperation among member countries to counter terrorism, separatism and extremism through information-sharing and coordination among relevant agencies.
