‘Can’t be both’: Bihar Raj Bhavan flags dual jobs of minister Ashok Choudhary
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Indian Polity and Governance-Constitution, Political System, Panchayati Raj, Public Policy, Rights Issues, etc.

Mains Examination: General Studies-II: Indian Constitution- historical underpinnings, evolution, features, amendments, significant provisions and basic structure, Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability.

What’s the ongoing story: Bihar Food and Consumer Protection Minister Ashok Choudhary may have to make a choice between retaining his Legislative Council seat or his post of assistant professor, after a Raj Bhavan note flagged his probationary leave as illegal and warned that holding the teaching post attracts disqualification under office-of-profit rules.
Key Points to Ponder:
— What is an ‘office of profit’?
— What constitutes an ‘office of profit’ under the Indian Constitution?
— Know the constitutional provisions governing the disqualification of legislators on the ground of office of profit.
— How do courts or the EC decide whether an MP or MLA has profited from an office?
— What is the underlying principle for including ‘office of profit’ as criterion for disqualification?
— What is the conflict of interest?
— What ethical issues arise when an elected representative simultaneously holds an academic or other public office?
Key Takeaways:

— Choudhary, who joined A N College under Patliputra University as an assistant professor of political science on February 17 this year, went on leave the very next day to continue his duties as a legislator and minister.

— The Raj Bhavan’s detailed note followed a meeting of the university Syndicate on August 19, after which its Vice-Chancellor referred the matter to the Secretariat of Governor Lt Gen Syed Ata Hasnain (retd) for guidance in the absence of clear rules.

— At issue were two questions: whether Choudhary, a senior JD(U) leader, was entitled to a lien — the legal right of a permanent employee to hold a substantive post while serving elsewhere — and whether the assistant professor post constitutes an office of profit even if he draws no salary from the university.

— In a detailed note on October 31, Deepak Kumar Singh, Additional Chief Secretary to Governor Hasnain, who is also the Chancellor by virtue of his post, wrote: “Dr Ashok Kumar is clearly not entitled to lien as it is not available to a person ‘on probation’. The note has examined this from the perspective of Bihar State Universities Act, Statutes as well as Bihar Service code. Hence, any question of ‘lien’ does not arise. Regarding Section 68(2) of the BSU Act, which gives a special privilege to university teachers and employees of ‘special leave’, if they are elected to state/ central legislature, it is pertinent to note that it applies one way only, that is when a university teacher/ employee (again meaning only permanent teacher/ employee and not a teacher/ employee on probation), while in service of the University, gets elected to Central / State Legislature, but not vice-versa.”
— The Raj Bhavan has sought the opinion of the Advocate General on the matter.

— Addressing the office-of-profit question, the note stated: “It is well settled that where the office carries with it certain emoluments or the order of appointment states that the person appointed is entitled to certain emoluments, then it will be an office of profit, even if the holder of the office chooses not to receive/ draw such emoluments. What is relevant is whether pecuniary gain is ‘receivable’ in regard to the office and not whether pecuniary gain is, in fact, received or received negligibly.”

— The Raj Bhavan note added that, hence, the post of assistant professor qualifies as an office of profit even if Choudhary draws no salary, adding that the Bihar Legislature Act also does not exempt this post under “office of profit classification”.
Do You Know:

— Basic disqualification criteria for an MP are laid down in Article 102 of the Constitution, and for an MLA in Article 191. They can be disqualified for: a) Holding an office of profit under government of India or state government; b) Being of unsound mind; c) Being an undischarged insolvent; d) Not being an Indian citizen or for acquiring citizenship of another country.

— The word ‘office’ has not been defined in the Constitution or the Representation of the People Act of 1951. But different courts have interpreted it to mean a position with certain duties that are more or less of public character.

— Articles 191 and 192 of the Constitution deal with “Disqualifications for membership” of a state Legislative Assembly or Council, and “Decision on questions as to disqualifications of members” respectively. Article 191(1) says that “a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member” of a state House “if he holds any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State…, other than an office declared by the Legislature…not to disqualify its holder”.

— Article 192(1) states that if “any question arises as to whether a member…has become subject to…disqualification…, the question shall be referred for the decision of the Governor and his decision shall be final”.
— Under Article 192(2), “Before giving any decision on any such question, the Governor shall obtain the opinion of the Election Commission and shall act according to such opinion.”

ECONOMY
Air fares, electronics, food: Price pressures becoming higher, wider
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Economic and Social Development-Sustainable Development, Poverty, Inclusion, Demographics, Social Sector Initiatives, etc.
Mains Examination: General Studies-III: Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilization, of resources, growth, development and employment.

What’s the ongoing story: October saw, for the first time in two years, household prices in a month rise more than 6% compared to the same month a year ago. The 6% figure is significant for one reason and one reason only: it is the upper limit of the Reserve Bank of India’s legally mandated tolerance range.
Key Points to Ponder:
— What is inflation targeting?
— How does the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement guide the Reserve Bank of India’s monetary policy decisions?
— What is the Consumer Price Index (CPI)?
— What is the difference between headline inflation, core inflation and core-core inflation?
— What are the causes of Inflation in the present situation?
— What is the impact of persistent food inflation and economic stability in India?
— What is chipflation?
— What is generalisation of inflation?
— What are the challenges faced by the RBI in balancing price stability and economic growth?
Key Takeaways:

— By law, if average inflation — as measured by the Consumer Price Index — is above 6% or below 2% for three consecutive quarters, then the central bank is deemed to have ‘failed’ in achieving its mandate.

— Three quarters is a long time. But some are already sounding warning signs: according to Tanay Dalal, an economist at Axis Bank, inflation is “likely to print above 6% until June 2027”. But what is driving inflation so hard that economists think prices will keep rising rapidly? We break it down here.

— In October, average airfares were a massive 43% higher compared to the same month last year. More importantly, of all the 358 goods and services in the CPI basket, airfares saw the largest increase in price (13.36%) from the previous month.

— Flying has become so expensive that the matter even reached the Supreme Court this month, with an application seeking a cap on fares ahead of the festival season. The court, however, declined to grant an urgent hearing, with Justice Vikram Nath saying ‘don’t travel by air’.

— As this newspaper has been pointing out for the better part of a year, the spiralling price of memory chips used in the manufacture of consumer electronics — or ‘chipflation’ — is increasingly becoming a driver of household inflation.

— In October, pen drive inflation jumped to 22%, phones and laptops to 9%, and other major electronic appliances to 4-5%. What will worry policymakers is that the global chip shortage, manufacturers say, is not going to end for several years.
— The first thing that households notice getting expensive is food items: in October, food inflation jumped to 8.94%. And if you want to dine out, throw in costlier cooking gas for restaurants.

— Prices of food and fuel items can be volatile — they can rise and drop sharply from one month to the next if supply suddenly improves for one reason or another. This is why, to understand the underlying price pressures, economists and policymakers like to also see how inflation is evolving by excluding food and fuel. This is called ‘core’ inflation.
— Even more refined versions of core inflation, which economists call ‘core-core inflation’, are rising. It excludes food, fuel, and jewellery.

— The problem, however, is that core inflation is also rising. The RBI predicted last month that core inflation will average 4.4% in 2026-27. With the October core inflation print already at 4.5%, the average for the first seven months of the fiscal year is 3.9%.

— The RBI will not just be worried about inflation rising, but also spreading to more and more items in the CPI basket, like consumer goods and services: 95 of the 358 items of the consumption basket recorded 6%-plus inflation in October versus 40 in January. Other measures also point to price pressures spreading wider.
Do You Know:

— Generalisation of inflation is the process when higher prices start to spread across the household consumption basket in a sustained manner. This requires the price rise to span different categories of items and move from ones that are most susceptible to price increases – such as food and fuel – to others, like consumer goods and services.

OPINION
DC in flux, open window to Beijing
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies-II: Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India’s interests.

What’s the ongoing story: P Vaidyanathan Iyer writes- “The US has consumed much of New Delhi’s diplomatic bandwidth over the last 12 months, with officers waking up to a fresh surprise every day. This is a relationship painstakingly nurtured by both the Congress and BJP governments over the last 25 years. It continues to remain ever so critical, but has of late required certain deftness to navigate the unpredictability.”
Key Points to Ponder:
— What is the status of India-China bilateral relations?
— What are the areas of cooperation between both the countries?
— What is a trade deficit, and how is it different from an overall balance-of-trade deficit?
— What are the major reasons for India’s persistent trade deficit with China?
— What are the challenges in bilateral relations?
— How do changing political dynamics in the United States influence India’s foreign policy choices?
— What measures should be taken to reduce India’s critical import dependencies on China?
— What is Productivity-Linked Incentive Scheme?
Key Takeaways:

— “The results of the mid-term elections in the US suggest the dynamics and engagement strategy will see a change. President Donald Trump no longer enjoys the advantage of a Republican-controlled Congress. With Democrats in majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, New Delhi will certainly look beyond the White House, and expand its outreach to the new Democrat lawmakers.”

— “While the challenge posed by the US over the last 12-18 months cannot be downplayed, where New Delhi really finds itself stuck and struggling to move forward is in the relationship with its big and powerful neighbour, China. It has never been an easy next-door neighbour, but India too has been slow to recognise the dependencies Beijing has been building over the years to gain strategic leverage.”

— “Under Deng Xiaoping, China started opening up in 1978, and became the factory of the world over the next three decades. Encouraged and aided by a benign and liberal multilateral trade order, it emerged as a global economic power and rivals the US now.”

— “As India continues to reform and push the pedal on economic growth, China has been aggressively pursuing what President Xi Jinping refers to as “new quality productive forces”. He spoke about it first on September 7, 2023, and elaborated on its contours over the next six months. It is necessary, he said, for China “to foster strategic emerging industries including new energy, new materials, advance manufacturing and electronic information, and nurture industries of the future.”

— “These are semiconductors, electric vehicles and batteries, artificial intelligence and robotics, renewable energy, critical minerals including rare earth, and future industries such as commercial spaceflight and quantum computing.”

— “These are all sectors where India will play catch up for a long time. The dilemma that New Delhi faces today is: Can it and should it really fast track business with Beijing. More than four years of deep freeze in bilateral relations after the military standoff in Ladakh, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi met on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in Russia in October 2024, endorsed a disengagement deal and decided to resume high level dialogues and restore predictability in relations.”

— “In the four years after the Galwan clashes in eastern Ladakh in June 2020, New Delhi had effectively shut its doors on China. Officials reckon that dismantling the restrictions and restoring normal processes pose considerable challenge. Can New Delhi quickly get back to allowing more business visas, can it expedite security clearances for investments, can it easily allow big Chinese industries to build factories? All this is easier said than done.”

— “But what is striking is even during one of the roughest patches in relations in recent years, India Inc’s appetite for imports from China did not diminish. Between 2020-21 and 2025-26, bilateral trade jumped 75 per cent to $151 billion from $86 billion. Significant though is the ballooning of India’s trade deficit with China — it almost tripled during the period to $112 billion in 2025-26  from $44 billion in 2020-21. This, in some way, also reflects on India Inc’s dependencies on China.”

— “Corporates are not unaware; many share the adverse impact felt by their businesses due to restrictions and export licensing by China. But building domestic capacity is still not seen as an imperative. It is true, imports are not bad, but the government feels cheap and easy imports have lulled India Inc to rising dependencies.”
— “The government is fully aware, and on its part has sought to support the industry in its capacity building efforts through programmes like the Productivity-Linked Incentive Scheme.”

— “Amid cooling of tensions, while engagement has resumed, it clearly needs to pick momentum. As India steps up its manufacturing capabilities, allowing Chinese investment, which brings technology along with it, is certainly an option. Security-related sensitivities need strategic calibration with different ministries sitting together on where procedures can be made simple. What Beijing does is not in Delhi’s control. It must do what is the need of the hour.”

ALSO IN NEWS
Study says to cut imports; key chemicals must be made locally from coal

— Hydrogen, Synthetic natural gas (SNG), methanol and ammonia should be prioritised for production from coal to reduce India’s dependence on imported fuels, fertilisers and industrial chemicals, according to a new study.

— The study by the Centre for Domestic Economy Policy Research (C-DeP) and the Centre for WTO Studies (CWS) ranks 23 coal-derived products across eight economic, industrial, and strategic parameters to guide investments under the government’s Rs 37,500-crore scheme for promoting surface coal and lignite gasification projects.

— Hydrogen emerged as the highest-priority product, followed by SNG, methanol, ammonia, dimethyl ether (DME), LNG, LPG, urea and diammonium phosphate (DAP), the study said. The recommendations come as India seeks to expand its coal gasification capacity to reduce its reliance on imported energy and fertiliser products.

— The government scheme aims to facilitate the gasification of an additional 75 million tonnes of coal and lignite annually, while the country’s target is to achieve 100 million tonnes of coal gasification capacity by 2030.
AI rockets to top of worries about financial system in US Fed survey
— Risks tied to the artificial intelligence sector surged to become the top-cited concern for –financial ​stability, according to a semi-annual report released by the Federal Reserve on Friday.
— The US central bank’s Financial Stability Report found potential risks from the ‌technology itself and the breakneck investment in the sector as the preeminent concern of survey respondents.

— Eighty-seven percent of contacts surveyed cited AI as a salient risk to the financial system, as respondents pointed to worries about cyberattacks, risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing, and the possibility of an AI earnings slowdown spurring a broad market correction. Just 50% of those surveyed cited AI as ​a risk in the May version of the Fed’s survey.

— Other top concerns cited in the survey also had heavy AI implications. The second most-cited concern was ​regarding a broad correction in risk assets at 52% of those surveyed, and cyberattacks specifically were flagged as a worry by 43% ⁠of respondents. Forty-eight percent of those surveyed also fretted about higher long-term interest rates, while 43% cited fiscal debt sustainability as a worry.
Transforming tribal education: From Eklavya to excellence

— C P Radhakrishnan writes- “Today, as we celebrate Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas on November 15 to mark the birth anniversary of Bhagwan Birsa Munda, one of the greatest tribal freedom fighters and a symbol of courage, sacrifice, and resistance against colonial oppression, I feel that a fitting way to pay homage to all our great tribal freedom fighters will be transforming the education and skilling system for tribal children, so that they not only empower themselves, but also society.”

— “As Bharat forges a new path ahead across almost every sector, the Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRS) are silently redefining the educational landscape of tribal children. These residential schools are established for tribal children within their own community setting, with the objective of ensuring their holistic development.. Through the EMRS Scheme, our tribal children are being provided institutional support, quality education, and opportunities to realise their dreams.”

— “The EMRS scheme is unique in its design and mandate. It has a strong focus on inclusive and equitable education for tribal children. Compared with the 7.5% reservation for Scheduled Tribes in other schools, at least 90% of students in the EMRS are from tribal communities. What is even more heartening is that 50% of seats are reserved for girls, an excellent positive step. Admissions are conducted through a state-level entrance test, with preference given to local students.”

— “If we look at the evolution of the EMRS, it can be traced in two phases. During the first phase from 1997-2018, a total of 288 schools were sanctioned. The first phase faced several structural challenges. The novelty of the EMRS 2.0, operationalised from 2018 onwards, lies in its addressing of limitations of earlier existing models.”

— “The scheme places special emphasis on first-generation learners and also recognises the learning gaps they may face. To address these challenges, structured academic support is provided through learning gap assessments, with bridge courses and remedial classes. In the initial classes, bilingual teaching is adopted, enabling children to learn comfortably in their familiar language, followed by a gradual transition to English as the medium of instruction. I was glad to learn from the Tribal Affairs Ministry that EMRS 3.0 has been operationalised from this year.”

Quad leaders meet today, signal to China before talks with US, Russia
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India’s interests.

What’s the ongoing story: The leaders of the Quad grouping — Prime Minister Narendra Modi, US President Donald Trump, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese — are set to meet in Manila on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the ASEAN and East Asia summits. This will be Trump’s first Quad leaders’ meeting since beginning his second term in January 2025.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Know these terms-QUAD, ASEAN, APEC and EAS
• What is Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD)?
• Know the Principles and the motive behind the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD)
• Who are member nations in Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD)?
• Who are observer nations in Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD)?
• What are U.S. interests in the Quad?
• What is Japan’s aims for the Quad?
• How is China’s relations with each of the Quad members?
• The QUAD in the Indo-Pacific region and its geopolitical implication-Know in detail
• How QUAD is Significant for India?
Key Takeaways:

• “On Tuesday evening in Manila, the President will participate in a multilateral meeting with Quad leaders to discuss shared interests of peace, prosperity and security in the Indo-Pacific region,” Olivia Wales, Assistant Press Secretary at the White House, said in Washington DC. She said under Trump’s leadership, the Quad has demonstrated that it is a partnership of action, tackling the region’s toughest challenges and driving opportunities to ensure a free and open Indo-Pacific.

• Sources said the Quad meeting, being held just ahead of the first-ever trilateral meeting between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on November 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, is a move to demonstrate the importance of the grouping which Beijing rejects.
• It also ties in with the position of the Quad countries, which have looked at China’s aggressive behaviour in the Indo-Pacific region as a challenge to maritime security.

• Trump, who revived the Quad grouping in 2017, has been giving mixed signals on China. The National Security Strategy in Trump 2.0 has been seen to be soft towards Beijing, a charge that the US administration denies.

• Sources pointed out that the four leaders will be meeting in a country which is not a Quad member for the first time since the grouping was upgraded to the level of leaders in 2021. Meanwhile, Modi reached the Philippines on Monday to attend the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit. “The visit reaffirms India’s partnership with ASEAN as a cornerstone to its Act East Policy and Indo-Pacific Vision,” the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said in a post on X.
Do You Know:

• The last Quad leaders’ meeting took place in September 2024, when then US President Joe Biden hosted the other three leaders in Wilmington, in Delaware. While it was India’s turn to host the meeting in 2024, Delhi swapped with Washington so that Biden could host it in the last year of his presidency.

• India was supposed to host the leaders’ summit in 2025, but the strained ties with the US over the tariffs, visa curbs and deportations, as well as Washington’s proximity to Islamabad, had cast a shadow. The situation has improved marginally, with Quad foreign ministers meeting thrice this year, including in Delhi in May, and twice in 2025. India is now expected to host the meeting next year, unless it passes the baton to another Quad member.

• India’s relationship with ASEAN countries is at the heart of its Act East Policy and occupies a central place in its MAHASAGAR vision, Modi said on Monday. MAHASAGAR, which translates to Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions, is India’s expanded global maritime doctrine.

• Founded in 1967, ASEAN has 11 members — Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Vietnam. India and several other countries, including the US, China, Japan and Australia, are its dialogue partners.

Bilkis Bano case: SC suspends life terms of two convicts, grants them bail
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance
Mains Examination:
• General Studies I: Social empowerment, communalism

• General Studies II: Structure, organization and functioning of the Executive and the Judiciary—Ministries and Departments of the Government; pressure groups and formal/informal associations and their role in the Polity.

What’s the ongoing story: The Supreme Court has suspended the life sentences of two convicts in the Bilkis Bano case and granted them bail, noting that they had been incarcerated for over 17 years and one of them has a “severe handicap”.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Who is Bilkis Bano?
• Bilkis Bano case and collective conscience of society-connect the dots
• What do you understand by pardon, suspension, respite, remission and commute?
• Bilkis Bano case: What Supreme Court Said?
• What was the issue before the court here?
• What is Rule of law?
• What is right to liberty?
• How right to liberty is granted by the Indian Constitution?
Key Takeaways:

• Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, currently lodged in a jail in Gujarat, were among the 11 men convicted in the case. Bilkis Bano, then 21 years old and five months pregnant, was gangraped and seven of her family members, including her three-year-old daughter, were killed during the Gujarat riots in 2002.

• “Having heard the parties, suffice it to state that the appellants have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years, and also the fact remains that one of the appellants has a severe handicap. Certainly, there are issues to be decided in the appeal, both on fact and law. In view of the above and considering the issues involved in this appeal, we suspend the sentence and grant bail to the appellants on such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the concerned trial court,” a bench of Justices M M Sundresh and P B Varale said in its order on October 28.
• Appearing for the appellants, Senior Advocate Siddharth Luthra said one of them was not named in the FIR and was implicated after nearly three years.

• Opposing the plea, Additional Solicitor General Raja Thakre said both the trial court and the Bombay High Court had taken into consideration the relevant material brought on record, especially as the offence committed was so serious.

• In August 2022, the Gujarat government had released the convicts under its remission and premature release policy. But in January 2024, the Supreme Court had quashed the remission, stating that the Gujarat government had no jurisdiction to pass such orders. The court had said that as the Bilkis Bano case was heard in a court in Mumbai, it was the Maharashtra government that had the powers to grant remission and Gujarat could not “usurp” the same. In its order on October 28, the Supreme Court directed that the duo’s appeal, challenging the Bombay High Court’s May 2017 order upholding their conviction and sentencing, be listed for hearing in due course.
Do You Know:

• In 2004, the Supreme Court transferred the gang-rape case from Gujarat to Mumbai over apprehensions of evidence tampering and the lack of a conducive situation for a fair trial. Four years on, a trial court in Mumbai convicted the 11 men of charges including murder, rape and rioting. The convicts appealed this order in the Bombay High Court, which upheld the punishment. The men then filed Special Leave Petitions before the Supreme Court which, on November 20, 2017, dismissed them, upholding the findings of the High Court as well as the sentence.

• In 2022, one of the convicts again approached the top court seeking directions to the Gujarat government for premature release, citing a 1992 remission policy for convicts who had completed at least 14 years in jail. The court asked the Gujarat government to consider the application “within a period of two months”, in line with the policy. Based on this, a government panel recommended their release and they were released from a Gujarat jail on August 15, 2022. They were felicitated upon their release by local leaders. Bano filed a petition against their release. Other petitioners, too, approached the court through public interest litigations.

• On January 8, 2024, a Supreme Court division bench said the Gujarat government did not have the authority or jurisdiction to consider the remission applications of the convicts to reduce their sentence as the trial was moved to Mumbai.
This is because such an application can only be taken up by a government within whose territorial jurisdiction the applicant was convicted — in this case, Maharashtra — and not where the offence took place (that is, Gujarat). The court also said that the pleas for remission should have been considered as per a 2014 policy which has a bar for grant of remission to convicts of heinous crimes.

• The bench said that in prior judgments, the Supreme Court has expressed scepticism over the convict’s claim to a second chance, particularly if the offence is a heinous one. The court also said this is not an indefeasible right.

• Unlike remission, the current release is on bail pending appeal. Two of the men, while serving their life sentence, filed a special leave to appeal, challenging their conviction altogether. The division bench was told that they had already spent 17 years in jail, that one of them was implicated nearly three years after the case, and that he was severely disabled.

• When the court hears the entire case in detail as part of the appeal, it will go into the specific details on the merits of the case. The bench said that pending the appeal, the two men should be granted bail on grounds including the 17-year incarceration as part of their life sentence. The court also suspended their sentence, which means that their punishment is stayed till the final decision on the appeal. The other convicts can also file separate appeals seeking bail on similar grounds of parity.

• According to the law, the court will decide on their pleas, and if it upholds the high court and trial court judgment, and sentences them, they will have to return to jail. The court has said that the appeal will be heard “in its due course”.

Let’s work to get back to 1.5° C target: COP31 draft agreement
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies III: Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, environmental impact assessment.

What’s the ongoing story: At the start of the second week of negotiations at the ongoing climate conference in the Turkish city of Antalya, host countries Turkey and Australia circulated the first draft of a cover decision that expresses deep concern at the scientific finding that the 1.5 degree Celsius target had gone beyond reach and urges every country to work harder to limit the magnitude and duration of temperature overshoot beyond that target.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Turkey and Australia circulated the first draft of a cover decision-What are key points?
• What is Just Transition Work Programme?
• “Countries strongly resist any attempts to force any new climate targets”—Discuss
• How the Just Transition Work Programme (JTWP) and Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) are different from each other?
• What are Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)?
• How Nationally Determined Contributions contribute to the Paris climate Agreement?
• Are Just Transition Work Programme legally binding?
• The COP 31 climate meeting-what has happened so far?
Key Takeaways:

• The 18-page draft decision, which is likely to undergo several amendments, also calls upon countries pursue efforts to bring back the levels of global warming to within 1.5 degree Celsius “as early as possible within this century”.

• The COP31 climate meeting in Antalya is being held in the backdrop of recent scientific assessments that it was no longer possible for the world to limit the rise in global temperatures to within 1.5 degree Celsius from pre-industrial times, one of the key objectives of the 2015 Paris Agreement. The scientific assessment, put out by the UN Environment Programme earlier this year, said a warming of 1.7 to 1.8 degree Celsius was now inevitable, and the best that the world could hope for was to bring it back to the 1.5 degree Celsius level through concerted efforts over the next few decades.

• The draft cover decision, which is supposed to serve as a political declaration from COP31, spends several paragraphs on the 1.5 degree Celsius target, urging countries to do more to fight climate change. It also calls upon the developed countries to strive to achieve net-zero emissions status by as early as 2030 and net-negative emissions by 2040.

• Each of these requests is highly unrealistic, considering the progress made by countries so far. None of the countries are on track to achieve net-zero status by 2030, and only a couple of relatively small nations, which account for a very small part of global emissions, have set targets for achieve net-zero status by 2040. A majority of developed nations are not on track to achieve this even in 2050.

• Countries strongly resist any attempts to force any new climate targets, and the success of voluntary commitments, on the sidelines of these meetings, have been very limited. The draft decision does not ask every country to try and achieve 35% electrification by 2035, but only calls upon every country to recognise this as a new global goal.

• Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav reiterated India’s position that a proposed Just Transition Mechanism must not create new obligations on countries. Just Transition refers to the efforts to ensure that transition to low-emission energy sources results in a fair, inclusive and socially equitable outcomes. Under a Just Transition Work Programme established three years ago, countries are currently negotiating the creation of a mechanism that would offer technical assistance, capacity building and knowledge-sharing
Do You Know:

• The draft decision proposes to set up a new technical ‘work programme’ on understanding the science of 1.5 degree with a particular focus on suggesting pathways to return to that level at some point. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a scientific body that produces comprehensive assessments of climate change every 5-7 years, had, in 2018, come out with a special report on 1.5 degree Celsius target, that dealt in detail, measures needed to be taken to meet this target.

• The draft decision also includes a reference to a new electrification target being pushed by Turkey and Australia, which seeks to increase the world’s share of electricity in total final energy consumption from the current 23% to 35% by 2035. Electrification is key to the global energy transition that the world has to go through to reduce its
greenhouse gas emissions.
• Turkey has been trying to convince countries to sign up to a voluntary commitment to this 2035 electrification target, but just about 30 countries had agreed to do so till the last count.

Why food inflation could be a major worry in 2027
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Economic and Social Development-Sustainable Development, Poverty, Inclusion, Demographics, Social Sector Initiatives, etc.
Mains Examination: General Studies III: Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilization, of resources, growth, development and employment.

What’s the ongoing story: India experienced an episode of high food inflation last during July 2023 to December 2024, when it averaged over 8.5% year-on-year. That was courtesy of a “strong” El Niño, which formed around June 2023 and ended by April 2024.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Know the Types of Inflation like Moderate Inflation, Galloping Inflation, Hyper-Inflation, Stagflation, Deflation, Core Inflation etc.
• What are the causes of Inflation in the present situation?
• How Inflation is Measured in India?
• What is food inflation?
• What are the factors responsible for the recent rise in food inflation in India?
• What is El Niño?
• How El Niño influences on India’s monsoon rainfall and agricultural production?
• Know the relationship between deficient monsoon rainfall and food price inflation in India, with reference to the developments highlighted in the article.
• What role do government buffer stocks of cereals play in controlling food inflation?
Key Takeaways:

• The current El Niño, officially confirmed from June 2026, has already developed into a “very strong” event. Most global weather agencies project it to persist in a “strong-to-very strong” form through January-March, before turning “moderate-to-weak” towards April-May 2027.

• The effects have been felt in rainfall for the country as a whole during this southwest monsoon season (June-September), being 12.6% below its “normal” long period average. The northeast monsoon season from October has also registered 33.6% below-normal precipitation as of November 16. The southern states, Maharashtra, Gujarat’s Saurashtra and Kutch regions, Rajasthan, western Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and the Northeast have borne the brunt of dry weather.

• The impact on food inflation is being seen too. The annual increase in the official consumer food price index crossed 5.3% in June, rising to 5.5% in July, 6% in August, 7.7% in September and a 23-month high of 8.9% in October.

• Going by the last food inflation episode — and the present El Niño being of much greater intensity than 2023-24, even tracking to be the strongest on record — one may expect a repeat, extending through 2027.

Do You Know:
Harish Damodaran Writes in “Why food inflation may creep higher in the months ahead”—

• El Niño – an abnormal warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean waters off the coasts of Peru and Ecuador – is associated with dry weather across India, Southeast Asia and Australia, while inducing heavy rains and destructive flooding in western Latin America, the US Gulf Coast and parts of the Caribbean. Sea surface temperatures in the east-central equatorial Pacific are currently 0.7 degrees Celsius above their 30-year-average. Any such deviation between 0.5 and 1 degrees is termed a “weak” El Niño. It is “moderate”, “strong” and “very strong” for deviations of 1-1.5 degrees, 1.5-2 degrees and above 2 degrees respectively.
• 2026 is seeing El Niño make a return after 2023-24, when it was a “strong” event that lasted from June 2023 to April 2024.

• This year has also witnessed a massive energy supply shock from the US-Israel versus Iran war. The closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz waterway since February 28 has led to global fertiliser prices skyrocketing. In April-May, India contracted urea and di-ammonium phosphate imports at port-landed prices of $935-959 and $930-935 per tonne respectively, as against their corresponding year-ago levels of $410-420 and $700-725.

• India’s last episode of high food inflation was during July 2023 to December 2024, which was courtesy of the “strong” 2023-24 El Niño event. El Niño is known to not only suppress rainfall, but also raise temperatures. If this El Niño turns out to be a “super/very strong” and peak through October-January, it could result in a relatively short and warm winter. The rabi (winter-spring) crops are the ones that would bear the brunt. El Niño apart, agricultural production can also take a hit from fertiliser shortages due to the West Asia conflict. An offsetting factor here could be a US-Iran deal to end fighting and reopen the Hormuz maritime chokepoint – through which roughly a third of the globally traded fertiliser products transited before the War.

Where India stands in fighting TB, despite missing 2025 target
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Economic and Social Development
Main Examination: General Studies II: Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources.

What’s the ongoing story: While India has not achieved its target of eliminating tuberculosis (TB) by 2025, five years ahead of the global deadline, it has been making strides. The incidence and mortality due to the bacterial infection has been on the decline.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Tuberculosis (TB) and India-Impact
• World Health Organisation’s Global TB Report 2026-what are the key takeaways?
• India has made tremendous progress in its fight against TB-What measures India adopted?
• Discuss the significance of India’s achievements in tuberculosis (TB) treatment and preventive therapy?
• What is India’s TB elimination target?
• What are the challenges and strategies in combating TB in India?
• What is the role of preventive healthcare in addressing communicable diseases like TB?
• Know India’s National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) in the context of WHO’s End TB Strategy.
• What are the socioeconomic implications of high TB incidence in India?
Key Takeaways:
• India has also seen an improvement in diagnosis — with more people accessing rapid diagnostics and getting tested for resistance to a commonly used antimicrobial.

• The country also saw a massive active case finding exercise over the last two years. Its incidence, however, remained uncalculated in this year’s Global TB report released by the World Health Organization (WHO) in view of new district-level surveillance data becoming available.

• India reported a 38% reduction in its TB mortality as compared to 2015 — breaching the 2020 End TB milestone of reducing it by 35%, albeit five years later. India’s TB mortality reduced from 28 per lakh population in 2015 to 18 per lakh population in 2025, according to the Global TB report. The 2025 target of reducing mortality by 75% still remains distant.

• This reduction came with WHO incorporating several different datasets to calculate the mortality. “Estimates of TB mortality in India for 2023–2025 were updated using recently released cause-of-death data from the sample registration system for the period 2022–2024, complemented by programmatic data for 2025,” the report said.

• India saw an increase in rapid diagnostic testing in 2025, with 46% of the cases being diagnosed using these. This is up from 38% the previous year. Quick diagnosis ensures timely treatment and prevents the further spread of the infection.

• The national programme has inducted several new testing methodologies under its TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyan. The programme which was started in November 2024, has already screened 25 crore people — 11 crore people being screened using chest X-ray that can diagnose asymptomatic cases. Another three crore were screened using the highly accurate molecular test. This exercise led to detecting nearly 49 lakh new cases, including almost 15 lakh asymptomatic cases that might not have otherwise been detected
Do You Know:
• With TB continuing to be the biggest infectious killer in the world, the WHO set End TB targets to bring down the incidence, mortality, and catastrophic costs associated with it.

• With 2015 as the base year, countries have been trying to meet targets of reducing TB deaths by 35% by 2020, 75% by
2025, 90% by 2030, and 95% by 2035. The target for TB incidence is reduction of 20% by 2020, 50% by 2025, 80% by 2030, and 90% by 2035. And, zero catastrophic costs across the years.

• While catastrophic cost data is unavailable for India and the incidence for the year is yet to be calculated, the mortality figures saw a decline but not to the levels targeted for 2025. “India, much like the rest of the world, is unlikely to meet the targets. But, this is not the time for complacency. There is a need for sustained efforts and proper funding to control the disease,” said Braj R, health expert who works in the domain of TB.

• The country’s estimated incidence is missing from this year’s Global TB report. This is significant considering India has not released its own TB report, which used to be released annually in March on the occasion of World TB Day. This report usually provides granular state-level data on various indicators.

• The report explained: “India has established a system for district-level sentinel surveillance (DLSS) of population-level trends in the prevalence of TB disease and TB infection. The system is based on a cluster sampling design and includes 300 clusters in 50 districts, with an eligible population (based on age and residency) of about 150 000 people. The first round of data collection was completed in 2025, with future rounds planned every 2–3 years. In addition to robust monitoring of trends in the prevalence of TB disease and infection, findings will be used to improve estimates of trends in TB incidence.”

LTCG tax debated by economists at pre-Budget FinMin meeting
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies III: Government Budgeting.

What’s the ongoing story:As the government began its pre-Budget consultations on Monday, the issue of Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax on equities was a keenly debated subject at a meeting of economists with officials from the Ministry of Finance.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax?
• What is the significance of Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax in India’s taxation system?
• Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) and Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG)-compare and contrast
• What are Foreign Portfolio Investments (FPIs)?
• What is the relationship between taxation policies and foreign portfolio investment flows?
• How can changes in capital gains taxation influence investment decisions?
• What is fiscal prudence?
Key Takeaways:

• The meeting, chaired by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, saw certain economists suggest that the LTCG tax on equities need not be reduced and concessions should not be made to foreign investors. At the same time, opposing views were also made.

• “It was debated a lot, but no consensus emerged,” a person aware of the discussions said. Another person who participated in the meeting said granular inputs came from all those in attendance and there was no one dominant view.
However, others said there were “not many takers” for cutting the LTCG tax now that circumstances have changed, with foreign inflows into India seeing a sharp turnaround in recent weeks.

• The first half of November has seen Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) buy $9.53 billion worth of Indian shares — the highest monthly purchase on record — marking a remarkable turnaround that has helped propel the Nifty 14% higher over the last five weeks. “The government officials did not say anything and heard the economists out. But the mood in the room was not in favour of cutting or giving concessions on LTCG tax to foreign investors,” another participant told The Indian Express.

• Ever since the Centre and the Reserve Bank of India took measures in June to support the rupee and encourage inflows by removing capital gains and withholding taxes on foreigners’ investments into government bonds, there have been calls from foreign investors, tax experts, and industry leaders that India should either remove or lower the LTCG tax on equities. This currently stands at 12.5%.

• Deliberations have also been held within the government on whether this relief should be provided. Speaking at an event last month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman had said the debate on LTCG tax is “healthy” and she is “keen” to hear about it. The Indian Express reported last month that the government’s internal deliberations in the run-up to next year’s Budget include lowering LTCG tax for both domestic and foreign investors and letting foreign investors pay this tax on the gains made in dollar terms as opposed to in rupee terms. So far in 2026-27 as a whole, FPIs remain net sellers of Indian shares to the tune of $7.67 billion. In 2024-25 and 2025-26 combined, FPIs’ net sales of domestic stocks were $34.32 billion.
Do You Know:

• The Union Budget for 2026-27 targeted a fiscal deficit of 4.3% of GDP. However, soon after the Budget was presented, the war in West Asia began, leading to a surge in global commodity prices, including those of energy and fertilisers — two of India’s key imports.

• On inflation, economists were of the view that the current high prints were not very disturbing, considering they are not expected to remain elevated on a sustained basis. Data released last week showed India’s headline retail inflation crossed 6% for the first time in two years in October.

Andhra Pradesh braces for third intense cyclone in a month
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Indian and World Geography-Physical, Social, Economic Geography of India and the World.

Mains Examination: General Studies I: Important Geophysical phenomena such as earthquakes, Tsunami, Volcanic activity, cyclone etc., geographical features and their location-changes in critical geographical features and in flora and fauna and the effects of such changes.

What’s the ongoing story: After cyclones Arnab and Murasu, another strong cyclone is headed towards the Andhra Pradesh coast, that too in less than a month. On Sunday, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said that a depression had formed in the southeast and adjoining southwest region of the Bay of Bengal. This system is set to intensify as it tracks northwestwards during the next couple of days.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Why back to back cyclones form in Bay of Bengal and travel towards India?
• Why are cyclones not forming in the Arabian Sea?
• After cyclones Arnab and Murasu, another strong cyclone is headed towards the Andhra Pradesh coast—what is the name, and who named it?
• Tropical cyclones and temperate cyclones—compare and Contrast
• What are the factors and the favourable conditions required for the cyclone formation over the Bay of Bengal?
• Know the process of cyclone naming in the North Indian Ocean region.
• How do successive cyclones affect the preparedness and response capacity of coastal states?
• Why are fishing communities particularly vulnerable during cyclonic conditions?
Key Takeaways:

• Once intensified into a cyclone, its will be called Akvan, a name proposed by Iran. The cyclone development is expected around November 16 and its further land-ward track likely to continue through November 18.

• The IMD said, “The system is very likely to move north-northwestwards, intensify further into a cyclonic storm over the central parts of South Bay of Bengal on November 16. It will further intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over westcentral Bay of Bengal on November 17. Thereafter, it is likely to intensify further and move northwestwards towards Andhra Pradesh coast during subsequent two days.”

• Akvan will will be third cyclone to develop in the Bay of Bengal this year and notably, the third in the post-monsoon season to form in the North Indian Ocean basin (comprising the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea).
Do You Know:

• A cyclone is a large-scale system of air that rotates around the centre of a low-pressure area. It is usually accompanied by higher temperatures, violent storms and bad weather. As per the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), a cyclone is characterised by inward spiralling winds that rotate anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

• It is also called a hurricane or typhoon in other parts of the world. India often witnesses tropical cyclones, known as such because they develop in the regions between the Tropics of Capricorn and Cancer. They are the most devastating storms on Earth. Such cyclones develop when “thunderstorm activity starts building close to the centre of circulation, and the strongest winds and rain are no longer in a band far from the centre,” the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) website said.

• The core of the storm turns warm, and the cyclone gets most of its energy from the “latent heat” released when water vapour that has evaporated from warm ocean waters condenses into liquid water. On the other hand, extratropical cyclones form outside of the tropic. They have “cold air at their core, and derive their energy from the release of potential energy when cold and warm air masses interact”, according to the NOAA.
• The Bay of Bengal is prone to large storm surges, in part because of its funnel-like shape that concentrates atmospheric activity, and its unique topography.

• An academic paper titled ‘Effect of landfall location and coastal topography on surge response in the Northern Bay of Bengal’, published in 2020, mentions that the destruction caused by storm surges also depends on the shape of the coastline. “A storm surge is highly dependent on local features and barriers that affect the flow of water. The Bay of Bengal has a complex coastal geometry, including estuary deltas, pocket-like bays, and straight coasts,” the paper says.

• Another important factor is temperature. Warmer the water, more intense the cyclone, and the Bay of Bengal has generally recorded higher temperatures than the Arabian Sea. Although, due to climate change-related disruptions of late, the western coast of India is also witnessing more frequent and stronger cyclones.

AI’s next frontier: From digital to physical world
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance
Mains Examination: General Studies III: Science and Technology- Developments and their Applications and Effects in Everyday Life.

What’s the ongoing story: At a time when renewed unease over artificial intelligence (AI) spending is weighing heavily on the technology sector, there are some answers to the related concern over how to tangibly monetise AI tools.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is physical AI?
• How does physical AI differ from conventional digital artificial intelligence applications such as chatbots and AI-based image generation?
• Explain the role of large language models (LLMs) and reinforcement learning in improving the capabilities of AI-enabled robots.

• “Physical AI could create a new industrial ecosystem involving the development, deployment and maintenance of autonomous machines”—Know its potential implications for manufacturing, logistics and industrial productivity.
• What are the potential of physical AI to create economic value by 2040?
Key Takeaways:

• Abu Dhabi’s state-owned oil company ADNOC, for instance, has signed a new deal earlier this week with AI firms G42 and OpenAI to deploy advanced AI capabilities across the energy major’s operations. The mandate: leverage AI to help improve operational efficiency and address complex engineering challenges in the oil sector.

• “For a long time, the AI industry has talked about what it needs from the energy industry. And now I think we can repay the favour,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday (November 2) after the signing of the agreement at the ADIPEC conference in Abu Dhabi. The agreement is a harbinger of what is to come next in the AI deployment strategy — “physical AI”, or AI systems that operate in and interact with the physical world, rather than existing only in digital environments or as pure software products.
Do You Know:

• Physical AI refers to the use of AI to enable autonomous systems such as robots, camera-bots, and self-driving cars to discern, comprehend, and perform complex actions in the physical world — effectively, AI systems that operate in the physical world. This involves the combination of AI models with sensors, actuators, and other control systems that allow models to act upon real-world environments.

• Most of the AI that humans interact with on a day-to-day basis today exists purely digitally: Things like talking with a chatbot, using AI for image generation, or using it as a code assistant – these all live in the world of bits and bytes. Physical AI, on the other hand, is the kind that crosses over into the world of atoms, things in actual physical space. These are AI systems that can perceive their environment, they can reason about it, and can take action. Take robotics, for instance. Before AI, robot behavior was typically scripted, and robots could only perform a predefined range of tasks within specifically engineered environments, like a robotic arm that welds the same seam a thousand times a day on an automotive production line.

• In contrast, robotic AI agents equipped with general understanding from large language models (LLMs) can be imparted with a powerful “common sense” about the world, according to IBM Think’s Cole Stryker. These models can be paired with reinforcement learning techniques in high-performance hybrid architectures so that robots can possess both general knowledge and a specialised understanding of a specific use case. So, these AI-infused robots get better with use. According to Stryker, physical AI “goes far beyond individual robots to entire AI-powered factories, energy-efficient smart grids or fleets of automated vehicles”.

• Generative AI models such as ChatGPT or Meta’s Llama are trained on huge amounts of text and image data, largely scraped off from the internet. While these AI models have significant capabilities in generating human language, visuals, and abstract concepts, they are limited in their grasp of the physical world. Physical AI extends current generative AI with an understanding of spatial relationships and the physical behaviour of the world by taking in multimodal inputs such as images, videos, text, speech, or real-world sensor data and converting them into insights or actions that an autonomous machine can then execute.

• The physical AI deployment push is also an attempt to tackle what has been the biggest bugbear for the AI sector: monetisation. “I think they are thrashing around for revenue ideas. You can’t vibe code a phone. It is a deep ecosystem. Others such as Amazon have tried,” a US-based technology analyst told The Indian Express.

Karakoram-2026: what deepening China-Pak ties mean for India
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India’s interests.
What’s the ongoing story:China and Pakistan’s longstanding partnership, while not a formal alliance, has emerged as a defining feature of the regional security architecture.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is Karakoram-2026?
• What is the significance of the first joint army-level exercise between the People’s Liberation Army and Pakistan Army?
• What is the strategic significance of Xinjiang in the context of China-Pakistan military cooperation and India’s northern security environment?
• Trace the evolution of China-Pakistan strategic relations since the 1963 Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement.
• What are the major pillars of China-Pakistan cooperation discussed in the article?
• How Karakoram-2026 represents a shift in China-Pakistan military cooperation from defence acquisitions towards operational integration?

• “The growing military integration between China and Pakistan has transformed India’s traditional two-front security challenge into a more complex operational problem”—Analyse this statement in the context of Karakoram-2026.
Key Takeaways:

• Over the years, their military cooperation has deepened, moving beyond defence acquisitions and joint exercises towards greater functional integration and interoperability. In this context, the countries’ recently concluded joint exercise, Karakoram-2026, marked a significant milestone — it involved the participation of regular army formations from both countries. Notably, the exercise was conducted in Xinjiang, which borders Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

• Phase One of the exercise, up to October 19, involved troops from both sides practicing specialised tactics, close-quarter combat and unmanned aerial vehicle (or drone) operations. Phase Two entailed joint command, mixed formations and combat teams undertaking counterterrorism clearance operations, joint manoeuvres and coordinated fire drills.

• The equipment used was Chinese, including small arms, armoured assault vehicles, infantry fighting vehicles and support systems, such as artillery, drones and anti-manned systems. The Chinese Ministry of National Defence described Karakoram-2026 as an opportunity to deepen cooperation and tactical integration between the two armies.

• The Karakoram-2026 exercise must be viewed against the expanding profile of the China-Pakistan defence cooperation — from a buyer-supplier arrangement towards deeper military integration. It follows a joint patrol conducted by Chinese and Pakistan security personnel at Mantika Pass, at an altitude of 4,700 metres (near Khunjrerab Pass), in the upper Hunza area of Gilgit-Baltistan, reflecting the operationalisation of the border management mechanism and a growing institutional engagement.

• In May 2025, when India launched aerial strikes (Operation Sindoor) targeting terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan, the collusion between Beijing and Islamabad came into sharp focus. There was strong evidence that China accelerated the deliveries of PL-15 E air-to-air missiles, air defence and electronic platforms into Pakistan’s military structure during the crisis.

• The change of government in Bangladesh also adds a new dimension to defence and diplomatic ties in the region. Islamabad, Dhaka and Beijing may not have formed a strategic trilateral, but they are leveraging the China-Pakistan strategic framework.

• Bangladesh has advanced plans to purchase J-10CE fighter jets from China and its pilots will be trained by Pakistan at Jessore airbase, near the Siliguri corridor. There are also discussions regarding integration of air defence radar systems and upgrading Bangladesh tank fleet with Chinese technology and Pakistani expertise. High-level exchanges between the Pakistani and Bangladesh militaries are a distinct departure from the past isolation.

• Karakoram-2026 takes the China-Pakistan relationship a step further. Beyond equipment familiarisation, the joint training facilitates the exchange of operational experience, standardisation of procedures, command and control coordination and interoperability. Incidentally, there are intelligence reports that Pakistan Army officers are posted in key Chinese military formations in the PLA’s Western Theatre Command and Joint Staff Department of the Central Military Commission (CMC).
Do You Know:
• Karakoram-2026, held from October 14-22 in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, was the first joint-army level exercise between People’s Liberation Army (PLA) and Pakistan Army.

• It expanded on the earlier naval, air and counterterrorism exercises (Sea Guardian, Warrior and Shaheen series). The focus was on challenging high-altitude operations, relevant to the PLA’s Western Theatre Command which oversees the border with India.

• The China-Pakistan nexus refers to the longstanding strategic, economic and military partnership between the two countries. It dates to the 1963 Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement under which Pakistan ceded the Shakasgam Valley, part of Gilgit-Baltistan, to China, thus cementing the strategic alignment.

• The subsequent decades witnessed China’s growing role in building Pakistan’s nuclear and missile programme which altered the regional strategic balance and security dynamics, primarily hedging against India. Today, China treats Pakistan a strategic priority, central to its South Asia policy.

• The core pillars of China-Pakistan nexus are:
—Military supplies: China is Pakistan’s dominant arms supplier, accounting for roughly 70-80% of its imported military hardware. Major acquisitions include J-10C and JF-17 fighter aircrafts, Type 054 A/P frigates, Hangor-Class Submarines, HQ-9, 16, 17 series air defence systems, and Wing Loom drones.
—Defence co-production: Both nations regularly collaborate on co-producing military equipment including fighter jets (J-10C and JF-17), main battle tanks (Al-Khalid), missiles, naval platforms, electronic and surveillance systems. Pakistan gets access to advanced technology while China gets to consolidate its defence-industrial outreach.
—Information: Information and space are other arenas of close cooperation; encompass intelligence sharing, cyber warfare, satellites (Bei Dou for navigation) and information cum narrative alignment, through initiatives like China-Pakistan Information Corridor.
—Infrastructure: The collaboration extends to infrastructure and strategic projects such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and Gwadar Port under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).
—Drills: The two countries regularly conduct bilateral and multilateral drills; the scope has significantly enlarged over the years.

• The significance of Karakoram-2026 lies in the changing character of the China-Pakistan military cooperation. The joint training of mixed formations, growing integration of the Chinese platforms into Pakistan’s military inventory and increasing military engagement in the Xinjiang-Karakoram region have critical strategic significance. India needs to closely monitor the evolving China-Pakistan military relationship, both as an integrated two-front challenge and in the larger regional context.

The Editorial Page
What AQI isn’t telling you about the air we breathe, the toll it takes
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: General issues on Environmental ecology, Bio-diversity and Climate Change – that do not require subject specialization.
Mains Examination: General Studies III: Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, environmental impact assessment.

What’s the ongoing story: Gautam I Menon Writes— The official AQI, as the CPCB in India calculates it, is represented by the pollutant with the worst sub-index. This can understate the combined risk of several pollutants. Other carcinogenic chemicals such as benzene, arsenic and nickel are left out altogether.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is the Air Quality Index (AQI)?
• What are the eight pollutants considered in India’s official AQI calculation?
• PM2.5 and PM10—Compare and contrast
• Why does India’s official AQI use the pollutant with the highest sub-index to determine the overall air quality category?
• Know the role of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) in monitoring air quality.
• What are temperature inversions?
• How the geography of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, changing wind patterns and temperature inversions contribute to winter air pollution?
• How limitations in India’s air-quality monitoring and reporting mechanisms can weaken evidence-based policymaking and public accountability?

Key Takeaways:
Gautam I Menon Writes—

• In north India’s autumns, particularly around the week of Diwali, smoke from crop burning adds to the annual Diwali spike in the air quality index, or AQI. The geography of the Indo-Gangetic plains, changes in the pattern of prevailing winds and temperature inversions common at this time conspire to trap the dirty air in place. In that week, and through much of the later winter season, India’s air pollution problem springs sharply into focus.

• A recent study showed that 83 of the 100 most polluted cities in the world were in this country. This isn’t a problem only in parts of northern India — whether in the north, south, east or west, air pollution levels are stubbornly high. Progress in reducing them has stalled even as the health toll rises.

• In India, the AQI is calculated based on the amounts of eight pollutants in the air we breathe. Of them, PM2.5 and PM10 represent the concentration, by mass, of particles of size up to 2.5 microns and up to 10 microns. The other pollutants are nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone, ammonia and lead. The first three are associated with the burning of diesel, coal and petrol, with biomass burning an additional major source of carbon monoxide and small particles in India.

• The official AQI, as the CPCB in India calculates it, is represented by the pollutant with the worst sub-index. This can understate the combined risk of several pollutants. Other carcinogenic chemicals such as benzene, arsenic and nickel are left out altogether. Further, values for the AQI are capped at 500, pulling the daily figure down during extreme episodes. Any hourly PM2.5 reading above 380 gives a sub-index of 500, so this Diwali’s peak of 3,744 at Mundka counted for no more than 380 would.

• An analysis of 2019 data attributed 1.67 million deaths to air pollution, about 18 per cent of all deaths in India. The State of Global Air 2025 report puts the figure at about 2 million in 2023, finding that about two-thirds of COPD deaths and 36 per cent of stroke deaths could be attributed to air pollution, as well as more than one in four heart disease deaths.

• Lower respiratory infections linked to air pollution caused four times the disease burden of those linked to tobacco in 2017, mostly affecting young children and older adults. An ICMR study of 33,213 patients in five cities linked higher-pollution days to more respiratory emergencies.
Do You Know:

• Air pollution is a wicked problem. It calls for cooperation across states, indeed countries, since it affects an airshed common to Pakistan, Nepal, the Indo-Gangetic plain and Bangladesh. What’s surprising is the public apathy towards the air pollution question, an apathy similar to that seen towards issues of climate change. Both may have their roots in the same thinking: That individuals cannot move the scale on what is essentially a collective action problem and, more cynically, that the incentives behind our politics will only reward short-term thinking.

• India’s clean air strategy needs to move beyond monitoring pollution levels to understanding and communicating their health consequences, says Dr Soumya Swaminathan, public health activist and former chief scientist at the World Health Organization (WHO).
—She believes thea National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) must correlate specific health impacts with individual pollutants and make the risks more visible to the public. “At present, the Air Quality Index (AQI) is calculated based on the highest concentration among the eight pollutants being monitored. However, this approach needs to change because different pollutants have different impacts on human health. They cannot be treated as equivalent. For instance, elevated levels of PM2.5 have different health implications from PM10, ozone or carbon monoxide. Each pollutant requires its own health-based benchmark, accompanied by a corresponding health advisory tailored to its specific effects,” Dr Swaminathan says.
—The health advisories should reflect the specific pollutant and the population groups most vulnerable to its effects. Although the health impacts of air pollution are already well documented, new evidence continues to emerge. For example, major studies published in 2026 have highlighted the relationship between PM2.5 exposure and dementia. According to Dr Swaminathan, the scientific evidence base is continually expanding. “We are learning more about the different ways air pollution affects the human body, the mechanisms through which these effects occur and the long-term consequences of exposure. PM2.5 triggers inflammation in the body, and once systemic inflammation develops, it can affect multiple organs and bodily functions,” she says.
—She also highlights the neurological impacts of air pollution, particularly on children. A study by the Institute of Economic Growth examined children aged 2–11 years and found that higher PM2.5 exposure during the preceding 12 months was associated with poorer performance in mathematics and reading.

At COP31, push for a more equal climate bargain
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Important International institutions, agencies and fora- their structure, mandate

What’s the ongoing story:Kamil Saiyed Writes—India must use its negotiating capital at the ongoing COP31 to advocate for a minimum annual amount of grant finance from developed countries. COP31 is framed as an implementation COP. Attention should turn to how developed countries will lead efforts to deliver the climate finance goal agreed at COP29: At least $300 billion annually by 2035.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is a Conference of the Parties (COP)?
• How is COP31 different from previous COPs?
• What is the significance of the pre-industrial temperature baseline in measuring global warming?
• What is the impact of El Niño on global temperature patterns, with reference to the warming trend highlighted in the WMO recent report?
• What is the significance of the 1.5°C temperature threshold under the Paris Agreement?
• Despite decades of international climate negotiations, global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise—Why?
• What is the Loss and Damage Fund?
• Know the importance of climate finance in implementing global climate commitments.
• What are Biennial Transparency Reports (BTRs)?
• Why Biennial Transparency Reports matters?
• Compare and Contrast—climate outcomes and voluntary initiatives under the COP Action Agenda.
• What are the three major voluntary 2035 climate targets highlighted in the COP31 Action Agenda?

Key Takeaways:
Kamil Saiyed Writes-

• Developed countries have mobilised finance towards the earlier goal of $100 billion through bilateral channels, multilateral development funds such as the World Bank, and multilateral climate funds such as the Green Climate Fund. These funds also unlocked private investments. They will have to substantially expand the financial flows to reach $300 billion. However, this expansion faces political headwinds in the US and fiscal constraints in Europe.

• Developed countries are likely to put greater emphasis on the role of private players and commercial investments in meeting the target, given that they seek returns on their investments. It makes these investments unsuitable for adaptation needs, most of which deliver public benefits without generating revenues for investors. A greater reliance on the private sector without a parallel rise in grant funding could leave adaptation needs unmet.

• We can observe this tension playing out in the debate over the loan-contribution policy of the Green Climate Fund. It is the biggest public green multilateral fund and has proposed to remove the cap on total aggregate loan contributions. It has also proposed to count guarantees as grants-equivalent. This means, if a donor provides a $100 million guarantee that has $15 million grant-equivalent value, it will count towards their contribution towards funds replenishment. The guarantee may provide a valuable risk cover, but no cash is transferred. This policy could inflate replenishment value with guarantees without increase in cash for grants.

• Developed countries’ financial obligation reflects their responsibility for historical emissions and their greater capacity to respond. These include helping vulnerable countries to address the problem to which they have contributed relatively little. Yet much of this support remains repayable — according to the OECD, loans accounted for 67 per cent of public climate finance in 2024, compared with 29 per cent for grants. This financing mixture can create problems for many countries.

• Currently, most of the climate-vulnerable countries are either small island states — with limited fiscal capacity — or poorer countries facing challenges with servicing interest on sovereign debt. They face an increasing number of climate shocks affecting their energy and food resilience, which needs more money to fix. At the same time, they spend an increasing amount of their budget for servicing sovereign debt owed to developed countries. This leaves less money than usual to meet domestic needs, let alone to absorb climate shocks.

Do You Know:
Kamil Saiyed Writes-

• India should therefore seek a quantified minimum amount of annual public grant finance for adaptation, with priority for vulnerable countries and activities without sufficient commercial revenue. Only grant disbursement should be assessed towards this goal. This commitment is in line with Article 9.4 of the Paris Agreement, which recognises the need for public and grant-based resources for adaptation.

• Climate COPs provide an opportunity for developing countries to come together for a measurable grant commitment. India has earlier helped in building coalitions to advance differentiated responsibilities. At the Conference of Select Developing Countries on Global Environmental Issues in 1990, India successfully advocated for developed countries to take responsibility for historical emissions and provide financial and technological support to developing countries.

• Since then, India has played a central role in developing the understanding of what constitutes Common but Differentiated Responsibility (CBDR). Advocating for a minimal annual grant commitment would continue India’s defence of CBDR.
