To understand women’s unpaid work, govt goes looking for data
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Economic and Social Development
Mains Examination:
• General Studies I: Role of women and Social empowerment,
• General Studies II: Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources.
• General Studies III: Inclusive growth and issues arising from it.

What’s the ongoing story: The government’s target to make India a developed nation by 2047 faces a major hurdle: getting enough women into the workforce. According to the World Bank, raising the female Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) to 50% — it was 34.6% in September — “could be the best way” for India to raise its GDP growth rate closer to the 8% needed to become a high-income country by 2047.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is the Female Labour Force Participation Rate (FLFPR)?
• Differentiate between paid work and unpaid domestic and caregiving work.
• Why has MoSPI proposed adding questions on unpaid domestic and caregiving activities to the PLFS?
• What is the significance of distinguishing between women undertaking unpaid household work by choice and those doing so because of social expectations or family obligations?
• How restrictions on women’s mobility, limited time for entrepreneurial activities and caregiving responsibilities affect the growth of women-led informal enterprises?
• How Tamil Nadu’s factory dormitory model has helped address accommodation and mobility constraints faced by women workers in the manufacturing sector?
Key Takeaways:

• “The argument that women don’t take up employment because of care duties, that there is a direct relationship between the two, has to be established first,” said Professor Neetha N of Centre for Women’s Development Studies. “So far, only broad analysis and claims have been made as there is not enough macro data that can establish this link.”

• And so, the government is now looking for this data, with the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) proposing changes to its flagship job and informal sector surveys following requests from academics, the Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises, the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, and the government’s top economic advisers.

• According to a statistics ministry official, the new questions will help capture the “magnitude of care work being performed”. And because care work can overlap with formal employment, they should also show how much domestic and caregiving work employed individuals undertake. “Among the unemployed, we also need to know how many are primary caregivers, or conversely, how many caregivers are unable to take up employment specifically due to care responsibilities.”
Do You Know:

• Last month, MoSPI suggested adding new questions to the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) to get more detailed answers on the unpaid work done by household members. This includes asking if the things they make and services they provide — such as cooking, feeding and taking care of children, and helping elders — are for their own consumption or for selling. It also proposed asking if people actively sought paid work in the previous 30 days, whether they want to do such work at present, and the main reason why they have not looked for such work. One of the answer options for the last question is family and household responsibilities.

• The PLFS already asks people not looking for work what the main reasons are, with the options including not being qualified, health and age, wanting to continue studies, and child care or personal commitments in home making. In response to this question, which experts say is “too generic”, 44.4% of women in 2025 cited child care or personal commitments in home making as the main reason for not looking for work.

• Unpaid domestic and care work is one of the major factors preventing women from taking up paid jobs. According to the government’s Time Use Surveys, working-age men (aged 15-59 years) spent 62 minutes a day on various unpaid activities in 2024, down from 74 minutes in 2019.

• In comparison, women in the same age bracket saw their time spent on unpaid activities — which includes caring for children and the elderly — go up slightly from 364 minutes per day in 2019 to 366 minutes in 2024. And yet, the female LFPR rose from around 26.5% to 43.6% over the same period.

title: Why SC said ‘creamy layer’ verdict can’t reopen past appointments

content.value: The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6) said its March verdict on the “creamy layer” among Other Backward Classes (OBCs) will not reopen selections and appointments already concluded but will apply to the pending Civil Services Examination (CSE) 2025 service allocation.
The “creamy layer” is a term used in India’s reservation system to describe wealthier, more advanced members of OBCs. Those included in the creamy layer are not entitled to OBC reservation benefits.

In March, the court had ruled that income cannot be the sole criterion to decide the OBC creamy layer, and settled the long-pending question of equivalence between public sector undertakings (PSUs) and private sector employees and those in the government sector.
The Centre then sought clarification on the verdict’s temporal reach, leading to the formation of a bench of Justices PS Narasimha and R Mahadevan.

That bench has now ruled: “The ratio laid down in the judgment shall not, by itself, furnish a ground for reopening selections or appointments already concluded prior to the judgment dated 11.03.2026.” It added that “the process of allocation remains pending and there is no convincing or reasonable justification for deferring the implementation” of the March verdict.
The court also refused the Centre’s plea for two years to establish equivalence of posts but extended the time for compliance with the judgement by two months.
What the Supreme Court’s March 2026 verdict on OBC creamy layer said

That case arose from an office memorandum (OM) of September 1993 which laid down the criteria for identifying persons from the OBCs who fall within the “creamy layer” and are thus excluded from reservation. Under category IV of the income/wealth test, income from sources other than salaries and agricultural land is excluded.

The Department of Personnel and Training clarified in a letter in October 2004 that where “equivalence” of posts in PSUs, banks and public employment had not been determined, those salaries would be assessed separately. If it crossed the prescribed limit for three consecutive years, the children would be under the creamy layer.

In March this year, the bench held that a clarificatory letter “cannot introduce a substantive condition that does not exist in the parent policy”. It held that income from salaries itself cannot become the sole criterion for determining creamy layer status. It said that treating children of PSU and private employees differently from those of government servants in similar posts amounted to “hostile discrimination”.
The court then directed the Centre to implement these principles within six months and create supernumerary posts as required for candidates who satisfy the non-creamy layer criteria.
Why the Centre needed clarification

The final result of CSE 2025 was declared five days before the March verdict. In its application, the Centre said that the retrospective implementation would unsettle concluded selections and service allocations, including those made in respect of earlier CSE.

It pointed to more than 6.69 lakh reserved vacancies, including 3.70 lakh OBC vacancies filled over the past 10 years. The government argued for prospective overruling, under which a court can limit a ruling to future cases, asked if the judgement operates prospectively, and also sought two years to establish equivalence of posts after consulting all states and Union Territories.
What the Supreme Court said

The court observed that the interpretation of the 1993 OM and the 2004 letter and the “rejection of mechanical exclusion based on salary income” were not open for reconsideration and said that the miscellaneous applications cannot be used as “a ruse to secure reconsideration of the merits of the judgment under the guise of seeking clarification”.

The bench then said that the original proceedings were between candidates before the court and the relief was confined to them. It said: “We find no observation or direction requiring the Union Government to revisit appointments already made, revise the seniority of any person, or undertake any selection, appointment or service allocation exercise afresh.”

The court said that the Centre’s application proceeded on an “erroneous assumption” that the benefit operated retrospectively. It said: “This Court did not direct the retrospective revision or reconsideration of selections, appointments, seniority or service allocations already concluded.” The six-month deadline in the verdict applied to considering the claims of the respondents and was not a general exercise to be undertaken covering all recruitment years.

The bench said that all selections, appointments, and roster allotments will follow the 1993 OM as the March verdict interpreted — that is, a clarificatory letter such as the 2004 one cannot override the OM, where equivalence of posts has not been established, the children of PSU and private sector employees are tested only under the income/wealth test, which does not count salary income; and income from salary can not be treated as a sole criterion for treating a candidate under creamy layer since the status and category of the parent’s post are also essential.

The court said that the government is free to frame policies on creamy layer criteria but refused to prescribe deadlines for establishing equivalence between posts as it falls “within the domain of the executive and the legislature”.

title: When can the Income Tax Department reopen a taxpayer’s assessment?

content.value: The Supreme Court has allowed the Income Tax Department to reopen assessments of Chetan and Nitin Sabharwal, sons of former Chief Justice of India YK Sabharwal, over shares sold for Rs 255 crore and subsequent property purchase in Delhi’s Sikandra Road.

A bench comprising Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran on October 28 upheld the 2015 notices that reopened the brothers’ earlier assessments. The court held that the notices were based on “tangible material”, citing the I-T Department’s investigative unit report.

It said that the alleged overvaluation of shares and the use of proceeds to acquire another asset could involve “a diversion of income, accessable to tax under the guise of sale proceeds.” Here is what the case is about, and what the law says on reopening taxpayers’ assessments.
What were the transactions in question?

In 2007, the brothers and two other shareholders signed share purchase agreements with GYS Real Estate Pvt Ltd, wherein they agreed to sell their shares in Pawan Impex and SVIIT Software Pvt Ltd for Rs 255 crore.
Each of the four sellers was entitled to a quarter of the consideration. The final payments were lower after the buyer deducted the company’s outstanding loans and other costs.

When Chetan filed for his income tax return in 2008-09, he declared a loss of Rs 90.37 lakh. The return also showed around Rs 37.64 crore received from the buyer under “sundry credit,” an accounting entry that included amounts payable by the buyer under the share sale transaction. The department examined the transaction and completed Chetan’s scrutiny assessment under Section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, accepting his declared income.

Nitin’s returns, however, were only processed under Section 143(1), which is a routine processing of returns that involves checks and certain permitted adjustments. It is not the same as a detailed scrutiny assessment of the taxpayer’s claims and transactions under Section 143(3).

The brothers used proceeds from the share sales for purchasing a residential property on Sikander Road. Chetan had also claimed exemption from long-term capital gains tax if the proceeds from the sale of certain assets were invested in a residential house.

The issue resurfaced after an I-T Department investigation raised questions about whether the shares had been sold at values substantially higher than the underlying land and buildings. In 2015, the assessing officer issued notices under Section 148 to reopen the brothers’ assessments, saying that a “substantial amount has escaped assessment during assessment years 2008-09 and 2009-10.”

The brothers challenged the notices, saying that the department was seeking to revisit already examined issues. The dispute before the SC was about whether the department had a legally valid basis to reopen the assessment.
When can a taxpayer’s assessment be reopened?

The I-T Department cannot reopen a taxpayer’s assessment simply because it wants another look at it. Section 147 of the I-T Act, 1961, allows an assessing officer to do so only when he “has reason to believe that any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year.”

The law sets a time limit on this power. If an assessment has already been completed after scrutiny under Section 143 (3), the department generally cannot reopen it after four years from the end of the relevant assessment year. But it can do so if the income escaped assessment because the taxpayer failed to make a return or “to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment.”

The law also requires the officer to record the reasons for reopening an assessment before issuing a notice under Section 148, to ensure that the decision is based on reason rather than vague suspicion.

An important safeguard is the rule against the Assessment Officer’s “change of opinion” in the case. In CIT v Kelvinator of India Ltd (2010), the SC said that without this check, “In the garb of reopening the assessment review would take place.” In ITO v Techspan India (2018), it said that Section 147 gives the department the “power to reassess and not the power to review.”

The distinction matters, as under Section 143(1), a return is only processed, and an intimation is sent to the taxpayer. That doesn’t mean that the department has examined every transaction or claim in the return. Under Section 143(3), the assessing officer examines the return, calls for information, and completes an assessment after scrutiny.
What the SC held

In the latest case, the court explained what the law means by an officer having “reason to believe” that income has escaped assessment. It said that when the officer does not have to prove at the time of issuing a notice that tax has definitely been evaded, the officer must have some material to support the belief that income may have escaped assessment.

The bench said “reason” means “cause or justification.” At the notice stage, the question is whether “there was relevant material on which a reasonable person could have formed the requisite belief.” The officer can only rely on direct and/or circumstantial evidence.

It said, “It is not any and every material, however vague and indefinite or distant, remote and far-fetched, which would warrant the formation of the belief relating to escapement of income. If there is no rational and intelligible nexus between the reasons and the belief, so that, on such reasons, no one properly instructed on facts and law could reasonably entertain the belief, the AO could not have reason to believe that income had escaped assessment.”

The brothers argued that the alleged overvaluation of shares could not by itself mean that income had escaped assessment. They also objected to the department relying on the treatment of capital gains in later years. The SC rejected this, saying that the recorded reasons covered not just the share valuation but also the gains being “adjusted in future years” and the exemption claimed.
The bench said that the transactions could involve “a diversion of income, assessable to tax under the guise of sale proceeds,” especially since the sale price was above the actual value of sale.

The brothers also argued that the department was revisiting matters it had already examined. The SC said that change of opinion arises only when the officer has applied their mind to an issue and formed a view during the original assessment. Merely accepting a return does not mean every transaction or claim in it was examined.

Both the brothers’ cases were treated differently. On Nitin’s returns being processed under Section 143(1), the court held that “the question of change of opinion, does not arise.” On Chetan’s return, which had to be scrutinised under Section 143(3), the court said the assessment order is “a bare acceptance of the returned income as it is.”

It found no indication that the officer had examined the share valuation, the purchase of property, or the treatment of capital gains. The assessment order from 2009-10 also contained no discussion of the long-term capital gains.

The court also noted that the information about the alleged undervaluation had emerged from a subsequent investigation and was not available to the officer during the original assessment and therefore held that reopening of assessments did not amount to a change of opinion.

title: Can states levy a tax on sales tax? The 30-year-old legal question SC has now settled, explained

content.value: Can a state impose a tax on a tax that a dealer already owes? The Supreme Court has reiterated that states can levy a surcharge calculated as a percentage of sales tax payable by dealers, holding that such a levy is essentially an additional sales tax and not a separate tax on tax.
In doing so, a seven-judge Constitution Bench has closed a reference that had been pending for nearly three decades, ruling that the question had already been settled by a 1974 judgment.
Background of the case

A surcharge is an additional levy imposed over and above an existing tax. The legal question before the Supreme Court was whether states could impose such a surcharge on the sales tax payable by dealers, or whether doing so amounted to an impermissible ‘tax on tax’.
The dispute arose from a 1990 amendment to Odisha’s Sales Tax Act, which required dealers with a gross turnover exceeding Rs 10 lakh to pay an additional 10% of the sales tax they owed.

The dealers challenged this provision, and argued that the surcharge was a “tax on tax”. They reasoned that the surcharge is measured on the tax payable and not on turnover, hence it is not a tax on the “sale or purchase of goods.” The dealers argued that it falls outside Entry 54 of list II of the Seventh Schedule, which empowers the states to tax the sale or purchase of goods but does not authorise them to impose a tax on sales tax that is already payable by the dealer.

The state maintained that the surcharge was only an increase in the rate of sales tax for a particular class of dealers. The fact that it was calculated as a percentage of the tax payable instead of turnover did not change the nature of the levy.
Previous cases

The Orissa HC upheld Section 5A following two Supreme Court rulings that had previously upheld a similar additional sales tax levies. Previous Supreme Court rulings have also adjudicated on similar points.

In S. Kodar v. State of Kerala (1974), a five-judge Constitution Bench upheld a Tamil Nadu law that imposed an additional tax of 5% on the sales tax payable by dealers whose annual turnover exceeded Rs 10 lakh. The court held that the levy was an increase in sales tax, not a separate tax on income. It said, “the fact that quantum of additional tax is determined with reference to the sales tax imposed would not alter its character.”

This position was reiterated in the Hoechst Pharmaceuticals (1983) ruling, in which a three-judge bench upheld a 10% surcharge on sales tax payable by dealers with an annual turnover exceeding Rs 5 lakh. It said a surcharge is “nothing but a higher rate of tax to raise revenue for general purposes.”

In the India Cement case (1990), a seven-judge bench struck down a cess imposed on mineral royalty, saying that “royalty is a tax” and a cess on royalty was beyond the State’s legislative competence. Dealers challenging the sales tax surcharges relied on this ruling to argue that a tax calculated on another tax was unconstitutional.

The Orissa HC bench referred the matter to a larger bench in 1998, seeing a possible conflict between Hoechst and India Cement rulings. In 1999, a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court in Arjun Floor Mills referred the matters to a seven-judge bench, noting that the earlier constitutional bench ruling in S. Kodar would also have to be considered.

In State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries (2004), a five-judge bench suggested that the observation in India Cement that royalty was a tax was an inadvertent error. The issue was eventually settled in the Mineral Area Development Authority ruling (2024) where a nine-judge bench held that “royalty is not a tax. Royalty is a contractual consideration paid by the mining lessee to the lessor for enjoyment of mineral rights.”
What the Supreme Court has now said

The bench held that the question of whether states could levy an additional sales tax as a percentage of the sales tax payable had already been settled by the Supreme Court in Kodar ruling and said there was no reason to revisit this decision.

The bench rejected the dealers’ argument that surcharge calculated on sales tax amounted to a “tax on tax”, saying the argument confused what was being taxed with how the tax was calculated. The subject of the levy remained the sale or purchase of goods. That the surcharge was calculated with reference to the sales tax payable did not change its character.

It said, “A surcharge of 10 per cent upon a sales tax levied at the rate of 10 per cent of the turnover is, in substance, nothing but an additional levy of 1 per cent upon the turnover. The subject of the surcharge remains the sale or purchase of goods; the only difference lies in the arithmetical route by which the quantum is reached.”

The court also rejected the argument that the surcharge was effectively a tax on dealer’s income. It said that the liability depended on turnover, not profit. Even a dealer who made losses would have to pay the surcharge if their turnover crossed the prescribed limit. The ruling said, “A levy which is payable irrespective of the existence of income, and which bears no relation to the quantum of income, cannot, by any stretch, be characterised as a tax on income.”

The bench also said that the India Cement ruling relied on by the dealers dealt with a different issue regarding a cess on mineral royalty and the limits of state power in a field covered by central legislation. It had not held that every levy calculated on another levy was unconstitutional. The nine-judge bench in the Mineral Area ruling had held that royalty was not a tax but a contractual payment for the right to extract minerals. The Supreme Court bench said that this removed the basis of apparent conflict between India Cement and S. Kodar.

The bench also noted that the reference concerned the state’s taxing powers under the pre-GST regime. The 101st constitutional amendment, which introduced the GST in 2016, narrowed Entry 54 of the state list to specified goods, replacing the broader power states’ previous ability to tax the sale or purchase of goods. Since the surcharge in question related to old sales tax laws, the bench said the reference had little prospective significance
The CJI, writing for the majority, declared the reference as infructuous since the legal question was already addressed in S. Kodar.

“The continued survival of a reference depends upon the continued existence of the doubt which occasioned it. Where the doubt has been authoritatively dispelled, in the interregnum, whether by a subsequent decision of a Bench of greater strength, by a legislative or constitutional amendment, or otherwise, the reference ceases to serve the purpose for which it was made. To answer it in such circumstances would be to render, in substance, an opinion on a question that no longer requires an answer, and to wastefully occupy a larger Bench’s time in restating the settled law,” the court said.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

The majority did not decide every individual challenge. It left open whether Punjab could impose a surcharge on industrial units exempt from sales tax under Section 30-AA, and whether proceeds of the Punjab Social Security Cess could be transferred directly to a separate fund without first being credited to the state’s Consolidated Fund under Article 266.

Justice K V Viswanathan authored a separate opinion holding that S. Kodar remained good law. He directed that the Odisha and Punjab sales tax appeals be placed before an appropriate bench for decision in accordance with S. Kodar. He said that the Punjab Social Security Act appeals should be separated and placed before an appropriate division bench.

title: Why SC is revisiting a 2003 ruling on two-child norm for panchayat polls

content.value: The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 4) referred its 2003 ruling in Javed v. State of Haryana, which upheld the disqualification of people with more than two children from contesting panchayat elections, to a larger bench for reconsideration.

A bench comprising Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said: “We are of the strong opinion that laws that penalise having more than two children have lost their relevance,” adding that the fear of overpopulation on which these laws rest “has crumbled due to demographic changes in the past few decades”.

“It is high time we recall Javed. We cannot ride into the future on a horse that is dead. It is not the strongest of the species that survives, nor the most intelligent, but the most responsive to change,” the bench said.
Background of the case

The case arose from the petitioner, Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, who was elected as the sarpanch of Kakoda gram panchayat in 2022. Her election was challenged on the grounds that she had three children, including a child born in 2014, which was in violation of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959, which disqualifies persons having more than two children.

In October 2024, the Additional Collector disqualified her under Section 14(1)(j-1) of the Act. Her appeal was subsequently dismissed by the Additional Commissioner in April 2025, following which she moved the Bombay High Court.
The High Court upheld those orders in August 2025, holding that the documents including the birth certificates of the three children supported the finding of her disqualification.
The legal framework

Maharashtra is among the several states that disqualify people from contesting or continuing in local body offices if they have more than two children. The provision was first introduced through a 1995 amendment to the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959, as part of a legislative approach to population control.

Section 14(1)(j-1) of the Act states that a person is disqualified from being elected as a member of a Gram Panchayat if they have more than two children. The carve-out is that a person who has already had more than two children when the amendment came into force is not disqualified, provided that the number of children does not increase thereafter.
Children born in a single delivery within one year of the amendment commencement are also excluded.
If a couple has one child and later has twins or more children in one delivery, they are counted as one for this law. Adopted children are excluded from the definition.
Similar two-child rules apply to local body elections in Haryana, Rajasthan, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh.
What Supreme Court said in Javed v. State of Haryana

The Supreme Court first upheld a two-child disqualification law in Javed v. State of Haryana (2003). The case concerned Section 175(1)(q) of the Haryana Panchayati Raj Act, 1994, which disqualified a person with more than two living children from holding the office of sarpanch, panch, or member of a panchayat samiti or zila parishad.

A three-judge bench held that disqualifying people with more than two living children from panchayat offices was a valid way of encouraging family planning. It said that the restriction did not prevent anyone from having more children but attached an electoral consequence to that choice.

It said, “If anyone chooses to have more living children than two, he is free to do so under the law as it stands now but then he should pay a little price and that is of depriving himself from holding an office in Panchayat in the State of Haryana. There is nothing illegal about it and certainly no unconstitutionality attaches to it.”

On the challenge under Article 21, the bench rejected the claim that personal liberty included a right to procreate without consequence for holding office, noting that it would be “futile to assume or urge that the impugned legislation violates right to life and liberty”.

The bench also held that the right to contest an election was a statutory right and not a fundamental right and could thus be subjected to legislative conditions. It said the provision “seeks to achieve a laudable purpose — socio-economic welfare and health care of the masses and is consistent with the national population policy. It is not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.”
What the Supreme Court has said now

The Supreme Court said that the demographic circumstances on which Javed was decided had changed. India’s total fertility rate (TFR) had fallen from 3.0 in 2003 to 1.9 which is below the replacement level, 2.1.
A replacement level is the TFR at which each generation exactly replaces itself, about 2.1 children per woman. Below it, a population shrinks over time and over it, a population grows.

The court said that ignoring this shift simply because India still has a large population “would be dangerously complacent…the stakes are too high,” adding that “the need of the hour is to have policies in tune with the present realities”.

The bench also questioned why such restrictions were only applied to elected representatives at the panchayat level but not those who are contesting elections to Parliament or state legislatures. It said that imposing such a measure only on grassroots representatives was “replete with prejudice and preconceived notions”.
It said that the right of representation and the right to hold office under the state are the two most important rights that make up a citizenship.

In Javed, the top court had said that the disqualification affected men and women equally. The bench disagreed, saying that such a reasoning “does not sit in accordance with the social realities of the country”. Referring to a 2009 study by the Ministry of Panchayat Raj, the bench noted that the two-child norm in a patriarchal society had “tended to weaken the position of women rather than empowering them”.

It held that women could face disqualification because of reproductive decisions over which they may have little or no control. The study had also documented instances of forced abortions, desertion of pregnant wives, and denial of paternity to avoid disqualification.

The bench further said that the law raised concerns about the right to reproductive autonomy under Article 21. It said: “The choice of whether, when, and how many children to have is a decision of the most intimate and personal character, which must ordinarily remain within the autonomous domain of the individual, free from external coercion.”

It noted that the law wrongly links access to elected office with population control, and unfairly singles out those seeking political representation at the village level, when higher fertility has far more complex causes.

By linking the birth of a third child to electoral disqualification, the law forced a person to make an “unconscionable choice” to choose “between the exercise of their reproductive autonomy and continued participation in democratic governance”. This, they said, impinged on Article 21 of the Constitution.

The bench said that allowing Javed’s reasoning to continue would “exclude an entire class of citizens from political representation on grounds bearing little rational connection to their capacity to hold public office”.
It said that laws that may have been justified when they were introduced could “become arbitrary and unreasonable” with the passage of time.

The bench also said that the validity of the Maharashtra provision and the ruling in Javed were not directly under challenge before it. However, it said that while courts cannot direct legislatures to repeal or amend laws, they can examine whether their continued operation remains constitutionally sustainable when the circumstances underlying it had already changed.

title: INDIA bloc’s Ramlila Maidan rally: Do we need to ‘pay to protest’?

content.value: On Sunday (November 1), the INDIA bloc is holding a rally in New Delhi seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.
The rally will be held at Ramlila Maidan — the first major demonstration at the newly designated protest site since the denotification of Jantar Mantar by Delhi Police in October.

While Jantar Mantar was just around 2 km away from Parliament, Ramlila Maidan is a 6-km drive from the nation’s supreme lawmaking body. The other two designated protest sites are even farther — the CBD ground in Shahdara is around 14 km from Parliament while the ground in Burari is about 23 km away.
Additionally, booking Ramlila Maidan costs between Rs 50,000 and Rs 1 lakh per day.

On October 15, the Supreme Court issued notice to the Centre and the Delhi Police on a writ petition challenging the October 11 standing order that denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.
Can a protest be held beyond a designated protest site? Is it a prerequisite under the right to protest? Two senior Supreme Court lawyers explain.
What is the need for a designated protest site?

Designated protest sites strike a balance between the right to protest and the need to minimise public inconvenience. They give people a space, ideally close to the seat of power, to make their voices heard while preventing traffic disruptions and the blocking of public roads, said Senior Advocate Shadan Farasat.
The practice of earmarking specific areas for protests was recognised by the Supreme Court in its 2018 judgment in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India.

“The case dealt with the rights of organisations, protesters, and residents impacted by prolonged agitation at Jantar Mantar. The case saw an intersection between the right to peaceful protest under Article 19(1)(b), freedom of movement under Article 19(1)(d), and the extended scope under the right to life (Article 21),” said Senior Advocate Nipun Saxena.

In this case, the Supreme Court held the right to protest in a democratic society to be sacrosanct and set aside an order by the National Green Tribunal that barred protests at Jantar Mantar. The Supreme Court said that Jantar Mantar would be the designated “protest site”, subject to a “few permissions, including the size of crowd”, to be obtained from the administration to “facilitate” protests.
Does the Constitution mandate designated protest sites?
There is no Constitutional or statutory mandate requiring designated protest sites. These sites are an administrative mechanism developed by governments to manage protests.
However, such sites must be accessible and close enough to the seat of power for protesters to be heard. If they are too far away, they defeat the purpose of the protest, said Farasat.
The right to protest is not absolute, and reasonable restrictions can be imposed to maintain public order, but these restrictions should not make peaceful protest ineffective, he said.

A designated protest site is also not a prerequisite to the right to hold a protest. This is a mechanism made to strengthen the right to protest as a convenience measure for all stakeholders. It is not “prohibitory” in nature; the right to protest is independent of a designated protest site, said Saxena.

The Supreme Court, in the Shaheen Bagh protest case of 2020 (Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police), held that the right to peaceful protest cannot be stretched to an extent where the daily lives of citizens, (commuters, in this case) are severely affected.

However, if no accessible site is available near the seat of power, or if even the designated site is closed to protesters, the balance shifts against the right to protest. In such circumstances, people may seek permission to protest in other public spaces, said Farasat.
What does a site booking fee mean for the right to protest?
Farasat said that designated protest sites should ideally be reserved for protests rather than routinely used for other events, rallies or public functions.

“While a ground such as Ramlila Maidan may naturally be occupied during Ramlila celebrations, the government should ensure that people have access to a suitable alternative… The idea of a designated protest site is different from that of a general-purpose ground used for political rallies or other events. If such sites are frequently unavailable because of other activities, they cannot serve their intended purpose,” he said.

On the question of booking fees, charging a substantial amount to use a designated protest site can make the right to protest inaccessible, particularly for workers, labourers and individuals who already struggle to get the government’s attention. A fee of Rs 50,000 for a protest involving 50 people, for instance, could be prohibitive for many groups. The right to peaceful protest should not depend on a person’s ability to pay, said Farasat.

Saxena said: “In the 2018 Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan case, one of the key concerns was that the alternative site proposed by the government, Ramlila Maidan, was a commercial venue that charged organisers Rs 50,000 per day at the time. This could prevent groups with limited resources, such as Anganwadi workers, pensioners, Dalits or ordinary citizens, from exercising their fundamental right to protest. Taking these concerns into account, the Supreme Court held in 2018 that Jantar Mantar would continue to be a designated protest site, subject to prior permissions. The underlying principle was that people should not be denied the opportunity to make their voices heard simply because they cannot afford to pay for a venue.”

He added: “Every citizen is free to assemble peacefully wherever they wish to. The only caveat would be the imposition of prohibitory orders in a specific geographical location. Protests cannot by any stretch of imagination be localised to one area alone. The denotification of a ‘protest site’ cannot by itself be a ground to let any peaceful protester who wishes to exercise the right to assemble peacefully and exercise freedom of speech be restrained in any manner.”

title: For voters deleted from rolls during SIR, why Form 6 remedy raises questions

content.value: When voters whose names were deleted from electoral rolls during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process are asked to apply afresh for reinstatement, can they be required to declare that they are first-time voters?

The Delhi High Court last week considered this question in a petition by two voters, who raised Form 6 for new voters in relation to the SIR exercise. While the bench comprising Justice Dinesh Mehta and Aditi Choudhary said the concern was “misplaced”, voters elsewhere have also earlier petitioned over the query, including in the Supreme Court.
Why is Form 6 under scrutiny?
Issued by the Election Commission of India (ECI), Form 6 is an application for inclusion in the electoral rolls and is meant for people who have never voted before.

In the case of voters who shifted homes and therefore could not be enumerated at their old addresses, resulting in their names being dropped from the rolls during the SIR process, the ECI provided the recourse of using Form 6. The form carries a declaration that an applicant is seeking enrolment for the first time.

However, petitioners point out that Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act of 1950 penalises any person with imprisonment of one year or a fine, or both, who makes “a statement or declaration in writing which is false and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true.”
The other concern is that the process treats an existing elector as a new one, as it does not restore the earlier enrolment.
What did the Delhi HC hold?

The petitioners contended that they could not complete the enumeration process because they had moved houses, leading to the deletion of their names. They said their names should be restored and their change of address processed through Form 8 rather than making them apply afresh. Form 8 is used to declare a change of residence or correct an existing entry.

The ECI told the court they could get their names added by submitting Form 6 with the help of the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO), but one petitioner argued that doing so would mean making a false declaration.

The bench dismissed the case, noting that the suggestion to use Form 6 came from the ECI’s counsel on the instructions of the ERO. The ERO is authorised to prepare and revise electoral rolls and is a local authority or government official designated as such by the ECI, after consultation with the state government.
What other courts have said

The Bombay High Court at Goa had also questioned why the ECI is asking voters to apply afresh through Form 6 when Form 8 allows them to update their addresses. The issue came up in a case filed by a family of five, whose names were left out of the electoral rolls despite applying through Form 8 after moving within the same Santa Cruz constituency.

The bench comprising Justices Amit S Jamsandekar and Valmiki Menezes orally asked the EC why Form 8 cannot be kept in abeyance (or halted) instead. It said, “Why must you (EC) reject it? Why can’t you just keep it in abeyance? Finish your roll. Publish your roll. Then deal with all those Form 8s, because that is the best information for you to understand where people are shifting.” The bench pointed out that rejecting Form 8 would mean “the roll will not have that person’s name.”
Plea before the SC

The Supreme Court is also examining the issue in a challenge to the Delhi SIR. The application states that Form 6 requires applicants to declare that they are “applying for the inclusion in the electoral roll for the first time.” The plea states that it creates a problem for already registered voters left off Delhi’s draft electoral roll.

One of the plea’s central arguments is the scale of voters deleted. Around 47.56 lakh electors were excluded from the draft roll published on August 31 (Delhi had around 1.45 crore electors before the SIR process began). Of these, 31.59 lakh were categorised as “permanently shifted.”

It states that “such persons were already enrolled as electors, and the statutory framework ordinarily contemplates the use of Form 8 for recording a change of residence or effecting a correction in an existing electoral entry.” The plea states that these voters must use Form 6, whose declarations do not reflect their circumstances.

The plea also raised concerns under Section 31 of the RPA of 1950. The application states that previously enrolled voters should not have to make a factually incorrect claim just to restore their names.

The plea also raises a question about the legality of the additional declaration that the EC requires applicants to submit during the SIR. The additional declaration states whether the applicant was included or had family members included in the previous SIR. The plea seeks to ask the court to declare the additional information as unenforceable and direct the ECI not to reject applications solely based on an unfilled additional declaration.

title: Can divorce abroad end an Indian marriage? What SC said in bigamy case

content.value: The Supreme Court has held that a person who is married under Indian law cannot use a foreign divorce decree to escape bigamy proceedings in India if the divorce was granted on a ground that’s not recognised in India.

A Supreme Court bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekar on November 3 held that a change in citizenship or the fact that the second marriage took place abroad cannot alter the legal consequences of a marriage that continues under Indian law.
Here’s what to know about the case, the legal framework governing foreign judgments, and what the top court ruled in this case.
Facts of the case

In the present case, the dispute arose after the marriage was solemnised under Hindu rites and customs in 2003. The couple eventually moved to the UK, and their relationship deteriorated. The husband then filed for divorce in a Guntur court, but his petition was dismissed. An appeal was filed in the Andhra Pradesh High Court, but that was withdrawn too.

After acquiring British citizenship in February 2013, he approached the Cambridge County Court in August that year. The court granted divorce in January 2014 on the ground of irrevocable breakdown of marriage. He eventually went on to marry another woman in the UK in March 2014.

His first wife eventually filed a complaint alleging bigamy under Section 494 of the Indian Penal Code (since replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2023), a punishment for which is either seven years imprisonment or a fine. She argued that she had objected to the UK jurisdiction and that irretrievable breakdown of marriage was not a ground for divorce under the Hindu Marriage Act (HMA), 1955, which governed their marriage.
Does Indian law recognise foreign judgments?
The recognition of foreign rulings in India is governed by Sections 13 and 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC).

Section 13 lays down six exceptions under which a foreign judgment would not be considered conclusive in India. These include cases where the foreign court lacked jurisdiction, the judgment was not granted on merits, or the order was obtained through fraud. Recognition can also be refused where the foreign court refused to recognise Indian law despite its applicability.
Section 14 provides that a foreign judgment is presumed valid unless the contrary is proved, but this presumption is easily rebutted when one of the exceptions in Section 13 is shown.

In matrimonial disputes, these provisions essentially mean that a divorce granted abroad does not automatically bring a marriage governed by Indian law to an end in India. The divorce decree must meet the requirements for recognition under the CPC.
Court precedents

The legal position on how India treats foreign divorce decrees was laid down more than three decades ago in Y. Narasimha Rao v. Venkata Lakshmi (1991). In that case, the Supreme Court held that a foreign divorce decree must be consistent with the matrimonial law under which the parties were married.

It laid down two principles: for a foreign divorce to be valid in India, the ground for divorce must first be recognised in India, and both spouses must have agreed to place themselves before the foreign court. If either condition is missing, the decree has no effect in India.

In Kishorekumar Mohan Kale v. Kashmira Kale (2026), the Supreme Court refused to recognise a US divorce decree on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage, which is not listed under the HMA. The court dissolved the marriage itself by exercising its powers under Article 142(1), which allows the top court “to do complete justice” in any matter before it.
What the Supreme Court held in the present case

The top court held that the husband had initially approached an Indian court for divorce but, after failing to obtain relief, had withdrawn his appeal and moved to a foreign court. The UK decree was based on a ground that the Indian law does not recognise.

It said, “The foreign divorce decree was passed in contravention of the existing matrimonial law in India and on a ground that is not even recognized statutorily. This not only violates the legal threshold of Section 13 of the CPC, which every foreign decree has to pass through, but also the observations made by this Court in Y. Narasimha Rao as to the conditions required to be fulfilled by a foreign decree to be enforceable in India.”

The bench further said that proceedings before the foreign court indicate that the wife raised objections and thus her participation could not be equated with “an unconditional submission to the jurisdiction of the foreign court”.
The husband also argued that he was a British citizen when he married the second time and the marriage took place outside India. Thus, the Indian law could not be applied to him.

The bench rejected this argument, saying that the inquiry into bigamy could not be restricted to where the second marriage took place, as it only had to consider whether the first marriage continued to subsist. “Legal consequences flowing from the subsisting marriage cannot be defeated by a subsequent change in the nationality of accused,” it said.

The husband argued that the FIR was filed after a long unexplained delay. The bench rejected this argument, observing that “bigamy is a continuing offence”, which means it’s an offence for as long as the second marriage persists.

The court also found that the material submitted before it was not sufficient to establish that the parents of the husband had participated in facilitating the second marriage, nor was it enough to establish whether the second wife knew that the first marriage was still subsisting.

title: SC says no distinction between arrest, detention: How it resets 24-hour clock

content.value: Underlining that “the Constitution does not recognize any detention dehors [outside] arrest,” the Supreme Court on Thursday (November 5) held that the 24-hour deadline to produce a person before a magistrate begins when the person is first detained and not when the investigating agency chooses to record a formal arrest.

A bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar said that searches, seizures and questioning that follow an interception cannot be treated as a pause in a Constitutional safeguard. “There is no such thing called temporary disruption of liberty,” the bench said, as it set aside the Tripura High Court’s refusal of bail in a drug smuggling case.

The court directed the magistrates to record when an accused’s liberty was first curtailed, and calculate the 24-hour deadline from that time. It said that the person is produced before them after the deadline has passed, they must order their release.

Magistrates should also examine whether the detention was reasonable. Even if the accused was produced within 24 hours, they can refuse remand if they find that the person was kept in custody on unreasonable grounds.

The ruling comes amidst large-scale detentions which police describe as preventive and can last up to 24 hours, which are a regular feature of policing in the capital. While the case arose under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985, it demonstrates that the label an agency uses for restraint does not decide when the clock starts.
Background of the case

The case stems from a major anti-narcotics operation conducted by the Divisional Preventive Force (DPF), Customs Division Agartala. On September 29, 2025, at 2 pm, customs officers intercepted the appellants, who were carrying a total of 60 kg of methamphetamine tablets.

Although the appellants were brought under physical control of the search team at 2 pm, the arresting officer did not sign the formal arrest memos until 11 am the following day. They were produced before the magistrate at 4.45 pm. A special judge and the High Court both refused bail.

The investigating officer had said that the men were “merely intercepted…not formally detained” at 2 pm and that the hours between their interception and formal arrest went into search, seizure, and questioning.
Legal framework
The law governing the detention of a person during a criminal investigation is laid down in three provisions in the Constitution, the Bharatiya Nyaya Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and the NDPS Act.

Article 22 is a fundamental right under the Constitution that provides for an accused to be informed about the grounds of arrest and to get legal representation. Clause (2) specifically states that a person “arrested and detained” shall be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours, excluding the travel time taken to reach the court. No person shall remain in custody for more than 24 hours without the approval of a magistrate.
Section 58 of the BNSS states that a person who has been arrested without a warrant cannot be detained for longer than “reasonable”.

In practice, the terms “arrest” and “detention” are often used interchangeably. “Arrest” is a formal act of police taking a person into custody in connection with an offence, marking the beginning of criminal proceedings. Once a person is arrested, a range of constitutional and statutory safeguards immediately come into play.

The BNSS does not define “detention” per se. Instead, it gives police a set of powers that allows them to stop, remove or temporarily hold people in certain situations, including when a crime has actually taken place.

The NDPS Act gives officers the powers to search, seize and arrest people suspected of drug-related offences — Section 37 specifically places restrictions on cases involving certain serious drug offences. It governs the conditions of bail too and does not extend the time the police can keep an arrested person in custody.
Arrest vs detention

At the heart of the judgment lies the court’s interpretation of Article 22(2). It said that the phrase “arrested and detained in custody” is “conjunctive and not disjunctive”, that is, the two words are joined by “and” not “or”.

The court said that because both the terms are joined together, they are synonymous. The court held that the “sacrosanct” 24-hour countdown to produce the person before a magistrate would begin the moment their liberty is curtailed. The only time period that is excluded from the 24 hour limit is the journey to the magistrate.

It said: “The prescription of 24 hours time period would commence the moment a person is detained by the arresting authority suspecting him to have committed an offence, when his liberty is effectively curtailed…any attempt to draw an artificial distinction between ‘arrest’ and ‘detention’ would dilute or negate the fundamental protection guaranteed by the Constitution.”
Buffer zones

The bench in its 97-page judgment disapproved of the views taken by the Orissa High Court in the Aryaman Pattnayak case, the Madras High Court in the Kannan case, and the Kerala High Court in the Arun K Thomas case, saying that these decisions “do not lay down the correct law”.
The High Courts had attempted to carve out investigative procedures for law enforcement before recording a formal arrest while calculating the 24-hour deadline.

Rejecting the Orissa High Court’s view that detention becomes arrest only after a “short investigatory hold”, the Supreme Court called it “constitutionally unsustainable” and said it delved “into a realm of uncertainty”.
It also rejected the Kerala High Court’s view that the 24-hour clock remains suspended during search and seizure, saying that “creation or contemplation of such buffer zone is unconstitutional”.

The bench said that the Constitution does not recognise the concept of “temporary disruption of liberty” and that High Courts cannot invent a statutory buffer zone that freezes or suspends the fundamental rights for executive convenience.
Informal custody

The bench also said that even if the suspect is produced before a magistrate within 24 hours, Section 58 of the BNSS imposes a dual limit, that is, a 24-hour limit and that the detention within those 24 hours must be “reasonable”. It said that there was an 18-hour gap between the completion of the search on September 29 and the formal arrest the next morning. The investigating officer had not explained this delay.

“18 hours in custody without judicial oversight is a long period with misuse and abuse of authority a clear possibility. Such a period certainly cannot be construed as a reasonable period,” the court said.

The court said that “remand is never a mechanical exercise” and held that if there is an unexplained gap that exists within the 24-hour window, magistrates are allowed to decline the police remand on the ground of unreasonableness alone.

On informal custody, the bench recalled Justice V R Krishna Iyer’s words in Niranjan Singh (1980) that reasons police have taken a person into informal custody but not arrested him are “terminological dubieties and unfair evasions of the straightforwardness of the law. He called such explanations as equivocatory quibblings and hide-and-seek niceties, describing those as a shady facet.”
Fundamental rights override special laws

The Tripura High Court had relied on the Supreme Court’s ruling in State of Punjab v. Sukhwinder Singh (2026), which held that the restrictions on bail under Section 37 of the NDPS Act had to be satisfied before bail could be granted.

The Supreme Court expressed reservations about this observation, saying that fundamental rights cannot be exercised under the framework of Section 37. The bench said: “These fundamental rights cannot be tinkered with so lightly, not even under the special statutes.”

It said that where there is a violation of Article 21 — which guarantees the protection of life and personal liberty — the restrictions under Section 37 “would have to give way”. It referred to the Supreme Court’s ruling in Union of India v. K A Najeeb (2021), which recognised that Constitutional rights could prevail over statutory restrictions on bail.
CCTV and custodial violence

The bench also linked the 24-hour limit to the need to prevent custodial violence, noting that the “worst violations of human rights take place during the course of investigation” when the police, in attempts to secure evidence or confessions, “resorts to third degree methods including torture”.

It also said that the Supreme Court directions laid down in previous rulings require CCTV cameras with audio- and video-recording and night vision in police stations and in offices of agencies such as the National Investigation Agency, the Central Bureau of Investigation, and the Enforcement Directorate, where interrogation and detention take place. The footage must be preserved for at least 18 months and longer if a complaint of custodial violence is made.

title: Why SC said Section 17A of anti-corruption law does not protect public servants in bribe cases

content.value: The Supreme Court last week held that public servants accused of demanding bribes cannot claim protection that requires prior approval for an investigation when the alleged act is unrelated to their official duties.

A bench comprising Justices S V N Bhatti and N V Anjaria dismissed an appeal by a Rajasthan police constable who had challenged the framing of a bribery charge against him. The court held that the alleged demand for a bribe of Rs 1.5 lakh was not linked to any official decision or recommendation he made.

It said, “The act of demanding a bribe is a pure criminal act, not connected with official functions and not relatable to or having any linkage with recommendation or decision of the appellant in his capacity, as public servant.”
Facts of the case

The case arose from a complaint by Devendra Kumar, a constable posted at Abu City Police Station in Rajasthan, alleging that Tejaram, another constable, had demanded a bribe of Rs 1.5 lakh on behalf of the Superintendent of Police. Tejaram disputed these claims and said they were filed in retaliation for his own allegation that Kumar had taken bribes from accused persons to help them escape.

Tejaram was eventually arrested in September 2021 and received a sanction in December 2023. Eventually, in 2024, the trial court framed charges against him for bribing a public servant. This was challenged before the Rajasthan High Court, but his plea was dismissed; he then approached the Supreme Court.
The legal framework
The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 lays down the offences for which public servants can be prosecuted and the safeguards that apply during an investigation and prosecution.
Section 7 concerns public servants who accept or attempt to obtain a bribe in return “to perform improperly or dishonestly a public duty.”
Section 7A deals with people who accept or attempt to obtain “undue advantage as a motive or reward to induce a public servant, by corrupt or illegal means.”

Section 17A requires prior approval before an investigation can look into allegations linked to a public servant’s decisions made during the course of discharging their duty. It states that “no police officer shall…investigate any offence punishable under this Act without the order” of the appropriate authority. The approval must come from the central or the state government depending on whether they work for the central, state, or any other authority. The authority must respond within three months, extendable by one month with reasons recorded. The carve-out is that approval is not needed if a person is arrested on the spot for accepting or attempting to accept a bribe.

Section 19 lays down the procedural safeguard that must be met before the court takes cognisance of the offence. It states that no court shall take cognisance of the specified offences under the Act without a prior sanction from the competent authority.

Section 17A concerns approval before an enquiry, inquiry or investigation in certain cases, but applies when an offence is linked to a particular decision made by the officer during the discharge of their official duties. By contrast, Section 19 concerns sanction before a court can take cognisance of specified offences. Both are procedural safeguards, but they operate at different stages of the criminal proceedings.
What the court held

The court held that Section 17A does not protect every act committed by a public servant. For the law to apply, the offence must be linked to a decision or recommendation made while discharging the official duty. It said, “The protection envisaged could be extended only if the conditions contemplated in the section are satisfied. The section cannot be viewed as to have an omnibus application.”

The court said the demand for a bribe was not linked to any decision made by the accused during the course of discharging his official duties. Since the allegation concerned a demand for illegal gratification rather than a decision taken in the discharge of official duties, the court held that Section 17A did not apply.

It also held that a sanction under Section 19 is required, requiring a competent authority’s approval before a court can take up certain corruption cases against a public servant. This is meant to prevent frivolous prosecutions. The Supreme Court held that the delay in granting sanction did not invalidate the criminal proceedings and that it was granted before the trial court took cognisance of the offence.

Earlier this year, a split verdict arose on Section 17A. Justice K V Viswanathan upheld the provision, whereas Justice B V Nagarathna struck it down as one that “protects the corrupt rather than seeking to protect the honest.” The matter has been referred to a larger bench.

The parties argued that the current case should wait for the outcome of the pending Supreme Court reference. The court said the reference had no bearing on the appeal because the provision was not applicable to the facts of the case in the first place.

title: Convicted of gangraping pregnant Bilkis Bano, killing family: Why bail now?

content.value: The Supreme Court on Monday suspended the life sentence of two convicts in the Bilkis Bano case from the 2002 Gujarat riots and granted them bail.
Bano, then aged 21 and five months pregnant, was gang-raped and seven of her family members, including her three-year-old daughter, were killed during the communal riots.
This came over two years after the top court struck down the remission granted to the two, and nine others, by the Gujarat government, and directed them to surrender and return to jail.
What does the latest Supreme Court order say?

Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, lodged in a jail in Gujarat, filed a Special Leave to Appeal, challenging the Bombay High Court judgment passed on May 4, 2017, which confirmed their conviction and sentence given by the trial court in 2008.

They told the Supreme Court that they had spent more than 17 years in jail. One of them said that he is severely disabled. The bench of Justice M M Sundresh and Justice Prasanna Varale considered these grounds and said: “Certainly, there are issues to be decided in the appeal, both on fact and law.”
The court then suspended the sentence and granted bail to the two, directing the trial court to impose terms and conditions. It then directed that their appeals be listed for hearing in due course.

In her response to the Supreme Court’s bail to the two convicts, Bano said she could not believe that the court passed an order “without hearing her”. She said she would fight this order, asking why their sentence was suspended without informing her. According to the law, a victim can be issued a notice and allowed to intervene and make submissions when hearing an appeal.
How were the 11 convicts released the first time around?

To understand this, we must go back to the origins of the legal proceedings. In 2004, the Supreme Court transferred the gang-rape case from Gujarat to Mumbai over apprehensions of evidence tampering and the lack of a conducive situation for a fair trial.
Four years on, a trial court in Mumbai convicted the 11 men of charges including murder, rape and rioting. The convicts appealed this order in the Bombay High Court, which upheld the punishment.
The men then filed Special Leave Petitions before the Supreme Court which, on November 20, 2017, dismissed them, upholding the findings of the High Court as well as the sentence.

In 2022, one of the convicts again approached the top court seeking directions to the Gujarat government for premature release, citing a 1992 remission policy for convicts who had completed at least 14 years in jail. The court asked the Gujarat government to consider the application “within a period of two months”, in line with the policy.
Based on this, a government panel recommended their release and they were released from a Gujarat jail on August 15, 2022. They were felicitated upon their release by local leaders.
Bano filed a petition against their release. Other petitioners, too, approached the court through public interest litigations.

On January 8, 2024, a Supreme Court division bench said the Gujarat government did not have the authority or jurisdiction to consider the remission applications of the convicts to reduce their sentence as the trial was moved to Mumbai.

This is because such an application can only be taken up by a government within whose territorial jurisdiction the applicant was convicted — in this case, Maharashtra — and not where the offence took place (that is, Gujarat). The court also said that the pleas for remission should have been considered as per a 2014 policy which has a bar for grant of remission to convicts of heinous crimes.
So how was the earlier release different from the current one?

In 2022, the 11 convicts were initially released on remission — which essentially means early release — with their life sentence considered complete. Under Section 432 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), state governments have the power to suspend or remit a sentence.

The criminal justice system has provisions such as remission or reduction of a sentence, taking into account that convicts can reform themselves. But the Supreme Court said in its 2024 order that this has to be balanced with the rights of the victim or her family.

The bench said that in prior judgments, the Supreme Court has expressed scepticism over the convict’s claim to a second chance, particularly if the offence is a heinous one. The court also said this is not an indefeasible right.

Unlike remission, the current release is on bail pending appeal. Two of the men, while serving their life sentence, filed a special leave to appeal, challenging their conviction altogether. The division bench was told that they had already spent 17 years in jail, that one of them was implicated nearly three years after the case, and that he was severely disabled.

When the court hears the entire case in detail as part of the appeal, it will go into the specific details on the merits of the case. The bench said that pending the appeal, the two men should be granted bail on grounds including the 17-year incarceration as part of their life sentence. The court also suspended their sentence, which means that their punishment is stayed till the final decision on the appeal. The other convicts can also file separate appeals seeking bail on similar grounds of parity.

According to the law, the court will decide on their pleas, and if it upholds the high court and trial court judgment, and sentences them, they will have to return to jail. The court has said that the appeal will be heard “in its due course”.

title: Why some judges are less likely to grant bail than others

content.value: Whether a person accused of a crime waits for trial at home or in prison often depends on one decision: bail. The Supreme Court’s position for decades has been that bail is the rule and jail is the exception. However, the law allows judges wide room to decide these individual cases of liberty. A new study that looks at 4,459 bail cases decided by the Delhi High Court asks whether a judge’s background is linked to how they use their discretion to grant bail.

The study, published in the Journal of Law and Courts, a Cambridge University Press journal, analyses 4,459 bail applications decided by 34 judges of the Delhi High Court between 2023 and 2024. It found that judges promoted from the district judiciary granted bail at lower rates than judges appointed from among practising lawyers, even after accounting for differences in the cases they heard. The authors describe this as “a robust descriptive association between professional pathway and bail outcomes.”
Simply put: a trial court judge who is subsequently elevated to the High Court is less likely to grant bail than a High Court judge, who was appointed directly from the Bar.

Currently, 40% of judges serving in the Delhi High Court are from the district judiciary. But the findings of the study matter beyond Delhi since every High Court draws judges from both routes, and their standing is equal as judges of a constitutional court. They could also go on to become judges of the Supreme Court. Article 217 of the Constitution sets the eligibility criteria for an individual to be appointed as a judge of a High Court: ten years at the Bar or ten years in judicial office. Conventionally, at least one-third of the sanctioned strength of the High Court is reserved for service judges. The number of serving judges from the district judiciary or the Bar varies at any given point in time depending on judges’ tenures and vacancies.
Why does it matter which judge hears a bail plea?
Nearly 70% of Indian prisons are filled with undertrials. Given the pace of trials, bail is the most crucial element in determining whether the process becomes the punishment for an accused.

A bail plea before the High Court is often filed after the trial court has rejected bail. In our three-tier legal system, trial courts are bound by rather strict statutory requirements and tighter processes, while High Courts, as constitutional courts, have greater room for discretion.

Speaking in 2024, then Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud said that trial court judges often choose to play it safe by not granting bail in criminal cases. For such applicants, the High Court bench is where liberty is decided. “People who should be getting bail in trial courts are not receiving it,” he said, forcing them to approach the High Courts.
What has the study found?

Of the 4,459 bail applications, 72.5 per cent were granted. Bar judges decided 3,102 applications and granted bail in 80.3 per cent. Service judges decided 1,357 and granted bail in 54.8 per cent. The raw gap is 25.5 percentage points.

After adjusting for case features such as bail type, whether the victim died, whether an earlier application had been rejected, the number of legal sections and whether a senior advocate appeared, the paper estimates that service judges were 23.7 percentage points less likely to grant bail.
If the law is the same, how can outcomes differ so much?

India doesn’t have one bail law, but bail provisions in different statutes set different standards. Judges have significant discretion to account for the particular facts of each case. Courts weigh the nature of the accusation, the likely punishment, the risk of tampering with evidence and the strength of the case, but no formula says how much weight each carries. It also depends on the accused, whether one is considered a flight risk.

The paper treats this flexibility as the reason differences can appear: “If bail were formulaic, professional background should be irrelevant; the discretionary latitude inherent in bail adjudication is what makes pathway-linked differences plausible.” In other words, where the law leaves more to judgment, the background of the person exercising that judgment has more room to show.

A plausible explanation is that trial court judges who spend most of their careers in district courts will likely carry their practices to high courts and give greater weight to the state’s case against an accused.

Advocate Bharat Chugh said it is difficult to shake off a habit built over a long career. “It’s difficult to let go of that hard-wiring that happens over a very long career of being slightly conservative. You become a HC judge if you’re a trial court judge, maybe 30 years after you join the service; you cannot suddenly become a different person. That is a possible hypothesis for the huge gap in the dataset.”

Chugh also pointed to what Bar judges bring with them. “When you practice for several years and represent individual clients, standing for their personal liberty in courts, then maybe you are slightly more aware of the very serious consequences that being in jail for even one day has for somebody’s life. You have sat with clients and families and seen families uprooted because somebody was arrested and not given bail.”
Do such biases matter?

Case outcomes have a direct impact on the lives of litigants. A 2023 study by Nitin Kumar Bharti and Sutanuka Roy in the Journal of Public Economics (2023) studied 668 judges deciding 323,380 bail cases in Uttar Pradesh and found that judges exposed to Hindu-Muslim riots in early childhood were about 16 per cent more likely to deny bail than the average judge. The study ruled out religious favouritism as the explanation but linked the effect of riots to judges’ relative trust in individuals versus state institutions.

If biases are apparent in an individual judgment, then they can often be rectified through an appeal. However, systemic inequities can be ascertained through large data sets. For example, a bench of judges comprising both those elevated from the Bar and those from the district judiciary could help address bias in bail decisions.

title: Why special MP-MLA court acquitted Rahul Gandhi of criminal defamation

content.value: A special MP-MLA court in Sultanpur on Monday (October 26) has acquitted Rahul Gandhi in a criminal defamation case over his 2018 remark describing the then BJP president Amit Shah as a “murder accused”. The court held that the complainant, BJP’s Sultanpur district vice-president (VP) Vijay Mishra, had failed to establish how the statement affected or harmed his reputation.
An MP-MLA court is a specialised or designated court set up to fast-track criminal trials and legal proceedings involving sitting and former MPs and MLAs.

Mishra had alleged that Gandhi’s comments humiliated him as a BJP worker. The Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Shubham Verma held that he was not an “aggrieved person” entitled to file the complaint in the first place and that the remarks that were made during the Karnataka Assembly election campaign did not meet the threshold for criminal defamation in the context of political discourse.
Here’s what to know about the background of the case, the legal framework surrounding criminal defamation, and what the court held in this case.
The case of criminal defamation against Rahul Gandhi

During the Karnataka Assembly election campaign in May 2018, a journalist at a press conference in Bengaluru asked Gandhi about Shah’s defence of BJP leader and former Karnataka Chief Minister B S Yediyurappa. The journalist referred to Gandhi’s allegations against Yediyurappa, noting that he had received a clean chit from the court and the Reddy brothers had also been acquitted.

Gandhi was responding to this question when he questioned Shah’s credibility, referring to the Sohrabuddin encounter case and the death of a CBI judge, B H Loya, who had been hearing the case. “Amit Shah has been accused of murder. The Supreme Court themselves have mentioned the Loya case, so I don’t think Amit Shah has a lot of credibility,” Gandhi said, and went on to describe him as a “murder accused”.
“The party that talks about honesty, decency, has a person who is accused of murder and he is President,” he added.

This forms the backdrop of Gandhi’s remarks. A special CBI court had discharged Shah in the Sohrabuddin encounter case in December 2014, and in April 2018 the Supreme Court dismissed petitions seeking an independent inquiry into Loya’s death, holding that the material before it indicated that he died of natural causes.
The complaint against Gandhi was filed by Mishra, who said that Gandhi’s comments had harmed Shah’s and the BJP’s reputation and, in a way, his own standing as a party worker.
The legal framework

Examining the case against the Constitutional guarantee of the right to freedom of speech under 19(1)(a) and the reasonable restrictions enumerated under 19(2), and the right to reputation under Article 21.

Under the Indian Penal Code (since replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023), Section 499 defines criminal defamation as any “words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations” intended to harm the reputation of a person, would amount to defamation. It allows any company or a group to claim defamation and requires that the statement made “lowers the moral or intellectual character of that person” in front of others.

Section 199 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC, since replaced by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) permits a criminal defamation complaint only by “some person aggrieved by the offence”.
