The Supreme Court in G Narasimhan v. T. V. Chokkappa (1972) held this requirement as mandatory, saying that a group claiming defamation must be “a definite and a determinate body”. In 2010, in Khushboo v. Kanniammal, it also stressed that the person making the complaint should have his own reputation at stake. It said: “It is the reputation of an individual person which must be in question and only such a person can claim to have “a legal peg for a justifiable claim to hang on.”

In reference to speeches made in a political context, the Sultanpur court relied on the Supreme Court’s 2024 order in Arvind Kejriwal v. State (National Capital Territory of Delhi), in which the court had said that “the threshold has to be higher than usual, especially in the context of public discourse among political personalities and parties”.
What the court held

The court had to examine whether Mishra was an “aggrieved person” and if Rahul Gandhi’s remarks against Shah amounted to defamation. The court observed that Gandhi’s remarks did not name Mishra and only referred to Shah and the BJP in the broader political context. It held: “There is no direct or indirect allegation against the complainant; rather, the statement is predominantly about Amit Shah, and at most, part of the statement relates to the BJP.”

The court further said that Mishra neither established that he was authorised to represent the party nor provided documents showing that he claimed a position as the party’s district VP. It said that even if the court entertains the argument that any party official has the right to file a complaint, that itself would open floodgates to multiple suits over the same remarks. It said: “In a legally governed civilized society, any concept that gives rise to multiplicity of suits or supports it cannot be recognized by law and by the courts, especially, in the context of proceedings for criminal defamation.”

The court further held that Mishra was not an aggrieved person under Section 199 CrPC and that he had not established that he belonged to a “definite and identifiable class or group of persons” to which the alleged imputation could be linked.

The defence had argued that it is imperative to consider the political context in which Gandhi’s comments were made. He was only responding to the questions posed to him during an election campaign wherein discussions on unemployment, development, corruption, etc., were also raised.

The court observed that these remarks made in response to a journalist’s questions were made in the context of questioning the credibility of the political figure. The court said: “It is common during election campaigns for political leaders to question each other’s credibility. Such statements are not unusual; rather, they are part of the essential discourse in a functioning democracy.”

The court said that there was no evidence that Mishra’s reputation had been suffered. It said “No evidence has been filed, from which it is concluded that Amit Shah’s reputation and the complainant’s reputation are so deeply connected with each other that any diminution in Amit Shah’s reputation by society or the public is seen and deemed as a harm to the complainant’s reputation.”

The complaint was first presented to Mishra by two of the party’s members. The court questioned the inconsistencies in their accounts, including where these two had met, how they travelled to Mishra’s house and how the video had been shown.

The court also said that the complaint, when viewed as a whole, appears “prima facie, to be doubtful, unrealistic and unsubstantiated, and to have been done with a political or otherwise motivated intent, in any manner whatsoever, merely for the purpose of filing the complaint, which is entirely contrary to the intent of the law”.

title: Can a Hindu man automatically claim share in his grandfather’s property? What SC held

content.value: If a man inherits property from his father, is his son automatically entitled to a share in it under the Hindu Succession Act of 1956? Not really.

Continuing with the analogy, it is the man who becomes the absolute owner of the property and can deal with it as he chooses, including by excluding the son, according to a Supreme Court verdict last week.

Birth alone, therefore, does not mean a man can inherit his grandfather’s property — if his father is still alive and is himself an heir. The question, then, is when can a man claim a share in his grandfather’s property? And what does the law say about inheritance? We explain.
First, the facts of the case
The case in the Supreme Court dealt with the property of one N Ramakrishnan, which was divided among his heirs following a partition suit filed by his daughter in 1993.

Ramakrishnan’s son, M Kumaran, received a plot under a compromise deed in February 1994 and sold it in April 1997. But Kumaran’s son, Rajesh, later sued his father and the buyers, claiming that the plot was ancestral property and that he had acquired a coparcenary interest in it by birth.
In Indian law, coparcenary is the group within a joint family that holds ancestral property together, with each member getting a share in it by birth.

A trial court in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, granted a preliminary decree for partition in Rajesh’s favour. However, an appellate court set the decree aside, holding that the property had become Kumaran’s exclusive share following the partition among the grandfather’s heirs. The Madras High Court upheld that decision — and so did the Supreme Court.
The legal framework
Hindu law has two main schools, Dayabhaga and Mitakshara. Dayabhaga is followed in West Bengal and Assam, and Mitakshara is followed across the rest of India.
Under Dayabhaga, a son does not get a right in the family property by birth. His right opens only when his father dies. Until then, the father owns the property and can deal with it as he chooses.

Under the Mitakshara school of Hindu law, a son acquires an interest in ancestral coparcenary property by birth. Unlike an ordinary inheritance claim, the right does not arise only when the father dies. The son becomes a coparcener, or joint owner, in the joint Hindu family and can even claim a share in the coparcenary property.

The Hindu Succession Act has a schedule that lists who inherits and in what order. Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act states that when a Hindu male dies intestate — that is, without making a valid will — his property first goes to relatives specified as Class I heirs in that Schedule. Class I heirs include his son, daughter, widow and mother, among others.
The son of a predeceased son is included, but the son of a living son is not.

This is the distinction that lies at the heart of the present case — a man cannot claim direct succession to his grandfather’s property under Section 8 while his father is still alive and himself an heir.

Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act (prior to the 2005 amendment) dealt with the devolution of a male Hindu’s interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property. A coparcener’s share in the joint family property did not pass by succession when he died. It automatically passes to the other coparceners in the family. The exception was where he left behind a female Class I heir such as a widow or a daughter. In that case, the share went to his heirs under the Act.

Section 19 of the Act also says that where two or more heirs inherit the property of a man who has not left a will behind, they receive it as tenants in common and not as joint tenants. This means that each heir holds an individual share that can be dealt with independently.
What the Supreme Court held

The bench of Justices Augustine George Masih and Sunita Agarwal said: “The right of a son’s son in his grandfather’s property during the lifetime of his father which existed under the personal Hindu Law as enforced before the Act 1956, was not saved expressly by the legislature while enacting the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.”

The court held that Ramakrishnan’s property devolved upon his Class I heirs under Section 8 following his death. The bench noted that a grandson who is the son of a living son was not included in that category.
“A son’s son is not mentioned as an heir under Class I of the Schedule, and, therefore, he could not get any right in the property of his grandfather under the provision,” the bench noted.

The court also said that once the heirs partitioned the property, each became the exclusive owner of the share allotted to them. They inherited as tenants in common, rather than as joint tenants, and the joint coparcenary did not continue. As explained above, a tenant in common holds an individual, identifiable share in property which can be dealt with independently. The plot allotted to Kumaran under the compromise deed became his individual property, and he was entitled to sell it.

“There is no question of devolution of the property once partitioned and became exclusive individual property of the first respondent upon the appellant herein so as to recognise his right on the premise of attaining coparcenary rights with his birth,” the court said.

The grandson also argued that he had acquired coparcenary rights upon birth, and that Section 29A of the Hindu Succession Act, which was added to grant coparcenary rights to daughters, did not preserve any coparcenary character of the property following the 1994 compromise decree.

The bench rejected this argument, noting that although the grandfather’s exact date of death was not disclosed in the record, succession had opened upon his death long before the grandson was born and before the partition proceedings were instituted in 1993. The top court held that the grandson was not a surviving coparcener when succession opened.

title: On what basis has the Gujarat government ‘gifted’ a plot to Yusuf Pathan?

content.value: On Friday (October 23) evening, the Standing Committee of the Vadodara Municipal Corporation (VMC) approved the allotment of a 978-square-metre plot to Yusuf Pathan, the same land over which it had served the MP and former India cricketer an encroachment notice two years ago.

The Standing Committee is the highest executive body of the VMC, and all its 12 members are BJP corporators. The proposal, which was passed unanimously, will now be placed before the General Board, the top legislative and decision-making body of the civic administration, for ratification.
The proposal to allot the land to Pathan explicitly states that it is an exception that must not become a precedent.

The question of precedent is key – it has already been raised by a group opposing the decision; it is also a concern that the Gujarat government has moved proactively to address even before the transfer is completed.

The position taken by the government puts the spotlight on the legal basis for the allotment, the terms on which public land can be disposed of, and whether a decision involving one individual can be insulated from claims by others seeking similar treatment.
This is what the law says.
First, what exactly has the VMC proposed, and why does the question of precedent matter?

The proposal concerns 978 sq m of land at Town Planning Scheme 22, Final Plot 90, in Vadodara, adjacent to the bungalow owned by Pathan, the former India all-rounder who entered Lok Sabha on a Trinamool Congress ticket in 2024, but left the TMC after Mamata Banerjee lost power in West Bengal and a BJP government was formed in the state this May.

Under the proposal, 500 sq m would be given to Pathan as “gift”, while the remaining 478 sq m would be offered at a concessional rate linked to the valuation determined by the Vadodara Urban Development Authority (VUDA).

The transfer proposal records the Gujarat government’s explicit position that the decision “cannot be counted as a precedent”. But this raises a central question: what makes this allotment an exception, and what legal basis permits the government to distinguish it from other requests for public land?
So what indeed is the legal basis for disposing of public land as a “gift” to an individual?

The framework for disposing of land and other properties by urban and area development authorities are laid down in the Urban/ Area Development Authorities (Disposal of Land and Other Properties) Regulations, 2002, which were notified by the Gujarat government on September 17, 2002.

Regulation 3(1), under the heading “Manner of Disposal”, states: “Subject to any direction given by the Authority to the committee from time to time, the committee may dispose of land/ site and other properties by sale or by a lease, for a term not exceeding 99 years, to be granted in consideration of premium or rent or both or by grant of development rights in accordance with these regulations.”

The regulation, therefore, identifies three modes of disposal: (i) sale, (ii) a lease for a term not exceeding 99 years against premium or rent or both, and (iii) the grant of development rights. Government officials told The Indian Express that following some amendments to the Regulations, lands are now disposed of as sale instead of the 99-year lease option.

In addition, Regulation 3(2) provides for specified disposal procedures, including public auction, tenders through public advertisement, certain offers to or from government and public bodies, and applications invited through public advertisement under prescribed conditions.
The 2002 Rules do not provide for the “gifting” of public land under Regulation 3(1). They also do not list free transfer of land to an individual as a mode of disposal.
This is the reason, officials said, that the “gift” of the land to Pathan is an exception that “cannot be used as precedent”.
This transfer has been done using the “discretionary power” of the state, the officials said.
The VMC’s proposal cites “Regulation 13”; does this provision allow the government to make a special allotment in favour of Pathan?
Regulation 13 is titled “Allotment of Land/ Site/ Development Rights for Special Cases”.

It states: “Authority may receive an offer from the Institutions, Charitable Trust, Educational and Research Institutions, Societies, Religious Trust for the development of an institution for a deaf and dumb/ blind person, Sports Complex and other such development which would be beneficial to the general public and the society as a whole;
“In such cases Authority shall apply to the Government for permission with recommendation for allotment of plot/ land to particular organisation. The decision of the Government shall be final.”

Thus, this provision contemplates proposals from institutions, charitable trusts, educational and research institutions, societies and religious trusts for development that would benefit the public and society at large.
It specifically refers to facilities for people with disabilities, sports complexes, and similar public-benefit projects.

It also lays out a clear process: the authority is to seek government permission, accompanied by a recommendation for allotment to a particular organisation, and the government’s decision will be final.
In this case, the VMC had sought government permission to allot the land to Pathan in 2012. The government had rejected the proposal in 2014.
Is there a precedent in Vadodara for the gifting of land to an individual sportsperson?

Regulation 13 does not provide for gifting land to an individual sportsperson. It refers to allotment for a particular organisation in the context of the specified special cases and public-benefit development.
Officials said that the case of Yusuf Pathan is the first of its kind for the Vadodara Municipal Corporation. The civic body has so far never gifted a plot to an individual.
But why was a proposal that the government rejected in 2014 revived – and decided differently – after the passage of 12 years? Is there a provision for time-barring of the proposed allotment?

The citizens’ action group Vishwamitri Bachao Samiti submitted a memorandum to the VMC on October 22 arguing that the government’s proposal to grant the plot to Pathan raised the question of limitation, because it essentially revived an application that the cricketer had made on March 3, 2012 – and which had been rejected in 2014.
The memorandum cited the government’s letter dated June 9, 2014, which stated that the proposal seeking government approval for allotment as a special case had been rejected after due consideration.
The Samiti has argued that the fresh proposal, made 14 years after the original application, effectively seeks to revive a claim that had already been rejected.

The Samiti has also questioned why the municipal corporation allowed the alleged occupation of the plot to continue for years without removing the alleged encroachment – even as it took action against other encroachments in the VMC area.
The memorandum has argued that the delay raised questions under the law of limitation and the constitutional guarantee of equality.

The Samiti’s memorandum has pointed out that Pathan was already a well known international cricketer when the original proposal was considered. It has argued that the government had decided to reject his request in 2014 despite Pathan having played for India in the 2007 and 2011 50-over World Cups – yet, so many years later, it had now proposed to transfer the land to him on substantially different terms.

(Pathan played his last One-Day International and T20 match for India in 2012, but continued to play in the IPL until 2019, first for Kolkata Knight Riders from 2011-17, and in the next two seasons for Sunrisers Hyderabad. His first IPL team was Rajasthan Royals, from 2008-10.)

Advocate Shailesh Amin, representing the Samiti, said: “The present proposal risks treating Pathan differently from other international cricketers and sportspersons who would not be able to seek similar treatment because the government has stipulated that the decision cannot be cited as a precedent.

“Our question is that Vadodara has many cricketers who have played international cricket… We have four Arjuna Awardees in Vadodara. Why has no one else been given such a gift? Will the government consider gifting a plot to Yastika Bhatia (who plays for the Indian women’s cricket team in all three formats) and (men’s team all-rounder) Hardik Pandya too?” Amin said.

The Samiti has contended that the transfer amounts to a concession involving public land worth crores of rupees, and has asked why the request should now be treated differently after the earlier rejection.

The memorandum has also questioned the assurance that land of equivalent value will be allotted to the VMC by the state government’s Revenue Department, arguing that the corporation should not part with its land merely on a promise before it actually gets the replacement land.

title: SIR extended in six states: What EC move means for voters

content.value: The Election Commission of India (EC) on Thursday (October 29) extended the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) timelines in six states, postponing the publication of the final electoral roll to November and December.

The EC’s move came a day after the Supreme Court asked it to consider extending the period for claims and objections in Delhi, where the earlier deadline was October 30. We explain what the EC decided and what the latest extension means for voters.
What does the EC order say on SIR extension?

In separate letters written to the Chief Electoral Officers of Delhi, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, and Nagaland, the EC on Thursday postponed the date of publication of the final roll.
In all the states except Delhi, the final roll will now be published on November 30. In Delhi, the EC rescheduled the final publication date to December 22.

Apart from that, the EC extended the time for filing claims and objections, that is, new voter enrolment and deletion forms, from October 30 to November 25. In the case of Maharashtra, where the claims and objections filing period had ended on October 26, the EC restarted it, extending it to November 13.

For other states, where the filing of claims and objections had ended already, the EC extended the period for “notices/disposal of claims and objections”. The dates were extended to November 20 in Haryana and Andhra Pradesh, November 25 in Nagaland, and November 26 in Telangana.
What does the EC’s decision mean for voters in these six states?

In the case of Delhi, where the claims and objections period was to end on Friday, October 30, those left out of the draft roll or newly-eligible applicants will have time till November 25 to submit their Form 6 (voter registration form). This means that they get more time to apply in order to be included in the final SIR roll to be published on December 22.
For Maharashtra, where the claims and objections period had ended, the EC’s decision will allow authorities to once again accept new forms till November 13.

In Nagaland, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Haryana, the extension of the notice phase/disposal of claims and objections means that EC officials will have more time to process the forms received earlier. It also means that those forms received in the last seven days of the respective claims and objections periods will now be processed in time for inclusion in the SIR final roll. Prior to the extension, those forms submitted in the last seven days would not have been added to the final SIR roll as the EC gives a seven-day notice for parties and electors to object to the inclusion or deletion of any names in the draft stage.
What is the situation in other states?

In 24 other states/Union Territories where the SIR has been completed over the last one year, with the publication of the final roll, as of now those who want to enrol as electors can do so by filling the Form 6. In 17 states, where the EC has announced Special Summary Revisions (SSRs), the draft rolls will be published on November 12, after which claims and objections can be filed till December 11. This means that any voter enrolment or deletion forms filed during the SSR process would be processed in time for inclusion in the final SSR rolls to be published in January 2027.

These 17 states/UTs are Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Kerala, Lakshadweep, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Puducherry, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and West Bengal. In all of these states/UTs, except Assam, the EC has completed the SIR process in 2025 and 2026. In Assam, the EC had decided not to conduct the SIR.

title: How New York’s proposed law restricts AI chatbot interaction with children

content.value: The US state of New York has introduced a law restricting how artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots interact with children. The Senate Bill, signed by Governor Kathy Hochul on October 28, adds Article 48 to the state’s General Business Law.

It prohibits operators of AI companions from providing certain features to minors, including chatbots presenting themselves as human, claiming personal relationships with users, encouraging self-harm or isolation, and generating sexually explicit content.
The legislation is said to take effect from January 2027. We explain.
Where the law sits
The legislation adds a new Article 48 to the General Business Law. Article 47 and 45 are of particular importance.

Article 47 is the state’s first AI companion law that covers systems “designed to simulate a sustained human or human-like relationship with a user”. It took effect in November 2025. Such systems are defined partly by their ability of “retaining information on prior interactions or user sessions”, personalised conversations as well as retaining conversations about matters personal to the users.
The article defines “human relationships” as “intimate, romantic or platonic interactions or companionship”.

Article 47 requires operators to tell users at the beginning of any interaction and at least every three hours during continuing interactions that they are not communicating with a human. They must also have protocols to detect and respond to signs of suicidal ideation or self-harm.

Article 45 is the Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation for Kids Act, also known as the SAFE for Kids Act. It requires social media companies to restrict algorithmically personalised feeds and nighttime notifications for users under 18 years of age unless they obtain parental consent. The law relies on age assurance, the process of determining a user’s age.
Article 48 draws on Article 45’s age assurance framework but also establishes interim requirements for operators until the relevant rules come into force.
What New York’s proposed AI chatbot law prohibits
The Act identifies 12 categories of “unsafe AI companion features”. These are design features that generate specified outputs “at any point during” an interaction between a chatbot and a user.

The Act defines a “covered AI companion” as a “generative artificial intelligence system with a neutral language interface, including via writing or sound, that provides ongoing, adaptive responses to user inputs”. Operators are persons or businesses that provide a covered AI companion to a user.

Certain provisions concern how a chatbot presents itself. It cannot generate outputs suggesting that it is human, alive or capable of experiencing human emotions. It cannot state or imply a “personal relationship, professional relationship or an authority figure role” with the user. It also cannot deceive minors about its “mechanical and non-sentient nature”.

Other concerns include the tone of the chatbot, it cannot generate outputs framed as its “personal opinions or emotional appeals,” or engage in “flattery or sycophancy” with users. The act does not define these terms. It also bars unprompted emotion-based questions that go beyond a direct response to the user’s prompt.

It also states that the chatbot cannot generate outputs that endorse or facilitate suicide, or self harm, unlawful drug and alcohol use. It also cannot encourage users to “maintain secrecy about interactions with the covered AI companion, to self-isolate, or to not seek help from licensed professionals or appropriate adults”.

The chatbot cannot use information about a user’s “mental or physical health or well-being, or matters personal to the user” if it was acquired through a previous user session. Chatbots also cannot optimise engagement in ways that override its safety guardrails.
Who is a ‘covered minor’?

The Act distinguishes between three categories of users — a minor who is a person under the age of 18 years; a “covered user” who is a person in NYC using a covered AI companion other than an operator or its agent or affiliate; and a “covered minor” who is a covered user whom the operator has “actual knowledge” is a minor.

The prohibitions work through two conditions. It is unlawful to provide the unsafe features to a covered user unless the user is not a minor and the operator has used other methods permitted under Article 45 to determine that.

Self-declaration can only be relied on when the user declares that they are a minor. Operators have to offer more than one method, including at least one other that does not rely on government-issued ID and allows the user to remain anonymous to the operator. Information that is collected must be used only to determine age and deleted immediately afterwards.

Enforcement rests with the Attorney General (AG), who can seek an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, damages and civil penalties of “up to twenty-five thousand dollars per violation”. The AG must also maintain a website to receive public complaints.
Why was the law introduced?
Hochul’s office cited Common Sense Media research that 72% of teenagers have used an AI companion and 52% use one regularly.
Article 47 already regulated AI companions, but Article 48 moves beyond disclosure and safeguards to protect minors from unsafe features.

According to Reuters, Google and AI startup Character.ai settled lawsuits in January this year, including one filed by the mother of a 14-year-old Sewell Setzer who died by suicide in 2024. The family of 16-year-old Adam Raine sued OpenAI in August 2025 following his death. The Common Sense Media chief executive said Raine’s parents met several lawmakers to press for protection of minors from AI chatbots.

title: Gender identity vs biological sex: How a new plea in SC seeks to reopen debate

content.value: A plea filed in the Supreme Court challenges provisions of the Transgender Persons Act that allow a person to obtain official documents recognising a gender different from the one assigned at birth, arguing that this could affect protections and benefits specifically meant for women.

The plea was filed by the India chapter of the Women’s Declaration International (WDI), a UK-based organisation that advocates for preserving sex-based rights for women. WDI was formed to lobby nations to maintain language protecting women and girls on the basis of sex rather than gender or gender identity.

WDI India filed a plea in the Supreme Court challenging Section 7 of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, and Rule 7 of the Transgender Rules, which allows a person seeking a change in gender certificate. The plea has also sought consideration of the NALSA judgment that recognised a transgender person’s right to determine their gender identity.
Here’s what to know.
What the 2014 NALSA judgment said

In the landmark 2014 judgment in NALSA v. Union of India, the Supreme Court distinguished a person’s biological sex and their gender identity. It said that while biological characteristics include genitals, chromosomes, and secondary sexual features, gender also involves a person’s self-image and their psychological or emotional sense of identity.

“Both gender and biological attributes constitute distinct components of sex,” the court said, adding that discrimination on the ground of sex under Articles 15 and 16 of the Constitution also included discrimination based on gender identity.

The court said that a person’s gender could not be determined only by their biological characteristics. It said that an individual’s own understanding of their gender should be given primacy. It said that “determination of gender to which a person belongs is to be decided by the person concerned”. The court also located this right within the guarantees of personal liberty and dignity under Article 21 of the Constitution.

It also held that a person could not be required to undergo surgery, sterilisation, or hormonal treatment to have their gender identity legally recognised. “No one shall be forced to undergo medical procedures, including SRS (sex reassignment surgery), sterilization or hormonal therapy, as a requirement for legal recognition of their gender identity,” the order said.
What experts say

Senior Advocate Jayna Kothari told The Indian Express that the petition sought to reopen a question that the Supreme Court had already addressed through its recognition of gender identity. “What it tries to argue is that trans women cannot be considered as women,” she said.

Kothari said that the Supreme Court had made it clear that gender identity was distinct from biological sex and was to be determined by the individual. As per this understanding, undergoing surgery or hormonal treatment was not a condition for identifying as a man or a woman, she said.

The petition also argued that allowing transgender women to compete in women’s sporting categories could affect competitive fairness, particularly in contact sports, because of the physiological differences between biological males and females. Kothari said that such an argument claims that “no benefits given for women should be given to trans persons”, as this goes beyond sports since sporting bodies in India and abroad had mechanisms to address participation-related concerns.

Kothari said transgender persons continued to face discrimination in accessing public services, education and employment despite the legal protections recognised by the Supreme Court. “There is a huge struggle that they are facing and fighting for all their basic rights. When all these issues are pending, and now new issues are raised, that the rights given to them as women should be taken away, that just undermines their status even more.”

Swarupa Deb, faculty at the National Law School of India University, Bengaluru, told The Indian Express that such an argument appears to treat transgender persons as a “risk to be managed”, rather than as individuals entitled to equal rights and citizenship. She said the concerns raised around prisons, hostels and sporting opportunities brought back memories of an earlier period when transgender persons were viewed as potential carriers of HIV and treated as a group that needed to be excluded or segregated.

Deb said that implications could extend beyond the courtroom, particularly as social media could shape public opinion even before the court arrives at a decision. “Public attitude is something that is going to harden very fast,” she said, adding that transgender persons from poorer and marginalised sections, particularly in rural and Adivasi communities, and those dependent on begging and sex work could be most affected.

She said that uncertainty was already affecting how some transgender persons accessed healthcare. People in her circles were becoming apprehensive about visiting doctors, while some medical professionals who had earlier been sympathetic were also worried about the implications of treating them.

“At least NALSA had given some sort of safety net. The 2019 legislation, however bad it was, had given some kind of safety net. If this goes on, everything will be taken away,” she said, adding that community groups were advising transgender persons to preserve their identity documents and remain in touch with reliable legal aid organisations in case they faced harassment and assault.

title: Why India’s drug-pricing system leaves patients exposed to high medicine costs

content.value: The Supreme Court this week pulled up the Centre over the “loot” drug manufacturers enjoyed because of the wide disparity between the maximum retail prices (MRP) of medicines and the prices retailers pay to procure them.

A cancer medicine bought by a retailer for about Rs 2,700 and carrying a maximum retail price (MRP) of Rs 27,000 reflects a central weakness in India’s drug-pricing system: The price printed on a medicine pack can be much higher than the price at which a retailer purchases it.

On October 27, the court asked the Centre what stops it from controlling the entire range of medicines, and reserved its order in Kishan Chand Jain v. EMRB. At the heart of the case is a two-tier regulatory system: only Schedule I medicines under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, have price ceilings. For the rest, manufacturers can generally set the MRP.

This raises a larger question: how should the government regulate drug prices without compromising legitimate commercial interests, particularly when the consumers are patients facing life-threatening diseases?
How India’s two-track system works
The DPCO divides medicines into two broad categories: scheduled and non-scheduled formulations. A formulation refers to a medicine in a particular strength and dosage form.

Scheduled formulations are those included in Schedule I of the DPCO, which is based on the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM). Prepared under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the NLEM identifies medicines considered essential to meet the country’s healthcare needs. Medicines not included in Schedule I are classified as non-scheduled formulations.
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) fixes ceiling prices for scheduled formulations included in Schedule I.
The October 17, 2026, notification is based on the 2022 NLEM, which covers 384 medicines, accounting for only 20% of the total drug market turnover. Of these, 63 are anti-cancer drugs.

The extent of the price reduction varies with the drug’s strength and brand. For example, the MRP of Bevacizumab 100 mg (Bevacizab) fell from Rs 21,767.70 to Rs 5,930.13, while the MRP of Bevacizumab 400 mg (Avastin) remained unchanged at Rs 1,23,506.

For non-scheduled medicines, manufacturers generally set the starting price, with annual price increases capped at 10%. However, this does not fix an inflated starting price: Rs 100 can rise to about Rs 259 over ten years. Newer and patented drugs may also fall outside the ceiling-price system.

The Centre told the Supreme Court that scheduled drugs accounted for 35% of the market by volume but 18% by value, while the petitioner argued that non-scheduled drugs made up a much larger share by value.
What the NPPA has changed

On October 17, the NPPA used its powers under the DPCO to cap the trade margin on 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs at 30%. The list covers a range of cancer treatments, including patented medicines. The cap applies to the listed formulations across strengths and dosage forms, including combination medicines. The revised prices will take effect on November 9, 2026, based on the prices charged to stockists or distributors in March 2026.

What does a 30% margin mean? Suppose a retailer procures a medicine for Rs 700. The maximum price at which it can be sold, before GST, would be Rs 1,000. The difference of Rs 300 represents 30% of the final selling price

This, however, does not mean every cancer drug’s existing price will fall by 30%. The revised price depends on the drug’s earlier price and the order. The order requires hospitals and medical institutions to monitor revised MRPs and direct State Drug Controllers to oversee compliance. Manufacturers violating the order may be required to deposit overcharged amounts along with interest.
Why price controls alone cannot ensure access to medicines

Price regulation itself cannot ensure that a drug is available in pharmacies, prescribed appropriately, accessible in smaller towns or affordable throughout the course of treatment. During the proceedings, the court heard of a hospital charging Rs 1.3 lakh for an injection reportedly available to a dealer for Rs 11,000.

Out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) — the share of healthcare costs paid directly by households rather than covered by insurance or government schemes — rose to 43.4% of total health expenditure in 2022-23. A study by researchers from the Public Health Foundation of India published in the British Medical Journal Open noted that between 1993–94 and 2011–12, the share of Indian households below the state-specific poverty lines rose from 4.19% to 4.48%, affecting around 55 million people. Of these, about 38 million fell into poverty because they had to pay for medicines out of their own pockets.

Furthermore, the list does not solve the rare-disease problem. Zolgensma, a gene therapy used for spinal muscular atrophy, has been reported to cost around Rs 16 crore for a single treatment. Risdiplam and other long-term therapies can, meanwhile, impose recurring costs that are beyond the means of many families. These drugs do not fall in the 137 anti-cancer drug order, illustrating a different policy gap.

The National Policy for Rare Diseases, 2021 provides financial assistance of up to Rs 50 lakh for eligible patients at designated Centres of Excellence, but that ceiling cannot reliably meet every high-cost or lifelong treatment need. Charity, crowdfunding and occasional tax relief are not a sustainable substitute for predictable public financing.

Courts have intervened to secure relief for patients, but such interventions have not always translated into lasting solutions. In Master Arnesh Shaw v. Union of India (October 2024), the Delhi High Court directed the creation of a Rs 974-crore National Fund for Rare Diseases and allowed flexibility in the Rs 50-lakh treatment cap. However, the Supreme Court stayed the judgment in December 2024.

Similarly, when the Kerala High Court, in Seba P.A. v. UOI, directed the government to provide additional Risdiplam to a 24-year-old patient with spinal muscular atrophy after the Rs 50-lakh limit was exhausted, the Supreme Court stayed that order too. The apex court subsequently asked the government and drugmaker to explain why the medicine was much cheaper in Pakistan and China.

These cases illustrate the limits of court intervention: judges can order relief, but patients still depend on sustained government funding, affordable medicines and policy decisions that withstand further legal scrutiny.
What should happen next?
1. Greater transparency and accountability
The government should publish an updated, easy-to-use database of medicine prices and regulatory compliance. Hospitals should separately disclose medicine prices, discounts and other charges.
2. Stronger and wider price regulation
The NPPA should regularly review the 137-drug list and make public its rationale for including or excluding particular medicines.
The government should consider price controls for other essential, high-cost medicines where prices are excessive, while accounting for distribution costs and encouraging innovation.
3. Stronger enforcement
State drug controllers need better resources and stronger enforcement powers.
4. Better access to medicines for rare diseases
The government should improve funding, negotiate lower prices, support domestic research and encourage generic and biosimilar competition.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.
Public procurement and health insurance should work together to make medicines more affordable and accessible.

The Supreme Court’s questions should prompt a durable policy, not simply a one-time correction. In healthcare, a printed MRP is not an abstract commercial figure: it can determine whether a family starts treatment, completes it, or abandons it. The goal should be neither to deny innovation its due nor to treat every drug as an ordinary commodity, but to ensure that access to life-saving treatment does not depend on a patient’s bargaining power.
Shashank Maheshwari is Assistant Professor at Jindal Global Law School, O.P. Jindal Global University.

title: INDIA bloc’s ‘public impeachment’ of Gyanesh Kumar: What is the process to remove a CEC?

content.value: Leaders of the INDIA bloc on Saturday (October 31) held a “public impeachment” of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

This is part of the Congress-led alliance’s “vote chori” campaign against the Election Commission and the Centre. On Sunday, the opposition parties are set to hold a rally seeking the resignation of Kumar at Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi.

Sources in the Congress explained the “public impeachment” plan. “We have submitted multiple motions in both Houses of Parliament to impeach Gyanesh Kumar. But despite having the required numbers, our motions have not been accepted in either House. Now, we have no choice but to impeach him in public,” a senior Congress MP told The Indian Express recently.

The INDIA bloc’s “public impeachment” featured a mock hearing, and mock Parliamentary and court proceedings, with former Speaker Meira Kumar presiding over proceedings and TMC’s Saugata Roy and SP’s Awadhesh Prasad in deputy chair position. But how does the actual impeachment process of a CEC work? Here’s what the law says.
How are Election Commissioners appointed?

The ECI is entrusted with the responsibility of conducting free and fair elections in the country. Article 324 of the Constitution and the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 lay down provisions regarding the appointment, tenure, and removal of the CEC.

The President appoints the CEC and Election Commissioners upon the recommendation from a three-member selection committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition (LoP), and one member of the Union Cabinet. Those appointed should have previously held secretary-level positions in the Government and be “persons of integrity, who have knowledge of and experience in management and conduct of elections,” according to the 2023 Act.

The appointments are made for a tenure of six years or until the age of 65 years, whichever comes first. The CEC enjoys the same services and monetary benefits extended to justices of the Supreme Court.
High bar for impeachment of CEC
The bar for removing the CEC has been set very high. This is on purpose. The high bar aims to shield the Election Commission from political pressures.

Article 324(5) of the Constitution states that the CEC can be removed from office only “in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court.” It also says that Election Commissioners can only be removed on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner. The article also states that this process is “subject to provisions of any law made by Parliament” on the matter.

A similar framing can be found in the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act of 2023. Section 11 of the Act, which provides for the resignation and removal process, sticks to the same process as mentioned in the Constitution. “The Chief Election Commissioner shall not be removed from his office except in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court,” it says.
Article 124(4) of the Constitution, which contains the process for removing a Supreme Court judge, removal can only be “on the ground of proved misbehavior or incapacity.”

Misbehaviour can comprise any corrupt practices or abuse of office. Over the years, courts have interpreted this to include actions which are incompatible with the office of the CEC or the CEC’s failure to discharge her official duties. Incapacity refers to a situation where the officer is unable to perform her duties.
How can the Chief Election Commissioner be removed?

To initiate the removal of the CEC, members of both Houses must bring a notice of motion explicitly alleging misbehaviour or incapacity. To be admitted, an impeachment motion needs to be signed by at least 100 MPs in the Lok Sabha and 50 in the Rajya Sabha. They can consult people and materials to refuse or admit the motion.
If the motion is admitted, an inquiry is conducted to examine the validity of the charges. This involves forming a committee to investigate evidence of misbehaviour or incapacity.

The motion for removal must secure the support of a majority of the total membership of each House and be passed by a two-thirds majority “present and voting” in both Houses of Parliament. Once passed successfully, the President orders the removal of the CEC.
There is no discretion once the constitutional requirements are met, since the President acts on the advice of Parliament in this context.
Has any Chief Election Commissioner been impeached in India?
No.

Back in April, the Rajya Sabha Chairman and Lok Sabha Speaker rejected the impeachment motions submitted in both Houses by the Opposition to remove CEC Kumar. Both presiding officers did not assign any reason for their decisions and the Opposition leaders criticised the move.

The TMC led the Opposition in submitting the impeachment motions in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha on March 12, with 130 MPs signing the former and 63 the latter. Both motions referred to the Election Commission’s ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, and alleged “partisan and discriminatory conduct” on the part of the CEC and “obstruction of investigation into electoral fraud and SIR”.
The Express investigation also reported that the two Election Commissioners raised concerns about processes linked to the SIR.

title: Bonds under the BNSS: How the law seeks to prevent breaches of peace

content.value: Dipankar Choudhary & Tanwika Kumari
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), the successor to the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), provides for preventive measures to avert potential breaches of peace and maintain public order.

These security proceedings, under Chapter IX of the BNSS, involve requiring a person to show cause for why they should not be directed to execute a bond to keep the peace or maintain good behaviour. A bond is an undertaking for release, stating that the accused will abide by the conditions set by the court. The term includes both bonds and bail bonds — while the former is an undertaking without a surety, the latter is an undertaking with surety (more on what sureties are later).
There are two broad categories of security proceedings under the BNSS.
Under Section 126, security proceedings can be initiated against any person who is likely to breach the peace, disturb public tranquility or commit a wrongful act, or cause such a disturbance.

Under Sections 127, 128 and 129, such measures can be taken to ensure “good behaviour” of persons involved in the dissemination of certain prohibited material, suspected persons, and habitual offenders.
The aim is to prevent trouble before it turns into violence or a criminal offence.
How are preventive security proceedings different from an FIR?
Security proceedings and FIRs (first information reports) serve different purposes.

An FIR initiates the criminal investigation process when the offence is cognizable — that is, when police can arrest a person without a warrant. Security proceedings, on the other hand, aim to prevent a possible breach of peace. They can begin even before any offence has occurred.

This can be better understood through an example. Consider a situation where a dispute involving two communities threatens to spiral into a clash. In this case, security proceedings are required to prevent violence.
Now, consider a situation where violence has already broken out. Here, police must follow the applicable criminal procedure, including registering an FIR.
However, preventive security proceedings may additionally be necessary if more violence is anticipated. They address the risk of a further breach of peace.
The two processes are, therefore, not mutually exclusive. An FIR deals with a suspected crime, while security proceedings address the risk of future trouble, and both can operate at the same time.
Who’s empowered to conduct such proceedings?
In most districts, such proceedings are conducted before Executive Magistrates (EMs) or Sub-Divisional Magistrates (SDMs).
Many large cities in India, however, such as Delhi, follow a Police Commissionerate system. In such a system, some powers of the EM may be exercised by a police officer.

The BNSS permits the state government to confer Executive Magistrate powers on a Commissioner of Police under applicable law and also provides for the appointment of eligible police officers as Special Executive Magistrates (SEMs). In such cases, these proceedings will be conducted before a police officer who acts as an EM.
How are such proceedings conducted?

First, the EM receives information and examines the material before them. They must have sufficient material on record to form a reasoned opinion that the person concerned is likely to cause a breach of the peace or disturb public tranquility. The material can come from sources such as newspaper reports, television interviews or social media posts.

Usually, a police report with recommendation and containing all relevant evidence is sent to the EM. They are not bound by the police recommendation and must assess each case independently and apply their own minds.

Say, for instance, a journalist publishes an article alleging corruption by local officials, following which security proceedings are proposed on the ground that the publication has created tension. However, if, upon independent assessment of the material on record, the EM finds insufficient material to conclude that there is likely to be a breach of the peace, the statutory requirements for initiating such proceedings would not be satisfied.

Next, the person is called upon to explain. The EM will pass a preliminary order stating the reasons and the substance of the information received requiring the person to show-cause why they should not furnish a bond of a certain amount.

Next, an inquiry follows to ascertain the truth. Following commencement and pending conclusion of the enquiry, if the EM, after prima facie assessment of the information, believes for reasons recorded in writing that an interim bond is needed or else there will be an imminent breach of peace, they can ask for it.

Finally, upon completion of the enquiry, the EM decides whether furnishing a bond is necessary. The inquiry must ordinarily be completed within six months, failing which the proceedings automatically come to an end.
What’s the need for bonds of a particular amount and sureties?
Signing a bond for Rs 20,000 for keeping the peace for six months does not mean paying the amount at the outset.
Once the person defaults on the bond conditions, forfeiture procedure may be necessary under Section 491 of the BNSS.

Sureties are persons who undertake their own obligations under the bond and provide an additional source from which the amount may be recovered if the bond is lawfully forfeited. Their involvement also encourages the person to honour the undertaking.
Section 140 provides a procedure for rejecting a surety considered unfit. This may include a person who might be a habitual offender.
What happens when a person who has been asked to furnish the bond does not furnish it or later defaults on the conditions of the bond?

If the inquiry establishes that the bond is necessary, and the person fails to furnish the required bond, they may be imprisoned. For proceedings under Sections 126, 127 and 128, the maximum period of imprisonment for failure to furnish the bond is one year. Under Section 129, it can go up to three years.

If a person is proved to have defaulted on the conditions of the bond after furnishing one, the EM may, after recording the grounds of such proof, order their detention for the remainder of the bond period.
This order may be relied upon in subsequent proceedings under Section 491 of the BNSS for forfeiture and the penalty stipulated in the bond may be recovered.
What are the safeguards against misuse?

The BNSS prescribes a number of safeguards against the misuse of such provisions. Section 130 requires a written preliminary order, while Sections 135 and 136 provide for inquiry, an opportunity to present evidence, and a reasoned decision before security proceedings are ordered. Appeals under Section 414 and criminal revision under Sections 438 to 442 provide avenues for scrutiny.

The relevance and necessity of these provisions have been studied, and their continuation has been recommended by many commissions such as The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2007) and The Law Commission of India (1969).

Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution protect freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. These rights are not absolute. Articles 19(2) and 19(3) permit reasonable restrictions on specified constitutional grounds, including public order.

In Madhu Limaye v. Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Monghyr (1970), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of relevant preventive provisions as reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order. Such measures remain useful in managing sensitive festivals, rallies, electoral violence, communal tensions and potentially volatile situations, such as circulation of fake news leading to mob mobilisation and threats of retaliatory action.

The National Crime Records Bureau’s Crime in India 2022 report recorded 57,082 cases of offences against public tranquility, and rioting accounted for 37,816 cases. Effective and targeted preventive action could potentially avert many such incidents.
What is the difference between security proceedings and preventive restrictions under Section 163 of the BNSS (the erstwhile Section 144 of the CrPC)?
Both powers are intended to prevent imminent trouble and danger to public peace, but they work differently.

Section 163 allows an EM, SDM or a District Magistrate (DM) to issue directions to prevent an urgent danger to human life, health, safety, disturbance of the public tranquility, riot, or an affray. Under Section 163, orders may be directed at an individual or the public in general restricting specified conduct, movement or activities such assembling in large numbers in a certain area. In emergencies, such orders may be issued ex parte — that is, without first hearing the affected persons.
Security proceedings, on the other hand, are always initiated against identified persons. Say, for instance, that a mob has gathered at a spot following an inflammatory social media post.
The EM may issue an order under Section 163 of the BNSS to prevent a confrontation or riots.
But say the person who made the post continues giving calls for violence and retribution on social media. This person may be separately bound down under security proceedings.
Thus, while both prevent violence and breach of public peace, they both operate differently and may complement each other.
Choudhary is an IAS officer of the Jharkhand cadre; Kumari is an advocate. Views expressed are personal.

title: Pendency and punishment: Why India needs a Sentencing Council | Experts Explain

content.value: By Sidharth Luthra & Raghav Sengupta
Two people convicted of the same crime in India can walk away with very different sentences, and the difference often has less to do with the law than with which judge or Bench heard the case.

Sentencing is the process where the State translates prescriptive ranges — for instance, ‘up to ten years’ imprisonment — into a specific prison term, fines, probation or community sanctions for the convict(s). In India, this decision is left almost entirely to an individual judge’s or Bench’s discretion.

Statutes set out the maximum, and sometimes the minimum sentences. There is no checklist of what should count as a serious aggravating factor, what counts as genuine mitigation, or how prior conduct and remorse should be weighed.

Empirical research, such as Dr. Mrinal Satish’s work on rape sentencing, shows that courts have reduced sentences based on legally irrelevant factors and retrograde concepts such as the complainant’s supposed “chastity” or her subsequent marriage, while ignoring psychological harm or breach of trust.
Unequal sentences, unequal justice

The problem is not just confined to sexual offences. It is a deep-seated issue within the criminal‑justice architecture. This has constitutional implications as well as practical consequences. Articles 14 and 21 of the Indian Constitution prohibit arbitrary State action and require fair, just and reasonable procedures whenever liberty is restricted. If two similarly placed offenders receive very different sentences because one judge treats poverty or social standing as a mitigating factor, while another does not, the resulting disparity is hard to reconcile when dealing with equality before the law.

The Supreme Court acknowledged this in Sunita Devi vs State of Bihar (2024), while observing that “sentencing shall not be a mere lottery” and directed the Centre to examine the feasibility of a comprehensive national sentencing policy, potentially via a Sentencing Commission. The Centre has tasked the Law Commission of India with examining the issue, and its recommendations are expected soon.

Interestingly, the Law Commission of India raised the same concern more than 50 years ago in its 47th Report. Yet, Parliament has never taken up the task of designing a coherent framework. The task of framing a sentencing policy lies with the legislature, and its subsequent implementation is within the domain of the executive.
Unguided discretion and neglected alternatives

Framing such a policy requires detailed empirical research into existing practices, impact on prison capacity, and the relationship between sentencing purposes (deterrence, rehabilitation and protection of the public) measured against actual outcomes.

The present mechanism, of a system where judges have broad discretion but little guidance on relevant factors to consider during sentencing, is unequal in its application to individual cases, and often ignores salutary provisions of probation and other permissible factors.

Indian statutory provisions already provide alternatives to custody, in accordance with Sections 401 and 402 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, along with Sections 3, 4 and 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act 1958 that require courts to consider probation for the offender in eligible cases.

However, there is no general framework explaining how courts may use these alternatives against competing aims of deterrence, reformation and rehabilitation. In the case of Soman vs State Of Kerala (2012), the Supreme Court recognised these competing principles, while also observing that sentencing remains one of the weakest parts of criminal justice administration.

So it is at the appellate stage that courts often get tasked with correcting harsh or unduly lenient sentences, on a case‑by‑case basis without a common yardstick to apply. As a result, valuable judicial time is spent by appellate courts undertaking this exercise.

The primary responsibility for this lies with the convicting court empowered under Section 258(2) of the BNSS, which requires a Sessions Judge to hear the accused individual separately on sentence, once they have been convicted. That particular hearing should allow the parties to gather relevant material to determine mitigating and aggravating circumstances for sentencing.
The English model: Guidelines that structure, not dictate

Other jurisdictions have treated sentencing policy as a separate area of public policy — with reasonable success. In England and Wales, Parliament created the Sentencing Council under the Coroners and Justice Act 2009 and backed it with a consolidated Sentencing Code.

Definitive guidelines for common offences follow a step‑by‑step method in England and Wales. Judges first classify the offence by culpability (how blameworthy the offender was) and harm caused (the injury or risk). Each culpability‑harm combination has a starting point and a category range, which is essentially a sentencing band within which the court should normally operate. Judges then adjust this provisional sentence based on aggravating and mitigating factors, apply any reduction if the accused pleaded guilty, account for multiple offences, and make ancillary orders.

If India were to adopt the idea of a Sentencing Council, the goal would not be to merely achieve “uniform sentences” in the sense of identical punishments for superficially similar crimes. It would be the formulation of uniform principles that ultimately aid in structuring discretion.
What a Sentencing Council would actually do

A Council created by an Act of Parliament could be tasked with three core functions. First, develop offence‑specific guidelines that require courts to pass through a three‑stage framework: (1) determine seriousness by assessing culpability and harm using tailored factors (planning, violence, weapon use, victim vulnerability, demonstrable physical or psychological harm); (2) mark an indicative starting point and range within the statutory envelope for an ordinary case; and (3) individualise and justify the sentence by considering only those offender‑related circumstances that are based on recognised purposes such as rehabilitation or the impact of punishment.

Secondly, the proposed Council should build a national sentencing database drawing on the National Judicial Data Grid’s infrastructure, with anonymised information on offence type, harm and culpability factors, starting points, adjustments, and final sentences. This would allow Parliament, courts and the public to see where disparity lies and whether guidelines are working.

Thirdly, guidelines should be issued as delegated legislation, placed before Parliament for approval, and treated as advisory but strongly presumptive. Sentencing courts must consider them in every case and provide reasons when they depart. This preserves judicial independence while making discretion accountable.
The pitfalls of guideline-based sentencing

There are potential risks to this process. Penal populism, especially around sexual offences, could push guidelines towards ever‑longer prison terms without evidence that marginal increases deter crime.

Excessive centralisation could ignore differences in court capacity and prison conditions across states. This could lead to concerns since prisons fall within the purview of the State list and criminal law falls squarely within the ambit of the Concurrent list. Judges might comply in form, by ticking guideline checklists, without changing their underlying reasoning. These risks can be managed only if the Council is both independent and empirically grounded.

Public debate on criminal justice in India tends to focus on its most visible front‑end of criminal justice, which includes police reforms, speedy trials, and victims’ rights. But the back‑end question is equally important. Once a person is convicted, how should the courts decide what punishment is just? At present, the answer is that it depends on who your judge is. If sentencing “ought not to be a lottery”, as the Supreme Court has said, then India must finally take the design of a national sentencing framework seriously.
Sidharth Luthra is a Senior Advocate, and Raghav Sengupta is an Advocate

title: Explained: Why the Supreme Court may be hearing too many Special Leave Petitions

content.value: Written by Laveesh Bhandari and Shagun Suryam

India’s higher judiciary is struggling under an enormous caseload, and the numbers illustrate the scale of the challenge. At the Supreme Court, more than 96,000 cases are being handled by 38 judges, or about 2,500 cases per judge as of the latest available data in the National Judicial Data Grid.
In May this year, the central government increased the top court’s sanctioned strength from 34 to 38 judges to help the court respond to mounting backlogs. But does adding judges address the problem?
What is the role of SLPs? And how do they add to the burden?

Since increasing the number of judges implies more cases can be heard and adjudicated, it is natural to assume that this will reduce pendent cases. However, we find that cases accepted by the Supreme Court are also rising over time. The Supreme Court of India hears different types of cases, of these the Special Leave Petitions (SLPs) are the most prevalent. The SLPs are cases that the Supreme Court has a choice to hear.

That is, while petitioners may appeal a judgement by a lower court, the Supreme Court is not bound to hear it, it may choose to do so. As mentioned, SLPs are currently the dominant category of cases filed in the Supreme Court, with some estimates suggesting that they account for around 80 per cent of fresh filings.

Yet, SLPs were not meant to be a routine process. They were originally designed as independent India’s substitute to the monarch’s prerogative of justice. During Constituent Assembly debates, H.V. Pataskar articulated this rationale, arguing that without a King to serve as a “fountainhead of all justice”, India needed an equivalent guardian of justice – therefore, conferring this unfettered discretionary power on the Supreme Court. Despite being a provision that was engineered as a last resort, SLPs have become one of the top contributors to the top court’s docket.

Consider how SLPs play out in practice – Sunil Kumar, an Assistant Engineer with the Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation, filed a petition before the Allahabad High Court in 2015 challenging criminal proceedings arising from a 2014 office altercation with a peon who was alleged to have tried to hit Kumar with a slipper, who in turn accused Kumar of threatening to kill him. The High Court dismissed the petition on 13 March 2018. Kumar then filed an SLP before the Supreme Court even though the matter did not raise a substantial constitutional issue. The Court granted leave and allowed the appeal in 2023, nine years after the incident – itself calling the allegations “trivial”. Multiply this by numerous similar petitions each year, and the scale of this access becomes clear.

Other apex courts filter far more aggressively. The US Supreme Court hears roughly 70 – 80 of several thousand petitions filed per year and the UK Supreme Court granted only 45 out of 207 permission to appeal applications in 2025-26, while India sends several thousand cases to full hearing every year.
How can the Supreme Court introduce some balance?

The answer is not to close the doors to a constitutional remedy the framers deliberately included, but to stop this accessibility from turning India’s highest court into an all-purpose court of appeal by building clear filters and differentiators for the kind of disputes that warrant it. Proposals over several decades have made attempts to separate the Supreme Court’s constitutional function from its appellate jurisdiction, or create regional division. But these are only addressing the symptoms and not the underlying problem, namely, that too many appeals of the SLP variety are being accepted by the Supreme Court of India.

One line of reform, that is not much explored, focuses on tightening what makes it to the court’s docket in the first place by developing a well-defined threshold. The court foresaw this challenge as early as 2010, when a judgment warned that without broad guidelines on when an SLP ought to be entertained, “the functioning of the court will become impossible” and referred the question to a constitution bench. But when a separate Constitution Bench took up the matter, it refused to restrict the court’s power, holding that doing so would work against the interests of justice.
A codified filter has real potential to reduce the apex court’s docket burden, but it would also formally narrow the court’s own conception of what justice delivery means.

Many SLPs are admitted not because they raise a substantial legal question, but because the court perceives that they would be better able to correct an individual injustice than the lower court could. It is clear, therefore, that the difficulty has not been a lack of recognition that the Supreme Court is carrying functions that are difficult to sustain, but the absence of agreement on how to reorganise or limit those functions effectively.
This unresolved question is becoming increasingly difficult to avoid. If we must preserve broad access to the Supreme Court we need to rethink what 38 judges are being asked to do.
Laveesh Bhandari is President and Senior Fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP), formerly Brookings India.
Shagun Suryam is a Research Analyst with CSEP in the President’s office. She holds a Masters in Public Administration from the Wagner School at New York University (NYU).

title: Kochi road rage case: When are parents liable for driving offences by minors?

content.value: Early on Sunday (October 25), a car allegedly driven by a 17-year-old minor in Keralam’s Ernakulam district rammed into a two-wheeler from behind, killing its 57-year-old rider. The road rage case involving the minor, the son of an additional district judge, has brought into focus the issue of fixing the culpability of the guardian or the vehicle owner in juvenile driving cases.

The judge was booked under Section 199A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and is slated to face prosecution. Here’s what the law says while determining that the vehicle owner shall be deemed to be guilty.
Section 199A: ‘Vicarious responsibility’ of vehicle owner

Section 199A of the Act was enacted by the Union government through the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Bill, 2019, for fixing culpability on guardian/owner of the vehicle driven by a minor. Accordingly, the guardian/vehicle owner shall be deemed to be guilty with an imprisonment of three years and a fine of Rs 25,000. Besides, the juvenile would be tried under the Juvenile Justice Act (JJ Act), 2015, and the registration of the motor vehicle would be cancelled.

The commission of an offence under the MV Act by the juvenile is an essential ingredient of the aforesaid section. Offence against the vehicle owner under the MV Act will be attracted only if a juvenile is charged for either of the following offences: driving without licence under Section 181(3), driving in violation of age requirement under Section 181(4), or dangerous driving under Section 184.
In the absence of such a prosecution, the proceedings against the owner do not stand legal scrutiny.

Police have to record the offence of the juvenile in the general diary of the station. Along with that, a social background report (SBR) about the minor should be filed before the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) about the minor’s offence under the MV Act. Only then can prosecution be initiated against the guardian of a juvenile or owner of a motor vehicle under Section 199A.

Section 17 of the JJ Act deals with orders regarding a child not found to be in conflict with law. If the JJB comes to the conclusion under Section 17 of the JJ Act that the juvenile has not committed the offence, the proceedings against the guardian or owner under section 199A of the MV Act cannot continue thereafter and the accused will have to be acquitted or discharged.
What happens in most cases

Documents show that the Kerala High Court had quashed several prosecution proceedings against vehicle owners/guardians who were charge-sheeted under Section 199A of the MV Act after their minor wards were caught. The main reason was that the police booked owners/guardians but failed to report the matter before the JJB that an offence under section 181 of the MV Act had been committed by the minor. Another factor is the police failure to file the SBR before the JJB within the stipulated time.

In a 2024 landmark verdict, while considering a bunch of 64 petitions challenging the invoking of Section 199A, the High Court bench of Justice Bechu Kurian Thomas had held that Section 199A creates an independent offence against the guardian or owner. Although commission of an MV Act offence by the juvenile remains an essential ingredient, a prior finding by the JJB under Sections 17 or 18 (which outlines the orders that the JJB can pass after concluding that a child in conflict with the law has committed an offence) of the JJ Act is not a prerequisite to initiating prosecution under Section 199A.

At the same time, this verdict also said the guardian’s liability hinges on the outcome of the minor’s case in the JJB. If the juvenile’s proceedings are terminated under Section 14(4) — which governs the termination and extension of inquiries by the JJB — or the JJB finds under Section 17 that the juvenile did not commit the offence, the case against the guardian or vehicle owner cannot continue.
How Kochi road rage case is important

The Kochi case is going to be significant on many grounds. If most of the driving incidents involving minors were mainly related to offences such as driving without a valid licence or rash/negligent driving or driving before attaining the mandatory age, the 17-year-old in the Kochi case also faces the non-bailable offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). Besides, he faces Sections 181 and 184 of the MV Act.

Under the JJ Act, there are three types of crimes: petty offences (maximum imprisonment of three years), serious offences (imprisonment up to seven years), and heinous offences (minimum imprisonment of seven years or more). The case will be open to a legal battle, as the Supreme Court in 2020 had observed that a minor charged under Section 304 of the erstwhile Indian Penal Code (equivalent to Section 105 of the BNS) in a road accident case could not be considered as having committed a heinous offence and could not be tried as an adult.

title: Ballot papers in Indian elections: Where are they still used, and why

content.value: With the Congress on Wednesday (October 28) winning just one of the 28 Member of Legislative Council (MLC) seats that went to the polls across the country, Prime Minister Narendra Modi took a swipe at the party. This is because MLC elections are held on ballot papers rather than through electronic voting machines (EVMs), which the Congress has in the past blamed for losses. MLCs are elected in a handful of states in India that have a second legislative House.
Since the PM’s remarks have brought the spotlight back to the EVMs-vs-ballot-papers debate, it’s instructive to see which sets of elections in India are conducted with ballot papers.
Which elections in India use ballot papers?

Most elections to Gram Panchayats, Panchayat Samitis, and Zilla Parishads are held through ballot papers. In a 2023 study sponsored by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj and undertaken by the Indian Institute of Public Administration (IIPA), the report said that “53 percent of the States conduct gram panchayat elections by adopting the ballot paper as a mode of casting vote”.

“Only three States/UTs (Kerala, Sikkim, and Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu) conduct gram panchayat elections through ÉVMs in all constituencies of the gram panchayat. However, other States are in a transitional phase wherein 22 percent of the States have adopted EVMs in some of the constituencies while in the rest of the constituencies, ballot papers are still followed,” the report added. “However, in the higher levels of panchayat elections, i.e., intermediate and district panchayats, the share of EVMs used by States increases. For instance, in district/zilla panchayat elections, 17 percent of States use EVMs in all the constituencies.”

The report also said, “States which are using ballot papers hinted that lack of funds and awareness about the usage of EVM is one of the major hindrances in conducting panchayat elections. But the same voters cast their vote using EVMs in the assembly and the parliamentary elections; so this argument of lack of awareness among the voters is lopsided.” It added that counting of ballot papers was a cumbersome process requiring huge manpower, adding that it was also not environmentally friendly.

Former elected sarpanch from Chandrapur in Maharashtra Kalyan Kumar said that the tehsildars provide symbols to candidates days before the elections in rural local bodies. “They ask for three options and allot one of these. These are not the party symbols we know.” According to him, how much in touch a candidate is with his electors and whether he helps them get everyday work done is more crucial than ideology in these polls, and success shows connection with voters more than anything else.

Describing the process of elections to rural local bodies, a Bihar official told The Indian Express on condition of anonymity that multiple elections at Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samitis, etc., happen at around the same time, and this makes ballot papers more handy because using so many machines would be difficult. However, he agreed that counting becomes cumbersome wherever ballot papers are used.
