Regarding how some states conduct Panchayat elections with EVMs if the symbols are not the conventional party symbols, former Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa told The Indian Express that there is a procedure called “symbol loading” that is used to load the required symbols onto the EVMs.

Regarding municipal corporations, Lavasa said that these elections lie within the purview of the State Election Commissions, and they can decide to use EVMs or ballot papers. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi elections, for instance, are conducted via EVMs, but Punjab decided to shift to ballot papers in 2026. The Punjab and Haryana High Court said that the Punjab Municipal Election Rules, 1994, allowed both ballot papers and EVMs, legally permitting the SEC to choose either of them.

Student union elections are also held either using EVMs or ballot papers. The Delhi University Students’ Union polls, for instance, use EVMs. “The EVMs display the names of the candidates in alphabetical order. Here, the name and the ballot number of the candidate is important,” said Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad national media convener Harsh Attri. The Jawaharlal Nehru University Students’ Union elections, however, use ballot papers.
Single, transferable vote

Elections held via a single transferable vote, however, have to use ballot papers. As per Article 171 of the Indian Constitution, elections to the legislative councils are held through a single, transferable vote. In this procedure, the voters have to mark their first, second, etc., preferences on the ballot paper, so that the vote is transferable. This happens on a ballot paper rather than an EVM.

Rajya Sabha elections also happen by a single transferable vote, where preferences are marked by the elector on a ballot paper. A formula is used here to calculate the quota required for a candidate to win. The total number of MLAs voting in a state is divided by the number of seats going for elections plus 1. Then, 1 is added to the resulting number to calculate the quota. Let’s understand this with the help of an example.

Say, the total number of MLAs voting in a state is 200 and elections are on for four seats. In that case, 200 will be divided by 4+1, or 5, which will result in a figure of 40. The quota thus will be 40+1, or 41. Any candidate getting 41 votes will be declared elected.
The system followed, however, is that of a single transferable vote. So, MLAs who vote — there is an open ballot in Rajya Sabha polls — can mark their first, second, third, etc. preferences.

In the above example, every candidate getting 41 first preference votes will be declared elected. If this does not fill all the seats, the surplus votes of those already elected are transferred to the second preference candidates of MLAs whose first preferences have already won.

Going back to the above example where 41 is the winning quota: If a winning candidate secures 45 votes, this would mean this candidate has four surplus votes. These four surplus votes will be moved to the second preference candidates.

If more than one victorious candidate has surplus votes, the largest surplus will be transferred first. If even this does not fill all vacancies, the candidate with the lowest number of first preference votes is eliminated, and the second preference votes in their ballot paper are transferred.
This process goes on until all seats are filled.

title: Why can’t satellite collars live-track cheetahs? Kuno director explains

content.value: Satellite collars fitted on cheetahs are not a live telecast and cannot provide continuous live tracking, Kuno National Park Director Uttam Kumar Sharma said – remarks that come as officials face the heat over lapses in monitoring following the death of a 19-month-old cheetah.

The explanation comes as the state government has suspended six forest department officials in connection with the death of KNG22, a male cheetah who was found seriously injured in the Sheopur territorial forest division on October 25 and died during treatment at the veterinary facility of Nanaji Deshmukh Veterinary Science University in Jabalpur on October 27.

The cheetah, an offspring of Nirva — a six-year-old female South African cheetah that is part of India’s Project Cheetah at Kuno — was found with multiple foreign bodies lodged in his body. Five firearm pellets were recovered during emergency surgery.

In his note recently written, Kuno director Uttam Kumar Sharma sought to explain the limitations of satellite-based wildlife monitoring, saying that a satellite location only provides the geographical position of an animal at a particular point in time. By the time the information reaches the monitoring team and personnel reach the reported location, the animal may have moved several kilometres away.
“Therefore, let us get rid of the misconception that a satellite-collared animal is available for continuous live tracking, like a live television broadcast,” Sharma wrote.

At Kuno, monitoring teams track around 15 cheetahs through a combination of satellite collars and radio receivers. Satellite collars provide location information over large and often inaccessible areas, while VHF equipment is used by field teams to locate animals more precisely on the ground.

The collars are generally programmed to transmit location information at six-hour intervals. Sharma said this frequency was chosen to maintain a balance between obtaining location information and ensuring the battery lasts sufficiently long.

However, if a scheduled transmission is missed for any reason, the gap between two location updates increases. If one update is missed, the gap can increase to 12 hours. If the next one is also missed, it can extend to 18 hours.

Sharma said satellite collars were expensive, generally costing around Rs 4-5 lakh each, and the frequency of transmission had to be determined by balancing monitoring requirements, battery life and the expected duration of collar use.

A temporary loss of satellite signal, he said, was not an unusual occurrence and could happen for several reasons. Dense forest canopy can interfere with the collar’s ability to obtain an accurate GPS location, while rocky terrain, caves and deep valleys may obstruct satellite visibility.

Temporary signal interference or poor satellite geometry can also affect location acquisition or transmission. An animal resting under dense vegetation, near water or in an area with poor satellite reception may not transmit its location at the scheduled time.

A missing location, therefore, does not necessarily indicate that a collar has malfunctioned or that something has happened to the animal. Sometimes, the collar simply cannot obtain or transmit a location at the scheduled time, and monitoring teams have to wait for the next successful transmission.
Why tracking cheetahs across Kuno’s terrain is difficult
Sharma said the limitations of satellite tracking were particularly significant at Kuno because of the extensive movement of cheetahs across the landscape.

Cheetahs are highly mobile animals and move an average of 6-8 kilometres a day. On many occasions, they cover 12-15 kilometres or even more, with their movements often concentrated during the early morning and late evening hours.

This means that by the time a monitoring team reaches the last reported satellite location, the animal may have moved several kilometres away and could have gone outside the team’s VHF radio range. “If the scheduled satellite transmission is also missed, the only option is to wait for the next successful location fix,” Sharma wrote.
Once a new location is received, the team moves towards that point and attempts to bring the animal back within VHF radio range.

Following a cheetah on foot is extremely difficult, while vehicles cannot move through forests in straight lines, as animals do. The actual distance covered by a monitoring vehicle can be several times the straight-line distance between two locations.
Moving on foot through dense forests in poor light also carries its own risks.

“Consequently, keeping an animal within visual or radio-tracking range throughout the day is an extremely demanding task. It requires continuous coordination, patience, technical understanding and tremendous physical effort from the monitoring teams,” Sharma wrote.
He said these challenges were part of the daily monitoring experience at Kuno and were not occasional or exceptional situations.

KNG22 was found injured in compartment No. 748 of the Sheopur Territorial Forest Division, near the Morena district border, on October 25. He was rescued and brought to Kuno for an initial medical examination before being shifted to Jabalpur for advanced treatment.

An X-ray revealed multiple foreign bodies at different locations in his body. A subsequent CT scan showed damage to his internal organs, musculoskeletal system and nervous system. Five firearm pellets were recovered during emergency surgery, but the cheetah could not be saved.

The state government has constituted a Special Task Force comprising forest and police officers to investigate the incident. Six forest department officials have been suspended in connection with the case.

title: How 2 major summits this week point to balance & bargain strategy in big-power diplomacy

content.value: Next week’s two summits are unlikely to set the world on fire. On Tuesday (November 17), the Quad leaders of Australia, India, Japan and the United States meet in Manila. On Thursday (November 19), Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping meet in Shenzhen. Taken together, they illuminate the rapidly changing nature of great-power politics: every major power is balancing and bargaining at the same time — simultaneously building coalitions, hedging against volatile partners and negotiating with adversaries.
This is not a world for the faint-hearted or those seeking ideological clarity. It rewards leaders who can navigate international contradictions and manage them to strengthen national capabilities.

Tuesday’s meeting in Manila of the leaders of Australia, India, Japan and the United States promises to resurrect a forum widely presumed dead. Thursday’s meeting in Shenzhen between Trump, Putin and Xi could give birth to a new format for consultations among the world’s three leading powers.
The Quad’s agenda

The sequence is accidental but significant. Trump will meet America’s Asian partners before engaging the Chinese and Russian leaders. His preference might have been to focus on the latter, but the American establishment sees value in reassuring its allies. It also recognises that the Quad could strengthen Trump’s bargaining position with Xi and Putin.

Until recently, many had written off the Quad. The obituaries were premature. Ministerial consultations and practical cooperation continued despite the absence of summit-level engagement. Manila has an interesting place in the Quad’s history. The forum first met there in 2007. After becoming moribund, it was revived in Manila in 2017. Nearly a decade later, Manila is once again the setting for its renewal.

The proposed agenda is practical: critical minerals, resilient supply chains, energy security and the protection of commercial shipping. Maritime security, emerging technologies and strategic infrastructure remain important areas of cooperation.
Why G-3 is not quite a new Yalta

If Manila is renewing an established forum, Shenzhen is about launching a new one. The prospect of the American, Russian and Chinese presidents sitting together has revived speculation about a “new Yalta”, recalling the 1945 meeting of American, British and Soviet leaders that helped shape the post-war European order.

But the historical analogy has limits. Yalta followed intensive cooperation among the Allies in defeating Nazi Germany. Trump, Putin and Xi are meeting amid expanding rivalry, with little agreement on the rules of the international order. Their immediate objective is to explore common ground rather than negotiate a grand geopolitical bargain.

Unsurprisingly, there is little clarity about the G-3 agenda. Nuclear arms control and cooperation in managing conflicts involving Iran and Ukraine are among the possibilities. Regulating artificial intelligence could be another. For Trump, the meeting reflects his faith in personal diplomacy and his ability to strike grand bargains. But much of the American foreign policy establishment remains sceptical of his approach to Putin and Xi. Any major concession by Trump to Russia and China with produce a vigorous American backlash.

For Putin, Shenzhen offers recognition of Russia’s enduring place at the global high table. Xi’s priorities are different. For Xi, trade, technology and strategic competition with Washington matter more than creating a trilateral institution. Yet Xi has little reason to reject a meeting that pleases Putin while consolidating Beijing’s status as the critical element of a global “triumvirate”.
The relevance for India

For India, the Quad’s revival offers an opportunity to reboot its troubled relations with Washington. But as part of the hedge against American unpredictability, Delhi will continue to deepen cooperation with Europe, Russia and Japan while seeking to manage the structural tensions with China.

Critics at home and abroad have often derided India’s foreign policy as excessively transactional, especially its attempt to ride several horses, including BRICS and the Quad. But the new reality is that the great powers are doing much the same— balancing and bargaining. That is now baked into the international dynamic today.

Russia is a vociferous critic of America, but it seeks accommodation with Trump. China wants to reduce American influence in Asia but also seeks recognition as Washington’s equal. Neither sees a contradiction in pursuing apparently competing objectives.

For India, strategic flexibility can’t be an end in itself. An open-ended foreign policy, strong international partnerships must go hand in hand with the purposeful modernisation and upgradation of national capabilities. Without domestic unity and strength, India’s multi-alignment runs the risk of remaining trapped in intellectual abstraction rather than becoming a transformative tool towards advancing national interest.

(C. Raja Mohan is a contributing editor on International affairs for the Indian Express. He is professor and director at the Motwani-Jadeja Institute of American Studies, Jindal Global University, Delhi).

title: Karakoram-2026: How China and Pakistan are deepening military ties — and what it means for India

content.value: China and Pakistan’s longstanding partnership, while not a formal alliance, has emerged as a defining feature of the regional security architecture.
Over the years, their military cooperation has deepened, moving beyond defence acquisitions and joint exercises towards greater functional integration and interoperability.

In this context, the countries’ recently concluded joint exercise, Karakoram-2026, marked a significant milestone — it involved the participation of regular army formations from both countries. Notably, the exercise was conducted in Xinjiang, which borders Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.
Why the Karakoram-2026 exercise matters
Karakoram-2026, held from October 14-22 in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, was the first joint-army level exercise between People’s Liberation Army (PLA) and Pakistan Army.

It expanded on the earlier naval, air and counterterrorism exercises (Sea Guardian, Warrior and Shaheen series). The focus was on challenging high-altitude operations, relevant to the PLA’s Western Theatre Command which oversees the border with India.

Phase One of the exercise, up to October 19, involved troops from both sides practicing specialised tactics, close-quarter combat and unmanned aerial vehicle (or drone) operations. Phase Two entailed joint command, mixed formations and combat teams undertaking counterterrorism clearance operations, joint manoeuvres and coordinated fire drills.

The equipment used was Chinese, including small arms, armoured assault vehicles, infantry fighting vehicles and support systems, such as artillery, drones and anti-manned systems. The Chinese Ministry of National Defence described Karakoram-2026 as an opportunity to deepen cooperation and tactical integration between the two armies.
The China-Pakistan Nexus: Its genesis and core pillars

The China-Pakistan nexus refers to the longstanding strategic, economic and military partnership between the two countries. It dates to the 1963 Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement under which Pakistan ceded the Shakasgam Valley, part of Gilgit-Baltistan, to China, thus cementing the strategic alignment.

The subsequent decades witnessed China’s growing role in building Pakistan’s nuclear and missile programme which altered the regional strategic balance and security dynamics, primarily hedging against India. Today, China treats Pakistan a strategic priority, central to its South Asia policy.
The core pillars of China-Pakistan nexus are:
Expanding architecture of military cooperation
The Karakoram-2026 exercise must be viewed against the expanding profile of the China-Pakistan defence cooperation — from a buyer-supplier arrangement towards deeper military integration.

It follows a joint patrol conducted by Chinese and Pakistan security personnel at Mantika Pass, at an altitude of 4,700 metres (near Khunjrerab Pass), in the upper Hunza area of Gilgit-Baltistan, reflecting the operationalisation of the border management mechanism and a growing institutional engagement.

In May 2025, when India launched aerial strikes (Operation Sindoor) targeting terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan, the collusion between Beijing and Islamabad came into sharp focus. There was strong evidence that China accelerated the deliveries of PL-15 E air-to-air missiles, air defence and electronic platforms into Pakistan’s military structure during the crisis.

Lt Gen A S Chaudhary, Director General of Pakistan’s Inter-Services Public Relations, had claimed in an interview with Bloomberg that China-made weapon systems performed extremely well during the four-day conflict with India.

The change of government in Bangladesh also adds a new dimension to defence and diplomatic ties in the region. Islamabad, Dhaka and Beijing may not have formed a strategic trilateral, but they are leveraging the China-Pakistan strategic framework.

Bangladesh has advanced plans to purchase J-10CE fighter jets from China and its pilots will be trained by Pakistan at Jessore airbase, near the Siliguri corridor. There are also discussions regarding integration of air defence radar systems and upgrading Bangladesh tank fleet with Chinese technology and Pakistani expertise. High-level exchanges between the Pakistani and Bangladesh militaries are a distinct departure from the past isolation.
Strategic implications

Karakoram-2026 takes the China-Pakistan relationship a step further. Beyond equipment familiarisation, the joint training facilitates the exchange of operational experience, standardisation of procedures, command and control coordination and interoperability. Incidentally, there are intelligence reports that Pakistan Army officers are posted in key Chinese military formations in the PLA’s Western Theatre Command and Joint Staff Department of the Central Military Commission (CMC).

The significance of Karakoram-2026 lies in the changing character of the China-Pakistan military cooperation. The joint training of mixed formations, growing integration of the Chinese platforms into Pakistan’s military inventory and increasing military engagement in the Xinjiang-Karakoram region have critical strategic significance. India needs to closely monitor the evolving China-Pakistan military relationship, both as an integrated two-front challenge and in the larger regional context.

The expanding China-Pakistan nexus, therefore, compounds India’s security threat on the Northern border. For Delhi, the challenge is no longer just to contend with two adversarial neighbours but to prepare for the strategic consequences with a coherent national security strategy that addresses the convergence of Chinese and Pakistani military capabilities.
The author is a war veteran, former Assistant Chief of Integrated Defence Staff, and served as Defence Attache in China. He is currently professor at Lal Bahadur Shastri Institute of Management.

title: Expert Explains | COP31: What’s at stake at UN climate summit in Antalya

content.value: Written by Indu K Murthy

Starting Monday (November 9), the next chapter of global climate action will unfold in Turkey at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) until November 20, with about 100,000 participants and heads of state gathering for a World Leaders’ Summit on November 11 and 12.

As the first COP since the United States’ exit from the Paris Agreement earlier this year, COP31 removes the largest historical emitter from finance conversations, sharpening developing countries’ demand that Europe and others fill the gap. Energy security, meanwhile, has taken centre stage. The war on Iran has pushed up oil and gas prices, raising the cost of fuel and food. Supporters of a faster energy transition argue that this shows the risks of fossil-fuel dependence, while importers such as India face more immediate pressure to keep supplies affordable.

The questions that matter are how much finance will actually flow to developing countries, how adaptation will be measured and paid for, and whether mounting pressure on coal and emission targets will respect the principle of “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities” (CBDR-RC).
What is a COP?

A COP is the annual meeting of countries that signed the 1992 UNFCCC. In Antalya, there will be three meetings in focus: COP31, the 21st session of the Conference of Parties serving as the meeting of Parties to the Kyoto Protocol (CMP21), and the 8th session of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of Parties to the 2015 Paris Agreement (CMA8).

The Paris Agreement asks every country to submit a nationally determined contribution (NDC), essentially its own climate plan, every five years, with the shared ambition of holding warming well below 2°C while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Because decisions require consensus, a single country can hold up an agreement.
How is COP31 different from previous COPs?

COP venues rotate among the UN’s regional groups, and 2026 was the turn of the “Western European and Others” group to host. Turkey bid with Antalya, and Australia bid with Adelaide, in partnership with Pacific Island nations.
The resulting standoff led to an unusual power-sharing deal last year, making COP31 the first summit where one country hosts the meeting while another runs the negotiations.

Turkey is the formal COP31 president and host, responsible for the venue, logistics, and the “Action Agenda” of voluntary pledges and initiatives, whereas Australia has “exclusive authority” over formal talks, drafting of texts, and steering decisions. This dual leadership model is untested, and questions remain about who would have the final word if there were disagreement in the closing hours.
What’s on the table?
COP31 is not expected to produce a landmark treaty text. The real fight is over delivery: mobilising finance, measuring progress, and accelerating the energy shift.

In terms of co-chairing consultations, India and Germany must decide on mitigation, as in how to press countries whose 2035 plans fall short of 1.5°C and what “transitioning away from fossil fuels” actually requires. On finance, France and the Philippines will work to build consensus on delivering existing finance commitments. On adaptation, the UK and Sierra Leone must chart a credible path to tripling adaptation finance and make enough headway for the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) to be finalised at COP32.

Taking on newer ground, Mexico and Poland must work out how the just transition mechanism will function and what money and technical help it will give affected workers and communities. Palau and Canada handle the ocean, where Pacific Island countries want commitments written into formal decisions.

Two more items will set the summit’s tone. Turkey wants countries to pledge to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use from about 23% today to 35% by 2035. Further, developing countries, including India, have pushed to include Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, the clause that obligates developed countries to provide finance, in the provisional agenda.
What Belém left behind

The COP30 in Belém, Brazil, closed with a package called the “Global Mutirão” (meaning, collective effort) and Antalya inherits this “to-do” list. It called for adaptation finance to be at least tripled by 2035, five years later than developing countries had wanted and without a clear baseline.

More broadly, it endorsed the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap to scale climate finance for developing countries to at least $1.3 trillion a year by 2035 from public and private sources, building on the $300 billion-a-year goal agreed at COP29 in Baku (Azerbaijan). It adopted a set of “Belém indicators” to measure progress on the GGA, created new vehicles for delivery, namely a Global Implementation Accelerator and a “Belém Mission to 1.5” to help countries carry out their plans, alongside work on a just transition mechanism.

The most conspicuous gap concerned fossil fuels. More than 80 countries backed a roadmap to move away from oil, coal, and gas, yet the final text left fossil fuels out entirely, referring only to the 2023 Dubai “UAE Consensus”. Brazil is now steering a voluntary roadmap process outside the formal talks, and Colombia and the Netherlands have initiated the Santa Marta process — an international, plurilateral climate initiative complementing the COP process launched in Santa Marta, Colombia — in April 2026 to identify pathways for the phase-out.
Where does India stand on its climate goals?
India goes to Antalya with a new climate plan and a central seat at the table, co-chairing mitigation consultations. India’s third NDC, covering 2031-2035, was approved and submitted in April.

The new plan raises the target for reducing the emission intensity of gross domestic product (GDP) to 47% below 2005 levels by 2035, up from 45% by 2030. Emission intensity of GDP, which measures the volume of greenhouse gases (usually carbon dioxide, or CO2, equivalent) emitted for each unit of economic output or GDP, acts as a key indicator of how carbon-efficient an economy is as it grows.

The plan increases the non-fossil share of installed power capacity from 50% by 2030 (already met) to 60% by 2035 and expands the promised additional carbon sink from forest and tree cover from 2.5-3.0 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent to 3.5-4.0 billion tonnes. A carbon sink refers to any natural or artificial system that absorbs more CO2 from the atmosphere than it releases, helping reduce the greenhouse gases responsible for global warming.

The NDC, however, ties any further ambition to “new and additional” finance and technology from developed countries. This conditionality runs through India’s negotiating line, which Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Bhupender Yadav set out at the Pre-COP in Fiji last month (October 5-8, 2026).

Yadav called for equal weight to be given to adaptation; mitigation; and the “means of implementation”, that is, finance, technology, and capacity-building. He insisted that the principle of CBDR-RC be upheld “in letter and spirit”, with no one-size-fits-all pathway imposed on countries. He backed the Article 9.1 finance discussion and argued that success should be measured by delivery on existing commitments rather than by new targets or declarations.
COP31: What to watch out for
Five questions will determine how Antalya is remembered.

The first is finance, and whether developed countries put numbers and a timeline behind tripling adaptation finance and give the $1.3 trillion roadmap a monitoring system.
The second is fossil fuels, and whether the negotiated text will include a transition away from them.
The third is Turkey’s electrification pledge, specifically how many countries sign on to the 35%-by-2035 target.
The fourth is the split presidency itself — the real stress test of a model that future COPs may copy.
The fifth is the Global South bargain, and whether India and other developing countries secure the Article 9.1 discussion and reforms to finance access in return for engaging on mitigation.
Ultimately, Antalya will be judged less on headline pledges and more on whether the promises of Paris, Baku, and Belém translate into meaningful action.
The author heads the climate, environment and sustainability sector at the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP), a research-based think tank.

title: An expert explains why fixing India’s air pollution crisis needs more than technical solutions

content.value: Air pollution is often discussed as if it were primarily a problem of Delhi NCR and winters, but much of India experiences unhealthy air throughout the year, both outdoors and indoors.

North India faces particularly severe outdoor pollution episodes because of numerous emission sources and unfavourable winter meteorology. And every winter, experts are called upon to decode these phenomena — atmospheric scientists explain the meteorology, engineers discuss pollution control, and doctors warn about health impacts.

After over a decade of the problem visibly worsening, it is worth examining how this knowledge has helped understand the situation, the limitations of the current approach, and the kind of information and scientific research that are still required.
The problems and solutions are not particularly mysterious

The sources of air pollution are known by now — fireworks and agricultural residue burning contribute during specific periods, while solid fuels such as firewood, dung cakes, and even waste are burnt for heating in colder months. Transport, polluting household fuels, waste burning, industry, power plants, and construction contribute year-round. Weather affects how emissions disperse and accumulate; it does not create them.
The major sources of pollution are well established, and we do not need to quantify every source precisely or measure every exposure before acting.

Fundamentally, reducing air pollution requires two clear actions: reducing the number of emitting sources and reducing emissions from those that remain. This means reliable public transport and less dependence on private vehicles, access to clean cooking and heating, viable alternatives to crop residue burning, functioning municipal waste management, and effective industrial regulation.

Stubble burning and firecrackers receive considerable attention during particular periods, but even addressing these requires looking beyond the immediate pollution episode and avoiding purely technological fixes.

Agricultural residue burning cannot be addressed without understanding farming practices, farmers’ economic constraints, and the availability of alternatives. Similarly, reducing pollution from firecrackers requires not only restrictions and enforcement, but also changing social attitudes, with schools, communities, and religious and spiritual leaders playing a role.
Neither problem can be solved by atmospheric scientists or enforcement agencies alone.
The relevance of scientific research

Uncertainties about source contributions, emission inventories, and atmospheric chemistry will always remain, to an extent, and sustained investment in science and monitoring remains essential. Our understanding of air pollution is indeed shaped by what we measure. Monitoring networks, emission inventories, and source apportionment studies help identify pollution sources for targeted policies.

It must also be noted that what we measure in the ambient atmosphere is not necessarily what people breathe. For instance, a rooftop monitor or a model forecast does not tell us the particulate matter levels inside a home while someone cooks with solid fuels. For those households relying on solid fuel for cooking and heating, household air pollution remains a major part of daily exposure. It additionally contributes to outdoor air pollution.
But research should help refine interventions, not become a prerequisite for starting them. We do not need to know the precise contribution of every source before acting on those already identified.

We need greater attention to studying personal exposure, particularly among the most vulnerable sections of society, but these gaps should not obscure what we already know. The solutions we need are often not those for which we lack expertise; they are those that lack institutional attention, political commitment, and sustained investment.
The question of expertise

This brings us to a more fundamental question: who exactly is an air pollution expert? The obvious answers are atmospheric scientists studying aerosols and meteorology, engineers developing pollution controls, doctors treating respiratory disease, and epidemiologists studying long-term health impacts.

Recognition of expertise is also shaped by institutional affiliation. Scholars from IITs and AIIMS may command immediate recognition, while equally valuable knowledge from less prominent institutions and practitioners working on the ground often receives less attention.

What about the agricultural economists studying farmers’ incentives, urban planners shaping transport systems, social scientists examining household energy choices and public behaviour, municipal officials responsible for waste management, and public health experts translating scientific evidence into preventive interventions?

Expertise is often recognised most readily when it comes with a technological solution. A new device is visible and presented as innovation, often as a silver bullet for a complex problem. More long-term, institutional and procedural changes, such as improving public transport, managing waste, or ensuring access to clean household energy, are less spectacular. They require sustained funding, institutional capacity, coordination, and often confronting vested interests.

Technological spectacle also raises the question of who scrutinises the claims made by those offering solutions. Every winter, proposals for smog towers, artificial rain, and other interventions are presented with considerable fanfare, despite questions about their effectiveness and scale. Such projects can consume substantial public resources, create lucrative opportunities for entrepreneurs, and offer governments the optics of action without meaningfully reducing emissions.

We need independent scientific scrutiny, as well as journalists, regulators, and civil society willing to question how public money is spent. Expertise must go beyond simply proposing solutions, and involve interrogating them as well.

We should also consider those living and working with the highest pollution exposure: street vendors, construction workers, sanitation workers, farmers, communities alongside industrial facilities, and women who spend hours cooking with polluting fuels. Exposure is often shaped by the work people do and the choices available to them. For someone dependent on daily wages, earning a livelihood may take precedence over concerns about pollution.

Similarly, household cooking is often borne disproportionately by women, whose exposure is rarely reflected in ambient air quality measurements. Effective interventions must therefore consider safer working conditions, viable livelihood alternatives, access to clean household energy, and better economic opportunities.

As an atmospheric scientist, I would argue that we need more science, not less. Understanding the atmosphere, however, is not the same as understanding everything that makes it polluted. We must continue filling knowledge gaps without delaying action on what we already know. The priority must be to translate that knowledge into cleaner transport, energy, waste management, and effective regulation. The real test of expertise is not how spectacular a solution sounds, or how prestigious the institution linked to the expert proposing it is, but whether it helps make the air cleaner for everyone.
Shahzad Gani is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Atmospheric Sciences, IIT Delhi.

title: E20 petrol row: Why Karnataka’s allegations could reignite the ethanol blending debate

content.value: India’s ambitious ethanol-blending programme, which the Centre has presented as a key pillar of the country’s energy security and decarbonisation strategy, is under renewed scrutiny after the Congress-ruled Karnataka alleged that petrol being sold at some retail outlets in the state contained significantly more biofuel than the prescribed 20% limit.
The public sector oil marketing companies (OMCs) and the Centre have rejected Karnataka government’s claims.

The three OMCs — Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum, and Hindustan Petroleum — dismissed the allegations, saying that E20 petrol supplied across India conforms to Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) specifications, and questioned the sampling and testing procedures used by Karnataka authorities. They sought independent testing of the samples as per the prescribed methodology in the presence of their representatives.

Nonetheless, the controversy has revived questions about the quality of E20 petrol, its impact on vehicle performance, the transparency in fuel blending, and whether the country’s transition to higher ethanol-petrol blends has been detrimental to the interests of motorists.

The issue has also acquired a political dimension as after Karnataka’s claims, Kerala has also ordered its own tests on petrol being retailed in the state. The issue could potentially develop into a confrontation between the Centre and states — particularly the opposition-ruled ones — over the implementation of the national ethanol blending programme.

The controversy, which had died down in recent months, could now fester politically. The credibility of India’s ethanol blending programme will depend on convincing motorists that the fuel they are buying meets the prescribed quality standards.

India achieved 20% ethanol blending in petrol last year, five years ahead of the original deadline, and E20 petrol — 80 parts petrol and 20 parts ethanol — is now the standard petrol blend being retailed across India.

The past few months saw opposition over the E20 fuel from various quarters, with claims ranging from notable reduction in mileage and engine component wear in older vehicles whose engines were not designed for higher ethanol blends.

On its part, the government has been attempting to allay fears, saying that the drop in mileage in older vehicles would be 3-5% at most, and would be outweighed by E20’s benefits as it is a superior fuel. It has also consistently rejected claims that E20 fuel could damage engine components. Questions have also been raised on why motorists aren’t being offered the choice of lower ethanol-petrol blends.
Karnataka’s allegations on ethanol-petrol blending

The controversy erupted on November 6 when Karnataka’s food, civil supplies and consumer affairs minister Rizwan Arshad announced the findings of tests conducted by the state on petrol samples collected from seven districts.

According to the Karnataka government, 63 samples were collected and their testing found ethanol concentrations exceeding the prescribed 20% limit in several samples. A few of the samples contained over 30% ethanol, alleged the Karnataka government. It also said that nearly four out of five samples showed blending of over 20%.

According to the state government, the samples were initially sent to the Indian Oil and Bharat Petroleum laboratories, but they did not provide reports on the extent of ethanol content in the fuel. The state then approached private labs accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) and those certified by ISO.

The Karnataka government alleged that motorists were effectively paying for petrol while receiving fuel containing substantially higher proportions of ethanol. It also raised concerns about the possible consequences for vehicle performance, fuel efficiency, and maintenance. The state government has now demanded greater transparency in the disclosure of ethanol content, action against companies found violating fuel-quality standards, and compensation for consumers.

Following Karnataka’s allegations, the Congress-led government in Kerala last week ordered inspections at petrol pumps across four districts. The state’s food and civil supplies minister Anoop Jacob said samples were being collected and would be tested at accredited laboratories Karnataka has urged other states as well to conduct inspections and called for independent testing nationwide.
How have the oil companies and the Centre responded?

The OMCs have strongly rejected Karnataka’s allegations. In a joint statement on November 6, the OMCs said that the inspection by Karnataka was conducted in the absence of their representatives, and that they were not provided with the retained samples, complete laboratory reports or technical details needed to verify the findings.
They also questioned the testing methodology, arguing that the certificates cited by Karnataka do not establish compliance with prescribed BIS testing standards.

“In view of the concerns raised, the three OMCs have requested the Government of Karnataka to share the complete sampling documentation, outlet-wise laboratory reports and details of the test methodology adopted for the reported findings. They have also sought access to the counterpart samples for independent testing at an authorised laboratory using the prescribed referee method, in the presence of representatives of the State Government and OMCs,” they said.

The OMCs also cited a joint quality-monitoring exercise with the Centre for High Technology, in which all 893 samples tested across 27 states and union territories, including 56 from Karnataka, met the prescribed ethanol range of 19-21%. The Karnataka samples recorded an average ethanol content of 19.3%. They maintained that E20 petrol supplied across the country, including Karnataka, complied with the Bureau of Indian Standards’ IS 17021 specifications.

“These results demonstrate that ethanol blending at OMC retail outlets is monitored and controlled within the prescribed specifications. The findings are inconsistent with the substantially higher ethanol levels reported in the Karnataka press release and reinforce the need for a transparent, technically sound and jointly verifiable testing exercise,” the OMCs said.

According to the companies, ethanol blending at refineries and fuel depots is undertaken through calibrated and controlled systems, and the process involves automatic calibration and proportioning arrangements, with blending governed by prescribed specifications and quality-control protocols.

“It is not a manual or arbitrary process of adding ethanol to petrol. The OMCs maintain established quality-assurance systems across their supply and distribution networks to ensure that the blended fuel meets the applicable BIS specifications before it reaches consumers,” the companies said.

The very next day, the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MoPNG) backed the oil companies’ position by issuing a similarly-worded statement. It also said that any suggestion that the OMCs have a commercial incentive to undertake blending beyond the prescribed target is “misplaced”. Ethanol procurement involves a significant cost, and every additional litre blended beyond the prescribed proportion would add to the OMCs’ procurement costs, which means that the OMCs have no commercial rationale to undertake arbitrary or excess blending, it said.
E20 controversy so far

India’s ethanol programme is primarily driven by three objectives — reducing crude oil imports, improving energy security and creating an additional market for agricultural produce. India imports more than 88% of its crude oil requirements, leaving its economy vulnerable to international oil-price fluctuations and geopolitical disruptions.

Replacing a portion of petrol consumption with domestically produced ethanol helps reduce the requirement for imported crude and saves foreign exchange. Ethanol blending in petrol also provides sugar mills and agricultural producers with an additional market for sugarcane, maize and other feedstocks.

Ethanol blending of 20% was achieved in 2025, and E20 became the standard petrol variant across the country. Within three years, the average ethanol blending level in petrol in India doubled from 10% to 20%. For older vehicles and those certified for E10 petrol — 90 parts petrol and 10 parts ethanol — this transition came about rather quickly, without sufficient warnings of the consumer-end pitfalls. The experience left motorists, especially those owning older cars and two-wheelers, feeling short-changed.

Consequently, the past few months saw a public backlash over the E20 fuel, with motorists complaining about reduced mileage, while questions were raised about the suitability of higher ethanol blends for older vehicles and the costs of transitioning to compatible models.
The question of the lack of choice for consumers emerged as a key point in the debate, with some opposition leaders calling for E10 and even unblended petrol to be made available to consumers.

But the Centre and the OMCs have been vehemently rejecting claims pertaining to mileage and engine wear. They added that E20 offers a higher octane rating, superior anti-knock characteristics, cleaner combustion and smoother engine operation. Nonetheless, amid the backlash, the government announced any decision to raise the blending levels beyond 20% will be taken only after detailed studies and stakeholder consultations.

According to the government, extensive laboratory studies and field trials conducted by the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), society of Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM), Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), Indian Institute of Petroleum (IIP) and automobile manufacturers covering parameters such as engine durability, drivability, startability, corrosion resistance, material compatibility, emissions and fuel efficiency confirmed that E20 is safe for use under prescribed standards.

The Centre also said that offering multiple grades 0f base fuel across the country would create an “enormous logistical challenge”, apart from raising costs and reducing operational efficiencies in India’s complex fuel retail network.

It also said that the current base fuel E20 is cleaner and superior than pure petrol and lower ethanol-petrol blends, has required massive investments, and reverting to a lower blend level wouldn’t be prudent on various counts.

There were, however, indications that a rethink was on the table. An opinion piece co-authored by Chief Economic Adviser V Anantha Nageswaran, which appeared in The Indian Express in August, called for lower ethanol-petrol blend, say E10, to also be available alongside E20 fuel.
While the views expressed in the article were personal, this is the first instance of a high-ranking government official publicly calling for more petrol options to be made available.

title: Sensex surges, but what will it take for a sustained rally? An expert explains

content.value: A buoyant Sensex jumped nearly 2,100 points to end at 79,373.18 on Thursday amid a fall in crude  prices and hopes for a resolution to the Iran war following the US midterm drubbing for the Republicans.

Before this upsurge, however, the Sensex had traded around the 74,000 mark for around three years. A combination of factors weighed on sentiment — a weakening rupee, volatile crude oil prices, geopolitical tension, slowing growth and uncertainty over a trade deal with the US.

Sankaran Naren, Executive Director and Chief Investment Officer at ICICI Prudential AMC, spoke to Sandeep Singh, National Bureau Chief at The Indian Express, on October 27, about what was holding the markets back and what risks should investors be watching out for. Edited excerpts from the Explained.Live interview.
What was holding the markets back?
Three years back, the markets were overvalued. That could be part of the explanation. But there are multiple reasons holding back the market.
First, is the geopolitical problem — war in Ukraine and the Gulf, and record high crude oil prices.

Second, artificial intelligence-related growth has been very high in some countries: US, South Korea, Taiwan, Japan, etc. The growth rate there has been much higher than the growth rate that India can ever give. People have moved to these markets, particularly in the last two years.

And the third reason is that after March 2023, once the money started coming into equity mutual funds, three sets of investors started to sell. One is Indian promoters who have been launching IPO after IPO because they know that the markets are overvalued. The second is private equity companies which had invested pre-2023, which had realised that you can sell these stocks to Indian investors at a good price. And the third was multinationals who had set up businesses in India over the last 20, 30, 40 years. They realised that they should list in India because here you get valuations much higher than in your home country.
Despite the huge amount of money that we collected, all that money primarily went into these three sets of people’s pockets. And that is why markets have not delivered returns.
Weakening rupee, volatile oil prices, rising interest rates, slowing growth: What is your biggest worry?

I am worried about the impact of AI on India, whether it will be negative or positive. It is the most important long-term view because at some point of time the war will end and when the war ends, oil will come down. At some point of time, people will not have IPOs.
But AI can be a structural trend. And no one knows what the long-term impact of AI will be. People believe that fund managers can correctly guess the long-term impact, but we also don’t know.
There is a talk of India becoming a $20-trillion economy say two decades from now. Are the grounds ready for that?
In the services sector, there are no other countries which are competing with us. In manufacturing, there are multiple countries that are competing, including Vietnam and Thailand.
To win in manufacturing is not as easy as winning in services. Is India working to become better every year over the previous year? Yes. But the competition is intense.

I think we need to create manufacturing employment on a very very large scale. And that is the solution for growth to increase. And I’m sure that the government is well aware of this issue and will focus on it. But it is not as easy to create a global manufacturing hub in every area as it has been to create a global services hub.
Assuming that the US-Iran war ends, which sectors should investors look at to maximise their returns?

I think banking clearly will benefit a lot because the sector has been hurt by inflation and the rupee has been depreciating. Oil marketing companies should certainly benefit because they are the people who are bearing the brunt of the higher oil prices. If you look at areas like aviation for example, they are going to be benefited. But overall, we have started rate hikes and they may continue if oil is like this. But if the war ends and oil crashes, the requirement for the Reserve Bank of India to keep hiking interest rates also goes down. But we require a good fall in oil. A good fall in oil actually lubricates all parts of the economy, not just a few areas.
These are external factors. On the domestic front, what gives you comfort and what is challenging?
The current account deficit is under control, fiscal deficit is under control. Credit growth is booming. The automotive industry has been booming over the last year. Power demand has been booming.
Some of the challenges include a subpar monsoon. And there is always the worry that El Niño will create more problems.

There are things that any country can do… the RBI realised that it is important to get insurance deposits. So, they floated an FCNR scheme and collected $127 billion of deposits. That takes care of all near-term foreign exchange issues.
Having said that, the problem of the war, and the problem of what AI leads to in the future, will remain.

Amid these challenges, does asset allocation become much more important, given we don’t know how things are going to shape, and how long the challenges will continue given the nature of them being external rather than internal?

Indians have got this love for equity at this point of time. And equity is inherently not a riskless asset class. That’s why if people start practising asset allocation, they will view volatility as an opportunity and not worry so much. But, if you are only invested in equity or you take positions in derivative markets on leverage, then you are very worried about everything that is happening.
Many investors have 15-20 schemes in their portfolio. Can you simplify and tell us three classes of schemes that investors must possess at all times?

I am of the view that if you create three categories — balanced advantage, balanced hybrid, and flexi cap — you would have covered substantially. Then you don’t need to worry day-to-day about what’s happening in the market. You just keep investing in these categories and keep saving and keeping put money in these three categories because our broad approach is very clear.
Can you take our readers through these categories briefly?

Balanced advantage is a very simple model: As the market goes up, you keep selling, and as the market goes down, you keep buying. So in 2023-24 when the market was more overvalued, it had less exposure to equity and higher exposure to debt and arbitrage. Today, because equity has become more fairly valued, it has a higher exposure to equity and a lower exposure to arbitrage and debt.

If you look at balanced hybrids, it’s even more simple. It says you can invest between 40% and 60% in debt, and 40% and 60% in equity. It is the quintessential asset allocation product where you’re choosing two products, and both the products have to be between 40% and 60%.

The third category is called “flexi” cap because you can invest in all kinds of things. You can invest in large cap, mid cap, small cap, micro cap and, therefore, you are entirely investing in the entire equity market. So we call it the most unconstrained fund.
For people who need gold, I would say multi-asset is the fourth category.
What’s your advice for retail investors?

For the first 10 years of people’s investing career, they should choose mutual funds so that they go through one cycle. They understand what is investing through balanced advantage or multi asset or flexi cap. After 10 years of investing, if you have learned quite a lot, then you do direct equity. And if you become an expert after 20, 30 years, you do derivatives.

But unfortunately, when we talk to stockbrokers, they say it is 25 to 30-year-olds who are actually trading derivatives. I do not know whether they have the knowledge and the temperament to handle it well.
Reader questions
Countries which have AI on their side, like the US, their markets are doing much better. Would you suggest that we try to invest in foreign markets?

Any market which is exuberant and where valuations are high is actually a riskier market. So, at this point of time we tell people to be careful if you are investing in the Nasdaq index because it is the best performing index in the world in the last 10 years.
I am currently investing in mutual funds. My SIP is around Rs 25,000 a month. Should I stop it because for the past 2 years, whatever I have invested giving negative returns?

We tell people to start a SIP in flexi cap category or balanced advantage category or multi-asset category. Forget closing, we tell people to add now. That is our view. Actually, that is what we have been trying to promote at this point of time. So, I think you know, for the best benefit of SIP, you actually have to invest when the markets are down.

title: 10 years after demonetisation, cash remains king despite India’s digital payments boom

content.value: Ten years ago, on November 8, the Modi government announced the demonetisation of high-value currency notes of Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 in a dramatic bid to curb black money and push India towards a cashless economy. A decade later, however, cash remains king, with currency held by the public having more than doubled since demonetisation.

Currency with the public, which stood at Rs 17.97 lakh crore on November 4, 2016, plunged to Rs 7.8 lakh crore in January 2017 following the November 8 announcement. It has since surged to Rs 42.55 lakh crore as of October 15, 2026, according to Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data, an increase of nearly 137 per cent over its pre-demonetisation level.

Though digital payments have jumped manifold, high cash holdings raise questions about the lasting impact of demonetisation on India’s dependence on physical currency. While the economy has expanded considerably over the past decade, growing at 6-7 per cent annually in several years, the currency-to-GDP ratio has also returned to around its pre-demonetisation level. In other words, despite the massive push towards digital payments and formalisation, cash has not been driven out of the economy. Instead, its circulation has recovered alongside economic growth.
The big announcement

Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced demonetisation at 8 pm on November 8, 2016, in a televised address to the nation. The announcement rendered the then-existing Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes invalid as legal tender from midnight on November 9. These two denominations together accounted for approximately 86 per cent of the currency in circulation at the time, triggering an unprecedented cash crunch that disrupted shops, offices, businesses and households across the country.

The government had projected demonetisation as a decisive strike against black money, counterfeit currency and the financing of illegal activities. It was also expected to accelerate digital payments, encourage formalisation and reduce India’s dependence on cash. Ten years later, however, the more than doubling of currency with the public tells a different story: demonetisation may have temporarily drained cash from the system, but it did not fundamentally alter India’s appetite for physical currency.
What was the impact?

The sudden withdrawal of notes roiled the economy in November 2016, with demand falling, businesses facing a crisis and GDP growth declining by nearly 1.5 percentage points. Many small businesses were hit hard and shut down after the note ban created a liquidity shortage. The shock of suddenly invalidated high-denomination notes disrupted daily commerce, forced people to queue for hours at banks and ATMs, and pushed individuals and businesses to rethink how they managed cash.

In the years that followed, the printing of new Rs 500 and Rs 2,000 notes (the latter was subsequently withdrawn from circulation), increased cash holdings and a persistent preference for cash across large parts of the economy drove the stock of currency with the public to levels well above the pre-demonetisation norm.

Cash holdings rose particularly sharply in 2020-21, primarily driven by a rush to hold cash as the government announced a stringent lockdown to tackle the spread of the Covid-19 pandemic. People began accumulating cash to meet their grocery needs, which were largely met by neighbourhood stores, and other essential expenses, including medical bills.
What’s currency with the public?

As per the RBI’s definition, currency with the public is calculated by deducting cash held by banks from total currency in circulation (CIC). CIC refers to currency notes and coins issued by the central bank within a country that are physically used to conduct transactions between consumers and businesses.
During the calendar year 2026 as of October 16, cash with the public increased by Rs 5.26 lakh crore, a rise of 14.1 per cent, according to RBI data.
How the currency to GDP ratio has changed
The rise in currency in circulation in absolute terms does not tell the full story, as GDP growth has remained strong and even touched 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of FY2026.

Since demonetisation in 2016, currency in circulation has risen steadily every year, with the CIC to GDP ratio having surged to 14.4 per cent in 2020-21 from 8.7 per cent in 2016-17. The ratio remained at 12.1 per cent in FY26 as against 12.1 per cent in March 2016.
However, when compared with other countries, the ratio is over 16 per cent in Japan, 7.3 per cent in the US, where the dollar also circulates internationally, and 10.2 per cent in China.

A high CIC-to-GDP ratio indicates that people and businesses rely heavily on cash for transactions, while a lower ratio reflects a shift towards digital payments, banking channels and formal financial systems. On the other hand, a lower CIC-to-GDP ratio, driven by increased digitalisation and reduced reliance on cash, generally enables smoother monetary policy transmission and better inflation control, experts say.

India’s currency-in-circulation-to-GDP ratio is relatively high compared with those of the US and China, but lower than Japan’s. However, a high ratio, while indicating greater dependence on physical cash, does not necessarily mean an economy is less developed or less financially sophisticated.
Cash is still king despite digitisation

Although the government and the RBI have pushed for a “less cash society”, promoted the digitisation of payments and imposed restrictions on the use of cash in various transactions, cash in the system has remained high. India’s total digital payments in FY2025–26 amounted to Rs 3,251.04 lakh crore, covering RTGS, retail bank transfers, card payments and prepaid payment instruments.

During FY2025–26, credit card, debit card and wallet transactions together accounted for approximately 151,611 lakh transactions, with a combined transaction value of Rs 30.31 lakh crore, RBI data shows. Credit cards dominated in terms of value, recording transactions worth Rs 23.62 lakh crore across 60,238 lakh transactions. Debit card transactions amounted to Rs 4.45 lakh crore, with a volume of 12,802 lakh transactions, while wallet transactions recorded the highest volume among the three instruments at 78,571 lakh transactions, amounting to Rs 2.23 lakh crore.

In FY2015–16, India recorded 10,038.67 million (approximately 1,003.87 crore) credit and debit card transactions, with a combined transaction value of Rs 29.39 lakh crore. Debit cards accounted for Rs 26.96 lakh crore, while credit cards contributed Rs 2.43 lakh crore.

The data highlight the growing role of electronic payment instruments in India’s financial ecosystem. Credit cards accounted for approximately 78 per cent of the combined transaction value of credit cards, debit cards and wallets during FY2025–26, reflecting their greater use for higher-value purchases. Debit cards contributed around 14.7 per cent of the value, while wallets accounted for the remaining 7.4 per cent. In terms of transaction volume, wallets dominated with a 51.8 per cent share, followed by credit cards at 39.7 per cent and debit cards at 8.4 per cent, reflecting their popularity for frequent, relatively low-value transactions.
Overall, the figures underline the growing adoption of digital payment instruments and the evolving preferences of consumers towards convenient cashless transactions.

title: What is Muhurat trading, and how will stock markets perform in Sunday’s session?

content.value: The Indian stock market enters the special Muhurat trading session on Sunday firing on all cylinders as it looks to extend its winning run for the eighth session. The Nifty 50 and the Sensex have gained around 10% during this run and remain just around 4% lower for the year, having been the worst-performing major market earlier.
While the special session on the occasion of Diwali usually ends on a positive note, is there any room for further gains during the session, and will the market be able to extend its winning streak?
What is Muhurat trading?

Muhurat trading is a special truncated session on the occasion of Diwali. Coinciding with Lakshmi Puja, it is considered auspicious and prosperous and marks the beginning of the Vikram Samvat, or the Hindu financial year.

This year, normal trading for the special session will start at 2:20 pm and will extend for just over an hour till 3:30 pm. The closing auction session will then last for another 20 minutes before overall trading for the day closes at 4 pm.

The benchmark Nifty 50 and Sensex have closed in the green in most of the past Muhurat sessions. “Over the last 20 Muhurat sessions, the Nifty has closed higher 15 times, including every year from 2018 to 2025. But 19 of those 20 moves were within 1% either way,” explained Tanvi Kanchan, associate director at Anand Rathi Share & Stock Brokers.
Last year, both benchmark indices gained 0.1%, marking the eighth straight year of ending higher during the special session.
Expectations this time

Most experts do not expect major gains from the session this time round. “The session is thin, mostly token buying for the new year, so festive sentiment and the recent momentum should keep the bias positive,” said Kanchan.

“The real test comes when markets reopen on Wednesday, after the Balipratipada holiday on Tuesday, by then, investors will have to absorb two days of moves in US tech and oil. What will matter for Samvat 2083 is whether earnings growth holds and oil stays contained,” she added.
Ajit Mishra, AVP of research at Religare Broking, believes that some consolidation after such sharp gains would be “healthy”.

“Following the sharp seven-session rally, some consolidation and sectoral rotation would be healthy. The Nifty’s ability to sustain above 24,500 will be important to preserve the positive momentum and pave the way towards the 25,200–25,500 zone,” Mishra said.
On Friday, the Sensex had gained 2.2% to close at 81,028.02. The Nifty 50 ended 2% higher at 25,030.35.
Outlook ahead

The Indian market looks in good shape while entering the new Hindu business year after some tough times so far in 2026. However, a lot is dependent on crude oil prices and, by extension, the situation in West Asia.

“As we usher into a new Samvat 2083, India stands at a point where a resilient domestic economy meets a challenging external backdrop. Samvat 2082 tested investors’ patience. Indian equities were weighed down by the West Asia conflict. After the correction (earlier this year), Nifty valuations of 17.5x forward earnings are 16% below the long-term average,” said a report by Motilal Oswal Wealth Management.

“Samvat 2083 begins on a cautious note, as an external energy shock overshadows a resilient economy. We perceive FY27 to mark a return to double-digit earnings growth, with Nifty EPS (earnings per share) expected to grow 16%/14% YoY in FY27/FY28 vs 5% in FY26,” the report said.

Thus, analysts remain positive on the Indian market for the longer run, even if the Muhurat trading session fails to light up the market after the rally. Earnings growth and a robust macroeconomic scenario continue to support the market.

Many experts recommended a host of stocks ahead of the new year. Many of these recommendations include banking and financial services stocks, which will benefit from a higher interest rate environment, and AI infrastructure stocks that have already skyrocketed multiple times so far this year.

title: ‘Very wrong signal to investors’: Behind Vedanta’s Anil Agarwal’s message to govt on ONGC transfer

content.value: Industrialist and chairman of the Vedanta group on Tuesday (November 17) cautioned that the Centre’s move to transfer operations of one of its oil and gas blocks to public sector major Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) could send a “very wrong signal” to investors at a time when the government is looking to boost private and foreign investment in India’s hydrocarbon exploration and production sector. He also urged the government to maintain regulatory stability.
Behind Agarwal’s comments, which he made through a post on LinkedIn, is a hydrocarbon block that the government asked ONGC to take over, and the ongoing legal dispute around it.

The block Agarwal was referring to is the offshore Cambay basin oil and gas block CB-OS-02, which is off the Gujarat coast. Vedanta held a 40% participating interest in the block, and was its operator as well. ONGC held 50% in it and Invenire Petrodyne held the remaining 10%. But ONGC has now taken over the block, after the government refused to extend Vedanta’s application for an extension of its production sharing contract (PSC), and the Delhi High Court upheld that decision.
The block in question and the story so far

The production sharing contract for the block expired on June 29, 2023, although Vedanta and its joint venture partners had applied for an extension on June 28, 2021, under the government’s 2017 PSC extension policy. The government, however, rejected Vedanta’s request in September last year and ordered the block to be handed over to ONGC.

Within days, Vedanta moved the Delhi High Court against the government’s decision. But on July 22 this year, its writ petition was dismissed by a single-judge bench of the court, which removed the interim stay that had earlier maintained status quo on the matter. Although Vedanta has appealed against the order before a division bench of the Delhi High Court, ONGC took control of the block and applied for a petroleum lease on July 28.

“Company (ONGC) has taken effective control of the said block with effect from July 22, 2026, consequent to Government’s directive to take control of the block. On July 22, 2026 Vedanta Limited has challenged the said order in Divisional Bench of the Hon’ble High Court of Delhi, and the matter is currently under adjudication.
The ultimate outcome of the litigation and its consequential impact, if any, cannot presently be determined,” ONGC said in a recent regulatory filing.

“…subsequent to decision of Single Bench of Delhi High Court, ONGC has taken over the Block. The company (Vedanta Oil and Gas) has filed an appeal against the said dismissal before the Division Bench of the Delhi High Court. The hearings have concluded on 1st October and the matter is reserved for judgement,” Vedanta Oil and Gas said in a regulatory filing.

It added that in view of the developments, absence of a valid PSC, and the resulting uncertainty regarding recoverability of assets and receivables relating to the block, it has recognised an impairment charge of about Rs 379 crore during the first quarter of the current financial year. Vedanta also stopped recognising revenue and related expenses from the block from July 22.
Anil Agarwal’s objections
“Recently, our running field has been given to ONGC which will send a very wrong signal to investors. We are seeing such great energy and enthusiasm from global investors.

This is the time to keep the policy hand steady and not disrupt any existing operator. That shall go a long way in building and boosting global investor confidence. Let us all together make a determined move to increase domestic production and reduce oil and gas imports drastically,” Agarwal said in his LinkedIn post.

“India is on the verge of something big in oil and gas. Like Guayana was ten years ago. We have a world-class policy ecosystem and a willingness to move from approvals to self-certification. Vedanta Oil and Gas, India’s largest private sector producer is committing USD 5 billion in investments to scale up production to 300,000-500,000 barrels per day. We have already moved into the deep sea Samudra Manthan programme,” he said.

The timing of the developments pertaining to the CB-OS-02 block and Agarwal’s comments are significant as they come amid the government’s push to increase participation from the private sector and global oil and gas firms in India’s upstream oil and gas sector. India is the world’s third-largest consumer of crude oil and depends on imports to meet over 88% of its requirement. It is also a major importer of liquefied natural gas (LNG) with an import dependency of about 50%.

A series of oil and gas block auctions have been held over the years, but the interest from global investors has been largely absent. Among domestic private sector investors, Vedanta has been the biggest in terms of bidding for new blocks, and the auctions have largely seen participation from public sector oil and gas companies.
The Samudra Manthan scheme, or the National Offshore Exploration Scheme, which Agarwal referred to is an ambitious Rs 84,084-crore programme that the green-lighted about three-and-a-half months ago.

The scheme will provide financial support for exploratory drilling in deep-sea and ultra-deep-sea areas and support building of common infrastructure for production of discovered hydrocarbons in offshore areas, apart from funding offshore data acquisition and developing hydrocarbon manufacturing and services zones. The Rs 84,084-crore outlay is for implementation till financial year 2030-31.

The Centre expects the Samudra Manthan scheme to catalyse reserve accretion of over 600 million tonnes of oil and oil equivalent gas (mtoe), while stimulating significant investments across the oil and gas exploration and production value chain.

The scheme will provide support of up to 50% of drilling cost or Rs 675 crore, whichever is lower, for every well drilled in deep-sea and ultra-deep-sea areas. Drilling at such depths is an expensive proposition, costing between $100 million and $250 million per well, as per industry estimates.

It is also risky as the drilling activity may not lead to any oil or natural gas discovery. In certain cases, even if hydrocarbons are discovered, it may not be commercially viable to exploit them. The scheme, officials expect, will mitigate some of the investment risks for upstream oil and gas players, and increase investment into the sector.

title: What is black mass, and why has India banned exports of this battery waste?

content.value: The Centre on November 10 banned the exports of lithium-ion battery black mass and related battery waste with immediate effect. This came just a day after China extended its restriction on critical mineral exports for two months amid its trade war between the US and Europe.

The government said that export prohibition is intended to ensure that black mass generated in India is recycled and refined within the country. The measure is expected to assure feedstock availability for domestic recycling, refining units and improve their capacity utilisation, encourage further investment and employment in the sector, an official statement said.

Black mass is a powder-like material that remains after waste lithium-ion batteries and consumer electronics are broken down. Apart from lithium, this powder contains critical minerals such as cobalt, manganese, silicon, tin, nickel, rhenium, and graphite, among others. Recycling of black mass can help recover these crucial materials, which can be reused to make new batteries.
Global push to retain critical minerals
India’s decision to restrict exports of black mass is in line with a global push to ensure availability and gain leverage in trade negotiations.

The US in August announced a year-long ban on exporting black mass along with restrictions on and scrap tungsten, which is used in defence supply chains. The EU is also set to introduce exports of black mass starting December 6.
While China and the US extended their trade truce earlier this month ahead of talks this week, China is also pushing for better market access in talks with the EU.

To be sure, Chinese restrictions have been impacting Indian industry too amid the steep dependence of Indian industry on China. Trade experts said that China could use its industrial dominance to gain more access in the Indian market even as India is ramping up anti-dumping measures on Chinese products across sectors.

Global Times, the mouthpiece of the Chinese Communist Party, in an editorial, earlier this month on India-China ties, said that “as long as India provides Chinese companies with a fair and non-discriminatory business environment,” the more advanced India’s infrastructure and manufacturing sectors become, the greater the potential market demand and opportunities for cooperation between India and China.
India’s dependence on imports raises supply concerns

India has limited domestic reserves of these critical minerals that are essential to manufacture batteries and remains heavily dependent on imports. Thus, waste streams from electrical and electronic equipment, as well as discarded lithium-ion batteries, are increasingly viewed as an important secondary source of these materials.

The ban comes as India is pushing to establish a domestic critical mineral processing ecosystem. Earlier this month, the government also approved a new scheme to provide capital expenditure support for lithium and nickel processing.

Notably, India has little processing capacity for these minerals and is almost 100% import-dependent for some key critical minerals such as cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earth elements (REEs) and silicon. At the same time, China controls 90% of global critical mineral processing and often uses it as leverage during times of trade tensions.
Given India’s limited critical mineral processing capacity and China’s dominance in the sector, the country remains vulnerable to supply disruptions.
Government concerns over black mass exports
India generates around 50000 tonnes of end of life lithium-ion batteries. Out of this, around 50% or 25000 tonnes of black mass can be generated, as per industry estimates.

There have been concerns within the government over the export of black mass, particularly at a time when several countries have imposed restrictions on its export to retain critical minerals and strengthen their domestic supply chains.

In January last year, the Technical Review Committee (TRC) of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) noted that black mass is considered hazardous waste, unless processed in the same premises for recovery of critical minerals.

So, any import and export of black mass needs to be regulated under Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules 2016 (HOWM). Accordingly, any import and export of black mass should be allowed only to actual users and after permission from MoEFCC as per the HOWM Rules, 2016.

In November last year, the Expert Committee of MoEFC deferred many applications seeking permission for export of black mass, stating that export of black mass reduces the availability of critical raw material for domestic recyclers and may adversely affect domestic recycling and resource-security goals.
Domestic recyclers stand to gain from the export ban
