While discussing an application for import of black mass, the committee noted that while some applicants reported difficulty sourcing black mass domestically, others had sought export permission citing a lack of domestic buyers.

Nitin Gupta, CEO & Co-Founder of Attero, one of the country’s leading e-waste & lithium-ion battery recycling companies, the ban on black mass exports is in line with the government’s push towards developing a domestic critical mineral capability.

“Essentially, what was happening is, a lot of interflight batteries in India, when they were collected, they were just sort of crushed, and a black powder, which is black mass, which contained cobalt, lithium, nickel, and graphite was exported to China or South Korea for refining,” he said, adding that the ban would help the domestic refining industry get access to this material and helps to build more capacity.

Chetan Jain, senior vice president at Lohum, another leading battery recycling company, said while the move will affect companies that dismantle batteries and carry out physical separation to generate black mass, by restricting their market to domestic buyers, it could benefit those that process black mass to extract metals in compound form, as well as companies that handle the entire process, from battery dismantling to metal refining.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

According to Jain, the move will have two benefits: it will boost domestic value addition by retaining critical minerals within the country and may also bring down black mass prices by limiting access to international markets.

“This is a step in the right direction which will help set up more capacities where people are just doing shredding, which is a minimum value addition and exporting the critical materials outside. This will help the industry to set up more refining capacities so that the complete consumption can happen within the Indian geography itself,” he added.

title: Why are more investors stopping their SIPs, holding off on new ones?

content.value: “I have discontinued three of my eight SIPs for now as returns had been negative for a few months. Maybe when conditions improve, I will start them again. For now, I have invested a bit in gold and fixed deposits,” said Saswati Chatterjee, a 56-year-old homemaker based in Kolkata.
Many retail investors have taken similar measures, even as the mutual fund industry appears to be powering through turbulent geopolitical conditions and a prolonged period of market stagnation.

Despite experts and industry executives remaining positive about investors’ resilience during difficult market conditions, systematic investment plan (SIP) discontinuations spiked in October, while new registrations slowed. Many investors like Saswati are sitting out for now. Does this signal a cause for concern for an industry that otherwise appears to be in good shape?
Headline numbers hold up

Contributions from SIPs to the industry’s monthly inflows remained above the Rs 30,000-crore mark for the eighth consecutive month in October, data from the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI) showed.

However, new SIP registrations fell nearly 20% month-on-month to 51 lakh in October, while the number of SIPs discontinued during the month rose 19% to 59 lakh. Both metrics recorded their worst performance since April 2025.

This took the SIP stoppage ratio, calculated as the number of SIPs discontinued as a proportion of new registrations, to nearly 117% during the month. This was the highest since the 353% recorded in April 2025.

A higher stoppage ratio can indicate increased churn in the industry or cautious investor sentiment. The elevated ratios between January and April 2025, however, were due to a one-time clean-up of the mutual fund system to remove dormant accounts.
There is no such one-time factor this time around. For context, the stoppage ratio over the past year has remained between 75%-101%.
Reading the spike
While uncertain market conditions may have contributed to the elevated numbers, experts have called for a more careful reading of the metric.

“The stoppage ratio needs careful reading, as it counts SIPs that completed their tenure along with those discontinued midway,” said Gaurav Goyal, chief business officer at Canara Robeco Asset Management Company.
It is “important to view these numbers in absolute terms”, as SIP stoppages can happen for multiple reasons, including market volatility or the achievement of financial goals, Goyal said.
“With nearly 10 crore SIP accounts still active, the base remains very large. This does not, by itself, point to any shorter holding periods or increased churn,” he added.

“This ratio measures SIP mandates and not how long investors remain invested or whether they have withdrawn their accumulated investments. And therefore the actual money being invested in market through SIP tells a different story,” said Shweta Rajani, head of mutual funds at Anand Rathi Wealth.
SIP investments in October stood at Rs 32,160 crore, just 1% below the record Rs 32,490 crore recorded in the previous month.
Uncertainty deters investors
SIP discontinuations and the slowdown in new registrations may be stemming from the same factor: market uncertainty.

“Investor sentiment was cautious, as evident from the fall in industry AUM in September 2026. AMFI data also shows that equity inflows moderated 14% month-on-month amid profit booking and market volatility in October. New SIP registrations tend to follow sentiment with a lag,” said Goyal.

Rajani shared a similar view. “One month’s slowdown should not be mistaken for a structural change in investor sentiment, as this number comes after two strong months, with registrations reaching 66.40 lakh in August,” she said.
“Some moderation in fresh registrations is natural, especially when markets have been volatile and new investors may prefer to wait before making fresh commitments,” she added.

While the benchmark Nifty 50 and Sensex indices have recovered 12-13% in a rally led by foreign money over the past three weeks, they had fallen as much as 16-17% at their lows this year, weighed down by the West Asia war, high fuel prices, a weakening rupee and an exodus of foreign capital.

Despite the rally, the near-to-medium-term outlook for Indian stocks depends considerably on fuel prices and the global artificial intelligence (AI) trajectory, both of which remain largely beyond India’s control for now.
Potential new investors may, therefore, be refraining from entering the market amid the uncertainty. Many investors whose fixed-tenure SIPs have matured have also preferred not to renew them.
MF executives remain positive
Despite these temporary challenges, industry executives maintain a positive outlook.

“What is encouraging is that even at the lowest level of the year, more than 50 lakh new SIPs were registered during October. Apart from this, the mutual fund industry added 15.80 lakh folios during the month,” said Rajani.

“This data shows that investors continue to participate in mutual funds, even if the pace of fresh SIP registrations has moderated temporarily. Monthly SIP contributions have the potential to reach Rs 50,000 crore over the next 5 years,” she added.
Such optimism stems from factors such as the continued expansion of the mutual fund investor base, increasing financial awareness and a growing preference for systematic investing.

title: Why Sri Lanka’s recent blackout has lessons for India’s rooftop solar push

content.value: On October 17, Sri Lanka’s national power grid collapsed, plunging the country’s 23 million people into darkness for more than five hours. As authorities scrambled to restore electricity, the National System Operator (NSO), which manages the country’s power grid, issued an unusual directive: rooftop solar operators were asked to switch off their systems until further notice.

The directive highlighted the challenges of integrating large volumes of rooftop solar into the power grid. This is not the first time Sri Lankan authorities have raised concerns about rooftop solar. During a similar blackout last year, rooftop solar was identified as a contributing factor.

The latest incident has renewed questions about how growing volumes of decentralised solar generation can be managed without compromising grid stability. The issue is relevant for India, too, as it rapidly expands rooftop solar capacity, which currently stands at 33.41 gigawatts (GW).
So, how can rooftop solar affect grid stability? What role did it play in Sri Lanka’s latest blackout? And what lessons does the incident hold for India? We explain.
What exactly happened in Sri Lanka’s blackout?

Sri Lanka’s installed power generation capacity comprises 51% renewable energy, with hydropower accounting for 21% of the total, followed by oil-based power plants at 17% and coal at 11%. Rooftop solar accounts for 48% of the country’s total installed renewable energy capacity, amounting to 2,499 MW.

While the extent to which distributed rooftop solar contributed to the grid failure remains unclear, the preliminary report on the October 17 power system failure, prepared by the NSO, has indicated the possible role of “non-dispatchable generation sources” in triggering the disturbance. Non-dispatchable generation sources include renewable energy sources such as rooftop solar and wind power, whose generation depends on weather conditions and cannot be ramped up or down by grid operators as easily as conventional power plants.
The report suggests that a sudden loss of generation from such sources may have triggered the sequence of events that eventually led to the nationwide blackout.

According to the report, the disturbance began at 11:43:29 am. Data recorded at the National System Control Centre showed that LVPP Unit 1 (Lakvijaya Power Plant), the country’s largest coal-based power plant, rapidly reduced its net power generation from 187 MW to 5 MW within 450 milliseconds. This was followed by a sharp decline in the grid’s frequency — a measure of the balance between electricity supply and demand. The frequency fell from 49.906 Hz to 48.75 Hz within just two seconds, the report noted.

The report noted that no dispatchable power generation units — conventional plants whose output can be controlled by grid operators — had tripped at the initial stage of the disturbance. It said the sudden drop in frequency might instead have been caused by the rejection of non-dispatchable generation sources such as rooftop solar connected to the grid at the time.

In a power system, frequency falls when electricity supply suddenly drops below demand. The preliminary report suggests that the initial disturbance may have triggered the disconnection of non-dispatchable generation sources, causing a further loss of supply and accelerating the decline in frequency.

Rooftop solar systems are connected to the grid through inverters, which convert the direct current generated by solar panels into the alternating current used by the power system. These inverters have built-in protection mechanisms that can disconnect the systems if grid voltage or frequency moves outside specified limits. If a large number of rooftop solar systems disconnect simultaneously, the resulting loss of generation can further destabilise the grid.

As the frequency continued to fall, all five stages of the Under Frequency Load Shedding (UFLS) scheme — which automatically disconnects selected loads to reduce demand and stabilise the grid — were activated. However, the safeguards failed to prevent a total system collapse. At 11:43:59 am, all dispatchable generating units tripped due to under-frequency or under-voltage conditions, except two units that remained connected but operated at no load.
Grid restoration began immediately, and the entire national transmission system was restored by 4:58 pm, five hours and 15 minutes after the blackout, the report said.
Why rooftop solar poses challenges to grid stability
Rooftop solar systems, particularly their inverters, had also come under scrutiny when Sri Lanka’s power grid suffered a similar failure in February 2025.

While rooftop solar was not identified as the initiating cause of the 2025 blackout, its high penetration and the response of its inverters were found to have contributed to the rapid escalation of the disturbance into a total system failure.

A report investigating the February 2025 blackout, prepared by the country’s Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB), found that a fault in a busbar — a rigid metallic strip or bar made of copper or aluminum that collects, carries, and distributes high-current electrical power — at the Panadura Grid Substation triggered localised voltage drops. This prompted a large number of rooftop solar inverters to automatically disconnect from the grid.

The report noted that some inverters had non-standard or overly sensitive protection settings, with disconnection thresholds set at frequencies as high as 49.5 Hz or voltage levels as low as 94% of the nominal value.

The nominal value here refers to the target or designed value of a characteristic (like voltage or frequency) that a system is built to operate at under normal conditions. It is the standard baseline from which tolerances and allowed variations are measured: so, a mere 6% drop in voltage levels means the inverter immediately disconnects rather than riding through the minor dip.

The sudden loss of rooftop solar generation increased the burden on the remaining conventional power plants, which had to compensate for the shortfall. This further strained the system and accelerated the decline in grid frequency, contributing to the cascading failure.

Following the February 2025 blackout, utilities required rooftop solar inverters to adopt low-voltage and frequency ride-through settings, said Kumar M, founder and CEO of Smart Grid Analytics, which provides grid management solutions to renewable energy operators. These settings allow inverters to remain connected during certain voltage and frequency disturbances instead of disconnecting immediately.

However, Kumar estimated that less than 50% of the installed rooftop solar capacity had adopted these settings. He attributed the gap to older inverters, firmware that could not be updated and weak enforcement.

“If a large share of non-compliant inverters tripped together, they would have deepened the generation deficit. The inquiry can settle this with disturbance recorder data, inverter OEM cloud logs and smart meter data,” he said.
What are India’s challenges with rooftop solar installation?

India, according to him, has already faced similar grid integration challenges at the utility scale, with the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) recording 68 disturbances in renewable complexes between January 2022 and June 2025, involving generation losses of 1 GW to 7 GW.
He said stricter enforcement had helped reduce such incidents, but managing distributed solar would be the next challenge as India rapidly expands rooftop installations.

Kumar said every state should assess how its electricity grid would perform on days when power demand is at its lowest and solar generation is at its highest. This would involve studying how much rooftop solar each local distribution feeder can safely accommodate, simulating how the grid responds to sudden disturbances using combined models of rooftop solar and other distributed resources, and setting limits on system inertia and on how fast grid frequency can change without destabilising the system.

States should also determine the impact of the sudden loss of the largest source of electricity supply that the grid may reasonably be expected to withstand. He said under-frequency load-shedding mechanisms need to be redesigned for feeders that export electricity during solar hours, as disconnecting these feeders could remove generation rather than reduce demand.

Black-start (the process of bringing an electrical grid back to life after a major blackout) and grid-restoration plans should also account for how rooftop solar systems reconnect after a blackout, he added.

title: How the government’s flagship PLI schemes are lagging in job creation

content.value: Launched in March 2020, the NDA-government’s flagship production-linked incentive scheme (PLI) achieved 76% of its investment target and 64% of its production target until March 2026. But its 14 schemes have generated just 8.49 lakh jobs — 28% of their target of 30.18 lakh — a NITI Aayog report showed.

Data released by the NITI Aayog showed that employment outcomes vary dramatically across sectors. While top job creators included the food products PLI scheme, generating 3.29 lakh jobs, the one for large-scale electronic manufacturing supported 1.69 lakh jobs, followed by 1.14 lakh jobs created by the scheme for manufacturing of pharma drugs (for complete chart, scroll to the end of the story).
Job generation under other schemes, however, did not cross the one-lakh mark.
Automobiles and auto components created 67,820 jobs, well below the projected five-year target of 1.48 lakh jobs.

White goods, on the other hand, created only 52,703 jobs. Telecom and networking created 33,610 jobs; textiles supported 33,427 jobs. Solar PV modules, speciality steel, bulk drugs, medical devices, IT hardware, drones and drone components, and battery manufacturing schemes created less than 15,000 jobs each.
Long gestation period

The report, prepared in partnership with IIM Ahmedabad, said that the divergence between cumulative employment and investment and production can be understood in the context of the gestation period of manufacturing investments.

The assessment said that the investment generally takes place before facilities become fully operational; production then ramps up as capacity is commissioned and utilisation increases, while employment can evolve further as operations reach commercial scale, and so the three principal outcome parameters need not progress at the same pace.

However, the authors of the report hinted that stringent targets for disbursement of incentives could be among the reasons for the weaker take-off of a few schemes, adding that industry participation is important in deciding the targets a sector faces.

Steep targets have been pointed out in several industries as an impediment to taking advantage of the scheme, which in its current form is a supply-driven scheme. The report has suggested modification in the scheme to include a demand-side support.
Stringent targets

“More stringent targets, especially in sectors where gestation periods are long, and there is a lot of demand uncertainty (owing to dynamics of international trade, changing geopolitical circumstances, etc.), will lead to lower adoption of the PLI scheme. Further, mechanisation of industry can also lead to the industry finding it difficult to reach employment targets. Therefore, the participation of industry in designing sector-specific policies becomes more imperative,” the report said.
The report said that the 14 PLI schemes have completed 58% of their aggregate implementation period, with 578 months completed against an aggregate duration of 996 months.

“A substantial 42% of the aggregate implementation period is remaining. The portfolio therefore represents a mix of schemes at different stages of maturity, with some having progressed substantially and others still moving through the investment and gestation phase. The current stage is consequently sufficiently advanced to assess emerging outcomes, but not sufficiently mature to judge the schemes solely against their ultimate full-tenure targets,” the report said.
Disbursements less than 20%

The assessment report of the scheme also pointed out that capital-intensive sectors may generate substantial investment without a proportionate increase in employment, while technology-intensive sectors may require a longer gestation period before production and export outcomes become visible.

“A cross-sector assessment highlights an important feature of the PLI framework: the schemes are not uniform in either their objectives or their implementation trajectory. In some sectors, the immediate priority is to establish domestic capacity and reduce import dependence; in others, the emphasis is on achieving scale, increasing exports and securing a position in global value chains,” the report said.

Cumulative incentive disbursements under the 14 PLI schemes notified in 2020 across key sectors also stood at 18.51% of the total outlay of Rs 1.91 lakh crore as of March 2026. Data released by the think tank showed that nine PLI schemes, including those for bulk drugs, automobiles and textiles, had disbursements of less than 10% of their respective outlays.

However, schemes for drones and drone components, large-scale electronics and food products saw disbursements ranging from 25% to 77% of their outlays. To be sure, all schemes did not come into effect in 2020, with some schemes having a longer gestation period.

title: A third front in US politics: Reading the rise of Democratic Socialists in capitalist USA

content.value: The US midterm election results have sent the Republican Party back to the drawing board. Florida Governor and White House hopeful Ron DeSantis described it as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” in many parts of the country.

The Democrats, meanwhile, will be strategising on how to best use their majority position in both houses of the US Congress. But beyond the two main parties, the elections have thrown up a third political force — one that could fundamentally alter US politics in the coming years. It is called the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the largest socialist organisation in the United States.

According to the DSA, it has fought 294 elections and won as many as 149 so far this year. To be sure, the DSA is not fighting elections as a separate political party, but working as a left-wing grouping within the Democratic Party.

Its members include some of the most well-recognised faces in US politics, such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (or AOC) and Rashida Tlaib (both members of the US House of Representatives), Zohran Mamdani (Mayor of New York) and Nithya Raman (who just won the Mayoral election in Los Angeles).
What is Democratic Socialism?

DSA members have often tried to encapsulate its vision as a system that provides everything a person needs to live a dignified life. That, in turn, means a society where no one goes without basic housing, food, healthcare, etc.
In more concrete terms, its ambitious agenda includes goals such as:
*Guaranteeing universal healthcare at no cost to individuals.
*Housing as a human right and, to that end, building new, publicly-owned social housing, strictly regulating investment properties, establishing universal rent control.

*Demilitarising police departments, disempowering police unions, and redirecting funding to public services as steps towards fully abolishing the police and prison system which, they argue, protects the rich and jails the poor.

*Green New Deal, which involves passing a federal jobs guarantee, implementing massive investment in sustainable, publicly-owned energy and transit infrastructure, phasing out the use of fossil fuels, and reclaiming and repairing Earth’s resources for all.

While this is not the full list of goals, many in the mainstream view the DSA as left-wing radicalism on steroids. The Trump White House has taken notice, and its Council of Economic Advisors released a brief, warning Americans about the cost of the DSA’s key demands . DSA representatives have called the White House calculations a gross overestimate, but have not provided estimates of their own.

Further, the DSA’s goals are not limited to economic matters. They also include sweeping political changes such as abolishing the Electoral College system of voting for the President, replacing the President and Supreme Court with an executive and judiciary chosen by — and subordinate to — Congress, and replacing the two-party system with a multi-party democracy.
How is Democratic Socialism different from Social Democracy practised in Europe?
While they sound very similar, the two concepts are quite different.

Social Democracy, as practised by many parties in several European countries, is a political ideology that tries to address the excesses of capitalism by attempting to make society more equitable through extensive regulation of the private sector, as well as wide-ranging social welfare programmes to ensure a fair distribution of wealth.

As Encyclopaedia Britannica put it, “While social democrats seek to improve capitalism through regulation and welfare, democratic socialists aim to fully abolish capitalism in favor of a decentralized socialist economic system where workplaces are under democratic control.”
Why is socialism gaining ground in the capitalist USA?

On the face of it, the US economy has done pretty well of late. For instance, since the global financial crisis of 2008, it has expanded the gap between itself and the other Western European economies. Per capita incomes, too, have expanded.

But these aggregate measures hide wide inequalities and an acute concentration of economic power in the hands of a few. Last year, Democratic Socialist Senator Bernie Sanders wrote: “In America today… while the rich get richer, the middle class struggles to pay the rent, put food on the table, and pay for health care. The poor live in desperation…One man (Elon Musk), worth nearly $400 billion, now owns more wealth than the bottom 52 percent of American households. The top 1 percent own more wealth than the bottom 93 percent. And the CEOs of large corporations make 350 times more than their average employee.”

Since then, Musk has become the world’s first trillionaire, and reportedly spent around $450 million in favour of Republican candidates in the midterms. Sanders has argued that the US has essentially become an oligarchy with just three huge Wall Street firms — Vanguard, BlackRock, and State Street — as major stockholders in 95% of S&P 500 corporations. The rise of DSA, then, can be read as a response to these excesses.

title: Jensen Huang resigns: Why his exit from Nvidia will be a test for the AI boom

content.value: Jensen Huang, the longtime face of Nvidia, has resigned as Chief Executive Officer of the world’s largest Artificial Intelligence chipmaker. This came amid reports of two extramarital affairs, one of which involved an alleged Chinese spy. The Nvidia board has named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO as it searches for a long-term replacement.

Even before his resignation, the scandal and his expected ouster had sent shockwaves through global financial markets, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars off the chipmaker’s valuation and prompting investors to turn towards rivals such as AMD and Broadcom.

But the implications of the crisis could extend well beyond the fortunes of Nvidia, given the company’s central position in the AI industry, in which it has emerged as the biggest supplier of computing infrastructure and an important financier of the technology’s expansion.

Jensen Huang’s ouster, and the resulting uncertainty for Nvidia, has come at a particularly delicate moment for the industry. Technology firms are committing hundreds of billions of dollars to building data centres and developing increasingly powerful AI models, which run on Nvidia’s highly advanced chips.
Much of this investment is flowing into the chipmaker. Any prolonged disruption at the company could, therefore, have consequences for the pace at which the industry expands.
Jensen Huang had two extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence agencies of spying for China.

And the controversy deepened after The New York Times reported that he had also been involved in a relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s Vice-President of Healthcare, who reported directly to him.
Nvidia crisis is exposing global stock market’s dependence on AI

Nvidia shares have witnessed sharp volatility amid the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang. While the stock recovered 2.92% during regular trading on Wednesday (November 11), it subsequently plunged more than 8% in after-hours trading following reports that the company’s board was considering removing him.

Nvidia’s announcement of Jensen Huang’s resignation came before US markets had opened for Thursday’s trade. But Nvidia shares (NVDA) already fell 10% in pre-market trading, with declines sharpening after the company announced Huang’s departure. At 8:30 pm India time Thursday, after Huang’s resignation, Nvidia shares were trading at $162.58 per share, down 6.4% from Wednesday, having recouped some losses after falling as low as $148.80. These swings have unsettled investors already concerned about the sustainability of the AI investment boom.

The reaction reflects how AI has become one of the most consequential investment themes in global equity markets. Nvidia alone accounts for roughly 6% of the S&P 500, making movements in its share price significant for the broader index. The concentration means that even investors without direct exposure to Nvidia can be affected by its fortunes through index funds and other investments.
The rise of A.I. spending

Perhaps the bigger concern is not what happens to Nvidia’s immediate chip sales, but whether its crisis could affect the financing arrangements driving the AI infrastructure boom. Nvidia has increasingly evolved from a supplier of computing hardware into an investor and financial backer of the companies building infrastructure around its products.

For instance, the company has disclosed approximately $164.5 billion in financial commitments, including an obligation capped at $105 billion relating to an OpenAI data centre in Ohio, alongside more than $50 billion in lease and capacity guarantees.

Such investments have helped accelerate the expansion of data centre capacity. However, they have also raised questions about the extent to which spending across the industry is being supported by financial commitments between companies that are simultaneously suppliers, customers and investors — creating a circular economy.

The leadership change at Nvidia could now complicate this model if Huang’s long-term successor decides to scale back investments, reconsider financial guarantees or adopt a more conservative approach towards supporting customers, given how central Huang, and his company, are, and have been, across the AI ecosystem stack.

Market intelligence firm Morningstar said before Jensen Huang’s resignation: “We’ve long considered Nvidia and Jensen Huang to be at the center of the AI ecosystem; his departure could lead to less AI dealmaking and financing, greater regulation, and more political backlash around artificial intelligence”.
Rival chipmakers could gain as AI companies seek alternatives to Nvidia
Not every company stands to lose from Nvidia’s troubles.

Shares of AMD, Nvidia’s closest rival, opened over 3% higher on Thursday (at around 8.30 pm IST). Broadcom, another AI chip supplier, was up more than 5%, as investors considered whether the companies could benefit from customers seeking to diversify their AI hardware suppliers.

AMD has been strengthening its position in AI accelerators, while Broadcom is a major supplier of custom chips and networking technology used by large cloud companies. In China, domestic GPU manufacturers Moore Threads, MetaX and Cambricon saw their shares surge nearly 10%, amid expectations that uncertainty surrounding Nvidia could create opportunities for local chipmakers.
However, replacing Nvidia is not straightforward. Its dominance extends beyond GPUs to software, networking and integrated systems, which form the technological backbone of many AI deployments.

Morningstar has maintained its Wide Economic Moat rating for Nvidia, reflecting the difficulty competitors face in challenging its position. It also retained its $310 fair value estimate despite the investigation. The research firm said demand for computing capacity continued to exceed supply and did not expect the controversy to materially affect Nvidia’s near-term or medium-term revenue.
Can the AI boom survive Jensen Huang’s resignation?

The distinction between the Nvidia crisis and the underlying strength of AI demand could prove crucial. Nvidia’s chips are deeply embedded in the infrastructure used to train and operate advanced AI models, meaning that a change in leadership would not immediately eliminate demand from cloud providers and AI developers.

But the company’s role in identifying emerging technologies, cultivating major customers and financing infrastructure has been closely associated with Jensen Huang, who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993. The immediate risk, therefore, may be to investor sentiment and valuations, while the longer-term risk concerns whether the industry can maintain its pace of expansion.

With Nvidia scheduled to report quarterly earnings on November 17, investors will be watching not only its financial performance, but also whether the company’s strategy of aggressively supporting the AI ecosystem remains intact.

title: Why US is tightening AI chip restrictions amid the Nvidia-China controversy

content.value: The Donald Trump administration has announced sweeping new restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies from accessing advanced American chips through data centres located outside China, as Washington faces growing questions over the effectiveness of its technology export controls.

The new regulations, announced by the US Commerce Department on Monday (November 16), seek to close a significant loophole in America’s restrictions on advanced AI chips. While Washington has largely restricted the direct shipment of its most powerful processors to China, Chinese companies have been able to access the same computing capabilities by renting servers in countries such as Malaysia and Singapore.

The move comes amid a widening controversy surrounding chipmaker Nvidia, following the resignation of its chief executive Jensen Huang over revelations of his relationship with a woman suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence. The woman, Alice Huang, was previously associated with Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner under investigation over possible violations of US chip export controls.

The restrictions also come as fresh research has raised questions over whether China’s leading AI developers, including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, have already gained access to Nvidia’s export-restricted Blackwell chips.
New restrictions target overseas data centres and remote computing

Under the new interim final rule, issued by the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), overseas data centres that provide significant computing capacity to companies headquartered in China and other countries of concern will require US government authorisation to receive certain advanced American chips.

Importantly, the restrictions also cover companies whose ultimate parent organisation is based in these countries, seeking to prevent Chinese entities from circumventing the rules through subsidiaries registered elsewhere.

The rule sets a threshold of more than 12 million aggregate Total Processing Performance (TPP), a measure of computing capability, for restricted remote access. It also covers computing capacity distributed across interconnected data centres.

Separately, Washington has introduced additional licensing requirements for exports of advanced semiconductors to five countries — Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil — which it identifies as presenting a higher risk of chip diversion. Certain shipments to US-headquartered companies are exempt, subject to reporting requirements.

Existing data centres providing restricted computing services will have 90 days from the rule’s effective date to obtain the necessary licences to continue doing so. The regulations exempt commercial recommendation systems, including those used by e-commerce and social media companies.
The rule also formally rescinds the Biden administration’s broader AI Diffusion Rule, which was never enforced, replacing it with more targeted restrictions.
Washington’s concerns extend beyond the physical movement of chips

For several years, the US has sought to limit China’s access to advanced semiconductors, arguing that the same powerful processors used to develop commercial AI applications could also strengthen Beijing’s military and intelligence capabilities.

These chips are critical to training increasingly sophisticated AI models, and Washington has sought to preserve America’s technological advantage by restricting China’s access to the most advanced hardware.

However, restrictions on the physical shipment of processors have created another challenge for US authorities. Chinese companies can potentially access powerful American chips without importing them, simply by purchasing computing services from overseas data centres.

The Commerce Department said the new controls were necessary because advanced AI systems could be used to develop sophisticated weapons, conduct cyber-espionage, disrupt critical systems and support military operations.
Nvidia’s Megaspeed controversy has intensified scrutiny

The announcement comes against the backdrop of growing scrutiny of Nvidia and the Commerce Department over their handling of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based provider of computing services with operations linked to Southeast Asia.
Megaspeed has faced allegations that it helped Chinese companies access restricted Nvidia processors, potentially undermining Washington’s export controls.

The controversy intensified following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, who previously worked with Megaspeed and was suspected by US intelligence officials of having connections to Beijing.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12. However, US authorities have not concluded that Alice Huang was engaged in espionage, and Beijing has rejected the allegations.

Singaporean authorities have separately investigated Megaspeed since February 2025 over possible false declarations relating to server purchases. On Monday, the US Commerce and Justice departments disclosed that Washington had initiated its own investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 over potential export-control violations.
Megaspeed has maintained that it complies with applicable laws, including US export-control requirements.
The episode has also triggered political scrutiny in Washington, with lawmakers questioning whether the administration had done enough to prevent American technology from reaching China.
Fresh evidence raises doubts over the effectiveness of export controls

The restrictions follow research published last week by Unemployment Labs, which found evidence suggesting that several advanced Chinese AI models were developed using Nvidia’s export-restricted Blackwell processors.
The researchers identified numerical fingerprints in models developed by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group that were consistent with the use of Blackwell hardware.

While the findings do not conclusively establish how or where the chips were accessed, they add to concerns that American export restrictions have not entirely prevented Chinese companies from obtaining advanced computing capabilities.
Separately, research organisation Epoch AI has estimated that around two million advanced AI chips entered China during 2024 and 2025 through arrangements designed to conceal their final destination.

title: ExplainSpeaking | Corporate investments are up, but their future depends on an old worry

content.value: Dear readers,

Since the day it came to power, the Narendra Modi government’s approach to the economy has been to pull back the role of the government and incentivise the private sector to play its part. To be sure, this is very much in line with the change in India’s approach since the 1991 economic reforms. Despite criticism of growing unemployment — it hit a 45-year high in 2017-18 according to the government’s own Periodic Labour Force Survey — the government stayed the course with its “Minimum Government, Maximum Governance” mantra.

The government’s view has been that the private sector must be incentivised to invest and, in the process, create jobs, economic growth and prosperity, while the government’s focus should be to make it easier for businesses to function.

To this end, it unleashed several reforms, such as the introduction of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) in 2016 and the Goods and Services Tax in 2017. The biggest such incentive was the historic cut in corporate tax rates introduced in 2019.
However, as the events since then have shown, investment rates, which had been trailing off since 2011-12, did not rise as the government had hoped.
What was the problem?

By the end of 2022, the government’s exasperation with corporate investments, despite subsidies such as the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Schemes, was made clear. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman even compared India Inc. to Hanuman from an episode in the Ramayana, where Hanuman displays diffidence about his immense abilities.
“Is it like Hanuman you don’t believe in your own capacity?” She had asked.

In the years since, and especially as the 2024 general elections loomed, the government’s approach shifted to addressing the underlying issue: weak consumption levels. In other words, if the average consumers did not consume at a fast enough rate, companies had no incentive to make fresh investments.

To address this issue, the government’s focus shifted to providing tax breaks to consumers — both personal income tax and GST — apart from substantial direct benefit transfers. The focus shifted from PLI to the Employment Linked Incentive (ELI) scheme — that is, the subsidy was tied not to production but to companies providing employment because without jobs, there can’t be much consumption.
Even when investments rose, they were patchy, reflecting the K-shaped recovery in consumption — when different parts of the economy are growing at different rates.
However, data suggests a turnaround may be underway.
What’s happening to corporate investments?

On Wednesday (November 11), Bank of Baroda published new research that looked at the balance sheets of more than 2,000 companies that have announced their corporate earnings so far, and it reveals a steady growth in gross fixed assets (read: investments into boosting the productive capacity of companies). BoB only looked at non-financial firms from the sample “to focus more on how investment has behaved for the manufacturing and services segments”.

Here’s what BoB’s study found. The 2,010 companies were categorised into 31 sectors, and 22 of them witnessed an improvement in the growth rate in fixed assets in the first half of the current financial year (see TABLE 1).
In the remaining sectors, the growth rate was lower than in the first six months last year. But in three of these remaining sectors (see TABLE 2), the growth rate was still in double digits.
In only about one-fifth of the total sectors, the growth in investments was lower than in the first half (H1) this year as compared to H1 last year (see TABLE 3).
“What is important here is to note that these are not investment intentions but actual investments,” says Madan Sabnavis, Chief Economist of BoB.
So, why have companies started investing more?

Typically, companies start making fresh investments when existing capacity starts getting used up because demand from consumers is up. Sabnavis says there is evidence that capacity utilisation is also going up.

To assess what is happening to capacity utilisation, the BoB researchers map the asset turnover ratio. This is the ratio of a company’s sales to its fixed assets. It is an indication of the utilisation of its existing assets (read machinery) in terms of total output generated.

A declining asset turnover ratio would mean that the industry has capacity to scale up production; as such, there may be less investment in physical capital in the short run. A rising ratio, on the other hand, would mean buoyancy in output relative to existing investments; as such, it could result in enhanced investment.

The BoB study finds that, for the sample companies considered, the asset-turnover ratio improved from 1.14 in September 2025 to 1.30 in September 2026. “This is a very good indicator of better utilization of capacity by India Inc. 23 of the 31 industries have witnessed an improved ratio which does indicate higher investments in future,” says the report.
Are we there yet?

The data shows two positive trends. One, actual investments by companies seem to be going up across a large number of sectors. Two, capacity utilisation is going up, which suggests a natural incentive for companies to invest in the future as well.

The immediate impact of these numbers could be that when the official GDP numbers for the second quarter are released by November-end, the actual growth rate can be expected to beat forecasts. For instance, RBI has pencilled in a growth rate of 7.2% for real GDP growth in Q2 (July, August and September), but more and more economists are expecting the actual rate to be higher — BoB expects 7.4%, State Bank of India expects 7.8%, and HSBC expects 7.5%.
But does that mean Indian companies can be expected to continue to invest from hereon, and that longstanding policy goal of higher investments by private companies has been achieved?
Here, the picture is a little hazy. That’s because while investments and GDP have grown fast in the first half of the year, the outlook for consumption is weak.
HSBC Global Investment Research pointed out that while rural demand has remained steady so far, “the decline in real rural wages cannot be ignored” (see CHART 4).

“Winter sowing has started on a weak note with low soil moisture and depleted reservoirs. If El Niño-related heat leads to pre-maturing of crops by shortening the grain-filling period, this will further impact yields and hurt rural demand. Tractor sales have slowed, and non-durable demand remains weak (see CHART 5),” states the HSBC report. In the urban informal sector too, real wages are barely growing.
In short, the old hurdle of weak consumption may hamper sustained investments by companies.
How do you look at the state of the Indian economy? Do you feel India’s economy is growing as fast as the official data claims?
Share your views and queries at udit.misra@expressindia.com

Take care,
Udit

title: India’s poverty rate has fallen, but challenges remain: Jobs, AI, ageing population

content.value: Extreme poverty in India halved to 2.6% in 2023 from a year ago, shows the World Bank’s latest ‘Poverty & Equity Brief’.

This measurement uses a $3-per-day poverty line. If one uses the Lower Middle-Income Country threshold of $4.2-per-day, the decline was from 23.9% to 16.1%. Whichever way one looks at it, these are significant declines.

The World Bank also estimates that the poverty rate, as per $4.2-per-day threshold, fell further to 14.2% in 2026 and may fall to 12.1% by 2028.  These figures will be updated as labour market and macroeconomic data are revised or new numbers become available.

But the projected decline in the poverty rate — by 2028 and beyond — hinges on a key development: India’s poorest states creating productive jobs. The World Bank noted that youth unemployment has increased over the past year to 15.9%, and real earnings have not moved much.
The ‘feeling’ of growth

To be sure, India has been posting rather impressive growth rates, with the 7.8% expansion of the GDP in the April-June quarter besting nearly all forecasts. And yet, questions have been raised about this rapid growth not being “felt” on the ground.

This isn’t unique to India, with the International Labour Organization (ILO) wondering a couple of weeks ago why life is “becoming harder to afford despite economic growth?” According to ILO Chief Economist Sangheon Lee, the relationship between higher productivity and wages has been weakening: globally, the share of income going to labour declined from around 54% in 2004 to 52.6% in 2025.
Government officials privately acknowledge the tough road that lies ahead, warning that India’s demographic dividend cannot be taken for granted.

“Our biggest problem is that we think demographic dividend is a tailwind for India. With social media, smartphones, and now AI affecting cognitive skills, ability to concentrate and read 10 pages at a time, and the impact on mental, physical, and social health, the question is whether the demographic dividend can be taken for granted. Probably not,” a government official said.
“Today’s ageing countries, when they were having demographic tailwinds, they did not have to worry about all these things, say till about 2000.”
A new BIMARU?
The World Bank estimates that 57% of India’s poor now live in a “contiguous belt stretching from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal”.
This is not particularly new information.

More than 40 years ago, the term BIMARU was coined by the late demographer Ashish Bose to describe the economically “sick” states of Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. The World Bank’s latest warning seems to suggest Rajasthan may have been replaced by West Bengal. Madhya Pradesh and Bihar, back then, were undivided.
The World Bank did not provide state-wise poverty rates.
Unofficial poverty line
Luckily, a Reserve Bank of India (RBI) staff paper last year updated India’s last official poverty line, set by a committee led by former central bank governor C Rangarajan.

The Rangarajan poverty line had caused a stir in 2014 when it estimated the national poverty line at Rs 1,407 in terms of monthly per capita expenditure for urban areas and Rs 972 for rural areas. What this meant was that anyone spending more than Rs 47 per day in urban areas or Rs 32 per day in rural areas was not poor. This led to India’s poverty rate being pegged at 29.5%.
So, when RBI economists updated the Rangarajan line for 20 major states using the 2022-23 Household Consumption Expenditure Survey, the results were striking.

In rural areas, the states with by far the highest poverty rates were Chhattisgarh (25.1%) and Jharkhand (16.6%). Rural Madhya Pradesh was fourth (9.6%), West Bengal seventh (7.5%), Bihar ninth (5.9%), and Uttar Pradesh 11th (5.7%).

The results were slightly more telling for urban areas. Chhattisgarh again had the highest poverty rate (13.3%), followed by Jharkhand (12.6%), West Bengal (12.4%), and Madhya Pradesh (11.6%). Uttar Pradesh was sixth (9.9%) and Bihar seventh (9.1%).

It was not all bad news for these states, because they had recorded huge declines in poverty levels between 2011-12 and 2022-23. For instance, the fall in poverty in urban Bihar was the highest of any state, from 50.8% in 2011-12 to 9.1% in 2022-23.
A new reckoning
While the World Bank noted that employment increased by 13.4 crore between 2017 and 2023 — nearly twice the increase seen in the working-age population — the problems are apparent too.

The advent of artificial intelligence and high youth unemployment rates mark a new challenging phase that India enters while targeting developed status by 2047 (as an aside, as per the World Bank’s poverty line of $8.3-per-day for Upper Middle Income countries, India’s poverty rate in 2023 was 80%).
The signs of the challenge for the Uttar Pradesh-to-West Bengal states are apparent. Consider the following facts:
* Wages of factory workers in Jharkhand declined 5.2% in 2024-25 against a 5.3% all-India rise. It was the only state to see a fall in wages.

* In 2025, 81% of districts in Bihar – the highest in the country – had more than a quarter of all youngsters aged 15-29 were neither employed nor in education or training. West Bengal was second at 75%, with Uttar Pradesh not far behind at 69%.
This is not to say these states aren’t making progress; Uttar Pradesh, for instance, saw the largest increase (12.8%) in the number of factories in 2024-25.

The government knows that we are now living in an age that is less forgiving of policy errors than previous ones. So, it has to not only get its decisions right but also, probably, to get them right at the first time of asking.

title: Paytm wallet to be back? What RBI’s initial nod means, and why it restricted Paytm Payments Bank

content.value: Over two-and-a-half years after placing debilitating restrictions on Paytm Payment Banks, which effectively shut down Paytm’s various services including prepaid payment instruments (PPIs) like digital wallets, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Friday (November 13) granted in-principle authorisation to Paytm Payments Services Ltd (PPSL) to set up and operate a payment system for issuing and operating PPIs in India.

While a final approval from the central bank is still awaited, the development paves the way for Paytm — once the poster boy of India’s fintech revolution — to again offer its once popular wallet services and other prepaid instruments. Before its wallet services — then housed under Paytm Payments Bank — were effectively suspended, Paytm had become India’s largest digital wallet provider. If the in-principle approval from RBI culminates into a final authorisation, Paytm wallet and other prepaid instruments will be back, this time under PPSL.

In April this year, the RBI scrapped Paytm Payments Bank’s banking licence, over two years after barring it from offering all its core services, which included accepting deposits or top-ups in any customer account, prepaid instruments, wallets, FASTags, National Common Mobility Card (NCMC), etc. While cancelling the license, the central bank said the bank’s operations were conducted in a way that was “detrimental to the interest of the bank and its depositors.”

Paytm had transferred its prepaid instruments business to Paytm Payments Bank in 2017 due to RBI guidelines governing payments banks and prepaid payment instrument issuers. The norms required Paytm to restructure its digital payments ecosystem and migrate mobile wallet users into the RBI-licensed payments bank.

Even as it was certain that the Paytm Payments Bank’s license was going to be scrapped, PPSL — a wholly-owned arm of Paytm parent One 97 Communications — had applied in December 2025 for setting up a payment system for issuance and operation of prepaid payment instruments, shows the RBI’s in-principle authorisation, which was shared by One 97 Communications with the stock exchanges on Friday. The company’s share rose on the development, closing 1.1% higher at Rs 1,945 apiece on the BSE.
What does the RBI’s in-principle approval for Paytm say?

The RBI’s in-principle approval does not allow PPSL to immediately commence wallet operations. The company can issue prepaid payment instruments, including wallets, only after receiving final authorisation or a Certificate of Authorisation from the central bank.

The RBI has laid down certain conditions that PPSL must fulfil before securing final approval. It has advised the company to undertake a system audit, including a cyber security audit, through an auditor empanelled with CERT-In or a qualified information systems auditor.

The audit must cover the requirements specified under the RBI’s Master Directions on Cyber Resilience and Digital Payment Security Controls for non-bank Payment System Operators, dated November 5, 2026. The company has also been asked to ensure compliance with the RBI’s April 6, 2018, circular on storage of payment system data.

The RBI has stipulated a six-month deadline from the date of its letter for submission of the system audit report. Failure to submit the report within this period will result in the in-principle authorisation automatically lapsing. In such a situation, the central bank will not consider granting final authorisation thereafter.

The RBI has further advised PPSL that any change in the company’s shareholding or ownership should be guided by its July 4, 2022, directions on obtaining prior approval in cases involving the takeover or acquisition of control of non-bank payment system operators, and the sale or transfer of payment system activities.
RBI actions against Paytm (2018-2024)

Paytm Payments Bank was under regulatory scrutiny since 2018 due to various compliance-related concerns. The central bank identified violations related to know-your-customer (KYC) norms — rules designed to verify customer identities and prevent financial fraud. One of the key issues flagged by the RBI was that the bank had linked a single Permanent Account Number (PAN) to multiple customer accounts.

This raised serious red flags, as such practices can potentially be used to bypass regulatory safeguards. Additionally, the RBI observed that the bank was allowing transactions beyond the prescribed limits for certain accounts, which heightened concerns around possible money laundering risks.

In June 2018, the RBI conducted an audit of the bank’s onboarding processes and found significant gaps in how new customers were being verified. The audit revealed that proper KYC procedures were not consistently followed during customer acquisition. As a result, Paytm Payments Bank was directed to halt the onboarding of new customers until it strengthened its compliance systems and addressed the identified deficiencies. These developments marked the beginning of sustained regulatory oversight, with the RBI closely monitoring the bank’s operations to ensure adherence to financial and compliance norms.

The bank was directed to stop onboarding new customers with effect from March 11, 2022. On January 31, 2024, the RBI barred Paytm Payment Bank from accepting deposits or top-ups in any customer account, prepaid instruments, wallets, FASTags and NCMC card after February 29, 2024 in the wake of persistent non-compliances and material supervisory concerns. The RBI had also imposed a penalty of Rs 5.39 crore on the bank in October 2023.

The actions were taken due to non-compliance of various regulatory guidelines including those related to know-your-customer (KYC) and not maintaining a Chinese wall with the group company, One 97 Communications.

The RBI action against Paytm Payments Bank triggered a sharp but uneven impact on One 97 Communications: its stock plunged 40–50% while its integrated payments ecosystem broke down, disrupting wallets, merchant settlements and services like FASTag and autopay.

Paytm was forced to partner with banks such as Axis Bank and YES Bank, migrate users and infrastructure and absorb higher compliance costs, leading to temporary user and merchant attrition to rivals like Google Pay and PhonePe, ultimately causing short-term disruption but a longer-term shift toward a leaner, partner-driven model.
Scrapping of Paytm Payments Bank license

While scrapping the Paytm Payments Bank’s license in April this year, the RBI said that the general character of the management of the bank is prejudicial to the interest of depositors as also the public interest. “Thus, the bank is not complying with provisions of Section 22 (3) (c) of the BR Act. No useful purpose or public interest would be served by allowing the bank to continue as envisaged in Section 22 (3) (e) of the BR Act,” the RBI said.

Section 22(3)(c) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, stipulates that a banking license is granted or maintained only if the general character of a bank’s proposed or existing management is not prejudicial to the public interest or the interests of its depositors.

The central bank said Paytm Payments Bank was prohibited from conducting the business of ‘banking’ as defined in Section 5(b) or any additional business specified under Section 6 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 with immediate effect.

title: Chemicals to capital goods: What is driving India’s push to indigenise 100 critical items

content.value: Amid China’s plans to introduce an export licensing regime from this month for capital goods used in key sectors such as solar equipment and heavy machinery, including tunnel boring machines, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) has begun a fresh push to indigenise 100 items spanning intermediates and capital goods across sectors. It has also begun discussions with the respective ministries on ways to boost their domestic production, a senior government official said.

The official said plans to begin domestic production of tunnel boring machines, which China’s Ministry of Commerce is expected to bring under a licensing mechanism from November 18, are also taking shape. A plant has been set up in Tamil Nadu, and production is expected to begin soon. Similar plans to indigenise select petrochemical products, drawn up against the backdrop of the West Asia crisis, have also begun to move forward.

As China proposed restrictions on exports of solar manufacturing technologies last month, the government has not only announced plans to expand domestic solar manufacturing capacity and reduce import dependence but is also preparing guidelines for recycling solar module waste. The Indian Express reported last week that the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has already held stakeholder consultations on module recycling.
Curbs on solar production
The proposed restrictions by China’s Ministry of Commerce come as India seeks to expand its domestic solar manufacturing capacity and reduce dependence on imports across the value chain.

According to industry estimates, India has around 233 gigawatts (GW) of annual solar module manufacturing capacity, but its solar cell manufacturing capacity remains relatively limited at around 30 GW. With the country adding about 50 GW of solar power capacity annually, much of its module manufacturing industry continues to depend on imported cells.
The gap is even wider further upstream. India has only around 2 GW of installed ingot and wafer manufacturing capacity, leaving a significant part of this segment dependent on imports.

The solar manufacturing value chain begins with polysilicon, which is processed into ingots and then sliced into wafers. These wafers are used to manufacture solar cells, which are subsequently assembled into modules.

“China has proposed certain export curbs, and we are expecting final provisions to come out by the end of November. Two things are important from our point of view. One, our cell capacity expansion is already complete, so we don’t have any exposure to cell technology imports. Second, the existing operations of the company are not expected to be affected because the proposed restrictions focus mainly on capital goods and technology for new plants. The main challenge is for people setting up new cell and ingot-wafer plants, but the Chinese capital goods manufacturers are likely to resist these changes as they will severely affect their business,” Vinay Rustagi, Chief Business Officer (CBO) at Premier Energies, told The Indian Express.

“There is limited availability of equipment outside of China. The cost of technology is higher, and in many cases, quality is also a compromise. Moving away from China and sourcing capital goods from Europe or Japan, etc., can push up costs by 20-40%,” Rustagi said.
Petrochemicals dependence

With global trade tensions on the rise, the government has been particularly pushing for domestic production of core petrochemical products, given their use across several industries, including textiles, pharmaceuticals and fertilisers, as well as in urea production.

Key petrochemicals targeted for domestic manufacturing include PVC, polyethylene (LDPE and LLDPE), polypropylene, polystyrene and ABS. These are the backbone of products such as packaging films, pipes, containers and consumer goods.

The list of critical items also includes high-value imports such as phosphoric acid, ammonia, acetic acid and toluene, which are used in agriculture, food production and industrial manufacturing. It also covers plastics and resins such as polypropylene, polycarbonates and propylene copolymers, which go into automotive components, packaging materials and medical devices.
In August, the Commerce and Industry Ministry imposed a minimum import price (MIP) of $0.766 per kg on PVC Suspension Resin (S-PVC).

While the Adani Group has announced plans to enter the sector and is setting up a PVC plant in Mundra, Gujarat, through its subsidiary Mundra Petrochem Ltd, Reliance Industries, which controls 51% of domestic manufacturing, currently produces PVC through the oil-derived ethylene route. It plans to expand its capacity to 1.5 million metric tonnes (MMT) per annum by 2026-27.
Trade imbalance

The renewed push for domestic production of critical items comes amid rising imports from China. While India has been imposing anti-dumping measures on Chinese goods at a record pace, its trade deficit with China has crossed $100 billion during the current fiscal year.
China’s global trade surplus reached $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is expected to surpass $1 trillion again this year.
According to a report by Rhodium Group last month, an increase in China’s share of global exports implies a decline in the share of other economies.

“We find that the countries that bear the greatest costs are those that are large trading economies in general, and have export profiles most similar to China’s. By 2030, we estimate that the US will lose 1.2 percentage points (pp) of its share of global trade, Indonesia 0.8pp, Canada 0.5pp, Germany 0.4pp, and the Netherlands 0.4pp. The rest of the world combined is projected to lose 4.6pp. Combined, these figures account for China’s estimated \~8pp gain,” the report said.

title: Why food inflation could be Modi government’s biggest economic and political challenge in 2027

content.value: India experienced an episode of high food inflation last during July 2023 to December 2024, when it averaged over 8.5% year-on-year. That was courtesy of a “strong” El Niño, which formed around June 2023 and ended by April 2024.

The current El Niño, officially confirmed from June 2026, has already developed into a “very strong” event. Most global weather agencies project it to persist in a “strong-to-very strong” form through January-March, before turning “moderate-to-weak” towards April-May 2027.

The effects have been felt in rainfall for the country as a whole during this southwest monsoon season (June-September), being 12.6% below its “normal” long period average. The northeast monsoon season from October has also registered 33.6% below-normal precipitation as of November 16. The southern states, Maharashtra, Gujarat’s Saurashtra and Kutch regions, Rajasthan, western Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and the Northeast have borne the brunt of dry weather.

The impact on food inflation is being seen too. The annual increase in the official consumer food price index crossed 5.3% in June, rising to 5.5% in July, 6% in August, 7.7% in September and a 23-month high of 8.9% in October (see chart).

Going by the last food inflation episode — and the present El Niño being of much greater intensity than 2023-24, even tracking to be the strongest on record — one may expect a repeat, extending through 2027.
The redeeming factor

Unlike 2023-24, however, stocks of cereals in government godowns are 3.3 times the required minimum buffer levels. Rice stocks alone, at 55.5 million tonnes (mt) on October 1, were an all-time high for this date, while the 46.3 mt of wheat were the highest in five years (see table).

Government agencies are, in addition, holding some 3.8 mt of pulses. That includes 1.6 mt of chana (chickpea), 1 mt of arhar/tur (pigeon pea) and 1.2 mt of other pulses – mainly moong (green gram), masoor (red lentil) and urad (black gram).

Adequate foodgrain stocks for now would enable the government to undertake market intervention operations to cool prices in the event of El Niño-induced crop failures. That leeway was less during 2023-24.

The better stocks position has been largely thanks to the back-to-back bumper harvests of 2024-25 and 2025-26. This was the case globally as well. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, world production of rice, wheat and corn/maize hit record highs of 545.7 mt, 844 mt and 1,334.7 mt respectively. So did that of soyabean (429.3 mt), rapeseed (96 mt), palm oil (82.1 mt) and sugar (186.1 mt).

The comfortable carryover stocks probably explain why global food prices haven’t really soared this time, notwithstanding the twin shocks from the Iran war and El Niño. The latest reading of the Food and Agriculture Organization’s (FAO) benchmark Food Price Index (having a base value of 100 for 2014-2016), at 133.9 points for October 2026, is still some way from the 155-160 peaks scaled during March-June 2022, just after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The downside
That respite may not last too long though.
To begin with, the kharif (monsoon) season crop hasn’t been too great.

Proof of it is the modal or most-quoted prices of maize in Karnataka’s Vijayapura wholesale market ruling at Rs 3,139 per quintal, as against Rs 1,700 a year ago. The same goes for soyabean in MP’s Dewas (Rs 7,000 versus Rs 4,200), cotton in Haryana’s Sirsa (Rs 9,060 versus Rs 7,500), bajra or pearl millet in Rajasthan’s Bhusawar Bair (Rs 2,600 versus Rs 1,950) and arhar/tur in Maharashtra’s Latur (Rs 10,200 versus Rs 6,700) mandis.

Second, sowing of rabi (winter-spring) crops has been poor, with the cumulative area reported as on November 13 being 15.3% down for wheat, 21.6% for chana and 8.4% for rapeseed-mustard, compared to the coverage of last year’s corresponding period. This is clearly due to the lack of soil moisture, and relatively low water levels in major reservoirs as well as ponds and underground aquifers, from subpar rains. Moreover, since El Niño is known to also raise the risks of warmer and shorter-than-usual winters in India, that can hurt crop yields on top of acreages.

Not surprisingly, all this is playing out at the retail price level too. As per the Department of Consumer Affairs’ (DoCA) data, the all-India modal price of arhar/tur dal has gone up from Rs 110 to Rs 140 per kg over the last one year, while similarly so for chana (Rs 85 to Rs 100) and urad (Rs 110 to Rs 130) dal; sugar (Rs 45 to Rs 60); groundnut (Rs 200 to Rs 214), mustard (Rs 198 to Rs 209), soyabean (Rs 143 to Rs 165), sunflower (Rs 165 to Rs 192) and palm (Rs 132 to Rs 159) oil; and onion (Rs 25 to Rs 50).

In the last one year, the Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation (Amul) and Mother Dairy have also hiked the retail prices of pouched toned (3% fat) and full-cream (6% fat) milk in the National Capital Region from Rs 58 and Rs 70 to Rs 62 and Rs 76 per litre, respectively.
The prospects
The FAO’s October 2026 index of 199.2 points for vegetable oils and 121.3 points for sugar are the highest since their levels of June 2022 and November 2024 respectively.

As stocks from the previous record harvests come down — and countries such as Indonesia and Brazil divert a growing share of their palm oil, sugar and corn production towards biodiesel and ethanol for blending in petroleum fuels — global food commodity prices could further harden in the coming months.
That, together with a strengthening El Niño and its more long-drawn effects, can present a significant economic and political challenge to the Narendra Modi government in 2027.

Take pulses, where the DoCA has made it mandatory for wholesalers, stockists, big chain retailers, millers and importers to declare the stocks held by them every Friday. Tamil Nadu has even imposed limits on how much arhar/tur and urad these entities can stock with effect from November 13.

These come amid field reports of the standing arhar crop in Karnataka (due for harvesting in November-end/early-December) and Maharashtra (from early to mid-January) being 40-50% of last year’s size, and the poor progress of chana plantings.

Under the circumstances, the government may have no option other than slashing import duties on all pulses (already 0% now on arhar and urad, 10% on chana and masoor, and 30% on yellow peas) and vegetable oils (11% on crude palm and soyabean, and 5.5% on sunflower). It might have to also consider extending the existing duty-free import window for raw sugar and cotton beyond December 31.

title: Jimmy Tata: Why Ratan Tata’s reclusive brother is at odds with Noel Tata

content.value: One member of the Tata family has always remained in the shadows, never uttering a word or expressing an opinion on developments within the Tata Group until this week. He is the 85-year-old Jimmy Naval Tata, the younger brother of Ratan Tata. Known for his low profile and quiet demeanour, Jimmy has consciously stayed away from the limelight surrounding one of India’s most respected business families.

For the first time, the low-profile Tata, a bachelor, went on record on Monday (November 16), expressing his views in a communication to a fellow trustee. In a clear departure from Noel Tata’s stance, he supported the RBI’s directive requiring Tata Sons to list on the stock exchanges and backed the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as Tata Sons chairman.
He also called on the government and the Charity Commissioner to intervene to safeguard the original objectives of the trusts and protect their public charitable character.

According to the trustee, Jimmy Tata said the trusts were created with the objectives of alleviating poverty and safeguarding Indian culture, and their trustees were merely custodians of public charitable trusts.

“What has transpired in recent times is that the trusts are being filled with family members of the present Tata Trust Chairman, thereby securing a degree of control over Tata Sons that was never the settlors’ intention,” Jimmy told the trustee.

Despite being a trustee of the Tata Trusts — the controlling shareholder of Tata Sons — Jimmy has never taken part in corporate discussions, public debates or boardroom decisions related to the group’s affairs. His silence has been consistent even during times of major turbulence, such as the ouster of Cyrus Mistry and other key transitions within the Tata empire.
“We don’t know whether his name was used to save the chair of some people,” said a Tata watcher.
Who is Jimmy Tata?

Jimmy Tata lives a simple, private life in Pune, far removed from the trappings of wealth and power. Unlike most business scions, he avoids social events, public appearances, and media interactions. Those who know him describe him as deeply private and content to stay away from corporate and social circles. His quiet detachment has only added to his mystique — the invisible Tata who chooses solitude over spotlight.

People who know him say he does not have an email ID or use WhatsApp. He had worked in various Tata companies but was never involved in management decisions. He retired in the 1990s and has since led a reclusive life.

He is a trustee of the Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT) and smaller trusts such as the Bai Hirabai Trust and the Sarvajanik Seva Trust. He has not participated in discussions involving the trusts or voted in recent times. He was also not a director of any Tata company.
What others say

RPG Group chief Harsh Goenka had played squash with Jimmy Tata in Mumbai. “Did you know of Ratan Tata’s younger brother Jimmy Tata who lives a quiet, reticent life in a humble two BHK flat in Colaba, Mumbai! Never interested in business, he was a very good squash player and would beat me every time. Low profile like the Tata group,” Goenka said in a post on X.

Most Tata officials do not have much information about Jimmy Tata’s life. “He stays in his own flat in Pune and seldom comes to Mumbai. Jehangir H C Jehangir is a close friend of his and reportedly his hospital provides medical help when required. I know very little about his past life, but he is very well informed and tracks the Tata universe closely,” said a Tata Group insider. Jehangir is also a trustee of SRTT.

According to people who know him, Jimmy follows developments within the Tata Group and has a sharp mind but has never interfered in the decisions of Tata Sons or Tata Trusts. The last time he was seen in public was during the cremation of his elder brother, Ratan Tata, on October 10, 2024.
Life with Ratan Tata

In a biography titled Ratan Tata: A Life, former IAS officer Thomas Mathew wrote that both Ratan and Jimmy Tata were ragged and humiliated by their peers at school, Cathedral and John Connon in Mumbai.
“Ratan recalls that they were made to feel ‘conspicuous and outclassed’. After his mother remarried, he says that boys of the school said ‘all kinds of things about both of them,” the author writes.

Their parents, Sooni Commissariat and Naval Tata, separated when the brothers were very young. Following the separation, Ratan and Jimmy became so insecure that they would try to accompany their father wherever possible, the author says. They would also accompany him for the Sunday lunches that Naval hosted for his friends at a small house in Juhu, Mumbai. They were the only children among the adults.

Ratan and Jimmy were subsequently brought up largely by their grandmother, Lady Navajbai Tata. Naval Tata later married Simone Dunoyer, and their son was Noel Tata, making Noel the half-brother of Ratan and Jimmy.
His assets

Jimmy Tata holds a 0.81% stake in Tata Sons, with 3,262 shares in the principal holding company of the Tata conglomerate. The dividend income from Tata Sons alone is sufficient to sustain him. In FY26, Tata Sons declared a dividend of Rs 1.11 lakh per share, which will fetch him Rs 36.20 crore for the year.

Apart from his flats in Mumbai and Pune, Jimmy Tata is entitled under Ratan Tata’s will to a 25% stake in the family’s Juhu bungalow in Mumbai, along with certain silver artefacts and jewellery from Ratan Tata’s personal collection.

The bungalow is jointly owned, with the remaining shares held by Simone Tata and Noel Tata. Valued at approximately Rs 16 crore, the property puts Jimmy’s inherited 25% stake at an estimated Rs 4 crore. This is in addition to the silverware and jewellery bequeathed to him.

title: Blue-chip stocks have performed poorly all year. How did they make a comeback?

content.value: Blue-chip stocks, also known as large-caps, have led the market’s rally over the past three weeks, after underperforming for nearly a year. As geopolitical concerns have eased, and other valuation and growth-related concerns have subsided for now, this premium section of the market has emerged as the most attractive risk-reward bet for investors.

Record foreign inflows have followed the recovery in sentiment in November. These have led to a sharp turnaround in the Indian stock market over the past few weeks, outperforming other major global markets.

From being down nearly 15-16% for the year at their lowest in October, the Nifty 50 and Sensex have rallied 11-12% over the last three weeks. Meanwhile, Nifty’s small- and mid-cap indices were up 3-8% in that period.

“Our view is that things are attractive in the next few quarters from an earnings perspective, and on top of that, valuations were attractive for large-caps. These factors are helping large-caps do better,” said Pankaj Pandey, Head of Research at ICICI Securities.
