So, why have blue-chips roared back to life lately after facing persistent issues earlier?
Why blue-chip stocks were performing poorly

Blue-chip companies are well-established and reliable, with massive market capitalisations, known for giving stable and safe returns over a long period of time. Broadly, all companies that are part of the Nifty 50 and Sensex fall under this category.
Mid- and small-caps are the other top 500 companies on the exchange, apart from the blue chips.

Since an all-time high in early January, the Nifty 50 had fallen as much as 15% by March. After remaining relatively stable post a brief recovery, it hit its lowest for the year in early October. Despite the recent rally, the index remains 3% below where it ended last year.

On the other hand, the mid- and small-cap indices had been on a roll as investors searched for more attractive bets. Despite undergoing a similar correction to the Nifty 50 and Sensex around March, these indices have soared and remain as much as 6% higher for the year.
In fact, almost all mid- and small-cap indices hit record highs around August and September even as the benchmark indices remained sluggish.
Blue chips turn attractive
The main reason behind mid- and small-caps outperforming blue chips was investors hunting for value deals and higher returns, as a host of problems bogged down the Indian market.
The war in West Asia was the biggest reason, triggering foreign outflows, exorbitant fuel prices, a battering of the rupee, and geopolitical uncertainty.

The focus thus shifted to mid- and small-caps, with the earnings of many of these companies still growing in double digits despite the overall market becoming unattractive, providing the potential of some returns for investors.

However, as things in West Asia have subsided a bit and India has gained from an “anti-AI” sentiment, blue-chip stocks have now overshadowed their counterparts. As the Nifty 50 and Sensex went on a seven-session winning run in early November, reflecting this exuberance, the small- and mid-cap indices were broadly positive but saw ups and downs.

Blue chips have also received strong inflows from foreign investors. Having dumped over $31 billion-worth of shares this year until last month, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) bought shares worth $9.5 billion in November as of Monday — the highest ever in a month.
The majority of this money has gone into blue chips, which are lower risk compared to the smaller stocks.

“After a prolonged phase of mid- and small-cap outperformance, investors are increasingly shifting towards quality businesses with strong balance sheets, consistent cash flows and reasonable valuations,” explained Mayur Shah, Portfolio Management Services (PMS) Fund Manager at Anand Rathi Advisors.
Earnings revival, valuation comfort
Strong earnings growth reported by blue chips for the July-September quarter and relatively comfortable valuations have turned the “risk-reward ratio” favourable for investors.

“From a valuation and earnings perspective, large-caps and small-caps are at reasonable valuations, while mid-caps are on the slightly higher side. From this perspective, the large-caps are more attractive in its risk-reward dynamic,” said Pandey of ICICI Securities.

The profit growth of companies part of the Nifty 50 grew by 27% year-on-year in Q2, which was the fastest pace in 17 quarters, according to Motilal Oswal. The profit growth of these blue-chip companies has been improving over the past couple of quarters, having seen single-digit growth for multiple quarters prior to that.
While smaller companies outside the blue-chip category have also delivered robust returns, the double-digit growth in the safer companies makes it an attractive “risk-reward” profile for investors.

title: Unorganised, gig workers’ welfare boards: Powers, duties & what changes for workers

content.value: The Ministry of Labour and Employment on Friday (October 30) notified the constitution of the National Social Security Board (NSSB) for unorganised workers with 40 members, and the National Social Security Board for gig and platform workers with 22 members to design, monitor, and recommend welfare schemes to bridge the social security gap for gig and unorganised sector workers.

The Code on Social Security, which was notified along with three other labour codes in November last year, merged nine social security laws to cover both organised and unorganised sectors. The Code defined gig and platform workers legally for the first time and stipulated a national registration system and a social security fund for unorganised and gig workers.
What’s the social security board?

The Code established a National Social Security Board for workers to advise the Centre on framing and monitoring suitable schemes for different sections of unorganised workers, gig and platform workers.

The government has now notified the setting up of the Board for unorganised sector workers with 40 members, including representatives of employees and employers. The membership is dominated by Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) linked unions and organisations such as Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) and Laghu Udyog Bharati (LUB), which has as many as six members on the Board.

The Board includes seven employees’ representatives from trade unions and seven employers’ representatives, with the remaining members drawn from various government departments and the Parliament. Among the trade unions, the RSS-linked BMS has three members, while Laghu Udyog Bharati, another RSS-linked organisation that works for MSME welfare, holds three of the seven employer seats.

In the 22-member National Social Security Board for gig and platform workers, the Union Labour Minister and Labour Secretary remain the Chairperson and Vice-Chairperson, respectively, as in the board for unorganised workers. The remaining membership includes aggregators and quick commerce operators such as Zomato’s parent company Eternal, Zepto, Swiggy and Urban Company. From the workers’ side, the members include BMS, the Indian Federation of App-Based Transport Workers (IFAT) and National Front of Indian Trade Unions (NFITU).
What will the social security boards do?

As per the Code on Social Security, the NSSB will meet at least thrice a year and will recommend that the Central government frame suitable schemes for different sections of unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers. The Code envisions the creation of a Social Security Fund for gig and platform workers with contributions from Central and state governments, corporate social responsibility, fines collected due to compounding, etc.

The Centre may, from time to time, frame suitable social security schemes for these workers on matters relating to: life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits, old age protection, and crèche facilities.

Aggregators like Amazon, Flipkart, Swiggy and Zomato will have to contribute 1-2% of their annual turnover towards the social security fund, with the total contribution capped at 5% of the amount payable by them to the workers.

The boards, presided over by the Union Minister for Labour & Employment, will also monitor social welfare schemes for unorganised workers and “review the expenditure from the fund and account” along with undertaking “other functions as are assigned to it by the central government from time to time”.

The Ministry also said that the board will also review the record-keeping functions related to the gig workers welfare scheme performed at the state level and also “advise the central government on such matters arising out of the administration of this Code as may be referred to”.
What will be the social security benefits for workers?

The provisions of the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) now apply to all establishments employing 20 or more employees, regardless of the type of industry. Earlier, the EPFO Act was applicable only to the establishments mentioned in Schedule 1 of the Act, primarily those in the manufacturing sector. This norm was removed under the Code on Social Security.

This expansion of coverage has brought all workers — organised and unorganised — under the ambit of social security. Social security schemes will be funded wholly or partly by central and state governments or corporate social responsibility contributions.

For gig and platform workers, who will get social security cover for the first time, the platforms will have to work with the government to register all gig and platform workers to ensure that they can access benefits. This registration will use an Aadhaar-linked Universal Account Number so benefits can move easily across states — a key need for gig workers who often travel for work. The benefits will be significant, as according to the NITI Aayog, the sector is expected to employ 2.35 crore workers by 2029-30.

title: Videocon and the Venugopal Dhoot case: What happens when a person is declared bankrupt

content.value: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) on November 5 declared former Videocon Industries promoter and director Venugopal Dhoot bankrupt. The tribunal found Dhoot liable as he was the personal guarantor for loans worth Rs 12,668 crore granted by the State Bank of India (SBI) to his companies.
This was a rare move — very few loan default cases in India have reached the stage of bankruptcy.

Once a business titan, Dhoot now stands to lose control of his companies and assets held in his name, unless the order is stayed or set aside by an appellate tribunal or court. Even holding the position of a company director requires one to not be bankrupt.

Another recent case relating to personal guarantees was that of Essel Group founder Subhash Chandra, whose repayment plan with a 99.97% “haircut” was approved by the NCLT in August. Later, a five-member special bench stayed the order.
What happens when a person is declared bankrupt? How often does a loan default case reach this stage? And how much money can be recovered once bankruptcy is declared? We explain.
How a person is declared bankrupt

First, let’s understand what the terms insolvency and bankruptcy mean. Insolvency occurs when a person or company is unable to repay debts when they fall due. Bankruptcy is the formal legal process through which an insolvent individual is declared bankrupt, allowing their assets to be distributed among creditors to repay outstanding debts.

In India, such matters are governed by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), which came into existence in 2016. While banks use the law to recover their loans, the government promotes it as a rescue ladder for a company in financial distress.

When a company fails to pay its loans, its creditors can approach the NCLT to initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) to recover their money. If this effort fails, the company is liquidated and its assets are sold to repay the loan.

Banks have one more option — to go after the person or promoter of a company who has provided a personal guarantee for the company’s loans. This is called the personal insolvency resolution process (PIRP), which came into force in December, 2019.
Now, the question that arises is: How do these different processes work? The answer: They work sequentially as well as simultaneously.
Say a company owes a bank Rs 100. The bank has two options. It can initiate CIRP and PIRP simultaneously, but its total claim in both processes put together cannot exceed Rs 100.
Alternatively, the bank can first initiate CIRP through the NCLT. Let’s say it recovers Rs 70 through the resolution process. The bank can then file a PIRP petition to recover the remaining Rs 30.
It is when these two processes fail to ensure recovery of money by creditors that the third stage kicks in — bankruptcy. In other words, bankruptcy is the liquidation of the personal guarantor.
What is the Venugopal Dhoot case?

Dhoot’s case relates to loans granted to Videocon Industries Ltd and Videocon Telecommunications Ltd between 2010 and 2012 by SBI and its associated banks, which were merged in April 2017. Dhoot had unconditionally guaranteed repayment of all the liabilities.
When the companies defaulted, the SBI issued demand notices to Dhoot in February 2018. The notices, however, yielded no relief for the bank.

Following this, the creditors filed a petition in the NCLT for the initiation of the CIRP, which was admitted in June 2018. Later, 12 more companies of the Videocon group were brought under the process by the tribunal. The creditors filed a claim of Rs 72,078 crore, of which around Rs 65,000 crore was admitted for the resolution process.

The NCLT approved a resolution plan submitted by Twin Star Technologies Ltd in June 2021. However, the NCLAT set it aside in January 2022, as it offered creditors only Rs 2,962 crore — a haircut of over 95%. The appellate tribunal sent the matter back to the committee of creditors for a fresh resolution plan. In the meantime, Twin Star challenged the NCLAT order in the Supreme Court, whose judgement is pending.
The bottomline, therefore, is that all of Videocon’s dues to the bank are still due.

Separately, after the NCLT approved the resolution plan in May 2021, the SBI, which has the highest outstanding exposure to the Videocon Group among lenders, filed a petition to initiate the PIRP process against Dhoot. Indeed, the tribunal initiated PIRP against Dhoot in April 2026 after he failed to submit a repayment plan in connection with SBI’s loans.
But this, too, failed. Dhoot’s offer of Rs 600 crore was rejected by creditors because it was contingent on the future development of a Siliguri project and offered nothing upfront.
The tribunal terminated the PIRP in July 2026 — and thus came the bankruptcy of Venugopal Dhoot.
What will happen to Venugaopal Dhoot now?
Dhoot’s entire estate will now be vested with a bankruptcy trustee appointed by the NCLT. What does this mean?

Essentially, Dhoot will have to submit details of all assets, sources of income and net worth held in his name to the trustee. These assets will then be sold, much like in a liquidation process, to repay creditors. Even in the case of Dhoot’s residential properties, there are limits to what he can retain.
An analyst, however, said that this IBC provision has largely remained untested so far since very few cases reach the third stage and the recovery is very low.

“The bankruptcy of a personal guarantor has largely remained untested under the IBC. It takes a very long time to reach this stage and recovery is also very low. In the case of companies they have hard assets and business on the ground, through which the lenders can recover their loans faster. In the case of an individual, discovery of their actual net worth continues to be a challenge,” said Prateek Kumar, a partner at corporate law firm Khaitan & Co.

Data from the IBC regulator, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), shows that bankruptcy cases are indeed few. Only 310 applications seeking to declare guarantors bankrupt have been filed since 2019, when the provisions relating to insolvency resolution and bankruptcy of personal guarantors were implemented.

On the other hand, 5,186 applications have been filed for the initiation of PIRP — a process that precedes bankruptcy. Of these, only 64 cases resulted in the approval of repayment plans, while creditors realised just 1% of their admitted claims.

In the case of company insolvency, the NCLT admitted 9,166 applications for the initiation of CIRP since 2016, according to IBBI. Of these, resolution plans were approved in 1,484 cases, while liquidation was ordered in 3,074 cases. A total of 1,333 applications were withdrawn under section 12A, 1,410 cases were closed on appeal or review or settled, and CIRP is ongoing in 1,865 cases.
Under resolution plans, creditors realised an average of 30.52% of their admitted claims, whereas in liquidation cases, the realisation was only around 4%.
Clearly, the data shows that the recovery in personal insolvency has remained low, in comparison to the resolution of companies.

title: Why Indians are investing billions abroad amid shaky domestic stock markets

content.value: Last week, artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed documents with the US capital markets regulator, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), for its Initial Public Offering (IPO). Interest is sky-high, with Anthropic aiming for a valuation of up to $2 trillion. And while Indians may find it difficult to directly invest in the IPO, some will surely look to snap up some shares once the company is listed, possibly as soon as in two weeks’ time. Why? Because it might ‘pop’.

Starved of returns in the domestic stock market — the Nifty is still down 6% in 2026 despite a 7% surge over the last week — Indians are increasingly investing abroad to the tune of billions of dollars. In fact, 2026-27 may see these investments in foreign equity and debt cross $4 billion for the first time.

According to data from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), investment in equity and debt under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) was at $1.73 billion in April-August 2026, averaging just under $350 million per month. More importantly, the $1.73 billion invested abroad in the first five months of the fiscal is more than double the $823 million in the same period last year. For 2025-26 as a whole, the figure was $2.65 billion — these numbers are much smaller than what individuals invest domestically. In September alone, around $3.4 billion was put in the domestic stock market via Systematic Investment Plans, or SIPs, of mutual funds.

Viram Shah, Founder and CEO, said business is brisk for global investment platforms such as Vested, which saw its new active users rise by 133% in 2024 and 79% in 2025, with the figure for 2026 until October already 33% higher than that of 2025. In terms of deposits, the rise has been similarly rapid: 250% in 2024, 140% in 2025, and 20% until October this year.

“Overall, annual deposits have grown nearly 10-fold since 2023, reflecting the increasing adoption of global investing among Indian investors. This suggests that international equities and other global assets are gradually becoming a more meaningful part of portfolio diversification,” Shah told The Indian Express.
Vested manages $1.5 billion worth of assets and has around 1.5 lakh active investors.
Capital outflow worries

But it’s not just individuals who have been investing abroad heavily in recent years. Even Indian companies’ direct investments abroad – or, outward Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) – have shot up. From $85 billion in the six years from 2018-19 to 2023-24, FDI by Indian companies has jumped to $82 billion in the subsequent two years and five months due to geopolitics and reshoring of production by developed economies.

Add these two outflows to foreign investors booking profits on past FDI into India and the widening trade deficit due to elevated energy prices, and the sharp weakening of the rupee over the last year-and-a-half is not hard to explain.

Which is why the authorities have looked to encourage inflows: eliminating withholding and capital gains taxes for foreign investments in government debt, bearing the exchange rate risk of banks’ Foreign Currency Non-Resident deposits, and floating the idea of removing long-term capital gains and transaction taxes on equities too.

Pressure on the rupee has also been alleviated through certain regulatory measures which have made it more expensive to get protection from a weaker rupee. But how tenable would it be to reduce the $250,000 per-year-limit on outward remittances under LRS?

Introduced in February 2004 with an initial annual cap of $25,000 per individual, only once has the RBI ever reduced the limit. This was back in August 2013, in the midst of the global turmoil caused by the US Federal Reserve’s taper tantrums. The move led to the RBI being accused of implementing ‘capital controls’ – or imposing restrictions on the outflow of money, something which no economy hoping to attract foreign funds wants to be seen doing.
Why invest abroad

Indians putting their money to work in overseas markets is not just to make higher returns but to diversify their portfolio with assets from across the world — no one wants to put all their eggs in one basket. And while foreign stocks are crucial, “there is growing interest in fixed-income strategies, private credit, private market funds and other alternative investments available through the GIFT City ecosystem”, said Gautami Gavankar, Head – NR Business at Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd’s Kotak Private Banking.

“Investors are using GIFT City or other routes to complement their India exposure by accessing global opportunities, diversifying currency risk and participating in sectors and themes that may not be readily available in domestic markets like AI infrastructure, semiconductor, defence technology, chip making, biotechnology, and space tech either through fund route or direct exposure to unlisted or listed companies,” Gavankar said.

The movement of non-stocks investments also shows up in data. With the US Federal Reserve raising interest rates sharply from nearly zero at the start of 2022 to over 5% by mid-2023, global interest rates surged. Consequently, Indians put in nearly $2 billion in foreign deposits in 2022-23 and 2023-24 combined.
Immovable property has also been a key asset of interest, with purchases worth a record $529 million being made under the LRS route in 2025-26.

There is also the fact that incomes in India are rising. And as people grow richer, their horizons extend beyond the domestic economy. Consider tourism: Indians spent $7 billion on foreign travels in 2019-20.  After the coronavirus pandemic induced lull of 2020-21 ($3.2 billion) and 2021-22 ($6.9 billion), 2022-23 saw the amount almost doubling to $13.7 billion before rising to a record $17 billion in 2023-24.

title: How AI made Taiwan the world’s fastest growing large economy

content.value: India, for several years, has been flying the flag of the world’s fastest growing large economy. But that won’t be the case this year. In 2026, it is Taiwan that is posting eye-watering growth numbers. All thanks to artificial intelligence (AI).

Data released on Friday showed Taiwan’s GDP grew by a stunning 14.36% in the July-September quarter, in real terms, which means after adjusting for inflation. This follows 15.43% in the January-March quarter and 12.93% in April-June. And according to Taiwan’s Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, growth in 2026 as a whole is expected to be 11.05% and 6.04% in 2027. In 2025, it had grown by 8.76%.
Economists think these are underestimates and growth will be close to 13% in 2026 and north of 6.5% next year.
In comparison, India’s GDP growth rate in the first two quarters of 2026 have been 8.6% and 7.8%, respectively – very high, but not a patch on Taiwan.

But is Taiwan even a large economy? India, for instance, is 90 times larger and 60 times more populous. But the difference in their GDP is not as big: almost $4 trillion for India and $1 trillion for Taiwan. In 2025, it was the 22nd largest economy in the world, ahead of the likes of Singapore, Norway, and South Africa. So, it’s certainly not a small economy.
The TSMC factor in Taiwan economy’s rise

Key to Taiwan’s astonishing growth is perhaps the most important company in the world: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC. It is the world’s largest manufacturer of semiconductor chips and the primary supplier to Nvidia, which was the world’s most valuable company until Apple overtook it on Friday. Both the companies have a market capitalisation of about $5 trillion.

But it’s the company in 6th place, with a market cap of $2 trillion, without which the world can’t function. The European Centre for International Political Economy estimated in January that TSMC is nearly a tenth of Taiwan’s GDP. But that was then: its net revenue in 2026 is seen at $175 billion, 43% higher than last year.
TSMC is one of the key companies at the centre of the global AI investment boom. And this spending spree is what is fuelling Taiwan’s growth.
In July-September, Taiwan’s investments were up 26.36% year-on-year and responsible for almost half the growth rate of 14.36%.

The other major driver was exports – after all, TSMC’s semiconductor chips have to be exported – which were up 21.12%, with net exports explaining a third of the headline GDP growth rate. In September, Taiwan posted a record trade surplus of $23.63 billion after exports jumped 61% to $87.22 billion.
Together, investments and exports were the reason for almost 80% of the growth.

“The composition suggests that the AI upcycle is increasingly spilling over from exports into local equipment spending, capacity expansion and broader economic activity,” OCBC Bank Economist Herbert Wong noted.
US, South Korea also sparkle
Taiwan, of course, is not the only country that is being driven by the AI investment boom.

In South Korea – dominated by tech giants Samsung and SK Hynix – growth in July-September was 3.4%, data released last week showed. This follows 3.8% and 3.7% in the first two quarters. While this doesn’t sound as impressive as Taiwan’s numbers, two things are worth keeping in mind: one, South Korea’s GDP is twice that of Taiwan; two, growth in 2025 was just 1.1%.

Again, the main drivers of growth were investments (up 4.3%) and exports (8.6%). Within investments, money spent on facilities was up a huge 9.4%, thanks to continued expenditure on things like semiconductor manufacturing equipment.

Third quarter growth in the other key AI market, US, also came in at 3.4%. This is perhaps even more impressive than South Korea’s number considering growth in the same quarter last year was 3.9% — developed economies just don’t grow so fast. Until now.

“We estimate the AI buildout, through capex and wealth effects, contributed about 0.7 percentage points to GDP growth over the past year, or roughly 30% of the total,” said Nancy Vanden Houten, Lead US Economist for Oxford Economics.

title: What Democrat-controlled US Congress means for AI, trade, immigration, oil

content.value: “Lawyer up”: that was the succinct two-word advice Robert Garcia, the American Democratic congressman set to chair of the oversight committee of the US House of Representatives, had for Republicans on Tuesday evening (November 3) after a decisive “blue wave” helped the Democrats wrest back control of both the Senate and the House.

As the House Democrats gear up to take on Donald Trump’s administration, with subpoenas, enquiries and investigations, the change of guard could potentially derail some of Trump’s legislative agenda. This could, in turn, probably make it a bit harder for the US President to hike tariffs, keep the war machine going and cut spending on things such as affordable medical care.

Democrats are generally less receptive than Republicans to overshooting of the federal debt ceiling, which could potentially mean a more range bound US dollar. All of these could have potential second-order impacts outside of the US, including in India.

The S&P 500 index of large American companies surged the morning after and ended the day over 1.5% higher even as the yields on ten-year US Treasury bonds slipped downwards, as did the US dollar. Despite the buoyant markets, there were some clear losers: the share price of CoreWeave, a major data-centre operator, dropped by 10%. Micron, which makes memory chips used by AI servers, ended well over 5% while Nvidia, the storied AI-chipmaker, slipped by around 3%.

Even in India, the markets opened significantly higher on Thursday (November 5): the benchmark index BSE Sensex opened 2.17% higher whereas the NIFTY50 opened 1.74% higher than the previous day’s respective closing figures.
AI buildout impact

Going forward, the big losers could be companies involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres across America. That could have potential stock valuation impact, which, in turn could serendipitously help India’s beleaguered stock markets. According to a Mumbai-based emerging equity fund manager, India is generally viewed as an AI loser and the wait for the AI hypercycle to turn for India to start attracting foreign capital again could potentially be on the cards.

There is yet another silver lining for India. The fact that the midterms delivered a vote that is interpreted as a pushback against the affordability crisis for the regular American, could mean a more calibrated approach by the administration against the factors that sparked the affordability crisis, which include the widely unpopular Iran war and the tariffs.

Sectors such as Indian pharma, which have so far escaped additional US tariffs, could see some upside. Trump had announced earlier that he plans to keep generic drugs tariff-free for only two years from August 2026, and intends to slap a 100% tariff on them from August 2028 for a year, hiking it then to 200% duty. If implemented, the plan could squeeze margins in Indian drugmakers’ largest export market. The sharp pushback against the cost of living crisis could mean these plans could be reconsidered. One of the first things on the legislative agenda for the Democrats would be to try to restore the funding that the Republicans cut for Medicaid, the health programme aimed at American lower income groups.
Trade talk upside?

But does all of this accommodation offer an immediate respite on trade talks with India? Unlikely, say experts. “Since Democratic lawmakers also support protective tariffs for local union workers, America’s overall trade posture will remain intact. To act without Congress, the president will continue to rely on existing powers — such as Section 232 and Section 301 — using executive orders, Treasury sanctions, and USTR (United States Trade Representative) rules to apply unilateral trade pressure,” Ajay Srivastava, founder of New Delhi-based think tank Global Trade Research Initiative said.

“The US midterm verdict does not hand Congress immediate authority over tariffs. The Section 301 and Section 232 duties rest on executive authority, and any rollback faces a presidential veto. What changes is the cost of unpredictability. With hearings and oversight likely to sharpen, the administration has less room for abrupt tariff escalation, giving India space to negotiate on substance rather than under deadline pressure,” Rituparna Kaushik, assistant professor of economics at Pune-based FLAME University told The Indian Express.

“Labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, apparel, leather, and gems and jewellery stand to gain most from greater tariff stability. Steel, aluminium and auto components are unlikely to see quick relief, as Section 232 protection enjoys bipartisan support. Generic pharmaceuticals could find a more receptive Congress focused on drug prices. Hence, India should use this window to lock in a more predictable and balanced tariff schedule, while holding firm on agriculture and dairy, where pressure from the US farm lobby cuts across party lines,” Kaushik added.

But there could be other pitfalls. With foreign policy leverage failing against Russia, China, and Iran, Trump needs a quick win and Srivastava expects heightened pressure on India for a trade deal for the US administration to prove American clout.

Also, immigration remains a problem and the concerns about immigration are now more or less bipartisan outside of states such as New York or California. So, the H-1B visa and that route of immigration is now on its way out. The good thing, though, is that Indian IT companies are slowly weaning away from their dependence on that route and there is the concomitant push for GCCs (global capability centres) in India that is likely to offer a policy counter to neutralise the waning effectiveness of the onshoring tech support model.
Oil markets

On the Russia front, there could be some fresh uncertainty. Trump was broadly much more amenable to accommodating Russia and its President Vladimir Putin, while the Democrats are unlikely to take that line. So, there could be a pushback against the diesel deal that Trump signed with Russia and, in all of this, there lies the possibility that India will remain a very visible scapegoat.

Brokerage Emkay expects the shift in power dynamics in Washington, DC to eventually reduce geopolitical risk premia in crude oil, although near-term policy uncertainty may keep prices volatile. “Broad voter fatigue with the Iran war, a sharp loss of political capital, and the risk of losing swing Republican votes before 2028 could push Trump toward a negotiated resolution with Iran in the coming quarters. Near-term policy swings may persist, keeping Brent volatile before it eases more durably. Brent is already down around 19% from recent Oct-26 highs to ~$95/bbl as the geopolitical risk premium unwinds. This is a clear macro positive for India, where the oil import bill is up ~24% FYTD, with Brent averaging ~$97/bbl”, it said in a note.

According to Gita Gopinath, the Gregory and Ania Coffey Professor of Economics at Harvard University, with Democrats taking control of Congress, there is a possibility that Jay Powell (former US Fed chair) will step out of the Fed as central bank independence will be more secure, the tariff policy will be “less insane” and that fiscal deficits will remain a problem.
All of this could have implications both for global capital and bond markets alike in the months to come, which could transcend American shores to impact most economies, including India.

title: Why everything from flight tickets to pen drives is getting more expensive

content.value: October saw, for the first time in two years, household prices in a month rise more than 6% compared to the same month a year ago. The 6% figure is significant for one reason and one reason only: it is the upper limit of the Reserve Bank of India’s legally mandated tolerance range.

By law, if average inflation — as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) — is above 6% or below 2% for three consecutive quarters, then the central bank is deemed to have ‘failed’ in achieving its mandate.

Three quarters is a long time. But some are already sounding warning signs: according to Tanay Dalal, an economist at Axis Bank, inflation is “likely to print above 6% until June 2027”. But what is driving inflation so hard that economists think prices will keep rising rapidly? We break it down here.
‘Don’t travel by air’

Anyone who has tried to book flight tickets to go home for Diwali would have noticed just how much prices have risen. And while the war in West Asia has made jet fuel very expensive, flying became sharply more expensive in October.

In October, average airfares were a massive 43% higher compared to the same month last year. More importantly, of all the 358 goods and services in the CPI basket, airfares saw the largest increase in price (13.36%) from the previous month.

Flying has become so expensive that the matter even reached the Supreme Court this month, with an application seeking a cap on fares ahead of the festival season. The court, however, declined to grant an urgent hearing, with Justice Vikram Nath saying ‘don’t travel by air’.
All about chips

As this newspaper has been pointing out for the better part of a year, the spiralling price of memory chips used in the manufacture of consumer electronics — or ‘chipflation’ — is increasingly becoming a driver of household inflation.
In October, pen drive inflation jumped to 22%, phones and laptops to 9%, and other major electronic appliances to 4-5%.
What will worry policymakers is that the global chip shortage, manufacturers say, is not going to end for several years.
Eat at home or out?
The first thing that households notice getting expensive is food items: in October, food inflation jumped to 8.94%. And if you want to dine out, throw in costlier cooking gas for restaurants.
“The surge in food prices continues, reflecting the impact of a weak monsoon as well as the festival season,” said Gaura Sen Gupta, IDFC FIRST Bank’s Chief Economist.
Core inflation rising

Prices of food and fuel items can be volatile — they can rise and drop sharply from one month to the next if supply suddenly improves for one reason or another. This is why, to understand the underlying price pressures, economists and policymakers like to also see how inflation is evolving by excluding food and fuel. This is called ‘core’ inflation.
Even more refined versions of core inflation, which economists call ‘core-core inflation’, are rising. It excludes food, fuel, and jewellery.

The problem, however, is that core inflation is also rising. The RBI predicted last month that core inflation will average 4.4% in 2026-27. With the October core inflation print already at 4.5%, the average for the first seven months of the fiscal year is 3.9%.
Higher… and wider

The RBI will not just be worried about inflation rising, but also spreading to more and more items in the CPI basket, like consumer goods and services: 95 of the 358 items of the consumption basket recorded 6%-plus inflation in October versus 40 in January. Other measures also point to price pressures spreading wider.

“The latest CPI data show that inflationary pressures are spreading beyond energy-related sectors,” ANZ economist Dhiraj Nim said. “Acute pipeline price pressures are also likely feeding through to consumer prices more visibly, beyond energy-sensitive CPI. With WPI (wholesale) and PPI (producer price) inflation still in double digits and growth broadly resilient, further passthrough to consumer prices is highly likely.”

title: How animal products are powering India’s farm exports

content.value: Livestock and fisheries contribute roughly 40% to India’s agricultural GDP today, as against 30% just over a decade ago. That is now getting reflected in exports as well. Latest data from the Department of Commerce shows marine products and buffalo meat to be the country’s two biggest agricultural export items.

Overall farm exports during April-September, at $27.1 billion, were up 4.7% over the $25.9 billion for the same period of 2025. But marine products and buffalo meat exports grew at a much higher rate of 13.2% (from $4 billion to $4.5 billion) and 53.8% ($2.2 billion to $3.4 billion) respectively.

The value of marine products exports from India crossed an all-time-high of $8.4 billion in 2025-26 (April-March), which came despite US President Donald Trump’s tariff shock. Even as it led to a fall in exports to the US (from $2.7 billion in 2024-25 to $2.3 billion in 2025-26), that to other countries such as China, Vietnam, Japan, Thailand, Belgium, Canada, Spain, Italy, Russia, Malaysia, the United Kingdom, and Taiwan rose.

The current fiscal has seen exports to the US recover (from $1.3 billion in April-September 2025 to $1.5 billion in April-September 2026), alongside continued buoyancy in that to China ($659.3 million to $753.4 million), Japan ($219.8 million to $318.4 million), Thailand ($138 million to $172.2 million) and Russia ($85.7 million to $137.8 million).
Bullish on buffalo

More impressive, however, is buffalo meat exports, which had actually dropped from $4.8 billion to $3.2 billion between 2014-15 and 2022-23. That figure topped the $5-billion mark for the first time last fiscal and is well on course to exceed $6.5 billion in 2026-27.
There are two significant features of Indian buffalo meat exports.

The first is the remarkable diversification of markets. Out of the $3.4 billion exports during April-September, the major destinations included Vietnam ($526.3 million), Egypt ($465.3 million), Malaysia ($346.6 million), Indonesia ($301.2 million), Saudi Arabia ($255.5 million), the United Arab Emirates ($212.5 million), Jordan ($192.4 million), Uzbekistan ($188.7 million), Iraq ($183.2 million), and the Philippines ($104.7 million).

Secondly, Indian exporters have also improved their value realisation per tonne. In 2022-23, the average value from every tonne of buffalo meat shipped from the country was only $2,716.8. That went up to $2,889.6 in 2023-24, $3,236.2 in 2024-25, and $3,591.4 in 2025-26. During April-September 2026, the average value realisation was $4,368.2 per tonne.

The higher unit value realisations indicate increased product acceptability of Indian buffalo meat in markets across Southeast, West and Central Asia; it is no longer perceived as a cheap number two alternative to regular cattle beef. This has also been enabled by government policy permitting exports to take place only from registered abattoirs and meat processing plants, which is conditional upon their meeting stringent safety, hygiene and infrastructure requirements.

From Table 1, it can be seen that barring the two animal product items, the growth in exports of all other farm commodities during the first half of this fiscal has been low (basmati rice and coffee) or negative (non-basmati rice, spices, tobacco, fruits and vegetables, oilseeds and oil meals).
Trends in India’s agricultural imports
India’s agricultural imports have traditionally been dominated by two big-ticket commodities where domestic production has trailed demand: vegetable oils and pulses.

The value of vegetable oil imports peaked at $20.8 billion in 2022-23 and by quantity at 169.4 lakh tonnes (lt) in 2025-26. Imports of pulses hit record levels in both value ($5.5 billion) and quantity (72.6 lt) terms in 2024-25. Imports of the two are unlikely to be anywhere near those highs in 2026-27, if trends for the first half are any indication (Table 2).

That could, nevertheless, change with a poor crop on the back of an intensifying El Niño. The Narendra Modi government has already slashed the import duty on crude palm and soyabean oil from 16.5% to 11%, and from 16.5% to 5.5% on sunflower oil, with effect from September 24. The need to augment domestic supplies and check food inflation may lead it to further cut these in the coming months and also remove the duty on imports of masoor (red lentils), chana (chickpea) and yellow peas similar to that on arhar (pigeon pea) and urad (black gram).

The one import item to have registered a notable surge in recent times is raw cotton. India, not long ago, was a massive exporter of this natural fibre, with the value of its shipments topping $4.3 billion, $3.7 billion and $3.6 billion in the three successive years from 2011-12 to 2013-14.

In 2024-25 and 2025-26, the value of imports ($1.2 billion and $1.9 billion) overtook that of exports ($809.7 million and $560.7 million). Imports have soared by over 50% during the first half of this fiscal too and are set to end up at $2 billion-plus.

Simply put, India has turned from a net exporter to an importer of cotton. Much of that is courtesy of stagnant, if not declining, domestic output due to no new yield-enhancing technologies after Bt cotton. The Modi government has allowed duty-free imports of cotton till December 31 and might extend that if this year’s crop turns out subpar due to drought in large growing tracts of Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.
Another commodity where India could be a net importer this year — and possibly next — is sugar.

The government, on May 13, banned the export of all sugar from the country, following an unexpected production drop and projected stocks for end-September depleting to a 17-year-low. On August 21, it also approved the import of 10 lt of raw sugar at zero for mills to process into white or refined sugar and sell in the domestic market.

Like with cotton, any shortage of domestic cane available for crushing by mills because of dry weather conditions in Maharashtra and Karnataka can force an additional quantity of duty-free raw sugar imports.

In all, one can expect the still unfolding El Niño to result in higher imports and reduced imports of farm commodities in the months ahead. That impact would, perhaps, be more on field crops and bulk staples than on animal products.

title: Jensen Huang’s scandal exposes Nvidia’s ‘key-man risk’. What does it mean?

content.value: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, already being billed as the most expensive extramarital affair in corporate history, is yet another reminder of a growing concern among big businesses on Wall Street — “the key man risk”.
Simply put, the key man risk refers to the potential impact stemming from the loss of a key employee, typically a founder or an influential CEO, whose contribution is critical to business success.

Some business owners see the company’s reliance on them as a badge of honour, and Huang, a key figure in the artificial intelligence revolution, pretty much fits the bill. A close adviser to US President Donald Trump, Huang has consistently spoken out against regulating the industry so as not to let China gain the upper hand in the AI race, while also relentlessly campaigning in favour of sales of advanced Nvidia chips to China.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon warned that the controversy has exposed substantial leadership concentration risk at the $400-price-target chipmaker. “The revelations over the weekend also highlight the considerable key man risk that NVIDIA faces,” the Bernstein analyst said in a November 9 report titled NVIDIA (NVDA): Stirring the (honey)pot?.

Mohamed El-Erian, the Rene M Kern Prof of Practice at Wharton, has said that “the so-called key-man risk looms large here (Nvidia)”, and that it was doubtful if markets had adequately priced this risk in. “This will not be easy for the board to navigate”, he said in a post on X Monday.
Why the controversy comes at a difficult time for Nvidia
The scandal couldn’t have come at a worse time, right when the AI trade is on really shaky ground, with a brutal industry-wide valuation slide underway after the US midterms results.

The risks for Nvidia are heightened given that the chip-maker increasingly resembles a family firm: Huang’s daughter and son hold senior executive positions, and Huang himself is the larger-than-life brand mascot in what is a purely business-to-business operation. If the AI race were a gold rush, Nvidia is currently the one selling most of the shovels. In that sense, Nvidia was seen as relatively insulated from the larger AI monetisation risk, which the large language model developers are faced with. But in Nvidia’s case, a lot rests visibly on Huang, and the big question mark is whether he will be forced to step down, given that the Federal Bureau of Investigation is now investigating the case.

The American government is said to have commenced its surveillance of the Chinese operative more than a year ago, when it first believed that her employer — Singapore-registered Megaspeed — was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s GPUs into China. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, reportedly readied a confidential note earlier this year warning officials in the administration in DC about Huang’s involvement with a suspected Chinese spy. Months later, when Trump took executives with him on a trip to China, Nvidia’s chief was initially left out, but then included at the very last minute.

Huang has consistently called for sales of advanced Nvidia chips to China, and this has been his position for many years, and something that likely precedes his meeting with the alleged Chinese spy. But his positions will be under fresh scrutiny given the revelations of the affair.

According to Isaac Stone Fish, CEO and founder of Strategy Risks and Visiting Fellow at the Atlantic Council, “Beijing usually dislikes when American companies receive massive press attention for being too pro-China. It wants the mechanics — around honey trapping and influence campaigns – to stay in the shadows. So far, Beijing has denied the allegations and claimed that this is a smear campaign against China. Nvidia needs to have a deep understanding of what its China exposure is and price out the risk of offending the US versus offending China”.

The global artificial intelligence (AI) boom has propelled Nvidia into becoming one of the world’s most valuable companies, as technology giants such as Google, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon spend billions of dollars building AI infrastructure powered by its advanced chips. Nvidia’s graphics processing units (GPUs), which were built for gaming consoles but serendipitously proved useful in AI server stacks, have gone on to become central to training and running sophisticated large language models, giving the chip-maker a dominant position in the market for AI computing hardware.
What is ‘key-man risk’, and why does it matter?

Ideally, no business of scale, especially with public shareholders, should be overly reliant on a single person. When a business owner, or a key figure running operations, is seen as disproportionately contributing to a company’s success, the inherent risks associated with this ‘key man’ are seen as posing a fundamental threat to the business. If this individual were to suddenly leave or is suddenly incapacitated, the company could flounder, both operationally and financially.

The key man risk is visible across the American corporate world. Would Tesla perform as well if Elon Musk quit? Or would Meta adapt to Mark Zuckerberg leaving? Or Jamie Dimon at JP Morgan Chase? Increasing numbers of systemically important companies are now overwhelmingly dominated by single individuals.
How Tesla illustrates the risks of dependence on one leader

Early last year, this risk was flagged in the American corporate sector after Tesla chief Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, managed to bulldoze the Austin-based automaker’s board and shareholders into approving a record-breaking pay package that could be worth up to $1 trillion.

While the scale of the potential payout has drawn widespread criticism, the Tesla board’s counterargument has been that Musk might leave the company if it was not cleared — and that Tesla could not afford to lose him. And that again went on to highlight ‘the key man risk’ and how some business owners see the company’s reliance on them as an indispensable feature that can be milked for eking out personal gains. Musk had built on a self-propagated assertion that the company simply cannot do without him. He’d threatened to resign multiple times earlier too.

The payout was predicated on Musk drastically raising the electric car firm’s market value over the next decade to $8.5 trillion from under $2 trillion, and getting a million self-driving Tesla Robotaxi vehicles into commercial operation.

Unlike Huang’s track record at Nvidia, the way Musk has run Tesla in recent years does not exactly inspire confidence: given that he has a solid track record of overpromising and underdelivering. Earlier last year, for instance, Musk promised to deliver driverless taxis in several American cities, secure regulatory clearances in Europe for his self-driving software and push sales up 30 per cent or so. Instead, his driverless robotaxis are restricted to just two US cities – Austin and San Francisco – and even in these places, they have human safety professionals inside. European regulators are still to approve his self-driving software, while Tesla sales continue to plunge across markets, including China and Germany. Tesla has failed to update its jaded line-up of cars and is being beaten hollow by Chinese upstarts including BYD and Xpeng.

Many investors have come out in open support of the Musk pay package, including New York-based Baron Capital Management, whose founder Ron Baron termed Musk “indispensable” to the company. Critics include the biggest American public pension fund, Calpers, and Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, which have argued that the pay is excessive. The Norwegian fund has even flagged concern that the Tesla board that cleared the proposal before it went to shareholders included Musk’s own brother and that it is not “independent enough”, the Associated Press had reported in 2025.

Even the Vatican has weighed in, admonishing the growing wealth inequality in the world and red flagging the trillion dollar pay package in particular. “If that is the only thing that has value anymore, then we’re in big trouble,” Leo said in the comments quoted by AP last year.

title: ChatGPT for teens: The limits of OpenAI’s new safeguards

content.value: OpenAI is rolling out a separate version of ChatGPT for teenagers, with tighter restrictions on conversations around self-harm, suicide, eating disorders and sexual content as concerns grow over the impact AI chatbots can have on younger users.

The move comes amid mounting scrutiny of AI companies over cases where teenagers who died by suicide had extensively interacted with chatbots before their deaths. Families in some of these cases have alleged that the bots encouraged emotional dependence, reinforced harmful thoughts or failed to intervene adequately when users expressed suicidal intent.

One of the most closely watched cases involves 16-year-old Adam Raine, whose parents sued OpenAI last year. They alleged that ChatGPT had validated his suicidal thoughts and discussed methods of self-harm before his death in April 2025. OpenAI subsequently acknowledged that some of its safety protections could become less reliable over the course of long conversations.

Similar concerns have emerged around other AI chatbot companies. Character.AI and Google this year agreed to settle a lawsuit filed by the mother of 14-year-old, who died by suicide in 2024 after extensively interacting with a Character.AI chatbot. His mother alleged that he had developed an intense emotional attachment to the bot.

These cases have opened the debate around AI chatbots because they work differently from conventional social media platforms. AI chatbots are programmed to be agreeable companions that validate users’ feelings. But this unchecked validation can intensify suicidal behaviors and self-mutilation among vulnerable children confiding their deepest fears.
What’s different about ChatGPT for teens?

Under its new system, OpenAI plans to place users it identifies as being under 18 into a more restricted ChatGPT experience. The company says the teen version will avoid romantic or sexual conversations, place stronger limits around self-harm-related content and discourage the chatbot from presenting itself as conscious or emotionally attached to the user.
Parents will also be able to link their accounts, set usage restrictions and receive alerts in certain high-risk situations.

A key part of the system is age prediction. OpenAI will use a combination of signals to estimate whether a user could be under 18. These include how an account is used, the subjects discussed, usage timings and how long the account has existed. ChatGPT can automatically place the account under the teen safeguards even if a different age was entered while signing up. Adults incorrectly classified as teenagers can verify their age to have these restrictions removed.

The challenge, however, remains enforcement. Age-detection systems are not foolproof, and several parental controls depend on families opting in. The teen version is therefore an attempt to reduce some of the risks emerging around AI companionship, rather than a complete fix for them.
AI chatbots expose kids to harmful content

Multiple incidents involving ChatGPT and other AI chatbots exposing children to harmful content have emerged in recent months. The US-based advocacy group Center for Countering Hate, in a 2025 study, found that ChatGPT provided dangerous responses to teens discussing self-harm, substance abuse and eating disorders, including instructions on hiding alcohol intoxication and even drafting suicide letters.

Research last year by Parents Together, a nonprofit focused on family safety issues, found chatbots suggested violence, self-harm and substance use approximately every five minutes during testing. Experts warn that children’s developing brains make them particularly vulnerable to AI systems that create dopamine responses.
Last year,  OpenAI introduced parental controls, though critics quickly demonstrated these could be easily bypassed.

title: Meta agrees to $17bn child safety settlement: What changes for teens on Instagram and Facebook?

content.value: Meta on Wednesday (August 26) agreed to pay states over $17 billion over the next decade to settle claims brought by 47 US states, as well as Washington DC and other territories. The company has also promised to place strict limits on how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram.

The agreement ends the states’ federal trial, in which Meta was accused of designing its platforms to encourage compulsive use among young people, misleading the public about associated harms, and improperly collecting data from children under 13. Meta denies wrongdoing.
A December 2025 Pew study found that 36% of US teens use at least one of YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and Facebook “almost constantly”.
What was Meta accused of?

The settlement comes amid a much wider set of lawsuits over alleged harms caused by social-media platforms to children and teenagers. In March, a Los Angeles jury in K.G.M. v. Meta et al held Meta and Google liable for $6 million in damages after finding that features of their platforms contributed to a young user’s mental-health harms.

Central to these cases is the design of these platforms themselves. Plaintiffs have pointed to endless feeds, recommendation algorithms, notifications and social metrics such as likes and views as features designed to keep young users engaged. In the KGM case, lawyer Mark Lanier compared social-media platforms to dopamine-seeking “slot machines”.

The states’ litigation forms part of a federal Multidistrict Litigation (MDL) encompassing roughly 3,000 lawsuits, which coordinates similar federal cases for discovery, common legal questions and test trials.

The states alleged that Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to keep young people compulsively engaged, knew about serious risks and misled the public about them. They also accused Meta of collecting personal information from children under 13 without complying with the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).
What has Meta agreed to change?

For the first five years of the settlement, Meta has agreed to impose a combined two-hour daily limit on Facebook and Instagram for users under 18, with direct messaging excluded from the limit. A verified parent can change the limit.

Teen users will also be blocked from most parts of the platforms between midnight and 6 am, with most push notifications disabled between 10 pm and 7 am. Notifications will also be muted between 8 am and 3 pm on school weekdays. Direct messaging will remain available during the nighttime block.

The agreement also provides for a non-personalised feed option, hides likes and reactions by default, restricts cosmetic-procedure filters, and requires stronger age-assurance, parental controls and safeguards around harmful content.

These provisions address an issue that had already surfaced during the earlier litigation: whether safety measures work when teenagers have to activate them themselves. At the KGM trial, an internal Meta document cited in court showed that only 1.1% of teen users used its existing daily-use limit.

The settlement makes some of these safeguards default settings, while others remain optional. Robbie Torney, Senior Director of AI Programs at Common Sense Media, said that distinction could determine how widely they affect teenagers.

“I’d expect the time and night-mode limits to have a real effect simply because they’re universal by default,” Torney told The Indian Express. “The recommendation and engagement changes will likely reach fewer teens because a parent must go into the settings menu to enable them.”

According to Carolina Rossini, Professor of Practice at UMass Amherst’s School of Public Policy, the settlement is the first instance in the US where a major platform has been forced to change the “architecture of its product”, rather than its policies alone.

“The dollar figure will get the headlines, but the consequential terms are those changes in design,” she told The Indian Express. “A safety tool a teenager has to find and turn on is fundamentally different from a constraint built into the product itself, and this agreement finally recognizes that distinction.”
Will these safeguards reduce harm to teenagers?
As part of the settlement, Meta will have to hire an independent auditor to assess its compliance with the safeguards for five years.

The auditor will have access to non-privileged information, personnel, systems and records relevant to assessing Meta’s implementation of the safeguards, including raw and aggregated data, internal documents and communications. Whether the measures are effective in reducing harm remains to be seen.
“Enforcement lives or dies on verification,” Rossini said, noting that the five-year audit period is shorter than the ten-year settlement timeline.

“Meaningful enforcement requires an auditor Meta doesn’t select, access to internal engagement and usage data rather than company self-reports, reproducible findings, and defined penalties for noncompliance,” she told The Indian Express.
Rossini also pointed to the possibility that teenagers could shift their activity to direct messages, which are excluded from the daily time limit, or to platforms outside the settlement.

“Compliance and harm reduction are different questions, and we should refuse to let the first substitute for the second,” Rossini said. “The real test is whether independent researchers get enough data access to measure outcomes: sleep, wellbeing, compulsive-use patterns, not feature checklists.”
Torney also cautioned against using screen time alone to judge whether the safeguards have worked.
“Time spent on screens is a proxy, not the primary outcome that matters. The real question is what happens during the time teens are still on the app,” he said.

Torney pointed particularly to recommendation systems, which Common Sense Media has previously rated as “high risk” on Instagram. “My biggest question is how turning off algorithmic recommendations changes what teens are shown and re-engage with,” he said.
What legal questions does the settlement leave unresolved?
The settlement ends the states’ trial without a judgment on the underlying claims against Meta, while thousands of other cases alleging harms to young social media users remain pending.
The agreement itself states that it does not establish a standard of care or serve as precedent in non-participating US states or international jurisdictions.

A recurring question in these cases concerns Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a 1996 law that generally protects internet platforms from liability for content posted by their users. As The Indian Express has previously explained, plaintiffs have sought to get around this protection by arguing that their claims concern the platforms’ own design choices, rather than content posted by third parties.

The settlement means that question will not be decided in the states’ trial. In a Stanford Law School interview before the settlement, professor Nora Engstrom said the Section 230 issue could eventually reach the US Supreme Court. While the outcome of this “bellwether trial” would not formally bind the other 2,900-plus cases in the multidistrict litigation, it could shape settlement expectations and litigation strategies.
Could the settlement affect other social media platforms too?

Rossini argues that the agreement also gives Meta a financial interest in seeing similar safeguards adopted by its competitors. Writing in The Conversation, she noted that states that participated in the trial are guaranteed about 70% of the $17 billion (about $12.7 billion) over the decade, while the remaining 30% (about $5.3 billion) will only be released if YouTube and TikTok adopt comparable teen protections and make matching payments.

The agreement defines Snap, TikTok and YouTube as “Core Industry Members”, and Rossini described the structure as a “workable template with a built-in confession”. If all three adopt comparable safeguards, the agreement provides for stricter restrictions, including a 60-minute daily limit on each platform.

Rossini noted that the settlement itself is expected to cost Meta barely 1% of its revenue over the coming decade. But if the new safeguards affect how much teenagers use its platforms, Meta has an interest in seeing its competitors adopt them too.

Torney also pointed to the consequences of teenagers moving between platforms. “Teens don’t use one app in isolation, so if one platform has strong defaults, a teen might shift their attention to another app without those same defaults,” he told The Indian Express.

An industry-wide standard, Torney said, could include measures to protect sleep, encourage time away from platforms and support real-world connections. But the measures themselves would have to account for differences between services.
“TikTok is not the same as Instagram is not the same as YouTube, so each platform will need different product-level design changes that support safe, healthy teenage development,” he said.
Rossini also pointed to a limitation of reaching such rules through a settlement. The agreement ends the trial before a fuller public record of Meta’s internal documents and testimony can emerge.

“But regulation by settlement is regulation by accident: negotiated behind closed doors, ending discovery before the public record is complete, and expiring on a contract timeline,” she told The Indian Express.

“It took state attorneys general stretching consumer-protection law to produce rules a functioning legislature should have written years ago. The settlement proves the design-accountability strategy works. It also proves we shouldn’t have to litigate our way to it, one company at a time.

title: Chinese robot sprints 100m faster than Usain Bolt: Why teaching robots to run matters

content.value: A Chinese humanoid robot has just done something that sounds both remarkable and faintly absurd: it ran 100 metres faster than Usain Bolt.

Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, covered the 100 metres in 9.39 seconds in a preliminary round at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on August 22. The human record is of 9.58 seconds, set by Bolt in 2009.

Tiangong Ultra wasn’t the only one. Another robot called Lightning, the made by the Chinese smartphone manufacturer Honor, finished in 9.47 seconds, although it had to then be carried away of a stretcher.
While this is a feat of science and another sign of China’s total dominance over the humanoid robot industry, why make a robot run at all? Who does it help, and how?
Racing to do what humans can

This is the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games, where, apart from racing, the humanoid robots will compete in football, and in tasks such as connecting cables, charging electric vehicles, and moving materials from one location to another.
The tasks are not just for the spectacle. They are a way of demonstrating how adept the robots are at handling real-world situations humans routinely face.
The human body is an extraordinarily good machine. It can move through a messy, unpredictable environment while constantly processing information from its eyes, ears, nose, and muscles.

Take something as mundane as tripping. A person catches a toe on an uneven surface. In a fraction of a second, the brain has to register that the body’s balance has changed, work out where the body is moving, decide how to correct it and coordinate dozens of muscles to put a foot down, shift the weight and stay upright. Sometimes we stretch out a hand or change our posture. Sometimes we simply take an extra step.
Thus, the seemingly clumsy act of tripping and righting yourself involves sensing, prediction, decision-making and physical action, in a fraction of a second.
Teaching a robot to do all of this reliably is enormously difficult.

A 100-metre sprint, or other games, are useful because they force engineers to solve several of these problems at once. The robot has to accelerate, coordinate its limbs, maintain balance, respond to tiny changes in its position and then decelerate.
Once a robot can do all this, it can perform a variety of tasks, from delivering food in restaurants to cleaning your house to sweeping a mine to rescuing people trapped under rubble.

Consider disaster response. A robot sent into a burning building, collapsed structure or hazardous industrial site needs to negotiate stairs, rubble and uneven surfaces. It may need to move on inclined surfaces, find something, pick it up, open a door or turn a valve.

The USA’s National Institute of Standards and Technology is running a project to develop robots that can help with disaster relief. Its website says, “Categories of elemental robot tasks include maneuvering, mobility, dexterity, sensing, endurance, radio communication, durability, reliability, autonomy, logistics, and safety.”
The same principle applies to warfare.

A drone is a good example of a machine capable of moving through the physical world while sensing and responding to it. A military drone can navigate, observe, carry equipment or operate in places where putting a human would be dangerous.
Physical dimension of Artificial Intelligence

While AI chatbots are becoming ubiquitous, as large language models become better and better at processing large amounts of information, the next frontier is giving machines more sophisticated physical capabilities — including ground robots that can move through terrain, carry supplies or potentially work alongside soldiers.

This is also why China is investing so heavily in robotics. The International Federation of Robotics says that China’s latest Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) places robotics at the “heart of its modern industrial system.” The report points out that even at present, 54% of annual industrial robots installed worldwide were in China.

In the new plan, the “aim is to pivot its AI research towards physical applications with robots as main drivers for economic growth. This is a next step in the country´s strong automation development,” the report says.

title: MG Hector Tomahawk is India’s first mainstream plug-in hybrid SUV. What is a PHEV?

content.value: The Tomahawk Land Attack Missile is an iconic American long-range, jet-powered, subsonic cruise missile that is used by the United States Navy in ship and submarine-based land-attack operations. The long-range analogy is perhaps what JSW MG Motor India wanted to play on when it decided to christen its newly launched Hector Tomahawk plug-in hybrid vehicle (PHEV), alongside an all-electric version of this new SUV, to emphasise range efficiency.

The vehicle is India’s first mainstream plug-in hybrid SUV, claimed to deliver over 115km of electric-only range and a combined fuel efficiency figure of over 40kmpl. MG claims the Tomahawk PHEV can cover over 1,100km with a full tank of fuel and a fully charged battery.
So, what exactly is a PHEV?

To understand this, it’s important to examine the textbook definition of an EV – a vehicle that can be powered by an electric motor, which draws electricity from a battery and can be charged from an external source.

Beyond this broad classification, though, across most parts of the world, a range of vehicle categories are subsumed as EVs. Globally, the EV segment covers, besides battery electric vehicles or BEVs, an alphabet soup of some other technologies that incorporate electrification in some form: HEVs or hybrid electric vehicles, PHEVs or plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, and FCEVs or hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicles. All these technologies are part of a broad basket of low-emission vehicular platforms that the Chinese now term as New Energy Vehicles.
How PHEVs differ from regular hybrids

Unlike BEVs, which are typically battery electric vehicles such as the Tesla Model S or the Tata Nexon electric that need to be plugged in before the battery is discharged, technologies such as HEVs and PHEVs bring together the best of both worlds.

For instance, HEVs, or conventional hybrid electric vehicles, such as strong hybrid variants of the Toyota Hycross Hybrid and the Honda City e:HEV in India, or the Toyota Prius HEV sold abroad, combine a conventional internal combustion engine (ICE) system, like in a regular petrol car, with an electric propulsion system to produce a hybrid drivetrain that substantially lowers fossil fuel usage.

The on-board battery in a conventional hybrid vehicle gets charged when the internal combustion engine is powering the drivetrain to produce forward or reverse motion, and this charge from the battery kicks in to offer motive power when it is fully juiced up. There is no need or provision to plug in these HEVs to recharge the batteries.

The PHEVs, or plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, such as the new Tomahawk or the Chevrolet Volt in the US market, also have a hybrid drivetrain that uses a combination of the internal combustion engine (ICE) and electric power for motive power, but is backed by rechargeable batteries, quite like the HEVs.

The big difference therefore is that a PHEV can be plugged into a power source, which offers an external option to charge the battery that is not available on an HEV. A plug-in hybrid car has a comparatively bigger battery and offers a longer electric range than a traditional HEV. The battery, which gets charged while driving and with regenerative braking, as in an HEV, can be recharged by plugging into a socket if that option is available. Effectively, a PHEV combines the positive attributes of internal combustion (range on long journeys) with those of plug-in electrics (a cleaner engine that typically costs less to run) in a single vehicle, resulting in a combination of features superior to those of a regular HEV.

A bigger battery means that a plug-in hybrid car can be driven completely on 100 per cent electric power far more frequently if it is recharged adequately at a charging point. And unlike a regular hybrid, it does not have to depend entirely on driving or braking for the on-board battery to get charged, given that external charging is an option in the PHEV that is not there in an HEV.

On the flip side, plug-in hybrids are comparatively more expensive to buy than their internal combustion counterparts, and they are also pricier than normal HEVs, given that the on-board battery in a PHEV is bigger than in an HEV. Running costs for a PHEV, on the other hand, are generally lower, especially if the batteries are charged from an external socket regularly. The important thing is that in the transition to emission-free vehicles, PHEVs offer a genuine progression from hybrids to BEVs, given that they address several concerns with battery electrics — range anxiety being the most important.
Why MG is betting on a multi-powertrain platform

The Tomahawk is one of the first iterations of MG’s ADAPT, or Advance Drive Architecture platform, which the Chinese SAIC-linked Indian entity claims is a modular, multi-powertrain platform designed to underpin MG’s next-generation vehicles in India, including new EVs, HEVs, PHEVs, and range-extender electric vehicles (REEVs). Both EV and PHEV models are built on the same ADAPT platform, but the company claims both have different use cases.

The EV variant is being pitched to commuters who drive largely within city limits, with a claimed 500 kilometres of range. The car also claims to bring the first practical use case scenario of the vehicle-to-home technology – so in case of a power outage, one can use the battery of the car to be able to run some electronics or a camper while vacationing. It also brings with it a very Chinese feature – karaoke inside the car.

With a claimed combined range of about 1,100 kilometres on a full tank and battery charge, MG is pitching the PHEV at buyers who make more outstation trips or might otherwise consider a diesel vehicle.
The charging problem PHEVs try to solve

The charging gap, which is now one of the major hurdles to the increased penetration of EVs in global markets, is an incipient problem in India too. According to Michigan-based data analytics and consumer intelligence company JD Power’s latest data, in the US, around 83 per cent of EV charging occurs at home, but one in three car consumers do not have a home charger nor the ability to install one. The most common reason people decide not to buy an EV is the lack of public charging and EV owners say public charging issues are the least satisfying aspect of the ownership experience. That is a problem that Indian EV owners are also incrementally facing. That’s where hybrids are seen as a superior solution, even if only for the transition period.

Hybrid technology is being seen as a good transitional step towards attaining the all-electric goal. Hybrids typically improve fuel efficiency through the electrification of the powertrain, but come with the advantage of not needing the charging infrastructure base that is essential for BEVs. Downsides include complicated engineering, given the fact that a hybrid packs in more equipment under the hood since both the ICE and the electric motor assembly are present together. That also makes hybrids pretty expensive (the Hector Tomahawk PHEV starts at nearly Rs 26 lakh ex-showroom, with a cheaper option available under the battery-as-a-service facility).

But manufacturers claim that a hybrid vehicle base can also potentially spawn a full-scale battery ecosystem, which can eventually be leveraged for a BEV push. PHEVs are a superior option among hybrids in this regard. So the Tomahawk could well be on target to fill in a much-needed technology gap in India.

title: The AI safety debate: Why ‘pacing the frontier’ comes with pitfalls

content.value: For an industry built around a race to make its models more powerful, calls from some of its biggest executives to deliberately slow down have opened up an unusual divide in Silicon Valley and Washington DC. Particularly over how real the dangers from advanced artificial intelligence (AI) are, who should regulate them, and whether the US can afford to apply the brakes while competing with China.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei’s proposal to “pace the frontier” has found support in places that would have appeared unlikely even a few months ago. OpenAI chief Sam Altman, one of Amodei’s fiercest commercial rivals, has said his company also believes frontier development may need to slow. Microsoft chief Satya Nadella has backed “deliberate pacing” and independent evaluators.

On the other side is US President Donald Trump, whose administration has increasingly treated AI as a technological contest in which American dominance over China takes precedence over new regulatory restrictions. Trump has called fears that AI could take over the world a “hoax”.
Meanwhile, some prominent technology executives and investors argue that warnings from the largest AI companies could end up giving those same firms a regulatory moat against smaller competitors.

The argument is therefore no longer simply between AI “doomers” and “accelerationists”.
