The scheme will provide central financial assistance (CFA) of Rs 1 crore per MW for each eligible project upon commissioning. For successful floating solar projects, feasibility studies and preparatory activities, including hydrographic assessments (to understand the physical characteristics of a water body, such as its depth and bottom contours) and environmental assessments (to assess potential impacts on aquatic life and water quality), are critical. Although these activities can be time- and resource-intensive, they are essential to de-risk project development. The scheme recognises this and provides additional CFA of up to Rs 0.5 crore per project for these activities.

It will also boost domestic manufacturing and generate employment opportunities across the floating solar value chain, with a 5-year implementation period and financial support available until 2032-33.
Factors necessary for success

The scheme’s success will depend not only on financial support but also on effective implementation, the bankability of eligible projects, and institutional coordination. Implementation will require clear identification of suitable water bodies and comprehensive feasibility studies for each site.

Floating solar systems are exposed to extreme winds, waves, and rapidly changing water levels, making climate-resilient system design crucial. It is also important to avoid any adverse effects on ecology and aquatic life. Ecologically sensitive water bodies, as well as areas important for biodiversity, bird habitats, and fisheries, should therefore be treated with caution and approved for floating solar development only after thorough assessments.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

Floating solar is generally more expensive than traditional ground-mounted solar because of the cost of floating platforms, anchoring systems, specialised electrical equipment, and installation. The inclusion of energy storage systems will further increase overall capital costs. While the CFA provided under the scheme will improve project economics, developers will still require access to affordable financing and clear revenue streams through long-term power purchase agreements.

For a floating solar system to be sanctioned, coordination among multiple institutions (including state agencies, municipal authorities, electricity utilities, water resources and irrigation departments, environmental authorities, and industries) is essential. Developing clear frameworks for identifying and allocating suitable water bodies, defining institutional responsibilities, and streamlining approvals will therefore be vital for successful implementation.
What lies ahead

Floating solar can complement ground-mounted and rooftop solar by providing an additional pathway for expanding India’s renewable capacity without placing further pressure on scarce land resources. PM-SSY provides an opportunity to move floating solar from a handful of large-scale installations towards systematic and widespread deployment. But converting financial assistance into actual projects will require careful site selection, environmentally responsible and climate-resilient designs, and effective institutional coordination.

India has already demonstrated the technical feasibility of floating solar at the MW scale. PM-SSY now provides an opportunity to build on this experience and make it a significant part of India’s renewable portfolio, while making better use of water resources and easing pressure on land.
The author is the sector coordinator for renewables and energy conservation at the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP), a research-based think-tank.

title: Different cobras have distinct venoms. How a new antivenom could treat them all

content.value: In a recent breakthrough, scientists from IISc Bengaluru’s Centre for Ecological Sciences (CES) and the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) have created an antivenom that could potentially be used to treat snakebites from the diverse cobra species of India. The scientists published their discoveries in the journal Science Translational Medicine, in a research paper titled “Oligoclonal nanobody-based recombinant antivenom protects mice challenged with venom from cobras and king cobras from India”, last month.
We explain how different cobra venoms affect humans, the challenges in treating snakebites, and how the CES-DTU collaboration developed the new antivenom.
What is the effect of various cobra venoms, and what are the challenges in treatment?

While there are many species of cobra in India, they generally kill their prey using “neurotoxins” in their venom that paralyse their prey and stop them from breathing. Cardiac issues and other side effects have been observed in some cases of attacks on humans.

In 2024, a Union Health Ministry statement had estimated the annual snakebite fatalities at 50,000. The spectacled cobra (Naja naja), one of India’s “Big Four” venomous snake species (the others being the common krait, the Russell’s viper, and the saw-scaled viper), accounts for at least 12.5% of these snakebite deaths — this number could be higher, as the snake is not always identified by the victim.

But it is just one of several cobra species in India — different species have different kinds of venom. In fact, venom from the same kind of cobra might vary in composition for cobras from different locations.

This poses a challenge when using antivenom. For example, while the Polyvalent antivenom is used in India to counter the venom of the Big Four snakes including the spectacled cobra, this would not have an effect in the case of king cobra venom. Even amongst king cobras, an antivenom developed for Thai cobras might not work on Indian king cobras.
Treatment is also complicated by the fact that rural victims often do not reach healthcare centres in time, or end up at centres which may not have the required antivenom.
According to Kartik Sunagar, an associate professor at CES who is part of the collaborative effort, antivenom treatment has essentially remained the same for the past century.
How was the new antivenom developed?

Previously, Danish scientist Andreas Laustsen and his colleagues at DTU had tested a new method on certain African snakes. They took the blood of domesticated animals such as alpacas and llamas, which had been exposed to the venom of these snakes.

Then, they extracted the antibodies that were formed. According to an IISc statement, the Danes “displayed the antibodies on bacteriophages, exposed them to venom from various snake species, and isolated specific antibody fragments that could bind to and neutralise the toxins in the venom”. A bacteriophage, also called a phage, refers to a virus that infects and replicates within bacteria.

A similar process was applied to create an “antibody cocktail” from India’s different cobra species. This was then tested on mice, which had been injected with venom from spectacled cobras, monocled cobras, and two species of king cobras. Even 30 minutes after venom injection, the antibody cocktail was able to save the test mice from death.
How could the discovery be applied in the future?

Previously, such use of antibodies to counter venom in mice tests required a large amount of antibodies, which might mean that a huge dose would be needed for humans. But the current research, Sunagar said, “showed that it is possible to neutralise venom using very small amounts of carefully selected and engineered antibodies”. This could potentially help address some of the cost and safety concerns associated with administering large quantities of antibodies, he added.

Further, such a method could be used to create cures for snakebite venom of species across the world. The IISc statement quoted Laustsen as saying, “This work provides a blueprint for how recombinant antivenoms can be tailored to different regions of the world by targeting the toxin families that drive disease in local snake species.”

title: Who keeps the internet running, and what happens when they can no longer afford to? An expert explains

content.value: When two critical security flaws in PHP, a programming language used by millions of websites, prompted organisations around the world to take services offline in October, Czech software engineer Ondřej Surý was among the maintainers who helped get the fixes to users.

The flaws, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, led to precautionary shutdowns on October 21 of services run by Japan’s Finance Ministry, US human-resources platform BambooHR, the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands, and the Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia.

Surý maintains widely used PHP software packages for Debian and Ubuntu, two Linux-based operating systems. He made patched versions available even for older releases of PHP that no longer receive official security updates.

Surý does much of this maintenance alongside his full-time job as Director of DNS Engineering at the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC), which develops software that helps translate website addresses into the numerical addresses computers use to communicate over the internet. He told The Indian Express that ISC had seen a sharp spike in vulnerability reports this year, although relatively few were serious. As AI tools make it easier to identify potential security flaws, assessing and fixing them still requires human expertise.

The experience raises a larger question about the sustainability of open-source software, whose underlying code is freely available for others to use, modify and distribute, and on which much of the internet depends. In an interview with The Indian Express, Surý discusses the PHP2Shell incident, the growing demands of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, and why he believes businesses that profit from open-source software must help fund its maintenance. Edited excerpts:
Why does PHP matter to the functioning of the internet, and what made the recent PHP2Shell vulnerabilities particularly serious?

PHP is a programming language mainly used to develop websites. Roughly 70% of the web is powered by PHP. The recently discovered vulnerabilities in PHP were in the most serious category, remote code execution (RCE). In short, an attacker can exploit such a vulnerability to execute a program of their own choosing on a remote machine, potentially gaining full access to the server (the computer running the website or service).

When researchers discover a serious security flaw in widely used software, what happens next? Who develops the fix, who ensures it reaches users, and which parts of this process still depend heavily on human work?

When ethical security researchers discover a serious security flaw, they contact the affected project or organisation privately. Any project or organisation that cares about security should have a mechanism through which researchers can report flaws in its software.

Fixing the vulnerability is usually no different from fixing any other defect in the software, but the process depends on the size of the project. The work could fall to a single person in a small project or a handful of people in a larger one. They might or might not be employed to do this work.

In the case of PHP, there are a handful of volunteers for whom this is a side project, and very few people are employed directly by the PHP Foundation. Most of the important work still depends on people. As for when and how AI is used, it is important to remember that AI is just a tool that might or might not be useful in specific cases.
How did the early disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities affect the release of security updates?

That was unfortunate because people who knew the original release schedule had made plans to properly release the software so that users could upgrade. The premature disclosure accelerated the whole process by a day.

Now, this is the bad part about AI: once details of the upcoming vulnerabilities were known, people started using AI to search for possible security flaws. It was no longer safe to stick to the original schedule because AI, as a tool, is quite good at finding security vulnerabilities, especially when guided by a skilled person.

AI tools are increasingly being used to discover vulnerabilities in software. Have you noticed any change in the number or complexity of vulnerability reports you receive, or in the work required to respond to them?

In my day job, I am the Director of DNS Engineering at ISC, responsible for BIND 9, a widely used open-source DNS server. There was a sharp spike this year in the frequency and depth of the vulnerability reports we received.
Fortunately, after the initial surge, things went back to normal. We still receive occasional security reports, but only very few of them are serious enough to be handled as security vulnerabilities.

That is the thing with AI: it needs to be guided by an expert with domain knowledge. Otherwise, you often end up with serious-sounding reports about ordinary software bugs, or issues that are not even bugs.
Could AI also help maintainers identify security vulnerabilities themselves?

Not only that, maintainers can also use frontier AI models to find security vulnerabilities themselves. That said, both offensive (finding and exploiting vulnerabilities) and defensive (finding and fixing vulnerabilities) uses of AI need to be supervised by an expert. Otherwise, you might end up with a pile of mediocre-quality reports or, worse, AI might miss something serious.

You’ve spoken about the difficulty of sustaining open-source maintenance. Why does so much essential software depend on the work of relatively few people, and what would it take to support them adequately?

When I joined university in 1995, free software was still very new, at least to me, and I found a purpose in making the fruits of my work freely available to others. It was a paradigm change, and I believe many people involved in the free-software movement are still driven by those ideals.
On the other hand, some people have built multibillion-dollar enterprises on top of open-source software and never even thought about supporting the software that allowed them to make money.

I think we need to find a balance. The free-software model is viable because it gives me and other developers freedom. On the other hand, if many people depend on that software for their livelihoods, we need a sustainable model that allows maintainers to continue working on the software they love without becoming exploited and exhausted.
Who should be responsible for funding the maintenance of open-source software?

That question can easily be turned around: if the people maintaining the open-source software your company uses were to simply walk away, how large would your losses be in the event of a serious security vulnerability like the recent one in PHP? This should give people running businesses the answer to who should fund the work.
Not every open-source project has an organisation, whether for-profit or non-profit, behind it, but some do.

For instance, Software in the Public Interest is a non-profit organisation that provides financial and administrative support to projects such as Debian. Smaller projects can raise funds through platforms such as Open Collective, while PHP development receives funding through the PHP Foundation.

My PHP packaging work can be supported through Freexian’s PHP Long Term Support (PHP LTS) project, which provides maintenance and security updates for older PHP releases, or through GitHub Sponsors, which allows individuals and organisations to fund developers directly.
At my day job, the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) offers paid professional support for open-source projects such as BIND 9 and Kea, among other projects I am closely associated with.

title: How India’s new IST rules aim to put the country on one clock

content.value: The Union Consumer Affairs Ministry on August 27 notified new rules that make Indian Standard Time (IST) the legally enforceable reference for official and commercial use. The Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026 now require time-dependent systems in government and critical sectors to use a “traceable”, authorised IST reference, with 180 days for compliance.
But India has already followed IST for decades. Why were the new rules needed and what changes with them?

People obtain time from many sources, often indirectly from GPS. A telecom provider provides the time maintained in its data centre, but there may be a lag of seconds or even minutes as people and organisations refer to different sources.

“It is like each person establishing their own starting point; you then cannot properly compare events or measurements,” said Poonam Arora, Head of the Time & Frequency Metrology Division at the Council Of Scientific And Industrial Research (CSIR)-National Physical Laboratory.
What do the new rules do?

The Department of Legal Metrology enforces measurements such as mass and volume. Inspectors can check the gauges at a petrol pump or verify the weights used by an establishment. They did not have an equivalent capability for time — until now.
The new rules seek to give time a legal status and make it comparable to these physical measurements.

The broader purpose of the new rules, that call for “traceability”, is to make IST the country’s common legal time reference for commercial and other purposes, including the display of time. “This can also improve cybersecurity, reduce crime and make critical infrastructure more resilient,” said Arora.
In the context of time, traceability means showing that a clock or time source is ultimately linked to IST maintained by NPL.
Who maintains time in the country?
The CSIR-NPL is mandated to maintain the country’s scientific standards, such as mass and volume. Maintaining (or “realising”) and disseminating IST is also part of its mandate.

A bank of extremely precise atomic clocks helps the NPL maintain the country’s time within a few nanoseconds of the international reference, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). According to the NPL website, these clocks are so accurate that they would lose or gain one second in about three lakh years.
“IST is a registered trademark of CSIR-NPL,” Arora said. “The NPL maintains UTC (NPLI), India’s realisation of UTC. Indian Standard Time is UTC (NPLI) plus five hours and 30 minutes.”
How is time ‘disseminated’?
Dissemination of time essentially refers to the transmission of the “realised” time scale across physical distances to external users and systems. There are different methods, with varying accuracy.
Your phone, for instance, shows you time indirectly derived from GPS.

Computers use network protocols, which synchronise the clocks of computers and devices over a network. The most common and accessible method — essentially how your computer shows you time — is a Network Time Protocol (NTP) server. The default server may be abroad, so it is not directly providing you the IST.
For more demanding applications, satellite links are used for highly precise time transfer. Given its strategic importance, ISRO has to be traceable to IST within nanoseconds.

Some Regional Reference Standards Laboratories now maintain secondary time scales traceable to IST, while ISRO also gets traceability from NPL, allowing IST to be disseminated from multiple locations, said Arora.

Traceability can be established through different technologies. NPL has an NTP service with a domain name. If you synchronise your computer with it, your computer becomes traceable to Indian Standard Time, said Arora.
In July 2026, the Union Consumer Affairs Ministry commissioned a White Rabbit Technology-based IST Dissemination Demonstration Network at the RRSL in Bengaluru.
White Rabbit is an open-source networking technology designed to synchronise computer clocks over fibre-optic networks.

Simply put, it sends a timing signal through a fibre-optic cable and measures how long the signal takes to reach another computer. Because that travel time can vary slightly, White Rabbit measures the delay and adjusts for it, allowing clocks in different locations to stay synchronised.
Who needs precise synchronisation?

Systems across multiple organisations — banks, telecommunications, power grids and even defence systems — need to coordinate. A unified time source helps establish the sequence of events, coordinate activities across locations and reconstruct failures, transactions or cyber incidents.
“At the very least, an organisation should be able to show that its systems are synchronised with IST,” Arora said.
The requirement is not only about display. There must also be synchronisation, so that the seconds start at the same time across applications and sectors.

Financial markets already operate under precise clock-synchronisation requirements. Since 2013, SEBI has directed stock exchanges to synchronise their system clocks with atomic clocks before the start of the market so that their clocks have precision of at least one microsecond and accuracy of at least +/- one millisecond.

This precision matters because financial systems can generate and process orders in fractions of a second. Accurate timestamps help establish the sequence in which orders and trades happened and can be important when regulators investigate unusual activity or disputes.
What changes for you?

Very little changes for the ordinary user. Arora noted that such changes would travel downstream as service providers comply with the rules, meaning the time supplied automatically to your device would be traceable to IST.

“Unless you have a business, you are unlikely to face any immediate requirement. But accurate time can matter if investigators or a court need to reconstruct events, for example in a fraud investigation,” Arora said.
Why is India now pushing for domestic timing infrastructure?
The push for IST uniformity comes along with India’s efforts to reduce its reliance on external satellite navigation systems and their timing signals.

Arora noted that most people currently obtain time through GPS, which the US owns and controls. A decision by the US to degrade or deny access to its services, as it did to India during the Kargil War, could pose a problem. That episode pushed India to build the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS) or NavIC, providing regional satellite-navigation coverage over India.

Alongside this, terrestrial systems such as White Rabbit can distribute IST over fibre-optic networks. Together, these give India more than one domestic route to provide precise time to critical infrastructure.

title: How hackers took control of supermarket fridges across Europe, and what it means for India’s cold chain

content.value: Overnight on October 11–12, hackers took control of refrigeration systems at around 700 retail sites in France, including stores run by Carrefour and Intermarché. They turned up the temperature settings used to melt ice off the cooling coils, causing food to spoil and starting at least 15 fires, according to France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI.

A second wave of such attacks followed in early November, affecting stores in eight European countries, including Belgium, Sweden and Ireland, and forcing retailers to throw away large quantities of food. Separately, an attack on a refrigeration equipment supplier affected the systems that monitor and control temperatures at three sites of France’s national blood service. Its alarm systems alerted staff, who moved the blood products before any were lost.

On November 9, France accused Shahid Kaveh, a unit linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), of orchestrating the October attacks, a charge Iran has denied. Authorities have not established that the subsequent incidents were carried out by the same group.

Refrigeration keeps food and medical supplies at safe temperatures as they are stored, transported and distributed. That temperature-controlled system is known as the cold chain. Connecting cooling equipment to the internet lets operators check temperatures, spot faults and adjust settings remotely. The attacks showed what can happen when someone else gains access to those controls.
First, how do cold storage systems work?

A cold-storage facility is a large, insulated refrigerator, often divided into rooms maintained at different temperatures depending on what is stored inside. Its insulated walls slow the entry of heat from outside, while refrigeration equipment continuously removes the heat that gets in. This preserves everything from fresh fruits and vegetables to frozen food, vaccines and blood products.
But how does a refrigerator actually cool a room?

It uses a refrigerant, a substance that circulates through pipes and changes between liquid and gas. As it passes through cooling coils inside the storage area, it absorbs heat from the surrounding air. A compressor raises the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant, which then releases heat through a second set of coils outside the cooled space.

Maintaining the required temperature involves constant monitoring. Sensors measure the temperature and send readings to an electronic controller. In industrial facilities, this may be a programmable logic controller (PLC), a rugged industrial computer that sends instructions to equipment such as compressors, fans and pumps.

For instance, when a loading door opens and warmer air enters, the sensors detect the resulting temperature change. The controller can then adjust the cooling equipment to bring the room back to the required temperature. It also manages defrost cycles, during which ice accumulated on the cooling coils is periodically melted. Without this process, ice can obstruct airflow and reduce cooling efficiency.
So, why connect refrigerators to the internet?

Traditionally, staff checked and recorded temperatures by hand. Connecting refrigerators to the internet allows businesses to monitor their performance remotely and manage several facilities through a single system.

“Businesses connect refrigerators to the internet to monitor temperatures and equipment performance in real time, receive alerts before stock spoils, diagnose faults remotely and manage many sites from one system,” Sandeep Kachhawa, an energy efficiency researcher, told The Indian Express.
Such equipment is part of the Internet of Things (IoT), where physical devices, including sensors and controllers, exchange information over a network.

Connected systems “also allow authorised staff or service providers to adjust temperature settings, alarm thresholds or defrost cycles remotely,” Kachhawa said “This improves response times, but creates a cyber risk if the controller is poorly secured.”
How can a cyberattack disrupt refrigeration?

Refrigeration controllers can become vulnerable when they are directly exposed to the internet or accessed through poorly secured remote connections. Attackers can identify such equipment online and attempt to gain access using weak or default passwords, or exploit vulnerabilities in outdated software.

“Many legacy systems used in Pharma, hospitals and industrial cold chains may have internet connectivity to enable monitoring and remote access so suppliers can undertake remote diagnostics,” Arun Rajagopal, principal consultant and managing partner at Cyber Forte UK, told The Indian Express.

Such connections could also allow attackers to move from an organisation’s corporate network into the systems controlling its physical equipment. “Time and time again, past security incidents have shown how easy it is for an attacker to pivot from Corporate IT Networks to OT or Industrial Environments,” Rajagopal said.

The risks are compounded by the long lifespan of industrial equipment. Xavier Bellekens, CEO of cybersecurity firm Lupovis, pointed out that while laptops might be replaced every three to five years, refrigeration equipment can remain operational for 15–20 years, sometimes long after manufacturers stop providing software security updates.
“The equipment may still work perfectly from a mechanical perspective, even though its software is outdated and its manufacturer no longer provides security updates,” he said.

Lupovis observed suspicious activity against its simulated Danfoss refrigeration controllers, known as honeypots, between October 20 and 30, following the first wave of attacks in France. These systems replicate real equipment, allowing researchers to observe attackers without exposing actual facilities.

“Over this ten-day period, we identified more than 250 attempts from 91 distinct sources, with activity peaking on 26 October,” Bellekens told The Indian Express. The attackers attempted to log in using default credentials and probed the controllers for vulnerabilities.

Bellekens had earlier told POLITICO that the activity could be linked to a Russian state-sponsored group, citing infrastructure previously associated with Russian hackers. Russia has denied involvement.
“We believe this activity may represent preparation for the second wave, but definitive attribution would require further investigation,” Bellekens told The Indian Express.
What could an attack mean for food supplies?

Farmers could lose income if their produce spoils or buyers cannot collect it. Food processors, retailers and logistics companies could face stock losses and supply delays, while consumers could experience shortages or higher prices.

“An attack on an individual facility would be unlikely to cause a nationwide food crisis, but disruption to a major distribution hub could affect supplies across several cities or regions,” Kachhawa said.

“If several facilities use the same refrigeration controls and automation vendor, a security weakness could affect multiple sites. This could turn a problem at one supplier or platform into a wider disruption,” he added. However, he cautioned that using the same technology does not automatically make every facility vulnerable; the security of the systems and their remote connections matters.
What does this mean for India’s cold chain?

India had 8,831 cold-storage facilities with a combined capacity of about 40.3 million metric tonnes, the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare said in a response to a Rajya Sabha question on February 6, 2026.
As these facilities adopt more automated and remotely monitored systems, they could also become exposed to the vulnerabilities seen in Europe.

In India, the risk is likely to be concentrated in cold-chain facilities that use internet-connected refrigeration controls, remote monitoring and external vendor access, Kachhawa said. These include organised retail chains, dairy chilling facilities, pharmaceutical warehouses, vaccine storage centres and large distribution hubs. Refrigerated transport may also be vulnerable where trucks use connected temperature-monitoring and fleet-management systems.

The exposure, however, is not uniform. Traditional potato cold storage facilities are less exposed to remote cyberattacks because most of their equipment is locally controlled and not connected to external networks, Kachhawa said.
Who is responsible for keeping these systems safe?

According to Arun Rajagopal, securing connected refrigeration systems is a shared responsibility, involving equipment manufacturers, software providers, maintenance contractors and the businesses operating them.

“This is a shared responsibility between product manufacturers, system integrators and asset owners and operators,” Rajagopal said. He pointed to network and information security rules in the UK and EU for operators, and to the EU Cyber Resilience Act’s requirements for product suppliers.
Manufacturers are responsible for secure equipment and software updates, while operators must monitor which devices are connected and who can access them.

For older equipment that no longer receives security updates, Bellekens said operators need additional protections rather than necessarily replacing entire refrigeration installations. “However, it must recognise that the controller presents a risk and restrict access to it accordingly.”
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

India is also encouraging greater automation in cold-chain infrastructure. The National Centre for Cold-chain Development’s (NCCD) Engineering Guidelines & Minimum System Standards (2025) encourage IoT-based monitoring, remote control and unified control systems for facilities supported under central government schemes.

However, Kachhawa said the guidelines do not appear to specify detailed cybersecurity requirements for these connected systems, including secure remote access, network separation, user authentication and software updates.

Separately, CERT-In’s May 2026 cybersecurity blueprint identifies operational technology (OT), which controls physical equipment, and cyber-physical systems as areas requiring protection. Its recommendations include restricting remote access, monitoring third-party vendors and managing supply-chain risks.
What should operators do? Rajagopal stressed the importance of strong passwords, multi-factor authentication and keeping critical controllers off the public internet.
“Cybersecurity and safety trumps operational flexibility,” he said.
Kachhawa also recommended independent temperature sensors and alarms, alongside procedures for manually monitoring temperatures and moving products if automated controls fail.
The French blood-service incident demonstrated why such precautions matter: its alarms detected abnormal temperature changes, allowing staff to move blood products before they were lost.

At the policy level, Kachhawa called for cybersecurity requirements to be incorporated into cold-chain infrastructure standards and government funding conditions, alongside regular assessments of facilities storing essential food and medical products.

title: India may end social media’s legal shield: What happens to Meta, Instagram, X?

content.value: Social media platforms decide what billions of people see online, amplify some posts over others through their algorithms, and enforce their own rules on what content is permissible. Yet, when it comes to legal responsibility for that content, they are largely treated as passive carriers of information. This distinction, which has helped companies such as Meta, Google and X build vast businesses, is now coming under scrutiny in India.

The Centre has begun preliminary discussions on whether social media companies such as Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and X should continue to enjoy legal protection from liability for content posted by their users, The Indian Express has reported. The deliberations, which are still at an exploratory stage, could eventually lead to a rethink of one of the most important legal provisions governing the internet in India.

At issue is the principle of “safe harbour”, which has allowed social media companies to host enormous volumes of user-generated content without being treated as the publishers of every post, video or comment appearing on their platforms.

A section of the government has questioned whether companies that use algorithms to determine the visibility and reach of content should continue to receive the same protections as services that merely transmit information. No decision has been taken, and it remains unclear whether these discussions will translate into a formal legislative proposal.

On Friday (November 6), IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw did not conclusively confirm or deny whether the government was considering withdrawing safe harbour protections for social media platforms, but stressed that such companies must take greater responsibility for preventing online harms.

“Today, social media platforms must take the responsibility for child safety, for women’s safety, for digital arrest, for the harms which come to the citizens… social media platforms must take proactive steps. Unlike the past, they must take proactive steps to make sure that our society is safe,” Vaishnaw said.
Why is safe harbour important for social media companies?

Section 79 of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000 provides conditional immunity to internet intermediaries from legal liability arising from information published or transmitted by third parties.

Under the provision, an intermediary can claim this protection if it does not initiate a transmission, select its recipient or select or modify the information being transmitted. It must also comply with prescribed due diligence obligations. The protection is not absolute, and intermediaries can lose it in specified circumstances, including involvement in unlawful activity or failure to act on legally valid directions concerning unlawful content.

In its landmark 2015 Shreya Singhal judgment, the Supreme Court clarified that the obligation to remove unlawful content under Section 79(3)(b) must be linked to a court order or appropriate government notification, consistent with constitutional restrictions on free speech.

Safe harbour is arguably among the most consequential legal protections underpinning the modern internet. Without it, platforms could potentially face legal proceedings over millions of posts made by users, even when the companies themselves did not create the content.

For companies such as Meta and Google, this protection has been fundamental to building businesses based on user-generated content at an enormous scale, while avoiding the liability traditionally associated with publishers exercising editorial control over material.
The central question emerging within sections of the government is whether today’s social media companies can still be described as neutral intermediaries.

Unlike internet service providers or telecom operators, social media platforms use recommendation systems to prioritise content, promote particular posts and determine what individual users encounter. They also enforce their own community standards, which may differ from requirements under Indian law.
One line of thinking being explored is whether safe harbour should be confined to relatively passive services, such as internet and telecom providers or certain peer-to-peer messaging services.
However, this remains a preliminary consideration, and a broad withdrawal of statutory protection from social media platforms would likely require amendments to the IT Act and parliamentary approval.
What developments have led to these discussions?
Several developments over recent months have brought intermediary liability into sharper focus.

In August, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), under the Home Ministry, submitted a status report before the Supreme Court during proceedings concerning digital arrest scams. Records of an inter-departmental committee meeting indicated that the government was examining a review of safe harbour protections and the possibility of explicitly holding intermediaries liable for misuse of their services, including through a victim-compensation mechanism.

Another flashpoint involved Meta. In July, Facebook temporarily withheld a video posted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi during nationwide student protests. The IT Ministry subsequently summoned senior Meta executives, including global affairs president Joel Kaplan, amid concerns over content moderation and compliance with Indian laws.

In August, BJP MP Nishikant Dubey, who chairs Parliament’s Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology, called for action against Meta and warned that safe harbour protection could be withdrawn. A communication from the parliamentary panel to the IT Ministry also sought accountability over the incident.

Separately, the Supreme Court, in an October 15 order concerning online child sexual abuse material, raised questions about the adequacy of Section 79’s existing framework. The court favoured proportionate penalties for violations, with withdrawal of safe harbour remaining an exceptional measure.
What could removing safe harbour mean for free speech?
Digital rights organisations have warned that weakening intermediary immunity could encourage platforms to remove content excessively to minimise their legal exposure.
The Delhi-based digital rights group, Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), has argued that greater intermediary liability can create a chilling effect on freedom of expression.

“Safe harbour is not a gift to Meta, Google or X. It is the legal foundation that lets ordinary Indians speak online without a platform’s lawyers deciding in advance whether their post is worth the risk and taking it down. If it is taken away, and every platform becomes liable for every post, comment and video. The rational response for any company is to remove anything that might draw a complaint, a notice or a summons,” IFF said in a post on social media platform X.

“Criticism of the government, reporting on protests, satire, and the speech of people without lawyers will be the first casualties which are already being censored by automated filters implemented pursuant to the IT Rules, 2021. The Supreme Court recognised exactly this in Shreya Singhal (2015), which is why it read down Section 79(3)(b) to require a court order or a lawful government direction before platforms must act,” it added.

title: Why a solar eclipse is the best time to study the ‘invisible’ part of the Sun

content.value: Europe is witnessing its first total solar eclipse in 27 years on Wednesday.

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth, blocking out some or all of the star’s light. The latter phenomenon happens during a total solar eclipse. It is a rare occurrence, requiring the Sun, the Moon and the Earth to line-up perfectly in space.
While not all of Europe will experience “totality” — the phase when the Moon completely covers the Sun’s surface — large parts of the continent will still experience near night-like conditions.
A solar eclipse also happens to be the best time for scientists to study the Sun. Here’s what they study at that time — and how they do it.
First, where is the total eclipse visible today?
The August 12 total solar eclipse is not visible from any location in India.
The total eclipse can be seen along the north of Russia, Greenland, west Iceland, northern Spain and a small area along northeast Portugal.
Together, these locations form the “path of totality” — the narrow strip on the Earth’s surface where the Moon can be seen completely blocking the Sun.
Large parts of the continent will witness a partial solar eclipse — most UK residents, for instance, will be able to see more than 90% of the Sun being covered by the Moon.
Outside of Europe, the partial eclipse would be visible over North America and northwest Africa.
The total solar eclipse is expected to last for two minutes and 18 seconds, occurring over Látrabjarg, Iceland.
In any total solar eclipse, the duration of “totality” is the longest near the centre of the path of totality widthwise and diminishes towards the edges.
Why do scientists need to study the Sun?

For scientists, observing the Sun’s corona and the inner corona is crucial. The corona’s magnetic field triggers solar flares and “coronal mass ejections”, which can disrupt satellites, GPS and other communication systems on Earth.
The corona is the Sun’s outermost atmosphere, extending millions of kilometres into space. The inner corona is the part of the Sun’s outer atmosphere that is closest to the star’s surface.

However, it is extremely faint. To study it, scientists need to block the solar disc artificially using an instrument called a coronagraph, which is usually placed on solar probes or missions. On many occasions, however, these instruments are affected by scattered light — making it impossible to observe the inner corona.
This is where an eclipse comes in.
How does a solar eclipse help in this study?
During a total solar eclipse, the Moon completely blocks the solar disc, making the inner corona visible in the form of a halo around the lunar body.
This provides helio-physicists with a valuable window to make ground-based observations of the solar atmosphere.

“When an eclipse happens, the bright inner disk gets blocked and the fainter outer atmosphere gets revealed, which is the solar corona. The eclipse thus gives us clues to the underlying magnetic structure of the Sun’s corona,” Dibyendu Nandi, an astrophysicist from the Raman Research Institute, told The Indian Express.

Another factor to consider is the solar cycle — the roughly 11-year cycle during which the Sun’s activity rises and falls, marked by changes in the number of sunspots, solar flares and other activity.
In the current solar cycle, which began in 2020, the Sun has already passed its maxima phase — the period when it is most active and when more structures in the inner corona are likely to be visible.
Owing to these reasons, scientists plan multiple experiments and solar observations during total solar eclipses, particularly from the location where the maximum eclipse is expected.
What can scientists observe during the total solar eclipse ?

During the eclipse, an Indian group of researchers at Centre of Excellence for Space Science India (CESSI), IISER-Kolkata, has predicted the possibility of spotting multiple large-scale streamers, which are petal-like structures.

“These are nothing but bright magnetic field structures rooted to the solar surface. There is no other way to see the magnetic fields, because the Sun’s disc is bright. During a natural eclipse, it is possible to see the Sun’s corona from the ground, too,” Nandi said.
If these magnetic field structures are spotted during the event, scientists expect them to be highly complex and spectacular.

title: Elon Musk says Starlink to serve rural India: Why its launch faces delays

content.value: Billionaire Elon Musk said on Friday (August 21) that his satellite communications company Starlink would help connectivity of Indians in rural areas, even as the service awaits formal launch, a year after securing necessary licences from the government.
“Starlink would help the least served in India, especially in rural areas,” Musk said in a post on X.

Musk’s Starlink is among the operators that have secured GMPCS (global mobile personal communication by satellite) licences and other statutory approvals needed to launch satellite communication, or satcom, services in the country. Others who have received it include Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Jio Satellite Communications Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of Jio Platforms. Jeff Bezos-owned Amazon Leo is also in contention for a licence.
Here’s why Starlink’s formal launch is facing delays, how satcom services work, and what statutory guidelines govern these services.
Why the delay in Starlink’s India launch

Last July, Starlink had received what industry executives said was the last regulatory approval needed to launch the service in India from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) granted authorisation to the satcom company for its satellite constellation. Before that, the company had received an operator licence from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), three years after first applying for one.
The Starlink Gen1 Constellation is a global constellation with 4,408 satellites orbiting earth in altitude varying between 540-570 km, capable of providing around 600 Gbps throughput over India.

Despite the regulatory clearance, it is understood the government is yet to green-light formal launch of these services over security concerns. The concern particularly stems from anxieties around foreign satcom operators potentially bypassing Indian gateways to offer their services, an event when the government might lose control over the service.

In satellite communication, Indian gateways refer to Satellite Earth Station Gateways physically located within Indian territory that interface between space-based satellite constellations and domestic terrestrial telecom networks. All traffic originating or terminating in India must process entirely through these local ground facilities.
How satcom services work

Satellite communication services rely on an array of satellites in orbit to offer connectivity to homes and businesses on the ground. They are an alternative to ground-based communication, called terrestrial networks, such as cable, fibre, or digital subscriber line, and they don’t require wires to transmit data. Starlink operates the world’s largest satellite constellation, with around 7,000 satellites in orbit.

For end-users, satellite-based communication and broadband services offer benefits on two key points: wider coverage, and a more resilient network. Even though the latency of satcom services can at times be higher than terrestrial broadband networks, they can cover vast swathes of areas with very little physical equipment needing to be installed.
DoT guidelines for satcom companies

Last May, the DoT had released guidelines for satellite communication companies. The norms call for companies to set up local manufacturing, data localisation, use domestic navigation systems, implement a blocking mechanism, and cooperate with law enforcement agencies.

According to the guidelines, satcom companies will have to share with the government a year-wise phased manufacturing plan aiming at indigenisation to a level of at least 20% of their ground segment of the satellite network that is established at the end of five years after launching commercial operations.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

The companies should also ensure provisioning of NavIC-based positioning systems in their user terminals on “best effort basis,” along with a transition plan to implement NavIC in a time-bound manner by 2029. NavIC, or Navigation with Indian Constellation, is India’s regional satellite navigation system, similar to GPS, which is a global system developed by the US.

Companies will have to provide real-time monitoring to ensure that no user traffic originating from, or destined for India is being routed through any gateway outside Indian territory. They will also have to submit an undertaking that they will not copy and decrypt Indian telecom data outside India.

Operators would need to implement service restrictions to “any individual, group of subscribers or certain geographical areas” during “hostilities”, the guidelines said. These companies will have to seek separate clearance (“from security angle”) for voice service and data service. Satcom operators will also have to ensure that their data centres are based within the geographical boundary of India and shall make provision to provide Domain Name System resolution within its territory.

title: Why a flat map fails to accurately depict Earth

content.value: The United Nations has adopted a resolution to shift away from the 16th-century Mercator map of the world towards one that more accurately depicts Africa’s vast size.

At a UN General Assembly session, 164 countries (including India) voted to adopt the 2018 Equal Earth design — with the US voting against the Togo-led resolution, and six countries abstaining. Since UN resolutions are not binding, it remains to be seen if or when governments, organisations and classrooms adopt it.

The Mercator layout has been the world’s most widely used projection for centuries. But it has also long been criticised for exaggerating the size of regions towards the poles relative to those closer to the equator. The most infamous example of these distortions is its depiction of the African continent, which appears similar to Greenland — an island 14 times smaller and about the size of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The 2018 Equal Earth design, developed by an international team of cartographers, also comes with its own limitations. But its supporters say it will help reverse “colonial” perceptions of Africa.
No flat map can accurately portray the three-dimensional Earth. Every projection involves trade-offs, depending on its purpose.
How did the Mercator map come to be the most commonly used depiction of the world? And why is it so difficult to map the world?
The Earth is not a sphere
The first thing we need to understand is that the Earth is not a sphere, though it is sometimes treated as one to make mathematical calculations easier.

It bulges in the middle due to its spin, the Moon’s gravity warps it, and the continents and oceans distort the shape, said Maj Gen (Dr) Siva Kumar Rachapudi (retd), a scientist who has played a key role in promoting geospatial technologies across government, academia and industry for decades. This means the best way to represent Earth is a spheroid, which is a three-dimensional shape created from a two-dimensional ellipse, Siva Kumar, who has also been a senior official at the Department for Science and Technology, told The Indian Express.

But carrying a globe around is impractical. This brings us to projections. The term refers to the transformation of a three-dimensional space onto a two-dimensional map. There are many different types of projections. Some of them are:
– Conformal projections (which preserve angles)
– Equal-area projections (which preserve areas, such as the newly adopted map)
– Equidistant projections (which maintain distance)
– Compromise projections (which balances distortions in area, shape, distance and direction rather than preserving any one of them exactly)
We shall explain what the terms area, shape, distance and direction mean in cartography further ahead. For now, suffice it to say that the Mercator layout is a conformal projection.
The origins of the Mercator projection
The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish (present-day Belgium) geographer and mapmaker Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the world.
It is a conformal, cylindrical map. This means Mercator projected the Earth’s surface as if unwrapped from a cylinder around the globe.
“In the 18th century, it became the standard map projection for navigation due to its property of representing rhumb lines as straight lines,” said Siva Kumar.

So, if you drew a straight line from Mumbai to Muscat on a Mercator map, you could point your ship in the same compass direction throughout the journey and reach your destination. This was a major advantage over other map projections, where a constant-direction route would appear curved.
The Mercator’s colonial lens

The Mercator projection has a grid pattern with longitudes and latitudes at 90-degree angles. The longitudes (vertical lines) are evenly spaced, but the distances between the latitudes (horizontal lines) increase as one moves away from the equator towards the poles.

This is deliberate. “To preserve shapes, the ratio of increase in the length of the parallels is kept exactly the same with respect to the increase in the length of the meridians,” said Dr Bimal Kumar Kar, president of the Indian National Cartographic Association and former head of Gauhati University’s geography department.

The result is that Mercator projection inflates the size of lands the farther they are from the equator. “Therefore, landmasses such as Greenland and Antarctica appear far larger than they actually are relative to landmasses near the equator,” said Siva Kumar.

Mercator’s projection helped Western cartographers easily mark towns, cities, and roads in their part of the world. “Its popularity also lies in its ease of construction, since all parallels and meridians are straight lines,” said Kar.
This Western-centric view is what has come in for criticism.

“…if you’re a humanist well versed in European imperialism’s harsh imprint on the Third World, the traditional Greenwich-anchored world map becomes a clear example of Western cultural hegemony…” wrote cartography professor Mark Monmonier in his 2004 book Rhumb Lines and Map Wars: A Social History of the Mercator Projection.

“The standard projection was a political tool that contributed to the scramble for Africa, also known as the partition of Africa when Western European powers colonised the continent,” Rabah Arezki, former economist at the World Bank, wrote in Le Monde.
The search for a better map

Every flat representation of the Earth distorts at least one property: area (how large a landmass is relative to others), shape (the true outline and appearance of a country), distance (the actual space between two points) and direction (the correct compass bearing from one location to another).
The one you pick depends on your purpose: representing data, navigation or general reference. This is why, as Kar cautions, one should not directly compare one type of map with another.
Attempts to create other projections began centuries ago.

In 1855, Scottish clergyman James Gall presented a new projection. In 1973, German historian Arno Peters unveiled a very similar map which gained widespread attention. While it preserves area accurately, it makes landmasses look stretched or squashed. In 2017, schools in Boston introduced it.

In 1963, geographer Arthur H Robinson devised the Robinson projection which tried to better balance the sizes and shapes of land masses and sought to solve the “Greenland problem”. It’s a compromise projection (which we explained above), with meridians curving gently towards the poles.

In 1921, German cartographer Oswald Winkel devised the similar Winkel Tripel projection, seeking to reduce distortion across area, distance and direction. In 1998, it replaced the Robinson projection in world maps made by the National Geographic Society. Schools and textbooks followed, as did the World Bank. This is also a compromise projection.
The Equal Earth map

The Equal Earth map, developed in 2018, is an equal area projection (there are others, too) that seeks to preserve the relative areas of landmasses. It, too, somewhat distorts shapes and distances, with meridians curving gently towards the poles.

“The Mercator projection heavily exaggerates regions closer to the poles, which visually diminishes the perceived scale of developing regions in the Global South, including South Asia. Equal Earth fixes this imbalance,” said Siva Kumar.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

But is the new map an improvement over previous maps such as the Robinson and Winkel Tripel? Kar says: “To me, it’s nothing special. It has simply drawn attention by comparing itself with Mercator’s projection, which was designed for a different purpose.” But since it is an equal area map projection with limited shape distortion, it can be used by all categories of users, he said.

According to Siva Kumar, the Equal Earth map is best used to represent thematic and statistical data. “For classrooms and research, it provides a mathematically accurate depiction of area, which is vital for visualising population density, climate impacts, and resource distribution across the Indian subcontinent,” he said.
A World Bank spokesperson told Reuters that they already use the Winkel Tripel or Equal Earth for static maps and are phasing out Mercator on web maps.
Google Maps offers you the option of either using a Mercator or a 3D globe view on desktop. On the mobile app, however, the Mercator projection remains the default, Reuters reported.

title: 2026 Chemistry Nobel: Mirror-image molecules and the chemistry of life

content.value: Certain molecules exist in two forms, each a non-superimposable mirror image of the other — like the left and right hands of human beings. Chemically, the two forms are the same in the sense that they are composed of the same set of atoms, connected in the same order. The difference is only in the relative three-dimensional arrangement of those atoms, such that one happens to be the mirror image of the other.

This structural asymmetry, called chirality, becomes particularly interesting in biology. Many of the fundamental molecules in biology, like the amino acids that make up proteins or the sugars in DNA, appear in only one form. The mirror image versions of these amino acids or the sugars do exist, but they are rarely used in these biological settings. This preference for homochirality in life forms has intrigued scientists for long.
This year’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to two scientists, Henry Kagan and Kenso Soai, for demonstrating how this homochirality can emerge.

The normal chemical processes used to produce a chiral molecule results in the production of both forms, called enantiomers. Kagan developed a way of manipulating these processes in such a manner that one form was produced in much greater proportion than the other. Soai took a step further and designed the first chemical reaction in which only one of the enantiomers was produced. Outside of biological processes, such a result had never been achieved.
The first breakthrough

The propensity of biochemistry to prefer one particular enantiomer over the other was initially thought to be something unique for life forms. After all, when chiral molecules were produced in laboratories, a mixture of both enantiomers was obtained in almost even proportions. However, way back in the early 1900s, German chemist Willy Marckwald had been successful in carrying out a chemical reaction in which the proportion of the yields of the two enantiomers was slightly asymmetric.

Marckwald had used a catalyst — a chemical that speeds up the reaction without itself getting consumed into it — which itself was chiral. And this had led to one mirror-image form being produced more than the other.

However, subsequent attempts to increase the asymmetry in the yields of the two enantiomers remained unsuccessful. Besides, scientists still did not understand how the use of a chiral catalyst was affecting the reaction in a manner that one enantiomer was produced in greater quantity.

It was Kagan, working in the 1980s, who eventually answered these questions. Before him, it was believed that there was a linear relationship between the catalyst’s chirality and the proportion in which the two forms of the product were produced. In other words, if the catalyst itself contained a disproportionate amount of one form, this would get reflected in the proportions of the final product as well.

Kagan was able to show that this was not true, and that much greater asymmetry in production could be achieved even if the catalyst was only mildly chiral. In the process he was also able to demonstrate the internal dynamics of how this was happening.
The next step

This breakthrough created a new excitement in the field. While studying one of the chemical reactions that had produced one particular enantiomer in large quantities, Soai realised that there were significant similarities in the catalyst used and the final product. That prompted him to explore autocatalytic reactions — chemical reactions in which the final products themselves act as catalysts.

None of the autocatalytic reactions known at the time Soai started experimenting with them in the 1990s were known to produce asymmetric formation of enantiomers. After about a decade of trying, he finally succeeded in carrying out an autocatalytic reaction that resulted in the production of one particular enantiomer, which then formed copies of itself in a self-replicating process. The final product contained 99.5% of one enantiomer, a result comparable to the kind of preference seen in biological processes for a particular version of a chiral molecule.
Mysteries of life

The work of Kagan and Soai has demonstrated that homochirality can be obtained in the laboratory as well. It was not exclusive to nature. Their work does not solve the origin of the puzzle of life — how biological processes themselves preferred homochirality. But it did open up fresh avenues for scientists to try and understand the chemistry of life.
Possibly the biggest practical implication of their work has been in the pharmaceutical industry. Many drug molecules are chiral, and it matters immensely which particular enantiomer has to be used.
This is because the human bodies prefer only those enantiomers. The other variety of molecule might not just be ineffective, they can even be harmful.

Before this Nobel Prize-winning work showed how one single enantiomer could be produced, pharma companies had been manufacturing the drug molecules as a mixture of both enantiomers, and then the desirable enantiomer was separated through a separate process. This was an expensive, wasteful and often technically difficult way of achieving the final result.

The asymmetric synthesis of a particular enantiomer, as shown by Kagan and Soai, is already being used widely by the pharmaceutical industry. This is relevant for the manufacturing of all other substances that are meant to interact with living organisms, including flavours, fragrances and agricultural chemicals like pesticides.

title: Nobel Medicine Prize 2026: How three scientists discovered a way to control brain cells with light

content.value: The Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine for 2026 was jointly awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discovery of an algae protein that react to light and its use as a switch to study the functions of nerve cells.
Their explorations led to the creation of a new field of study called optogenetic, which may finally help scientists understand how the brain forms memories, feelings and behaviours.

“We were able to precisely pace the heart and look at the effects that different heart rates have on brain states… Communication across the body, from the body to the brain, but with the precision of a gain of function in a peripheral organ allowing us to see the effects on brain and behavioural state … this ability to execute a precision intervention in one organ and read out the effects in complex behaviours — this is something that people have wanted for a long time to be able to do,” said Deisseroth.

In simple terms, they found a way to control cells with light. Imagine that the brain is a vast electrical network containing billions of tiny cells called neurons. These neurons communicate by sending electrical signals, allowing us to move, see, remember, feel pain and experience emotions.

Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel helped scientists develop a remarkable way of controlling these electrical signals: using light. Their research led to the discovery and development of light-sensitive proteins, called opsins, that can be placed in specific cells. When light is shone on those cells, the proteins act like tiny switches, turning the cells’ activity on or off. This technology is known as optogenetics — essentially, using light to control genetically modified cells.
What is optogenetics?

It is basically a field of research that uses light to manipulate the activity of neurons or other types of cells and study the resulting effects. This is done by expressing the light-sensitive protein in the targeted cells. Within the brain, it has contributed towards identifying neural circuits responsible for sense of pain, social behaviours, thirst, food consumption, reward and attention or the understanding of how memories are created.
How did the discipline evolve?
Interestingly, the field rests on a theory proposed by Francis Crick, the molecular biologist who was behind the discovery of and was awarded the Nobel prize for the double helix structure of DNA.
He envisioned activating individual nerve cells in a brain to investigate the mechanisms that underlie human consciousness.

With nerve signals being extremely rapid, he realised it would only be possible if scientists were somehow able to manipulate the nerve cells with light. He himself admitted that the idea sounded far-fetched.

But it was made possible by the work of Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel on the alga Chlamydomonas. These are famous for their ability to quickly swim towards a light. Hegemann found that it reacted extremely quickly, within half a millisecond after the light reached a tiny orange dot called eyespot that the alga used to detect light. To compare, it takes 10 milliseconds for the human eye to react to light. Hegemann wondered how could the response to light be more than twenty times faster in Chlamydomonas?

He hypothesised that a single protein complex both captured light and acted on it in the alga as opposed to the multi-step process in the human eye. Yet, finding this protein was a challenge because when the proteins in the algal eyespot were removed from their natural setting, they became unstable and easily damaged. This is when he discovered that Japanese researchers had mapped the DNA of Chlamydomonas, among which were the codes for two genes that had similarities to light-capturing proteins.

Enter Nagel. He used egg cells of frogs to express the two proteins and confirm that Hegemann’s hypothesis was actually correct. The alga detected and reacted to light using the protein channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR-2). They then introduced the cells in different types of cells and found that they all became light sensitive.

Karl Deisseroth found that ChR-2 could control the activity of specific nerve cells in the manner proposed by Francis Crick. He used it to control rat nerve cells in a petri dish and later in the rats. With Deisseroth’s lab at the forefront, researchers soon found more proteins that can turn nerve cells on and off, and which are activated by different wavelengths of light.
How does it help to study the brain?

“Imagine the brain to be a building with lots and lots of rooms — now there was no way for us to know what happens if the light is switched on in just one room. Optogenetics has given us an extremely powerful way to switch on and off the neurons and see what happens. It has allowed us to manipulate nerve cells and study its effects with unprecedented level of precision. It has completely changed the scale at which discoveries are happening in neurosciences,” said Vidita Vaidya, senior professor at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research.

While optogenetics is still largely used in the laboratories to see which set of neurons regulate what type of behaviour in animals — it helps us look into the black box, she says — it is still ways away from therapies to help those with spinal cord paralysis.
Dr Sanjeev Kumar Mahto, professor at IIT BHU, said it has allowed scientists to see the functions of the brain and enhance the understanding of what causes certain conditions.

Deisseroth’s research group introduced the gene for ChR-2 in 2006 and successfully used a light to activate neurons to control movements of the mouse whiskers.The same year he used the technique to wake sleeping mice by manipulating a recently discovered type of nerve cell that was suspected to control wakefulness. His team also studied the brains of mice as they experienced fear, and noted which nerve cells appeared to form the memory. When they later reactivated these nerve cells, the mice showed signs of fear, despite not being in danger at the time.
What kind of therapies are being developed based on this field?

There are ongoing clinical trials on restoring vision in people who have become blind due to retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys the eye’s rods and cones. Using special glasses emitting light, the person was able to discern and grasp objects on a table. There are also hopes that optogenetics could improve cochlea implants. Currently, these implants stimulate the auditory nerve using electricity.

title: Microsoft offers voluntary exit to 60,000 employees: What it means for India staff

content.value: Microsoft, which employs around 23,000 people in India, has extended to the country a global voluntary exit programme covering approximately 60,000 employees. People in India working in roles across Copilot, AI experiences, Windows and Devices, Xbox, finance and human resources, could be impacted by the move.

Announcing the Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) on Monday (October 26), Microsoft said the scheme would be available to eligible employees at level 70 and below across participating teams in India, the US, the UK and Canada. Level 70 is an internal hierarchical structuring within Microsoft, and could cover employees with vice-president titles. While the company has not disclosed how many of its India-based employees would be eligible for the scheme, it hires Indians across software engineering, research and development, artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure, sales, customer support and corporate functions.

“This is a time-limited, voluntary programme that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organisations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs,” Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer, said in a blog post.

The development comes amid increasing concerns over AI-led disruptions to employment, particularly in the technology sector, where companies are deploying AI tools to automate tasks traditionally performed by human workers. Several major technology firms have announced workforce reductions, hiring slowdowns and organisational restructuring in recent months, with some explicitly citing productivity gains from AI. While the technology is creating demand for new skills and specialised roles, its growing adoption has also raised questions about the future of conventional software development, customer support and other white-collar jobs. Microsoft, however, has not explicitly attributed its latest voluntary exit programme to AI replacing human workers.
Impact on Microsoft’s Indian workers

Microsoft’s decision to offer voluntary exit packages to around 60,000 employees globally could also affect a section of its workforce in India, where the American technology giant employs approximately 23,000 people. A senior industry source said not all roles will be impacted, and those that receive an email from the company about their eligibility to participate in the voluntary exit scheme would have until December 1 to decide.

The programme will cover employees at Microsoft’s internal level 70 and below, including certain senior executives, but only in participating business divisions. It is understood that employees in divisions such as Copilot, AI experiences, Windows and Devices, Xbox, finance and human resources are among those eligible. This means that not all Microsoft employees in India will receive the offer, with eligibility depending on the business division to which they belong.

A significant part of Microsoft’s India operations is its India Development Center (IDC), one of the company’s largest research and development facilities outside its headquarters in Redmond, Washington. With operations in Hyderabad, Bengaluru and the National Capital Region, the centre develops technologies for Microsoft’s global businesses, including Windows, Azure, Microsoft 365 and AI products. Its Indian teams also contribute to Copilot Studio, Azure AI Search, AI agents, speech and translation technologies and machine learning platforms.

For Indian employees, the voluntary exit package is understood to be broadly similar to Microsoft’s standard severance arrangements, including one month’s base salary for every completed year of service, along with health insurance and career transition assistance. Eligible employees in India will have until December 1 to decide whether to accept the offer, with departures expected by the end of December. However, the company has not publicly specified how many employees in India it expects to take up the scheme.

The move comes as Microsoft seeks to reorganise its workforce while significantly increasing investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure, with the company stating that its India plans remain unchanged.

“Microsoft continues to invest in India’s talent and technology ecosystem and is backing the country’s AI ambitions with $20.5 billion in committed investment between 2025 and 2029 across cloud and AI infrastructure, skilling and operations. We are also on track to fulfil our commitment of equipping 20 million people across India with AI skills by 2030,” a Microsoft spokesperson said in a statement.

The programme could also have implications for Indian technology professionals employed by Microsoft in the US, particularly those working on H-1B visas. While the company has not clarified how the scheme would apply to foreign workers on temporary visas, employees choosing to exit without securing alternative employment could face immigration-related challenges. Unlike US citizens, H-1B visa holders are generally required to find another sponsoring employer, change their immigration status or leave the country within an applicable grace period, typically up to 60 days following termination of employment. These concerns come amid tightening US immigration regulations and greater scrutiny of employment-based visa and permanent residency programmes.
AI-led job disruptions

Microsoft’s move comes amid a broader restructuring of workforces across the global technology industry, with several companies either reducing their headcount or slowing hiring as AI tools take over tasks previously performed by employees. While some companies have explicitly linked job cuts to AI-driven productivity gains, others have cited the need to redirect resources towards AI investments and reorganise their operations.

One of the most prominent examples came in February 2026, when Block, the financial technology company founded by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, announced plans to cut more than 4,000 jobs, nearly half its workforce. Dorsey directly attributed the decision to improvements in AI tools, saying that smaller teams could now accomplish significantly more work. In September 2025, enterprise software company Salesforce disclosed that it had reduced its customer support workforce from around 9,000 to 5,000 employees as AI agents increasingly handled customer queries. CEO Marc Benioff said the company needed fewer people for these functions.

In India, home interiors platform Livspace laid off around 1,000 employees, or approximately 12% of its workforce, in February 2026 as it shifted towards an AI-led operating model. The Bengaluru-based company’s restructuring affected employees across design, sales, operations and marketing. Livspace said it was integrating AI agents and automation across these functions, reducing the need for certain manual roles. Earlier, in 2023, Indian e-commerce startup Dukaan had attracted controversy after its founder announced that the company had replaced 90% of its customer support team with an AI chatbot.

India’s larger IT services industry has also faced pressure to reorganise its traditional labour-intensive business model. In July 2025, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), India’s largest IT services company, announced plans to reduce its workforce by around 12,000 employees, primarily in middle and senior management positions. While the company cited skill mismatches and changes in business requirements, the announcement came amid increasing adoption of generative AI in software development, testing and maintenance. However, TCS did not directly attribute the job cuts to AI replacing workers.
