The spike in inflation has been such that it has robbed average US workers of any real earnings growth. Chart 4 shows the growth rate of earnings of US workers when adjusted for inflation. As the data shows, since the start of March, the growth rate of real earnings has turned negative every month.

Further, the government’s own debts have continued to grow to alarming levels, leading to investors demanding higher interest rates for lending money to the US government. That shift, in turn, has made loans costlier for the average American — in several cases the mortgage rates are higher by almost 50%.
In other words, things are costlier to buy with cash in their pockets and loans are costlier to finance. In real terms, most Americans are worse off than a year ago.
This explains the anger that many opinion polls are capturing notwithstanding a fast growing economy and a booming stock market.
Upshot

President Trump has never accepted that his policy choices are hurting American citizens. For months after taking charge, every time he was asked about the worsening economic state, he would blame his predecessor Joe Biden. In May last year, in an interview to NBC News, he even said that “the good parts are the Trump economy and the bad parts are the Biden economy”.

A key aspect of what distinguishes a democracy from a monarchy is the voter’s ability to force the government to be accountable, and the midterms are the American voter’s best chance to tell President Trump whether they are happy with his policy choices or would they like a change.
Do you think Trump’s Make America Great Again approach has worked for the US? Do you think other countries and leaders should learn from Trump and his approach?
Share your views and queries at udit.misra@expressindia.com
Take care,
Udit

title: France high school students’ protest: What sparked violence, what’s next

content.value: France Student Protests: Around 500 schools stayed shut across France on Monday (October 5), amid raging students’ protests. According to the French government, around 500 high schools, out of the country’s 3,700, are fully or partially closed.
The country’s education minister, Édouard Geffray, has announced a feedback programme for high school students, along with an action plan to quickly hire more teachers beginning today.

The protesters have blockaded schools, set fire to waste bins, and in some cases smashed furniture, doors and windows. According to French officials, damage across 40-odd schools is worth around €3million (Rs 32.5 crore).
Among the high school students’ complaints is that there are up to 40 students in a class.

The unrest has taken on political colours, coming around six months before the Presidential elections and coalescing with grievances across other sections of the public. On Tuesday, more protests by different unions are planned in support of the students.
What is the scale of the students’ protests in France?

The protests began on September 17 at the Saint-Exupéry high school in Créteil, a Paris suburb, where students joined teachers protesting a lack of staff and resources. They quickly spread through the Paris region and then to cities including Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours and Lille.

The demonstrations have increasingly involved fires, thrown projectiles and clashes with police. In some places, rubbish bins and other objects were set alight, while police used tear gas and rubber bullets.

The Education Ministry said 65 education staff, including 40 school principals, had been injured; students have also been injured. More than 4,000 people had been arrested since Monday, according to the Interior Ministry.
The government has said the students’ grievances are legitimate but that violence cannot be tolerated. Students, meanwhile, have accused police of using excessive force.
What do the protesting French high school students want?

The major grievances are overcrowded classrooms, fewer teachers, no nurses or social workers in some schools, and crumbling infrastructure. Inequality is also a factor, with students from poorer suburbs saying their address is impacting their education.

A French government report on education from April this year says, “During the 2024-2025 school year, 9.8% of teaching hours were not provided in public secondary schools, of which 7.5% was due to the non-replacement of absent teachers and 2.3% was due to the total closure of the establishment.”
The report adds that the “proportion of teaching time not provided increased by 0.7 points compared to the previous year due to a greater number of days of school closures.”
Some of the protesting students have said there are 40 of them packed in a classroom, when the average for French high schools is around 30 in a class.
The length of the school day is another complaint — French high school days can extend from 8 am to 5 pm, with a lunch break, which many say is too long.

The extreme heat wave France saw earlier this year has added another dimension. Students have complained about having to sit examinations in classrooms reaching 35°C to 40°C, while others said classrooms became unbearable during the heatwaves in May and June.

French public schools are often not air-conditioned and built to keep heat in rather than out, so 40°C in poorly ventilated classrooms for children not accustomed to such temperatures can feel difficult.
What is the political angle behind France school protests?
While in many schools, teachers have protested side by side students, in other cases, school staff have said the protesters are not from among their pupils.

This, the scale of the violence, and flags of Palestine and Algeria at some of the protests have led those on the right wing and even the centre to claim that the hard left party France Unbowed (LFI) is playing its part in the protests.

France will go to polls next year as the centrist government of Emmanuel Macron is under unprecedented stress from both the right and the left, over the issue of migration and identity politics on one hand and rising inequality and spending cuts by the government from the other.

While support for the hard right party National Rally led by Marine Le Pen has surged, the LFI’s presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is popular among the youth. However, the French youth often do not turn up to vote in large numbers. Some analysts believe that the LFI is fuelling the high school students’ protests to rally the youth and make them vote for it next year.

For the government, it is a tight spot. In its 2027 budget, education spending is set to rise by 1.7% to €65.53 billion, excluding teacher pensions — an increase below inflation. Now, it has to balance students’ demands while remaining committed to its programme of cutting government spending.

title: Rare shooting highlights Switzerland’s relationship with guns: High ownership, low violence

content.value: On August 30, an annual electronic music festival in Aarau, a canton in Northern Switzerland, was the site of a shooting which left a 22-year-old-woman dead and injured five people.

The music festival was hosted at the Schachen horse racing track in Aarau and local police said that all the victims of the shooting were in their 20s. The shooting happened later into the night when the crowd had thinned down. Maria Spinelli —an Italian national — succumbed to her injuries after being struck in the back by a bullet.

The perpetrators of the crime remain unidentified and preliminary investigations have indicated that the victims did not share any prior connection with one another. Aarau’s Police Commander has indicated that the end to this investigation is not yet in sight and a manhunt is currently being conducted.

The incident comes as a shock to the nation given the rarity of systemic mass shootings and gun-related violence in the country. Despite that, however, Switzerland still maintains one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in Europe. For a nation that has adopted a neutral stance, why is the civilian gun ownership rate so high and what is Switzerland’s relationship with guns? We Explain.
High gun ownership, low violence in Switzerland

Switzerland simultaneously maintains one of the lowest rates of gun-violence alongside a population that owns firearms. Geneva-based Small Arms Survey reported in 2017 that approximately 2.33 million civilian-held firearms were in circulation within a population of 8.4 million. This equates to a rate of 27.6 guns for every 100 residents.

This degree of civilian ownership is tied to the model of citizen-militia and reserve military service framework observed in the nation. Able-bodied Swiss nationals undergo mandatory conscription and retain their service weapons at home to ensure rapid national mobilisation in the event of a foreign aggressor.

Civilian armament for personal defence, however, is strictly regulated. Gun culture in the Alpine nation shares deeper ties with national defence and target sports than with the protection of personal freedoms. Historically, Switzerland has experienced very low rates of firearm related homicides which have hovered around 0.2 for every 100,00 residents. In contrast, the United States has an estimated 120.5 firearms per 100 residents with a homicide rate of approximately four to ten for every 100,000 residents.
Rules and regulations

Switzerland follows stringent regulations governing the acquisition and possession of weapons. Publicly carrying a firearms is essentially prohibited for citizens and the purchase of one requires a shall-issue permit that is accompanied by extensive criminal background checks. In 2007, a national reform banned the distribution of ‘Taschenmunition’ or pocket ammunition. This is a sealed tin of 50 cartridges that used to be kept with militiamen at home but was discontinued due to a series of high-profile homicides that employed service weapons.

Additionally, in 2019, Swiss voters overwhelmingly passed a referendum to tighten gun laws, restricting high-capacity semi-automatic weapons and improving the traceability of firearm components to comply with the European Union’s Schengen directives.

The last event of comparable shock was the Zug massacre on September 27, 2001. A lone gunman named Friedrich Leibacher who was armed with legally acquired weapons (including a SIG SG 550 and a pump-action shotgun), stormed the cantonal parliament, and killed 14 politicians before committing suicide.
Interestingly, the Aarau shooting now left behind cartridge casings that pointed to two different calibers of ammunition used. This complicates the profiling of the perpetrator(s) of this crime.
Containment

The Aarau canton police are evaluating terrorism, mass shooting and targeting criminal feuds as equally probable motives. The investigation is complicated due to a lack of information about the shooter and the motive.

The shooting took place a full thirty minutes after the music festival had wrapped up. Of an estimated 3,500 attendees, only about a 100 were still present. The perpetrator also escaped in a timely manner without engaging the police, which was the case in the 2001 Zug massacre. The use of heavy weaponry, multiple firing locations, and a clandestine escape aligns closely with organised criminal violence.

The entire constabulary of the Aarau police was mobilised and a manhunt remains underway. Specialised state assets like Argus special intervention unit and the Cantonal Disaster Response Element were also deployed. The Swiss army’s Super Puma helicopters are assisting with reconnaissance and monitoring escape routes up to 30 kilometers away.

Aarau’s location near the South German border has extended the investigation into neighboring areas and police from Freiburg, Germany are linked to this case. Cooperation relies on the Schengen information system (SIS), a large database used by European nations to share border security data.

title: Why Europe’s summer of reckoning has just begun

content.value: A dense, yellow-orange pall hung over Bordeaux on Sunday, blotting out the sun and blurring the spires of the cathedral in this French city. A swirl of tiny ash particles stung eyes and stuck in throats. Twenty miles west of town, a mammoth forest fire burned so ferociously that it generated its own weather system.

“We’ve never seen anything like it,” said Roger Peuron, 89, a retired engineer born before World War II who was driven out of his home by the approaching flames. He could have been speaking for millions of people across Europe.

Ravenous fires. Searing heat waves. Freakish storms. The summer of 2026 has already shattered meteorological records in several European countries. On a continent that has weathered centuries of upheaval — ruinous wars, deadly pandemics — it is the weather itself that now has Europe feeling close to a breaking point.

It has displaced more than 300,000 people in France and Spain, where the largest fires in those countries’ modern history have led to their largest peacetime evacuations, with villages destroyed and hundreds of thousands of acres incinerated. It has left millions more desperate for relief from temperatures that routinely soar above 40 degrees Celsius, or 104 degrees Fahrenheit.

It has forced the cancellation of concerts and festivals, curtailed the final stage of the Tour de France cycling race and closed the Louvre Museum and Eiffel Tower early. It brought wildfires to the Scottish Highlands. It led organizers in London to call off a conference on how to cope with extreme heat. And it caused at least 10,000 heat-related deaths across Europe in June alone — a number that may turn out to be an undercount.
“Europe is ground zero when it comes to impacts” from climate change, said Johan Rockström, a Swedish scientist who is the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany.
“2026 is just the beginning,” Rockström added. “It will inevitably get worse. It will get worse and worse and worse to the point where, I’m afraid, we’ll be passing the limits of adaptation.”
Why Europe

Europe is not alone, of course. Heat waves gripped Australia and Japan this year. Floods devastated Kenya and Angola. A snowstorm paralyzed the Eastern United States. Developing countries in the Southern Hemisphere are still more vulnerable than wealthy Europe to the effects of a changing climate.

Yet no other continent has warmed as rapidly as Europe, at nearly twice the global average since the mid-1990s. That has forced Europeans to confront, more starkly than others, the harsh realities of a changed climate, particularly in the summer, when their once-mild days have given way to furnace like heat.

Though still cooler than other parts of the world, like the American Southwest or the Persian Gulf region, Europe is less able to cope because its buildings are often without air conditioning and were built to retain heat. The homogeneity of the trees on its hillsides and coastal plains, many of which were planted during cooler, wetter periods, make them dangerously flammable during fire season.
“With this heat wave and these fires, you can say it starts to become unbearable,” said Sonia Seneviratne, a Swiss climate scientist at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich.
Whether it leads to drastic new measures — either to mitigate the effects of a warmer climate or to adapt to them — is another question.
What are governments saying

In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared a “climate emergency,” which he said would necessitate a state pact to “attack the root of the problem in a structural way.” In France, President Emmanuel Macron vowed to replant the vast pine forests that were burned in the Gironde region over the last week with different species of trees that are better suited to a dry, hot climate.
“The situation we’re in today is the most difficult we’ve ever recorded, the most difficult since World War II,” Macron said.

Yet for all the urgency, Europe’s commitment to reduce carbon dioxide emissions — a goal that scientists say is the only conclusive way to curb climate change — is in danger of being watered down. This month, the European Union proposed to adjust rules so that some industries could pollute at slightly higher levels, further into the future.

“Net zero” policies, which aim to balance the greenhouse gases put into the atmosphere with the amount removed, have become inviting targets for critics, particularly on the right, who condemn them as a luxury Europe can’t afford during a period of weak economic growth and energy insecurity. And no matter what Europe does, the global trajectory depends on China and the United States, where President Donald Trump has called climate change a “con job,” as well as on energy-hungry developing countries.
What temperatures are looking like

Europe’s status as the fastest-warming continent is a consequence of both changing weather patterns and its proximity to the Arctic, where reduced snow and ice lead to more dark surfaces that absorb heat.

The continent is more than 1.6 degrees Celsius, or 2.9 degrees Fahrenheit, warmer than it was three decades ago, and the rise in temperature is swift enough to be noticeable over a single generation. By the start of this week, France had recorded 53 heat waves since 1947; 28 of them occurred in the last 15 years.

Bordeaux never experienced a day with temperatures at or above 39 degrees Celsius (102.2 degrees Fahrenheit) between 1921 and 2000, according to Météo-France, the national climate and weather service. This summer, it has happened eight times, including Wednesday, and the season is not even half over. Bordeaux’s winemakers, already beleaguered by the heat, now worry about smoke tainting their famous vineyards.

Friederike Otto, a German climatologist at Imperial College London, said “jet stream” wind patterns and high-pressure systems once could lock in days of “nice-ish summer weather” in Europe. Now, she said, those same dynamics produce excruciating conditions because they occur in tandem with a warmer climate.

The most frightening aspect of Europe’s summer, scientists say, is that it could appear tame in retrospect. The planet is already on course to breach the central goal of the Paris Agreement of 2015: to stop the planet from heating more than 2 degrees Celsius, or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, higher than preindustrial levels.

Far from moderating, some experts say the pace of warming appears to be accelerating. France’s weather and climate service has painted a dystopian picture, saying that by 2050, heat waves could be five times more frequent, while temperatures could hit 118 degrees Fahrenheit.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

title: 9/11 attacks: An Expert Explains how it changed warfare, terrorism

content.value: It was September 11, 2001, when 19 terrorists associated with al-Qaeda hijacked four civilian airliners — two struck the twin towers of New York City’s World Trade Center (WTC) and one the Pentagon, while the fourth aircraft crashed in Pennsylvania. The WTC was completely destroyed, and a total of 2,977 people were killed in the 9/11 attacks. The dastardly act demonstrated a new face of the asymmetric warfare, wherein “non-state actors” (NSAs) operating from the distant sanctuaries could inflict strategic shock on a global superpower.

The US responded swiftly by launching “Operation Enduring Freedom” a month later, on October 7. The aim was to dismantle al-Qaeda, remove the Taliban regime that had provided haven to the terrorists’ outfit, and capture or kill top leadership and high value targets — including al-Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden — by employing overwhelming force. Local Afghan forces like the “Northern Alliance” formed part of the US-led international coalition. The Taliban regime was quickly overthrown and what followed was the strategic expansion of counter terrorism operations.
Global War on Terror to ‘Forever War’

The GWOT became the organising framework of US national security. It basically entailed creating unprecedented global intelligence networks, special forces (small teams central to counterterrorism), intelligence-led precision strikes by armed drones, and scrutiny of terrorist funding. While the initial objectives were quite specific, the mission gradually expanded to counter-insurgency, regime change, and eventually nation-building. This fundamentally changed the complexion of war to “Forever War’.

The US forces enjoyed overwhelming tactical and technological superiority. The satellites, signal intelligence, cyber capabilities, and networked command systems compressed the “sensor to shooter” cycle, from days to hours or even minutes. The al-Qaeda core leadership was dismantled, and bin Laden was eliminated in 2011 in Abbottabad-Pakistan. Even when the extremist group Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) established the “Caliphate” (a self-proclaimed Islamic state spanning parts of Iraq and Syria), it too was annihilated.
Tactical edge, however, could not compensate for strategic outreach. The adage “winning battles does not necessarily mean winning the war” stood vindicated.

The Iraq invasion in 2003 opened another theatre, diverted resources, and created vulnerabilities which were subsequently exploited by the extremist outfits. Although major combat operations under “Operation Enduring Freedom” concluded on December 28, 2014, broader involvement of US-led coalition forces continued subsequently.

After two decades, the US forces withdrew from Afghanistan, having incurred enormous expenditure and extensive human cost. The departure of Major General Christopher Donahue, Commander of the 82nd Airborne Division, along with the last of US forces personnel on a C-130 aircraft from Kabul on August 30, 2021, marked the literal end of US military presence in Afghanistan.

The most enduring lesson of the US’s Afghan experience and perhaps of GWOT was: external military power can destroy terrorist infrastructure but cannot substitute for legitimate politics, effective governance, and indigenous institutions. Military interventions can create strategic space and the environment for political process but cannot ensure political legitimacy.

The principal error in the GWOT was not the use of force — which was inevitable to destroy the al-Qaeda network — but losing sight of specific aims and missions. Terrorism is a tool of political violence, so it is crucial to address the political and socio-economic issues in which the extremist narrative thrives.
Terrorism transformed

Two decades ago, terrorist organisations were comparatively hierarchical, with recognisable leadership, known sanctuaries and training camps, financing networks, and centrally planned operations. Currently, the terrorists’ outfits are networked, decentralised, digitised, and individualised lone actors.

Outfits like al-Qaeda and ISIS have not totally disappeared but dispersed into parts of Africa, West Asia, and South Asia. New havens are weak states and civil war-prone regions or ungoverned spaces. The training is being imparted on smartphones instead of camps. The recruitment and radicalisation are now through encrypted communications and social media, without physical contact or formal organisation. Lone wolves or small autonomous cells can undertake violent acts with minimal warning.

Technology is playing a significant role in this transformed terrorism. Commercial drones are being employed for reconnaissance and delivery of explosives. Artificial intelligence is being effectively employed for propaganda as well as psychological and cyber warfare. Cryptocurrencies and dubious financial channels make tracking complicated. Terrorism is increasingly becoming faceless, anonymous, and high-tech. The distinction between domestic and foreign terrorism is also becoming blurred.

The US may finally close the chapter on 9/11, which began 25 years earlier. During the “war on terror”, while the US forces decimated al-Qaeda leadership and severely degraded the core, it did not end terrorism. Jihadist ideology, affiliates, and radicalised elements survived. But it changed the very nature of warfare and transformed terrorism. As things turned out, when the American forces pulled out, the Taliban were back in Kabul. Iraq proved that regime change is easier than building a stable political order. Tactical dominance did not translate into strategic outcomes — a paradox which shuns a simplistic analogy.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

The US paid a heavy price for being involved in West Asia and Afghanistan. While it was embroiled in GWOT, China rose rapidly and Russia reasserted itself, with great power competition returning to the centre stage. Ironically, the US is once again stuck in West Asia. History vindicates that ignoring past lessons turn out to be future blind spots.

With technology as the new battlespace, inexpensive autonomous systems lend NSAs and proxy outfits significant capability to undertake operations that can generate strategic effect. Today, there is considerable overlap between conventional war and terrorism, leading to hybrid warfare. Only prevention and pre-emptive measures can eliminate the perpetual “never ending wars”. For this, coordinated real time intelligence, border management, financial disruption, and precise counterterrorism actions are key. So are good governance, counter radicalisation, and addressing conditions that extremist organisations tend to exploit.
All said, 9/11 changed the very face of terrorism. The wars that followed exposed the limits of military power.

The author is a war veteran and served as defence attache in China, North Korea, and Mongolia. He is currently professor of international relations, management at Lal Bahadur Shastri Institute of Management.

title: Pakistan’s ‘Form 47 government’: Why India uses the term as criticism

content.value: India on Saturday (October 24) accused Pakistan of attempting to “paint a propagandist picture” of India during a dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on Minority Issues at the UN General Assembly. The remarks followed Pakistan’s claims about Kashmir.

Raghoo Puri, the First Secretary at the Permanent Mission of India to the UN, said the government of Pakistan makes statements criticising India based on “instructions” from the Pakistan Army, calling it a “Form 47 government”.
The term first gained prominence during the 2024 Pakistan elections. Here is what happened then and why it has since been used to criticise the Pakistani State.
What is Form 47 in Pakistan?

Following polling in early 2024, allegations of rigging and result manipulation marred Pakistan’s election results. Raoof Hasan, a close aide and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) Central Information Secretary, then tweeted that former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s “mandate has been stolen in the dark of the night”.

At the heart of the controversy were Forms 45 and 47, meant to provide official documentation of election results. The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) provides several forms to document results in a constituency, and Form 45, also known as the ‘Result of Count’ form, is a key document.

This form formally records votes polled at a polling station and is crucial for compiling results at the constituency level. It contains essential information on the polling station, including the station number, the constituency it falls under, the total number of registered voters, the total number of votes cast, and a breakdown of the votes secured by each candidate.

It is signed not just by the presiding officer of the polling station, but also by the polling representatives of candidates present, who act as witnesses to the process. Thus, Form 45 acts as the most basic record of electoral outcomes in Pakistan. By law, polling stations have to publicly display copies of the form in order to ensure accountability and transparency.
Form declaring ‘unconfirmed results’

After voting is completed and ballots are counted at a polling station, the Presiding Officer fills Form 45 and submits it to the Returning Officer of the constituency. The Returning Officer then gathers and tallies results based on Form 45 for every polling station in the constituency to determine the final results.

Prior to official confirmation of final results, Form 47 documents the unconfirmed results in a constituency. This includes the number of votes polled in the constituency, a candidate-wise breakdown of votes, and the number of votes cancelled/rejected. Form 47 is prepared by tallying results obtained from Form 45s.
After all votes are counted and results come in, Forms 48 and 49 publish the full and final vote tallies, and act as official declarations of the election results.
Discrepancy between Form 45 and 47
The two forms were at the centre of the controversy surrounding poll results in Pakistan.

On election night, various reports said that candidates and their representatives were being denied Form 45s by the presiding officers. PTI expressed serious concerns over the non-provision of Form 45 to its polling agents, even after the lapse of several hours, “seemingly under a malicious plot to change the results”, Pakistan Today reported.

Moreover, the party later claimed that the results tallied in Form 47s, in several cases, showed a major discrepancy with regard to the granular data provided in Form 45s. PTI Secretary General Omar Ayub said on February 11 that the Form 47 (provisional results) of 18 National Assembly seats were “falsely changed”.

Imran Khan, in an AI-generated statement of victory, claimed that PTI won “170 seats” according to Form 45s. Form 47s, however, show PTI-backing independents only winning 92 seats (since PTI was barred from contesting following a court order). This was the largest win among parties but still fell short of a majority.

Subsequently, the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) formed a coalition, with Shehbaz Sharif of the PML-N as the Prime Minister. As has long been the case in the country, the Army was seen to have backed the government formation, leading to allegations of unfair elections. India has since used Form 47 as a reference to criticise Pakistan’s position on India’s internal issues, arguing that it lacked any standing to do so and should manage its own internal political and constitutional processes first.
The poll results were then challenged in Pakistani courts. In late February 2024, the Sindh High Court disposed of around 50 petitions against the provisional results, Dawn reported.

title: Why India should observe China’s Fifth Plenum, as Xi Jinping tightens political control

content.value: A key political meeting that recently concluded in China reflected President Xi Jinping’s resolve to tighten political control and reinforce the supremacy of the Communist Party of China (CPC).

The Fifth Plenary Session of the Party’s 20th Central Committee, held in Beijing from October 26–29, also addressed institutional vulnerabilities, which matter ahead of next year’s Party Congress — an all-important meeting held every five years. According to the official communiqué, the conclave focused on internal Party discipline, leadership adjustments, and preparations for the next political cycle.

For India, the implications are strategic rather than merely political. Understanding China requires looking beyond its economic strength and military hardware to its political architecture, the mindset of its leadership, and strategic behaviour.
Significance of the Plenums

During its five-year tenure, the CPC Central Committee, elected by the National Party Congress (NPC) or the national legislature, holds seven plenary sessions. These serve as important instruments for translating the NPC’s political directions into policies and decisions.

Although each plenum follows an established agenda, the 20th Central Committee (established during the 2022 Party Congress) witnessed some deviations. The First and Second Plenums focus on top leadership appointments and state institutional structures. The Third Plenum addresses major economic policies and reforms; this time delayed and held in July 2024.

The Fourth Plenum, associated with Party building, was held in October 2025 and took up the task of finalising guidelines for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030), an exercise normally reserved for the Fifth Plenum. Consequently, the Fifth Plenum shifted its emphasis towards strengthening CPC governance structures ahead of the 2027 Party Congress. The Sixth traditionally centres on ideology and Party discipline, while the Seventh prepares the agenda for the next NPC.

The Fifth Plenum must be viewed against the evolution of Xi’s leadership since 2012. Anti-corruption and Party discipline have been defining features of his tenure. The 20th Party Congress in October 2022 consolidated Xi Jinping’s position as China’s paramount political leader and reaffirmed his vision of national modernisation and rejuvenation. His term as the general secretary, or top leader, of the CPC was extended for a historic third time.

The record-low attendance at the latest meeting also came amid continuing leadership upheaval, marked by investigations and disciplinary action against civilian officials and People’s Liberation Army (PLA) commanders.
Fifth Plenum: Highlights and key outcomes

The communiqué outlined several guiding principles, including strengthening of Party leadership, enforcing rigorous governance across organisations, improving institutional oversight and ensuring governance through Party regulations.

A consequential outcome was the adoption of a resolution reinforcing the CPC’s position that its capacity to govern itself is fundamental to its ability to govern China. The emphasis on top-down control was particularly significant.

Perhaps the most consequential development remains the continuing upheaval within the PLA. The Plenum confirmed the expulsion of 33 officials from the Party. These included senior military figures such as Zhang Youxia, former Vice Chairman of the apex military decision-making body, the Central Military Commission (CMC), Liu Zhenli, former Chief of Staff of the Joint Staff Department, Ma Xingrui, former Politburo member and Wang Haijiang, former Western Theatre Commander. This theatre also concerns the border with India.

The shrinking military leadership is evident from the CMC’s composition. Constituted with seven members in 2022, it has since seen five members removed, leaving only Xi as Chairman and General Zhang Shengmin, who oversees military discipline. The Plenum did not announce appointments to fill the vacant positions. This could reflect an effort to retain direct control and avoid potential internal challenges, particularly amid suspicions concerning officers associated with the purged figures.
The political signal

The Plenum formally announced that the 21st Party Congress would be held in Beijing in the latter half of October 2027. It will determine the composition of the CPC’s senior leadership for the next five-year cycle.

Xi’s position remains firmly at the centre of the political system and he is widely expected to seek another term. No succession arrangements have been announced. In China’s opaque political system, personnel changes and purges offer important, though not definitive, indicators of leadership priorities. In this context, Zhang Shengmin’s elevation to Politburo merits attention, although it does not settle the succession question.

The Fifth Plenum was primarily an exercise in reinforcing the foundations of Xi’s political system before the Party Congress. The underlying proposition is that the Party must strengthen and discipline itself to lead China’s rejuvenation. The unprecedented removal of senior functionaries, particularly within the PLA, highlights the continuing emphasis on political control.

However, tighter political control cannot, by itself, resolve China’s economic challenges. Weak domestic consumption, property-sector stress, local government debt, demographic decline and external technology restrictions remain structural constraints. The 15th Five-Year Plan seeks to address these issues. Excessive political control can constrain private enterprise and discourage innovation. The challenge, therefore, is to balance political authority with the flexibility required for sustained economic growth.

The centrality of national security in China’s governance framework was also reinforced. Domestic governance and external policies are increasingly interconnected. Against the backdrop of intensifying US-China competition, the leadership is expected to accelerate efforts towards technological independence, military modernisation and strategic outreach.

Closer to home, China’s territorial claims and emphasis on national security will continue to shape the environment along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). The removal of senior PLA commanders should not be interpreted as a moderation of China’s strategic objectives or a dilution of its military capabilities. India must closely monitor changes in the PLA’s command structure and operational readiness while strengthening its own defence preparedness as part of a coherent China policy.
The writer is a war veteran and former Assistant Chief of Army Staff (Strategy). He has served as Defence Attaché in China and is currently a Professor at Lal Bahadur Shastri Institute of Management.

title: 50,000 migrants, 48 hours: How the border crisis in Ceuta reveals divides within Europe

content.value: The Spanish territory of Ceuta, located on the North African coast, witnessed a surge of more than 50,000 migrants in just a few days late last month. The city has a total population of around 84,000.

As of August 3, the vast majority of the migrants from neighbouring Morocco have been escorted back, with Spanish authorities executing over 48,000 returns within 48 hours. But the events have had a human cost, with at least 72 people dying while attempting to migrate to Ceuta.

The incident also reflects the broader tensions running through the European Union, at a time when migration has become a particularly polarising political concern. On Saturday (August 1), the leaders of 22 European states, led by Italy and Denmark, submitted a letter to urgently discuss the situation and decide on a coordinated response. Ireland, which holds the rotating EU Presidency, announced a videoconference for Tuesday.

Notably, the letter singles out the Spanish government’s recent move to grant legal status to unauthorised migrants as a “pull factor”, arguing that it affects the entire continent. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has spoken out against this assessment by citing data to highlight that Ceuta remains one of the least porous migration points in the region.
Contested territory in focus

Ceuta and Melilla are Spain-controlled autonomous cities on the coast of North Africa and constitute the EU’s only land borders with Africa. Both are exclaves, or parts of a nation cut off from the mainland by another country.

Historically, Morocco has claimed the two as occupied African land while Spain has retained control of Ceuta since 1580 and Melilla since 1497. In 1978, the two exclaves were enshrined within the Spanish constitution as integral parts of the kingdom’s territory.

The dispute has been a flashpoint in Spanish-Moroccan relations. In 2021, Spain provided medical treatment for Covid-19 to Brahim Gali, the leader of the Algeria-based Polisario Front that actively seeks the ‘liberation’ of the Western Sahara from Morocco.

Subsequently, Spain-Morocco ties worsened, and a month later, between 10 and 12,000 migrants crossed into Spain through Ceuta owing to relaxed border security in Morocco, despite a bilateral agreement to control migrant arrivals.

Dr Divya Balan, Faculty of International Studies at FLAME University told The Indian Express that “Historically, the Moroccan government has used the exclave borders as leverage… This time, however, the June ruling of the Spanish Supreme Court seems to have been the lever which was abused.”
Spain’s ‘pull factor’ for migrants
Some important policy and court decisions in Spain of late have concerned migrants:

*On June 29, Spain’s Supreme Court ruled that summary returns — also known as “hot returns” — were inapplicable for rejecting migrants on the high seas, intercepted while swimming into Ceuta and Melilla. An important part of Spain’s Aliens Act, summary returns allows authorities to turn back undocumented migrants.
*At the same time, the court invalidated clauses from earlier regulations that enforced strict child welfare standards for migrants who were minors.

*Earlier this year, under a Royal Decree, the Spanish government ran a widespread labour regularisation program. It granted thousands of undocumented migrants work permits and temporary residence across all sectors. Spain has an aging population and this drive was touted by the government as a pragmatic approach for solving two problems at once.
Along with the ruling government’s pro-migration stance, these policies have invited scrutiny as a pull factor to the continent, particularly from Europe’s far-right parties.

“Migration within the EU boils down to an issue of sovereignty and burden sharing. Frontier countries, like Spain, are stuck between a rock and a hard place. Where there is a pull factor, there is a complementary push factor which must be considered as well,” Dr Balan said. In this case, high rates of youth unemployment and climate change-related shifts in Morocco are driving migration.

The leap from a localised court ruling to a 50,000-strong surge, however, was catalysed by immediate misinformation. Sánchez has publicly blamed criminal trafficking networks for weaponising the ruling and spreading false rumors that swimming around the breakwaters guaranteed entry to Europe without the risk of summary rejection.
Dr Balan said that the use of social media by smuggling rings to spread disinformation was a concern this time, and the younger demographic of the migrant movement was indicative of it.
Fallout within the EU

Several EU nations have framed the Ceuta incident as undermining collective Schengen security. Italy’s Interior Ministry ordered a temporary suspension of its free movement agreement with Spain on July 30, introducing “targeted and selective” checks on non-EU travellers.

This move has drawn praise from far-right parties, including France’s National Rally and Germany’s Alternative for Germany (AfD). The trend is reflective of larger immigration-related anxieties projected by centrist and right-wing parties in Europe over the last decade, spurred by the 2015 migrant crisis.

Today, the debate centres around the structural demands that will be made of Madrid, with EU allies likely expecting it to adopt harsher posturing on borders. Dr Balan said that migration was and will remain a significant issue for Europe to contend with, even as synchronicity on the issue has been hard to achieve among members. “The rising demand for labour in Europe is a reality, which even the anti-migration right-wing governments shall have to eventually recognise”, she said.

The lack of consensus also points to an unsustainable paradox in European governance. The friction between sovereign domestic economic priorities, such as Spain’s need to address labour shortages, and the collective mandate of Schengen border security forces frontier nations to negotiate between their own demographic needs and broader geopolitical realities.

title: Behind India’s Russia-Ukraine peace proposal: Grain, crude oil — and Trump

content.value: Four years after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, India, for the first time, is said to have put forward a “comprehensive” and “broad” proposal to end the war.
This was revealed by Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha last week, after Russian President Vladimir Putin had said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi has some “very good ideas”.

The broad contours of the proposal revolve around easing the especially intense fighting since July around the critical Black Sea region, which would allow Ukraine’s agricultural products to reach the world. Russia would halt attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, while Ukraine would refrain from attacking Russian positions along the line of contact.
This “limited” and “partial” ceasefire is what has animated the conversation between India, Russia and Ukraine.

Over the last four-and-a-half years, India emerged as a major buyer of discounted crude oil from Russia as much of the West shunned the country — much to Ukraine’s anger. Yet, it has kept communication channels open with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has also told Putin that “this is not an era of war”.

This engagement with both sides is what has put India in a good position to put forward such a proposal. Here’s why the move matters, how India’s involvement has deepened, and the larger signal it sends — especially to the US.
The Black Sea hotspot in the Russia-Ukraine war

Of particular interest in the proposal is the larger Black Sea region — a key grain-export hub for the world. The fighting there could put at least 400 million people in Africa, West Asia and Asia at risk of food shortages, malnutrition and hunger.

Ukraine, in particular, is a major agricultural exporter. Russia has targeted Ukrainian port facilities and vessel operations around the Greater Odesa region on the Black Sea coast. Ukraine has three key deep-water ports there — Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi — which handle around 90% of its agricultural exports.

Between July 22 and August 31, the operations at these three ports declined sharply: average daily cargo handling fell from approximately 215,300 tonnes to around 14,000 tonnes, according to the Ministry for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport of Ukraine.
In the 2025-26 marketing year, agri-food products accounted for more than 56% of Ukraine’s merchandise exports, generating $22.5 billion in export revenues. This revenue is essential for its economy.

For the 2026-27 marketing year, Ukraine expects to produce approximately 81 million tonnes of grain and oilseeds, of which around 64.4 million tonnes will need to be exported. A complete blockade would undermine global food security. Additionally, under a prolonged disruption, the storage deficit in Ukraine could increase to almost 11 million tonnes by the end of autumn.

It’s not just Russia that is attacking such facilities, though. Since mid-July, Ukraine has also stepped up attacks on grain vessels, maritime infrastructure and ports on the Sea of Azov and the vital Kerch Strait that connects it to the Black Sea.
Russia exports significant volumes of grain through the Azov-Black Sea region — approximately 42-44 million tonnes, or 77-81% of its total grain exports, is transported through this area.
Western intelligence inputs also indicate that Russia is planning to accelerate attacks on Ukraine’s electricity grids and power plants ahead of the harsh winter.
How New Delhi stepped in
In such a delicate and volatile situation, New Delhi’s proposal has many takers and supporters.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said on October 4 that India has gone “beyond advocacy” to be a “little more involved” in the efforts to end the war.

Jaishankar said that New Delhi has been in conversations with both Moscow and Kyiv, trying to be “helpful” on the safety of shipping in the Black Sea, grain and energy exports and on “non-attack possibilities”.

The latest round of conversations began in July, when there were attacks on civilian shipping by both Russia and Ukraine. In the course of those attacks, some Indian sailors were killed while others were injured.
With five deaths of Indian seafarers in the region in the second half of July, India summoned diplomats from both Russia and Ukraine and lodged a strong protest.

Indians constitute almost 12% of seafarers in the world — roughly one in every 10 seafarers is an Indian national. This means that an Indian national is likely to be present during any attack on a ship.

Before this, India had mostly been involved in advocacy: On August 31, Modi had urged Putin to move from “endless war” to “end of war” when they met in Bishkek on the sidelines of the summit of SCO leaders.

Modi has been raising this issue with Putin ever since 2022 when he first said, “This is not the era of war.” In a meeting with Putin in Moscow in July 2024, Modi said “peace talks do not succeed amid bombs, guns and bullets”, and a “solution cannot be found on the battlefield”.
The Trump factor
The evolution from advocacy to actual deal-making has a broader implication — with respect to the US administration under President Donald Trump.

In recent weeks, the US Congress has empowered Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy (India is one of them). Yet, just weeks later on Friday, Trump announced a surprise deal under which Russia will supply hundreds of thousands of tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets.
Amid these contradictory signals — and a trade deal hanging in limbo — India’s efforts convey a seriousness as well as a signal that it is not taking sides in the war.

Meanwhile, Russian crude continues to make up a significant chunk of India’s crude oil imports. It surpassed $43 billion in 2025 and rose 25% during the first half of 2026, peaking at a record share of over 50% (about 2.47 million barrels per day) in July. The imports moderated to around 1.82 million barrels per day by September.
India is, of course, looking to avoid another round of US tariffs over its purchases of Russian oil. Last year, half of the exorbitant 50% tariffs imposed by Trump were for these imports.

In this scenario, the proposal buys India the time and diplomatic space needed to negotiate the long-pending deal with the US on bilateral trade. With Prime Minister Modi expected to travel to the US for the G20 Leaders’ summit in December, this is an important move to secure some diplomatic space.

For many external observers, New Delhi is also perceived to be an idle bystander in the diplomatic chess board, even as Pakistan briefly stole the spotlight by brokering a US-Iran truce — which swiftly collapsed.

While New Delhi doesn’t want to be seen as being compared to Pakistan in deal-making, any possible truce in a limited peace deal between Russia and Ukraine will serve the Indian interest in securing its national economic and strategic interests, apart from taking care of Indian nationals on board the ships across the world.

title: China This Week | Is China cheating on AI, going overboard with manufacturing, and other debates

content.value: At a time when the US-China AI race routinely invites discussion, raising questions of how strong the US’s lead is, the question of whether the competition itself is fair is increasingly cropping up. Interestingly, it is the leader of this race that is levelling accusations of improper behaviour against its fast-moving competitor.

Reuters recently reviewed over 80 Chinese academic papers and found that “Chinese military researchers have used outputs from leading U.S. artificial intelligence models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic to train domestic AI systems.” This is in line with broader allegations made by US tech giants against rising Chinese AI companies.

But the United States government is not the lone participant in this chain of action and retaliation. On Wednesday (August 5), the Chinese government announced economic countermeasures, including export controls on drones and sanctions on six American entities, in response to recent restrictions imposed by Washington.

Finally, we examine a document released by the government, titled “China’s Position on the So-called Excess Capacity Issue”. It addresses questions raised about Chinese manufacturing in many parts of the world, and the cheap goods that reach the rest of the world. The fact that the paper itself refers to the charge as a “so-called” issue speaks to China’s overall interest in challenging those questions.
Here is a closer look at these developments:
1. China, US, and AI distillation

The Reuters report said documents showed widespread use of a technique known as “model distillation,” where responses from a more powerful AI model (here, the likes of ChatGPT) are used to train smaller ones. This is seen as a more efficient and cheaper way of building models from scratch, and one without requiring large datasets.
The review also showed that “distillation is widely used by researchers linked to the People’s Liberation Army and other military institutions.”

UPSHOT: Distillation is not a banned method in itself. But reports of Chinese AI models building on their capabilities through it, also reportedly with the help of advanced chips that the US has banned from exporting, have led to a strong response.

As we earlier detailed in this explainer, another complicating factor is that this is a new domain — what exactly constitutes illegal distillation is unclear, as is the extent to which Chinese companies have engaged in the practice.

But with some US officials also supporting claims of American companies like Anthropic, and new reports of military use, there could be a greater push for defining the limits of the practice and challenging China on this basis.
2. China’s counter, weeks before Trump’s trip

In late July, the US government added 43 companies based in China to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List. According to the government, this is a “key tool” aimed at “preventing the importation into the United States of goods made with forced labor and leveling the playing field for American companies.”

China has historically denied claims of forced labour or religious persecution of its Uyghur Muslim minority. It said that the “restrictive measures seriously violated the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and severely infringed upon China’s legitimate rights and interests, leaving China no choice but to respond.”

UPSHOT: In its official statement, the Chinese government drew attention to the US having “repeatedly overstretched the concept of national security” to impose restrictions on Chinese goods, including “advanced robotic devices and power inverters” more recently.

Its decision to impose countermeasures, however, marks a change while building on a more aggressive stance. For instance, in 2024, China moved beyond simply denying allegations of human rights abuses in Xinjiang, the home province of the Uyghurs. It opened an investigation against the parent company of apparel brands Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger over its boycott of cotton from Xinjiang over the alleged use of forced Uyghur labour.
The measures and their response also come weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to visit the US for an official trip, after US President Donald Trump arrived in Beijing in May.
3. Chinese paper on excess manufacturing
The 40-page paper from China’s Commerce Ministry covers a range of topics — the historical shifts in global trade, the relationship between subsidies and industrial capacity, and so on.

In its conclusion, it notes: “China cannot develop in isolation from the rest of world, nor can the world as a whole maintain prosperity without China. China stands ready to work with all parties to safeguard the global free trade system…”

UPSHOT: The Economist described the paper as “both rigorous and disingenuous.” It added that while “some parts bring healthy scrutiny to the concept of overcapacity”, “The deep insincerity of other sections suggests contempt for countries facing waves of Chinese exports.”

On the issue of insincerity, it is also important to note that Chinese officials have themselves acknowledged the related problem of involution. The word has been used to describe a situation where excess manufacturing, coupled with low demand, leads to manufacturers dropping the prices of their goods to an unsustainable extent. Xi himself has called for curbing “disorderly” price competition.

As Chinese goods again pose concerns about a “China Shock”, or the loss of jobs due to rising exports, the timing of the paper assumes significance. That a paper is seeking to counter criticism has been released itself indicates that for all its posturing, China is concerned about a negative global perception of its manufacturing, the sector which propelled it to an economic giant and continues to aid its economy at a time of weak domestic demand.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil: The cases and investigations against him explained

content.value: Flávio Bolsonaro investigations: Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil’s presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has fled the country for the United States, where he declared himself Brazil’s “true president” before withdrawing the claim.

Bolsonaro arrived in Miami with his family on Wednesday (October 28). Shortly afterwards, he published a letter claiming to be the “true president”, despite his own party recognising Lula’s victory. He later deleted the letter and issued another describing himself as “the leader of Brazil”, The Guardian reported.

The escape had been planned as a contingency in case he lost, Brazilian newspaper O’ Globo reported. Flávio’s brother, Eduardo, a former congressman, has been in self-imposed exile in Texas since February 2025 and secured a green card last July.

The US State Department on Tuesday (October 27) said it would grant visas to Flávio and his family. However, US immigration records obtained by Brazilian newspapers Folha de S.Paulo and O Globo show that Bolsonaro entered the country under a temporary humanitarian authorisation, allowing him to remain until October 2027. This is distinct from a visa or a grant of asylum. US President Donald Trump also said he would approve their move to the country, calling the election “very strange” and “terrible”.
Bolsonaro had disappeared for over 24 hours until Argentina’s migration authorities said on Tuesday night that he had entered the country.

The Brazilian senator fled after Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports in connection with a money laundering investigation. After he failed to comply, the Federal Police cancelled his Brazilian passports. He reportedly crossed into Argentina using an Italian passport before travelling to Miami via Ecuador.

Flávio Bolsonaro, who had won the first round of the election earlier this month and was widely considered a favourite for the presidency, was defeated in a runoff by the 81-year-old Lula. Lula’s victory also bucks a regional trend in which seven consecutive Latin American presidential elections were won by conservative candidates.

Bolsonaro’s loss also dealt a major setback to US President Donald Trump’s ambitions to expand Washington’s influence in the region. Trump has repeatedly clashed with Lula over the years, and considers Bolsonaro, as well as his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, close allies.
The cases against Flávio
Flávio is involved in three investigations concerning his own alleged conduct, while a fourth inquiry ordered on Tuesday is examining possible foreign interference benefiting his campaign.
‘Dark Horse’ financing controversy
One case pertains to the financing of the film Dark Horse (2026), an English-language semi-fictionalised biopic about Jair Bolsonaro.

Flávio negotiated a deal worth R$134 million (US$24 million) with disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro to finance the film. Investigators are examining possible irregularities in the funding, including the source of the money.

Vorcaro’s private bank, Banco Master, was liquidated, leaving behind over $7 billion in debts, and he was charged with fraud. Bolsonaro was formally included in the inquiry this July. The senator has denied any wrongdoing.

According to an investigation by The Intercept Brasil, at least US$10.6 million was paid in six transactions between February and May 2025. The investigation uncovered messages and audio of Flávio pressuring Vorcaro to release funds.

A follow-up report by The Intercept this month traced the first US$2 million payment to a company owned by Fabiano Zettel, Vorcaro’s brother-in-law, which is also under investigation in the Banco Master fraud case. The developments raise scrutiny over Bolsonaro’s claim about the film being funded entirely through legal means.
Money laundering case linked to disgraced lawyer
Bolsonaro is also under investigation over suspected money laundering involving lawyer Willer Tomaz, who is himself accused of involvement in a wider financial fraud scheme.

According to the Federal Police, Bolsonaro was the “master user” of a bank account linked to Alcazar Holdings, an offshore company owned by Tomaz, which held a stake in a company that owns an executive jet linked to Vorcaro. This access allegedly granted him a “high level of access and management” and “significant operational access” to the account.

The inquiry originated from a probe into unauthorised deductions from pension payments by Brazil’s social security agency. As the investigation progressed, investigators examined suspected money laundering involving betting platforms and financial transactions linked to Tomaz.
The Federal Police identified illegal financial transactions amounting to R$ 130 million between March and May 2025, according to CNN Brasil.
Times Brasil reported that a person working for Tomaz reportedly asked the bank to remove Bolsonaro’s access to the account in May 2025.
Both Bolsonaro and Tomaz have denied wrongdoing, or even sharing financial ties.
Slander case against Lula
A third investigation concerns a social media post in which Flávio allegedly linked Lula to crimes including international drug and arms trafficking and money laundering.

The post was published on X on January 3, following the illegal capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro by the US. In June, the Federal Police concluded that Flávio had falsely attributed criminal conduct to Lula. The matter was sent to the Prosecutor-General’s Office, which must decide whether to seek charges, request further investigation or recommend that the case be closed.
Allegations of foreign funding

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court ordered the Federal Police to investigate possible foreign funding or other forms of assistance to Flávio’s campaign, including alleged links to the US conservative donor network Rockbridge Network.
The wider probe also covers paid political content attributed to foreign-based accounts and possible manipulation of online platforms. Rockbridge has denied involvement.
Like father, like son

Flávio Bolsonaro’s departure from Brazil has drawn comparisons with his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who also fled the country before Lula’s inauguration in 2023. In February 2024, Jair spent two nights at the Hungarian embassy in Brasília after police seized his passport during a coup investigation, raising suspicions that he was seeking asylum. The former president was later convicted of attempting a coup after losing the 2022 election.

In January 2023, Jair Bolsonaro’s supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia and attempted to rally military support in an attempt to overturn the election result. The insurrection attempt drew comparisons with the events of January 6, 2021, when Trump’s supporters, fired by his “STOP THE STEAL!” campaign, stormed the US Capitol in Washington DC, after his defeat to Joe Biden.

Jair Bolsonaro was subsequently banned from running for office till 2030, and was charged in three separate criminal cases, including one in which he had “planned, acted in, and had direct and effective control over” an attempted coup.

Flávio Bolsonaro has not been formally charged in the three cases he has been named in, has denied wrongdoing and claimed the investigations are political persecution against him. With his Senate term set to expire in February 2027, he will lose his office and the privileges associated with it. The investigations could continue regardless of his election defeat, and their outcome will depend on the evidence and decisions by prosecutors and the courts.
In Trump, we trust
Since his first presidency, Donald Trump has cultivated close ties with the Bolsonaro family.

Jair Bolsonaro’s time as president (2019-23) overlapped with Trump’s first term (2017-21) and marked a period of close ties between Brazil and the US. The senior Bolsonaro modelled himself on Trump, and earned himself the moniker “Trump of the Tropics”. Commentators have seen the friendship between the two men as being built on mutual respect, and a shared disdain for legacy media and scepticism about science and scientists.

Both Jair and Trump have been implicated in legal cases, and have accused their political rivals of targeting them unfairly. More significantly, both have responded to electoral defeats in similar fashion – alleging electoral fraud, refusing to concede the presidency, and instigating insurrections.

In his second term, Trump has sought to implement the “Donroe” Doctrine, his riff on the Monroe Doctrine of 1823. The latter is a foreign policy position first articulated by President James Monroe in 1823, which holds the Western Hemisphere — specifically the Americas— as the United States’ zone of influence.

Over the following centuries, the US has relied on Monroe, and the Cold War-era Truman Doctrine, which meant to curtail the spread of communism, to justify installing (or attempting to install) friendly regimes in a dozen Latin American countries… including Brazil.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

The Trump iteration has also been accompanied by the US President’s willingness to use economic pressure to extract concessions from trading partners. This was exemplified by Trump’s 50% tariff levy against Brazil in a bid to influence the outcome of the ongoing criminal trial against Jair Bolsonaro.

The Trump administration has expressly stated its intent to fight a new war on drugs in Latin America, even citing this as its reason for its capture of Maduro in January. The US State Department has already labelled 21 criminal groups in the region as terrorist organisations, while the Pentagon has conducted 71 strikes on boats in waters around Latin America, The New York Times reported.

A Bolsonaro victory would have given US President Donald Trump a crucial ally in the region’s largest economy. Flávio had pledged to join Washington’s anti-cartel coalition, the Shield of the Americas, which Lula has resisted over concerns about Brazilian sovereignty.

title: What is China’s Singles’ Day, and how is AI changing the world’s biggest shopping festival?

content.value: In China, November 11 has been a day for single people to celebrate their relationship status. What began as a celebration among university students over three decades ago has become one of the world’s biggest shopping events and has drawn millions of consumers to online platforms with discounts and celebrity-led promotions.

The festival, however, is changing. It has expanded to include a month-long sales campaign while e-commerce companies are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to persuade shoppers to make purchases. Chatbots recommend products, while virtual try-on tools offer shoppers a more personalised experience.

The technology push comes at a time when Chinese consumers are becoming more cautious about spending. A prolonged property downturn and fatigue with year-round discounts have made it harder for retailers to generate the excitement that once defined the festival.

The Associated Press reported that sales during the 2026 Singles’ Day campaign had crossed 1 trillion yuan ($154 billion) by October 31, broadly in line with the corresponding period last year. The festival’s record sales in 2025 were nearly 1.7 trillion yuan ($254 billion).
So, how did a celebration of singlehood become a global retail phenomenon, and what does Singles’ Day look like today? Here’s a look.
What does Singles’ Day in China entail?
Celebrated on November 11, Singles’ Day takes its name from the date 11/11, with the four ones representing people without partners.

It is believed to have originated at Nanjing University in 1993 and was initially termed Bachelors’ Day. Male students began marking the occasion by treating themselves to gifts, organising social gatherings and celebrating their single status.
The observance spread beyond university campuses over time and came to be an occasion for all single people — including women — to celebrate their independence.

The occasion also offered an alternative to festivals that traditionally placed greater emphasis on couples and families. For many young people, it became a way of celebrating singlehood rather than viewing it as a social disadvantage.
How did Singles’ Day evolve into a commercial staple?
The transformation into a consumer-focused celebration began in 2009, when e-commerce giant Alibaba turned November 11 into a day-long online shopping festival.

The marketing pitch played on the original idea of the day by suggesting that even without a partner, people could treat themselves by shopping. According to a Quartz report, Alibaba promoted the event with the message: “Even if you don’t have a boyfriend or girlfriend, you can at least shop like crazy.”

The strategy drew criticism. Zhang Hailan, a folklore researcher at East China Normal University, argued in 2015 that Alibaba had turned an occasion associated with the social stigma of being single into a celebratory shopping experience.

The strategy worked. Other retailers joined in, and the event grew in scale, with companies investing in advertising, celebrity appearances, livestreamed performances and interactive shopping experiences.

In 2023, Alibaba kicked off its Singles’ Day campaign with a group of livestreamers, including popular online influencer Austin Li Jiaqi, known as the “Lipstick King”, and actor-singer Allen Lin Yilun. During the first evening of presales, 12 livestreamers each generated more than 100 million yuan ($14 million) in sales volume by midnight, according to figures released by Alibaba.

Such large-scale shopping events are not limited to China. In 2019, Amazon hosted a live concert for its Prime members featuring performers including Taylor Swift and Dua Lipa ahead of its Prime Day sale.
Over the years, Singles’ Day expanded beyond Alibaba to include rival platforms such as JD.com and social commerce platforms such as Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.
Is Singles’ Day big today?
Singles’ Day is widely regarded as the world’s largest online shopping festival, having grown far beyond its origins as a one-day sale.

Alibaba’s gross merchandise value (GMV) rose from 52 million yuan ( 7.6 million) in 2009 to 168.2 billion yuan (25.3 billion) in 2017. The festival subsequently expanded beyond Alibaba, with third-party estimates tracking sales across China’s major e-commerce platforms.
According to Bain & Company, total Singles’ Day GMV rose from 840 billion yuan in 2020 to 1.115 trillion yuan in 2022 and 1.442 trillion yuan in 2024.

Retailers have extended the promotional period from a single day to several weeks, making year-on-year comparisons less straightforward. Alibaba and JD.com have also stopped disclosing their overall festival transaction values.

The AP reported that total Singles’ Day sales in 2025 reached nearly 1.7 trillion yuan. For the 2026 campaign, cumulative sales had exceeded 1 trillion yuan by October 31, according to retail data platform Syntun, broadly matching the pace of the previous year.

The event’s expansion has also changed how its success is measured. Rather than a single day’s shopping frenzy, it is now a prolonged contest among e-commerce companies to attract consumers, retain merchants and increase purchases across multiple platforms.
How is AI changing Singles’ Day shopping?
One of the biggest changes to the festival is the growing integration of artificial intelligence into the shopping experience.

According to a November 11 Reuters report, Alibaba, JD.com and PDD Holdings are increasingly using AI-powered tools to attract consumers. These include chatbots that recommend products, virtual try-on features, automated discount searches and shopping assistants that can help customers complete purchases.

Alibaba’s Taobao and Tmall platforms have incorporated AI tools that allow shoppers to research products and find deals. JD.com’s AI shopping assistant, Dongdong, attracted nearly 80 million users seeking shopping advice during this year’s festival, more than three times the figure recorded last year.

The shift is also visible on social commerce platforms. On Douyin, AI-generated chatbot links accounted for around 5% of purchases in October, according to data from WPIC Marketing + Technologies. For more considered purchases, such as dietary supplements, the proportion exceeded 20%.

AI is also emerging as a product category in its own right. Alibaba said sales of AI toys on its platforms crossed 100 million yuan within a year of the category’s launch. Sales of AI companion robots increased nearly fivefold year-on-year in the second half of October, while sales of AI token packages, prepaid credits that allow customers to use AI services, rose more than 700% between October 15 and November 5, compared with September 15 to October 5, according to Alibaba’s Tmall platform.
However, the growing dependence on AI also presents challenges for retailers. Brands that fail to appear in AI-generated recommendations or product searches could lose visibility among consumers.

Whether these technological changes will translate into significantly higher overall spending remains uncertain. Reuters reported that Singles’ Day sales rose just 2.4% between October 7 and October 31, according to Syntun.
The festival’s enormous scale has also raised environmental concerns. The volume of deliveries generates transport-related emissions, while discarded plastic packaging adds to waste.

Chinese authorities and retailers have sought to address these concerns by promoting recyclable packaging and more sustainable delivery practices. JD.com, for instance, introduced measures to reduce packaging waste during earlier editions of the festival.

title: Why US midterm results could make oil cheaper, but complicate India’s Russian crude imports

content.value: The Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the US midterm polls, which handed it control of both chambers of Congress, has raised expectations of a potential diplomatic breakthrough in the Iran conflict, restoration of energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and consequently, a sustained decline in global crude oil prices.

For India — the world’s third-largest oil importer and fourth-largest refiner — lower oil prices would offer substantial economic relief by reducing the country’s ballooning oil import bill, ease external inflationary pressure, and improve the finances of oil marketing companies.

But the poll results may also carry a rather uncomfortable implication for New Delhi as a Congress controlled by the Democrats could make it politically harder for the Donald Trump administration to ease sanctions on Russia, and lead to calls for imposing a higher cost on Moscow over the war in Ukraine. Any such development could complicate India’s oil imports from Russia, its largest source of crude.
As election results came in, global benchmark Brent crude fell 8.7% to $94.62 a barrel on Wednesday. As of Thursday afternoon, oil prices were largely flat over Wednesday’s levels.

However, these are still early days, and despite the optimism, an end to the conflict is far from guaranteed. US President Donald Trump retains considerable authority over foreign policy, and there is also a fear that the electoral setback could encourage him to adopt a more aggressive posture in the West Asia conflict.
Iran conflict is the immediate energy market concern

Market participants and experts expect the Republican Party’s dismal performance in the polls to increase pressure on Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict. There are growing fissures within the Republican camp over the Iran war. US Vice President JD Vance publicly broke with the Trump administration’s foreign policy stance by blaming the war for the election debacle.

“The president retains full discretionary authority over military strikes, blockades and sanctions licenses. No war powers resolution has ever overcome a presidential veto, and the Democrats’ margins in both chambers will not be large enough to override one. What a unified Democratic Congress can do is make escalation considerably more costly: both chambers can pass resolutions, attach conditions to war spending and hold back confirmations of key officials. With war funding and appointees now subject to a hostile majority, the administration faces greater institutional pressure to pursue a Hormuz deal rather than a further round of strikes,” Rystad Energy said after US midterm election results.

Abu Dhabi-based energy analyst Natalia Katona cautioned that while there is growing optimism for an end to hostilities in West Asia and normalisation of energy flows, there is a risk in being too optimistic.

“Trump acknowledged the political cost of the war, but he still defended the decision to go ahead with it. The day after the vote, November 4, Washington sanctioned a network that helped tankers carrying Iranian oil get false flags. Democrats can begin to ask tougher questions and make it harder to secure fresh military funding once they take office on January 3. But until then, Trump still has room to turn up the pressure, and I don’t see any reasons why this time he should become predictable and more cautious with his actions,” she said.
If oil prices fall, India gains

For India, the disruption in energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz exposed the longstanding vulnerability of its dependence on energy imports, and the concentration of a substantial share of those imports in West Asia.

Prior to the war, about 40% of India’s oil imports, 60% of its LNG imports, and a whopping 90% of its LPG imports regularly came from West Asia through the Strait of Hormuz. The country’s dependence on imports stands at over 88% for oil, 60% for LPG, and about 50% for natural gas.

Although Indian refiners have diversified their suppliers in recent years, with Russia becoming the biggest supplier, Gulf crude remains central to the country’s energy mix. And while availability of West Asian crude has improved considerably in recent months from the dismal levels seen in the initial few months of the war, those barrels are still quite expensive due to war risk premiums on shipping through from the region.
“For India, the clearest upside would come from an easing of Gulf tensions. That could make supplies more reliable and bring down tanker freight”, said Katona.

For India, the distinction between political signals and actual shipping conditions is crucial. Until tanker movements return to normal and the threat of further disruption recedes, India will continue to face uncertainty and high landed prices of oil and gas, even if the underlying prices of the commodities themselves fall and flows improve.
