In the first six months of the current financial year, India’s oil import bill jumped 46.4% year-on year to $90.6 billion, as per provisional data from the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MoPNG). Notably, oil imports in the whole of last financial year stood at about $135 billion. LNG imports in April-September rose 23.2% year-on-year to $8.5 billion.

The country imports 1.8-2 billion barrels of oil a year, and every $1-per-barrel increase in price bumps up its oil import bill by up to $2 billion on an annualised basis. According to a March report by Nomura, India is among the three Asian economies most vulnerable to high oil prices. It also said that every 10% increase in oil price typically widens the country’s current account deficit by 0.4% on the GDP. Crude oil alone is the country’s largest merchandise import.
The midterm polls’ potential ramifications for Russian energy

While lower global oil prices would benefit India, the possibility of tougher US sanctions against Russia could complicate things for New Delhi. In September, India imported 1.9 million barrels per day (bpd) of Russian crude and it accounted for over 35% of the country’s total oil imports for the month, even as West Asian oil imports saw notable recovery, according to tanker data from commodity market analytics firm Kpler. In the preceding months, the import volumes from Russia were even higher, with an all-time-high of 2.8 million bpd seen in July.

India’s oil imports from Russia really took off after the Ukraine war broke out. With much of the West shunning Russian crude following Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Moscow started offering discounts on its oil to willing buyers. Indian refiners were quick to avail the opportunity, leading to Russia—earlier a peripheral supplier of oil to India—emerging as India’s biggest source of crude, displacing the traditional West Asian suppliers.

While the Trump administration had targeted India regularly over hefty purchases of Russian crude, Washington’s stance on Moscow and Russian energy exports has softened considerably in recent months. Just weeks ago, Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports, saying that the US will also be buying diesel from Moscow. He also waived the implementation on some key clauses of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act which stipulated up to 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy, like India and China.

But a Congress controlled by the Democrats could push for a tougher approach towards Moscow to limit Russian oil revenues. The commercial attractiveness of Russian oil depends on factors other than just the price of crude. Payment arrangements, shipping availability, insurance costs and compliance with sanctions all influence the final landed cost of Russian oil for Indian refiners.

Experts expect the Democrats to pressure the Trump administration to reconsider its existing sanctions relief, and even impose additional restrictions on Russian energy companies, banks, and shipping networks. Harsher sanctions could make it more difficult and expensive for Indian refiners to arrange payments, secure tankers or obtain insurance for Russian cargoes.

“On Russian oil, the Graham Act tariff waiver has no fixed expiry date, and the President’s administration still decides whether to lift it under the current law. I’d expect Democrats to push for tougher sanctions directly on Russian oil companies and banks — that will keep Russian barrels discounted, but with payments harder to arrange and Black Sea freight already expensive and risky. So a cheaper Russian barrel at the loading port may offer Indian refiners little saving by the time it lands,” said Katona.

title: Abdul El-Sayed to be US’ first Muslim Senator: Why his win matters beyond that

content.value: Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan’s Senate race in the 2026 US midterm elections, a historic victory that will make him the country’s first Muslim Senator when he takes his seat in January 2027.

An outspoken critic of Israel, El-Sayed defeated former Representative and Republican candidate Mike Rogers, who was making his second run for the Senate, in a closely watched and bitterly fought campaign. President Donald Trump even described him as a “jihadist lunatic”.

El-Sayed — whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed — responded to Trump’s emphasis on his middle name, calling attention to his religious identity, by saying: “I’ll be Senator Mohamed to you, bro.”
Now that he will indeed become “Senator Mohamed”, his election holds relevance beyond his identity — for his party, US politics and possibly the world. Here is why.
Who is Abdul El-Sayed?

El-Sayed, 42, was born in Michigan and raised by his Egyptian immigrant father and Michigan native stepmother. He attended public schools and played football, wrestling, and lacrosse, later studying medicine at the University of Michigan and Columbia University. He then earned a second doctorate at Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar.

Some ambiguity over him allegedly presenting himself as a practising doctor has come under scrutiny. According to a Politico report, El-Sayed earlier said he decided not to practice medicine after treating a patient during medical school and “decided he wanted to address systemic issues, instead of individual patients.”
He has written books about public health and held academic positions. He is married to Sarah Jakaku, a psychiatrist whose parents were Indian immigrants.
What was Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign about?

El-Sayed has not described himself as a democratic socialist — a tag embraced by other young, non-White politicians of the Democratic Party, including New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York House representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Yet, he has focused on issues relevant to the working classes, such as cost of living and free medical care. El-Sayed’s website says: “No one should have to choose between getting the care they need or going into debt in the richest, most powerful country in the world. I will fight to expand Medicare (the government’s health insurance programme) to cover all necessary healthcare… without premiums, copays, or deductibles.”

Interestingly, he has echoed some of Trump’s own talking points, such as bringing back US manufacturing jobs outsourced elsewhere, and opposing the existing political establishment. His website says, “Trade deals, like NAFTA, have been a disaster for American manufacturing and have rotted out our towns… Trump’s incoherent, self-serving version of tariffs have only made the problem worse. I support targeted, smart tariffs that would help protect Michigan manufacturing and incubate the industries of the future with unions at the forefront.”
Michigan is among the US’s “rust-belt” states in the northeast, which were known as leading manufacturers in sectors like steel, but they faced decline beginning around the mid-20th century.

El-Sayed has also criticised Israel and US support for the nation over its war in Palestine that has resulted in the decimation of the Gaza Strip. This has been a point of contention given the traditional Jewish support for Democrats in the state.
This stance was one of the factors behind his fallout with Michigan’s Democratic Representative Haley Stevens who, in a widely criticised last moment U-turn, backed his Republican opponent Rogers.
And it has brought additional scrutiny over his religious identity. But El-Sayed has responded strongly to comments like Trump’s.

When Rogers spoke about his name, he replied: “Mike, listen man, if you can’t say the name — it’s Abdulrahman — keep the name out your damn mouth.” He then said to the crowd he was addressing: “My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries. You know what is? Their B.S. policies.”
Why does El-Sayed’s candidacy matter?

Ahead of the midterms, the Republicans controlled both legislative bodies that comprise the US Congress — the House of Representatives, which is the lower house, and the Senate, the upper house. All 435 seats in the former, and 35 of the 100 Senate seats, went to the polls.

But the contest always seemed like the Democratic Party’s to lose. Polling among voters showed dissatisfaction with rising fuel prices and inflation, alongside opposition to the underlying reason for these events — Trump’s war against Iran.

Those sentiments have borne themselves out in the results. In the stunning “blue wave”, Democrats, according to the latest figures, secured 54 seats in the Senate (they needed 51 to reclaim the majority) and 225 House seats (they needed 218 to take control of the lower chamber).

These decisive results, therefore, deal a serious blow to how the Republicans and Trump can pass their agenda. This could also influence US policy on tariffs and visas in relation to countries like India.
In the Senate, Republicans earlier held a 53-47 advantage. Michigan had a Democratic senator who vacated his seat.
It is the upper house alone which has the power to confirm presidential appointments, including Cabinet members and federal judges, and approve treaties by a two-thirds majority.

El-Sayed’s Senate victory, therefore, has solidified Democrats’ control over Senate and would add to the argument made by a section of the party’s younger leaders towards a platform focused on welfare and the economy — rather than wars and support for Israel. It also indicates that such campaigns do resonate among voters outside liberal strongholds like New York and can now be adapted for other parts of the country.

title: China This Week | FM Sitharaman to Europe, growing focus on Chinese trade surplus

content.value: From the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, prominent global figures had critical words about the Chinese economy this week.

While Sitharaman flagged the growing imbalance in bilateral trade, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva advised China to move from exports to domestic consumption to boost growth. A common thread runs through these arguments that China’s own trade data, also released this week, attested to.

We then look at China’s relationship with North Korea. A bridge inauguration took place this week, coming as the two nations have been attempting to deepen their relationship. Chinese President Xi Jinping’s first foreign trip this year was also to North Korea.
Here is a closer look at these developments:
1. Europe to India, China’s trade surplus in focus

Sitharaman said at the IMF-World Bank annual meeting in Thailand, “The trade imbalance is something which we have been talking with China now for several years. We are denied market access even for those goods for which there are immense market opportunities in China.” She identified sectors such as pharmaceuticals and bovine meat as having export potential.
Mao Ning, a Chinese spokesperson, responded that “China never aims for trade surplus” and that it stood ready to work with India and address mutual concerns.

Zooming out, the IMF MD also made note of China’s massive exports in the context of discussing the steps that major economies must take: “For (trade) surplus countries, what they need to do is increase domestic consumption. That clearly applies to China’s ‌growth model. Shift ⁠from exports more toward domestic consumption.”
UPSHOT: China’s trade data showed that its exports increased by around 36% compared to last year, indicating that the overall figures this year will be higher, too.

In 2025, China hit a record trade surplus of $1 trillion — a figure no country has ever registered. While it was a clear reflection of the country’s rise as a manufacturing powerhouse across product categories, from cheap consumer goods to semiconductors and tech products, it also highlighted just how reliant the country has become on the rest of the world to power its economy.

Apart from the sense of instability that it lends to the Chinese economy, it also results in a large trade gap with other countries, which have all tried to manage it in different ways. For the United States, the solution under the Trump administration has included tools like tariffs and mandating that China buy certain commodities from it. One big example is soybeans, which hold importance for President Donald Trump in securing the political support of farmers and the rural voter base.

For Europe, it has meant a rising number of Chinese automobile exports, especially much-cheaper Hybrid Electric Vehicles, posing a threat to the continent’s flagship carmakers. Earlier this month, trade talks led to a cap imposed on the number of such vehicles reaching Europe, after years of complaints. But automobiles are only part of the picture —  the EU’s ⁠goods trade deficit with China stands at around 1 billion euros per day.

On Friday (October 16), European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said European industries have called for action, and they would respond with more safeguards in other sectors, adding, “We need to act.”

Spurring domestic demand is easier said than done for the Chinese State, with problems ranging from youth unemployment to a long-running real estate crisis. But the chorus of disapproval could hint at more room for some accommodation that has been a long time in the making.
2. New China-North Korea bridge

The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) tabloid Global Times described the bridge over the Yalu River as a “cross-border transport link” between the city of Dandong in Northeast China and Sinuiju in North Korea. Visuals from the event showed trucks with flags of both nations and a Reuters report called it “the largest and most significant ​land crossing for trade between the two countries.”

Li Qiang, the Premier of China, quoted the President during a video address, saying, “Xi has pointed out that no matter how the international landscape evolves, the firm position of China’s Party and government to attach great importance to the traditional friendship between China and the DPRK will remain unchanged.”

UPSHOT: The bridge adds another route that could aid the countries’ economic ties. China has long been crucial to the North Korean economy amid the sanctions imposed by much of the world, even as the hermit kingdom has developed a closer relationship with Russia in recent years.

This strategy is part of a diversification that the country has attempted, balancing the two major powers. What further complicates the dynamic are Russia-China ties, which are marked by managing competition, economic and diplomatic reliance on one another, and strategic considerations against the West. At times, the three nations have been clubbed together as part of the larger informal “CRINK” (China, Russia, Iran and North Korea) grouping, encapsulating this mix of commonalities and divergences.

title: Why the EU is deepening security ties halfway across the world

content.value: On July 24, the European Union and the Philippines signed a statement announcing that they were significantly expanding their cooperation on defence, maritime security and strategic resilience.
This also comes as the EU negotiates a free trade agreement with the Philippines.

Why is the EU deepening ties with the Philippines at this moment? The answer lies in the archipelagic nation’s location — the South China Sea, an area where China has long made territorial claims. And as the US slowly takes a backseat in the Indo-Pacific, the EU appears to be taking on a greater role.
Why is the South China Sea so important for a grouping in a different part of the world? How is the EU getting involved? We explain.
First, what is the South China Sea dispute?

The South China Sea is situated just south of the Chinese mainland and is bordered by Brunei, China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam. The countries have bickered over territorial control in the sea for centuries, but tensions have soared to new heights in recent years as an increasingly powerful China looks to assert more power over the region.

In 2016, the Philippines filed an arbitration case in an international tribunal, seeking to strike down China’s expansive territorial claims in the sea, and won. Ten years on, however, that has done little to dissuade China from flexing its muscles. Both countries’ vessels have had several tense face-offs in the region for years now.
What is the EU doing?

Security is a key part of the EU-Philippines agreement. As part of the pact, the EU has approved its first-ever security assistance measure in the Indo-Pacific under the European Peace Facility (EPF), worth €15 million (about $17 million).

The assistance measure is expected to strengthen the Philippines’ “maritime domain awareness” while supporting freedom of navigation and respect for international law, an EU Spokesperson at the European Commission’s (EC) offices in Brussels told The Indian Express.

Simply put, this is an investment in the Philippine Navy’s non-lethal capabilities — especially surveillance and monitoring. This may help the coastal state to independently track and deter “gray-zone coercion” in contested waters of the South China Sea.

“Gray-zone coercion” refers to actions just short of open conflict that are meant to pressure or intimidate another country. These include using coast guard vessels, water cannons or aggressive manoeuvres in disputed waters — an apt description for China’s playbook over the years.

The Philippines is not an isolated partner. Rather than building a formal military alliance, Brussels is developing a network of security partnerships across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean, focused on areas such as maritime security and information-sharing. India is also a partner.
So what’s in it for the EU? To understand that one must understand the importance of the South China Sea.
What’s the importance of the South China Sea?
There are 11 billion barrels of oil and 190 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in deposits under the South China Sea, according to the estimates of the US Energy Information Agency.

Moreover, the sea is home to rich fishing grounds — a major source of income for millions of people across the region. The BBC reported that more than half of the world’s fishing vessels operate in this area.

Most significantly, the sea is a crucial trade route. The UN Conference on Trade and Development estimates that over 21% of global trade, amounting to $3.37 trillion, transited through these waters in 2016.
What is the EU looking to achieve here?
Around 40% of the EU’s external trade passes through the South China Sea, the spokesperson quoted above said.

“This assistance measure for the Philippines reflects the EU’s growing engagement as a security partner in the Indo-Pacific. The region is increasingly important for the European Union because its stability, maritime security and respect for international law directly affect our own security and economic interests,” the spokesperson said.

Importantly, these strategic moves come at a time when the US’s relationship with the Indo-Pacific is changing. Its role as the region’s main security guarantor is being challenged as it deals with crises around the world. The country has also been calling upon its allies to step up their defence engagements.

Ken Moriyasu, Senior Fellow at the Hudson Institute, told The Indian Express: “The Donald Trump administration is otherwise preoccupied with their engagements in Iran and Ukraine. It currently doesn’t possess the capacity — diplomatically, militarily or economically — to sustain heightened tensions with China. Naturally, the US is unlikely to raise tensions with China over the Philippines simply because their priorities dictate otherwise.”

This is where the EU comes in. Manjeev Singh Puri, former Indian ambassador to the EU, told The Indian Express: “They are trying to become a pole — an interesting development since it might lay a possible foundation for the start of multi-polarity within a Western context.”

“The EU is trying to signal to the international community that they are no longer seeking shade under the American security blanket. This is visible through their push for strategic autonomy in conjunction with their NATO commitments,” Puri said. “This step, however, doesn’t diminish their relations with China but is a signal that they are more than just an economic power in an evolving world.”

“The trajectory of the US-China relationship has not changed”, Moriyasu said. “The EU stepping in to offer their support to the Philippines is surely to be viewed favourably by both the US and more importantly, the Philippines, considering their positioning in the region.”
Still many hurdles
The way forward for the EU in its hopes of establishing permanence to a rules-based order in the Indo-Pacific still faces many hurdles.

“At the 10th anniversary of the South China Sea arbitration award, there were a host of countries that publicly supported the ruling. Interestingly, what stood out was the countries that were absent — of which there were a fair few. It was telling that specific nations did not engage with the joint statement”, Moriyasu said.

The abstinence of key regional countries like Vietnam, Malaysia, South Korea and India (among many others) underscores the complexities the EU is likely to face in a theatre where legal arguments are not enough.

title: After US midterm wipeout, will Trump resume Iran war? An expert explains

content.value: The US midterm polls have left the Democratic Party in firm control of both Houses of the US Congress, with the Republican Party suffering historic losses even in traditional strongholds.

Behind the Blue Tsunami was the cost of living crisis in the US, exacerbated by President Donald Trump’s tariffs and, crucially, the war he started against Iran — which drove up fuel prices domestically and globally.
Indeed, after the results, Vice President J D Vance acknowledged on X that “the reason we lost is the war [with Iran]”. Trump has himself called this “largely true”.
The question now is whether a defeated Trump will lash out by resuming the war with Iran or pursue a deal instead.

The signals seem mixed. Early after the polls, he seemed disinclined towards more war, saying: “We seem to be getting everything we want… we’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it.”

But, on Thursday, he tried to keep the possibility open: “Do we want to go further (with military action)? I would rather not destroy the rest of the country, if possible, but maybe I will have to. You’ll know soon enough.”

Vance, perhaps driven by the need to distance himself from Trump before the 2028 Presidential elections, has been clearer. He said that for voters to return to the party, the administration would have to “end the war, focus on inflation, put America first (and) change our relationship to Israel”.
With the new Congress set to take office in early January, the US now appears simultaneously on the verge of both war and a deal with Iran. What are the pathways ahead?
The path to war

As has been explained before in these columns, the Trump administration’s military actions against Iran later in the year were essentially an attempt to improve its bargaining position for a deal. But this prolonged entanglement in West Asia has significantly affected its domestic standing, as proved by the midterm polls. The President’s approval rating now stands at 38%.

In recent months, Vance has reportedly privately accused Israel’s (now caretaker) Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, of being “wrong on everything” about Iran. This shows Washington DC’s loss of faith in the military approach that has long been pushed by the Israeli leader.

If anything, the US’s post-midterms predicament has strengthened Tehran’s bargaining position, reflected in Iranian leaders’ rhetoric following the results. This, in turn, may force the US President to save face through yet another visible show of force, even if a deal remains the ultimate objective.
But Trump’s principal challenge, even before the midterms, has been that Tehran retains as much agency as Washington in determining when a round of strikes ends.

In the run-up to the polls and ever since, Tehran has consistently asserted that there is not a single US military pathway — whether swift or prolonged — that will not result in escalatory retaliation, especially with potentially longer-range missiles being used without “geographic restraint”.
This significantly cuts into Washington’s space for calibrated military action that absorbs the cost of Iranian retaliation but still keeps Tehran at the table.

The regional Arab states, which faced the brunt of Iran’s retaliatory attacks earlier this year, know that another round of fighting will hobble them economically. Recognising both Washington’s dilemma and Tehran’s resilience, Qatar, Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and UAE are proactively pushing for any possible interim arrangement.

The US achieved no strategic objective through the war it started with Israel in late February. Resuming it would do even less for its bargaining position in the ongoing negotiations for an interim deal.
The path to a deal
In the run-up to the midterms, it was the aforementioned lack of an achievable objective that prevented US military action, or support for Israeli action.

Iran remains interested in forcing the US to return to the core terms of the collapsed interim peace deal from June. This is reflected in its seven demands — including cessation of hostilities, end of the US blockade, sanctions relief, release of frozen Iranian funds and reparations, among others.

Iran also wishes to retain the pathway to peace that was set out in the June memorandum of understanding — the US meeting these seven demands, followed by Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz (retaining the right to coordinate shipping with Oman), and then both sides then moving to nuclear talks.
For Tehran, this interest supersedes the need to preempt hostilities with Washington (as it has rhetorically been threatening to do).

Iran refrained from responding to Israel’s large-scale aerial provocation close to Iranian airspace in October. It is also now reportedly amenable to a two-day implementation window for an interim deal — Day 1 would see Iran admitting International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors in return for a lifting of the US blockade and release of frozen Iranian funds; Day 2 would see Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and the initiation of talks over its reported 440 kg stockpile of 60% enriched uranium.
This is a marked step-down from Iran’s seven-day roadmap presented to the US in September.
However, if the midterm results dissuade the Trump administration from military action, it would need Iranian nuclear concessions (related to the 60% enriched uranium) even in the interim deal.

This is unlike the June MoU, which effectively agreed to defer nuclear negotiations for 60 days. This is untenable for Tehran, especially as it blames Washington for undermining key provisions of the June MoU, such as guaranteeing Iranian/Omani control of the Strait of Hormuz.
The clock is ticking
For the Trump administration, time is running out for a smooth path to removing sanctions on Iran — a core part of Tehran’s demands.

On September 18, Trump had signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. This statute had extended the expiry of the original 1996 Iran Sanctions Act from December 2026 to December 2031. For permanent sanctions relief, a Congressional vote is inevitable.

Moreover, it was a Republican-led House and Senate which had passed the 2015 Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act that sought to review Barack Obama’s nuclear deal. Now, this same Act binds the Trump administration to submit any nuclear deal with Iran to Congress with a 60-day review period. For a Republican-led Congress to oversee this review period, a comprehensive deal for full sanctions relief would ideally need to have been submitted by November 7.

Hence, notwithstanding the actual complexity of Congress-linked options facing President Trump for whenever a nuclear deal is on the table, an interim agreement remains the only viable path presently.

But Trump is not the only one facing the difficult question of releasing funds to Iran. Democrats, too, will soon have to choose — back a Trump-led deal, or be seen as prolonging the war. That, however, remains a problem for after January, when the new Democrat-controlled Congress takes charge.

Ironically, it is also this closing “lame duck” window which arguably presents the last opportunity for Washington to attempt another military-led attempt at forcing early nuclear concessions from Tehran.
Ultimately, it will be Iran’s willingness (or lack thereof) to offer nuclear concessions during an interim deal that will determine whether Washington turns to the military to save face.

This is notwithstanding a ‘Black Swan’ scenario where Israeli caretaker PM Netanyahu or his successor conducts fresh unilateral strikes on Iran and allows Washington to intervene, declare a ceasefire, and secure credit for “ending” the war — which it had started.

title: US backing for Israel has long been bipartisan. Will a Democrat-held Congress change that?

content.value: The morning after the Republican wipeout in the US midterm elections, Vice President J D Vance posted a lengthy postmortem on social media site X. The following was his prescription for Republicans to win back voters: End the Iran war, bring down the cost of living, focus on America — and “change our relationship to Israel”.

The Democratic wave — marked by a key Senate victory for a staunch Israel critic (Abdul El-Sayed) and Vance’s partial attribution of defeat to Israel — have brought the US-Israel relationship, and voters’ growing scepticism of it, into sharp focus.
Over the decades, Israel has largely been the one issue on which both Democrats and Republicans have largely been on the same page.
Multiple polls this year, however, have shown that public opinion is changing in the US, with people and politicians across the political spectrum questioning the uncritical backing for the country.

Indeed, just before the midterm polls opened, President Donald Trump said the US would cut off around $4 billion in annual aid to Israel, though it was not clear if this was an attempt to sway disillusioned voters.

Will the new political realities reshape the special ties between the US and Israel? What will be the attitude of the Democrats towards Israel? Will they shun their traditional position and assume a critical stance? We explain:
Formative years

The Democrats embraced the newly formed state of Israel in 1948 despite President Harry S Truman facing opposition from within his own administration. The US Department of State as well as the Department of Defence argued that recognising Israel would alienate oil-rich Arab monarchies, jeopardise the stance against the Soviet Union in the emerging Cold War and instigate prolonged regional instability.

Truman recognised Israel just a few minutes after David Ben-Gurion declared independence. His decision was said to have been driven by a combination of personal moral convictions regarding Holocaust survivors, historical sympathy for Jewish statehood, and domestic pressure from American Jewish leaders and Democratic political strategists.

Democrats have traditionally served as a haven for American Zionism as well as pro-Israel advocacy for several decades. In contemporary international relations, Democrats’ policies towards Israel are defined by a “two-tiered realism”.
At the institutional level, the mainstream Democratic leadership maintains a commitment to Israel’s fundamental security, defence assistance and right to self-defence.

At the ideological level, however, a widening partisan and generational rift has emerged. Foreign policy experts such as Amnon Cavari and Shibley Telhami have noted that progressive Democrats increasingly view the Israeli-Palestinian conflict through the lens of civil rights, human rights universalism, and anti-occupational norms. Consequently, a section of the current Democratic leadership (the progressives) rejects unconditional support for Israel.
Republican realignment

In the late 1970s, Republicans began to forge a strong alliance with White Evangelical Christians, who supported Israel due to their belief in dispensationalist theology, which professes that the modern gathering of Jewish people in the Land of Israel and the re-establishment of the Israeli state in 1948 are literal fulfilments of Biblical prophecy — and necessary precursors to the Second Coming of Christ.

By the 1990s, the Republican leadership adopted an approach that closely aligned with Israel’s right-leaning Likud party. Hence, they prioritised unconditional diplomatic protection at the UN in opposition to a negotiated two-state solution that requires Israeli territorial concessions and strong support for Israeli sovereignty claims over Jerusalem and the West Bank.
Democratic divergence
While Democrats at the core remain pro-Israel, the party’s broader base has questioned the favours extended to the Jewish state at the cost of US taxpayers.

US assistance to Israel is managed through structured statutory frameworks, primarily Foreign Military Financing. Since the 2016 Memorandum of Understanding negotiated under the Obama administration, the US has provided Israel with around $3.8 billion annually.

However, contrary to the belief that US military aid to Israel has always been unconditional, several presidents have repeatedly frozen, delayed, suspended, or leveraged aid to compel Israeli strategic compliance (see box below).
What the future holds

As the Democrats have secured a majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, and at a time when there seems to be a deadlock in Israeli electoral politics, bilateral ties are likely to be subjected to rigorous Congressional scrutiny.

With the Democrats in the majority in key committees, the Congress is likely to introduce stricter compliance mechanisms under existing legislation, including the Leahy Laws that prohibit the US military assistance to foreign security force units credibly implicated in gross violations of human rights. It can also invoke Section 620I of the Foreign Assistance Act, which restricts aid to countries that prohibit or restrict the transport or delivery of US humanitarian assistance.

Moreover, settler violence in the occupied West Bank and the expansion of outposts have resulted in friction between Democrats and Israeli leadership. The settler-related violence, which was once treated as  a secondary diplomatic issue, is now seen by Democrats as a threat to US national security interests and the viability of a two-state solution.
But it would be premature to count on the new US Congress (it takes charge in January) forcing a sweeping shift in policy stance for two reasons.
First is Trump’s veto power, which would take a two-thirds majority in both Houses to overcome — something the Democrats don’t have despite their sweeping gains in the midterms.

Second, it is establishment Democrats — who have not exactly been strident in their criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza — who appear poised to take up the top Congressional leadership positions: Hakeem Jeffries as Speaker of the House of Representatives and Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader. Jeffries, to be clear, recently called for a “dramatic change” in the US policy on Israel, though it remains to be seen whether he follows through on the rhetoric.

But what is worth remembering is that Israel’s war on Gaza began in 2023, when Joe Biden was president. And Biden, an establishment Democrat, repeatedly backed Israel with arms shipments and aid despite the widespread humanitarian disaster that was unfolding in Gaza (see box above).
Israel, meanwhile, does anticipate some systemic pressure to condition military assistance on human rights compliance and territorial restraint. It also expects more open criticism of settlements.
Additionally, US foreign policy is likely to prioritise broader regional security arrangements — including Saudi-Israeli normalisation — related directly to progress on Palestinian sovereignty.
But it is unlikely to abandon its historical commitment to Israel’s core security and existence, even if the strategic baseline has shifted.

title: Saudi Arabia has defence pacts with Pakistan, Turkey, US: Why aren’t they fighting the Houthis?

content.value: The fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis has sharply escalated in the past two weeks, with the militia making their biggest territorial gains in years.

On September 10, they captured the strategic Red Sea port of Mocha (after which Mocha the coffee is named) along with other territory along Yemen’s western coast. By September 17, Ansar Allah, the official name of the Houthi militia, effectively controlled much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

Thus, while the Houthis are gaining more power against Yemen’s official government, which Riyadh backs, they are also in the position to disrupt Saudi oil flow on its western coast, at a time its eastern coast shipping is already suffering because of the Strait of Hormuz blockade. The global oil price has already crossed $100 per barrel, up from $70 in June 2026
The Houthis have also launched missiles and drones at Saudi territory, including attacks on energy infrastructure. Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes and warnings of stronger action.

On paper, Saudi Arabia has defence partnerships with multiple key players in the region. The US-Saudi Strategic Defense Agreement was signed on November 18, 2025; Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed their Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) on September 17, 2025; and Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, 2026. The Makkah agreement says an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack on all three.
So why have Pakistan, Turkey, or the US not joined the fighting against the Houthis?
Why aren’t Pakistan and Türkiye fighting alongside Saudi Arabia?

While the Makkah agreement is supposed to be a defence treaty, few details about its actual operational structure are available publicly. It does not delineate the escalation ladder, or what sort of response is expected from a member at which stage when another is facing attacks.
Both Pakistan and Turkey have said that Saudi Arabia has not requested them to send combat forces to Yemen. Turkish officials have said their Parliament is yet to approve the defence treaty.

Pakistan, of course, also has another mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia. However, barring a few fighter jets it sent in April when Iran was attacking US military assets in the kingdom, Pakistan hasn’t intervened militarily. Nor has Saudi Arabia come to Pakistan’s aid against Afghanistan, with both countries prioritising their own immediate concerns.

In the past few days, Pakistan has said it will extend all help to Saudi Arabia, but hasn’t given details. Recently, defence minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif told a Pakistani news channel that, “Under the trilateral agreement, if the territorial integrity of a country comes under threat, the agreement will be activated and the other two countries will proceed to protect it in fulfilment of their obligations.” But when asked specifically about military involvement against the Houthis, Asif said the government’s strategies couldn’t be made public at this stage.
Both Pakistan and Turkey are using diplomatic channels to calm the fighting. Pakistan specially has asked Iran, the Houthis’ main benefactor, to rein in the militia.

Retired IFS officer Anil Trigunayat, who has served as Director General of the Gulf and Haj Divisions in the Ministry of External Affairs, explained another reason. “Pakistan, Turkey and the Makkah Pact are stuck in a competing conundrum as they do have a good relationship with Iran and are not convinced that this time, the war was initiated by Houthis,” he told The Indian Express.

Pakistan has a big reason to not antagoise Tehran too much — it shares a 900-km border with the Shia country, passing through the restive Balochistan region, and has the world’s second largest Shia population in the world, after Iran itself.
Why isn’t the US fighting the Houthis?
US President Donald Trump has reportedly declined Saudi requests for direct military intervention against the Houthis.

The US has participated in the Yemen conflict in the past. It reached an understanding with the Houthis in 2025, under which it stopped its bombing campaign in return for a Houthi commitment not to attack American vessels.

That arrangement is still relevant. Right now, the Houthis are threatening only Saudi ships in the Red Sea, but they have the power to completely disrupt navigation in this crucial water body. With the world still reeling from the economic shock of the blocked Strait of Hormuz, the US would not want this. Also, US munitions are running low as the war with Iran grinds on. The Trump administration would not want to open another front in the Middle East when midterm elections are approaching and the Iran war is anyway unpopular.

Then is the Iran factor. The Houthis have largely been trained and armed by Iran. If other countries were to enter active fighting on Saudi Arabia’s behalf, Iran and its allied militias might get behind the Houthis openly, adding another dimension to the US-Israel-Iran war and risking a much wider conflagration in the region.
Why doesn’t Saudi Arabia simply fight the Houthis alone?

Because Riyadh has already tried that. The Houthis are Zaidi Shias, and Yemen’s civil war began because they felt marginalised under the Sunni government. In 2014, they captured the capital, Sanaa.
Saudi Arabia, a major Sunni power, intervened militarily in 2015. The rich Saudi Arabia has a modern, well-equipped military, but the Houthis survived years of pressure, while the war produced enormous humanitarian and political costs.

A UN-mediated truce in 2022 significantly reduced the fighting, although it was never turned into a permanent settlement. The current escalation came because the Houthis want Saudi Arabia to remove its blockade of the territories they control.

Today, the Houthis are far better trained and equipped, especially with missiles and drones. A direct confrontation, thus, could be prolonged and messy, with both economic and security costs for Saudi Arabia, at a time the Iran situation is anyway volatile and Riyadh would like to prioritise its growth ambitions.

“The history of the Yemen war indicates that Saudis and the 27-member Sunni alliance led by a retired Pakistani general was unable to overpower the Houthis. If an all-out attack is carried out with land forces, perhaps the Houthi resistance can be overcome, but winning against powerful non-state actors needs innovative strategies. Hence, the Saudis are seeking mitigation, including Chinese intervention with Iran,” Trigunayat said.

title: US midterms 2026: How Trump’s India trade deal pitch, peace claims ran into reality check

content.value: US Midterm Elections Results 2026: After months of to-and-fro on a trade deal triggered by harsh tariffs on India, the Donald Trump administration, in the run-up to the 2026 US midterm elections, showcased a “new and improved trade agreement” with India among key trading partners as a win for the US, which could foster industrial growth in the country.

The Trump administration also sought votes for “leveraging his dealmaking ability” to achieve peaceful resolution of the several conflicts throughout the world, including between India and Pakistan (New Delhi has contested the involvement of a third party in the ceasefire reached in May last year).

Yet, the Democratic Party has regained control of the Senate, the upper house of the US Congress, and the House of Representatives, the lower house, after voting in the 2026 US midterm elections concluded on Tuesday. In fact, the Democrats have won in several states that have traditionally voted Republican. This reveals a major rebuke for Trump — and his claims on the economy and peacemaking.
What Trump and claimed and promised

The White House on November 2 said that US President Donald Trump had “promised” that he would be a champion for the American worker, who suffered under lopsided trade deals. “President Trump has delivered better terms for American workers, farmers, and manufacturers by levelling the economic playing field with our trading partners,” the White House claimed.

“By using tariffs as leverage, President Trump secured new and improved trade agreements with major US trading partners covering more than half of global GDP — including the United Kingdom, European Union, Japan, China, India, Republic of Korea, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Cambodia,” the statement read.

The White House statement said that Trump had promised that warmongering would be expelled from the government. “President Trump has achieved remarkable success, leveraging his dealmaking ability to achieve unprecedented peace in eight conflicts throughout the world,” it said.

According to the US government, the Trump administration resolved conflicts between India and Pakistan, Israel and Iran, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, Egypt and Ethiopia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, and Israel and Hamas and that Trump is “now driving the push for trilateral talks to end the war between Russia and Ukraine”.

After the India-Pakistan ceasefire Minister of External Affairs of India, S. Jaishankar had said, “I can tell you that I was in the room when Vice President [JD] Vance spoke to Prime Minister Modi on the night of May 9,” Jaishankar said. “There was no linking of trade and ceasefire.”
What US citizens actually face
Trump came to power on promises of addressing the cost of living crisis in the US. However, the concerns on this front have only flared up.
The inflation rate in the US was 2.4% when Trump took charge. But it has not come back to that level since. At last count, it was at 3.7% — almost double of the US central bank target of 2%.
The results showed that the economy proved to be the single-most important issue on which votes were cast.

The AP Voter Poll, conducted by SSRS, found that 39% of voters considered the economy the country’s most important issue, followed by the state of democracy (32%) and immigration (14%). Nearly three-quarters rated the economy poorly, while 65% believed Trump’s policies had worsened economic conditions. Another 62% blamed his policies for higher-than-usual prices.
Trump’s policy choices have directly contributed to the spike in inflation rate, which has robbed average US workers of any real earnings growth.
He has pursued his sweeping tariff war despite a Supreme Court setback. But research has shown that it is the US consumer who has actually ended up paying for these tariffs.
And then there’s the war he launched in Iran, which further spiked fuel prices. Since the Iran war, retail fuel prices have gone by almost 50%.

The continuing war in Iran also directly contradicted his claims of bringing about peace across the world. The AP Voter Poll found that 62% of voters believed the US had been wrong to launch military action against Iran, while 74% said the conflict was a major or crucial factor in their Congressional vote.
India-US trade deal

While India and the US signed a framework agreement earlier this year in February, both countries are yet to officially sign an agreement. As per the framework agreement, the US and India agreed on a framework for an Interim Trade Agreement aimed at lowering tariffs, opening markets and reshaping energy and technology ties, as both sides work towards a full bilateral trade pact.

Under the framework agreement, India had agreed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on all US industrial goods and a broad range of US agricultural and food products, including animal feed, nuts, fruit, soybean oil, wine and spirits. But the framework agreement is yet to be implemented.

And the US agreed to apply a reciprocal tariff rate of 18% on many Indian goods, including textiles, clothing, leather, footwear, plastics, chemicals and certain machinery, under existing executive orders. It also agreed to remove tariffs on certain aircraft and aircraft parts, generic pharmaceuticals, gems, and diamonds and provide preferential market access to India in sectors of respective interest.
India had also agreed to buy $500 billion worth of US goods over five years, including energy products, aircraft, precious metals, technology products and coking coal.

Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told The Indian Express last month that the two countries were “incredibly close” to signing the deal, and that “99 per cent of the work” had been done. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal also said that the US free trade deal is sometimes sought to be politicised by a few elements, but India will get a competitive advantage when the US deal is signed.

title: As China’s leaders huddle for ‘Fifth Plenum’, an expert explains its significance

content.value: Beginning today (October 26), the Communist Party of China (CPC) is holding a four-day meeting of its top leaders in Beijing, known as the fifth plenum. Such meetings have previously heralded key policies — including the 1978 liberalisation of the Chinese economy.

This year, the meeting comes as the rest of the world keenly watches China’s position in sectors ranging from artificial intelligence (AI) to manufacturing. At the same time, its economy is no longer growing at the rates it did a few years ago, and corruption within the CPC has been touted as a major reason for purging senior military leaders.
What can the closed-door event reveal about the priorities of Chinese leaders? G Venkat Raman, professor at IIM Indore and fellow at the Institute of Chinese Studies (ICS), New Delhi, explains.
What are CPC Central Committee plenums?

The CPC holds a National Congress every five years to set its broad political direction and elect a Central Committee. Comprising around 200 members and 175 alternate members, this committee then elects the Politburo (around 24 members) and its Standing Committee — China’s apex political leadership of seven leaders. At the very top is the general secretary, the position Xi Jinping holds.
Between these congresses, it convenes plenary sessions, or plenums, to deliberate on major political, organisational and policy questions.

Although the State Council (similar to a Union Cabinet) and National People’s Congress (the national legislature) perform administrative and legislative functions, the CPC exercises overarching political leadership. Plenums translate the leadership’s priorities into authoritative decisions guiding ministries, provincial governments, state-owned enterprises and other institutions.

Their agendas range from economic reforms and development plans to Party discipline, ideology and senior appointments. The first plenum after a Party Congress generally establishes the new leadership; subsequent meetings set policy priorities and address institutional challenges.

The forthcoming Fifth Plenum of the CPC’s 20th Central Committee is unusual. Whereas Fifth Plenums have generally focused on economic development planning, this meeting is expected to consider a draft decision on comprehensive and rigorous Party self-governance, signalling a distinct internal emphasis.
How have previous plenums shaped China’s political and economic direction?
Several plenums have marked turning points in contemporary Chinese history. The Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in 1978 initiated the reform era associated with Deng Xiaoping.

The Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee in 2021 adopted the Party’s third historical resolution, consolidating Xi’s political and ideological position. The Fifth Plenum of 2015 announced the universal two-child policy.

Notably, the Fourth Plenum in October 2025 adopted recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030), departing from the usual sequence in which Fifth Plenums address development planning. Another relevant precedent is the Sixth Plenum of 2016, which adopted regulations on internal Party political life ahead of the Party Congress in 2017.
The 2026 meeting similarly precedes a Party Congress by approximately a year, making its emphasis on discipline and organisational cohesion particularly significant.
What does this emphasis mean in practice?

Since assuming leadership in 2012, Xi has made comprehensive and rigorous Party self-governance (quan mian cong yan zhi dang) central to his political programme. It encompasses combating corruption, enforcing political discipline, supervising officials and ensuring compliance with central directives.

The underlying principle is the Party’s self-revolution (dang de zi wo ge ming): the CPC’s conviction that it must continuously correct internal weaknesses to preserve its governing authority and maintain the Party’s legitimacy and effectiveness.

The disciplinary vocabulary is revealing. The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) has warned against ‘duplicitous’ officials (liang mian ren) who profess loyalty while acting otherwise, and ‘nice-guyism’ (hao ren zhu yi), whereby officials avoid confronting misconduct to preserve personal relationships. Both expressions highlight concerns about superficial loyalty and weak accountability.

On October 23, the Politburo acknowledged continuing problems in central Party and state institutions and demanded substantive rectification. The timing underscores that the forthcoming Plenum concerns not merely political loyalty but also the institutional capacity to implement central decisions effectively.
Could this also affect China’s economic growth?

China’s economic transformation historically relied on provincial experimentation, local entrepreneurship and competition among regional governments. Under Xi, however, political authority has become increasingly concentrated, narrowing the autonomy traditionally enjoyed by local officials.

This tension is acute amid weak domestic demand, local government debt and pressures for technological upgradation. Beijing needs provincial governments to attract investment, support private enterprise and implement reforms. Yet intensified anti-corruption investigations and political supervision can encourage risk aversion, with officials prioritising compliance over initiative.

Recent official discourse emphasises adapting policies to local conditions (yin di zhi yi) and encouraging officials to take responsibility and act (dan dang zuo wei). It acknowledges that effective governance requires administrative initiative alongside political discipline.

The emerging approach resembles selective decentralisation. However, administrative delegation within centrally prescribed boundaries is not equivalent to political decentralisation. The test is whether tighter Party supervision can coexist with meaningful local discretion. China’s economic performance depends not only on central decisions but also on whether local governments have the confidence and capacity to implement them creatively.
What could the Plenum signal about Xi Jinping’s authority, and the 21st Party Congress?

Recent investigations and personnel removals make this Plenum particularly consequential. The anti-corruption campaign has reached senior Party officials and military commanders, including individuals previously considered close to Xi.

According to the Asia Society Policy Institute’s estimates, nearly a quarter of the Central Committee’s original 2022 membership may be unable to attend on account of potentially being purged. Even the highest levels of the Central Military Commission (CMC), China’s apex military leadership body, have not been spared the anti-corruption campaign, with only two of the seven members still standing, raising questions about institutional stability and military leadership.

These developments reveal a paradox: disciplinary enforcement may consolidate Xi’s personal authority while exposing weaknesses in the institutions and personnel responsible for implementing his decisions.

The next Party Congress will determine the leadership lineup. Xi, at 73, is widely expected to seek a record-extending fourth term as Party general secretary. Leaders before him served two terms, and he broke from tradition in 2022. Any appointments, promotions or confirmed expulsions at the Plenum will attract scrutiny, although major leadership decisions may be deferred until 2027.

The larger question is whether Xi can rebuild an experienced and trusted leadership team after extensive removals. Rather than a formal succession meeting, the Plenum may indicate how he intends to manage political continuity and institutional renewal.
What are the wider implications of tighter Party governance for China?
Although the Fifth Plenum focuses on Party governance, its implications extend to China’s economic priorities and international standing.

Stronger Party supervision could improve accountability, curb corruption and ensure consistent implementation of national priorities. However, political discipline alone cannot resolve structural economic problems or stimulate domestic demand. China’s governance system will ultimately be judged by its ability to translate industrial ambitions into sustainable economic growth.

Internationally, greater political cohesion could strengthen Beijing’s capacity to pursue long-term technological and strategic objectives amid geopolitical competition. Yet foreign investors and trading partners will assess whether tighter Party control improves regulatory predictability or further concentrates decision-making, reducing transparency and flexibility.

The wider significance of the Fifth Plenum will depend on how its decisions reshape the relationship between Party supervision, institutional accountability and policy implementation. The central question is whether tighter political control can strengthen China’s governing capacity while sustaining economic dynamism and confidence among its international partners.

title: How the US midterm results reflect the Constitution’s distrust of majorities

content.value: Two years into Donald Trump’s second term in the White House, US voters made clear their sentiment toward the former businessman who had earlier urged the nation to treat the 2026 US midterms as a “referendum on his presidency”.

For a President that ascended to power in 2024 with a landslide win against his contender, Kamala Harris, an increase in Congressional oversight is likely to be an unwelcome — yet unavoidable —feature of his remaining two years in office given that as of 04:37 pm IST, the Democratic party led the race with a +25 gain in the House of Representatives and a +7 gain in the Senate.

The midterms as a measure to alleviate distrust are, however, baked into the fabric of American democracy. “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition”, wrote James Madison, a principal architect of the Constitution and fourth President of the US.
How is this distrust of majoritarianism reflected in the Constitution? And why are the 2026 midterm results a good way to understand it? We explain.
First, why majority rule was insufficient
Madison’s argument rationalising his distrust was rooted in understanding “factions” in society.

A faction, he operationalised, was a “majority or minority number of citizens” united by a common interest which was “adverse to the rights of other citizens or interests of the community,” as noted in the Federalist Papers, Letter No. 10. His problem lay in the fact that their competing interests could become a threat to the rights of others when given political legitimacy — regardless of whether the faction was a majority or minority.

He concluded hence in a later letter (no.51) that , “if men were angels, no government would be necessary”.  The great difficulty that lay in framing a government, was that one must first “enable the government to control the governed” while simultaneously “oblige it” to control itself.

While a minority faction could be defeated through a regular vote, a majority faction possessed the numbers to translate its interests into public policy. It could, in Madison’s words, sacrifice both “the public good and the rights of other citizens” to its own ruling interests.
This was the central dilemma the Constitution’s framers had to address: how could a system of government preserve majority rule while preventing a majority from exercising power without restraint?
So, is this visible in the US Constitution?
The Constitution then went ahead by ensuring a separation of powers, creating a bicameral house structure, ensuring federalism and a strong system of checks and balances.
The Congress — composed of the House of Representatives and the Senate — made the laws while the President was the primary executor of those laws.

The first three Articles of the Constitution lay out the separation of powers between the legislative, executive and judiciary. Article 1, Section 1 vests the Congress with legislative power while Article 2, Section 1 similarly assigns executive powers to the President.
The Constitution also places checks and balances between these branches.

Art.1/Section 7 specified that any bills passed by Congress must be “presented to the President” and allows him to “return it, with his objections” to the House which proposed it. Yet, both chambers may override such a veto with a two-thirds majority. Similarly, Art.2/Section 2 requires the President to seek “the advice and consent” of the Senate for several Presidential appointments — including that of Supreme Court judges. In this manner, the Constitution balances decision and reservation within its government branches.

Federalism, meanwhile, distributes authority between the national government and the 50 states. The Tenth Amendment, ratified in 1791, explicitly reserves powers not delegated to the federal government by the Constitution, nor prohibited to the states, to the states or the people respectively.
Congress itself is divided into two chambers under Article I.

Members of the House serve two-year terms and representation is based on population comprising 435 voting members. The Senate, conversely, has two senators from each state serving staggered six-year terms — with one-third of its membership elected every two years and totals a 100 members.

The distinction indirectly makes the House more immediately responsive to changing public opinion. Meanwhile, the Senate provides continuity and equal representation to states regardless of population.
What makes the midterms part of this reasoning? Do the results matter if Trump is still President?
The US midterms are the electoral expression of this constitutional arrangement.

The US President serves a fixed four-year term. Voters can, however, change the composition of Congress — as displayed in 2026 — midway through the President’s term which effectively divides the government.

More so than a deviation from majority rule, the 2026 blue wave sweep may have an answer rooted in John Locke’s concept of a social contract forged between an individual and government. In his Second Treatise of Government, Locke argued that political authority derives from the consent of the governed, who entrust government with the protection of their rights.

Consent, however, is not unconditional or permanent. The midterms offer one way in which this accountability is exercised. By changing the composition of Congress without changing the presidency, voters have altered the institutional balance through which the executive is held to account. This brings Locke’s idea of consent into conversation with Madison’s concern about the concentration of political power.
With Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress, Trump is likely to face greater congressional scrutiny.

Federal appropriations — the authority to authorise withdrawals from the Treasury — are controlled by Congress under Article I, Section 9 of the Constitution. The Senate also has a constitutional role in confirming presidential appointments under Article II, Section 2, while the House can initiate impeachment proceedings under Article I, Section 2.

Trump has not yet, however, lost his executive authority. The Republican President retains the power of veto legislation which mandates a two-thirds majority in both houses to be overruled. His party still retains control over Congress until January 2027 until the new members are sworn in, giving some respite.

Nearly 240 years after Madison articulated his concerns while advocating for the ratification of the Constitution, the midterms remain central to the American constitutional principle of allowing the majority to govern while ensuring that no electoral victory confers unlimited power.

title: Brazil elections: Why a jailed ex-president’s son is leading race, and the Trump factor

content.value: Brazil voted in the first round of its presidential elections on Sunday (October 4), with incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro receiving 45% and 47% of the vote, respectively.
Since neither won over 50% of the vote but still secured the most votes among all candidates, they will go head-to-head in another round of voting on October 25.

Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who won the 2018 elections and rejected the 2022 poll results after losing to Lula. His supporters stormed government offices in the capital, Brasília, evoking visuals of US President Donald Trump’s supporters attacking the US Capitol building in 2021. This is only one of many ways Bolsonaro and Trump are linked, with Trump backing him strongly over the years and expressing solidarity with him over supposed “witch hunts” for not accepting the results.

Today, Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence in relation to the attempted 2023 coup. How did his son become the frontrunner to lead Brazil? And what has been Trump’s role in the elections for the continent’s biggest country and economy?
Who is Flávio Bolsonaro?

Flávio, 45, is a lawyer by training and Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son. A senator from Rio de Janeiro, he bears a striking physical resemblance to his father, which may or may not lend him a political advantage given Bolsonaro Sr.’s reputation as a polarising figure. Take the 2022 election, the closest in Brazil’s history, where Lula received 50.9% of the votes against Bolsonaro’s 49.1%.

When Jair first came to power as the leader of Brazil’s Liberal Party (LP), his supporters saw him as a conservative, pro-business politician who would “tell it like it is”, similar to other populist right-wing leaders globally. Among his key policies was relaxing protections for the Amazon rainforest to encourage commercial activities.
He vowed to combat corruption, which was noteworthy since his own political rise was fuelled by mainstream political figures in Brazil getting implicated in major corruption scandals.

Bolsonaro is also known to make homophobic and misogynistic statements, telling a woman legislator who accused him of being a rapist: “I wouldn’t rape you because you don’t deserve it.” He was also criticised for his handling of the Covid-19 pandemic, with Brazil having the second-highest death toll among countries, after the United States.

As the Financial Times put it in a profile of the Bolsonaro family, “Flávio is the self-styled moderate of the family: a “vaccinated Bolsonaro”, in his own words. In the constant shadow of his father, he treads a difficult line… He all but acknowledges being an inferior substitute. “How can you compare Pelé’s son to Pelé himself?” Flávio asked the FT in an interview earlier this year during which he refused to sit behind his father’s desk in the party HQ.”

The Bolsonaros have enjoyed voter support among more well-off groups, the more conservative Evangelical Christians, and the country’s southern regions. On the other hand, Lula, 80, is a veteran socialist leader now contesting for a fourth term with supporters such as Catholics, progressives and poorer groups. Flávio has criticised Lula for not being tough enough on crime and drug gangs.
Lula was also president when the first BRIC meeting comprising Brazil, Russia, India and China was held in 2009 (South Africa was not a member of the grouping then).
And what is Trump’s role in the Brazilian elections?

Since Jair Bolsonaro’s first term, which partly overlapped with the first Trump administration, Trump has publicly supported him owing to their similar ideology and disdain for critics. He met Flávio earlier this year, calling him a “smart young man, who loves his country, Brazil, very much.”

Within months of his second term, Trump announced 50% tariffs on imports from Brazil in July 2025 for “threats” to the US. The executive order also noted that Brazilian officials were “persecuting” Bolsonaro and that this “contributes to the deliberate breakdown in the rule of law in Brazil.”

Trump has earlier warmed up to other strongman leaders globally, with vocal support for those from South America. Another prominent example is Argentina’s Javier Milei. This approach is also in line with the US National Security Strategy, released in November 2025. It laid out intentions for the US to be dominant in the Western Hemisphere, and its effects were seen in the military capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January this year.

As The New York Times said of South America in a recent report, “Candidates aligned with President Trump on issues like fighting drug gangs and “woke ideology” have won the last seven elections in the region, with Brazil the biggest remaining prize.” This period of rightward political shift comes not too long after a “pink tide” around 2022. The term was first used around the early 21st century, with the election of Hugo Chavez in Venezuela, followed by a roughly decade-long period that saw many countries reject neo-liberalism in favour of socialism (hence “pink”, rather than Communism’s red).

Oliver Stuenkel, Visiting Scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington, wrote back in 2022 for Americas Quarterly that this wave would be more short-lived. His reasons ranged from greater geopolitical instability translating into tougher economic circumstances for governments to their declining interest in maintaining a sense of regional unity and convergence.

“Today’s leftist presidents are less likely to prioritize ties to their neighbors because they are less relevant from an economic point of view. Intraregional trade amounted to over 20% of Latin America’s total exports in 2008, but this share has declined by a third and is set to fall further as commodity exports to China are on the rise,” he wrote.

title: Pakistan restricts foreign media in most of the country: What new rules say

content.value: Pakistan has unveiled sweeping new rules governing foreign media that require mandatory registration and accreditation for journalists and others working with international news organisations, while also placing new restrictions on where they can report.
The move comes days after international outlets covered protests taking place amid elections in Pakistan-Occupied Kashmir (PoK), coverage that drew a sharp response from the government.

The local media in Pakistan has blanked out the crackdown, which has led to around 40 deaths. On social media platforms, however, many, including Pakistanis, had criticised the State’s actions in PoK. The new guidelines state, “These guidelines shall be applicable to all foreign or international print, electronic and digital media including social media & web-based platforms.”
What are the new restrictions for foreign media in Pakistan?

The Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines, 2026, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting’s External Publicity Wing (EP Wing), make registration compulsory not only for foreign correspondents but also for Pakistanis working with foreign media in almost any capacity.

The guidelines apply to “foreign media houses, organizations and outlets working in Pakistan and all eligible journalists, media owners, media professionals, sources, freelancers, sponsors, fixers, attached persons, assignees etc., of Pakistan working or contributing for them.”
All of these terms are then explained in detail, covering translators, printers, distributers, and even those performing tasks of a “managerial/administrative” nature.

“Sources” are explained as “any book, publication, person or organization that discloses information forming the substance/subject of work undertaken by any journalist, reporter or media professional”.
“Foreign content” means a content that is produced under direct or indirect creative control of foreigners, foreign companies or foreign broadcasters.”
Thus, almost any journalistic work on Pakistan undertaken by a foreign media organisation can be impacted by the rules.
Journalists’ movement curbed
Foreign journalists also need the government’s No Objection Certificate for “official assignment especially for the work outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi.”

Of Pakistan’s four provinces, Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the latter two are in the grip of major, violent opposition movements to the Pakistani State. Waiting for an NOC will severely impact coverage of breaking news events or developing stories.

Of the cities foreign journalists are freely allowed in, Lahore is in Punjab, the comparatively prosperous Karachi is in Sindh, and Islamabad is federally administered, though geographically in Punjab.
Even for “leisure trips to Abbottabad and Murree”, an NOC is required from the EP Wing, which may be granted “within three working days”. Muree is in Punjab, while Abottabad is in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Suspension of accreditation or registration

While journalists need the accreditation for almost any work they do in Pakistan, it can be taken away if they are found misusing it, if their documents were forged, or if they are involved in “acts against the ideology, sovereignty, security, or public order of Pakistan.”
The guidelines offer no definition of what those terms mean or how such a determination would be made, raising fears of arbitrary application.
Context of the guidelines
Pakistan is ranked 153 out of 180 on the World Press Freedom Index, and curbs on journalism are not new.
The timing of the rules has attracted particular attention, coming into force after international media covered the deadly protests amid the ongoing elections in PoK.

Pakistani authorities had earlier criticised the BBC and Al Jazeera’s coverage of PoK. On August 4, the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting had accused Al Jazeera of “yellow journalism”, which refers to sensationalised and exaggerated reportage.

“We have taken note of Al Jazeera’s selective reporting from handpicked polling stations in Muzaffarabad today… Such yellow journalism only confirms the agenda of external actors with vested interests,” it had posted on X. Journalists working for foreign media were also instructed to leave the region and obtain an NOC before returning.
People in Pakistan had reported not being able to access Al Jazeera.

The guidelines themselves do not mention Kashmir or explain the circumstances in which they were introduced. However, the sequence of events has led media organisations and press freedom advocates to view the rules as part of a broader tightening of oversight over international reporting.

The guidelines have led to criticism within Pakistan too. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan posted on X that the guidelines “will invariably institutionalise bureaucratic control over news gathering and risk deterring independent reporting on matters of public interest… The requirement that journalists obtain state approval to report from large parts of the country sends a chilling message: that critical reporting is unwelcome.”

The Rawalpindi Islamabad Union of Journalists also “fiercely condemned” the notification. In a statement posted on X, it said the new rules would “only bring disrepute to Pakistan” and also “affect the employment of Pakistanis working with international media outlets.”

title: Nord Stream pipeline blasts: Why a Ukrainian man is on trial in Germany

content.value: In late September 2022, four underwater explosions ripped through the two Nord Stream gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany.

The suspicion immediately fell on Russia. Its invasion of Ukraine, launched just seven months back, had strained relations with Europe and the West, which had begun weaning themselves from cheap Russian energy and imposing sanctions on Moscow.

Four years later, it is a Ukrainian man — a former army officer no less — who is set to go on trial in Germany for his alleged involvement in one of Europe’s biggest acts of sabotage since World War II.
What are the two pipelines? How did the attack happen? And why? Here’s a refresher:
What is Nord Stream?
Before the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Germany was Russia’s biggest European gas consumer, and most of it came through the Nord Stream.

Nord Stream, meaning “North” stream, is a pair of underwater gas pipelines, majority-owned by the Russian energy giant Gazprom. Each pipeline comprises two separate pipes (or a total of four pipes) that run around 1,200 km through the Baltic Sea.

The first pipeline, Nord Stream 1, runs from Vyborg in northwest Russia to Lubmin in northeastern Germany. Announced in 1997, it was inaugurated in 2011, becoming the primary route through which Russian gas reached Germany. Nord Stream 1 transported 55 billion cubic metres of gas a year, most of which went directly to Germany, while the rest travelled west and southwards through onshore links to other countries and into storage caverns.

In 2015, Gazprom and five other European firms decided to build Nord Stream 2, valued at around $11 billion. This pipeline, running from Ust-Luga in Russia to Greifswald in Germany, was also meant to carry 55 billion cubic metres of gas per year and was completed in 2021.
The US and some of its allies had criticised the pipelines long before the invasion, pointing to how they increased Europe’s dependence on Russian gas.

Russia had already switched off Nord Stream 1 in August 2022, a month before the explosions ruptured it. Nord Stream 2, which was also damaged, never started operations because Germany suspended its certification process shortly before the invasion.
How did the attack happen?
It was Sweden that first discovered the leaks in the pipelines near the Danish Island of Bornholm on September 26, 2022.

While neither pipeline was transporting gas to Europe, they still contained pressurised gas. So, the ruptures in three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines released huge plumes of methane — a harmful greenhouse gas — into the atmosphere. Videos and photographs from that time show methane bubbling up to the surface of the Baltic Sea, measuring up to a kilometre in diameter.
While the cause was initially unclear, investigators concluded in November that the damage had been caused by four explosions.

While international observers initially blamed Moscow, investigators turned their focus to allegations that Ukrainian state security agencies may have been involved.
