Another voice counts down to zero, followed by a nuclear blast after which Lyndon B Johnson is heard saying: “These are the stakes—to make a world in which all of God’s children can live or to go into the dark. We must either love each other or we must die.” A narrator then urges viewers to vote for Johnson, warning that the stakes are too high to stay home.
Johnson’s Republican opponent, Barry Goldwater, who was implicitly targeted, condemned the advertisement for suggesting that his election could lead to nuclear war.

More than two decades later, the infamous 1988 Willie Horton ad directly attacked a candidate’s record. It was also widely condemned as racist for playing on fears and stereotypes about Black men and crime.

During a presidential campaign in which crime became a major issue, a group supporting Republican presidential candidate George H W Bush released the ad, linking Willie Horton, a convicted murderer who committed further violent crimes while on furlough from prison, with Michael Dukakis, Bush’s Democratic rival.

The ad meant to show Dukakis as being “soft on crime”, linking his opposition to the death penalty to a Massachusetts prison furlough programme that operated during his governorship and permitted prisoners serving life sentences to leave prison temporarily. “Horton received 10 weekend passes from prison. Horton fled, kidnapped a young couple, stabbing the man, and repeatedly raping his girlfriend,” the ad says.

The advent of social media also gave an unprecedented reach to the kind of fabricated allegations associated with “dirty tricks”. The 2016 presidential campaign notably witnessed “Pizzagate”, in which a conspiracy theory spread across social media alleging that Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton’s campaign manager’s emails had coded references to a child sex ring run by high-ranking members of the party. The fabricated claims centred on a Washington DC pizzeria.

Following the 2020 election, Donald Trump’s campaign released television advertisements alleging widespread electoral fraud, including one titled STOP THE STEAL! The claims were false. In 2024, baseless allegations that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were abducting and eating neighbourhood pets circulated widely online and were even featured on billboards commissioned by the Arizona Republican Party.

By 2026, artificial intelligence (AI) has added another dimension to political advertising, allowing campaigns to create everything from minor visual enhancements to convincing but fabricated depictions of candidates. Citing research by the Wesleyan Media Project, The New York Times reported that over $137 million was spent promoting over 220 advertisements featuring AI-generated content during the US midterm campaigns. Nearly 70% of these advertisements did not disclose the use of AI. The technology has also made elaborate campaign videos considerably cheaper, while making it harder to distinguish genuine footage from fabricated material.
Do negative political ads work?

A 1999 meta-analysis by political scientists Richard Lau, Lee Sigelman and colleagues found little evidence that negative advertisements were more effective than positive ones, or that they significantly discouraged political participation. A 1990 study by Gina Garramone and colleagues, meanwhile, suggested that negative advertisements could sharpen voters’ perceptions of differences between candidates without necessarily affecting their likelihood of voting.

However, a 2016 study by Jared Barton, Marco Castillo and Ragan Petrie found that negative campaign letters increased turnout among supporters compared with positive letters in two local elections. More recently, a 2022 study by Yingying Chen and Luping Wang found that hostile exchanges in the comments on a misleading Trump campaign video on YouTube tended to continue, showing how such advertisements could fuel hostility online.

A candidate’s use of negative campaigning also need not cost them support, even when voters disapprove of their tactics. In a post-election survey in November 2024, the Pew Research Center found that 68% of Trump voters considered the presidential campaign too negative. Yet 82% said they had voted primarily in support of Donald Trump, rather than against Kamala Harris.

Voters have overlooked controversial conduct before. During his successful 1983 campaign for Louisiana governor, Edwin Edwards famously declared that he could lose only if he was caught in bed with “either a dead girl or a live boy”.

In Ohio, recent opinion polls show Acton ahead of Ramaswamy. The RealClearPolling average puts Acton at 48.5% and Ramaswamy at 44.9%, while an October 15–19 Fox News poll found a narrower 50–48% margin. On October 24, the Kalshi betting market priced an Acton victory at approximately 82%, against 19% for Ramaswamy.

In Ohio, however, the negative strategem appears to have backfired on Ramaswamy. Though Acton’s prospects had already been improving, Ramaswamy’s odds nosedived further following the airing of the advertisement — which has attracted criticism even from Republicans — according to the popular betting site Kalshi. As per Kalshi, Acton’s chances increased from 68% on October 14 to 76% on October 20, following the controversy, and climbed further to 81% by October 22.

title: Eisenkot gets mandate to form Israel’s government: 3 scenarios, and Netanyahu’s options

content.value: Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Sunday (November 8) formally tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming the country’s next government, following an inconclusive parliamentary election in which neither Eisenkot nor Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority.

Eisenkot received the mandate after 67 lawmakers, including those from two Arab-majority parties, recommended his candidacy. He now has 28 days, extendable by another 14, to assemble a governing coalition.

However, deep divisions among Eisenkot’s prospective allies remain an obstacle. While the Arab parties have offered their support, several right-wing opposition leaders remain unwilling to govern with them. Eisenkot, meanwhile, has called for a national emergency government, acknowledging that compromises would be necessary.
Should he fail to put together a coalition, Netanyahu could remain caretaker prime minister as Israel faces another round of negotiations or fresh elections.
What options does Eisenkot have, and how could Netanyahu benefit from a prolonged deadlock? Here are three possible scenarios.
First, who stands where in Israel?
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority in the 120-member Knesset.

Netanyahu’s right-wing and ultra-Orthodox coalition won 53 seats, while Eisenkot’s fractious alliance comprising his centrist Yashar party, as well as right-wing and centre-left factions, got 48 seats.

But two Arab-led alliances together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters. While the United Arab List (Ra’am party) won eight seats, the Joint List — an alliance of Hadash, Ta’al and Balad parties — won 11.
With both the Joint List and Ra’am recommending Eisenkot for prime minister, he secured the backing of 67 lawmakers for the mandate to form a government, exceeding the majority mark of 61.

Meanwhile, the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) party, a longstanding ally of Netanyahu, declined to recommend any candidate to President Herzog, leaving the Prime Minister with the backing of just 46 lawmakers.

Herzog formally handed Eisenkot the mandate on Sunday (November 8), after concluding consultations with party representatives. Eisenkot now has 28 days to assemble a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension. However, the recommendations of 67 lawmakers do not guarantee their support in a parliamentary confidence vote.
How might Eisenkot and his alliance stake a claim to the government?
Scenario 1 – Allying with Arab-majority parties

Eisenkot’s Yashar party could form a minority government with outside support from the Arab-majority Joint List and Ra’am parties. Both parties have now endorsed Eisenkot for the mandate to form a government, although this does not guarantee they would support him in a parliamentary confidence vote. Ra’am is willing to join a coalition, while the Joint List has expressed interest in extending outside support, conditional on protections for Israel’s Arab communities.

These parties’ 19 seats could theoretically give the Eisenkot bloc 67 seats. However, Eisenkot has long ruled out forming a government with the support of the Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.

In a statement issued on October 31, he reiterated four conditions for a prospective government, including recognising Israel as a Jewish, democratic, liberal and equal state; upholding the values of the Declaration of Independence; requiring all citizens to undertake military, national or civilian service; and dismantling Hamas’s military and governing power in Gaza.

Eisenkot said any elected lawmaker accepting these principles could join his government. However, the conditions are likely to complicate negotiations with the Arab-majority parties, particularly over Israel’s character as a Jewish state and the Palestinian conflict.

Allying with the Arab parties could also pose a challenge to other anti-Netanyahu leaders, such as Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman, who had campaigned against forming a government dependent on Arab parties. Liberman reiterated his opposition to an Arab-backed minority government as Eisenkot began coalition negotiations on Sunday.
As The Indian Express previously explained, Israel’s Arab parties have emerged as potential kingmakers despite longstanding resistance to their inclusion in governing coalitions.
Scenario 2 – Allying with the Haredim

Alternatively, Eisenkot could seek support from the ultra-Orthodox UTJ. A longstanding Netanyahu ally, the party has been frustrated by his Likud party’s failure to preserve military-service exemptions for Haredi religious students following judicial intervention.

According to a Channel 12 report on October 29, UTJ figures had considered supporting Eisenkot’s coalition from outside the government, in exchange for compromises on military-service exemptions. One possibility would be for its seven lawmakers to abstain from a confidence vote, leaving Netanyahu with 46 votes against Eisenkot’s 48, provided the Arab parties and other lawmakers also abstain. This could allow the latter to form a government without the Arab parties’ support.

The possibility has gained renewed attention after Liberman reportedly softened his longstanding opposition to governing alongside ultra-Orthodox parties. Channel 12 reported on Thursday (November 5) that he was open to cooperation with UTJ, potentially under a power-sharing arrangement with Eisenkot. However, no agreement has been reached.

A government can win the Knesset’s confidence vote with a simple majority of lawmakers voting, even without securing 61 seats. However, Eisenkot would still need reliable parliamentary support to pass legislation and budgets, leaving a minority government vulnerable to collapse.

The obstacle is military conscription: Eisenkot has made national service for all Israelis a condition for joining his government, while UTJ wants to preserve exemptions for Haredi students. Liberman has also insisted on military-service requirements, making the terms of any compromise crucial. Any agreement would require the prospective partners to compromise on a central electoral position.
Scenario 3 – A unity government… with Netanyahu

A third alternative could be a national unity government that brings together Eisenkot and lawmakers from parties currently aligned with Netanyahu. After receiving the mandate on Sunday, Eisenkot appealed to members of Likud and Religious Zionism to support a government under his leadership, saying that the political circumstances demanded compromise.

He has called for a national emergency government and promised to pursue unconventional approaches to building a coalition. His invitation to lawmakers from Netanyahu’s bloc could potentially expand the pool of parties willing to support him.

A separate possibility would be a unity government involving Netanyahu himself, potentially under an arrangement to rotate the premiership. President Herzog has long favoured such an arrangement to avoid repeat elections, but it would require opposition leaders to abandon their central campaign promise of removing Netanyahu from power.

There are precedents for cooperation between political rivals. Following the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, for instance, former IDF chief turned lawmaker Benny Gantz and Eisenkot joined Netanyahu’s emergency wartime government, despite their political differences. An earlier power-sharing arrangement between Netanyahu and Gantz in 2020, however, collapsed before Gantz could serve as prime minister.

Eisenkot, however, has repeatedly ruled out serving under Netanyahu, and the opposition camp has largely campaigned on removing the prime minister from power. His latest appeal therefore leaves open the possibility of cooperation with lawmakers from Netanyahu’s bloc, without indicating a willingness to serve alongside Netanyahu himself.
How Netanyahu could benefit from a prolonged deadlock

Despite receiving the mandate following recommendations from 67 lawmakers, Eisenkot still faces the challenge of turning their endorsements into a viable governing coalition, given the deep ideological divisions among his prospective allies.

Under Israel’s Basic Law, the outgoing government continues to exercise its functions until a new one takes office. Netanyahu will therefore remain caretaker prime minister while Eisenkot attempts to form a coalition.

If Eisenkot fails to form a government within 28 days, extendable by another 14, Herzog can either give another lawmaker 28 days or inform the Knesset that no government can be formed. In either case, lawmakers may subsequently seek a final 14-day mandate for a candidate backed by at least 61 members. Continued failure would trigger fresh elections.

Netanyahu has benefited from such political deadlock before. Between 2019 and 2020, he headed successive caretaker governments as Israel held repeated elections that failed to deliver a stable governing majority. The prolonged stalemate allowed him to remain prime minister despite his inability to secure a durable coalition.

The October 27 verdict offers another opportunity. As The Indian Express previously explained, Israeli voters weakened Netanyahu’s coalition without decisively rejecting his leadership. His Likud party emerged as the single largest party with 27 seats, even though his wider alliance fell short of a majority.

Fresh elections could give Netanyahu another opportunity to regain his parliamentary majority, although there is no guarantee of a more favourable result. More immediately, Eisenkot’s failure to assemble a coalition could give Netanyahu an opportunity to seek the mandate himself, while prolonging his tenure as caretaker prime minister.

title: Nobel Prize in Economics 2026: How Hall, Woodford reshaped modern economic policy

content.value: The Nobel Prize in Economics — officially the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 — was awarded on Monday (October 12) to Robert E. Hall (Stanford University) and Michael Woodford (Columbia University) for their work in micro foundations that deliver macro insights.

The Academy said that the laureates’ work in developing new models to better implement stabilisation policy would be helpful in devising fiscal and monetary policy measures to weather periods of economic fluctuations.
The winners’ work in developing new Keynesian models is “now used” by central banks and finance ministries to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles.
First, what is a stabilisation policy? And why is it needed for new Keynesian models?

In economics, stabilisation policies are measures enacted by the government or central banks to smooth out economic fluctuations, ensuring steady economic growth and keeping unemployment to a minimum.

In fiscal policy, the government intervenes by adjusting public spending or tax levels to influence aggregate demand, which is the total amount of spending on finished goods and services in an economy at a given price level and time over a given period. Monetary policy measures, by contrast, involve interventions by the central bank, such as adjusting the interest rate, reserve requirements and conducting open market operations.

In either route, the aim is to reduce fluctuations in unemployment and economic growth so that the economy does not enter or remain in a “situation with very high unemployment or uncontrolled inflation.”

The concept of stabilisation was developed in the work of economist John Maynard Keynes during the Great Depression (1929-39). The period, regarded as one of the worst economic downturns in modern history, was marked by high rates of unemployment and poverty, as well as global bank and business failures. Keynes’ call for interventionism challenged the dominant principle of classical economics principle of the time — that free markets automatically correct themselves.

Keynes argued that total demand for goods and services from households and businesses does not automatically match the production capacity of the economy. Hence, when aggregate demand drops during a crisis, governments and banks can simply step in with public spending or rate cuts to smooth the downturn.
What was the critique that stabilisation policy faced?

Traditional Keynesian models relied on the assumption that statistical relationships between key macroeconomic variables — such as inflation, consumption, unemployment and production — remained stable. This notion was heavily tested during the oil crises of the 1970s, which resulted in stagflation, a period marked by stagnant or negative economic growth, high unemployment and persistent inflation.

In 1976, economist Robert Lucas — who won the Nobel Prize in 1995 — argued that the biggest, and simplest, problem with Keynesian models was that they assumed that the relationship between variables was stable and proportionate. He essentially argued that human behaviour could not be treated as a fixed system.

Consider the case of a highway where speed cameras are to be installed. If the speed limit is set at 80 km/h on the assumption that this is the average speed, one might expect accidents to decrease by a certain percentage. In reality, however, drivers may slow down near speed cameras and accelerate after passing them.

Lucas’ critique rests on this very principle. When central banks try to influence the economy based on past relationships, consumers and businesses may change their behaviour, altering the relationships on which policymakers based their decisions and potentially weakening the intended effects of policy.
Macroeconomic phenomena like GDP and unemployment can therefore be understood more fully by studying the behaviour of individual actors and examining how their decisions shape the wider economy.
Why Hall’s research was a breakthrough

Robert E. Hall’s central idea was that current household consumption reflects people’s expectations about their future lifetime wealth. He argued that people change their consumption only if their assessment of the future changes in response to new, relevant information: if they were optimistic about future income, they would consume more than if they were pessimistic.

Hall thus established that instead of looking for indicators to forecast household consumption, past economic variables were not reliable indicators of future consumption. In what came to be called the random walk hypothesis, he posited that shifts in spending occur only in response to unexpected information, causing changes in consumption to follow a “random walk”. Thus, future changes in consumption became inherently unpredictable from past economic data.
He also demonstrated that labour markets suffer from search frictions which may help explain why unemployment often lingers for long after periods of recovery begin.
Consider the example of a 12-year old named Rahul receiving a fixed allowance of 500 rupees which is used for his recreational purchases.

On the first of the month, he receives the sum and goes about his month with no deviations in his spending habits. Now, let us assume that on the first of the next month, Rahul receives a surprise visit from his grandmother — who brings him a gift of Rs 5,000.

Rahul does not spend the entirety of the excess Rs 5,000 which is complementing his allowance of Rs 500. He does, however, change his spending habits and instead of a Rs 25 chocolate, he buys one that costs him Rs 50. Similarly, his spending changes across purchases.
And what Woodford brought to the mix
Woodford’s development of a macro model built on microfoundations became the prototype for subsequent New Keynesian models.

Woodford revolutionised central banking by pairing Hall’s discovery — household consumption depends on forward-looking expectations — with Swedish economist, Knut Wicksell’s concept of neutral interest rates. The Wicksellian neutral rate (or natural rate) is the ideal interest rate where the economy achieves full employment and stable prices.

Woodford advanced modern central-bank theory by combining Hall’s insight — that household consumption depends on forward-looking expectations — with Swedish economist Knut Wicksell’s concept of neutral interest rates. The Wicksellian neutral rate (or natural rate) is the interest rate at which the economy operates at its potential, with stable inflation.

Central banks steer economies by adjusting policy rates, with the natural rate serving as a benchmark, rather than relying on changes to the physical money supply alone. Prices remain “sticky” because firms face costs when updating price tags. Businesses must therefore set prices based on expectations of future costs and interest rates.

This sets up the idea of forward guidance by central banks, in which transparency and clear communication act as policy tools to anchor public expectations. If a central bank clearly announces, “We plan to keep interest rates low for the next two years,” long-term borrowing costs may drop immediately, stimulating investment today without the bank having to cut policy rates further.

Woodford’s model showed how central banks can use interest-rate policy to manage demand and inflation, including in response to supply shocks — an important contribution to the framework used by modern central banks to handle global economic crises compared with the stagflation era of the 1970s.

Consider an ice-cream shop. The owner prints glossy menu cards that cost money to replace, so her prices remain fixed (‘sticky’) for months at a time. When deciding whether to borrow money to expand her shop, she listens to the central bank. If the central bank issues “forward guidance”— publicly committing to keep interest rates low for the next two years — the owner doesn’t wait two years to act. Knowing future borrowing costs are expected to remain low, she takes out a loan and expands her business today.
Why this matters enough to have won the prize

The work of Hall and Woodford has helped transform how central banks understand and manage economic fluctuations. By accounting for how households and businesses form expectations and respond to policy decisions, their research has helped policymakers better anticipate the effects of interest-rate changes, communicate policy intentions and stabilise economies. According to the Nobel Committee, this framework has also helped central banks navigate crises, with inflationary episodes becoming less prolonged.

title: Taylor Rule: What is the math equation Iran invoked in jibe at Trump?

content.value: In the ongoing US-Iran war now underway for over six months, one of the biggest fallouts has been the global energy supply. With the Strait of Hormuz — a key maritime route through which one-fifth of the global oil and gas supply passes — largely shut to maritime traffic, Iran-backed Houthis have now set their eyes to another crucial maritime route: the Bab al-Mandeb Strait linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.

The disruptive oil trade has not just hurt the energy suppliers, but also strained economies thousands of miles away in the United States, where the interest rates have been raised this week to control the rising prices.

Iran, which has also been waging an internet war aimed at social media influence and perception management, recently posed a mathematical equation — the Taylor Rule — to US economic challenges. Here’s what the equation means, and the extent of its application to the US’ current economic situation.
Ghalibaf’s jibe at US interest rates

In a post on X on Wednesday (September 16), Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf invoked a 1990s mathematical equation to pose a question regarding the US economy: if soaring inflation can be curbed by hiking interest rates.

Using the Taylor Rule, an equation introduced by the American economist John Taylor in a 1993 paper to determine interest rates, Ghalibaf suggested that the impact of monetary policy would be limited as long as the Strait of Hormuz remains blocked.
Straits Taylor Rule:
i = r* + π* + 1.5(π−π*) + 0.5(y−y*) + α(SOH−SOH*) + β(BEM−BEM*), α,β > 0
Let’s see if a hike could open SOH or produce a single barrel :)
You can’t 25bp a chokepoint and r* isn’t neutral. It’s SOH risk premium, and We set it.
Stay unanchored !
— محمدباقر قالیباف | MB Ghalibaf (@mb_ghalibaf) September 16, 2026

“Straits Taylor Rule: i = r* + π* + 1.5(π−π*) + 0.5(y−y*) + α(SOH−SOH*) + β(BEM−BEM*), α,β > 0 Let’s see if a hike could open SOH or produce a single barrel,” Ghalibaf’s post read. The post highlighted two geopolitical “shocks” in the equations: the Strait of Hormuz (SOH) and Bab el-Mandeb (BEM).

He added, “You can’t 25bp a chokepoint and r* isn’t neutral. It’s SOH risk premium, and We set it.” The SOH risk premium here apparently referred to the risks emanating from the halted energy exports flowing out of the Strait of Hormuz.
Hours after Ghalibaf’s post, the US Federal Reserve did raise the interest rates from 3.75% to 4% by 25 basis points — the first such hike in over three years.
What Taylor’s equation means

The Taylor Rule is an equation John Taylor introduced in a 1993 paper that prescribes how central banks should set interest rates in response to inflation and economic activity. In simple terms, the rule suggests that a central bank sets a higher rate when inflation is above target and a lower rate if inflation is below target. Similarly, real GDP growth above a target would mean a higher interest rate, while weaker growth would dictate lowering it.
A commonly used version of the equation is: i = r∗ + π + 0.5(π−π∗) + 0.5(y−y∗), where:
i = recommended short-term interest rate
r∗ = estimated “neutral” real interest rate: the rate that neither stimulates nor slows the economy
π = current inflation
π∗ = the central bank’s inflation target
y−y∗ = the output gap: the difference between actual and targeted growth in real GDP. If the output gap is 0, then the economy is operating at its potential.
For instance, consider a hypothetical scenario where the real interest rate is 2%, current inflation rate is 4%, the inflation target is 2%, and output gap is 0. Then the equation is —
i = 2 + 4 + 0.5(4−2) + 0.5(0), where i equals 7. So, the rule suggests an interest rate of 7%.

The Taylor Rule, however, is not a law but more of a rule of thumb: it offers a framework to central banks for deliberating monetary policy. When it comes to real-world applications, central banks such as the Fed consider many other factors while setting interest rates.

The rule has also been seen generally less effective in times of economic crises, forcing central banks to deploy alternative policy tools, as the Fed noted in a 2022 report. In the years since 1993, alternative versions of Taylor’s original equation have been used.

In his post, Ghalibaf also used a modified version of the equation, accounting for two variables in the form of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb. The point he appeared to be making was that while the rule suggests setting interest rates after considering inflation and an economy’s strength, the Fed raising rates wouldn’t solve a physical oil-supply problem caused by the two Straits turning into chokepoints.
Does Ghalibaf’s formula make sense?

Although Ghalibaf altered John Taylor’s equation giving it a ‘Hormuz’ twist, does it really make any sense? Rahul Menon, associate professor at the Jindal School of Government and Public Policy, told The Indian Express that while the social media post shared by the Iranian speaker is “rhetorical”, the main factor remains the oil flowing out of the Gulf.

“Essentially he’s (Ghalibaf) saying that the interest rate changes right now are just tinkering at the margin, because the main factor that’s going to drive up prices for the American population is the fact that Iran is not letting any oil pass through the Strait of Hormuz,” Menon said.
“I don’t think we should look too strongly at the mathematical nature of that equation. What matters is the fact that you don’t have any oil coming through these places,” he added.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

Highlighting the importance of the US interest rates, Menon said the inflation rate matters for common Americans and for US President Donald Trump, especially ahead of the mid-term elections slated for November.

“The US electorate is very sensitive to inflation rates. We have seen the effect of inflation on the last US Presidential election, which brought Trump back to power on the promise of greater growth and employment. But the rising inflation will play a role in affecting the midterms and I think higher inflation will definitely affect the Republicans in the midterm,” he added.
Oil supply remains hit

Even as the US and Iran battled over the control of Strait of Hormuz, the maritime traffic remained largely hit, with sporadic instances of vessels getting attacked while transitioning the narrow waterway.
According to Reuters, the 10-day average of vessels commuting through the Strait of Hormuz was around 16, while the number was 26 for Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have strengthened their grip over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait with rapid advances over the past week. The Houthis have been firing at Saudi oil facilities and tankers, threatening Saudi’s exports.

title: How a routine router upgrade grounded flights across the US, and what went wrong

content.value: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday (November 13) night after a communications outage halted most departures for more than four hours, stranding thousands of passengers at airports across the country.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said technology upgrades had “overwhelmed” the existing, antiquated system.

The ground stop began shortly before 4 pm Eastern Time and was lifted at 8.15 pm (6.45 am IST on Saturday). It was the first nationwide halt since January 2023, when a failure in the system that sends safety alerts to pilots paused departures for about 90 minutes.

It was the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11, 2001 attacks, when hijackers flew two passenger planes into the twin towers of New York’s World Trade Center. US airspace reopened to commercial flights about two days later.
“This isn’t another 9/11,” Mullin said. “This is a telecommunication outage.”
Here is what we know.
What caused the US air traffic control outage?

At a press briefing after the FAA lifted the ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said radar communications at air traffic control centres became unstable at 3.36 pm ET. He said the fix pointed to a problem with an older network.

“We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines,” Duffy said, adding that switches and routers on the FAA’s older network had been overloaded with data. What caused the overload remained unclear, Reuters reported.
CBS News, citing multiple sources, reported that an update to the private communications network linking air traffic control facilities prompted a reboot, after which the system crashed.

Separately, The Washington Post, citing a person briefed on the outage, reported that the FAA’s internal network was having trouble with its timing system, which could prevent messages from reaching their intended destinations.
Investigators have since narrowed their attention to two facilities: a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas.

At the Arkansas facility, contractor L3Harris was carrying out routine work to replace ageing copper connections with fibre-optic cables. A router began sending an unusually high volume of connection requests across the FAA’s telecommunications network, while officials also detected similar activity at the Texas facility, where upgrades had been completed weeks earlier.
According to the FAA, the network received around 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting communications and radar feeds at 17 of its 22 regional air traffic control centres.
Investigators have yet to determine whether the initial problem arose from faulty equipment or an installation error. The FAA said it had found no indication of a cyberattack.
How do pilots talk to controllers, and why were flights grounded?

On a typical US commercial flight, the airport tower clears the plane for take-off and hands it over to a departure controller, who guides it as it climbs. Regional air traffic control centres then guide it along its route. Near its destination, an approach controller takes over before handing it to the airport tower for landing. At each handoff, the controller tells the pilot whom to contact and which radio frequency to use, unless that frequency is already known.

Once a plane is en route, the controller speaking to its pilot can be hundreds of miles from the ground station that relays the conversation. The pilot communicates by radio with that station, which must be within range of the aircraft. Ground links carry the conversation between the station and the controller’s centre, according to the FAA.

A telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to be among the systems affected, The Wall Street Journal reported. The network supports radio communications between pilots and controllers. L3Harris also says it is replacing decades-old copper connections across FAA facilities with fibre, satellite and wireless links as part of a wider overhaul.
Duffy said the disruption was intermittent, and controllers were still able to reach pilots. “It wasn’t a complete blackout in communication or radar,” he said.

Voice radio is the main way pilots and controllers talk, with backup and emergency frequencies available. Controllers can also send text messages to pilots, and many commercial aircraft have satellite communications for use in remote airspace, The New York Times reported.
Holding departures limited the number of aircraft controllers had to manage while they guided planes already in the air.
How far has the US progressed in modernising air traffic control?

In 2024, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported that the FAA had classified 51 of its 138 air traffic control systems as unsustainable and another 54 as potentially unsustainable. Congress approved $12.5 billion in July 2025 to upgrade infrastructure including telecommunications and radar.
In September, however, the GAO warned that the FAA risked prioritising speed over costs and potential disruptions, having failed to coordinate the schedules of more than 11,000 upgrade projects.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy demanded on Friday that Congress provide another $50 billion for air traffic control upgrades by the end of the year. The request has drawn questions from lawmakers, particularly as Congress had already approved $12.5 billion for modernisation, nearly two-thirds of it for telecommunications upgrades and radar replacements.

The administration said on Friday that 68% of the FAA’s legacy copper telecommunications network had been replaced with high-speed fibre, Reuters reported. But FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had warned in September that replacing copper alone would do little to prevent outages without an overhaul of the wider network. That month, a communications fault prompted a switch to a backup fibre line serving a Philadelphia air traffic control facility. A construction crew then accidentally cut that line, compounding the disruption.
Did the FAA’s new AI tool play a role?

Three days before the outage, the FAA announced it had expanded SMART, an AI-assisted flight planning tool, to all 22 US air route traffic control centres. The tool uses flight schedules, weather and airport capacity to flag potential bottlenecks and recommend routes and departure times. Controllers remain responsible for keeping aircraft safely apart.
Mullin did not identify SMART as the cause. Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes SMART, said its tool was not involved in the ground stop.
How long could US flight delays and cancellations last?

The nationwide ground stop lasted nearly five hours on Friday, November 13, but its effects continued through the weekend. According to the FAA, approximately 12,462 flights were cancelled on Friday, including 9,082 by major airlines, although not all cancellations were directly attributable to the ground stop.

By Sunday, more than 17,000 flights had been cancelled since Friday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium, as cited by The New York Times. Nearly 40% of the 74,696 scheduled flights over the three days had been delayed.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said he expected flight operations to return to normal by Monday  (November 16). However, officials had yet to establish the root cause of the network failure.

title: Expert Explains: What the fresh Houthi offensive in Yemen means for Saudi Arabia

content.value: On September 11, Houthi forces in Yemen seized the strategically vital port town of Mokha, about 60 km from the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait. They said they had also captured the Perim and Zuqar islands, both in the Red Sea, and now had control of the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait area.

Forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognized government (in exile) withdrew from these areas after days of escalated fighting which began on September 3. The principal government-aligned militia controlling Mokha was the National Resistance Force (NRF), led by Lt Gen Tareq Saleh.

Following the port’s capture, the Houthis asserted that they would not threaten international shipping but would continue targeting Saudi-linked vessels transiting the Strait — a position the Houthis had announced in July after a Saudi-backed Yemeni government strike on Sana’a airport. That strike also sparked Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Abha airport, Saudi oil tankers and oil refineries in Jizan, along with Saudi strikes on Hodeidah and other Houthi-controlled positions.

By August, this renewed breakdown of a de facto UN-backed 2022 ceasefire meant that the other actors in Yemen’s civil war also clashed with the Houthis, especially in Taiz province. In these first two weeks of September, this fighting reached a crescendo with both the civil war elements within Yemen, as well as Saudi-Houthi strike exchanges, escalating most significantly in over 10 years, until the Houthi capture of Mokha. On the same day, Saudi Arabia also shut down its East-West oil pipeline after drone strikes which Riyadh said originated in Iraq.
The US-Iran context

The Yemeni Houthis always had the capability to control the Bab-el-Mandeb, as they proved during the shipping blockade they imposed in 2024 citing Israel’s war in Gaza. The control of Mokha only reinforces this capability, apart from strengthening their position in Yemen’s civil war.

While Iran has leveraged this threat to deter Saudi Arabia from upscaling its involvement in the US’s war on Iran, there has arguably been no novel threat to Iran arising from Saudi Arabia which would require immediate mitigation.

The last Iranian strike on Saudi Arabia was a single strike on Prince Sultan Air Base (a US military hub) in July, with the strike before that being in April. In any case, Iran has been negotiating with both Oman and Saudi Arabia vis-à-vis Hormuz while intermittent kinetic action with the US has been largely restricted to the Strait itself where both sides now focus on striking oil tankers and coastal infrastructure.

Moreover, the Houthis’ specific commitment to not target international shipping (but only Saudi Arabia’s) differs from Iran’s strategy in Hormuz which requires coordination by all shipping with Iranian authorities. Iran’s preference is a blanket deterrent aimed at imposing international costs for US action.

The Houthis’ differing approach in the Red Sea proves that the developments in Yemen are linked principally to the dynamics of Yemen’s civil war. It further proves a peculiar characteristic of the Axis of Resistance (Iran-backed groups in Yemen, Iraq and Lebanon) — their “nexus” with Tehran has a significant degree of flexibility, with these actors also retaining their local agency even as Iran furnishes their capabilities (with Russian support).

While the first Houthi action in July was triggered by an incident with an Iranian-link (the Saudi-backed Yemeni government preventing an allegedly Iranian plane from landing in Sana’a), that development has long been overtaken by the fighting on the ground between the Houthis and other Saudi-backed Yemeni groups.

Hence, the Houthi action arguably occurs in a context that resembles 2018-19, when the group targeted Saudi (and then Emirati) oil facilities with unprecedented strikes while improving their positions on the ground in Yemen, and at a time when the Strait of Hormuz was open with no US-Iran kinetic action. Combined with the proven Houthi ability to hold Saudi energy facilities directly at risk, Riyadh’s imperative need for regional stability (for its large-scale vision 2030 projects) had pushed Saudi Arabia to explore alternative approaches to mitigate the Houthi threat to its Southern borders.
Saudi Arabia’s lens to view the Houthis

In the months of the UN-backed ceasefire between April and October in 2022, the Saudi logic had shifted to containment and ensuring homeland defence. But even then, the Saudi route to ensuring stability on the Yemen front ran through Tehran, as it focused on a political settlement in Yemen during negotiations for its China-brokered rapprochement with Iran in 2023. In that year, Iran’s UN mission had also raised hopes for institutionalising the UN-backed ceasefire in Yemen.

Note that even in the 2023-July 2026 period, as regional instability became linked more to Israel’s wars than the Yemen conflict, Riyadh proved that it was not interested in any immediate redrawing of the lines where the war had frozen in 2022. In early 2024, Riyadh had also dissuaded the US from launching a maritime campaign against the Yemeni Houthis, due to their threats to Israel.

Moreover, reflecting fractures within the Gulf anti-Houthi coalition itself, Saudi Arabia also took unprecedented kinetic action against the UAE-backed Southern Transition Council in Yemen which attempted to leverage regional instability to improve their positions (even as Abu Dhabi remained theoretically aligned with Riyadh).

Since the Yemen civil war’s dynamics precede the US-Iran war’s context by a decade, they have involved motley non-state actors, each of whom have guarded their own interests, even within the larger coalitions they fight with.

Take Gen Saleh — he is the nephew of Ali Abdullah Saleh, the Republic of Yemen’s first President (1990-2012) who oversaw the most significant military campaigns against the Houthis in Northern Yemen (the Sa’dah Wars). Ali Abdullah Saleh was forced to transfer power to his GCC-backed Vice President (Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi) in 2012. He later allied with the Houthis, his former arch nemeses, to topple the Hadi government in 2015. And then he broke this new alliance, prompting the Houthis to ambush and kill him in 2017.

His nephew’s NRF, while formally aligned with the Yemeni government exiled in Riyadh (led by Hadi as President until 2022), operates within a similar context — aligned against the Houthis but focused on maximising its own power.

Ultimately, it is the Houthi superiority in fighting tactics and a proven resilience across decades that has consistently yielded them military gains. Their abilities were proven beyond Yemen’s borders when the US declared a joint ceasefire with the Houthis in mid-2025 after a protracted campaign to weaken their ability to threaten Red Sea shipping.
The modern Saudi state’s ‘Black Swan’

Now, for Saudi Arabia, the older Houthi threat’s evolution has created a Black Swan that no Saudi state has ever faced historically — a loss of unimpeded access to both the sea routes of Hormuz and Mandeb, as well as its interceding land pipeline which allowed it to bypass the Hormuz blockade since March. During the US-Iran war, Iran’s targeting of Saudi Arabia was unprecedented, but its lesser focus on Saudi targets (compared to UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Israel) meant that the kingdom could continue pushing oil through its Western ports using its East-West pipeline; the Houthis near the Bab-el-Mandeb remained a threat-in-being.

In any case, even as Iran retained plausible deniability vis-à-vis the Houthis, it refrained from leveraging the Houthis directly during the war, which some also attributed to Tehran’s need to respect the sensitivities of the Saudi-Pakistan defence pact signed in September 2025.

Now, given the fact that the Houthi action against Saudi Arabia has escalated alongside an expansion of that pact to include Turkey, it also proves that that pact cannot (or will not) act against a longstanding non-state threat to Saudi Arabia.

Hence, even as Houthi actions seemingly generate strategic dividends for Tehran in the context of the US-Iran war, the Yemen war’s own dynamics mean that these developments would arguably have occurred even without this specific US-Iran context. For Saudi Arabia, the double blockade of Straits to its East and West (even if each have their own distinct dynamics), forces it to act kinetically against at least the Houthis through targeted strikes.

However, in the long term, the increased Saudi need for regional stability (especially as Vision 2030 projects struggle financially), will likely push it towards freezing negotiated tactical lines in Yemen, rather than grand military efforts (beyond targeted strikes) to displace the now-further-strengthened Houthis.

title: Israel’s Arab parties are kingmakers, yet no one wants them. Here’s why

content.value: The results of the Israeli general elections, with no clear winner, once again shine the light on a democracy functioning in a deeply divided society. Every section of the Israeli society voted for their representatives, which resulted in a fractured mandate.

While the coalition led by Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud managed to secure the maximum number of seats (53), it is not enough to form the government. The Gadi Eizenkot-led (Yashar) Opposition could manage 48 seats, despite thousands of its supporters flying in to vote for change. The surprise was reserved for the Arab parties, who received an unprecedented number of votes and seats (19) in the 120-member Knesset.

To form a government, the arithmetic looks simple: either of the two major Jewish political blocs could take the support of the Arab parties — such as the United Arab List (Ra’am) or the Hadash-Ta’al alliance — to assemble a majority. Yet, neither side appears willing to do so.

Understanding why both the right and centre-left exhibit such structural aversion requires examining how Israel balances its democratic institutions with its identity as a Jewish state. To analyse this issue, historian Alan Dowty has examined the precise nature of the democracy that Israel has maintained over time.
Democracy with a difference

Applying Dutch-American political scientist Arend Lijphart’s theory of consociational democracy, Dowty ranks Israel among consensus-based regimes on several metrics while acknowledging its majoritarian features. Consociationalism suggests that a stable democracy in deeply divided societies relies on power-sharing, grand coalitions, mutual vetoes, and proportional representation.

However, in the Israeli context, these consociational features have historically been restricted to intra-Jewish politics—accommodating ideological divides among secular, religious, Ashkenazi, and Sephardic factions.

While Israeli Arabs enjoy the formal rights of citizenship, including voting and access to the political system, on most occasions, they have been placed outside the sphere of traditional Jewish politics. Despite progress in several fields, it took 40 years for the Arabs to establish their first independent parliamentary party – the Arab Democratic Party (Mada, 1988).

Summarising this institutional exclusion, political scientist Ian Lustick notes that Israel lacks a traditional Arab negotiating partner in the elite bargaining processes characteristic of consociational systems. Lustick argues that, despite Arabs constituting approximately 20 per cent of the population, Jewish and Arab political elites do not engage in systematic ethnic bargaining or proportional resource allocation, as is typical of classic consensus democracies.

There is another way of looking at Israeli politics beyond majoritarianism and consociationalism. Israeli sociologist Sammy Smooha suggests that Israel belongs to a category of “ethnic democracies” that combine a dominant ethnic character with democratic rights for all. According to this theory, the way Israel defines its public space and national interests only reflects the wishes of a Jewish majority while undermining the Arab minority’s participation in national affairs.

Moreover, legislation such as the 2018 Basic Law further formalises this condition by legally prioritising Jewish self-determination. The law specifies that the right to exercise national self-determination in the State of Israel is only for the Jewish people. Arab politicians, civil rights organisations, and non-Jewish communities (including the Druze) have criticised the law for omitting explicit guarantees of civic equality. Opponents argued that it legally codified structural hierarchy, aligning directly with Smooha’s model of ethnic democracy.

In July 2021, the Supreme Court of Israel upheld the law in a 10–1 ruling, determining that while the Basic Law anchors Israel’s national identity as a Jewish state, it does not nullify individual human rights guaranteed under other Basic Laws.
Insider-outsider
While Netanyahu has framed the Arab bloc as a threat within, Opposition leaders too, during poll campaigning, had said they would stay away from those parties.

A primary factor behind this is the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The Zionist parties accuse Israeli Arab citizens of extraterritorial loyalty. For most Jewish leaders, the Israeli Arabs occupy a complex position as an “enemy-affiliated minority”—a population linked by geography, history, and kinship to Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, while maintaining political citizenship within Israel, notes Smooha.

Amid the ongoing attacks on Gaza, most Israeli parties see reliance on Arab parties as a direct national security risk. In contrast, the Arab parties reject the Zionist definition of Israel as an explicitly Jewish state. Instead, they advocate their full rights and representation in Israel while supporting a Palestinian state along the 1967 borders, a position supported by many Jewish compatriots. When military operations escalate, Arab parliamentarians face intense pressure from their constituencies to denounce IDF actions.

After the counting of votes, a chorus has been growing that the Opposition bloc should join hands with the Arab parties to unseat Netanyahu. However, partnering directly with factions like Hadash-Ta’al risks alienating right-leaning coalition partners (such as Yisrael Beiteinu or Yamina successors), whose votes are equally vital to secure a 61-seat parliamentary majority.

There is recent precedent to this. In 2021, the 36th Israeli government – led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid – was formed with the support of the Ra’am party led by Mansour Abbas, who had secured just four seats. Abbas and his party members prioritised civil rights, housing, crime prevention, and economic development in Arab towns over broader debates on political sovereignty. However, the government fell in 2022 over ideological issues, including the illegal settlements in the Occupied West Bank.
Impact beyond borders
The 19 seats the Arab parties have won show that Arab citizens have embraced the Israeli democracy and want to extend their political participation beyond voting rights.
If the Zionist parties still keep them at arm’s length, it can impact Israel’s efforts to normalise relations with neighbouring Arab and Muslim states through the Donald Trump-backed Abraham Accords.

title: Yes to Iran, no to Palestine: Can US decide visas to UN General Assembly attendees?

content.value: The United States has granted visas to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and other members of the core Iranian delegation to attend the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) next week at the UN headquarters in New York. This came even as the war in West Asia, ongoing since February, shows no signs of ending.

The US State Department, however, denied visas for a high-level delegation of Palestinian officials, including Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, to attend the UNGA. The UNGA voted Thursday (September 17) to allow Abbas to address the body via a prerecorded statement.

The UN is an international body with its headquarters located on US soil. So, can the US approve or refuse visas to foreign leaders and officials visiting the UN on official business? Here’s what to know about what a 1947 agreement says about the extent of US jurisdiction.
The cases of Palestine and Iran

According to the US State Department, the denial of visas to Palestinian officials — for the second year in a row — is owing to Palestinian officials failing to live up to their commitments under previous agreements to seek peace with Israel. In August 2025, the department had revoked visas for members of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) and the Palestinian Authority (PA) for “undermining the prospects for peace” ahead of last September’s UNGA, forcing PA chief Abbas to appear by video thereafter.

The PLO is a political coalition internationally recognised as the official representative of the Palestinian people, whereas the PA is the government body that exercises partial civil control over the Palestinian enclaves in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

In a statement Wednesday (September 16), the department said the PA had continued to pursue legal action against Israel at the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court and kept paying stipends to the families of prisoners convicted of attacks against Israelis. It also mentioned officials tied to the PLO.

In the case of Iran, although its leaders and top officials have been granted visas, State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products.

“We will not let the Iranian regime’s elites exploit UNGA for a luxury retail splurge paid for by the Iranian people’s suffering, all while the regime funnels Iran’s wealth to support its terrorist proxies,” Pigott posted on X. He also told New York shops to “be on guard” against selling goods to the delegation.
The 1947 Agreement

According to the “Agreement regarding the Headquarters of the United Nations” signed by the UN and the US government on June 26, 1947, the US is generally required to allow access for foreign diplomats to the UN in New York.

Under Article IV governing “Communications and Transit”, Section 11 states that the federal, state or local authorities of the US “shall not impose any impediments to transit to or from the headquarters district of (1) representatives of Members or officials of the United Nations, or of specialized agencies as defined in Article 57, paragraph 2, of the Charter, or the families of such representatives or officials…”

Section 12 reiterates the provisions under Section 11, saying they “shall be applicable irrespective of the relations existing between the Governments of the persons referred to in that section and the Government of the United States”.

Also, Section 13(a) says: “(a) Laws and regulations in force in the United States regarding the entry of aliens shall not be applied in such manner as to interfere with the privileges referred to in Section 11. When visas are required for persons referred to in that section, they shall be granted without charge and as promptly as possible.”

In the past, however, Washington has said it can deny visas for “security, terrorism, and foreign policy” reasons. For instance, the previous Joe Biden-led US administration had initially delayed granting visas to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and his delegation ahead of the UNGA in September 2022, before it relented with days to go for the annual gathering. At the time, relations between the US and Russia had nosedived after the latter invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

Last year, when the US denied PA chief Abbas a visa to attend the UNGA, it had cited “national security interests”. Also, the PA, which represents the Palestinian people at the UN, where ⁠the delegation is officially known as the State of Palestine, is not a full member and has no vote in the UNGA. It is an observer state, holding the same status as the Vatican. The Palestinians will now be represented at the UNGA by their diplomats who are already accredited to the UN.

title: United no more? How the UK came together, and may come apart

content.value: The First Ministers of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland signed a joint memorandum of understanding on Monday (September 14) to signal their intent of putting their respective nations on the path to referendums towards independence from the United Kingdom. The three nations, along with England, make up the UK.

At a summit in the Welsh capital of Cardiff, the three leaders — Wales’ Rhun ap Iorwerth, Scotland’s John Swinney, and Northern Ireland’s Michelle O’Neill — as well as the Republic of Ireland’s leader of the opposition Mary Lou McDonald affirmed in the “Cardiff Agreement” that “the political landscape across these islands is changing”.

“For the first time ever, there are First Ministers in Scotland, in Wales and in the North of Ireland who are all committed to independence from the United Kingdom… there could be no clearer sign that Westminster’s time is coming to an end,” the memorandum read. “Our nations have the right to self-determination: No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.”

The Cardiff Agreement came on the back of two recent developments: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham expressing that referendums for Scotland and Northern Ireland were not on the cards, and US President Donald Trump saying on Saturday (September 12) that he would “love” to see the reunification of Ireland.
We explain how the UK came to be in the first place, and what British law has to say about conducting a referendum in its constituent nations.
Acts of Union

The British Isles, a group of over 6,000 islands located in northwestern Europe, comprises the two major islands of Great Britain and Ireland besides several smaller islands. Great Britain consists of three nations — England, Scotland, and Wales — whereas Ireland is made up of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland.
The name “Great Britain” assumed significance only in the 18th century, when the kingdoms of England and Scotland were united in 1707 by an Act of Union, becoming the United Kingdom of Great Britain.

Wales, which is also located on the island of Great Britain, was conquered by the English in the late 1200s, but was legally annexed and made a part of the Kingdom of England only in 1536 through an Act of Union.

Meanwhile, the island of Ireland had been under British control since the late 12th century but entered the UK as a political entity only in 1801, following a failed Irish rebellion (1798) and the Acts of Union (1800). Thereafter, the UK came to be officially known as the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.

The name, however, lasted for over a century until 1922, when the majority of Ireland — barring six counties that make up Northern Ireland — gained independence from the British after the Anglo-Irish War (1919-21). With Northern Ireland choosing to remain part of the UK, the latter became the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
The question of separation

Notably, the three First Ministers signed the joint memorandum not in their capacity as heads of their respective governments but as party representatives: ap Iorwerth as leader of Plaid Cymru, McDonald as president of Sinn Féin and Michelle O’Neill as vice president of Sinn Féin, and Swinney as leader of the Scottish National Party (SNP).

After the SNP, which considers Scottish independence its core political plank, came to power with an outright majority in the 2011 Scottish Parliament election, it pushed for a Scottish independence referendum. Through a Section 30 order under the 1998 Scotland Act, powers were transferred to allow the Scottish Parliament to legislate for the referendum.

On September 18, 2014, the Scottish independence referendum was conducted with the single-point question “Should Scotland be an independent country?”, with voters having to choose yes or no. The result: 55.3% voted No and 44.7% voted Yes, and Scotland remained with the UK.

In 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament doesn’t have the power to unilaterally call a second referendum on Scottish independence, with the subject “reserved” for the UK Parliament in Westminster, London. Although SNP’s Swinney said Monday that he wants to hold a second Scottish independence referendum by 2031, the 2022 ruling could pose a major obstacle since major British parliamentary parties such as Labour, Conservatives, and Liberal Democrats remain opposed to it.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

Both Wales and Northern Ireland are yet to hold an independence referendum in the traditional sense, but the latter in 1973 conducted a border poll to decide on its constitutional status: whether it should remain part of the UK or join with the Republic of Ireland to create a united Ireland. Irish nationalists, who were in the minority and favoured a united Ireland, boycotted the poll: 98.9% of the votes chose to remain in the UK.

Latest polling reported by The Guardian suggests 47% of Scottish voters would opt for independence in a referendum held tomorrow, along with 36% in Northern Ireland and 32% in Wales. Since the 2014 referendum, support for independence in Scotland has stayed around 45-50%. Data suggests a rise in Wales and Northern Ireland as well.

As things stand, the UK Parliament retains exclusive legal authority to hold a referendum in any part of the UK. Only constitutional changes — in the form of the UK Parliament transferring powers to the respective three national parliaments — can facilitate independence referendums, using an order similar to the one granting the Scottish referendum in 2014. This explains why the Cardiff Agreement calls on the British government “to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction”.

title: Why Trump wants to cut US military drills with South Korea over Iran

content.value: US President Donald Trump on Sunday (August 16) announced that the US would substantially scale back its annual joint military exercise with South Korea, a long-term ally, for not participating in the “Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

In a social media post, he also said that North Korea, by contrast, had been “unthreatening and respectful” to him. North Korea condemned the drills last week, calling it a provocation that heightens tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

South Korean joint chiefs of staff told Reuters that the drills started on Monday as scheduled. The latest development comes mere days after South Korean President Lee Jae Myung proposed talks with North Korea to officially end the Korean War.
Why has Trump sought to scale down the exercise?

Trump has long sought to scale back joint US-South Korean military exercises, and has also questioned the cost of the US military presence in the country. The US President has repeatedly expressed his disappointment with several of the US’ long-time allies not contributing military or logistical support to aid the US in its ongoing war with Iran.
Trump has previously objected to what he sees as excessive US military spending on South Korea’s defence, arguing that Seoul does not contribute enough towards the cost.

The exercises are an important part of the US-South Korea alliance, allowing their militaries to practise how they would operate together in the event of a conflict with North Korea. Seoul has therefore traditionally viewed regular exercises as necessary to maintaining military readiness and deterring an attack from the North.

Pyongyang has long taken the opposite view, describing US-South Korean exercises as rehearsals for an invasion. Trump has shown some sympathy for this argument: during his first term, he called the exercises “provocative” and suspended major drills after his first summit with Kim Jong Un in Singapore in 2018.
South Korea has attempted to appease the US President, committing $350 billion in investments in the US.
What are the Ulchi Freedom drills?

Ulchi Freedom Shield is an annual summertime exercise conducted by South Korea and the US to test their ability to respond jointly to a conflict or other security crisis on the Korean Peninsula. It combines computer-simulated command-post training with field exercises and South Korea’s government-led Ulchi civil defence exercise.

This year, about 18,000 South Korean troops are expected to participate alongside US forces. Personnel from 11 of the 18 member states of the United Nations Command (UNC) — the multinational body that oversees the 1953 armistice that halted hostilities of the Korean War — are also expected to participate. The exercise got its latest rebrand in 2022 when it was rechristened the Ulchi Freedom Shield to reflect the multifaceted nature of threats.
Why are the two Koreas still at war?
North Korea and South Korea have been in a state of war since 1953.

After Japan announced its intent to surrender in 1945, the Korean Peninsula, previously under its control, was divided into two: The Soviet and the Chinese communists propped up the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea in the North, while the Americans supported the creation of the Republic of Korea in the South.

In 1950, North Korean forces under founder Kim Il Sung invaded the South, triggering the three-year-long Korean War. Despite making major initial gains, US troops helped the South fight back. Eventually, neither side secured a decisive victory, and an armistice was signed in 1953, leaving both sides technically still at war.

Since then, both Korean nations have spoken of “reunification”, by force if necessary. But the likely human and material cost of an all-out war has meant that the status quo has, by and large, prevailed. Since the 1970s, both sides have held negotiations towards achieving a “peaceful reunification”, with agreements in 2000, 2007, and 2018 significant in this regard. However, very little tangible progress has been made.

Meanwhile, North Korea has also pursued the development of nuclear weapons, inviting heavy sanctions from the UN Security Council, the US, and its allies. Last week, it launched a ballistic missile towards the Sea of Japan.

Things came to a head in 2019 when Trump, then the US president, met with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Hanoi, Vietnam. The Hanoi summit ended without an agreement after the two sides failed to bridge differences over sanctions relief and denuclearisation. Diplomatic engagement subsequently stalled, while North Korea continued to expand its nuclear and missile capabilities.

Tensions between North and South Korea have only escalated since then. In 2024, Kim notably announced a shift in DPRK’s outlook towards South Korea. Renouncing further attempts at reunification, Kim said that the South was now to be viewed as the “primary foe and invariable principal enemy”.

In recent years, both countries have resorted to escalating tactics, ranging from defence posturing to balloon diplomacy: North Korea sends trash-laden helium balloons in response to South Korean activists sending “propaganda-laden” balloons to the North. The two sides have also used loudspeakers across the border.
North Korea maintains a close strategic partnership with China, which has opposed the expansion of US-led military cooperation in the region.

Russia has also emerged as a North Korean ally, trading weapons with the largely isolated ‘hermit’ kingdom. North Korean troops have participated in Russia’s war against Ukraine and have reportedly gained “crucial experience”, according to an official with US and South Korean Combined Forces Command quoted by The New York Times on Monday.

title: India-Turkey ties: Why discord over Kashmir and Pakistan hasn’t stopped sporadic cooperation

content.value: Days after Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan raked up Kashmir during his address to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly, India secured the extradition of drug kingpin Navpreet Singh from the country, a development hailed by Union Home Minister Amit Shah as a “historic milestone”.
These twin developments were, in some ways, emblematic of India’s relationship with Turkey for years — sporadic cooperation amid fraught ties.

Both countries had, in fact, suspended foreign office consultations from 2022 until this year. Bilateral ties came under further strain following the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack and India’s subsequent retaliation against terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Erdogan had then expressed solidarity with Pakistan and called for de-escalation. In August, Turkey entered the Mecca pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
We explain the differences between the two sides, ​the avenues for cooperation despite ​discord, and the seeming contradictions in India-Turkey ties.
Kashmir remains the biggest irritant

The biggest issue between the two sides — which has often caused strain — is Turkey’s repeated references to Kashmir, especially on international fora, and its constant siding with Pakistan in asking for a third-party solution to the “Kashmir issue”. New Delhi maintains that Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are integral parts of India, and dismisses calls for third-party intervention.

In the last week of September, Erdogan said that “all disputes in South Asia, including Kashmir”, should be addressed through dialogue within the framework of the UN Charter and relevant resolutions. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) quickly issued a rebuttal, saying that Jammu & Kashmir is an integral part of India and that external parties have no role in an internal, bilateral matter.

Erdogan spoke extensively about the issue in 2019 after India abrogated Article 370 of the Constitution, which provided special status to Jammu & Kashmir. He also raised Kashmir at the UN General Assembly in 2020 (in a video statement at the General Debate) as well as in 2021.
Turkey’s close relationship with Pakistan

On August 7, Turkey entered into the Mecca pact — a collective defence agreement — along with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Experts say the pact may entail the risk of Turkish drone and military technology reaching Pakistan. Indian defence planners are evaluating potential technology and military-industrial cooperation between Ankara and Islamabad, particularly concerning advanced drone technology and electronic warfare systems.

It also risks potential diplomatic friction with Ankara or Riyadh regarding future cross-border anti-terror operations on the lines of Operation Sindoor. New Delhi says it’s tracking the trilateral arrangement and remains fully prepared to take all necessary steps to protect its national interests.
With alignments in West Asia reshaping in the wake of the Mecca (or Makkah) pact, the India-UAE-Israel alignment may offer a strategic counterweight.
Where interests converge: crime and security

Despite recent diplomatic strain, legal and law-enforcement cooperation has acted as a stabilising factor. This was recently evidenced by Turkey’s active assistance in extraditing high-profile fugitive criminals, such as drug trafficker Salim Dola, back to India. Both were wanted by Indian agencies such as the Narcotics Control Bureau for running international syndicates smuggling heroin and synthetic drugs into India from Afghanistan and other regions.

Experts say India’s 2001 extradition treaty with Turkey mandates a legal basis for cooperation on serious criminal offences, even amidst broader geopolitical differences. The Indian intelligence agencies worked to unmask the forged documentation and fake foreign citizenships of these fugitives, utilising Interpol red notices and prompting Turkish authorities to block citizenship-by-investment bids and detain the individuals.

Turkey itself faces issues with narco-terrorism primarily because of its unique geographic position as a bridge between Asia and Europe, sometimes going against its own security interests. Cracking down on narco-terrorism fundamentally helps Ankara’s own national security, geopolitical stance, internal stability, and economic health, as per experts.
Beyond the disagreements, a pragmatic relationship

This April, both sides resumed foreign office consultations after being in abeyance for four years. Ankara dispatched Turkish Deputy Foreign Minister Berris Ekinci, who co-chaired meetings with Sibi George, the Ministry of External Affairs’ (MEA) Secretary (West).

According to the MEA, both sides focused on trade, investment, tourism, technology, innovation, energy and educational cooperation. Discussions also touched upon security matters, including the fight against cross-border terrorism.

“We believe dialogue is better than not talking and deepening disagreements and misunderstandings. And the conversations have been satisfactory,” former Ambassador Muktesh Pardesi had told The Indian Express.

In fact, after the economic backlash in India, Turkey began to actively insulate its broader economic interests in Asia from its Pakistan alliance. Ankara also assured New Delhi that it had no inherent bilateral dispute with India.

Turkey stands to gain economic, geopolitical and infrastructural benefits from its relations with India. For India, a working relationship with Ankara offers crucial geopolitical leverage in the Islamic world, a strategic gateway to European and Central Asian markets.

title: Trump says US will cut military aid to Israel: Why now, and what can actually happen?

content.value: US President Donald Trump has said Washington will stop providing nearly $4 billion in annual military assistance to Israel by the end of 2026, claiming that the country no longer needs the money. In a Fox News interview on November 3 (Tuesday), as Americans voted in the midterm elections, Trump said he had reached an agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to end the funding. The US would still sell weapons to its Middle East ally and help them when needed, Trump said.

The announcement on the face of it sounds momentous, coming specially from a US President who is a steadfast Israel backer. But Trump offered no details on how the cutoff would be implemented, and the existing US-Israel military aid agreement runs until September 2028.
Why is Trump talking of cutting aid to Israel now?
Trump said aid to Israel had become a “bad talking point” for Democrats, singling out Abdul El-Sayed, the new Democratic Senator from Michigan.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said, arguing that Israel was prosperous enough to do without American funding.

His remarks came amid declining US public support for Israel, particularly among Democrats, following the war in Gaza. A Quinnipiac University poll found that 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believed the US was too supportive of Israel, compared with 16% and 20%, respectively, when the question was first asked in 2017.
The issue has also become contentious within Trump’s own political movement.

The timing, on Election Day, therefore suggests a domestic political calculation: removing an issue Democrats can use to attack Republicans. Trump has said Netanyahu himself proposed ending the aid. However, the Israeli prime minister had previously discussed phasing it out over a decade, rather than stopping it abruptly.
After the midterms, now that Democrats have control over both Houses of the US Congress, pushing through new aid for Israel would anyway be more difficult.
How much aid does the US give Israel?
Israel has received more US aid, including military aid, since its creation, than any other country in the world.

The current arrangement stems from a 2016 memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed under President Barack Obama. It provides for $38 billion in military assistance over 10 years, from fiscal years 2019 to 2028.

This amounts to $3.3 billion annually in Foreign Military Financing (FMF), alongside $500 million for joint missile defence programmes, taking the annual total to $3.8 billion. Additional assistance has been provided outside this framework, particularly following the October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel and the ensuing war.

Crucially, this is not simply a cash handout. Under FMF, Israel uses American financing to purchase US-made military equipment, services and training. The arrangement therefore also benefits American defence manufacturers.
What could US curtailing aid to Israel mean?

Netanyahu has himself acknowledged that American assistance cannot be taken for granted. In an interview with The Economist in January 2026, he said he wanted to taper off US military aid over the next decade. Being tied to US aid makes Netanyahu vulnerable to US lawmakers’ opinion, especially if he comes to power again and continues his bloodshed in Gaza.
But an abrupt cutoff would be a different proposition. Opposition leaders have already criticised Netanyahu over Trump’s announcement.
