Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who is Netanyahu’s main rival for the top job, posted on X after Trump’s comments, “Israel’s special relationship with the United States is a key component in its national security. The fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a genuine danger. We can no longer rely on him and must replace him.”

Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, had a similar warning. “Precisely at a time when Israel’s defence expenditures have reached enormous proportions, when Israel needs to replenish its offensive weapons stockpiles, and when its air defence capabilities have eroded after such a prolonged war — Netanyahu chalks up yet another colossal failure on his record. The halt in American aid is a severe blow to Israel’s security and to the quality of life in the country…,” he posted.
Thus, Trump’s remarks come at an awkward time for Netanyahu, knee-deep in negotiations to cobble up the numbers for the next government. His closeness to Trump has been one of his big selling points.
Can Trump actually stop the aid?
Not simply by making an announcement. The existing MoU runs until 2028, and Congress plays a central role in appropriating the funds each year.

The more plausible outcome may be a negotiated transition towards reduced direct assistance, potentially alongside deeper cooperation in defence technology and weapons manufacturing. Discussions about the future of US-Israel security cooperation are already under way. This has also raised concerns within the US, from quarters who don’t think Israel learning to build bigger and better bombs on its own is a good idea.

title: Trump’s midterm defeat: Good news or fresh trouble for India’s trade deal?

content.value: The Democratic Party has pulled of a sweeping victory in the 2026 US midterm elections, taking firm control of both legislative bodies that comprise the US Congress — the House of Representatives, which is the lower house, and the Senate, the upper house. The decisive results — driven by a cost-of-living crisis worsened by President Donald Trump’s tariffs and war on Iran — have now fueled hopes of a more predictable trade policy in the US.

This will also come as some relief to India, which among the handful of countries that faced steep tariffs but managed to avoid getting entangled in a one-sided trade agreement that would have imposed several one-sided demands on digital trade and pushed for access into politically sensitive sectors such as agriculture. The increased scrutiny from a Democrat-controlled US Congress, experts said, could result in more practical asks from American negotiators.

However, Trump’s second term has been marked by an unusually frequent use of executive orders, which could continue to spell trouble for trade partners across the globe. In fact, soon after the results, Trump posted a photograph of a red cap emblazoned with the word “VETO” on his Truth Social platform. Indeed, he told Fox News that he would work with Democrats on issues such as ⁠immigration, but threatened to veto any “insane” bills they passed.
Midterm results could actually embolden Trump

With the elections out of the way, the United States Trade Representative (USTR) is expected to release the findings of its investigation into “overcapacity” — a situation when a sector or a country’s production capacity exceeds the demand in the market — under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974. This is the Trump administration’s latest route to resurrecting its tariff architecture.

Currently, tariffs on most countries except China remain in the 10 to 12.5% range. But the new tariffs will determine the final rates and form the basis on which trade deals with global partners, including India, will be renewed.
So, after the midterm setback, will Trump tamp down such actions?

Unlikely. Mohan Kumar, a former Indian ambassador, said that a domestically constrained President in the last term feels, if anything, more free to do things abroad. So, the President’s scope to do good and inflict harm abroad either remains the same as before or may even increase. “We will have to wait and see how this affects the relatively unpredictable occupant of the White House,” he said.

“Congressional imprimatur has not been sought by successive Presidents for several policy initiatives. Obama issued 35 executive orders, George Bush issued 42. Biden issued 162 executive orders in just one term. President Trump has already issued a whopping 166 executive orders in just two years. So expect rule by executive decree, whether the Congress likes it or not,” said Kumar, who is the Director General of the Motwani Jadeja Institute for American Studies, OP Jindal Global University. (Kumar was speaking in his personal capacity).

The former ambassador also said that there is no such thing as a “lame duck” American president when it comes to foreign, security or even trade policy. “President Trump will likely continue to do things he did before. For example, in June of this year, both the House and the Senate passed a ‘War Powers Resolution’ directing President Trump to end hostilities with Iran. In September, Congress passed sanctions on Russia with veto-proof majorities. President Trump used a national interest ‘waiver’ to nullify the sanctions. So, expect President Trump to resort to more of this for the remaining two years of his mandate,” he said.
So what could be the impact of a Democrat-controlled Congress?

One of the main factors behind the election results is the anger among Americans over the cost of living and high diesel prices. Behind these high prices are Trump’s tariffs — whose burden, as research has shown, was mostly passed on to US consumers — and his war on Iran, which resulted in the effective closure of the vital energy passage of the Strait of Hormuz.
Exit polls suggested the economy was the top concern among American voters, prompting even key Republican strongholds like Texas to side with Democrats.

Several US polls also showed that public opinion in the US has shifted when it comes to tariffs. An ABC News poll found 64% of respondents said the use of tariffs had gone too far. A Council on Foreign Relations poll showed 83% blamed high tariffs for at least partially driving inflation, a major negative factor for Trump.

A US-based think tank, Hudson Institute, said that Democrats have clearly signalled their intent to undermine Trump’s dominance of trade policy while reclaiming the prerogatives of the legislative branch. In preparation for their improved, post-election political position, Democratic leaders have already surfaced ideas for reclaiming control over trade policy, the think tank said.

“The likely new chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over trade, Ron Wyden, and the presumed Majority Leader, Charles Schumer, have introduced bills to invalidate Trump policies. Schumer’s bill would repeal several of the laws invoked by Trump, as well as the widely used Section 301 authority on ‘unfair trade practices’, to justify his trade actions,” the report said.
Bipartisan policy on trade
Trade experts, however, pointed out that both Republicans and Democrats have often been on the same page when it comes to trade policy and on dealing with China.

While Trump is believed to have abandoned multilateral organisations, including the World Trade Organization (WTO), it was under the Obama administration that the appointment of judges to the trade body began to blocked. This eventually resulted in the WTO becoming dysfunctional — thus paving the way for unilateral measures under the Trump administration. Trump’s protectionist measures, however, have been far more unconventional and erratic.

“The adverse midterm results won’t change President Donald Trump’s trade direction because both Democrats and Republicans now favour economic nationalism, domestic manufacturing, and strong supply chains,” said Ajay Srivastava, former trade officer and founder of the think tank Global Trade Research Initiative.
Since Democratic lawmakers also support protective tariffs for local union workers, America’s overall trade posture will remain intact, Srivastava said.

To bypass Congress, Trump will likely continue to rely on existing powers — such as Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 and Section 301 (already mentioned above) — using executive orders, Treasury sanctions and USTR rules to apply unilateral trade pressure.
Section 232 allows the President to impose restrictions on goods imports if it is found that the quantity or other circumstance of those imports “threaten to impair” US national security.
“With foreign policy leverage failing against Russia, China, and Iran, Trump needs a quick win. Expect heightened pressure on India for a trade deal to prove American clout,” said Srivastava.

title: France protests blow up: What exactly is wrong with its economy?

content.value: France protests: France is witnessing some of its worst unrest in years, as a month-long student protest movement widens into nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services.

More than half a million people have joined marches across the country, while violent groups have clashed with police, looted shops and set public buildings on fire. Around 1,800 people across the country have been arrested.

The unrest has put President Emmanuel Macron’s government under renewed pressure ahead of the 2027 presidential election. At the heart of the crisis are two interconnected problems: political fragmentation and economic strain.
The political problem in France

France is divided between the far right, which emphasises immigration clampdown, national identity, and stricter controls on welfare, and the left, which argues for stronger public services, redistribution and workers’ rights.
Questions of immigration, secularism and the place of minorities have deepened these divisions.

Macron’s centrist camp has lost its parliamentary majority, leaving governments struggling to pass budgets and reforms. The result is a political stalemate over who should pay for the country’s problems, and what should be protected or cut.
France’s economic problem: Spending more than it earns

France has an extensive welfare state, which provides pensions, healthcare, education and other social benefits. These services are funded largely through taxes and social contributions. The problem is not simply that the government spends a lot: it is that expenditure persistently exceeds revenue, even without an exceptional emergency, like war for example, to justify the gap.

According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025, while public debt stood at 115.5% of GDP. GDP measures the value of goods and services produced in a country; the deficit is the annual shortfall between government revenue and spending, while debt is the accumulated amount the government owes.

When a government runs a deficit, it borrows to cover the difference. Borrowing year after year adds to its debt, and the government must pay interest on that debt. France’s economy has continued to grow, but modestly: the OECD says average growth has been around 1.4% since 2023. Slower growth makes it harder for tax revenues to rise quickly enough to ease the debt burden.

For France, multiple things are going wrong at once. Weak economic growth, high public debt and pressure on living standards are feeding political polarisation and social unrest already present. In turn, political instability is deepening economic uncertainty, making businesses more cautious about investment and complicating efforts to address the country’s fiscal problems.
Why high pension costs are central to the problem in France

Pensions are one of the biggest pressures on public finances. France has an ageing population, and people are living longer. This means the state must fund retirement benefits for longer, while the proportion of working-age people contributing taxes and social contributions does not necessarily keep pace. In fact, while France’s education budget is sizeable, a large share goes in paying salaries of retired teachers, leaving a smaller amount to spend on infrastructure and hiring new teachers.

The retirement age is politically contentious. Macron’s government sought to raise it gradually from 62 to 64, but opposition from both the far right and far left stalled the reform. Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman, in a substack post from October 8 titled ‘What’s the Matter With France?’, argues that the country’s difficulty in confronting this issue is central to its fiscal troubles. He writes: “France does stand out, even among fiscally troubled nations, in one main way: its persistent inability to get realistic about retirement.”

“…the fiscal pressure caused largely by France’s very generous government pension plan has led to cutbacks in other spending, notably on education. France is effectively handing over large subsidies to older French at the expense of everyone else,” Krugman writes.

Students protesting over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings are therefore confronting the visible consequences of a wider budget squeeze. But cutting pensions or raising the retirement age affects people’s livelihoods, making reform politically difficult.
Why can’t France simply not borrow more?

Investors who lend money to governments expect to be repaid, with interest. If they become concerned that a government’s debt is growing too quickly, they may demand higher interest rates to compensate for the risk. This makes new borrowing more expensive and leaves less money available for public services.

France’s borrowing costs have risen amid concerns about its finances and political uncertainty, although this does not mean that a default is imminent. Krugman warns that France’s membership of the euro adds a complication: France cannot independently create euros to meet its obligations, while a country with its own currency can print more of it.
The way out is political as much as economic

It is not like France’s economy doesn’t have strengths. The challenge is that tough measures needed to sort out the economic problems run into political problems. Raising taxes, cutting expenditure, reforming pensions or stimulating growth each comes with costs and opposition.

That is the central dilemma: citizens are demanding better services and protection from rising costs, while investors want credible plans to control the debt. With a fragmented Parliament and a presidential election approaching, reaching a compromise has become harder.

title: Expert Explains | India-China boundary talks: Some progress, but a long road ahead

content.value: The eight-point consensus reached at the 25th round of talks between Special Representatives (SRs) Ajit Doval and his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing is a welcome step ahead of the expected visit of President Xi Jinping to India for the BRICS Summit.

Some of the outcomes concern the maintenance of peace and tranquillity in the border areas, and advancing negotiations on a framework for the settlement of the boundary question in accordance with previous agreements. There is a specific reference to advancing discussions through an Expert Group and Working Group respectively, to explore an “early harvest” of boundary delimitation in appropriate sectors, and effective border management.

Last year, there was agreement in principle on working towards setting up additional General-Level Mechanisms/Senior Highest Military Commander (SHMC) meetings in the Eastern and Middle sectors akin to the existing mechanism in the Western sector at Chushul/Moldo.

This time, the two sides agreed to implement that understanding along with establishing two hotlines in the Eastern and Middle Sectors. Going forward, the implementation will have to be handled carefully.
The past as prologue

In 1992, the Joint Working Group (JWG) on the Boundary Question decided on confidence building measures (CBMs) such as border personnel meetings (BPMs), complementing forward movement on border trade.

A sub-group of the JWG was created following the border peace and tranquillity agreement (BPTA) of 1993 — the India-China Expert Group of Diplomatic and Military Officials (EG), a precursor to the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (WMCC), an institutional mechanism for border management set up in 2012.

After the success achieved in 1995 on disengagement at Sumdorong Chu (along the India-China Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh), Lipulekh (Middle Sector) and Dichu (Eastern Sector) were subsequently identified as additional military meeting points. The plan for BPMs at Lipulekh was abandoned due to lack of infrastructure and adverse weather conditions. A trial meeting at Dichu in the Kibithu sector in Arunachal Pradesh was finalised. Dichu is a sensitive area in Anjaw district, and the site of a famous battle in 1962 at Hill 100, in which the Kumaon Regiment did the Indian Army proud. The site chosen for the BPM on Madan Ridge proved contentious. No further meetings could take place.

It was not until 2014 that the proposal for additional points for BPMs was revived. Eventually, it was decided to have regular BPMs at Wacha/Kibithu in the same sector opposite Damai on the Chinese side, in addition to existing venues across Bum La in Arunachal Pradesh and Nathu La in Sikkim.

Together with BPMs across the Lungnak Lungpa stream at Daulat Beg Oldie (DBO) and Tianwendian (TWD) in the Chip Chap valley, and at the Chushul–Moldo meeting point in the Spanggur Gap, these have contributed to the two militaries maintaining direct contact.
Additional meetings would further the cause of peace.

Existing hotlines at DBO and Chushul, some informal communication at Demchok in the Western Sector, and similar hotlines at Nathu La (Sikkim) and Bum La and Kibithu in the Eastern Sector have provided the two militaries with channels for direct contact. The two additional hotline channels agreed to for the Eastern and Middle sectors could strengthen this capacity and help defuse local tensions.
The road ahead
The SRs are working to realise the consensus reached between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi at Kazan in October 2024 and at Tianjin in August 2025 on improving ties.
Recent developments such as the resumption of the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, direct flights, and border trade are meaningful steps in the right direction.

However, the road ahead, especially on the task of “early and substantial harvest of boundary delimitation and border management” may be long and arduous, requiring patient negotiations. It would be premature to suggest that substantive boundary delimitation has already begun in earnest. After all, the Expert Group and Working Group under the WMCC are now explicitly tasked with finalising their respective Terms of Reference. That means the framework is being created and the process is being activated incrementally.

There is also the issue of making piecemeal progress as against a more holistic settlement of differences along the Line of Actual Control. Neither the Sikkim sub-sector nor the Middle Sector are free from the burden of differences. The negotiators must be empowered to engage in meaningful discussions. They must have sufficient experience in handling a matter that has proved vexatious for previous generations.

If taken in the right direction, the guidance provided by the political leadership can lead to lasting peace and offer a window for substantive cooperation between two large and populous neighbours in an era of global flux.

(The author is Director General, Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses. He was also head of the Indian side in the Expert Group of Diplomatic and Military Officials negotiating with China between 1996 and 2000)

title: As Israel’s exit polls point to tight finish, can Arab parties become kingmakers?

content.value: Close to 5.7 million Israeli voters cast their ballot on Tuesday (October 27) out of approximately 7.3 million eligible voters — a turnout of 77.7% — for the Israeli parliamentary election. According to exit polls released until now, no single party or bloc is projected to win a clear majority in the 120-seat Knesset — both the right-wing bloc led by the incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the opposition (“Change”) bloc fall short of the 61 needed.

Arab citizens, who are 21% of Israel’s population, make the Arab parties pivotal. Poll averages put the Joint List — a three-party alliance of Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad — at about 11 seats and the Ra’am party (also known as the United Arab List) at about seven.

The war and destruction in Gaza — especially after the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel orchestrated by the militant group Hamas — have made Arab participation harder. We explain who the Arabs are in Israel, where they stand in the Israeli electorate, and what electoral representation can and cannot do for them in a country divided over national identity, security, and Palestinian statehood.
Who are the Arabs in Israel?

Arab Israelis refer to citizens or permanent residents of Israel of Arab descent, mostly composed of Palestinians who remained inside Israel’s borders after establishment of the State of Israel on May 14, 1948, and the Arab-Israeli war (1948-49).

The war forced around 700,000 to 800,000 Palestinians to flee their homeland. The Palestinians who stayed back — roughly 150,000 — became citizens, although they lived under military rule until 1966. Today, Israel’s Arab citizens include Muslims, Christians, Druze, and even Bedouin communities. Although they have had the right to vote since the first election in 1949, they remain unequally represented and marginalised in housing, infrastructure, public safety, and public resources.

Also, Israel has no single written constitution. While its Declaration of Independence promised equality of political rights, a 2018 law (called the “Nation-State Law”) defined the right to national self-determination as exclusive to the Jewish people.

Palestinians in Israel regularly complain that they are treated as “second-class” citizens. According to the Palestinian non-profit Adalah, there are over 65 laws in place that discriminate directly or indirectly against Palestinian citizens in Israel and residents of the Occupied Palestinian Territories.

The law governing elections is another constraint. As Israel is a democracy with a proportional representation system of elections, it has several lists and parties. Simply put, a party is an institution that seeks power within the established rules of elections, whereas a list is a list of candidates prepared for the elections sponsored by a party or by a group of parties.

Under Israel’s Basic Law, lists can be barred if they reject Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, incite racism, or support armed struggle. In September, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar the Joint List and Ra’am under these provisions, but the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the bans. However, Balad’s leader, Sami Abou Shahadeh, withdrew his individual candidature before the court ruled on his own disqualification.
Arab parties in government

Arab parties have sat in the Knesset for decades, but power has remained elusive. For Arabs, representation came first through the Communist party and Arab lists allied to Mapai, the forerunner of Labor. Independent parties such as Hadash, Ta’al, Balad and Ra’am came later.
Until 2021, the closest Arab parties had come to power was Labor leader Yitzhak Rabin’s second government. Rabin’s coalition survived on the outside support of five Arab Members of Knesset (MKs).

In 2021, Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am had joined the coalition government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. It was the first independent Arab party to enter an Israeli governing coalition. Abbas bargained for investment in Arab towns, housing, infrastructure and action against organised crime. But the coalition collapsed in 2022 after some right-wing MKs defected. Bennett has since apologised for governing with Ra’am.

Alvite Ningthoujam, who teaches international relations at Symbiosis School of International Studies, Pune, said the Arab camp is split on strategy. “Ra’am’s approach offered a route to practical gains, but it also drew criticism that it came at the expense of wider Palestinian political demands,” he told The Indian Express. “The Joint List has taken a more oppositional line, emphasising Palestinian national identity and resistance to the occupation.”
The contrast is “not simply pragmatism versus principle”, according to Ningthoujam. “It reflects different judgments about where Arab parties can gain leverage.”
Shrinking political space after October 7

The Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza (still ongoing) have hardened the divide. Arab citizens have had to press for equality at home while living with the daily toll and gruesome imagery of killing and displacement across the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.

“The Gaza war has deepened the historical trauma of occupation, killing and expulsion of Palestinians, across Arab populations inside and outside Israel,” said Omair Anas, associate professor of international relations at Ankara Yildirim Beyazit University.

The political room for Arab parties has narrowed, as opposition to Palestinian statehood has spread across most of Israel’s political spectrum. “The right wing and the centre differ only cosmetically on the future of a Palestinian state and on the Gaza crisis,” Anas said.

The liberal centre is weak, he added. “Most European nations have actively supported Israel’s right-wing parties in Netanyahu’s Gaza war, and that has weakened Israel’s already shrinking liberal and centrist space. It might take time for Israel to revive liberal politics.”
For Arab voters, disillusionment lowers the incentive to vote, but staying home would weaken representation further. “They are realistic about their isolation within the system,” Anas said.
What does the data show?

The arithmetic matters. Parties must win at least 3.25% of the vote to enter the Knesset, which amounts to about 165,000 to 170,000 votes this election. If a party fails to reach this minimum threshold, all votes cast for its slate are discarded, producing “wasted votes” that are reallocated among the parties that succeeded.

In 2022, a split in the Arab vote left Balad below the line, and its votes were wasted. The revived Joint List, which includes Balad, is meant to stop that from happening again. In the March 2021 Israeli election, the two main Arab-led electoral lists — the Joint List and Ra’am — together received 379,647 votes, or approximately 8.61% of all valid votes cast, winning 10 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.

Pointing to the “volatile” Arab voter turnout, Ningthoujam said, “It fell from 64.8% in 2020 to a low of 44.6% in 2021, then recovered to 53.2% in 2022, still well below the national rate of about 70%. Disillusionment, anger over unchecked crime in Arab towns and doubt that a vote can change policy all depress it.” Fragmentation of votes also matters, he added.

Political acceptance is a bigger obstacle. Most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc have ruled out joining forces with the Arab-led parties. The election could hand Arab parties the numbers to shape the next government, but no formal way to use them.

According to Ningthoujam, Arab parties may exercise influence even without joining a government. He cited how the Joint List offered the possibility of a parliamentary safety net — supporting a government in confidence votes without taking ministerial responsibility, in return for policy commitments.

The election will test more than whether Arab parties can become kingmakers, he said. “It will show whether parliamentary strength can become a real influence, even as their legitimacy as partners in government remains contested. Representation alone does not guarantee equal partnership.”

title: Lindsay Clancy case: What is postpartum psychosis — and can it drive a mother to kill her children?

content.value: A closely watched legal case in the US, involving a mother killing her three young children, was declared a mistrial last week. Lawyers defending Lindsay Clancy, 36, had argued that jurors should find her not guilty by reason of insanity, arguing that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings.

With the jurors unable to reach a unanimous verdict, prosecutors could seek a retrial with a new jury. The trial has also raised questions about what postpartum psychosis is, how it can affect a person’s behaviour, and whether it can affect criminal responsibility for killing one’s children.
What is postpartum psychosis? What can it do to a person’s state of mind?

“A most basic description of psychosis is that someone is out of touch with reality,” Susan Hatters-Friedman, forensic and reproductive psychiatrist at Case Western University, told The Indian Express.

Postpartum psychosis is a state in which mothers who have recently given birth may experience delusions, hallucinations, irritable or depressed mood, insomnia, and confusional states, she added. “Postpartum psychosis tends to come on quickly as opposed to over weeks to months. And postpartum psychosis symptoms wax and wane.”

It is currently unclear why postpartum psychosis occurs. According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), risk factors include bipolar disorder, a previous episode of postpartum psychosis, a history of psychosis, a family history of psychotic illness, sleep deprivation, discontinuation of bipolar medication and prior pregnancy loss.

Hatters-Friedman contrasts this with postpartum depression, saying it is “much more common than postpartum psychosis, fortunately.” In postpartum depression, mothers experience symptoms of depression such as depressed mood, loss of enjoyment in activities, difficulty with focus, energy, sleep, and appetite, for example.

Clancy’s symptoms have been described in court as including hallucinations and delusions, which began after the birth of her third child. Her ex-husband, Patrick, testified Clancy had become “very depressed” after giving birth, and her mental health only got “worse and worse”, saying the month before the children’s deaths “was really where her big spiral started”.

But psychosis does not necessarily mean that a person appears disorganised at all times. “A lot of it comes down to how organised the person’s mind is in their state of psychosis — in any psychotic disorder (also such as schizophrenia). For example, someone could still be hearing voices and experiencing delusions, but be able to plan behaviour,” Hatters-Friedman told The Indian Express. With postpartum psychosis, she added, there may be periods of organised thinking alongside periods of less organised thought.

Hatters-Friedman also referred to the five-point framework introduced by Dr Phillip Resnick in the 1960s for mothers killing their children. She said that, in her research and forensic experience, the “altruistic” and “acutely psychotic” motives are the two most commonly found among mothers who are legally insane.
However, a postpartum psychosis diagnosis is not synonymous with violence.
When does postpartum psychosis become legally relevant?

A postpartum diagnosis does not automatically imply that a person is legally insane or not criminally responsible. In Massachusetts, the legal question is whether a defendant is criminally responsible, under what is commonly referred to as the insanity defence. Under state law, “mental disease or defect” is itself a legal term and does not have to correspond to a formal medical diagnosis.

“Particularly relevant in legal insanity evaluations are whether they were experiencing hallucinations or delusions — signs that the person was out of touch with reality at the time of their offending,” Hatters-Friedman told The Indian Express.
The question is what effect the illness had on the person at the time of the offence.

In Massachusetts, the burden of proving criminal responsibility rests with the prosecution, which must prove “beyond a reasonable doubt” that the defendant was criminally responsible at the time of the alleged offence. The defendant has no burden to prove that they lacked criminal responsibility. Under the state’s standard, the prosecution must establish either that the defendant did not have a mental disease or defect at the time of the alleged offence, or that, despite having one, the defendant retained the substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of their conduct and to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law.

“So, it is not that we as a society are finding anyone not criminally responsible merely because of having a mental illness — it is about the specific effects of the mental illness,” Hatters-Friedman told The Indian Express.

As Hatters-Friedman noted, a person can be experiencing hallucinations and delusions while still being able to plan apparently purposeful behaviour, including planning or concealment. The fluctuating nature of postpartum psychosis can also mean that organised and less organised thinking occur at different times.

The difficulty is that the court is assessing a person’s state of mind after the fact. Psychiatric experts can offer opinions on whether a defendant was experiencing psychosis and how it may have affected them, but the jury ultimately decides whether the prosecution has proven criminal responsibility.

In Clancy’s case, the jury weighed evidence of her mental illness alongside evidence of her actions and behaviour, and decide whether the prosecution has met the legal standard for criminal responsibility.
What happens after a mistrial?

After seven days of deliberations, the jury remained unable to reach a unanimous verdict, and Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial on September 4. Clancy remains charged, and prosecutors must now decide whether to retry her before a new jury, pursue lesser charges, or seek another resolution such as a plea agreement.
Clancy remains at a state psychiatric hospital while the charges are pending. A hearing is scheduled for September 29.

If Clancy is eventually found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, that would not mean she is simply acquitted and released. Under Massachusetts law, a person found not guilty by reason of mental illness or mental defect may first be ordered to undergo up to 40 days of observation and examination.
The state may then seek a commitment order, initially for up to six months, with further periods of commitment possible if the statutory requirements are met and subject to legal review.

“The issue is not so much about fitting into legal frameworks—the issue is a lack of knowledge by many people about postpartum psychosis,” Hatters-Friedman said. “If the court, and the jury, understand that postpartum psychosis is a mental illness, then legal insanity criteria may be met just as it may be met with another mental illness.”

title: Why Turkey is seeking to end the long-simmering conflict with Kurds now

content.value: The Turkish government on Wednesday (August 5) submitted to parliament a 12-article draft law, 2-article draft law, titled “Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration”, aimed at achieving ‌peace with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), offering protection from prosecution to several former militants and ending prison sentences for others. According to Reuters, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s ruling AK Party, ⁠its nationalist MHP allies, and the pro-Kurdish DEM Party backed the “national solidarity and social integration” bill. Even the main opposition has voiced support.

Despite broad support, the draft seeks to address a conflict whose roots predate the PKK. The Kurdish question can be traced back to the Treaty of Lausanne (1923), when the newly founded Turkish Republic adopted a centralised nation-state model that marginalised ethnic minorities, including the Kurdish population.

These policies led to Kurdish resistance and several uprisings during the 20th century, including the Sheikh Said and Dersim rebellions. The current armed conflict began in 1984, when the PKK, founded by Abdullah Öcalan in 1978, launched a guerrilla campaign against the Turkish state. So why is Ankara pushing for peace now, and what does each side stand to gain?
Turkey’s renewed urgency

Kadir Yildirim, a non resident fellow at the Baker Institute for Public Policy, Rice University, in his article, The New Peace Initiative and Kurdish Perspective, attributes the renewed urgency to electoral politics. Yildirim notes that President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s AKP and its coalition partner, the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), seek Kurdish political backing—specifically from the pro-Kurdish DEM Party—to secure parliamentary support for constitutional amendments or other electoral pathways for another presidential term.

Besides politics, decades of counter-insurgency operations, defence spending, and regional instability in southeastern Anatolia have cost the Turkish economy billions of dollars. Resolving the conflict is expected to bring economic relief amid Turkey’s broader macroeconomic pressures, according to an ETH Zurich report. An agreement could also reduce vulnerabilities across Turkey’s southern borders in Iraq and Syria, where Kurdish armed groups operate.

The conflict has claimed over 40,000 lives since 1984. According to the London-based Campaign Against Arms Trade, the casualties include Turkish military and security personnel, PKK fighters, and thousands of Kurdish and Turkish civilians. Reports by the International Crisis Group and Amnesty International suggest that between 350,000 and 1 million people were internally displaced, primarily during the forced evacuation of thousands of villages in southeastern Turkey during the 1990s and the urban battles of 2015–2016. The International Crisis Group has recorded approximately 6,000 deaths since 2016, including PKK militants, Turkish security forces and civilians.
Kurdish response

According to Yildirim, Kurdish society and political representatives display a complex mix of strong aspirations for peace and deep institutional scepticism. He notes a strong desire for a peaceful resolution among Kurdish civilians, who have borne much of the cost of military conflict, displacement, and economic neglect in the southeast. Yildirim also argues that imprisoned PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan’s call for disarmament, and the group’s willingness to disarm, suggest a greater inclination towards democratic politics and constitutional rights rather than armed struggle.

At the same time, Kurdish activists remain cautious due to past failures—including the 2013–2015 peace process and the current status of pro-Kurdish politicians. They emphasise that, without guarantees of democratic reform and cultural and linguistic rights, lasting peace will remain difficult, Yildirim notes.
Peace amid West Asia crisis

The ongoing conflict in West Asia, involving Israel, Iran, the United States and regional proxies, appears to have added urgency to Ankara’s calculations. Turkey fears that escalating proxy warfare in Iraq and Syria could create power vacuums, enabling external actors to weaponise autonomous Kurdish armed groups against Turkish interests.
A peace agreement could therefore help insulate Turkey from the spillover of armed conflict in the region.

Turkey had hoped to advance this process in early 2025. However, with the escalation of regional conflict, key state institutions tasked with executing the peace process, specifically the Turkish Armed Forces, the Interior Ministry, and the National Intelligence Organisation (MİT), shifted their priorities from domestic peace negotiations to immediate national defence.
Kurds in Iran, Iraq and Syria
While the Turkish-PKK agreement directly addresses the insurgency in Turkey and northern Iraq, its impact on Kurdish communities elsewhere in the region is less direct.

In Iraqi Kurdistan (KRG), peace is likely to improve conditions by ending decades of Turkish military operations against PKK strongholds in Qandil and Dohuk. The disarmament of the PKK could also more closely align the interests of the ruling Kurdish Democratic Party (KDP) in Erbil and Ankara.

In Rojhelat, or Iranian Kurdistan, the demilitarisation of the PKK is expected to reduce cross-border armed activity along the Iran-Iraq-Turkey tri-border region, shifting the Kurdish struggle in Iran more towards political and civil rights movements rather than armed insurgency.

Meanwhile, in Rojava, or northeastern Syria, the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF/YPG) share ideological roots with the PKK. A successful disarmament framework in Turkey could create pathways for political normalisation and local autonomy agreements in northeastern Syria.
2013–2015 process versus current framework

While the 2013–2015 “Solution Process” relied mainly on informal, executive-driven negotiations conducted by intelligence officials and informal delegations without a legal framework, the current initiative has been submitted to parliament as legislation. By embedding surrender procedures, probation terms, and oversight mechanisms into law, supervised by a multi-ministerial executive committee and a parliamentary commission, the state aims to give the peace process a legal foundation that its predecessor lacked.

Moreover, during the 2013–2015 process, Turkish nationalist actors, particularly Devlet Bahçeli’s MHP, fiercely opposed negotiations with the PKK. Today, the MHP is part of Erdoğan’s governing coalition and backs the initiative, giving the process nationalist support it previously lacked.

The regional balance has changed too. While the earlier process coincided with the expansion of autonomous Kurdish governance in Rojava, Turkey now has a substantial military presence in northern Iraq and Syria.

title: Trump bats for a ‘unified’ Ireland: What led to its partition?

content.value: US President Donald Trump said on Saturday (September 12) that he would “love” to see a “unified” Ireland. “I don’t want ⁠to cause any problems, but ‌I will ‌tell you, I’d love ‌to see it unified… The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now,” Trump, who was on a two-day visit to Ireland, told reporters in Dublin.
Trump was referring to the reunification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland — the latter is part of the United Kingdom.

His comments drew diverse responses from the UK government as well as parties across the political spectrum in both Ireland and Northern Ireland. It came two weeks after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that a referendum on unification was “off the table” during a visit to Northern Ireland.
Here’s how Ireland came to be partitioned after centuries of British rule and whether Irish reunification is still a possibility.
Struggle for independence

From the 13th century, Ireland had been ruled by Great Britain. But over time, there had been some form of resistance to British rule, which was expressed both in peaceful parliamentary representations as well as violence on the streets. This was partly driven by the fact that most of the Irish population was Catholic, as opposed to the Protestants dominating Britain and parts of present-day Northern Ireland.
Broadly, there were two major strands in pre-independence Irish politics, which exist even today:

Irish nationalists, who mostly belonged to the majority Catholic population and wanted a separate Irish state. On several occasions, they advocated for “Home Rule” — the process of transferring the right to govern from British to Irish hands — but the idea finally gained momentum only in the late 19th century. By the turn of the 20th century, Irish “Home Rule” began to look like a real possibility.

Unionists, the minority, largely Protestant population that believed Ireland should remain part of the UK. Loyal to the British and located largely in the north-eastern province of Ulster, the Unionists actively resisted the idea of Home Rule, since they feared being a Protestant minority being ruled by a Catholic majority in an independent Ireland.

After three attempts in Parliament, Home Rule finally became law in 1914, granting the Irish the right to govern themselves. But it excluded the six mainly Protestant counties of the Ulster province (which eventually became Northern Ireland). Although tensions almost boiled over into civil war, hostilities were suspended owing to the outbreak of World War I (1914-18).

By the time WWI ended, Sinn Fein (which translates to “We Ourselves”) emerged as the dominant party among the Irish nationalists. In the 1918 UK general election, it became the largest political party in Ireland. In a bid to boost the independence movement, its MPs abstained from the British Parliament in London’s Westminster, choosing to establish a rival parliament in Dublin instead in January 1919.
The same month, the Irish Republican Army began a guerrilla war against the British, also known as the Anglo-Irish War or the Irish War of Independence (1919-21).
The partition of Ireland

As even the Anglo-Irish War dragged on for over two years, the British government attempted to find a political solution. This led to the passage of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, which stated that while Ireland would remain part of Britain, a “Home Rule Parliament” in Dublin would be given some control over their own affairs. It also partitioned the island into Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland — the latter eventually came to be known as the Irish Free State.

Jane Ohlmeyer, a leading historian of early modern Ireland and empire, earlier told The Indian Express: “The legislation that partitioned Ireland was the same legislation later used to partition India and Pakistan, and also informed partition elsewhere, including Israel and Palestine.”

Of Ireland’s 32 counties, six were allocated to Northern Ireland whereas Southern Ireland comprised the remaining 26. Both regions would have their local parliaments to deal with local issues such as education and health, while Britain would continue to look after major policies, such as foreign policy and the military.

In his book The Partition: Ireland Divided, 1885-1925, the British historian Charles Townshend wrote: “A clean cut six-county bloc would inevitably contain a large nationalist minority, and in any case it would preserve ‘British rule’ in part of Ireland. The (British Cabinet) committee dismissed the idea of a single parliament with ‘safeguards’ for Ulster. This it decided would be ‘unworkable’: it was simply no longer ‘within the power of the Imperial Parliament to impose unity on Ireland’…”

To ensure minorities were adequately represented, proportional representation would be used in elections. A Council of Ireland, comprising representatives from North and South, would be set up to discuss issues of mutual interest and to work towards establishing a single parliament for the whole of Ireland.
“The ‘Council of Ireland’ concept was a token of the government’s reluctance to let go of an all-Ireland settlement of some kind,” Townshend wrote in The Partition.

Although the Unionists in the north accepted the Act, Sinn Fein (Irish nationalists) rejected the Act completely owing to their objection to the lack of provisions pertaining to complete independence, besides partition.

Meanwhile, the escalating military and economic costs of the Anglo-Irish War forced both the British government and most Irish nationalists to call a truce in July 1921. Negotiations finally culminated in the Anglo-Irish Treaty signed in December 1921, bringing the war to an end.

Under the treaty, Southern Ireland came to be known as the Irish Free State. Although it would be a dominion within the British Commonwealth, the treaty granted the south a greater degree of independence, with its own parliament in Dublin and an army. It also decreed that Northern Ireland had the right to opt out of the Irish Free State, which its representatives eventually did.
By 1937, the Irish Free State adopted a new constitution and renamed the country Éire, or Ireland. In 1949, it became a republic and left the Commonwealth.
Is reunification possible?

In the years since, the island has witnessed a fair amount of violence within its borders. From the late 1960s until the 1990s, “The Troubles” in Northern Ireland saw militant groups belonging to both Unionist and nationalist factions carry out bombings and shootings in pursuit of their political ends. It finally ended with the signing of the Good Friday Agreement between the UK and Irish governments on April 10, 1998.

Although the Agreement set up a new parliament and representational government (comprising both Unionists and nationalists) for Northern Ireland with devolution of powers in key areas, it also stipulated the provision of a referendum towards reunification: that both the governments of the UK and Ireland “recognise that it is for the people of the island of Ireland alone… to exercise their right of self-determination on the basis of consent, freely and concurrently given, North and South, to bring about a united Ireland, if that is their wish, accepting that this right must be achieved and exercised with and subject to the agreement and consent of a majority of the people of Northern Ireland”.
Follow our daily newsletter so you never miss anything important. On Wednesday, we answer readers' questions.

Professor Stewart Weaver, who teaches history at the University of Rochester, said in a Q&A in 2021 that “the strong referendum in favor of the Good Friday Agreement” on both sides of the border suggested that “there was a political will, if not toward unification, at least toward reconciliation”.

He added that although the 2016 Brexit — when the UK voted to leave the European Union (EU) — had complicated the issue of cross-border trade between the north (part of the UK) and the south (still an EU member), changing demographics in Northern Ireland as well as growing liberalisation and secularisation in Ireland meant that reunification remains a possibility.

title: What is the White House press pool, what its boycott of Trump can mean

content.value: For decades, whenever the US President travels anywhere in the world, he is accompanied by a group of journalists and a news channel crew, complete with technicians and camera operators. When he addresses the UN General Assembly on Tuesday (September 23), these journalists will be absent — the White House press pool, as it is called, is boycotting Donald Trump.
When Trump inaugurated a helipad on Monday, his remarks were barely audible because the press pool’s sophisticated cameras were not on him.

Trump had last week announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would no longer be allowed inside the White House, accusing the outlets of unfair and false coverage. In solidarity with them, the press pool as a whole — which includes Fox News, generally warm towards Republicans — has decided not to cover the President.
Meanwhile, CNN, MS NOW and Politico have sued the Trump administration, arguing that the ban violates their constitutional rights.

Trump has responded by posting on social media that, “Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown “sources,” shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
The White House has also launched a new video platform, Trump TV, offering a stream of presidential content.
What is the White House press pool?

The press pool was created to solve a logistical problem: the President cannot be accompanied by every journalist who wants to cover him. The system dates to the 1950s, when the White House under Dwight Eisenhower and news organisations developed an arrangement under which a small group of reporters, photographers, radio journalists and television crew would physically accompany the President and then share what they saw and heard with the wider press corps.

The decision of which reporters should be in the press pool was taken by the White House Correspondents’ Association, created in 1914. This changed last year, when the Trump administration started exerting greater control on which individual journalist could be in the pool.

The are separate pools for different forms of media. The television pool currently consists of ABC News, CBS News, CNN, Fox News and NBC News. The five networks take turns sending a crew to Presidential events and share their footage with one another and with other news organisations. In the present case, it was CNN’s turn to cover the President, and when it was banned, the other outlets decided to not accompany Trump at all.

Covering the American President involves constant movement and entry into restricted spaces. The TV pool crew can travel on Air Force One, accompany the President in the motorcade and enter places such as the Oval Office. Apart from covering events, the pool is always on standby in case the President needs to address the nation suddenly.
Why can’t the press pool simply be replaced by other journalists?

Following the President is extremely expensive. News organisations have to pay for journalists’ travel, hotels, food, internet and ground transportation. A foreign presidential trip can cost a television network thousands of dollars. Smaller digital outlets, individual journalists, or content creators generally cannot sustain that kind of operation.
The five major American TV networks therefore spread the burden among themselves: each takes its turn paying for and operating the crew, while everyone else gets access to the resulting footage.

In case of the Tuesday UN event, for example, a newspaper, website or smaller broadcaster may have a journalist at the UN, and the UN will have its own cameras. But that will not guarantee access to every room Trump enters or speaks in. Also, if the journalists aren’t from the press pool, they are under no obligation to share their footage with others. And smaller networks or independent journalists can hardly match the reach of the five major TV networks put together.
Why is there a First Amendment lawsuit?

CNN, MS NOW and Politico argue that the government cannot selectively deny journalists access because it dislikes what they publish or how they cover the President. Their lawsuit invokes the First Amendment, which protects freedom of speech and of the press, and the Fifth Amendment, which includes protections relating to due process. They are asking a federal judge to restore their access while the case proceeds.

title: Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death: How the Syrian civil war unfolded, and ended

content.value: Syria’s toppled leader Bashar al-Assad, who fled to Russia after rebel forces overran the capital Damascus in December 2024, has been sentenced to death in absentia for crimes during the country’s 14-year conflict that left about half a million people dead.
The Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus also handed the death sentence to Assad’s younger brother, Maher, and his maternal cousin, Atef Najib.

The sentences are a landmark, marking the first judicial action against key ruling figures from the country’s previous government, whose five decades in power ended less than two years ago. Here’s a look at what Assad and his relatives were accused of, how the civil war in Syria unfolded and ended, and the challenges it continues to face.
What are the charges against Assad and his relatives?
The Damascus Criminal Court found that Assad, who was toppled in 2024 and now lives in exile in Russia, guilty of premeditated murder, torture and crimes against humanity, Al Jazeera reported.
“Bashar Assad used state agencies to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity,” said judge Fakhareddine al-Aryan during a court session that was aired live on state TV.

Maher, also now living in Russia, was also convicted in absentia of premediated murder and torture, the report said. He was a former commander of the Syrian military’s 4th Armored Division — which Syrian opposition activists have accused of killings, torture, extortion and drug trafficking, in addition to running its own detention centers, AP reported.
Both had fled to Russia after a lightning offensive by rebel group Hay’et Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) overwhelmed government forces in December 2024 in just around 14 days.

Also sentenced to death was Assad’s maternal cousin Atef Najib for “crimes against humanity”. Unlike the other two, who found political asylum in Russia, Najib was detained and became one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial.
Najib is a former Syrian army brigadier general who was head of the Political Security Branch in southern Syria’s Daraa province under Assad in 2011.

In that role, he led the crackdown in the southern province that led to the uprising and later the civil war. Amid tight security, Najib stood inside a cage wearing a prisoner’s uniform as the judge read the sentence, AP reported. His crimes include murder, “the intentional killing of children under 15” and “torture leading to death”, according to the court, Al Jazeera reported.
How did the Syrian conflict begin?

Since 1971, Syria was under the control of Hafez al-Assad, the all-powerful president seen by many as a dictator. After Hafez died in 2000, his son, Bashar, took over. In 2011, the Arab Spring began, resulting in a number of movements calling for authoritarian leaders to be toppled across West Asia. Syria would not remain untouched.

Assad belongs to the Alawite community, a sect of Shia Islam. Many in Syria believed that while Sunnis were the majority, power and resources were concentrated in the hands of the Alawaites. After coming to power, Assad had opened up the economy, but the gains had largely been limited to the elites.

During the tenure of Assad’s cousin Najib, more than a dozen teenagers who scrawled anti-government graffiti on a school wall in Daraa were arrested and tortured. The case became a catalyst for mass protests against the repressive policies of Assad’s security forces. Price rise and unemployment were also among the major issues.
Soon enough, these protests morphed into an armed conflict as defectors from the army turned rebels. And unlike the protests, the civil war reflected sectarian divisions.
Who was fighting whom, and why?
The leader of the group that captured Damascus was the HTS, led by Abu Mohammad al-Jolani — formerly a sanctioned al-Qaeda terrorist with a $10-million bounty on his head.

The HTS was founded in 2011 as Jabhat al-Nusra, the al-Qaeda’s branch in Syria. In 2016, it broke away to form the Jabhat Fateh al-Shaam, standing for the liberation of al-Shaam, or the Levant (the sub-region of the Middle East lying near the Mediterranean Sea, including Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, Israel and Palestine). The HTS wanted to overthrow Assad and establish a Sunni-Islamic rule.

The other significant players were the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), a collection of Kurdish militias that sought greater autonomy and rights for the Kurds. They were not a major enemy of Assad. Then there was the Turkey-backed Syrian National Army, opposing both Assad and the Kurds.
Other countries were drawn in to the conflict. The governments of Shia-majority Iran and Iraq, and Lebanon-based Hezbollah, supported Assad. Russia, too, supported Assad.
The US and Turkey backed the anti-Assad forces, though Turkey’s dispute is mainly with the Kurds, including those within its own borders.

The rebels had taken control of areas to the northeast and northwest of the country. However, Assad was in control of a large section of Syria. This was made possible thanks to a major offensive in 2015, when Russia provided air support and Assad’s forces, with the help of Iran, beat back the rebels. Since 2020, the civil war had remained a frozen conflict, till the anti-government forces mounted a quick and surprisingly effective campaign from November 27, 2024.
Syria under Assad was a staunch supporter of Palestine, and thus Israel, too, has conducted strikes over it.
How did the Syrian civil war end?

The rebels had taken control of areas to the northeast and northwest of the country. However, Assad was in control of a large section of Syria. This was made possible thanks to a major offensive in 2015, when Russia provided air support and Assad’s forces, with the help of Iran, beat back the rebels.
Since 2020, the civil war had remained a frozen conflict, till the anti-government forces mounted a quick and surprisingly effective campaign from November 27.

With Iran, Hezbollah, and Russia all distracted with their own wars in Gaza and Lebanon, and Ukraine, respectively, Assad was missing critical support. As the rebels ran over the country, they met little effective resistance from the official Syrian Army.
After his forces captured the capital, al-Jolani — now going by Ahmed al-Sharaa — took over as president. In the process, he rebranded himself as a modern, soft-speaking, linen-suit wearing leader.
The challenges ahead for Syria

In November 2025, al-Sharaa became the first Syrian president in 80 years to visit the White House, where he received US President Donald Trump’s stamp of approval. “I think this leader can do it,” Trump said.

Al-Sharaa has the unenviable task of leading a country that is fractured on ethnic lines and left economically impoverished by the lengthy civil war. While the establishment of the National Commissions for Transitional Justice (NCTJ) and for Missing Persons last year was hailed as a welcome step, much more still needs to be done.

Since the fall of the Assad regime, there has been widespread ethnic violence, with Sunni groups aligned to the new regime targeting minority communities, notably, Shia Alawites (Assad’s community), the Druze, and Kurds.

Al-Sharaa has been criticised for not doing enough to control this violence. Certain actions have been viewed as explicitly fanning tensions: The failure of Syria’s interim constitution to guarantee Kurdish rights is being seen as a betrayal by the Kurds, who, too, fought Assad.
Human Rights Watch has criticised the NCTJ for focussing on the Assad regime, and overlooking war crimes committed by others, including al-Sharaa’s own HTS.
With al-Sharaa as President, Syria has also been trying to distance itself from Iran’s network and gain international legitimacy after decades of intertwined connections with Hezbollah and Iran.

There are clear difficulties in doing so, such as the leader’s own past role as a former al-Qaeda commander. His attempts at portraying himself as a leader focused on rebuilding Syria and making the nation a serious international player, and in seeking out the US as an ally, come against this backdrop.
During the current West Asia conflict, the Iranian military has also launched attacks on US military sites in Syria.

title: What are US midterms, why these elections matter to India

content.value: US midterms: On November 3, the largest economy in the world — the United States — is scheduled to conduct its midterm elections. The outcome of these midterms dictates the balance of power in the American national legislature, state governorships, and thousands of local offices. Both the American Senate and House of Representatives — the two bodies which comprise Congress — are set to witness strong competition.

India functions as a Parliamentary democracy and does not follow the system of midterm elections, but in the US, they can have a major impact on policy decisions even when the government remains the same. We explain.
First, how is the US political system structured?
The US federal — or central — government is divided into three branches.
The Executive comprises the President — currently Donald Trump — and his administration.

The Legislative, directly elected by the people, is the US Congress composed of the US Senate and the US House of Representatives. Lastly, the judiciary is the Supreme Court and federal judiciary. The US operates on a strict separation of powers.
The President is elected independently of the legislature, which is bicameral.

The lower chamber, termed the House of Representatives, consists of 435 voting members, directly elected, who serve two-year terms. The seats in this House are allocated on the basis of the population of the state. For example, California and Texas hold more seats than states like Wyoming or Iowa. The upper chamber — referred to as the Senate — consists of 100 members. Here, regardless of the population, each state is represented by two Senators serving six-year terms.

When a federal bill — applicable to all 50 states — has to be passed, it must be approved by both the House of Representatives and the Senate before it is elevated to the President, who signs it into effect.

The party with the most seats in the chamber is referred to as the majority party, which grants it the power to select leadership. The Speaker of the House, currently Lousinia’s Mike Johnson, is the presiding officer of the House and controls the lower chamber’s legislative agenda. In the Senate, the Majority leader dictates the proceedings.

The two chambers of Congress have distinct powers. The House of Representatives must initiate bills to raise federal revenue and has the exclusive power to impeach federal officials. The Senate confirms presidential appointments, approves treaties, and conducts impeachment trials.
Both chambers must pass a bill for it to become law, making control of either chamber consequential for the President’s legislative agenda.
What are midterms elections in the US?
Midterm elections occur exactly halfway through a president’s four-year term.

During these elections, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one-third of the 100 Senate seats (33 or 34 seats) are contested. These elections widely serve as a referendum on the sitting president’s administration and performance.
American elections are also highly decentralised in nature.

Elections are conducted using a first-past-the-post system, where the candidate with the highest number of votes wins the seat. Before the general election, the Republican and Democratic parties — the two main national parties — select their candidates through state-level “primaries” or “caucuses,” where registered party members vote for their preferred nominee.

For voters, there are state-wise voter registration rules which vary. Furthermore, because local, state, and federal elections occur simultaneously, no two voters across the country receive the exact same ballot. Depending on their state’s laws, Americans can cast their votes via postal ballots, early in-person voting, or traditional Election Day voting. Because of this, final results can take days.
Election results determine how the country is governed through 2028 when the general elections are scheduled.

A win by the Republican party would empower Trump to advance his agenda whereas a Democratic House would introduce legislative gridlock and oversight to Trump’s policy leanings. A steep enough win for the Democrats may empower them to raise the process of impeachment which requires a two-thirds conviction vote in the Senate to oust the sitting President.
So, what is the 2026 midterm arena looking like?
The 119th Congress is currently defined by razor-thin margins. Midterm elections inevitably serve as a referendum on the sitting president, and 2026 is no exception.

The field is highly competitive, though historical trends consistently penalise the president’s party. Over the last 23 midterm cycles, the incumbent president’s party has lost an average of 27 House seats and three Senate seats due to anti-incumbency sentiment and voter fatigue.

In the Senate, Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage. Democrats require a net gain of four seats to flip the chamber, navigating difficult toss-up races in states like Texas, Maine, Ohio, and Alaska. In the House, the Republican majority is fragile, and generic ballot polling suggests Democrats possess a tangible path to reclaiming control.

Since beginning his second term in 2025, Donald Trump’s administration has aggressively implemented his campaign agenda. Fulfilling his promise to dismantle the federal bureaucracy, Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) initiated dramatic budget cuts, eliminating approximately 264,000 positions from the federal workforce.

While this delivered on conservative pledges, the broader economy is experiencing turbulence. Despite strong corporate earnings, core inflation recently rebounded to 2.6%, ensuring the cost of living remains a paramount concern for voters.
Economic friction has also been compounded by conflicts such as the ongoing Iran War and aggressive trade policies — especially the ‘Trump Tariffs’.

Following joint US and Israeli military strikes against Iran in February this year, retaliatory measures in the Strait of Hormuz have severely disrupted global energy supply chains. This has pushed US gas prices to a peak of $4.50 a gallon.

Simultaneously, Trump has rapidly executed his protectionist trade agenda via executive orders, establishing a 10% baseline global tariff on imports and elevating tariffs on Chinese goods to a punitive 125%. On the domestic front, while his promised mass deportation programs face friction from Supreme Court rulings limiting executive emergency powers, the administration has curtailed legal immigration and asylum.
Why does India, and the world at large, care about US midterm elections?
The US Constitution grants Congress the power to regulate foreign commerce and approve budgets. For India, the main buckets of interest are across technology, trade and defence ties with the US.

In September 2025, the Trump administration overhauled the H-1B visa program to protect domestic workers, imposing a staggering $100,000 fee on new applications. Because Indian nationals account for over 70% of all H-1B approvals, this unilateral policy dealt a severe blow to India’s $200 billion IT services export industry, triggering a sharp decline in Indian student enrollment and workforce mobility.
Trade relations have been equally volatile.

The Trump administration levied a punitive 50% tariff on Indian goods in 2025 as a measure against India’s continued purchase of Russian crude oil. Following fraught bilateral negotiations, these tariffs were conditionally reduced to an interim 18% in early 2026, tied to reciprocal Indian concessions.

Conversely, technological defense cooperation has deepened via the newly established TRUST (Transforming Relationship Utilising Strategic Technology) initiative, aimed at countering Chinese semiconductor dominance.

A Democratic takeover of the House could introduce rigorous oversight over Trump’s policies over tariffs and Middle East interventions. This may potentially provide diplomatic and economic relief to Indian exporters.
Neither US party, however, has been publicly eager to dismantle protectionist frameworks entirely, reflecting a bipartisan shift toward prioritising American supply chains.

title: How hackers overheated French supermarket fridges — and the lessons for India

content.value: This week, hundreds of supermarkets in France were hit by a cyberattack that spiked the temperatures of their fridges and freezers, causing food worth millions of euros to spoil.

The attack exposed a vulnerability that extends beyond the financial or retail sector: the ability of hackers to interfere with physical equipment through vulnerable internet-connected control systems.
France’s cybersecurity agency has warned that attacks on the equipment may still be under way, highlighting the risks posed by outdated software and exposed industrial systems.
What happened in France?
The cyberattack affected refrigeration systems at supermarkets belonging to several major retail chains.

Reports suggest that compromised refrigeration control systems allowed attackers to manipulate their temperature and defrost settings, forcing some fridges to warm up to 50 degrees Celsius overnight into Monday morning. Many supermarkets were forced to discard fresh and frozen products.
French minister Roland Lescure told parliament on Tuesday: “700 of the 10,000 sites spread across the country have been affected. These 700 sites have disconnected the platform.”

In an alert issued on October 12 and updated on October 13, France’s national cybersecurity response team, CERT-FR, identified equipment made by Danish company Danfoss, as well as systems associated with Copeland and Dixell, as among those affected.
Significantly, the agency warned that the threat might not have ended. “Attack campaigns are probably still ongoing,” the alert said.

Although the precise mechanism by ‌which attackers ⁠compromised the refrigerators is not clear yet, cybersecurity experts quoted by Reuters said that all signs pointed to a basic stunt enabled both by the failure to adopt Danfoss’ software updates and by exposing device interfaces to the internet.
How are French authorities responding?

French prosecutors have opened a cyber-crime investigation into the incident. However, no person or group has taken responsibility yet, puzzling investigators — cybercriminals usually raise ransom demands to monetise their hacks.

CERT-FR issued an advisory for supermarkets across the country. For supermarkets whose equipment was not compromised, it suggested that they disconnect their refrigeration units from the internet, and then reconnect them securely after checking their settings.

“Restore service only through a secure VPN or protected network. Emergency firewall filtering of authorised service providers’ IP addresses may be used temporarily but is not a long-term solution,” it said.
For supermarkets with compromised equipment, it advised disconnecting units from the internet, resetting them to remove unauthorised changes, and securely configuring them before reconnecting.
Lessons for countries like India

The French incident highlights risks for countries such as India which are increasingly connecting their infrastructure to digital networks. India’s power networks, factories, transport systems — such as metros, flights and trains — hospitals, smart cities, and food and pharmaceutical supply chains increasingly depend on operational technology to monitor and control physical processes.

Traffic signals, water treatment systems and industrial control equipment could be vulnerable. Compromised refrigeration and temperature-monitoring systems could damage food, medicines, vaccines and blood products.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issues cybersecurity advisories, while the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre protects designated critical infrastructure. However, officials have stressed the need for security measures covering individual devices, older equipment and third-party systems.

“Organisations should remove unnecessary internet exposure, apply security updates and replace equipment that cannot be adequately secured. The attack in France shows that such incidents can disrupt physical systems and threaten essential services. For India, the lesson extends beyond supermarkets to any connected system whose failure could disrupt supply chains or endanger public safety,” said an officer who has served in the past with the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre.

With public utilities, industries, hospitals and supply chains increasingly dependent on connected systems, the incident offers lessons for India at both the individual-system and infrastructure-wide levels, including for assets not traditionally considered part of the cybersecurity landscape, the officer added.

title: China This Week | Rumours about Xi Jinping’s health, US jets arrive in Taiwan, and more

content.value: Over the last few days, analysts and longtime China watchers have tried to make sense of the bilateral leaders’ meeting in Washington, DC, in late September. What stood out was the pageantry surrounding Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit, even as many argued that the trip itself fell short on substantial outcomes.

A report from The Wall Street Journal has now claimed that Xi’s staff requested several breaks during the visit and to cut down the duration of some events, raising questions about the 73-year-old’s health. It also follows similar rumours that swirled during Xi’s trip to India for the BRICS summit in New Delhi earlier in September.

Another noteworthy event this week was the delivery of two American F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan. The Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) tabloid, Global Times, commented on the fact that it came years behind schedule. The jets have also come as a major arms sale from Taiwan to the US hangs in the balance.

Finally, we look at a recent Reuters report that used satellite images to find that China is building a full-scale runway at the Antelope Reef in the disputed South China Sea. “Military attaches and security analysts say [it] could be one of China’s most important offshore bases in the region,” the report said.
Here is a closer look at these developments.
1. Why Xi Jinping’s health is often the centre of rumours
The WSJ report cited former US officials involved in planning state visits and analysts, who said that the nature of China’s requests for Xi was unusual.

“Chief among the requests was a private room inside the West Wing [of the White House] for Xi to take a break between events, with only his wife, Peng Liyuan, permitted to join him, the people said. No others from the Chinese delegation were allowed to use the ‘hold room,’ as it was called,” the report said.

UPSHOT: Such rumours are not exactly new. In fact, back in 2012, months before Xi was elevated as the general secretary of the CCP — the most powerful position in China — he was not seen in public for a while, sparking speculation over his health.

Xi is not alone, in that many key public figures in China often draw such scrutiny given the lack of transparency in the country’s political and media systems. Information flows are heavily regulated by the government, which, in turn, heightens curiosity among observers. With a leader like Xi, who has concentrated power at the top and bypassed term limitations, China watchers are particularly interested in observing the tiniest body language shifts and movements to understand his health condition, including Xi reportedly clasping his wife’s hand while using the stairs in Washington, SC.

This incident may turn out to be about Xi simply requiring rest given his age and the long-duration flight to the US. The rumours of his supposed ill-health in India were also not found to have a strong basis, at least so far, but are indicative of how China’s political system, in an attempt to project strength and infallibility, can damage those very perceptions.
2. Taiwan gets new jets, with some delays
