During Donald Trump’s first presidential term in 2019, the United States approved an $8 billion sale of Lockheed Martin F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan, but issues such as software problems delayed delivery, Reuters reported.

The arrival of the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70s strengthens Taiwan’s defense capabilities and safeguards our skies. We thank the United States for its longstanding support and continued security cooperation.
As President @ChingteLai has said, investing in defense is investing in peace. Taiwan remains committed to defending our homeland and to contributing to regional peace and stability.
— DPP U.S. Mission (@TaiwanDPP_DC) October 2, 2026

The jets were to reach Taiwan between 2023 and 2026, but only two of the 65 F-16V Block 70 jets have been delivered. Commenting on the news, Global Times noted the positive reactions from Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), calling it “political performance”.

The article spoke of “The DPP’s alarm over the rising prevalence of ‘abandoning Taiwan’ and ‘doubting the US’ sentiments, particularly as China and the US have sought greater strategic stability in their relationship. Under this narrative, the arrival of two F-16Vs in Taiwan has been… cited as proof of continued US support for Taiwan island.”

UPSHOT: The article touches on a subject that has worried some stakeholders in the US of late: the country’s longstanding relationship with Taiwan. While the latest jet delivery may have been approved years ago, its delivery comes when Trump has held off on approving a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan. Once signed, it would be the biggest such package to date.

Amid the visit, Lyle Morris, Senior Fellow on Foreign Policy and National Security at the US-based Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, told The Indian Express that Trump’s delay could be an attempt to accommodate China. Xi and the Chinese State have criticised such arms sales as part of the broader objection to any conception of Taiwanese independence.

But Trump’s more recent statements have also diverged from the more assured US support for Taiwan over the past few decades. In that context, it would be understandable why the DPP would see the jets as evidence of US support, and why the CCP would describe it critically.
3. New activity in South China Sea

Reuters reported that a ​completed base at Antelope Reef would be “China’s most significant military expansion in the South China Sea in ⁠a decade, extending the reach of Chinese naval ships and military aircraft in a waterway that is an increasingly militarised ​arena of competition between Beijing and the United States and its allies over Taiwan.”
It would also help protect the approaches to Hainan Island, where China keeps its nuclear-armed ballistic missile submarines, the report said.

UPSHOT: In the last decade or so of increasingly assertive Chinese foreign policy, the South China Sea has been a major component. Apart from the region’s vast oil and gas resources, it has also become a source of territorial contestation, with claims upto various points made by countries such as Vietnam and the Philippines.

For the US, it could also emerge as a region where China incrementally increases its presence through the deployment of smaller vessels and forces, creating a strategic threat. In July, the US government issued a joint statement with countries including Japan, Australia and the Philippines on the tenth anniversary of the Philippines-China South China Sea Arbitral Tribunal Award. That award had criticised China’s claims to the region, while China has said the tribunal was not eligible to adjudicate on the subject.

“We reaffirm that the Award rendered ten years ago by the Arbitral Tribunal is a significant milestone and is final, legally binding, and definitive between China and the Philippines… We reaffirm the Arbitral Tribunal’s decision that there is no legal basis for China’s expansive maritime claims in the South China Sea, including those based on ‘historic rights’,” it said. With continued Chinese activity even a decade after the ruling, however, there is little to suggest that tribunals and other means of adjudication will influence China to slow down its work there.

title: How Xi Jinping’s sweeping military purge echoed at a top Chinese leaders’ meeting

content.value: At the conclusion of a four-day closed-door meeting of senior Chinese Communist Party (CCP) leaders on Thursday (October 29), it was difficult to miss the main messaging that emerged — “full and rigorous party self-governance”.

Underneath the jargon commonly spotted in official communiques was the goal that CCP general secretary and Chinese President Xi Jinping has pursued over nearly 15 years in power: ridding the Party of corruption. Of late, however, it has taken the shape of major leaders being removed across key bodies, including military ones.

The recent meeting, known as the Fifth Plenum, saw a record number of members expelled. It also saw the elevation of General Zhang Shengmin into the Politburo, which is a 24-member body of top party leaders.

In January this year, General Zhang Youxia, holding the top rank in the People’s Liberation Army (PLA), was purged from the Central Military Commission (CMC) — China’s apex military decision-making body, involved in procurement, testing and other key functions. Nearly all of the CMC’s top leadership have come under corruption investigations in recent years, and only Zhang Shengmin and Xi remain now.

And it’s not just the CMC. Suyash Desai, a Non-Resident Fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute in Philadelphia and an analyst of the Chinese military, told The Indian Express that within the PLA, “over 55% of its top leadership (three-star and above) has been purged” to date. The fact that the purge has affected “every section of the PLA” makes it unique in terms of its scale, scope, and nature, he added.
Major gaps

Since Xi assumed power as the general secretary of the CCP in 2012, he has described tackling corruption as a top priority. In fact, his first few years also saw senior military leaders purged, including CMC Vice Chairman Guo Boxiong, who was then the highest-ranking general to ever face a corruption charge. He is currently serving a life sentence.

Initially, some analysts in the West saw the campaign as a means for Xi to remove rivals and consolidate power, but over the years, not even his loyalists and appointees have been spared. The campaign has taken the shape of sudden removals and investigations.

Defence has increasingly come under focus. Key posts are now vacant (see chart) in many top bodies, while others have witnessed a churn. Five of the seven CMC positions remain unfilled, and while the political head of defence has historically been part of the body, current Defence Minister Admiral Dong Jun has yet to be made a member.

In May, former defence ministers Wei Fenghe and Li Shangfu were sentenced to death ‌with a two-year reprieve (meaning the sentence would be converted to life imprisonment after that period) over graft charges.

Desai said that across the five theatre commands, almost all commanders and commissars (who handle major political responsibilities) have been purged on multiple occasions over the past three years. He added that this also includes the Eastern and Western Theatre Commands, which are responsible for Taiwan and India, respectively.

Anushka Saxena, a Staff Research Analyst at the Takshashila Institution in Bengaluru who tracks the PLA, also laid out the case of the PLA Rocket Force. Responsible for managing China’s conventional and nuclear missiles, the force saw senior leaders removed in 2023. Ex-defence ministers Wei and Li had ties with the PLARF, too.

Saxena termed it the “pillar of China’s long-range strategic deterrent and the arm that would open a campaign against Taiwan and threaten US naval vessels”. “After former PLARF Commander Li Yuchao was pulled in 2023 and replaced by Wang Houbin, who was parachuted from the Navy, Wang himself was expelled in October 2025… the PLARF has been decapitated twice in barely two years, and no successor commander has surfaced in public since,” she told The Indian Express.
Why the removals matter

Desai said, “There are direct implications of these purges for military operations and effectiveness… For instance, the PLA’s operational textbooks divide the Taiwan contingency scenario into three parts: Joint Strike, Blockade, and Amphibious Landing Operations. The Joint Strike is the first operation led by the PLARF to clear the ground for the invading Chinese forces. However, these purges have set back the PLA’s operational effectiveness by a few years.”

Saxena added that when seen in relation to the PLA’s equipment development ecosystem and the removal of leaders at major defence State-Owned Enterprises, it is clear that layers of dishonesty run deep. “The command architecture for a joint operation has been altogether disrupted at the top. That is corrosive to the trust, continuity and rehearsed coordination on which jointness actually depends,” she said.

Apart from the military, another senior figure to have been abruptly removed was Qin Gang, the Foreign Affairs Minister who served a tenure of less than a year and was one of the youngest people ever appointed to the post. His ouster was suspected to be linked to personal reasons rather than corruption, but it again raised questions about Xi’s picks.

With his rise, Xi at times elevated officials with links to two major factions in Chinese politics — the so-called Shaanxi and Fujian “gangs”. These are the names of the two provinces where Xi has served, the former during the Cultural Revolution and the latter as Governor.

While the CMC’s Zhang Youxia was part of the Shaanxi grouping, other purged CMC members, including He Weidong and Miao Hua, were part of the Fujian gang. Factional rivalries have previously been cited as a potential driver for the purges.

Yet another probable theory for the sudden revival in purges in the last few years is the question of Taiwan. Several US analysts have argued that Xi wants the PLA to be ready for a potential battle scenario by 2027 — the centenary year of the PLA’s founding, and when Xi seeks a record-extending fourth term as general secretary of the CPC at another major party meeting next year. Xi has also earlier stated the goal of turning the PLA into a “world-class” military by 2027.

However, Desai was of the view that these theories only made sense up to a certain point: “It is very clear now that the purges are not related to any single contingency, since all theatre commands are affected and all factions are chopped.”

The most likely explanation for these purges, he said, was the corruption within the PLA. While Xi ordered several rounds of restructuring upon assuming power, the PLA’s power base remained intact. “And over the past two tenures before Xi, the PLA gained significant commercial autonomy, making it one of the most corrupt armed forces in the world. It reached the point where it began to impact military effectiveness,” Desai said.

It could point to a leader who, despite commanding the top of the leadership as few Chinese leaders have, remains concerned about inefficiencies and how they could affect his — and the party’s — standing in a real-world battle.

Saxena noted that while Mao Zedong’s purges were about ideology and factional loyalty, the current purges are “formally centred on corruption in procurement and modernisation, striking at the very credibility of the ‘world-class military by 2027’ project.”

She said that while political disloyalty might be a worry, paramount concerns may be related to “mediocrity, inefficiency, and graft, which is also important at a time when China is competing with the world’s biggest superpower — the US.”

She pointed out that “A striking share of the CMC-level purge does cluster around a Taiwan-facing network,” referring to the Fujian faction. The region is also the closest to Taiwan in mainland China. Saxena said that many of the clique’s now-purged members “oversaw war planning vis-à-vis Taiwan… That so many fell together does suggest something went wrong.”

But, she cautioned, one should avoid a “siloed reading.” “It can be both a cleanup before contemplated action and a symptom of rot in the Taiwan mission, and neither is mutually exclusive. And much of the wider churn doesn’t map neatly onto just Taiwan.”

title: How Starlink, Starshield pause exposed Ukraine’s drone warfare vulnerability

content.value: Starlink Starshield Ukraine: In mid-October, Ukrainian forces experienced restrictions on Starlink and Starshield satellite communications for fast-moving equipment, disrupting frontline operations and efforts to intercept Russian attack drones. The restrictions reportedly caused connections to fail when equipment travelled faster than about 160 kmph, affecting drones that depend on satellite links to operate.

US President Donald Trump said on October 22 that the problem had been resolved, but Ukrainian officials reported that restrictions remained the following day. On Saturday (October 24), however, Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said that both systems were operating at speeds exceeding 400 kmph.

The most important thing today is that Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored to the speeds we had before the restrictions. The speeds are now where they need to be. The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient. This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered “shaheds.”
I thank all Americans and all our partners who took this seriously and truly helped – members of Congress, senators, all the media, the State Department, and the President. Protecting lives matters.
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 24, 2026

SpaceX chief Elon Musk subsequently accused Ukraine of violating commercial Starlink’s terms of service by using it for offensive drone strikes. He denied responsibility for the restrictions affecting Starshield, SpaceX’s military-oriented service.

The restrictions came amid worsening relations between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump pressing Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and accept concessions in peace negotiations. It remains unclear whether the restrictions were part of this wider pressure, but the episode exposed a vulnerability: nearly five years into Russia’s war against Ukraine, its military relies heavily on satellite communications over which Kyiv does not have complete control.
First, what are Starlink and Starshield, and why does Ukraine need them?

Starlink is a satellite internet network comprising thousands of small satellites in low-Earth orbit. SpaceX first began sending them into space in 2019 and now operates more than 11,000 satellites that provide internet connectivity through receivers on the ground.

Unlike conventional broadband, Starlink does not depend on cables reaching a user’s location. A portable satellite dish connects to orbiting satellites, allowing users to access the internet even where local communications networks have been damaged or destroyed. This has made Starlink especially valuable to Ukrainian forces coordinating troops and operating drones amid the war with Russia.

Starshield, by contrast, is Starlink’s military counterpart, developed primarily for government and military applications. According to SpaceX, Starshield relies on Starlink’s technology and operational infrastructure. Its applications include encrypted communications, gathering images and other information about the Earth, and carrying specialised surveillance or communications equipment aboard satellites.

Although Starshield serves different purposes from commercial Starlink, the two share underlying technology. Some Starshield communications services use dedicated equipment and additional security protections while relying on the larger Starlink satellite network to transmit information.
How did the speed restrictions affect Ukrainian drones?
Ukrainian forces use satellite terminals mounted on some drones to maintain contact with their operators during flight.

Unlike conventional radio links, which have a limited range, Ukrainian drones on Starlink or Starshield can maintain this connection over much greater distances. These connections allow operators to receive information from the drones and, where applicable, control them remotely.

On October 13–14, Ukrainian forces reported that Starshield connections had begun dropping when the terminals moved faster than about 160 kmph. While the drones could still fly, those depending on satellite communication could lose contact with their operators upon exceeding this speed.

This was particularly problematic for interceptor drones, which must fly fast enough to catch incoming Russian attack drones, and longer-range strike drones, some of which need to reach high speeds during launch or flight. Slowing down to maintain connectivity could prevent an interceptor from catching up with an incoming Russian drone, while accelerating risked severing the connection with its operator. Ukrainian units reported interruptions lasting 10–20 seconds even at lower speeds of 110–120 kmph, forcing some missions to be cancelled.

Ukraine does not rely on Starlink for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including strikes on oil refineries, presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said. Such drones operate at speeds of 70-90 kph, he added.
On October 24, Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said stable connections had been restored at movement speeds exceeding 400 kmph.
Who controls these systems?

While SpaceX operates the commercial Starlink network, the US government is Starshield’s largest customer. The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services, including dedicated satellites for military and intelligence purposes.

However, the precise division of control between SpaceX and the US government remains unclear, and the October restrictions highlighted this ambiguity. Reuters reported, citing two US officials and a Western official, that the order to restrict Starshield originated inside the White House. The Wall Street Journal, however, reported that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown.

Musk has maintained that Starshield is controlled by the US government, and that restrictions on its use could only be authorised by the US military or the President. Trump has denied responsibility, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said decisions about Ukraine’s commercial Starlink access rested with SpaceX.

The dispute has unfolded amid worsening relations between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump pressing Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and accept concessions in peace negotiations. However, the conflicting accounts have left unanswered who authorised the restrictions and whether they were connected to Washington’s wider pressure on Ukraine.

title: Brazil election: 2 reasons Lula trumped predictions of defeat to win historic fourth term

content.value: Brazil election 2026: In a stunning upset, Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected for a historic fourth term on Sunday (October 25), securing 51.79% of the vote against his rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who won 48.21%.

In the first round earlier this month, he had finished behind the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated in 2022. Flávio won the first round with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, and has thus far refused to concede and called for the election results to be annulled.
The result was historic for another reason: since Brazil returned to direct presidential elections in 1989, no candidate who finished second in the first round had gone on to win the runoff.

Lula’s victory also bucks a regional trend that saw right-wing candidates win seven consecutive presidential elections across Latin America, dealing a setback to US President Donald Trump’s ambitions to expand Washington’s influence in the region.
“Brazil is no one’s backyard. We will change the way we run this country; we will make people participate more in the decision-making process,” Lula said.
How did Lula turn the election around?
1. Higher turnout and voter mobilisation
Lula’s narrow loss to Bolsonaro in the first round initially dismayed his supporters but prompted a renewed mobilisation effort ahead of the runoff.

Following the initial defeat, Lula’s campaign intensified efforts to mobilise voters who had abstained, cast invalid ballots or supported other candidates. Young Brazilians organised demonstrations across the country, while Lula held rallies in key battlegrounds, including Belo Horizonte in Minas Gerais, Brazil’s second-largest electorate, days before the runoff.

The 80-year-old president, who does not own a mobile phone, also stepped up his digital campaign. On the advice of younger politicians, Lula began recording selfie videos, while millions joined a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”. Congressman André Janones used the channel to coordinate supporters and encourage them to circulate pro-Lula content, The Guardian reported. According to Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, Lula’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s during the runoff campaign.

Lula also announced welfare measures, including increased and early payments under the Bolsa Família cash-transfer programme, and secured congressional approval for a shorter working week, reducing the maximum from 44 to 40 hours without cutting pay. The constitutional amendment was formally promulgated on October 16, nine days before the runoff.

The result was a significant increase in voter turnout: Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court reported that nearly three million more Brazilians voted in the runoff, reducing abstention from 21.08% in the first round to approximately 19.2% in the second round. Although it is unclear how these additional voters cast their ballots, their number exceeded the gap of just over 2.2 million votes between Lula and Bolsonaro in the first round.
2. Lula retained his strongholds and made gains elsewhere
Lula won all nine states in the country’s northeast, his traditional voter base. But his victory depended on gains in areas that had favoured Bolsonaro in the first round.

An analysis by CNN Brasil noted that 213 municipalities across 18 states that voted for Bolsonaro on October 4 switched to Lula in the runoff. These included 76 municipalities in Minas Gerais, 33 in São Paulo and 20 in Paraná.

Crucially, Lula also overturned Bolsonaro’s first-round lead in Minas Gerais, Brazil’s second-largest electorate and a key battleground. He secured 50.43% of the vote there in the runoff, against Bolsonaro’s 49.57%.
The geographical shifts show how Lula expanded his support beyond his traditional strongholds, even in states where Bolsonaro remained ahead overall.
What challenges lie ahead for Lula?
A conservative Congress and economic pressures

Despite his victory, Lula now faces Brazil’s most conservative Congress since its return to democracy in the 1980s. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies are set to control both chambers, complicating Lula’s efforts to expand social welfare programmes and pursue his economic agenda.

He must also address Brazil’s public debt, which has risen by more than 10 percentage points during his present term to over 82% of its GDP. Amid high interest rates, which stood at 13.75% in September, nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million businesses are behind on debt payments, according to credit bureau Serasa. The debt crisis has fuelled public dissatisfaction despite record-low unemployment and wage growth outpacing inflation.
A disputed result and judicial tensions

Flávio’s challenge to the election result centres on a decision by Supreme Federal Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting by two hours on Sunday, following requests from both campaigns over transport and weather-related disruptions. The order, issued just before polls were due to close, caused confusion because some polling stations had already shut. Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court subsequently clarified that the extension applied only to stations that remained open.

The dispute has also revived longstanding tensions over the expansive powers of Brazil’s judiciary, which has faced criticism for its interventions in elections and online speech, even as it maintains that these are necessary to safeguard democracy.
The Trump factor

A Bolsonaro victory would have given Trump a crucial ally in Latin America’s largest economy, particularly as Washington seeks closer security cooperation with right-wing governments across the region.

Flávio had pledged to join Washington’s anti-cartel coalition, the Shield of the Americas, and work more closely with the US against Brazilian criminal gangs. Lula has resisted joining the coalition over concerns about Brazilian sovereignty.

Trump has repeatedly clashed with Lula, imposing tariffs of up to 50% on Brazilian goods in 2025 in an attempt to pressure his government over the prosecution of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The New York Times reported that Washington also imposed sanctions on Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw Bolsonaro’s coup trial.

Lula used these interventions to frame the election partly around Brazil’s sovereignty and resistance to foreign pressure. While it is unclear how much Trump’s involvement influenced voters, the result denies Washington an opportunity to bring Brazil into closer alignment with its regional security strategy.
Although many of the tariffs were later eased, Lula’s re-election leaves Washington dealing with a Brazilian government that has resisted its expanding military and security role in Latin America.

title: Why US has suspended Indian IT firms Cognizant, TCS, Wipro, HCL from Green Card filings

content.value: US Green Card Suspension News Explained: The US government is suspending several large Indian IT firms from a key programme that allows skilled foreign workers to gain ‌permanent residency. The administration has cited alleged fraud, and claimed that foreign workers got jobs in the US at the cost of American workers.

US Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said, “I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world — Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini”.  The move is a major blow for Indian professionals looking to work at some of these companies in the US.

The Permanent Labour Certification Programme in the US, also referred to as PERM (Program Electronic Review Management), is a key provision used by American employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency, with several Indian IT companies also relying on the system.

Last month, the US had announced it was suspending Cognizant from the process, but had not mentioned the specific allegations against Cognizant, the number of applications affected or the duration of the suspension.

.@Sonderling47: “I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world — Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini — and also, due to multiple active federal investigations, @USDOL is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the program.”
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 8, 2026

The latest action is a clear broadening of the crackdown on foreign workers that has become a central policy under US President Donald Trump. Technology and IT services companies are particularly facing greater scrutiny over their reliance on foreign workers. Apart from the IT services firms, the US has also suspended Microsoft and Adobe from the programme.

US authorities have stepped up investigations into alleged misuse of the H-1B and PERM programmes, including claims of wage undercutting, fraudulent filings and displacement of American workers. The scrutiny is especially significant for Indian professionals, who account for a large share of H-1B beneficiaries and employment-based Green Card applicants.
Why is US cracking down on Indian IT giants?

The key reason behind the suspensions is the US administration’s belief that foreign workers hired by these companies were resulting in fewer jobs for American workers. “…we are ending the fraud that has fuelled reliance on foreign labour. President Trump’s Department of Labour will ensure that American businesses now look first to the most talented workforce in the world, and that’s the American worker,” Sonderling said.

“ This administration knows that American workers are the best and brightest in the world. These jobs that were stolen from them should have gone and will now go to Americans first, not foreigners, and especially not foreign fraudsters… We are cutting off the head of the snake,” he added.
Vice President JD Vance announces the suspension of the PERM Program for Microsoft:

“Thanks to an ongoing investigation, we have decided to suspend the PERM program for Microsoft, which means they will no longer be able to take those H-1Bs and apply for permanent resident status within the United States of America. Now our message to Microsoft and to any other foreign or domestic corporation is quite simple. We obviously want you to thrive in the United States of America. We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector. We’re the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers. And so our message to Microsoft is, you’re great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
— Vice President JD Vance (@VP) October 8, 2026

He said that since 2009, the impacted companies have requested permanent residency for almost 3 million foreign workers. “They’ve received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals, and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications – that’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” Sonderling said.
What is PERM?

PERM, or Program Electronic Review Management, is the system through which employers generally obtain labour certification before sponsoring a foreign employee for an employment-based Green Card. Unlike a visa application, which is primarily made by an individual, the PERM filing is done by the employer on behalf of the worker.

Before filing, an employer must obtain a prevailing wage determination for the position and carry out prescribed recruitment. Broadly, the process is intended to establish that hiring a foreign worker permanently will not adversely affect the job opportunities, wages or working conditions of US workers. Once the Labour Department certifies the application, the employer can proceed to the next stage of the Green Card process.

The date on which the Labour Department accepts the labour certification application also generally becomes the worker’s “priority date”, which is effectively their place in the queue for an employment-based immigrant visa. This is particularly important for workers from countries such as India, where demand for Green Cards far exceeds the number available.
How does PERM differ from H-1B visa?

PERM and H-1B visa are different things. H-1B visa is a temporary, non-immigrant work visa that allows US employers to employ foreign professionals in speciality occupations. PERM, in contrast, is part of the process for obtaining permanent residency.
How will action against Cognizant affect Indian workers?

For employees of these IT giants whose Green Card process has not yet reached the PERM filing stage, the immediate consequence is a delay. The suspension means they cannot make fresh PERM filings while the suspension remains in place, meaning affected employees cannot secure a priority date and begin moving through the employer-sponsored Green Card process.

That can be particularly consequential for Indians because they already face a severe backlog. In the US State Department’s September 2026 Visa Bulletin, the employment-based second preference, or EB-2, category for India was listed as “unavailable” for final action, while the EB-3 final-action date was January 1, 2014. The system also imposes limits on the number of employment-based Green Cards available to nationals of any one country.

There can also be an H-1B implication for some workers approaching the normal six-year limit on that visa. US rules allow certain H-1B holders to extend their stay beyond six years where a labour certification was filed sufficiently early. An inability to get the PERM process started could therefore become more serious for employees nearing that deadline. Workers who already have approved petitions and are waiting because a Green Card number is unavailable are in a different position and can, subject to the rules, qualify for H-1B extensions of up to three years at a time.

title: Why a meme landed footballer Mbappé in trouble with China over Mao Zedong

content.value: What’s in a meme? A great deal, as French footballer Kylian Mbappé has lately discovered.

For a jesting remark about a meme featuring the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong, Mbappé has found himself in a whirlwind of controversy. Beneath the surface lie larger questions: why the backlash was so fierce, the place Mao holds in China, and why the Chinese State has reacted to similar instances in the realm of sports.
What is the Mbappé controversy?

When asked to name his favourite Mbappé meme on the French online show The Bridge, the footballer chose one that superimposes his face on Mao’s. He said it features “Some guy… I think he’s a Chinese dictator.”

The clip went viral and drew flak in China. Mbappé apologised on October 27, saying his comment was “ill-judged” and had hurt many people. The same day, Chinese companies Dongpeng (beverages), Mengniu (dairy) and Milkground (cheese) ended their partnerships with him, each saying it opposed words and actions that hurt national sentiment.

Renmin Ruiping, the commentary platform of the People’s Daily, the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) mouthpiece, delivered its own verdict: “Smashing the rice cooker after eating from it will not be tolerated.”

China Media Group (CMG), which oversees the state broadcaster CCTV, also suspended La Liga broadcasts, along with other games and advertisements involving Mbappé on October 26. It said that apologies from La Liga, Real Madrid and Mbappé were a prerequisite for any talks.

La Liga also said that it “deeply regrets” the offence caused to Chinese fans and that the remarks were made in a personal capacity. Its president, Javier Tebas, also wrote to CMG, condemning Mbappé’s conduct. Real Madrid apologised to the Chinese people on October 28.
Why did such a framing of Mao draw criticism?

China has often bristled at remarks it deems a threat to its sovereignty. In the latest case, what adds to the sensitivity is Mao’s complicated but lasting legacy. It was under him that the People’s Republic of China was founded in 1949 as a communist State.

Professor Abanti Bhattacharya of the Department of East Asian Studies, Delhi University, told The Indian Express that in 1981, under reformist leader Deng Xiaoping, the Party acknowledged Mao’s mistakes in policies such as the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. Focused on agricultural and industrial progress and deepening the Party’s presence across all facets of society, respectively, they caused massive upheaval.

Under President Xi Jinping, Bhattacharya argues, that stance has somewhat shifted. “There is a perception, both among sections of the Chinese public and in the West, that Xi Jinping is Mao 2.0, that China is returning to the Mao era. There is also a popular sentiment, including among sections of the younger generation, that China was better off during Mao’s time. Today, you can see young people spending nights near Mao Zedong’s mausoleum. There is a certain emotional attachment to him and to the period he represents,” she said. Elements of Xi’s increasing centralisation of power have also been compared to Mao.

After the liberalisation of the Chinese economy under Deng in 1978, the Mao era lost some of its sheen, said Bhatacharya. Today, however, Mao and his legacy are returning to the picture and the CCP is increasingly sensitive to criticisms.

“Calling Mao a dictator is completely taboo in China. He is not generally viewed in those terms. After the decline of the Soviet Union, there was a period in China where Mao was barely publicly discussed. But now, Xi has revived the connection with history, something which Mao regarded as very important. He is bringing back sentiments of China’s civilisational history and its glorious past, where Mao is seen as the leader who helped China stand up again and reclaim its place,” Bhattacharya said.
The precedents: China and global sports
This is not the first time that Chinese displeasure has set off a cascade of apologies, given China’s increasing weight in the global sports economy.

Take football. During the FIFA World Cup Qatar 2022, the total amount of Chinese sponsorship reached $1.4 billion, making it the top sponsor among all nations, according to CCP tabloid Global Times. Leagues have learnt the price of souring their relationship with China the hard way.

The NBA, perhaps, knows it better than most. In October 2019, Houston Rockets’ then general manager Daryl Morey posted an image on X that read: “Fight for Freedom. Stand with Hong Kong.” The Chinese Special Administrative Region was then witnessing protests against the government.

Subsequently, China’s state broadcaster supended airing NBA matches, and Tencent, the league’s major digital streaming partner in China, followed. The NBA issued a statement calling Morey’s tweet “regrettable”, and Rockets owner Tilman Fertitta publicly distanced the franchise from it. Commissioner Adam Silver later said the loss would run to around $400 million.

Football has its own example. China is the Premier League’s most lucrative overseas broadcast market, with rights sold for $700 million in a three-year deal that ran through 2022. On December 15, 2019, Chinese television pulled an Arsenal and Manchester City match after Mesut Özil criticised China’s treatment of Uyghur Muslims in Xinjiang. Arsenal distanced the club from Özil’s views.

title: Nobel Peace Prize 2026: How Navi Pillay’s work on genocide ‘held states and leaders accountable’

content.value: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded on Friday (October 9) to South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, 85, whose work — from the apartheid regime in her home country to the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Gaza — has helped shape legal precedents on key global issues.

Her Indian Tamil grandparents reached Africa as indentured labourers, and she grew up at a time when racial discrimination was systemically ingrained into the law. Pillay went on to become the first South African to earn a doctorate in law from Harvard University and would later defend compatriot Nelson Mandela, the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, in court during apartheid.
In its official citation, the Norwegian Nobel Committee spoke of her “exceptional courage and integrity”, stating that she led the way “towards a more comprehensive global legal order.”

It is not often that the committee rewards jurists. But the citation stated that through this award, it wanted to “remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice.”
Career of firsts, landmark cases

The committee noted that Pillay “has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.” Early in her career, though, her very presence in institutions marked several firsts — she became the first Black woman to start a law practice in Natal Province, South Africa, in 1967, and the first to serve in the High Court. Mandela nominated her to the court.

She had earlier fought for the rights of anti-apartheid prisoners like him, such as access to lawyers. Pillay recalled later, “When Nelson Mandela was first charged, he refused to plead as he had no trust in an apartheid court. The magistrate responded that it was a white man’s court and that it would remain that way… We were taught that apartheid law even if immoral, could never be questioned.”

Reading about the Nuremberg Trials after World War 2 gave her a framework for understanding how the law could tackle state-sponsored violence and inequality. Nuremberg marked a historic first where “judicial power backed by punishment was exercised by the international community to achieve justice and accountability,” she said.

Pillay was elected as a judge to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda for eight years. The Rwandan genocide of 1994 is considered among the most brutal in modern history, where a period of genocidal killings extended over 100 days and left 800,000 people dead. People were egged on through hate speeches and political propaganda.

The tribunal found a man guilty of genocide, which was the first time an international tribunal entered a judgment for genocide and interpreted it under the Geneva Conventions against war crimes. Crucially, the tribunal also defined the crime of rape in international law and recognised it as a means of perpetrating genocide.

Pillay later said the UN tribunal wanted to “send out a strong message that rape is no longer a trophy of war.” A UN News report noted, “As the Rwandan women sat behind a curtain in a tiny court… and recounted in painful detail the brutal and violent sexual assaults they endured… they had no idea they would make history. And that by doing so, they would give hope to survivors like them.”
The tribunal was also the first to recognise the role of propaganda in aiding genocide, and it held members of the media responsible for intentionally inflammatory broadcasts.
International law today

Today, Pillay is an ad hoc judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in a case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide against the Rohingya Muslims. She also chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory from 2021 to 2025. It stated that “Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank.”

While recognising her work, the Nobel announcement noted that the prize comes amid “existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time”. Despite criticism of bodies like the UN and the ICJ for having little power to stop acts of violence, it said that recent events show international law is an “absolute necessity” for peace and security.

Pillay earlier said that “Justice as integral to the peace process in the aftermath of great conflicts is still a relatively new development. It needs nurturing and greater support from states.” She held out hope for it. In 2023, she said, “I’m 82. Many people asked me: “When are you going to stop?” As long as there are human rights violations and someone is suffering, why wouldn’t you care? We have to continually recite the principles… That’s what keeps me optimistic, that we have a duty.”

She also said, “As Nelson Mandela said when he thanked the world for helping end apartheid: “Thank you, you chose to care”. So that’s my call upon all states: they should care and act collectively to address all these new and emerging challenges that we will be facing.”

title: Why Spain’s snap election could be make-or-break for the progressive left

content.value: Earlier this week, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who leads one of Europe’s few socialist governments today, called for snap elections on November 29.

His decision came after his minority government’s proposed housing reforms failed to pass in Parliament, with several parties joining hands against it. The proposed reforms were introduced after massive protests, triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid from her home of seven decades. She died on Wednesday (October 7).

This is the latest in the government’s failed attempts to push through legislation in Parliament. Sánchez’s call for polls may be an attempt to “turn a political setback into an advantage,” Professor Jose Ismael Crespo Martinez, Director of the Department of Political Science at Spain’s Universidad de Murcia, told The Indian Express.
How exactly will this snap election help? And why is Sánchez’s position as the key progressive-left leader on the continent worth understanding as the country heads to the polls? We explain.
What is a snap election?
In any country, snap elections are polls held before the routinely scheduled end of a parliamentary term, usually when Parliament is dissolved early.

Researchers Semra Sevi and Ruth Dassonneville note that snap elections are called when political leaders “try to capitalise on electoral gains”, assuming that “public opinion is on their side.” A stronger mandate can allow for a smoother path towards enacting policies.
Why has Pedro Sánchez failed to pass major legislation?

Sánchez’s time in power has been characterised by frequently making concessions to regional and left-wing parties. His party, the PSOE or the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party, is formally allied with the left-wing electoral platform Sumar. But it has needed outside support from parties in the Catalonia and Basque regions, with diverging political alignments.

For instance, a proposal to reduce the 40-hour work week to 37.5 hours without docking pay ran afoul of PSOE’s parliamentary ally Junts per Catalunya, a Catalan centre-right party. It also shot down the housing reforms.
Additionally, the conservative People’s Party (PP), which is the largest party in the Lower House (PSOE is the second-largest), controls the Upper House. This poses a significant hurdle to the passage of legislation cleared by the Lower House.
Why is Spain seeing housing protests?

Sánchez’s bid for a snap election is predicated on the issue of affordable housing that has “gripped the country”, said Manjeev Singh Puri, India’s former Ambassador to Brussels and the European Union. His call for a vote is “deeply rooted in the struggle of the Spanish middle-class whites”, Puri told The Indian Express.

Data show that the Spanish economy is doing well. According to the Spanish National Statistics Institute, Spain recorded its unemployment rate at 9.87% in the second quarter of FY26 — the lowest since the 2008 financial crisis. The EU’s fourth-largest economy is forecast to grow by 2.1% in 2026 — almost thrice the rate for the wider euro area — according to Goldman Sachs Research.

So why is there anger against rising rent and evictions? That is because while GDP growth and unemployment measures “are accurate data citations,” they are still “macroeconomic in nature,” Martinez said. “Much of this growth also came from the EU NextGeneration funds (a post-pandemic programme for EU nations), loose control over the deficit and Spain’s rising public debt,” he added.

Through the EU’s funding program, the €102 billion package for Spain reached the end of its core targets on August 31 this year. As a result, public capital expenditure is likely to sharply decline going forward.

With inflation reaching 5%, there is a widespread “sense of economic unease” about the future, Martinez said. Public figures close to the PM have also come under fire over corruption cases and misappropriation of public sector contracts. In that regard, the timing of a snap election is favourable since these perceptions could have complicated things for Sánchez over time, he added.
Where does Sánchez’s foreign policy stand in Europe?

At a time when much of Europe has embraced a restrictionist stance on the issue of border control, Sánchez has strongly championed pro-immigration policies, citing labour shortages and a negative population growth rate, said Martinez. The issue has also been used “as a cultural battleground to polarise opinion against the Vox party”. The rising far-right party could be among the biggest gainers of the snap polls.

Puri said the rise of parties like Vox across Europe stems from the idea of nativism, essentially “a clawback from globalisation, which is taking a toll on the way politics has generally been conducted here over the past 50 years”. This, however, ignores “The objective reality that a country with negative population growth rates could not remain viable without immigrants.”

For Sánchez, positioning himself as a global progressive voice, often the lone one among major European leaders, has also allowed him to project power and leadership through domestic political deadlocks. This has included criticism of US President Donald Trump and of Israel.
What are Sánchez’s prospects now?
This is not the first time Sánchez has called — and survived — a snap election. The 2023 snap elections saw him retain his post despite PSOE not emerging as the largest party.

But that could change, and this is where Vox enters the equation. In the 2023 general election, Vox won 12.4% of the vote. Current polling puts its support at around 18%. The significance of that rise is that the party is increasingly occupying the political space created by dissatisfaction with both the mainstream right and the fragmented left. The People’s Party and Vox could come together to form a right-wing government after the polls.

Sánchez’s hope is to win enough seats to recover some legislative room, even if PSOE is still not the largest party. For Europe, his performance in November will also be a test of whether a progressive government can translate upward economic movement into political legitimacy, when its survival depends on smaller parties unaligned with the larger political project.

title: Meet Trump aide Natalie Harp, the ‘human printer’ everyone is suddenly talking about

content.value: There has recently been an unusual amount of attention on Natalie Harp, a relatively little-known but highly trusted aide to US President Donald Trump. Harp has been close to Trump for years, frequently travelling with him and helping manage the information he sees and the posts he puts out. So why has she suddenly become a subject of political controversy?
The answer lies in a remark by Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff — and in the furious response it provoked from the Trump administration.
Who is Natalie Harp?

Harp, 35, grew up in California and graduated from Point Loma Nazarene University, a Christian liberal arts college in San Diego, in 2012. She then earned an MBA from Liberty University, an evangelical university in Virginia, in 2015.

She first came into national prominence because of her experience with cancer. In 2019, Harp wrote a LinkedIn post titled “I’m Living Proof – the Party of Healthcare is Trump’s”, describing her battle with bone cancer and crediting Trump’s 2018 Right to Try law with helping her new treatments.

The Right to Try law allows terminally ill patients to access experimental treatments that have passed only Phase 1 safety testing, without needing the FDA’s approval. She said Democrats focused more on living with pain and ‘dying with dignity’ than cure. “According to the Democrats, healthcare is a right. But a right to what — all of the above? No, thank you. Donald Trump would change a letter of that. Healthcare is a fight,” she said in her post.

This attracted the attention of Fox News, which invited Harp to discuss her experience. Trump subsequently praised her publicly. She was then invited to speak at the 2020 Republican National Convention, where she told Trump: “I wouldn’t be alive today if it wasn’t for you.” A later Washington Post report questioned whether the treatment she received could actually be attributed to the Right to Try law, with experts disputing the timeline.
How did she get so close to Trump?

After her appearance at the Republican convention, Harp moved deeper into Trump’s political orbit. She and her mother left California for Florida, close to Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate. In 2020, she joined One America News Network, where she worked as a presenter and promoted Trump’s claims that the 2020 election had been stolen. She left OANN in 2022 and began working directly for Trump.

During Trump’s campaign to return to the White House, she became known among colleagues as the “human printer”. According to The New York Times, she followed Trump with a portable printer and battery pack, supplying him with printed news and information because he prefers reading things on paper.

Today, Harp is officially a special assistant to the president and executive assistant to the president, with an annual salary of $150,000, according to The Guardian. She is frequently at Trump’s side and is involved in his communications, including showing him proposed Truth Social posts and publishing material on his account.
Why is she in the headlines now?

Her proximity was highlighted last month when Trump secretly switched aircraft in Turkey because of an alleged Iranian assassination threat. Harp was among the small group of aides who accompanied him on the military plane, while other staff and journalists remained on the plane supposedly at risk.

The issue blew up after comments by Ossoff. At a campaign speech recently, the Georgia senator accused Trump of preferring to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie” rather than doing his job as President.

The Trump administration reacted furiously. Trump attacked CNN reporter Kristen Holmes when she asked him about Ossoff’s comments, while the White House’s “Rapid Response” account accused Holmes of asking a “disgusting and inhumane” question.

Political analysts believe that Ossoff’s rather provocative comments were meant to get him limelight and increase his profile. The Trump administration’s response seems to have had that exact effect, with more limelight on both Harp and Ossoff.

title: How did the far-right AfD move from Germany’s fringes to becoming a mainstream power?

content.value: The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (Alternative for Germany or AfD) came within reach of power at the state level for the first time since World War II on Sunday (September 6), recording its strongest-ever electoral performance in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. It won 43.8% of the vote and 39 of 83 seats, just three short of an outright majority.

The result was also a severe blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which had governed Saxony-Anhalt since 2002 but won just 17.2% of the vote. Whether the AfD can form a government, however, remains unclear, as other major parties have so far refused to work with it.
The victory marks the latest milestone in the AfD’s transformation from a fringe Eurosceptic party to one of Germany’s largest political forces.
Who are the AfD and how did they become a major political force?

The AfD, previously the Electoral Alternative 2013, was founded in 2013 by Bernd Lucke, Alexander Gauland, Frauke Petry and Konrad Adam, a Eurosceptic band of economists opposed to the then-German government’s decision to bail out poorer European countries during the Eurocrisis.

The party took a hard-right pivot in the following years. As a record 1.3 million refugees, mainly from Syria, Iraq and Afghanistan, sought asylum in Europe in 2015, the AfD rode a wave of anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim sentiment to make electoral gains regionally. By 2017, it had entered the Bundestag, winning 94 of 709 seats and finishing third.

The AfD has doubled down on these views since. It advocates “remigration”, a controversial policy that implies the forced deportation of immigrants and their European-born descendants not deemed “ethnically” European by ethnonationalists. It is also deeply Eurosceptic, has campaigned for a “Dexit” from the European Union, and opposes Germany’s climate policies.

Members of the party have also sought to distort the significance of the Holocaust. Björn Höcke, the AfD leader in Thuringia, called the Holocaust memorial in Berlin a “monument of shame” in German history in 2017.

The party has found particularly fertile ground in the former communist east. Post-communist eastern regions have long lagged behind western Germany in incomes, employment and productivity, while voters have also expressed resentment at a lack of political representation and the perceived failure of mainstream parties to address economic stagnation, inflation and migration.

But the grievances behind the AfD’s rise have broadened beyond immigration. Gurjit Singh, who served as India’s Ambassador to Germany, points to economic anxiety, deteriorating infrastructure and pressure on the welfare state as factors behind the growing protest vote.

“The basic life of a German is no more as good as it used to be,” Singh told The Indian Express, citing frustrations over public infrastructure and the strain on the welfare system. He said that while immigration had been an initial source of discontent, social anxiety, poor economic performance and deterioration of infrastructure were now important drivers of AfD support.
In September 2024, the AfD became the first far-right party since World War II to win a German state election, taking 32.8% of the vote in Thuringia.
So why is this significant?

Sunday’s victory goes considerably further than the AfD’s previous electoral successes. In Saxony-Anhalt, the party more than doubled its vote share from 20.8% in 2021 and came close to securing enough seats to govern without a coalition partner. Voter turnout was also unusually high at 77.8%.

The result also shows how far the AfD has grown at the national level: it is already the largest Opposition party in the Bundestag, with recent national polling putting it at around 28%, ahead of the parties in the governing coalition.
But Saxony-Anhalt is also part of a longer pattern of AfD success in eastern Germany. The party has drawn on long-standing economic and political discontent in the region.

The east-west divide has long shaped the party’s rise. Establishment parties such as the CDU and SPD, which are rooted in western Germany, have struggled to establish themselves as firmly in the post-communist east. The region has also lagged behind western Germany in economic development, while the lack of eastern representation in successive governments since reunification has fuelled a sense of political alienation.

Unlike voters in the west and south, eastern voters have also tended to switch political allegiances more frequently between elections, creating greater space for newer parties such as the AfD. The divide has also been visible in attitudes towards Russia and the war in Ukraine, with voters in the east generally more sceptical of sanctions on Moscow and military support for Kyiv than those in western Germany.

Singh said the factors driving AfD support were not necessarily the same in every state. “I wouldn’t put immigration necessarily at number one in every state that the AfD is popular because in some states … there are not so many immigrants but other issues are more important,” he said.
What is Germany’s firewall? Can AfD govern?
Given Germany’s Nazi past, mainstream political parties have maintained a “firewall”, a political commitment not to cooperate with far-right parties such as the AfD.

This has so far kept the AfD out of government even when it has emerged as the single-largest party. After it won 32.8% of the vote in Thuringia in 2024, other parties combined to prevent it from taking power.

But the firewall has come under increasing strain. In January 2025, Merz relied on AfD support to pass a non-binding parliamentary motion calling for tougher immigration rules, triggering accusations that he had broken a long-standing political taboo.

The Saxony-Anhalt result shows how complicated the political arithmetic has now become: The AfD needed 42 seats for a majority, and won 39. The CDU has 15 seats, while the Social Democrats, Greens and Left each have eight, and the leftist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance has five. With the other major parties continuing to rule out cooperation with the AfD, forming a stable alternative government could prove difficult.

The question, then, is whether the firewall can hold as the AfD continues to gain support. Singh argued that its continued rise could eventually force other parties to reconsider how they deal with it. “If AfD is going to keep getting popular, other parties need to learn to work with it rather than ignore it,” he said, suggesting that a major party such as the CDU could eventually seek to engage the AfD on a coalition agenda.

title: Saudi-Houthi conflict and the Mecca pact: What Pakistan, Turkey can and cannot do

content.value: Saudi Arabia said it faced fresh missile and drone attacks on Monday (October 12), even as the Riyadh airport remained shut two days after a missile strike by the Houthis, the Iran-backed rebel faction in Yemen.

Operationally distinct from the US-Iran war, the Yemen theatre has seen a Houthi takeover of key positions near the Bab-el-Mandeb chokepoint in September, a counteroffensive by Yemeni anti-Houthi forces since early October (backed by Saudi air support), and recurring strikes across Saudi Arabia and Yemen ever since.

Months earlier, Saudi Arabia had signed a trilateral defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan, called the Mecca pact. This pact partners held an ‘emergency meeting’ earlier in October and “decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of collective defense commitments”.

However, two days later, as the New York Times reported the participation of Pakistani jets in Saudi air support operations in Yemen, Pakistan’s Information & Broadcasting Ministry issued a swift denial, calling the NYT report ‘fake and fabricated’.

By October 8, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also re-characterised Turkey’s position, asserting that the pact’s defensive nature means that Ankara will not send troops to Saudi Arabia for attacking another country. This further meant that Turkish assistance to Riyadh remains restricted to bilateral technical and defensive support.
These developments do not signal a ‘failure’ of the Mecca pact but rather reinforce how each member state is positioned vis-à-vis each other.

To unpack Pakistan’s and Turkey’s postures towards Riyadh’s needs in Yemen, it is essential to distinguish the September 2025 Saudi-Pakistan Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) from the 2026 Mecca Defence Alliance.
Pakistan and the SMDA
Pakistan’s public rebuke of any attempt at showing its direct intervention in Yemen follows a historic trend.

While Pakistan’s operational support for Riyadh in its southern theatre has been well known since the 1960s, Pakistan’s public positioning has consistently attempted to show balance and neutrality. For instance, it is well documented that Pakistani fighter pilots flew the Royal Saudi Air Force’s English Electric Lightning jets to bomb South Yemeni forces in Al Wadiah in 1969. However, the Pakistani military regime under Yahya Khan firmly denied such action then.

Nearly 50 years later, as the Pakistan military sent over 1000 personnel to Saudi Arabia during Riyadh’s active coalition operations in Yemen in 2018 (and supplementing an existing 1500+ Pakistani troop contingent already present in the Kingdom), Pakistan’s official position remained tied to its 2015 Parliamentary consensus against an intervention in Yemen. In part, this historic duality in Pakistan’s posture is tied to two characteristics.

First is Pakistan’s sensitivities vis-à-vis its western neighbour Iran, who remains the principal state backer of the Houthis and shares a friction-ridden border with Pakistan. Regardless of Pakistan’s overt neutral positioning, its practical pro-Saudi tilt has consistently led Tehran to warn against fresh escalation in Yemen (as Tehran did afresh after the Mecca pact’s ‘activation’).

This time, Iran’s adverse view of Pakistan is enhanced by its institutional distrust of Pakistani good faith in the mediation channel with the United States. Iranian MP Mohsen Zanganeh’s jibe on October 10 that even the Pakistan PM’s tweets are written by Steve Witkoff is a case in point.

This Iran-centric concern, combined with Pakistan’s desire to project itself as a state interested in preserving ‘Muslim’ interests at large, has historically necessitated a position that covers for its operations to preserve Saudi security.
Second, is Pakistan’s deference to Saudi leadership of the Islamic world, which is combined with a projection of Islamabad’s own invaluable utility for Riyadh to sustain this leadership.

Islamabad proves the former often, such as when it kept away from a Malaysia-based attempt at developing a non-Saudi based alternative for global Muslim leadership in 2019. The latter has been proved operationally, through the Pakistan military’s special relationship with Riyadh.

Compared with Pakistan’s public-facing political institutions, the Pakistan Army has shown strong sensitivities to Saudi needs and concerns. Riyadh itself routes most of its concerns through the Pakistani military and has been a recurring destination for past Pakistan Army Chiefs for standalone visits, sometimes without the civilian leadership present. This is until COAS/CDF Asim Munir broke that pattern by widening his international engagement profile since June 2025.

Hence, when the Pakistani Parliament desisted from sending troops to Saudi Arabia in 2015, it was the Pakistan Army under COAS Qamar Bajwa which undercut the legislature through limited troop deployment to the Kingdom (but justified it to Parliament later by downplaying their role).

In such deployments, the following operational logic has largely held true — protective operations requiring troop presence are officially restricted to Saudi soil, while force multiplication for Saudi offensive/defensive operations are unofficially ensured for operations not on Saudi soil (such as Yemen or Bahrain).
Turkey and the Mecca Pact

By 2025, it is this historic pattern of Saudi-Pakistan engagement which was institutionalised in the SMDA. The Mecca pact only broadens the defence cooperation architecture of the SMDA to include an additional state for long term joint capacity building, Turkey.

The logic of combining Turkish defence industrial depth, Saudi financing, and Pakistani operational experience is a template that has been firming up since 2023, given Ankara’s need to expand its regional military footprint, Riyadh’s recognition of the need to build an indigenous military industrial complex, and Islamabad’s need to mitigate its abject economic crises by leveraging its ability to take geopolitical risks.
This logic was decisively driven home by 2026, given the fallout of American, Israeli, and Iranian military operations on Arab states that have traditionally rented out security to external powers.

Hence, the long-term technical goals of the Mecca pact are not meant to subsume or gloss over specific political alignments or differences between each partner state. Within the MDA, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan as SMDA partners have a special political alignment that allows Pakistan to assist Saudi Arabia along a well-established historic template. This template’s need is now further enhanced due to the normalisation of Houthi strikes against critical infrastructure in the Saudi mainland.

However, Turkey’s own regional outlook remains a poor fit in the Saudi-Pakistan template. In Yemen itself, Turkey’s longstanding anti-Houthi position has hardly ever meant neat alignment with Saudi Arabia. Rather, Ankara under Erdogan has viewed Yemen as a theatre of geopolitical competition with Riyadh. While Turkey has rhetorically backed the Saudi-led anti-Houthi coalition since 2015, it has refrained from participating with any troops or major combat platforms, restricting support to occasional logistical/intelligence cooperation.
This is another template that the Mecca pact has evidently not disturbed, despite increased Turkish strategic engagement with Saudi Arabia.

Historically, Ankara’s focus has also remained on expanding its own influence in Yemen through the Muslim Brotherhood-affiliated Yemeni Congregation for Reform (Al-Islah), which has a dual presence in both Istanbul and Sanaa.

More broadly, and especially after Turkey’s own geopolitical successes in Syria since December 2024, Ankara’s involvement in the Mecca pact allows it to share in Riyadh’s claim to Islamic leadership, rather than to take operational risks to help preserve it (as Pakistan does). This is the definitive characteristic of the Mecca Defence Alliance.

title: Israel elections: Why only coalitions have ruled so far, could this time be different

content.value: About 7.3 million eligible Israeli voters are expected to vote on Tuesday (October 27) to elect the 26th Israeli Knesset (parliament). The 26th general parliamentary election, since the founding of the State of Israel in 1948, is taking place exactly on its legally mandated, statutory date, as the Knesset has completed its full term this time.

As many as 38 registered parties are competing for seats in the 120-member legislature, though only around 11 are projected to clear the strict 3.25% electoral threshold required for parliamentary representation.

This election assumes immense significance because it is the first Israeli parliament since 1988 to complete a full four-year mandate without early dissolution. The vote follows years of intense societal turmoil, including contentious judicial reform debates, the traumatic security crisis following October 7, and protracted wartime conditions. Beyond choosing a prime minister, this election is expected to be a critical national referendum on Israel’s governance, domestic civil cohesion, state security architecture, and long-term democratic character.
Who are the key contenders in the 2026 Israel elections?

Being a democracy with a proportional representation system of elections, Israel has several lists and parties. The difference between parties and lists is that a party is an institution that seeks power within the established rules of elections, whereas a list is precisely what it says it is: a list of candidates prepared for the elections sponsored by a party or by a group of parties.

Any registered party or list may contest elections. Under Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset, the Central Elections Committee (CEC), or the Supreme Court may disqualify a political party list or an individual candidate if their platform or actions express denial of the existence of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, indulge in racism, or support armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organisation against Israel.
Once the registrar determines that the party’s platform and behaviour are consistent with democracy and that it keeps proper records of its accounts, the party is approved to contest elections.
The key electoral lists in this election are as follows:
Government coalition & right-wing blocs
Likud: Led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, running on a consolidated national-conservative list that merged with Gideon Sa’ar’s New Hope.
Otzma Yehudit: A far-right party list headed by Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Religious Zionist Party – Zehut: A joint list led by Bezalel Smotrich (Religious Zionism) and Moshe Feiglin (Zehut).
Shas: Ultra-Orthodox Sephardic party list led by Aryeh Deri.
United Torah Judaism (UTJ): Ultra-Orthodox Ashkenazi joint list between Degel HaTorah and Agudat Yisrael, led by Ya’akov Asher.
Amcha Yisrael: A new right-wing list formed by former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) general Ofer Winter and activist Yoseph Haddad.
Noam: A far-right, religiously conservative list headed by Avi Maoz.
Opposition and centre-left blocs
Together (Beyachad): A centre-right and centre joint list combining Naftali Bennett’s new movement with Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid party.
Yashar!: A broad centrist list led by former IDF Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot and former Shin Bet chief Yoram Cohen.
The Democrats (HaDemokratim): A merger between the Labor Party and Meretz, headed by Yair Golan.
Yisrael Beitenu (“Israel [is] Our Home”): A secular right-wing party list led by Avigdor Liberman.
Blue and White (Kahol Lavan): A centrist list headed by Benny Gantz.
The Reservists & The Economic Party: A joint list formed by Yoaz Hendel (The Reservists) and economist Yaron Zelekha (New Economic Party).
Arab sector parties
The Joint List: A united electoral list bringing together the Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad factions, headed by Yousef Jabareen and Ahmad Tibi.
United Arab List (Ra’am): An Islamist Arab-Israeli party list headed by Mansour Abbas.
Parliamentary regime
Israel is a parliamentary democracy with three main branches of power: the legislative, executive, and judiciary.
The country has a unicameral (single-house) parliament, composed of 120 members. Members of the Knesset (MKs) are elected nationally for four-year terms.

The prime minister holds the executive power. The government depends directly on the confidence of the Knesset and must maintain a working majority (at least 61 seats) to govern. Headed by the Supreme Court, the judiciary acts independently to interpret basic laws and review legislation. National elections in Israel are administered and overseen by the CEC.
Electoral threshold

In Israel’s party-list proportional representation system, the electoral threshold is the minimum percentage of the total nationwide vote a political party must receive to enter parliament. The threshold is currently set at 3.25% — a standard established by Knesset legislation in 2014. Crossing this hurdle grants a party a baseline of at least 4 seats out of the 120 total Knesset seats. If a party fails to reach the 3.25% mark, all votes cast for its slate are discarded, producing “wasted votes” that are reallocated among the parties that succeeded.

The main purpose of the threshold is to balance representation with political stability by preventing extreme parliamentary fragmentation and keeping micro-parties out. Historically, the threshold started at just 1% in 1951 before being gradually raised to 1.5% (1992), 2% (2003), and finally 3.25% (2014), notes Prof. Ofer Kenig, a researcher at the Israeli Democracy Institute.

This high barrier incentivises smaller ideological factions or niche parties to merge into joint electoral slates before election day, ensuring they pass the threshold together. As a result, the 3.25% rule plays a decisive role in shaping coalition arithmetic and determining which political bloc can form a government, he adds.
How does government formation work in Israel?

Since no single political party in Israel’s history has ever won a 61-seat majority on its own, every Israeli government has been a coalition. In such a situation, the process of forming a government, with both old and new allies, takes time.

Following election day, the CEC certifies the final count and seat distribution. The President holds discussions with representatives of party lists that cleared the electoral threshold regarding the possible PM candidates. After discussions with party lists, the President grants the mandate to form a government to the party candidate who is most likely to ensure a 61-seat majority.

The President grants 28 days to the chosen candidate to form a coalition. A single 14-day extension, if extra time is required, can be given to the candidate. If one candidate fails to get the required support, the President can either transfer the mandate to a second candidate for a 28-day attempt.

Once coalition agreements are finalised, the prime minister-designate presents the new government, its policy guidelines, and cabinet ministers to the Knesset for a formal vote of confidence. If approved by at least 61 votes, the ministers take their oaths of office.

title: How Cornell rape case throws a harsh spotlight on fraternities — and their pattern of violence

content.value: A former student of Cornell University in the US filed a civil lawsuit in the New York State Supreme Court on September 16, alleging that she was raped by seven members of a university “fraternity” house in 2024. The lawsuit names, among others, seven students of Cornell who belonged to one of the chapters of the national “Chi Phi” fraternity. They are now being referred to as the “Cornell 7”.

The case has sparked anger in campuses across the country, especially over how Cornell handled it back in 2024. New York Governor Kathy Hochul, who said on Friday that the survivor was “failed” at “every turn”, appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead the case.

The incident also shone a harsh light on a ubiquitous aspect of college life in the US — fraternities, which are male student organisations built around shared social, academic or professional interests. Many have voiced anger over the autonomy and freedoms enjoyed by fraternities (also called frats) across the country, relative to their status as a student-led group.

In fact, the mayor of Ithaca, where Cornell is situated, has called for a moratorium on fraternity life (also called Greek life because frats are named after Greek letters), with the Chi Phi fraternity’s Cornell chapter shut down pending investigation.
Around a million students are estimated to be currently part of such organisations across the US, according to Fraternity Advisor, a website that documents US college fraternities.

Why are fraternities, or for that matter sororities (their female equivalent), so common in the US? Why do they attract so many students? Why are they always named after Greek letters (such as Chi Phi)? And, what exactly do they do? Here’s a primer on their evolution and significance.
How college fraternities evolved
Until the late 1700s, student-led groups in the US were dominated by literary societies.

Nicholas L Syrett, author of the book A History of White College Fraternities, told The Indian Express: “Almost everyone who wanted to be in one (literary society) was able to join.” Indeed, at some schools “students were basically required to join one of two societies. In that sense, they weren’t exclusive at all”.
In 1776, however, a fraternity called Phi Beta Kappa at the College of William and Mary in Virginia came up as an alternative.

Fraternities, unlike literary societies, were a solution for engaging in discussion and were, from the very beginning, “by definition exclusive,” said Syrett, who is Gender Studies Chair at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

As fraternities expanded into the 19th century, they solidified to serve a specific social function. “One of the reasons was also to separate out the wealthier or secular students from the poorer students studying for the ministry”, said Syrett.

Some universities, like Harvard, “banned traditional fraternities” (1850s) or limited the presence of “Greek life” on campus. “In some instances, these groups re-emerged anyway,” and groups like the finals clubs that Harvard houses “are not all that different from fraternities in that they are generally more open to wealthier students,” according to Syrett.
