Additionally, a presidential pardon does not supersede state-level prosecutions. States such as Louisiana, Alabama and Florida are reportedly in the midst of investigating Fauci for his Covid conduct.
Legal and political precedent

Simply put, no one can be legally tried (or convicted) for invoking the Fifth Amendment. The US Constitution prevents silence from being treated as an admission of guilt. This makes the case of Fauci a potential landmark moment in the making.

Republican figures like Senator Josh Hawley argue that the refusal to answer non-incriminating questions during the original hearing were a sign of proof that his plea was a pre-meditated attempt to evade oversight. This allows a pardoned official to defy Congress which, in turn, cripples legislative power.

Democrats such as Senator Maggie Hassan and Richard Blumenthal, conversely, warn that punishing the exercising of a constitutional right is a far graver precedent to set. The prosecution of Fauci would only serve to dissuade future witnesses from appearing before committees — regardless of their innocence or guilt.

Legal scholars, however, can view this as a test case. Mark Osler, a former state and federal prosecutor, noted the precedent this hearing might set and anticipates that future presidents may issue similar pardons to administrators. Should courts rule that pardoned individuals cannot “plead the Fifth”, it shall reshape how congressional investigations conduct business in the future.

Ultimately, the resolution of Dr Fauci’s case will not only determine his personal legal fate but could fundamentally redefine the boundaries between executive pardons, congressional subpoenas, and the Fifth Amendment.

title: Palestinian elections postponed again: What it means, what happened last time

content.value: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday (October 10) postponed elections to the Palestinian Legislative Council (PLC) slated for November this year to September 2027, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.

In an official decree, Abbas cited worsening conditions within the Palestinian territories and announced September 11, 2027, as the date for legislative elections. The 90-year-old Abbas, who has served as President since 2005, said in the decree that presidential elections are scheduled for the same day.

The Palestinian territories last witnessed national elections in 2005-06, although the Palestinian Authority (PA) — the government body that exercises partial control over the Palestinian enclaves in the Israel-occupied West Bank — conducted municipal elections in April ​in the West Bank and in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, the only city in the Gaza Strip to participate.

We explain what the presidential decree said, what it means for the political scenario in the Palestinian territories, and what happened the last time elections were conducted more than two decades ago.
Why are Palestinian elections being postponed?

In his decree, Abbas cited “obstacles posed by Israeli measures” to holding elections ⁠in ​November and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for “free, fair and inclusive elections”. It called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to participate ​in the ​polls.

Abbas’s decree said that Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence, and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with ⁠Israel’s continued withholding of ⁠Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections on the previous date.

It also pointed to “exceptional security and humanitarian conditions” in Gaza, ​the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and ‌police. According to the decree, Israeli restrictions on ​access for ​election ​commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem had also complicated preparations.

Earlier on Friday, Reuters had reported that a letter dated October 8 (Thursday) from Palestinian Vice President Hussein Al-Sheikh to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot had indicated that a delay in holding elections was likely.

“The assessment concluded that the anticipated political, security and economic conditions, on which the scheduling of the legislative elections for 28 November 2026 was based, have not materialized,” said the letter. “Holding them under the current circumstances faces fundamental obstacles affecting their ​inclusiveness, freedom of participation and the integrity of the electoral process.”
What does the delay mean for Palestinian politics?

The ​decision to postpone the November polls came after a resolution ⁠by the Palestine Liberation Organisation’s (PLO) executive committee and consultations with different Palestinian factions and political forces. The PLO, currently represented by the PA, is internationally recognised as the official representative of the Palestinian people in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The postponement means that incumbent Palestinian leaders will remain entrenched in power for over two decades. The PA, which has faced allegations of corruption and criticism over security cooperation with Israel over the years, has grown increasingly unpopular among ordinary Palestinians during Abbas’s tenure.

The PA, which is controlled by Abbas’s party Fatah, receives diplomatic and financial support from global partners including the US, the European Union (EU), and several Arab states. In recent years, Abbas has attempted to convince the US and the EU that he can reform the Palestinian political system. The delay in conducting elections means that Abbas’s own credibility continues to erode especially among the PA’s donors.

Mustafa Barghouti, who leads Fatah’s rival party Palestinian National Initiative, told Al Jazeera that it was “totally unacceptable” that Palestinians have been denied elections for two decades and Abbas’s decision had caused great disappointment among the Palestinian people.

“At this moment, everything is concentrated in the hands of the executive authority… There is no independent judiciary, no parliament, that can issue laws and legislations,” Barghouti, who finished second to Abbas in the 2005 presidential elections, said.
What happened in the 2005-06 Palestinian elections?

Abbas was elected as President in January 2005 after his predecessor, Yasser Arafat, died in November 2004. Although his tenure expired in 2009, Abbas has continued to rule by executive fiat since then.

Over two decades, he has consolidated power at the PA’s helm by pushing out political rivals and allegedly interfering with the judiciary. The decision of postponement, according to geopolitical analysts, was partly out of fears among senior officials that elections would confirm the PA’s eroding legitimacy.

Legislative elections were last held in January 2006, when Change and Reform — the name used by the Palestinian militant group Hamas as its political front — won a majority (74) in the 132-seat PLC, defeating Abbas’s incumbent Fatah. This was only the second time elections were held to the Council, the first being 1996. The PLC’s members had been elected by Palestinian residents across the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

But Hamas’s victory meant that while it dominated the PLC, the PA was still controlled by Abbas. What followed was a period of uneasy power-sharing for the next 17 months, as a unity government faced external pressures in the form of sanctions imposed by the US, the EU, Israel, and other Western countries. Hamas, which has been designated as a terrorist organisation by several countries, also refused to accept demands such as giving up violence.

In June 2007, a brief civil war broke out in the Gaza Strip between Hamas and Fatah, which ended with Hamas ousting Abbas’s loyalists and seizing control of Gaza. This split also led to the PLC’s activities being suspended — it has remained so since then.

title: Can Trump rename Lake Ontario as Lake America?

content.value: US President Donald Trump on Thursday (August 27) signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, situated on the US-Canada border, as “Lake America”. The order said the lake was a “tremendous asset to the United States and part of our Nation’s heritage.”
In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote in a post on X that the name Ontario (also the name of a Canadian province) comes from the indigenous Wendat people.

“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he wrote.
What’s behind Trump’s order, and can countries unilaterally change the names of water bodies? In Trump’s case, there is precedent for the move, which also involved a neighbouring nation.
What is Lake Ontario, and why is Trump renaming it?

Lake Ontario is part of the Great Lakes system, along with Lake Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie, spanning the US-Canada border. According to the US National Ocean and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the lakes system holds about 90% of the freshwater in the US and approximately 20% of the world’s freshwater supply. Forty million people across the two countries depend on it for clean drinking water.

In his executive order, Trump cited a range of reasons for the decision — including the US’s investments in the lake to keep it open for free shipping, Canada spending comparatively less on it, and the lake’s history as an “asset to American exploration, settlement, commerce, and defense.”

But more pressingly, it comes amid heightened trade tensions between the countries. Trade talks collapsed last week and led to the US imposing tariffs on Canada, with Carney promising to match them “dollar for dollar” against American imports. The US is Canada’s largest trading partner, while Canada is the US’s second-largest trading partner.
So how will Lake Ontario be addressed now?

The name change will apply to how the US officially refers to the lake, but it will not affect how Canada or the rest of the world choose to call it. No single global organisation is tasked with ensuring uniformity among names of water bodies, and the decision to use a certain name is often based on historical precedent.
In a social media post, Trump stated that the US Geological Survey was officially changing the name to have it reflect in all official USGS electronic documents.
This is not the first time that disagreements over trade and other issues have prompted Trump to use nomenclature as a tool.

In January 2025, the day Trump took office in his second term, he signed a slew of executive orders. These included one on renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, amid tensions with Mexico over immigration and tariffs. According to Reuters, it took about two weeks for the US government to update the official federal nomenclature to reflect those changes. The change was also reflected on Google Maps.
Google Maps is now reflecting the changed name for Lake Ontario too.

According to Google, the names seen on Maps are based on information such as a user’s country location and phone operating system (e.g., iOS and Android). Users in Mexico saw “Gulf of Mexico” on Maps while those in the US saw “Gulf of America”. For other users, both names are visible. For example, in the present case, users in India can see ‘Lake Ontario (Lake America)’. This is seen in some other features with disputed names, too, like the Persian Gulf, which is followed by “Arabian Gulf” in brackets on Google Maps.

title: Can Eisenkot unseat Netanyahu: Path ahead, and one major roadblock

content.value: Gadi Eisenkot, Israel’s former military chief, has been given a chance to form a new government, after he was recommended for the task by parties that won 67 seats in the 120-seat parliament.
But completing that mission and replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may well be the toughest assignment of Eisenkot’s career so far.

The ideologically and ethnically diverse factions that recommended him for prime minister include left-wing, right-wing, centrist and predominantly Arab parties. Most would have to break seemingly ironclad campaign promises to unite behind Eisenkot, no matter how he arranges them into a governing coalition.
But the pressure is on him and his allies to do just that because the alternatives, in their view, are far worse.

A failure to form a government could send Israel to another round of elections. It would leave Netanyahu in his job as prime minister in the meantime, with all of the advantages of incumbency. And the opposition would be unlikely to perform as well as it did in October, when thousands of expatriate Israelis flew home to vote.

A unity government in which Eisenkot and Netanyahu share power, such as by taking turns as premier, seemed far-fetched before Election Day and seems unthinkable now. Some of Eisenkot’s campaign promises left wiggle room, but he was adamant in saying that Netanyahu, as the person with ultimate responsibility for defending the country on Oct. 7, 2023, when it suffered its worst attack in history, was unfit to continue in government.
But what kind of government can Eisenkot form?

He starts with 48 members of parliament, thanks to his own center-right Yashar party (21), Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s centrist Together party (12), Yair Golan and the left-wing Democrats party (8), and Avigdor Liberman’s right-wing but secular Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) party (7).
That is more than Netanyahu’s coalition can count on: After an ultra-Orthodox party, United Torah Judaism, refused to recommend him for prime minister, Netanyahu’s coalition has only 46 seats.

To form a bigger coalition, let alone a majority in parliament, Eisenkot’s options include partnering with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which together have 13 seats, or the Arab parties, which won a record 19 seats. Either route is deeply problematic, according to opposition lawmakers, operatives and advisers, most of whom insisted on anonymity to discuss coalition talks.
Here is a look at Eisenkot’s possible path forward, and at one major roadblock standing in his way.
First, Take Control of Parliament

Until a new government is formed, Netanyahu remains a caretaker prime minister. But parliament is another story. Lawmakers will be sworn in on Tuesday, and Eisenkot is working to arrange for the election of a new speaker to replace Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu loyalist.

If he is successful, that could put Eisenkot’s allies in charge of key legislative committees. And it could allow his anti-Netanyahu bloc to begin enacting legislation — fulfilling key campaign promises and demonstrating Eisenkot’s ability to get things done.

The lowest-hanging fruit, insiders say, would be to repeal laws passed by Netanyahu’s coalition, such as controversial judicial changes allowing more political control over the appointment of judges and curbing the attorney general’s powers.

Equally important would be to deliver on a core campaign promise by all the opposition leaders to establish a national commission of inquiry to investigate the security failures that preceded the Oct. 7 attack.
Liberman Rules Out the Arab Parties
Eisenkot this past week began speaking of the need to form a “national emergency government” — an important rhetorical shift.
“If it’s an emergency, you do things you wouldn’t do otherwise,” said Nimrod Novik, a senior fellow of the Israel Policy Forum who was an adviser to former Prime Minister Shimon Peres.
The Arab parties’ 19 seats would give Eisenkot a solid majority, but bringing them into a government could cost him other allies.

For now, the question is moot: The Joint List, an amalgam of three smaller Arab parties that together won 11 seats, has ruled out joining a government, though it could provide support from the outside and enable a minority government to function. The United Arab List, or Raam, which won eight seats, has not. But Eisenkot has insisted that any party joining his government must declare Hamas a terrorist organization.
Raam’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has refused to do so, though he condemns all terrorist acts. But he did say Thursday that Hamas and all other Palestinian factions should be disarmed.

Even if Abbas were to satisfy Eisenkot, however, Liberman, the Yisrael Beiteinu leader, has repeatedly ruled out a government that includes Arab parties or even relies on their support from the outside.
That leaves relying on the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties.
A Deal With the Ultra-Orthodox?

This, too, is fraught with peril. The most important issue for the Haredim is to protect their young men, who now account for about 1 in 4 draft-age teenagers, from conscription into the military and punishment for draft evasion. But with the Israeli army overstretched, a core campaign promise of Eisenkot and his opposition allies was to compel Haredi men to share the sacrifice of defending the country.
Liberman has now chosen to break that promise but not his vow to keep Arab parties out of government.

On Friday, he wrote on social media that while he remained dead set on replacing Netanyahu, avoiding new elections and spurning any partnership with the Arab parties, “on all other issues, it is permissible and desirable to be flexible and compromise, and to understand that you cannot have it all. This includes the issue of the conscription law as well.”

Eisenkot was not entirely absolutist in his campaign rhetoric about drafting the ultra-Orthodox, but Bennett, of the Together party, was adamant about it and would have to accept going back on that pledge.

Eisenkot could also find it difficult to strike a deal with the Haredi party leaders, who are far more experienced at coalition negotiations than he is, and whose voters have grown steadily more right-wing and nationalist in recent years.
Eisenkot Considers a Minority Government

With 48 votes to Netanyahu’s 46, Eisenkot said Friday that he planned to form a minority government, at least initially. That would mean that the Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties abstain from the vote to form the government.

But he also said he would invite every political party — without exceptions — to join his government, now or later, provided it embraced his terms: recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accepting the values in the Israeli Declaration of Independence, requiring universal national military or civilian service, and agreeing that Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be dismantled.
Liberman, however, is again standing in the way. On Friday, he ruled out forming a government with anything less than a 61-seat majority.

Should Eisenkot fail to form a government, Netanyahu would be given a chance next. But if he failed, there would be a short period before new elections are called in which anyone in parliament — including Liberman — could become prime minister by enlisting the support of 60 other lawmakers.
On Friday, Eisenkot appeared to allude to Liberman’s resistance — and possible ulterior motives.

“Anyone who seeks to delay or sabotage the formation of a government for personal rather than substantive reasons,” he wrote on social media before the start of the Sabbath, “will be remembered by history as someone who failed to rise to the occasion and failed to act to save Israel in a time of national emergency. They will not be forgiven.”
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

title: China This Week | With Xi set for US state visit, the 2 items on top of the agenda

content.value: This Wednesday (September 23), Chinese President Xi Jinping will arrive in Washington, DC, for a state visit to the United States. US President Donald Trump, in a rare move, is expected to personally greet Xi at the Joint Base Andrews military base in Washington.

Ten years after Xi last met Trump in the US for a state visit, much has unfolded in bilateral ties and the world at large, including several rounds of tariff wars and two major ongoing wars in Europe and Asia. Over the last few years, analysts have avoided predicting that such meetings might result in any breakthroughs or landmark agreements. As one headline for an opinion column in the Financial Times put it, “The main Trump-Xi summit achievement will be it happening at all”.

While China-US relations have remained significant for the world at large over the decade, they have witnessed increasing instability and disagreements. In that context, the muted expectations make logical sense.

That the two largest economies should find room for cooperation matters as a goal in itself. What makes the US and China’s case all the more important is the sheer scale of the brute power they wield. Looking at the simple metric of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), the US stands at $32 trillion, the Chinese economy trails with a large gap at $20 trillion, and Germany stands in third position with an even larger gap at over $5 trillion.

Their economic might ensures that no matter the concern at hand — wars, emerging technology, climate action, or anything else — these countries can shape global debate and action. Going into this meeting, two main areas of concern stand out.
Here is a closer look.
1. Tariffs and trade

Ahead of Xi’s visit, Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng will lead a delegation to the US for economic and trade consultations with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent from September 19 to 23. Throughout 2025, too, when tariffs imposed by the US marked the beginning of a long-drawn tit-for-tat tariff war, these leaders were involved in negotiations.

The trade war revealed the US’s capacity to withstand pain and inflation concerns to an extent. Chinese producers, too, were able to deal with the rising costs to send goods to a major market in multiple ways, including frontloading (shipping goods early, before the tariffs came into effect) and turning to other markets. There were also allegations of transhipment (shipping goods through third countries, which paid lower tariffs to the US).

However, China was seen as having emerged victorious thanks to rare earth minerals — used in industries ranging from defence to automobiles. Its dominance in processing them led it to use the minerals as tools of leverage. The restrictions it imposed on exports in 2025 affected countries across the world, and the supply eased only after an October summit with Trump in Busan, South Korea. The US agreed to a pause in escalating tariffs until November 2026, contingent on China easing its export controls on minerals.

UPSHOT: The Busan summit will mark a year soon. Since then, Trump’s tariffs have been struck down by the US Supreme Court, but that has not stopped the Trump administration from exploring and deploying other means to impose levies on countries, including China.

A senior US official told Reuters that China had also “not been up to par” on easing critical minerals’ supply and that this would be a topic for discussion ahead of the Trump-Xi summit. How these disagreements are navigated will determine what the next few months have in store for trade — bilateral and global. For now, the hope is that the status quo should, at least, be maintained.
2. Artificial Intelligence

The other domain that has triggered intense debate — and has the US and China as central players — over the past few months is AI. Whether companies should pause the pace of their development, in the face of some AI models going beyond the limitations set for them, is just the latest question.

Just this week, Reuters reported that AI agents from OpenAI (the company behind ChatGPT) hijacked the platform Hugging Face’s user accounts. This is only the latest in a series of similar incidents from other major AI companies. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for slowing advancements, and other heads of big companies, including OpenAI, have concurred.

Tech leaders, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk and Google’s Sundar Pichai, will also meet the presidents this week (as many of them did during Trump’s May state visit to Beijing).

But there are several stakeholders here, including Trump, who has equated limitations on AI to slowing progress, and AI companies themselves, who have invested billions into their products. In the US, concerns about China closing in on the gap with the US in the AI race are also raised to downplay risks.

China, for its part, regulates AI in that, like all parts of the market, the state has ultimate control. More targeted regulations may be expected soon. Its major models have been open-weight, meaning that they allow developers to gain some insight into their code and modify them to run their own programmes. This further allows for easier adoption of Chinese models, helping their spread.

China has also sought to rally other countries, usually of the Global South, and take the lead in the contested area of creating common global agreements on AI. During the recent BRICS summit in New Delhi, Xi proposed setting up a BRICS open-source AI community, offering to support cooperation among member countries on developing and deploying AI models. However, despite these attempts at “openness”, the Chinese systems of governance lack the openness associated with American ones, which allow breaches to be made public at all.

China may also have something to lose if the pace of development slows in the US, critics say. Anthropic has earlier claimed that Chinese AI models used American models to train at a fraction of the cost.

UPSHOT: That AI is fast-developing and already deeply embedding itself into the lives of people globally is indisputable. The two most influential countries in the world, however, often view it as a zero-sum game, and calls for slowing down its progress have often been deemed a barrier to national progress.

At a time when nationalism is on the rise on both sides, it would be difficult to convince either side of the case for cooperation. This is the task at hand this week. Even if countries are reluctant to put the brakes, the frequency of AI-related concerns coming to light, for one, is making a strong case for finding common ground.

title: Palestine, Iran, Yemen: What BRICS Delhi Declaration tells us about the shifting sands in West Asia

content.value: Of the 140 paragraphs in the BRICS New Delhi Declaration adopted last week, 11 paras were devoted to recent developments in West Asia.

Each BRICS declaration expresses the in-principle position of any state at the time and does not create any binding obligation. But since they are passed by consensus, each document acts as a broad yardstick to identify shifts in the postures of particular states.

In this light, the 2026 New Delhi Declaration is the first consensus document from a multilateral grouping featuring China, Russia and Iran that mentions the UN Security Council’s Resolution 2803 — the Donald Trump-backed Gaza peace plan that was adopted on November 17 last year with China and Russia abstaining and Iran subsequently condemning it.
The declaration also reflects subtle shifts in the Iranian, Emirati and Saudi positions on key conflict variables in West Asia. Both are considered below.
On Palestine

The New Delhi Declaration, in paragraphs 30 and 31, takes “note of the adoption of UNSC Resolution 2803” and reaffirms the “Arab Peace Initiative that includes the establishment of a sovereign, independent and viable State of Palestine within the internationally recognised 1967 borders, which included the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, with East Jerusalem as its capital”.

The Arab Peace Initiative, a “land-for-peace” arrangement outlined in 2002, is a result of Arab positions turning more pragmatic after the failure of the Oslo Peace Process and the onset of the Second Intifada.

It made Arab recognition of Israel contingent on verifiable Israeli steps towards recognising a Palestinian state with borders before the expansion of Israeli occupation during the Six-Day War of 1967.

For Israel, the 1967 requirement has long been a deal-breaker, with its positions hardening since October 2023. Israeli diplomatic resistance to the ‘1967’ obligation (reiterated in at least 13 legally binding UNSC Resolutions) has since been reinforced by Israel’s increasing occupation of Gaza and illegal settlements in the West Bank.

However, UNSC Resolution 2803 was the first Security Council resolution on Palestine that omitted Israel’s obligation to return to 1967 borders and the UN’s foundational principles on Palestine. The resolution reflected an American position peculiar to both Trump administrations, causing both Russia and China to abstain.

Trump‘s Comprehensive Peace Plan for Gaza, endorsed in the resolution, omits both Israel’s obligation to revert to its 1967 borders or aid the establishment of a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital. It also refrains from terming Israel’s control of Palestinian territories as “occupation”.

Note that the first Trump administration was the first world government to recognise undivided Jerusalem as Israel’s capital, reversing Washington’s decades long sensitivity to the Arab posture and alignment with past UNSC resolutions.

No Gulf Arab state was present at the UNSC November session, with Pakistan and Algeria being the sole Islamic countries to assent. However, motivated largely by a then-urgent need to support a US-led effort to force a ceasefire in Gaza, Arab states later assented to the resolution, its endorsement of Trump’s peace plan, as well as the Board of Peace.

However, unlike the American-Israeli posture, Arab states convened multiple times in the immediate aftermath of UNSCR 2803. The 46th Session of the Gulf Cooperation Council’s Supreme Council (December 3, 2025), the Joint Summit of the African Union, Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, and the Arab League (December 16, 2025), and the OIC’s Emergency Executive Committee Meeting (February 26, 2026) all referenced UNSCR 2803 alongside a reiteration of “the need to end the Israeli occupation and establish an independent Palestinian state on the 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital”.

In fact, the OIC emergency session references all 13 UNSC Resolutions since 1967 which declare East Jerusalem as Palestine’s capital — a customary invocation in all UNSC Resolutions on Palestine (except 2803).

The New Delhi Declaration, then, is an institutionalisation of the Arab effort to ensure that resolution 2803’s implementation is not seen as divorced from the 1967 need. Moreover, it reflects China, Russia, and Iran’s implicit acknowledgement that UNSCR 2803 and the Trump peace plan can act as a roadmap for Gaza, as long as the 1967 obligation is respected, thus restoring greater balance in the positions of major stakeholders on the theoretical road to Palestinian statehood. This is notwithstanding Israel’s continued rejection of such positions.
The Iran war

In the months leading up to the September declaration, India’s BRICS presidency was fraught with the challenges of an unprecedented geopolitical context in West Asia — the US-Israeli war on Iran and Tehran’s strategy of retaliating against targets in Arab states.

India became the first BRICS chair in the grouping’s history to issue a Chair’s Statement at the end of the BRICS Foreign Ministers’ Summit in May that included mentions of member-specific reservations to key paragraphs. Across March, April and May, the decisive breakdown in the détente between Iran and its Arab Gulf states had meant that they disagreed specifically over the situation in West Asia — enough to prevent consensus.

In the months since, as US military efforts to dislodge the Islamic Republic or its control over the Strait of Hormuz failed, Gulf Arab states have shown an openness to engaging with Tehran, even as skirmishes between American and Iranian forces continue in Hormuz.

This was particularly evident in President Masoud Pezeshkian’s meeting with the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi on BRICS sidelines where they “agreed to put the past behind us and look to the future”, despite Iran having targeted the UAE more than any other Gulf Arab state in its retaliatory strikes.
A crucial Yemen omission

While the UAE has historically maintained its own unique forms of engagement with Iran to mitigate threats, it is Saudi Arabia’s assent to the New Delhi Declaration which presents the most prominent shift.

This is particularly due to the document’s omission of any reference to the Yemen conflict, despite unprecedented Houthi reciprocal strikes against multiple Saudi cities, as well as a Houthi-imposed blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait since July.

This omission becomes more conspicuous when set against the Chair’s Statement in May which both expressed support for a UN-led Yemeni peace process as well as the need to ensure freedom of navigation for all states in the strait.

As Saudi-Houthi escalation continues and Riyadh faces a historic double blockade in the straits of both Hormuz and Mandeb, it is evident that this omission favours the unnamed member state (arguably Iran) that expressed reservations to the Yemen/Bab-el-Mandeb reference in May and indicates a Saudi concession.

Moreover, the New Delhi Declaration also endorses South Africa’s case against Israel — which is named explicitly — at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) as well as an overt call for Israel “to withdraw its occupying forces from all of the Lebanese territory”. States such as the UAE have traditionally adopted quieter postures (especially vis-à-vis South Africa’s ICJ case), than Iran or Saudi Arabia.

The actual positions of Arab states will ultimately be determined by the contours of the ongoing conflict of the region. However, consensus for the 2026 New Delhi Declaration reflects three crucial characteristics — India’s success as a convenor, as it oversaw the reconciliation of crucial reservations from May; Iranian, Russian and Chinese sensitivity to the Gulf Arab approach over Palestine; and Saudi-Emirati recognition of the need to engage Iran for long-term regional stability despite the Yemen escalation.
The author is Senior Research Associate at the Council for Strategic and Defense Research, New Delhi

title: Experts Explain | How the European Union’s carbon tax works, and why BRICS pushed back against it

content.value: By Nimish Singh & Shivang Agarwal

On September 12, the leaders of the 11-member BRICS bloc adopted the New Delhi Declaration. Paragraph 108 of the declaration opposes “unilateral, punitive, discriminatory and protectionist measures” — naming carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM) as an example.
No country is named, but the Global Trade Research Initiative said the reference was plainly to the European Union (EU), the only bloc charging such a carbon tax today.
What is CBAM? How will it affect Indian exports?

Europe charges its own factories for the carbon dioxide they release. But imports that may not have paid such a fee would be cheaper. So, from January 1, 2026, the EU began applying a charge on that carbon at its borders (which importers will start paying from February 2027). This tax is the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM, and covers six kinds of goods: iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity.

When an Indian mill sells any of these to Europe, the European buyer must buy certificates for the carbon dioxide released in making them. The certificates track Europe’s own carbon market and cost a little over €75 (per tonne) each in the first two quarters of this year. Each certificate covers a tonne of carbon dioxide, not a tonne of the product.

Making a tonne of steel in India releases 2.54 tonnes of carbon dioxide, against a world average of 1.9 tonnes. So, a tonne of Indian steel carries carbon roughly worth €190 on paper. The charge will climb each year as Europe withdraws the free permits it gives its own mills.
Importers do not have to pay this yet, as mentioned above: they will start purchasing these certificates from February 2027, covering goods shipped during 2026.
India’s exposure is narrow, yet deep. Of the $6.3 billion of CBAM-covered goods India sold to the EU in 2024, iron and steel accounted for $5.4 billion.

Therefore, India’s CBAM bill is, in effect, a steel bill. ICRIER estimates that the tax could cut India’s steel exports to the EU by 24%. Commerce Ministry figures already show a 13% fall in iron and steel shipments to the bloc in the first four months of the new regime.
BRICS countries have called CBAM protectionist and discriminatory. How true are these claims?

ICRIER finds that emissions from the world’s steel industry would fall by about 1%, while the EU’s own emissions would rise by 0.29%. European mills would simply make more steel to fill the gap. Production would shift from India to Europe, and the atmosphere is left where it was.

The money does a great deal for European industry, however. European steel, cement and aluminium plants still receive free permits for their own emissions, which are meant to be withdrawn between 2026 and 2034. The European Commission has also proposed a €100-billion Industrial Decarbonisation Bank for European factories. Brussels wants 75% of CBAM revenue, about €1.4 billion a year, to go to the EU budget.

The countries being charged CBAM have done the least to cause the problem. India has produced about 3.6% of all the carbon dioxide emitted since 1751, and the EU’s member states almost a fifth. Paragraph 110 of the New Delhi Declaration says developed countries shall give developing ones money to adapt. But this tax sends it the other way altogether.
What is the EU’s stance?

Europe’s concerns are valid. Its own factories pay for their carbon, and the EU does not want them undercut by imports that pay nothing for theirs. Brussels would also point out that the BRICS declaration expects fossil fuels to keep playing an important role in the energy mix of developing economies. And whatever a summit says, it cannot repeal a European law. Collection will begin in February 2027 either way.
Can India reduce the impending bill?
There is a line in the existing European law India can use. Article 9 of the CBAM regulation deals with carbon prices already paid at home.
If India charges a domestic mill for carbon, the European importer can subtract the amount from the bill at the border. So, India can decide whether this carbon payment happens at home or in Europe.

But, so far, India has left it to Brussels, and the reason is the way its carbon market is built. Unlike the EU model, the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme does not charge a factory for every tonne it emits. Rather, it sets every plant a limit on emissions per unit of output. A plant that crosses this limit must buy certificates to cover the excess.

A mill that stays within its limit would, therefore, pay nothing domestically. But with nothing paid at home, there is nothing for the European importer to subtract, so the mill will have to pay the full bill in Europe. A mill that emits more than allowed does pay in India, and that is the payment Article 9 recognises, so its European bill will come down on the tonnes it overshot.
The result, therefore, is that plants following India’s rules would end up paying Brussels in full while plants that break these would get a discount.

Europe, therefore, needs to recognise the Indian scheme — which it has not. The UK, meanwhile, has moved faster: on September 8, its treasury put the Indian scheme on its list of qualifying carbon pricing schemes for its own border tax starting in January 2027.
What can India do to offset negative impacts before February 2027, when CBAM collection begins?
Three things are in India’s hands before the bills arrive.

First: Address steel, which carries nearly all of the exposure and is the last big sector being brought into the scheme. The Environment Ministry issued draft targets for 255 iron and steel plants only on June 26, skipping the 2025-26 compliance year, with a median cut in emissions per tonne of about 5.5%. Finalising those targets, and putting a clear price per tonne on any shortfall, would give exporters a payment to show at the border.

Second: Leverage the trade agreement which India closed with the EU in January, which is a ready channel to press India’s case. In the agreement, both sides agreed to work on recognising each other’s carbon prices, and the EU promised India any flexibility it grants another country.

Third: Turn up in Brussels. When the Commission asked for comments on those draft rules, India sent three responses, all of them from private firms. Brazil sent 12, two filed jointly by federal ministries. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency and the commerce, steel and environment ministries should be filing these responses.

Beyond that, paragraph 109 of the declaration supports a BRICS Carbon Markets Partnership. Common standards among members would make it harder for Brussels to decide alone whose price counts. Europe will start collecting regardless. How much of that money leaves India depends on rules written in Delhi this year.
Singh is Director, Science, Gateway Research Foundation, and Agarwal is Senior Fellow at the Institute for Governance & Sustainable Development.

title: China This Week | China as ‘anchor of BRICS’, potential of ties with India: How Chinese media reported on summit

content.value: Chinese President Xi Jinping departed New Delhi on Sunday (September 13) at the end of the two-day BRICS Summit, also capping off his first visit to India in over seven years.

The final New Delhi declaration signed by the member countries did not result in any unexpected outcome, largely sticking to the grouping’s common concerns on issues like “unilateral protectionist measures” (likely referring to US tariffs).

But the fact that a common consensus was reached among members is also being read as an achievement of sorts. Iran, for instance, has targeted US military bases in the UAE amid the war that began in February. Both their leaders met on the sidelines of the summit.

China will next host the BRICS summit and hold the rotating presidency from 2027. With the Chinese State and the Communist Party heavily regulating its media landscape, commentary on Chinese websites can provide a sense of the messaging China seeks to convey and its priority areas. Here is what major media outlets said.
China Daily

China Daily is an English newspaper. Its coverage largely included routine news reports of Xi’s visit and the summit. One editorial spoke of 2026 marking the 20th anniversary of BRICS cooperation in glowing terms: “Over the past two decades, the BRICS cooperation mechanism has become the world’s most influential platform for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries.”

Making thinly veiled criticism of the US, it said, “With the countercurrents of unilateralism and power politics surging, multilateralism and the international order are coming under strain.” BRICS countries should thus be inspired to “steer the international order toward greater justice and equity,” it added.
The article also described China taking over the presidency as happening at a time when BRICS’ third “golden decade” begins.
Global Times
Global Times, a tabloid newspaper, is considered to have a more aggressive tone than many other Chinese papers and is seen as aimed more towards a foreign audience.

Its reports covered a wide range of topics, from India-China ties to a separate story on the summit’s effect on bilateral trade ties. An editorial presented China as the star of the show: “China has always been a key force making BRICS more substantial, more significant, and more influential, and is a well-deserved ‘anchor of BRICS cooperation’ in both name and reality.”
It credited Xi for “pioneeringly” putting forward a series of important proposals, including the “BRICS Plus” cooperation model for increasing BRICS countries’ outreach to other nations.

Another article spoke of the meeting between Xi and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, noting that this was “the third consecutive year that the Chinese and Indian leaders have met, following Kazan meeting in 2024 and Tianjin meeting in 2025, underscoring the steady stabilization of bilateral ties.”

It quoted a Chinese expert as stating that “If Kazan marked a turning point and Tianjin helped put relations back on a stable track, the New Delhi meeting can be seen as a new phase of confidence-building, focused on turning strategic consensus into concrete mechanisms and results.”

The report on business ties struck a positive tone: “India’s ongoing manufacturing expansion has generated steady demand for Chinese mechanical and electrical products, active pharmaceutical ingredients and industrial components.

Meanwhile, India’s agricultural products, mineral resources and characteristic consumer goods also have ample room to enter the Chinese market. The two-way movements of supply and demand have built a stable foundation for trade, proving that China-India economic and trade cooperation rests on a solid, realistic footing.”

It spoke of the trade imbalance as well — a concern that the Indian Foreign Ministry also noted in its statement. “Some may worry that deeper economic ties with China could worsen India’s trade deficit or lead to excessive reliance on China in certain strategic sectors. While such worries are understandable, the right way to address them is not through erecting barriers – it is through dynamic structural adjustments as cooperation deepens.
The problem of the trade deficit between China and India has emerged gradually through development, and it will ultimately find its resolution in more robust development,” it said.
CGTN
China Global Television Network, or CGTN, is available in more than 160 countries and regions worldwide through its TV and social media channels.

Its website also shared expert commentary aligned with BRICS talking points put forward by China. “BRICS members differ in development stage and comparative advantage, which creates favorable conditions for building a more resilient regional production network. Tariff and non-tariff barriers should be further reduced… Greater use of local currencies and cross-border payment cooperation can also lower transaction costs,” one opinion article said.

Another article similarly built up India-China ties, while noting challenges. “Strategic mistrust will not disappear after a few successful meetings. Differences over the boundary, trade imbalances, investment and regional security will continue. Domestic political pressures can also complicate the relationship…”

“The answer is not to pretend differences do not exist, but to manage them responsibly. That requires more strategic communication, institutionalized dialogue and fewer worst-case assumptions. Both sides should respect each other’s development paths and resist allowing third-party factors to dictate their bilateral relationship,” it added, likely referring to US-India ties.

“The world does not need China and India to agree on everything. It needs them to learn how to disagree without confrontation and cooperate without demanding uniformity. That may be the most important lesson of the New Delhi meeting,” the report said.
Upshot

In the last few years, amid concerted efforts by the governments of India and China to improve ties since the low of the 2020 Line of Actual Control (LAC) standoff, Chinese media have reflected the State’s line. This has often resulted in coverage that speaks of positive potential and familiar refrains like ‘the dragon and the elephant dancing’.

But for all these prospects, long-term differences in the ties are also similarly highlighted in times of disagreement. This was seen during the 2025 Operation Sindoor conflict, where Chinese media sites published reports that at times only reported the Pakistani view.

And for all the reporting now, parts of the commentary can still reflect longstanding biases. For instance, the fact that India-US relations were referenced speaks to an age-old concern: China still views its relations with India through the lens of the United States. Experts have traced its roots to Cold War-era politics, when India’s stance as a non-aligned nation made it seem unusual, and even untrustworthy, in the eyes of the leadership of the Communist State.

Ultimately, given the absence of independent media within China, such commentary can offer a window into how the Chinese State perceives the bilateral relationship, covering both its possibilities and revealing what the hurdles to achieving them might be.

title: Jobs, housing, corruption: Why angry youth are protesting across Europe

content.value: In Serbia, a student movement has just unseated a President who had consolidated power for around a decade. Around 400 km away, in Albania’s capital of Tirana, students have launched major anti-corruption protests against the government. And in France, students held demonstrations for weeks demanding more resources for schools. Neighbouring countries Belgium, Italy and Germany saw similar protests.

Over the last month, several nations across Europe — also including Spain, Bulgaria and Portugal — have seen citizens, especially the young, protesting against public institutions. The catalysts for each country are different — rising costs, discontent with the state of schools, declining public services and a housing crisis. But they point to broader pressures — distrust towards the government and uncertainty for the future.

The current unrest flaring up across borders can be geographically categorised under three geographical clusters: the Mediterranean and Southwest, parts of Western Europe and the Balkans regions like Serbia and Albania.
What’s going on in the Balkans?
The Balkans, situated at the continent’s periphery, were in some ways, the initiators.

In late 2025, the Bulgarian government’s proposed budget for 2026 triggered protests over planned tax increases and higher social security contributions to fund increased public spending. Despite the suspension and eventual withdrawal of the budget, protests continued and widened to encompass broader concerns over corruption. Rosen Zhelyazkov’s government eventually resigned on December 11, 2025.

The European Commission’s 2025 Rule of Law Report and the OECD’s Economic Surveys: Bulgaria 2026 report include corruption as a constraint on competition and business conditions, as well as a shrinking working-age population, skills shortages and mounting pension pressures that threaten the country’s long-term economic prospects.

Similarly, in Albania, the student protesters have been demanding action against corruption, greater investment in education and accountability over a controversial luxury tourism project planned by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

The European Commission’s 2025 Albania Report identifies an education system hampered by outdated curricula, insufficient teacher training and inadequate infrastructure. The outcry against environmental disregard fuels “hostility towards our generation,” Alan Bollard, former Governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand told The Indian Express. “It is seen effectively as having taken advantage of the environment without paying the price for it.”
What about the Mediterranean?

In the south-west, closer to the Iberian Peninsula, discontent over the unaffordability of urban life and real estate prompted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election for November 29, 2026, ahead of the general election originally scheduled for 2027. Sánchez’s bid for re-election is “deeply rooted in the struggle of the Spanish middle-class whites”, former Ambassador to the EU and Belgium, Manjeev Singh Puri, told The Indian Express.

Eurostat data from 2025 showed that 9.1% of EU residents aged 15-29 lived in households spending at least 40% of their disposable income on housing. It went on to say that 26.9% of young people lived in overcrowded conditions, pushing the average age at which Europeans leave the parental home to 26.3 years.

At 26.4% for individuals aged 15-29, Greece’s youth housing-cost overburden rate is one of the more severe.  Historically, economic growth meant making “successive cohorts richer,” Bollard explains. “But there are areas where they clearly do not feel better off. Homes are increasingly being used as financial assets, driving prices up and making the market harder to enter. Younger people are finding it harder and harder to buy a home.”
This is not, however, the only lever. In Italy and Greece, the property crisis is compounded by reduced public education funding.

The OECD’s Education at a Glance 2025 report provides evidence for this argument. Greece invested just 3.9% of GDP in education, compared with the OECD average of 4.7%, while education’s share of public budgets fell from 6.2% in 2015 to 5.9% in 2022.  Italy, meanwhile, saw education’s share of public budgets decline from 7.1% to 6.7% over the same period.

Indeed, it is clear “this generation is facing an inordinate amount of uncertainty”, said Jean-Pierre Landau, Professor of Economics at Sciences Po and former Second Deputy Governor of the Banque de France.

“I can feel that with my students and when we recruit for admissions,” he told The Indian Express. “When you have UN leaders or global figures saying the planet is burning or there are expected job losses, it creates an unnecessary amount of anxiety and fear.”
How does this connect to Western Europe?
In the wealthier economies of France, Belgium and Germany — among others — the fracture lies in the failure of the State to execute on its promises.

In mid-September, students in the Paris suburb of Créteil began agitations against the teacher staffing shortages and disproportionate allocation of the education budget to pensions. A report released by the French Ministry of Economy revealed that 32% — almost €28.5 billion — of the education budget funded pensions for retirees.

The OECD’s Education at a Glance 2025 report also found that 39% of French secondary-school teachers were aged 50 or older in 2023, highlighting the challenge of renewing the teaching workforce. For students, these pressures mean unfilled teaching positions, aging school buildings, and overcrowded classrooms.

That local dispute over staffing in Créteil subsequently spread to schools elsewhere in France, with students demanding better-funded institutions and more equitable access to education. By September 29, protests had affected 180 schools, according to the French Interior Ministry. The underlying grievance, therefore, is not simply a lack of money. It is the perceived disconnect between the taxes citizens pay, the public services they are promised, and the services they actually receive.

In Southern and Eastern Europe, protests have reflected concerns over corruption, opportunities and declining trust in institutions. In richer European economies, the discontent is more visibly tied to public-service delivery, the cost of living, and competition over how public resources are allocated.
Upcoming European election cycle
On November 29, Spain is set to hold snap elections. In 2027, France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Slovakia and Estonia among others shall have their general elections.

The ousting of Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić and the preemptive snap elections called by Spain’s Pedro Sánchez highlight how incumbents are being questioned for systemic stagnation. When traditional parties fail to address the core grievances of the youth — ranging from unaffordable housing to decaying public infrastructure — voters are increasingly willing to voice their frustrations.

Historically, however, disillusionment with mainstream institutions has paved the way for populist and fringe movements, which often promise radical disruptions to the system. If the youth feel that traditional center-left and center-right coalitions are merely trading power while protecting the interests of older generations, their votes may migrate to the extremes.

title: Behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair lies a much bigger China controversy

content.value: Chipmaking giant Nvidia has launched an investigation into reports that Chinese intelligence targeted its chief executive, Jensen Huang, through a woman who was a former executive at the firm Megaspeed. The controversy puts renewed scrutiny on the Singapore-based data centre operator, which American authorities have separately investigated since 2024 over suspicions that it was helping China access restricted artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

On being asked about the allegations, US President Donald Trump said, “I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he’s a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on,” he told reporters. “I hope everything’s fine,” he said, adding that Huang was an “honourable guy” and that “he probably has an excuse for ​it. ⁠You have to hear it.”

The row has spotlighted Megaspeed’s Chinese origins, its purchase of billions of dollars worth of Nvidia equipment, and allegations that the company has received financing from Chinese technology giant Alibaba, despite being registered in Singapore.

The company has also been at the centre of concerns in Washington over whether American export restrictions can effectively prevent Chinese businesses from accessing advanced AI computing power through data centres in third countries.
What are the allegations against Jensen Huang?

Recent media reports claimed that Huang had a relationship with a woman named Alice Huang. In a message on Sunday (November 8), he confirmed the claims, stating, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The same day, Nvidia said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel, would investigate the allegations. While the board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security had been compromised, it would examine all available information.

The allegations have also brought renewed scrutiny to Huang’s lobbying of the Donald Trump administration to ease restrictions on Nvidia’s chip exports to China. This position has drawn criticism from US lawmakers and national security officials concerned that Beijing could use advanced American AI technology to strengthen its military capabilities. Huang has repeatedly argued that supplying inferior quality chips to China would help stem the growth of its domestic industries and innovation.

But after the spying allegations, the possibility that a suspected Chinese intelligence operative had personal access to Huang has further heightened concerns over whether Beijing could have sought to influence his advocacy for easing these restrictions.

While American export controls prohibit the unauthorised shipment of certain advanced chips to China, Chinese companies can potentially obtain access to comparable computing power by renting infrastructure housed in other countries. Such arrangements are not necessarily illegal, but they have complicated Washington’s attempts to restrict Beijing’s AI capabilities.

The global AI boom has propelled Nvidia into becoming one of the world’s most valuable companies (currently valued at over $4.5 trillion), as technology giants such as Microsoft, Google, Meta and Amazon spend billions of dollars building AI infrastructure powered by its advanced chips. Nvidia’s graphics processing units (GPUs) have become central to training and running sophisticated AI models, giving the company a dominant position in the market for AI computing hardware.
What is Megaspeed, and what are its alleged links to China?

Megaspeed is a Singapore-registered company that provides AI computing capacity through data centres in Southeast Asia, including Malaysia and Indonesia. Its origins, however, can be traced to 7Road, a Chinese gaming and cloud-computing company that US lawmakers have described as having links to the Chinese government. Megaspeed was previously incorporated as 7Road International before adopting its present name in 2023.

Despite Nvidia maintaining that Megaspeed has no Chinese shareholders and is operated outside China, its business dealings have raised questions about the extent of its links with Chinese technology companies.

According to trade records cited by The New York Times, a Malaysian affiliate of Megaspeed purchased at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia technology between June 2024 and February 2026. The company has reportedly supplied computing capacity to Alibaba and other Chinese businesses, allowing them to access Nvidia-powered infrastructure located outside China.
American authorities had begun examining Megaspeed’s operations well before the alleged Chinese intelligence operation involving Huang came to light.

The US Commerce Department started investigating the company in late 2024, after an official visiting one of its data centres in Malaysia reportedly found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising suspicions that the chips could be shipped elsewhere rather than installed at the facility.

According to reports, American officials subsequently examined whether Megaspeed was diverting chips to China in violation of US export controls. The investigation was transferred to the US Department of Justice earlier this year.

In October 2025, Republican Senator Tom Cotton also wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, calling for an investigation into Megaspeed’s ownership, affiliations and potential violations of American export restrictions. Cotton flagged the routing of Nvidia equipment through intermediaries, including a US subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese technology company whose parent had been placed on Washington’s trade blacklist.
What Nvidia, Megaspeed argued

Singaporean authorities have also confirmed an ongoing investigation into Megaspeed for suspected breaches of domestic laws. However, neither the American nor Singaporean investigations have publicly established that Megaspeed illegally diverted chips to China. The company has denied wrongdoing, while Nvidia has maintained that its checks found no evidence of diversion.

In May 2026, short-selling firm Culper Research published a report alleging that Megaspeed had received financial backing linked to Alibaba through intermediary companies, despite claims that it was not Chinese-owned.

Citing corporate filings, Culper said Megaspeed’s balance sheet expanded from $33 million at the end of 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, driven largely by $2.9 billion in refundable deposits from an undisclosed source.

The report also pointed to filings showing that Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, had pledged its business as collateral to Singapore-based Apex Enterprise Solutions, whose parent company was Alibaba. Culper alleged that these arrangements suggested Alibaba-linked financing was being channelled into purchases of Nvidia-powered servers.

More broadly, Culper alleged that over 20% of Nvidia’s FY2026 compute revenue was ultimately driven by Chinese demand through Southeast Asian intermediaries and illegal chip diversion. The firm disclosed that it held a short position in Nvidia, meaning it stood to benefit from a fall in the company’s share price. Its allegations remain unproven.
The Chinese espionage allegations

The latest allegations centre on Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen and former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence officials reportedly concluded was passing information to Beijing.

The New York Times reported that she had developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive, while reports have suggested that China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited her to gather information about Huang and potentially influence his position on chip exports. In his message to Nvidia employees, Huang apologised and accepted responsibility for his conduct. He did not identify the other person in his statement.

China has rejected the espionage allegations. Singapore, on its part, has clarified that it did not investigate Alice Huang over alleged intelligence ties, distinguishing that allegation from its ongoing investigation into Megaspeed.

Singaporean authorities are separately investigating Megaspeed for suspected violations of domestic laws, although the Singapore Police Force has not disclosed the specific offences under examination. The authorities have said Singapore does not enforce unilateral US export restrictions, but will act against companies using the country to circumvent foreign controls through fraudulent practices. On October 31, Singapore clarified that the Megaspeed investigation was unrelated to allegations involving former executive Alice Huang’s suspected links to Chinese intelligence, which it said it had not investigated.
Why this matters for the US-China AI race

The controversy comes amid Washington’s efforts to restrict China’s access to advanced AI technology, particularly Nvidia’s most powerful processors, which can have military and intelligence applications. Huang’s close relationship with Trump and his lobbying for exports are also under the scanner.

Three Republican chairmen of US House committees have requested a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18, citing significant national security concerns over China’s access to American technology and information.

title: Ilhan Omar: Why the US democrat is being targeted by Donald Trump

content.value: “Ilhan Omar, whatever the hell her name is, with the little – with the little turban, I love her. She comes in, does nothing but bitch.”

“Ilhan Omar is garbage. She’s garbage. Her friends are garbage. […] These aren’t people that work. These aren’t people that say, let’s go. Come on, let’s make this place great. These are people that do nothing but complain.”

“She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right.’ She’s telling us about the constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.”

These are just three of Donald Trump’s many attacks on US Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar. Few people have been targeted as ferociously by the US president. But why has Trump singled her out for such hostility?
Who is Ilhan Omar?

lhan Abdullahi Omar, 44, was born in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia. She fled the civil war in the country while still a child, and spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She finally came with her family to the US in 1995, at the age of 12, and became a US citizen in 2000. She joined the Democratic Party, and made a career as a politician on the party’s left wing. Since January 2019, she has served as representative for the state of Minnesota and is one of the first two Muslim women to enter the US Congress.

Ilhan Omar is a practising Muslim who wears a hijab. Congress altered a 180-year-old rule for her that prohibited head coverings in the chamber of the House of Representatives. Politically and socially, Omar champions progressive values, and often makes a connection between her faith and her commitment to social justice, human rights, and the protection of minorities.

Omar campaigns on issues such as universal health insurance, increasing the minimum wage, climate protection, and the cancellation of student debt. She is also one of Donald Trump’s most prominent and outspoken critics, repeatedly accusing him of racism and systematically fomenting hatred against minorities, immigrants, and Muslims. She has frequently condemned raids by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which she describes as a “militarized campaign of fear.” She has also accused the president of corruption in office.
Ilhan Omar’s criticism of Israel and accusations of antisemitism

Young, outspoken, female, Muslim, and a left-wing Democrat — politically, Ilhan Omar is almost the polar opposite of the 80-year-old Republican Trump. But she is also a controversial figure within her own party.

Omar is one of the fiercest critics of Israel in US politics, and has repeatedly called Washington’s support for the country into question. She has been accused of antisemitism, and of supporting the movement BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions), which encourages people to boycott Israeli businesses. Omar has defended BDS as a legitimate form of non-violent protest and freedom of expression. In 2019, she even introduced a resolution in the US Congress that aimed to strengthen the right of Americans to boycott, with a view to countering laws that restrict what the BDS movement can do.

In early 2023, Republicans removed her from the House Foreign Affairs Committee over a number of controversial tweets, including a comment she made in 2021 that seemed to equate the actions of the US and Israel with those of the Taliban in Afghanistan, and the Palestinian group Hamas. The latter is classified as a terrorist organization by the US and many other countries around the world.
Accusations of embezzlement, immigration fraud against Ilhan Omar

Her critics also tried to link Omar to a corruption scandal in her home state of Minnesota. During the COVID-19 pandemic, around $250 million (€220 million) were misappropriated from a government-funded food program for children. Omar had previously called for the rules of the program to be eased.

Many of those convicted were from the state’s Somali community, something that political opponents, including Trump, seized on to claim Omar was involved. No law enforcement authorities have ever accused her of any wrongdoing.

The most recent accusation against Omar concerns her immigration to the US. For years, her opponents have claimed that she made false statements during the procedure, even alleging that she entered into a fraudulent marriage with her biological brother to help him secure a US visa. On October 12, federal officials ordered a search of Omar’s home, investigating allegations that Omar’s father lied about her age on her immigration application.
Ihan Omar’s controversial house search

Omar has repeatedly denied the accusations, describing them as part of a “campaign of political intimidation” and “an attempt to target political enemies.” Several leading Democratic politicians have come to her defense, accusing the Trump administration of weaponising the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security against its political opponents.

Former immigration officials told the Reuters news agency that it is extremely unusual for a house search to be conducted as part of such an investigation, as the government should already have all the relevant immigration documents.

Many see a raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress over a formality from 26 years ago as excessive, and have been especially critical of the timing of the raid, just three weeks before the Congressional elections in which Omar is standing for re-election.

The long-standing, unwritten “60-Day Rule” holds that authorities do not take any public action against political candidates in the two months before an election, so as not to influence the outcome. Critics see the fact that this practice has been ignored in Omar’s case as amounting to election interference.
Other Muslim politicians also targeted

With the midterm elections looming, Trump is battling plummeting approval ratings, and Omar is not the only Muslim politician the president has been attacking. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Senate election in Michigan, is another.

At a rally last Saturday in Tennessee, Trump said of El-Sayed: “I call him Mohammed. Somebody said, ‘His name isn’t Mohammed, it’s Abdul.’ I said, ‘To me, it’s Mohammed.’ I’m the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he’s Mohammed, and he’s a radical jihadist.”

There is no intelligence whatsoever to suggest that El-Sayed has any extremist connections. The 41-year-old epidemiologist was born and brought up in Michigan. He went to university there, then won a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, where he gained a doctorate in public health. For many years, he was the health director of the city of Detroit. Like Omar, he too belongs to the progressive left wing of the US Democratic Party.

During the election campaign, El-Sayed has repeatedly emphasised that he is not the one responsible for the rise in food prices, the expensive rents, and other political grievances. He has placed the blame on what he describes as the failed policies of the administration in Washington.
This article has been translated from German.

title: Why a labour rights activist’s detention has put a broad China law under scrutiny

content.value: The detention last month of Feng Rui, a labour rights activist in Guangzhou, has sparked rare criticism in China of a broadly worded law used against people who document social grievances. His case has prompted questions about the invocation of the offence of “picking quarrels and provoking troubles”.

According to information available in the public domain as of October 8, Feng was criminally detained by the Yuexiu District Public Security Bureau on September 14 and held at the Yuexiu District Detention Centre. It remains unclear whether his detention is connected to his labour rights activities or to a “survey and annual review” he released earlier this year.
Who is Feng Rui?

Feng Rui, whose actual name is Xiao Wu, is the editor of the independent platform “Chiapas Dongfeng TV”. He graduated in 2017 from the Chinese Department of Beijing Normal University in Beijing. Rather than pursue a conventional white-collar career, he chose to work with marginalised workers at a workers’ home in Picun, a settlement where hundreds of rural migrant workers live.

A few years later, he founded Chiapas Dongfeng TV to document the lives and struggles of migrant and low-wage workers. He also established a labour law support group and criticised the “996” work system, under which employees are expected to work from 9 am to 9 pm, six days a week.

Over the years, Feng has documented labour disputes involving unpaid wages, layoffs, unemployment, workplace injuries and excessive working hours — issues affecting workers who rarely feature in mainstream narratives. He has also conducted annual reviews of labour rights.

A Chinese online current affairs platform, described as Maoist and radical leftist, reported his detention. The account said he had been criminally detained on suspicion of “picking quarrels and provoking troubles”. The precise connection between his work and the allegations against him remains unclear.
A broad offence under scrutiny

“Picking quarrels and provoking troubles” (寻衅滋事, xunxin zishi) is a broadly worded offence that has been used in cases involving independent reporting and civil activism. The term appears in two distinct legal contexts: the Criminal Law and the Law on Public Security Administration Punishments.

Under the latter, the relevant provisions cover acts such as gang fights or arbitrary assaults; chasing or intercepting others; forcibly taking, damaging or occupying public or private property; and other acts of provoking trouble that disturb others or disrupt social order.

Under the law in force before January 1, 2026, Article 26(4) contained the catch-all provision for other acts of picking quarrels and provoking troubles. The revised Public Security Administration Punishments Law, which took effect on January 1, 2026, places the corresponding provision under Article 30(4). Criminal proceedings under the Criminal Law are separate from administrative punishment under this law.

The broad wording has prompted criticism from lawyers, activists and commentators concerned about arbitrary enforcement. A September 2025 commentary on the issue, published by Guangming Daily and republished on People’s Daily Online, asked how the offence should be defined and how administrative law enforcement could avoid abuse of power.

“In the Internet age, the Internet has become a public space for social activities. Because current laws lack a clear definition of what constitutes ‘social order’ on the Internet, and there is also a lack of clear standards for determining what constitutes ‘disorder,’ this may lead to law enforcement actions exceeding legal boundaries and infringing on the public’s right to free expression,” wrote Wang Jinfu.

The commentary also questioned whether authorities could invoke the offence simply because a person’s remarks were unwelcome or drew attention to social conflict. “Can someone be labelled as ‘picking quarrels and provoking troubles’ just because the person said something that made the relevant authorities uncomfortable or brought social conflicts to the public’s attention,” it asked.

A post on Chinese social media, criticising the wide range of conduct to which the law could be applied, warned that “a criminal charge that should be targeted at a specific illegal act can easily become a ‘pocket’ with a lot of room for interpretation”.
Detentions for online criticism
The concerns are not limited to labour activists. Two cases involving online comments have drawn attention after courts found the administrative penalties unlawful.

Deng, a 36-year-old man from Ning County in Gansu Province, was administratively detained for seven days after posting videos questioning the quality of his son’s school uniform. The Qingyang Intermediate People’s Court subsequently found the police penalty unlawful, citing procedural violations and insufficient evidence.

In another case, Xiao Xinliang, a resident of Xiangyin County in Hunan Province, was detained for five days after posting a 12-character comment under a video about street renovations. On June 25, 2025, the Hunan High People’s Court overturned the penalty on retrial, finding insufficient evidence that the comment had disrupted public order.

The cases illustrate the concerns raised by critics about the breadth of the offence and the possibility of its use against online expression. They also show that administrative penalties imposed under the provision can be challenged in court.
From public order to online speech
The offence predates Xi Jinping’s rise to the leadership of the Communist Party in 2013. Critics argue that its application expanded as the authorities increasingly used it to address online speech.

In May 2015, The New York Times wrote: “Previously, this charge only applied to disrupting public order, but in 2013 a judicial interpretation expanded the scope of this charge to include the internet, allowing prosecution of those who publish and widely disseminate false information or rumours online.”
The newspaper described “picking quarrels and provoking troubles” as a “catch-all” crime, one with an exceptionally broad scope of application.

Feng Rui’s detention has brought these concerns back into focus. The September 2025 commentary in Guangming Daily warned against treating reports of labour disputes as offences merely because the underlying events were unpleasant or uncomfortable for the public.
