“The labour incidents that have already occurred should not be compiled and interpreted as picking quarrels and provoking troubles simply because they are unpleasant to the public. Otherwise, what will truly disappear in the end will not be a single article, but rather people’s courage to face reality,” the article said.
Hemant Adlakha, formerly a professor of Chinese at Jawaharlal Nehru University, is Vice Chairperson of the Institute of Chinese Studies, Delhi.

title: How Serbia’s student movement won national elections within two years

content.value: A student-led movement in Serbia won parliamentary elections on Sunday (October 25), unseating incumbent President Aleksandar Vučić after more than a decade in power.

The development comes as countries around the world, including in Europe, have witnessed student-led movements of late, calling for fixing systemic issues ranging from corruption to the education system.

How did Serbia go from a student movement to unseating the president in two years, and what effect could this have on the region? Gulshan Sachdeva, Professor and the Jean Monnet Chair at the Centre for European Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, explains.
What led to the Serbian student movement?

The student movement was triggered by the tragic collapse of a canopy at a railway station in the city of Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people. The disaster soon became a symbol of alleged institutional corruption and lack of accountability.

It was followed by campus blockades that gradually escalated into mass protests. Students made decisions about the movement through open campus assemblies, where they debated and approved their course of action. What began as weekly protests and campus blockades soon became a national movement, as other parts of society, including teachers, actors, and farmers, joined the demonstrations. Allegations of collusion between the ruling party and organised crime also gained prominence, inspiring one of the movement’s slogans: “Serbia or the Mafia?”

With snap elections announced in September, the movement sought to translate nearly two years of protest into an organised electoral platform: “Student List – Students Win.” The List brought together 250 candidates from diverse backgrounds, including more than 160 PhD holders. It excluded students and individuals previously associated with the ruling party or other political parties. Its candidates included university teachers, actors, farmers and singers. Collectively, they developed a programme outlining their vision for the country.

To broaden its appeal and avoid internal divisions, the movement prioritised domestic issues, including media freedom, anti-corruption measures, institutional reform and education. It called on all opposition parties to support its candidates rather than field their own. The List ultimately won 141 of the 250 seats, forcing Aleksandar Vučić to concede defeat.

It is noteworthy that the movement adopted a cautious approach to more contentious foreign policy questions. The List maintained that Kosovo remained part of Serbia, despite its declaration of independence in 2008. While around 100 countries have recognised Kosovo’s independence, India, China, Russia and five EU member states continue to withhold recognition. It also proposed holding a referendum on Serbia’s membership of the European Union (EU), and opposed imposing sanctions on Russia over the war with Ukraine.
Why is Aleksandar Vučić’s defeat significant?

Aleksandar Vučić has dominated Serbian politics since 2014, first as Prime Minister and later as President. He emerged as a prominent ultranationalist leader during the Yugoslav wars and NATO’s bombing of Serbia in 1999. He later co-founded the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and repositioned himself as a more pragmatic leader.

In power, Vučić pursued a multi-vector foreign policy, engaging with the EU while maintaining close ties with Russia. He also opened Serbia to Chinese investment, established a strategic partnership with Beijing, and signed a free trade agreement with China. Serbia has also benefited from China’s Belt and Road Initiative, including the Belgrade–Budapest high-speed railway project.

This was shaped by its EU accession ambitions, dependence on Russian energy and diplomatic support over Kosovo, and growing economic ties with China — often described as a “four-pillar” foreign policy. Under his administration, the Serbian economy recorded reasonably strong economic growth.

However, persistent protests over the past two years posed a serious challenge to Vučić’s leadership. In September, he announced his resignation as President five months before the end of his second and final term. With control over the media and state institutions, Vučić appeared confident of retaining power by returning as Prime Minister.
The election results mark a watershed moment for Serbia. This is not merely a change of government; it marks the collapse of the political order under Vučić.
How did the movement survive the strong Serbian State?

The decentralised structure of decision-making within the movement made it difficult for Vučić’s administration to discredit it or arrest a prominent figure. Its independence from established political parties also helped preserve public trust.

Students went beyond campus protests, engaging in door-to-door canvassing and reaching out to villages that had traditionally supported Vučić. They prepared a list of 250 candidates, including respected individuals without political baggage. Crucially, the movement remained peaceful and focused primarily on domestic issues. By using national symbols rather than EU flags, the protesters also made it harder for the administration to portray the movement as externally driven or foreign-funded.
And what does it mean for Europe?

The students’ victory could provide a significant boost to student movements across Europe. It could inspire other movements, demonstrating how sustained, peaceful mobilisation can challenge deeply entrenched political regimes and bring about political change without violence.

It also has implications for the Russia-Ukraine War. No government in Belgrade can afford to ignore Serbia’s deep historical, cultural, religious and economic ties with Russia. Both countries share the Orthodox Christian tradition. The List has announced that Serbia will halt arms supplies to all conflict zones, including to those western countries that subsequently supply weapons to Ukraine.
Serbia’s European integration remains a major challenge. A candidate country since 2012, Serbia has opened 22 of the 35 negotiating chapters, of which only two have been provisionally closed.

Accession progress has been held back by concerns over the rule of law, judicial independence, media freedom, the normalisation of relations with Kosovo and Serbia’s limited alignment with EU foreign policy, particularly its refusal to align fully with EU sanctions against Russia. This may change, depending on the new government.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen responded immediately, stating: “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union.” The new government may adopt a more cautious approach towards Chinese infrastructure investments.
How will they govern now?
This will be the movement’s crucial test. One advantage for the List is its clear majority, which eliminates the need for coalition negotiations.

The question now is how the List will choose its prime minister. Cardiologist Dr Ilija Srdanović tops the list of 250 candidates, while other prominent figures, like Dejan Šoškić, an economist and former governor of the National Bank of Serbia, are also likely to play important roles.

According to one member of the List, its first task will be the “social and psychological detoxification” of the country. As outlined in its programme, the priorities include ensuring media freedom, replacing key officials associated with the Vučić regime, and reforming education and healthcare. Major shifts in foreign policy appear less likely, although the List could announce a date for a referendum on EU membership.

title: As Europe sees protest wave, understanding the economics of social unrest

content.value: France is not the only country witnessing an outpouring of discontent on the streets. Be it Albania, Belgium, Italy or Portugal, a wave of social unrest appears to be sweeping across the European Union.
Like in France, where the protests started with student dissatisfaction with school facilities, most of these protests are eventually turning into a broader cry about the cost of living crisis.
In other words, while the timing is often political — several countries such as France and Italy are set for national elections in 2027— the issues are in fact economic in nature.

It is often argued that growing economic inequalities in an economy lead to such social unrest. This applies to arguments that are often advanced by those who oppose immigrants as well; that is, it is argued that more immigrants rob a country’s citizens of economic benefits.
So, have economic inequalities risen in France?

The most established data in this regard is from The World Inequality Report of 2026, which, in turn, provides data until 2024. The table below maps the broad measure of inequality called Income Gap. The WIR 2026 defines it as follows: “The top 10% to bottom 50% average income gap is the ratio between the income share of the top 10% and the bottom 50%.”

In other words, the income gap is a ratio and it measures the average income difference between the poorest half and the richest tenth within a population. The higher the ratio, the greater the inequality.
For France, the income gap has increased between 2014 and 2024, as indeed it has for Italy. But in many other peer countries, it has fallen as well. For instance in the UK, Germany and Spain.

It is also relevant to note that while the income gap has increased in France, by itself it is among the lowest among peers such as Germany. In India, for instance, the income gap is 38 and in South Africa it is 118.
What are the other predictors of unrest?

Economic inequality alone cannot explain social unrest. As Philip Barrett and Sophia Chen wrote for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in 2021: “Although inequality has crept up slowly in recent decades, it has not significantly worsened over the past decade in a way that would explain the recent surge of discontent.”

So what else could one look at? IMF economists Sandile Hlatshwayo and Chris Redl have used machine learning techniques to assess the ability of more than 340 economic and social indicators to predict unrest. “A central finding is that past turmoil — both domestically and in neighboring countries — is by far the most important variable for predicting future strife. It is about 10 times as informative as the most revealing economic or social factors,” they wrote.

Barrett and Chen explain: “This idea has much in common with a bank run, when people rush to withdraw deposits because they see others in line. As a result, factors signaling that others are more willing to protest — such as past protests or protest in culturally similar neighboring countries — can act as coordinating signals.”

Other factors that the IMF researchers identified as predictive of unrest are digital access and social media penetration, suggesting that the ability to communicate and coordinate on a large scale might be essential to protest activity.
Can social unrest have economic consequences?

So while economic factors are not irrelevant — “prices particularly of food and fuel, seem to be particularly important” — they are not necessarily the biggest predictor of social unrest. But IMF’s researchers have found that economic factors play a much more prominent role when it comes to the consequences of unrest.
IMF economist Metodij Hadzi-Vaskov and colleagues have found a close link between unrest and subsequent economic performance.
On an average, major unrest events are followed by a one percentage point reduction in GDP, six quarters after the event (see the chart below).

“Unrest motivated by socioeconomic factors is associated with sharper GDP contractions than unrest associated with political motives. Yet events triggered by a combination of both factors correspond to the sharpest GDP contractions,” they point out.

title: Saudi East-West oil pipeline shut: Why it matters for global oil markets, and India

content.value: Saudi Arabia has temporarily shut its East-West oil pipeline after multiple attacks on the crucial network on Thursday, raising fresh concerns over global oil supplies already strained by disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. The pipeline, also called Petroline, is one of the most important Hormuz-bypass routes for exporting Saudi Arabian crude.

This came even as Yemen’s Houthi rebels seized the strategically vital Mayun Island located at the entrance to the Red Sea — developments that mark a dangerous new front in the wider war with Iran. Both Saudi Arabia and Iraq have said that the attack originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate.

An official source at the Saudi Ministry of Energy said the attacks took place in the Riyadh and Madinah regions on the morning of Thursday, September 10. The pipeline was shut down while emergency and technical teams moved to secure it and assess its safety. The attacks also caused an unspecified number of injuries. Saudi authorities described the shutdown as a precautionary measure.
#Statement | East–West Pipeline shut down as a precaution following multiple attacks. pic.twitter.com/I9LWwsi53Z
— وزارة الطاقة (@MoEnergy_Saudi) September 11, 2026

A CNN report citing US officials and satellite imagery separately confirmed that pumping stations along the pipeline were struck and that fires were visible at the sites. The extent of any damage to the pipeline system itself, and how long the shutdown may last, remain unclear. The attacks on the pipeline system came from Iraq, most likely from Iran-backed militias there.

The timing of the suspension of the pipeline’s operations is critical. Apart from attacks on the pipeline system itself, Iran-backed Houthi forces have tightened their grip around the Bab el-Mandeb and Red Sea shipping route, which could further reduce oil flows, particularly from the world’s largest exporter,  Saudi Arabia. Riyadh has relied upon for its oil exports amid the effective halt in shipping from the Persian Gulf.

The development is also likely to push up oil prices, which are anyway at their highest levels in over three months. The immediate effect on Saudi oil exports, and consequently on international supplies and prices, will depend on the extent of the damage and how quickly the pipeline can resume operations. For energy-import-dependent India, too, there will be ramifications affecting supplies, and more importantly, prices.
East-West pipeline’s importance amid Hormuz crisis

The East-West Pipeline runs roughly 1,200 km across Saudi Arabia, from the Abqaiq oil processing centre in the kingdom’s oil-rich east to the Red Sea port of Yanbu in the west. From Yanbu, oil tankers usually sail east to Asia through the Bab el-Mandeb, while those headed west go through the Suez Canal.

Operated by Saudi Aramco, the pipeline allows Saudi Arabia to move crude oil overland from its main producing region to the Red Sea, rather than shipping it from terminals on the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz. In fact, the pipeline was built partly to hedge against risks arising from disruptions in oil flows through Hormuz.

The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that accounted for a fifth of global oil flows before the West Asia war started over six months ago. It is the main outlet from the Persian Gulf. Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the UAE have traditionally depended heavily on it to reach global markets, particularly top oil importers China and India.

The Petroline has the capacity to transport around 7 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude, of which about 5 million bpd is available for exports, while the remaining carrying capacity is for feeding the Kingdom’s domestic refineries, according to the EIA.

This makes it Saudi Arabia’s principal route for rerouting crude exports amid disruption in shipping through the Strait of Hormuz since the West Asia war began late February. Before the conflict erupted, the pipeline operated at just a fraction of its capacity, as exports from the regular route through the Strait of Hormuz were normal. But with maritime traffic through the chokepoint grinding to an effective halt, Aramco started pumping more oil through the Petroline.

While the actual volume of crude moving through the pipeline has been lower than its capacity, with estimates ranging around 4-5 million over the past few months, it is still significant and represents 4-5% of global oil supplies. This route has therefore served as an important safety valve for global oil supplies during the current crisis. Its targeting, however, has demonstrated that alternative routes themselves can become targets in a wider regional conflict.
Likely impact on oil market

Brent crude had already moved above $100 a barrel earlier this week, triggered by the recent sharp escalation in the West Asia conflict, including attacks on oil tankers and petroleum infrastructure in the region. The $100 threshold was breached on Wednesday, and Brent futures continue to trade above that level till Friday, closing at about $105 per barrel, the highest since May. The Petroline shutdown arrives when traders are already nervous.

The duration of the shutdown will be critical in the prevailing circumstances. If Saudi Arabia is able to restore the pipeline quickly, the market impact could remain largely psychological and short-lived. Tankers can be redirected, inventories can be drawn down, and Saudi Arabia can use its other export infrastructure. But if the shutdown lasts weeks, the consequences become much more serious.

From here, there are three broad possible scenarios that industry analysts and experts are taking into consideration. If the pipeline is repaired or reopened within days, and attacks on Saudi infrastructure do not continue, oil prices could retreat from their current elevated levels.

If the shutdown lasts several weeks while dangers around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb persist, oil prices could move higher. The scenario that the markets fear most is a further widening of the conflict. If attacks spread to additional Saudi oil facilities, Yanbu, tankers or other Gulf export infrastructure, the disruption could turn into a wider supply shock, which would certainly push up oil prices.
The worry for India

Saudi Arabia had traditionally been among the top sources of crude oil for India. While supplies from Riyadh have fallen notably amid the Hormuz crisis, Saudi oil still accounted for 7-8% of India’s total oil imports over the past couple of months. And a vast majority of these came from the Yanbu export facility. In August, India imported about 332,000 bpd of Saudi oil, accounting for 7.2% of New Delhi’s total oil imports for the month, as per tanker data from Kpler. In July, oil imports from Riyadh stood at about 414,000 bpd and made up 8.2% of India’s oil imports.

The first impact of the Petroline’s shutdown for India would be on supplies, and Indian refiners will have to find replacement volumes. While that can be managed, given India’s highly diversified crude import slate, higher prices for those alternative barrels will be the bigger headache. Amid the West Asia conflict, India’s crude oil import bill surged by over 56% on a year-on-year (y-o-y) basis in April-July to $63.4 billion, even as import volumes rose slightly to 81.9 million tonnes — or about 600 million barrels — from 81.5 million tonnes, as per data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC).

Energy imports are a major component of India’s overall imports, and any meaningful increase has ramifications for the country’s trade balance, current account, inflation, and the rupee’s exchange rate, among others. India is the world’s third-largest consumer of crude oil and depends on imports to meet over 88% of its requirements. Put simply, an oil shock can be considered an external tax on the Indian economy.

Given its high oil consumption and import dependency, India is already bearing the brunt of high oil prices. The country imports 1.8-2 billion barrels of oil a year, and every $1-per-barrel increase in price bumps up its oil import bill by up to $2 billion on an annualised basis.

It also said that every 10% oil price increase typically widens India’s current account deficit by 0.4% of the GDP. Crude oil alone is the country’s largest merchandise import. According to Commerce Ministry data, crude oil imports in 2025-26 stood at about $135 billion. If oil prices sustain at $100 per barrel in the current financial year and import volumes don’t decline, the oil import bill could be upwards of $200 billion for the year. If the price sustains at a much higher level, the implications would be even graver.

title: Israel elections: Why Netanyahu was punished, but not rejected

content.value: Israel Election Results 2026: In one of Israel’s most significant elections ever, voters so far seem to have weakened Benjamin Netanyahu without rejecting him, underlining the country’s post-October 2023 dilemma: many want a change from his orthodox, muscular, polarising vision of Israel, but have no clear picture of what should replace it.

With the counting of votes still underway, on Wednesday (October 28) afternoon, the bloc led by Netanyahu was projected to win 54 seats in the 120-member Knesset, according to a partial count reported by The Times of Israel. The bloc led by opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot was projected to win 47, while Arab-led parties were projected to win 19. Thus, neither side has the 61 seats needed for a majority.
What do right and left mean in Israel?

The terms “right” and “left” in Israel do not map neatly onto their counterparts in India or elsewhere. While the opposition bloc positions itself as more secular, liberal, and democratic, in terms of foreign policy, there is a broad alignment after the Hamas attack of 2023.

The Israeli political spectrum is shaped particularly by national security, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, the future of settlements in the occupied West Bank, and the relationship between religion and the state.

The right has generally opposed Palestinian statehood and supported settlements, while the left has been more open to territorial compromise and negotiations. Over time, positions once associated with the right have gained wider acceptance in Israeli Jewish politics.

An October 2025 survey by Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies found that 72% of Israelis were dissatisfied with the government’s handling of the Gaza war, while 57% were satisfied with the military’s handling of it. This distinction matters to the election. A voter can favour a forceful military response and still oppose Netanyahu’s leadership, question his government’s conduct or want a different approach to governing. Equally, a vote against Netanyahu does not necessarily signify support for Palestinian statehood or a fundamental shift to the left.

Three years ago, a major issue in Israel had been Netanyahu’s proposed “reform” of the judiciary, which led to huge street protests. While the issue was pushed back by the October 2023 attacks and its aftermath, the government did manage to pass in March 2025 a law that allowed it greater control over judicial appointments. A second part of the “reform package” involves legislation that will allow the Knesset to reinstate laws the Supreme Court strikes down. This is yet to be passed.

Yonatan Touval, an analyst with the Israeli think tank Mitvim, told The Indian Express: “An Eisenkot-led government, whatever its composition, will be materially different from the current one, especially in restoring competent, professional government, strengthening democratic institutions and reversing years of cronyism, corruption and political interference.”

On foreign policy, Touval said such a government “might be more disciplined in distinguishing achievable security objectives from grandiose military ambitions” in Iran, and “more willing to translate military gains into political arrangements that permit Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction” in Gaza.
The right and left in Israel also differ on how much violence settlers in West Bank can be allowed to get away with.
Touval said an Eisenkot government “would likely curb settler violence and resist outright annexation, but would continue to support settlements and oppose Palestinian statehood.”
Why Arab parties will do more than play kingmaker

The Arab-led parties’ performance could determine not only who forms the next government, but also whether Israel’s political establishment is willing to accept Arab citizens’ elected representatives as legitimate partners in power. Their role therefore goes beyond the familiar arithmetic of coalition formation.

Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party and a former deputy chief of the Israel Defense Forces, argued on Wednesday that the opposition should work with Arab parties to form a government of change. In a post on X, he wrote: “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count to 120. 65 is more than 55. That’s how Israeli democracy works. Period. We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes.”

Netanyahu, meanwhile, is already raising the tempo against aligning with Arab parties. During the campaign, even his opponents had said they wouldn’t join hands with the Arab faction. Thus, on one hand, a government propped up by Arab parties would be a rejection of a more exclusionary vision of Israel, while on the other hand, it would be under pressure from its own constituents.

“The opposition bloc failed in its mission to rout out Bibism. Still, it succeeded in weakening the Netanyahu bloc from 64 to 55 or 56 seats, short of a majority. Netanyahu can no longer do whatever he wants with his bloc in the Knesset, in the judicial system, in the media, and so on. The opposition bloc must leverage this now into real achievements or its failure will turn into a historic defeat,” Touval said.
Why it could be months before Israel knows its next PM

Israel does not directly elect its prime minister. Voters elect 120 members of the Knesset, and the government must command the confidence of a parliamentary majority. The president, after consulting representatives of the elected parties, assigns the task of forming a government to the member of the Knesset considered best placed to succeed. The largest party does not automatically get to govern.
The law sets out several stages for government formation:

· 28 days: The member of the Knesset assigned the task has 28 days to form a government. The president may grant an extension of up to 14 additional days, making the first period a maximum of 42 days.
· A second attempt: If the first attempt fails, the president may assign the task to another member of the Knesset. This person gets 28 days, without an extension.

· A final opportunity: If that attempt also fails, or the president concludes there is no possibility of forming a government, Knesset members have 21 days to request that the task be assigned to another member who agrees to try. If a request is made, that person has 14 days to form a government.
· Fresh elections: If no such request is submitted, or the final attempt fails, the Knesset is deemed to have decided to dissolve itself, and elections must take place within 90 days.

These are successive stages, not a single 90-day deadline for coalition negotiations. If negotiations fail, the process can ultimately lead to another election. Until a new government is formed and takes office, Netanyahu’s outgoing government continues as the caretaker government.

title: Expert Explains | What the BRICS 2026 summit achieved — and what challenges remain

content.value: By Vrinda Sahai

The 18th BRICS Summit, marking two decades of the group’s formulation, concluded on September 12-13. The summit, hosted by India, brought together the heads of states of all 11 member nations, providing an opportunity for both multilateral deliberations and significant bilateral engagements. It also tested the effectiveness of an expanded and increasingly diverse BRICS, questioning whether and to what extent consensus could be formulated.
What were the most notable outcomes of the BRICS Summit?
Two elements stand out from India’s 2026 BRICS presidency: the New Delhi Declaration and the diplomatic activity on the sidelines of the summit.

The summit navigated sharp differences among members, adopting the 140-point New Delhi Declaration. Despite significant divergences over ongoing conflicts, the document used carefully calibrated language and avoided naming individual countries as offenders, allowing members with competing positions to remain within a common framework. The declaration also endorsed China as the 2027 chair.

For India, an important outcome was the reference to the April 2025 terror attack in Pahalgam. Unlike the Rio Declaration last year, the New Delhi Declaration explicitly condemned the attack: “We condemn in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured.”

It also addressed the continuing conflict in West Asia. With Iran and the UAE now both BRICS members and directly affected by the conflict, the text expressed concern over the escalation of tensions, without naming any parties, yet reaffirming the UN Charter and calling for exercising maximum restraint. The Rio Summit had also addressed the situation in West Asia, but none of the countries directly involved in the conflict were BRICS members at the time.

At the bilateral level, the summit provided an important platform to engage key partners. Most notably, the meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping signaled continued efforts to stabilize India-China ties, following the 2020 Galwan Valley clash leading to severe deterioration in the relationship. The two sides discussed areas of cooperation, including trade, business links, supply chains, and people-to-people exchanges, while also reiterating that peace and tranquility along the border remain essential to the development of bilateral ties. The statements from the two sides, however, differed in emphasis and tone.

India also sought to address a larger problem within BRICS — the tendency for initiatives launched during one presidency to lose momentum under the next. PM Modi proposed the BRICS Continuity and Implementation Mechanism under which the troika (outgoing, current and incoming chairs) will track progress and systematically follow-up on outcomes. The proposal’s real test will come after the handover to China for the 2027 chairship.

India’s chairship also tried to move BRICS beyond leader-level statements and towards mechanisms with a more direct impact on trade, investment and businesses. This included advancing the BRICS Economic Partnership 2030 and working on development finance, infrastructure and investment. The practical significance of these initiatives, however, should not be overstated. Several proposals, including the investment platform, remain under development.
How was India’s 2026 presidency different from its previous chairship in 2021?

There are three important differences between India’s 2021 and 2026 presidencies of the BRICS. First, the composition of the grouping has changed substantially. In 2021, the group comprised only the five original members whereas in 2026 it has expanded to 11 members and 10 partner countries. This has increased the group’s economic weight but made consensus more difficult.

Second, the two presidencies took place in very different contexts. The 2021 Summit was held virtually following the outbreak of Covid-19 pandemic and against the backdrop of the India-China border standoff. In 2026, India was able to host an extensive programme of over 350 meetings across 30 Indian cities. Substantively, the 2021 Summit New Delhi Declaration focused on Global Health Challenges and combating the pandemic, particularly focusing on vaccine production and distribution.

In 2026, however, India placed greater emphasis on science and technology, agroecology, fintech, and economic cooperation, alongside its continued push for UN and multilateral reform around representation, responsiveness, and rulemaking.

Third, the economic relationship within BRICS has deepened. Indian trade with BRICS members has more than doubled from $203 billion in 2020-2021 to $417 billion in 2025-2026. Recognizing this expanded potential for intra-bloc trade and market opportunities in these developing economies, the group emphasised customs cooperation, trade finance, supply chains and digital payments while also addressing trade asymmetries.
What are the developments in the cross-border payments systems?
While efforts to boost intra-bloc trade and streamline payment mechanisms have expanded, BRICS does not yet have an operational system for cross-border trade in national currencies.

The BRICS Payment Task Force will continue to explore practical solutions for efficient cross-border payments and enhancing interoperability of payment and messaging channels. This builds on the BRICS Cross-Border Payments Initiative referenced in the Kazan and Rio Declarations.

India pushed for a more ambitious approach, including linking the fast-payment systems of BRICS countries and examining interoperability between central-bank digital currencies. The objective is to make payments faster, cheaper and more reliable. Implementation is complicated by the fact that members have different exchange rate regimes, capital controls, exposure to sanctions, banking regulations, and payment standards. Intra-BRICS trade is also highly asymmetric, with China’s dominance accounting for a substantial share and several members running large trade deficits with it.

The discussions on trade in national currencies also help distinguish what BRICS is realistically pursuing from the often-repeated misconception of a common BRICS currency. Still, the members have not agreed on a common technical architecture, a shared settlement mechanism, or the launch of the payments platform, BRICS Pay, to materialise trade in national currencies beyond the existing initiatives at bilateral levels.

India’s attempt was to keep the group focused on its core concerns of development, trade and practical cooperation in technology, while securing meaningful language on conflicts despite a fragmented geopolitical environment. It is now increasingly necessary for these ambitious efforts to witness materialisation — such as on payment systems interoperability, MSME financing, greater investment announcements, and meaningful bilateral development under future presidencies.
The author is a Research Analyst at Carnegie India

title: US suspends Cognizant’s Green Card filings: What is PERM, why does it matter for Indian workers?

content.value: The US Department of Labor has suspended IT services giant Cognizant’s filings under PERM, a key system used by American employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency, as authorities investigate alleged fraud and misuse of employment-based immigration programmes.

Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito announced the action on September 8, saying Cognizant’s PERM filings had been suspended and that his office was working with other Labor Department officials and the White House Fraud Task Force. Similar action was announced against software company Cloudera. US authorities have not yet disclosed the specific allegations against Cognizant, the number of applications affected or the duration of the suspension.

The action comes amid a broader crackdown by the Donald Trump administration on employment-based immigration, with technology and IT services companies facing particular scrutiny over their reliance on foreign workers.

US authorities have stepped up investigations into alleged misuse of the H-1B and PERM programmes, including claims of wage undercutting, fraudulent filings and displacement of American workers. The scrutiny is especially significant for Indian professionals, who account for a large share of H-1B beneficiaries and employment-based Green Card applicants.
What is PERM, how is it different from H-1B, and how can Indian workers be affected?
What is PERM?

PERM, or Program Electronic Review Management, is the system through which employers generally obtain labour certification before sponsoring a foreign employee for an employment-based Green Card. Unlike a visa application, which is primarily made by an individual, the PERM filing is done by the employer on behalf of the worker.

Before filing, an employer must obtain a prevailing wage determination for the position and carry out prescribed recruitment. Broadly, the process is intended to establish that hiring a foreign worker permanently will not adversely affect the job opportunities, wages or working conditions of US workers. Once the Labour Department certifies the application, the employer can proceed to the next stage of the Green Card process.

The date on which the Labour Department accepts the labour certification application also generally becomes the worker’s “priority date”, which is effectively their place in the queue for an employment-based immigrant visa. This is particularly important for workers from countries such as India, where demand for Green Cards far exceeds the number available.
How is PERM different from H-1B?

An H-1B is a temporary, non-immigrant work visa that allows US employers to employ foreign professionals in speciality occupations. PERM, in contrast, is part of the process for obtaining permanent residency.

The two can, therefore, run alongside each other. An Indian engineer, for instance, could be working for Cognizant in the US on an H-1B visa while the company separately files a PERM application to sponsor the employee for a Green Card. A PERM suspension, on its own, does not cancel an employee’s existing H-1B status or an already-issued Green Card.
How will action against Cognizant affect Indian workers?

For Cognizant employees whose Green Card process has not yet reached the PERM filing stage, the immediate consequence is a delay. Cognizant cannot make fresh PERM filings while the suspension remains in place, meaning affected employees cannot secure a priority date and begin moving through the employer-sponsored Green Card process.

That can be particularly consequential for Indians because they already face a severe backlog. In the US State Department’s September 2026 Visa Bulletin, the employment-based second preference, or EB-2, category for India was listed as “unavailable” for final action, while the EB-3 final-action date was January 1, 2014. The system also imposes limits on the number of employment-based Green Cards available to nationals of any one country.

There can also be an H-1B implication for some workers approaching the normal six-year limit on that visa. US rules allow certain H-1B holders to extend their stay beyond six years where a labour certification was filed sufficiently early. An inability to get the PERM process started could therefore become more serious for employees nearing that deadline. Workers who already have approved petitions and are waiting because a Green Card number is unavailable are in a different position and can, subject to the rules, qualify for H-1B extensions of up to three years at a time.

The scale of Cognizant makes the action particularly notable. The US-headquartered IT services company had 3,56,700 employees globally as of June 2026 and reported $21.1 billion in revenue in 2025. At the end of 2025, more than 2,50,000 of its employees were based in India, accounting for nearly three-fourths of its workforce.

This does not mean all of them are affected by the US action, but Cognizant’s large Indian employee base and its long-standing use of US employment-based immigration routes mean Indians are likely to make up a significant share of workers exposed to any prolonged restrictions.

title: From London to local: How Andy Burnham’s ‘Manchesterism’ could transfer power away from Westminster’s corridors

content.value: Before he formally assumed the office of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom last week, Andy Burnham had in a June 29 speech referred to the concept of “Manchesterism” as an important guiding needle in terms of political philosophy.
This was a reiteration of what he said earlier in February and March this year, detailing the concept as business-friendly socialism and a model of regional devolution that leads to growth.
So, what does Manchesterism entail? We explain.
Tragic roots

Conceived in the 19th century, Manchesterism was a school of thought which championed free trade and argued that wealth is best created by individuals as far removed from state interference as possible.

In 1996, the Irish Republican Army detonated the largest bomb the UK had witnessed since World War II. This explosion ripped through Manchester’s city centre, causing $700 million worth of damage and destroying structures within a mile’s radius.

This tragedy set the stage for the modern revival of Manchester. Council Leader Sir Richard Leese proposed the city centre’s overhaul, which was largely delivered by private capital. Today, a major criticism the city centre faces is that it resembles a mini-London amidst all the glass and steel. But it was the focus on building a successful public-private partnership — with investments derisked by public money — that catalysed this northern renaissance.
Key elements

Burnham’s vision of Manchesterism insists that a greater degree of public control over assets like housing, transport, and energy is an essential pre-requisite to growth. He shares the original movement’s defiance of a London-centric order and has long advocated for devolution of political and fiscal power concentration in the South.

This concept has also been said to embody collaboration between governments, businesses, and trade unions, given its focus on investing in public services and building more social housing — both areas of deep focus for Burnham from his time as the former mayor of the Greater Manchester Area (2017-26).
Some of the major points in Burnham’s interpretation of Manchesterism are:

Devolution: In the UK, devolution refers to the transfer of power from the Parliament in Westminster, London, to national assemblies in Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, and English regional local authorities. By devolving power, budgets, and accountability to local areas, public services can integrate around the citizen rather than the UK’s institutional boundaries.

Linking economic and social progress: Burnham has openly dictated that economic progress without social change is a fallacy. In his book, Head North: A rallying cry for a more equal Britain, Burnham rejects the idea of trickle-down economics. Instead, he demands good growth in every postcode as an outcome of growth while questioning why this change should only be observed in urban centres.

The international angle: Burnham has also expanded the concept to foreign policy. Recognising that global shocks — from energy market convulsions to supply-chain fragility — are felt most acutely at the local level, this model dictates foreign policy and trade agreements explicitly protect regional manufacturing, lower local household bills, and secure jobs in lagging regions. This is meant to ground international dialogues in everyday, local issues.
Policy examples
Burnham has attempted to boost his agenda’s credibility by citing the real-world feasibility of relevant instances during his mayoral tenure, such as:

‘The Bee Network’:.Reversing the 1980s deregulation of the UK’s buses, Burnham utilised statutory mechanisms to bring Greater Manchester’s transport system back under local authority control. The region capped fares at £2 and reduced operational costs by a third per kilometre by integrating buses, trams, and travel routes under a public umbrella.

Reindustrialisation push: Burnham organised the city-region’s economic future around five “growth clusters”: Digital/Cyber/AI, Life Sciences, Creative/Media, Low Carbon, and Advanced Manufacturing. By aligning local universities, innovators, and skills providers within these specific sectors, Manchesterism attempts to build a £100 billion regional economy from the ground up in a town once in the doldrums of deindustrialisation.
As Burnham takes charge, it remains to be seen whether a national executive can use the levers of the centralised British state to dismantle and devolve that very power.

title: US immigration crackdown: How Indian IT giants have long prepared for this moment

content.value: Long before the Donald Trump administration suspended several Indian IT companies from a key US green-card programme, these firms had begun reducing their dependence on American work visas, increasingly hiring locally and building delivery centres in countries closer to their biggest overseas market.

For years, Indian IT services majors followed a relatively simple business model — executing routine work for overseas clients from India while sending experienced engineers to client offices for more complex projects and to build relationships. However, as the US tightened regulations around H-1B visas, and Indian IT companies expanded their global operations, they began shifting more work offshore while stepping up local hiring in markets such as the US and Europe.

The shift has helped shield these companies from the immediate business impact of the US Department of Labor’s decision on Thursday to suspend eight major technology firms, including TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech and Cognizant, from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme (PERM), a key step in obtaining employment-based green cards for foreign workers.
Vice President JD Vance announces the suspension of the PERM Program for Microsoft:

“Thanks to an ongoing investigation, we have decided to suspend the PERM program for Microsoft, which means they will no longer be able to take those H-1Bs and apply for permanent resident status within the United States of America. Now our message to Microsoft and to any other foreign or domestic corporation is quite simple. We obviously want you to thrive in the United States of America. We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector. We’re the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers. And so our message to Microsoft is, you’re great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
— Vice President JD Vance (@VP) October 8, 2026

The groundwork for this transition had been laid over several years. Improvements in subsea cable connectivity in the early 2000s and the rise of cloud computing in the following decade reduced communication and data-transfer costs, making it easier to deliver technology services remotely. The Covid-19 pandemic further accelerated acceptance of offshore work among clients.

The Trump administration’s decision in September 2025 to introduce a $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B petitions became another trigger for companies to reduce their dependence on sending employees to the US. The fee was subsequently blocked by US courts, though the administration has proposed a new, separate cap-subject fee of $103,265.
How Indian IT companies changed their hiring trend

Historically, Indian IT companies maintained a 70:30 offshore-to-onshore employee ratio. Following the announcement of the H-1B fee hike, an analysis by Kotak Neo projected that this could shift to 85:15 by FY27, with nearshoring gaining traction in Canada, Mexico and Latin America. It also expected US-based hiring to increase 12-18% between FY26 and FY27.
Industry estimates suggest that around a fifth of the workforce at major Indian IT companies works onshore, with only a small proportion dependent on H-1B visas.

“We’ve seen our IT companies investing heavily in creating hubs in Latin America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific in order to be nimble without the regulatory hurdles. This has especially picked up over the past 2-3 financial years, in what is called a ‘hybrid’ global delivery model,” an analyst tracking the sector at a domestic brokerage said. “So, I am not very concerned by it (the US’ actions). The groundwork to protect against this started a while back.”
Company disclosures provide evidence of this shift. Let’s look at the situation with some major companies
HCLTech: In its FY26 annual report, HCLTech said approximately 80% of its US workforce comprised local hires, reducing its dependence on visas.

Its FY25 sustainability report showed that its global operations had expanded to 20 locations across the Americas, Europe and other markets. The workforce at these locations increased from 24,797 in FY24 to 26,083 in FY25, while local hiring rose 47% to 7,731 employees during the year.

Tech Mahindra: Similarly, Tech Mahindra chief executive Mohit Joshi said during an earnings call in October 2025 that fewer than 1% of the company’s global workforce was on H-1B visas, while its visa dependence in the US was below 30%. The company was strengthening its operations in Canada, Mexico and Brazil to deliver work for clients from locations outside the US.

Tata Consultancy Services: TCS, India’s largest IT services company, opened an AI-driven operations centre in Mexico in August 2025, its eighth in the country. It said it had built a workforce of more than 11,000 employees in Mexico over the previous 22 years.
The company’s management has consistently emphasised the importance of hubs in Latin American countries such as Mexico, Brazil and Colombia, which act as “time-zone bridges” for US clients.

During its July-September FY26 earnings call, TCS chief human resources officer Sudeep Kunnumal said: “We have significantly localised our workforce in the US…we believe our business model will be able to adapt quickly to any changes in immigration policy.”

Following the latest PERM suspension, TCS reiterated that its limited use of the programme would insulate its operations. “Our PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years and hence we do not expect the suspension of the program to impact our workforce strategy and customer engagements,” the company said on Friday. It also reiterated plans to hire 15,000 people in the US over the next five years.

.@Sonderling47: “I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world — Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini — and also, due to multiple active federal investigations, @USDOL is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the program.”
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 8, 2026

The limited exposure is reflected across the industry. According to an ICICI Securities analysis, Indian IT firms accounted for less than 2% of PERM applications filed in the US between October 2024 and September 2025.
Wipro: Wipro has also undertaken similar steps to reduce its dependence on US immigration policies.

“More than 80% of people are localised and we are looking at 250-odd H-1Bs in the past five years. So, we have been progressively reducing our dependence on H-1Bs,” the company’s human resources head Saurabh Govil said during its post-Q2 FY26 earnings call.

The company has also expanded its delivery capabilities across the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific. Infosys, HCLTech and Tech Mahindra have adopted similar strategies, combining local recruitment with offshore and nearshore delivery centres.

The market reaction to the PERM suspension reflected expectations of a limited immediate impact on operations. Indian IT stocks rose on Friday, with the Nifty IT index gaining around 3%. TCS shares rose about 5.5%, also supported by its September-quarter earnings, while Infosys, Wipro and HCLTech gained around 3%.

However, analysts have warned that prolonged uncertainty over permanent residency could make it harder for these companies to retain experienced foreign workers in the US, even if the immediate impact on project delivery remains limited.
Drop in H-1B approvals
The changing employment model is also visible in the sharp decline in new H-1B approvals for Indian IT companies over the past decade.

According to an analysis of US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) data by the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP), the seven largest India-based IT companies received just 4,573 H-1B petition approvals for initial employment in FY25 — a decline of 70% from FY15 and 37% from FY24.

Only three Indian companies figured among the 25 largest recipients of new H-1B approvals in FY25. US technology companies Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Google occupied the top four positions, marking a shift from the period when Indian IT services providers were among the biggest users of the programme.

While IT companies do not typically disclose a detailed breakdown of their overseas workforce by immigration status, the decline in new H-1B approvals points to their reduced reliance on bringing employees from India to work at client locations in the US.

Companies such as Wipro, LTIMindtree, HCLTech and Tech Mahindra have progressively expanded local recruitment and offshore delivery capabilities, while US multinational companies have increasingly established global capability centres (GCCs) in India to directly employ skilled technology workers.
The latest PERM suspension nevertheless creates fresh uncertainty for employees seeking permanent residency in the US, particularly those whose applications have not yet been completed.

title: Expert explains: Why is Kenyan President William Ruto targeting Indian companies?

content.value: Kenyan President William Ruto’s recent public announcement ordering Tata Chemicals to leave its Lake Magadi soda-ash operation has raised a larger question in India: Why are two major Indian companies, earlier Adani and now Tata, finding themselves on the wrong side of Ruto’s government?

Back in 2024, Ruto cancelled the proposed Adani Group concession for upgrading and operating Nairobi’s Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. So, is Kenya turning against India? And if Tata is being pushed out now, who does Ruto want to bring in?

The short answer is that there is no evidence yet of a deliberate Kenyan policy to replace Indian companies with companies from another country. But there is increasing evidence of a more assertive Kenyan economic nationalism in which foreign investors are expected to deliver much greater local value, employment and industrialisation.
Why Tata?

Ruto’s immediate complaint is clear. Tata Chemicals Magadi extracts soda ash (or sodium carbonate, used in industries such as glass manufacturing) from Lake Magadi in Kajiado County, much of which is exported. It is the largest such plant in Africa. Ruto argues that Kenya has allowed a foreign company to exploit an important natural resource for decades without creating enough downstream industry in the region.

During his visit to Kajiado on September 3, Ruto said Tata had held rights to the resource for about a century but had not built factories or generated sufficient local economic activity. He said Kenya would instead bring in new investors required to establish a large glass factory and a chemical-processing plant in Kajiado. The next day, he said a bidding process would be introduced.

However, Tata Chemicals only acquired Magadi Soda in 2005 from Brunner Mond Ltd., which had held the 1911 concession from 1991 onwards, taking it from the UK’s Imperial Chemical Industries. This timeline is important, in that it shows how Ruto’s target is not simply Tata’s ownership but the broader business model. He wants Kenya to move from extracting and exporting soda ash to processing it locally and capturing more of the value chain.

There is also a regulatory dimension. In July, Kenya suspended Tata’s operations and exports, citing issues including mineral-beneficiation plans, royalty reconciliation, export reporting and community-development obligations. Tata subsequently submitted the requested documentation and says it is fully compliant and awaiting the ministry’s direction. While this is underway, an unverified announcement emerged.
Thus, Tata’s position is that this is a regulatory dispute which should be resolved through due process. Ruto has elevated it into a question of national economic sovereignty.
But why Indian companies?
That two Indian companies have come under the government’s lens of late becomes politically uncomfortable for India.

In 2024, Ruto cancelled the approximately $2.5 billion Adani Group proposal, which became highly controversial in Kenya because of concerns over the concession terms. The new contract with China Communications Construction Co. (CCCC) is nearly 50% more expensive than the original Adani proposal, shifting the financial framework from a private investment-led model to one that depends on commercial loans and future user levies.

The Tata case is different in substance. Tata has operated Magadi since 2005, and its legal rights derive from a much older lease arrangement. The company also points to substantial investment, employment and community programmes, as well as recent investment in a 5-MW solar plant and an electric calciner.

Yet the political optics are striking: within two years, two of India’s best-known corporate groups have encountered major reverses under the same Kenyan president who is otherwise seen as friendly to India. He had a state visit in December 2023. While seeking more Indian Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) into Kenya, Ruto invited Indian companies to ‘take advantage of the conducive and attractive environment to invest in Kenya.’ The events since then naturally raise questions.
Who might Ruto want to favour?

So far, it is not known which companies Ruto wants to bring into Magadi. It would therefore be premature to argue that Ruto is deliberately replacing Tata with Chinese or Western companies. They may well be local interests looking to explore the other critical minerals expected to be found in the Magadi basin.

In the past, Ruto has publicly courted investors from many countries, including Chinese businesspeople, but his investment agenda has been broader: manufacturing, agro-processing, ICT, healthcare, energy and other sectors. In March 2026, he announced more than $2.9 billion in investment deals involving 20 investors.
Kenya’s stated objective now is to find investors willing to undertake downstream industrialisation, rather than simply continue the existing export-oriented model.
What could this mean for India-Kenya ties?

India remains an important economic partner for Kenya, and Indian business has a substantial presence there. Bilateral trade was about $4.31 billion in 2025–26, while Indian companies continue to invest in Kenya. Recent involvement includes major infrastructure and power-sector projects.

But Ruto may be signalling that Kenya’s relationship with foreign investors is changing. For decades, African countries often accepted an investment model in which foreign companies extracted resources, exported them and provided employment, taxes and royalties.

Increasingly, African governments are asking different questions: Why should we export the raw material when we can process it ourselves? Should foreign investors receive long-term access to strategic resources or infrastructure without demonstrating tangible benefits to Kenyan citizens?

For India, the lesson is that its investment in Africa is entering a new political environment. African governments increasingly want investment that visibly creates local industrial capacity, skills, technology, supply chains and jobs. Tata’s may have made substantial contributions by conventional corporate standards, but Ruto is demanding local value addition on a much larger scale.

There is also the matter of precedent. If Kenya can force Tata out after decades of operation, and if the Adani airport concession can be cancelled amid political controversy, Indian companies may reasonably ask whether their contractual rights and long-term investments are sufficiently secure.

India’s answer should probably be neither confrontation nor retreat. It should be a new investment compact: Indian capital and technology, but with deeper local processing, employment, skills and community development; Kenyan access to investment, but with predictable rules, transparent regulation and respect for contracts. And to do this through due process and quietly rather than through public pronouncements.
Rather than a rupture, the Tata-Kenya episode warns that the terms of India’s economic engagement with Africa are changing, and Indian companies may need to adapt.
The author is a former Ambassador to Ethiopia and the African Union.

title: What Saudi Arabia’s execution of Bangladesh nationals tells us about Islamic law

content.value: The Bangladesh government issued a note verbale — an unsigned diplomatic letter — to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia on October 15, requesting clarification about the execution of a Bangladeshi man and woman earlier this week (October 14) in Mecca — an action of which Tarique Rehman’s government was unaware.
The execution was carried out under ta’zir, which is a form of punishment where the determination of the offence and sentence are left in the hands of a judge.

The Saudi Press Agency confirmed the execution of the individuals in a statement, with the Interior Ministry stating that it would enforce Islamic law against any individual found to be violating the sanctity of its mosques.

While the Bangladesh government awaits a response regarding the details of the incident, a question arises about how Saudi Arabia determines which crimes are punishable by death. How much of the system is rooted in Islamic law besides judicial and State discretion? And how have death penalty rulings worked in the past? We explain.
First, what is known about the incident till now?
The complete facts surrounding this incident have not yet been released.

What is known, however, is that a Bangladeshi man and woman were executed on October 14 after a court found them both guilty of an allegedly indecent act inside a mosque in the holy city of Mecca. They had come to Saudi Arabia some time back, according to a Gulf News report.

The following day, the Bangladesh diplomatic mission in Jeddah sent the note verbale to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs seeking clarity on the execution. On October 18, another letter was sent to the Saudi Ambassador in Dhaka.

The ministry has not yet complied with the request for more information, such as the specific mosque, the exact act of “indecency” or the date when the two were arrested. It has been stated that they were tried under ta’zir law.

Earlier, Bangladesh’s The Daily Star newspaper also reported that the consulate general from Bangladesh in Jeddah had sought information about Bangladeshi prisoners in the region. The names of both the deceased were on the list, though it had no information regarding their sentences. Gulf News, however, confirmed that the capital punishment verdict was confirmed after a judicial authority upheld it and a royal order sealed the fate of the two.
How should we understand ta’zir as a part of Islamic Law?
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Bangladesh are both predominantly Muslim nations.

Bangladesh’s system is structured like that of a secular democracy and Islamic Law does not dictate its legal system. Over 90% of the population is Muslim according to the 2022 Population and Housing Census.

Saudi Arabia, on the other hand, predominantly follows the Sharia Law system and the country decides criminal, civil and personal cases based on the same. Yet, state legislature also plays a part in governance, and this varies from nation to nation. For example, the restrictions around women driving are not derived from Islamic law.
The nuance to note here is that Islamic criminal law is not a single uniform code and is deeply subject to interpretation.

Saudi Arabia’s judicial interpretation has largely been rooted in the Hanbali school of interpretation — there are four schools of thought in total — since 1932, when the kingdom was first unified. The Hanbali school affords the least amount of autonomy to the judge and is deeply dependent upon the text of the Quran and hadith, the sayings and traditions of the Prophet Muhammad captured in the Sunna, in its rulings.

For criminal law specifically, classifications broadly agree upon three categories termed hudud, qisas, and ta’zir. Legal scholar Chibli Mallat, in his study Mapping Saudi Criminal Law, describes a system in which certain offences are addressed through legislation while others are dealt with through the classical categories of hudud, qisas and ta’zir.

Hudud laws refer to offences for which Islamic law prescribes fixed punishments. They have been traditionally grounded in the Qur’an and hadith. Commonly cited hudud offences include zina (unlawful sexual intercourse), theft, and, in some interpretations, apostasy or disaffiliation from the religious system.

The classification of seven offences as hudud crimes is based on scholarly interpretation, rather than an explicit list of seven crimes in the Qur’an. The application of hudud punishments is subject to strict evidentiary requirements, which may include eyewitness testimony and specific kinds of proof, depending on the offence and the legal school. These requirements, alongside the principle that hudud punishments should be avoided where reasonable doubt exists, can make convictions difficult to establish, particularly in cases carrying the most severe penalties.

Qisas, colloquially translated as retaliation, provides the victim an avenue to seek retribution. Punishment is varied and specified in the Qur’an. Punishment may include ‘Diya’ or restitution. It is logically different from discretionary punishment. Crimes include murder, both premeditated and non-premeditated, or broader offences against human life.

Ta’zir, meanwhile, refers to discretionary punishment for offences that do not attract a prescribed hadd punishment or fall under the rules of qisas. It can cover a range of conduct, including acts considered harmful to public order or the interests of society. The judge determines the appropriate punishment within the applicable framework.
This last category is particularly significant in Saudi Arabia.

Ta’zir is not confined to a fixed list of offences carrying predetermined penalties and historically judges have been given considerable discretion in deciding the severity of both the crime and the sentence. Indeed, simply because a case is tried under ta’zir does not mean that it shall automatically prescribe the death penalty.
The question, therefore, which the Bangladesh government is likely to have is: what about the conduct of their citizens warranted an execution — especially one that remained undisclosed?
So why did it result in death? And how does Saudi Arabia apply capital punishment?
In 2021, the Saudi government recognised the need for greater predictability in its legal systems, and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman announced a programme of legal reforms in February that year.
The announcement, however, remains different from implementable legislation.

In this case, the central controversy — besides a lack of communication — surrounds ta’zir and the breadth of discretion it can permit. Discretionary punishment is used for a wide range of offences and punishment ranges from imprisonment to fines or, in some cases such as this, execution.

The use of the death penalty for ta’zir offences is particularly contentious because the punishment is not tied to a single, universally accepted list of offences carrying fixed penalties. The questions asked then become about the conduct constituting an offence, the legal principle pointing to the specific sentence, and the safeguards provided to the accused. The scope of ta’zir has been contested by scholars, and modern Saudi legal practice has developed through both inherited jurisprudence and state intervention.

In the wider context, the kingdom executed at least 356 people in 2025 according to Amnesty International’s annual report on capital punishment. The figure for 2024 was 345, with 122 drug offence executions. In 2025, drug-related offences accounted for 240 of the 356 total executions.

For countries such as Bangladesh, whose citizens form a substantial part of Saudi Arabia’s migrant workforce, the stakes extend beyond one case. Access to legal assistance, effective consular communication, and reliable information about criminal proceedings can be critical for citizens facing serious charges abroad.

title: Gautam Gambhir’s ‘right decisions, not popular decisions’: What lessons in ethics can we learn?

content.value: (UPSC Ethics Simplified, a special series under UPSC Essentials by The Indian Express, examines ethical dilemmas through contemporary issues. This edition uses Gautam Gambhir’s remarks on team selection to explore ethical leadership and the principles that guide decision-making.)

“My job is not to make everyone happy. My job is to take the right decisions, not the popular decisions. And that is what I’m there for,” India’s head coach Gautam Gambhir said while defending the team’s selection decisions amid questions over young batter Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s limited opportunities.
The dilemma raises three questions:
1. What are the ethical issues involved in this situation?
2. Should public opinion have any role in the selection process?
3. How can the committee ensure fairness while balancing merit, potential and institutional objectives?

Gambhir’s remarks bring this dilemma into focus: Should decision-makers prioritise public approval or uphold what they believe is right? Ethical decision-making requires more than seeking popularity. It calls for fairness, objectivity and sound reasoning, even when these lead to uncomfortable choices.

Being popular and being right are not mutually exclusive, but they are distinct. Player selection, for instance, requires decision-makers to balance individual merit, potential, performance and the team’s collective interest. Consider this: if MS Dhoni had not been entrusted with the captaincy at a young age, would the world have witnessed the extraordinary leader and sporting legend he became?

Providing opportunities must be guided by merit, potential and the team’s objectives, rather than popularity alone. Ethical decision-making begins with moral sensitivity, followed by moral judgement, moral motivation and moral character. These elements help decision-makers recognise dilemmas, determine the right course of action and find the conviction to act.
Aristotle’s idea of justice: Giving everyone what they deserve

Aristotle believed that justice means giving each person what they deserve. But how do we determine what an individual deserves? His answer is to consider the telos, or the purpose of the thing in question.

Suppose we have excellent flutes. To whom should they be given? Not the wealthiest person, because wealth has no bearing on the ability to play. Nor should they go to someone who simply enjoys possessing them. The purpose of a flute is to be played well. Therefore, Aristotle argues, the flutes should go to the most skilled players.

This reasoning can be applied to institutions and opportunities. If a tennis court exists for playing tennis, the best players should get priority. If a university aims to foster academic excellence, academic merit should inform admission. Aristotle’s idea of distributive justice is relevant whenever limited resources or opportunities must be allocated. Fairness does not always mean treating everyone identically. It means using criteria that are relevant, justifiable and consistent.
Merit, popularity and fairness in sports

In team sports, selectors and coaches have a responsibility to protect the team’s collective interest. Jofra Archer’s inclusion in England’s 2019 World Cup squad after his strong IPL performances is an example. His selection meant dropping a more established option and generated considerable debate. Archer went on to take 20 wickets in the tournament and bowled the Super Over in the final. The decision proved successful.

Similarly, Virender Sehwag’s promotion to the opening position under Sourav Ganguly was an aggressive call. It unlocked one of the most destructive opening batters of the modern era and changed India’s approach to Test cricket.

These examples show that an unconventional decision can become popular and deliver results. However, its ethical worth cannot be judged by the outcome alone. A favourable result may follow an unfair process, while a fair and well-reasoned decision may sometimes produce an unfavourable outcome.

Selectors, coaches and captains must therefore assess players on their contributions, potential and the team’s requirements, rather than seek external praise. Giving high-performing players a consistent run, often described as giving them a long rope, can foster fairness and trust. But this should not become an unconditional entitlement. Past achievements must be balanced against current performance, consistency and team needs.

Decisions driven solely by public pressure can be unjust to players who have demonstrated their abilities. At the same time, disregarding public sentiment entirely may mean overlooking emerging talent or missing an opportunity to strengthen the team. Popularity is neither moral nor immoral in itself. It is one consideration to be weighed against a player’s ability, expertise and the team’s objectives. If a 15-year-old batter can dominate the best players in a league, that talent deserves recognition. An opportunity, however, must also be supported by objective assessment and the team’s requirements.
From sports selection to public administration

The same dilemma arises in public administration. Civil servants may face pressure while selecting welfare beneficiaries, recruiting personnel or allocating limited resources. Decisions must be guided by objective criteria, impartiality and established rules, while remaining sensitive to vulnerable groups. Resisting undue pressure and remaining accountable reflect moral courage and ethical leadership.

Ultimately, ethical leadership is not about making decisions everyone likes. It is about decisions that can be justified on grounds of fairness, merit and the larger public interest. Whether in sport or public administration, decision-makers must balance individual aspirations with collective objectives and remain accountable for their choices, even when challenged publicly. The true test lies not in the applause a decision receives, but in the values and reasoning behind it.

Ethical Takeaway: A decision is not necessarily ethical because it is popular or produces a favourable outcome. Its ethical worth also depends on the principles, fairness and reasoning underlying the decision-making process.

(The writer is the author of ‘Being Good’, ‘Aaiye, Insaan Banaen’, ‘Kyon’ and ‘Ethikos: Stories Searching Happiness’. He teaches courses on and offers training in ethics, values and behaviour. He has been the expert/consultant to SAARC countries, UPSC, Central Bureau of Investigation( CBI),National Judicial Academy, ATI, RAKNPA, Haryana Institute of Public Administration, ISA MountAbu, National Centre for Good Governance,Competition Commission of India (CCI), etc. He has PhD in two disciplines and has been a Doctoral Fellow in Gandhian Studies from ICSSR. His second PhD is from IIT Delhi on Ethical Decision Making among Indian Bureaucrats. He writes for the UPSC Ethics Simplified (concepts and caselets) weekly.)
