Front Page
Blow to Netanyahu as rival Eisenkot gets chance to form new govt in Israel
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Comparison of the Indian constitutional scheme with that of other countries.

What’s the ongoing story: For Benjamin Netanyahu, the battle to remain Israel’s prime minister has entered a new phase. President Isaac Herzog has chosen former military chief and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to make the first attempt at forming a government after an election that left neither side with the numbers to rule.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Know the composition and role of the Knesset in Israel’s parliamentary system.
• How does government formation work in Israel?
• What are the main features of Israel’s parliamentary system?
• Compare and Contrast single-party majority government and a coalition government. (Illustrate your answer with reference to the Israeli election and India’s parliamentary experience)
• What is the electoral threshold in Israel?
• What can be the implications of a prolonged government-formation process for political stability and continuity in Israel?
• How Israel’s 2026 election and the subsequent government-formation process illustrate the opportunities and limitations of coalition politics in a parliamentary democracy?
Key Takeaways:

• Eisenkot, 66, emerged as Netanyahu’s principal challenger in the October 27 election, which ended without a clear parliamentary majority. While Netanyahu’s Likud remained the largest single party, his wider religious-nationalist coalition fell short of the numbers needed to govern.

• Eisenkot’s appointment gives the opposition its first opportunity to put together an alternative government, although the difficult negotiations ahead mean Netanyahu’s departure is far from certain.

• News agency Associated Press reported that representatives of most of Israel’s major political parties recommended Eisenkot during consultations with Herzog this week. The Israeli president subsequently announced that he would give the former military chief the first opportunity to assemble a governing coalition.

• News agency Reuters reported that Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government, with a possible extension of another 14 days. The appointment marks an important moment for a politician who entered electoral politics only in 2022 but has since emerged as one of the most prominent challengers to Netanyahu.
• The October 27 election produced a fragmented Knesset, Israel’s 120-member parliament, with neither of the two main political camps securing the 61 seats required for a majority.
Do You Know:

• The Knesset has 120 seats, so a government needs 61 to hold a majority. Israel uses proportional representation, which means parties win seats in line with their share of the vote. For that reason, every Israeli government has been a coalition of several parties.
• If no bloc can reach 61 seats, a minority government is possible. If that fails too, new elections can be called, and Netanyahu would stay on as interim prime minister until then.

• Eisenkot formed his Yashar Party only last year, and part of his appeal is his military record and his status as a newcomer to politics. His son, a soldier, was killed in the first months of the Gaza war. Eisenkot sat in Netanyahu’s war cabinet until he resigned in 2024 over how the war was handled, and his campaign calls for accountability over the failures that led to October 7.

• Israel is a parliamentary democracy with three main branches of power: the legislative, executive, and judiciary. The country has a unicameral (single-house) parliament, composed of 120 members. Members of the Knesset (MKs) are elected nationally for four-year terms.

• The prime minister holds the executive power. The government depends directly on the confidence of the Knesset and must maintain a working majority (at least 61 seats) to govern. Headed by the Supreme Court, the judiciary acts independently to interpret basic laws and review legislation. National elections in Israel are administered and overseen by the CEC.

• In Israel’s party-list proportional representation system, the electoral threshold is the minimum percentage of the total nationwide vote a political party must receive to enter parliament. The threshold is currently set at 3.25% — a standard established by Knesset legislation in 2014. Crossing this hurdle grants a party a baseline of at least 4 seats out of the 120 total Knesset seats. If a party fails to reach the 3.25% mark, all votes cast for its slate are discarded, producing “wasted votes” that are reallocated among the parties that succeeded.

• The main purpose of the threshold is to balance representation with political stability by preventing extreme parliamentary fragmentation and keeping micro-parties out. Historically, the threshold started at just 1% in 1951 before being gradually raised to 1.5% (1992), 2% (2003), and finally 3.25% (2014), notes Prof. Ofer Kenig, a researcher at the Israeli Democracy Institute.

Explained
The Centre-state divide in food safety regulation
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources.

What’s the ongoing story: The Maharashtra government, through its Food Safety Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, recently went to the Bombay High Court against the national regulator, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), alleging that it had created a parallel regulatory mechanism and encroached on the state’s powers.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What are the objectives and major provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with reference to the regulation of food businesses in India?
• Know the respective roles of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and State Food Safety Commissioners in ensuring food safety.
• What are the functions of Food Safety Officers and Designated Officers under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006?
• How are food businesses classified into registration, State licensing and Central licensing categories?
• Why has Maharashtra challenged the FSSAI’s May 2023 order concerning inspections of centrally licensed food businesses?
• How can ambiguity in determining the turnover of food businesses affect licensing, regulatory compliance and enforcement of food safety standards?
Key Takeaways:

• Mundhe — known for taking strict action against food businesses and highlighting huge markups charged by hospitals on medicines and consumables — has said that the Centre has put restrictions on the powers of the commissioner and his officers.

• The petition has put the spotlight on how food safety is regulated in India at both Central and state levels. We explain the division of responsibilities in terms of monitoring food safety, the points of contention in Maharashtra’s plea, and the challenges that arise out of the division of responsibilities.
• The Maharashtra government’s petition raises several important issues in the implementation of the 2006 Act.

• The petition says that while the enforcement of the Act should have rested with the state Commissioners, FSSAI created a parallel mechanism through its May 2023 order. The order, which was meant to clarify the procedure for enforcement on Centrally licensed food businesses, said that inspections of such facilities will be carried out by the “Central food safety officers”.
Do You Know:

• Section 31(3) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, states: “Any person desirous to commence or carry on any food business shall make an application for grant of a licence to the Designated Officer in such manner containing such particulars and fees as may be specified by regulations.” A Designated Officer, as defined under Section 36, is responsible for food safety administration of a specified area (usually a district), who is appointed by the Commissioner of Food Safety, who is responsible for the entire state.

• The Act also empowers the Commissioner to appoint Food Safety Officers (FSOs) for specified local jurisdictions to carry out inspections and seizures in case of complaints or contraventions. These FSOs report to the district-level Designated Officer.

• In its order dated March 13, 2026, the FSSAI said that food businesses with annual turnover of up to Rs 1.5 crore can get a registration, those with turnover up to Rs 50 crore need a state licence, and those above Rs 50 crore need a Central licence. Before this, companies with annual turnover of Rs 12 lakh needed a registration, those with Rs 12 lakh to Rs 20 crore needed a state licence, and those with turnover of more than Rs 20 crore needed a Central licence. This included food businesses with large footprints, those operating across state lines, those dealing with large quantities of high risk foods such as milk and meat products, and those manufacturing food products for export.

• The FSSAI, in an earlier order dated May 12, 2023, had said that all Centrally licensed food businesses have to be inspected by the Central FSOs. The state officers are allowed to carry out inspection only in certain cases:
—when there is an incident or emergency where immediate action is necessary;
—when the state authority is carrying out any special drives, only with prior permission of the state Commissioner and prior intimation to the Regional Director of FSSAI; and
—in case of VIP duty where time is of the essence.

• Even in cases where inspection is carried out and samples collected by the state food officers, the reports have to be submitted to the Central licensing authority, with the consequent proceedings and appeals undertaken by the Central authority.

Meet the Siddis: Tribal Gujaratis from Kathiawad, natural athletes of African stock
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Indian Polity and Governance-Constitution, Public Policy, Rights Issues, etc., Economic and Social Development
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections of the population by the Centre and States and the performance of these schemes;
What’s the ongoing story: Fifteen-year-old Khushbu Rajakbhai Darjada made history this week, becoming the first Siddi athlete – and only the second Indian – to win a Youth Olympics medal in judo.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Who are the Siddis of Gujarat?
• What is the historical origins of siddis and the different accounts associated with their migration to India?
• Know the geographical distribution of the Siddi community in Gujarat.
• Know the historical and cultural significance of the Siddi community’s traditional dhamal dance.
• How African ancestry, Gujarati language and Kathiawadi traditions influenced the cultural identity of the Siddis.
Key Takeaways:

• Siddis – also known as Siddi Badshah, apparently because of their “free-bird” attitude towards life – are one of the five primitive tribes of Gujarat who are physically identifiable by their distinct East African features and hair.

• But their appearance is literally skin-deep – an identifier of genetic descent, but little else. The Siddis are Kathiawadis who speak Gujarati with a Kathiawadi accent, and eat and dress like other Gujaratis. Members of the community also live in Maharashtra, Goa, Diu, and Daman.

• The Siddi population of Gujarat is concentrated in 18 villages of Talala taluka in Gir Somnath district. Some members of the community also live in the districts of Junagadh, Jamnagar, Bhavnagar, Rajkot, Porbandar, Amreli and Surendranagar.

• The central government told Rajya Sabha in July 2025 that according to a survey carried out among the community, the population of Siddis in Gujarat who are classified as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG) is 12,959.

• The Siddis of Gir Somnath live in close proximity to the Gir National Park, the only natural home (along with some other parts of Gujarat) of the Asiatic lion. The forest sustains many Siddi livelihoods – members of the tribe are often employed as guides, drivers, and labourers in the national park and wildlife sanctuary.

• Among the Siddi villages of Talala taluka, Talala and Jambur are the best known. Jambur, located around 25 km from Gir National Park, is often called “Mini Africa” for its prominent Siddi community. Sirvan, Javantri, Madhupur, Surva, Moruka, and Hadmatiya are among the other villages with considerable Siddi populations.

• Overall, Gujarat’s Siddi population is small. The 1991 Census recorded 6,336 Siddis in the state, which rose to 8,662 in 2001, with roughly equal numbers of males and females. The 2011 Census found almost the same number of Siddis in Gujarat.
Do You Know:

• “There are various views on how the first Siddis came to India, but there is no definitive record of their arrival,” C C Chaudhari, Executive Director of the Gujarat Tribal Research and Training Society (GTRTS) under the
state’s Tribal Development Department, said.

• “There is a view that the first Siddis were brought to India from Africa by the Portuguese colonists who enslaved them. Others believe that the Siddis were purchased as slaves and brought to India by overland routes by the various invaders from Central and West Asia who came to India during the medieval period,” Chaudhari told The Indian Express.

• The GTRTS’s note on the Siddis on its website says: “According to Census (1931), the Siddis appear to have been brought to India by the Portuguese towards the end of 17th century, presumably as slaves; while Russel and Hira Lal (1916) state that they have come to India in the middle of 15th century.”

• Some members of the Siddi community believe their ancestors were invited to Gujarat by the nawabs of Junagadh, who settled them in their kingdom.
“Around 700 years ago, a nawab of Junagadh travelled to Africa and was impressed by the physical strength of the members of the native population. He brought along a few African families to act as his ‘balwaans’ (strongmen) or ‘angrakshaks’ (bodyguards), and to take care of captive lions. Since the king was Muslim, our ancestors too adopted Islam,” Sadikbhai Makwana, a ‘patel’ or leader of the Siddi jamaat (traditional community council) in Talala told The Indian Express.
• According to ‘Primitive Tribal Groups of Gujarat’ published by GTRTS, there are “several stories” about the “Siddis’ habitation in Gujarat”.

• Researcher Pravin Patel told this newspaper that like many other tribal communities, the Siddis were essentially simple folk who liked to live happy, uncomplicated lives. They are predominantly non-vegetarian, whose food is typically Kathiawadi.
“They are considered to be very kindhearted and simple in nature; people who believe in living as free birds, careless about tomorrow’s worries and happy to be by themselves. Perhaps that is why Siddis are known as ‘Siddi Badshah’, or ‘carefree kings’. Siddis themselves address each other by this name,” Patel said. According to the
Oxford Dictionary, the word ‘Siddi’ probably derives from the Arabic ‘Saiyad’, loosely meaning a ‘prince’.

• Siddis are often considered synonymous with ‘dhamal’, the traditional folk dance that is believed to have African origins. The popular and auspicious dance is performed by groups of 8-10 dancers, and is dedicated to Baba Gor.
Dancers dress in clothes made of animal skin and feathered headgear, and move energetically to the beats and rhythm of large and small drums, mimicking the calls of animals such as tiger, deer, and goat.
While both men and women participate in other kinds of Siddi dance, the ‘dhamal’ is performed only by men.

• In 1956, the central government declared Siddis as a Scheduled Tribe (ST), and identified Siddi populations based on where they lived: “in the districts of Halar (North West region), Madhya Saurashtra (Central), Zalawad (North East), Gohilwad (South East), and Sorath (South West)”.

• In 1982, the Government of India declared the Siddis and Padhars as “primitive tribal groups”. The Kotwalias and Kathodis had been declared primitive tribes a few years earlier in 1978. Today, Gujarati Siddis residing in Saurashtra – including in the districts of Junagadh, Amreli, Rajkot, Jamnagar, Surendranagar and Bhavnagar – are included in the list of STs, but members of the community who live outside the Saurashtra region, in places such as Bharuch, are not. Siddis living outside Saurashtra are classified as a Socially and Economically Backward Community (SEBC).

The Editorial Page
Net Zero transition brings opportunity to build, not just import, technology
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: General issues on Environmental ecology, Bio-diversity and Climate Change – that do not require subject specialization.
Mains Examination: General Studies III: Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, environmental impact assessment.

What’s the ongoing story: Ramakrishna R Sonde Writes— There is a persistent weakness in India’s technological ambitions: The difficulty of taking research from the laboratory to industrial deployment.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is net zero?
• Why is net zero important?
• How can net zero be achieved?
• Is there a global effort to reach net zero?
• Are we on track to reach net zero by 2050?
• Difference between ‘Net Zero’ and ‘Carbon Neutral’?
• How can net zero be achieved?
• How the transition towards Net Zero can create opportunities for India’s industrial and technological development?
• What are Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs)?
• Why does the transition from laboratory research to industrial-scale deployment remain a major challenge for India’s scientific and industrial ecosystem?
Key Takeaways:
Ramakrishna R Sonde Writes—

• Why does a country with excellent scientific institutions and a strong industrial base struggle to turn its intellectual capital into technologies of its own? Atmanirbhar Bharat cannot just mean manufacturing equipment in India while importing the underlying process know-how, critical materials, catalysts, membranes, engineering designs and intellectual property. Such manufacturing creates jobs and economic value, but it does not necessarily deliver technological independence.

• True atmanirbharta must mean progressively moving from know-how — from importing technologies — to know-why in India (generating IPRs — intellectual property rights), show-how in India (design thinking capabilities), develop how in India (integration of many sub systems) and then improve in India (more IPRs for technology protection) — in addition to Make in India.

• One, technology development takes time. In sectors such as energy, steel, cement, chemicals and fertilisers, laboratory discoveries must progress through pilot plants to industrial demonstration. Laboratories have to become pilot plants. Pilot plants must become demonstration plants. Equipment fails, materials behave differently at scale, and processes must become safe, reliable and cost-competitive. This requires patient capital and a willingness to accept failure.

• Two, industry understandably wants proven technology. Companies cannot risk production or commit unlimited resources to untested ideas. This creates a paradox: If everyone wants proven technology, who will prove a new Indian technology for the first time? The answer lies in sharing development risks rather than leaving industry or academia to shoulder them alone.

• Three, technology development is a complex process, commonly described through nine technology readiness levels, or TRLs. A scientific idea begins at lower levels and progresses through laboratory validation, pilot demonstration and finally commercial deployment.

• Four, collaboration hasn’t been sufficient. Scientists, engineers, equipment manufacturers, plant operators and policymakers must work together throughout technology development, not merely meet periodically as consortium partners. Academia must understand industrial problems; industry must recognise what research can contribute. Universities, too, must break disciplinary silos.

• Five, nobody owns this journey. Government funds research, academia generates knowledge and industry commercialises technology. But who takes responsibility for carrying promising ideas through demonstration? India needs mechanisms that bring all three together from the outset, with shared responsibilities and financial contributions that evolve as technologies mature.

Do You Know:
Ramakrishna R Sonde Writes—

• The transition to Net Zero emissions offers India an extraordinary opportunity. Green hydrogen, carbon capture and utilisation, energy storage, sustainable fuels, new materials and circular manufacturing are not merely environmental necessities. They represent perhaps the largest industrial technology transition since the Industrial Revolution, which will reshape steel, cement, chemicals, fertilisers, transport and power over the coming decades.

• AI can accelerate materials discovery, process modelling and equipment design. But it cannot eliminate the need to demonstrate and operate real industrial hardware. We should use this transition to create Indian technology.

• India’s atomic energy programme offers important lessons. Faced with restrictions on access to advanced technologies, the country developed capabilities of its own. In hindsight, perhaps technology denial brought out the best in us. Something else was equally important: Scientific leadership. Our leaders created a sense of national mission, freedom for scientists and engineers, trust in young people and acceptance of failure as part of technological progress.

• That spirit needs to be renewed, not by isolating India from global technology, but by building domestic capabilities alongside it. India has the scientists, industries, entrepreneurs, capital and the target market. It lacks a reliable bridge between scientific discovery and industrial application. Deep-tech incubators and demonstration centres bridge the gap between academia and industry.

• Atmanirbhar Bharat must be measured not just by how much equipment India manufactures, but by how much technology it develops, owns, improves and confidently deploys. Building that bridge holds the key to the ambition of becoming Viksit Bharat.

The Ideas Page
With decline in poverty, shift focus—from free food to nutritional security
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Economic and Social Development-Sustainable Development, Poverty, Inclusion, Demographics, Social Sector Initiatives, etc.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Government policies and interventions for development in various sectors and issues arising out of their design and implementation.

What’s the ongoing story: Ashok Gulati, Ritika Juneja, Sulakshana Rao Writes—Nutritional security also demands that our basic staples are biofortified with iron and zinc, as wheat and rice have become deficient in these. This is a result of impoverished soils, starved of soil organic carbon.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What are the key takeaways from the World Bank’s India Poverty and Equity Brief?
• How food security is different from nutritional security?
• Why is access to adequate calories alone insufficient to ensure nutritional well-being?
• What is the significance of the World Bank’s poverty estimates in assessing India’s progress in poverty reduction?
• What is multidimensional poverty?
• How indicators relating to health, nutrition, education and living standards provide a broader understanding of poverty?
• Know the objectives of the National Food Security Act, 2013, and its role in ensuring food access for vulnerable sections of society.
• What is biofortification?

Key Takeaways:
Ashok Gulati, Ritika Juneja, Sulakshana Rao Writes—

• The World Bank’s India Poverty and Equity Brief, released in October 2026, has renewed the debate on poverty in India. It shows extreme poverty, measured at the international line of $3.00 per person per day (2021, Purchasing Power Parity or PPP), falling from 27.1 per cent in 2011 to 2.6 per cent in 2023.

• At $4.20 a day, poverty fell from 57.7 per cent to 16.1 per cent over the same period, which the Bank calls one of the fastest declines in the world. The estimates draw on three official household consumption and expenditure surveys (HCES): The 2011–12, 2022–23 and 2023–24 HCES. The Bank cautions that part of the latest gain reflects better measurement, not just better lives.

• The World Bank’s long series on poverty status tells a more interesting story. In 1983, 78 per cent of Indians lived below $4.20 a day (PPP). By 2004, after two decades that included the 1991 economic reforms, the figure was still at 74.5 per cent, a decline of just 0.2 per cent a year.

• At $3 a day, poverty fell from 46.4 per cent in 2004 to 2.6 per cent in 2023, about 14 per cent a year, against 0.4 per cent during 1983–2004. NITI Aayog’s multidimensional poverty index, built from 12 indicators of health, nutrition, education and living standards, also tells a similar story: Poverty fell from 55.3 per cent in 2005 to 11.3 per cent in 2022. Statistically, 2004 is the inflection point in India’s poverty.

• The Labour Bureau’s data also show that real farm wages grew at 5.4 per cent between 2004-05 and 2013-14. However, this has slowed down drastically since 2014-15, and yet it has reduced poverty. That seems somewhat paradoxical. An uncomfortable fact is also that employment in agriculture rose from 42.5 per cent in 2018-19 to 46.5 per cent in 2020-21, as lockdowns pushed workers back to villages, before settling at 43 per cent in 2025-26.

Do You Know:
Ashok Gulati, Ritika Juneja, Sulakshana Rao Writes—

• Welfare measures such as MGNREGA, rolled out in 2006, and the National Food Security Act of 2013 (rechristened as PM-Garib Kalyan Yojana, or PM-GKY) may have also played a role in reducing poverty. This is especially true when food allocations were enhanced to 10 kg/person/month during the Covid period.

• The Centre has since extended PM-GKY for five years, from 2024 to about 81 crore beneficiaries. However, now with the economy back on track and extreme poverty down at 2.6 per cent, this extensive coverage under PM-GKY is hard to justify. The cost is steep: PM-GKY is budgeted at Rs 2.27 lakh crore in 2026-27. It raises a fundamental question: If extreme poverty is down to 2.6 per cent, why give free food to more than half the population? This needs rationalisation. Late PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s formula of giving free to antyodya (the poorest of the poor) and charging at least half the procurement price to others may be a useful one today. As the adage goes, it is better to teach a person how to catch fish than to hand out a free fish every day.

• Reform is a continuous process, and the time has come to rationalise the food subsidy bill and reorient it towards nutritional security. Our malnutrition numbers, especially of children below the age of five, are still very high. India cannot become Viksit Bharat if malnutrition remains high, and PM-GKY, in its current form, by giving wheat and rice, cannot solve this problem.

• India’s SOC hovers around 0.3 per cent as against a desirable level of 1.5 to 2.0, according to World Food Laureate, Rattan Lal. Diversifying diets and the production basket can improve nutrition. Can the Modi government bite the bullet and improve the nutrition of soils, crops and people? Only time will tell.

Economy
AI has made Taiwan the world’s fastest growing large economy
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies III: Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilization, of resources, growth, development and employment.

What’s the ongoing story: India, for several years, has been flying the flag of the world’s fastest growing large economy. But that won’t be the case this year. In 2026, it is Taiwan that is posting eye-watering growth numbers. All thanks to artificial intelligence (AI).
Key Points to Ponder:
• How does growing global demand for AI technologies influence investment, manufacturing and exports in semiconductor-producing economies?
• What is the relationship between investment, exports and GDP growth with reference to Taiwan’s economic performance in 2026?
• What is the significance of advanced semiconductor manufacturing for the development of high-performance computing and AI infrastructure?
• What are semiconductors?
• What is the role of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) in the global semiconductor supply chain?
• What is the relationship between investment, exports and GDP growth with reference to Taiwan’s economic performance in 2026?
Key Takeaways:

• Data released on Friday showed Taiwan’s GDP grew by a stunning 14.36% in the July-September quarter, in real terms, which means after adjusting for inflation. This follows 15.43% in the January-March quarter and 12.93% in April-June. And according to Taiwan’s Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, growth in 2026 as a whole is expected to be 11.05% and 6.04% in 2027. In 2025, it had grown by 8.76%.
• Economists think these are underestimates and growth will be close to 13% in 2026 and north of 6.5% next year.
• In comparison, India’s GDP growth rate in the first two quarters of 2026 have been 8.6% and 7.8%, respectively – very high, but not a patch on Taiwan.

• But is Taiwan even a large economy? India, for instance, is 90 times larger and 60 times more populous. But the difference in their GDP is not as big: almost $4 trillion for India and $1 trillion for Taiwan. In 2025, it was the 22nd largest economy in the world, ahead of the likes of Singapore, Norway, and South Africa. So, it’s certainly not a small economy.

• Key to Taiwan’s astonishing growth is perhaps the most important company in the world: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC. It is the world’s largest manufacturer of semiconductor chips and the primary supplier to Nvidia, which was the world’s most valuable company until Apple overtook it on Friday. Both the companies have a market capitalisation of about $5 trillion.

• But it’s the company in 6th place, with a market cap of $2 trillion, without which the world can’t function. The European Centre for International Political Economy estimated in January that TSMC is nearly a tenth of Taiwan’s GDP. But that was then: its net revenue in 2026 is seen at $175 billion, 43% higher than last year.

• TSMC is one of the key companies at the centre of the global AI investment boom. And this spending spree is what is fuelling Taiwan’s growth. In July-September, Taiwan’s investments were up 26.36% year-on-year and responsible for almost half the growth rate of 14.36%.

• The other major driver was exports – after all, TSMC’s semiconductor chips have to be exported – which were up 21.12%, with net exports explaining a third of the headline GDP growth rate. In September, Taiwan posted a record trade surplus of $23.63 billion after exports jumped 61% to $87.22 billion.
Do You Know:
• Taiwan, of course, is not the only country that is being driven by the AI investment boom.

• In South Korea – dominated by tech giants Samsung and SK Hynix – growth in July-September was 3.4%, data released last week showed. This follows 3.8% and 3.7% in the first two quarters. While this doesn’t sound as impressive as Taiwan’s numbers, two things are worth keeping in mind: one, South Korea’s GDP is twice that of Taiwan; two, growth in 2025 was just 1.1%.

India ready to help set up food corridors, says Zelenskyy after phone call with Modi
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Main Examination: General Studies II: Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India’s interests.

What’s the ongoing story: Ahead of the US-brokered two-day peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi starting Tuesday, India on Monday reached out to the top political leadership in Kyiv and Moscow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy while External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar spoke to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What are the major takeaways from the India’s proposed approach to easing tensions in the Black Sea region?
• Why India’s willingness to mediate in establishing food corridors is significant?
• How the Russia-Ukraine conflict has transformed the relationship between maritime security, agricultural exports and humanitarian concerns?
• How have disruptions to grain exports through the Black Sea affected global food security, particularly in Africa, West Asia and Asia?
• Map Work- Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi
• Know the significance of Ukraine’s three major Black Sea ports — Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi.
• Discuss the historical and geopolitical factors that led to the Russia-Ukraine war.
• What has been India’s stance in the Russia-Ukraine conflict?
Key Takeaways:

• In a post on X after his phone call with Modi, Zelenskyy said they discussed “Russia’s blocking of grain exports via the Black Sea” and added that India was ready to “mediate in establishing food corridors”.

• This is the first time Zelenskyy has spoken out on the Indian proposal to broker a ceasefire in the Black Sea, which has witnessed attacks on Ukrainian grain exports. In a post on X, Modi said he “reiterated India’s firm commitment to contributing in every possible way towards a peaceful resolution”.

• “Glad to have had a productive telephone conversation with President Zelenskyy. We reviewed our wide-ranging bilateral cooperation and agreed to further strengthen India-Ukraine ties,” Modi said. “I thanked President Zelenskyy for sharing his perspectives on the ongoing conflict, its humanitarian aspects and various efforts to restore peace,” he said.

• Zelenskyy said that he briefed Modi on the latest diplomatic developments. “It is important that India identify what steps it can take and what dialogue it can pursue with other leaders to help bring the war to an end. Food security could be one such area. We discussed Russia’s blocking of grain exports via the Black Sea. India is ready to mediate in establishing food corridors, and we are counting on these efforts to continue,” Zelenskyy said in his post.
Do You Know:

• Ukraine, in particular, is a major agricultural exporter. Russia has targeted Ukrainian port facilities and vessel operations around the Greater Odesa region on the Black Sea coast. Ukraine has three key deep-water ports there — Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi — which handle around 90% of its agricultural exports. Since mid-July, Ukraine has also stepped up attacks on grain vessels, maritime infrastructure and ports on the Sea of Azov and the vital Kerch Strait that connects it to the Black Sea.
• Russia exports significant volumes of grain through the Azov-Black Sea region — approximately 42-44 million tonnes, or 77-81% of its total grain exports, is transported through this area.

• The broad contours of the proposal revolve around easing the especially intense fighting since July around the critical Black Sea region, which would allow Ukraine’s agricultural products to reach the world; Russia halting attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure; and Ukraine refraining from attacking Russian positions along the line of contact. Of particular interest in the proposal is the larger Black Sea region — a key grain export hub for the world. The fighting there could put at least 400 million people in Africa, West Asia and Asia at risk of food shortages, malnutrition and hunger.

Hasina seeks fresh passport, Bangla minister for extradition
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: India and its neighbourhood- relations.

What’s the ongoing story: Three months after she expressed a desire to return to her country, former prime minister of Bangladesh Sheikh Hasina on Monday requested a new passport to facilitate that journey in December.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What legal and diplomatic considerations must India take into account when it comes to former prime minister of Bangladesh Sheikh Hasina?
• How can the presence of a former head of government in a neighbouring country create diplomatic complications, particularly when the home country seeks extradition?
• What are the key highlights of the India-Bangladesh Extradition Treaty?
• How can India maintain stable relations with Bangladesh amid political changes in Dhaka?
• India and Bangladesh Bilateral Relations-Know in Detail
• India and Bangladesh Bilateral Relations after August 2024-how things changed drastically?
• What are the areas of cooperation between India and Bangladesh?
• What are the issues and challenges between India and Bangladesh?
• How can India and Bangladesh strengthen their relations?
• What is the significance of Bangladesh for India?
• How external influences is shaping domestic policies in Bangladesh?
Key Takeaways:

• Hasina, who fled Bangladesh in August 2024 after a student-led mass uprising, has been living in India for more than two years. On August 5 this year, which marked the second anniversary of her government’s collapse, she made public her intention to return.

• In a letter to Bangladesh’s Acting High Commissioner to India, Preeti Rahman, in Delhi, Hasina’s lawyers wrote, “In view of the reported revocation of her existing Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card by the interim government and other authorities,… respectfully request that you take the necessary steps to issue a new Bangladeshi passport and NID for our client.”

• The letter also asked for the application to be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of her Bangladeshi nationality and in accordance with “obligations arising under international human rights instruments”.

• However, Bangladesh High Commission’s spokesperson Saidur Rahman, responding to questions about the letter, told The Indian Express on Monday, “Former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was ousted following the student-people uprising, has not applied for a new passport or National Identity Card (NID).”

• “We have received an email from a law firm requesting the issuance of a new passport and NID in the name of Sheikh Hasina. However, we are not sure whether the request is genuine. There is no way for us to verify whether the request was actually made on behalf of Sheikh Hasina, as the email sent by the law firm did not include any authorisation letter or supporting documents proving that the firm was authorised by her to make such a request,” Rahman said.
• The Bangladesh government led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has been seeking Hasina’s extradition and the Indian government had said earlier that this request is “being examined”.
Do You Know:

• The India-Bangladesh Extradition Treaty was signed on January 28, 2013, and later amended in 2016. It allows both nations to extradite individuals charged or convicted of offenses punishable by a minimum of one year in prison, operating under the core principle of dual criminality.

• Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since fleeing a student-led uprising in August 2024. Her presence in New Delhi remains a sensitive diplomatic issue. While Dhaka has requested her extradition and expressed concern over her political statements from Indian soil, India maintains that private virtual events hosted for her carry no government endorsement.

Pumped hydro project in tiger corridor gets in-principle forest nod
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance
Main Examination: General Studies III: Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, environmental impact assessment.

What’s the ongoing story:A Union Environment Ministry panel has recommended an in-principle approval to divert 511 hectares of forest land within the Panna-Ranipur Tiger Corridor to make way for the 1,800 MW Panari Pumped Storage Project.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is a pumped storage hydropower project?
• Map Work- Panna-Ranipur Tiger Corridor
• Know about Panna-Ranipur Tiger Corridor
• How do tiger corridors help in maintaining landscape-level conservation?
• What are the challenges involved in balancing Panari Pumped Storage Project development with wildlife conservation?
• What is the significance of the Panari Pumped Storage Project for renewable energy integration and electricity grid stability in India?
• What is the role of the Forest Advisory Committee (FAC) in examining proposals for diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes?
Key Takeaways:

• The Forest Advisory Committee (FAC) recommended clearance for the project by Sri Siddharth Infratech and Services spanning Satna and Panna districts during its October 23 meeting, chaired by the Director General of Forests and Special Secretary, Environment Ministry.
• The tiger corridor connects the forests of the Panna Tiger Reserve, across the Satna and Panna districts, to the Ranipur Tiger Reserve in Chitrakoot, Uttar Pradesh.
• Incidentally, the Ranipur Tiger Reserve was notified in 2022 to compensate for the forest submergence in Panna’s core zone caused by the Ken-Betwa river linking project.

• “A total of 211.7 hectares of the proposed area falls under compartment P-132, 133, 135, 136, 137, which is part of NTCA-approved North Eastern Tiger Corridor of Panna Tiger Reserve,” the meeting’s minutes noted. As per tentative enumeration figures, approximately 1.32 lakh trees are proposed to be felled, including 70,240 in Satna and 62,278 in the North Panna forest divisions.
Do You Know:

• The project was first taken up for appraisal on February 27, but a decision was deferred to await recommendations from the Standing Committee of the National Board for Wildlife. Later, the SC-NBWL, chaired by the Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav, recommended the project for wildlife clearance with specific conditions during its July 9 meeting.

• The project will consist of two reservoirs, which are to be constructed afresh. The upper reservoir is planned in Panari village under Devendra Nagar Range of North Panna Forest division in Panna district, and the lower reservoir is planned on the Baghain river, in Barondha range of the Satna forest division, the FAC minutes noted.

• A pumped storage project uses the elevation difference between an upper and a lower reservoir. During periods of low electricity demand, water is pumped from the lower reservoir to the upper reservoir to store energy. When electricity demand peaks, the stored water is released back down through turbines to generate power.

• The NBWL had appraised the project as it lies within an “ecological sensitive tiger landscape and supports movement of tigers, leopards, dholes, wolves, sloth bears, gaurs, sambar and chital”, with some components overlapping the satellite core areas of the Panna Tiger Reserve.

• The conditions specified included the construction of three 30-meter-wide wildlife overpasses across the frequently used Baghain River. While recommending the project, the SC-NBWL also noted reservations expressed by field officers regarding the possible fragmentation of the wildlife corridor.

Climate meet begins, report says 2026 among warmest years ever
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination:
• General Studies II: Important International institutions, agencies and fora- their structure, mandate
• General Studies III: Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, environmental impact assessment.

What’s the ongoing story: The annual year-ending climate meeting opened in the Turkish city of Antalya on Monday with another sobering reminder from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) about the steadily worsening climate situation.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What exactly did the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warn?
• What are the key takeaways from annual State of the Climate Report, 2026?
• What is a Conference of the Parties (COP)?
• How is COP31 different from previous COPs?
• What is the significance of the pre-industrial temperature baseline in measuring global warming?
• What is the impact of El Niño on global temperature patterns, with reference to the warming trend highlighted in the WMO recent report?
• What is the significance of the 1.5°C temperature threshold under the Paris Agreement?
• Despite decades of international climate negotiations, global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise—Why?
• What is the Loss and Damage Fund?
• Know the importance of climate finance in implementing global climate commitments.
Key Takeaways:

• In its annual State of the Climate Report, released on the opening day of the COP31 climate meeting, the WMO said 2026 could end up as one of the warmest ever, almost certainly among the top four warmest years.

• The average global temperature between January and September this year was 1.47 degrees Celsius higher than pre-industrial times (the average of the 1850-1900 period), the WMO report said. It is higher than the full-year averages in 2025 and 2023, and only slightly lower than 2024, which remains the warmest year on record.

• The remaining three months of this year are unlikely to bring down the average so far, considering the prevailing El Niño conditions, which have a general warming impact on the planet. Thus, it is very likely that 2026 ends up as the second warmest year.

• Like all previous COP hosts, Turkey decided to launch a few voluntary initiatives to create momentum for greater climate action. The most important initiative seeks to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to at least 30 per cent by 2035 from the current levels of about 20 per cent. It is not very evident, but electricity serves only a small fraction of the world’s energy needs even today. Most of the energy consumption happens in non-electric forms, like oil and gas.
Do You Know:

• The State of the Climate Report, considered one of the most authoritative assessments of global climate change, also revealed that greenhouse gas emissions—the main driver of rising global temperatures—were still going up and reached new record levels in 2025. Measurements from benchmark monitoring stations indicate a continued increase in 2026 as well. Even after three decades of global discussions, international legal arrangements, and resource allocation, the world has not even begun reducing its emissions.

• For the climate negotiators assembled in Antalya for the two-week conference, this is no new information. They have been getting similar messages for several years now, with every climate assessment pointing to the steadily worsening situation. But the negotiators are now more helpless than ever in changing the situation in any significant manner in the short term, at least.

• COP31 is one of the most low-key climate conferences in years. No major decisions or outcomes are expected. Most discussions are likely to focus on finding ways to speed up the implementation of promised climate actions. But that too runs into a familiar stalemate—the need for more money.

Used vehicles: Ease of transactions depends on state
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies III: Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, environmental impact assessment.

What’s the ongoing story: The sale of pre-owned or used vehicles has emerged as a strong market in India, growing significantly every year. Used cars are even expected to outsell new ones at a ratio of 1.7:1 by 2030, thanks to lower upfront costs for middle-income households.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is the Ease of Vehicle Ownership Index (EVOI)?
• What are the major findings of the Ease of Vehicle Ownership Index?
• What are the major procedural difficulties faced by individuals while buying and selling pre-owned vehicles in India?
• Know the role of VAHAN, DigiLocker and mParivahan in facilitating digital vehicle ownership transfers.
• Why is the used-vehicle market becoming increasingly important for middle-income households and first-time vehicle buyers in India?
• How differences in road tax across states affect the inter-state movement and resale of pre-owned vehicles?
Key Takeaways:

• According to the new Ease of Vehicle Ownership Index (EVOI), released by the minister on November 4, Andhra Pradesh is the leading state in terms of a smooth process involving used vehicle transactions.

• The report, prepared by startup industry body IndiaTech.org in partnership with consumer organisation Consumer VOICE, gave Andhra Pradesh a score of 5.91 out of 10, followed by Kerala at 5.74 and Tamil Nadu at 4.58. Uttar Pradesh came last at 2.47, just behind Bihar (2.51) and West Bengal (2.56). Delhi is at fourth place in the ease of vehicle ownership index, with 4.58 score out of 10.
• Karnataka ranks fifth in terms of ease of vehicle transfer among the 15 states covered in the index, followed by Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Telangana, Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana.

• None of the states crossed a score of six, showing that even the top performers do not have the entire ecosystem in place to help people buy and sell pre-owned vehicles. Only two states achieved an overall score above 5.5, while eight states scored between 3.8-4.3, showing that most of them face similar structural challenges.
Do You Know:

• The report is based on the performances of states on six metrics: clarity and consistency of ownership transfer rules; functional availability and reliability of online systems; speed, predictability and procedural burden; fee clarity, application tracking and grievance mechanism; consumer protection, dealer support and trade infrastructure; and official fees versus actual all-in market cost of transfer.

• The index covered 15 states — Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Delhi, Karnataka, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Telangana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana, West Bengal, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh — which account for more than 85% of India’s organised used-car market.

• According to the report, the cost is the weakest pillar in the pre-owned vehicle market. This is an area in which 12 out of 15 states scored below 3.5. This means people have to pay well above the cost prescribed for the transfer of vehicles, thanks to multiple manual stages, court notaries, MV inspection and multiple departmental signings.

• It said registration certificate (RC) transfer times run from seven to 10 days in Andhra Pradesh, where buyer, seller and lender authenticate biometrically, to more than 30 days in Uttar Pradesh. In 13 of the 15 states, applicants file online and are still asked to deliver physical copies to the RTO. The uneven road tax among states adds to another layer of problem for the pre-owned vehicle market. “The road tax on a Rs 6 lakh petrol car ranges from 3% in Uttar Pradesh to 14% in Karnataka, a difference of over Rs 66,000 on the same vehicle. Only Andhra Pradesh and Telangana run a working refund for vehicles that leave the state,” it said.

• According to the report, India’s pre-owned vehicle market was valued at $36.4 billion in 2024-25 and is expected to grow to $73.5 billion in 2030. If this happens, the sale ratio of used and new vehicles will also increase from 1.3:1 to 1.7:1 by 2030. While the projections are impressive, it is well below the 2.5:1 to 3:1 ratio seen in mature markets like the US and Europe, signalling that there is room for expansion.

• The report recommends that a stepwise timeline for the transfer of vehicles should be fixed through an amendment to the Motor Vehicle Act. It also said that DigiLocker and mParivahan documents should be accepted as primary evidence at every RTO to end the dual online and physical submission.

War or peace: How Trump can deal with Iran next
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India’s interests

What’s the ongoing story: The US midterm polls have left the Democratic Party in firm control of both Houses of the US Congress, with the Republican Party suffering historic losses even in traditional strongholds.
Key Points to Ponder:
• How the 2026 US midterm election results will impact President Donald Trump’s policy towards Iran?
• What were the major economic consequences of the US-Iran conflict?
• What is the strategic significance of the Strait of Hormuz in the context of the US-Iran conflict?
• Know the significance of Iran’s reported stockpile of 440 kg of uranium enriched to 60% in the ongoing negotiations with the United States.
• What were the seven major demands put forward by Iran for an interim agreement with the United States?
• What are the factors that have strengthened Iran’s bargaining position following the US midterm elections?
Key Takeaways:

• Behind the Blue Tsunami was the cost of living crisis in the US, exacerbated by President Donald Trump’s tariffs and, crucially, the war he started against Iran — which drove up fuel prices domestically and globally. Indeed, after the results, Vice President J D Vance acknowledged on X that “the reason we lost is the war [with Iran]”. Trump has himself called this “largely true”. The question now is whether a defeated Trump will lash out by resuming the war with Iran or pursue a deal instead.

• The signals seem mixed. Early after the polls, he seemed disinclined towards more war, saying: “We seem to be getting everything we want… we’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it.”

• But, on Thursday, he tried to keep the possibility open: “Do we want to go further (with military action)? I would rather not destroy the rest of the country, if possible, but maybe I will have to. You’ll know soon enough.”

• Vance, perhaps driven by the need to distance himself from Trump before the 2028 Presidential elections, has been clearer. He said that for voters to return to the party, the administration would have to “end the war, focus on inflation, put America first (and) change our relationship to Israel”. With the new Congress set to take office in early January, the US now appears simultaneously on the verge of both war and a deal with Iran. What are the pathways ahead?
Do You Know:

• The Trump administration’s military actions against Iran later in the year were essentially an attempt to improve its bargaining position for a deal. But this prolonged entanglement in West Asia has significantly affected its domestic standing, as proved by the midterm polls. The President’s approval rating now stands at 38%.

• In recent months, Vance has reportedly privately accused Israel’s (now caretaker) Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, of being “wrong on everything” about Iran. This shows Washington DC’s loss of faith in the military approach that has long been pushed by the Israeli leader.

• If anything, the US’s post-midterms predicament has strengthened Tehran’s bargaining position, reflected in Iranian leaders’ rhetoric following the results. This, in turn, may force the US President to save face through yet another visible show of force, even if a deal remains the ultimate objective.
But Trump’s principal challenge, even before the midterms, has been that Tehran retains as much agency as Washington in determining when a round of strikes ends.

• The regional Arab states, which faced the brunt of Iran’s retaliatory attacks earlier this year, know that another round of fighting will hobble them economically. Recognising both Washington’s dilemma and Tehran’s resilience, Qatar, Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and UAE are proactively pushing for any possible interim arrangement.
• In the run-up to the midterms, it was the aforementioned lack of an achievable objective that prevented US military action, or support for Israeli action.

• Iran refrained from responding to Israel’s large-scale aerial provocation close to Iranian airspace in October. It is also now reportedly amenable to a two-day implementation window for an interim deal — Day 1 would see Iran admitting International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors in return for a lifting of the US blockade and release of frozen Iranian funds; Day 2 would see Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and the initiation of talks over its reported 440 kg stockpile of 60% enriched uranium.

10 yrs. after demonetisation, cash remains king despite booming digital payments
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Government policies and interventions for development in various sectors and issues arising out of their design and implementation.

What’s the ongoing story:Ten years ago, on November 8, the Modi government announced the demonetisation of high-value currency notes of Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 in a dramatic bid to curb black money and push India towards a cashless economy. A decade later, however, cash remains king, with currency held by the public having more than doubled since demonetisation.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is Demonetisation?
• Demonetisation of Rs 500 and 1000 currency notes-Know the background
• How demonetisation impacted on the GDP for the current year? (Know short-term and Long term effect)
• Does demonetisation served the purpose of curbing black money and terror funding? (What economic survey said about it?)
• Demonetisation has been implemented twice in the past-When, why and how?
• Demonetisation in 1946 and 1978 and Demonetisation in 2016-compare and contrast
• Demonetisation in 2016 was the decision taken in haste and not gone into the nitty-gritties of this step-Do you agree?
• Demonetisation in 2016-How it impacted common man?
Key Takeaways:

• Currency with the public, which stood at Rs 17.97 lakh crore on November 4, 2016, plunged to Rs 7.8 lakh crore in January 2017 following the November 8 announcement. It has since surged to Rs 42.55 lakh crore as of October 15, 2026, according to Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data, an increase of nearly 137 per cent over its pre-demonetisation level.
• Though digital payments have jumped manifold, high cash holdings raise questions about the lasting impact of demonetisation on India’s dependence on physical currency.

• While the economy has expanded considerably over the past decade, growing at 6-7 per cent annually in several years, the currency-to-GDP ratio has also returned to around its pre-demonetisation level. In other words, despite the massive push towards digital payments and formalisation, cash has not been driven out of the economy. Instead, its circulation has recovered alongside economic growth.

• As per the RBI’s definition, currency with the public is calculated by deducting cash held by banks from total currency in circulation (CIC). CIC refers to currency notes and coins issued by the central bank within a country that are physically used to conduct transactions between consumers and businesses. During the calendar year 2026 as of October 16, cash with the public increased by Rs 5.26 lakh crore, a rise of 14.1 per cent, according to RBI data.
Do You Know:

• Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced demonetisation at 8 pm on November 8, 2016, in a televised address to the nation. The announcement rendered the then-existing Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes invalid as legal tender from midnight on November 9. These two denominations together accounted for approximately 86 per cent of the currency in circulation at the time, triggering an unprecedented cash crunch that disrupted shops, offices, businesses and households across the country.

• The government had projected demonetisation as a decisive strike against black money, counterfeit currency and the financing of illegal activities. It was also expected to accelerate digital payments, encourage formalisation and reduce India’s dependence on cash. Ten years later, however, the more than doubling of currency with the public tells a different story: demonetisation may have temporarily drained cash from the system, but it did not fundamentally alter India’s appetite for physical currency.

• The sudden withdrawal of notes roiled the economy in November 2016, with demand falling, businesses facing a crisis and GDP growth declining by nearly 1.5 percentage points. Many small businesses were hit hard and shut down after the note ban created a liquidity shortage. The shock of suddenly invalidated high-denomination notes disrupted daily commerce, forced people to queue for hours at banks and ATMs, and pushed individuals and businesses to rethink how they managed cash.

title: Knowledge Nugget| Global Carbon Budget: Why does the latest emissions assessment matter?

content.value: Written by Sanju Singh

Take a look at the essential events, concepts, terms, quotes and developments shaping current affairs every day and brush up your knowledge. Here’s your UPSC Current Affairs Knowledge Nugget for today on global CO₂ emission trends and key climate developments at COP31.
Knowledge Nugget: Global Carbon Budget Study and COP31
Subject: Environment and Ecology
Why in the news?

A new Global Carbon Budget study, released at the COP31 climate meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, projects a 0.4% decline in global fossil fuel-related CO₂ emissions in 2026 to 38.2 billion tonnes, from 38.4 billion tonnes in 2025.  India, however, is the only major emitter projected to record an increase.

Beyond this development, the Global Carbon Budget provides an opportunity to understand global CO₂ emission trends, the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal, and the significance of COP31 in advancing global climate action and India’s climate commitments.
Key takeaways:
1. The marginal decline is attributed partly to supply shocks caused by the ongoing US-Iran conflict and the growing contribution of renewable energy sources.

2. India is the only major emitter projected to record an increase in fossil fuel-related CO₂ emissions in 2026, rising by 4.4% over 2025 (higher than its preceding decade’s average annual growth of 3.5%).

3. In contrast, China, the US, the EU and Japan are expected to record declines. The projected decline in fossil fuel-related CO₂ emissions in 2026 would be the first since 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic caused a 2% drop, the largest year-on-year decline recorded so far.

4. Researchers caution that a one-year decline does not signal a lasting peak. Sustained reductions require structural energy-system changes, faster adoption of clean energy and reduced fossil fuel dependence.
5. The WMO’s Greenhouse Gas Bulletin reported that atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases reached record highs in 2025, with further increases in CO₂ concentrations expected in 2026.

—The WMO’s State of the Global Climate report covers broader climate indicators, including temperatures, ocean heat, sea levels, glaciers and sea ice, while the Global Carbon Budget focuses on CO₂ emissions, atmospheric accumulation and natural carbon sinks.
6. Paris agreement:

— Scientific assessments indicate that global annual greenhouse gas emissions need to be reduced by almost half from 2019 levels by 2030 to give the world a minimal chance of limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
— However, current projections suggest that even in the best-case scenario, annual emissions would decline by no more than 2% by 2030.
7. What is the Global Carbon Budget?
— It is an annual scientific assessment coordinated by the Global Carbon Project (GCP).

— First published in 2006, it accounts for CO₂ emissions from fossil fuel combustion, industrial processes such as cement production, and land-use change such as deforestation. It also estimates atmospheric CO₂ accumulation and absorption by natural carbon sinks, mainly land ecosystems and oceans.

— Remaining carbon budget: The remaining carbon budget is the additional CO₂ that can be emitted while retaining a specified chance of limiting warming to 1.5°C or 2°C. The GCB 2026 estimates the 1.5°C budget at around 150 billion tonnes, or less than four years of emissions at current rates.

— Global Carbon Project is a Global Research Project of Future Earth and a research partner of the World Climate Research Programme. It studies the global biogeochemical cycles of three major greenhouse gases-carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O)-including their natural and human-induced sources, sinks and drivers.
FYI: COP31-The United Nations Climate Change Conference

— COP31 is the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), 1992.  Three parallel meetings are taking place: COP31 (UNFCCC), CMP21 (Kyoto Protocol) and CMA8 (Paris Agreement).
— COP has been held annually since 1995 and it provides a platform for countries to negotiate global climate action and review commitments.
Why is COP31 significant?
— COP31 is the first UN climate conference since the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement took effect in January 2026.
— The US is a major greenhouse gas emitter and climate finance contributor and its absence has intensified calls for other developed economies, particularly European countries, to fill the gap.
— Energy security is another key concern amid the Iran conflict and rising oil and gas prices, bringing renewed attention to fossil-fuel dependence and the transition to cleaner energy.
— Türkiye has proposed increasing electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from around 23% to 35% by 2035.

— Developing countries, including India, are also seeking progress on Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which requires developed countries to provide financial resources to developing countries for climate action.
What does COP31 inherit from COP30?
— COP31 will build on COP30 outcomes in Belém, Brazil, including the Global Mutirão package.

— Key outcomes at COP 30, included a call to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035, the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap targeting at least $1.3 trillion in annual climate finance by 2035 from public and private sources, and indicators to track adaptation progress.
— However, COP30 did not establish an explicit roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. This remains a major issue for COP31 negotiations.
BEYOND THE NUGGET: What are India’s climate commitments?
1. India’s updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs):
The Union Cabinet approved India’s third NDC for 2031–2035 on March 25, 2026. It builds on the country’s earlier commitments for 2030 and sets three principal quantitative targets:
— Emissions intensity: Reduce the emissions intensity of GDP by 47% by 2035, from the 2005 level.
— Non-fossil electricity capacity: Ensure that 60% of cumulative installed electric power capacity comes from non-fossil fuel-based energy resources by 2035.
— Carbon sink: Create an additional carbon sink of 3.5–4 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent through forest and tree cover by 2035, from the 2005 level.
2. India’s net-zero target by 2070:
— At COP26, Glasgow (2021), India announced its commitment to achieve net-zero emissions by 2070 as part of its Panchamrit climate commitments.

— The Panchamrit commitments include achieving 500 GW of non-fossil energy capacity, meeting 50% of energy requirements through renewable sources, reducing projected carbon emissions by 1 billion tonnes and cutting the economy’s carbon intensity by 45% (from 2005 levels), all by 2030.
— Net zero means balancing greenhouse gas emissions released into the atmosphere with removals through sinks or other measures.
— India submitted its Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS) to the UNFCCC in November 2022, outlining its approach to low-carbon development.
Post Read Question
Consider the following statements with reference to the Global Carbon Budget 2026:
1. India is the only major emitter projected to record an increase in fossil fuel-related CO₂ emissions in 2026.
2. The Global Carbon Budget accounts only for CO₂ emissions from fossil fuel combustion.
3. The remaining carbon budget refers to the amount of additional CO₂ that can be emitted while retaining a specified probability of limiting global warming to a particular temperature threshold.
Which of the statement(s) given above is/ are correct?

(a) 1 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 3 only 
(d) 1 and 3 only
Answer: (d)

(Source: CO2 emissions from fossil fuels projected to decline in 2026: Study, COP31: What’s at stake at UN climate summit in Antalya, Why climate summits still matter, even as the world misses its targets, India’s new climate targets are modest, but significant. Here’s why?, globalcarbonbudget.org, wmo.int/publication-series, pib.gov.in)

title: Knowledge Nugget | Mahabharata to Arthashastra: 3 Indian manuscripts earn UNESCO recognition

content.value: Take a look at the essential events, concepts, terms, quotes, or phenomena every day and brush up your knowledge. Here’s your UPSC Current Affairs knowledge nugget for today on Indian manuscripts in UNESCO’s Memory of the World Asia-Pacific Regional Register.
Knowledge Nugget: Indian epics in UNESCO’s Memory of the World Asia-Pacific Regional Register
Subject: Art and Culture
Why in the news?

The Manuscripts of the epic Mahabharata, Rajatarangini and Arthashastra have earned a place in UNESCO’s Memory of the World Asia-Pacific Regional Register. In this context, let’s know about these manuscripts and their significance.
Key takeaways:
Mahabharata

1. The world’s longest epic Mahabharata by Vyasa, stands as a unique documentary heritage of humanity. The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute preserves a 400-year-old rare birch-bark manuscript of the Mahabharata written in the Sharada script.

2. According to Memory of the World Committee for Asia and the Pacific, “It preserves India’s civilizational memory while offering profound reflections on Dharma (moral ethics), Artha (material prosperity), Kama (pleasure), and Mokṣa (liberation), alongside explorations of Kartavya (duty), Rajadharma (principles of statecraft), Darsana (philosophical thought), and Niyati (the human destiny).”
3. Far more than a narrative of dynastic conflict, the text serves as an encyclopaedia of human experience and ethical inquiry.

4. The influence of the Mahabharata extended far beyond India’s borders, shaping the life and art of Asia for centuries. Its presence is etched into the bas-reliefs of Angkor Wat, which vividly depict episodes from the epic, and it inspired adaptations such as the Japanese Kabuki play Naru-kami and narrative traditions in Mongolia.

5. In Thailand, it emerged in the form of Krishna Son Nong, while in Indonesia it was transformed into the Bharatayuddha, integral both to the shadow-puppet theatre (Wayang Purva) and to courtly literary traditions.
Arthasastra

1. The Arthasastra, composed two millennia ago, is a foundational Sanskrit treatise that integrates statecraft, economics, administration, diplomacy, law and military strategy into a systematic science of governance.

2. Arthasastra is attributed to Kautilya, also called Chanakya or Vishnugupta, the adviser to Chandragupta Maurya. It is structured into fifteen adhikaranas (books), one hundred and fifty adhyayas (chapters), and one hundred and eighty prakaranas (sections).
3. The text articulates judicial procedure, rules of evidence, and graded punishments; establishes a professional gupta-cara (secret-agent) system for intelligence and counter-intelligence.

4. It formulates foreign policy through the mandala (circle of states), Shadgunya or Shadgunya Niti (six diplomatic measures), and the four Upayas – sama (conciliation), dana (gifts), bheda (dissension), and danḍa (force), integrating internal order with external strategy to secure stability and prosperity.
5. The text survives in a complete sixteenth-century palm-leaf manuscript in Grantha script at the Oriental Research Institute, Mysore.

6. Rediscovered in 1905 by R. Shamasastry, it transformed understanding of ancient Indian polity and inspired extensive editions, translations, and comparative studies. Its insights remain relevant in governance, business, management, sustainable development, and contemporary fields.
Rajatarangini

1. The manuscript of Kalhaṇa’s Rajatarangini, preserved at the Oriental Research Library, Srinagar, stands as one of the rare extant works of Sanskrit literature that embody the character of a true historical text.

2. Composed in the 12th century C.E., Rajatarangini interweaves historical narratives, royal genealogies, political events, and socio-cultural elements of Kashmir within the aesthetic framework of poetry. The text stands as a vital effort to restore a continuous and coherent history of Kashmir.

3. The Rajatarangini is a repository of the cultural essence of Kashmir. Demonstrating Kalhaṇa’s critical method, his use of sources, innovative chronological framework, and ethical reflections, the manuscript evinces an early historical consciousness rare in South Asian literature.
4. Written in Sharada script on old Kashmiri paper, the manuscript is a direct copy of the lost codex archetype, making it the closest surviving link to the original source.
Other literary works were added to the list in 2024
1. Notably, three Indian literary works—Ramcharitmanas, Panchatantra, and Sahṛdayaloka-Locana—were added to UNESCO’s Memory of the World Asia-Pacific Regional Register in 2024.
2. This recognition was announced during the tenth meeting of the Memory of the World Committee for Asia and the Pacific (MOWCAP), held in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia.
3. Ramcharitmanas: This manuscript was authored by Goswami Tulsidas.
4. Panchatantra: Attributed to Vishnu Sharma, this is an ancient Indian collection of interrelated animal fables in verse and prose.
5. Sahṛdayaloka-Locana: Written by 15th-century Kashmiri scholars Acharya Anandvardhan and Abhinavagupta, it was chosen for its aesthetic significance.
Indian Manuscripts on UNESCO’s Memory of the World (MOW) Register
1. Manuscripts of the Bhagavad Gita and Bharat Muni’s Natyashastra were added to UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register last year taking the total number of inscriptions from India in the list to 14.

2. Natyashastra: Natyashastra is an ancient Sanskrit treatise on performing arts. It is traditionally attributed to the sage Bharata. Comprising 36,000 verses, the “Naṭyashastra embodies a comprehensive set of rules that define natya (drama), abhinaya (performance), rasa (aesthetic experience), bhava (emotion), sangita (music),” the UNESCO citation says.

3. Bhagavad Gita: Bhagavad Gita is a Sanskrit scripture comprising 700 verses that are organised in 18 chapters, embedded in the sixth book (Bhishma Parva) of the epic poem Mahabharata. It is traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa.
BEYOND THE NUGGET: What is the UNESCO’s Memory of the World (MOW) register?

1. UNESCO’s MOW programme is an international cooperation strategy aimed at safeguarding, protecting, and facilitating access to and the use of documentary heritage, especially heritage that is rare and endangered.

2. According to its charter, UNESCO launched the initiative in 1992 “to guard against collective amnesia” by calling upon the preservation of invaluable archive holdings and library collections all over the world and ensuring their wide dissemination.
3. The programme recognises documentary heritage of international, regional and national significance, maintains registers of it, and awards a logo to identified collections.

4. It facilitates preservation and access without discrimination. It campaigns to raise awareness of the documentary heritage to alert governments, the general public, businesses and commerce to preservation needs and to raise funds.

5. Inscription on the register affirms the significance of the documentary heritage, makes it better known, and allows for greater access to it, thereby facilitating research, education, entertainment, and preservation over time.
6. Beginning in 1997, the Register has been biennally updated, with the exception of a lengthy gap between 2017 and 2023. In any year, at most two submissions from a country are added.
6. The MoW register operates on regional levels as well. The Memory of the World Asia-Pacific regional register celebrates Asia-Pacific achievements in genealogy, literature, and science.
Post Read Question
Consider the following statements:
1. The UNESCO’s Memory of the World (MoW) programme was launched in 1992.
2. The Arthashastra manuscript is a sixteenth-century palm-leaf manuscript written in the Sharada script.
3. The Rajatarangini was composed by Kalhaṇa in the 12th century CE is an important historical account of Kashmir.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 1 and 3 only
(c) 2 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
Answer Key
(Sources: Ramcharitmanas included in UNESCO’s Memory of the World Regional Register: Its significance,  UNESCO’s Memory of the World (MOW) Register)
