title: UPSC Essentials | Daily subject-wise quiz : Science and Technology MCQs on pollutants in Air Quality Monitoring Stations, cloud seeding and more (Week 188)

content.value: UPSC Essentials brings to you its initiative of subject-wise quizzes. These quizzes are designed to help you revise some of the most important topics from the static part of the syllabus. Attempt today’s subject quiz on Science and Technology to check your progress.
🚨 Click Here to read the UPSC Essentials magazine for October 2026. Share your views and suggestions in the comment box or at manas.srivastava@indianexpress.com🚨
QUESTION 1
Which of the following is/are used in cloud seeding to trigger artificial rain?
1. Silver iodide
2. Silver Nitrate
3. Sodium chloride
4. Potassium Nitrate
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
(a) 1 and 3 only
(b) 2 and 4 only
(c) 3 only
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 only

Relevance: The question is relevant to weather modification techniques and emerging applications of atmospheric science. It links Science and Technology with cloud physics, precipitation processes and artificial rain generation.
Explanation
— Cloud seeding refers to introducing substances such as silver iodide or sodium chloride into a particular class of clouds to artificially trigger rain.

— Cloud seeding experiments began to be carried out around the world after American chemist Vincent Schaefer and his colleagues at General Electric in New York made the first snowstorm in a laboratory freezer in 1946.

— Generally, water vapour condenses around small particles in the air to form the droplets that make up a cloud. These droplets collide and grow; as they get heavy and the cloud gets saturated, it rains.

— In case of cloud seeding, the seed particles are “cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), a particle on which water vapour condensates” or “ice nuclei particles, a particle on which water freezes”, the 2024 document said. CCNs have an affinity for water vapour to form cloud droplets or ice particles, respectively. Ice crystals grow faster than drops, and they enlarge and fall.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
To read more: How cloud seeding carried out? and How cloud seeding improve air quality?
QUESTION 2
With reference to the kamikaze drones, consider the following statements:
1. These are weapon systems that can hover or circle a target area, searching for a suitable target before attacking.
2. They are more expensive than traditional missiles.
3. These drones are designed primarily to return to their launch platform after completing a strike mission.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
(a) Only one
(b) Only two
(c) All three
(d) None

Relevance: The question is relevant to emerging defence technologies and the modernisation of military capabilities. It links Science and Technology with unmanned aerial systems, precision-guided weapons and their applications in modern warfare.
Explanation

— The Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) is planning to acquire kamikaze unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that are capable of striking targets up to 15 km away while livestreaming video of the ground beneath. The Directorate General of CRPF has circulated draft qualitative requirements and trial directives for what it calls OFC+RF-based FPV kamikaze drones — first-person-view UAVs — that fly to a designated objective carrying a high-explosive warhead, transmit surveillance imagery back to the operator, and then destroy themselves on impact.
According to pib.gov.in,

— “Loitering munitions also known as “suicide drones” or “kamikaze drones”, are weapons systems that can hover or circle a target area, searching for a suitable target before attacking. Hence, statement 1 is correct.
— They are generally considered a relatively cost-effective alternative to conventional precision-guided missiles. Hence, statement 2 is not correct.
— Kamikaze drones are designed to destroy themselves along with the target on impact. They are not primarily designed to return to their launch platform.” Hence, statement 3 is not correct.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 3
The term “Physical AI” refers to:
(a) The use of artificial intelligence to simulate human intelligence and emotions in virtual environments.
(b) The application of AI to analyse large datasets and generate predictions without interacting with the physical environment.
(c) The integration of AI into digital platforms to automate administrative, financial and business-related processes.
(d) The use of AI to enable autonomous systems such as robots or camera-bots to discern, comprehend, and perform complex actions in the physical world — effectively.

Relevance: The question is relevant to emerging technologies and recent advances in Artificial Intelligence. It links Science and Technology with robotics, autonomous systems, machine perception and human-machine interaction.
Explanation

— At a time when renewed unease over artificial intelligence (AI) spending is weighing heavily on the technology sector, there are some answers to the related concern over how to tangibly monetise AI tools. Abu Dhabi’s state-owned oil company ADNOC, for instance, has signed a new deal earlier this week with AI firms G42 and OpenAI to deploy advanced AI capabilities across the energy major’s operations.

— Physical AI refers to the use of AI to enable autonomous systems such as robots, camera-bots, and self-driving cars to discern, comprehend, and perform complex actions in the physical world — effectively, AI systems that operate in the physical world. This involves the combination of AI models with sensors, actuators, and other control systems that allow models to act upon real-world environments.

— Most of the AI that humans interact with on a day-to-day basis today exists purely digitally: Things like talking with a chatbot, using AI for image generation, or using it as a code assistant – these all live in the world of bits and bytes. Physical AI, on the other hand, is the kind that crosses over into the world of atoms, things in actual physical space. These are AI systems that can perceive their environment, they can reason about it, and can take action. Take robotics, for instance. Before AI, robot behavior was typically scripted, and robots could only perform a predefined range of tasks within specifically engineered environments, like a robotic arm that welds the same seam a thousand times a day on an automotive production line.
Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 4
With reference to the measurement of pollutants in Air Quality Monitoring Stations, consider the following pairs:
1. Sulphur dioxide – measured by UV photometry
2. Ozone – measured by UV fluorescence
3. Carbon monoxide – measured by non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) absorption
How many of the pairs given above are correctly marked?
(a) Only one pair
(b) Only two pairs
(c) All three pairs
(d) None of the above pairs

Relevance: The question is relevant to environmental monitoring technologies and scientific methods used to assess air pollution. It links Science and Technology with the measurement principles and applications of analytical instruments used in Air Quality Monitoring Stations.
Explanation

— Particulate matter is measured using Beta Attenuation Monitors (BAM), which rely on the beta ray attenuation principle. A small Carbon-14 or Krypton-85 source emits beta rays through a clean patch of filter tape. After air is drawn through and dust collects on the tape, the instrument re-measures the spot. Fewer beta rays pass through, and the decline in signal is used to calculate PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations.
— Sulphur dioxide is measured by UV fluorescence, which detects the weak glow SO2 emits under ultraviolet light. Hence, statement 1 is not correct.
— Ozone is measured by UV photometry, which tracks how much UV light it absorbs. Hence, statement 2 is not correct.
— Carbon monoxide is measured using non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) absorption, based on how much infrared light CO absorbs. Hence, statement 3 is correct.
— Nitrogen oxides are measured through chemiluminescence, where instruments detect the faint light produced when the gases react with ozone inside the analyser.
— Ammonia is measured using optical spectroscopy based on its characteristic absorption of light.

— These methods are approved under the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) of 2009, which list “gravimetric, wet-chemical (for manual stations) and automatic instrument-based techniques” to ensure comparable data across India.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 5
With reference to PJ.2.1, recently seen in the news. It is a:
(a) SARS-CoV-2 variant
(b) Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) strain
(c) Mpox virus variant
(d) Ebola virus strain
Relevance: The question is relevant to emerging infectious diseases and developments in virology. It links Science and Technology with the evolution, classification and genetic lineages of viruses.
Explanation

— A new SARS-CoV-2 variant, PJ.2.1, is drawing attention after being identified in Canada in May 2026 and subsequently detected in several countries, including the US, Singapore, Australia, France and Spain. A study published in the Journal of Infection in October 2026 documents its spread, characteristics and how well antibodies generated by variant-adapted booster vaccines can neutralise it.

— The researchers noted that Covid-19 continues to circulate globally and remains a cause of considerable illness and death. PJ.2.1, described in the paper as a “novel saltation variant”, originated from MC.10.1.7, a descendant of the JN.1 lineage that circulated until May 2025, and was first detected in Ontario, Canada, on May 2, 2026, before cases were reported in other Canadian provinces.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.

title: UPSC Mains Answer Practice — GS 1: Geomorphological processes of the Himalayas and temperature inversion (Week 180)

content.value: UPSC Essentials brings to you its initiative for the practice of Mains answer writing. It covers essential topics from both the static and dynamic portions of the UPSC Civil Services syllabus across various GS papers. The questions are carefully selected on the basis of their relevance to the UPSC examination and current developments, helping aspirants focus on themes that matter most for Mains. This answer-writing practice is designed as a value addition to your UPSC CSE Mains preparation. Attempt today’s GS-1 questions and check your progress.

QUESTION 1
Discuss the role of glacial lakes and moraine-dammed lakes in shaping the hydrological and geomorphological processes of the Himalayan region.
QUESTION 2
What is temperature inversion? Explain how this atmospheric phenomenon contributes to the accumulation of pollutants over the Indo-Gangetic Plain during winter.
QUESTION 1: Discuss the role of glacial lakes and moraine-dammed lakes in shaping the hydrological and geomorphological processes of the Himalayan region.

Relevance: The question links with the physical geography of the Himalayas, particularly glacial processes and landform development. It is relevant to understanding the evolving geomorphology and drainage systems of the Himalayan region.
Note: This is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers.
Introduction:

— Glacial lakes are bodies of water formed in front of, above, or beneath melting glaciers. They form when meltwater pools in glacier-eroded depressions or behind natural barriers. Moraine-dammed lakes arise when unconsolidated glacier debris, such as rocks, sand, silt, and boulders, serves as a natural barrier to water buildup.
— These lakes help shape the Himalayan landscape by affecting river hydrology, sediment movement, and mountain geomorphology.
Body:
You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer:
Role in shaping hydrological processes
— Glacial lakes serve as natural reservoirs, retaining meltwater from glaciers and seasonal snow, adding to the freshwater resources of Himalayan river systems.
— Water held in glacial lakes adds to downstream river discharge, which influences seasonal water availability.
— The creation and extension of glacial lakes can disrupt local drainage networks by altering the channels through which meltwater moves.
— Breaching of natural glacial or moraine dams can result in Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs), which release massive amounts of water into downstream rivers.

— Glacial lake outbursts in upstream Himalayan regions can disrupt river systems and populations across national borders. For example, the 2026 GLOF in Bhutan’s Shintaphu Lake generated flood warnings in Assam and West Bengal along the Sankosh River.
Role in shaping geomorphological processes
— Glacier erosion causes depressions in the mountain landscape, which then fill with meltwater to form glacier lakes.
— Glaciers carry and deposit unconsolidated materials, resulting in lateral and terminal moraines. These deposits can serve as natural dams, influencing the formation of mountain landscapes.
— Retreating glaciers reveal loose sediments and unstable slopes. Temperature, rainfall, and ice conditions can all influence the slopes’ susceptibility to landslides and erosion.
— Sudden outbursts convey significant amounts of glacial debris downstream, resulting in sediment deposition, channel change, and the formation of new landforms.
Conclusion:

— Glacial and moraine-dammed lakes are critical components of the Himalayan hydrological and geomorphological systems. While they help to store freshwater, regulate river flows, and shape the landscape, glacial retreat and natural dam instability raise the risk of dangerous changes. Understanding these processes is critical for analysing the Himalayas’ developing physical geography.

(Sources: Bhutan GLOF explained: What are glacial lake outburst floods, and why are such events recurring in Himalayas?, How glacial lake expansion adds to the growing concerns about GLOFs, Flash floods in Nepal again: Warning bells for Himalaya, lessons for India, Why Nepal flash floods resemble 2021 Chamoli disaster, with greater impact)
Points to Ponder
How do moraine-dammed lakes contribute to landscape evolution and changes in mountain drainage patterns?

QUESTION 2: What is temperature inversion? Explain how this atmospheric phenomenon contributes to the accumulation of pollutants over the Indo-Gangetic Plain during winter.

Relevance: The question links with climatology, particularly atmospheric temperature distribution and vertical air circulation. It is relevant to the study of seasonal climatic variations and their influence on the geographical distribution of air pollution.
Note: This is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers.
Introduction:

— Temperature inversion is a meteorological phenomenon in which the typical vertical temperature profile of the atmosphere is reversed, resulting in warmer air above cooler air near the Earth’s surface.

— Under normal conditions, temperature drops with altitude, allowing warmer air near the surface to rise and promote vertical mixing. During inversion, vertical movement is hindered, causing contaminants to accumulate closer to the ground.
Body:
You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer:
Temperature inversion and winter air pollution

— During winter, the Earth’s surface loses heat quickly, especially on clear nights. The air near the ground grows colder and denser, while relatively warmer air remains above it, resulting in an inversion layer.

— The warmer air above prevents the colder air near the surface from rising freely. Consequently, pollutants released by vehicles, industries, construction activities and biomass burning remain trapped in the lower atmosphere.
— During the winter, the planetary boundary layer thins. This lowers the vertical area available for contaminants to disperse, resulting in higher concentrations near the surface.
— Weak winter winds limit horizontal dispersion and ventilation. Pollutants might remain concentrated in the location for long periods of time.

— The Indo-Gangetic Plain is primarily landlocked and surrounded by the Himalayas. Its geographical location, combined with adjacent topographical factors, limits the flow and dispersal of contaminated air.
— The collection of particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), along with fog and other atmospheric pollutants, causes dense winter haze that limits visibility.
— Falling temperatures, weak winds, and atmospheric stability during the winter all contribute to the persistence of inversion conditions.
— The wide landlocked plains and the Himalayan barrier prevent pollutant dispersion.
— High population density, urbanisation, industrial activity, and agricultural burning all contribute to area pollution levels.
Conclusion:

— Temperature inversion is a natural atmospheric phenomena, but its combination with significant anthropogenic emissions and adverse geographical conditions exacerbates winter air pollution over the Indo-Gangetic Plain. To address the issue, pollution must be controlled at its source while also comprehending seasonal climatic and regional geographical characteristics.

(Sources: What is smog and why does it blanket Delhi every winter?, Explained: Why Delhi air quality deteriorates in October, How local topography contributes to air pollution, UPSC Issue at a Glance | Delhi’s toxic air and beyond: Understanding air pollution for UPSC Exam)
Points to Ponder
How do wind speed, planetary boundary layer height and atmospheric stability influence pollutant dispersion?
Why does the Indo-Gangetic Plain experience persistent winter pollution compared to regions with stronger atmospheric mixing?

title: UPSC Weekly Current Affairs Quiz (November 08 – November 14): 10 key questions with detailed answers for Prelims 2027

content.value: As UPSC CSE Prelims 2027 is still ahead, building a strong foundation alongside regular current affairs preparation is essential. UPSC Weekly Quiz is a current affairs–based quiz on relevant topics from the past week, curated for aspirants of competitive examinations. Attempt the weekly quiz every Saturday and review the detailed answers with explanations to strengthen conceptual clarity and exam readiness.
🚨 Click Here to read the UPSC Essentials magazine for October 2026. Share your views and suggestions in the comment box or at manas.srivastava@indianexpress.com🚨
QUESTION 1
With reference to tuberculosis (TB), consider the following statements:
1. India’s TB mortality reduced from 2015 to 2025.
2. India has not achieved its target of eliminating tuberculosis (TB) by 2025.
3. Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (NPY) provides direct benefit transfer (DBT) financial assistance to support the nutrition of TB patients.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
(a) Only one
(b) Only two
(c) All three
(d) None
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?

The topic is relevant to understanding ENSO and its influence on global climate and atmospheric circulation. It covers regional variations in rainfall, droughts, floods and wildfire patterns across different geographical regions.
Explanation

— While India has not achieved its target of eliminating tuberculosis (TB) by 2025, five years ahead of the global deadline, it has been making strides. The incidence and mortality due to the bacterial infection have been on the decline. India has also seen an improvement in diagnosis — with more people accessing rapid diagnostics and getting tested for resistance to a commonly used antimicrobial. Hence, statement 2 is correct.

— India reported a 38% reduction in its TB mortality as compared to 2015 — breaching the 2020 End TB milestone of reducing it by 35%, albeit five years later. India’s TB mortality reduced from 28 per lakh population in 2015 to 18 per lakh population in 2025, according to the Global TB report. The 2025 target of reducing mortality by 75% still remains distant. Hence, statement 1 is correct.

— India saw an increase in rapid diagnostic testing in 2025, with 46% of the cases being diagnosed using these. This is up from 38% the previous year. Quick diagnosis ensures timely treatment and prevents the further spread of the infection.
— Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (NPY) provides direct benefit transfer (DBT) financial assistance to support the nutritional needs of TB patients during treatment. Hence, statement 3 is correct.
Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 2
The principle of collective defence is mentioned in:
(a) South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation
(b) Association of Southeast Asian Nations
(c) International Atomic Energy Agency
(d) North Atlantic Treaty Organisation
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?

The question is relevant to understanding regional and international security arrangements and military alliances. It covers the concept of collective defence and the institutional framework of major international organisations.
Explanation

— US President Donald Trump announced that he had met with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy at the White House and that a “big, beautiful agreement” over the war in Ukraine was on the horizon.

— This Turkey-mediated meeting was marked by a 28-point US-Russia peace plan that included Ukraine permanently denouncing NATO membership and a total prohibition on Ukraine’s long-range arsenal — a demand that was denied by Zelensky. It was also met with a swift counter-proposal by the European bloc, which demanded a “robust, Article 5-style security guarantee” mirroring that of the NATO agreement. Article 5 encapsulates the principle of collective defence, where an attack on any member is considered an attack on all.
— Russia’s proposal also outlined sweeping domestic reform, such as an armed personnel cap, and ultimately, no common ground was reached.
Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 3
Consider the following statements:
1. The I-T Department cannot reopen a taxpayer’s assessment simply because it wants another look at it.
2. Section 147 of the I-T Act, 1961, allows an assessing officer to do so only when he has reason to believe that any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
(a) Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct and Statement 2 is the correct explanation for Statement 1.
(b) Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct and Statement 2 is not the correct explanation for Statement 1.
(c) Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.
(d) Statement 1 is incorrect but Statement 2 is correct.
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?

The question is important for understanding the statutory powers and limitations of tax authorities under the Income-tax Act. It covers the legal framework governing income tax reassessment and safeguards against arbitrary administrative action.
Explanation

— The I-T Department cannot reopen a taxpayer’s assessment simply because it wants another look at it. Section 147 of the I-T Act, 1961, allows an assessing officer to do so only when he “has reason to believe that any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year.” Hence, statements 1 and 2 are correct.

— The law sets a time limit on this power. If an assessment has already been completed after scrutiny under Section 143 (3), the department generally cannot reopen it after four years from the end of the relevant assessment year. But it can do so if the income escaped assessment because the taxpayer failed to make a return or “to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment.”

— The law also requires the officer to record the reasons for reopening an assessment before issuing a notice under Section 148, to ensure that the decision is based on reason rather than vague suspicion.

— An important safeguard is the rule against the Assessment Officer’s “change of opinion” in the case. In CIT v Kelvinator of India Ltd (2010), the SC said that without this check, “In the garb of reopening the assessment review would take place.” In ITO v Techspan India (2018), it said that Section 147 gives the department the “power to reassess and not the power to review.”
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 4
With reference to the Loss and Damage Fund, consider the following statements:
1. The fund aims to provide financial assistance to nations most vulnerable and impacted by the effects of climate change.
2. The Loss and Damage Fund was finalised during COP 27.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?

The Loss and Damage Fund is an important component of international climate finance and global climate governance. It is relevant to understanding the UNFCCC process, climate justice and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.
Explanation
— In terms of expected outcome and impact, COP31 could turn out to be one of the most inconsequential COPs in recent years, though not because of any shortcoming of its own.

— COPs, in general, have always underperformed. These annual year-ending two-week conferences, which attracted the largest gatherings of global leaders until not so long ago, have only produced low-ambition outcomes. In the last two decades, its most important success has been finalising the 2015 Paris Agreement, which defined the climate targets and framed the broad rules for international climate action.

— But COPs have had a poor record in convincing the member countries — virtually the entire world till the United States decided to walk out — to do enough to achieve those targets. COPs take decisions only through consensus, and there is no way to force laggard nations to do more.

— Climate change has largely disappeared from the agendas of other major global and regional forums, thanks to multiple wars, rapidly evolving technological threats, and new demands for energy use. While several immediate challenges have emerged in recent years, the problem of climate change has not disappeared, as evidenced by the growing number of large-scale climate disasters. COPs remain the only major global stage that continues to focus on climate change.

— The COPs are still the only forum where developing countries can demand greater accountability from the developed world, which bears the primary responsibility for addressing climate change. Nepal was recently promised US$ 20 million from the newly-established Loss and Damage Fund for recovery and reconstruction efforts after the devastating flash floods in August.

— The establishment of a Loss and Damage Fund was, for many, the highlight of the United Nations Climate Conference (COP 27) and the culmination of decades of pressure from climate-vulnerable developing countries. The fund aims to provide financial assistance to nations most vulnerable and impacted by the effects of climate change. Hence, statements 1 and 2 are correct.
Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.
(Other Source: http://www.unep.org)
QUESTION 5
With reference to the ‘surcharge’, consider the following statements:
1. It is an additional levy imposed over and above an existing tax.
2. It falls under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?

The question is relevant to understanding the constitutional provisions governing taxation and the distribution of financial powers between the Centre and States. It also links fiscal federalism with the principles of tax revenue sharing and the Consolidated Fund of India.
Explanation

— Can a state impose a tax on a tax that a dealer already owes? The Supreme Court has reiterated that states can levy a surcharge calculated as a percentage of sales tax payable by dealers, holding that such a levy is essentially an additional sales tax and not a separate tax on tax. In doing so, a seven-judge Constitution Bench has closed a reference that had been pending for nearly three decades, ruling that the question had already been settled by a 1974 judgment.

— A surcharge is an additional levy imposed over and above an existing tax. The legal question before the Supreme Court was whether states could impose such a surcharge on the sales tax payable by dealers, or whether doing so amounted to an impermissible ‘tax on tax’. Hence, statement 1 is correct.
— The dispute arose from a 1990 amendment to Odisha’s Sales Tax Act, which required dealers with a gross turnover exceeding Rs 10 lakh to pay an additional 10% of the sales tax they owed.

— The dealers challenged this provision, and argued that the surcharge was a “tax on tax”. They reasoned that the surcharge is measured on the tax payable and not on turnover, hence it is not a tax on the “sale or purchase of goods.” The dealers argued that it falls outside Entry 54 of list II of the Seventh Schedule, which empowers the states to tax the sale or purchase of goods but does not authorise them to impose a tax on sales tax that is already payable by the dealer. Hence, statement 2 is not correct.

— The state maintained that the surcharge was only an increase in the rate of sales tax for a particular class of dealers. The fact that it was calculated as a percentage of the tax payable instead of turnover did not change the nature of the levy.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 6
Which of the following events are associated with El Niño?
1. Alteration in rain patterns
2. Incidents of wild fires
3. Flooding in Asia and Australia
4. Drought in the Horn of Africa region
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 1 and 3 only
(c) 3 and 4 only
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?

The question covers the geographical distribution of climate variability and its impact on regional weather patterns. It links climatology with extreme weather events, ecological vulnerability and disaster management.
Explanation

— El Niño will continue to remain ‘strong’ to ‘very strong’ during the first quarter of 2027, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said. The UN organisation further said that the current El Niño event continues to intensify, and would become the “strongest ever since 1950”. It is set to shatter all previously known records with respective to the sea surface temperatures along the equatorial Pacific Ocean.

— El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon associated with warm seas along the equatorial Pacific Oceans. El Niño alters rain patterns, spikes temperatures, increases incidents of wild fires, leads to extreme weather in the form of fluids or droughts across the world.

— It is one of the three phases of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the other two being ENSO neutral and La Nina (cool). The ENSO phase is subject to the Relative Ocean Nino Index (RONI) value — the sea surface temperature measured over the Nino 3.4 region. An El Niño event is declared when the average RONI value surpasses 0.5 degree Celsius, an average considered over three months.
— Heavy Rainfall and Flooding in Asia and Australia, and droughts in Horn of Africa, are associated with La Nina.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 7
The Karakoram Exercise is a joint army-level exercise between:
1. India
2. China
3. Tibet
4. Pakistan
5. Afghanistan
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
(a) 1 and 3 only
(b) 1 and 5 only
(c) 2 and 4 only
(d) 1 and 2 only
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?

The question is relevant to India’s neighbourhood security environment and evolving military cooperation in South and Central Asia. It covers joint military exercises, defence diplomacy and strategic partnerships among neighbouring countries.
Explanation

— China and Pakistan’s longstanding partnership, while not a formal alliance, has emerged as a defining feature of the regional security architecture. Over the years, their military cooperation has deepened, moving beyond defence acquisitions and joint exercises towards greater functional integration and interoperability.
— Karakoram-2026, held from October 14-22 in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, was the first joint-army level exercise between People’s Liberation Army (PLA) and Pakistan Army.

— It expanded on the earlier naval, air and counterterrorism exercises (Sea Guardian, Warrior and Shaheen series). The focus was on challenging high-altitude operations, relevant to the PLA’s Western Theatre Command which oversees the border with India.
Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 8
The ‘classical’, ‘rapid’, and ‘blitz’ are the three formats associated with:
(a) Scrabble
(b) Swimming
(c) Chess
(d) Hockey
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?
It covers basic knowledge of internationally recognised sporting formats and their governing institutions. It also links sports terminology with major national and international sporting events.
Explanation

— Chess has never been a particularly television-friendly sport. Over the years, organisers and officials have tried to introduce elements such as live screens and commentary to bridge the gap with the viewer.

— The latest attempt, however, is a reimagining of chess competitions themselves. Meet Total Chess — a plan for a “complete” new world championship in the sport. An ongoing pilot event in Hungary’s capital of Budapest is laying the grounds for the new format, trying to turn it into a made-for-TV product.

— The Total Chess World Championship Tour that starts next year will have four events around the year in different cities, with the first three events having 24 players each and the finale having four players fighting it out to become the FIDE World Combined Champion. The idea is to crown the most complete chess player in the world.

— Chess currently has three formats — classical, rapid and blitz. And each has its own world championship: the Classical World Championship (the most prestigious, and chess’s equivalent of Test cricket), the Rapid World Championship (comparable to ODIs) and the World Blitz Championship (closest to T20s, with players starting with 10 minutes or less on the clock).
Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 9
Consider the following statements about the Sessions of the Indian Parliament:
1. India has a fixed parliamentary calendar.
2. The Monsoon Session is the longest.
3. The Constitution specifies that six months should not elapse between two parliamentary sessions.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
(a) Only one
(b) Only two
(c) All three
(d) None
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?

The question is relevant to understanding the constitutional provisions governing the functioning of the Indian Parliament. It also tests conceptual understanding of legislative functioning and the constitutional framework of parliamentary democracy.
Explanation

— The power to convene a session of Parliament rests with the government. The decision is taken by the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs, which currently comprises 10 ministers, including those for Defence, Home and Finance. The committee’s decision is formalised by the President, in whose name MPs are summoned to meet for a session.

— India does not have a fixed parliamentary calendar. The Constitution specifies that six months should not elapse between two parliamentary sessions. The framers of the Constitution borrowed it from the Government of India Act of 1935. Hence, statement 1 is not correct and statement 3 is correct.

— By convention, Parliament meets for three sessions in a year. The longest, the Budget Session, starts towards the end of January and concludes by the end of April or the first week of May. The session has a recess so that Parliamentary Committees can discuss the budgetary proposals. Hence, statement 2 is not correct.

— The second session is the three-week Monsoon Session, which usually begins in July and finishes in August. The parliamentary year ends with a three-week-long Winter Session, which is held from November to December. This Winter Session is expected to begin in late November or early December.

— The summoning of Parliament is specified in Article 85 of the Constitution. Like many other Articles, it is based on a provision of the Government of India Act, 1935. This provision specified that the central legislature had to be summoned to meet at least once a year, and that not more than 12 months could elapse between two sessions.
Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.
QUESTION 10
With reference to the National Planning Committee, consider the following statements:
1. In 1938, the Congress established the National Planning Committee under Subhas Chandra Bose, during the presidency of Maulana Azad.
2. The committee sought to envision India’s economic and industrial future.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2
Why this question for UPSC Prelims 2027?

The National Planning Committee is relevant to understanding the evolution of economic planning in pre-independent India. The topic provides a historical link to post-independence planning, the Planning Commission and India’s development strategy.
Explanation

— The idea of placing science at the centre of India’s development had also begun to take shape before Independence. In 1938, the Congress established the National Planning Committee under Jawaharlal Nehru, during the presidency of Subhas Chandra Bose. The committee sought to envision India’s economic and industrial future, drawing on the expertise of scientists, industrialists and economists. Among those associated with it were scientists Meghnad Saha and J C Ghosh, and industrialists Purshottamdas Thakurdas, Walchand Hirachand and Ambalal Sarabhai. Hence, statement 1 is not correct and statement 2 is correct.

— The outbreak of World War II in 1939 and the launch of the Quit India Movement in 1942 disrupted the committee’s work. However, many of its members remained committed to the cause of scientific, technological and industrial development in the years that followed. Nehru had articulated his own faith in science even earlier. In 1937, he declared: “The future belongs to science and those who make friends with science and seek its help for the advancement of humanity.”
Therefore, option (b) is the correct answer.

title: Knowledge Nugget | India’s proposed largest Agriwaste-to-Fuel project: Why does biofuel production matter?

content.value: Written by Sanju Singh

Take a look at the essential events, concepts, terms, quotes and developments shaping current affairs every day and brush up your knowledge. Here’s your UPSC Current Affairs Knowledge Nugget for today on agricultural waste-to-bio-crude technology and India’s biofuel ecosystem.
Knowledge Nugget: Greenjoules’ Agriwaste-to-Fuel Project and Bio-Crude
Subject: Science and Technology and Environment
Why in the news?

Greenjoules Private Ltd plans to set up a plant at Khed City, near Pune, to produce up to 2 lakh litres of bio-crude daily from agricultural residues. The company claims to use its proprietary Integrated Catalytic Thermo Cracking (ICTC) technology to convert these residues into bio-crude for further processing into renewable diesel and bio-naphtha.

Beyond the development, the project offers an opportunity to understand the science of converting agricultural waste into biofuels, the role of second-generation biofuels in addressing the food-versus-fuel debate and India’s biofuel policies.
Key Takeaways:
1. Greenjoules claims that every litre of bio-crude refined yields approximately 75% renewable diesel, which can be used in existing vehicles without modification.

2. Greenjoules has secured total financing of Rs 250 crore for the proposed Khed City plant. This includes Rs 100 crore from the Technology Development Board (TDB) under the Union Ministry of Science and Technology and Rs 150 crore through a Series B funding round.

3. Unlike biofuel production based on food crops such as sugarcane and cereal grains, the proposed project uses agricultural residues as feedstock. This can reduce direct competition between food production and fuel production.
4. What is Integrated Catalytic Thermo Cracking (ICTC)?

— Greenjoules claims to have developed a proprietary Integrated Catalytic Thermo Cracking (ICTC) technology that uses multiple catalysts at approximately 600°C to convert agricultural residues, such as paddy straw and husk, groundnut and cashew shells, and sugarcane bagasse, into bio-crude.
— This bio-crude serves as an intermediate that can be further processed in conventional refineries to produce renewable diesel and bio-naphtha.
5. What is Bio-crude and how it is different from Bio-diesel and Renewable-diesel?

— Bio-crude is a liquid intermediate produced by thermochemical conversion of biomass. In hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL), biomass is processed in water under high temperature and pressure to produce an organic liquid, which is separated from the aqueous phase.

— Generally viscous but thermally stable, it is easier to pump, store and process than solid biomass. However, it is not readily miscible with petroleum. Its density is slightly higher than petroleum but considerably lower than bio-oil.

— Bio-crude is an intermediate liquid product derived from biomass that requires further upgrading before it can be used as a fuel. Biodiesel is generally produced by chemically processing vegetable oils or animal fats, while renewable diesel is a hydrocarbon fuel obtained by upgrading biomass-derived feedstocks and designed to meet conventional diesel fuel specifications.

6. National Policy on Biofuels, 2018,  categorises biofuels as “Basic Biofuels” viz. First Generation (1G) bioethanol & biodiesel and “Advanced Biofuels” – Second Generation (2G) ethanol, Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) to drop-in fuels, Third Generation (3G) biofuels, bio-CNG etc.
— First-generation (1G) biofuels: Produced from food-based feedstocks such as sugarcane, maize, rice and vegetable oils.

— Second-generation (2G) biofuels: Derived from non-food biomass, including agricultural residues, crop stalks, husks, bagasse and other lignocellulosic materials. The proposed Greenjoules project falls under this category as it uses agricultural residues as feedstock.
— Third-generation (3G) biofuels: Primarily derived from algal biomass, including microalgae and macroalgae.
7. Environmental significance of biofuels:

— Agricultural residue management: Paddy straw and other agricultural residues are often burnt after harvesting due to limited disposal alternatives. This releases particulate matter and gaseous pollutants, contributing to regional air pollution. Converting crop residues into biofuels can provide an alternative economic use for biomass and potentially reduce stubble burning.

— Circular economy and Waste valorisation: A circular economy minimises waste and maximises resource use through reuse, recycling and recovery. Waste valorisation converts discarded materials and industrial by-products into useful products such as biofuels, chemicals and fertilisers. Agricultural and organic waste can be converted into bio-crude, bio-CNG and biogas.

— Climate change mitigation: Biofuels can potentially reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by substituting fossil fuels. Utilising agricultural residues may also help avoid emissions from open-field burning. However, their climate benefits depend on feedstock collection, transportation, processing energy, chemical inputs, hydrogen consumption and refining.

— Food-versus-Fuel debate and sustainable feedstock utilisation: First-generation biofuels use food crops such as sugarcane, maize and rice, potentially creating competition between food and fuel production. Second-generation biofuels use non-food biomass, including crop residues, husks and bagasse, reducing direct competition.
— However, residues also serve as animal feed, compost and soil amendments. Excessive removal can reduce soil organic carbon, affect nutrient recycling and undermine soil health.
FYI: Technology Development Board (TDB)
— Technology Development Board (TDB) is a statutory body under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), Ministry of Science and Technology.
— It was constituted under the Technology Development Board Act, 1995.

— TDB provides financial assistance to Indian industrial concerns and other agencies involved in the commercial application of indigenous technologies, as well as the adaptation of imported technologies for wider domestic applications. It provides financial assistance through three principal modes:
— Investment Committee (IC) of TDB:
BEYOND THE NUGGET: How is India building its biofuel ecosystem?
1. National Policy on Biofuels, 2018 (amended in 2022):
— The policy promotes biofuels to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, boost domestic production and diversify feedstocks.
— It covers bioethanol, biodiesel and advanced biofuels derived from agricultural and other lignocellulosic residues.

— The 2022 amendment advanced the indicative target of 20% ethanol blending in petrol from 2030 to Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025–26. The indicative target for biodiesel blending in diesel remains 5% by 2030.
2. Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN Yojana:
— The scheme provides financial support to integrated bioethanol projects, particularly those using lignocellulosic biomass and other renewable feedstocks.
— Modified in August 2024, it expanded to cover agricultural and forestry residues, industrial waste, synthesis gas and algae, and was extended by five years, up to 2028–29.
— It promotes advanced biofuel technologies, adds value to agricultural residues and strengthens energy security.
3. GOBARdhan initiative:
— Launched in 2018, GOBARdhan (Galvanising Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan) promotes converting cattle dung and other biodegradable waste into biogas, bio-slurry, compost and bio-CNG/CBG.

— It links waste management with clean energy, organic manure and rural livelihoods. In August 2026, the Union Cabinet approved a new national scheme for the CBG sector, with an outlay of ₹23,731 crore over ten years (FY 2026–27 to FY 2035–36).
— It includes assured CBG offtake, pricing support, capital assistance and pipeline connectivity.
4. Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme:
— Implemented through public-sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs), the programme promotes ethanol blending with petrol.

—The government advanced the 20% ethanol blending (E20) target from 2030 to ESY 2025–26, achieving it five years ahead of schedule (as per the Government update). Under the EBP Programme, blending increased from less than 1.5% in 2013–14 to 20% in 2025–26.
Best Practices: Brazil’s ethanol model (lessons for India):
Key factors behind Brazil’s wider adoption of ethanol-blended fuels:

— Flex-fuel vehicles (FFVs): Brazil encouraged the widespread adoption of FFVs, which can run on different petrol-ethanol blends, including high-ethanol fuels. This gave consumers greater flexibility in fuel choices.

— Consumer choice and price incentives: Brazilian motorists can choose between ethanol-blended petrol and nearly pure ethanol (E100), depending on availability and price. Government support and price incentives have encouraged ethanol adoption.

India needs a phased transition, greater availability of flex-fuel vehicles, adequate vehicle-readiness standards, consumer awareness and transparent communication about fuel efficiency and compatibility. Blending targets must be aligned with vehicle technology, infrastructure and consumer interests
Post Read Question
With reference to the classification of biofuels, consider the following statements:
1. First-generation biofuels are generally derived from food crops such as sugarcane, maize and vegetable oils.
2. Second-generation biofuels are produced from non-food biomass, including agricultural residues and lignocellulosic materials.
3. Algae-based biofuels are generally classified as second-generation biofuels.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 2 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
Answer: (c)

Defiant Hegseth slams efforts to impeach him
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.

Main Examination: General Studies II: Comparison of the Indian constitutional scheme with that of other countries and Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India’s interests, Indian diaspora.

What’s the ongoing story:The bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has failed in the 435-member US House of Representatives. The impeachment notice was moved in the House by Republican congressman Thomas Massie. He accused Hegseth of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation and misusing his official position.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is impeachment under the US constitutional system?
• Who is Indian counterpart to US Defence Secretary?

• What are the constitutional relationship between the US President, Congress and the Secretary of Defence in matters concerning national security and military operations? (Compare this with Indian Scenario also)
• What were the principal allegations contained in the eight articles of impeachment introduced against Pete Hegseth?
• What is the role of the US House of Representatives and the Senate in the impeachment process?
• Know the procedure for impeachment in the Indian Constitution.
• Compare the impeachment procedures of the United States and India with reference to the initiation of charges, investigation and final removal from office.
• The US Constitution provides for impeachment of the President, Vice-President and other civil officers, whereas India’s Article 61 specifically deals with impeachment of the President—Discuss
Key Takeaways:
• In the US, its Constitution impeachable offenses are “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors

• The House majority has agreed to refer the impeachment articles to a separate committee instead. Only Massie voted against sending the resolution to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, reported the BBC.
• Hegseth later described the effort to impeach him as “farce” and “sabotage”.

• The bid to remove Hegseth, one of US President Donald Trump’s closest aides, failed in a 211-204 vote in favour of sending the motion to the Judiciary committe. Several Representatives skipped vote. This included 11 Democrats.
Do You Know:

• Massie’s 34-page resolution lists eight articles of impeachment, covering military operations in Iran, Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean and Pacific, as well as allegations involving civilian casualties and freedom of speech.

• Under the US Constitution, Congress has the power to declare war, while the President serves as commander-in-chief of the armed forces. The War Powers Resolution of 1973 was enacted to place limits on a president’s ability to conduct military operations without congressional authorisation.
The law requires the President to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying troops into hostilities. Unless Congress authorises the operation, US forces must generally be withdrawn within 60 days, with a possible additional 30 days for their safe withdrawal.

• Trump subsequently argued that the April 7 ceasefire with Iran had ended hostilities and effectively stopped the 60-day clock, which was set to expire on May 1.
Legal scholars, however, questioned this interpretation. Jasmine Farrier, a political science professor at the University of Louisville, pointed to the difficulty Congress faces in enforcing the law following a 1983 Supreme Court ruling against legislative vetoes. Congress must now pass legislation to stop military operations, which the President can veto.

• The continued US military presence near Iran also raised questions about whether hostilities had actually ended. On April 19, a US warship fired at an Iranian-flagged cargo vessel attempting to breach the American blockade, despite Trump’s assertion that there had been no exchange of fire since the ceasefire.

• Massie’s resolution now accuses Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution on three counts: initiating hostilities without congressional approval, continuing military operations despite a congressional direction to withdraw, and disregarding the statutory deadline for ending unauthorised hostilities.

• Under the US Constitution, federal officials, including Cabinet secretaries, can be impeached for “treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanours”. The House of Representatives can impeach an official by a simple majority, formally bringing charges against them. Removal from office, however, requires a separate Senate process, where conviction needs a two-thirds majority of senators present. The Senate can also vote to disqualify a convicted official from future federal office.
Only two Cabinet secretaries have been impeached so far: William Belknap in 1876 and Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. Neither was convicted by the Senate.

Sci-Fi breaks Booker barrier as M John Harrison wins prize for ‘The End of Everything’
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.

What’s the ongoing story: M John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for his novel The End of Everything, published by Serpent’s Tail. The winner was announced in the early hours of Tuesday, November 10, IST, at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate in London, which was livestreamed on the Booker Prize’s channels. Harrison receives £50,000 (about ₹62 lakh) and a trophy named Iris.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is “New Weird”?
• What is the Booker Prize?
• Who is M. John Harrison?
• What is science fiction as a literary genre?
• What is dystopian literature?
• Why is M. John Harrison’s 2026 Booker Prize victory considered a milestone in the recognition of science fiction as literary fiction?
Key Takeaways:

• At 81, Harrison becomes the oldest winner in the prize’s history. The End of Everything, his 13th novel, is set in a near-future, post-catastrophe Britain, where Phillip Tennent makes his living scavenging the Kent coastline as the sea washes up strange artefacts left behind by the iGhetti, mysterious entities that arrived with an unexplained “Event”. When he fishes out a shapeshifting object he cannot keep, he must carry it inland before it destroys everything he thinks he knows.

• The Booker Prize Foundation describes the book as a “slyly satirical and unsettling post-apocalyptic adventure into the limits of human understanding.” Harrison has described it as a satire on gentrification.

• Reviewing the novel for The Indian Express, Shalini Langer called it “a bleak account of such a post-apocalyptic England, which is now more than ever an isolated island,” a world in which “death has seeped into everything, living and non-living.” She also read it as a parable for the age of artificial intelligence: “As we stand at the brink of a life to apparently be determined by Artificial Intelligence, which side really lies the artifice?”
Do You Know:

• A genre-defying British author and critic, Harrison sold his first story in 1965 and later edited the speculative fiction magazine New Worlds. He is known for the Viriconium stories and the Kefahuchi Tract trilogy, and has previously won the Boardman Tasker Prize, the James Tiptree Jr Award, the Arthur C Clarke Award and the Goldsmiths Prize. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 2025 and was himself a Booker judge in 2022.
• A panel chaired by classicist Mary Beard chose the winning novel from 163 submissions, alongside poet Raymond Antrobus, musician Jarvis Cocker, critic Rebecca Liu and novelist Patricia Lockwood.

• The other five shortlisted authors each receive £2,500 (about ₹3 lakh): Marlon James for The Disappearers, Luke Kennard for Black Bag, Rebecca Perry for May We Feed the King, Elizabeth Strout for The Things We Never Say, and Douglas Stuart for John of John.
• Harrison succeeds David Szalay, who won the 2025 prize for Flesh.

• Traditional fantasy typically features heroes who triumph so readers can imagine they lived happily ever after, but the New Weird turns this trope on its head. Women in Science Fiction and Fantasy (2009), edited by literary scholar Robin Anne Reid, describes the New Weird as fiction that subverts the clichés of the fantastic “in order to put them to discomfiting, rather than consoling ends.”

Ukraine talks begin, India pushes for safe Black Sea, quick end to war
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Main Examination: General Studies II: Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India’s interests.

What’s the ongoing story:As US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine began in Abu Dhabi Tuesday to try and end the nearly five-year war, India said it was “in touch with both sides” and other “interested parties” to “contribute” towards the “return of peace” to the region.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Map Work-Ukraine, Black sea region
• What is the strategic and economic significance of the Black Sea in international trade?
• What is the importance of Ukraine’s major Black Sea ports—Odesa, Chornomorsk, and Pivdennyi?
• What is meant by a food corridor in the context of an armed conflict?
• What are the major elements of India’s proposals for de-escalating the Russia-Ukraine conflict, as highlighted in the article?
• Know India’s stated position on resolving the Russia-Ukraine conflict through dialogue and diplomacy.
Key Takeaways:

• Ahead of the talks, which were last held in February this year, Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said India was ready to “mediate in establishing food corridors” in Ukraine. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, meanwhile, spoke to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

• India’s proposals revolve around easing the intense fighting since July around the critical Black Sea region – this will allow Ukraine’s agricultural produce to reach the world; Russia halting attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure; and Ukraine refraining from attacking Russian positions along the line of contact.

• The larger Black Sea region is key to trade and security interests of both Ukraine and Russia. It is the grain export hub of Ukraine, a major agricultural exporter. Russia too exports significant volumes of grain through the Azov-Black Sea region, an area it considers vital for military power projection.
Do You Know:

• In May-June 2025, Ukrainian and Russian officials met for their first direct talks after the 2022 war began in Istanbul, Turkey. This Turkey-mediated meeting was marked by a 28-point US-Russia peace plan that included Ukraine permanently denouncing NATO membership and a total prohibition on Ukraine’s long-range arsenal — a demand that was denied by Zelensky. It was also met with a swift counter-proposal by the European bloc, which demanded a “robust, Article 5-style security guarantee” mirroring that of the NATO agreement. Article 5 encapsulates the principle of collective defence, where an attack on any member is considered an attack on all.
Russia’s proposal also outlined sweeping domestic reform, such as an armed personnel cap, and ultimately, no common ground was reached.

• The next meeting came about in February 2026 in Geneva. Here, Moscow firmly insisted that Ukraine formally cede the entire Donbas region before it would even entertain a cessation of hostilities. Kyiv explicitly rejected these terms, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s delegation demanded an unconditional ceasefire, and the talks stalled again. Any further action was marred by the fact that only days later, the US — alongside Israel — was embroiled in a conflict against Iran, severely depleting its diplomatic capacity and shifting its focus elsewhere.

• The two days of negotiations in Abu Dhabi are expected to focus on the three broad questions of territory, post-war security guarantees and the future security architecture of Europe. Notably, Russia — and Putin — have remained steadfast in insisting that no European delegation be present, despite the Trump administration having suggested that a new European security “framework” may be tabled. The most immediate sticking point remains the question of territory. Russia currently controls Crimea, which it annexed from Ukraine in 2014, and substantial parts of eastern and southern Ukraine. Moscow has also claimed the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions as Russian territory. Their principal demand remains that Ukraine withdraw from Donbas, allowing the surrender of territory that may have otherwise not been captured.

• A day before the Abu Dhabi negotiations began, Zelenskyy spoke to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, briefing him on preparations for the trilateral meeting. Hours later, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar also spoke to his Russian counterpart.
Zelenskyy specifically urged India to identify the steps it could take, and the dialogue it could pursue with other world leaders, to help bring the war to an end. He also pointed to food security as a possible area of cooperation, with India expressing readiness to mediate in establishing food corridors through the Black Sea.

Retired officials rehired also come under model code: EC
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Salient features of the Representation of People’s Act.

What’s the ongoing story:The Election Commission on Monday directed authorities in five election-bound states that restrictions under the model code of conduct (MCC) that apply to government officials should extend to retired officials re-employed or engaged by state governments.
Key Points to Ponder:
• How Election Commission described MCC?
• What is the Model Code of Conduct?
• When does the Model Code of Conduct come into effect?
• What restrictions does the Model Code of Conduct impose?
• Is the Model Code of Conduct legally binding?
• Who comes under the Model Code of Conduct?
• Know the constitutional position and powers of the Election Commission of India under Article 324 of the Constitution.
• What restrictions does the Model Code of Conduct impose on government servants during elections?
Key Takeaways:

• Writing to the chief secretaries and chief electoral officers of Goa, Manipur, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, and Uttarakhand, where Assembly elections are expected early in 2027, the EC said it previously issued instructions that government employees must not participate in election campaigns or support any individual or party during elections.

• “The provisions of the Model Code of Conduct apply to all organisations/committees, corporations/commissions, etc. funded wholly or partially by the Government, and their employees. Further, the relevant Conduct Rules, in the States, prohibit the Government servants from taking part in political activities and elections,” the EC said.

• The EC added that the same restrictions should extend to retired government employees engaged or re-employed in various capacities by the states, noting that there were “no specific guidelines or rules relating to their political neutrality and conduct during MCC period”.
Do You Know:

• The Election Commission’s Model Code of Conduct is a set of guidelines issued to regulate political parties and candidates prior to elections. The rules range from issues related to speeches, polling day, polling booths, portfolios, content of election manifestos, processions and general conduct, so that free and fair elections are conducted.

• According to the Press Information Bureau, a version of the MCC was first introduced in the state assembly elections in Kerala in 1960. It was largely followed by all parties in the 1962 elections and continued to be followed in subsequent general elections. In October 1979, the EC added a section to regulate the ‘party in power’ and prevent it from gaining an unfair advantage at the time of elections.

• The MCC comes into force from the date the election schedule is announced until the date that results are out. As a result, it will kick in from today evening and will remain in effect until the election process is concluded. The MCC contains eight provisions dealing with general conduct, meetings, processions, polling day, polling booths, observers, the party in power, and election manifestos.

• As soon as the code kicks in, the party in power — whether at the Centre or in the States — should ensure that it does not use its official position for campaigning. Hence, no policy, project or scheme can be announced that can influence the voting behaviour. The party must also avoid advertising at the cost of the public exchequer or using official mass media for publicity on achievements to improve chances of victory in the elections.

• The code also states that the ministers must not combine official visits with election work or use official machinery for the same. The ruling party also cannot use government transport or machinery for campaigning. It should also ensure that public places such as maidans etc., for holding election meetings, and facilities like the use of helipads are provided to the opposition parties on the same terms and conditions on which they are used by the party in power. The issue of advertisement at the cost of public exchequer in the newspapers and other media is also considered an offence. The ruling government cannot make any ad-hoc appointments in Government, Public Undertakings etc. which may influence the voters.

The Editorial Page
Court dismantles unconstitutional buffer zone between detention & arrest
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Indian Polity and Governance-Constitution, Political System, Panchayati Raj, Public Policy, Rights Issues, etc.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Indian Constitution—historical underpinnings, evolution, features, amendments, significant provisions and basic structure.

What’s the ongoing story: Faizan Mustafa Writes—Every arrest deprives liberty and, therefore, must be a last resort in a liberal democracy. Even words may amount to arrest if they are calculated to bring to a person’s notice that he is under compulsion and he, thereafter, submits to such compulsion. Indeed, the word “arrest” is a legal term of art.
Key Points to Ponder:
• Know the Terms- Arrest, Detention, Remand, bail, Punitive detention and Preventive detention
• Why is communication of the grounds of arrest considered an essential constitutional safeguard?
• What is meant by ‘due process’ in the context of arrest and criminal investigation?
• How does judicial oversight help prevent arbitrary deprivation of liberty?
• What Article 22 of the Constitution says?
• What is the significance of the Supreme Court’s judgment in Sujit Das v. Union of India?

Key Takeaways:
Faizan Mustafa Writes—

• At a time when there is a widespread conversation about institutional decay, with some expressing concerns that the Supreme Court has become an executive-minded court, a two-judge bench led by Justice Ujjal Bhuyan — Justice A S Chandurkar was the other judge — has given a bold judgment that drastically restricts the power of the police to detain people before their formal arrest.

• In Prabir Purkayastha (2024), too, a violation of Article 22(1) for not supplying grounds of arrest was the basis of his release. In last week’s verdict, the right to production before a magistrate within 24 hours under Article 22(2) was in question.

• Unfortunately, the 44th constitutional amendment (1978) that was aimed at humanising preventive detention in Article 22(4) has not been notified even after 48 years. This shows successive governments’ lack of commitment to due process. Interestingly, Article 22(1) and (2) in essence incorporated guarantees — right to counsel of choice and production before a magistrate within 24 hours — that were already part of the colonial government’s Code of Criminal Procedure,1898.

• Justice Bhuyan is showing, time and again, that every appointment to the apex court is extremely important. Judges sitting even in smaller benches not only greatly contribute to our constitutional jurisprudence but can help reinforce the people’s trust in the judiciary.

• Criminal law is the most direct expression of the relationship between a state and its citizens. Criminal sanction is the most coercive method of regulating an individual’s behaviour that a state can deploy.
Do You Know:

• As per the National Crime Records Bureau, in 2024, we recorded 58,85,867 cognisable crimes, with 35,44,608 under IPC/BNS and 23,41,259 under special and local laws. In most crimes, there are several suspects and accused who are arrested. About 72.6 per cent of prisoners are undertrials — they have not been convicted of any crime.

• Article 22 is a fundamental right under the Constitution that provides for an accused to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, to be informed about the grounds of arrest, and to get legal representation.

• Article 22(1) applies across the spectrum including offences under the BNS or under special enactments. It is not statute specific. It is not a mere formality or a matter of procedure. It is a mandatory binding constitutional safeguard. When there is violation of the Constitution, question of prejudice or demonstrable prejudice does not arise. The safeguards adumbrated in Article 22(1) are not mere procedural safeguards; these are fundamental principles which are required to be followed in the event liberty of a person is sought to be curtailed,” the court said.

The Ideas Page
World Bank’s poverty estimate does not pass the thali test
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Economic and Social Development
Mains Examination:
• General Studies I: Poverty and developmental issues,
• General Studies II: Issues relating to poverty and hunger
• General Studies III: Inclusive growth and issues arising from it

What’s the ongoing story: Pulapre Balakrishnan, Aman Raj Writes— The latest poverty estimates could create complacency in economic policymaking — if extreme poverty is almost nonexistent, policies are needed to remedy it. But our finding of a low level of food consumption for a significant section of Indians imparts an urgency to it.
Key Points to Ponder:
• The World Bank recently released estimates of poverty in India—What has the latest World Bank data shown on poverty in India?
• What is the point of a poverty line?
• How poverty is Defined by World Bank?
• Extreme poverty definition by World Bank?
• Classifications of poverty-Know in Detail
• Poverty estimation in India-How Poverty is defined in India?
• Why is India using the World Bank’s poverty line to estimate poverty?
• How World Bank calculates poverty line?
• What is the Thali Index?
• What are the major findings of the Thali Index regarding the ability of rural and urban Indians to afford two meals a day?
• Differentiate between monetary poverty and food deprivation.
• What were India’s domestic poverty lines in the past?
• Why are poverty estimates about India contested by many?
• What do you understand by the term ‘head-count ratio’?
• Alagh Committee (1979) Lakdawala Committee (1993), Tendulkar Committee (2009), Rangarajan committee (2012) and their poverty estimation.
• What do understand by Private Final Consumption Expenditure (PFCE) and Government Final Consumption Expenditure (GFCE)?
Key Takeaways:

• The World Bank recently released estimates of poverty in India, pegging “extreme poverty” at 2.6 per cent. If true, that would be good news, as it would imply that high levels of economic deprivation are now a thing of the past. We argue that such a conclusion would be premature.

• The WB’s poverty estimate is a headcount ratio — the ratio of the number of poor to the population. It estimates the number of poor by applying a poverty line to data reported in the NSS’s Household Consumption Expenditure Survey for 2023-24 (HCES). The poverty line translated into goods represents the minimum acceptable level of consumption, below which an individual is deemed poor. The report does not mention the set of goods and their prices that the World Bank used to construct its poverty line for India. The Survey is a rich source of consumption across the population and reveals granular information on the standard of living, which can be used to assess a headcount poverty estimate, as we demonstrate.

• In 2025, we proposed a simple measure of the standard of living in India (‘The Thali Index’, IE, July 1, 2025). Termed the “thali index”, it measures the number of thalis an individual can afford to buy based on the monthly per capita expenditure on food reported in the HCES.

• The latest poverty estimates could create complacency in economic policymaking — if extreme poverty is almost non-existent, policies are needed to remedy it. But our finding of a low level of food consumption for a significant section of Indians imparts an urgency to it. The level of food consumption is directly affected by food prices, and controlling the price of food is central to safeguarding the well-being of the population.
Do You Know:

• Poverty line is the level of income used as a cut-off point for deciding who is poor in any economy. It is important to note here that the context (both time period and location) is critical to arriving at a meaningful poverty line.
For instance, an Indian receiving a salary of Rs 1,000 a month may not have been considered poor in 1975, but today that income (Rs 33 a day) will barely buy anything.
Similarly, a monthly salary of Rs 1,00,000 (or Rs 3,333 a day) in today’s Patna will be comfortable for a person to live by, but the same salary in Paris or New York may not buy the same lifestyle.

• Governments, especially in developing and poor countries, want to identify the extent of poverty in their countries. This has two uses. One, to help them gauge the extent of poverty and shape welfare policies for the poor. The second use is for governments, policymakers and analysts to understand whether a set of policies has actually worked over time to reduce poverty and improve wellbeing.
• Historically, India had been a leader in poverty estimation and India’s poverty line methodology and data collection influenced the rest of the world in how to study poverty.

Study: CO2 emissions from fossil fuels to decline this year
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Main Examination: General Studies III: Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, environmental impact assessment.

What’s the ongoing story:Global carbon dioxide emissions from burning fossil fuels are projected to be slightly lower than 2025, in part because of supply shocks created by the US-Iran conflict and the growing footprint of renewable energy sources, reveals a new study by the Global Carbon Budget.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What are fossil-fuel-related CO₂ emissions?
• What are the major sources of carbon dioxide emissions discussed in the Global Carbon Budget study?
• What are the principal findings of the Global Carbon Budget study regarding projected global fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions in 2026?
• Why is the projected decline in global fossil-fuel emissions in 2026 significant?
• What is the significance of the 1.5°C temperature target under the Paris Agreement?
Key Takeaways:

• Released at the COP31 climate meeting in Antalya, Turkey, on Tuesday, the study said carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels in 2026 was expected to be 38.2 billion tonnes, 0.4% lower than the 38.4 billion tonnes measured for 2025.

• India was the only major emitter whose fossil fuel emissions were expected to grow in 2026. The study said India’s fossil fuel emissions in 2026 were likely to be 4.4% higher than the previous year, while China, the United States, European Union and Japan are expected to see declines, the study said. India’s growth this year is higher than the 3.5% average annual growth it registered over the last one decade, it said.

• While the small dip of 0.4% in global CO2 emissions might appear to be an encouraging signal from a climate change perspective, researchers behind the study clarified that it is most likely a short-term consequence of the ongoing conflict.

• “A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, who led the study.

• The expected marginal decline in CO2 emissions from fossil fuels this year would be the first since 2020, when the Covid19 pandemic had resulted in a 2% drop, the biggest year-on-year decline measured so far.
Similar small declines have been witnessed in 1992, 2009, 1981, 1974, and 1998, all associated with some kind of global churn that affected industrial activity and led to reduced fuel usage.
• Such reductions in fossil fuel emissions have remained single-year aberrations, caused by some temporary disruption, and have resumed on their upward trajectory after that.
Do You Know:

• The Global Carbon Budget study restricts itself only to measuring carbon dioxide emissions from burning of fossil fuels and some other sources. It is only the fossil fuel-related CO2 emissions that have shown a decline.

• The overall emissions of greenhouse gases are still rising, as pointed out by the State of the Climate Report released on Monday. That report, an annual publication of the World Meteorological Organisation, which, too, is released to coincide with the climate conference, said that the greenhouse gas emissions had touched a new high in 2025, and early indications for 2026 suggested that it would continue to increase this year as well.

• Scientific assessments had found that the world needed to cut its annual greenhouse gas emissions by almost a half from 2019 levels by 2030 to give itself minimal chance to keep the rise in global temperatures within 1.5 degrees Celsius from pre-industrial times, a target defined in the Paris Agreement. However, the annual emissions are still rising and current projections show that even in the best case scenario, not more than 2% reduction in annual emissions would be achieved by 2030.
