Discoms’ finances emerge as key concern amid energy storage push
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Economic and Social Development-Sustainable Development, Poverty, Inclusion, Demographics, Social Sector Initiatives, etc.
Main Examination: General Studies III: Infrastructure: Energy, Ports, Roads, Airports, Railways etc.

What’s the ongoing story:As the government works on a mandate requiring electricity distribution utilities (discoms) to add energy storage capacity, concerns are emerging over the ability of financially stressed discoms to shoulder the additional investment burden, given their already stretched finances and limited capacity to fund new infrastructure.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What are electricity distribution companies (discoms)?
• How discoms are backbone when it comes to electricity supply chain?
• What are Energy Storage Systems (ESS)?
• How Energy Storage Systems help address the intermittent nature of solar and wind energy.
• Why has energy storage become increasingly important as India expands its renewable energy capacity?
• What is an Energy Storage Obligation (ESO)?
• Why is the Centre considering making energy storage procurement mandatory for electricity distribution utilities?
Key Takeaways:

• While the specific storage capacity that utilities will be required to procure has not been finalised yet, the proposed mandate is at an early stage of formulation, with its contours still being worked out.

• The development comes as energy storage systems are becoming vital as the country rapidly scales up its renewable energy capacity to meet its climate goals. However, the growing share of intermittent renewable sources such as solar and wind is posing a challenge for the power system: generation is often abundant during certain hours but insufficient to meet demand at other times.
• Energy storage systems can address this mismatch by storing surplus electricity when renewable generation is high and releasing it when demand rises or generation from these sources falls.

• The government has already proposed making battery storage mandatory for all new government solar and wind power projects from July 2027. The proposed mandate is expected to extend the storage requirement beyond project developers to electricity procurers, including discoms, which purchase power from generating companies. This would mean that utilities may also have to factor storage capacity into their power procurement plans.
Do You Know:

• A growing financial imbalance is placing electricity distribution companies in the country under mounting strain, highlighting the need to redesign retail electricity tariffs, the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has flagged in a new report in May 2026.

• The strain is mainly because of the widening mismatch between the fixed costs incurred by electricity distribution companies, or DISCOMs, and the fixed charges they recover from consumers through electricity bills, the report noted.

• While a large share of a DISCOM’s expenditure remains fixed and must be paid regardless of how much electricity is sold, the bulk of its revenue continues to depend on variable energy consumption. The electricity bill a consumer pays does have a fixed component and another depending on the actual units used, but the former is too small to recover a DISCOM’s expenditure.

• A DISCOM’s fixed costs include capacity payments to thermal power generators, transmission costs, employee salaries, and infrastructure maintenance. These expenses have to be paid on a lumpsum basis, irrespective of DISCOM’s energy sales.

Why a floundering COP still matters
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Current events of national and international importance.
Mains Examination: General Studies II: Important International institutions, agencies and fora- their structure, mandate
What’s the ongoing story:The annual United Nations Climate Change Conference, or COP31, this year comes amid a troubling reality check.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is the Conference of the Parties (COP) under the United Nations climate framework?
• What are the stakes for COP31?
• How is COP31 different from previous COPs?
• What are the principal temperature goals established under the 2015 Paris Agreement?
• What are the major findings of the 2026 United Nations Environment Programme reports regarding the feasibility of limiting global warming to 1.5°C?
• Explain the consensus-based decision-making process followed at COP meetings.
• Despite more than three decades of international climate negotiations, the world remains far from achieving its climate targets—Why?
• Why is COP31 unlikely to produce a major breakthrough in global climate action?
Key Takeaways:

• According to two reports released by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) earlier this year, the window of opportunity to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels is firmly shut now. The best the world can now hope for, the reports say, is to restrict the temperature rise to 1.7-1.8°C. This is the first time that any scientific assessment of climate change has made such an assertion.

• One might have therefore expected the COP31 climate conference, which began in the Turkish city of Antalya on Monday (November 9 and runs till November 20), to focus on finding ways to put the world back on track. However, the conference is unlikely to deliver any outcome that can be considered a breakthrough on this front.

• The 1.5°C target did not suddenly become unattainable this year. It was always a difficult target, and years of inadequate climate action have finally led scientists to conclude that it can no longer be achieved. No outcome from COP31, however ambitious, can reopen that window of opportunity.

• In terms of expected outcome and impact, COP31 could turn out to be one of the most inconsequential COPs in recent years, though not because of any shortcoming of its own. COPs, in general, have always underperformed. These annual year-ending two-week conferences, which attracted the largest gatherings of global leaders until not so long ago, have only produced low-ambition outcomes. In the last two decades, its most important success has been finalising the 2015 Paris Agreement, which defined the climate targets and framed the broad rules for international climate action.

• But COPs have had a poor record in convincing the member countries — virtually the entire world till the United States decided to walk out — to do enough to achieve those targets. COPs take decisions only through consensus, and there is no way to force laggard nations to do more.

• The result has been a widening gap between what is required to achieve the targets set in the Paris Agreement and the actions actually taken by individual countries. The gap has grown so large that COPs no longer seem interested in even pretending to catch up. Any outcome that enables incremental progress towards reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and prevents further backsliding, is now considered a good outcome.
By this metric, the success of COP31 would rest on being able to build on the decisions taken in past COPs, particularly in Brazil last year, to keep pushing for decarbonisation and energy transition.
Do You Know:

• Climate change has largely disappeared from the agendas of other major global and regional forums, thanks to multiple wars, rapidly evolving technological threats, and new demands for energy use. While several immediate challenges have emerged in recent years, the problem of climate change has not disappeared, as evidenced by the growing number of large-scale climate disasters. COPs remain the only major global stage that continues to focus on climate change.

• The COPs are still the only forum where developing countries can demand greater accountability from the developed world, which bears the primary responsibility for addressing climate change. Nepal was recently promised US$ 20 million from the newly-established Loss and Damage Fund for recovery and reconstruction efforts after the devastating flash floods in August. While the allocated sum is only a fraction of what Nepal needs to rebuild after the disaster, there is no other international forum where it could have demanded and received this kind of funding without any strings attached and within a short span of time. There is also a possibility that Nepal could receive more money from the Fund.

• Most countries appear to have reconciled with the reality that not just the 1.5℃, but even the 2℃, target might be breached in the coming decades, unless some really unexpected technology intervention takes place.

OBC reservation: What determines creamy layer status
Syllabus:
Preliminary Examination: Indian Polity and Governance-Constitution, Political System, Panchayati Raj, Public Policy, Rights Issues, etc.

Mains Examination: General Studies II: Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections of the population by the Centre and States and the performance of these schemes; mechanisms, laws, institutions and Bodies constituted for the protection and betterment of these vulnerable sections.

What’s the ongoing story: The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6) said its March verdict on the “creamy layer” among Other Backward Classes (OBCs) will not reopen selections and appointments already concluded but will apply to the pending Civil Services Examination (CSE) 2025 service allocation.
Key Points to Ponder:
• What is creamy layer?
• Why has the service allocation of 958 candidates who cleared the Civil Services Examination 2025 been delayed?
• What is the Supreme Court’s March 11, 2026 judgment?
• Who will benefit from the Supreme Court ruling?
• Why did the Supreme Court hold that parental salary income alone cannot be the sole criterion for determining whether an OBC candidate belongs to the creamy layer?
• Why was the creamy layer introduced?
• What are the criterion for deciding creamy layer for OBC reservation?
• What was the SC ruling in the Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)?
• How Article 14, 15, and 16 of the Constitution indirectly associated with affirmative action?
• What are the DoPT OM of 1993 and the clarification of October 2004?
• What was the impact of the DoPT clarification?
Key Takeaways:

• The “creamy layer” is a term used in India’s reservation system to describe wealthier, more advanced members of OBCs. Those included in the creamy layer are not entitled to OBC reservation benefits.

• In March, the court had ruled that income cannot be the sole criterion to decide the OBC creamy layer, and settled the long-pending question of equivalence between public sector undertakings (PSUs) and private sector employees and those in the government sector.
• The Centre then sought clarification on the verdict’s temporal reach, leading to the formation of a bench of Justices PS Narasimha and R Mahadevan.

• That bench has now ruled: “The ratio laid down in the judgment shall not, by itself, furnish a ground for reopening selections or appointments already concluded prior to the judgment dated 11.03.2026.” It added that “the process of allocation remains pending and there is no convincing or reasonable justification for deferring the implementation” of the March verdict.
Do You Know:

• That case arose from an office memorandum (OM) of September 1993 which laid down the criteria for identifying persons from the OBCs who fall within the “creamy layer” and are thus excluded from reservation. Under category IV of the income/wealth test, income from sources other than salaries and agricultural land is excluded.

• The Department of Personnel and Training clarified in a letter in October 2004 that where “equivalence” of posts in PSUs, banks and public employment had not been determined, those salaries would be assessed separately. If it crossed the prescribed limit for three consecutive years, the children would be under the creamy layer.

• The final result of CSE 2025 was declared five days before the March verdict. In its application, the Centre said that the retrospective implementation would unsettle concluded selections and service allocations, including those made in respect of earlier CSE.

• It pointed to more than 6.69 lakh reserved vacancies, including 3.70 lakh OBC vacancies filled over the past 10 years. The government argued for prospective overruling, under which a court can limit a ruling to future cases, asked if the judgement operates prospectively, and also sought two years to establish equivalence of posts after consulting all states and Union Territories.

• The court observed that the interpretation of the 1993 OM and the 2004 letter and the “rejection of mechanical exclusion based on salary income” were not open for reconsideration and said that the miscellaneous applications cannot be used as “a ruse to secure reconsideration of the merits of the judgment under the guise of seeking clarification”.

title: Knowledge Nugget | How has Madhya Pradesh’s Panari project put a tiger corridor in focus?

content.value: Written by Sanju Singh

Take a look at the essential events, concepts, terms, quotes, or phenomena every day and brush up your knowledge. Here’s your UPSC Current Affairs knowledge nugget for today on the Panari Pumped Storage Project and the Panna-Ranipur Tiger Corridor.
Knowledge Nugget: Panna-Ranipur Tiger Corridor and Wildlife Conservation
Subject: Environment and Ecology
Why in the news?
The FAC, under the Union Environment Ministry, recommended in-principle approval for the diversion of 511.91 hectares of forest land in Madhya Pradesh for the 1,800 MW Panari Pumped Storage Project.

Beyond this development, the project brings into focus the ecological significance of tiger corridors, the geography of Panna and Ranipur Tiger Reserves, and the institutional and legal framework governing forest diversion.
Key takeaways:

1. The project spans Satna and Panna districts. Around 211.7 hectares of the project area falls within the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)-approved North Eastern Tiger Corridor of Panna Tiger Reserve, which connects Panna with Ranipur Tiger Reserve in Uttar Pradesh.

2. The proposal was deferred earlier, pending recommendations from the Standing Committee of the National Board for Wildlife (SC-NBWL). The committee recommended wildlife clearance with conditions on July 9, 2026.

3. The project will have two reservoirs: an upper reservoir at Panari village in the North Panna Forest Division and a lower reservoir on the Baghain River in the Satna Forest Division. A pumped storage project uses the difference in elevation between the two reservoirs to store and generate electricity.
4. Impact of the project:
— The project may lead to the felling of approximately 1.32 lakh trees across the Satna and North Panna forest divisions, affecting wildlife habitats and ecological balance.

— The project falls within the Panna–Ranipur Tiger Corridor, which facilitates wildlife movement between the two reserves and supports tigers, leopards, dholes, wolves, sloth bears, gaurs, sambar and chital. Some project components also overlap with Panna Tiger Reserve’s satellite core areas.

— A Divisional Forest Officer (DFO) warned that the project could block the corridor, which has seen increased wildlife movement following the Ken-Betwa project, with no alternative dispersal route available.
5. Panna Tiger Reserve:

— Situated in the Vindhyan ranges of northern Madhya Pradesh, the reserve extends across Panna and Chhatarpur districts. The Ken river enters the reserve from the southern end and passes through it for almost 55 km.
— Panna National Park was established in 1981 and brought under Project Tiger in 1994. It was the fifth tiger reserve in Madhya Pradesh and the 22nd in India.
— The reserve is mainly characterised by dry deciduous forests, including dry teak and mixed forest types. Important tree species include teak, mahua, tendu and dhaw.
— Major wildlife species include tigers, leopards, sloth bears, wolves, hyenas, wild dogs, sambar, chital, nilgai and chinkara.
6. Ranipur Tiger Reserve:
— Situated in Chitrakoot district of Uttar Pradesh, in the Vindhyan hill ranges of the Bundelkhand region, the reserve comprises dry deciduous forests.
— Notified in October 2022, Ranipur became the fourth tiger reserve in Uttar Pradesh and the 53rd in India.
— The reserve is home to teak, mahua, bamboo, tendu, palash, khair, salai and amla. Its wildlife includes tigers, leopards, sloth bears, wolves, hyenas, wild dogs, chinkara, sambar and chital
— Ranipur is connected to Panna Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh through the Panna-Ranipur Tiger Corridor.
7. Significance of wildlife corridors: Wildlife corridors are natural or connected stretches of habitat that link two or more wildlife habitats or protected areas.
— Maintaining genetic diversity: Movement between isolated populations supports gene flow and reduces the risks associated with inbreeding.
— Habitat connectivity: They connect fragmented forests and protected areas, allowing wildlife to access larger landscapes.
— Ecological balance: They support the movement of different species and help maintain ecological processes.

— Human–wildlife coexistence: Corridors also support local communities that depend on forests and natural resources for their livelihoods. Therefore, conservation efforts must consider both wildlife movement and community interests.
FYI: Ken-Betwa Link Project (KBLP)

— The project aims to transfer water from the Ken river basin to the Betwa river basin to address water scarcity and irrigation challenges in Bundelkhand, covering parts of Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
— It is the first project under the National Perspective Plan for Interlinking of Rivers to enter the implementation stage.
— The project includes the Daudhan Dam on the Ken river, the Lower Orr Project, Kotha Barrage and Bina Complex Multipurpose Project, along with modernisation of irrigation infrastructure.
— Bundelkhand faces recurring droughts, water scarcity and inadequate irrigation. The project aims to improve water availability for irrigation and drinking purposes and provide hydropower benefits.

— The KBLP Authority is the implementing agency, while the National Water Development Agency (NWDA), established in 1982, is the nodal agency for interlinking studies. The foundation stone was laid on December 25, 2024.

— Environmental concerns: The Daudhan Dam and reservoir involve submergence of forest areas in the Panna landscape. Concerns include habitat loss, wildlife displacement and disruption of ecological connectivity, making the project’s impact on Panna Tiger Reserve and surrounding forests an important conservation issue.
BEYOND THE NUGGET: Institutions and bodies involved in environmental governance and wildlife clearances
1. Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC):
— It administers key laws, including the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980, Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
— It oversees forest and wildlife conservation policies and the relevant clearance processes.
— The Ministry administers the central forest diversion approval process.
2. Forest Advisory Committee (FAC):
— The FAC is an advisory committee constituted by the Central Government under Section 3 of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980.
— It examines proposals for diverting forest land for non-forest purposes and advises the Central Government on forest conservation.

— It assesses the impact of proposed projects, considers alternatives and recommends safeguards to minimise damage to forests. Its recommendations are not final forest clearance. The approval is granted by the Central Government.
3. National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA):

— The NTCA is a statutory body established under Section 38L of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, through the 2006 amendment. It functions under the MoEFCC and provides statutory backing to Project Tiger.

— Its functions include approving Tiger Conservation Plans, monitoring tiger populations and habitats, prescribing conservation standards, addressing human-wildlife conflict and assessing activities that may affect tiger reserves and their ecological sustainability.
— Its mandate also covers the protection of corridors connecting protected areas.
4. National Board for Wildlife (NBWL):
— The NBWL is a statutory body constituted under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. The Prime Minister is its Chairperson, while the Union Environment Minister is its Vice-Chairperson.

— It advises the Central and State Governments on wildlife conservation, protected area management, habitat protection and measures to control poaching and illegal wildlife trade. It also reviews the progress of wildlife conservation programmes.

— The NBWL can constitute a Standing Committee to exercise powers and perform duties delegated by the Board. It examines proposals involving wildlife-related considerations, including the potential impact of development projects on wildlife and their habitats.
Post Read Question
With reference to Ranipur Tiger Reserve, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. The reserve is situated in the Vindhyan ranges of northern Madhya Pradesh,
2. It became the 53rd Tiger Reserve in the country.
3. It is connected to Panna Tiger Reserve through a wildlife corridor.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
(a) 2 only
(b) 1 and 2 only
(c) 1 only
(d) 2 and 3 only
Answer: (d)

title: Knowledge Nugget | Pioxaniliprole: What makes India’s first indigenously developed insecticide significant?

content.value: Written by Sanju Singh

Take a look at the essential events, concepts, terms, quotes and developments shaping current affairs every day and brush up your knowledge. Here’s your UPSC Current Affairs Knowledge Nugget for today on Pioxaniliprole and India’s pesticide regulatory framework.
Knowledge Nugget: Pioxaniliprole and Insecticide Regulation in India
Subject: Agriculture / Science and Technology
Why in the news?

PI Industries Ltd’s Pioxaniliprole, India’s first indigenously discovered insecticide molecule, has received approval from the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIBRC) for use on rice, chilli, tomato and chana (chickpea) crops. Belonging to the anthranilic diamide class of insecticides, it targets ryanodine receptors in insects, causing feeding cessation, muscle paralysis and eventually death.

Beyond this development, Pioxaniliprole offers an opportunity to explore the mechanism of the insecticide, India’s regulatory framework under the Insecticides Act, 1968, and the role of CIBRC in regulating insecticides.
Key takeaways:
1. Pioxaniliprole is India’s first insecticide molecule to be indigenously discovered. It has been developed by PI Industries Ltd.
2. PI Industries plans to launch the molecule under the trade name ‘Pioxazon’ in the coming Rabi (winter-spring) crop season.
3. The molecule has received approval from the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIBRC) following regulatory studies and multilocation field trials.
4. Pioxaniliprole belongs to the anthranilic diamide class of insecticides, which acts on calcium-releasing channels in insects.
5. Target insect pests: The insecticide is effective against yellow stem borer, leaf folder, fall armyworm, tobacco cutworm, fruit borer and pod borer.
6. Pioxaniliprole’s chemical composition and mechanism of action:
— Pioxaniliprole is an insecticidal active ingredient belonging to the anthranilic diamide class of insecticides.
— It is designed to control insect pests, particularly caterpillar-type pests (larvae of moths and butterflies), affecting agricultural crops.
— It is registered as a 20% weight-by-volume (w/v) suspension concentrate (SC) formulation. It is a carboxamide compound containing chlorine, nitrogen, oxygen and sulphur atoms.
— Formulation:
— Mechanism of action:

The indigenous development of Pioxaniliprole highlights India’s growing research and innovation capabilities in agrochemicals and its potential to develop proprietary crop-protection solutions, reducing reliance on foreign innovations.
FYI: Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIB&RC)

— CIB&RC operates under the Directorate Plant Protection, Quarantine & Storage (DPPQ&S), Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India.
— Its headquarter is located in Faridabad, Haryana. It operates under the Insecticides Act, 1968 and the Insecticides Rules, 1971.
— The CIB&RC comprises two statutory bodies: the Central Insecticides Board (CIB) and the Registration Committee (RC).
— The Central Government appoints a Secretary to the Board, who also serves as the Secretary to the Registration Committee.

— The manufacture, import, sale or distribution of insecticides in India requires regulatory approval and a Certificate of Registration from the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIB&RC).
— Central Insecticides Board (CIB):
— Registration Committee (RC):
BEYOND THE NUGGET: Legal and Institutional Framework for Insecticide Regulation in India
1. Insecticides Act, 1968:
— The Act provides the legal framework for regulating the import, manufacture, sale, transport, distribution and use of insecticides in India to prevent risks to human beings and animals.

— It provides for the registration of insecticides based on their efficacy and safety, regulates their manufacture and sale through licensing, and prescribes mechanisms for inspection, sampling, testing and quality control. It also establishes the Central Insecticides Board (CIB) and the Registration Committee (RC).
2. Insecticides Rules, 1971:
— Framed under the Insecticides Act, 1968, the Rules lay down procedures and standards for its implementation.

— They prescribe requirements for the packaging, labelling, storage and transport of insecticides, specify safety precautions and toxicity classification, and provide for residue tolerance limits and minimum intervals between pesticide application and harvesting.
— They also cover licensing and quality-control requirements.
3. Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage (DPPQ&S):
— An attached office of the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, the DPPQ&S was established in 1946 and is headquartered in Faridabad, Haryana.
— It coordinates plant protection activities through Integrated Pest Management (IPM), which promotes biological, cultural, mechanical and need-based chemical methods of pest control.

— Its other functions include preventing the introduction and spread of exotic pests through plant quarantine measures, supporting pesticide regulation and residue monitoring, undertaking desert locust control operations, and conducting training programmes to promote the safe and judicious use of pesticides.
Post Read Question
With reference to the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIB&RC), consider the following statements:
1. The CIB&RC operates under the Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage.
2. The Central Insecticides Board (CIB) is responsible for registering insecticides after scrutinising their formulae and verifying their efficacy and safety.
3. The Registration Committee (RC) advises the Central and State Governments on technical matters relating to the administration of the Insecticides Act, 1968.
4. The CIB advises on residue tolerance limits and pre-harvest intervals under the Insecticides Rules, 1971.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
(a) 1 and 2
(b) 2 and 3
(c) 1 and 4
(d) 3 and 4
Answer: (c)

(Source: First developed-in-India pesticide molecule soon for rice, chilli, tomato farmers, Biostimulants that aid plant growth, now under the Centre’s scrutiny, piindustries.com, pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, ppqs.gov.in )

title: UPSC Mains Answer Practice — GS 2: Emerging global order and Inter-State Council (Week 180)

content.value: UPSC Essentials brings to you its initiative for the practice of Mains answer writing. It covers essential topics of static and dynamic parts of the UPSC Civil Services syllabus covered under various GS papers. This answer-writing practice is designed to help you as a value addition to your UPSC CSE Mains. Attempt today’s answer writing on questions related to topics of GS-2 to check your progress.

QUESTION 1

The emerging global order is increasingly characterised by bi-multipolarity, with the United States and China as dominant powers and several middle powers shaping international relations. Examine its implications for India’s foreign policy.
QUESTION 2

The Inter-State Council was envisaged as an important institutional mechanism for strengthening cooperative federalism in India. Highlight its constitutional mandate and assess the reasons for its limited effectiveness.

QUESTION 1: The emerging global order is increasingly characterised by bi-multipolarity, with the United States and China as dominant powers and several middle powers shaping international relations. Examine its implications for India’s foreign policy.

Relevance: The question examines the changing global balance of power and its implications for India’s foreign policy. It is relevant to GS2 under International Relations, particularly India’s interests in the changing global order.
Note: This is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers.
Introduction:

— The global balance of power is shifting from the post-Cold War unipolar order to a bi-multipolar system dominated by the United States and China, as well as numerous influential intermediate powers.
— In this changing world order, India must strike a balance between its strategic interests, economic goals, and diplomatic relationships to avoid becoming completely allied with any country.
Body:
You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer:
Implications for India’s foreign policy

— India cannot rely solely on the United States to counterbalance China, and it cannot ignore China’s strategic and territorial issues. Maintaining stable relations with both powers while safeguarding national interests is critical. India should explore issue-based relationships rather than rigid geopolitical alignments.

— India has to strengthen ties with Russia, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Japan, Brazil, and South Africa. Such collaborations can broaden India’s diplomatic options in trade, technology, defence, and global governance.

— India’s historical character as a postcolonial democracy allows it to represent the concerns of developing countries. Advocating for reforms in global institutions and resolving developmental inequities can boost India’s diplomatic standing. Support from poor countries is especially vital for India’s ambitions to gain a permanent membership on the UN Security Council.

— Economic expansion, scientific improvement, and industrial capacities all affect a country’s potential to influence international affairs. India needs to improve manufacturing, R&D, technical innovation, and infrastructure.

— Competition between the United States and China has the potential to destabilise global trade, supply networks, technological access, and regional security. India must diversify its economic partnerships and lessen its reliance on specific countries. It must also strengthen its position in the Indo-Pacific and maintain positive relations with regional groups.
— India’s weaker growth rate compared to China inhibits its chance to emerge as a significant global force.
— Balancing relations with Washington and Beijing while resolving border and security concerns is still difficult.
— Unfulfilled global leadership goals can widen the gap between India’s aspirations and actual capabilities.
— Middle powers may emphasise individual national interests over collective viewpoints, making long-term coalitions problematic.
Conclusion:
— India’s emergence as a global power will be determined not just by its diplomatic ambitions, but also by its economic strength, technological capabilities, and international reputation.

— Rather than hastily projecting itself as a third major power, India should leverage its position as a middle power to form strategic alliances, represent the Global South, and maintain strategic autonomy in the evolving bi-multipolar system.

(Sources: India’s time will come. For now, it is a middle power in a bi-multipolar world, C Raja Mohan: The multipolar world India wants may be a distant reality, India has demonstrated strategic autonomy, but its record is not perfect, Between Trump’s US and Xi’s China, the trap India must avoid, US-China are recalibrating ties. Five things India needs to keep in mind amid the change)
Points to Ponder
How does US-China strategic competition influence India’s foreign policy choices?
How can India strengthen strategic autonomy while deepening partnerships with major powers?
Related Previous Year Questions

“The reform process in the United Nations remains unresolved, because of the delicate imbalance of East and West and entanglement of the USA vs. Russo-Chinese alliance.” Examine and critically evaluate the East-West policy confrontations in this regard. (2025)
“The USA is facing an existential threat in the form of China, that is much more challenging than the erstwhile Soviet Union.” Explain. (2021)

QUESTION 2: The Inter-State Council was envisaged as an important institutional mechanism for strengthening cooperative federalism in India. Highlight its constitutional mandate and assess the reasons for its limited effectiveness.

Relevance: The question examines the constitutional and institutional framework governing Centre-State relations in India. It is relevant to GS2 under Federalism, particularly constitutional provisions and institutional mechanisms for Centre-State coordination.
Note: This is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers.
Introduction:
— India’s federal structure necessitates ongoing communication and coordination between the Union and state governments.

— The Inter-State Council (ISC), established under Article 263 of the Constitution, was envisioned as an institutional tool to promote discussion, resolve disagreements, and build cooperative federalism. Despite its constitutional significance, its functioning has been restricted.
Body:
You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer:
Constitutional mandate of the Inter-State Council
— Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council when it appears that public interest would be served by doing so.
— To inquire into and advise upon disputes that may arise between States.
— To investigate and discuss subjects in which the Union and States, or two or more States, have a common interest.
— To make recommendations for better coordination of policy and action on such subjects.
— The Sarkaria Commission (1988) recommended establishing the Council as a permanent body. It was formally constituted through a Presidential Order in 1990.
Reasons for its limited effectiveness
— Despite the necessity for regular engagement, the Council has not operated consistently, reducing its importance as a forum for discourse.
— Its operating under the Union Ministry of Home Affairs has curtailed its institutional autonomy.
— Its recommendations are advisory, which limits its ability to assure effective execution.
— Differences between the Union and State governments frequently impede consensus-building.
— The Council has received insufficient attention and operational assistance, resulting in institutional atrophy.
— Important policy choices impacting states were not usually preceded by proper international engagement.
Conclusion:
— The Inter-State Council must transform from an underutilised consultative group to an effective platform for interstate interaction and consensus-building.
— Its resurrection is critical for strengthening cooperative federalism and preserving the constitutional balance between the Union and the states.

(Sources: For federalism to be truly cooperative, revive the Inter-State Council, Can M K Stalin’s committee help deepen ‘cooperative federalism’?, This is the moment for a new federal compact, What is the Inter-State Council?)
Points to Ponder
How does the Inter-State Council differ from the Zonal Councils and the GST Council?
Related Previous Year Question
Constitutional mechanisms to resolve the inter-state water disputes have failed to address and solve the problems. Is the failure due to structural or process inadequacy or both? Discuss. (2013)

title: The back end of 55

content.value: I’ll admit it up front: I don’t like procedures. I’m fine doing them to other people. Having one done to me is different. For 10  years I treated my colonoscopy the way some people treat a check-engine light. I knew it was there, I knew what it meant, and I kept driving.
Every birthday there was a reason to wait. I was too busy, I had no symptoms, I’d get to it next year. I’m 55 now, which means I spent a full decade telling patients to do what I wouldn’t.

Two groups finally wore me down. The first was my wife, who is persistent and usually right, a combination I find exhausting. The second was my colleagues, who brought it up in the lounge more often than you’d think. Once a doctor’s wife and his co-workers are on the same side, the argument is over.
Seeking counsel
Before any big decision, I call my senior partner. He’s been my mentor for years, and he has the sharpest wit of anyone I know. He’s also, as I learned that day, almost no help at all.
I told him I’d finally decided to schedule the colonoscopy. He paused, and then  said: “It’s a good thing you called. Now I’ll know why you’re walking funny the next day.”

I hung up, wondering why I keep calling him. I also quietly saved the whole speech, word for word, so that I can pass the same useless advice to the younger doctors in our group. Some traditions deserve to continue.
Why we do this at all

Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide, accounting for approximately 10% of all cancer cases and the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths globally. . In India, it accounts for  about 65,000 new cases a year and  is rising, especially in cities, and with no national screening programme, too many cases are found late. Nearly 38,000 Indians die of it every year. It is also one of the few cancers we can actually prevent, not just catch early.

Most colon cancers start as polyps, small growths on the lining of the colon. Over roughly 10  years, some become malignant. That long, quiet stretch is the opportunity. If you find a polyp and remove it, the cancer never gets a chanc’e to start. A colonoscopy is one of the few screening tests that also serves as treatment.
A brief history

Colonoscopy is younger than you might guess. In the late 1960s and early 1970s,  William Wolff and Hiromi Shinya in New York used new flexible fiberoptic scopes to examine the whole colon. Dr. Shinya also developed the wire-loop snare to remove polyps through the scope, so they no longer had to be removed through open abdominal surgery. That was a revolutionary change.

The landmark evidence came from the National Polyp Study. In 1993, Sidney Winawer and colleagues reported in the New England Journal of Medicine that removing adenomatous polyps sharply cut the rate of colorectal cancer compared with what would otherwise be expected. In 2012, a long-term follow-up in the same journal showed that removing polyps reduced colorectal cancer deaths by about half. Our whole screening approach rests on those two papers.
The recommended starting age in the United States has also come down. Rising rates in younger adults led guidelines to lower it from 50 to 45. That leaves people like me with no excuse.
The alternative

Think about what skipping it looks like. A polyp grows unnoticed for years, and colon cancer often gives no warning until it’s advanced. Then the symptoms come: bleeding, a change in bowel habits, weight loss, fatigue, anaemia. By that point the conversation is about surgery, chemotherapy, and staging scans.

For some patients it means a colostomy, where the bowel is brought out through the abdominal wall and stool goes into a bag, sometimes permanently. For too many, it means dying of a disease that a simple screening test could have prevented.
Put that way, a day of inconvenience looks like a bargain.
The prep and the procedure
Every patient will tell you the procedure is easy and the prep is the hard part. They’re right.

I’ll spare you the details. You either already know, or you’ll find out soon enough. The good news is that the prep has come a long way. The dreaded jug is no longer your only choice, and tablet preps have made the whole thing far more bearable. If your doctor offers them, take them.
The next morning was close to anticlimactic. I checked in at the outpatient centre, changed into a gown that and got an IV. A nurse went through the usual checklist, and we chatted about nothing.
Then came propofol.

If you’ve never had it, here’s what it’s like. A warm flush rises up your arm, a brief awareness that something is about to happen, and then nothing. No dreams and no sense of time passing. One moment you’re listening to the anaesthesiologist, and the next you’re in recovery with a cup of juice, asking whether they’ve started yet.
The verdict

My gastroenterologist is also a friend, and he was completely professional from start to finish. He was calm and thorough, and he put me at ease. He came by recovery to tell me he’d found one polyp and removed it. It will go to pathology, and I’ll come back for surveillance on whatever schedule the results call for.
That polyp had probably been growing for years while I made excuses. Now it’s gone. That’s the point of screening: find it before it becomes cancer.
The bottom line

It really isn’t that bad. The prep is unpleasant for a single night, and easier than it used to be. The procedure takes less time than your commute, and the sedation is the best nap you’ll take all year. It may keep you from getting cancer. That’s a pretty good trade.

If you’re 45 or older and you’ve been putting it off as I did, talk to your doctor about getting screened. Colonoscopy isn’t the only option. You can do stool tests at home, and your doctor can walk you through other options. The best test is the one you’ll actually do. Doing nothing is the only wrong answer.
(Dr. Dinesh Arab is Director, Interventional and Structural Cardiology, AdventHealth Daytona Beach and Clinical Assistant Professor of Medicine, Florida State University dinarab@yahoo.com)

title: Licences of three Mumbai blood banks suspended for offering gifts

content.value: The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has suspended the licences of three blood banks in Mumbai for three to five days after an investigation found that Titan watches were distributed as gifts to donors at a blood donation camp held in April this year, in violation of National Blood Transfusion Council (NBTC) guidelines.
Also Read : Maharashtra FDA Commissioner made recommendation to NPPA on pricing gap of hospital consumables

The three blood banks are the Indian Red Cross Society Blood Centre, Mumbai; Dean Grant Medical College and Sir J.J. Group of Hospitals Blood Centre, Byculla; and B.Y.L. Nair Charitable Hospital Blood Centre, Mumbai Central. Their licences were suspended for five days, three days, and three days, respectively, under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.
However, the blood centres at Sir J.J. Group of Hospitals and Nair Hospital have appealed against the suspension orders before the State Government and secured temporary stays on the orders.

According to the FDA, the blood donation camp was organised by the Young Star Committee, Altamount Road, towards the end of April 2026. Advertisements for the camp stated that donors would receive Titan watches as gifts. However, the NBTC’s Guidelines for Voluntary Blood Donation prohibit offering gifts to donors at voluntary blood donation camps.

During the initial inquiry, the organisers and participating blood banks denied knowledge of the distribution of gifts. However, FDA officials subsequently contacted several blood donors, who confirmed that they had received watches.

Following these findings, the FDA inspected the three blood banks on August 22 and issued show-cause notices on September 2 over the violations detected. Personal hearings were conducted on September 22, during which the blood banks submitted their explanations.
The FDA found their explanations unsatisfactory and subsequently ordered the suspension of their licences under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.
FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe said blood donation was an important act of social responsibility and service to humanity, and that gifts or inducements should not be used to encourage donations.

“The FDA is committed to ensuring that no gifts or inducements are used to encourage blood donation and that the relevant guidelines are followed. Blood banks must strictly comply with the applicable legal provisions and guidelines,” Mundhe said.

title: 161 confirmed measles cases, one death reported in Kozhikode

title: Limiting warming to 1.8 degree C could prevent loss of 1.89 billion years of healthy life: Analysis

content.value: ) Limiting global warming to around 1.8 degrees Celsius, instead of allowing it to reach 4.4 degrees Celsius, could prevent the loss of 1.89 billion years of healthy life to causes such as extreme heat and air pollution, according to a new LancetCommission.

Researchers said that the true burden could be even greater and that without sharp cuts to emissions, health losses would continue to compound beyond 2100, increasingly intensify other threats, such as migration, in ways not yet reflected in these numbers.
The authors of The Lancet Commission on "21st Century Global Threats to Health", launched at the World Health Summit 2026 in Berlin, Germany, examined hundreds of possible threats.

They identified 17 threats posing the greatest danger to human health and survival between 2025 and 2100. These are also the threats that can be averted through policy changes, funding decisions and innovation, they said.

The 17 interlinked "catastrophic" threats spanning diseases, social and economic conditions, environmental change, technology and conflict will shape the health of the next generation, the team added.
If current trends continue, the 17 catastrophic threats collectively could account for tens of billions of years of lost health, the analysis found.

Every country faces significant risks, even as the scale varied by threat and region. Within each country, people with limited resources and marginalised communities bear the greatest burden, compounded by existing inequalities, it said.
Nuclear conflict and the malicious use of artificial intelligence (AI) were identified as the two threats with a potential for extinction, even as their likelihood of occurring were deemed 'low'.

Accounting for both their potential impact and probability, the commission's assessment found that action to prevent nuclear conflict could avert an estimated 133 million deaths and 9.35 billion years of healthy life lost by 2100, while action to reduce the risk of malicious AI could avert an estimated 10.4 billion years of healthy life lost.

"The estimates highlight how much health loss could be avoided in each area. Some are already imposing substantial health burdens today, while others carry a real danger if they materialise. Crucially, all 17 threats are interconnected, which is why they must be addressed together, not in isolation," commission co-chair Christopher JL Murray, director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington, said.

"The striking finding is not only the scale of these threats, but that humanity still has the agency to act. Across all 17 catastrophic threats, the decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation. But delaying action will only serve to shift and increase the costs into the future," Murray added.

The other catastrophic threats to health are air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition, conventional conflict, a declining development assistance for health, high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics, obesity, poor mental health, smoking and unhealthy ageing, the authors said.

The commission also puts forth a framework to inform action before harm becomes embedded -- create and fund threat-ready health systems, increase investment in innovation and reassess threats regularly and independently, they said.

title: Pope Leo XIV undergoes surgery for cancer: What is lung adenocarcinoma?

content.value: Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer, according a statement by the Vatican on October 13, 2026

The 71-year-old spiritual leader of the Roman Catholic Church was in the operating room for about 3 hours, and the surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. The lower lobe of his right lung has been removed after the diagnosis.
The surgery was successful and there were no complications.
The pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, according to a bulletin by the Vatican.
It added that tissue tests conducted during the operation confirmed what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), lung cancer is a disease in which cells in the lung grow out of control.
Lung cancers are grouped into two main types called non-small cell and small cell.
The CDC website adds that “non-small cell lung cancer is the most common type of lung cancer” and “it grows more slowly and often doesn’t cause symptoms until it is advanced.”

The website adds that adenocarcinoma, the type of cancer Pope Leo XIV is suffering from, is the “most common type of non-small cell lung cancer” and “begins in cells in the alveoli, which are tiny air sacs in the lungs that make mucus.”
Current status of Pope Leo XIV’s health
The Pope regained consciousness normally after the operation and later returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, Reuters reports, while citing the Vatican’s medical bulletin.
It added that the Vatican had said earlier this week that he was expected to remain in hospital for about a week, and all his public events have been cancelled until October 20.

Pope Leo was seen waving to a supportive crowd of well-wishers before heading to Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. Several of his supporters shouted “auguri” (best wishes) to their religious leader before his surgery.
The Christian leader is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru from November 6 to 17, 2026, but it was not clear if the trip would still go ahead.
With inputs from Reuters

title: DR Congo Ebola vaccine trial to begin within weeks: WHO

content.value: The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine is expected to begin in the Democratic Republic of Congo by the end of October, World Health Organization experts said Tuesday.
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,000-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,000.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the outbreak.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will go through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
"We have got strong reassurances that... it should be starting before the end of this month," said Anthony Scott, chair of the WHO's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunisation (SAGE).
The group said insights that Ervebo might offer cross-protection against Bundibugyo were no match for evidence from standardised vaccine trials.

The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC -- a single trial framework that can test the efficiency of multiple vaccines -- should also eventually incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are moving through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Need for data
The Tumaini trial "will generate urgently-needed data on the efficacy of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease, and will help formulate the policy decisions we need", Scott told a press conference.
"In addition, we welcome the accelerated development of vaccines that are specifically targeting Bundibugyo.
"They're both progressing rapidly through early clinical development."
SAGE said it was deeply concerned about the ongoing challenges in controlling the Ebola outbreak.

"The key elements here are insecurity and population displacement, and they're hindering access to care, disrupting surveillance, and delaying critical research, including, from our perspective, research on vaccine trials," said Scott.

Kate O'Brien, director of the WHO's immunisation department, said a WHO technical advisory group would be meeting to review evidence from the small-scale trials of the Oxford and Moderna candidate vaccines.

She suggested the Oxford jab could drop into the broader Tumaini trial fairly swiftly -- as doses are ready to roll -- if the safety and the immunogenicity data from the first trial is "positive and reassuring".
Therefore "everything is lined up for at least two products to be moving quickly", she said.

The medical charity Doctors Without Borders is conducting a data-gathering study -- not a full clinical trial -- of Ervebo's effectiveness in frontline health workers in DRC provinces hard-hit by the Bundibugyo outbreak, with the jab being offered to volunteers as an interim measure.

title: Jonathan, the giant tortoise, is 198 years old. Here is his secret

content.value: Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise who lives at the residence of the governor of St Helena. He is 194 years old, the oldest living land animal on Earth today: the upper limit of the life expectancy for Aldabra tortoises is 93.68 years, making him some 100 years older than the typical upper lifespan limit for his species.

The longevity of Jonathan, who was likely a contemporary of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria, has confounded scientists: but now the enigma may have been partly unravelled in a study published in Science Advances. It isn’t just “good genes” but his “epigenome” (chemicals and proteins that turn genes on or off), that keeps Jonathan youthful, scientists found.

Researchers analysed Jonathan’s genome and his epigenome to understand his extraordinary longevity: and they found as many as 287 unique gene variants, which control DNA damage-repair, reduce inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer, thereby reducing the process of ageing.

This is not for the first time that long-lived species have been studied through comparative genomic analysis: the naked mole rat, the bowhead whale, Brandt’s bat and immortal jellyfish being a few examples. These studies have offered important insights into genes markers that slow ageing or curb cancer in these species.

This study, the first of its kind, was led by scientists who study longevity at the non-profit Kallel in the US. “Nature has already solved the puzzle of ageing in remarkable ways, and Jonathan’s genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience,” said Stephen Clark, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study, in a release.

From Jonathan’s genome, scientists found ‘positively selected genes’ (genes that have, over time, accumulated advantageous mutations) involved in DNA repair and insulin regulation. A further investigation found genes involved in development, metabolism, and immunity. Another study indicated a substantially low resting heart rate of 21 beats per minute.

Aldabra tortoises are believed to have dispersed out of Africa, first from the eastern African coast to Madagascar, then to Granitic Seychelles, and lastly to the Aldabra atoll, located in the Indian Ocean. Today, the Aldabra atoll, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is home to around 1,00,000 tortoises.
Dr. Clark added that their goal was to take these evolutionary insights and translate them into “practical, affordable treatments for everyday people.”

While humans live for about 80 years (and rare individuals 100 years), there are some animals, plants and fungi that can live for several hundred or even several thousand years, and often show negligible senescence (biological process of growing older), said a 2014 study published in Ageing Research Reviews. “The longest living animals are also among the simplest ones,” said the paper, citing corals, jellyfish, comb jellies, hydras, and sea anemones, which “can become in some cases potentially immortal.”

title: Old doubts linger, yet new Microsoft quantum chip raises the stakes

content.value: In February, the Microsoft Quantum research group announced a new kind of computer processor called Majorana 1. According to the tech giant, the processor contained the world’s first topological qubits, built with a new material it called a ‘topoconductor’. Majorana 1 contained eight qubits, with Microsoft Quantum saying it would in future hold a million.
The group published its paper in Nature the same day, and that stoked the early concerns about what Microsoft Quantum had actually demonstrated.

Foremost, the paper was considerably more circumspect than Microsoft’s press release. The researchers had built devices made of indium-arsenide-aluminium and discussed a way to measure, in a ‘single shot’, the parity of an electronic state, i.e. whether the number of electrons was odd or even in the state, in the wire.
The team called this measurement a “necessary ingredient” for a highly sought after form of quantum computing.

However, there was a significant gap between the scopes of the paper and of the press release, prompting concerns in the scientific community that Microsoft was trying to lay claim to a commercially lucrative technology without first proving that it actually worked.
Zero modes

Quantum computing is a new, more powerful form of computing that scientists believe can solve some problems much better than conventional devices can. However, the quantum bits, or qubits, these machines are based on are notoriously fragile.

A qubit stores information in a quantum state, which can be disturbed by even the slightest interactions with stray heat or stray magnetic fields. Another technology called quantum error correction can compensate but not without imposing additional technological hurdles.
Many leading quantum computers encode qubits in superconducting circuits, while others use atoms, ions or light. At least on paper, topological quantum computing shows another way.

In this domain, Microsoft Quantum has been trying to build a quantum computer with qubits based on particles called Majorana zero modes (MZMs). Technically, MZMs are ‘emergent quasiparticles’. The physicists Sankar Das Sarma, Roman Lutchyn, and Jay Sau had predicted in 2010 that they would occur at the ends of specially engineered superconducting wires.

Two MZMs separated by some space constitutes a particular quantum state, and whether that state is occupied or not can encode information, like 0 and 1. This way, each MZM pair stores information in both particles together.

This is less like one half being stored in each particle and more like both particles storing the information together: many small disturbances affecting only one end cannot destroy the information, yet both ends are required to access it. The space between the two MZMs of a pair is crucial to achieve this.
MZMs also follow some strange rules. For example, carrying out one exchange of MZMs and then another can create a different quantum state than performing the same exchange in the reverse order.
Airtight inference

But a big problem today is to ascertain if a device with the necessary superconducting wires and other parts also has MZMs. This is because there are many impostor states that are easier to create but which lack the MZMs’ unusual properties. There is no way to directly spot an MZM with some kind of microscope and claim success. Instead, scientists and engineers have to measure the device’s properties in different ways, and from that infer the presence of MZMs.
This inference has to be airtight, and the dispute in the Microsoft case is that its inference is not.

The matter is still on, in fact: on June 2 this year, Microsoft Quantum announced a new processor called Majorana 2 and uploaded a new preprint paper. Here, the team replaced aluminium with lead, whose superconducting state is harder to disrupt, to make the desired state more robust. It also switched to a gallium-antimonide substrate and redesigned the semiconductor stack to reduce disorder.

The upgrade was apparently dramatic: in Microsoft’s telling, the topological gap — the energy needed to excite the system out of its protected state — had increased from around 30 microelectron-volts to 70 microelectron-volts. The parity switching time had also increased from a few milliseconds to around 20 seconds.

The group presented this as proof of topological quantum computing’s promise because the new numbers were indicative of the encoded information being more robustly protected from disturbances. On the back of these reported advances, the company said it would build a scalable quantum computer by 2029 — a significantly shortened deadline considering how complex the  technology still is.
Rebuttal and response

However, not everyone is convinced Microsoft learnt the bigger lesson from last time. As University of Pittsburgh professor Sergey Frolov has said, Microsoft’s previous record has left him unwilling to treat the new work as resting on a well-understood foundation.

MZMs are very difficult to create and detect. For example, researchers from TU-Delft in the Netherlands published a paper in Nature in 2018 claiming they had spotted MZMs. But it had to be retracted three years later after independent scientists found problems in the data analysis.

In its 2025 paper, the Microsoft Quantum team used the topological gap protocol it had presented in a 2023 paper: a way to use electrical conductance data to identify combinations of magnetic field and gate voltage that are consistent with gapped MZMs. The team then used a technique called radio-frequency interferometry to check one region of the device, and where the team said the data had evidence of parity switching.

But at an American Physical Society meeting a month later, scientists remained sceptical. The Microsoft team had demonstrated one measurement on one wire in the paper and itself presented additional measurements of a different kind, but many physicists still had doubts.

Cornell University professor Eun-Ah Kim said the data was quite weak while Argonne National Laboratory physicist Kartiek Agarwal called the paper’s claims premature, even if not deserving to be dismissed. Henry Legg, a lecturer at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, in particular said the headline data came from a small number of measurements on one device.

Then, on June 24 this year, Nature published a rebuttal by Dr. Legg alongside a response from Microsoft Quantum (physicist Chetan Nayak was the corresponding author). In his rebuttal, based on his own work over the last year, Dr. Legg contended that Microsoft’s device itself may not have been qualified to host MZMs, that the underlying data of how electric currents move in the device appeared consistent with a gapless and highly disordered system, and that the topological gap protocol was sensitive, rather than agnostic, to how a researcher chose to analyse the system.
In response, Nayak et al. disputed Dr. Legg’s logic and said its claims were based on the radio-frequency measurements, not the protocol.

Many physicists believe Microsoft’s attempts are promising and commend its transparency with data. But many physicists also remain unconvinced that the qubits in Majorana 1 and Majorana 2 are working topological qubits.

title: Why are the whites of human eyes white?

content.value: A: The tough outer covering of the eyeball is called the sclera. In humans, the sclerae (in both eyes) are white. This allows someone standing a distance away to easily say which way a person is looking.

Scientists are not sure why human sclerae are white. Chimpanzees may have white, brown or darker sclerae. Bonobos and Sumatran orangutans have light brown sclerae. On the other hand, researchers have documented pale sclerae in golden langurs and southern pig-tailed macaques and some leopards and sea lions.

title: IISER researchers make solid material that releases two fuel gases

content.value: Scientists at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram, have developed a chemical compound that releases hydrogen and methane when heated moderately. Per the team, the work is a step towards new, better methods to store and transport these fuel gases.
The findings were published in Science Advances on October 7.

Both in India and around the world, hydrogen is emerging as an important new fuel because its combustion does not directly release carbon dioxide. However, because of its very low density, hydrogen is very difficult to store and transport and demands the use of expensive technologies.

Scientists have previously proposed blending hydrogen with methane as an intermediary step: while hydrogen burns faster than methane, methane can reduce the risk of flames travelling back into burners or triggering violent detonations. They have also devised ways to store the two fuels as compressed gases and solid materials that can release one or the other gas.

In the new study, researchers developed a compound of magnesium, zinc, hydrogen, and carbon called magnesium hydridomethylzincate. When the compound was heated in solution to 100° C, it released hydrogen — and when its crystals were heated in the absence of a solvent, at 80-110° C, it released both hydrogen and methane.

“The broader significance of the work is that organometallic compounds could potentially provide molecular platforms for the storage and controlled release of fuel gases,” chemistry professor and study lead Ajay Venugopal told The Hindu.

The team established that methane emerged before hydrogen, indicating the compound was releasing the gases through successive chemical reactions. Further analysis also revealed that each unit of the compound’s paired molecular structure could produce two molecules each of hydrogen and methane.

Since magnesium hydridomethylzincate is a solid at room temperature, it could offer an alternative to transporting methane and hydrogen as compressed gases. This together with the relatively low temperature required to liberate the gases merit more research on the compound, the paper said.

More research attention is warranted considering, as the team has acknowledged, the compound is also highly sensitive to moisture and it is not known whether it can be ‘replenished’ once its gaseous contents have been depleted.

“Although we are yet to demonstrate reversibility in our system, the study provides a starting point for exploring molecular compounds that can reversibly uptake and release fuel gases using main-group elements,” Prof. Venugopal said.
The study’s other authors were Sheetal Kathayat Bisht, Poorna Gomathisankaran, and Alex Andrews.

title: Mining project threatens future of rare Jeypore ground gecko

content.value: In the crevices of boulders and beneath the rustle of leaf litter in the hills of the Eastern Ghats in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh lives a tiny population of the strikingly-patterned Jeypore ground gecko, which was presumed extinct for 130 years until it was rediscovered in 2010 by an Indian scientist.

Just four individuals of this endangered species have been documented in the past year in Odisha’s Balda hills, worryingly, within the site of a proposed bauxite mining project by an Adani-linked group.

The nocturnal gecko, some 3.6 inches long, with a comparatively large head, and a yellow-orange body, was originally described as far back as 1878 by the British naturalist Richard Henry Beddome. It was only in 2010 that herpetologists Ishan Agarwal and Aniruddha Datta-Roy sighted a specimen in Odisha’s Koraput district.

Later, happily for the herpetologists, there were more sightings: one in 2025, and three this year, including one this month. One of the least studied reptiles in the country, this gecko’s behaviour, habits and lifecycle continue to elude scientists.

What is known, however, is that its habitat is fast shrinking, owing to its transformation to coffee plantations, hydropower projects and mining. In fact, the habitat where it was first sighted in the 1870s, Potangi in Odisha, has already been lost to bauxite mining by the National Aluminium Company Limited (NALCO), where the animal is believed to be now extinct.

And today, the spectre of Adani’s opencast bauxite mine proposal, covering 147 hectares of forest in the Balda hills, within the Nageswari reserve forest, threatens the very future of this vulnerable species.
Adivasi uprising

The bauxite mining project has also been the site of much contention among resident Adivasis of the Nageswari reserve forest, who have protested the proposal for the past two years. The Bondo and Porja Adivasis, whose ancestral land this is, lodged a complaint against the Adani-subsidiary Kalinga Alumina Ltd. in February, but to no avail.

“The communities have also applied for forest rights over the hill, which the government has refused to recognise,” naturalist Yuvan Aves told The Hindu. “There was a demonstration earlier this month too, and when the Adani group flew drones to scope the area, the Adivasi people stopped the exercise, asserting that this is their ancestral land,” he added.

Ecologist Ishan Agarwal, who rediscovered this gecko in the Eastern Ghats in 2010, said that the gecko is “an ecologically and biogeographically significant species having split from its closest relatives over 20 million years ago.” This is a relatively range-restricted species that is only found in high-elevation (900–1,400 metres) forests in the northern Eastern Ghats. “Anything that threatens their habitat is the major risk. Coffee [though we don’t understand to what extent], hydel, mining are all potential threats,” he told The Hindu.

The Balda hills are a treasure-trove of biodiversity and host a unique assemblage of species, including the unique limbless amphibian, Gegeneophis orientalis, said Dr. Agarwal. Another endemic species likely to be found in the region is the Araku worm gecko, he added.

The Jeypore ground gecko is a “flagship species of the area,” said the renowned herpetologist Romulus Whitaker and added that the proposed mining project will most definitely see the end of the habitat of this important species, as well as others, including some yet undescribed. “I strongly advise against the mining of bauxite in the Balda hills and insist on prioritising the conservation of biodiversity of the area, in particular the Jeypore ground gecko,” Mr. Whitaker said in a release.
