title: Apple unveils HomeView smart display in renewed home push

content.value: Apple on Tuesday unveiled HomeView, a voice-driven smart display built around its revamped Siri AI assistant, as the iPhone maker makes a fresh bid for a place in living rooms and kitchens.
The device, which pairs a square seven-inch touchscreen with a speaker base, will sell for $299 in the United States starting November 13.
Apple has struggled for years to gain ground in the smart home, where its HomePod speakers have trailed Amazon's Alexa and Google AI-amped devices.
Analysts see the new hardware as an effort to deepen customers' ties to the Apple ecosystem as AI rivals, including OpenAI, eye devices of their own.
The launch is one of the first under John Ternus, Apple's former hardware engineering chief, who took over as chief executive from Tim Cook on September 1.
HomeView is meant to act as a family command center, controlling connected features such as lights, locks, thermostats and cameras.
It also handles FaceTime video calls, plays music and video and doubles as a digital picture frame when idle.
In addition, Apple has also formed partnerships with South Korea's LG and France's Schneider for door locks and thermostats.
The release's centerpiece is Siri AI, the overhauled version of Apple's assistant powered by Apple Intelligence, which the company is pitching as a more conversational helper than the original Siri.
Siri AI is central to Apple's effort to catch up with rivals in generative artificial intelligence, and it is built on AI technology from Google Gemini.
The company said that HomeView would not be sold in the European Union for the time being as the company finds ways to make Siri AI compliant with Europe's competition rules.
Apple stated that it is working constructively with the EU to find a way for these products to enter the European market.

title: What is New York City’s ‘Click to Cancel’ rule, and does India have a similar policy?

content.value: On October 1, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the enforcement of the city’s ‘Click to Cancel’ rule that essentially lets residents cancel any subscription just as quickly as they can sign up — ideally with a single click.

“No one should need 45 minutes of hold music to stop paying for something they never wanted,” said Mr. Mamdani. “If a company can take your money with one click, you should be able to get your money back with one click.”
What’s the need for a ‘Click to Cancel’ rule?

It can feel effortless to sign up online for a gym membership, a grocery subscription, a mobile phone plan, or a magazine delivery. When one wants to cancel the same service, however, the process is often so convoluted and time-consuming that customers end up keeping a subscription they’d prefer to eliminate.

This unethical retention is commonly achieved through digital “dark patterns” that make it hard for customers to act in their own best interests. For example, subscription cancellation or account deletion buttons might be obscured by multiple menus and sub-menus designed to confuse users. Or, they may require the user to “click” through pages and pages of text, wasting their time and making them likely to give up.
Sometimes, customers may not even know they are locked into a subscription, as a free trial is converted into a paid commitment without clearly seeking consent.

Alternatively, many merchants who allow easy online subscriptions arbitrarily require buyers to send personalised emails or letters, spend time on the phone, or even visit the business in person just to end their subscription. This lack of parity ends up keeping reluctant customers locked into bad services.

Consumers such as time-pressed workers, minors, vulnerable adults, seniors, and non-literate customers face extra hurdles when struggling to offload unwanted subscriptions. In extreme cases, customers may even have to cancel their credit cards and get new ones in order to end a subscription.
The problem is so pervasive that media outlets have reported people are resorting to AI agents — such as Meta’s Muse — in order to identify and get rid of unnecessary subscriptions on their behalf.

‘Click to Cancel’ rules would force sellers to make cancellation processes easier, quicker, transparent, fairer, and customer-friendly, so that buyers don’t need to depend on external tools and services.
As per one estimate cited by the NYC Mayor’s office, the ‘Click to Cancel’ rule could save New Yorkers up to $162.5 million per year.
Who is covered by the ‘Click to Cancel’ rule?

The rule gives the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) citywide authority for enforcement, adding on to the New York state’s existing regulations that govern subscription terms. The ‘Click to Cancel’ rule covers subscriptions for any type of goods or services meeting the definitions of “automatic renewal” or “continuous service offer,” with exceptions for government-linked businesses and several licensed financial institutions.

“A person making an automatic renewal or continuous service offer to a consumer must provide the consumer with the option to cancel at any time using a simple cancellation mechanism that is as easy to use as the mechanism that the consumer used to provide consent and that is through the same medium that the consumer used to provide consent,” stated the ‘Click to Cancel’ rule.

For example, an internet-based sign-up process cannot require a call-based or in-person cancellation process. New York City residents can also file complaints in order to seek mediation, while companies could face civil penalties starting at $525 for violations.
Does India have a ‘Click to Cancel’ policy?

India has a bank-based regulation that is meant to protect customers from deceptive subscription practices. Even so, the reality is that many consumers are often manipulated by the merchants they rely on for their daily needs.

Take the Reserve Bank of India’s ‘Digital Payments – E-mandate Framework’ from this April. It directs an issuer (of a mandate/recurring transaction) to send a pre-transaction notification to the customer at least 24 hours prior to the actual charge/debit. The issuer must share the merchant’s name, transaction amount, date/time of debit, reference number of the e-mandate, and the reason for the debit. A post-transaction notification to the customer is also required.

In other words, merchants cannot silently deduct funds from customers’ accounts and hope that they don’t notice. However, a lack of regulation targeting “dark patterns” creates avenues for Indian consumers to be exploited by merchants.

According to Datum Intelligence’s Dark Patterns Consumer Perception Study dated June 2026, e-commerce platforms Nykaa, Myntra, Flipkart, and Amazon, as well as quick commerce platforms Big Basket, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, and Blinkit did not offer pre-renewal reminders for free trial billing. The study further noted that cancellation required more than 4 steps on most of the listed platforms.
In essence, Indian shoppers are far from being able to click to cancel.

title: OpenAI fires employee after finding recording device in conference room

content.value: OpenAI has fired an employee after discovering a “sophisticated” recording device hidden in one of its offices, and using its own models to “understand” the gadget and where it had come from, announced the ChatGPT-maker on October 14.
OpenAI stated that a specific employee had planted it a few days ago and that the U.S. FBI was investigating the matter.
The U.S. Justice Department confirmed that a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had been arrested on October 9.
He had been working at OpenAI since July 2025.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” stated OpenAI, adding that the case showed how AI could help address security threats.

The discovery was made towards the end of September, when OpenAI personnel found a recording device hidden in toilet paper and inserted into a TV’s USB port in an office conference room in San Francisco, per an official complaint.

CCTV footage featured Mr. Alfozan near that location despite not being authorised to take part in meetings there. Other factors that aroused suspicion were his use of a productivity tool to track company meetings, and the use of a chatbot account associated with his spouse, where there were prompts related to recording devices.
According to the complaint, another similar recording device was found in Mr. Alfozan’s bag, while there was an image of Mr. Alfozan appearing to look at the place where the device was hidden.

“According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” said FBI Director Kash Patel.
“This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said.
If he is convicted, Mr. Alfozan faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release.
The investigation is ongoing.
