title: Why Keralam has launched India’s first ecosystem Red List assessment

content.value: Driven by dam construction, invasive plantations, and escalating climate extremes, Keralam’s tropical riparian evergreen forests in the southern Western Ghats have suffered a devastating 83% loss over the past century. This alarming decline places these vital natural habitats on a path toward potential collapse within the next 20 to 40 years, earning them a Critically Endangered status status under International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) criteria.

Other irreplaceable habitats across the State, including delicate myristica swamps, high-altitude shola-grassland mosaics, and coastal mangroves, face similar existential threats from rapid urban expansion and rising sea levels.

In response to this crisis, the Kerala State Biodiversity Board (KSBB), has launched a pioneering Red List Assessment of Ecosystems (RLE) project. This initiative marks a first for any Indian State, aiming to transition conservation efforts from isolated species preservation to proactive, landscape-wide ecosystem management.

Funded by KSBB, the one-year project is being jointly executed by the Kerala Forest Research Institute and the Centre for Ecology, Taxonomy, Conservation and Climate Change at MES Asmabi College, led by researchers Dr. Amitha Bachan K.H. and Dr. Deepu Sivadas.
Systematic evaluation

The scientific initiative systematically evaluates ecosystem collapse risks across all 14 districts, spanning high-altitude mountain summits, densely populated midlands, and vulnerable coastal stretches.

Dr. N. Anil Kumar, chairperson, KSBB, says the goal is to build strong empirical evidence of environmental degradation through a comprehensive, year-long scientific study. By examining natural habitats across the State from forests and rivers to coastal belts, the project will pinpoint both climate-driven and human-induced threats.

“Ultimately, this research powers nature-based climate adaptation by repairing fragmented landscapes, analysing historical loss, and safeguarding natural resilience. True resilience demands that we restore our ecosystems in their entirety, which is why we are simultaneously assessing the red list of species alongside this initiative,” he says

According to Dr. Amitha Bachan, major landscapes like Periyar river basin have never been properly classified according to international guidelines, nor have their specific risks of collapse been formally measured. “By evaluating core habitats against the five standardized criteria of the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List of Ecosystems framework, the team aims to establish the State’s first standardised baseline documentation of historical loss, habitat fragmentation, and hydrological disruption. The project addresses this long-standing research gap by identifying risks of collapse and the factors governing it,” he says.

The findings will yield an official Risk Register, an Ecosystem Typology Atlas, and ecorestoration priority maps, all of which will be integrated directly into State planning portals. By placing this actionable spatial intelligence into the hands of local Biodiversity Management Committees and panchayats, the project aims to empower grassroots decision-makers. Armed with detailed mapping, local authorities can strengthen natural barriers against floods and landslides, guide sustainable development, and implement nature-based climate adaptation strategies tailored to their specific landscapes.

This initiative also gives scientific structure to Keralam’s vision of becoming India’s most biodiversity-friendly State by guiding community-led restoration and climate resilience across all major ecosystems.

title: Thailand floods villages to protect capital

content.value: Stilt houses in villages north of Bangkok are no longer high enough to stay dry as Thai authorities deliberately flood riverside communities to spare the capital.

Inside the home of Kamonchanok Sathaphonamonwut, raised more than three metres above the ground in Ayutthaya province, her family of three sleeps on makeshift platforms and cannot use the waterlogged toilet.
Her village has been flooded six years in a row, pushing some to move away, while others have raised their houses higher.
“Our area simply cannot cope with this much water anymore,” the 34-year-old said, wading through her soaked home.
But while authorities prioritise protecting Bangkok and other business hubs from floods, “when it comes to our residential communities, they neglect us”, she said.
Thailand experiences flooding every year during the monsoon season, and scientists say human-made climate change has made heavy rain and floods more frequent and severe.

After devastating floods in 2011, the government expanded embankments, water gates and other infrastructure to direct water away from Bangkok, the historic city of Ayutthaya and industrial zones along the Chao Phraya River, which flows through the capital.
The defences have largely kept commercial centres safe, but residents of other areas have been left to fend for themselves.

Around 20 km from Ayutthaya’s centuries-old temple ruins, a UNESCO heritage site, residents say floods that once reached their knees now rise above their heads in some areas and can take several months to recede.
Office worker Kamonchanok has been forced to commute by boat, and hoist her household appliances and other belongings above the waterline.
“All we can do is deal with the consequences,” she said.
‘Cruel’ but effective

Thai irrigation department spokesman Thanet Somboon said climate change, low-lying geography and recently built embankments that altered the natural flow of the Chao Phraya have contributed to more severe flooding of downstream communities.
“Even when water is released from the Chao Phraya Dam at the same rate as before, the impact is greater than it used to be,” Thanet told AFP.
And after irrigation channels were completely full of diverted water, he said authorities had “no choice but to discharge the remaining water downstream”.
But Thanet acknowledged that officials may need to review infrastructure to “ensure floodwater can be kept within the intended limits”.
Environmental conservationist Sasin Chalermlarp said the government has done “an excellent job” managing floods across the central plains.
But its efforts were “cruel” to those bearing the brunt of the flooding.

In low-lying riverside districts that serve as flood retention zones, AFP journalists saw stretches of villages underwater this month, with some homes abandoned and others submerged up to their roofs.
Sasin said floodwater that once spread across much of Ayutthaya is now concentrated in just “five to 10 percent” of the province.
Rising costs
As flooding in hard-hit districts has become more severe, many who remain have paid to lift their stilt houses higher and keep their living space dry.
Kamonchanok’s family raised their home twice in the 1990s, the second time by 1.5 metres.
But floodwater reached their house in 2011, and again for the past six consecutive years.
Raising a house can cost between 100,000 and one million baht ($3,000-$30,000), depending on its size and height, residents say.
Some families have lifted their homes twice in just a few years, exhausting their savings and borrowing to get by.
‘Flood-free tax’
Sasin acknowledged that the area’s low-lying land made it a natural route for floodwater.
“But the villagers have no choice. They are being forced to make sacrifices,” he said.
Sasin, who lives in a protected part of Ayutthaya, has proposed a “flood-free tax” on those who benefit from the defences, to help impacted families raise their homes and repair damage.
Thanet from the irrigation department said the idea warranted further study to determine “how to support people who sacrifice their land to accommodate floodwater”.

The government’s flagship fix is a $780-million flood diversion canal, designed to carry 1,200 cubic metres of water -- around half the volume of an Olympic-size swimming pool -- per second around the bottleneck where the Chao Phraya narrows through Ayutthaya.
It is expected to be completed by 2030.

Until then, Kamonchanok said her community was not even demanding an end to intentional flooding, but rather a cap on water levels and financial support for those whose homes sit below the flood line.
“All we’re asking for is to be able to live comfortably in our own homes,” she said .“Why can’t they give us that?”

title: India’s problem of overtreatment and overmedication

content.value: Modern medicine has never been more capable than it is today. Tests detect illness earlier, scans reveal invisible abnormalities, medicines prevent and treat diseases, and interventions and procedures can save lives within minutes. Yet, the same system that can do more is increasingly tempted to overtreat and overmedicate.
Also read |Lifestyle, not medicine, is key to good health

Overtreatment and overmedication are not simply the use of an unnecessary medicine but often a chain: a test detects an incidental abnormality, which leads to another test, a diagnosis and then a prescription that may become permanent. What begins as prevention can end in long-term medication or surgery. Then, in India, overtreatment coexists with undertreatment: unnecessary interventions are offered to some, while many others still lack essential primary care, affordable medicines and timely treatment.
Health packages and tests

The rise of overtreatment is the result of a convergence of several factors. The first driver of overtreatment is unnecessary and excessive testing — both screening and diagnostic — which creates a cascade of care. A review article in the prestigious National Medical Journal of India in 2016 found that routine health-check packages often include unwarranted tests that can lead to false-positive results, anxiety, further investigations, overdiagnosis and overtreatment. The truth is that the ability to test has expanded faster than our ability to decide who actually needs testing.

The second driver is the fragmentation of health and medical care. Its most visible manifestation in India is an excessive focus on specialist and super specialist care. A person with a common health problem often goes directly to a specialist or superspecialist. A person with chronic conditions may consult several specialists, each optimising one part of care without necessarily paying attention to the person’s other health problems. The patient is treated in parts, while the human body does not live in specialties.

This matters particularly in older adults. A systematic review and meta-analysis of Indian studies, published in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2021, reported polypharmacy in about 49% of older adults. Another study, published in Scientific Reports in 2025, found that roughly one-third of older adults were taking five or more prescribed medicines (polypharmacy), with potentially inappropriate medicines identified in 28.8% of cases.
These figures do not mean that everyone taking several medicines is being overtreated. They do, however, show why medication reviews and deprescribing must become routine.

A third force is the transformation of health care into a marketplace. Laboratory tests, radiological investigations, procedures, supplements and monitoring devices have become products to be sold — sometimes products in search of potential customers. As a result, the boundaries between those who genuinely need these interventions and those who do not can become blurred. A linked aspect is that much of health care and medical care in India operates on a fee-for-service model, which can reward activity rather than restraint. Many patients consider a medical consultation complete only when several medicines and investigations have been prescribed.

Health insurance is a proven solution for financial protection from health-related expenses, as the cost is borne by the insurer. However, it can create both ‘ex-ante’ and ‘ex-post’ moral hazards, discouraging preventive care and encouraging hospitals and patients to favour costlier interventions. What is forgotten is that while someone else may bear the financial cost, it is the patient’s body that undergoes the intervention. Paying insurance premiums for years does not mean that one must ‘recover’ the money by undergoing a relatively unnecessary procedure or surgery.

Fourth, patient beliefs and expectations arising from advances in medical care where people want certainty when they are worried and may feel that something tangible should follow a consultation. Reassurance can look like inaction; observation can feel inferior to a scan; lifestyle advice can appear less serious than medication. Doctors may respond to these expectations, particularly in crowded clinics where explanation requires time.

The fifth driver is the rise of ‘defensive medicine’, in which clinicians, fearing that they might miss a rare diagnosis, may consider ordering another test as the safer option. What is often forgotten, however, is that every test carries potential risks, both from the test itself and from the discovery of abnormalities that may never have caused harm.
Choosing wisely

India is not alone in facing this problem. Overtreatment first became widely recognised in high-income countries and is now increasingly visible across many middle-income nations. This gave rise to the global Choosing Wisely movement, which encourages people to choose health-care interventions more carefully. It is against this backdrop, between 2012 and 2023, that nearly 80 specialty societies worldwide published close to 700 recommendations identifying hundreds of tests and treatments that clinicians and patients should question. The message is that medicine requires stronger mechanisms for self-correction. The solutions are about practising better medicine. Halting and reversing overmedicalisation requires the engagement of all stakeholders, including individuals, communities, professional societies and health policymakers.

First, India needs to rebuild stronger and functional primary care and restore the family physician as the first point of contact for most non-emergency health needs. A general physician can decide which problems require specialist expertise, reconcile multiple prescriptions and recognise when treatment can safely be reduced. Initiation of care by a general physician, followed by continuity through the referral pathway, protects patients against overmedication and excess surgeries.

Second, every medical prescription should carry a review date and, where appropriate, a possible stop date. Medicines should not become lifelong simply because nobody asks whether they are still needed. Older adults and people taking five or more medicines should periodically undergo a structured medication review assessing indication, benefit, duplication, interactions and opportunities for deprescribing.
Develop India-specific lists

Third, professional medical societies and the Indian Council of Medical Research should develop Indian lists of low-value tests, treatments and procedures — similar to Choosing Wisely — and embed these principles in medical training, accreditation and quality-improvement programmes. Hospitals should measure not only whether recommended care was provided, but also whether unnecessary care was avoided.

Fourth, before starting any test or treatment, patients should note that these four questions matter: Why do I need this? What happens if I wait? What are the possible benefits and risks? What are the alternatives? These questions can substantially improve clinical conversations and outcomes.

Fifth, payment systems and health insurance must reward outcomes, clinical reasoning and continuity of care rather than volume alone. A health-care system should not make it financially easier to order a scan than to explain thoughtfully why that scan may be unnecessary.

Medical advances will continue — and they should. However, the next stage of medical progress will come not only from discovering more tests, medicines and procedures, but also from learning when not to use them. Good medicine requires action when action helps. In an age of medical abundance, it increasingly requires something more difficult — restraint.
Dr. Chandrakant Lahariya is a practising physician and the author of ‘Pill-Free: You Don’t Need Everything You Have Been Prescribed’ (2026)

title: Two Assistant Professors, two PG students suspended for medical negligence at Kakinada GGH

content.value: Two gynaecology Assistant Professors and two postgraduate students have been suspended for one month on charges of medical negligence after a cannula was allegedly left inside the abdomen of a pregnant woman during a surgery at the Kakinada Government General Hospital (GGH).
The incident occurred during a delivery-related surgery on September 26, when the 31-year-old woman delivered a baby girl. She was discharged on September 30.
On October 10, the woman was readmitted to the hospital with a complaint of stomach pain. Medical examinations revealed a cannula inside her abdomen.

Rangaraya Medical College Principal Dr. Usha Kiran told The Hindu on Tuesday that Assistant Professors Dr. Vamsi Priya and Dr. S. Sravanthi and two postgraduate students had been suspended for one month based on the inquiry report submitted by the GGH authorities.

Kakinada GGH Superintendent Dr. Lavanya Kumari said the cannula was removed safely during a subsequent surgery. The woman’s condition was stable, and she was recovering. She was also able to breastfeed her baby and remained under medical observation, she said.
Dr. Lavanya Kumari took charge as the hospital superintendent a few days after the incident.

title: Pathogens, pandemics and parleys

content.value: (In the weekly Health Matters newsletter,  Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)

Time and time again as we celebrate achievements in health care, a measurable pinnacle of which could be the Nobel for Physiology/ Medicine, a sobering dose indicating the power of pathogen is delivered to us. This time, with the reported case of all things, the plague, in Russia. This week we discovered that the entire issue is mired in mystery, with not much information being shared by the nation. What was clear during the COVI-19 pandemic was the absolute criticality of sharing information globally, but with every squeak about the break out of infectious disease. In fact the Pandemic Agreement includes an aspect of Pathogen Sharing and Benefits among member nations. However, practically, sometimes nations find it difficult to easily share information with the global community.

Initially, the WHO cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. A WHOOfficial said the global organisation doesn’t know exactly how lab worker in Russia died in plague case. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the agency doesn’t know the “causative agent” behind the woman’s October 2 death, and urged Russia to share more information. The EU also urged Russia to be ‘transparent’ on plague reports - The Hindu

On its part, in tersely-worded statements, Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, does not link the case to pneumonic plague, maintaining that “extensive” testing found no evidence the lab worker’s illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Russia earlier said she died of pneumonia — a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection — and its health authorities have found no cases of plague recently. Moscow also denied sanitary measures over plague reports.
For an idea of what we actually know for sure now, do read this explainer: Pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia?

In addition, there was a fresh scare from Ebola-affected Africa: Kenya confirms first Ebola case imported from Congo after patient dies in Nairobi. Why is this significant? I explain here: Ebola death recorded in Kenya after victim travelled from DRC. The victim had been living in DRC for years, and was reportedly already ill before he took a road trip, and then, a flight back home to Nigeria. He was admitted to a hospital in Nigeria by a relative, but succumbed to his illness. This is the first case of an Ebola death that has occurred in a country, outside of the DRC and Uganda, during the outbreak raising significant concern regarding transmissibility for public health authorities. Kenyan authorities have called for stricter controls at the airports and also undertaken efforts to spread awareness and urge citizens to test if they notice symptoms. While the WHO has not issued a travel ban to the affected countries, self declaration by travellers has become mandatory at all international ports.

The past week also saw some hectic health-related activity in India. The most significant among them was easily the Supreme Court calling for a cap on trade margin for all essential medicines and medical products, as Aaratrika Bhaumik reported. As the government declared that it had proposed a 30% trade-margin cap on patented and non-patented cancer medicines, but top court asks why a margin cap cannot be extended to all medicines and medical products; the court says the government has to ensure that DPCO-approved medicines, whose price is legally regulated, reach patients. That is jumping the gun though, first read Bindu Shajan Perappadan’s article: Centre to cap trade margins on non-scheduled cancer drugs to 30% of MRP.

She also reported on the Centre’s direction to the States toDisplay rates of healthcare services prominently. Clearly visible display will enable patients to take informed decisions, build trust, prevent billing-related disputes; the Health Ministry also urged clinical establishments to display package rates for international patients visiting India on medical and Ayush visas. Another significant decision taken in the country last week: NMC brings doctors’ digital patient acquisition under ethics rules. In regulatory terms, the Centre proposing tighter curbs on advertising of prescription drugs was also a development of note.

Moving on to mental health issues, Afshan Yasmeen reported a NIMHANS study that found loneliness linked to psychological distress, excessive series watching among parents of children who had emigrated.The study examined 64 ‘empty-nest’ parents aged between 45 and 65, whose adult children had emigrated and lived away from home for at least two years.

Athira Elssa Johnson wrote on Treatment-resistant depression and what happens when antidepressants do not work, while Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula took us through Dental anxiety, particularly important, because here, fear becomes a barrier to care.

Looking at the Indian health care system and the larger stage, Rajendra Pratap Gupta argues that to retain and grow its advantage,  India needs a smarter healthcare margin policy, explaining the role of MRP in the sale of drugs and health care consumables. A lesson or two here for India’s drug price regulators, surely.
K. VijayRaghavan and Archish Mittal discuss how Indian research can shape the worldwhile Priyadarshini Singh reemphasisesIndia’s stakes in the Global Pandemic Agreement
And more…
Zubeda Hamid on the In Focus podcast, discusses the fact thatNew research has linked 12% of cancer cases to infections
Dr. Priya Chockalingam writes on Why it is essential to improve cardiac rehabilitation completion rates in India - The Hindu
Further in our explainer series, there iscoronary thrombosis, Epstein-Barr virus, stem-cell donor registries and how they work
The Hindu’s editorial on breaking the chain in leprosy in India
And before we sign off, we leave you with a link to our Health Wrap episode from last Sunday, where we discuss the 2026 Nobel Prize, brain research, and healthcare access.
(There is much more, do head to ourhealth pageand subscribe to the health newsletterhere)

title: Towards an age-ready Keralam: translating rights into care

content.value: The Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026, presents an opportunity to strengthen Keralam’s response to population ageing. The Government of Keralam’s initiative to introduce this first-of-its-kind legislation in the country is a welcome step towards protecting the rights and well-being of senior citizens.

By recognising dignity, independence, safety, participation and access to care, the Bill provides a foundation for moving beyond welfare and towards a comprehensive, entitlements-based approach to ageing.
Central principle

A central principle of the Bill is ageing in place, enabling older persons to remain in their homes and communities for as long as possible, with institutional care as a last resort. This requires supporting families through accessible health care, community-based services, trained caregivers, rehabilitation, and social support. Care must be organised as a continuum, responding to changing needs rather than only during crises.

Equally important is the shift from managing dependence to preventing or delaying avoidable functional decline. The Bill’s provision for standardised care assessments, incorporating intrinsic capacity and functional dependency, is particularly relevant. Linking these assessments with primary and community health care could enable earlier identification of changes in mobility, cognition, sensory function and daily activities, followed by timely interventions that help preserve independence.
Addressing critical gaps

The Bill also addresses critical gaps in the care ecosystem through provisions for registration and regulation of care institutions, caregiver training and certification, and minimum standards of service delivery. These measures must be accompanied by appropriate supervision, continuing education, fair working conditions, and support for family caregivers.

The proposed district-level institutional mechanisms offer an opportunity to strengthen accountability, grievance redressal, and coordination. The Bill also introduces penalties, including fines and imprisonment, for specified violations, reinforcing the importance of compliance and protection of senior citizens’ rights.
The effectiveness will depend on clear responsibilities, adequate resources, effective enforcement, and convergence across health, social welfare and local self-government systems.

An age-ready Keralam must be measured not only by the institutions and services established but also by whether older persons can maintain their functional ability, remain connected to their communities and live with dignity, independence, security and purpose.

The next priority is translating legislative provisions into accessible, equitable and quality services, particularly for older persons living alone, those with disabilities or dementia, and those without adequate family support.
Overall, the Bill presents a robust framework for geriatric care. Its efficient implementation can help set an effective precedent that can be replicated nationwide.
(Prof. (Dr.) Sudha Chandrashekar is CEO, Swasti - The Health Catalyst, a not-for-profit global organisation in the field of public health).

title: Pope Leo has lung cancer, lower lobe of right lung removed: Vatican

content.value: Pope Leo XIV's surgeon confirmed that he has lung cancer, and he had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, the Vatican said Tuesday (October 13, 2026).

The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.
Pope Leo XIV undergoes surgery for cancer: What is lung adenocarcinoma?

The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about 3 hours, the statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said.

Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli Hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.

The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localised nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
The Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo's audiences through Oct 20.

But the decision to have the operation clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.

title: Brain damage to toddler: Health Department refers medical negligence case against hospital to Karnataka Medical Council

content.value: In a case of alleged medical negligence involving a 14-month-old boy who suffered brain damage following routine ear surgery, the Bengaluru Urban District Health Officer (DHO) and the Karnataka Private Medical Establishments (KPME) Grievance Redressal Authority have officially referred the matter to the Karnataka Medical Council (KMC) for an inquiry and report.

The decision follows a complaint lodged by Sampath Kumar K.P., whose son was taken to Cloudnine Hospital, Nagarabhavi, on July 26, 2026, for emergency surgical repair of a full-thickness ear laceration. During the procedure, the toddler suffered a cardiac arrest in the operation theatre and subsequently sustained severe brain injury due to lack of oxygen.
Lapses in anesthesia administration

A detailed inquiry conducted by an expert medical panel — comprising Raghunatha M. (anaesthesiologist) and Nagaraju (paediatrician) from the State-run Sir C.V. Raman General Hospital — said there were critical lapses during the administration of anesthesia.

According to the technical committee’s report submitted by doctors to the KMC, the operating room was satisfactorily equipped, but the attending anesthesiologist was “not well trained to administer anaesthesia for small children”.

Describing how the lapse led to oxygen levels plummetting, the report states that the doctor attempted to intubate the child with an uncuffed tube, leading to hypoxia, bradycardia, and eventual cardiac arrest.

While hospital logs claimed cardiac arrest was reversed within seven minutes, the expert committee stated in the report that brain hypoxia persisted for 15 to 20 minutes, causing severe, irreversible brain damage. An MRI scan performed three days later confirmed partial prolonged hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury.
Current condition and referral
Following initial resuscitation, the toddler was transferred to the Paediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) at Cloudnine Hospital, Jayanagar, for advanced critical care.

The clinical evaluation conducted by Dr. Nagaraju noted that while the child has been weaned off mechanical ventilation and is currently hemodynamically stable, he suffers from profound neurological sequelae. The toddler remains unresponsive to verbal commands, has lost his sight, exhibits decerebrate posturing, and is dependent on Ryle’s tube feeding. He requires ongoing multidisciplinary care.

During the hearing held on October 8, the DHO and KPME Authority reviewed the expert panel’s findings and the parents’ submission. Noting that the medical panel’s findings explicitly indicate prima facie medical negligence, the Bengaluru Urban DHO, formally transferred the case files to the KMC president on October 12, for disciplinary proceedings and further action.

title: Osteoporosis awareness, detection camp on Oct. 20

content.value: Shri Physio & Rehab Centre at Adyar in Chennai will conduct an osteoporosis awareness camp on October 20, marking World Osteoporosis Day. Led by Shriram Krishnamoorthy, consultant orthopaedic and joint replacement surgeon, the initiative aims to raise awareness of bone health and the importance of early assessment and preventive care.

The camp will offer free bone density assessments, Vitamin D3 tests, and physiotherapy consultations. Participants will also receive guidance on simple exercises to strengthen bones, maintain mobility, and support bone health as part of their daily routine.
The camp will be held at the Wellness Hall on the first floor of Shri Physio & Rehab Centre on  October 20, from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. Walk-ins are welcome.

title: Keralam Senior Citizens Bill referred to Assembly Subject Committee

content.value: The Keralam Assembly on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) referred the Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection) Bill, 2026, which aims at ensuring the rights and protection of the elderly, to the Finance Subject Committee for further scrutiny.

The Bill, piloted by Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, aims at promoting healthy and active ageing, registration and regulation of senior citizen care centres, capacity-building for family and care givers, and protection of rights, dignity, and social security of the elderly.
Opposition alleges Constitutional breach

However, the Opposition alleged that the provision that a copy of a Bill to be tabled in the Assembly should be made available to members at least three days before had not been fully complied with. N.K. Akbar, MLA, in a point of order, alleged Constitutional violation, failure to calculate the financial burden correctly, violation of Supreme Court directives on advanced medical directives with regard to the Bill’s provisions on execution of ‘living will.’

The LDF government had brought out a policy for the elderly, set up a commission for them, and prepared an elderly budget. “So, the Opposition is not against the Bill. But, serious legal issues exist,” he said.

The Chief Minister, who holds the portfolio of the Department of Senior Citizens, contended that special Acts could contain penal provisions. Moreover, the finance memorandum in the Bill clearly specified recurring and non-recurring expenditure. The government would not incur any particular expenditure in setting up senior citizen unit and forums as proposed in the Bill. The Supreme Court guidelines would be incorporated when Rules for the Act were framed, he said.
The Speaker ruled that the Bill was published in the Gazette on October 10 and its copies circulated among members the same day.

During the discussion on the Bill, the Chief Minister reiterated that “the measure of a civilised society was how it treated its senior citizens”. If the Bill were to be passed, the Keralam Assembly would become a model for the world, he addded.
Focus also on silver economy

Referring to demographic changes and migration of children and youth outside Keralam, he said the population of the elderly in the State was expected to be double the national average by 2036. However, the government was focussing not only on the welfare of the elderly, but also “silver economy” so as to transform the challenges posed by the rising elderly population into an opportunity.

The United Democratic Front (UDF) government had set up a dedicated department for the elderly. Government interventions were planned to ensure active and healthy ageing, tapping into the skills and knowledge of the elderly, conducting a survey of all elderly in the State and their health status, setting up a volunteer corps, registration and monitoring of care homes, and training and certification of care-givers, he said.
“No one should feel they are alone. They should be protected and their rights ensured,” the Chief Minister said.
He also explained the rights and principles that informed the drafting of the Bill.

title: What intestinal gas can tell us about our gastrointestinal health

content.value: Food, from the moment it’s in the mouth until it’s excreted as poop, goes through digestion—and this process is a wild journey.  Food containing carbohydrates, proteins, or lipids is chewed into a mush in the mouth, where some degree of starch and lipid digestion occurs before it is swallowed. In the stomach, the swallowed ‘ball’ of chewed food is continuously ground and churned until the food particles are small enough to enter the small intestine. Simultaneously, hydrochloric acid (HCl) and pepsin (an enzyme) in the stomach break down complex proteins in the food.

The food, now in a semi-liquid form, reaches the digestive enzyme-rich small intestine, where its fate is sealed for major chemical digestion before being converted into absorbable nutrients. Enzymes in the small intestine break down the partially digested macronutrients—carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids—into smaller molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream, along with vitamins and minerals.

What remains is indigestible food, along with leftover digestive fluids and cellular waste, which enters the colon (large intestine), where digestive enzymes are lacking. However, the gut microbiota—the body’s dynamic ‘organ’—in the colon compensates for this dearth by fermenting indigestible food, including dietary fibres and indigestible proteins.  Enzymes produced by the gut microbiota break this indigestible food into useful metabolites and gases before the remainder is expelled as poop.
What are intestinal gases?

In humans, intestinal gases include nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>), oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>), carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>), hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>), methane (CH<sub>4</sub>), and trace amounts of hydrogen sulphide (H<sub>2</sub>S)—the gas with the rotten egg smell. While N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> mostly reflect swallowed air, H<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub> are odourless gases produced by gut microbiota. It is H<sub>2</sub>S that is primarily responsible for the smell of gas.

The colon—which hosts the highest microbial densities—harbours microbes that prefer indigestible carbohydrates as food, or as an energy source. These indigestible-carbohydrate-loving microbes (carbohydrate-fermenting) flourish in the colon region close to the small intestine (proximal colon), where their energy source availability is higher. Microbes including Bacteroides scavenge (ferment) human-indigestible carbohydrates such as dietary fibres and resistant starch, producing substantial quantities of hydrogen as a major by-product.

Also thriving in this oxygen-poor, hydrogen-rich ecosystem are microbes that compete for, and convert hydrogen to methane, like methanogenic archaea. Likewise, sulphate-reducing bacteria (SRB) in these regions of the colon convert hydrogen into hydrogen sulphide in small amounts. As the food passes through the colon, the availability of indigestible carbohydrates decreases over time. Microbes like SRB in regions of the colon close to the rectum (distal colon) also ferment human-indigestible proteins for energy, producing hydrogen sulphide in the process.
Studies so far suggest that host cells (through distinct mechanisms) and microbial cells utilise intestinal gases. Excess gases are eliminated as exhaled gas (from the lungs) and flatulence.
What do intestinal gases do?

Recent studies suggest intestinal gases are more than just gas. They can, in fact, serve as markers of gastrointestinal (GI) health, and can regulate gut motility and transit time. Gut motility refers to the muscle contractions in the digestive tract that move the food, and gut transit time is the time it takes for food to move through the gastrointestinal tract before being excreted.

Advancing research reveals that hydrogen can influence gut motility and, in experimental models, shorten transit time. Methane, by contrast, has been shown to slow gut motility and increase transit time. However, findings on the effect of hydrogen sulphide on gut motility and transit time have been mixed.
Microbiota research has also pointed to links between imbalances in gut microbiota and intestinal gas levels and gastrointestinal(GI) diseases/symptoms.

A real-world study measured hydrogen, methane, and hydrogen sulphide levels using breath testing in 3,004 participants with GI symptoms, especially excessive bloating and flatulence, from the United States. The study found associations between intestinal gas levels and GI symptoms: higher hydrogen levels (≥20 ppm above baseline) with diarrhoea; higher methane levels (≥10 ppm) with constipation; and higher hydrogen sulphide levels (≥2 ppm) with severe diarrhoea and abdominal pain. The study also suggested dysregulated hydrogen sulphide production was associated with greater diarrhoea, urgency, bloating, and symptom severity.

Animal models and clinical studies have reported similar associations between intestinal gases and GI symptoms. However, these studies lack identical methodologies and comparison with healthy participants as controls.
Monitoring gases for diagnosis

The most commonly adopted method for measuring intestinal gases is breath testing—measuring gases in exhaled breath. Microbial fermentation activity and gut motility are also assessed indirectly with this method.

However, new techniques are being devised for non-invasive, real-time continuous monitoring of intestinal gases. To capture eliminated intestinal gases (exhaled gas and flatus), researchers have designed respiration/fermentation chambers (airtight rooms with gas sensors and continuous air supply) to explore microbial fermentation activity, track intestinal gases, and monitor the effects of therapeutic interventions.

Alternatively, as flatus has relatively higher concentrations of intestinal gases, researchers at the University of Maryland have developed a device that can be attached to underwear. The device, designed to objectively measure hydrogen in flatus, monitors real-time gas profiles and gas-release patterns, providing insights into gut microbial activity and digestive health.
Why this is important

Measuring and monitoring real-time gas profiles  could enable researchers to expand gut microbiota research: define ‘normal’ and ‘abnormal’ levels in intestinal gases, establish mechanisms behind gas effects, and study diverse populations, involving both healthy people and people with GI diseases, over long periods. Doctors could also potentially tailor a treatment plan—diet or gas-targeted medication—to rebalance the gut microbial ecosystem and modulate gas production and track GI health progress.

Therefore, the next time someone lets one rip, remember that intestinal gases have uses beyond popular humour or emptying out a room.  These gases are part of a dynamic system that shapes the gut microbiota and influences digestive health, including how one poops, and can serve as markers of GI health.
(Smruthi Prabhu is an independent science writer from Mangalore. smruthigp@gmail.com)

title: India’s water plants are failing to catch elusive ‘forever chemicals’

content.value: Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are synthetic chemical compounds that contain multiple carbon-fluorine bonds. PFAS materials are used in coatings, textiles, and several industrial products. They are also notorious for resisting degradation and can contaminate the environment for a very long time.

Many studies from different parts of India have already found PFAS in water sources. Conventional water treatment systems that can remove these compounds are not yet commercially available even as the extent of PFAS contamination across India remains unclear.

title: What are type I and type II errors?

content.value: A: The null hypothesis is a cornerstone of scientific experiments. It is the hypothesis that an experiment tests. For example, if a hospital is testing a new drug, the null hypothesis will be that the drug has no effect.

In this scenario, scientists are vulnerable to making two kinds of mistakes. One, the type I error, happens when a scientist rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true: they conclude the drug works when in fact it does not. This is called a false positive. In a type II error, a scientist does not reject a null hypothesis even though it is actually false, i.e. a false negative.

There are different ways to measure, and prevent, these mistakes. Often the most effective one is to ensure all involved parties have more information during the test. This way, scientists do not have to work with a too-tight false positive limit or a too-loose false negative error limit.

The Election Commission of India (ECI) is currently conducting a ‘Special Intensive Revision’ (SIR) where both these errors are in play. Say a registered voter is eligible. A false positive error happens if ECI officials wrongly remove that voter’s name from the electoral rolls. A false negative error occurs if officials include a name on the rolls whereas that person is ineligible to vote (e.g. if they have died).

A good way to reduce both types of error rates would be for all stakeholders — including the ECI and the people — is to have more information, e.g. data from the new Census, opportunities to challenge decisions, and independent audits.

title: Elon Musk and Mukesh Ambani’s feud over Starlink | Explained

content.value: SpaceX owner Elon Musk has never shied away from starting a social media spat, be it with his own family members or U.S. President Donald Trump.

Mr. Musk has now taken aim at India’s billionaire Mukesh Ambani, accusing the chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries of being the real “boss” of India, and playing a role in keeping Starlink’s satellite internet out of the Indian market to favour Jio.

title: Meta says its new AI models on par with OpenAI, Anthropic

content.value: Meta on Monday unveiled two new "frontier" artificial intelligence models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude.
"Muse Spark was our first family of models, and now Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier," CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X.

Zuckerberg has pushed Meta to compete with leading AI labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic over the past year or so amid a race to win over customers and diversify beyond advertising, which has historically been its main source of revenue.
In June 2025, the company made a $14 billion investment in Scale AI, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and poached its co-founder Alexandr Wang as part of the deal.
Zuckerberg subsequently made Wang the company's chief AI officer overseeing its newly formed division called Superintelligence Labs.
Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry.
The new models can soon be used in Meta's new personal agent app, known as Muse, for paid subscribers only.
Wonder is "our largest and most capable model yet" and "rivals the big (boys)," Wang posted on X, presumably referring to leading labs OpenAI and Anthropic.

In a blog post, Meta touted so-called benchmarking data from an independent firm called Artificial Analysis that appears to show that Meta's newest Wonder models outperform its own previous models, Spark, as well as various models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.
Artificial Analysis's website shows that Wonder is also among the most expensive models.
Meta has committed billions towards competing in the global race to dominate AI, despite growing concerns about safety and security.
In July, the Facebook and Instagram maker said its spending on AI-related investments could reach $145 billion this year.
The company has more than 3.6 billion daily active users around the world.
In its early years, Facebook was known to operate under a philosophy of "move fast and break things," but more recently, Zuckerberg implied Meta would balance safety with speed.
"Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would," Zuckerberg posted on X last month.
In August, Meta launched Muse Code, a product intended to compete with similar automated coding tools offered by OpenAI and Anthropic.
Then in September, it launched an agentic app called Muse. Agentic software can autonomously perform specific tasks such as coding, research, shopping, booking reservations or shopping.

At its annual developer conference Connect last month, Meta also revealed a new handheld AI hardware product called Muse Charm that allows users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone.
Developers have been racing to design agentic apps that will capture users' attention, time and wallets. AI-powered hardware remains an elusive goal for the industry as well.
While Silicon Valley heavyweights OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta dominate the landscape, young startups like Instinct are also becoming breakout hits.
Zuckerberg sped up Muse's launch due to Instinct's popularity, the New York Times reported.
Some competitors have called for an industry-wide slowdown to address and mitigate safety concerns.

In September, Zuckerberg was one of six American tech executives to sign what President Donald Trump described as a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards around ever more advanced AI models.
Executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Nvidia also signed the agreement but there is no consensus among politicians or industry leaders around how to best move forward.

Leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have encouraged "pacing" or slowing down development after models created by all three were found to have escaped their testing environments or taken actions without authorisation.
"We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the United Nations last month.

title: Interview | ‘Tiger man’ K. Ullas Karanth on protecting India’s wildlife habitats

content.value: The walls of K. Ullas Karanth’s office in Bengaluru are lined with striking photographs of tigers, unsurprising for a man who has spent decades studying the striped phantom of the forest. One shows his younger self in camouflage gear, posing with a tranquillised tiger. It was taken in January 1990, when he had captured and collared the tigress labelled as T-02, nicknamed Sundari.

This picture, and the incident behind it, are both part of Tiger Memories: My Life in Wildlife Conservation, Karanth’s latest book, co-authored with Bengaluru-based writer Joshua Mathew. It traces the tiger expert’s lifelong passion for the natural world, his pioneering contributions to tiger research and conservation in India, and the successes, challenges, regrets, and disappointments he encountered along the way.

Karanth, a recipient of numerous honours, including the Padma Shri, is the founder of the Centre for Wildlife Studies, a conservation, research, and education organisation based in Bengaluru. In this interview, he explains why he emphasises less on co-existence and more on protecting habitats, enforcing laws, and reducing dependence on forest resources. Edited excerpts:

You push back on the emphasis on co-existence and community conservation, arguing instead that effective forest departments, land protection, strong laws and policies, and the voluntary relocation of people are more important. Could you elaborate?

In the Brazilian Amazon, where human population densities are low, that sort of co-existence between humans and wildlife is possible as long as bio-resource consumption rates don’t exceed nature’s capacity to replenish itself. But this doesn’t work in India, where local populations run into lakhs in and around tiny nature reserves. We can’t change the availability of resources or human population density, but we can reduce biomass dependencies using modern technologies in energy generation and agriculture.

The number of animals that a piece of land can support is driven largely by three things: the animal’s body size, its energetic requirements or diet, and its habitat needs. And we can’t radically alter these determinants if the goal is to preserve wild nature.

When modern humans evolved around 3,00,000 years ago, we had no domesticated animals or farmed crops. So, our total biomass was only 3% of all mammalian biomass. After we started domesticating animals, mastering agriculture, and later venturing into modern industrial development, this changed. Today, humans and domestic animals together account for 95% of total mammalian biomass. Which means that in a densely populated country such as India, where dependence on biological resources is so high, our protection measures have to be pretty drastic if we really want to hang on to our wildlife. Protected areas in India cover just 4% of the country’s land, which is nothing.
But doesn’t context matter? In the Northeast, for instance, where so much of the land is under customary community ownership, isn’t community conservation the best way to protect wildlife?

Conservation definitely needs to vary depending on context. And we are fortunate that we have this tradition of tolerance in some parts of India. But this is a unique feature of Indian culture, unlike in most parts of the world, including even Buddhist countries of Southeast Asia. For instance, in Gujarat and Rajasthan, you will see herds of antelopes grazing in the fields. Of course, there are contrary examples — across vast forested areas of India, including the Northeast, such tolerance for wildlife is not the norm, but traditional mass hunting is.

But even if you accept all these big-picture arguments, and even if 90% of people turn benign towards wildlife, a small fraction will still hunt or get involved in commercial wildlife trade and smuggling. In any society, you need some regulatory power over such crime; you need laws and somebody to enforce them. The question is: who should do that?

In the Northeast, the model that we have of the forest department and enforcement doesn’t work. So, I agree we need multiple models. But ultimately somebody has to enforce the law wherever you go. And to say that you don’t need enforcement at all, and people will not use wildlife and only tolerate it, is unrealistic.

Recently, a tigress from the Valmiki Tiger Reserve in Bihar was airlifted and released in West Bengal’s Buxa Tiger Reserve, part of the National Tiger Conservation Authority’s larger translocation programme. What are your thoughts on this, given that you have often said the country could support far more tigers than it does today?

The moving of highly territorial cats between reserves is mostly unwarranted. If you look at all the translocation records, only some 5% are successful; most have failed, but nobody talks about these.

Right now, India has roughly 4 lakh sq.km. of forests where tigers can potentially exist, but only one-fourth of this area has tigers in reasonable numbers. If we manage it properly, we can have 15,000-20,000 tigers within government forests. Of course, it is a slow process. Tigers were almost extinct, but by bringing around 1 lakh sq.km. or so in different areas under some protection after the 1960s, their numbers have increased. Instead of reintroducing tigers, if you recover more potential tiger habitat through protection and build up prey densities, tigers will spread out automatically.

The case for physical translocation is extremely rare. Only if you have recovered the prey base in an area with no connectivity does it make sense to introduce some tigers, preferably pregnant females. If you simply dump tigers without ensuring there is enough prey, it causes conflict and leads to local hostility towards tigers.
Do you think the rise of wildlife tourism could play a significant role in conservation, especially given that the tiger is the primary marketing magnet in this sector?

Wildlife tourism, in general, has not played a positive role in expanding our wildlife habitats. I think it has tremendous potential in India because it can boost the rural economy, which can help people who live around these protected areas. If a farmer next to a protected area can make more money from having wildlife on his land than from, say, growing ragi, she will automatically switch to more wildlife-friendly land uses.

We have seen this happen in Africa, where farmers get together, form a conservancy, and enter into an agreement with lodges that bring in tourists and a lot of money. But right now, in India, tourism companies aren’t expanding the land base for wildlife; they are pressuring the same areas that are already protected.

We need to push protected areas to 10%-15% of our land, and that can only happen through economic incentives and development, not government diktats. If this money goes to people who own land next to the reserves, land use changes will expand wildlife habitats as well as reduce conflicts with humans.
preeti.zachariah@thehindu.co.in

title: Forest ‘violations’ in Keralam’s Chalakudy division come under scrutiny

content.value: Alleged unauthorised tree marking for a proposed solar fence and the felling of trees on forest land diverted for a school playground in the Chalakudy Forest Division in Keralam have raised environmental concerns, with environmentalists claiming that up to 20,000 trees could be affected.

Greens have warned of potential forest destruction and disruption of elephant corridors in the absence of a cumulative ecological impact assessment. They have demanded immediate intervention by the relevant authorities and a halt to work on the proposed fencing, which is intended as a human-elephant conflict mitigation measure.
The activities related to the fencing works are reportedly continuing even as the matter is under consideration by the Supreme Court-constituted Central Empowered Committee (CEC).
Two complaints filed

The Animals and Nature Ethics Community (ANEC) Trust has filed two complaints with the CEC alleging irregularities in the Chalakudy Forest Division, including proposed large-scale tree felling in the Kodassery Notified Reserve Forest and illegal diversion of forest land at Nayarangadi, both in Pariyaram range.

The first complaint alleged that tree marking and felling along a 30-km stretch for vista clearance and restoration of a solar-powered electric fence had begun without statutory approvals. It also alleged that the work was split into smaller proposals to evade scrutiny of its cumulative ecological impact.

The second complaint alleged the illegal diversion of 0.84 hectares of forest land at Nayarangadi for a school playground, involving quarrying and rock removal, the felling of hundreds of trees, including sandalwood, and irregularities in timber valuation and auction.
The complainant submitted photographs and other evidence. The CEC directed the Forest department and the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) to jointly submit their response.

T.S. Santhosh, legal representative of ANEC Trust, said the proposed solar fence would span about 38 km across the Chalakudy Forest Division, including 30 km in Pariyaram and another 8 km in the Vellikulangara range.

“More than 6,000 trees have reportedly been assigned serial numbers, with around 20,000 potentially affected,” said Mr. Santhosh. “The key question is whether felling so many mature trees is necessary when less destructive alternatives, such as existing clearings and modified alignments, may be available. Large-scale tree removal and fencing could damage wildlife habitats, affect drainage and riparian vegetation, fragment ecological connectivity and obstruct elephant movement routes.”
When contacted, Joseph Thomas, divisional forest officer, Chalakudy, told The Hindu that the project was still at the planning stage.
“No work is currently under way. We are only assessing how many trees may need to be felled for the fencing. No marking is being done,” said Mr. Thomas.

Environmentalists have urged the Forest department to submit complete project records to the CEC and comply with its directions. They also sought an independent expert assessment and a VACB inquiry to establish violations, fix responsibility and initiate action against officials found guilty of irregularities.

title: Top AI researchers demand action to prevent models going ‘rogue’

content.value: More than 200 artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity researchers have called for immediate action to prevent further cases of AI models going rogue and posing a risk to critical infrastructure.

The letter signed by luminaries in the field including Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton and Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio, called for models relating to cybersecurity to be physically cut off from the internet during testing.

Leading U.S.-based AI firms have disclosed over recent months a series of incidents where models under development have escaped containment measures to access the internet and have gone on to hack websites, including gaining unauthorised access to Australian government sites.

“Without immediate changes in AI development and deployment practices, such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure,” they warned.
Their letter called for organisations developing, deploying, and testing cyber-capable AI models to be air-gapped, i.e. physically cut off from the internet, to ensure they do not escape.
It also called for the creation of an international body that standardises best practices regarding security.

The letter urged companies to be required to report containment failures to the body, which would be responsible for tracking and recording them. “This transparency is required for both learning and accountability purposes,” the letter said.
The rogue incidents amplified calls to slow AI development, but the industry and governments are divided on tapping the brakes as well as regulating the sector.
In the U.S., the Trump administration has opposed any binding regulation that could hinder innovation, amid fierce competition with China.

title: What is coronary thrombosis? Explained

content.value: The death of actor Nana Patekar, 75, has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, a condition in which a blood clot forms in an artery supplying the heart. What causes these clots, who is at risk, and how is the condition diagnosed and treated?
The story so far:

According to published accounts of the autopsy report, actor Nana Patekar died after a blood clot blocked the left main coronary artery, which supplies blood to a large part of the heart muscle. A blockage in this artery can severely restrict blood flow to the heart and cause a heart attack. The reported finding has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, the formation of a blood clot within a coronary artery.
What is coronary thrombosis?

Coronary thrombosis occurs when a blood clot forms in one of the arteries that supply blood to the heart muscle. These arteries carry oxygen and nutrients that the heart needs to function. When a clot partly or completely blocks an artery, less blood reaches the heart muscle. If the blood supply is cut off for too long, the heart muscle can become damaged, leading to a heart attack. The severity depends on how much of the artery is blocked and how quickly blood flow is restored.

This form of thrombosis  is often associated with atherosclerosis, in which fatty deposits, cholesterol and other substances build up in the artery walls. These deposits, called plaques, can remain unnoticed for years.

When a plaque ruptures or its surface is eroded, platelets gather at the site and a clot may form. The clot can then obstruct blood flow, sometimes suddenly. Damage to the inner surface of an artery can trigger the process of clot formation. Additionally, at rupture,  the material beneath the plaque’s  surface comes into contact with blood, prompting platelets to gather and the clotting process to begin. A clot may grow quickly and block the artery.
What are the warning signs?

A clot that significantly restricts blood flow through a coronary artery may cause chest discomfort, pressure or tightness. Pain may spread to the arms, shoulders, back, neck or jaw. Breathlessness, sweating, nausea, dizziness and unusual fatigue may also occur.

The symptoms depend on the artery affected and the extent of the blockage. Some people may have less typical symptoms or no obvious warning signs before the blockage becomes serious. Symptoms alone cannot confirm coronary thrombosis; medical assessment and investigations are needed.
Suspected coronary artery blockage accompanied by chest pain or breathlessness requires emergency medical attention.
Who is at risk?

People living with coronary artery disease are at greater risk of coronary thrombosis because fatty deposits can build up in their arteries and trigger clot formation if a deposit ruptures. Smoking, high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes, physical inactivity and an unhealthy diet can increase the risk of developing this artery disease.
In some cases, a clot may form in an artery affected by other conditions, including inflammation or injury to the blood vessel.

Older age and a family history of heart disease at a younger age are also risk factors. However it can occur even in people who have not been diagnosed with coronary artery disease. The underlying plaque build-up may have gone undetected until it triggers the formation of a clot.
How is this condition diagnosed?

Doctors assess symptoms and medical history and use tests to determine whether a coronary artery is blocked and whether the heart muscle has been damaged. An electrocardiogram (ECG) records the heart’s electrical activity, while blood tests measuring cardiac troponin can help identify damage to the heart muscle.

Coronary angiography uses a contrast dye and X-rays to show the coronary arteries and identify the location and extent of a blockage. This can help doctors decide how best to restore blood flow. Other tests may be used depending on the patient’s condition.
How is it treated?
Treatment aims to restore blood flow and prevent the clot from growing or new clots from forming. The approach depends on the location and severity of the blockage and the patient’s condition.

Angioplasty may be used to reopen the affected artery. A thin tube is guided to the blockage, where a small balloon is inflated to widen the artery. A stent, a small mesh tube, is often placed to help keep it open.

Doctors may also use antiplatelet medicines, which reduce the tendency of platelets to clump together, and anticoagulants, which interfere with the blood-clotting process. In selected cases, clot-dissolving medicines may be used. Coronary artery bypass surgery may be considered when the pattern of blockage makes it a more suitable option.

Preventing further clots involves managing the underlying risk factors and following the prescribed treatment plan. This may include controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, stopping tobacco use, maintaining physical activity appropriate to the person’s condition and taking prescribed medicines.

title: Display rates of healthcare services prominently, Centre tells States

content.value: The Union Health Ministry has asked all States and Union Territories to ensure the prominent display of rates charged for services and facilities offered by clinical establishments.

In a move aimed at strengthening transparency, accountability and patient-centric healthcare delivery, Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava, in a letter to the Chief Secretaries of all States and Union Territories, called for compliance with regulatory provisions, and ensuring information on service charges was clearly visible to patients and their attendants.
ALSO WATCH 2026 Nobel Prize, brain research, and healthcare access | Health Wrap | Episode 54

“Display of rates would help patients and their families understand the likely cost of treatment, make informed healthcare decisions, and plan their medical expenditure,’’ Ms. Srivastava said, adding that greater transparency would also help minimise avoidable confusion and billing-related disputes.
The letter refers to the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 and the Clinical Establishments (Central Government) Rules, 2012.

Under the Rules, clinical establishments in States and Union Territories where the Act is applicable are required to display the rates charged for each type of service provided, along with facilities available, at a conspicuous place, in the local language as well as in English.

Since health is a State subject, in States and Union Territories where clinical establishments are regulated by their own respective frameworks, several of which also contain provisions relating to the display of rates, the Health Secretary has called upon Chief Secretaries to ensure effective compliance.
The letter also places particular emphasis on transparency in healthcare pricing for international patients.
States and UTs have been requested to encourage the prominent display, wherever applicable, of package rates offered to foreign patients travelling to India on medical or Ayush visas.

“This would enable international patients to make informed choices, help minimise pricing and billing-related grievances and further strengthen India’s position as a trusted destination for medical and Ayush care,’’ the Ministry said.

title: Supreme Court wants cap on trade margin for all essential medicines and medical products

content.value: Even as the Centre informed the Supreme Court on Monday (October 12, 2026) that it had decided to cap trade margins at 30% for non-scheduled cancer drugs, the court questioned why the benefit of such price regulation should be confined to cancer drugs and not extended to other essential medicines and medical products.

The development comes after a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta expressed concern over stark disparities between the price to retailer (PTR) and the maximum retail price (MRP) of certain medicines, particularly cancer drugs, with mark-ups in some instances soaring to 1,000%. The Bench had flagged that such exorbitant mark-ups constituted “broad daylight dacoity” and placed an enormous financial burden on patients.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, informed the Bench that the proposed 30% trade-margin cap would cover both patented and non-patented cancer medicines, with an expert committee headed by the Director General of Health Services tasked with identifying the drugs to be brought within its ambit. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) will examine the committee’s recommendations before issuing a price notification to implement the cap.

The Bench, however, said that while the intervention was commendable, it was inadequate, and questioned why other medicines and medical devices could not also be brought within the 16% retailer margin prescribed under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013.
“This is just the tip of the iceberg... this has come around only because of the unduly hard observations we made during earlier hearings. What about other drugs,” the Bench asked.

The top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha seeking stricter enforcement of price controls under the DPCO to curb disproportionate margins across the pharmaceutical supply chain.

Justice Mehta drew attention to steep markups on medical devices and consumables, pointing out that an India-made cardiac stent costing around ₹5,000 was being sold by hospitals for more than ₹25,000. He cited the example of a saline drip line carrying an MRP of ₹11 being sold for ₹270.

“We understand that there are transportation costs, raw material costs, R&D costs and other ancillary costs, but all these are included in the MRP. What is the logic behind allowing them to sell at 400 times the actual cost? How can you allow this? What is the benefit for the patients?” the Bench observed.
‘Balance in pricing’

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, also appearing for the Centre, cautioned against a uniform cap across medicines, arguing that low-value products often required higher margins to remain commercially viable for retailers. Excessive regulation, she said, could discourage retailers from stocking such medicines and affect their availability, particularly in rural areas.
Ms. Bhati stressed the need to preserve some room for market forces rather than subject the entire pharmaceutical sector to price controls.

“Higher margins in such cases are important for ensuring the availability of such medicines to consumers… Our concern is that there has to be a balance in pricing. There has to be some level of market play available for drugs. We do not want to control the entire ecosystem of drugs. The policy was framed with the outlook that there should be intervention only when necessary,” she submitted.
The Bench, however, was not persuaded, observing that ensuring the availability of price-controlled medicines was the government’s responsibility.

“If the DPCO -approved medicines do not reach customers, then it is the duty of the government to ensure it reaches [sic] the patient. The actual dispute is over which medicines should be on the DPCO-controlled list and which should not,” Justice Mehta observed.
Accordingly, the Bench gave the Centre until October 27 to work out the modalities for capping medicine prices, when the matter will be heard next.
Centre’s affidavit

The Centre, in its 551-page affidavit, said the proposed trade-margin rationalisation (TMR) was expected to reduce the MRP of anti-cancer drugs by 20% to 70%, translating into estimated annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore. It said the measure would reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure and improve the affordability and accessibility of cancer medicines, while retaining a 30% trade margin for the distribution chain.

The Centre cited a similar intervention by the NPPA in 2019, when a 30% trade-margin cap was imposed at the first point of sale on 42 select non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines. The margin was based on an industry-practice assumption of 10% for distributors and 20% for retailers.

The measure, it said, led to a substantial reduction in the MRP of 526 brands and annual savings of around ₹984 crore for patients, based on information furnished by pharmaceutical companies. The Centre said the 2019 exercise provided a policy and operational precedent for extending trade-margin rationalisation to a wider range of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines.

Detailing the existing price-control mechanism, the Centre said the ceiling price of medicines listed in Schedule I of the DPCO is determined by taking the simple average of the price to retailer of brands and generic versions with a market share of at least 1%, and adding a 16% margin.

“The ceiling price so fixed becomes the MRP, i.e., the price above which the drug cannot be sold in the market. However, the manufacturer is at liberty to give an appropriate margin to the wholesaler and the retailer within the ceiling price,” it said, adding that ceiling prices had so far been fixed for 935 formulations.

For non-scheduled formulations, manufacturers are free to determine the initial launch price, subject to the NPPA’s regulation of subsequent price increases. The Centre said competition in the pharmaceutical market generally acted as a restraint against arbitrary pricing.

title: New research has linked 12% of cancer cases to infections: what does this mean? | In Focus Podcast

content.value: We’re used to thinking of cancer as something for which there is no known cause and we know that risk factors include using tobacco and excessive alcohol as well as obesity. And while of these factors are true, what we may not have realised is that infections could also, in some cases, lead to cancers. A new study conducted by the International Agency for Research on Cancer or IARC, has now found that infections were responsible for 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024, or 12% of the total cases globally that year.
What infections? A bacterium and several viruses were linked cancer cases, and what is significant is that a large proportion of these cases were found in low- and middle-income countries.

What are the cancers caused by infectious agents, and how common are they? Could vaccines eliminate these sorts of cancers? Are there vaccines available for all the viruses and bacteria that cause cancers? What kind of screening programmes and preventive measures should we take?
Guest: Dr. Rajeev Jayadevan, Convener Research Cell Kerala State IMA Physician and gastroenterologist
