title: What the Skin Observatory reveals about access to dermatological care in India

content.value: A skin problem can begin with something familiar. An itch that persists. A rash that returns. A patch that looks different from the rest of the skin. What happens next often depends on where a person lives and whether appropriate care is within reach.

The Global Access to Skin Health Observatory is a landmark global study led by Esther Freeman in collaboration with the International League of Dermatological Societies (ILDS) and L’Oréal Dermatological Beauty. Published in JAMA Dermatology, it brings together data from 158 countries representing 97% of the world’s population.
For India, the findings raise questions about where specialists practise, how patients reach them and what happens when treatment is delayed.
What the numbers miss

The study proposes a benchmark of 5.63 per lakh, derived from countries reporting adequate access to dermatological care. This, however, is  a reference point, rather than a universal staffing prescription. Dr. Freeman, who is associate professor of dermatology at Harvard Medical School and director of global health dermatology at Massachusetts General Hospital, places India’s dermatologist density well below the benchmark at around 0.5 to 1 per lakh people.

Ramesh Bhat, the Indian co-author of the study and professor at Father Muller Medical College and head of research at Father Muller Research Centre, Mangalore,  cautions against directly comparing India with Europe or the Americas, because their health systems differ. What surprises Prof Bhat is that shortages persist despite the number of postgraduate dermatology training seats. He points to the urban-rural divide, with a concentration of specialists in urban areas,  and in many cities in southern India, while rural communities face a different reality, where access even to a doctor may be limited.

The study reports that, globally, 79% of dermatologists practise in urban areas. National averages can therefore conceal substantial local gaps. “Dermatologist density gives us an important starting point, but it does not tell us whether a patient can actually receive care,” Dr. Freeman says.
When care is delayed

For Prof Bhat, the consequences are visible in clinical practice. He identifies “delay in diagnosis, wrong treatment, steroid abuse” among the problems arising when appropriate care is unavailable. He singles out leprosy as a condition where delayed diagnosis has implications beyond the individual patient. His concern brings the discussion back to what happens before someone reaches a specialist and whether the treatment they receive along the way is appropriate.

Dr Freeman emphasises the breadth of skin disease, from common infections to chronic inflammatory conditions and neglected tropical diseases. She argues that skin health must be recognised as an essential part of healthcare, with investment directed towards services that already reach communities.
The question is, how to make those services capable of recognising and managing skin disease safely.
Bringing expertise closer

“We need more dermatologists, but we cannot train our way out of this problem with specialists alone,” Dr Freeman says. Primary-care physicians and health officers already manage substantial amounts of skin disease. She advocates practical training, essential medicines and clear referral pathways, allowing common conditions to be treated locally while complex disease and uncertain diagnoses reach specialists.

Prof Bhat also proposes that medical colleges adopt villages, strengthening their links with surrounding communities. He also sees a role for the district residency programme, which takes residents into district settings, and for health camps in reaching rural and tribal populations.

These approaches sit alongside his call for rural specialist clinics and teledermatology. His emphasis is on extending the reach of existing teaching institutions and services, while giving residents the training needed to work effectively beyond major urban centres.
Making remote advice useful

“Teledermatology can be implemented,” Prof Bhat says. But he cautions that training healthcare workers must not result in unqualified practice or drug misuse. Expanding access requires clarity about who can manage a condition and when specialist assessment is necessary.

Dr. Freeman makes a related point.  Teledermatology and Artificial Intelligence use need trained frontline providers, available treatment, and reliable referral arrangements. A patient requiring a biopsy, urgent assessment or specialist therapy must still be able to obtain it. “The goal is not to replace dermatologists, but to make their expertise reach much further,” she says.
A remote consultation  needs to connect with treatment and follow-up. Advice alone cannot resolve the practical difficulties of obtaining medicines or reaching a referral centre.
What progress should look like
In 2025, the World Health Assembly recognised skin diseases as a global public-health priority. The next step is translating that recognition into national funding and delivery plans.

Prof Bhat’s priorities include an adequate health budget and insurance coverage for dermatological medicines such as biologics and for procedures. He also calls for better training of dermatology residents and dermatology nursing as a separate speciality within nursing education. These proposals bring together workforce development, treatment affordability and rural services, addressing several barriers to appropriate dermatological care.

Measuring progress will require listening more closely to patients. Dr. Freeman acknowledges that the Observatory relied on national leaders and health-system informants, rather than patients directly. Future work should examine waiting times, travel, affordability and diagnostic delays, alongside outcomes and quality of life.

Her planned next phase will examine selected countries more closely to understand where clinicians choose to train and practise, what retains them in underserved areas and which models improve access in different settings. “Five years from now, success should not simply mean there are more dermatologists,” she says. “It should mean that where someone lives is less predictive of whether they can get appropriate care for their skin disease.”
For India, that would mean earlier recognition, appropriate treatment and dependable referral, with fewer patients left to navigate the gaps themselves.
(Dr. Monisha Madhumita is assistant professor, department of dermatology, Saveetha Medical College and Hospitals, Chennai. mail.monisha.m@gmail.com)

title: T.N. achieves target of National AIDS Control Programme-Phase V: Health Minister

content.value: Tamil Nadu has achieved the National AIDS Control Programme-Phase V (NACP-V) target of 95-95-95 during 2026-27 under which 95% of people living with HIV know their status, 95% of those diagnosed are on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and 95% of those receiving treatment achieve viral suppression, Health Minister K.G. Arunraj said on Monday.

Officials said the State achieved the target in September this year. The Minister, while participating in an event on a State-level intensified IEC campaign on HIV/AIDS, said the prevalence of HIV/AIDS was down by half in the State; it has dropped from 0.40% in 2010 to 0.19% in 2023 as a result of sustained and intensive awareness efforts by the State government and NGOs.

The aim, he said, was to increase awareness and achieve a HIV/AIDS-free Tamil Nadu by 2030. Currently, 1,63,151 people are under treatment in the State, he added. He said a total of 311 integrated counselling and testing centres (ICTC) functioned in the State with funding support from the National AIDS Control Organisation, while 403 ICTCs functioned through financial assistance from the National Health Mission. A total of 2,656 testing facilities functioned at primary health centres and government hospitals, a press release said.
Free HIV testing

Free testing for HIV, prevention, and treatment services are provided through ART centres in 58 government health facilities, including government medical college hospitals, district headquarters hospitals, and government hospitals, and 28 ART centres in private medical colleges hospitals and 172 linked ART centres. As many as 104 NGOs and social organisations have been working to bring about behavioural changes among high risk groups in the State. This includes sex workers, men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, transpersons, heavy vehicle drivers, and migrants, he added.

The Minister said eliminating mother-to-child transmission of three infections — HIV, Syphilis, and Hepatitis B — was another key priority. Babies born to HIV-positive women were given a prophylactic dose of ART soon after birth to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV, he added.

Taking into consideration the need to provide social protection for children living with HIV/AIDS through nutritious food, uninterrupted education, and continuous treatment, the State government enhanced the monthly financial assistance provided to children affected by HIV/AIDS.

The revised monthly assistance was ₹3,000 for children living with HIV who have lost both parents, ₹2,000 for children who have lost one parent, ₹1,500 for children who live with their parents, and ₹1,500 for children who have lost both parents to HIV/AIDS but are not infected. An additional ₹1.21 crore has been allocated for this scheme and the enhanced assistance will benefit children from November onward, the Minister said.

He said the intensified awareness campaign on HIV/AIDS must reach every section of the society. Through the Tamil Nadu State AIDS Control Society (TANSACS), Red Ribbon Clubs have been set up in 2,329 colleges to create awareness among students about HIV/AIDS, sexually transmitted infections, and behavioural change. To create awareness on HIV/AIDS prevention among adolescents, life skills education training is being imparted to students studying in classes VIII, IX, and XI in 9,830 schools through the State Council of Educational Research and Training, Dr. Arunraj added.
Health Secretary Darez Ahamed and Project Director of TANSACS R. Seethalakshmi were present.

title: Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection) Bill to focus on protection of rights, dignity of elderly

content.value: The Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection) Bill, 2026, that will be tabled in the Assembly on Tuesday aims at promoting healthy and active ageing, registration and regulation of senior citizen care centres, capacity-building for family and caregivers, and protection of rights, dignity, and social security of the elderly.

The Bill underscores the principles of right to dignity, ageing in place and home-based care, safety and social care ecosystem, and senior citizens’ participation in policy making. Thrust is also given to rights such as access care, safe public spaces, digital inclusion, legal aid, reporting of abuse, and access to dignity-preserving products.

The Bill points out that the population of the elderly has been increasing in Keralam. However, modernisation and globalisation had paved the way for nuclear families, adversely affecting the living conditions of the elderly. In order to accommodate their needs, various systems need to be put in place and long-term forward planning is required.
It calls for urgent policy intervention to integrate and standardise home-based health-care services and create a legal framework for their operation.
The government also aims at ensuring that older persons are not marginalised or left unprotected, advocating for their financial security, health care, shelter, and protection of rights.
Protection unit

According to the Bill, the government will set up a State Senior Citizen Protection Unit, besides a District Senior Citizen Protection Forum in each district. A District Senior Citizen Protection Unit will also be formed in each district to assist the District Senior Citizen Protection Forum.

The forum will monitor the policies and schemes of the government implemented through the District Senior Citizen Protection Unit, activities of care centres, mobilise local organisations to carry out activities related to care and protection of the elderly, and take suo motu action on complaints.
The Bill deals with registration of senior citizen care centres in detail.

It requires every home-care service agency that operates or engages caregivers through a digital platform, mobile application, website or other online intermediary to maintain an accurate and updated list of caregivers deployed through it.

Training to caregivers, with phased certification compliance, is another aspect. It proposes that the government establish a ‘Keralam Geriatric Care Certification Framework’ providing progressive certification pathways for caregivers. A ‘State Register of Caregivers’ is also mooted in the Bill.
Other mechanisms proposed include Senior Citizen Cyber Fraud Cell in all cyber police stations and a State reserve fund for protection, care, welfare and social security of the senior citizens.
The Bill also lays down punishment for violation of provisions of the Act and rules and guidelines issued under it.

title: Your cells keep a record of every workout you’ve ever done – and those gains persist even after a break from exercise

content.value: Have you ever taken months off training – maybe due to an injury, a new baby or crushing work deadlines – and come back convinced you were starting from zero?
Research from our team has some good news: At the cellular level, you probably weren’t.
We found that muscle and liver cells store memories fromevery training session in ways that may help improve endurance, control blood sugar levels and even slow weight regain after inactivity.
Use it or lose it? Maybe not

For most of the past century, long before fad diets and fancy workout trends took off, exercise was considered one of the most effective lifestyle changes to lower the risk of heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, several cancers and early death for people of all ages. But people typically understood exercise as something whose beneficial effects fade away over time: You use it or lose it.

When you stop training, your maximum oxygen uptake, muscle gains and insulin sensitivity drift back to where they started, often within weeks. Physical activity guidelines are built on this fact, which is why they emphasise consistency above all else.

Consistency, however, is a luxury that roughly 3 in 4 American adults aren’t able to enjoy. People can experience injuries, illness, pregnancy or jobs that limit their time for or ability to exercise. If adaptation really resets, every time you step into the gym would be as if you’ve never been there before. But that scenario doesn’t match what coaches and returning athletes typically describe: In practice, people who have trained before can get fit again faster than those who haven’t undergone similar training.

In recent years, however, scientists have started challenging the concept of “use it or lose it.” New research hints that your cells might keep a record of your training history so all of your gains are not completely lost.
More than muscle
We areexercise physiologists who study how cells remember exercise. Our lab and others have shown that the body is able to store a form of exercise memory across different organs.

To study how this exercise memory works, our team of researchers use an ON-OFF-ON exercise training protocol in mice, which involves an initial four- to eight-week training period, followed by detraining – a period of no exercise – and a second training bout. This method allows us to examine how cells form a memory of exercise, maintain a record of exercise through detraining, and recall memories of prior training when exposed again to exercise.

Using this strategy, our team found that skeletal muscle memory accelerates muscle growth. Compared to mice with no training history, mice who retrained grew bigger muscles, and the individual muscle fibers inside those muscles grew too. Larger muscle fibers meant that the working cells were themselves getting bigger, rather than the surrounding tissue.

Looking more closely at these muscle cells, we found that retrained muscle is better at matching energy production to demand – meaning, the muscles were better at drawing from energy stores when it’s needed most – and this ability persists without further exercise. This memory held even when the mice ate a high-fat diet, suggesting that prior training can still offer benefits even when diet is working against those gains.
Muscle isn’t the only body part that learns from exercise. Working muscle needs fuel, and the liver supplies it during and after training sessions.

My colleagues and I found that liver cells also store exercise memory and uses it to feed muscle more efficiently. In both mice and people who trained, stopped, then trained again, their livers released higher levels of a family of enzymes called carboxylesterases. These enzymes chop up lipids circulating in the blood, delivering fat in a form that muscle can take up and burn as it grows.
A record that outlives you
Recorded cellular memories of exercise may even be passed down to future generations.

In mice, we found that three to four weeks of maternal and paternal endurance exercise can have a lasting effect on their offspring. Compared to offspring born to sedentary parents, parental exercise granted protection against poor blood sugar levels and excess weight gain for an entire year after birth.

Researchers have hypothesized numerous ways that prenatal exercise may affect offspring. For example, maternal exercise might allow offspring to spend more time developing in the womb or lead parents to producer higher quality milk.
But there remains much to be discovered on how parents influence the health of their children and whether their lifestyle could provide a fitness advantage across generations.
Every cell remembers

Biology has traditionally granted memory to a short list of cells. Neurons store memory in the connections between them. Immune cells store memory so they can recognize pathogens faster and more strongly the next time they encounter them.

Researchers previously considered all other cells to be memoryless; a cell responds to a signal, then returns to baseline without keeping a record of that interaction. But that assumption is now coming apart.

Skin stem cells can keep a record of inflammation, allowing them to heal a new wound faster months later. Human fat cells keep a record of obesity that persists even after substantial weight loss, which may account for why you gain weight faster when switching back to a high-calorie diet – the so-called yo-yo effect.

We propose that every cell in the body remembers exercise, regardless of how little or how much someone trains. The question is how long these records are stored and whether researchers could prolong or expand each cell’s storage capacity. Better understanding of how cells learn and remember exercise, where they store memories and how those memories are preserved could help improve exercise guidelines for those who cannot exercise for prolonged or consistent periods of time.

To be clear, none of these findings are evidence for skipping the gym; nothing in our data suggests the effects of past training can substitute for present training. But there is hope that the work you put into getting in shape isn’t completely lost over time.
Somewhere, deep in your cells, there is a record waiting to be replayed the next time you lace up your running shoes, pick up a pair of dumbbells or want to fulfill a New Year’s resolution.
Diego Hernandez-Saavedra, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Yi-Heng (Hank) Huang, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

title: Indian researcher recalls lifechanging mentorship of late Nobel laureate Ada Yonath

content.value: In science, some discoveries change the way we understand life. Others change the lives of the people who make them. For Tanaya Bose, her years in the laboratory of late Nobel laureate Ada Yonath were marked by both. Yonath passed away on August 31, 2026 at 87.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)

Yonath, the Israeli structural biologist who shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studies of the structure and function of the ribosome, is known for helping unravel one of biology’s most fundamental molecular machines. But for Dr. Bose, now a scientist at the CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Biology in Kolkata, the lasting influence of Yonath lies as much in her approach to mentorship as in her scientific achievements.

Over seven years, from November 2016 to September 2023, Dr. Bose witnessed a scientist who was willing to take risks on young researchers, give them difficult problems to solve, and, perhaps most unusually, step aside to let them receive recognition for their work.
Join THEdge LinkedIn group
“She was not afraid of giving away the spotlight,” Dr. Bose recalled. “In fact, she seemed to believe that the spotlight was meant to be passed on.”

It is a lesson Dr. Bose hopes to carry into her own laboratory. Every living cell depends on proteins. They perform a remarkable range of functions, from catalysing biochemical reactions and transmitting signals to providing structural support. Yet proteins cannot be made without ribosomes, the molecular machines that translate genetic instructions carried by messenger RNA into chains of amino acids.

Understanding the ribosome’s structure is therefore central to understanding how life operates at the molecular level. When Yonath began investigating the ribosome in the 1970s, determining its three-dimensional structure presented a formidable scientific challenge. Ribosomes are enormous molecular assemblies, comprising ribosomal RNA and proteins arranged in intricate configurations. Their complexity made it exceptionally difficult to obtain crystals suitable for structural analysis and to interpret the resulting X-ray diffraction data.

At the time, many scientists regarded the task as extraordinarily difficult. Yonath persisted, developing approaches to crystallising ribosomes and investigating their structure using X-ray crystallography. Her work helped make possible the determination of ribosomal structures at atomic resolution, revealing how the ribosome is organised and how it participates in protein synthesis. In 2000, Yonath and other research groups reported landmark structural advances that transformed the field.

These discoveries also had important implications for medicine. Several antibiotics work by targeting bacterial ribosomes, disrupting the production of proteins essential for bacterial survival. Structural knowledge of the ribosome has helped scientists understand how these drugs bind to their targets and how their action can be improved.

In 2009, Yonath shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and Thomas A. Steitz for studies of the structure and function of the ribosome. Her scientific career is a testament to the value of pursuing difficult questions long after their answers appear out of reach. Yet the story of her work also has another dimension: the people she encouraged to ask questions of their own.

When Dr. Bose arrived in Israel in September 2016, she had recently completed her Ph.D. in chemistry. Her husband was a postdoctoral researcher at the Weizmann Institute of Science, and she had followed him there without a clear idea of what she would do next. After several weeks of looking for postdoctoral opportunities, she decided to write to Yonath.

The prospect was intimidating, she said. Dr. Bose was an organic chemist, while Yonath was one of the world’s leading structural biologists. The Nobel laureate’s stature made a reply seem unlikely. Instead, Yonath responded almost immediately and invited her for a meeting.

Dr. Bose remembers barely sleeping the night before the interview. She was anxious about the questions she might be asked and whether she would be able to answer them. But when she entered Yonath’s office in the Kimmelman Building, her first surprise had little to do with science.

“It was a simple room tucked away in one corner of the sixth floor of the Kimmelman Building. I had imagined a grand office befitting a Nobel Prize winner, perhaps surrounded by students and visitors. Instead, there was simply Ada,” she said.

Coming from an organic chemistry background, Dr. Bose was entering an unfamiliar area of structural biology. But Yonath did not treat that difference as a limitation. Instead, Dr. Bose was able to bring a new way of thinking to the problem. Within a couple of months, the work produced a result. Yonath travelled frequently, sometimes moving between continents within days. Yet when she heard about the breakthrough, she appeared at the office the following day, Bose recalled.

“There is a familiar pattern in academia where a young scientist makes an important discovery in a laboratory, but the principal investigator becomes the face of that discovery. Ada did the opposite,” Dr. Bose said. She pushed the young scientist forward. It was the beginning of a scientific relationship in which the young researcher was given not only a demanding problem, but also the freedom to approach it in her own way.

For Dr. Bose, one of the clearest demonstrations of Yonath’s character came at a ribosome meeting in Bordeaux, France. Yonath was scheduled to deliver the keynote lecture. A few days before the conference, she told Dr. Bose that she thought the younger scientist should give the lecture instead.

The organisers refused. The audience had come to hear a Nobel laureate. Yonath could have accepted their decision. Instead, she devised another plan. The lecture was scheduled for 25 minutes. Yonath instructed Dr. Bose to remain ready near the podium. She would begin the keynote, speak for ten minutes and then invite Dr. Bose onto the stage to deliver the remaining 15 minutes.

She was unsure whether Yonath was serious. “But to my surprise, she was”, Dr. Bose said. At the conference, Yonath began the lecture as planned. Ten minutes later, Bose joined her on stage and delivered the rest.
For the audience, it was a keynote address by a Nobel laureate. For Dr. Bose, it was an experience that would shape her understanding of what scientific leadership could mean.

In academia, the principal investigator often becomes the most visible face of research conducted by a laboratory, even when a young scientist has made a substantial contribution. Yonath, Dr. Bose says, repeatedly did the opposite. She put her researchers forward for lectures, scientific meetings, and opportunities to present their own work.

Yonath could easily have occupied the stage herself. Instead, she made space for someone who was still establishing her scientific identity. The gesture was not simply an act of kindness. It was a lesson in independence, confidence and the importance of allowing young scientists to become visible in their own right, Dr. Bose said. “To me, she was the mentor who opened doors I did not even know existed,” she said.
Opening doors beyond the laboratory
Yonath’s support did not end with scientific presentations or research opportunities.

Towards the end of her postdoctoral years, as Dr. Bose began looking for an independent faculty position in India, she encountered another difficult transition: moving from working within an established laboratory to building a research programme of her own.

She had assumed that a Nobel laureate would have little time to concern herself with the career uncertainties of a young researcher. Yonath, once again, proved her wrong. She reached out to members of the Indian scientific community on Dr. Bose’s behalf, contacting senior professors who had been her longstanding friends as well as younger principal investigators who had only recently established their laboratories. She did more than recommend Dr. Bose. She sought advice, connected her with scientists who could guide her, and helped her navigate the unfamiliar process of applying for faculty positions. For Dr. Bose, the significance of this support lay in the effort behind it. Yonath was lending not only her time but also her reputation and personal relationships to help a younger colleague find her footing.

“A mentor’s greatest achievement is not always the discovery made in their laboratory. Sometimes it is the scientist who leaves the laboratory more confident, more independent and more visible than when they arrived. That is what Ada did for me,” Dr. Bose said.

Today, as a scientist leading her own research group, Dr. Bose often reflects on the example Yonath set. She cannot repay what her mentor did for her, she says, but she can extend the same generosity to the young scientists who will one day enter her laboratory. That, perhaps, is how mentorship becomes a lasting scientific legacy: not merely through the transfer of knowledge from one generation to another, but through the willingness of each generation to make the path easier for the next.

Dr. Bose’s memories of Yonath bring into focus a dimension of scientific achievement that is less easily measured than publications, discoveries or awards. Yonath’s determination helped open a window into the molecular machinery responsible for protein synthesis. Her work contributed to a deeper understanding of how antibiotics interact with bacterial ribosomes, advancing a field with important implications for medicine.

But her influence on Dr. Bose demonstrates another way a scientist can shape the future: by recognising potential in someone whose background differs from her own, giving that person the freedom to think independently, and ensuring that the credit for scientific work reaches the people who have done it.

For Dr. Bose, the memories remain vivid: the anxious young chemist waiting outside a Nobel laureate’s office; the difficult research problem that became an opportunity to think differently; the unexpected invitation to share a keynote stage in Bordeaux; and the personal effort Yonath made to help her find an independent position in India.
To the world, Yonath is a Nobel laureate whose research transformed structural biology. To Dr. Bose, she is also the mentor who opened doors she had not known existed.

The measure of that mentorship may ultimately be found in what Dr. Bose does next. As she builds her own research group, she hopes to create the same space for young scientists to explore unfamiliar questions, develop confidence, and receive recognition for their work. It is a way of honouring Yonath that requires no grand gesture: only the decision, made repeatedly, to help another scientist move forward. And so the spotlight passes on.
(Nibedita Sen is an independent journalist specialising in defence, with over 15 years of experience covering diverse topics like rural India, healthcare, education, and women’s issues.)

title: Why science’s contract with society needs citizens as research partners

content.value: For hundreds of years, science has operated with a social contract: science develops knowledge that improves the human condition and expands the range of what is possible while society provides public funds, infrastructure, and institutional support. Sustained investments in research have paid dividends to society, in the form of inventions and discoveries, new technologies, and more innovation in general.

Today, this contract is being strained. Governments are increasingly demanding measurable returns from public investments in research while public trust in institutions is reducing. As a result, science can no longer afford to remain an activity conducted largely for society but without society. The next phase of scientific progress must involve citizens as beneficiaries and taxpayers as well as as partners in deciding which questions science should address and how scientific knowledge should be used.
Patrons of science

Curiosity-driven research often produces unexpected discoveries that eventually transform society. Yet governments, as major patrons of science, are increasingly asserting their right to determine where research money should go. There are legitimate reasons for this. Governments are obligated to resolve national priorities because public resources are finite. But governments misstep when their policy-driven management becomes intrusive.

When funding decisions are mainly influenced by short-term political priorities or economic returns, research areas that are not easily measurable, such as parts of the social sciences, humanities, climate research, and fundamental science, become vulnerable to being seen — unjustifiably — as producing too little bang for the buck. Yes, science must serve society, but science also works better when it retains the intellectual freedom required to challenge prevailing assumptions and explore questions whose value may not be immediately apparent.

Governments, as the patrons, are entitled to establish broad priorities and expectations, but they should not use science policy as an excuse to politically micromanage research. But the answer is also not to isolate science further from society. Instead, the answer is in the middle: scientists must build a broader constituency for science by bringing society into the research process.
To achieve this, scientists need compelling narratives about why research matters, and allies across communities, civil society, industry, education, and public institutions.
What citizens know

Inviting citizens into research does not mean replacing scientific expertise with popular opinion. A scientist trained in epidemiology knows considerably more about disease transmission than the average citizen. A climate scientist understands atmospheric processes in ways that a farmer may not. However, the reverse is also true. A farmer may possess knowledge about changing soil behaviour and crop resilience that a scientist in a laboratory may not. A forest-dwelling community may possess detailed knowledge of medicinal plants, forests, and biodiversity that is absent in formal databases.

Scientific knowledge and community knowledge are different — and they can be complementary. The challenge is to bring them together. This is particularly relevant to a country like India, which is one of the world’s most biologically and culturally diverse countries. Indeed, India is too geographically vast and ecologically diverse for professional scientists alone to be able to understand every landscape by themselves. A network of citizens can provide observations across locations and seasons that conventional research is not designed to capture. For instance, a school student studying a butterfly or a birdwatcher recording a migratory species can contribute to ecological knowledge. Citizen science can transform the relationship between the public and scientific institutions.

India’s long tradition of community-based conservation reveals another aspect of this argument. Sacred groves, community forests, germplasm conservation, traditional systems of resource management, and so on demonstrate that local communities have often developed sophisticated ways to understand and protect ecosystems. One of the key success metrics in research is observation, which many local communities excel at. So instead of merely entering a village to collect traditional knowledge and leaving with a publication, researchers can, and should, establish long-term partnerships with communities. Local knowledge bearers should participate in framing research questions, identifying species, help interpret the findings, and decide how knowledge is documented and used.
Rebuilding trust

Under the European Union’s Horizon 2020 programme, citizens from numerous countries participated in developing research priorities. Here, while expert-led foresight exercises tended to emphasise technological advancement, citizens placed greater emphasis on strong communities, health and well-being, education, and local economies. A similar approach in India could have significant implications. Research priorities relating to groundwater, urban pollution, agricultural resilience, coastal erosion, public health, biodiversity, nutrition or climate adaptation, for example, can be developed through structured dialogue among scientists, policymakers, and the most affected communities.

Another compelling reason for citizen participation is trust. Specifically, public trust in governments and institutions is becoming increasingly fragile. Scientists and universities are sometimes portrayed as distant elites disconnected from the concerns of ordinary people. At the same time, misinformation spreads rapidly through social media and emotional narratives can compete successfully with carefully established scientific evidence. The instinctive response is often to communicate more science. But perhaps the deeper problem is a lack of participation and ownership.

People are more likely to support a process when they believe their voices have been heard. They may not agree with every conclusion but they are more likely to accept decisions when the reasoning is transparent and their concerns have been seriously considered. This is particularly important for contentious issues such as climate change, vaccination, genetic modification, artificial intelligence, and biotechnologies. Science cannot promise that every citizen will agree with every scientific conclusion — nor should it. But it can promise a fair opportunity to question, participate, deliberate, and understand.
Humility from scientists

At present, many researchers are trained to design experiments, analyse data, and publish papers but not necessarily to build long-term relationships with communities. That must change. Community engagement should be integrated into research training. Academic recognition should extend beyond publications and citations to include meaningful societal engagement and co-produced research. Funding agencies should also encourage researchers to explain, wherever appropriate, how communities will participate in setting priorities, conducting research, interpreting results and disseminating findings.

To be sure, not every laboratory experiment requires citizen participation. The objective is also not to impose participation mechanically. Public involvement should instead become the default expectation for research with significant societal implications, with researchers explaining why participation is inappropriate when it is not used. Should an emerging technology be deployed rapidly or cautiously? How much privacy should society sacrifice for technological convenience? How should the benefits and risks of artificial intelligence be distributed? How should climate-transition costs be shared? Such questions can benefit enormously from community engagement.

This transformation also requires some humility from scientists. Scientists must learn to listen, be willing to hear uncomfortable questions, acknowledge uncertainties, and recognise the values embedded in their own recommendations. At the same time, the public must recognise that scientific evidence cannot always provide simple answers to complex social questions.
Biju Dharmapalan is  the dean, Academic Affairs, Garden City University, Bengaluru,  and an adjunct faculty member at the National Institute of Advanced Studies, Bengaluru.

title: IISc study says strong magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to grow beyond the Chandrasekhar limit

content.value: Simulations by researchers of Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and their collaborators show that strong internal magnetic fields could allow some white dwarfs to grow to substantially higher masses than determined by the Chandrasekhar limit.

When a dying star runs out of fuel and sheds its outer layers, its remaining core can become an approximately Earth-sized, extremely dense stellar remnant called a “white dwarf”. For a white dwarf that is not strongly rotating or magnetised, there is a well-known upper mass limit of about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun, known as the “Chandrasekhar limit”.
In one of their simulations, the researchers found that a magnetised carbon-oxygen white dwarf can reach about 2.4 times the mass of the Sun – well above the limit.

“The idea started in 2011, when a summer student came to me and I gave him a problem quite casually: to check whether the Chandrasekhar limit can be violated by a magnetic field,” said Banibrata Mukhopadhyay, professor at the Department of Physics and corresponding author of the study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
Predicted for decades

The IISc said that theorists have predicted the possibility of such “super-Chandrasekhar” white dwarfs for decades. Observations of unusually over-luminous Type Ia supernovae have added support, hinting at the possibility of progenitor white dwarfs having masses, and the mass limit as high as 2.8 times the solar mass.

“The important question was not simply whether a super-Chandrasekhar white dwarf is possible, but whether a star can actually evolve into one. Our simulations allowed us to follow that evolutionary pathway from the main-sequence star to the white dwarf, and show that under certain conditions, such a pathway is possible,” said Zenia Zuraiq, first author of the study and PhD student at the Department of Physics.
How they tracked

To track this evolution, the team modified STARS, a computer code developed at the University of Cambridge to model how stars evolve. They incorporated magnetic field effects and white dwarf cooling, which allowed them to follow magnetised stars from the main sequence – the long phase when stars generate energy by fusing hydrogen – through their later evolution into white dwarfs. Then, they modelled a binary system in which the white dwarf gains additional matter from a companion star.

The simulations showed that a magnetic field that is initially too weak can become increasingly important as the white dwarf gains mass. As matter accumulates, the white dwarf becomes denser and contracts, strengthening its magnetic field. The stronger field provides additional pressure inside the star, helping it withstand its own immense gravity and supporting more mass. This changes the usual relationship between the white dwarf’s mass and size with a new limit(s) of mass, depending on the exact physics of magnetic fields.

title: Berlin to BITS Pilani: How Nobel-winning optogenetics connects to parasite research in Hyderabad

content.value: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”, has brought renewed attention to using light to investigate fundamental biological processes. These include memory formation, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders, as well as processes involved in infectious disease.
Editorial | Let there be light: On the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology/Medicine

For Nishith Gupta, professor of Biological Sciences at BITS Pilani, Hyderabad, and founder of the Intracellular Parasite Education and Research Labs (iPEARL), the recognition has a personal significance in his own scientific journey.

Mr. Gupta’s decades-long collaboration with Hegemann at Humboldt University of Berlin, where Hegemanna is Hertie Senior Professor of Neuroscience, helped extend optogenetic approaches beyond neuroscience into his study of Toxoplasma gondii, an intracellular parasite that infects humans, mammals, and birds.
Interactive Guide | Nobel Prize 2026
Professor of Biological Sciences at BITS Pilani-Hyderabad Campus, Nishith Gupta with Peter Hegemann, 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine laureate.
Optogenetics enables scientists to control selected cells or biological processes using light-sensitive proteins.

The Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine stated: “It all began with Peter Hegemann’s curiosity. He wondered how Chlamydomonas, a single-celled alga, is able to swim towards a light source. In the early 2000s, he and Georg Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, an algal protein with unique properties, found on the surface of the cell. When it is illuminated by blue light, a channel opens through the protein. Charged ions then flow into the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that regardless of which cell they put the protein in, those cells became light sensitive.” In 2005, Deisseroth showed that introducing channelrhodopsin into rat neurons allowed blue light to trigger nerve signals. In 2007, he showed light-based control in mice.
A researcher at iPEARL, BITS Pilani-Hyderabad Campus with Peter Hegemann, 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine laureate.

In contrast, Mr. Gupta, Mr. Hegemann and others used light-regulated enzyme adenylate cyclase, which converts adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy of a living cell, to produce cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate (cAMP). This molecule acts as messengers, helping transmit signals within cells.

Put simply, the researchers showed that light controls the enzyme, the enzyme produces cAMP, and cAMP helps regulate what happens inside the parasite (Toxoplasma gondii): how it enters cells, moves, and exits cells. This landmark study was published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry in 2013.

While Mr. Deisseroth, Mr. Hegemann, and Mr. Nagel’s optogenetics “solves one of humanity’s great mysteries, how our incredible brain works”, Mr. Gupta, Mr. Hegemann and others’ found light-regulated signalling to investigate parasite’s lifestyle, and infection.
A researcher at iPEARL, BITS Pilani-Hyderabad Campus with Peter Hegemann, 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine laureate.

Mr. Gupta says that working alongside Hegemann in Berlin, with their laboratories in neighbouring departments, was an important part of this scientific journey. Joint funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) supported their collaboration.

After Mr. Gupta relocated to India, Mr. Hegemann continued to support his research through Mr. Gupta’s Wellcome Trust–DBT Senior Fellowship project at BITS Pilani. Researchers from his team continued to visit Hegemann’s group in Berlin.
Peter Hegemann, 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine laureate.

For Mr. Gupta, the Nobel Prize awarded to Mr. Hegemann and his fellow laureates underscores the far-reaching consequences of fundamental research. A protein that evolved to help an alga sense light has become a tool for probing the brain, investigating infection and understanding how cells function. He says the broader lesson is that technologies developed to answer one biological question can open entirely new avenues of research.
“Light has become more than a means of observation; it is a way to intervene, test, and uncover cause-and-effect relationships,” Mr. Gupta says.

title: Warming Himalayas demand a rethink on development

content.value: For decades, the fight for sustainable, climate-resilient, hazard-averse development in the Indian Himalayan Region (IHR) has gone unheeded, and the region is witnessing frequent and severe climate-induced disasters.

The catastrophic Nepal floods of August 26 are a warning that the ‘global natural commons’, stretching from the Hindu Kush and Karakoram to the Himalayas, are in an existential crisis. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) have warned that warming in the high mountains of Asia is occurring at 0.3°C per decade, nearly twice the global average, “leading to glacier retreat, decreasing in turn the stability of mountain slopes and the integrity of infrastructure, threatening water security, livelihoods, ecosystems, and increasing disaster risk.”

Reports released on March 21, 2026, by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) found that ice-loss rates across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) have doubled since 2000. “We are trying to navigate a rapidly changing future with an incomplete map,” said one of the authors of the report. Warming is not uniform across this 3,500-kilometre range. According to the Journal of Earth System Science, the western Himalaya is warming consistently faster than the central and eastern stretches, with night-time minimum and winter temperatures rising at the most extreme rates.

Cryosphere crisis: glaciers, water scarcity, and a race to adapt in the Himalaya
90% of Himalayas face year-long drought at 3 degrees global warming: study
Nepal is paying the price for a crisis it did not create. As it produces roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, it is right to demand compensation for loss and damage.
Rising temperatures, effect on glaciers

Rising atmospheric temperatures shift the balance between winter snow accumulation and summer melt, causing glaciers to retreat and thin steadily. Ice that once had a thermal profile of −6°C to −20°C now has temperatures closer to −2°C, making it far more susceptible to melting.

Meltwater pools atop glaciers in supraglacial lakes and carves vertical shafts called moulins, plunging hundreds of metres through the ice to the bedrock, where it forms a pressurised liquid layer between the rock and ice. This layer lubricates the glacier, allowing it to slide downslope faster, while the resulting subglacial (between the glacier and bedrock) and englacial (within the glacier) water channels generate mechanical forces intense enough to fracture the ice.

In high-altitude environments such as the Himalayas, permafrost — ground or rock that remains at or below 0°C — acts as geological cement, holding steep rock walls together by filling fractures, joints and pores with solid ice. As temperatures rise, permafrost melts into water, triggering rock avalanches, landslides and debris flows that threaten downstream valleys.

In Nepal, a shaking equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 seismic event was recorded by the United States Geological Survey (USGS) on August 26, when a 600-metre-wide section of ice and rock broke away from the northern flank of Langtang Himal at an elevation of 5,600 m and fell 1.2 km into the valley below. Researchers from the British Antarctic Survey recorded unusually high ground temperatures two days before the collapse, using sensors located 10 km from the site.

This mass of ice and rock landed in the Lhende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, damming it. When the dam broke, it unleashed a flash flood of concrete-like mud and debris — “an inland tsunami” travelling 170 km down the Bhote Koshi Valley into central Nepal. This was no isolated event. Such collapses can happen anywhere in these mountains and warming makes them more likely.
What can be done

There is no technology to prevent such collapses. The only real option is to mitigate their impact on downstream communities, which requires regional cooperation and a shared system for real-time data exchange. High-altitude satellite and drone surveillance is urgently needed to detect early signs of cliff fracturing, permafrost thaw and glacial instability. Real-time acoustic and hydrological sensors along glacier-fed rivers could detect sudden subsurface movements or flash surges and alert downstream communities immediately. Glacial lakes need continuous monitoring and, where feasible, engineered drainage.

River flood zoning must account for valley slope. Steeper slopes concentrate damage vertically, requiring infrastructure to be located much higher above the riverbed, while gentler slopes spread destruction horizontally, demanding an entirely different zoning approach.

Hydropower policy needs to be rethought, with a firm ban on construction above a defined elevation. The Avay Shukla Committee (Court on Its Own Motion vs State of Himachal Pradesh and Others) and the Ravi Chopra Committee both recommended restricting major hydropower projects or subjecting construction activities above 2,200 metres to detailed expert review.

The proposed Chenab-Beas river-linking project — an 8.7-km tunnel through the steep slopes of the Pir Panjal Range in Lahaul and Spiti district, near Koksar village in Himachal Pradesh, at an elevation of 3,140 metres (10,300 feet) — needs serious rethinking. The rationale for diverting more water from the western rivers of the Indus system may appear logical on paper, but the project is located in a fragile Himalayan ecosystem, and its likely environmental impacts make it eminently avoidable.

Every development activity in the IHR must be evaluated in light of the changing geological realities of the Himalayas. There should be a moratorium on all development projects until each is rigorously reassessed for its environmental impact, hazard-averseness and climate resilience.
Archana Vaidya is an advocate and the founder of the Forum for Environment Legal Policy Research (FELPR)

title: Restrictions on firecrackers: Supreme Court urges balance between religious sentiments and public health

content.value: The Supreme Court on Monday (October 12, 2026) highlighted the need to balance religious sentiments with public health concerns while considering restrictions on firecrackers in the national capital and neighbouring regions.

“We will not hurt religious sentiments but at the same time, people should themselves come forward and opt for it. The whole exercise should involve a balancing approach,” Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, heading a three-judge Bench, said.
During the hearing, Justice Joymalya Bagchi questioned the religious basis for bursting firecrackers.
Health risks

Senior advocate Aparajita Singh, who is the amicus curiae in the case, expounded on the health risks associated with air pollution, particularly for children, senior citizens, and those suffering from health vulnerabilities. Ms. Singh suggested that the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), the statutory body responsible for air quality management in the region, should be asked to turn its attention to the medical concerns related to air pollution.

The Bench, however, cautioned against imposing restrictions that could prove difficult to enforce on the ground. “We have to make people wiser, bring awareness, and tell them which firecrackers are harmful and which are less harmful,” the CJI said.
He suggested promoting a culture centred on traditional practices, such as lighting lamps and using sparklers, along with restrictions on the availability of more harmful cracker varieties.
The matter will be heard next on October 15.

title: Drought report: On southwest monsoon, drought in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh

content.value: A substantial drought seems to be inflicting Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh after the crucial southwest monsoon concluded with a significant deficiency in the most-affected regions. The national drought framework combines agricultural and hydrological indicators and ground-truthing studies, including before a distressed State can access additional support from the NDRF. In June-September, Karnataka reportedly suffered a close to 35% rainfall deficit. The government has since declared 217 of 240 taluks to be drought-hit with extensive damage to red gram, maize, cotton, and sugarcane cultivation. Andhra Pradesh experienced a shortfall of 53% in June-August and 388 of 688 mandals have been declared drought-hit. Horticulture crops over nearly 18,000 hectares are now at risk. Karnataka has also petitioned the Centre for ₹11,000 crore from the NDRF along with higher input subsidies. Andhra Pradesh has set aside ₹190 crore to protect horticultural crops and has directed drinking water conservation. The summer monsoon had its poorest showing since 2015 this year. There have been warnings of the effects of the strengthening El Niño, although an attribution study elucidating the strength of causal relationships in the present instance is pending.

In a previous era, drought declarations were beset by subjective claims, sometimes exaggerated to maximise state support. Since 2009, however, the Manual for Drought Management and updates to it and Finance Commission decisions have tightened the process. While States still have some incentives to expand their declarations, the Centre has also resisted releasing NDRF assistance before, including with Karnataka in 2024, while also increasing their own relief obligations. The Centre must desist from frustrating States and release support as soon as the findings of the Inter-Ministerial Central Team have been publicly verified. In addition to mitigating indebtedness among farmers and expanding access to relief beyond land ownership, the States also need more discipline vis-à-vis storing water and rationalising consumption. Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka have offered incentives and advisories, including to adopt micro-irrigation and to cultivate less water-intensive crops, but have not imposed binding limits. The Centre may also consider incentives to resist drought, even in the face of a deficient monsoon, because the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has been warning of expanding drought-like conditions in South Asia, and broadening agricultural insurance. It must certainly not use the prospect of the more protracted, more imprudent river-interlinking project as an excuse to overlook pro-resilience aims such as sustainably using groundwater and choosing crops based on local rainfall and aquifers and availability of income support.

title: OpenAI film 'Artificial' turns lens on creators of 'new world,’ Andrew Garfield says

content.value: Curiosity and fear powered actor Andrew Garfield’s performance in Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI movie “Artificial”, which premiered at the London Film ​Festival on Sunday.

Garfield plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in the film, which unfolds over ‌two decades and chronicles the conception and growth of the artificial ​intelligence company behind ChatGPT and Altman’s dramatic firing and rehiring ⁠in 2023.

“I think the reason I was drawn to it was just pure curiosity and fear and really trying to understand as deeply as possible the people ‌who are ushering us into this next phase of the world,” said Garfield.

“There’s a sense of courage and imagination and ‌resilience these people at the top of these companies must have, ‌the ability ⁠to withstand so much criticism and such a microscopic lens on ⁠them as people. And it’s important that we do that because we need to know who’s in power and who’s creating our new world,” he said.
Garfield, who also starred ​in 2010’s Facebook origin film “The ‌Social Network”, did not contact or meet with Altman in preparation for the role.

“I don’t know Sam and I have a lot of compassion for a person who’s my age, almost, and there’s a movie ‌being made about him,” Garfield said. “It’s not him, but it’s an ​idea of what this story is and his part in it.”
OpenAI did not respond to a Reuters request for ⁠comment. In an interview with Vanity Fair, Altman said he was not expecting an “accurate depiction”.

With a screenplay by Emmy-winning “Saturday Night Live” writer Simon Rich, “Artificial” stars Russian Oscar-nominee ‌Yura Borisov as OpenAI co-founder and former chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, who left the company after his involvement in Altman’s brief ouster. It follows the ethical differences and conflict over AI safety between Altman and Sutskever, who trained under Geoffrey Hinton, known as the “Godfather of AI”, portrayed in the film by Mark Rylance.

The film also stars Ike Barinholtz as Tesla CEO Elon ‌Musk. Monica Barbaro plays Mira Murati, OpenAI’s former technology chief. It was shot in 2025 ​and comes at a time of mounting concerns triggered by recent incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic that have sparked fears rogue ⁠AI systems may slip beyond human control.

“It’s so fascinating making a film like ⁠this when the topic is so relevant right now,” said Barbaro. “We’d be on set, watching two people argue with each other on ‌Twitter, who we were portraying in this movie. It was really wild to have that experience. It’s exciting and it’s also really daunting ​because you want to be truthful, but the truth seems to change every month.”

title: Startups are betting on AI to predict the future

content.value: Several startups are betting that they can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to make better forecasts than even the most specialised experts when it comes to topics as varied as stock market movements, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, or how a Shakira song will perform on music charts.
By 2030, "we're going to feel that what we were doing for our decision-making was complete Stone Age thinking," Dan Schwarz, cofounder of the forecasting company FutureSearch, said.

AI forecasting models are already on par with the best "superforecasters,” or gifted individuals whose estimates are markedly superior to those of ordinary people, thanks to troves of data acquired from both public and private sources.
In early September, two AI models made history when they took the top spots in the Metaculus Cup, a competition among prediction champions, both human and nonhuman.
FutureSearch's in-house human wizard, superforecaster Tom Liptay, is aware that "he's not secure in his job" in the medium term, Schwarz said. "He knows that these things are going to surpass him."
Theo Summer, who cofounded Preseen with Veniamin Veselovsky, used AI tools to turn $35 into $1.9 million in just seven months on the American prediction-making site Kalshi.

The idea is not to guarantee a result but to define a probability of occurrence, with the ability to cross-check assumptions related to several interconnected events; for example, changes in the price of oil and the war in the Middle East.
"Right now, the quickest buyers are normally the hedge funds, just because if they think they can make money off something, they can move pretty fast," Veselovsky said.
Algorithms have shaped Wall Street for more than a decade, but the rise of AI forecasting is likely to further increase the automation of financial markets.

"I think it's probably already having a small impact because we already have customers who use it when making trading decisions," said Toby Shevlane, the cofounder of another forecasting startup called Mantic.
Now-famous prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket, which are used by millions of Americans, are also becoming inundated by AI use.

It might soon be too late for retail investors, who don't have access to expensive AI tools, to profit on those types of consumer-oriented trading sites because "they will soon just be dominated by AI forecasting systems," Veselovsky said.
The most advanced models no longer just predict events, either.
They can also formulate their own questions about the future and then assign probabilities based on the different possible outcomes, Shevlane said.

Their sphere of influence is beginning to extend beyond finance, as well, with potential applications in government policy, corporate decision-making, scientific research, and insurance risk assessments.
Mantic provides a large American company with likely scenarios of regulatory developments in its sector and has also worked for the British government.
Companies "are interested in risks and how to monitor them," Shevlane said.
Meanwhile, other customers might be more interested in medical research, particularly to help make decisions around which types of treatments would be best to fund, Schwarz said.
Widespread access to these types of tools can come with costs, though.
"I think that good can be derived from this," Veselovsky said, but "I'm also a little bit scared because, you know, maybe Russia or China has better systems."

title: Slew of events planned in memory of K.V. Thiruvengadam in centenary year

content.value: A year-long celebration of renowned clinician, teacher, and humanitarian, the late K.V. Thiruvengadam will kick off in his centenary year on Sunday (October 11, 2026). The celebrations, in memory of Prof. Thiruvengadam’s extraordinary impact on medicine both in Chennai and beyond, will focus on restoring the art of listening to the patient, examining at the bedside, thinking before ordering a test, and finally, and dwelling on the fundamental question of what it means to be a good physician in an age of extraordinary technology.

K. Vardachari Thiruvengadam, fondly known as KVT, was born in 1926. He graduated from Government Stanley Medical College in 1950 and taught for 31 years both at his alma mater and at Madras Medical College, and subsequently at private institutions. His core areas of specialty were chest medicine, allergies and infectious diseases. His career coincided with a period when medicine was rapidly expanding, but his students remember that he did not teach bedside examination as a ceremonial ritual — he taught it as a way of thinking, listening to the patient, and asking the right questions.

Prof. KVT was a scientist as well as a clinician. He received formal training in chest diseases in the U.K., under the Colombo Plan. He published nearly 100 papers in national and international journals. Among the many areas of his research were chikungunya fever, neurological complications following influenza and amoebiasis. He also investigated traditional medicines in allergic lung and skin diseases. He worked for decades in the government system, among the poorest in society, and believed that government service could achieve extraordinary things when doctors had the willingness to serve. For him, medicine was a social responsibility.
Enduring legacy

Prof. KVT’s awards and recognitions were numerous, and included the Padma Shri in 1981 and the Dr. B.C. Roy Award for Eminent Medical Teacher, alongside multiple other distinctions. But perhaps the most enduring aspect of his legacy is in the number of students who remember him and his teachings and went on to become teachers and leaders themselves, committing to his principle of what you learn and experience must be passed on to the next generation.

The centenary year celebration’s objective is not merely to celebrate him, but to translate his philosophy into medical education. The commemoration is not an argument against technology, but an argument against technology without context, and for the need for human clinical reasoning to be paramount.

The proposed celebration aims to take to medical students and postgraduate doctors the importance of history-taking, clinical examination, clinical reasoning and their role not only in diagnosis and management, but also in medical research.

On October 31, the third Prof. K.V. Thiruvengadam Memorial Oration will be delivered at Sree Balaji Medical College and Hospital, by S.R. Chandra, on ‘The Patient Speaks, the Doctor Thinks and the Research Begins’, alongside a national conference on movement disorders.
For details, contact Dr. Ramachandran at 9443238315 or Dr. Basheer at 9840217486.

title: Pope Leo to undergo surgery for growth on lung

content.value: Pope Leo said on Sunday (October 12, 2026) that ⁠doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery ‌this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff’s tenure.
Leo told pilgrims ‌in St. Peter’s Square for his weekly Sunday ‌prayer ⁠that the growth was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.
“Recently, ⁠during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung,” said the pontiff. “It was detected at a very early stage and ​is well contained.”
“The doctors ‌believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” he said. “The operation is already scheduled for ‌the next few days.”

A nodule on the lung is ​a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than ⁠5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors.
Leo, elected pope by the ‌world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to previously have had health issues.
The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years.
The Vatican press ‌office said Leo’s recovery from surgery was expected to take about ​a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope’s health.
Leo keeps a ⁠busy schedule and is due to make an 11-day tour of ⁠Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6-17.
Before mentioning his health issue in his address on ‌Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers “for the pastoral visit I will undertake.”

title: U.S. health secretary Kennedy launches new push on vaccine injuries

content.value: U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week launched ​an agency-wide effort to study and document any health problems ⁠reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services said on Thursday.

The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group ‌before taking office, to reshape federal immunization policy. The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and ‌monitored for safety after approval.

The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 ‌compensable injuries ⁠across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a ⁠no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded roughly $5 billion across about 12,300 injury and death claims.

The new moves, which appear to be part ​of Kennedy’s decades-long efforts to sow ‌skepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter US childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunisation rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the ‌US since last year. The effort centers on a National Institutes ​of Health clinic
opened on Monday to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement. Other ⁠measures include a proposal by the Centers for

Medicare & Medicaid Services to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccine Adverse ‌Event Reporting System, or VAERS; a CDC effort to update VAERS; and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.

Kennedy has said U.S. children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which has been echoed by President Donald Trump. Kennedy has long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no ‌evidence of harm.
In his first year heading HHS, he fired all 17 independent expert members of ​the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.

In January, the CDC announced a revamped ⁠childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, ⁠hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.

A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts ‌of the proposed changes, finding that Kennedy and HHS had violated federal law in reshaping the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunisation Practices. The injunction has prevented ​ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunisations often needed for insurance coverage.

title: Of being young at heart: A platform for elderly in Thiruvananthapuram to rediscover life

content.value: Priya cannot remember a time when her mother was not busy. Apart from her work, there were always social engagements to attend, friends to visit or new books to read. But something changed after retirement.

“She seemed to lose some of her sparkle. She became a little inward and moody at times, as though an inertia had taken over. Her outings became less frequent. She no longer went shopping, as everything could be home-delivered. The fact that my father preferred to stay at home further reduced her opportunities to socialise. This transition from a busy, active person to a listless and diffident individual was quite shocking and sad,” she says.

When she opened up to her friends about this, Priya discovered that they had similar stories to share. Parents who had once led full, active lives were now confined to the quiet routines of home. They had not lost their zest for life, but age had caught up with them, sapping their energy and enthusiasm to get out and about.

“Then it struck us that, in a few years, this could be our lives too. Why should we allow the years to steal all the colours from our lives?” says Dimple Mohan, who runs a consultancy service in the city.
Five women

And so, Young at Heart (YaH) was born — a dream that took wings when five women entrepreneurs and working professionals in Thiruvananthapuram came together to explore how they could help their parents rediscover the joy of living and embrace ageing with enthusiasm.

Envisioned as a platform for senior citizens and those in their 50s, YaH hopes to bring people together to rediscover life’s little pleasures — new friendships, new learning experiences, evenings out, and a little fun and frolic. Growing older, the founders believe, should never mean compromising on emotional happiness and mental well-being.

“We all have successful careers, active social lives and wide networks of friends. But living with our parents, we have seen how their personalities and attitudes towards life change as they grow older, even when they are financially secure and have no major worries,” says Ms. Mohan, who is one of YaH’s founder.

“It made us think that, regardless of age, we should be able to embrace life with gusto and live it to the fullest in the company of good friends. YaH is an initiative to help senior citizens and people in their 50s connect, forge friendships, share interests and build a community that helps everyone lead more fulfilling lives. Many have the money and time, but are hesitant to venture out on their own,” she adds
On October 16
A formal launch event of YaH, featuring music and entertainment, is planned in the capital on October 16. The event  will also offer participants an opportunity to meet and get to know one another.

YaH plans to organise regular entertainment and recreational activities, while creating opportunities for like-minded people to discover, share and nurture their talents. Events will be tailored to the interests, hobbies and leisure preferences of those who have registered with the initiative.
The group has also identified areas such as diet and nutrition, physical fitness, digital literacy and financial planning as important components of healthy, active ageing.

“We had several women register with us and we asked them what has been on their bucket list. One wants to learn to speak English fluently so she can converse with her grandchildren abroad. Another has always wanted to design dresses, while someone else simply wants to travel — something she could never manage while working. We hope to facilitate the fulfilment of some of these dreams,” says actor Manju Pillai, who is spearheading the initiative along with Devi Mohan, Sankari Unnithan and Maya Menon.
Younger volunteers
In time, YaH hopes to involve younger volunteers, building bridges between generations. They could take senior citizens to the beach or the movies, or simply spend an afternoon playing chess.

As age-related frailties set in, many older people find themselves increasingly disconnected from the world around them. The resulting isolation can take a toll on their emotional health and leave them vulnerable to depression.
Young at Heart hopes to address this often-overlooked need for socialisation and companionship first and help them embrace life, wholeheartedly.

title: Ruling parties sweep all six seats in by-election, Starlink row, Nobel Prize 2026, and more: The week in 5 charts

content.value: (1) Ruling parties sweep all six seats in by-election

Ruling parties in three States and a Union Territory won all six seats in the by-elections for which results were declared on Friday (October 9, 2026). The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won both Assembly seats in West Bengal and wrested the Nagaon Lok Sabha seat in Assam from the Congress. In Tamil Nadu, Chief Minister Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) won both seats it contested, while the All India NR Congress (AINRC) retained the Thattanchavady Assembly seat in Puducherry.

In Tamil Nadu, TVK candidates K. Maragatham Kumaravel and P. Sathyabama won the Madurantakam and Dharapuram Assembly constituencies, respectively. The victories marked the party’s first electoral test since its surprise victory in the Assembly elections in May, taking its strength in the 234-member House to 109. With five seats vacant, the effective majority mark stands at 115. The TVK’s ally, the Congress, has five seats.

In West Bengal, BJP candidate Shankharavh Sarkar defeated Aam Janata Unnayan Party (AUJP) candidate Golam Nabi Azad, son of party chief Humayun Kabir, by 75,816 votes in Rejinagar. The result marked the first time a non-Muslim candidate had won the constituency in Muslim-majority Murshidabad district. In Nandigram, BJP candidate Hasirani Rath defeated Congress nominee Milan Pradhan by 1,22,753 votes. The seat had been held by Adhikari since 2016.
In Assam, the BJP wrested the Nagaon Lok Sabha constituency from the Congress, which had won the seat in both the 2019 and 2024 general elections.

In Puducherry, AINRC candidate Ashok Anand defeated Congress nominee E. Vinayagam by 8,482 votes in Thattanchavady. The bypoll was necessitated by Chief Minister N. Rangasamy’s resignation from the constituency after he won the Mangalam seat in the April 9 Assembly elections.
(2) Elon Musk alleges ‘oligarch’ interference in Starlink’s India launch

After years of efforts to secure permission to operate its satellite broadband service in India, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has accused “certain oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s launch to protect their monopolies. Mr. Musk made the allegation on X, formerly Twitter, hours after a company executive said she hoped the service would be operational in India by 2027.

Responding to a user demanding Starlink’s launch in India, Mr. Musk said, “Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are … This is a crime against the people of India!”

Although Starlink has obtained a Global Mobile Personal Communications by Satellite (GMPCS) authorisation from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), it is yet to receive the security clearances required to begin operations. The requirements, some of which were amended in May, mandate that SpaceX disable Starlink receivers purchased outside India and terminals sold in India but operated abroad. These conditions are in addition to extensive surveillance requirements applicable to the telecommunications and broadband sectors.
