On Friday (October 9, 2026), Mr. Musk escalated his public spat over Starlink’s entry into India by sarcastically addressing industrialist Mukesh Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani”. He accused Mr. Ambani of seeking to protect a monopoly and questioned whether he would allow Starlink to compete in the Indian market.

The Ministry of Communications had rejected allegations of discriminatory treatment in a statement on Thursday (October 8, 2026). “The Government has put in place a fair and non-discriminatory authorisation framework for all telecommunication services, including satellite communication services,” it said, adding that licences had been granted to three providers of satellite communications based on non-geosynchronous satellite orbits.

Union Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia reiterated the Department of Telecommunications’ position on Friday, saying Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti-backed OneWeb were at the same stage of the licensing process.

Responding to Mr. Musk’s allegations, Mr. Scindia said India did not allow monopolies in any sector and that the DoT remained technology-agnostic. “Our job is to be able to provide the bouquet of services to every single customer. It is for the customer to choose, in a free market, which service he or she prefers, and within that service bouquet, which company’s service he or she prefers,” he said.
(3) Nobel Prize 2026

This year’s Nobel Prizes were announced from Monday, October 5, with the announcement of the laureates in Physiology or Medicine, and concluded on Monday, October 12, with the announcement of the Economics prize.

The Economics Nobel was awarded to Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday (October 12, 2026).
Nobel prize 2026: An interactive guide

The prestigious award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final prize to be announced this year. It carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).

The Economics prize was announced three days after South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday (October 9, 2026). With the announcement of the Economics laureates, the 2026 Nobel season came to a close.

A trio of scientists — Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel — was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries that led to the development of optogenetics, a technique that allows scientists to control specific nerve cells using light. The Nobel Assembly said the laureates’ work enabled neuroscience to move beyond observing correlations and to test how particular neurons and neural circuits are linked to different behaviours and emotions.
Two women were honoured during this year’s Nobel season: Pillay, who won the Peace Prize, and Canadian-Icelandic writer Anne Carson, who received the Nobel Prize in Literature.
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to French scientist Henri Kagan and Japanese scientist Kenso Soai, while the Physics prize went to Belgian physicist Francis Halzen.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Francis Halzen for his contributions to IceCube, a neutrino observatory at the South Pole, and for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.

The laureates will receive a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million). The awards will be presented on December 10, Nobel Day, which marks the death anniversary of Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel. In his will, Nobel stipulated that his estate should be used to fund prizes for those who, during the preceding year, had “conferred the greatest benefit to humankind”.
(4) Trump administration freezes green cards for Microsoft, Indian IT firms

The U.S. on Thursday (October 8, 2026) suspended IT firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme, which allows companies to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers.
The announcement was made by U.S. Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling, with Vice-President J.D. Vance, the head of the U.S. Anti-Fraud Task Force, by his side.

Since taking office, US President Donald Trump has pursued a broad effort to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship. Thursday’s twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs — potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers — while putting some of the country’s top research universities on notice.

Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, or the permanent labor certification process, according to data from the US labor department. Under PERM, which most employment-based ​green cards require, employers must show a foreign hire will not hurt US workers’ wages or jobs.

The company said in a statement that about 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers. In July, the company said it would cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1% of its global workforce.
(5) Almost 75% of buildings in Gaza damaged or destroyed

On Wednesday (October 7, 2026), which marked the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks, Israel carried out new strikes in Gaza killing at least three people. Just four days before, an airstrike on an apartment building in Gaza killed five, including four women. Since October 7, 2023, Israel’s total siege on Gaza has killed around 74,200 Palestinians, with about 60% of the Strip directly under the control of the Israeli military.

A satellite-based analysis by Conflict Ecology at Oregon State University estimates that 2,45,981 buildings, or 74.5% of Gaza’s pre-war building stock, have been damaged or destroyed between October 2023 and August 2026.
The northern governorates of North Gaza and Gaza have suffered the most extensive destruction, with 87% of buildings affected.

Despite a U.S.-brokered ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes have continued, with further damage reported on both sides of the Yellow Line. The analysis, based on Sentinel-1 radar imagery, documents the widespread destruction of Gaza’s built environment over nearly three years of war.
Read the full article here

title: Mystery surrounds young worker's death at Russia lab studying severe diseases

content.value: The World Health Organisation (WHO) said Saturday it still doesn't know what caused the death of a young worker at a lab in Russia that focuses on plague and other illnesses.

The UN health agency has cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person, causing a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time.
WHO, in its first full Disease Outbreak News since the case emerged earlier this month, called for a continued investigation.
Russian health officials, it said, had conducted more than 5,500 tests and found no evidence of any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.

“Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment,” WHO said.

WHO continued to refer to “a purported second case” that, in emailed explanations to The Associated Press, it previously attributed to two tabloid news outlets in Britain and Serbia that cited unspecified reports in Russia.
Russia has denied any such second case.

title: Health Wrap Episode 54 discusses Nobel 2026, brain research and healthcare access

content.value: In the 54th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, discuss the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, experimental approaches to studying human brain development, and incidents from Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya that highlight barriers to healthcare access.

The episode begins with the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The discussion explains how optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control the electrical activity of selected nerve cells. By activating or inhibiting specific neurons, researchers can investigate how neural circuits influence movement, memory, emotions and behaviour. The technique has become an important tool in neuroscience research, including studies of neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, it remains largely a research tool and is not a routine treatment for brain disorders.

The next segment examines an experimental approach described as ‘xenocortication’, in which human brain tissue is transplanted into the brains of mice. Researchers have been exploring this approach to study aspects of human brain development that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory-grown cells or animal models alone. The discussion looks at how the transplanted tissue may receive a blood supply, develop connections and interact with its surroundings within a living brain. The approach could help researchers investigate human neuronal development and mechanisms involved in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. However, it remains experimental, and findings from such models cannot be assumed to reflect human brain development fully. The work also raises ethical questions about the use of human neural tissue in animal research.

The episode then turns to barriers to healthcare access, examining how social discrimination and inadequate infrastructure can prevent people from receiving medical care. In Uttar Pradesh, a Dalit woman was allegedly denied admission to a government hospital while in labour and was forced to deliver outside the facility. Her family alleged that untouchability was involved. The incident highlights how discrimination can obstruct access to care even when a health facility is physically available.

Another incident in Meghalaya’s West Khasi Hills district, an ill child died in his mother’s arms while his parents were making a three-hour trek to reach the nearest hospital. According to the village headman, the family had tried to arrange a vehicle after the child’s condition deteriorated, but no driver was willing to travel to the village because of the poor road conditions. The incident draws attention to the difficulties faced by people in remote areas, where distance, road connectivity and the availability of transport can delay access to emergency medical care.
The episode ends with a fun-fact segment on why mice are widely used in laboratory experiments. The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

title: World’s top climate body deadlocked over inclusivity concerns

content.value: The decision was expected to take ​minutes. But after nearly three years of debate, members of the world’s leading authority on climate change still can’t agree on a timeline to publish its next review of the latest science on the warming planet.

Such assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) have ‌informed every major United Nations climate agreement for three decades. But the impasse over publication dates could leave countries to decide the next phase of action without consensus on critical issues – ​including the extent to which some global warming might be reversible – according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former IPCC scientists, government negotiators and meeting observers.

On October 12, representatives from the IPCC’s 195 member states are expected to have convened in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital, for a plenary meeting many see as the last chance to agree publication dates falling before UN climate talks in November 2028. That’s when governments are due to assess progress toward goals set out in the landmark agreement reached in Paris in 2015.

The possibility the IPCC’s reports might not be ready in time for ‌the 2028  talks has alarmed a coalition of countries pushing for more robust action. Those discussions are intended to guide decisions on climate financing and national targets to bring down greenhouse gas emissions.

Countries including India, Kenya, Saudi Arabia, Russia, and China are pressing for more time to prepare the IPCC’s next reports to ensure scientists from less-resourced countries can make meaningful contributions. Some struggle to publish new research in time to be included or to take time off from their regular jobs for unpaid IPCC work, they say.

The deadlock – unprecedented in the IPCC’s history – comes as the organisation faces increasing pressure from governments critical of climate policies they say hurt industrial competitiveness or restrict the ‌ability of emerging economies to use cheaper, more polluting fuels to meet development needs. The United States, the IPCC’s biggest funder, quit the organisation in January.

The IPCC will publish three key reports: one on ​the extent and causes of climate change, another on vulnerabilities and how countries can adapt, and a third on options to avoid warming getting worse. Scientists chairing groups preparing the reports have proposed a work plan that would see all three approved by September 2028.

Robert Vautard, a French co-chair, said the proposal was based on the anticipated workload rather than the timing of the 2028 UN ⁠summit. Report timelines are typically approved in “a matter of minutes,” he added.
Opponents of the chairs’ proposal want the second and third reports pushed into 2029.
Thiagarajan Jayaraman, a scientist who represents India at the IPCC, said it was “short-sighted” to suggest the value of the body’s work rests solely on contributing to the 2028 UN talks.

Developing countries have long argued their perspectives are not sufficiently reflected in IPCC reports because they do not have enough experts involved and because their researchers have fewer resources to publish peer-reviewed studies.
The result, Thiagarajan said, ​is that issues of “equity and inclusivity” are in some instances “simply ducked.”

title: Global warming is turning frogs’ sex reversal into an extinction risk

content.value: Some fish can switch sex more than once over a lifetime. In lizards, genetically male hatchlings can be born looking and functioning as females. In some frogs, genetically female individuals can develop into fertile males.

This phenomenon is called sex reversal. It is well documented in the animal kingdom, from invertebrates to amphibians to birds, where an individual can begin life with one sex and later switch to another.

But a warming planet is making these changes more frequent and potentially more consequential for animals. In a population skewed towards one sex, individuals may run out of mates to reproduce with, slowing population growth, reducing genetic diversity, and ultimately raising the risk of extinction.
Agile frogs

Around 40% of amphibian species face the risk of extinction, which makes them the most threatened vertebrates on the earth. As temperatures continue to climb, scientists are asking whether increased sex reversal could affect the long-term survival of amphibian populations.

To answer this, a group of researchers turned to agile frogs in Hungary. They found that sex-reversed wild males sire fewer offspring — which are in turn more vulnerable to heat and infectious disease. These disadvantages could together speed up population declines as the planet keeps warming.
The results were published in Science Advances on September 3.

In agile frogs as in mammals, the sex at birth is determined by chromosomes. Two X chromosomes make a genetic female whereas an X and a Y make a genetic male. But excessive heat in the tadpole stage can override that genetic recipe and turn some genetically female tadpoles into physically normal and fertile male tadpoles.

“Theoretical models suggest that this threat can be mitigated, up to a certain severity of climate change, for example XX males siring all-XX offspring,” said Veronika Bokony, the study’s lead author and researcher at the HUN-REN Centre for Agricultural Research. However, “this mitigating effect can be lost if sex-reversed individuals cannot participate in reproduction.”
Chance of mating

Bokony et al. first looked at whether animals whose sex differs from their genetic sex reproduce just as successfully in the wild. They paired 20 sex-reversed males with 20 sex-concordant males, matched for body size and arrival time at the breeding ponds, two traits known to affect mating success. They let each male mate with a female.
The team then tracked whether the female laid eggs, how long it took, and whether the eggs developed into tadpoles.
The team found that sex-reversed males were just as capable of winning mates and fertilised eggs did develop into tadpoles.

However, sex-reversed males did not have an equal chance at mating. About one-third of females paired with sex-reversed males laid only part of their eggs, called the split clutch strategy in which they saved the rest for a better mate.
In an experimental set-up, females had no choice, so sex-reversed males could still coerce the female into mating and sire a clutch.
“Had they been free in a real mating aggregation, this could have allowed the female to find another male who could replace the sex-reversed male by fighting,” Dr. Bokony said.
Artificial heatwave

So the researchers turned to breeding ponds in the wild. They sampled more than a hundred egg masses from 16 different populations and found that even though the sex-reversed male agile frogs made up roughly 20% of the wild populations, only 4% of egg clutches belonged to them.
“This suggests that when the frogs mate freely, the sex-reversed individuals are not as successful at becoming sires as the sex-concordant males,” Dr. Bokony said.

The few offspring they did sire were also not in the clear. As researchers tracked the development of lab-reared tadpoles, they found that 61% of the offspring of sex-reversed males underwent sex reversal, developing as males despite being genetically female. Only 17% of offspring of sex-concordant males did, however.
“We were suspicious that sex reversal might have negative consequences on individual fitness and on population viability,” Dr. Bokony said.

A warming climate is also amplifying the threat of infectious diseases. The pathogen ranavirus is of particular concern: in some instances, it has wiped out more than 90% of tadpoles in a single event.

To understand how well these offspring could withstand such climate-driven stressors, researchers exposed eggs from sex-reversed and sex-concordant males to an artificial heat wave along with ranavirus. Under high temperatures, tadpoles of sex-reversed males carried higher viral loads.

With lower paternity, higher rates of sex reversal in offspring, and greater disease susceptibility all being plausible outcomes, the team turned to computer models to test how these combined pressures could affect wild agile frog populations.
Higher extinction risk

“What happens in the laboratory and what occurs in the field are two different matters, and the strength of this study lies in the assessment of the impact of sex reversal in the wild,” University of Canberra professor Arthur Georges, who was not involved in the study, said.
Their results showed small populations were especially vulnerable, since losing even a few breeding females could affect a population’s ability to reproduce.

While some populations may already have begun declining, others could disappear within 60 to 70 years as heat-driven sex reversal pushed populations towards more males with fewer females to mate with.
When the model factored in the mortality from ranavirus among the offspring of sex-reversed males, population decline began roughly 10 years earlier and extinction came about 9.5 years sooner.
Without ranavirus, populations still declined about eight years earlier — but the extinction occurred only about two years earlier.
“We, as scientists, underestimate the number of sex-reversed individuals in populations and species,” Dominique Potvin, associate professor at the University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia, said.

She added that scientists need to know how the environment is affecting sex reversal and affecting the long-term survival of species to update their interpretations and management strategies for conservation.
Rupsy Khurana is science communication and outreach lead at the National Centre for Biological Science, Bengaluru.

title: Science Snapshots: October 11, 2026

content.value: Unusual rains of 2024 could be earth’s new normal

The year 2024 experienced a record-breaking number of heavy and extreme rainfall events worldwide, a new study has confirmed. But unlike previous strong El Niño years, 2024 also featured unusual simultaneous warming across the Atlantic and Indian Oceans that, together with a warmer atmosphere, brought extreme rainfall around the world and later into summer. Models also suggest that while 2024’s pattern is currently rare, it could become a typical year by 2050 if current warming trends continue.
Why people with high BP have worse osteoarthritis

Doctors have known for a time now that people with hypertension often suffer from more severe osteoarthritis. Researchers have now found that high blood pressure increases vasopressin hormone levels in the blood. Meanwhile, ageing primes the joint to cause cartilage cells to produce vasopressin receptors. When vasopressin in the blood meets the receptors, cartilage breaks down and damages the joint. The team also found blocking these receptors with specific drugs would stop the hastened damage.
AI model, proof-checker combo can do math unaided

Researchers have developed an AI tool called AlphaProof Nexus they say can autonomously make mathematical discoveries. AI has struggled with advanced maths because it often hallucinates or makes small mistakes. The team paired advanced language models with Lean, a rigorous proof-checking software that verifies every step. Astonishingly, the tool solved nine open problems posed by mathematician Paul Erdős, including two unsolved for 56 years, proved 44 open conjectures, and made an advance in optimisation theory.

title: ‘Overemphasis on MCQs’: Ramanujan Prize winner, Mahesh Kakde, on maths education in India

content.value: The 2026 Ramanujan Prize has been awarded to Mahesh Kakde, Professor, Department of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Science (IISc), for his contribution to algebraic number theory. It honours Prof. Kakde’s fundamental work on non-commutative Iwasawa theory and his outstanding research on the Gross-Stark and Brumer-Stark conjectures, with implications for Hilbert’s 12th problem — one of the 23 renowned and unsolved problems posed by David Hilbert in 1900. He is the fifth Indian to receive this award.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)

Each year, the Ramanujan Prize is awarded to a young mathematician from a developing country jointly by the  International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) and the International Mathematical Union (IMU) in honour of the Indian mathematical genius Srinivasa Ramanujan.

Born in 1983 in Akola, Maharashtra, Prof. Kakde knew from childhood that mathematics was his calling. He fondly recalls being motivated to solve problems, especially after an older cousin told him, “Maths is hard.” He would also solve problems from mathematics textbooks even before the corresponding topics were covered in school. “I realised that you don’t need to know a lot of things to start doing mathematics as long as you understand some definitions. That aspect of mathematics just attracted me—that you could start doing it without knowing a lot.” Prof. Kakde said.
Join THEdge LinkedIn group

In Class 10, he attended a mathematics workshop for high school teachers, led by a local professor. He remembers being fascinated by concepts that went beyond his math textbook. He later met the professor, who encouraged him to aim for the Math Olympiads and also gifted him relevant textbooks. The textbooks included the authors' addresses, prompting Prof. Kakde to write to them and seek guidance in choosing maths as an academic option.

“One of the authors replied, suggesting I should pursue mathematics. He recommended I explore a place called Chennai Mathematical Institute,” recalled Prof. Kakde. Through networking, he also learned about the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI) in Bengaluru. He received a Bachelor’s in mathematics from ISI, becoming only the second in his family to complete university education.

With a profound interest in number theory, he went on to do a Certificate of Advanced Study in Mathematics (CASM Part III) and further pursued a Ph.D. at the University of Cambridge under the supervision of Professor John Coates. He previously taught mathematics at Princeton University and served as a reader at King’s College, London.

He joined the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in 2019, where he has worked ever since, mainly on classical and non-commutative Iwasawa theory and Stark’s conjectures. He considers IISc a fantastic place that provides a conducive environment, particularly with a reasonable administrative and teaching load, supportive colleagues, and ample time for research and research visits to different places.
Prof. Kakde has received several prestigious awards and honours, including the 2022 Infosys Prize in Mathematics and the 2023 Whitehead Prize by the London Mathematical Society.

His work is directly influenced by Srinivasa Ramanujan’s work on modular forms, which has been quite influential in number theory. He further explains that modular forms act as a crucial bridge between analytic and algebraic mathematical objects in his field. “I think there’s hardly anything in algebraic number theory that hasn’t been influenced by modular forms. My work in non-commutative Iwasawa theory and Stark’s conjecture uses these congruences a lot,” Prof. Kakde said.

India has a rich history of mathematicians who have contributed to the field, spanning the period before and after Ramanujan. Prof. Kakde explains that after independence, mathematics education and research were mainly concentrated in fewer centres. However, the past 25 years have seen an expansion in mathematics with the inception of several institutes such as IITs and IISERs. Despite this, the number of institutes remains small for the size and population of India compared to Europe. He calls it a “chicken-and-egg problem”, further explaining, “In these places that you are building, until you train a lot of people, you won’t have enough people to hire, and without building those places, maybe you cannot train enough people.”
A strong mathematical ecosystem can only be built with students’ enthusiasm for learning and engagement with mathematics. The way students think can tremendously affect the ecosystem, he said.

Prof. Kakde is a staunch advocate for open-ended thinking and is worried that the overemphasis on multiple-choice questions in entrance examinations hinders exploration — an essential process for conceptual understanding, creativity, and problem-solving in mathematics. He acknowledges that the NCERT textbooks are well-written and provide ample scope in the form of open-ended questions, but “neither the school nor the student has incentive to solve any of those because eventually, the admissions to universities are based on multiple-choice question-based entrance exams,” Prof. Kakde says.

He is also deeply concerned about the under-representation of women in mathematics and describes it as a “universal problem”. He gives an example of policies in Europe, where maternity leave or not treating childcare-related career breaks as career gaps can work as possible ways to address the gender imbalance in India, and he is optimistic about the impact. “This will not solve the whole problem (of the gender gap), but at least it’s a step in the right direction,” Prof. Kakde said.
(Rohini Karandikar works with the TNQ Foundation and is a science communicator and educator.)

title: El Nino sets temperature record in key Pacific zone: EU monitor

content.value: An intensifying El Nino broke a temperature record in a key zone of the Pacific in September, the EU’s climate monitor said on Monday (October 12, 2026), in another sign the weather pattern is gaining exceptional strength.

Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Nino would likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode’s expected peak later this year.

The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in a tell-tale El Nino monitoring region of the Pacific, known as Nino3.4, had reached an “all-time high” of 29.70C last month.
This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Nino events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, “underscoring the exceptional intensity of the current El Nino”, the EU monitor said.
But in a statement to AFP, Copernicus said it “cannot yet say that the current El Nino is the strongest ever recorded”.
As climate change raises ocean temperatures, it can make recent El Nino events appear stronger than past ones, complicating historical comparisons.
Copernicus said it had adopted a new index, which accounts for the warming of tropical oceans, that suggested the current event is not yet stronger than past ones.
But the values observed in September “point to an already exceptionally strong El Nino, especially given that the event has not yet reached its peak”, Copernicus told AFP.
Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino.
On Friday, Japan’s weather agency said that El Nino conditions had reached their “strongest intensity on record”, with temperatures in the phenomenon’s monitoring area 4C above normal.
Record ocean temperatures
As El Nino gathers strength, global average sea surface temperatures hit a record 21.05C for September, topping the previous high of 20.92C for the same month in 2023, according to Copernicus.
Overall, the world experienced its second hottest September on record, with surface air temperatures averaging 16.27C, the EU service said.
September was 1.63C hotter than the pre-industrial average, a period defined as 1850-1900.

Nations agreed at the 2015 UN climate talks in Paris to keep global warming “well below” 2C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5C, in order to limit the effects of climate change.
But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5C target would be missed in a matter of years.
“We are in a new run of months above 1.5C, and with a strong El Nino still intensifying it is likely to last into 2027,” Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo said in a statement.
“Crossing the Paris Agreement’s long-term limit is only a matter of time. How far we overshoot, and for how long, is still up to us,” he said.
Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of “overshoot” above 1.5C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.
Experts have warned that this El Nino would likely push global temperatures to a new record in 2027.
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.

title: Roundglass Sustain’s short film A Spring Against All Odds to be showcased at international film festival

content.value: Roundglass Sustain’s short film A Spring Against All Odds opens with a poignant couplet by 18th-century Urdu poet Mir Taqi Mir: “My heart and my Delhi may both be in ruins; There are still some delights in this ravaged home.”

Centuries later, the words still ring true, setting the tone for this layered, deeply introspective film, one of the 48 films selected for Film SouthAsia (FSA), an international documentary film festival to be held in Kathmandu from November 27–29, 2026. Based on a story and script by Radhika Raj and directed and edited by Samreen Farooqui, both associated with Roundglass Sustain, the film captures the three years Radhika spent obsessing over the red silk cotton tree, or semal, outside her window in her Delhi home.

A Spring Against All Odds features an eclectic cast: Radhika, her partner Saptak, house help Swati, and cats Chutney and Chikki, plus the semal tree itself and the pair of grey hornbills who inhabit it. Opening in 2021, when Radhika and Saptak move into a new home overlooking this tree, the film shows how the tree becomes a constant witness to multiple crises, including a mismanaged pandemic, a winter thick with pollution, a monsoon of floods, an oppressive summer, a political shift, and a personal loss, as the film’s release states. “It was a very difficult time. My life was unravelling in many ways, along with the city. I was struggling emotionally…grieving,” says Radhika, who believes that the tree outside her window held her together during this challenging period. “It became an antidote to what was happening in my life,” she says.

For Samreen, the idea for the film originated from Radhika saying she had moved into this house with a tree and was looking at hornbills all day. “She was just ecstatic and couldn’t believe her luck.” It got them talking about making a short natural history video about the semal and the birds nesting in it, recalls Samreen. But the more she heard Radhika talk about the tree, the more she realised it could become a full film, not just a video. “We started to think about the tree and the city and decided to expand on that idea, because the city is full of red silk cotton trees,” she says. As Radhika’s life, too, went through ups and downs, it became clear that “there was no escaping or separating her from the tree or the city,” says Samreen, a firm believer that a film makes itself. “I think that is what happened. The film directed us towards it. And then, it started to unpeel and unfold; various layers came in.”

Radhika, who thinks of the film as almost “accidental, started by doing what Samreen had told her to do: put a camera on the window and capture what was happening. “Every time I told her something new was happening, she would tell me to get that as well. And this just kept going on,” says Radhika, recalling how they just could not look away from the tree after a point. “So, it very naturally expanded into this unintentional three-year project.”

While the tree is central to the film, it does not just remain about the tree. Instead, it became “a microcosm of everything happening in our lives, the natural life of the city and the city itself,” says Samreen. While politics is different from nature, as is our inner life from the tree outside a window, “it is all really interconnected, and all comes together. That is what the film became: it is about the tree, but also about everything,” she says, adding that as a filmmaker she has always tried to explore what holds us together in the kind of world we live in today. “I think I am exploring that in the film, too.”

The film is also an unusual exploration of Delhi, a city filled with these trees and one that both Samreen and Radhika hold dear, in very different ways. “I am not from Delhi, but from Mumbai, and came here for college, work and then got married to someone from here,” says Radhika, who ends up falling in love with the city, though she agrees it is a difficult place to live in. “In a way, the tree offered an alternate lens to look at the city, experiencing it through trees, time and seasons. It allowed me a second chance to love Delhi.”

Samreen, on the other hand, grew up in Delhi and lived there for most of her life. “But now I have left it and live in Bengaluru, which is increasingly becoming my city. But Delhi has kind of made me, so I have a complicated, love-hate relationship with it,” she says. The film helped her witness the city again and, in the process, find the city she wanted, she says. “Radhika would throw all her research at me, and it really struck me that Delhi is also the city of the 17th-century poets, and Delhi became their muse. So the poetry became very pivotal to the film.”

While she agrees that much has gone wrong in Delhi — the pollution, political uncertainty, and public apathy have made it a shadow of what it once was, it also refuses to be undone by them.  “That became very clear to me while I was editing the film,” says Samreen, who began editing in 2024 and took nearly a year to finish it.

In her opinion, A Spring Against All Odds is not just an intimate narrative of South Asia highlighting the relationship between a tree and a woman, but “really the story of cities all over South Asia,” says Samreen, pointing out that they wanted an international premiere because the film resonated at so many levels and needed a diverse audience. “We are really thrilled that it is going to be screened in Kathmandu. We couldn’t have asked for a better premiere.”

title: How Jodrell Bank turned a corner

content.value: The scale of a project often determines the size of the problems too. Agreed, all or most projects are confronted with hurdles, but overcoming them is often easier in the case of smaller projects. When the stakes are higher and things take a downward turn, problems might seem insurmountable on occasions.

The Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire, England is one such project that almost went under just as it was almost ready for operation. Thanks to an unexpected turn of events, however, it survived, going on to play a crucial role in radio astronomy.
Humble beginnings

The observatory had humble beginnings, thanks in large to one man: Bernard Lovell. Having been called up for wartime work on centimetric radar during World War II, Lovell learnt about radar’s potential. He was quick to realise that it wasn’t limited to detecting enemy vessels, but could actually be employed to detect natural phenomena that were happening at a distance.

Having returned to the University of Manchester after the war in 1945, Lovell’s efforts at radar experiments outside his lab in the city proved unsuccessful as there was interference from Manchester’s electric trams. As the university’s botany department owned land in Cheshire, Lovell decided to use it to continue his experiments to see if radar could be used to study cosmic rays. They couldn’t, but there was success nevertheless.

On a cold day in December, Lovell drove a trailer to the remote location — with the area around the gardener’s hut serving as the perfect setting for him to set up shop. While the results were good, it didn’t meet his initial objectives. Instead, he had luck finding meteors and work soon shifted in the direction of studying meteor trails, the moon, and different planets. It marked the beginning of radio astronomy in Jodrell Bank.

For what remained of the decade, Jodrell Bank turned into a hubbub of activity in radio astronomy. Studying radio waves from space to understand the universe was still a fledgling field and the excitement was palpable for the scientists who joined Lovell to work in this new branch of science. Using army surplus, they built their own equipment, including the “Searchlight Aerial” in 1946 and “Transit Telescope” in 1947. Lovell, however, knew that they needed a bigger telescope to be at the forefront of the field.
Building the Lovell Telescope

Preliminary ideas for a 250-foot steerable parabolic dish were shot down by many engineers, and it was only after Sheffield engineer Charles Husband came on board that they had a workable design. Funding agencies gave the initial go-ahead for ‘Mark 1’ — now known as Lovell Telescope — on June 22, 1950 and the final approvals came through by March 1952. Construction began later the same year.

It was far from smooth sailing as the project faced deep financial stress. It wasn’t until May 1953 that the concrete foundations were completed, and it was only in March 1954 that circular tracks enabling telescope movement in azimuth were laid. The electric drive motor system for the telescope proved harder to develop than imagined, and it was only in the spring of 1957 that this system was finally delivered following multiple delays, including a change of contractor. By now, the construction of the telescope had gone way beyond the initial estimated budget, plenty of people had lost hope in the project, and Jodrell Bank’s future was teetering on the brink.
“I was in the laboratory where the receiving apparatus was and suddenly, before midnight, I saw the most dramatic echo”Sir Bernard Lovell

It was in such a climate that hope came from unexpected quarters — the launch of Sputnik 1 by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The first artificial Earth satellite not only sounded the start gun for the Space Race between the Soviet Union and the U.S., but also marked the rebirth of Jodrell Bank, offering it renewed purpose.

While any simple equipment could be used to listen to the bleeps from Sputnik 1, it soon became obvious to anyone with passable knowledge of the subject that the near-complete Mark 1 at Jodrell Bank was the only instrument with the capacity to locate and track the intercontinental ballistic missile that had served as Sputnik 1’s launch rocket. Soon fully operational, the radar equipment built to detect echoes of natural phenomena was looking instead for a missile. It succeeded on October 12.
“Wonderful echo”

“I was in the laboratory where the receiving apparatus was and suddenly, before midnight, I saw the most dramatic echo,” Bernard recalled, years later, according to the BBC. “A huge echo — the echo of the intercontinental missile travelling over the lake to a distributed speed of 17,000 miles an hour. This wonderful echo, the only instrument in the Western world which could detect the launching of the Sputnik.”

While this brought credibility to Jodrell Bank, sponsors weren’t queuing up yet to save it from financial distress. Its size and capability, however, turned out to be an asset, and soon both the U.S. and the Soviet Union were seeking Jodrell Bank’s help, and it started playing a pivotal role in the Space Race. Funding soon followed.

In the decade that followed that turning point, Jodrell Bank served as a focal point to confirm both success and failure. In 1959, the Soviet Union roped in its service when Luna 2 became the first human-made object to crash into another cosmic body, our moon. Luna 9’s first images from the surface of the moon were received at Jodrell Bank in 1966. When the Apollo 11 astronauts took the first steps on the moon, Jodrell Bank was listening in throughout, right from the descent stage.
Also read: Luna 2: touched by humans, touches the moon

Even though there were complaints from certain quarters about these tracking escapades costing valuable research time, there was no denying that it only amounted to just a small fraction of all the work it was doing. Additionally, tracking these probes also enabled exploring regions of space wherein Jodrell Bank had a scientific interest.
Immense contributions

Jodrell Bank, in fact, has probably contributed beyond Lovell’s wildest dreams when he set out on his trailer in 1945. From quasars to black holes, and pulsars to gravitational lenses, Jodrell Bank has played a crucial part in our better understanding of the universe.

While the Lovell Telescope is still one of the largest telescopes of its kind, Jodrell Bank was recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019. Things aren’t all rosy with the observatory at the moment though, with the institution losing funding for the future in July 2026 — a step that could lead to its closure in March 2028. “There must be a way to save Jodrell Bank,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on September 1, vowing to find a solution to this pressing problem. If that happens, it wouldn’t be the first time Jodrell Bank has turned a corner.

title: TRISHNA satellite is in advanced stage of realisation, says ISRO official

content.value: The Indo-French satellite TRISHNA (Thermal Infra-Red Imaging Satellite for High-resolution Natural Resource Assessment) will be launched in the next 12-16 months, said Jasvinder Singh Khoral, Director (Projects), U.R. Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), on Sunday (October 11, 2026).
He said this was the third satellite that India and France are developing after Megha-Tropiques and SARAL (Satellite with ARGOS and ALTIKA) satellites.

“This particular project has been around for a decade or so in its conceptualisation and formalisation. Now it has come to the realisation stage. It is at a point where, in the next 12 -16 months, we will be due for launch,” Mr. Khoral said while speaking at the TRISHNA Water for Tomorrow workshop.

“We at the URSC will be responsible for the realisation of the bus along with the payloads our partners in CNES [France’s space agency] would be delivering the other half of the payloads and I understand the data will be processed jointly both in France and in India,” he added.
ALSO WATCH Gaganyaan Episode 10: Can reusable rockets shape India’s future in human spaceflight? | The Scope
Nagalakshmi A.M., Project Director, TRINSHA, said the main objective of the mission is better management of water resources, visible shortwave and thermal infrared Earth observation.
“We will have an open data policy where science data is disseminated to the entire globe seamlessly,” she said.
The TRISHNA mission, a collaborative endeavor between ISRO and CNES, will be launched by the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle.

ISRO and CNES are jointly developing TRISHNA, which is engineered to deliver high spatial and high temporal resolution monitoring of the earth’s surface temperature, emissivity, and biophysical and radiation variables for surface energy budgeting at regional to global scale.
The satellite will have two primary payloads, the Thermal Infra-Red (TIR) payload, developed by CNES, and the Visible-Near Infra-Red Short Wave Infra-Red (VNIR-SWIR) payload, developed by ISRO.

title: Shigella cases ring alarm bells in Thrissur as 10 infections surface in nine days

content.value: A cluster of Shigella infections linked to a temple festival has put health authorities in Thrissur on alert, with 10 cases reported in the district in the first nine days of October. Seven of the cases, including that of a seven-month-old child, were reported from Tholur among people who had attended a festival at a temple there.
The suspected source of the infection has been traced to a well at the temple, from which water was drawn for rituals. The well has since been chlorinated, District Medical Officer M. Sujatha said.

“The seven Shigella cases reported from Tholur were among people who attended a festival at a temple in Tholur. The source of infection has been identified as the temple well from which water was taken for rituals. The well has been chlorinated,” Dr. Sujatha said.

Health teams are closely monitoring the situation, while hospitals have been instructed to respond immediately if any further cases are detected. Awareness campaigns have also been conducted in the area, with people advised to seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms, she said.
All those who tested positive for Shigella have sought treatment, and most have recovered. The remaining patients are also recovering, according to the DMO.
The other three Shigella cases reported during the nine-day period were from Wadakkanchery, Arimbur and Adat.

The Shigella cluster comes amid a wider surge in fever cases in the district. As many as 4,914 people sought treatment for fever between October 1 and 9. During the period, 39 dengue cases and four cases of leptospirosis were also confirmed.

Dengue cases have been reported from several parts of the district, including Kodakara, Mattathur, Meloor, Thrissur Corporation, Avinissery, Chalakudy municipality, Kaiparamba, Kodassery, Pananchery, Puthukkad, Adat, Alur, Puthur, Mullurkara, Pariyaram, Tholur, Orumanayur, Thalikulam and Choondal.
Leptospirosis cases were reported from Pananchery, Pazhayannur, Porkulam and Kuzhur.
Dengue cases

The DMO said a significant number of dengue cases had been detected in migrant labour camps and among their contacts. “Most of the dengue cases have been reported from migrant labour camps and their contacts. We are keeping a close watch on them and monitoring the situation,” she said.

Health authorities have stepped up surveillance and preventive measures across the district. The DMO urged people with fever to take adequate rest, drink sufficient water and consume nutritious food, while vulnerable people, particularly those with compromised immunity, should take extra precautions and seek medical care when necessary.

With Shigella cases emerging in connection with a common gathering and dengue continuing to surface across multiple locations, health officials are keeping a close watch on possible further transmission and urging the public to maintain strict hygiene and food and water safety.

title: Dental anxiety: when fear becomes a barrier to care

content.value: During my 10+ years of clinical experience in various States and with numerous patient populations, I have seen that dental anxiety is a constant challenge. I have seen this phenomenon in children clutching their parents’ hands before their first cleaning and in accomplished professionals quietly cancelling appointment after appointment in the hope that the problem will somehow resolve itself.
It doesn’t.

In my experience, the longer you leave a fear unchecked, the greater the clinical and human cost becomes. Dental anxiety is not a moral failing. This is a well-documented psychological response—and one with important, measurable public health consequences.
How severe is it?

Roughly a third of people have significant dental anxiety, and roughly a tenth have a clinical phobia. That’s not a little footnote. That means a lot of the population is actively avoiding or delaying care that could prevent serious disease. The downstream consequences of this avoidance are visible daily in my clinical work: infections tolerated for months, decay advanced far beyond what early intervention would have required, and patients presenting with pain that could have been prevented years ago.
Knowing where it starts

Dental anxiety typically has a definite source. A painful or poorly done procedure in childhood can be a source of dental anxiety. A provider who was in a hurry or didn’t tell the patient what was happening. The specific sensory environment of a dental office—the sounds, the smells, and the physical vulnerability of lying back with your mouth open—can leave powerful imprints, especially in young patients. That memory is not just wiped out; it impacts behaviour for decades. For some, it’s not just one event but an accumulation. Years of avoidance layered on top of embarrassment about how their teeth look now, and a fear of judgment prevents them from asking for help. This cycle of shame avoidance is one of the hardest patterns I see clinically. When these patients do come in, they need much more intervention than if they had come in sooner, and this becomes an instance of the very fear that kept them away.
The health price of avoidance

Research literature teaches us, that oral health is not an island. Untreated dental disease is a chronic inflammatory load on the body. It has been linked to cardiovascular risk, dysregulated blood sugar, and impaired immune function. When a patient avoids dental care for years, it is not just their smile that is at risk;  they are carrying a preventable health load that will rise elsewhere in time.

In addition to the system effects, the impact on quality of life is immediate and real. A toothache interferes with sleep. It impacts nutrition, concentration, and the ability to speak with confidence. These are not trivial consequences; they affect how people show up in their professional and personal lives every day.
What works in practice

The most significant change I’ve made in my practice is making communication a priority before any procedure begins. When patients feel informed and in control, it  greatly reduces their dental anxiety. A stop signal—a raised hand that stops everything instantly—can alter the psychological dynamic in the room.  It shifts the patient from passive recipient to active participant, and that shift matters enormously. I also allow extra time for anxious patients. The problem is not that procedures take longer, but that rushing them increases anxiety. I explain everything before it happens, check in frequently, and never minimise what a patient is feeling. These should not be  luxury accommodations; they should be  routine parts of effective care.

For patients with more severe anxiety, pharmacological support is appropriate. Nitrous oxide is safe, effective, and rapidly reversible. There are also oral sedation choices if needed. These are clinical tools, not last resorts, and patients should feel comfortable asking about them.
A message to patients

If fear has kept you from the dentist, remember  you are not alone, and you are not too far gone to be helped. What I ask of patients in this situation is one small step—not a treatment plan, not a procedure, simply a conversation. Come in and tell us about your nervousness. A good provider is a good listener and  will start there.  There is no need to be afraid of the dental chair. With the right approach, it can be a place where you take difficult things and make them manageable—and where the relief on the other side is worth it.

(Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula is a U.S.-licensed dentist with international training who focuses on preventive and evidence-based oral healthcare and contributes to advancing community and public health dentistry. sowji.gunukula@gmail.com)

title: Karnataka seeks wider price caps beyond cancer medicines on other high-cost life-saving drugs

content.value: Karnataka has urged the Centre to extend price-control measures beyond cancer medicines to other high-cost, life-saving drugs used to treat cardiac and kidney diseases, following the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s (NPPA) in-principle approval to cap trade margins on certain non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines at 30% of their maximum retail price (MRP).

Addressing presspersons in Bengaluru, Health Minister U.T. Khader said price rationalisation should translate into direct savings for patients, and urged the Union government to extend similar measures to other essential medicines where high treatment costs place a burden on patients.

At its meeting on October 8, the NPPA gave in-principle approval to rationalise trade margins on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines identified under Paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. The measure is subject to finalisation of the list of medicines to be covered.

The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has been asked to constitute an expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services to recommend the anti-cancer medicines to be brought under price control. The committee is expected to submit its report by October 14.

The Centre estimates that the measure could reduce the MRP of several anti-cancer medicines by 20% to 70%, potentially saving patients around ₹2,500 crore. “The financial strain of cancer treatment often pushes families into debt, making it inevitable for them to exhaust their savings and sell assets to meet medical expenses,” Mr. Khader said.

Citing examples, the Minister said a cancer drug/injection costing around ₹3,250 was reportedly priced at ₹23,347. Medicines with a landing cost of about ₹3,000 are being sold at a cost of ₹27,000. Under the 30% trade-margin cap, the maximum price of a medicine would depend on its applicable pricing base and can substantially reduce out-of-pocket expenditure for patients, he explained.
Also Read: Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
Karnataka’s representation to the Centre

In a letter dated September 23 to Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda, the Karnataka government had sought national-level action after inspections in the State found substantial differences between the procurement costs of medicines and the prices charged to patients. The State identified pricing concerns involving 253 medicines and consumables with mark-ups.

Karnataka had sought the inclusion of advanced chemotherapy, targeted therapy and other expensive cancer medicines under the ambit of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, along with a comprehensive cap on trade margins for high-cost and life-saving medicines.
The State had also called for expanding the NPPA’s price-control oversight and strengthening enforcement against excessive charging and profiteering.
Disclosure of medicine costs in hospital bills

The State has also sought greater transparency in the prices charged to patients. A circular issued on October 1 asked healthcare institutions to disclose both the purchase or landing cost and the MRP of medicines in patient bills. The instructions are advisory in nature and are proposed to take effect from November 1.

Karnataka’s call follows observations by the Supreme Court questioning why the MRP of essential medicines, including cancer drugs, could not be capped at 16% above the price to retailers, as is applicable to scheduled medicines under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013.

The State said the proposed 30% trade-margin cap on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines should be followed by wider action to cover other essential, high-cost medicines, including those used in cardiac and kidney treatment, so that the benefits of price rationalisation reach patients directly.

title: ‘Operation Thelima’ makes headway in Kozhikode district

content.value: Food safety inspections in Kozhikode district have resulted in fines over ₹16 lakh against eateries over the past three months, with officials detecting violations including unhygienic food preparation, storage of stale ingredients and failure to follow basic hygiene requirements.

The aggressive inspections mostly covered hotels, bakeries, wayside eateries and other local food establishments. The action comes amid directions from the Food Safety Department requiring food handlers to wear gloves and hair caps while preparing and serving food.

Officials have also exposed food being prepared in unhygienic vessels and with corroded equipment, as well as food sold in areas where contaminated water accumulates. Poor handling practices have also been found to increase the risk of contamination by bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella, which can cause serious illness.

“A recent inspection at a food establishment near Malabar Christian College in the city found food items that had reportedly been stored for several days. The items included stale curries, spices, spice mixes, fruits, vegetables, bread and chapatis,” said an official who was part of the inspection. He said similar violations were detected during recent inspections at the Beach Food Street in which one outlet was ordered to shut down, while six others were served notices.

According to the Food Safety Department squads, the inspections are being conducted as part of ‘Operation Thelima’, a special drive launched by the State government across the State. Six mobile squads have been deployed for checking violation on a regular basis and initiate instant action.

Officials make it clear that under the Food Safety and Standards Act, penalties vary according to the nature of the violation. The reported provisions include fines of ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh for supplying food that does not meet prescribed standards and penalties for unhygienic food preparation, misleading advertisements, adulteration and operating without a valid licence or registration. More serious offences involving food poisoning or death may attract imprisonment and fines, depending on the circumstances and applicable provisions, they warn.

title: Family rejection, hunger and a court battle: Hyderabad’s Ruth John Paul becomes India’s first transgender PG doctor

content.value: There were days when Dr. Koyyala Ruth John Paul struggled to find food. Estranged from her family after coming out as a transgender woman, she spent years trying to make ends meet, searching for jobs while refusing to give up on her dream of becoming a doctor. When the path to postgraduate medical education was blocked by the absence of clear admission procedures for transgender candidates, she turned to the courts.

On Saturday (October 10, 2026) her perseverance culminated in a milestone. Dr. Ruth John Paul cleared all subjects in the recently announced MD/MS examination results, completing her postgraduate degree in Emergency Medicine at the ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar, Hyderabad, where she studied during the 2023-26 academic session. She has become the first transgender person in India to complete a postgraduate medical course. “I am feeling very happy. It is a matter of pride for me and my community. It is a great achievement in my life,” she said.
A childhood marked by loss

The youngest of three siblings, Dr. Ruth John Paul hails from Khammam district and grew up in a family with limited financial means. She lost her father when she was eight years old and was raised by her mother. She completed her schooling and intermediate education in her native district before clearing the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) and pursuing undergraduate medical education. She came out as a transgender woman during her undergraduate years. This led to her family rejecting her, leaving her separated from them for nearly six years.

The period that followed was marked by financial insecurity and the struggle to survive independently. “There were times when I did not even have food. I struggled to survive and looked for jobs,” she said.

In 2021, she found part-time work at Mitr Clinic (now Sabrang Clinic), which is India’s first transgender clinic. She worked there for around two years while continuing to prepare for postgraduate medical entrance examinations.
A legal battle to pursue her dream

Clearing the entrance examination was not the end of her struggle. Dr. Ruth John Paul said she encountered difficulties during postgraduate medical counselling because there were no clear protocols for accommodating transgender candidates.

With the assistance of transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli, she approached the Telangana High Court seeking relief. The legal proceedings continued for nearly two years. An interim order from the High Court eventually enabled her to proceed with admission. In 2023, she secured a seat in Emergency Medicine at ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar.
Her admission marked a turning point, but the challenges did not end there. She said she continued to encounter stigma and apprehension from people who were unfamiliar with transgender individuals.
From apprehension to acceptance

Working in a clinical environment brought its own challenges. As an emergency medicine trainee, she had to interact with patients during some of their most vulnerable moments, while also navigating the prejudices that transgender people can face. She recalled how some people were initially hesitant or uncomfortable around her. “Initially, some people were scared and did not know how to respond. But when I interacted with patients and treated them with care, they began to appreciate me. People who were initially apprehensive have now become comfortable with me,” she said.
A doctor with a larger purpose

Now that she has completed her postgraduate course, Dr. Ruth John Paul wants to use her medical training to help people in need, particularly transgender individuals who require emergency and critical care. “I want to serve everyone, especially transgender people who face critical medical emergencies. I want to provide care without discrimination based on gender identity or sexuality,” she said.

title: Frederick G. Banting and John J.R. Macleod’s Nobel-winning discovery of insulin

content.value: Frederick G. Banting and John J.R. Macleod were awarded the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of insulin, a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels. Their work helped establish insulin as a treatment for diabetes, a disease that, in its severe forms, had often been fatal before insulin therapy became available.

The prize was shared equally. Banting and Macleod were recognised “for the discovery of insulin”. The award acknowledged research conducted at the University of Toronto in the early 1920s, when investigators developed pancreatic extracts that could lower blood sugar in diabetic animals and subsequently demonstrated their therapeutic potential in humans. Charles Best, who worked with Banting, and biochemist James Collip, who helped purify insulin for clinical use, also made important contributions to this work.
Research on pancreas and blood sugar

Diabetes had been linked to the pancreas decades before insulin was isolated. In 1889, researchers Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering demonstrated that removing the pancreas from dogs produced diabetes. Subsequent research established the importance of the islets of Langerhans, clusters of cells within the pancreas, in regulating blood sugar.

The challenge was to identify and extract the substance responsible for this effect. Several researchers attempted to prepare pancreatic extracts, but obtaining a preparation that could be used safely and consistently in patients remained difficult.

Frederick G. Banting was a Canadian physician and surgeon whose interest in diabetes led him to investigate the role of the pancreas in regulating blood glucose. After serving in the First World War, he returned to Canada and worked in medical practice before pursuing research.

John J.R. Macleod was a Scottish-born physician and physiologist who had built his career around teaching and research in physiology, including carbohydrate metabolism. By 1920, he was a professor of physiology at the University of Toronto.

Banting approached Macleod in 1921 with a proposal to isolate a substance from the pancreas that could regulate blood glucose. Macleod provided laboratory facilities, scientific guidance and access to experimental animals. Banting began the work with Charles Best, a medical student who assisted with the experiments. Their collaboration brought together Banting’s research hypothesis and Macleod’s experience in physiology, setting the stage for the experiments that led to the development of insulin as a treatment for diabetes.

The researchers tied off the pancreatic ducts of dogs, allowing the enzyme-producing tissue to degenerate while attempting to preserve the islets. They prepared extracts from the pancreas and tested them in dogs whose pancreases had been removed. The extracts lowered blood sugar and improved the animals’ clinical condition.

These experiments provided evidence that an extract from the pancreas could help compensate for the loss of its normal blood sugar-regulating function. However, the early preparations were not suitable for prolonged use in humans because they contained impurities that caused adverse reactions.
Purifying insulin for treatment
In 1922, biochemist James Collip joined the research team to improve the purity of the pancreatic extract. His work helped produce a preparation suitable for clinical testing.

In January 1922, insulin was administered to Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old boy with severe diabetes, at Toronto General Hospital. The first injection produced limited results, and an abscess developed at the injection site. After the preparation was further purified, a second course of treatment produced a marked improvement in his condition, with a substantial reduction in blood glucose and urinary glucose.

Thompson’s response demonstrated that insulin could be used to treat diabetes in humans. The development of more reliable preparations and the expansion of production subsequently allowed treatment to reach more patients.

Insulin did not cure diabetes, but it changed the outlook for people living with the disease. Before its introduction, severe diabetes was often managed through restrictive diets that could prolong life only for a limited period. Insulin enabled patients to use glucose more effectively and helped prevent the severe metabolic disturbances associated with insulin deficiency.
The role of Best and Collip
The Nobel decision remains a significant part of the history of insulin research. Although Banting and Macleod received the prize, the work involved a larger research team.

Banting was unhappy that Best had not been included among the laureates. He shared half of his prize money with Best. Macleod, in turn, shared half of his prize money with Collip, recognising his contribution to the purification of insulin.
Later historical assessments of the discovery acknowledged the importance of contributions made by researchers who were not included in the award.
Laboratory discovery,modern diabetes care

The introduction of insulin marked a turning point in the treatment of diabetes. It allowed many people living with severe insulin deficiency to survive and helped establish hormone replacement as a major approach to treating endocrine disorders.

Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy or stored for later use. When the body produces insufficient insulin, or cannot use it effectively, blood glucose levels can rise.

Insulin remains essential for people with type 1 diabetes, in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce the hormone. It is also used by some people with type 2 diabetes when other treatments do not adequately control blood glucose.

The treatment has evolved considerably since the first pancreatic extracts were administered. Modern insulin preparations are manufactured under controlled conditions, with different formulations developed to vary how quickly they begin working and how long their effects last.
The Nobel recognition

Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for 1923. Banting delivered his Nobel lecture, titled ‘Diabetes and Insulin’, on September 15, 1925, while Macleod’s lecture, ‘The Physiology of Insulin and Its Source in the Animal Body’, followed on May 26, 1925.

The discovery also has a lasting connection to World Diabetes Day, observed on November 14, the birthday of Banting, who was born in 1891. More than a century later, insulin remains a cornerstone of diabetes treatment, changing a condition that was once often fatal into one that can be managed with sustained treatment.

title: Adhventha Hospital announces fellowship in interventional radiology

content.value: Adhventha Hospital, Bengaluru, has announced admissions for its 2026-2027 RGUHS-accredited Fellowship in Neuro and Vascular Interventional Radiology. The 18-month programme, offered by the hospital’s Department of Radio-diagnosis and Interventional Radiology, is led by Bhaskar M.V.,course director, chairman, senior Consultant in interventional Radiology.

The fellowship offers hands-on training in non-vascular, vascular and neuro-interventional procedures, including embolisation, onco-interventions, laser treatment for varicose veins, acute stroke interventions, aneurysm coiling and arteriovenous malformation (AVM) embolisation.
Two seats are available. Candidates with an MD or DNB in Radiology are eligible to apply. Selection will be based on a merit examination and interview.
The last date to apply is October 19. The examination will be held on October 22, and the merit list will be announced on October 23. The programme will commence on November 1.
Application forms are available on the hospital’s website at https://www.adhventhahospital.com/

title: Kidwai’s home-based palliative care in Karnataka reaches over 3,000 patients and caregivers

content.value: For patients with advanced cancer and other life-limiting illnesses, palliative care often needs to extend beyond hospital wards to their homes, where families grapple with pain, emotional distress, and the demands of long-term caregiving.

At the State-run Kidwai Memorial Institute of Oncology (KMIO), the Department of Palliative Medicine has made home-based care a key part of its services, reporting more than 750 home-care visits, over 12,000 km travelled and more than 3,000 beneficiaries, including patients and caregivers.
These services were highlighted while observing World Hospice and Palliative Care Day on October 10, which this year carried the theme ‘Pain management: An essential part of palliative care’.

“With the help of volunteers and NGOs, we also extend financial support for children’s education. We provide waterbed and airbed, ration kits, and nebuliser machines for use at home. It is not just about treating the patient,” M.K. Yadhuraj Gowda, Head of the Department of Palliative Medicine at KMIO, told The Hindu.

The home-care service is intended for patients who find it difficult to travel to the hospital because of advanced illness, reduced mobility, or other challenges. Multidisciplinary teams provide medical assessment, symptom management, nursing care, and support in familiar surroundings, helping reduce the burden of repeated hospital visits.

The department’s approach also recognises that serious illness affects entire families. Caregivers may need help managing the practical demands of looking after a patient, as well as support in coping with emotional and financial pressures, Dr. Gowda said.
Beyond death

Palliative care also includes bereavement support for families after the death of a loved one. KMIO’s department provides guidance to help family members cope with grief, manage emotional distress and access support during the grieving process.

The service reflects the broader role of palliative care, which addresses not only physical pain and other symptoms but also the psychological, emotional, social and spiritual needs of patients and their families. Volunteer services add another layer of support for families navigating serious illness and loss.
Pain relief and care for children

Institute director R. Krishnappa said the department provides inpatient palliative care for patients who require specialised management of pain and other distressing symptoms, with capacity for more than 30 patients. Its services include medication and interventional procedures such as nerve blocks and neurolysis for selected patients with severe cancer-related pain that remains inadequately controlled with conventional treatment.

It also provides paediatric palliative care, with age-appropriate pain and symptom management, emotional support and guidance for families caring for children with cancer and other serious illnesses, he said.

Music and sound therapy sessions are conducted for inpatients on Wednesdays, while yoga therapy sessions are held on Thursdays to promote relaxation and emotional well-being alongside medical treatment.
Teleconsultations extend specialist support

The department has relaunched its ‘Call for Care - Neravina Kare’ service to connect patients living outside Bengaluru and in distant locations with specialist palliative care. Through telephone and video consultations, a team comprising a palliative care physician, nurse and clinical psycho-oncologist offers guidance on symptom management and emotional support. Patients and caregivers can contact the service on 9008441708.

title: Berlin to BITS Pilani: How Nobel-winning Optogenetics connects to parasite research in Hyderabad

content.value: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”, has brought renewed attention to using light to investigate fundamental biological processes. These include memory formation, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders, as well as processes involved in infectious disease.
Editorial | Let there be light: On the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology/Medicine

For Nishith Gupta, professor of Biological Sciences at BITS Pilani, Hyderabad, and founder of the Intracellular Parasite Education and Research Labs (iPEARL), the recognition has a personal significance in his own scientific journey.

Mr. Gupta’s decades-long collaboration with Hegemann at Humboldt University of Berlin, where Hegemanna is Hertie Senior Professor of Neuroscience, helped extend optogenetic approaches beyond neuroscience into his study of Toxoplasma gondii, an intracellular parasite that infects humans, mammals, and birds.
Interactive Guide | Nobel Prize 2026
Professor of Biological Sciences at BITS Pilani-Hyderabad Campus, Nishith Gupta with Peter Hegemann, 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine laureate.
Optogenetics enables scientists to control selected cells or biological processes using light-sensitive proteins.

The Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine stated: “It all began with Peter Hegemann’s curiosity. He wondered how Chlamydomonas, a single-celled alga, is able to swim towards a light source. In the early 2000s, he and Georg Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, an algal protein with unique properties, found on the surface of the cell. When it is illuminated by blue light, a channel opens through the protein. Charged ions then flow into the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that regardless of which cell they put the protein in, those cells became light sensitive.” In 2005, Deisseroth showed that introducing channelrhodopsin into rat neurons allowed blue light to trigger nerve signals. In 2007, he showed light-based control in mice.
A researcher at iPEARL, BITS Pilani-Hyderabad Campus with Peter Hegemann, 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine laureate.

In contrast, Mr. Gupta, Mr. Hegemann and others used light-regulated enzyme adenylate cyclase, which converts adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy of a living cell, to produce cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate (cAMP). This molecule acts as messengers, helping transmit signals within cells.

Put simply, the researchers showed that light controls the enzyme, the enzyme produces cAMP, and cAMP helps regulate what happens inside the parasite (Toxoplasma gondii): how it enters cells, moves, and exits cells. This landmark study was published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry in 2013.
