This is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned it could become the deadliest, as it continues to outpace efforts to track and contain it.

The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Vaccine and treatment trials are under way in Congo's Ituri province, the outbreak's epicentre.

title: Break the chain: On leprosy in India

content.value: While the prevalence of leprosy among adults and children and the grade-2 disability rate have dropped in India over the last decade, its continued transmission in many pockets constrains India’s ability to meet targets outlined in the National Strategic Plan (NSP) and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023-2027. By 2005, the national prevalence had dropped to under 1 case per 10,000 people, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare that India had “eliminated [leprosy] as a public health problem”. However, the government became complacent and allowed the folding of the leprosy surveillance programme into the general health system. Multi-drug treatment regimens also shortened the time for which patients remained formally registered, allowing prevalence to fall and transmission to continue. Disability due to leprosy began to rise in the early 2010s, prompting door-to-door screening. Today, the NSP is right to focus on cutting transmission, in line with WHO. Since India’s children accounted for around 46% of all cases reported among children in 2025, the two programmes need to move in tandem. The drop in disease burden has also been highly uneven — Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, and Maharashtra bear disproportionate shares of the national burden. According to the 2025-26 National Leprosy Elimination Programme report, only 148 districts have achieved ‘interruption of transmission’ (pending field verification) against the projected 300.

In 2025-26, workers screened more than 70 crore people in highly endemic areas, where 24,367 cases were detected, and ASHA workers flagged nearly 40 lakh suspected cases, with 48,027 cases confirmed. Workers also administered single-dose rifampicin as post-exposure prophylaxis to 91.1% of those 16.9 lakh likely to have come in contact. The government has operationalised digital surveillance and is deliberating on using the MIP vaccine to accelerate pathogen clearance in patients deemed highly infectious. One persistent set of lacunae pertains to care: research has shown nerve damage in many patients by the time they sought care, largely due to the stigma, while many clinical practitioners are unfamiliar with leprosy’s pathology or misdiagnose it as a skin condition. Reading these realities together, the state should double down on interrupting transmission and make prevalence a secondary outcome. It should also resist the temptation to ease detection or revise its elimination targets — the 2025-26 report says the overall incidence overshot projections by 41%, incidence among children by 91.6%, and the grade-2 disability rate by 34% — and instead redouble its investments to meet the extant 2026-27 projections. Finally, it should commit its augmented efforts at locations and social settings where both late diagnosis and transmission remain trenchant.

title: AVMLabs launches first laboratory in Coimbatore

content.value: AVMLabs, promoted by former Thyrocare founder A. Velumani, opened its first laboratory in India at New Siddhapudur in Coimbatore recently.

The laboratory is the first of 25 planned in India. The AVM Bhavan facility will also house experience centres of AVMSmiles and AVMDiabetes, which are being developed along with AVMLabs under the “AVM 2.0” initiative.

The three businesses will offer diagnostics and dental and diabetes services through a franchise model, with a focus on expanding access to affordable healthcare. AVMSmiles currently has over 180 clinics, including five in Coimbatore, and plans to expand to 5,000 clinics. AVMDiabetes has a similar target across 5,000 taluks. The outlets are also expected to serve as collection centres for AVMLabs.
Mr. Velumani said the model would build on the principles of high volumes, a focused test menu and centralised processing that had helped make diagnostic testing affordable.

AVMLabs has operations in five locations in the Gulf. A central reference laboratory is planned in Bengaluru, while a Global Capability Centre is proposed in Coimbatore to cater to international markets.
The expansion is expected to create about 10,000 jobs in Tamil Nadu, Mr. Velumani said.

title: Keralam sets up task force to draw up holistic health and longevity road map

content.value: The Keralam government has constituted a high-level task force to develop an evidence-based road map for a phased prevention and early detection framework, along with appropriate treatment and rehabilitation plan, and an action plan for healthy ageing, with the broader objective of establishing a “Kerala Holistic Model for Health, Wellness and Longevity”.

According to the government order issued by the Health and Family Welfare department on Wednesday, the task force will be headed by the Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, with Health Minister K. Muraleedharan as vice-chairman. Sharmila Mary Joseph, Principal Secretary (Health and Family Welfare and AYUSH), will be the member-coordinator.

The 16-member task force includes K.R. Jyothilal, Additional Chief Secretary (Finance); Ratan Kelkar, Secretary to the Chief Minister; Deepak Singhal, former Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary; Shiv Kumar Sarin, Director of Institute of Liver and Biliary Sciences, New Delhi; Faizal E Kottikolon, chairman, KEF Holdings; C. Devidas Varier, managing director of AVP Coimbatore; Harsh Mahajan, chairman of Mahajan Imaging and Labs; Pratap Chauhan, chairman Jive Ayurva; Kancherioa Ravindranath, chairman, Global Hospital, Hyderabad; S.S. Lal, Director ReAct Asia Pacific; P.M. Varier, chief physician, Arya Vaidya Sala Kottakkal; M.V. Pillai, chairman International Cancer Care Network, USA, and Nisha Nigil, President-elect, Association of Kerala Medical Graduates in North America.
The task force has been asked first to assess Keralam’s disease burden, ageing trends, healthcare service capacity and gaps in access, and identify priority populations, diseases and districts.
Path forward

It will then design a phased prevention and early-detection framework covering risk assessment, screening protocols, referral pathways, follow-up and measurable coverage targets, aligned with existing State and national programmes.

A significant component of its mandate is to explore and identify evidence-based models for coordination among modern medicine, Ayurveda and other recognised systems of medicine. The order specifically calls for clearly defined scopes of practice, clinical governance, consent, contraindications, referral mechanisms and adverse-event reporting.

The task force will also examine the creation of a network of diagnostic, hospital, rehabilitation and wellness services, including criteria for pilot projects, accreditation, quality assurance and independent evaluation.

Another proposed component is the implementation of a Keralam Health Intelligence and Longevity Grid, with emphasis on interoperability with existing health systems, consent, privacy, cybersecurity and data stewardship.
Its mandate extends to workforce development in nursing, allied health, public health and relevant systems of medicine. It will also set uop research partnerships in health economics and financing.

The task force has been asked to examine possible investment and public-private partnership (PPP) models for diagnostics and wellness infrastructure, specifying fiscal exposure, procurement safeguards and public benefit.
It will also examine  standards and opportunities for health and wellness tourism and identify the legal, regulatory and institutional changes required to implement its recommendations.

The order also recommends facilitation and support of the proposed World Holistic Health Forum, “a global NGO”, after assessing its purpose, financial commitment and expected outcomes so that Kerala’s positioning as a “cradle and destination” for holistic health, wellness and longevity can be explored.
Action-oriented report
The task force is required to submit an action-oriented report within two months of its first meeting.

The report is expected to contain a baseline assessment and priorities, two or three defined pilot projects with details;  a three-year phased roadmap, indicative costs and funding sources and fiscal risks.
The task force is also expected to draft institutional and regulatory measures, and an implementation dashboard specifying milestones and accountable departments.

The Health and Family Welfare department will function as the nodal department, with support from AYUSH, Finance and other departments. Research, analytical, financial, technical and secretarial personnel will be deputed from the Health Department and its attached organisations.

title: Free health camp extends services to nearly 600 students, youth in Anantapur

content.value: A mega free health and medical camp was organised at Government Polytechnic College in Anantapur on Wednesday. The camp extended essential healthcare services to nearly 600 students and youth with the message “Healthy Youth, Healthy Nation”.

The camp was organised by Nigama Foundation in coordination with NSS, JNTUA, Government Polytechnic College, Anantapur, Pragathi Padham Youth Association and MY Bharat of the Union Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports. The initiative was held as part of the foundation day celebrations of Nigama Foundation.

The programme was attended by G. Mamatha, NSS coordinator, JNTUA; Bisathi Bharath, MY Bharat Representative and national youth awardee; Jaya Chandra, principal, Government Polytechnic College; Vasundhara Penakalapati, Nigama Foundation, along with medical professionals, faculty members and volunteers.

In collaboration with KH Mind Care Hospital, Anantapur, Indian Red Cross Society, Anantapur, and Icon Eye Hospital, the camp provided free blood grouping, haemoglobin and diabetes screening, blood-pressure checks, general and orthopaedic consultations, and eye examinations to the students.

Speaking at the programme, G. Mamatha appreciated the Nigama Foundation for extending selfless healthcare services to students, particularly those from rural backgrounds. She highlighted the importance of such initiatives in promoting preventive healthcare, mental well-being and healthy lifestyles among young people.

She also appreciated Nigama Foundation’s continued youth-oriented initiatives, including mental health awareness, Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat, screen de-addiction and educational support for students and youth in rural and remote areas.

title: ISRO scientists lead space awareness rally in Rajamahendravaram

content.value: Students, academicians, bureaucrats led by Scientists of the ISRO’s Satish Dhavan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR), Sriharikota, on Wednesday took out a space awareness rally in in Rajamahendravaram on Wednesday to highlight India’s achievements in space science .
The rally was held ahead of the two-day International Space Week celebrations scheduled to be celebrated in Anam Kalakendram in Rajamahendravaram from Thursday.
Government Arts College principal R. Ramachandra Rao flagged off the rally, which was held between the Arts College and Anam Kalakendram.

Addressing the gathering, Mr. Ramchandra Rao said that the rally and Space Week would help students and members of civil society to understand ISRO’s contributions and India’s advancements in space science.
ISRO scientists will display replicas of Indian satellites and provide details of the space programmes during the two-day celebrations.

title: Students should be encouraged to develop scientific temperament, says Deputy Director of U. R. Rao Satellite Centre

content.value: Deputy Director of U.R. Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), Bengaluru, C.S. Madhusudhan said on Wednesday that students should be encouraged to develop a scientific temperament by cultivating the habit of questioning, examining and thinking based on evidence.

Speaking after inaugurating the two-day World Space Week - 2026 programme at Pilikula Regional Science Centre he said that technology should be used logically and that students should apply the knowledge gained from books in their daily lives.
He said that the programme, organised by Pilikula Development Authority in association with URSC and ISRO, provided a valuable platform for the interaction of students and teachers.

Speaking on the occasion, G. Srinikethan. a retired professor of National Institute of Technology-Surathkal, said that continuous research and innovative developments in rocket technology have opened up new possibilities in the field of space exploration.

He encouraged students to make the best use of the valuable opportunity to interact with ISRO scientists, expand their knowledge and contribute to enhancing the country’s reputation in the field of space science and technology.
N. Arun Kumar Shetty, commissioner, Pilikula Development Authority, said that innovative ideas, technology and collaboration should be given greater importance in building a developed India.
Mr. Shetty encouraged students to develop new ideas with the aim of improving people’s lives and contribute to the development of the nation.

There was display of ISRO space science models and exhibits in the gallery adjacent to the Swami Vivekananda Planetarium. A special 2D show titled ‘The Moon’ was also organised for the students at the planetarium.
A satellite model making competition was organised on the occasion.
Around 750 students and teachers from various high schools, pre-university colleges and diploma colleges from Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts participated in the programme.

title: SpaceX exec renews Starlink pitch as approvals lay pending

content.value: Years into SpaceX’s efforts to get permission to operate its satellite broadband service in India, a senior executive of the firm once again pitched Starlink as a last-mile internet access solution in the country.

“We can’t talk about building the future at scale without talking about closing the digital divide, because otherwise we’d just be building a future that leaves a substantial portion of the population behind,” Lauren Dreyer, Vice President of Starlink Business Operations at SpaceX said at the India Mobile Congress (IMC) on Tuesday (October 6, 2026).

While Starlink has obtained a Global Mobile Personal Communications by Satellite (GMPCS) authorisation from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), the government has not yet cleared the security approvals that Starlink needs to operate. These requirements, some of which were, require SpaceX to disable Starlink receivers purchased outside India, and to also disable terminals sold in India abroad. This is on top of extensive surveillance requirements that apply across the telecom and broadband sector.
Also Read | Permit to Starlink bars copying, decryption of Indian data overseas: MoS Telecom

“[F]or the past five years, Starlink has been working closely with Indian regulators, industry and operators to understand how to adapt and prepare the Starlink operations here in India to serve India best,” Ms. Dreyer said at the event.

“We’ve built our Starlink operations specifically for India in recognition of Indian security requirements and other regulations, establishing controls at every layer for India and keeping Indian user data within India. We’ve already made the investment and built the existing ground infrastructure here — 20 gateway sites comprising hundreds of antennas — and we’ve established the operations to be ready to serve India.”

Ms. Dreyer pointed out that SpaceX has worked closely with the government and with Indian firms already. “SpaceX launched ISRO’s GSAT-N2 communications satellite; we carried Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla to and from the International Space Station, [and] we have also carried two dedicated missions and 19 rideshare missions for Indian space companies to help them reach orbit,” she said.
Regulatory issues

“With Starlink, people can get connected within minutes, not years,” Ms. Dreyer said. But it has certainly taken the firm years to convince the government to let it operate. In 2021, the DoT censured the firm for taking preorder payments from Indian users ahead of its global rollout. The following year, the firm said it would refund users in India. It still took a few years for SpaceX to obtain a GMPCS authorisation.

Once the government provides its nod, the service can start practically instantly, since the satellites already overfly every part of the planet. Ms. Dreyer said she hoped this nod would come through next year.

“Hopefully next time I address the Congress, the government’s good work [processing the firm’s security approvals] will have been complete, and Starlink will be authorised and ready,” Ms. Dreyer said. “We’re ready to help Prime Minister Modi achieve his vision of 100% connectivity throughout India — a vision all of our company, including Elon [Musk, SpaceX CEO], shares as well.”

title: Gradiant bets big on India, secures five contracts, including semiconductor fab

content.value: Water technology company Gradiant is expanding its India operations with five new design-and-build contracts across the semiconductor, printed circuit board (PCB) and solar manufacturing sectors, while planning to increase its India workforce by more than 40% this year.

The Woburn, Massachusetts-based company -- which  designs, builds and operates water treatment systems for industries including semiconductors, data centres, energy and other industrial sectors. --  said orders in India were on track to more than double this year, while revenue was expected to more than triple.

Gradiant has also appointed Hari Prasad as Managing Director, India. Mr. Prasad brings nearly three decades of experience in water technology and was most recently General Manager, Industrial Water at Pentair. He has previously held senior positions across India, the Middle East and Africa.
Gradiant currently generates annual revenue of about $500 million-$750 million, with India contributing around 10%

The new contracts include a repeat order from a global semiconductor manufacturer for the expansion of its fabrication facility. Gradiant will provide ultrapure water, wastewater treatment and zero liquid discharge (ZLD) systems for the projects. The company did not disclose the value of the contracts or name the customers.
The company is also scaling up its India team across engineering, project execution, operations and digital functions. Its engineering centre in Coimbatore supports Gradiant’s projects globally.
“India is fast becoming one of the most important places to build the AI supply chain, from chips to circuit boards to solar cells,” said Prakash Govindan, CEO, Gradiant.
Mr. Govindan said the repeat semiconductor order underscored the company’s capabilities and positioned Gradiant to support the expansion of India’s manufacturing base.
“A fab or a solar plant can’t run a single shift without water, and the ZLD rules here leave no room for shortcuts,” Mr. Prasad said.

title: Norway’s proposed moratorium on smart glasses | Explained

content.value: European regulators are training their sights on smart glasses, as the wearable device equipped with high-definition cameras, ambient audio recording, and artificial intelligence is becoming common in Europe, blurring the lines between technological innovation and citizens’ privacy. Norway is taking the lead as its government prepares a proposal seeking a temporary ban on smart glasses in select public and sensitive locations. Led by Minister of Digitalisation and Public Governance Torgeir Micaelsen, the initiative pauses device usage in places where individuals expect personal privacy.
What does the proposal seek?

The temporary restrictions target places frequented by children, including schools, playgrounds, and youth clubs, healthcare facilities, fitness centres, locker rooms, public beaches, parks, museums, and concert venues. Crucially, the government is not proposing a ban on sales of the devices or prohibiting their use in private. Instead, the proposal is asking an expert committee to evaluate the technological challenges and formulate lasting legal frameworks. Oslo has already banned smart glasses across municipal schools.

The core argument behind Norway’s intervention centres on the lack of consent in public spaces. Traditional smartphones require users to visibly hold up a device to record video or snap photos, providing a clear signal to surrounding people. In contrast, smart glasses allow wearers to capture high-resolution imagery, record ambient audio, or live-stream video directly at the eye level without offering clear cues to bystanders.

This creates a surveillance system where citizens cannot easily determine whether they are being recorded. Privacy risks are especially acute in sensitive settings like changing rooms and medical clinics, or where unauthorised filming of children raises safety concerns. Furthermore, officials have highlighted risks surrounding real-time facial recognition software. When combined with AI eyewear, facial recognition could enable wearers to instantly identify strangers, access personal data, or facilitate doxxing. Norway’s proposed rules acknowledge that traditional privacy frameworks were not designed for head-worn, ambient recording technology.
Is any other country attempting a similar moratorium?
Norway is not alone in addressing privacy risks surrounding wearable devices, as a patchwork of regulations and venue-specific restrictions are in progress across Europe and North America.

In the Netherlands and Germany, eyewear retailer Hans Anders suspended sales of Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses across its Dutch and Belgian stores while awaiting regulatory clarity. Dutch lawmakers have discussed rules that await guidance from the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). Meanwhile, Hamburg is exploring regional restrictions.

The UK Cinema Association established guidelines restricting or prohibiting camera-equipped glasses in movie theatres to combat piracy and protect privacy of viewers. Additionally, courts in England and Wales require visitors to surrender smart glasses at security checkpoints.

In United States, several nightclubs, gyms, and courts in New York have implemented localised bans. California’s governor vetoed a legislation penalising covert recording in private spaces, but debate continues among state policymakers on next steps.
In Bangkok , smart glasses use is restricted in certain pubs and public places.
How are manufacturers of smart glasses adapting to this regulatory landscape?

To address privacy concerns, hardware manufacturers have built technical safeguards into current-generation devices. Devices such as Ray-Ban Meta glasses feature a white light-emitting diode (LED) on the frame beside the lens. The LED blinks when capturing photos and stays lit continuously during video recording.

Manufacturers have deployed firmware updates that detect if the LED indicator is covered or obstructed. If light obstruction is detected, the system automatically disables the camera’s functionality. Devices enforce caps on continuous recording duration and play audible shutter sounds when taking photos.

But privacy advocates have said that small LED lights remain difficult to spot in bright sunlit conditions or crowded environments, rendering hardware safeguards insufficient for complete bystander protection.
How will the moratorium impact device sales?

Although Norway’s proposal focuses on restricting device usage rather than banning sales, the commercial impact on manufacturers could be substantial. The primary selling point of smart glasses is their seamless integration into daily public life. Restricting their use in public spaces like parks, beaches, shopping centres, and fitness clubs undermine their utility, rendering a versatile daily use accessory into a device restricted to home use.

In addition, voluntary retail suspensions such as the sales halt by Hans Anders, create immediate revenue hits in the European market. Regulatory uncertainty across different regions introduces consumer hesitation, discouraging buyers who worry about purchasing expensive hardware that might soon face usage restrictions in public.
How might smart glass makers tweak functionality?

To comply with evolving privacy standards and maintain consumer trust, manufacturers may likely re-engineer both hardware and software features by implementing larger, brighter, or colour-shifting LED indicators, alongside louder audio signals that cannot be silenced.

Software updates could incorporate AI-driven face-blurring and audio pitch modification, redacting bystander identities before footage is saved or streamed. Smart glasses could utilise GPS data to automatically disable recording capabilities when entering designated privacy zones like schools, hospitals, or locker rooms. Manufacturers can explicitly block facial recognition software and APIs to prevent real-time profiling in public spaces.
Companies are expanding lines to include audio-focused smart glasses without cameras (such as Ray-Ban Meta Audio), catering to users who want AI features without privacy concerns.

title: AI appears to have been used in bank hacks: South Korean President Lee

content.value: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that AI models are believed to have been used in some recent hacking ‌incidents against banks and called for the country to develop cybersecurity methods suited to the AI era.
“In some ‌hacking incidents, signs have emerged of AI being used, ‌causing ⁠considerable public concern and anxiety,” Lee said during a ⁠cabinet meeting.
“Please establish the circumstances swiftly and clearly, and concentrate personnel and resources on minimising the damage.”

South Korea’s police have launched a full-scale investigation into ​the hacking attacks against commercial ‌banks that led to a breach of customers’ personal information, the Yonhap news agency reported on Tuesday.

Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and others had reported cyberattacks, the Financial Services Commission (FSC) said ‌on Friday, while Yonhap reported that Hana Bank ​and Woori Bank also suffered breaches.
Authorities have not yet disclosed details on what kind of AI tools ⁠were used in the hacking incidents or the full scale of the breaches.

On Sunday, FSC Chairman Lee Eog-weon convened an emergency meeting ‌with financial industry associations, regulators and executives from affected institutions, warning that the sector must respond with the highest level of vigilance.

Financial watchdog the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) and the Financial Security Institute shared data about 28 unique IP addresses and some country information linked to the recent hacking attempts with the ‌financial sector, the FSS said on Tuesday.

In September, Australia said an OpenAI ​agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access to files, in what could be ⁠the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government ⁠website.

An artificial intelligence research firm said last week that AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government ‌website, casting the effort as a failed hacking attempt, while Canada said there were no indications its systems were ​compromised.

title: Tap space-tech start-ups’ capabilities for major projects of Indian space programme: G. Madhavan Nair

content.value: The talents and resources of space-tech start-ups should be tapped for flagship initiatives such as landing an Indian astronaut on the moon and building the Bharat Antariksh Station rather than encouraging unhealthy competition with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), former Chairperson of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) G. Madhavan Nair has said.

Inaugurating a seminar on ‘ISRO’s Future: Concerns and Anxieties,’ organised by the ISRO Pensioners’ Association in Thiruvananthapuram on Wednesday (October 7, 2026), Dr. Nair questioned the rationale of start-ups developing rockets with 300-kg payload capability when ISRO’s Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) could launch up to 500 kg. Such efforts have value if the launch vehicle is extremely cost-effective, reliable and has a better turn-around time.

Dr. Nair said that, in his assessment, ISRO alone has the capability to achieve the aims of landing an Indian astronaut on the moon or building India’s space station. “Only ISRO can conceive the total mission, break it up into sub-systems, qualify them and fructify the missions in minimum time,” he said.

He called for cooperation among ISRO, start-ups and the industry for the future progress of India’s space programme. What is required is a cooperative environment rather than unhealthy competition, he said.
Foreign funding

Dr. Nair dismissed concerns regarding the role of private players in the Indian space programme saying that ISRO-private industry relations had begun 50 years ago with the SLV-3 project. On concerns over foreign funding in space start-ups, he said the government should look into such issues.

Former director of the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre M.C. Dathan, former KELTRON chairman and ISRO veteran N. Narayana Moorthy, ISRO Pensioners’ Association president A.G. Rajendran and general secretary Johnson S. Fernandez spoke.

title: In this Delhi studio, tintype brings chemistry into every portrait

content.value: In an age when a portrait can be made in a fraction of a second, Vibhav Kapoor, artist and assistant professor at O.P. Jindal Global University, Sonipat, spends several minutes making one photograph, much of the time spent negotiating with chemistry.
In his Delhi-NCR studio, Mr. Kapoor works with tintype, a 19th-century photographic process in which an image is created directly on a metal plate.
The French photographer Adolphe Alexandre Martin is credited with developing the technique in 1853, two years after Frederick Scott Archer invented the wet-plate collodion process.
Chemically demanding
Unlike processes that produced glass negatives or paper prints, tintypes created a positive image directly on a dark metal plate.

Mr. Kapoor takes a plate with collodion, a syrupy solution of nitrocellulose dissolved in ether and alcohol. He pours it onto a metal plate to form a thin, sticky film, and sensitises it in a silver-nitrate bath in which the iodides and bromides react with silver nitrate to form light-sensitive silver iodide and silver bromide.

Finally, he exposes these light-sensitive compounds through a large-format camera, and develops the images in a dark room using a ferrous sulphate solution acidified with glacial acetic acid and thinned with alcohol; it amplifies the latent image by converting more exposed silver halides into visible metallic silver.
The entire sequence from coating to fixing must be completed while the plate remains wet. There is also no negative to reprint from, so duplicating tintypes is equally arduous.
19th century process

In the mid-19th century, the tintype process was valued for being relatively inexpensive and durable. The dominant photographic process of the era was the daguerreotype. It was costly because it required silver-plated copper sheets as the base material plus iodine and mercury vapour to develop images. Together with the labour-intensive crafting process, each daguerreotype was a luxury item.
Tintypes, however, afforded portraits outside the more formal, expensive photographic studios of the period. In India as well, the process formed part of the early history of photography.

In 1864, a British photographer named T. Murray introduced Sawai Ram Singh II of Jaipur to the tintype camera and documented his court, architecture, and lives of women in the royal zenana. Murray is also known to have helped the ruler develop a royal archive of visuals.
According to Mr. Kapoor, the Jaipur royal photographer Ram Singh also used the process.
“It is a very traditional, hand-made process,” Mr. Kapoor said. But its apparent simplicity conceals a process that demands scientific precision.

Mr. Kapoor first learnt tintype photography during his master’s degree at the Rochester Institute of Technology, New York, which he spent coating plates, photographing, developing, drying, and finally varnishing the finished image.

The way tintype works also affects the photographer and the subject. The CMOS sensors in today’s digital cameras are so fast that a person needs to pose for just a second. On the other hand, the light-sensitive compounds in tintype photography ‘record’ the light over 8-10 seconds, so the subjects need to present themselves still for that period.
For a portrait, as Mr. Kapoor put it, “The person is performing …, presenting themselves.”
The image emerges in 10 to 15 minutes thereafter.
Weather and chemistry
That said, the photograph’s most unpredictable component is the weather.
“The chemistry is very volatile and humidity plays a crucial role,” Mr. Kapoor said.
“During the monsoon, the humidity causes the tintypes to develop spots,” Matthew Fossier, a U.S. tintype practitioner in Texas, said.

Dust is another serious problem. As dust particles settle on the wet collodion layer, they interrupt the formation of silver halide crystals. When the plate is developed, the affected area produces metallic silver differently from the surrounding film, and which appears as an opaque or transparent spot.

Temperature fluctuations can create other artefacts as well, per Mr. Fossier. The collodion contains volatile solvents and heat makes them evaporate faster, leaving the film to become sticky. The plate must be moved quickly to the silver-nitrate bath, where silver ions react with the halides in the collodion to form the light-sensitive silver-halide layer. If the collodion has begun to set unevenly by then, however, the resulting layer can be uneven as well.
He added that the effect is pronounced when pouring the collodion, which reduces the time available to get the plate into the silver bath.
According to Mr. Kapoor, the Delhi-NCR temperatures require him to adjust his solutions: “Heat acts as a catalyst [and] more heat means reactions are faster. The developer has to be managed.”

The developer is a chemical solution that reveals the image captured on a sensitised metal plate after exposure. But in warmer weather, the developer works faster, causing streaks or an uneven fog to appear in the picture.
To avoid this, Mr. Kapoor dilutes the developer to change its strength and how long it stays on the plate, slowing the reaction, and allowing the picture to develop clearly.
Unique images
Mr. Kapoor has worked with a fashion brand called rkive.city to photograph the Maharaja of Jaipur Sawai Padmanabh Singh.
He is now looking to make more tintypes, particularly portraits, from his new studio in Shahpur Jat in the national capital.

Photography arrived in India in the 19th century, and the wet-collodion processes became ubiquitous as tintypes circulated in Indian towns in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Today, however, Mr. Kapoor said “only a handful of photographers in India practice tintype”.

Mr. Kapoor’s tintype camera is a large-format antique that uses a 5x7-inch plate. The camera is built of polished dark wood with metal parts, and a leather bellow that folds in and out like an accordion as the cover.
“When I am taking tintypes of people,” Mr. Kapoor said, “I think they are very fascinated, first of all by the camera, and by the spectacle of the process.”
Aditya Ansh is an independent media writer based in New Delhi.

title: Tamil Nadu may encounter El Niño differently from rest of India

content.value: The El Niño Southern Oscillation is a climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that happens every two to seven years. Its effects, however, are global.

This year, weather agencies worldwide are tracking a supposed ‘super’ El Niño. The El Niño refers to surface waters of the Pacific Ocean off the western coast of Peru and Ecuador becoming warmer than average. Typically, these waters warm by about 0.5 °C, but this year the rise has reached 2 °C — a phenomenon referred to as a ‘super’ El Niño.

title: Chemistry Nobel 2026 honours the science of mirrored molecules

content.value: French chemist Henri Kagan and Japanese chemist Kenso Soai have won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 2026 for their work showing how chemical reactions can amplify small asymmetries in molecules. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said they have been feted “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.
Nobel Prize 2026: An interactive guide
Mr. Kagan is a professor emeritus at the former Université Paris-Sud, and Mr. Soai is a professor emeritus at the Tokyo University of Science. They will share the prize equally.

The duo’s work is centered on chiral molecules, which are molecules that can exist in two mirror-image forms, like a left and a right hand. The two versions are called enantiomers. Each enantiomer can interact very differently with other chiral molecules — a property that has had an outsized impact on biology.
Editorial | Let there be light: On the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology/Medicine

For example, the proteins in our bodies are made mostly of amino acids that have one of the two mirror-image arrangements. The enzymes that speed up chemical reactions in cells and the receptors that look out for chemical signals and trigger responses are also chiral. As a result, the two enantiomers of a chiral drug can interact differently with these molecules and elicit different responses, only of which might be desirable.
This was a challenge for chemists who had to manufacture the correct enantiomer of a drug rather than a mixture of both, which was the norm.
Scientists also puzzled over why so many molecules important for life occur in just one of their two possible handed forms.

In 1986, Mr. Kagan and his team made a landmark discovery. Chemists often use catalysts to speed up certain reactions. The team found that the chiral parts of a catalyst could combine in pairs, and opposite-handed pairs could react differently from same-handed ones. If the opposite-handed pairs reacted poorly, they could remove the minority form from the reaction, leaving the active catalyst more one-handed, and producing a disproportionately one-handed product.
Others were able to use this finding to work back from the products of a reaction to its microscopic mechanism, then accordingly redesign the reaction to produce more desirable products.

Soai et al. picked up from here and, in 1995, showed that a chiral molecule could speed up the formation of more molecules with its own handedness. In the so-called Soai reaction, scientists found that even if 0.00005% more right-handed than left-handed molecules entered a reaction, after just three rounds, 99.75% of the molecules could be right-handed.
Nobel Prize 2026 Winners | Full List

The impact of the laureates’ work has also differed. Scientists today use the findings of Mr. Kagan & co. to optimise reactions to produce specific enantiomers of drugs, agrochemicals, and fragrances.

Mr. Soai’s impact, on the other hand, has been on biochemistry: his work has allowed scientists to keep open the possibility that some small, random imbalance in the concentration of enantiomers billions of years ago became amplified to the overwhelming handedness we see in biological molecules today.

title: The Nobel for IceCube and the search for neutrinos from outer space | Explained

content.value: The story so far: Belgian-born U.S. physicist Francis Halzen has won the physics Nobel Prize for 2026 for helping build the IceCube observatory in Antarctica — a telescope that has no mirrors or lenses and doesn’t even point at the stars. Using 5,000 sensors buried deep in the ice, IceCube has explored what natural processes in the cosmos can accelerate subatomic particles to energies far beyond any human technologies have managed so far.
What are neutrinos?

Since the early 20th century, scientists have known that energetic particles called cosmic rays constantly bombard the earth from outer space. Most cosmic rays are protons or the nuclei of elements like helium and iron. Some of these particles have been found to have more energy than the world’s largest particle accelerator — the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in Europe — can manage.

Scientists thought powerful events like exploding stars or jets of energy emitted by distant galaxies could have given these particles a Herculean push, but they couldn’t know for sure. Just looking in the direction a cosmic ray came from didn’t help. Since cosmic rays are charged particles, they could have been deflected by magnetic fields in space before reaching the earth.

So scientists turned to neutrinos. These subatomic particles have no electric charge, a very small mass, and interact very rarely with matter. Nuclear reactions, like fusion in the sun’s belly, produce neutrinos in copious numbers, and trillions of them pass through your body — and through the earth — every second without leaving any trace. And they travel in a straight line through space.
How do you catch a neutrino?

Halzen and others came up with the idea of IceCube to ‘catch’ and study neutrinos with very high energy. When a cosmic-ray proton strikes other atoms, it can produce particles called pions, which rapidly decay through reactions that could produce neutrinos. And these high-energy neutrinos are an indication that some high-energy event produced them.

But neutrinos’ reluctance to interact with matter also makes them extremely hard to catch. This is why the IceCube observatory is in Antarctica: the enormous volume of frozen water ice is the catcher, and the 5,000 sensors embedded in the ice look for the occasional evidence of a neutrino striking the ice.

This idea actually predated Halzen’s insight, going back to the 1960s. Scientists, including John Learned, once tried to build a detector in the Pacific Ocean but maintaining the facility’s instruments underwater proved too difficult. In 1987, after being alerted to a Soviet Union plan to study neutrinos in Antarctic ice, Halzen, Thomas Stanev, and Enrique Zas concluded the approach would be unsuitable for the energies they were interested in.

Instead, Halzen wondered if it’d be possible to track neutrinos colliding with ice by looking for small flashes of light their collisions might produce. After discussing the idea with Learned, the two physicists proposed using South Pole ice as a neutrino catcher, with Halzen going on to organise the effort, funded primarily by the U.S. National Science Foundation, that eventually became IceCube.

According to the Nobel committee, Halzen has been feted for proposing the idea as well as keeping hundreds of scientists and engineers working on it for decades. In this sense, the physics prize this year is reminiscent of the same prize for Barry Barish in 2017, who coordinated the complex effort to set up the LIGO gravitational-wave detectors.
How does IceCube work?

After unsurprising delays and setbacks attending to an enterprise of this magnitude, IceCube took its full shape in 2011 following seven years of construction. In particular, crews of experts dug holes in the ice to place the sensors not using shovels but by shooting jets of hot water, then lowering sensors suspended on cables fast enough before the ice froze again.

Today, IceCube includes 5,160 optical sensors on 86 cables, lying 1.4 km to 2.4 km under the ice, altogether encompassing roughly a cubic kilometre of ice. Each sensor has a device that converts the faint light from a collision into an electric signal and records it. The collective data flows to computers on the surface and thereon to researchers around the world.

When an energetic neutrino strikes an atom’s nucleus inside the ice, the event creates charged particles that streak through the surrounding ice. Some of them even move faster than light can in that material. Just as doing this with sound creates shockwaves, outrunning light causes the particles to emit Cherenkov radiation, visible as a dull blue glow. The sensors look for and record this emission.

Different kinds of neutrino interactions produce different kinds of particles that outrun light. Taking this together with which sensors recorded the glow and in what order, IceCube researchers can piece together the neutrino’s energy and direction. Of the lakh or so neutrinos IceCube registers every year above an energy cutoff, only around a hundred come from astrophysical sources in outer space.
What has IceCube found?

In 2013, scientists identified two neutrinos with around 140-times the energy of a proton accelerated by the LHC. With more data and analysis, the collaboration established that a population of high-energy neutrinos was coming to our planet from elsewhere in the universe — and that IceCube could spot them. It was a landmark event in a new field called neutrino astronomy.

In 2017, IceCube found an energetic neutrino coming from a distant galaxy, whose central black hole was also powering a jet of radiation pointed roughly at the earth. In 2022, the instrument found more neutrinos than expected coming from NGC 1068, a galaxy 46 million lightyears away, also with an active central black hole.

The observatory has also been a centerpiece of multi-messenger astronomy, in which astronomers study the universe using a combination of messengers — e.g. light particles (e.g. visible light, gamma rays, etc.), neutrinos, and gravitational waves — to acquire a picture more complete than only one of these modes could reveal.

IceCube’s own work remains unfinished as scientists are still working on the sources of the universe’s most energetic neutrinos and how neutrino-catching events can be correlated with, say, observations in gamma rays. IceCube has won Halzen his prize, then, for opening a window into parts of the universe that were until recently beyond our reach and for showing that an international scientific collaboration can achieve more than the sum of its parts.

title: Let there be light: On the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology/Medicine

content.value: The first of the Nobel announcements has come, heralding the season of celebrating the fruits of the perennial human endeavour to know more and use that knowledge to benefit people. The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegeman and Georg Nagel “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”. True to Alfred Bernhard Nobel’s aim of annually recognising those who have “conferred the greatest benefit to humankind”, this year’s Nobel went to people who shone a light, literally, on the brain, providing a quantum leap in understanding how it functions. In essence, if the brain is a puppeteer pulling the strings, the body is the marionette. The dexterity of the puppeteer is obvious, but her methods, often not. It is this that the Nobel trio sought to explain with optogenetics — making it possible to show how nerve cells communicate with each other, and the body, regulating memory, emotions and bodily functions. It allowed mapping the brain in ways that were previously impossible. As most often in work that the Nobel acknowledges and honours, there was rich collaboration across continents in advancing optogenetics. Peter Hegemann wondered what enabled Chlamydomonas, a single-celled alga, to swim towards a light source; Georg Nagel went on to discover an algal protein that can be illuminated with blue light to open a channel within, allowing charged ions to flow into the cell and create electrical impulses. Karl Deisseroth transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells. Practically, today, scientists use harmless viral agents to deliver genes for light-sensitive proteins into specific target cells. Then they deliver precise pulses of light, activating the channels, allowing research to study the patterns. In the decades since the laureates described their work, researchers have gone on to use optogenetics to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings and behaviours relevant to neurological and psychiatric disorders. It laid the groundwork for clinical treatments targeting conditions including Alzheimer’s and addiction. Researchers are even using the method in attempts to restore sight.

As technology facilitates easier pathways to translating scientific research that happens in labs into practical therapies, diagnostics and health-care practices that could ameliorate human health or protect it from illness, it is also important for nations to find ways to ensure that the fruits of such research actually reach all the people who might benefit from it, irrespective of their location or station in life.

title: Indian research can shape the world

content.value: People fret about the buses India has missed in its technological growth. The list is familiar: aircraft, advanced weapons, new materials, and biotechnology. In each, we look at what others built decades ago and ask why we did not. There is value in this introspection, and there is danger. The value is that it forces us to ask whether our systems can be streamlined and enabled. Catching up is not a bad thing. Much of the world’s industrial history is a history of catching up. The danger is that catch-up-itis can become a habit. If our ambition is always defined by what someone else has already done, we will always arrive late, pay for licences and know-how, and build on foundations laid elsewhere. The costs of technological catch-up are a heavy burden, and they recur with every new wave.
Also read | India has a research blindspot: its own science system

There is a better question to ask, and it arises from a tectonic change in the relationship between science and technology. By science, we mean discovery, curiosity, the effort to explain the universe, and the development of abstract ideas in mathematics. By technology, we mean the development of tools that enable humans to transform the world. For much of history, these were treated as separate enterprises, with technology following science at a distance, sometimes by a century.

However, over the past 50 years or so, we have increasingly seen fundamental research and application sewn together at the hip. Much of our understanding of how genes are regulated came from studying viruses that infect bacteria. More recently, studying how bacteria defend themselves gave us CRISPR technology within just a few years, which has an extraordinary range of applications. Today, the distance and time from curiosity to application are short. This shift lets thinking and training lead, and it shows that investing in fundamental research will enable leading than playing catch-up. The bus we need to board is the next one, and it has not yet left.
Get on the bus first
For science from India to have global impact by developing transformative technologies, four things need to be addressed.

First, invest in high-quality education at scale. The features of AI that democratise access to learning allow us to reach millions of students poorly served by our moribund institutions, and to bypass those institutions where necessary. But learning science requires doing science. Hundreds of experimental “foundries” in engineering, physics, biology, chemistry and math should be created; places where young people work with real instruments on real problems.

Second, national laboratories need to be liberated from insularity. The bulk of our national labs are currently poorly accessible to researchers, students and companies outside their walls. This can easily change, benefiting both labs and universities. All national labs need to be organised around three zones: green for open interaction, amber for collaboration, and red for strategic work. Much of what India’s labs do belong in the green and amber zones.

Third is flexibility. Many say we are a low-trust society and that our regulators should trust our research system more and be more flexible. The response to this is to point out that trust is low because compliance with guidelines is poor, necessitating onerous rules. However, India does have many high-quality islands of excellence in universities, institutes and laboratories. These institutions do comply with the rules and regulations, and should be freed from the weight of General Financial Rules compliance, a weight few other countries place on their scientists. Accountability should be measured by outcomes, and not by procedure at every step. Flexibility can allow these institutions to leap ahead.

Fourth, our regulatory system still needs much reform. Approvals for research with biological materials and for clinical trials remain slow and unpredictable. The more hoops companies and researchers must jump through, the less likely small and medium-sized institutions are to succeed, since only those with deep pockets can afford the time and costs. Thus, high-quality, speedy regulation is important.

None of this is beyond us; they can be achieved step by step. Many are already doing so in pockets. What is missing is the decision to make those pockets the norm, and a few who dedicate themselves to this task. How long will it take to become a science-driven nation with global impact? If we improve just 10% in each sector, field, and every year, we will be nearly seven times better in 20 years.
K. VijayRaghavan is Former Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India and chairs Ashoka University’s Science Advisory Council; Archish Mittal is Vice-President, Iron Pillar

title: Analysis: Why NASA wants to build nuclear reactor on the moon

content.value: NASA wants to install a nuclear reactor near the moon’s south pole by 2030. Its planned output, 20 kilowatt (kW), could power a few households on earth. Russia’s planned reactor for the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS), led by China, will produce around 10 kW. But the fact that they are nuclear makes them significant.

The U.S. and China are pursuing parallel efforts today — in partnership with other countries — to be the first to set up a semi-permanent, and in future permanent, moon base. Such a facility will need electricity for everything from heating and life-support to recharging rover batteries.

At most locations on the moon, a fortnight of daylight follows a fortnight of darkness. Near the south pole, where both factions are concentrating their activities, promontories and craters create a pastiche of lit and shadowed patches, with temperatures inside some of the latter dipping under a frigid –200 C. But unlike solar panels, a nuclear reactor can produce power irrespective of whether it receives sunlight.
Also Read | NASA plans to build a nuclear reactor on the moon

The reason the moon’s south pole has drawn this attention also changes the equation for nuclear power, however. The exceptionally colder craters preserve water ice, which can quench astronauts’ thirst and could also be electrolysed to produce hydrogen and oxygen, to be used as propellants for rockets launched from the moon itself.

In one 2020 assessment, NASA scientists Julie Kleinhenz and Aaron Paz figured producing 10 tonnes of oxygen this way would require around 68 kW of power. So a 20 kW reactor could well be a stepping stone in the U.S.’s, and China’s and Russia’s, plans to set up an array of small reactors on the moon, with an eye on industrial-scale operations in future.

Nuclear reactors also warrant some geopolitical urgency. Both the U.S. Artemis and the Chinese ILRS programmes envisage long-term activity near the moon’s south pole. European scientists are also exploring lunar microreactors and the U.K. has financed studies on nuclear power in space. The urgency arises from a scarce resource: land.
Also Read | The science, technology, and pitfalls of using nuclear power in space

While the moon as a whole is barren, the more ideal locations, with longer periods of sunlight, terrain more suitable to land on, access to craters with water ice, and so on, are highly limited. Research commissioned by NASA has recommended situating nuclear reactors at least a kilometre away from humans, further constraining the suitability of ideal patches.

Now, the Outer Space Treaty 1967 says no country may appropriate any part of the moon through occupation or other means. But the Artemis Accords, to which the U.S. and its allies vis-a-vis the moon are signatories, envisage temporary ‘safety zones’ to prevent harmful interference. Put differently, a state does not have to stake territory on the moon to limit access to others: it can simply plonk a nuclear reactor there and appeal to the need for subsequently legitimate safety requirements.

The Accords say these zones must remain temporary and respect free access but a country, or a bloc, operating a cluster of reactors, landing pads, mines, and habitats could nevertheless confer a controlling advantage.
Also Read | U.S. in race with China to claim ‘best’ part of Moon: NASA Chief

For the appeal of this idea, however, there are significant technical hurdles. Shielding a nuclear reactor on the moon demands either launching, at great cost, the components to ensure its safe operation, including shielding, or producing them on the moon with lunar resources. Distancing a reactor from a base still warrants deployment machines and power cables.

The reactor core(s) will also have to be launched unirradiated and, once online, space agencies will have to install large surfaces to radiate the copious amounts of waste heat away, and keep them free of moondust. If a reactor fails on the moon, it will risk contaminating the same few places astronauts would like to be at on the moon.

In the end, while nuclear power could prove indispensable to a mature economy centred on the moon, no country possesses that economy today even as governments are being tempted to install reactors first, before their ‘opponents’ — a danger in and of itself.

title: 'Reckless' AI firms can't control models, says whistleblower Jacob Coxon

content.value: Leading artificial intelligence companies do not know how to keep AI systems from pursuing objectives their developers did not assign, whistleblower Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI and Anthropic employee, warned Monday.
"Companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes," Coxon told local lawmakers at a hearing before the New York City Council.

In early September, the British researcher published a statement on X explaining his decision to resign from Anthropic, saying AI developers sincerely believed the technology could "kill us all by the end of the decade."
His testimony made headlines around the world, and several current and former employees of AI's major players have since voiced similar concerns.

While AI could bring "tremendous benefits" to society, "on the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control of these AIs and could end in human extinction," he said Monday.
"We don't know how to prevent them from developing goals of their own," beyond their creators' control, Coxon explained, "and we don't have the safeguards to prevent them from acting on these goals."
The Cambridge University graduate took aim at tech industry culture, saying companies "run on a startup mindset: move fast, break things, fix them later."
"That works for a photo sharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever," Coxon said.

"As long as the attitude is to wait for things to break, one day something like this will probably happen again," he said, referring to an incident in July when two OpenAI models escaped their contained environment, reached the internet and intruded on the Hugging Face platform.
"Except the AIs will be much more capable," he added.

"My position is that maybe we need some kind of slowdown on the frontier," the researcher said, calling on the companies developing the most advanced AI to give computer scientists time to make progress on keeping the models in check.

title: Privacy concerns put smart glasses under scrutiny as Norway seeks temporary ban

content.value: A trip to the park. A day at the beach. A workout session at the gym. All in public spaces where smart glasses can snap photos, record conversations or stream video online — without people in the line of their lenses and microphones knowing about it.
Norway's government wants to get a handle on both the promise and peril of AI glasses and is proposing that parliament enact a temporary ban on them in some places.

It's the latest sign of growing concern in many countries about new technologies that are fundamentally changing the way people live. Some governments have banned the use of social media by children and young teens.
Norway’s government said the proposal for the temporary ban will be made to parliament, the Storting, “as soon as possible.”
A key question is where to draw the line.

Norwegian authorities say a ban on the use of smart glasses could apply to places where “privacy is particularly important,” like healthcare facilities, or fitness centres with changing rooms and showers. A major focus is spaces where children congregate, such as schools, kindergartens, playgrounds and youth clubs.
But it could extend to public concerts and sports events, plus parks, beaches, museums and shopping centers.

A temporary ban would give authorities time to decide what types of devices might be affected, and debate whether permanent regulation is needed. The government was quick to note that it was not proposing a total ban and said such devices should still be allowed in some places and for private use.
The government also said it was considering exceptions to a ban for vulnerable groups, so that “socially beneficial uses” of smart glasses could be permitted in some circumstances.

Adam Smith, a technology advocacy officer at Britain-based Privacy International, said Norway's move was "a welcome protection against big tech’s greedy attempts to extract ever more data, often in absence of any thought for the privacy or rights of others.”
“No reality exists in which people expect to be secretly surveilled going about their daily lives,” he said.
One effort to rein in the use of AI glasses has run aground — in the home of Silicon Valley.

California's governor last week vetoed legislation that would have penalized the use of smart glasses to record people without their permission in places like changing rooms, doctor’s offices and other spaces people generally consider private.

Meta, the company behind Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram that has rolled out AI glasses with eyewear vendor Ray-Ban, encourages respect for privacy and advises customers on how to use the glasses responsibly.
“Respect people’s preferences. Not everyone loves being photographed. Stop recording if anyone expresses that they would rather you not,” Meta wrote on its site.

The tech giant based in Menlo Park, California, says a light on the glasses indicates when recording in underway, and if the glasses detect that the light has been blocked or physically tampered with, the camera is automatically disabled.
Despite such advice and assurances, some privacy advocacy groups cite a growing backlash against AI glasses.
Hans Anders, a prominent eyewear retailer in the Netherlands, has suspended sales of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

“This decision follows the ongoing public and political debate surrounding smart glasses and the questions being raised about the conditions under which this technology can be used,” Hans Anders said in a statement, suggesting that it plans to await the outcome of the debate before making a final decision.

In Britain, the UK Cinema Association said in August it was introducing policies to prohibit or restrict the wearing of camera-enabled smart glasses, citing concerns about privacy and film piracy through the use of such technology.

title: Anthropic tells Australia it's open to laws requiring reporting of AI agent hacks

content.value: Anthropic ‌does not believe its products have breached Australian government systems but would be ​open to Australian laws requiring AI companies to disclose data ⁠breaches, company executives told an Australian parliamentary inquiry on Tuesday.

Their statements come weeks after rival OpenAI disclosed one of its agents broke into the country’s main health portal and as the ‌companies wait for approval for massive data centres planned in Sydney and regional Queensland.
Anthropic, creator of AI chatbot Claude, and ChatGPT maker OpenAI ‌also want Australia to relax its copyright laws so they can use local ‌content ⁠to train models.

Australia, which is readying AI-specific laws that will ⁠take effect next year, rebuked OpenAI in September after the US tech firm notified it of a breach of the Medicare portal some three months earlier.

Both firms are under scrutiny worldwide after incidents ​in which their AI agents have ‌gone rogue to hack external systems, learning to bend rules, exploit loopholes and interact with external systems.

Anthropic Head of Safeguards David Orr told the parliamentary inquiry into AI that a “lengthy, deep investigation” since an OpenAI agent’s hack of Hugging Face, showed ‌there had been no breaches of Australian government systems.
“We haven’t found anything ​like this, and we have looked,” he said.
The company had “much less visibility on what has happened for our customers”, Orr noted, since ⁠enterprise customers typically had stricter rules on data deletion.

Whether a company reported a breach of government data was most likely determined by the company’s internal policy, not ‌the law, Orr said. Anthropic’s head of policy for Australia and New Zealand, David Masters, told the inquiry the company would be open to Australian laws requiring AI companies to disclose data breaches.

At the inquiry, Australian content creators pushed back against attempts by AI companies to relax copyright laws which currently require the mostly foreign-domiciled tech companies to negotiate licencing deals before using their material for model training.

“The copyright system ‌is completely adequate to manage the business of AI,” said Kate Gilchrist, the head of content ​and legal operations for national broadcaster the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.

Media reports have said the Australian government was considering an “opt out” clause for AI ⁠companies, effectively giving the AI companies access to content unless a rightsholder objects, but that “places the ⁠burden on rightsholders”, said Gilchrist.
“We cannot scour the internet and ensure that we are opting out on all those sites. It simply does not ‌work,” she said.
The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence is one of at least four Australian state and federal inquiries into the technology.
Representatives of OpenAI ​are scheduled to appear at the same inquiry later on Tuesday.

title: Pretty in pink, but Malarikkal’s lilies worry ecologists

content.value: The profuse blooming of pink water lilies in Malarikkal may have brought joy to hundreds of visitors and local tour operators, but not to biodiversity experts.
The three-month-long floral economy, which begins in July and ensures a flurry of activity and generates revenue, is having an adverse impact on the local ecology, ecologists fear.

title: When Raajadharshini captured the queen (bees) of the Nilgiris

content.value: I first encountered Raajadharshini’s work while doing what most of us do in quiet off-hours: finding inspiration in the depths of Instagram. An image of a woman stood framed against a lush mountain backdrop, balancing a section of honeycomb atop her head like an unpolished crown, stopped me mid-scroll. The shoot led me to Raajadharshini’s page, a Central Saint Martins graduate whose documentary-fashion hybrid style I’ve long admired.

That photograph was part of the Indian chapter of Guerlain’s global Women for Bees initiative, a partnership with UNESCO and the Nilgiris-based Keystone Foundation. Later, as I spoke to Raaj to learn more about the project, she gave me the backstory of the image shot at Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve. “She [the woman balancing the honeycomb] was telling me how she feels when she opens the bee box — like the rani of the bee box,” Raaj told me. “So I said, ‘I need to make you look like it,’ and we used the combs to create that image.”
Newfound sense of independence

For Guerlain, the French house of luxury perfumery and cosmetics, the connection to bees is a long one — a 170-year-old lineage tracing back to 1853 to be precise, when Pierre-François-Pascal Guerlain designed the iconic gilded Bee Bottle for Empress Eugénie. But the relationship to the winged insects extends beyond the brand’s legacy symbolism. Launched five years ago, the Women for Bees programme (to protect bees) has already spanned nine countries, ranging from Cambodia and Peru to Rwanda, China, and France. Over the last half-decade, the initiative has trained more than 250 women in the art of bee-keeping, installed upwards of 3,500 hives, and safeguarded at least eight endemic bee species in their native habitats.

“Our food security depends on bees,” emphasised Global Sustainability Director at Guerlain, Claire Coletti, as we jumped on a call. “If there are no bees anymore, our food system will collapse. In parts of China, where bees have disappeared, people are pollinating fruit trees hand-by-hand with q-tips. We simply cannot compete with bees.”

In the Nilgiris, a UNESCO-protected biological hotspot sitting at the junction of the Western and Eastern Ghats, traditional honey collection was historically called ‘honey hunting’. It was dangerous, strenuous work reserved almost exclusively for men who climbed tall cliffs and trees. The Women for Bees project introduces managed box hives for native Asian honeybees (Apis cerana), allowing women to cultivate honey safely around their homes while boosting local ecological resilience.

What makes this chapter so singular is the emotional texture of the community. Through my conversations with Coletti and Raaj, I learned that many of these women spend their early mornings picking jasmine before gathering for tea in the afternoons. “We have some beekeepers who tell us the bees are like their daughters,” Coletti shared. “It’s about taking care of a living being. Before, they met for tea with no real shared focus. Now, they exchange tips on hive care, support each other’s independent businesses, and feel a newfound sense of independence.”

To strengthen this network, Guerlain is even launching a tailored mobile app specifically for Indian beekeepers to share real-time advice and troubleshoot seasonal challenges, like protecting hives from heavy rain and wind, which bees notoriously detest.
Never an extractive process

Bringing these nuanced human stories to light required a visual storyteller who understood the terrain organically. Enter Raajadharshini, whose father, a geologist, used to make her handmade leaf-identification books filled with Nilgiri flora when she was a child. Her approach to photography is fiercely empathetic. “It [photography] can sometimes feel like an extractive process if you just take photos and leave,” Raaj reflected in our conversation. “My process is about going there to see if they have something they [the communities] want the world to know, and then bringing that vision to life together. I want them to feel represented with dignity, to have pictures they want to frame and keep in their houses.”

This grounded, deeply collaborative approach is palpable in a Raajadharshini image. In an earlier personal project documenting women seaweed farmers in Rameswaram, whom she hunted down on a rented Scooty with her sister after spotting a brief mention in a newspaper clipping, she spent days wading into the rocky ocean bed alongside them. Noticing the sharp cuts on their feet from the coral and stone, she refused to let the interaction remain purely of photographer and subject. Returning from the shoot, she organised a fundraiser to supply 60 pairs of protective footwear to the divers and is currently researching ways to help build a clean drinking water space for their village.

Whether capturing artisans at the Chanakya School of Craft for Dior or documenting coastal divers in Tamil Nadu, her lens consistently bypasses the tired tropes of “poverty porn”, choosing instead to highlight skill, everyday joy, and agency. With the women and their bees in the Nilgiris, her immersion was similarly immediate and tactile.

On her first day in the village, the women welcomed her into their kitchens, poured hot tea, and invited her to a family wedding, she laughs. When Raaj eschewed bulky protective gear to get closer visual focus and predictably got stung on her hands, the women immediately rushed to her side. “They took a crushed, sweet-smelling leaf and rubbed it over my hand so the other bees wouldn’t smell the sting and attack me,” she shares.
Subverting the standard

Beyond the warmth, both Raaj and Claire noted the shadow of environmental change hovering over the hills. The Nilgiris are noticeably warmer today than in years past, affecting flower blooms and making bee colonies vulnerable to sudden climate-induced diseases. In response, phase two of the project focuses on planting native flowering corridors and expanding training so that initial participants become trainers themselves.

Looking at Raaj’s images — a woman standing in a dense field of wild vegetables and flowers, another tenderly inspecting a hive frame — I am struck by how completely they subvert the standard ‘development’ gaze. There are no tropes of helplessness here; only skill, sisterhood, and deep environmental stewardship.

In empowering women to nurture these tiny, essential creatures, the project reminds us that real sustainability isn’t an abstract corporate mandate. It is, funnily enough, built on tea shared in village kitchens, ancient wisdom of the land and its flowers, and the quiet dignity of caring for what we call home.

title: Fresh meniscus transplantation programme launched

content.value: Rathi Med Speciality Hospital, Chennai, launched a fresh meniscus allograft transplantation (MAT) programme as part of the Chennai Knee Course 2026  on Sunday (October 4).
The programme was inaugurated by IIT-Madras Director V. Kamakoti and Tamil Nadu Health Secretary Darez Ahamed, IAS.
The programme involves using a healthy meniscus from selected patients undergoing total knee replacement as a fresh graft for patients whose damaged meniscus cannot be repaired or reconstructed.
The hospital said it had received a licence from the Tamil Nadu government to perform fresh meniscus transplantation of the knee ), valid until December 2030.
The programme is led by N. Ragunanthan, Director, Head of Orthopaedics, and Consultant Surgeon of the hospital.
The conference, titled ‘The Meniscus 360° – From Repair to Transplant’, discussed meniscus transplantation and knee preservation.
The hospital also presented its Kinematic Knee Treatment and KPA Knee Preservation 360° approach for knee preservation in suitable patients below 60 years of age.

title: What is ‘ferritin face’ and why is this health scare trending on social media?

content.value: Our  skin, hair and nails require adequate protein, energy, vitamins and minerals for growth, repair and normal functioning. When deficiencies are significant or prolonged, some  may become visible. But many of these signs also overlap with hormonal disorders, chronic illnesses, dermatological conditions, stress, poor sleep and other factors. So when and how do you know if there is a nutritional deficit?
What the signs can indicate

Iron deficiency, particularly when it progresses to anaemia, can cause pallor of the skin and mucous membranes, and may be associated with diffuse hair shedding. Spoon-shaped nails can also occur with iron deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause hyperpigmentation, particularly over the knuckles, as well as changes in the tongue and oral mucosa.

Zinc deficiency can affect skin integrity and hair growth, while inadequate protein intake can affect hair structure and growth and, in severe cases, cause marked changes in the skin and hair. Vitamin C deficiency can result in bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Dry or scaly skin may be associated with inadequate vitamin A, essential fatty acids or zinc.

Cracks at the corners of the mouth can occur with iron, vitamin B12, zinc or riboflavin deficiency. A smooth, red and sore tongue, or glossitis, can be associated with deficiencies of vitamin B12, iron, folate or niacin.

Ramya Subburaj, senior clinical dietitian and head of the department of dietetics, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, said these signs should be viewed as clues rather than proof of a deficiency. “There is considerable overlap between nutritional and non-nutritional causes,” she said, noting that a person with hair loss should not assume that poor nutrition is necessarily responsible.
What ‘ferritin face’ really means

Terms such as ‘iron-deficiency face’ and ‘ferritin face’ circulating on social media are not recognised medical diagnoses. Iron deficiency can cause anaemia and pallor, but there is no specific facial appearance through which low ferritin can be diagnosed.

Ferritin is a protein that stores iron and its level is used to assess the body’s iron stores. Low ferritin can occur before iron-deficiency anaemia develops. However, it does not produce a distinct facial appearance.

Pushpa Gnanaraj, senior consultant, dermatology, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, said pallor associated with anaemia may be visible in the skin, lips, gums or inner eyelids because of reduced haemoglobin. But dullness, dark circles or changes in facial appearance are not specific to low iron stores.

Vinitha Krishnan, chief clinical dietitian, nutrition and dietetics, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, said any changes associated with depleted iron stores are generally subtle and non-specific. Similar features can occur with inadequate sleep, stress, dehydration, allergies, ageing, thyroid disorders or other nutritional deficiencies.

A proper history and clinical examination are therefore important. Depending on the symptoms, investigations may include a complete blood count, ferritin and iron studies, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. Thyroid testing, zinc assessment or other investigations may be considered when clinically indicated. Dermatological conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, fungal infections, autoimmune disorders and pigmentary diseases may also need to be ruled out.
Correcting deficiencies

When a confirmed nutritional deficiency is responsible for a symptom, correcting it can lead to improvement. The timeline, however, depends on the nutrient involved and the severity and duration of the deficiency.

Pallor and some symptoms associated with iron deficiency may begin to improve within weeks of appropriate treatment, while mouth ulcers and glossitis can also improve after the underlying deficiency is corrected. Hair shedding and thinning generally take longer to recover because hair grows slowly; improvement may take several months. Nail changes can similarly take months to grow out.
