Finally, we are exploring the All of Us dataset to identify systematic differences – for example, in patients’ cultural background or income level, specific health system practices, urban versus rural settings – that might be linked with whether menopause data gets recorded in medical records. These associations can point to targeted ways to encourage its collection.
It’s impossible to research, and treat, what’s not measured. Capturing the menopause transition is an essential step to improving healthcare for women in midlife.
Audrey Hendricks, University of Colorado Anschutz and Nanette Santoro, University of Colorado Anschutz

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article here: https://theconversation.com/menopause-is-a-major-health-milestone-yet-health-records-barely-track-it-new-research-292227.

title: Rethinking suicide prevention in Adivasi communities

content.value: Prem* is a young mathematics graduate from a village in Jharkhand. He was known as an energetic and supportive young person. Children from the village often approached him when they had difficulties with mathematics. When he was selected for a job with the Indian Railways, it was expected to be a moment of happiness. But the thought of leaving his parents, friends, village and the life he shared with them was difficult for him.

In the weeks following the job offer, Prem began having sleepless nights, worrying about how he would cope with a new life and new responsibilities. Gradually, he stopped talking to his family. He began to feel helpless and worthless, lost interest in everyday life and reached a point where he attempted to end his life.

What helped was having people around him who could understand not only what he was going through, but also the world he was coming from. A neighbourhood facilitator working in a community-based organisation was able to sit with him, listen to his worries and share his dukh-sukh. They understood why leaving his parents, friends and village felt so difficult and gave him space to talk about the fears he was carrying.

The support was not about asking him simply to adjust or move on. It helped him think about what mattered to him, what he wanted for his future and how he could remain connected to the people and place that were important to him while taking up the new opportunity. He eventually wrote to the department asking for another opportunity to join. He was invited again and went to work,  while continuing to receive support.

Prem’s experience highlights  that what looks like a positive life event from the outside can sometimes become overwhelming. A suicidal act can often  happen suddenly, during a moment of intense crisis. But the distress behind that moment may have been building for much longer.
For Adivasi communities, distress can be shaped by circumstances that may never appear in a psychiatric consultation.
When distress is accumulates

A recent study in Jharkhand examined psychosocial distress and help-seeking among Adivasi Ho adolescents. It found that distress was often linked to family conflict, pressure around education and work, financial hardship, violence, separation and loss, and difficulties in relationships. Some adolescents withdrew and stopped sharing what they were going through; for some, this included thoughts of self-harm or suicide

These accounts do not offer a single explanation for suicide among Adivasi communities. They show how distress can accumulate across everyday life — in family conflict, having to leave school temporarily or reduce schooling to help with agricultural or household work, substance use, untreated illness, violence, displacement, loss of livelihood, lack of mentorship, identity-related stigma and self-doubt, or the erosion of community and belonging.
When communities are disrupted

Belonging is an important part of suicide prevention. Stereotypes, exclusion, humiliation, discrimination and pressure to hide one’s identity can affect how people see themselves and how connected they feel to society. Historically, Adivasi communities stayed together. But modern development, alongside education and employment opportunities, have in some cases, uprooted  Adivasi people from their culture. Mainstream schools do not teach Adivasi children in their own mother tongue; their history is woefully under-represented in the school curricula.

Sandip Sing, a radiologist from the Munda  community practising in rural West Bengal and a first-generation learner, says,  “There is a rapid transition in accessing and navigating educational and professional spaces, often amid gaps in resources, networks, and institutional familiarity. Bridging these gaps can be challenging, particularly with unfamiliar systems.”

Many educated Adivasis may also have had fewer opportunities to engage with their community’s history, culture, language and traditions, and may have complex or evolving relationships with their Adivasi identities.  This matters for mental health because belonging itself is a source of strength. When people are uprooted  without finding a new sense of belonging, distress can deepen.

This does not mean that development itself causes mental illness or suicide. The concern is what happens when rapid social change is accompanied by displacement, loss of livelihood, cultural disconnection and weakening social support.
Collective strength, mentoring

The strength of Adivasi life also lies in ways of expressing emotions and sharing knowledge. Songs and dances are not simply cultural performances; they are ways of expressing emotions, maintaining connection and making sense of life. The Adivasi dance itself is a powerful metaphor. People dance in a chain, holding one another. The village headman, Majhi Baba, dances alongside everyone else. An 80-year-old and an eight-year-old can dance together. There is no hierarchy; the strength is in the circle. For suicide prevention, this collective strength matters.

Young people also need places where they can be themselves without constantly having to explain or defend who they are. Lilibiti Saren, a medical officer from the Santhal community working in  tribal areas of Bankura, West Bengal, notes that she often finds young people in these communities lacking direction. “There is a need for proper mentorship,” she says.

Locally organised Adivasi youth spaces can help. Such spaces can offer young people opportunities to speak in their own language, share experiences, learn from peers and elders and explore what Adivasiyat — identity, history, relationships and belonging — means to them.
Access and pathways in care

Clinical care remains essential. A person experiencing suicidal thoughts may need assessment for depression, substance use, trauma, psychosis, previous attempts, suicidal intent, access to means and immediate safety. Treatment and follow-up can save lives.
But access to mental health care is itself a major challenge in many Adivasi areas. Services are often limited, distant and unevenly available.

And even when services are available, the pathways into care may not be optimal. An Adivasi person with lived experience of mental healthcare says: “I felt like the psychiatrists and the psychologists were not speaking to me. They were judging me for what I had done and they were trying to find symptoms instead of trying to understand me, my pain and my situation.”
This raises an important question: are our mental health systems listening as carefully as they are diagnosing?

When formal services are scarce, difficult to reach, or experienced as unfamiliar or judgmental, people may seek support elsewhere—including from family, community networks, faith healers or indigenous systems. These spaces may offer something that the formal system does not: familiar language, relationships, cultural understanding and a sense of belonging.
Adivasi mental health therefore cannot be treated simply as another category within rural health. Representation matters — from schools to healthcare institutions and policy making.
Models that could work

In Adivasi communities of Jharkhand, particularly among the Ho, Munda and Santhal communities, Madait refers to a tradition of voluntary help and collective support for someone who needs it or is in distress. It reflects an understanding that some difficulties are too large for one household to manage alone.

This may be  a useful way to think about mental healthcare too. The question is not simply how services can be delivered to Adivasi communities, but how communities themselves can shape, participate in and lead the care they need.

The same principle can be seen in Dukhu-Sukhu Baithaki — community support group meetings where people experiencing mental health difficulties and their families can meet, share experiences and support one another. This model works in West Singhbhum, Jharkhand, where people living with mental health conditions come together each month. These spaces do not replace professional care. They bring community knowledge, relationships and mutual support into the process of recovery.

Education without a knowledge of one’s roots; development that comes with displacement and mental healthcare that does not see or hear the people who need help is no longer enough. For suicide prevention, we must ask not only, “What is wrong with the individual?”, but also, “ Where is the community support? Where is the system that understands them?”
Perhaps suicide prevention in Adivasi communities must begin there — not by doing things for Adivasis, but by doing them with Adivasis.
*Name changed to protect privacy
(People in distress can reach out to Tele-MANAS (14416 or 1-800-891-4416) or the helplines listed here)

(Dr. Sachin Barbde is a public health physician working with Adivasi communities in Jharkhand barbdesachin@gmail.com; Dr. Christianez Ratna Kiruba is an internal medicine physician and a freelance health journalist from Guwahati christianezdennis@gmail.com; Dr. Debasmita Saren, is a Santhal Adivasi psychiatrist debasmitasaren5@gmail.com)

title: Tennessee execution survivor Christa Pike on ventilator, attorneys say

content.value: Convicted murderer Christa Pike is unconscious, intubated and receiving breathing assistance ​from a ventilator after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her, ‌her attorneys said on Friday (October 2, 2026), providing the ​first detailed account of the extent of ⁠injuries she suffered during the lethal injection.

Hospital staff are working to save Pike’s life and clear the lethal drug pentobarbital from ‌her system, her attorneys said in an emergency court filing seeking an order requiring ‌Tennessee’s Department of Correction to preserve evidence from ‌Wednesday night’s ⁠botched execution.

Pike remains in critical condition, her ⁠lawyers said, two days after the state administered two doses of pentobarbital but failed to kill her. She has suffered significant ​injuries to both arms, they ‌added.

“At no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown ‌and that the pentobarbital was, in whole ​or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” Pike’s lawyers said in a filing in the ⁠Chancery Court for the State of Tennessee Twentieth Judicial District.

The filing provides the fullest picture yet of the ‌medical consequences of an attempted execution that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said followed the state’s established protocol. It was the state’s second botched execution this year and Lee has halted any further state killings for the rest of 2026 and ordered an independent review ‌of what happened.
Pike’s attorneys have said the execution team’s difficulties ​administering the drug were related to intravenous access, an issue they had warned the state ⁠and courts about before the execution.

Pike, 50, was convicted of ⁠killing her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when Pike was 18. She had been scheduled ‌to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than two centuries.

title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak records more than 4,000 deaths

content.value: Congo’s Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.

The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday (October 1, 2026). They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases, making up for nearly half of the confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.

The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.

A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation’s 17th Ebola outbreak.

Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons ranging from how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

title: International organisations form alliance for diabetic foot survival and limb preservation

content.value: Eight organisations from different parts of the world have come together to form the Global Alliance for Diabetic Foot Survival and Limb Preservation. This was announced at the Diabetic Foot Society of India’s (DFSI) national conference held in Bengaluru on Friday, October 2, 2026. The founding organisations also signed a joint declaration calling for diabetic foot ulceration to be recognised as a global public health priority.

The eight organisations are the DFSI, King’s College London, the International Association of Diabetic Foot Surgeons, D-Foot International, the Pan African Diabetic Foot Study Group, the American Limb Preservation Society, the International Federation of Podiatrists and the Podiatric Surgeons’ Society.

A 2023 review cited in the alliance proposal estimated that about 18.6 million people worldwide are affected by diabetic foot ulceration annually. It reported a five-year mortality of about 30% following a diabetic foot ulcer and over 70% following a major amputation.

The proposed alliance will focus on research, workforce training, comparable data collection and advocacy with the World Health Organization and national governments to secure greater policy recognition of diabetic foot disease.

The proposed framework also emphasises the involvement of people living with diabetes, those who have experienced foot ulcers and people living with amputation or disability in decision-making and programme design. It envisages regional demonstration programmes, a common measurement framework and an annual report on progress.

The DFSI Scientific Committee is proposed as the alliance’s interim secretariat, with a governing council representing the founding organisations overseeing strategy, finances and activities. The members are expected to meet within 30 days to discuss governance, collaboration, resource mobilisation and implementation.

title: Allahabad HC to hear suo motu PIL on noise pollution after student’s death

content.value: The Allahabad High Court has initiated suo motu proceedings on noise pollution following reports of the death of a 7-year-old Class 2 student at a school in Balrampur while a procession carrying loudspeakers and a music system was passing nearby.

The incident occurred on September 22 at Divine Public School on City Palace Road in Bhagautiganj, Balrampur. The deceased was identified as Vaishnavi Tiwari. According to reports, the procession was part of the 10-day Ganpati Utsav, which started on September 14.

Observing that the incident raises larger questions over the unchecked menace of noise pollution, a Division Bench of Justice Rajan Roy and Justice Manjive Shukla on Wednesday (September 28) ordered the registration of a separate suo motu PIL while hearing an existing case concerning the use of pressure horns, modified silencers and hooters.
The court, however, clarified that it had not established any connection between the alleged loud noise and the child’s death.

The Bench maintained that the broader problem of noise pollution and the enforcement of statutory safeguards required separate consideration. It observed that violations of the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, were frequently witnessed in public spaces despite the existing legal framework.
The PIL will examine the authorities responsible for controlling noise pollution, the enforcement measures currently in place, and whether regular monitoring is required, The Bench said.

The court also stressed the need for greater public awareness, observing that a lack of awareness may contribute to violations. At the same time, the Bench said continued violations despite enforcement measures should attract accountability under the applicable law.

The court made the Uttar Pradesh Director General of Police, the Uttar Pradesh Pollution Control Board (UPPCB), the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Lucknow civic authorities and officials from key government departments parties in the matter. The Balrampur District Magistrate, Superintendent of Police and Chief Medical Officer were also directed to be impleaded. The State was asked to obtain reports on the incident and submit details of measures taken or proposed to enforce noise-control laws.
The court also expressed hope that the child’s parents and school authorities would not face unnecessary pressure or interference. The matter will now be heard on October 12.

title: Pakistani cosmetics seized in Hyderabad traced to Mumbai’s Crawford Market

content.value: Pakistan-made cosmetics that continued to find their way to Hyderabad more than a year after India shut the door on imports from the neighbouring country have now led investigators to Mumbai’s Crawford Market, pointing to a wider supply chain behind the banned products.

The development comes amid a separate public-health concern over some of the skin-whitening products. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) last month specifically warned consumers against two Pakistan-made creams after tests found excessive levels of heavy metals.
Both ‘Goree Beauty Cream’ and ‘Chandni Whitening Cream’, named in the September 8 CDSCO alert, were among the products found during raids on three shops in Hyderabad this week.

An officer involved in the investigation said the cosmetics seized in Hyderabad were allegedly being sourced from Crawford Market in Mumbai. “Investigators are now looking further up the chain to establish how the products entered India and reached wholesale and retail markets despite restrictions on their import.
Imports from Pakistan prohibited since May 2025

India prohibited the direct or indirect import or transit of all goods originating in or exported from Pakistan on May 2, 2025. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade imposed the restriction through a notification, citing national security and public policy.
The prohibition extends to goods entering India indirectly, meaning routing Pakistan-origin products through another country does not by itself make their import permissible.

Cosmetics imported into India are additionally governed by the Cosmetics Rules, 2020. Products must be registered with the Central Licensing Authority before import and are required to comply with prescribed quality and safety standards.

The CDSCO had stepped up scrutiny even before the latest Hyderabad seizure. In July, it directed its zonal offices, State licensing authorities and officers at ports to maintain enhanced surveillance following instances of imported cosmetics being sold in domestic markets without valid import registration certificates.
Heavy metals found in two creams

The health regulator followed this with a more pointed warning on September 8. After testing Goree Beauty Cream and Chandni Whitening Cream, it said neither had been issued a registration certificate for import and that the products contained heavy metals beyond specified limits, which could pose health risks, including toxic effects. Consumers were advised not to purchase or use them.

The Hyderabad investigation has meanwhile opened another line of inquiry. According to the officer, investigators found that an ointment originating from the United Kingdom was allegedly being mixed with cosmetic products and the resulting preparation sold for skin-lightening purposes.
Samples of the products have been sent for forensic examination, and investigators are awaiting the laboratory findings to establish their composition and determine the substances present in them.

Officials have raised concerns about potentially carcinogenic substances, but the forensic results are awaited. The precise health implications of the seized preparations are therefore yet to be established.

The latest investigation follows raids by the Hyderabad police and CDSCO at Beauty Ladies Emporium, Beauty Queen Shop and S.J. Medical Shop in the Habeeb Nagar and Nampally areas, where cosmetics valued at about ₹7 lakh were seized.
The stock included several Pakistan-made whitening creams, soaps and other cosmetic products. Five persons were identified in connection with their alleged sale and distribution.
The Crawford Market link also comes against the backdrop of enforcement action in Mumbai itself, where Pakistan-made cosmetics valued at about ₹12 lakh were seized during a raid in July.

title: The ‘WarGames’ problem: Computer science has long understood what it takes to keep AI under control

content.value: AI agents don’t go rogue. That’s something only humans do.
Nevertheless, a New York Times article – representative of much news coverage of AI – described an OpenAI hacking as “A.I. bots going rogue and independently spearheading a cyberattack.”

Name-brand artificial intelligence agents have been on a hacking spree in 2026. OpenAI’s software agents hacked software company Hugging Face and government sites, Anthropic’s Claude hacked four companies’ systems, and in cybersecurity experiments Google’s Gemini hacked three companies.

The AI companies are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving their agents, according to a report in Axios. These episodes have heightened fears about AI agents taking actions without human prompting.

The problem with headlines proclaiming that AI agents have gone rogue goes beyond anthropomorphising the technology. It creates the impression that the agents were beyond the control of the AI companies that made them and there was little the companies could do about it.

As a technology law and ethics scholar who studies the effects disruptive technologies have on society, I know that’s not the case. If you don’t specify the limits of what software is allowed to do, you should not be surprised when the software pursues all possible options to achieve its goal. This behavior – an AI pursuing a fixed objective – is what I call the “WarGames” problem, and it’s been recognised in the field of computer science for decades.
Been there, seen that

In the 1983 movie “WarGames,” a teenager, David, hacks into a computer to play a new video game, Global Thermonuclear War. David doesn’t know that the computer is the government’s AI machine tasked with defending the United States from Russian nuclear attacks and can launch the U.S.’s missiles. When David and his friend start the game, they select Las Vegas as the first target. While the North American Aerospace Defense Command goes on alert, launching bombers and warming up intercontinental ballistic missiles, David’s parents make him turn off the game. It’s over. Or is it?

The next day, David’s phone rings and he connects it to his computer. The caller is the government computer, which updates him that the game was interrupted, the primary goal has not yet been achieved, but a solution is expected in the next 52 hours. Like a modern software agent, the program has been running since David started the game and will work until the task is done.

Chess provides another view of the problem. Conquering chess was a goal for early AI. The rules of chess are well defined, including what winning looks like. So, programming a machine to play chess is straightforward. But imagine you let the software reason and act beyond the confines of the chessboard. The software might pursue options such as blackmailing its opponent or grabbing more compute time.

This example comes from one of the most assigned textbooks on AI, “Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach.” As the authors explain, you might be tempted to see those actions as rogue, but they “are a logical consequence of defining winning as the sole objective for the machine.”
What to do about it
The AI hacking events involving OpenAI, Anthropic and Google underscore a few lessons that draw on years of computer science research.

First, given the increasing use of AI agents, every organization involved in internet infrastructure, from large technology companies to small websites, needs to conduct audits and tighten up its internal security systems. As my colleague Mark Riedl and I explain in our work on AIagents, application programming interfaces, or APIs, are a vital part of managing AI agents. APIs facilitate communication between different software systems. But as more people use AI agents, the agents are likely to reveal and exploit poor API construction and security.

Second, it’s important for AI agents to be designed to identify and authenticate themselves to third parties. What if you gave your AI agent your credentials? Website operators will need to know whether a human or bot is making a reservation, selling a product or making a purchase. They may want to limit automated systems that overwhelm their sites or reject AI agents because of high rates of buying errors and refunds. Just as in laws covering human interactions, it’s important for third parties to be able to assess whom or what they are dealing with so they can allow or deny access.

Third, it’s important for AI agents to have a default setting to slow down and check in with the human user. In the corporate AI hacking cases, the user appears to have launched their AI agents with the mistaken idea that the agents had a perfect specification of what to do and not to do. I believe it would have been better had it explored options and reported back to the user.

Google’s Gemini appears to have had a safeguard that detected the system was outside the simulated environment and so stopped its attacks. Slowing down and verifying actions, especially when a system detects it is exploiting a security hole, would be a big step in managing AI agents.

Fourth, AI companies could have strong controls akin to those biomedical researchers use, including ways to check what is happening and how the experiment is working. AI executives have claimed that their software is as or more dangerous than fission and could end humanity. At the same time, they have not built safeguards commensurate with that level of risk.
Reality check

At one point in “WarGames,” David asks the computer, called Joshua, whether it is still playing the game. Joshua responds, “Of course.” It proceeds to update the time when it will launch its missiles and, much like a chatbot, asks, “Would you like to see some projected kill ratios?” David asks, “Is this a game? Or is it real?” Joshua replied, “What’s the difference?”

AI models, of course, don’t have any understanding of reality and are simply attempting to complete the tasks they’ve been assigned. Executives at AI companies, on the other hand, can’t claim that excuse.

As of September 2026, luck has so far prevailed. The AIs have attacked nonvital government sites and harmed smaller companies. If the AI companies – and government regulators – don’t take the “WarGames” problem seriously, I believe that we risk serious disasters. Tomorrow it could be taking out a hospital’s power system, wiping out a bank’s account system, breaking air traffic control, or worse.

Regarding the AI industry’s approach of rapidly developing powerful models, talking about the massive risks they pose, and at the same time failing to prevent harm, the movie’s climax offers a response: “A strange game. The only winning move is not to play.”
(This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.)

title: Nepal plans to drain four glacial lakes after deadly floods

content.value: Nepal will kick off a high-stakes effort this fiscal year to drain four ​glacial lakes perched high in the mountains, as it scrambles to reduce flood risks, ⁠officials said, after a recent disaster that killed more than 1,400.
Rescuers are still searching for more than 5,000 people missing in the border region with China after August’s glacier collapse unleashed landslides and a flash flood that tore through ‌valleys.

“Our aim is to lower the risk of the lakes breaching their natural dams and reduce the risk of downstream floods,” said Subash Tuladhar, an expert with a government ‌research centre tasked with overseeing the new project.

Canals will drain water into nearby rivers in ‌a ⁠regulated way, he said, adding that workers faced health risks as a result of the ⁠lengthy periods of high-altitude work required, in addition to the dangers of sudden flooding.

Design work and detailed studies targeting the central and eastern lakes of Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho and Hongu II, will begin in the fiscal year that runs ​until mid-July 2027, authorities said.

The lakes, at heights ‌ranging from 4,050 m to 5,483 m (13,280 ft to 18,000 ft), rank among Nepal’s most potentially dangerous, the United Nations Development Programme and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said in a 2020 report.

Nepal had the skills and experience required for the $50-million project to be ‌funded by the Green Climate Fund, the UNDP and the government, added Tuladhar, of Nepal’s ​Centre for Hydrology and Water Resources Research.
Draining project could take six years
The work of draining “through gated structures” will start after a detailed study, and could take up ⁠to six years to complete, said Sanjeeb Baral, the Centre’s executive director.
It will encompass installation of sensors, a flood forecasting and warning system, and efforts to build downstream resilience and prepare communities for the risks.

In similar ‌previous efforts, Nepal lowered by 3 m (10 ft) the level of the central Himalayan glacial lake of Tsho Rolpa by in 2000 and that of Imja in the vicinity of Mount Everest, the world’s tallest peak, 10 years ago.
Urgency after recent floods

Nepal’s disaster served as a warning to the world, Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 36, told the United Nations in an impassioned speech last month that blamed climate change despite his country’s negligible emissions.
Retreating glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and increasingly unpredictable rivers showed Nepal was ‌paying a heavy price, he added.

Nepal, which has reported about 26 Glacial Lake Outburst Flood events in the past four ​decades, loses more than 300 lives and property worth millions of dollars to extreme climate events annually on average.
The latest floods devastated a dozen hydroelectric plants, roads, bridges, farms ⁠and settlements. Cash-strapped Nepal would need nearly $5 billion for early recovery, officials have said.
Climate scientists say as temperatures ⁠rise glaciers in the Himalayas retreat, leaving behind unstable glacial lakes held back by little more than loose rock and ice, above valleys home to millions.
Lowering the lakes by 3 ‌m (10 ft) would significantly reduce the threat, said Samjwal Ratna Bajracharya, a retired ICIMOD expert on glaciers, glacial lakes and outburst floods.
“They are growing fast, are high up in the Himalayas and could ​cause outbursts any time, due to earthquakes, avalanches, climatic conditions and unplanned human-induced activity,” he told Reuters.

title: Pay the Global South for climate damage, but only if it prices carbon, says economist Greenstone

content.value: Rich countries should pay people in developing countries for the climate damage their emissions cause, on condition that those countries put a price on carbon. That is the central proposal of a forthcoming book, Just Economics, by University of Chicago economist Michael Greenstone, with Nobel-Prize winning economists Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo.

“We’re proposing Indians receive money unencumbered,” Mr. Greenstone, who is Director, Energy Policy Institute, University of Chicago, said in an interview. “Spend it on whatever you want. That is based on the amount of damage the OECD countries’ emissions are doing.” The payment, he said, “would go directly to the people, not to the government.”

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), is a grouping of mostly wealthy, industrialised countries that has contributed to most of the accumulated carbon in the atmosphere driving global warming. This contrasts with the “Global South”, meaning low- and middle-income countries but whose emissions are fast rising.

“82% of the emissions going forward are projected to be outside the OECD and moral appeals have failed,” he reckoned, “the better angels-argument ain’t working.” However the transfer would be “contingent on the Global South adopting carbon pricing. It’s not for free. It’s a deal. You have to give something to get something.”

Mr. Greenstone said it was possible to calculate the damage from carbon emissions to India. “However the exact parameters of that will have to be negotiated. Such a deal did not require the whole world and could be struck between, say, the European Union and India, he argued.

He pointed to “the more or less complete failure of climate finance to the Global South” and said “it’s time to think about a new approach.” Next month countries are expected to convene in Turkey for the annual climate meet.
Market-based solutions

Much of Mr. Greenstone’s work is around designing market-based solutions to address pollution. Most prominent is the Surat Emissions Trading Scheme for controlling particulate matter, first mooted with the Gujarat Pollution Control Board in 2010. In a randomised trial, 150 textile plants were assigned to a market and 150 stayed under conventional regulation. Compliance in the market was “99%”, against about a third of industries out of compliance at any time under the status quo. This happened because researchers could see what firms bid to buy and sell pollution permits: “The price I want for that has got to be at least what it cost me to do it. From those bids, we were able to infer how expensive it was to achieve different levels of total emissions. Cutting emissions proved cheap, because the guys had all the equipment and just had to start operating it or maintaining it,” he explained. Enforcement mattered. When firms fell short of permits, the regulator levied a fine of ten times the permit value. “Once the industry saw that the rules were going to be enforced then everything changed,” he said.

While the Surat system was designed to reduce particulate matter from textile mills, the next stop is Maharashtra, where the market will cover sulphur dioxide — a gaseous pollutant — and include large power plants. He said that a “mock trading period involving an actual market, without real money, was under way to get firms used to trading permits before the real market opened.

Similar conversations are on with Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Haryana. Gujarat’s Pollution Control Board has itself asked for help designing a water market and a Statewide sulphur dioxide market. If States get their own markets working, he said, “one could imagine linking those markets”.

The challenge that enforcement agencies faced is the inability to track a plant’s emissions second by second. Industries, for competitive advantage, frequently resorted to turning off pollution monitoring equipment. “ This is the Achilles heel of environmental regulation around the world.” Finding the upper limit to the pollutants that industries could be permitted to emit is the other big challenge. “It is a judgement about the right trade-off between economic costs and environmental quality.”

title: Multiple factors to determine cotton crop for 2026-27

content.value: Cotton planting for the 2026-27 marketing season (October to September) has been higher. However, scattered rainfall and the growing conditions in each of the cotton-growing States will determine the crop size for the new cotton season, said Nishant Asher, secretary of the Indian Cotton Federation, at the annual meeting of the Association held on Wednesday (September 30).
On the market front, international prices, currency value, price movement of other fibres and various other factors will continue to influence the demand for cotton, he added.

Speaking at the meeting, president of the Federation J. Thulasidharan said the total cotton production for the 2025-26 that ended on September 30 this year stabilised at 320 lakh to 325 lakh bales, with steady arrivals from the southern States and Maharashtra.

Over the past two months, domestic cotton prices surged by nearly 25%, driven by deficit rainfall in Gujarat and Telangana and fears about the standing crop. Global ICE benchmarks have softened from earlier 86-cent averages down toward the 80–82 cent range now. “This widening disparity between elevated domestic prices and softer overseas futures has squeezed spinning mill margins and hampered downstream export competitiveness,” he said.

The national average yield has drifted downward from 565 kg per hectare in 2013–14 to around 430 kg per hectare today. It is imperative for the stakeholders to work for reversing this yield stagnation.
The government should provide total relief from import duty for cotton and establish preferential, low-interest credit windows for seasonal cotton procurement by ginners and spinning mills.
Mr. Thulasidharan, Managing Director of Rajaratna Mills, was re-elected president of the Association.

P. Nataraj, Managing Director of KPR Mill, and Aditya Krishna Pathy, Managing Director of Lakshmi Mills, were re-elected vice presidents and Nishant Asher of Ravji Shamji Asher was elected again as secretary of the Association.

title: Wildlife photography exhibition to showcase Andhra Pradesh biodiversity in Vizag

content.value: The forests, wetlands, grasslands and coastal habitats of Andhra Pradesh will take centre stage at Hawa Mahal this weekend.  A wildlife photography exhibition at Hawa Mahal on October 3 and 4 will showcase 150 photographs documenting the varied biodiversity of Andhra Pradesh.

Organised by WildVizag in collaboration with the Andhra Pradesh Forest Department and Nagarjunasagar Srisailam Tiger Reserve (NSTR), the exhibition is being held as part of World Wildlife Week 2026. It will bring together 23 wildlife photographers from Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, with their photographs offering glimpses of the State’s forests, protected areas, habitats and wildlife.

The exhibition has been planned as an information-rich display rather than a collection of photographs alone. A dedicated display on various wildlife sanctuaries of Andhra Pradesh will explain their ecological significance and the species they support.

“The idea is to showcase the rich biodiversity of Andhra Pradesh and spread awareness. The show is intended to help visitors understand the forests and protected areas behind the photographs and the conservation work being undertaken there,” says Arunkumar Thyadi, a documentary filmmaker who has been closely associated with the Andhra Pradesh Forest Department.

A significant component of the exhibition will come from the Nagarjunasagar Srisailam Tiger Reserve team. Visitors will be able to see some of the equipment used by forest personnel in the field, including surveillance cameras, drones, tranquilisers, camera traps and other specialised gadgets and equipment. The display will offer an insight into the practical side of wildlife monitoring and protection, complementing the photographic account of the State’s biodiversity.

Among the individual displays, Arun Thyadi’s Project Black will draw attention to one of the less understood groups in the wild: snakes. The project documents 18 species of snakes found in Andhra Pradesh, bringing together species as different as the king cobra and the Brahminy blind snake, one of the smallest snake species. The collection is expected to provide visitors with a closer look at the diversity of snakes found across the State and the habitats they occupy.
The exhibition will also include a souvenir stall offering caps and T-shirts.

title: Wildlife week at Vizag zoo: Workshops, competitions and conservation activities

content.value: What does it take for a butterfly, a bird or a wild animal to thrive beyond the boundaries of a zoo? This is the question that Wildlife Week at Indira Gandhi Zoological Park seeks to explore through a series of competitions, workshops and conservation activities from October 2 to 8.
This year’s theme, ‘Connecting Habitats, Thriving Wildlife’, places emphasis on habitat protection, coexistence and the role of people in conserving biodiversity.

The programme opens on October 2 at the Zoo Bioscope with a drawing competition from 10.20am to noon. The competition has three categories, with children from classes 1 to 5 working on ‘Wildlife in My Neighbourhood’, classes 6 to 10 exploring ‘Wildlife Corridors: Connecting Forests’ and intermediate to postgraduate participants taking up ‘Connecting Habitats, Thriving Wildlife: Building a Future of Coexistence’.

The week will also use speech, art and performance to introduce different aspects of conservation. An elocution competition on October 3 will invite participants from class 1 to postgraduate level to speak on either the role of zoos in wildlife conservation or wildlife and tribal communities. Participants will have three to five minutes to present their speeches, with the organisers encouraging the use of facts, examples and original ideas.
Conservation through participation

On October 4, International Zoo Keeper’s Day will be marked with a photography competition for animal keepers. A fancy dress competition for children aged three to 12 will be held at the Zoo Bioscope from 10am to noon with participants invited to dress as wildlife, birds, veterinarians, forest officers, animal keepers or other Nature-related themes.

The following day, the zoo will turn its attention to conservation education and outreach. A session introducing participants to Indira Gandhi Zoological Park and wildlife management will be followed by a quiz competition. On October 6, participants will take up wildlife-human coexistence, examining the challenges that arise when people and wild animals share landscapes and considering possible solutions. The poster presentation competition, open to participants aged seven to 22, will give them two minutes to explain their ideas and key messages.
Looking closely at butterflies

The butterfly workshop on October 7 is among the more hands-on programmes in the week’s schedule. Held from 10am to noon at the Zoo Bioscope and open to all age groups, it will introduce participants to butterflies, their life cycle, butterfly rearing and the identification of host and nectar plants.

Participants will be introduced to the distinction between host plants, on which butterflies lay their eggs and caterpillars feed, and nectar plants, which provide food for adult butterflies. Understanding this relationship also explains why a butterfly-friendly garden needs more than flowering plants with the right vegetation at different stages of the insect’s life.

The zoo already uses its butterfly park as a conservation education space. According to the zoo curator G Mangamma, the park has endemic host and nectar plants that attract butterflies to feed and breed. Around 30 butterfly species can be observed in the garden, while more than 120 species have been recorded across the zoo premises.
For details, contact zoo education officer at 7893632900 or mail at igzpeo@gmail.com.

title: Tigress released in Bengal’s Buxa Tiger Reserve; plans afoot for three more by end of year

content.value: Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav on Friday released a tigress in the Buxa Tiger Reserve in West Bengal's Alipurduar district with Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari in attendance.
Addressing the event, Mr. Adhikari said three more tigers will be released in Buxa Tiger Reserve in the next two months.

The three-year-old tigress was brought from Bihar's Valmiki Tiger Reserve to populate the Buxa reserve with big cats. Although the reserve did not have any big cats, camera traps have spotted a tiger, which experts believe had wandered into the region from either Bhutan or Assam's Manas National Park.
The release of the big cat into the Buxa reserve coincided with the start of World Wildlife Week, 2026.

In a post on X, Mr. Yadav said, "Inspired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's push for landscape conservation and species protection, today we have fulfilled the significant promise to reintroduce a tiger in Buxa. T138 has been brought from Valmiki Tiger Reserve in Bihar to Buxa."
He thanked the Chief Ministers of Bihar and Bengal "for their support in this successful reintroduction".

Mr. Adhikari also thanked Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary for the smooth translocation of the tigress from the Valmiki Tiger Reserve to Buxa. He also alleged that the previous Trinamool Congress government in Bengal had no inclination to save wildlife and only wanted to quarrel with the Centre.
West Bengal Forest Minister Manoj Oraon described the translocation as a significant step towards augmenting tiger population in Buxa.
The translocation is part of a five-year project planned for financial years 2023-24 to 2027-28, officials said.

The Proposal for Tiger Augmentation and Soft Release of Tiger in Buxa Tiger Reserve envisages not only bringing tigers to the reserve but also improving prey availability, developing suitable habitats, strengthening wildlife corridors and reducing human-wildlife conflict.

title: World's 90% health burden of chewing tobacco concentrated in 10 countries, including India: Study

content.value: ) India is among the top countries with 90% of the world's chewing tobacco-related health burden, and South Asia is the "epicentre" of chewing tobacco, according to new research published in The Lancet Global Health journal.

Researchers estimated that chewing tobacco contributed to 251,000 deaths globally in 2023 -- there were 241 million chewing tobacco users globally, with use peaking among individuals 60 to 64 years old, they said.

The analysis, part of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023) and covering 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, distinguishes the burden of chewing tobacco from that of other forms of smokeless tobacco, the team said.

"Chewing tobacco is not a uniform public health problem, and our findings show that a relatively small number of countries bear an overwhelming share of its health burden," lead author Gabriela Gil, research scientist at Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), University of Washington, US, said.
"Understanding how patterns of use differ within these populations is critical to designing more effective prevention and tobacco control strategies," Gil said.

The researchers said despite decades of progress in tobacco control, the global prevalence of chewing tobacco use has remained relatively unchanged. Stroke and lip and oral cavity cancer were found to comprise much of the health loss attributable to chewing tobacco use globally.
South Asia had the highest concentration of chewing tobacco use, with 14.6% of people aged 15 years and above chewing tobacco products in 2023.
The region accounted for 2,10,000 chewing tobacco-related deaths -- about 84% of the global total, the study estimated.
However, more than 90% of chewing tobacco-related deaths and disability burden among men was found to occur in 10 countries, including India, Bangladesh, China, Pakistan and the US.
Among women, more than 90% of the burden was concentrated in countries, including India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia, Myanmar and China.
The researchers said the figures reflect total deaths and disability, meaning countries with larger populations may account for a greater share of the burden even if their rates are not the highest.
Patterns of chewing tobacco use also varied substantially by age and sex.
"These findings show why chewing tobacco control cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach," senior author Emmanuela Gakidou, professor in the department of health metrics sciences at IHME, said.

"Prevention and cessation strategies need to reflect how patterns of use differ by country, age, and sex, as well as the cultural and social factors that shape tobacco use in each setting," Gakidou said. PTI KRS

title: Temperament, childhood adversity may offer clues to psychiatric vulnerability: NIMHANS study

content.value: Temperamental traits and adverse experiences during childhood may together offer clues to vulnerability to major psychiatric disorders, a transdiagnostic study by researchers at NIMHANS has found.

The study, published recently in the Journal of Affective Disorders, examined 1,162 adults, including 532 people with psychiatric disorders, 457 unaffected first-degree relatives (FDRs) and 173 healthy controls. The participants were drawn from 393 multiplex families - families in which multiple members had been diagnosed with psychiatric disorders - involving schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD).

The researchers examined four broad dimensions of adult temperament - negative affectivity, extraversion/surgency, effortful control and orienting sensitivity - along with adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).

“Our findings suggest that temperament does not map onto psychiatric disorders in a simple, one-to-one manner. Rather, different combinations of temperamental characteristics are associated with different disorders, and some of these characteristics are also seen among unaffected family members,” said Srinivas Balachander, corresponding author and one of the lead researchers of the study.
Temperament shared within families

Using data from the erstwhile Accelerator programme for Discovery in Brain disorders using Stem cells (ADBS) project, (funded by the Department of Biotechnology and Pratiksha Trust), now known as the Rohini Nilekani Centre for Brain and Mind, at NIMHANS, the researchers found evidence of familial sharing across all four temperamental domains.

This was observed despite considerable variation in the psychiatric diagnoses within the same families. The finding is of interest because temperament is known to have a substantial heritable component, although the study did not directly establish that the temperamental characteristics observed were caused by specific genetic variants.
“In our study, considering the significant within-family heterogeneity in terms of different diagnoses, there was still a significant degree of shared temperament,” Dr. Balachander said.

Among affected participants, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder were associated with lower extraversion/surgency and orienting sensitivity. OCD was associated with higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity, along with lower effortful control and extraversion/surgency. Participants with AUD showed higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity and lower effortful control.

Some of these patterns were also observed among unaffected first-degree relatives. Relatives of people with schizophrenia showed lower extraversion/surgency, while relatives of people with OCD showed higher negative affectivity and lower effortful control.

“These findings are particularly interesting because some temperamental characteristics were evident even in individuals who did not have the disorder but belonged to families carrying a higher degree of familial risk,” Dr. Balachander said.
Childhood adversity and alcohol use disorder
The researchers also examined whether adverse childhood experiences altered the relationship between temperament and psychiatric disorders.

The clearest evidence for an interaction between temperament and childhood adversity emerged in alcohol use disorder. The overall ACE score was significantly associated with AUD, and interactions between childhood adversity and two temperamental domains - extraversion/surgency and effortful control - were also observed.

“Childhood adversity appears to add another layer to the relationship between temperament and psychiatric vulnerability. In our study, the evidence for this interaction was particularly apparent in alcohol use disorder, rather than uniformly across all four disorders,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers, however, cautioned against interpreting the findings as evidence that a particular temperament or childhood experience causes a psychiatric disorder.

The study was cross-sectional, meaning that the assessments were made at one point in time. The adult temperament measures were self-reported and could be influenced by current illness, treatment, illness duration or an individual’s perception of their own past Reports of childhood adversity may also be affected by recall and measurement biases.
Testing the findings

To examine whether the findings extended beyond the genetically enriched family sample, the researchers tested their statistical model using an independent community-based cohort from the Consortium for Vulnerability to Externalizing Disorders and Addiction (c-VEDA).
The analysis included 2,485 adults aged 18 to 23 years for whom the relevant temperament, ACE and psychiatric assessments were available.

The model showed an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.822 for alcohol use disorder, 0.742 for bipolar disorder and 0.752 for OCD. Its performance for schizophrenia was close to chance level, with an AUC of 0.526.

“The external validation gives us some indication that the associations identified in the family-based sample may extend to community populations for some disorders. However, the findings for schizophrenia did not replicate well, which is an important limitation and needs further investigation,” Dr. Balachander said.

The researchers said the findings point to the need for prospective studies that follow unaffected family members over time. Such studies could help determine whether particular temperamental characteristics precede the onset of psychiatric illness or are partly consequences of illness and its treatment.

“Temperament and childhood adversity may eventually become useful components of broader risk assessment frameworks, but we need prospective longitudinal evidence before we can say that they have predictive or preventive value,” Dr. Balachander said.

The researchers said that studying temperament alongside childhood adversity could eventually provide a more nuanced understanding of psychiatric vulnerability than considering family history alone. However, they stressed that the present findings do not establish that these measures can predict who will develop a psychiatric disorder.

The researchers said continued longitudinal follow-up of the cohort would be important to establish whether the observed temperamental patterns have value in identifying individuals at increased risk before the emergence of clinically significant symptoms.

title: Why Kerala’s groundwater is increasingly at risk of contamination | Explained

content.value: The story so far

The groundwater resources of Kerala have been under severe stress due to changes in rainfall pattern following climate change, high population density as well the fact that approximately 62% of the population relies on groundwater from an estimated 6.5 million open wells for their domestic needs. The State’s fragmented wastewater management system and the unscientific construction of septic tanks and pit latrines at homes close to shallow and open wells have resulted in persistent faecal contamination of ground water in the State, which has been documented by several studies.

A 2024 study in the Journal of Environmental Management reported that 7.4% of the State’s population could be making do with poor quality of groundwater and estimated that 0.59 million people in 252 local self government bodies in the State could be continuously exposing themselves to health risks from consuming ground water from wells which may not be chlorinated regularly.

And the latest report on E.coli contamination comes from Pala, where a water quality assessment conducted in flood-affected areas along the Meenachil river detected E. coli bacteria in 67% of the samples, raising concerns over the safety of drinking water sources in and around Pala.
Researchers attributed the spike in bacterial contamination to the recent floods, which may have allowed contaminated surface water to enter water sources.
How is contamination taking place?

It is a dangerous combination of high population density, unplanned urbanisation with hundreds of septic tanks and wells sitting close to each other in small plots and the State’s natural hydrogeological features that allow surface pollutants to reach the water table quickly. In recent years, unpredictable and heavy rainfall has been adding to the State’s woes, as oversaturation of the soil and the overflow of drainage systems can quickly allow pollution and microbial contamination to infiltrate ground water.

Environmental scientists explain that groundwater is drawn mostly from shallow, unconfined aquifers, which are recharged directly by rainfall and surface infiltration. In most areas the local water table might be sitting just below the level of the river bed and it naturally leaks water downwards to recharge the underlying unconfined aquifers. If rivers are polluted, then all groundwater resources in the surrounding area would also be carrying the same pollutant.
What is the extent of groundwater contamination in Keralam?

A community-level GIS study of 449 households in an urban area of Thiruvananthapuram in 2018 had reported that most of the wells were in an intermediate-high contamination risk state, with more than 77% of wells having a septic tank within 7.5 m radius. Coliform contamination was prevalent in 73% of wells, and the groundwater was predominantly acidic with a mean of 5.4, rendering it unfit for drinking.

This picture could be true for the rest of the State also. Because of the State’s unique geography and highly dispersed, continuous rural-urban settlement pattern, just about 5-6% of major urban zones are connected to a centralised pipe-based sewerage network system. The State’s sanitation strategy relies heavily on onsite sanitation systems, with individual household septic tanks and soak pits for sewage disposal.
Unscientific construction of these household sanitation systems has rendered much of the groundwater resources unsafe for human consumption, unless properly treated.
What are the health impacts?

Safe drinking water is one of the crucial social determinants of health. It is thus unfortunate that a State which has made enviable strides in developing its public health sector has paid little attention to ensuring that people have access to safe drinking water. While people in urban areas have to a large extent, access to treated water supply, in many rural areas of the State serviced by local small water supply schemes, water distribution lines often run close to sewerage lines and even small breaks in the pipelines can lead to the contamination of drinking water

Recurrent outbreaks of water-borne diseases like Hepatitis A, Shigellosis and norovirus outbreaks have been the bane of the State in recent years, especially in the northern districts of the State, indicating the scale and impact of groundwater contamination. Hepatitis A in particular has been taking a heavy toll on the State since the last three years, with significant mortality and in many instances, leaving people with severe morbidities

Epidemiological studies conducted by the ICMR and Health department into amoebic men­in­go­en­ceph­al­itis, which has emerged as a significant public health problem in Keralam in recent times, has traced the infection to the use of non-chlorinated well water which has high concentration of E.coli, in which free-living amoeba thrive
What is the sewerage infrastructure status?

To modernise sewerage infrastructure, the State is executing projects under the AMRUT 2.0 Mission, a Central initiative aimed at ensuring universal access to safe water and reliable sewerage connections across urban areas. The CAG’s 2025 report stated that at the closure of the AMRUT Mission (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), Kerala’s overall achievement was just 11.25% and only 0.13% households got sewerage connections.

Keralam’s geography, population density, lack of vast tracts of uninhabited land means that many proposed treatment plants end up being close to residential areas, which triggered huge public protests. Such protests led to the cancellation of multiple approved septage treatment plant projects in many parts of the State. There are also reports about the State’s financial crunch affecting project payments leading to delays in implementation

title: Shortage of drugs to treat NCDs in govt. hospitals in Keralam

content.value: Hospitals across the State are up against a shortage of drugs for treating non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Several commonly prescribed drugs for blood sugar management (metformin), hypertension (telmasartan), and cholesterol (atorvastatin) are in short supply in hospitals, even as authorities have assured that these will be back in stock within a week.

“It is not as though we are running short on all drugs. But NCD drugs are medicines that people should be taking without fail as a matter of routine and disruptions in its supply can be worrying. We anticipated this shortage last month  and  moved fast to make local purchases so our patients do not  miss the medication,” the medical officer at a family health centre in Thiruvananthapuram said.

“NCD drugs are in short supply but we have not had any issues because our hospital management committee has adequate funds, apart from the substantial resources that our block panchayat sets aside every year for purchasing drugs, for making local purchases.  If a substantial amount of drugs has to be purchased, then we float a tender. However, there are also health institutions in smaller panchayats which might be struggling to make local purchase because of insufficient funds,” the superintendent at a taluk hospital in the suburbs said.

Ideally, when a patient registered at the NCD clinic of a particular healthcare institution comes for review, the hospital should have at least 30 days’ stock of the NCD drugs for the patient to take home. In the present situation, many hospitals are not able to ensure that.

Medical officers said this year, the  Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) released only the drug supplies of the first quarter and that the second quarter release of June did not happen at all which led to the shortage of some drugs, including NCD drugs.

The KMSCL purchases around ₹700-800 crore worth of medicines every year for supplying to around 8,000 government healthcare institutions. In its last procurement exercise, 180 items reportedly received no bids, while suppliers quoted higher prices for another 171 items. This resulted in re-tendering and delays in placing fresh orders.

According to sources, the supply orders given in January-March, for some 18 non-bidder drugs, were cancelled by the new government because  the prices quoted were considered far too high, which triggered the present shortage. However, fresh procurement orders have been placed and the supplies are expected to arrive within a week, it was pointed out.

The fact that the KMSCL owes over  ₹2,200 crore to various pharma firms, for drugs purchased for hospitals as well as the drugs purchased by hospitals for patients under the Karunya Arogya Suraksha Padhati, has not helped the situation. The massive delays in payment is one of the reasons why many pharma forms do not respond to tenders floated by the KMSCL.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan had directed that the procurement procedures for the next financial year begin in October itself and that the entire process be completed by the end of December.

He also directed that middlemen be removed from the tender processes and that agencies dealing directly in imported medicines also be allowed to take part in tenders. He said a comprehensive overhaul was under way at the KMSCL

According to sources, there are also efforts to form a consortium  with medical service corporations of other States so that common purchase tenders can be floated, which might likely bring prices further down.

title: Massive markup on high-cost drugs: Raids to continue, Karnataka writes to Centre

content.value: The Karnataka government has flagged the disparity between the institutional landing costs and the Maximum Retail Prices (MRP) of high-value medicines, cancer drugs, antibiotics and hospital consumables supplied to hospitals across the State.

The department has raised the issue with the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA). Health and Family Welfare Minister U.T. Khader, in a letter dated September 23, wrote to the Union Health Minister seeking action.
Massive markup

Recent investigations by the Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) have revealed that pharmaceutical companies are supplying medicines to hospitals at heavily discounted institutional (landing) prices, while patients are being billed at or near the printed MRP, resulting in markups ranging from 10 times to over 52 times the actual procurement cost.
During inspections, the FSDA found extreme pricing anomalies in 253 drugs. For the cancer drug Cytax 100 mg, the landing cost was ₹342, while the MRP was ₹3,836, reflecting a markup of 11.2 times.
In the case of Gufipol, manufactured by Criticare, the markup was as high as 52.6 times, or 5,165%.
11-point letter

The Karnataka government has requested the Centre to mandate transparency in institutional pricing by requiring hospitals to display both the landing cost and MRP on patient bills, expand the list of drugs under price control under the Drug Price Control Order (DPCO), and regulate trade margins on essential high-value medicines and consumables.
The State has also sought the constitution of an inter-ministerial expert group, a national data study, and amendments to, or supplementation of, the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013.

Other demands include rationalisation of trade margins, mandatory cost-to-MRP transparency, expansion of the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), and creation of an audit and enforcement mechanism.
Drive to continue

Another special verification drive was conducted on September 25 and 26, 2026, at various wholesale premises, hospitals and other establishments in Bengaluru and district headquarters across Karnataka. According to the FSDA, preliminary observations indicate substantial differences between the landing cost, the MRP and the actual sale price of certain high-cost drugs, medical devices and hospital consumables. The inspections covered more than 768 consumable items and 189 high-cost drugs. The findings will be brought to the notice of the Central Government, the FSDA said in a statement.

According to the FSDA, the special verification exercise will continue in a phased manner. In the next phase, enforcement and verification activities will focus, among other categories, on antiretroviral drugs, higher-generation and critical antibiotics, medical devices and hospital consumables with substantial financial implications for patients.
Khader unveils SuMi
Health and Family Welfare Minister U.T. Khader released the new mascot for the Karnataka State AIDS Control Society on Thursday.
The mascot, SuMi, short for Suraksha Mitra, was selected from around 1,500 entries. The winning mascot was designed by Navya of Athena College of Nursing, Mangaluru.
The competition was organised by the AIDS Control Society to raise awareness about HIV/AIDS. It was conducted across all districts for people above the age of 16.

title: The last act of dignity: Sumira Roy on National Award-winning documentary Bhangaar

content.value: A decade ago, actor Deepika Padukone said in an ad campaign: ‘My body, My choice.’ But, in reality, when it comes to older people, society often wrests that agency from them. Last week, as the world observed both International Day of Older Persons (October 1) and Gandhi Jayanti (October 2), Mumbai-based Sumira Roy’s documentary film Bhangaar (Obsolete), raised the question of dignity in death and the right to die for the elderly.
The yet-to-release Marathi film, which won the National Film Award for Best Non-Feature Film last month, was screened by the Kriti Film Club in Delhi NCR.

Bhangaar trains the lens on Narayan and Iravati Lavate, an octogenarian Maharashtrian childless couple, who petitioned for active euthanasia in 2018. Iravati succumbed to cancer in 2023, Narayan lives in an old-age home. His eyesight and memory, too, have deserted him. After the news of the National Award came in, Royb wanted to share the moment with Narayan. She rang up Prakash Joshi, the brother of Iravati, who also appears in the film. Joshi told her that due to Narayan’s present old-age health and impediments there of, nothing would register with man.

While Nilesh Maniyar and Shonali Bose’s documentary A Fly on the Wall (2024) is also on the same subject and travels with Chika Kapadia to Switzerland for his last days, Roy’s documentary shows how only privilege can afford that right.

Monisha Advani, Bhangaar’s producer and partner, Emmay Entertainment, calls the film personal, “My late mother was a Maharashtrian and while growing up, the frugality of my maternal grandparents’ lives somewhere was mirrored in the Lavates. Sumira has given me the opportunity, in a private way, to pay tribute to my familial pedagogy."
Excerpts from an interview with director Roy:
You are from an advertising background; how, when and why did you transition into filmmaking and documentary films at that?

Since I’ve been a student, I’ve been passionate about films and documentary films and had even sat for the FTII entrance examination. But the women in my family were against me going to Pune and feared the casting couch in the film industry. Years later, when I went to Japan for work, I did a postgraduate course in Japanese cinema, theatre and painting. I was just hooked on when I saw [films by Yasujirō] Ozu and all the greats there. So, I thought, there’s a roundabout way to do films through advertising films. There’s a great amount of discipline in ad films; you shoot minimally and you have only 30-40 seconds to tell your story. Ad films [at Ogilvy and JWT] also gave me a lot of exposure to a lot of things that you need in documentaries. For instance, understanding human behaviour. And then, in documentaries, I learnt how to listen… to people’s stories. I went on foreign location shoots and for post-production. All that’s helped me now. In 2011, I left advertising and started two agencies, mainly for production. I was a little bit jaded and cynical, trying to do these falsehoods to make people buy things they didn’t need.
Did the Central Board of Film Certification raise any objections in Bhangaar?

Only to the title. The censor board didn’t like the word bhangaar [obsolete] and called it insulting. I had to keep going back to explain to them that the word is what Narayan uses [in life and in the film]. It’s his, not mine. After some time, they agreed but asked me to carry a disclaimer in Marathi at the start of the film that this is the character’s interpretation of the title. That was fine by me.
There seems to be a thematic continuity between your documentaries Last DaysLast Shot (2017) and Bhangaar. Tell us about the earlier film.

I have an idea, and then I make a film. I don’t just go and make documentaries, because I’m not an activist or an investigative filmmaker. As Narayan says in the film [Bhangaar], the day you’re born is the beginning of death. He echoes the Myth of Sisyphus when he says there’s no purpose to life; it’s absurd. I am drawn to existentialism, and like diving into the interior of minds.

For my earlier film, I was interested in exploring the philosophy of moksha and nirvana. I went to Banaras [Hindu] University, and walked around in the gullies and ghats. People would pop out from the woods to say, ‘Come listen to my poem.’ There, I found a Bengali poet-artist who had gone to Japan and become famous. He returned to Varanasi with his Japanese wife [they ran the Kumiko Guest House]. By the time I shot him, he looked like Rabindranath Tagore. He was about 80 or 81. He told me his idea of moksha: to dissolve the ego. Then I met a 26-year-old Dom in Harishchandra Ghat cremation ground, who [told me he] hardly got a chance to light the fire, and couldn’t make money with it. So, he bought a camera and started shooting the relatives of the dead. He said from his experience that a good person’s corpse burns faster than a sinner’s.
Narayan and Iravati Lavate in a still from Bhangaar.
What drew you to Iravati and Narayan Lavate’s story?

It’s a personal reason. My long-widowed mother was quite active in life. She’d drive, have a social life, her body and mind intact. A year before she passed away, she started saying, ‘I want to die with dignity.’ I was a documentary filmmaker, but I never listened to her nor asked her what she meant. I was petrified of her dying. [After] she passed away, I was stricken with grief and regret. I came across the Lavates’ story in Mid-Day; they asked for the right to die together with dignity. That struck me, and I went to meet them in their 12x12 room in a Mumbai chawl, to get closure for what I hadn’t done with my mother. They taught me so much about Marathi literature and theatre. Narayan looked like Picasso to me. He knew the Constitution by heart. I asked, how could they want to die. He said, ‘It’s time to go.’

They had this fixed spiel they would rattle to the media/news channels. They would do the same during our initial days of shoot. I just told them not to look at the camera and go about their days. I had to be a fly on the wall and filmed them over four years. Afterwards, they forgot there’s a camera. My DOP (cinematographer Ishani Roy) is brilliant because it was a boot camp for her, with no lights, no space to set up the camera. The aerial shot of them playing cards was shot from atop a washing machine.
In India, the elderly population is growing rapidly even as the birth rate declines. What did your research throw up about ageing and caregiving?

The elderly are growing three times faster than the population of the youth. Palliative care exists only for the rich. There’s no geriatric care and no focus on what is going to happen to the elderly population. All of us are in some stage of caregiving. We are either watching our parents or grandparents.
A still from Bhangaar.

Gandhi spoke of self-rule. Swaraj is not just political self-rule but also the rule/autonomy over oneself. Does that idea of self-determination versus duty get complicated when it comes to an older person’s choice to die?

Loss of personhood and loss of autonomy, which older people fear, is exactly why they [Irawati and Narayan] asked for it [active euthanasia]. We do not connect with our families. Our conversations revolve around whether they have taken their medicines, if the oxygen tank is running low, if the nurse administered the injection. That’s our only conversation with them. The elderly feel like they are [outdated] machines. We have moved away from joint families to nuclear families. As a society, we have forgotten how to respect someone who has lived longer than expected. We keep talking about Gen Z and loneliness, but loneliness is far worse among the older generations. We hardly talk about it. Even our films don’t.

We’ve read about the Aruna Shanbaug case. This year, the Supreme Court gave its landmark judgment permitting passive euthanasia for Harish Rana who was in a vegetative state for over 13 years. What has been the impact of the Lavates’ petition?
Narayan and Iravati are the pioneers of this, at least in our country, or in South Asia. The courts are getting more and more petitions since. The press doesn’t cover many of these.
A still from Bhangaar.
Bhangaar (Obsolete) screens on October 1 at the India Habitat Centre, Delhi, and on October 4 at Museo Camera, Gurugram at 4.30 pm.
