title: CSIR-CCMB develops India-specific tool to predict Sickle Cell severity

content.value: Doctors may soon have a more reliable way to predict how severely sickle cell anaemia (SCA) will affect Indian patients, thanks to a new India-specific disease severity score developed by scientists at the CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB).
Potential impact of the India-specific tool

The new tool, developed using clinical data from Indian children, could improve treatment decisions and disease management as existing international scoring systems do not accurately reflect the clinical profile of Indian patients with SCA, whose disease patterns often differ from those seen in African and Western populations.
What is Sickle Cell Anaemia?

SCA is an inherited blood disorder caused by a mutation in the beta globin gene, which produces abnormal haemoglobin causing red blood cells to assume a sickle shape, leading to anaemia, severe pain episodes, organ damage and other complications. India is among the countries with the highest burden of the disease, according to Giriraj R. Chandak, physician-scientist and Sir J C Bose Fellow at CSIR-CCMB.
He and fellow scientists including Suraj S. Nongmaithem, Amitabh Biswas, Swaroop Iyer, Jandhayala Vyshnavi, Archana Wath and Dipty Jain conducted this study.
Early identification helps to alleviate suffering

SCA is caused by a single genetic mutation, yet its severity varies considerably. While some patients experience relatively mild symptoms, others endure repeated hospitalisations and life-threatening complications. An early identification of those at risk of severe clinical course can help devise targeted strategies and alleviate the suffering.

Indian patients are said to have a milder disease profile than many African populations, partly because of higher levels of foetal haemoglobin, which helps reduce disease severity. Complications such as leg ulcers, pulmonary hypertension and ‘priapism’, commonly reported in African populations, are comparatively rare here. However, nutritional deficiencies, infectious diseases and environmental stressors can worsen anaemia.

Researchers analysed the medical records of 171 SCA children aged up to 18 years and receiving treatment at the Government Medical College and Hospital, Nagpur, to develop a more suitable assessment tool. Two experienced paediatricians independently classified the patients into mild, moderate and severe categories based on their clinical condition.

The study found that the widely used Paediatric Severity Score (PSS), developed using international patient data, matched expert clinical assessments in only about 67% of cases. The score was modified adding four clinical features frequently observed among Indian patients — recurrent blood transfusions, severe anaemia requiring hospitalisation and acute febrile illnesses.
Improvement in clinical assessments

The revised model — ‘ISS1’ (India-specific Severity Score), improved clinical assessments to nearly 83%. A second version, ‘ISS2’, replaced the laboratory measurements with easily observable clinical indicators to achieve an overall concordance of about 85%, correctly identifying all patients in the mild category and improving performance in moderate cases. This enables clinicians to decide the management without the need for many laboratory investigations.

The findings highlight the importance of developing population-specific tools rather than relying solely on models designed for different ethnic groups and healthcare settings. It was also found that painful vaso-occlusive crises were the most common complication among the children while frequent blood transfusions, severe anaemia and recurrent fever-related illnesses led to hospital admissions.

“We believe the new scoring systems could help doctors make quicker and more informed decisions on treatment, including the use and dosage of hydroxyurea, one of the primary drugs used to manage SCA. This study adds to the comprehensive efforts by CSIR-CCMB in making a difference in the lives of Indian SCA patients, under CSIR-Sickle Cell Anaemia Mission”, said Dr. Chandak.

This could be applicable to other low- and middle-income countries with similar genetic backgrounds, disease patterns and healthcare challenges. However, further validation in larger and more diverse populations will be needed before the tool can be adopted more widely, added researchers.

title: G.P. Talwar at 100: scientist, institution builder, lifelong researcher

content.value: At any gathering, you could easily spot him by his colourful printed shirt or jacket. His tall stature, smiling face, and warm handshakes have put generations of students, researchers, and scientists at ease.

Since 1956, when he joined the founding faculty of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, he has never stopped working at the bench. Along the way, he developed the world’s first leprosy vaccine and a hormonal birth control vaccine, founded India’s first immunology institution, mentored hundreds of students, and continues his research work at a private R&D institution he established after retirement. That’s Gursaran Prasad Talwar, Pran to friends and colleagues, who turns 100 on October 2, today.
Gaining experience

Talwar had a troubled childhood. His mother passed away a week after delivering him in 1926, at her mother’s place in Hisar, then in undivided Punjab. His father, a science postgraduate from the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore (now Bengaluru), ran a small pharmacy and dispensary in Lahore, where he shifted after remarrying. After a few years of schooling at a madrasa in Hoshiarpur, his father admitted Talwar to the Central Model School in Lahore. His excellent performance in the matriculation exam got him into the Government College Lahore, where he did his BSc Honours and MSc (tech).

As part of the postgraduation course, Talwar came to work at a pharmaceutical manufacturing unit in the Kangra Valley in the summer of 1947 but was caught in the communal frenzy that followed the partition of Punjab. He somehow made it to Lahore only to find that his family had migrated to India. Thus he landed in Delhi in late 1947 and started looking for jobs.

At this time, European countries began offering scholarships for higher education to Indian students via the Government of India. Talwar applied, and he was shortlisted and given a choice. “I chose France. Their national echo ‘Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité’ appealed to my leftist leanings,” Talwar recalled. He joined the fermentation laboratory of the Pasteur Institute, but soon shifted to the biochemistry wing. He completed his Docteur es Sciences degree in 1953. After two years of postdoctoral work in Germany and working in an industrial concern in Milan in Italy, Dr. Talwar returned to India in 1955. His idea was to gain necessary experience for starting a pharmaceutical or chemical business in India.
Great excitement

But life took a different turn as Dr. Talwar was selected to join the proposed biochemistry department of AIIMS as an associate professor in 1956. “In medical colleges, biochemistry was then a minor part of physiology. I tried against all odds and succeeded in making it an independent course with a separate compulsory paper,” Dr. Talwar said. Simultaneously, he established a research lab and began working on growth-promoting hormones like estradiol. He published papers on mechanisms that enable hormones to activate gene transcription and translation.

The 1960s were a period of great excitement in modern biology, with landmark discoveries being made. Pushpa Mitra Bhargava, then at the Regional Research Laboratory Hyderabad, teamed up with Dr. Talwar to form what came to be called the Guha Research Conference. Bhargava organised an international symposium on nucleic acids at the Regional Research Laboratory, Hyderabad, in January 1964, which several newly minted and future Nobel laureates, such as Francis Crick, Gerhard Schramm, Charles Heidelberger, Seymour Benzer, and Roger Monier, attended. The trio of Bhargava, Dr. Talwar, and Obaid Siddiqui themselves constituted the rising stars of modern biology in India.

In 1970, the World Health Organization (WHO) proposed to start a regional training centre in immunology and initiate research in leprosy at AIIMS. Dr. Talwar was hesitant since his work on hormones was going on satisfactorily. “Howard Goodman, who was leading the WHO team, said India had the largest burden of leprosy in the world and asked me bluntly: ‘Do you think Americans will come and solve this problem?’ I knew nothing about leprosy but then started studying why people get leprosy and found that it was their inability to react immunobiologically to some key antigens of M. leprae,” Dr. Talwar said.

This fundamental understanding eventually led to the first curative vaccine against leprosy. It was a long process but resulted in an effective vaccine that not only cured the disease but also healed the scars. It also has the ability to react with key antigens of M. tuberculosis. The mycobacterium used to make the vaccine was later sequenced and named MIP or Mycobacterium indicus pranii, combining Pran and ‘National Institute of Immunology’, or NII.
Founding NII

Another landmark contribution by Dr. Talwar was the birth control vaccine, which has undergone extensive human trials and has been found to be safe, but is still to go into commercial production. “I found that all available birth control methods like vasectomy and intra-uterine devices were not yielding desired results because of various reasons. I wanted to develop a vaccine which could prevent pregnancy without derangement of menstrual regularity and hormonal profiles. So the target molecule should have a key role in sustaining pregnancy,” Dr. Talwar explained as to why he chose human chorionic gonadotropin to develop the vaccine.

Dr. Talwar revealed that the idea of the NII emerged from a discussion with Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. In 1980, the Jawaharlal Nehru Memorial Fund selected Dr. Talwar as a Nehru Fellow; during the fellowship, Indira Gandhi, who was the Fund’s chairperson, used to meet the Fellows to learn about their work. Dr. Talwar told her about the leprosy vaccine and also explained how childhood immunisation could save millions of lives. She asked Dr. Talwar if India had enough vaccines, and he said ‘no’. Ms. Gandhi told him to give him a one-page note in ten days on how India could develop new vaccines.

Dr. Talwar happened to travel to New York the next day for a scientific meeting. “While sipping champagne along with caviar, on the plane, I wrote a note and submitted it to her upon my return. It was this note that became the basis for founding NII just two years later, in 1983,” Dr. Talwar said.

After retiring from the NII and a stint with the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, New Delhi, Dr. Talwar founded the Talwar Research Foundation in 1999, where he continues to work with a small band of researchers on hormones, antigens, and antibodies. He says he has no regrets in life as he begins his second century.
Dinesh C. Sharma is a New Delhi-based journalist and author.

title: Multiple Indian payloads launched by Space X’s Falcon 9

content.value: Multiple payloads developed by Indian companies were successfully deployed in orbit by Space X’s Falcon 9 in the early hours of October 2 from the Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, U.S.A., as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission.

Dhruva Space’s Launching Expeditions for Aspiring Payloads (LEAP-2), hosting multiple In-Orbit Demonstration (IOD) missions, which includes a star tracker by France-based Sodern ArianeGroup, and TAPAS-1 by India-based Satleo Labs, were part of the Transporter-18 mission.

Dhruva Space stated that LEAP-2 was successfully deployed in orbit at 1 a.m. IST on October 2. It has undertaken the end-to-end launch integration of the LEAP-2 satellite with SpaceX’s Falcon 9 launch vehicle, building on its experience with LEAP-1, where Dhruva Space became the first private Indian company to undertake the launch vehicle integration of its satellite in-house.

“This extends Dhruva Space’s role beyond satellite manufacturing into launch integration and end-to-end mission delivery, reinforcing its full-stack space engineering approach. LEAP-2 will be supported by Dhruva Space’s growing global ground infrastructure, including its owned and operated ground station in Luleå, Sweden; the first NGE-owned and operated ground station outside India, authorised by the Government of India to provide Ground-Station-as-a-Service,” the company stated.

TAPAS-1 (Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions), developed by SatLeo Labs, is India’s first dedicated commercial CubeSat-category thermal payload, and the opening flight of the country’s first full-stack commercial thermal intelligence platform.

The Ahmedabad0based SatLeo Labs said that using Thermal Infrared (TIR) sensing, TAPAS-1 captures temperature information invisible to conventional optical imagery, enabling in-orbit demonstration and validation of SatLeo’s thermal sensing technology, payload performance, and data-processing capabilities. The mission marks a category-first for India in dedicated commercial thermal (LWIR) Earth observation.

Also part of the mission was TakeMe2Space, which launched its MOI-1A satellite that enables customers to run AI models on Earth-observation data directly in orbit, processing imagery before transmitting the resulting insights to the ground.

“The 14 kg satellite carried 117 trillion operations per second (TOPS) of onboard computing capacity, 2 TB of storage, and a nine-band multispectral imager. These capabilities are designed to reduce the need to download large volumes of raw imagery for processing on Earth, supporting applications such as agricultural monitoring, mining and supply-chain intelligence,” according to TakeMe2Space.

Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (INSPACe) Chairperson Pawan Kumar Goenka said that the deployment of the payloads as part of SpaceX’s Transporter-18 mission is a big day for India’s private space sector.

“Genuinely big day for India’s private space sector. SpaceX’s Transporter 18 is carrying two Indian satellites and an Indian hosted payload into orbit, all authorised by IN-SPACe. Among them, @satleolabs TAPAS-1, India’s first commercial thermal imaging payload built by a private company. Thermal sensing picks up what ordinary optical cameras cannot, from crop stress to forest fires to urban heat. A new layer of Earth intelligence, now opened up by Indian industry. Alongside it, @tm2space‘s MOI-1A brings AI computing to orbit, running models on the satellite itself, and @DhruvaSpace ‘s LEAP-2 flies four payloads, demonstrating its platform for hosting others in space. Orbital computing, thermal intelligence, and a homegrown hosting platform, all on a single flight. This is the range and ambition of India’s private space ecosystem today. Congratulations to all three teams. Wishing you a clean deployment and a long innings in orbit,” Goenka posted on X.
In total, the 18th Transporter rideshare mission carried 130 payloads.

title: Ig Nobel Prizes 2026 awarded to serious work in amusing areas

content.value: On September 3, a dozen people from various countries were declared to be the recipients of the Ig Nobel Prizes for 2026. Some readers may wonder what an Ig Nobel Prize is. The Ig Nobel Prizes are a light-hearted parody of the actual Nobel Prizes. They were instituted in 1991 by Marc Abraham, editor of The Journal of Irreproducible Research.
For example, last year, a group from Nigeria worked on how lizards like to eat pizza, and another group was feted for showing that when a lactating mother eats garlic, the baby drinks more milk.

title: Poor diet, sedentary habits contribute to rising metabolic disorders among young people, says expert

content.value: Poor diet, sedentary habits, and prolonged screen use are contributing to metabolic disorders among young people, said Challa Suresh, Scientist ‘G’ and Director Grade, Head of the Cell Biology Division, AcSIR Coordinator at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, at an oration organised by Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research recently.

Delivering the Prof. S.P. Thyagarajan Endowment Oration on ‘The Modern Lifestyle Paradox: Why are Young People Developing Metabolic Disorder Earlier?’, Prof. Suresh stressed the importance of nutritious food and healthier lifestyle habits in preventing lifestyle-related illnesses.

He advised young people to choose wholesome, nutrient-rich foods, and limit processed and packaged foods, which he linked to rising obesity. He also called for reducing screen time, noting that prolonged use of digital devices encourage sedentary behaviour and affect memory and overall well-being.
The event was attended by university officials, academicians, clinicians, researchers, and students.

title: What human brain tissue transplanted into mice showed us

content.value: A study published in September in Nature by neuroscientist Sergiu Pașca’s group at Stanford University reports an experiment that sounds almost like science fiction. Human brain tissue grown from stem cells was transplanted into mice in which much of the cerebral cortex had been genetically prevented from forming. The transplanted tissue grew into this vacant space, produced several types of human brain cells, became electrically active, connected with the mouse nervous system and was associated with measurable differences in behaviour.

Yet, an important limitation must be stated at the outset. The researchers have not created a human brain inside a mouse. The transplanted tissue remained immature, lacked the ordered structure of a normal human cortex, and the study cannot establish that human neurons directly caused any particular behaviour. What the experiment offers is a narrow glimpse of human brain development as it unfolds inside a non-human living nervous system.
Our blind spot

Understanding how the human brain develops matters both for evolutionary biology and for medicine. The cerebral cortex expanded greatly during human evolution, developing specialised cells and connections involved in language, planning and complex social behaviour. Studying how these features emerge may help explain what makes the human brain distinctive.

It is also medically important because many neurological and psychiatric disorders may begin during development, long before symptoms appear. The main challenge is access. Scientists cannot experimentally manipulate a developing human brain as they can in laboratory animals. Imaging can track structural changes, while foetal and post-mortem tissues provide useful snapshots. Still, neither allows researchers to alter a gene or developmental process and observe the consequences over time. Human developmental neuroscience has therefore long faced a major experimental blind spot.
Growing brain tissue

Stem cell technology opened up another avenue to study the developing human brain. Scientists can take ordinary human cells, re-programme them into an earlier, flexible state called induced pluripotent stem cells, and guide them to become nerve cells. When these cells are grown together in three dimensions, they can organise into structures called organoids. A brain organoid is a small piece of laboratory-grown neural tissue that reproduces some features of early brain development. Organoids allow researchers to observe how human neurons develop, introduce disease-related genetic changes and test responses to drugs.

However, tissue grown in a lab dish lacks key features of a living brain, including normal blood circulation, sensory inputs and long-distance connections with other parts of the nervous system. Researchers, including the  Stanford group, have therefore transplanted human brain organoids into rodents, where the living environment supports better survival and maturation. Yet this creates another constraint: the rodent already has its own cortex, so the transplanted human tissue must compete for limited space and neural connections, and has never amounted to more than a fragment of the host’s brain.
A third window

The Stanford researchers opened up a third possibility. Instead of engineering a better graft, they re-engineered the host. Using genetic techniques, they produced mice in which much of the neocortex and hippocampus never formed. Because the mice were also bred to lack a functioning immune system, the human tissue would not be rejected. Human cortical organoids were then transplanted into the vacant space soon after birth. The researchers call the approach xenocortication. ‘Xeno’ refers to something originating from another species, while the cortex is the outer region of the brain involved in many higher functions.

In the Stanford experiment, freed from much of the competition from mouse cortical tissue, the human grafts expanded substantially, and by three months, they made up about 92% of the animal’s cortical tissue. They produced several types of developing cortical neurons, along with progenitor cells and astrocytes, at a stage of maturity roughly equivalent to that of the human cortex late in the second trimester of pregnancy. The grafts generated deep-layer neurons carrying the molecular signature of von Economo neurons, large, distinctively shaped cells found in humans and a few other large-brained mammals, but absent in rodents, and long associated with social cognition and psychiatric illness. Such neurons are almost impossible to grow in a dish.

The grafts also became electrically active, producing slow waves that swept across the tissue every few minutes, a pattern characteristic of developing, rather than mature, cortical networks. They formed connections with surviving parts of the mouse nervous system, and human nerve fibres reached as far as the cervical spinal cord, something not seen in mice with an intact cortex.  This is the conceptual leap of the study: human neural tissue was no longer a fragment lodged inside a rodent’s brain, but tissue occupying almost all of the space where that animal’s cortex would have been.
Reading behaviour

The next question was whether this integration had any functional effect. The starting point was itself surprising. Mice lacking most of their neocortex and hippocampus (roughly half the brain by volume) remained active and mobile, ran at normal speeds and responded normally to heat and touch. To detect subtler differences, the researchers combined conventional behavioural tests with a machine-learning system called Motion Sequencing (MoSeq). A depth camera recorded freely moving mice, while the software divided their movements into 60 recurring sub-second patterns, such as rearing, pausing, and turning, creating a detailed behavioural fingerprint rather than relying solely on speed or distance travelled. By this measure, mice lacking much of their cortex behaved differently from normal animals. Xenocortical mice showed an intermediate pattern, suggesting that transplantation altered behaviour without fully restoring it.  In a Y-shaped maze used to test working memory, normal and xenocortical mice performed above chance, whereas mice lacking much of their cortex did not. This suggests possible partial functional compensation, but does not prove that human neurons restored memory.
Why this matters

To show what the platform can do, the researchers exposed the mice to five hours of severe oxygen deprivation. The response was confined to the human tissue: a molecular marker of oxygen stress appeared in the graft but not in the adjacent mouse brain, and not at all in animals without a graft. Two days later, the xenocortical mice walked differently, shifting to a more stable stance without any change in their speed. Imaging 10  days on showed changes in the graft’s blood vessels. Under the microscope, the graft’s supporting cells had multiplied and become more complex.

This creates a potentially powerful experimental pathway. Scientists could introduce a disease-related mutation into human cells, allow the resulting neural tissue to develop within a living nervous system, observe changes in cells and circuits, assess whether behaviour is affected, and then test possible treatments. Such models could help study developmental brain disorders, the oxygen deprivation around birth that can lead to cerebral palsy, human-specific neuronal diseases and evolutionary differences between human and animal brains. They may also provide a platform for drug testing and, eventually, for evaluating regenerative or cell-based treatments for severe early brain injury.
Limits and ethics

The model is still far from reproducing a developing human brain. The grafts  did not reproduce the full balance of excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Human neurons also mature far more slowly than mouse neurons, creating a mismatch between the developmental timelines of graft and host. Although anatomical connections were observed, this does not prove that they directly controlled behaviour. Any behavioural changes, therefore, arise from a hybrid system in which human tissue interacts with the remaining mouse brain.

These scientific limits also shape the ethical questions. There is no evidence that the animals developed human consciousness or a human-like mind. However, future models may contain larger, more mature, and better-organised human neural tissue, with greater integration into the host brain. At what point might this alter an animal’s cognition, perception or capacity for experience in ethically significant ways? The researchers anticipated this  question and  consulted bioethicists at Stanford before beginning. The paper argues that going further towards grafts with mature cortical layering, or transplantation into embryos or into non-human primates, will require a greater degree of scrutiny before such experiments begin.
Ultimately, xenocortication is important not because it creates a human brain in another species, but because it may provide a third window to study human brain development.

(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com; Dr Veera Rajagopal is a physician-scientist & geneticist working in drug discovery. veera.scientist@gmail.com)

title: The Hindu to release documentary Gandhi for GenZ today

content.value: On the occasion of Gandhi Jayanthi on Friday (October 2, 2026), The Hindu is releasing a documentary Gandhi for GenZ: The Mahatma is suddenly cool again that highlights the relevance of the Father of the Nation to the struggles of the youth of India today.
With interviews of Gandhi historians and GenZ activists and archival footage, the 30-minute documentary is both a tribute to and an assessment of the Mahatma.
It will be published on The Hindu’s website and on YouTube.

title: Super Intelligence and Trump’s AI Accord with Big Tech leaders | Explained

content.value: The story so far: On September 29, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump stood surrounded by the leaders of American AI giants. He announced that they had come together and signed something akin to a constitution.

The page-long document, titled ‘White House Accord and the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities’, was an agreement on AI safety commitments by tech companies that are developing frontier models. The accord misspelled “United States”; an error that was widely circulated on the internet.
What is U.S. President Trump’s AI accord?

The pact stresses the need for tech companies to build safe AI products and foster public trust. It outlines four steps to make it happen, starting with robust internal controls to prevent unintended AI hacking, developing an internal team to manage safety operations and resolutions at the company, partnering with an independent external auditor for assessments, and designating an independent committee of the board of directors to address reports.
The document noted that “participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems.”

The tech leaders who signed the AI accord were Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI Co-founder/President Greg Brockman, XAI CEO Elon Musk, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
A notable omission was Microsoft, even though CEO Satya Nadella was included in a luncheon with the U.S. President, alongside other tech leaders.

Several technologists who signed the agreement shared their thoughts on AI regulation with Mr. Trump and the press. Nvidia’s Huang insisted that there was no conflict amongst innovation, technology, and safety. By contrast, Anthropic’s Amodei highlighted that the technology had very real risks, but called for collaboration nonetheless.

Some tech leaders took to social media to share their perspectives. Google’s Pichai posted on X that the company is “focused on building the right way” and releasing models “only after they’ve been thoroughly reviewed.”

Meta’s Zuckerberg posted that leaders of every major American AI company “committed to implementing robust internal controls and multiple layers of audits and reviews” to boost people’s trust in the technology these firms are building.
Critics pointed out that the accord lacks any penalty clause in the case of potential violations of the agreement.
Is the AI accord binding?
Not really. The very first sentence of the AI accord notes that “every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public.”
Mr. Trump referred to the agreement as being “morally binding,” and called it a “form of protection.”

In other words, companies are being left to police themselves, apart from linking up with an external auditor. These are by no means groundbreaking regulations or directives. Rather, they are highly generalised guidelines and many were already in place.
The AI accord further noted that “over time, it may make sense to codify ‌these steps into laws or regulations.”

At the present moment, the four specified controls are not legally enforceable or mandated; as per the wording of the AI accord, the White House merely “believe[d]” that each company should implement the four listed audits.
The White House noted that implementing controls and audits was “critical” for a safe future and the companies that had signed the document were committed to their actions.
What will be the effect of the AI accord?
The White House’s AI accord largely serves as a show of unity amongst AI companies and the President of the United States.

This comes in the face of criticism from lawmakers across the European Union and Australia, who seek to regulate built-in-America AI models by implementing more guardrails to protect user privacy and children’s mental health.
There is also mounting backlash over AI agents “going rogue” and attempting to hack secure online platforms. Anthropic, OpenAI, and now Google have been named after their models were identified.

In late September, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese reported that OpenAI’s AI agent had hacked into the country’s healthcare platform this June, but the incident was not formally reported until September 10.
The Australian PM confirmed he had taken OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to task over the delayed report, adding that the investigations were ongoing and promising there would be legal consequences.

The U.S. President is also shaping the way the world discusses AI. Mr. Trump on September 29 passed an executive order to inaugurate the era of “super intelligence,” calling on the executive branch of his administration to use this term and “SI,” instead of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI.”
This was to better capture the capabilities of the technology, according to him.
U.S. diplomats have been instructed to make the change in their communications, reported AP.

title: Trump formally replaces ‘Artificial Intelligence’ with ’Super Intelligence’ in an executive order

content.value: U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) signed an executive order directing executive departments and agencies to begin using ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in place of ‘Artificial Intelligence’ and ‘AI.’

While the U.S. President mulled over the idea for around a week, an executive order now means that the new terminology will have to be formally defined and adopted across the relevant U.S. government offices and departments.
Mr. Trump claimed that the change was appropriate when taking into consideration the “promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities” of AI technologies.
The AI-to-SI update is set to apply to official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents, per the executive order.
U.S. diplomats have been instructed to make the change in their communications and official correspondence, reported AP.
Media outlets reported earlier in the week that the Chinese foreign ministry had acknowledged the change in terminology and signalled its respect for the policy update.

“The terminology used by the [U.S.] Federal Government should reflect the transformative capabilities of these technologies and the limitless opportunities they create for the American people.  Accordingly, the term “Super Intelligence” more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies,” stated Mr. Trump in the executive order.

title: WhatsApp rolls out parental controls for teens

content.value: WhatsApp on Wednesday (September 30, 2026) announced that it was introducing parental controls for teens.

The new features will allow parents and teens to customise their privacy settings on WhatsApp, with a parent-set PIN helping make sure that the teen does not bypass the controls without the adult’s approval.
As a result, parents can now decide who can see their teen children’s profile photos or add them to groups.

Furthermore, parents will be notified about their teens joining or exiting groups, as well as when groups grow in size. Parents can further control their teen’s use of Channels, the Status updates they view and share, and the Meta AI experience.
For AI, they can choose between a default 13+ setting and a stricter ‘Limited Content’ setting.
The settings are optional, WhatsApp noted in its blog post, so they can be both adjusted and turned off.
WhatsApp confirmed that even with the parental controls in place, teens’ chats would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption.

“This is just the start. We’re building these controls step by step, based on what families tell us they need. All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone’s personal messages private,” said WhatsApp in a blog post.

title: Frame SOP governing participation of elephants in temple events, religious functions, Madras HC directs Tamil Nadu government

content.value: The Madras High Court on Thursday (October 1, 2026) directed the Tamil Nadu government to formulate a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) governing the use of elephants in religious functions and temple festivals strictly in compliance with animal welfare and safety standards.

First Division Bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan directed the Environment, Climate Change and Forests secretary and the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) secretary to first constitue a Joint Working Group (JWG).

The JWG should consist of the Chief Wildlife Warden, HR&CE Commissioner and expert veterinary officers and it shall draft and submit a comprehensive and standardised SOP governing all aspects related to the participation of elephants in religious events and temple festivals, the Bench ordered.

The judges said, the SOP should provide for pre-festival health & microchip verification process by making it mandatory to obtain veterinary fitness certification, physical inspection, and verification of microchips/DNA profiles prior to granting permission for participation of the pachyderms in any festival.
ALSO WATCH Sacred and shackled: Tamil Nadu’s temple elephants

Concurring with the submissions made by senior counsel V. Raghavachari and S. Prabakaran for Seva Trust which had filed a public interest litigation petition and Special Government Pleader (Forests) Mohammed Fayaz Ali, the judges said, district level committees (DLCs) should also be formed for granting approval.

The Division Bench said, it should be made mandatory for registering the animals and obtaining prior clearance from the DLCs. It also wanted tranportation protocols such as strict regulations with respect to maximum travel duration, compulsory rest intervals, veterinary transit support, and use of specialised transit vehicles.

Authoring the order, the Chief Justice said, the SOP should also cover safety & environmental thresholds by prescribing decible limits for loudspeakers/firecrackers, maintaining safe physical buffer zones between elephants and crowds, and prohibiting the display of elephants in close proximity to pyrotechnics.

Directing the JWG to lay down handler & mahout standards too, the court said there must be verification of qualified mahouts and strict prohibition of heavy tethering, spiked chains, or any form of physical cruelty. The judges ordered that the draft SOP must be placed before the court on October 30, 2026.

“Elephants hold a significant place in the cultural, historical, and religious traditions of the State, where they participate in rituals and processions governed by ancient temple customs. However, the integration of captive animals into religious ceremonies cannot exist in a legal vacuum,” the Bench wrote.

It said: ”Scriptural traditions must strictly accord with constitutional values, statutory safeguards, and the fundamental duty enjoined upon the State and as well as the citizens under Article 51A(g) of the Constitution of India to show compassion to living creatures.”

title: Gen-2 joined green crackers | Explained

content.value: Story so far: On September 30, the Supreme Court ruled out a nationwide firecracker ban and accepted CSIR-NEERI’s recommendation for a “limited and conditional relaxation”. This allows the manufacture of next-generation joined green crackers that meet noise, emission and safety norms ahead of Diwali. The Bench said it would not permit 24-hour bursting and would consider fixed time windows.
What are Gen 2 ‘green’ crackers?

They are crackers whose chemistry has been reworked to release less particulate matter than conventional ones, without losing brightness, sound or shelf life. NEERI’s (CSIR-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute) changes include additives such as zeolite, water-releasing compounds that act as dust suppressants, and metallic composites that improve combustion. Conventional crackers rely on barium nitrate, antimony and other metals linked to respiratory disease.

The label is a misnomer, as there is nothing environmentally friendly about these crackers. NEERI’s own scientists have called them “reduced emission fireworks”. NEERI claims that the earlier generation of ‘green crackers’ saw a 30% cut in particulate matter. Its newer analysis says that the newer variants, called ‘Gen-2’, reduce pollution 45%-60% for PM10 and PM2.5, using formulations with less barium. However, these are laboratory figures, not verified in real-world conditions. Only manufacturers with a licence from the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), the central explosives regulator, can register with NEERI.
Why are we discussing green crackers now?

The Court has put a time-limited, conditional endorsement on a specific product, the “joined” cracker, a string of crackers burst in sequence. The “joined” crackers are colloquolly known by many names — garland crackers, lari crackers, wala crackers, saram, and so on. NEERI says the new version bursts five braids a second instead of 25, stretching the burn fivefold. Smaller shells have cut solid waste by 4% to 32%. Noise must stay within 125 dB(AI)/145 dB(C) peak, and barium-based ingredients are restricted.

The science is still unfinished. NEERI is modelling how barium from Gen-2 crackers disperses in Bhopal, Delhi, Kolkata and Chennai, with results due by October 15. The Court has also given the Central Pollution Control Board and the Centre more time for barium and decibel tests.
What prompted their development?

Delhi-NCR’s winter smog and the cracker ban. Petitions were filed in the Supreme Court in 2015 over Delhi-NCR’s winter smog. In November 2016, the Court suspended licences for firecracker sales in the region, and in October 2017 it banned sales. The next year, it  laid down the framework that, until now, allowed only reduced-emission ‘green’ crackers and barred barium salts and ‘joined’ crackers.
From 2025: Have ‘green’ crackers brought down pollution?

The September 30 order relaxes that framework for a redesigned version of the joined cracker, subject to NEERI’s conditions. NEERI began developing the formulations that year. In January 2025, the Court extended the firecracker ban to the NCR areas of Uttar Pradesh and Haryana. However, the ban hit a largely small-scale informal industry. Green crackers, the Centre has argued in the past,  are meant to balance public sentiment during festivals, pollution and livelihoods.
Does Delhi’s winter-pollution plan say anything on crackers?

The Delhi Government announced its Winter Action Plan 2026-27 on September 29. Reported measures include 50% work from home from November 1, doubled parking charges and a full construction and demolition ban from December 10 to January 20. Non-BS-VI vehicles registered outside Delhi will be barred from November 1. There are no strictures on firecracker dos and don’ts.
From 2025: Fire in the sky: on Deepavali and the battle for clean air
What is IMD’s latest outlook?

In 2024, IMD warned that firecrackers and stubble fires could push Delhi’s air into the “severe” category when dispersion conditions are unfavourable. The monsoon’s withdrawal is expected to be complete from India by mid-October, which will see the onset of atmospheric conditions such as a cessation of high-altitude winds (that flush pollutants), lower temperatures and an inversion layer that traps pollutants. With Diwali expected in the first week of November, it remains to be seen how all of this will play out with ‘green crackers’ in the mix.

title: Supreme Court questions steep mark-ups on cancer drugs, calls pricing disparity ‘carnage’

content.value: The Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) expressed concern over the sharp disparity between the prices charged to retailers and consumers for essential medicines, particularly cancer drugs, observing that steep mark-ups placed an enormous burden on taxpayers and amounted to “carnage”.

A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta questioned the Centre on why the 16% retailer margin provided for under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013 should not be applied uniformly to essential medicines to curb steep mark-ups over the price to retailer (PTR).
“Why not keep the 16% margin on MRP, which is prescribed in the DPCO, on everything? ... Ultimately, the loser is the taxpayer. This is carnage, as simple as that,” the Bench remarked.

The observations came while the top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha, seeking its intervention to regulate the prices of drugs, medical equipment, and generic medicines, and make them more affordable.

Justice Mehta pointed, in particular, to the nearly ten-fold mark-up on an essential cancer drug, which was supplied to retailers for around ₹3,000 but sold to consumers for ₹27,000. He questioned who ultimately benefited from the nearly ₹24,000 difference. “You tell us why this difference... Where does this chunk of money go? Ten times...” Justice Mehta remarked.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, acknowledged the concern and said the government would have to find a way forward while “balancing equities”. He, however, said it was private hospitals, rather than pharmaceutical companies, that benefited from the steep mark-ups. “The pharma company is not the gainer. The gainer is the private hospital,” the Solicitor General submitted.

The Bench also flagged the practice of private hospitals insisting that patients purchase medicines from their in-house pharmacies, leaving them with little choice to procure the same drugs at lower prices elsewhere.

It also pointed to the impact of such inflated prices on public finances, observing that when treatment is covered under government-funded health schemes such as Ayushman Bharat, the cost is ultimately borne by taxpayers.
“Suppose the patient is taking treatment through government services... The government doesn’t pay, the taxpayer pays. This affects a larger section of society,” the Bench remarked.

Mr. Mehta sought time to place before the court details of the existing mechanisms governing drug pricing and assured the Bench that he would make his submissions on the next date of hearing. The Bench accordingly posted the matter for further hearing on October 12, 2026.

The petitions have sought directions to make drug formulations more affordable by curbing alleged overpricing of essential medicines by pharmaceutical companies and retailers. They have also sought stricter enforcement of price controls under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 to prevent violations of the prescribed pricing mechanism and disproportionate profit margins across the drug supply chain.

Earlier, the top court had described the wide difference between the price to retailers and the MRP of medicines as “dacoity”, while drawing attention to the financial distress faced by patients struggling to meet treatment costs.
“The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what is it? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment,” the Bench had remarked.

title: All you need to know about: Swyer Syndrome

content.value: Swyer syndrome is a rare condition in which a person is born with XY chromosomes, the combination usually associated with males, but their reproductive organs develop along a typically female pattern. The person typically has female external anatomy and a uterus and fallopian tubes.

The condition often goes unnoticed during childhood and comes to light during adolescence, when puberty does not progress normally or menstruation does not begin. It can also be diagnosed later during investigations for infertility. Here’s all you need to know about Swyer syndrome.
What is Swyer syndrome?

Swyer syndrome is a rare difference of sex development, medically known as 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis. According to the US’ Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center, a person with the condition has a 46,XY chromosome pattern, but the gonads do not develop into functioning testes. Instead, they remain as small, non-functioning structures called “streak gonads”. The person generally develops female external genitalia, while the uterus and fallopian tubes are usually present. The condition is estimated to occur in about one in 80,000 people,

Swyer syndrome results from disruption of the genetic pathway involved in testicular development during early embryonic development. The SRY gene, located on the Y chromosome, plays an important role in initiating this process. However, an SRY mutation is not found in every person with Swyer syndrome.
What are the symptoms?

Swyer syndrome may not be apparent during childhood and often comes to light during adolescence, when puberty does not progress normally. One of the most characteristic signs is primary amenorrhoea, meaning that menstruation does not begin.

Delayed or incomplete development of secondary sexual characteristics can also prompt investigation. Because the streak gonads do not produce sufficient sex hormones, spontaneous breast development may be limited. The condition can sometimes remain undiagnosed even when a person reaches adulthood.
How is Swyer syndrome diagnosed?

Diagnosis usually involves looking at the person’s chromosomes, hormone levels and reproductive anatomy. Karyotyping, a test that examines the number and structure of chromosomes, typically shows a 46,XY pattern in Swyer syndrome. Blood tests generally show evidence of gonadal failure, including low levels of sex hormones and elevated levels of hormones such as follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone. Ultrasound or MRI can be used to examine the uterus and the gonads.

Genetic testing can be used to investigate the underlying cause, including variants in SRY and other genes involved in gonadal development. However, not finding an SRY mutation does not exclude Swyer syndrome. In some patients, even more extensive genetic testing may not identify the precise molecular cause.
Can Swyer syndrome be treated?

There is currently no treatment that can change the 46,XY chromosome pattern or turn the streak gonads into functioning ovaries. However, the effects of Swyer syndrome can be effectively managed. Hormone replacement therapy, usually involving oestrogen and subsequently an appropriate progestogen regimen when indicated, is used to induce and maintain puberty, support development of secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone health.

The streak gonads also need to be assessed because they carry an increased risk of gonadoblastoma, a type of germ-cell tumour. Decisions about gonadectomy and its timing are now generally individualised according to the underlying diagnosis and tumour risk.

Fertility is another important consideration. Because the streak gonads cannot produce eggs, people with Swyer syndrome cannot conceive using their own eggs. However, if the uterus is present and sufficiently developed, pregnancy can be possible through IVF using a donated egg or embryo. Research shows that patients with Swyer syndrome can have successful pregnancies following endometrial preparation with hormones and IVF using donated eggs. Following pregnancy and delivery, continued hormone replacement is important for maintaining bone health.

In other words, Swyer syndrome itself cannot currently be reversed, but its effects can be managed. Hormone replacement can address the absence of normal gonadal hormones, removal of the streak gonads can reduce the risk of tumours, and assisted reproductive techniques can make pregnancy possible for some patients.

title: Diabetic Foot Society of India calls for global alliance

content.value: The Diabetic Foot Society of India (DFSI), under the aegis of its national president V.B. Narayanamurthy, has written to Zulfiqarali G. Abbas, president of the Pan-African Diabetic Foot Study Group (PADFSG), proposing the formation of a global alliance on diabetic foot survival and limb preservation.

The letter, a copy of which was shared with The Hindu, notes that diabetic foot ulceration is an under-recognised cause of premature death, major amputation, recurrent illness, disability, and social exclusion. Available evidence shows that its five-year mortality is comparable to that of some cancers. And yet, global investment, policy attention, organised pathways, and post-amputation support remain substantially below the scale of the problem, the letter notes.

The DFSI, therefore, has proposed that institutions, including itself, King’s College London, International Association of Diabetic Foot Surgeons, D-Foot International, American Limb Preservation Society, Federation of International Podiatrists, and PADFSG, come together to form a Global Alliance for Diabetic Foot Survival and Limb Preservation, to create a sustained, scientific, and policy platform for prevention, limb preservation, improved survival, rehabilitation, surveillance, research, and engagement with governments and the World Health Organization (WHO).

The letter further stated that DFSI would announce the shared intention to form the Alliance at its next national conference, slated to be held on October 2, 2026. This, it said, would be an announcement of intent rather than a representation that the Alliance had been legally constituted or that any institution had accepted a financial or contractual obligation.
The letter urged the PADFSG to provide in-principle concurrence with the formation of the Alliance and the proposed conference announcement.

Apart from the proposal for the alliance, the letter also contained a draft Joint Global Declaration for joint consultation and unveiling, and asked for comments on the proposal and draft declaration from the PADFSG.
The DAFSI also stated that subject to the PADFSG’s concurrence, it proposed to convene the first founding meeting of the Alliance within 30 days of its conference.
The proposal

The proposal noted that the Alliance would provide a common platform for scientific leadership, policy advocacy, regional demonstration programmes, and responsible resource mobilisation. Its objectives would include advocacy with the WHO and national governments to secure explicit recognition of diabetic foot disease as an important medical condition; to improve survival and quality of life through multi-disciplinary care and patient-centred research; to promote prevention, early detection, and rapid referral; to advance surveillance and support the development of registries; to strengthen post-amputation rehabilitation; to promote research and training programmes; and to ensure the meaningful participation of people living with diabetes in governance and programme design.

The proposal also detailed membership and governance, standing bodies, the Secretariat, proposed activities of the Alliance, donor engagement, and financial management, as well as a performance framework and a risks safeguard.
The declaration

The draft declaration called for diabetic foot disease to be recognised as a major cause of premature death, disability, and exclusion. It called upon the WHO Director-General, regional directors, and member states to make diabetic foot prevention, limb preservation and survival a visible part of diabetes policy, establish common indicators and baseline registries, and support flagship programmes in at least two WHO regions.
It also proposed a goal to reduce risk-adjusted five-year mortality after a new diabetic foot ulcer by 30%, and potentially avoidable major amputations by 50% by 2030.
The draft declaration called for coordinated action that keeps people alive, mobile, included, and able to live with dignity.

title: Scientists can now measure the damage each new coal mine can do to people, nature

content.value: Scientists have long known every tonne of carbon dioxide matters to the climate. But governments keep approving new fossil fuel projects – even as climate change worsens.

Until now, it’s been difficult to say how much damage and extra warming a specific project will do. Fossil fuel companies – and government agencies approving their projects – have often relied on what’s known as the “drop in the ocean” defence.

While backers concede a new project will add more carbon dioxide emissions to the atmosphere, they say these are tiny compared to the global tally and that it’s almost impossible to track damage attributable to the emissions of an individual project.

This defence won’t work any more. In recent years, attribution science has advanced rapidly, allowing scientists to pinpoint the role of climate change in making disasters and extreme weather more likely.

The new open-source climate tool – the Carbon Impacts Tracer – goes one step further. It shows how much a new project will warm the planet – and how much damage it will do across eight areas, from loss of crops to heatwave deaths in Europe.
This will help make fossil fuel companies and governments approving these projects accountable for the damage they will do.
How did scientists get here?
To measure the damage attributable to a single fossil fuel project, scientists connected the dots between emissions produced, extra warming and the damage done to people and the environment.

Last year, experts from six universities in Australia and the United Kingdom released research on the damage that corresponds with emissions from the newly approved Scarborough gas project in Western Australia. Three of this article’s authors were involved.

This found that 876 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions from the Scarborough project would expose an extra 516,000 people worldwide to unprecedented heat. They would also result in 484 heat-related deaths in Europe by 2100 and destroy millions more coral colonies during every future mass bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef.
The new tool gives users the ability to use the same robust methodology on any fossil fuel project.
How can scientists track the damage from one project?
The more carbon dioxide scientists add to the atmosphere, the hotter the planet gets.

The relationship is nearly linear. For every trillion (thousand billion) tonnes of carbon dioxide emitted into the atmosphere, the globe will warm about 0.45°C, according to the latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assessment report. As of 2019, cumulative global emissions are about 2.4 trillion tonnes.

The Carbon Impacts Tracer uses this relationship to calculate the extra warming caused by a new project’s publicly documented carbon emissions. It then calculates the damage it will do across eight areas, including how many more people will be exposed to dangerous heat globally, how much glaciers will melt and how many Europeans will die due to heatwaves.

The tool uses only published studies robust enough to quantify the link between higher global temperatures and a specific type of damage. This high evidence threshold is why scientists only include eight types of damage at present. We will add more types of damage once the evidence base is robust enough.

For instance, the link between European heatwave deaths and climate change is robust and reproducible. But scientists don’t yet have research which meets the criteria for heatwave deaths in Australia or elsewhere.
What the tool does is bring together crucial scientific findings to measure how emissions lead to warming and subsequent damage.
Tracking the damage
The tool lets users see the damage that will flow from five proposed Australian fossil fuel projects and one in the United Kingdom.

For example, Woodside’s proposed Browse to North West Shelf gas project will add 1,597 megatonnes of CO₂ over its lifetime. It will warm the planet 0.00072°C, which translates to almost 200,000 more people enduring an extra week of dangerous heat every year.

The tool also tracks future damage from 16 major fossil fuel companies between 2024 and 2050. For instance, ExxonMobil’s future emissions of 5,245Mt represent an extra 0.0024°C of warming which means an extra 127km² of glaciers will melt.

Users can also input carbon emissions from any project, company or country around the world to quantify the damage and generate reports showing the impacts, as well the underpinning science and references.
From the courtroom to the boardroom
For years, the difficulty of tracing a direct link between emissions and resulting damage made it harder to launch climate legal cases.

Last year, the world’s top court – the International Court of Justice – found fossil fuel production and expansion “may constitute an internationally wrongful act”, attributable to the nation where extraction is happening. The court recognised it was possible to establish a causal link between emissions and climate harms.

The Carbon Impacts Tracer shows the robust causal links between project and harms. It will be useful to communities and organisations seeking to attribute legal responsibility for climate harms to governments and fossil fuel companies, as well as to insurers and decision-makers assessing climate impacts.
Time for accountability
For decades, fossil fuel producers have been able to extract oil, gas and coal and emit pollution to the atmosphere with virtual impunity – even as climate change worsens and damages mount.

But we are entering a new era of accountability. Now that climate attribution science has come of age, it’s no longer possible to hide behind the argument that a new gasfield is just a drop in the ocean.
Scientists can now see just how much damage that drop will do to the climate, nature – and to us.
(This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.)

title: After great apes, scientists find African elephants self-medicate too

content.value: Wild animals have for long been known for their intuitive pharmacological knowledge: orangutans balm their wounds with plants; chimpanzees consume bitter antibacterial leaves; Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins queue up to rub against selected corals; and birds smear their nests with insecticidal plants to fend off anaemia-causing mites.

Scientists term this behaviour zoopharmacognosy, where animals seek out plants to treat endoparasite infestations, respiratory and fungal infections, wounds, and gastrointestinal problems. While most of these medicinal resources are plant-based, for example barks and leaves and resin, animals also treat themselves with charcoal, clay and insects.

title: Why do we make noises like ‘oof’ when we lift something or bump into furniture?

content.value: A: When you physically exert while doing a task, you may also briefly hold your breath, releasing it as the effort eases. Your body may also contract the muscles around the trunk, making the torso more rigid and giving your arms and legs a more stable base from which to work. When the trunk stiffens, the abdominal muscles brace while briefly holding or restricting the breath. When you release that pressure, air is forced through the partly closed vocal cords, producing a grunt that sounds like ‘oof’.

This said, the noise you make after bumping into furniture has a different origin. A sudden impact, like stubbing your toe or hitting your shin against a wooden beam, prompts the nervous system to respond quickly. You might gasp, tense your muscles, pull away, and vocalise before you have actually decided to do any of these things. A sound like ‘ow’ or ‘ah’ is thus part of the body’s startle response.
The exact sound is not automatic. People learn to react a certain way from those around them, so those speaking different languages and from cultures exclaim somewhat differently.

title: Ancient grasslands, once destroyed for development, can take 100 years to grow back

content.value: (This article forms a part of the Science for All newsletter that takes the jargon out of science and puts the fun in! Subscribe now!)

Ancient grasslands, one of the least valued ecosystems, support a phenomenal diversity of wildlife, create livelihoods of billions of pastoralists, and store one-third of Earth’s terrestrial carbon. But they are often considered “wastelands,” ripe for development, mining, power projects or afforestation drives.

Now a new global study has found that once destroyed, grasslands that grew for millennia can almost never regenerate the same way, at least for a century. When they do “recover,” the secondary grasslands consist of different species that are taller, with greater leaf area, found a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

This phenomenon, said the paper, owes to altered ecological conditions, including soil nutrients and pH levels that are no longer suitable for old grassland flora. In their place are established plants that are taller, had higher specific leaf area, and lower dry-matter content, and non-native annuals, found the scientists, including a researcher at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research in Pune.

For the study, researchers gathered data on 742 plant species from species in India, Australian, and Brazilian savannas and the iconic “big four” prairie grasses of the United States and compared old-growth grasslands flora with secondary grasslands species. “Notably, these trait differences that make old-growth grassland plants more resource conservative and secondary grassland plants more resource acquisitive persisted over a century,” said the scientists.

Old-growth plant species include fire-prone, megafauna-grazed ecosystems such as North American prairies, Australian savannas and Indian savannas, while secondary grasslands consist of a mix of native and non-native species, the paper stated.

Secondary grasslands, on the other hand, contain fewer plant species than the old-growth grasslands they replace. The paper provides examples: many native perennial grasses and forbs that are characteristic of old-growth grasslands can be missing or replaced by non-native weedy annuals in secondary grasslands, particularly in the initial decades of recovery.
These findings underscore the importance of old-growth grassland conservation, said the paper, which also provides guidance to recover grassland biodiversity through ecological restoration.

Alas, natural grasslands cannot entirely be restored. However, in the Thar desert, Kutch, the Deccan, the Terai and in the Assam flood plains “I have seen restoration and the return to grassland obligated species, Asad Rahmani, a leading Indian conservationist and an ornithologist told The Hindu.

For example when the Solapur grassland was restored, it brought back the endangered bustard; in Kutch the grassland restored by the Corbett Foundation, brought the back lesser florican and many larks, warblers, white-browed bush chat; and on the Orange grasslands in Assam, the pygmy hog has been successfully reintroduced, Prof. Rahmani told The Hindu . “We need a National Grassland Restoration Programme along with the National Grazing Policy, he added.

With 15 per cent of the livestock of the world in four per cent of surface area of the world, India does not have any programme or policy to restored the grasslands. “This needs to change for our livestock and wild animals that live in grasslands,” Prof. Rahmani told The Hindu.

title: Subatomic ambitions take five Indian school students to CERN

content.value: A group of Indian school students are among the five winning teams of the 13th edition of the ‘Beamline for Schools’ competition, a physics competition for high school students from all around the world organised by CERN, the European Laboratory for Particle Physics, in Geneva.

The Indian team, named “attoPION”, comprises Nenavath Abhay Vivek, Sidhartha Aniket Jaiswal, Ayush Bhardwaj, Aarush Mandala, and Aritra Sadhukhan. They are from Bansal Junior College Nizamabad; Greenwood High International School, Bengaluru; The Shri Ram Global School, Greater Noida; and Purv International School, Durgapur.
They found each other through different science competitions they participated in.
Tracking pions

A beamline is a facility that provides high-energy fluxes of subatomic particles that can be used to conduct experiments in different fields, including fundamental physics, material science and medicine. The other four winning teams are from Bangladesh, Türkiye, the U.K., and the U.S.

The Indian students’ project was based on a process called pion charge exchange. In particle physics, pions are subatomic particles that can have a positive, negative or neutral charge. The students tried to measure how often a charged pion turns into a neutral one when it hits “light” atoms like lithium and beryllium, and they looked at this change of charge at specific energy levels.
These readings are of interest for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, a large physics experiment under construction in the U.S.

When neutrinos hit an atom, they produce pions. If the pions change their charge before they even leave the atom, it can mess up the data scientists see, the students said. Recording how often this change takes place in lithium and beryllium will allow scientists to model it correctly in their simulations.
Learning the basics
When the students started, they did not have any formal training in particle physics.

“We were just a group of 11th and 12th graders who were obsessed with the subject,” they said. “In the beginning, it felt like we were trying to solve a high-level puzzle without having the box with the picture on it. We spent so much time reading papers and talking to mentors just to get our heads around the theory.”

The students said they spent several hours every day in the three to four weeks before the competition. While the first week was mostly about recruiting and forming a team, the next three weeks were a complete grind.

The team started with the basics, with Griffiths Introduction to Elementary Particles (1987) serving as their main reference book. They also said A Tour of the Subatomic Zoo (1992) gave them their first big picture and that YouTube lectures by experts at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, and courses on the National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning (NPTEL) kept them going.

“Once we had the basics, we moved to CERN documentation and research papers from CERN and other institutions,” they continued. “For the Geant4 simulations, we used CERN’s official documentation and some of their preloaded models, which we then tweaked to test our own idea in the initial stages.”

Sometimes, understanding just one research paper or one detector concept would take them days.  “We just kept going until the physics finally started making sense,” one of the students said. “We were pulling all-nighters to finish the proposal before the deadline.”

“Sometimes understanding just one research paper or one detector concept would take us days. We feel once you start counting hours, your focus shifts from learning to the clock. We just kept going until the physics finally started making sense.”
Physics that could make sense to high-schoolers was one constraint. Two others were that the participants had to design an experiment from scratch and that it could actually be run at CERN.
So the students proposed a setup to collect data across different energy levels and different types of atoms to see the variations.
“We were nervous because we were so new to this, but after a lot of collaboration and refining the technical details, we felt confident enough to hit the submit button,” they said.
A love for physics in particular was a strong motivation. “We thought of it as an opportunity to try something new and unconventional and learn something during that process,” they added.
Mentoring helps
Once the team was in place, the students hunted for mentors to guide them. They started by cold-emailing several PhD scholars, postdocs, and graduate students across universities in India and abroad.

They struck luck with Manu Srivastava, a doctoral scholar at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the U.S., and received additional feedback on their experimental design from Laxman Mekala at IIT-Bombay.

“My role was purely a supervisory one,” Mr. Srivastava said. “The students came up with different ideas and worked out all the calculations themselves.” He added: “I only had to guide them about which ideas would be more worthwhile to pursue, so in a way just providing direction and giving minimal feedback on their work.”

The students’ discussions among themselves and with Mr. Srivastava were online. “To me, that is a powerful example of how technology is becoming a unifying force at the grassroots level in India, allowing talented students from different regions to come together around a shared scientific goal. Such collaborations would have been much more difficult to imagine even a decade ago,” Mr. Srivastava said.

He added that the students’ achievement was made more remarkable by the competition’s scale. Beamline for Schools is a prestigious international science competition for high-school students and this year attracted more than 700 proposals from around the world.
‘Just the start’
A lot of students think competitions like this are too tough and not for them, the students said.

“We want to tell them that sometimes the biggest opportunities start from a very simple question or a crazy idea,” they said. “Curiosity is enough to start. If you are curious enough to try, keep learning and do not give up when it gets difficult, you might end up in places you never imagined.”

Looking ahead, the students would like to keep the momentum going, stay connected as a team, and collaborate with other physicists. They would also like to engage in outreach for the BL4S program to help other students.
“All of us are definitely planning to pursue careers in STEM and keep doing our own research. Being at CERN is just the start for us,” they said.
T.V. Padma is a science journalist based in New Delhi.

title: The question of access

content.value: (In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Athira Elssa Johnson writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)

A treatment can make a difference only when patients can access it. The cost of medicines, their safety and regulation, and whether people can get the care they need are all part of that question. This week, our coverage also looks at vaccination, infectious diseases, artificial intelligence, prevention and new medical research.

Questions around the cost of medicines came into focus after the Supreme Court described the overpricing of essential cancer drugs as “broad daylight dacoity”. The report examines concerns around medicine prices and what they mean for access to treatment.

A regulatory warning against the indiscriminate use of painkillers and antibiotics highlighted the risks of inappropriate medicine use, including kidney disease. India has also ordered a crackdown on nicotine pouches, citing health risks.

Food regulation also featured this week. Krishnadas Rajagopal reports on FSSAI telling the Supreme Court that front-of-pack nutrition labelling will be rolled out in a single phase.The regulator has also proposed that only milk-derived products be represented as ‘paneer’. Bindu Shajan Perappadan explains what analogue paneer is and why FSSAI is acting against it.
Vaccination and infectious diseases
Vaccination has been another focus, with attention on missed doses, vaccination records, catch-up vaccination, adult immunisation and changing needs across different stages of life.

In our Health Webinar, experts discussed childhood and adult vaccination, travel vaccination and common concerns around vaccines. The discussion also looked at the importance of maintaining vaccination records and understanding changing immunisation needs.
Ahead of winter, Sayesha Gupta, Megha Jacob and Karan Babbar looked at vaccination among older adults and why Delhi’s grandparents may need protection alongside their grandchildren.
The wider question of preparedness also remains important. India stressed the need for resilient health systems and pandemic preparedness at the United Nations.

On the infectious disease front, reports showed that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to two new health zones. An mpox case has also been confirmed in a northeastern Congolese city at the centre of the Ebola outbreak.
In India, C. Maya reports on scientists at IAV, Keralam developing a dengue early-warning system to forecast trends and help anticipate outbreaks.
AI and healthcare

Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in medical imaging, clinical decision-making and drug and vaccine development. Its expanding role also raises questions around patient safety, inaccurate information, data and the potential misuse of AI in biology.
The latest Health Wrap examines these issues in ‘AI in healthcare: promise, risks and patient safety’.

Other developments include a partnership between Anthropic and OpenEvidence to expand access to medical AI; Afshan Yasmeenreported on HEADS, an initiative using AI to help address gaps in mental healthcare. In Assam, inputs from ASHAs are being used to develop an AI-enabled training platform for cervical cancer screening.
Health data is also coming under scrutiny, with the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic called to appear before an Australian AI probe following a breach involving a health database.
Nutrition and prevention

Nutrition and preventive health also featured prominently. A study found that consuming an additional 100 grams of ultra-processed food a day was associated with a 14% higher risk of a heart event. The findings add to research examining the relationship between ultra-processed food and cardiovascular health.
Suparna Mukherjee looks at what people should know about artificial sweeteners and health, particularly as their use becomes more common.
Managing conditions, new research
Several stories this week examine conditions that can be difficult to recognise, diagnose or manage.
I look at GERD and why persistent reflux symptoms need to be distinguished from what is commonly described as heartburn.

Another report looked at research linking pregnancy-related forgetfulness, popularly called ‘momnesia’, to disruption in a brain circuit, offering another possible explanation for cognitive changes during pregnancy.
Swagata Yadavar reported on village health centres in Haryana screening people for heart disease and identifying those who need further care.
Divya Gandhi reports on a study found that deaf adults have distinctly superior peripheral vision, adding to research into how sensory systems adapt to differences in sensory input.

Dr. V. Divya Sai looks at what happens when cancer treatment is no longer working and treatment options change. Dr. C. Aravinda examines why male contraception continues to lag behind other forms of contraception.

Researchers at RGCB in Keralam have developed nanopore sensors aimed at detecting biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, while IIT Palakkad researchers have developed sensors for faster heparin monitoring.

Another report looks at the U.S. FDA’s approval of an AbbVie drug for Parkinson’s disease. The Health Ministry’s latest advisory on stem cell therapy for autism has also drawn attention, read our explainer here.

In our all you need to know series, Meenakshy S. explains Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a group of connective tissue disorders that can affect multiple systems of the body
President’s call puts spotlight on celebrity endorsements of harmful products
Serish Nanisetti reports on a UN finding that five crore Indian children still lack access to sanitation services in their schools.
Rajlakshmi Ghosh explains how the new NCAHP regulations could affect allied and healthcare professionals.
