title: Southwest monsoon ends with 12% deficit

content.value: India’s 2026 southwest monsoon ended with 759.4 mm of rain, 12.6% below the 868.6 mm normal, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Wednesday. At 87% of the Long Period Average (LPA), this is the lowest rainfall recorded during the monsoon season since 2015, which was a tad drier at 758.2 mm.
The east and northeast region, which recorded 1,017.1 mm of rainfall, had its driest monsoon since 1901, or since the IMD started to keep systematic records.

The subdued rainfall was in line with forecasts by global weather agencies, including the IMD, which anticipated one of the strongest El Ninos in recent history. The IMD had, since April, predicted a subdued monsoon rainfall and overall, reality corresponded to what was forecast. On April 13, for instance, it anticipated the June-September rain to be at 92% of LPA, with an error window of 5%. The May 29 update lowered that to 90% with a 4% error window. The IMD’s final estimate sits within this range.
June rains fell short

However, its regional and monthly forecasts were much farther off the mark. June, which got only 65% of normal rainfall, was far drier than the 92% forecast. July rainfall, which was expected to be below 94%, ended up with 1% more, thanks to rains in central India, which got 33% more rain than normal. August came in at 84% of the LPA, in line with the “below 94%” that was forecast. September, at 92.4% finished a little above the forecast of “below 91%”.
IMD director general M. Mohapatra told journalists on Wednesday that the IMD’s predictions matched conditions in “many regions, except some parts of northwest and adjoining central India”.
Diminishing trend in the east

The largest deviations from normal rainfall were in east and northeast India (25.6% below normal). Mr. Mohapatra said that there was a “marked trend” of diminishing rainfall in this region “in recent years”. Rainfall in the southern peninsula was 24.3% below normal, and at 542 mm, this was the fourth lowest monsoon rainfall recorded in the region since 1901. Northwest India ended 5.9% below normal and central India stood at 2.6% below normal, according to an IMD statement.

Punjab, Arunachal Pradesh, and the Assam & Meghalaya subdivisions were rain-deficient in every month from June to September. Nationally, 17 of 36 subdivisions (covering 42% of the country’s land area) saw deficient rainfall, 18 were normal, and one had excess rain. Of 741 districts assessed, 282 were deficient and 34 were “large deficient”.
Hotter, drier October expected

The southwest monsoon this year is in the process of withdrawal and is likely to completely exit within the first weeks of October, Mr. Mohapatra said. The country will then see the advent of the northeast monsoon.

With the El Nino still gaining strength, rainfall for the country in October is likely to be below 85% of the LPA of about 75.4 mm. Most regions are expected to get below-normal rain, except parts of northwest India, southern peninsular India, and isolated pockets of the east, which may see normal to above-normal rain.

“Parts of Punjab, Haryana and northern states may see good rainfall because, in El Nino years, western disturbances are likely to increase. We’ve seen some good rain in these regions in the last week and this means soil-moisture is high, which will help the forthcoming winter crop,” Mr. Mohapatra added.

Maximum and minimum temperatures are likely to be above normal across most of the country. The exceptions are in parts of the northeast, where normal to below-normal minimums are likely, and pockets of central and northwest India, where normal maximums are expected.

title: What are the new guidelines set by IN-SPACe for Indian and foreign hosted-payloads? | Explained

content.value: The story so far: The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) on September 17, 2026, released a document titled Norms, Guidelines and Procedures for implementation of the Indian Space Policy 2023 in respect of authorisation for establishment and operation of hosted-payloads.

IN-SPACe, which is the single-window agency for all space sector activities of private entities in the country, has released this document due to the increasing number of private participants, which it refers to as Non-Government Indian Entities (NGEs). These NGEs over the last few years have been developing and deploying payloads for Earth observation, space science, communications, technology demonstration and other space-based applications. IN-SPACe says the guidelines will help the Indian companies to access space-based infrastructure through hosted-payload opportunities, while ensuring compliance with applicable technical, safety, security, spectrum, orbital and other regulatory requirements.

title: Apple Pay goes live in India with Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard cards

content.value: Apple on Wednesday (September 30, 2026) launched Apple Pay in India — a payment feature that lets iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch users make payments using Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard cards.
Support for Mac is coming soon, according to an official press release.

With Apple Pay, users can make payments without having to type in PINs or OTPs. To make the payment, users will have to activate their devices and verify their identity if needed, before holding the device near a contactless reader.

Concerning safety, Apple Pay customers’ card numbers are not stored on the device or Apple servers, with the service instead using a unique Device Account Number and encryption in order to store payment information securely.
Apple also will not retain user-identifying transaction information, while there are mechanisms in place to remotely control payments even if the device is lost.
To activate the service, customers can add their eligible credit card to the Apple Wallet via the Axis Bank app, or through the Wallet app on their iPhone.
Customers can continue to avail the rewards and benefits offered by their cards.
Some sellers and retailers that will accept Apple Pay include Apple Store locations, Blinkit, Chaayos, Comet, Croma, Interflora, Ixigo, Le15 Patisserie, Reliance brands, Tata 1mg, Zomato, and others.

“India is home to a dynamic and digitally savvy population that continues to embrace a cashless future while expecting the highest standards of security and privacy, and we’re so excited to bring Apple Pay to users in India today. Apple Pay makes everyday payments with a card easy, secure, and private — from simply tapping to pay in stores without an extra app, PIN, or OTP to checking out online without repeatedly entering payment information,” said Jennifer Bailey, Apple’s vice president of Apple Pay and Apple Wallet.

“We are at a significant inflection point in payments, where technology, security and changing customer expectations are reshaping how people transact. At Axis Bank, our aspiration is to remain at the forefront of this transformation by building payment experiences that are progressive, trusted and deeply relevant to our customers,” said Amitabh Chaudhry, MD & CEO, Axis Bank.

title: Cabinet approves hike in Rabi minimum support prices for 2027-28 season

content.value: The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) on Wednesday approved the increase in the Minimum Support Prices (MSP) for all mandated Rabi crops for the marketing season 2027-28, with safflower receiving the biggest increase, the government announced.

“Under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the government has a clear policy decision that farmers should get a profit of at least 50% or more over their average cost of production,” Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said at a press conference following the Cabinet decision. “In line with this, the MSP announced for rabi marketing season 2027-28 carries a margin of 50% to 106% over the all-India weighted average cost of production.”

The MSP for safflower was increased by ₹675 per quintal to ₹7,215 per quintal, an increase of 10.3% over its level in the previous year. Rapeseed and mustard saw their MSP increase by 6.7% or ₹413 per quintal to ₹6,613 per quintal.
The MSP for barley was increased by 6.3% to ₹2,286 per quintal, masur dal by 5.6% to ₹7,390 per quintal, gram by 1.4% to ₹5,958 per quintal, and for wheat by 1% to ₹2,610 per quintal.

“The increase in MSP for mandated Rabi crops for marketing season 2027-28 is in line with the Union Budget 2018-19 announcement of fixing the MSP at a level of at least 1.5 times of the all-India weighted average cost of production,” the government said in its release.

It added that the expected margin over the all-India weighted average cost of production is 106% for wheat, followed by 96% for rapeseed & mustard, 92% for lentil, 59% for gram, 58% for barley, and 50% for safflower.
“This increased MSP of rabi crops will ensure remunerative prices to the farmers and incentivise crop diversification,” the government added.

The government said that its procurement of wheat over the period  2014-15 to 2025-26 increased to 3,715 lakh metric tonnes (LMT) as compared to an increase of 2,254 LMT during the 2004-05 to 2013-14 period.
Similarly, it said that the procurement of six Rabi crops during 2014-15 to 2025-26 increased to 3,921 LMT as compared to an increase of 2,302 LMT during 2004-05 to 2013-14.
“The MSP amount paid to wheat-growing farmers during 2014-15 to 2025-26 has increased to ₹7.31 lakh crore as compared to ₹2.56 lakh crore during 2004-05 to 2013-14,” the release said.
For the six Rabi crops, the MSP paid to the respective farmers in total stood at ₹8.36 lakh crore as of 2025-26 as compared to ₹2.65 lakh crore in 2013-14, it added.

title: India to have more elderly people later this century as fertility falls, age structure shifts: Moody’s

content.value: India is likely to have a much older population later this century, as the country’s age structure is beginning to shift and fertility has fallen “below replacement,” Moody’s Ratings said on Tuesday (September 29, 2026).
Moody’s said population growth has long been a tailwind for economic growth and creditworthiness, but falling fertility is now changing that picture.
Fewer workers will limit productive capacity, while fewer households and consumers will weaken demand. As a result, countries will have to rely more on productivity to sustain growth.
Moody’s said the global fertility rate had declined from 4.9 children per woman in 1950 to about 2.2 today, only slightly above the replacement rate of 2.1.

“What makes this episode particularly significant is that many of the world’s largest economies are ageing at the same time. In fact, more than 70% of the world’s population now lives in countries with fertility rates at or below replacement level,” Moody’s said in a report on global demographics.
It said fertility rates across much of Latin America were now comparable to those of Europe and Japan, while several East Asian countries had some of the lowest fertility rates ever recorded.
Japan has the most top-heavy population structure, with nearly 30% of its population over 65 and about 11% under 15.
South Korea is close behind, while China is moving rapidly in the same direction. Emerging markets, including Brazil, India, Thailand and Türkiye, are also progressing along the same path.

“Although India’s population remains relatively young, fertility has already fallen below replacement and the country’s age structure is beginning to shift, setting the stage for a much older population later this century,” Moody’s said.

Declining fertility ultimately reshapes age structures as well as population growth, it said. Countries experiencing the steepest fertility declines today will also age most rapidly in the coming decades.

title: Fever cases see spurt in Kozhikode, alert issued against measles

content.value: Fever cases are seeing a spurt in Kozhikode in recent weeks. On average, between 600 and 900 people are seeking outpatient treatment in government hospitals and health centres almost every day. This is apart from the hundreds of influenza cases reported from various places in the district this month.

According to doctors, high body temperature, headache and sneezing are the most common symptoms of fever, while those with influenza have fatigue, muscle pain, and chest congestion. While it could take at least three days for the fever to subside normally, severe cases may take up to a week to recover. Dengue fever, leptospirosis, and malaria are being reported from various places.

Meanwhile, the district medical officer has issued an alert against measles cases as well. Health department sources say that it is being reported in neighbouring districts too. According to them, measles, a viral disease primarily affecting children, is transmitted through the air and through contact with an infected person. It can lead to complications such as pneumonia, diarrhoea, and brain infection, and may even result in death.

The sources say that the fatalities are reported among those who have not been vaccinated. Its symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, red spots on the body, and redness in the mouth. They appear within 10–14 days after getting infected.

Doctors say that those with symptoms should seek immediate medical attention. Infected children should not be sent to schools or anganwadis. Since measles is a viral disease, there is no specific treatment for it, and medical care focuses on managing the symptoms, they say.

Health department officials, however, point out that the disease can be completely prevented through vaccination. The first dose should be administered between 9 and 12 months of age, and the second dose between 16 and 24 months. Administering two doses of the Measles-Rubella vaccine will help protect children’s health and save their lives. Those who may have missed any dose can receive the vaccine up to the age of five. It is available for free at all government health centres, they add.

title: Understanding vitiligo

content.value: A chronic autoimmune skin condition in which the body’s immune system mistakes melanocytes (cells which produce melanin, giving colour to your skin, hair and eyes) as enemies and attacks them. This leads to patches of depigmentation anywhere in your body. This condition is known as vitiligo.
Types of vitiligo
The main types of vitiligo are non-segmental and segmental vitiligo.

Non-segmental vitiligo is the most common form, where colour loss appears symmetrically on both sides of the body, such as both hands or both knees. Segmental vitiligo, on the other hand, often starts at a younger age and affects only one side or a single specific area of the body.
What causes vitiligo?
While the primary reason for vitiligo is not fully understood, it is seen to be caused by various factors, from genetics to immune dysfunction.

Research has shown that vitiligo is primarily a T-cell–mediated autoimmune disease where CD8+ cytotoxic T cells attack and destroy skin pigment cells called melanocytes, leading to white patches on the skin.

Having a family member with vitiligo or other autoimmune diseases is shown to have an increased risk, suggesting shared genetic susceptibility. Environmental factors like oxidative stress, skin trauma, and certain chemicals can sometimes trigger or worsen vitiligo in genetically susceptible people.
Vitiligo is also often associated with other autoimmune conditions, especially autoimmune thyroid disease, so clinicians may screen for these in some patients.
Symptoms of vitiligo

The main symptom of vitiligo is depigmentation and the appearance of patches on your body. This can be anywhere from your face and hands to your knees or feet. Hair in the affected area may also turn white.

There are various ways through which doctors can help you diagnose vitiligo and determine what type of vitiligo you may have. One major examination done is the Wood’s lamp examination, where ultraviolet light is used to distinguish vitiligo from other hypopigmented conditions.
Treatment options
Treatment for vitiligo is mostly connected to re-pigmentation, or slowing progression, depending on the type of vitiligo and patient preference rather than a guaranteed cure.

There are various types of topical treatments (like creams for external use) which can often help with inflammation, as well as medical light treatments like narrowband UVB phototherapy and excimer laser or lamp. Availability of certain treatments also changes from country to country and by the patient’s age group. There are situations where oral medication is also used for the short term. People with stable vitiligo can also consider surgical options if other treatments are not working, and depigmentation therapy if a major part of the person’s natural pigmentation is lost.

title: Painkillers, antibiotics, and kidney disease: Why has drug regulator issued a fresh warning?

content.value: The story so far: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has warned against the indiscriminate, repeated, or prolonged use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics, linking inappropriate use to avoidable renal complications and chronic kidney disease (CKD).
In its September 21 circular, it also reminded doctors, pharmacists, hospitals, and the public that these medicines are subject to prescription and other regulatory safeguards.
What does the latest directive mean?
The CDSCO circular is, in significant part, a reminder that existing rules already require medical supervision for these medicines and doesn’t amount to any new ban on painkillers or antibiotics.

Most NSAIDs are classified under Schedule H of the Drugs Rules, 1945. Most antibiotics are under Schedule H1. These medicines are therefore not meant to be sold at retail without a prescription from a Registered Medical Practitioner.
Schedule H1 medicines also carry a specific warning that they should be taken only on and according to medical advice.
The regulator has asked the public not to take NSAIDs or antibiotics indiscriminately, repeatedly or for prolonged periods without medical advice.
“Antibiotics should not be self-medicated or used for illnesses where they are not clinically indicated,” it said.

Also, doctors have been asked to prescribe them only when clinically justified, in the appropriate dose and for the appropriate duration, and to follow antimicrobial stewardship principles. Pharmacies, hospitals, and healthcare institutions have also been put on notice.

The kidney warning is particularly relevant to NSAIDs. These drugs can reduce blood flow to the kidneys and are associated with acute kidney injury, particularly among people who already have kidney disease, diabetes, or hypertension. Longer-term use has also been associated with CKD occurrence or progression.
Importantly, the warning does not mean that all painkillers or antibiotics are inherently unsafe. The concern is inappropriate selection, dose, duration, and unsupervised use.
How extensive is antibiotic misuse?
There is no single national figure that captures all inappropriate antibiotic use in India. Available studies, however, show that self-medication remains a significant problem.

A systematic review covering 66 Indian studies and nearly 30,000 participants estimated overall self-medication at 64.4%, although this included medicines generally and not antibiotics alone. Analgesics, antipyretics, antibiotics, and cough remedies were among the commonly self-medicated drug categories.

A community study from South-East Delhi found that 35% of 200 participants reported antibiotic self-medication. Fever, cold, and flu were common reasons, while pharmacies were the main source of antibiotics.

While these studies cannot be interpreted as a national prevalence estimate and represent different populations and locations, together they illustrate why prescription enforcement and antibiotic stewardship remain concerns.
What does antibiotic misuse do?
Antibiotics work against bacterial infections. They do not treat viral illnesses such as most common colds and influenza.

When antibiotics are used unnecessarily, incorrectly or for an inappropriate duration, bacteria can be exposed to the drug without being eliminated. Resistant organisms can then survive and multiply. This contributes to antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
The consequences extend beyond the individual who takes the antibiotic. Resistant organisms can spread to other people and through healthcare and environmental pathways.

WHO estimates that bacterial AMR was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021. In 2023, approximately one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections globally was resistant to antibiotics. WHO says misuse and overuse of antimicrobials are important drivers of the problem.
What does WHO say about antibiotic use?
WHO has increasingly moved towards antimicrobial stewardship — ensuring that antimicrobials are used only when necessary and that the right drug, dose and duration are selected.

Its AWaRe classification divides antibiotics into three groups: Access, Watch and Reserve. Access antibiotics are generally preferred for common infections because they have a narrower spectrum and lower resistance potential. Watch antibiotics have greater resistance potential and therefore require more careful use. Reserve antibiotics are intended for infections caused by multidrug-resistant organisms when other options are inadequate.

WHO’s analysis of 2022 antibiotic-use data found that only about one in three reporting countries/territories/areas met the target of having at least 70% of antibiotic consumption from the Access group. WHO has called for stewardship policies to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use and encourage Access antibiotics when they are clinically appropriate.

WHO’s 2025 global AMR surveillance report, based on more than 23 million laboratory-confirmed cases reported by countries, also underlines the continuing global burden of resistance and the need for better surveillance.
Which drugs are commonly misused, and who is most vulnerable?
NSAIDs are among the medicines of concern because they are widely used for headaches, fever, body pain, arthritis, dental pain, and other painful conditions.

Common NSAIDs include ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen, and similar anti-inflammatory painkillers. Their risks become more important with prolonged or high-dose use and in people with kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, dehydration or other risk factors.

Indian pharmacovigilance data, although based on reported adverse events rather than population prevalence, provide an important signal: in one analysis of NSAID-associated CKD reports, 82% of cases were among people aged 40–80 years, with diclofenac implicated in 43% of the reports.

For antibiotics, children are an important vulnerable group, largely because parents or caregivers may administer medicines based on previous prescriptions or advice from pharmacies and family members. The recent Indian meta-analysis found substantial antibiotic self-medication among children.
Older adults and people with chronic diseases also require particular caution because kidney function may already be reduced and multiple medicines may be involved.
What measures is the government bringing in?

India has been working on AMR for more than a decade. The National Programme on AMR Containment was launched in 2013, with surveillance, monitoring of antimicrobial consumption, infection prevention and control, and promotion of rational antimicrobial use among its objectives.

India launched its National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2.0 (NAP-AMR 2025–2029) in November 2025. It adopts a One Health approach, bringing human health together with animal, agricultural, and environmental sectors. It includes surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention and control, research and monitoring.

The government has also used the Drugs Rules to control antibiotic sales. Schedule H1 requires records of the supply of listed medicines, including details of the prescriber and patient, with records maintained for three years.
There is also a recent regulatory development in August 2026, when CDSCO issued a draft notification proposing four additional drugs for inclusion in Schedule H1.
Why have rules not worked so far?
The central difficulty is that regulation has existed for years, but implementation has been uneven.

India’s NAP-AMR documentation itself records earlier CDSCO awareness and enforcement drives concerning Schedule H and H1 medicines, including restrictions on selling antimicrobials without prescriptions. Yet studies continue to document antibiotic self-medication and access through pharmacies.

Similarly, antimicrobial stewardship programmes have been part of India’s AMR strategy since the first National Action Plan. The 2017–2021 plan called for stewardship programmes, treatment guidelines, multidisciplinary stewardship committees, and training.

The continuing problem, therefore, is less about the absence of rules and more about translating those rules into routine practice — ensuring that prescriptions are actually required at the point of sale, that doctors prescribe antibiotics appropriately, that patients do not demand or reuse medicines, and that hospitals monitor antibiotic consumption.

title: What is brain fog and when does it need investigation

content.value: ‘Brain fog’ is used to describe a feeling of mental slowness, difficulty concentrating, finding words, remembering information or processing things as quickly as before. But it is not a medical diagnosis, and persistent cognitive difficulties should not automatically be attributed to brain fog.
What brain fog feels like

Brain fog is a subjective description of changes in cognitive functioning. People may feel that their thinking has become slower or more effortful, that they cannot concentrate on a task, lose their train of thought, struggle to find words or read something without absorbing the information.

“Brain fog is basically a subjective feeling that you are cognitively slow, that you are mentally slow, that you are not able to do your daily activities as quickly or as deftly as before,” says  Srividhya S., associate consultant, department of neurology, Rela Hospital, Chennai.

It is different from the occasional forgetfulness that occurs when a person is tired, distracted or stressed. Forgetting where the keys were kept or briefly forgetting a name, for instance, does not by itself indicate a cognitive disorder. Tiredness is also not the same as brain fog. Fatigue is primarily a feeling of reduced physical or mental energy, while brain fog refers more specifically to difficulties with attention, memory, processing or mental clarity.

T. Swathi, consultant, neurology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai, says people with brain fog are often aware that they are not functioning as efficiently as before. This also distinguishes it from some memory disorders, where relatives may be the first to notice changes such as repeated questions, difficulty managing regular  tasks or getting lost in familiar places.
Health factors

The causes of brain fog can be varied, and more than one factor may be involved. Poor or inadequate sleep is a common contributor. Sleep apnoea can also disrupt sleep repeatedly without the person being aware of it.

Stress, anxiety and depression can affect attention and processing speed. Other possible contributors include thyroid disorders, diabetes, anaemia and nutritional deficiencies such as vitamin B12 and folate. Migraine and hormonal changes, including those during pregnancy, the postpartum period and menopause, can also be associated with cognitive symptoms.

Medicines should also be considered. Sedatives, some sleeping medicines, antihistamines, anticholinergic medicines and some anti-seizure drugs can affect alertness or cognitive function. Alcohol and dehydration may add to the symptoms.

“Brain fog has several possible causes and can be due to more than one,” says  Arulselvan V.L., senior consultant in neurology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. “It is crucial to not think that all brain fog is neurological.”

Cognitive difficulties can also occur during or after infections. A recent systematic review of 47 studies involving more than 25,000 people with long COVID estimated the pooled prevalence of brain fog at 30%. However, various studies use different definitions and assessment methods. There is so far no comparable prevalence estimate because brain fog is a symptom description and not a defined medical diagnosis.
When tests are needed
There is no fixed duration after which every case of brain fog requires investigation. Persistence, progression and its effect on daily functioning are  important.

Doctors advise evaluation when symptoms continue despite adequate sleep and lifestyle measures, recur frequently or gradually worsen. Repeatedly forgetting important information, struggling with previously familiar tasks, difficulty following conversations or unusual changes in work performance are also reasons to consult a doctor.

Symptoms lasting for several weeks without an obvious explanation, particularly when they affect work, studies or relationships, should be assessed. New symptoms such as persistent fatigue, weight changes, breathlessness, tingling, low mood or excessive daytime sleepiness can provide additional clues.
Evaluation usually begins with a detailed history. . A neurological examination may then be performed.
Depending on the history and examination, doctors may check blood counts, blood sugar, electrolytes, thyroid function, kidney and liver function and nutritional markers such as vitamin B12.

A brief cognitive assessment may be useful when there are concerns about memory, attention or language. Brain imaging such as an MRI is also not routinely required for uncomplicated brain fog. It may be considered when symptoms are progressive, the neurological examination is abnormal or there are other features suggesting a structural or neurological cause. A sleep study or EEG may be considered in selected cases.

Certain symptoms, however, require prompt attention rather than being attributed to brain fog. Sudden difficulty speaking, facial drooping, weakness or numbness on one side, sudden problems with vision or balance, seizures, fainting or severe confusion can indicate an acute neurological problem such as stroke. A sudden, severe or unusual headache also requires urgent assessment.

title: Epidemic prevention to be strengthened through coordination committees in Keralam

content.value: Coordination committees, chaired by District Collectors, will be formed to strengthen local-level prevention of epidemic diseases such as dengue and chikungunya.
The Principal Secretary (Health) has been tasked to take necessary steps regarding this, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan announced after the epidemic review meeting here on Monday.

The meeting also directed that committees be formed at the grassroots in local bodies, by including councillors/panchayat members, residents’ association office-bearers, and health workers. Dengue hotspots will be identified and mosquito control activities, among other measures, will be intensified.

To prevent water stagnation from intermittent rains and to eliminate mosquito breeding, Dry Day should be observed on Fridays in educational institutions, on Saturdays in workplaces, and on Sundays in households, wherein all potential breeding sources for mosquitoes should be eliminated. An action plan will be prepared for this  in consultation with the Local Self-Government Minister.

Directions were also issued to step up preventive activities according to the epidemic calendar, to strengthen fever clinics in fever-affected areas, and to start new ones where needed. The Minister said that meetings of District Medical Officers and District Programme Managers will be convened to review day-to-day grassroots activities in the coming days.

Those who attended the review meeting included the Principal Secretary (Health), Sharmila Mary Joseph; the Chairman, Health Department High-Power Committee, S. S.Lal; the Director of Health Services, V. Meenakshy; the Director of Medical Education, K.V. Viswanathan; Head, Infectious Diseases Department,  Thiruvananthapuram Government Medical College, Aravind R.; Special Officer, Kerala Centre for Disease Control, A. Althaf, among others.

title: India’s river interlinks may carry invasive species farther

content.value: The National River-Linking Project is the world’s most ambitious project of its kind to date, proposing to link 37 major river basins across India using 30 links, potentially redistributing around 174 billion cubic metres of water from ‘surplus’ to ‘deficit’ basins while generating some 34,000 MW of power.

Yet the Project has also raised serious concerns about its environmental costs. Experts have said the idea of ‘surplus’ and ‘deficit’ basins can mask seasonal and year-on-year variations in river flows, and that transferring water between basins can alter downstream flows, sediment transport, floodplains, deltas, and the habitats that depend on them. Dams, reservoirs, and canals can also break ecosystems up into pieces and disturb fish migration and other ecological processes.

Climate change has also been complicating assumptions about how much water a basin will reliably have available to transfer in the decades ahead. But it seems river-linking also poses another, less obvious problem.
‘Ecological highways’

Recently, researchers from the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE), Bengaluru, assessed the Project also possibly creating “ecological highways” that invasive species can travel on to new, ecologically sensitive areas.
Their findings were recently published in Scientific Reports.

Because of the ways in which India’s river basins are isolated from each other, many species in each one are endemic, meaning they inhabit a small area and are not found elsewhere on the planet. River links may then threaten them more than native species.

“There is no public or verifiable scientific basis that backs any of the claims of benefits of the National River-Linking Project, but more of a notional basis that if you connect a drier part to a wetter part of the country, there will be water balance, as opposed to how ecology actually works,” Siddharth Agarwal, director-founder of the Veditum India Foundation, a nonprofit working on environmental governance, said.
In the paper, the team showed that all Northeast and peninsular Indian basins are more vulnerable to biological invasions than those in Central and North India.

The Southwestern Ghats, Kaveri, Krishna Lower Ganga, and Brahmaputra basins support diverse habitats and complex ecological niches that host native species, threatened species, and invasive alien species.
‘Invasion hotspots’

“Right now, [the invasive alien species] are isolated, restricted to individual river basins,” the study’s lead author and ATREE senior fellow Aravind Neelavar Ananthram said. “By connecting rivers, we would not only introduce new species which are not naturally found but also increase the vulnerability of the native species that cannot compete with the invasive alien species.”

This finding is consistent with research worldwide, which has suggested that biodiversity hotspots can accumulate more invasive alien species, thus compromising the long-term prospects of native species and themselves turning into ‘invasion hotspots’.

For example, the Lower Ganga basin hosts 13-15 invasive alien species, and could become a major source of invasives for the Mahanadi, which is home to 69 threatened species. In fact, this is one of the Project’s most ecologically sensitive links, and it could increase the risk of extinction for the threatened species.
Water connections under the Project could also help aquatic pathogens to spread, disrupt the migratory routes of fish, and flatten the unique biota that individual river basins boast today.

“Fishes in one river basin may be well adapted or immune to the pathogens it harbours, while species in other basins may not be able to protect themselves against such pathogens,” Dr. Ananthram said. “If one reduces the water flow by taking out water from one river and putting it into another, the downstream water flow will be reduced. As a consequence, the downstream biodiversity will be severely affected and there is a high chance that the endemic species in the lower reaches might go extinct.”

“The river linking project is being sold as a solution (at least for the Ken-Betwa) to water scarcity (in Bundelkhand), but can it really serve the objectives that it is proposing?” Mr. Agarwal asked. “There is no way for us to verify. It is more of a capital investment than an ecological one.”
In need of foresight

“Rivers like the Ken have sand of great ecological value. But when the Ken-Betwa link is live, large quantities of water will be moved away from the river, lowering the flow volume and reducing sediment production rates in the river,” Mr. Agarwal said. “That could ultimately reduce the biodiversity in the river and potentially even trigger a food chain collapse.”
The Project’s consequences may also extend to downstream nations.

“Right now, we have only considered 15 freshwater invasive species for which data is available,” Dr. Ananthram said. “If one looks at all species across India, including terrestrial and marine systems, it would be approximately 350 to 400 species in different stages of invasion. Developed economies like Australia and in Europe have very strong policies for invasive alien species. It is an urgent need that India comes up with a specific policy targeted to regulate, manage and control” such species.
Embedding evidence-based management of river basins into national infrastructure planning could provide ecological foresight.

“The health risks, biodiversity, wildlife, and economic costs of [the Project] to India, especially for the agro-economy, farmers’ livelihoods, and fisheries, are matters of urgent attention,” he added. “While the government’s intention might be good to address water deficit, development plans and policy decisions should be holistic, addressing the ecological impact, the effect on biodiversity, and people’s lives.”
Jhinook Mitra is an independent researcher and ecologist, currently with the Nature Conservation Foundation, Bengaluru.

title: Highly educated professionals are vulnerable to financial cybercrime, finds IIT-Madras study

content.value: A study led by researchers from the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT-Madras) has found that financial cybercrime victims in India are often highly educated professionals, challenging the perception that victims are primarily careless, financially unaware or greedy. The study found that high digital literacy does not necessarily protect individuals from cyber fraud. Victims included IT professionals, bankers, doctors, management and finance professionals, public-sector officers and individuals with cybersecurity certifications.

The researchers found that victims were often targeted during periods of stress or life disruption, including illness in the family, retirement, job searches, or workplace pressure. Fraudsters exploited fear, financial expectations, and reputational concerns to create an “engineered brain freeze,” with victims describing a state of “mind arrest” that impaired their ability to think clearly. Financial losses ranged from a few thousand rupees to more than ₹1 crore, while victims also reported shame, insomnia, depression, and damaged family trust. The study also found that institutional responses varied, with some banks and cybercrime cells responding quickly while others lacked the required technical capabilities and coordination.

The study was led by retired IPS officer P. Kandaswamy and Nandan Sudarsanam, from IIT Madras in collaboration with Akanksha Jaiswal, Associate Professor, The University of Western Australia, Chennai Campus and Ameeta Fernando from Loyola Institute of Business Administration, Chennai. The research received support from the Wadhwani School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence at IIT Madras.

The study sample comprised victims of financial cybercrime residing in various Indian cities including Chennai, Bengaluru. Hyderabad, New Delhi and Mumbai. The team contacted the cybercrime cells in these cities, sharing the study’s purpose with police officers who, in turn, shared victims contact details and provided an initial brief to the victims about the research study. The final details included 11 females and 22 males, mostly married with dependents. Among them, 12 were senior citizens, including one visually impaired individual.

Mr.Kandaswamy IPS (Retd), Adjunct Faculty, Department of Data Science and Artificial intelligence, Department of Management Studies, IIT Madras said, “The response to cybercrime must move beyond blaming victims. Banks and law-enforcement agencies need stronger systems for early detection, rapid intervention, and coordinated response, along with better support for victims.”

Nandan Sudarsanam, Wadhwani School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, IIT Madras, said, “Our findings show that financial cybercrime is not simply a problem of inadequate digital literacy. Even highly educated and digitally experienced individuals can become vulnerable when fraudsters exploit fear, stress, and urgency. Understanding these factors is essential to designing more effective prevention strategies.”

India’s rapid digital transition near-universal mobile access, UPI, and the wider Digital India push has brought hundreds of millions of first-generation users into digital finance within a decade, opening an unusually wide attack surface for investment and stock-trading frauds, task and job scams, digital payment frauds, malware attacks, and the distinctly Indian “digital arrest” scam.

While official statistics from the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) record the transactional breach, they remain silent on the human trauma behind the numbers, prompting the research team to ask a human question rather than a technical one.

title: What are Dots, OpenAI’s new AI agents?

content.value: OpenAI, on Tuesday (September 29, 2025), unveiled Dots, the company’s new agentic capability that completes a range of tasks for users. The company also introduced several major updates focused on AI agents and developer tools.

Dots, which reads like a play on “bots”, are always-on AI agents that  can handle complex tasks by accessing your files, apps, and context. They can be delegated responsibility for projects like monitoring bugs, drafting code, or managing calendars.

Unlike traditional virtual assistants that handle simple tasks, Dots, per OpenAI, are engineered to understand complex workflows and context, and operate with the agency of a “chief of staff” or a “high-level engineer”.

These intelligent bots can learn how you work over time by gaining access to your files, and communicate with platforms like Slack, Teams, calendars, and other development environments, allowing them to proactively manage your workflows.
They are capable of performing multi-step tasks like monitoring bug reports, drafting code fixes, or managing project timelines, without needing constant oversight.

They work with over thousands of apps, per OpenAI, via existing connectors and have their own cloud-based computers and browsers, enabling them to execute tasks, build apps, and test workflows independently.
Users can interact with the AI agent with their voice, text, or phone call, and they are accessible accessible round the clock.

CEO Sam Altman, during the DevDay 2026 keynote, listed a few examples of how Dot agents can be used in various organisational scenarios like application migration, product launches and administrative delegation.

He explained that the agent can trace dependencies within a codebase to migrate an application from a legacy API.  This involves writing the required code running tests and then submitting a pull request for the team’s review.

The agent is also capable of updating calendars, analysing user feedback from testing, and even implementing last-minute design changes by building them directly into the app using Codex, OpenAI’s coding tool.
The generative AI bot can help with rescheduling meetings to accommodate personal priorities, and handling complex vendor communications.

Mr. Altman noted that these intelligent bots operate within defined safety boundaries, allowing users to control their level of responsibility, and are powered by Astra, the company’s most advanced AI model.

Apart from Dots, Mr. Altman also showcased a collaborative platform for teams called Spaces. It lets users and their respective Dots to work together on documents, research, and data visualisation. It supports dynamic content like interactive charts and live prototypes.

The usage cost of Dots is included directly in existing ChatGPT subscription plans, and the service is available to ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise users at “no additional cost” and the conversations users have with their Dots do not count toward their standard ChatGPT usage limits.
The San Francisco-based company also introduced GPT-6.1 Sol that, per the firm, offers near-Astra intelligence at a significantly lower price point, and is optimised as a daily workhorse.
The company also unveiled UltraFast, an amped up model, that provides a speed boost for faster execution across API, ChatGPT, and Codex.
Codex is now fully cloud-based, and it allows seamless transitions between devices, the company said during the keynote.

Lastly, OpenAI announced the Marketplace, a new platform where developers can sell their products and companies can buy using for developers to distribute their products, allowing enterprise customers to purchase these tools using existing OpenAI commitments

title: SpaceX Starship engine failure could hit NASA moon mission plans

content.value: The Starship engine failure that nearly foiled the orbital debut of SpaceX’s next-generation spacecraft on its 14th uncrewed test flight may complicate NASA‘s ‌ability to meet its time frame for astronaut missions to the moon.

Starship, designed in part to carry ​large payloads to space, is one of two vehicles vying to become the first craft that NASA will use ⁠as early as 2028 to land humans on the moon and bring them safely home, a feat last achieved in 1972 at the end of the Apollo era.
While Starship accomplished a number of key objectives in its latest test launch from Texas on Monday, the mission was cut short by ‌several hours after a malfunction of its propulsion system.

Despite the unexpected shutdown of one of its three main Raptor engines following Starship separation from its lower-stage booster rocket, flight controllers proceeded with sending the spacecraft to orbit for its ‌first-ever commercial satellite deployment.

Determining what caused the engine glitch remains critical to SpaceX’s bottom line. But the stakes are potentially ‌higher for ⁠NASA, as a Starship moon-landing vehicle would rely on the same engine system for transporting astronauts through space ⁠to and from the lunar surface.

How big a blow to Starship’s development progress the engine snafu becomes depends on whether it turns out to be “a one-off failure of a single part” or points to a larger design problem that requires upgrades “across the fleet,” said Dean Sladen, an aerospace engineer for Accu Components.
“Any engine fix that holds ​up the next flights, including the planned attempt to ‌catch the ship with the launch tower’s arms (after re-entry), eats into that schedule,” he said.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

A NASA spokesperson did not address questions for comment on the engine issue or its Artemis programme, instead pointing to a post on X from the head of the space agency, Jared Isaacman, saying Starship ‌had “achieved an important milestone.”
‘The real pressure is the moon’

A longer delay would pose not only a greater setback ​to SpaceX’s commercial ambitions to rapidly expand its Starlink broadband satellite network, but its pivotal role in NASA‘s Artemis moon programme.

Raptor engine and propulsion-system issues have contributed to several previous Starship setbacks, including an engine that failed to ignite as planned during Starship’s 12th flight in May. The methane-fuelled engines ‌are among the most complex and expensive components on the rocket.
During some previous flights, SpaceX scrubbed plans to test-ignite the Raptor engine in space. But all of the engines successfully fired during ascent on Starship’s 13th flight in July.
SpaceX is competing with Blue Origin, the rival rocket company from fellow entrepreneur Jeff Bezos, to usher in an era of lunar exploration under NASA‘s Artemis programme.

While SpaceX was originally contracted to provide the first crewed lunar lander for Artemis, Isaacman said in April that NASA would go with whichever lander was ready to fly first. NASA saw the added competition as healthy ‌for progress in light of mounting delays in Starship’s test flight programme.
NASA officially aims to return astronauts to the moon’s surface by 2028, a target widely seen ​as overly ambitious, to get there ahead of China, which plans a crewed lunar landing by 2030.

title: MeitY IndiaAI Centre of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence to be launched on Wednesday

title: Buzz on space privatisation upstages ISRO’s moment of glory

content.value: This article is part of Space Wrap, a round-up of space news and developments in and related to India every month

The successful predawn launch of the advanced earth observation satellite EOS-05, on board the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle rocket on September 4, 2026 from the spaceport in Sriharikota brought considerable relief for the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO): it had finally successfully launched a rocket and place a satellite in orbit after a gap of nearly eight months.

However, even before it could celebrate the success of the F17 mission, a group of employees working in various centers of the space agency wrote to the ISRO chairman, V. Narayanan, seeking a clarification on the official government policy regarding privatisation, the transfer of ISRO manufacturing and operational functions, its future role in the Indian space programme, and the impact on serving and future employees.

Also, on the same day of the GSLV-F17 launch, the Joint Action Council (JAC), representing nine ISRO employees’ associations, sought clarification from Dr. Narayanan on a statement by Pawan Kumar Goenka — the chairman of Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) — at a media summit: that “ISRO will not make any launch vehicles and will not manufacture any launch vehicles. That will all be done by the private sector or public-sector undertaking.”

The JAC also wrote in a strongly worded letter that while they were not against private participation, they would also not accept without debate a policy that they said could reduce ISRO to a residual R&D boutique.

In response, ISRO — which had until then maintained a studied silence on various issues pertaining to the agency’s functioning as well as the findings of the Failure Analysis Committee (FAC) report on the two launch failures that created the launch hiatus — issued a clarification. It dubbed the assertions to be completely baseless and incorrect, and said ISRO will neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished.

Mr. Goenka also said ISRO will continue to remain the bedrock of the Indian space sector while IN-SPACe will facilitate greater non-governmental participation and NewSpace India, Ltd. (NSIL) would help with commercialisation. In addition to this, Dr. Narayanan also addressed ISRO employees in a video conference.

However, these outreach efforts did not quell the JAC’s concerns, and the body issued another notice seeking an official inquiry into the allegations of sabotage in the two consecutive PSLV failures, which happened on May 18, 2025, and January 12, 2026.

This second notice also said private participation must strengthen ISRO, not replace it, and sought expanded production capabilities at the organisation without also weakening it, and strengthening its R&D and administrative systems. The associations also demanded that the Joint Consultative Machinery be reinstated, that the Central Civil Services (Recognition of Service Associations) Rule 1993 be rescinded, and to endeavour against the erosion of promotional avenues and to not act against association activists.
International efforts

Aside from dealing with the HR situation back home, ISRO also strengthened its international cooperation. Dr. Narayanan participated in the International Space Summit in Paris and signed documents with the European Space Agency to extend the longstanding cooperation agreement between the two space agencies for five more years, until January 8, 2032.
The agencies have included space weather, human and robotic exploration and sustainability of space activities as new areas of cooperation.

At the BRICS New Delhi Declaration 2026, the participating countries recognised the importance of international cooperation in the peaceful exploration and use of outer space and of space systems. They also reiterated their commitment to reducing existing asymmetries in space capabilities among the BRICS countries.
The BRICS bloc today comprises Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates.

IN-SPACe also engaged in dialogue with the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), the Myanmar Space Agency, the National Space Agency of Singapore, and the Ambassador of Italy to India to strengthen bilateral ties and expand collaboration across commercial space, technologies, investments, and industry partnerships.
Two tests

Next, ISRO also carried out a couple of crucial hot-tests involving cryogenic and semi cryogenic engines. Specifically, it hot-tested the cryogenic engine identified for the seventh operational mission of the LVM-3 launch vehicle, called (LVM-M7), before its flight acceptance.
In this test, the liquid oxygen tank pressurisation module, meant for the C32 engine stage for the Gaganyaan mission, was also successfully demonstrated.

The other hot-test successfully qualified the semi-cryogenic engine power head test article (PHTA) at the full thrust level of 200 tonnes. This marked the first time the PHTA had been tested at 100% of its level. Previous tests had been conducted at 47% (94 tonnes), 60% (120 tonnes), and 88% (175 tonnes).
The PHTA contains all the semi-cryogenic engine’s systems except the thrust chamber.
Private sector

On the private front: GalaxEye, the space technology startup incubated at IIT-Madras, reported that it had been granted a patent in the U.S. for the core technology behind its OptoSAR imaging capabilities. As a result, it became the first Indian startup to receive a U.S. patent for a satellite imaging technology.

The U.S. patent covers GalaxEye’s invention of the architecture and systems used to align and synchronise optical and microwave sensors for the instrument’s spatially and temporally matched data acquisition.

Another firm, Pixxel, based in Bengaluru, announced that it had closed its Series C funding round at $100 million, co-led by Temasek and Seraphim, with participation from new investors 360 ONE Asset and IMM Investment, plus existing investors Radical Ventures and growX ventures.
The round brought Pixxel’s total funding to $195 million.
Finally, IN-SPACe has released the norms, guidelines, and procedures towards implementing the Indian Space Policy 2023 — this time vis-à-vis Indian payloads on Indian and foreign launch missions.

title: Why Rayalaseema farmers fear a bumper crop more than drought; can the ₹1-lakh-crore horticulture hub change that?

content.value: Ask tomato growers in Madanapalle or mango farmers in Chittoor what they fear most. It is not drought but a bumper crop.
That is Rayalaseema’s paradox. Farmers toil for months and reap a good harvest, but lose money because everyone else in the region has a similar yield.

In July, 13,000 tonnes of tomatoes flooded markets in a day, and the price crashed to ₹14.70 a kg. Lower grades fetched ₹8 to ₹10. After spending on crates and transport, farmers got barely ₹3. In kharif 2025, farmers in Annamayya and Anantapur districts resorted to distress sales, selling tomatoes at ₹4 a kg against a cost of ₹6.

The plight of mango farmers is no different. In 2025, Totapuri growers in Chittoor faced rain damage yet had a bumper harvest, and still ended up at the receiving end. The government announced a minimum support price (MSP) of ₹12 a kg plus a ₹4 subsidy, but it never reached the yard. In 2026, prices fell from ₹120 in May to ₹30 in June.
Horticulture scientists cite three problems. First is water. Rayalaseema is rain-fed. Groundwater falls, borewells fail.

“Farm ponds, check dams and micro-irrigation coverage are still patchy. When Handri-Neeva water reaches late, sowing is delayed and harvests bunch together,” a horticulture official in Rajampeta said.

Second is marketing. On a peak day, 300 farmers rush to Madanapalle or Punganur in the same hour. There are no prior buyers, no grading and weak farmer producer organisations (FPOs). Middlemen who give crate advances dictate the price.
Third is logistics. When it comes to perishability, tomatoes have a two-day window and mangoes ten. The region has no cold storage units or pack houses even to meet the minimum needs of farmers.

“If transport fails to arrive on time, or the yard is full, farmers must sell at whatever is offered or simply throw the produce away. Incidents of tomatoes dumped on the Madanapalle-Punganur Road in 2025 were not about overproduction, but about nowhere to store and no one to buy,” laments Rajasekhar, 38, a farmer from Gurramkonda.

The ₹1-lakh-crore Rayalaseema Integrated Horticulture Hub project seeks to fix this. Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman are to lay its foundation stone at Madanapalle on October 2. The project envisages ₹40,000 crore from the Centre under the Purvodaya scheme and ₹60,000 crore in private investment across 201 clusters in 10 districts.
Rayalaseema to become global horticulture hub with launch of ₹1 lakh-crore project: Collector
Sri Sathya Sai district to play key role in transforming Rayalaseema into global horticulture hub, says Collector
Works worth ₹8,022 crore give fillip to Rayalaseema development: Pawan Kalyan
Rayalaseema: India’s new industrial hub

Each cluster will have collection centres, grading, cold storage and market linkages. An Indian School of Agriculture, being set up at Ramireddypalli by Reliance, will bring AI tools and issue market alerts.

“If this project is implemented in true spirit, tomato farmers need not bring all their produce on day one. They can grade and store the produce for three to four days, and send them to Chennai, Bengaluru or Hyderabad based on demand. For mango, it could mean pulp units, pack houses for export and direct linkage to processors instead of dependence on the local mandi during a three-week glut,” said Kothur Babu, president of the Chittoor District Mango Producers’ Association.

“The multi-crore project should compulsorily address farmers’ issues first and those faced by the food processing industry as well. Importantly, we need a separate Central Mango Board on the lines of the Tobacco Board,” said Kattamanchi Govardhan Bobby, chairman, All India Food Processors Association, South Zone.

Farmers recall the promises made by Narendra Modi. In April 2014 at Tirupati, Mr. Modi, then the BJP’s prime ministerial candidate, said Rayalaseema tomato could become world-class ketchup if adequate cold storage facilities were available. He described poverty as not only the lack of rain but also the absence of value addition. He promised agro-industries.

“Mr. Modi had spoken about cold storage and the tomato industry in Rayalaseema in 2014. Now, there is the double-engine government. We are still waiting for the promise to be fulfilled,” said Manjunath, 42, from Valmikipuram.

title: AIKMS calls for united movement against corporatisation of agriculture

content.value: All India Kisan Mazdoor Sabha (AIKMS) president Vemulapalli Venkataramaiah has called for a sustained mass movement to address the problems faced by farmers and agricultural labourers in the country.

Speaking at a public meeting in Khammam on Monday marking the beginning of the three-day fourth national conference of the AIKMS, he said there was an imperative need to build a united struggle along the lines of the farmers’ movement which forced the BJP-led Central government to repeal the three farm laws in 2021.
