The second burn to reach orbit is "the hardest part," requiring "more forces and more complex calculations," explained Kathleen Curlee, a senior analyst at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, before the launch.
To reach the necessary altitude and speed, "the rocket has to do different things when it's experiencing different levels of gravity," she told AFP.
On this flight, SpaceX is aiming for a circular orbit about 275 km (171 miles) above the Earth, requiring a speed of about 28,000 km/hour.
Once in orbit, the spacecraft began deploying next-generation Starlink satellites designed to expand the company's already massive satellite internet constellation.
Public expectations
The plan calls for the rocket to finish its journey in the Pacific Ocean after orbiting the Earth six times.
The huge first-stage booster, called "Super Heavy," fell shortly after launch into waters of the Gulf of Mexico.
From an engineering point of view, "just achieving flight and getting data" would be considered a success, Curlee said.
But spectators and investors have different expectations.
"They need to have flashy tests" because anything less would be seen as a failure, she added.
The development of Starship has faced repeated delays, and a Chinese company has recently made progress in the field of reusable rockets.
Still, SpaceX continues to dominate the global space launch market, thanks to its partially reusable Falcon rockets, and has made risk-taking its mantra.

Whether or not it is successful, this 14th test flight will be followed the same week by three other SpaceX rocket launches, one of which will carry a crew of astronauts to the International Space Station.

title: U.P. focuses on utilisation of Gram Sabha ponds, reservoirs, rivers to make fisheries backbone of rural livelihood

content.value: The Uttar Pradesh government on Sunday (September 27, 2026) said it was aiming to make fisheries a reliable source of income for farmers and fishing communities by improving the utilisation of Gram Sabha ponds, reservoirs and rivers.

The State government said more than 80,000 hectares of Gram Sabha ponds had been leased for fisheries activities, 2,205 km of rivers had been brought under organised leasing frameworks, and 342 reservoirs were now actively supporting fish production.

"Our structured approach has brought transparency, efficiency, and stronger community participation in fisheries management," Mukesh Kumar Meshram, Additional Chief Secretary, Animal Husbandry, Dairy Development and Fisheries Department, told The Hindu. He said the expansion in scale and coverage had significantly increased fish output while creating employment opportunities for thousands of rural households. Fish production had risen from 6.29 lakh tonnes to 15.90 lakh tonnes in the past eight years, he said.

Mr. Meshram, a 1995-batch Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer, said the focus on scientific fish culture and improved resource management was also helping farmers achieve sustainable growth without depleting ecological resources. Access to government schemes, modern practices and collective investment models had led to higher productivity and better income stability, he said.

"Our initiative strongly aligns with long-term goals of utilising underused water resources efficiently, enhancing farmers' incomes through targeted schemes, promoting sustainable fisheries management practices and balancing economic growth with ecological sustainability," the Additional Chief Secretary added.

title: Dental trauma affects over a billion globally, remains overlooked health concern: AIIMS experts

content.value: More than one billion people globally have experienced traumatic dental injuries, making it a significant yet often overlooked public health concern with potentially long-term consequences for oral health and quality of life, AIIMS experts said.

Observed annually on September 21, Global Dental and Oral Trauma Day is supported by the Indian Society of Dental Traumatology to raise awareness about prevention, timely management and equitable access to care for traumatic dental injuries.
A study published in the Dental Traumatology journal in 2018 reported that more than one billion living people worldwide have experienced traumatic dental injuries (TDI).

Researchers highlighted that TDI represents a neglected condition of substantial global burden, noting that, if included among the world’s most frequent acute and chronic diseases and injuries, it could rank fifth in terms of prevalence.

"Dental trauma can happen anytime, anywhere and to anyone. It can have both immediate and long-term consequences. It is not simply a broken or displaced tooth. For many patients, a traumatic injury can initiate a lifelong cycle of treatment, follow-up and rehabilitation," said Ajay Logani, professor of endodontics at the Centre for Dental Education and Research (CDER), AIIMS Delhi.
Dr. Logani stressed the emphasis has to shift from treating trauma only after it occurs to preventing injuries. The public should also know what to do immediately after an accident, he said.
Falls, road traffic accidents, sports injuries, domestic violence and everyday accidents are among the common causes of dental trauma.
Children are particularly vulnerable to dental trauma, and the first few minutes after an injury can be critical, Nitesh Tewari, professor of paediatric dentistry at CDER, AIIMS Delhi said.

"For a child, a traumatic injury can affect not only the tooth but also facial development, appearance, psychological trauma and quality of life. Parents should know that dental trauma requires timely assessment and should not be dismissed as 'just a broken tooth'," said Dr. Tewari.
Experts said awareness about immediate first aid remains inadequate, despite the fact that the response in the first few minutes can influence the outcome of an injured tooth.

"The first person to handle a dental injury may be a parent, school teacher, sports coach, or even a bystander. A few simple fact -- what to do with an injured tooth, what not to do, how to transport it and where to seek care -- can potentially make a lifelong difference," said Sidhartha Sharma, associate professor of endodontics, CDER, AIIMS, Delhi.
Dental trauma education therefore needs to move beyond dental clinics and into schools, sports facilities, emergency services and the community, Dr. Sharma underlined.

"Teachers, coaches and parents should be equipped with basic information on recognising serious injuries and taking appropriate immediate steps. This can help reduce avoidable complications and improve the chances of preserving an injured tooth," he stated.
Dr. Tewari said prevention should include safer sports practices, use of appropriate protective equipment, road safety measures and greater awareness of risks in children and young people.
Experts stressed that dental trauma should not be viewed merely as a cosmetic problem, as injuries can have long-term consequences for oral health, function, appearance and quality of life.

The observance carries a message extending beyond the dental profession: prevent injuries where possible, know the correct first-aid response when trauma occurs, and ensure timely access to evidence-based care.

title: Scientists at IAV, Keralam develop dengue early warning system to forecast trends

content.value: Scientists at the Institute of Advanced Virology (IAV) in Keralam are developing a dengue forecasting system that integrates epidemiological and weather data on a machine-learning platform to predict dengue incidence trends in advance.
The aim is to help public health managers plan resource allocation and preventive measures proactively, rather than responding only after outbreaks occur.
Climate factors are important early warning indicators for dengue because they directly influence the biology of the Aedes mosquito and the replication of the dengue virus.

Warm temperatures accelerate mosquito development, shorten the virus’s extrinsic incubation period—the time required for the virus to become transmissible inside the mosquito—and can increase transmission efficiency. Moderate to high humidity can prolong mosquito survival, while moderate rainfall creates breeding habitats. Torrential rain, however, can flush out mosquito breeding sites.
Favourable climate

Keralam, which remains warm and wet for much of the year, therefore has climatic conditions favourable to Aedes proliferation and dengue transmission. This has prompted considerable interest in developing forecasting models that combine meteorological and epidemiological data to enable disease surveillance to stay ahead of outbreaks.

“Our machine learning model integrates six years of epidemiological data (March 2020 to February 2026) with climatic variables, including rainfall, temperature and average humidity, to generate weekly dengue forecasts,” says Abhinand C.S., scientist in the Department of Virus Genomics, Bioinformatics and Statistics at IAV, who developed the model.

The Dengue Early Warning System (DEWS), the current version of the system, is accessible at https://dews.iav.res.in, and uses epidemiological data from the State Surveillance Unit (SSU) of the Directorate of Health Services and meteorological data from the India Meteorological Department.

The dengue case trends predicted by DEWS showed a positive correlation with actual case data from the Health department, Dr. Abhinand says. Further evaluation using the SSU data for March-July 2026 has indicated the model’s potential for early prediction of district-wise dengue trends.

The model incorporates daily epidemiological and climatic parameters, including temperature, rainfall and humidity, allowing a more granular representation of disease dynamics. Each district is treated as an independent unit, taking into account district-specific geographical and environmental characteristics, including waterbodies and drainage systems. This enables the model to be trained and optimised for individual districts.

For easier interpretation by public health managers, predicted disease burden is classified into four risk levels—very high, high, moderate and low, based on predefined prediction ranges. This provides a district-wise indication of the expected risk.
Prediction difficulties
Dengue is among the more difficult infectious diseases to predict because its transmission is multidimensional and can vary substantially between locations.

Beyond climate, factors such as urbanisation, human mobility, water-storage practices, population immunity to the four dengue virus serotypes and changes in vector biology can alter transmission dynamics. Models relying heavily on climatic variables may therefore struggle to capture sudden changes in these factors.

Under-reporting is another major challenge. A large proportion of dengue infections are asymptomatic or mild and may be mistaken for other viral fevers. Differences in testing and reporting practices can also create geographical biases. Thiruvananthapuram, for instance, has long been regarded as Keralam’s dengue hotspot, although public health experts have argued that its high reported burden also reflects stronger surveillance and testing.

The IAV acknowledges these limitations. Since DEWS is trained on historical data, sudden or substantial changes in climatic parameters could affect its accuracy. Variations in the reporting of confirmed dengue cases by the Health department could similarly influence observed disease patterns and the reliability of predictions, Dr. Abhinand says.
Yearly updation

“For the model to evolve from a research model to a routinely functioning public health forecasting system, DEWS will have to undergo yearly updation and further refinement, and perhaps be trained with more variables. DEWS is the first disease forecasting model of its kind to be developed for use by the State,” says IAV Director E. Sreekumar.

The platform could eventually be extended to other Aedes-borne diseases such as chikungunya and Zika, potentially strengthening Keralam’s disease surveillance capacity and enabling more timely, data-driven public health interventions.

title: Beyond borders and difficult roads, government hospitals in Telangana’s Bhadradri Kothagudem keep specialised care going

content.value: When Meghana’s family in YSR Kadapa district was told to wait for months for a sinus procedure and private hospitals quoted costs running into lakhs of rupees, they looked beyond Andhra Pradesh for an alternative. They eventually travelled to Yellandu in Bhadradri Kothagudem district of Telangana, where a government hospital performed the specialised surgery.

Meghana, a resident of Busireddypalli village in Veerapunayunipalli mandal, had been suffering from severe sinus-related problems and nasal obstruction caused by tissue growth inside her nose. Coming from a financially disadvantaged family headed by a single mother, the prospect of paying lakhs of rupees at a private hospital was difficult for the family.

Hospitals in Andhra Pradesh and Hyderabad had advised the family to wait for nearly three months for the procedure. It was through an acquaintance that the family came to know of Bhadradri Kothagudem District Coordinator of Hospital Services (DCHS) Dr G. Ravi Babu, who referred Meghana to the Area Hospital at Yellandu.

At the hospital, ENT specialist Dr. Ravi Tejaswi performed Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS), along with septoplasty, bilateral turbinectomy and middle meatal conchoplasty. The procedures were aimed at treating her sinus disease and relieving the nasal obstruction. “For the family, the treatment offered at a government hospital in a relatively remote part of Telangana meant that they did not have to wait several months or incur the high costs quoted by private hospitals,” said Dr. Ravi Babu.

The effort to keep essential healthcare services available in remote areas is also visible at the Community Health Centre (CHC), Charla, in the same district, where the medical team conducted eight deliveries within 24 hours recently, including four normal deliveries and four Caesarean sections. The deliveries were managed by gynaecologist Dr. Sravani, anaesthesiologist Dr. Krishna Prasad, OT team member Sneha, nursing officers Shailaja and Dayamani, Abrar, labour-room nurses and other hospital staff.

The achievement came despite heavy rains in the region over the past three days and difficult road conditions. “The medical team has been travelling nearly 60 km every day to provide maternity services at Charla, ensuring that pregnant women do not have to depend entirely on hospitals located farther away,” Dr Ravi Babu added.

Charla is around 56 km from the Area Hospital at Bhadrachalam, making the availability of local maternity services particularly significant for residents of the remote mandal. The continuation of 24x7 services has also helped improve confidence among local residents in using the government hospital.

Dr. Ravi Babu said that the hospital had earlier faced a shortage of nursing personnel. Following recent recruitment, adequate nursing staff are now available. Doctors were also recruited, although several have not joined duty because of the hospital’s remote location.

title: Study flags E. coli in 67% of water samples in Keralam’s Pala region

content.value: A water quality assessment conducted in flood-affected areas along the Meenachil river has detected E. coli bacteria in 67% of the samples, raising concerns over the safety of drinking water sources in and around Pala.

The study, conducted by the PG and Research Department of Zoology of Alphonsa College, Pala, in collaboration with local administrations, analysed water samples collected from water bodies in Pala Municipality, Karoor, Bharananganam, Erattupetta, Poonjar, Mutholy and Kidangoor. The assessment was undertaken as part of efforts to mitigate the risk of waterborne diseases in flood-affected areas.

The study evaluated nine physicochemical and microbiological parameters, including pH, electrical conductivity (EC), total dissolved solids (TDS), alkalinity, chlorinity, total hardness, sulphate, faecal coliform and E. coli.

The findings showed that TDS and pH levels exceeded the normal permissible range in the samples tested. E. coli was detected in 67% of the samples, with researchers attributing the spike in bacterial contamination to the recent floods, which may have allowed contaminated surface water to enter water sources.

The assessment has recommended scientific chlorination of water sources and mandatory water quality testing after every flood as key remedial measures. The recommendations have been shared with local stakeholders for follow-up action.
The report, along with the recommendations, was handed over to the Pala municipality at a function attended by Water Resources Minister Mons Joseph the other day.

Meanwhile, the college has launched a one-year pilot study to track seasonal variations in water quality during the pre-monsoon, monsoon and post-monsoon periods. The study is expected to provide a broader assessment of changes in water quality across the region.
The college has also initiated steps to transform its research laboratory into a certified facility, with efforts under way to secure recognition from the Kerala State Pollution Control Board.

title: Cancer, kidney, AIDS drugs sold at up to 70 times procurement cost: Karnataka Health Minister

content.value: Pointing out that high-cost medicines used to treat cancer, kidney ailments, and AIDS are being sold at prices up to “70 times higher” than the rates at which dealers and stockists procure them, Karnataka Health Minister U.T. Khader has written a letter to Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda, seeking national action against “abnormal gaps” in drug prices.

The Minister said dealers and stockists purchase advanced pharmaceuticals from manufacturers at heavily discounted wholesale landed rates, while the MRPs printed on the medicines are fixed at “inflated, highly disproportionate levels”. The letter said the gap between the procurement price and MRP was “sometimes 30 times to more than 70 times”.

Mr. Khader said that the issue was particularly concerning for in-patients, emergency and intensive-care patients, oncology patients, and those requiring implants, surgical consumables, and other hospital-based treatment, as they cannot realistically compare suppliers or defer purchases.

The letter said that while the existing MRP framework prevents medicines from being sold above the printed MRP, it does not address situations where the MRP itself has little relation to the actual institutional transaction price, adding that hospitals retain an excessive undisclosed margin.

Mr. Khader sought a national study comparing the printed MRP, manufacturer/importer price, hospital’s net acquisition price, and the price ultimately billed to patients for selected high-value medicines, medical devices, and consumables. He also proposed that the patient-facing price of products supplied through hospitals be capped at the lower end of the applicable statutory price, MRP or the hospital’s net acquisition cost plus a notified and reasonable service margin and applicable taxes.

The Minister said Karnataka would “cooperate with any pilot or national framework” and could, within its powers, make private hospitals disclose more information, require detailed bills for patients, and set up a system to handle complaints locally. However, he said the Centre needs to fix the basic problem — the large difference between what hospitals pay for medicines, the MRP printed on them and what patients are finally charged.

title: OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs called to appear at Australian AI probe over health database breach

content.value: The CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic have been called to appear at an ​Australian Senate inquiry on AI, the head of the probe ‌said on Sunday, September 27, 2026, days after the revelation that ​a rogue OpenAI bot had hacked ⁠the country's health-system database.
The Medicare breach, condemned by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing ‌external systems outside the U.S.

OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have been sent ‌written requests to appear at the inquiry, ‌which ⁠is to hold public hearings in the capital ⁠Canberra on Thursday, said a spokesperson for Senator Sarah Hanson-Young of the Australian
Greens party, who chairs the probe.
OpenAI and Anthropic ​did not immediately respond ‌to requests for comment outside business hours.

The OpenAI agent's incursion on one of the country's most used government agencies may prompt Albanese's Labor government
to toughen ‌AI-specific laws it is readying for next ​year, adding pressure to Australia-US relations already tested by Canberra's ban on social media for ⁠teens, tech policy experts say.

The Senate inquiry is examining the potential impacts of AI and data centres on ‌Australian communities, industries, water
and energy. It is one of several state and federal probes into AI.

"There are serious questions for Sam Altman to answer about the OpenAI hack of Australian government websites," Hanson-Young said in a statement. Altman and Amodei "must front up, ‌face the Senate's questions and have an honest conversation about ​what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should look like", she said.
Albanese, who revealed the June ⁠breach of Medicare on Thursday, called it "unacceptable", saying he had ⁠voiced "extreme concern" to Altman.

OpenAI says it only learned of the breach — one of at ‌least four of Australian government websites — in August. It says the incident was not intentional and did ​not compromise any private information.

title: Ahead of winter, why Delhi needs to vaccinate its grandparents alongside their grandchildren

content.value: The winter season in Delhi usually results in poor air quality, outbreaks of seasonal influenza, a heavy burden on hospitals and increasing medical expenses. Hidden within the yearly air quality reports is a health problem that is preventable, and yet costs the city’s citizens lakhs.  Among the elderly, especially those who have diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart disease or a suppressed immune system, a viral infection can develop into bacterial pneumonia and  require hospitalization. Industry estimates suggest that the average cost of a hospital stay is about ₹50,000, while intensive care can amount to ₹1 lakh. A single such incident can erase months’ worth of income and cause households relying on pensions and daily wages to slip down the income scale.
The battle against pneumonia

India has achieved real advances in the fight against pneumonia, mainly as a result of introducing the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) as part of the Universal Immunisation Programme in 2017 and through Mission Indradhanush. Free three-dose vaccinations are provided to infants, and by 2023, vaccination rates among infants in India had reached 83%, according to the WHO/UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC).

The grandparents of these infants, however, are almost completely unprotected: National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) 80th Round Data on Health reveals that vaccination coverage among people aged 60 and over is only 0.40 per cent. While one generation is covered by the national programme, the other is left to avail of vaccines from a private market  they may struggle to  afford.
This gap is most significant in Delhi, since in the winter, the conditions can turn common respiratory infections  into serious health issues.
Toxic winters

In December 2025, the city experienced its most toxic month in six years, with an average Air Quality Index of 351. Colder months naturally place a greater strain on the respiratory system. Winter air, which tends to remain stagnant, traps particulate matter near the ground: prolonged exposure compromises the lungs’ defensive abilities.

Government records show that there were more than 2,00,000 cases of acute respiratory illness and 30,000 hospital admissions in just six Delhi government hospitals between 2022 and 2024. When the pollution lasted throughout December 2025, doctors reportedly noted a 20% to 30% increase in the number of patients with respiratory problems, including some who had never before had such a condition.

These figures do not reflect the full extent of the problem, as they exclude people treated in private clinics, those who take medication on their own, infections that have never been confirmed by a laboratory test, and cases recorded as pneumonia rather than influenza.
Vaccine present, policy absent

What makes the number of hospitalisations and their resultant expenditure tragic, is that a a significant portion of this could perhaps be avoided with a vaccine that is already available. The 2026 Indian consensus guidelines concerning immunisation in adults recommend pneumococcal vaccination based on age and level of risk. It recommends the PCV20 vaccine for all adults between the ages of 18-49 years with chronic medical conditions or those considered at risk based on their health and lifestyle, or a single dose of the vaccine for all adults aged 50 and above. The guidelines also include adults who have immunosuppression and chronic diseases. For residents of Delhi, in winter when pollution makes the air toxic, this could mean the difference between a minor ailment an episode of hospitalisation.

India has no National Adult Immunisation Policy, and as a result, vaccination rates rely on individual awareness, access to a doctor, and the ability to pay out of pocket, a situation that systematically excludes older people in lower-income families.   While this a critical problem ahead of winter in Delhi, it is not merely a Delhi problem:  in 2022, India was estimated to whom were 149 million people aged 60 and over, a large number of whom are still economically active and support households.The Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (2017-18) showed that of Indians aged 45 and over, only around 0.6%  had received a pneumococcal vaccine, a figure that has not changed much since then.
The proportion of adults aged 45 years and over who have been vaccinated in Delhi. Source: LASI Wave 1
The burden in lives

The figure for deaths due to pneumonia recorded by India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death in 2024 was 35,987, making it the leading cause of respiratory deaths, although it remains relatively out of the spotlight compared to other causes. Even this figure is an under estimate since the system covers only about one fifth to one quarter of all registered deaths nationally, and older people who die at home rather than in a hospital where certification takes place almost never get included at all.

Data on a year-by-year basis from Delhi shows that this is not an isolated occurrence but a consistent pattern, affecting precisely the group for whom a vaccine is already available but for whom no public system provides it.
The number of institutional deaths in Delhi caused by pneumonia from 2005 to 2024. Source: Directorate of Economics & Statistics and Office of the Chief Registrar (Births & Deaths), 2024
Pollution raises the stakes

It is impossible for Delhi to solve its problem of air pollution by vaccination, and there is no suggestion here that it should. Reducing emissions at the source must continue to be the main course of action. However, the two measures operate at different stages of the same risk pathway. In the winter of 2025, the AQI reached 450 at a number of monitoring stations and people suffering from respiratory and cardiac conditions were told to remain indoors, a recommendation that  is not a policy. When pollution increases baseline vulnerability, the removal of an additional infectious trigger becomes all the more important.

Before winter sets in this year,  there is a concrete option available. Delhi could provide free pneumococcal vaccination to adults aged 60 and over who have recorded comorbidities via its present dispensary and mohalla clinic network and then assess both the uptake and the hospitalisation outcomes. The cost of each dose, at a few thousand rupees, is significantly lower  compared to ₹65,000 for a hospitalisation episode.
Delhi already vaccinates the grandchildren; the medical case for vaccinating the grandparents is no different, it is merely administratively missing.

(Sayesha Gupta is a research student at the economics department, Jesus and Mary College, University of Delhi, sayeshagupta08@gmail.com; Megha Jacob is assistant professor of the department, mjacob@jmc.du.ac.in; and Karan Babbar is an assistant professor of economics at XLRI Jamshedpur, phd17karanb@iima.ac.in)

title: China’s space diplomacy brings Pakistani astronauts closer to orbit

content.value: Two Pakistani pilots are memorising Mandarin, spinning in centrifuge drills, and learning to eat, sleep and repair equipment while weightless ​as a decision nears on which one will become the first foreign astronaut aboard China’s Tiangong space station.

The voyage into space would be a first for the ‌South Asian nation. It is part of broader cooperation with Beijing that straddles the Belt and Road Initiative and has produced Chinese-launched Pakistani satellites, a joint satellite-navigation system and a Pakistani-built rover due to fly on China’s Chang’e 8 lunar mission around 2028.

Pilots Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud have spent months training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Center in Beijing for a mission that was conceived by the two countries in 2019, said Amer Gilani, who ​oversees human spaceflight cooperation at Pakistan’s space agency, SUPARCO.
China has not said which of the two will fly or when, but Gilani said a final astronaut selection decision is expected ​in mid-to-late October.

Whoever is chosen will not return to Pakistan before launch, setting off into space directly from training in China and returning home ⁠after a recovery period following the return to Earth, Gilani said in an interview.
Training includes intensive Chinese-language instruction, learning spacecraft systems, and adapting to both the microgravity of orbit and the g-forces ​of liftoff, he added.

“You cannot easily find scientists who are familiar with travelling and facing high-level g-forces,” SUPARCO’s director of ​artificial intelligence Uzair Ansari said, explaining this is why the two men with backgrounds in high-speed flying were chosen.
The details shared by Gilani and Ansari are the first insight provided by SUPARCO to foreign media since the pilots were selected and deployed to China.
China’s space agency did not respond to a request for comment about ​the selection process.

Once in space, the chosen pilot will carry the title of “payload specialist”, which is astronaut-speak for someone whose job in orbit is running Pakistan’s science experiments rather than flying ​the ship, Ansari said.

Of more than 300 proposals SUPARCO fielded from universities in Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad after a year-long campaign, Gilani said Chinese institutes picked four for this flight: biotechnology experiments that will help combat food ‌insecurity and ⁠climate change.
Every experiment is built and pre-tested in SUPARCO’s own labs before Chinese engineers sign off.
The scientific payload is modest next to a station that has already hosted more than 180 experiments and produced over 500 research papers and 150 patents, Ansari added.
Tiangong’s three modules weigh about 77 metric tonnes combined and house roughly 14 experiment racks spanning life sciences, materials, fluid physics, combustion and radiation exposure, Gilani said.
The astronaut will fly aboard a ​Chinese-built spacecraft, launched from a Chinese site, ⁠trained by Chinese instructors and communicating in Mandarin in orbit.
Pakistan has no independent launch vehicle or crewed spacecraft of its own, and the stay itself will last a week.

The Pakistani astronaut is due to return with two ​members of a Chinese crew that arrived at the space station in May because the third member is expected to stay for a year ​to enable the study of ⁠long-duration human physiology in space.

title: Brain mapping of students and teachers uncovers when learning happens best

content.value: To help us retain the information about the Second World War, Rani Miss, our History teacher, divided the class into three groups. A few students were the Axis powers, another set was the Allied powers, and the rest were bodies like the League of Nations and the UN. A History class that could have been just about remembering the dates and names of people turned into a journey. As we took on the roles of Hitler, Mussolini, Churchill, and Stalin, the textbook became part of our lives, and information stayed well beyond the class tests. The debates that took place also made us understand the distance between the leaders waging wars and the human cost.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)

This is a teaching technique known as scaffolding, which is a kind of storytelling where the listener is also a character. Unlike passive storytelling, scaffolding helps students engage more with the information presented, thus improving retention and comprehension.

In a 2026 study published in Nature, titled ‘Enhanced word learning and neural synchrony during children’s storytelling ’, scientists found that learning outcomes in school-going children significantly improved through social experiences like storytelling and scaffolding. And during these teaching processes, the brain wave patterns in teachers and their students were in sync or aligned with each other – a situation scientists call neural synchrony.
Join THEdge LinkedIn group
Scientists say that when neural synchrony occurs between teachers and students during a session, it is an indication that students are comprehending and engaging.

In the study, researchers tested passive storytelling, where the child is the listener, and scaffolding, where the child is a character in the story. They used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), a brain imaging method, to record neural activity in the frontal lobes, the temporal lobes, and the parietal lobes of the child and the instructor.
Regions of the brain engaged

Through neuroimaging, it was found that during a scaffolding session, synchrony occurred mainly between the child’s left prefrontal cortex, which controls language, decision-making, planning, attention, and retention; and the teacher’s right hemisphere which is tied to spatial awareness, empathy, and nonverbal communication.

In passive story-listening, synchrony predominantly engaged the child’s right premotor cortex, which is associated with planning and organising movements and actions. “The premotor cortex is known for its part in perceiving and predicting others’ actions within goal-directed contexts, which is essential for social learning,” the authors said in the study. Here, the child was primarily in the receptive role.

“This is extremely important from a learning outcome point of view. Simply put, children learn better when there is active engagement from the teacher, which probably tunes several other networks beyond language comprehension, namely attention, arousal, emotion, saliency, and flexible decision-making,” Arpan Banerjee, a scientist and professor at the National Brain Research Centre, told The Hindu (he was not involved in the study). He added that engagement of brain regions involved in social communication is also a key player in improving learning outcomes and gets more optimally involved in an in-person setting.

The study found that children were able to pick up new words significantly better in the scaffolding session, as it involved spontaneous dialogue and the left prefrontal cortex was more actively engaged. Several studies have found that children’s vocabulary improves in social learning environments, with storytelling an effective medium of instruction. The sessions have to be instructor-led, with the child given space for responding and answering. “These findings may point to the relation between neural synchrony and the active engagement of both instructor and learner, as they collaboratively build a shared understanding,” the authors wrote in the study.
Remote setting not as effective

However, when the child attended a remote storytelling session online, they were found to be less engaged. The scaffolding effect also disappeared. This is significant as remote classes have become a common phenomenon following the COVID-19 pandemic. Several studies have shown that for active learning, face-to-face interaction plays a vital role in comprehension and mutual understanding between the educator and the child.

For educators, it is also essential to test whether children understood the concepts taught in class. The study found that both passive storytelling and scaffolding had an equal impact on test scores. It also showed that neural synchrony does not automatically translate to better outcomes in tests. “The ideal way to test the students would be via an active approach; for example, give them real-life situations where they can project themselves and answer questions akin to solving puzzles,” Dr. Banerjee said.

The manner of instruction also has a major impact on the child’s comprehension. A recent study conducted by researchers from the University of Iowa found that combining gestures with speech through scaffolding helps improve neural synchrony and learning. The study found that it does not matter how much time is spent on a particular topic, but the nature of the interaction is what matters for effective learning. The researchers saw that when parents used gestures, blood flow rose in the problem-solving areas of the child’s brain and the adult’s perception region, which senses when someone understands you.

The relationship a student shares with the teacher also influences the learning outcome. A study published in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, conducted among high school students,found that students who reported higher social closeness had more neural synchrony during lectures than other students. In terms of retention, the social closeness the student had with a teacher had more influence on the learning outcome than neural synchrony. This helps in predicting students' performance and shaping course outlines.

When facts and figures are presented in an isolated manner, it is difficult for children to retain and comprehend the information. Presenting the matter through creative methods like storytelling and scaffolding becomes important to ensure that learning occurs in the classroom. Dr. Banerjee also said it is important to test how such techniques can be applied for children who are within the neurodiversity spectrum. “For example, designing a scaffolding paradigm from brain activations that enhances the learning outcomes in kids or young adults who fall under the spectrum will help to understand how these techniques can work for everyone,” he said.

title: COP31 hosts Australia and Türkiye face the fossil-fuel question

content.value: The next United Nations climate change conference, COP31, will be held in Antalya in Türkiye in November this year. Türkiye will be hosting the event, with its environment minister Murat Kurum serving as COP31 president. Australia will oversee the negotiations process, with its energy and climate change minister Chris Bowen as the vice-president of COP31.

This is a novel arrangement — a result of both Australia and Türkiye not being willing to concede their demand to host, and where both countries share crucial responsibilities. In previous editions, the COP’s physical host has differed from the president only for logistical reasons.

A pre-COP event will be held in Fiji on October 5-8, where Pacific Island countries and Australia will discuss preparations for the main event, including what to negotiate. These pre-COPs are a routine affair before the annual summits.
Domestic fossil reliance

Both Türkiye and Australia are heavy users of fossil fuels. Australia is the world’s third-largest fossil fuels exporter, after Russia and the U.S. Domestically, Australia as well as Türkiye rely on coal, gas, and oil to generate respectively around 90% and 80% of their energy needs. Three weeks ago, Australia also came under fire from climate groups for approving the expansion of a coal mine.
The primary goal at COP31 is a target to electrify industry and vehicles and in turn “to raise the share of final energy demand met by electricity from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035”.
‘Oceans and Seas’ are also a priority agenda: Türkiye hosted a ‘Blue Dialogue’ on September 10-11 whose focus was on protecting marine resources.
However, none of the themes listed as a priority for the event make direct reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels.

That said, various industries in Australia, including iron-ore mining, are trying to decarbonise by investing in hybrid or electric heavy machinery. Local governments are also pushing for electric vehicles (EVs), which recently overtook petrol car sales for the first time in Australia.

Türkiye, on the other hand, is working to augment recycling and so eventually reduce methane emissions. In fact, the country has listed ‘zero waste and a circular economy’ on the COP31 priority list. The fortunes of a local EV brand, Togg, has ballooned so much that the government hopes it will herald a new era in the automobiles market.
Loss and damage financing

At the COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last year, the European Union pushed for a “fossil fuel roadmap” to help countries worldwide transition away from fossil fuels. While many countries supported the call, observers have said it took the focus away from developing countries’ calls to triple adaptation finance and developed countries’ resistance to that.

That said, most countries involved in the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) did not oppose the call for the “fossil fuel roadmap” at COP30. India did not oppose either, on the condition that it incorporate the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and that countries are not expected to follow uniform energy transition pathways.

Beyond the UNFCCC framework as well, and partly because of the slow pace of negotiations at the COP summits, there have been calls for concrete action to transition away from fossil fuels. In April this year, the first conference on ‘Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels’ was held in Santa Marta in Colombia, co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands. The second conference is scheduled for 2027, to be co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Given such momentum, there is likely to be pressure on the COP31 presidencies to include fossil fuel language as part of the agenda. The catastrophic floods in Nepal on August 26, boosted no doubt by climate change, and the damage they wrought are also set to add momentum to both mitigation action, including the language surrounding fossil fuels at COP31, and to loss and damage financing. But as with their not mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels, the joint Australia-Türkiye presidents have also included no loss and damage financing, or even the broader climate finance question, among the priority topics.

“We know there are strong views on all sides of this topic,” the Türkiye presidency said in response to questions from the author about whether this will change. “We will create space for Parties to discuss the transition and listen carefully to the positions they bring forward to see what we can agree by consensus. But listening to Parties’ views on negotiations does not mean we are standing still. We are taking the next logical steps in the energy transition by making electrification the flagship thematic priority of the COP31 Presidency’s Action Agenda, because electrifying buildings, transport and industry is key to reducing emissions and should be accompanied by complementary efforts to expand renewable energy.

Likewise, the reply said on mitigation financing: “we have been clear that we need to close the climate finance chasm, and we are holding donors to the financial commitments made at past COPs, while also introducing innovative new mechanisms, such as the ‘Climate Implementation Bridge’, to address the gap between ambitious climate plans and the finance needed to make them a reality.”
The Australian presidency did not respond.

Countries participating at COPs can propose new agenda items for consideration during negotiations. For example, the European Union introduced the “roadmap” in the formal negotiations agenda at the last minute at COP30. That said, it remains to be seen whether countries will do so at COP31, and if so what the items will be — and ultimately how the event’s two fossil fuel-heavy stewards will navigate negotiations.
The author was in Türkiye September 8-13 at the invitation of the government for a COP31-themed media tour. She also visited Australia in October 2025 on a similar official tour.
Rishika Pardikar is a freelance journalist.

title: Health Wrap Episode 52 examines AI in healthcare, its potential and patient safety risks

content.value: The 52nd episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu examines the growing use of artificial intelligence in healthcare, including its potential applications in drug and vaccine development, medical imaging and clinical decision-making.

Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, speaks to Abdul Gaffur, infectious diseases expert, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, about the opportunities and limitations of AI in healthcare and the questions its growing use raises for patients and healthcare professionals.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly being explored across healthcare and medical research. The episode discusses how AI could help researchers identify potential drug candidates, analyse large volumes of information and accelerate some stages of medical research.

The conversation also looks at the possible use of AI in vaccine development and other areas of biomedical research. While these applications could support research, the discussion examines the need to consider the limitations of AI-generated outputs and the importance of scientific and clinical validation.

A key focus of the episode is the use of AI for health-related information. AI systems can produce answers that appear confident and authoritative but may contain incorrect information. The episode discusses why patients should be cautious about relying on AI-generated responses for medical advice and why such information needs to be assessed against reliable medical sources and professional advice.

The discussion also examines the use of AI in clinical care. AI-powered clinical intelligence could potentially bring together information from radiology, laboratory investigations, pharmacy records and medical records to support doctors in screening and triaging patients.

The episode looks at how such systems could assist healthcare professionals without replacing clinical assessment. It also considers the importance of understanding the limitations of AI when it is used in decisions that can affect patient care.

Data is another aspect of the discussion, particularly as healthcare AI systems may involve large amounts of medical information. The episode considers questions around the use of health data and the need for appropriate safeguards as AI becomes more integrated into healthcare.
The conversation also touches on the potential misuse of AI in biology and why advances in artificial intelligence need to be considered alongside questions of safety and responsible use.

The discussion focuses on both the potential applications of AI in healthcare and the limitations that need to be considered as these technologies are increasingly used in research, clinical settings and the communication of health information.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

title: Two arrested with musk deer pods in Assam

content.value: A special team of the Assam Police recovered six musk deer pods from two Arunachal Pradesh-based men during an operation near Guwahati on Saturday (September 26, 2026).
Police intercepted Moga Doye, 48, of Lower Siang district, and Nokphua Wangsa, 44, of Changlang district, while they were transporting the pods, which weighed 158 grams.
A musk deer pod is a specialised scent gland found in the abdomen of a male musk deer. It produces a strong-smelling, reddish-brown secretion used in traditional perfumes and medicines.
“A team of our Special Operations Group and the local police foiled the suspected wildlife trafficking attempt at Medhikuchi, about 30 km east of Guwahati,” a police spokesperson said.
A preliminary investigation suggested the pods were being transported out of Assam, raising concerns about illegal wildlife trade through the State.

The musk deer, which belongs to the family Moschidae, is listed in CITES Appendix I, which covers plants and animals at the highest risk of extinction and threatened by international trade. CITES stands for the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora.
The deer is also covered under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972.

“Legal action has been initiated in connection with the seizure. We are investigating the case further to establish what species these pods are from, their source and intended destination,” the spokesperson said.

title: Experts discuss vaccine schedules, missed doses, and common misconceptions

content.value: Vaccine schedules, catch-up vaccination, and common misconceptions about immunisation were among the issues discussed by doctors at The Hindu’s Health Webinar Series on ‘Vaccines: Armour Against Infectious Diseases’ held on Sunday.

Janani Sankar, medical director, Kanchi Kamakoti CHILDS Trust Hospital, Chennai, explained the recommended vaccination schedule for children, the importance of completing the required doses and what parents can do when a child misses a scheduled vaccine. She also addressed questions about vaccination during minor illnesses, such as a cold, cough or fever, and concerns about children receiving multiple vaccines.
Dr. Sankar discussed common reactions following vaccination and symptoms that may require medical attention, as well as vaccines recommended for children in specific situations.

Dilip Mathai, senior consultant in Infectious Diseases, Naruvi Hospitals, and Professor of Medicine and Adult Infectious Diseases, discussed vaccination in adults, including how vaccination needs may change with age and individual circumstances. He explained options for adults who do not have records of earlier vaccinations, and the role of catch-up vaccination. He also discussed travel vaccination, including the need to consider recommended vaccines based on the destination and travel plans.
Vaccination during pregnancy and considerations for people taking long-term medicines or living with chronic conditions were also discussed.
The doctors also addressed questions on vaccine safety, side-effects, information circulating on social media, vaccination after an infectious disease, and immunisation during outbreaks.
The webinar was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, senior reporter, The Hindu.
The webinar can be viewed at https://newsth.live/vaccination.

title: From idol immersions to funeral rites, Maharashtra faces the drought pinch

content.value: The vibrant beats of dhol-tashas and chants of ‘Ganpati Bappa Morya’ faded into a sobering reality across Maharashtra this week as the 10-day annual Ganesh festival concluded on Friday and the State government on Saturday declared drought in 265 of the 358 talukas, including several parts of the Marathwada and Vidarbha regions.

In Kalamb town, Dharashiv district (Marathwada), the local administration scrambled ahead of idol immersion day. Because the local Manjara river and surrounding water bodies were completely dry due to a glaring monsoon deficit, civic authorities had to resort to filling temporary ponds using water tankers. For idols taller than four feet, desperate pleas were made to reroute processions to a nearby stone quarry holding residual water.
“We didn’t even have water to immerse the idols. You can only imagine what is going to happen until the next monsoon,” said Balaji Adsul, a Kalamb resident.

The crisis extends far beyond a single town. According to India Meteorological Department data, 20 out of 36 districts in Maharashtra have recorded deficient rainfall. The severity is starkly reflected in reservoir levels. Marathwada dams are currently sitting at just 46% capacity compared to 81% at this time last year, while those in Amravati division in Vidarbha hace dropped to 64% from 85%.

Faced with fast-depleting reservoirs, G. Sreekanth, Divisional Commissioner of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, a division covering eight Marathwada districts, had urged Ganesh mandals to avoid traditional water immersions entirely, suggesting instead that idols be donated, saved for the following year, or subjected only to symbolic immersion.

However, the appeal found little resonance among tradition-bound communities. In Renapur taluka of Latur district, frustration boiled over when one Ganesh mandal carried their large idol directly to the tehsil office, asking where was the water to immerse the idol.

“The situation here is grim, though some water in the Wardha river allowed for idol immersions,” said Madhuri Khadse, a farmer from Yavatmal in Vidarbha. “We have submitted a memorandum to the District Collector urging immediate aid for farmers to prevent a surge in suicides.”
Meanwhile, in Amravati, the local civic body deployed numerous water tankers to ensure Ganesh mandals had enough water for idol immersions.
Parched rites
As festivities fade and crops wither in parched fields, thousands of farmers across Maharashtra are urgently seeking relief.

The crisis extends far beyond agriculture, deeply affecting personal and cultural lives. Sominath Gholwe, a farmer and social science researcher from Beed, highlights how severe water shortages force families to rely on tankers even for sacred rituals like dashkriya vidhi (the tenth-day funeral rite). “One of my relatives in Pathardi (Beed) passed away. We had to bring water via tankers from borewells, store it in a well, and then perform the rites,” he said.

With rivers entirely dry and groundwater depleted, signs reading ‘Water tankers for dashkriya vidhi available here’ have become a grim reality across Marathwada. Having travelled through five districts in the region, Mr. Gholwe notes that 85% of crops have failed, creating a dire humanitarian situation.

“This is a big drought. The State government has earlier waived off loans and electricity bills. Now we will pay compensation in cash. We will ensure they get water, foodgrains and children continue their education,” said Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis while touring the drought region in Marathwada earlier this week

title: OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs called to appear at Australian AI probe over health database breach

content.value: The CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic have been called to appear at an ​Australian Senate inquiry on AI, the head of the probe ‌said on Sunday, September 27, 2026, days after the revelation that ​a rogue OpenAI bot had hacked ⁠the country's health-system database.
The Medicare breach, condemned by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing ‌external systems outside the U.S.

OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have been sent ‌written requests to appear at the inquiry, ‌which ⁠is to hold public hearings in the capital ⁠Canberra on Thursday, said a spokesperson for Senator Sarah Hanson-Young of the Australian
Greens party, who chairs the probe.
OpenAI and Anthropic ​did not immediately respond ‌to requests for comment outside business hours.

The OpenAI agent's incursion on one of the country's most used government agencies may prompt Albanese's Labor government
to toughen ‌AI-specific laws it is readying for next ​year, adding pressure to Australia-US relations already tested by Canberra's ban on social media for ⁠teens, tech policy experts say.

The Senate inquiry is examining the potential impacts of AI and data centres on ‌Australian communities, industries, water
and energy. It is one of several state and federal probes into AI.

"There are serious questions for Sam Altman to answer about the OpenAI hack of Australian government websites," Hanson-Young said in a statement. Altman and Amodei "must front up, ‌face the Senate's questions and have an honest conversation about ​what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should look like", she said.
Albanese, who revealed the June ⁠breach of Medicare on Thursday, called it "unacceptable", saying he had ⁠voiced "extreme concern" to Altman.

OpenAI says it only learned of the breach — one of at ‌least four of Australian government websites — in August. It says the incident was not intentional and did ​not compromise any private information.

title: ‘Vaccines: Armour Against Infectious Diseases’ webinar to be held on September 27

content.value: Vaccination plays an important role in preventing infectious diseases and reducing the risk of serious illness and complications. While childhood immunisation is a key part of disease prevention, vaccination needs can continue into adulthood depending on age, health conditions, occupation, travel and other factors.
The Hindu is hosting a free webinar, “Vaccines: Armour Against Infectious Diseases,” on Sunday from 11.30 a.m. to 12.30 p.m.

The discussion will look at the importance of timely childhood vaccination, completing the recommended schedule and what parents should do when doses are missed. It will also address vaccination when a child is unwell, vaccines recommended in specific situations, and common concerns about vaccine safety and side-effects.

The session will also examine adult vaccination and how immunisation needs may change with age and health conditions. It will cover vaccination for older adults and people living with chronic illnesses, catch-up vaccination for those who are unsure of or do not have records of previous doses, vaccines recommended for international travel, and vaccination during pregnancy.
The discussion will also address how people can review their vaccination requirements and stay up to date with recommended vaccines.

title: India stresses resilient health systems, pandemic preparedness at UN

content.value: Representing India at the United Nations high-level meeting on 'Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response' in New York, Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava reaffirmed the nation's commitment to strengthening global health security through international cooperation.
She stressed the need to translate lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic into sustained investment, institutional capacity and resilient health systems.

Addressing the meeting at the United Nations Headquarters on Friday, September 25, 2026, Ms. Srivastava outlined India's coordinated approach to pandemic prevention and response across government and society, which covers a wide range of potential health emergencies.

She spoke of the country's efforts to expand laboratory networks, emergency coordination, health workforce, stockpiles and clinical care capacity to ensure systems are equipped to respond effectively to health emergencies.
She noted that these efforts must be rooted in national health systems, development plans and domestic financing, with international assistance complementing national responsibility.
Drawing on India's experience during COVID-19, Srivastava called for digital public infrastructure to be recognised as a global public good.
She noted that digital solutions played an important role in surveillance, vaccination, risk communication, supply chains and continuity of health services during the pandemic.

Ms. Srivastava also underscored the importance of solidarity and fair access to essential health products. During the COVID-19 pandemic, India supplied 300 million vaccine doses to around 100 countries and two UN entities, while providing medical assistance to over 150 countries. She said this reflected India's commitment to the principle of ‘One Earth, One Health’ and to the Global South.

Referring to the WHO Pandemic Agreement adopted in May 2025, the Union health secretary described it as an important milestone and stressed that its credibility would depend on a fair Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing (PABS) system.

She emphasised that countries contributing pathogens and biological resources must receive timely access to vaccines, diagnostics, therapeutics, technologies and other benefits, while respecting national sovereignty.

Srivastava further stated that the political declaration should not prejudge ongoing negotiations on the PABS annex and should be implemented in accordance with national circumstances and capacities. On the 'One Health' approach, she called for its implementation, as appropriate, in accordance with domestic law, international law and national circumstances.

She also underlined the importance of member states' role in reviewing and consolidating pandemic prevention, preparedness and response tools, assessments and data, noting that such processes should be undertaken in consultation with member states given their policy implications.

Concluding her speech, Ms. Srivastava highlighted that preparedness is a shared responsibility and that equity must remain central to efforts to address future pandemics and outbreaks. "Global solidarity must be demonstrated through action," she said.

WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus pointed to the progress made in strengthening the global health security architecture since COVID-19, including the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations.
He stressed the urgency of concluding negotiations on the PABS system, noting that delays could affect the world's ability to respond to future pandemics.

title: Match sickle cell status, not horoscopes before marriage, say experts in Odisha

content.value: Malini (name changed) from Odisha’s Angul district did not have a conventional arranged marriage. Instead of matching horoscopes with her prospective husband, she and her family relied on the couple’s medical reports before agreeing to the marriage.

Malini, 42, has lived with sickle cell disease (SCD), a genetic disorder affecting red blood cells, since birth. Yet, she went on to have a successful marriage and is now the mother of a healthy 12-year-old son.

Asish, a manager with public-sector Mahanadi Coalfields Limited (MCL), was not as fortunate. Despite having a stable and well-paying job, he could not convince his girlfriend’s family that there was no harm in marrying her. Even a renowned haematologist tried to mediate, but the couple’s nine-year relationship eventually failed to culminate in marriage.

Odisha is among the 17 states with a high prevalence of SCD. According to available data, around 10.61% of the population screened in the state has either sickle cell trait (SCT) or sickle cell disease.
Asish, a Homozygous Sickle Cell Anaemia patient, said he could endure the excruciating pain caused by the disease, but found it far more difficult to overcome the stigma associated with it.

“Social stigma affects people with sickle cell disease more than the disease itself,” members of the newly formed National Alliance for Sickle Cell and Thalassemia Control (NASCETC) said at its first meeting held on the sidelines of the 16th annual congress of the Odisha Haematology Association here on Saturday (September 26, 2026). The voluntary forum has been formed to create a stronger support system for people living with SCD and thalassemia.

The Union government launched the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Programme (NSCAEP) on July 1, 2023, across 17 high-prevalence states, including Odisha, with the goal of eliminating SCD as a public health problem by 2047.

“The programme is one of India’s largest initiatives to control a genetic disease and is being closely watched internationally because of its scale and comprehensive community-based approach. Besides medical interventions, we also need to address the taboos and social stigma surrounding the disease. People living with SCD themselves must take the lead in creating awareness about the condition,” said Professor R. K. Jena, a renowned haematologist.

Experts, including Ruby Khan, Deputy Director of the National Health Mission, Madhya Pradesh, and Manoranjan Mohapatra, Head of the Department of Haematology at AIIMS, Delhi, advised patients and their families that people living with sickle cell disease can lead a healthy married life if their partner does not have either sickle cell trait (SCT) or sickle cell disease.

“Kundli milao ya na milao, lekin sickle cell reports milana zaruri hai (Match horoscopes or not, but matching sickle cell medical reports is a must). Pregnant women should also undergo prenatal diagnosis, while screening of family members should be carried out as a preventive measure,” said Dr. Khan.
Prof Mohapatra said that, unlike thalassaemia, people with SCD can lead normal lives and that, not every patient requires a bone marrow transplant.
“Not every patient will require a bone marrow transplant. Patients must follow the advice prescribed by their doctors and overcome their fears,” he said.

Although medicines such as hydroxyurea, which helps reduce the frequency and severity of pain episodes, are available at government hospitals, and haematology departments have been opened at several government and private hospitals, patients and their families continue to face social stigma associated with the disease.

“In Kandhamal district, where we are studying the social stigma attached to blood disorders, we have found that some people collect medicines from places far from their homes to conceal their condition from neighbours. Marriages also take place without families disclosing the medical condition of their sons or daughters,” said Debarpita Mohanty, a scientist at the ICMR’s Regional Medical Research Centre, Bhubaneswar.

title: Mpox case confirmed in northeastern Congolese city at center of Ebola outbreak

content.value: A laboratory-confirmed case of mpox was identified in the northeastern Congolese city of Bunia, ​the director of a local hospital and two health ‌officials said, raising concerns about a resurgence of ​the disease as the country battles its ⁠worst Ebola outbreak on record.

The epidemic caused by the Ebola outbreak was declared on May 15 in Ituri ‌province, where Bunia is located, and has infected 7,890 people and killed 3,799, according to ‌government data published on Thursday, September 24, 2026.
Mpox is a ‌viral ⁠disease that causes fever and skin ⁠lesions and spreads through close physical contact.

Congo declared an end to mpox as a national public health emergency in April after ​a three-year outbreak that ‌resulted in more than 34,000 confirmed cases nationwide. Authorities cautioned at the time that the virus had not been eradicated and could resurge.

The latest case ‌involves a 21-year-old woman who was admitted to ​hospital on Thursday with lesions across her body consistent with mpox, hospital director Davin ⁠Ambitapio Musungufu said. She tested positive on Friday, he and two health officials told Reuters.

A second woman, ‌aged 32, has been identified as a suspected mpox case and is awaiting laboratory results, Musungufu said. She and the confirmed patient have been isolated and are being cared for by a dedicated medical team.
Investigations are underway to trace contacts and ‌identify the source of infection, Musungufu said.
Adelard Lofungola, a ​health official who served as deputy incident manager for Congo's mpox response, said five suspected ⁠mpox cases in Bunia were currently under investigation.
Health officials ⁠have reported an increase in mpox cases in several parts of the country over the ‌past month, he said.
Dr. Lofungola said the Ebola outbreak's impact on Congo's health system was complicating ​efforts to monitor other infections.

title: Science Snapshots: September 27, 2026

content.value: IIT-Madras tool bridges quake science and dam safety

An IIT-Madras team evaluated 6,545 dams under India’s National Dam Safety Authority and found standard seismic zone maps misjudge earthquake risks. For Himalayan ‘mega-dams’ like Tehri and Bhakra, site-specific modelling revealed previously projected ground accelerations were too conservative. The team achieved this using a combination of a tool it built to perform “probabilistic seismic hazard analysis”, a catalogue of 68,000+ earthquakes from 2,600 BC to 2019, and maps of India’s major faultlines.
‘Forever chemical’ disrupts immune system’s antiviral action

PFOS, a widespread industrial ‘forever chemical’, weakens the body’s ability to fight viral infections, a study has found. Researchers found that it binds to an immune protein called IRF3, which keeps it from triggering the release of interferons, our immune system’s top antiviral defence. As a result, viruses can multiply faster. Tests in human cells and mice showed that everyday levels of PFOS exposure led to more severe infections from viruses like influenza and hepatitis B.
Hot-spring eukaryote sets record for warmest reproduction

Scientists have found a new species of amoeba, Incendiamoeba cascadensis, in hot springs in California that has set a record for the upper temperature limit of eukaryotic life. Scientists previously thought these lifeforms couldn’t reproduce above 60° C. However, I. cascadensis replicates at 63° C. To survive such heat, it activates genes to repair DNA and cell membranes. Its proteins’ chemical properties are such that they don’t clump together, a trick heat-loving bacteria use as well.

title: How the science Nikolai Vavilov built changed how we save crops

content.value: Nicolai Ivanovich Vavilov (1887-1943) was a remarkable agricultural scientist in the former USSR. His name is familiar to some as an ‘Indiana Jones’ who roamed around the world collecting crops and seeds, as someone who established the first global seed bank, as a martyr who died in prison despite his extraordinary accomplishments, and as the person who inspired so many scientists to sacrifice their everything to save a priceless seed bank during the Second World War.
Such a list, however, does not capture his intellectual contributions, which were fundamental to the utilitarian development of the seed bank.
Centres of origin

One of Vavilov’s major contributions was his paper titled ‘Studies on the origin of cultivated plants’, published in 1926. Even today, one century later, it continues to be the foundation for the study and use of crops and livestock. In fact, this work has been critical to preserving plant genetic resources and to protect the rights of farmers who had initially developed crop diversity. It is also central to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity and related discussions.

Humans use the plants they find where they live. But If they see something new and it does not grow nearby, they have also been known to go to extremes to get it. A familiar example is pepper, which ancient Rome traded for gold. We know about pepper because there are records that tell us the history of its spread. But what about in pre-historic times, say 6,000 years ago? We can find out from archaeological remains, which tell us about the prehistory of different peoples and cultures. We can also find out using good-old-fashioned taxonomy.

This was what Vavilov did, combined with the (then) new methods of genetics and evolutionary biology. Just like Charles Darwin and Alfred Russell Wallace, Vavilov travelled around the world, in his case looking for crop varieties.

He observed that varieties and their closest wild relatives tended to be confined to a geographic region. This is what we expect under evolution: every species originates at a particular time and place, and undergoes changes as it spreads to other regions. Vavilov went further than others, like Alphonse de Candolle, and examined not just one or two crops but an array, as well as the prehistoric cultural conditions in which they were modified.

Vavilov thus found that most of our crops came from just eight regions of the world, which he was also the first to demarcate, and called the ‘centres of origin’. The foods on our plate today may thus have come from very different places.
Seed bank

Time is as important as geography. We know that the potato originated in Peru and spread to other parts of South America. We know from historical records that it had been transported to the rest of the world, including India, in the post-Columbian period. So if you went back to the times of the Cholas in the ninth and tenth centuries, you would not have been able to savour potato chips.

For thousands of years, human beings selected crops for the features they wanted. These needs varied according to factors such as the climate, soils, landscape, and cultural history. Vavilov explored and collected seeds of a large number — some 2.5 lakh — of crop varieties and species. The seeds were maintained in a facility that he built into a global seed bank in 1921 in Leningrad (now St. Petersburg).

He and his associates also conducted careful, methodical studies in a large number of  field stations located in different climatic and geographical regions of the former Soviet Union. It was a large-scale experiment that allowed the scientists to analyse crop variations in diverse conditions at the field level. These efforts speeded up the rate at which varieties with suitable features could be identified for introduction or breeding in different regions.
A giant himself

Vavilov stood on the shoulders of giants — botanists, geneticists and breeders who preceded him. The scientist Eduard Regel had already put Russia on the forefront of applied botany. Regel also recognised Vavilov’s talents and placed him in positions that allowed Vavilov to interact with leading scientists across the world.

His concept of the centres of origins of crops also holds, broadly. Modern approaches, especially molecular biology, have suggested that the centre of diversity may not always be the centre of origin of a crop, as initially conceived. Thus, centres of diversity continue to be important in discussions on biodiversity and bioresources.
Undoubtedly, Vavilov was a giant himself, and deserves to be more widely recognised and remembered today.
R. Geeta is retired professor, Delhi University.

title: Six years on, ringed Eurasian whimbrel resighted on Keralam coast; marked Tibetan sand-plover also recorded

content.value: With the winter migratory bird season under way, two marked shorebirds recorded along the Keralam coast earlier this month offer clues to migration routes, stop-over sites, links between breeding and wintering grounds, and the movements of individual birds.

A Eurasian whimbrel (Numenius phaeopus) ringed at Kadalundi-Vallikkunnu Community Reserve more than six years ago has been resighted on the Elathur beach, about 20 km from the reserve, in Kozhikode, while a Tibetan sand-plover (Anarhynchus atrifrons) spotted on the Chavakkad beach had been banded in Mumbai in 2025.
Black flag and ring

Abdulla Paleri, a Kozhikode-based ornithologist and Assistant Professor at Dignity College of Arts and Science, Perambra, photographed a Eurasian whimbrel on the Elathur beach on September 19. According to him, the bird had a ‘black flag’ bearing the alphanumeric code ‘0J3’ on its left leg and a metal ring on its right leg. The black flag, fitted on the upper part of its leg, indicated that the bird had been marked in south India under a bird-banding programme of the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), which uses a single ‘black flag’ with a unique alphanumeric code for waders marked in southern India.

On September 12, a Tibetan sand-plover was seen on the Chavakkad beach in Thrissur with two ‘white flags’ on its right leg, one above the other, bearing the code ‘HZN’, and a metal ring on its left leg. The bird was photographed by birdwatcher P.P. Sreenivasan from Guruvayur in Thrissur. The use of two white flags, according to him, is associated with the bird-marking programmes conducted by the BNHS in rest of India.
Photographs of both the birds were sent to the BNHS to obtain further information about their ringing and banding history.
Mr. Paleri said, according to information provided by the BNHS, the Eurasian whimbrel had been ringed on January 29, 2020, at the Kadalundi reserve by S. Sivakumar, a scientist at the BNHS.

“The observation is noteworthy as it documents an individually marked Eurasian whimbrel returning to the Keralam coast more than six years after it was ringed. The bird may have returned to its breeding grounds in Europe or Central Asia after being ringed in 2020 and subsequently migrated back to the Kozhikode coast,” said Mr. Paleri.
In Mumbai
According to information provided by the BNHS, the Tibetan sand-plover was banded on March 27, 2025 in Mumbai by researcher Kiran Dalvi.

“One possibility is that, during its migration from the Himalayas or Tibet, the bird first reached Mumbai, where it was banded, and subsequently travelled approximately 1,000 km to reach the coast of Thrissur. Another possibility is that after visiting Mumbai, it returned to its Himalayan or Tibetan breeding grounds and subsequently migrated to Keralam for the winter,” said Mr. Sreenivasan.
A second sighting of a marked shorebird can tell a larger story about its migration.

“Individual bird sightings recorded at different locations can reveal much more than the presence of a species. When a marked shorebird is sighted again, it provides a glimpse into the bird’s journey — where it travels, its stopover site, and how different parts of its migratory range are connected. Such records are crucial for piecing together migration patterns and understanding the journeys shorebirds undertake between their breeding and wintering grounds across seasons,” P.O. Nameer, Dean of the College of Climate Change and Environmental Science at Kerala Agricultural University, told The Hindu.

title: How Haryana’s village health centres are screening heart patients and helping save lives

content.value: On  July 15, Raj Rani, 52, an ASHA worker  in Yamunagar, Haryana had just completed her tasks for the day when she  felt a throbbing pain in her left arm and in the middle of her chin. Since this pain had persisted for a few days, she went  to the Community Health Centre (CHC) in  Vyaspur to get an electrocardiogram (ECG) done.

The Additional Senior Medical Officer at the centre,  Gunjeet Singh, saw the results of the ECG, gave her a dose of drugs including blood thinners and clotbusters, called a ‘loading dose’, and asked her to rush to the district hospital at Ambala Cantonment, two hours away, for further treatment.

Raj Rani had single-vessel disease, with  a major coronary artery  blocked. “At the district hospital, they scheduled my angioplasty the next day and I got one stent in my heart,” said Raj Rani. “I told my doctors to give me good treatment so I could resume my work as an ASHA.
