They reassured me that I would be able to  do my duties, because I was lucky: I came in time,” she said.

Had this happened even two months ago, Raj Rani would not have received the diagnosis that would have led to quick treatment. Even though the Vyaspur CHC had an ECG machine, there was no technician to conduct it and while the medical officers could interpret the results, they were not very confident.
What changed

On May 29 this year, the  Haryana government tied up with Sunfox Technologies, a health-tech startup, as part of Public-Private Partnership (PPP), to set up a tele-ECG network called Spandan One. Each medical centre in Haryana received a tele-ECG device that connects to smartphone and tablets, can be operated by frontline workers and gives a clinician-reviewed result in less than three minutes.

To date, nearly  600 government health facilities including primary health centres (PHCs), CHCs, sub-divisional hospitals and district hospitals have been equipped by a tele-ECG device along with training in using it. As of September 17,  33,854 ECG tests were conducted; 9,287 ECGs were abnormal and 1,342 critical cases were detected according to the Spandan dashboard.

In the remote Ranjitpur PHC in Yamunagar district, there is a steady increase in the footfall of patients due to the tele-ECG service available. “This is a new building  we started using just six months ago; there is no fixed nurse or staff or even furniture,” said  Varun Singh, medical officer who has been running the centre with staff on deputation and through borrowed furniture from other centres. “Ever since we got the tele-ECG, people have been coming to the centre asking for it,”  he said.

One recent morning,  Ram Saran, 75, come to the PHC with his son Mangaram to get his reports examined by Dr.  Singh. Mr. Saran had been experiencing a feeling of his heart racing and breathlessness for many months. He had gotten an ECG and blood tests for  ₹1200 at a private hospital at Vyaspur but wanted confirmation from the government doctor. The nursing officer at the PHC put the electrodes on Mr. Saran and  an ECG graph formed  in the tablet in her hands, with a message that the report was being analysed. Two and half minutes later, the report was ready to be downloaded. Mr. Saran had an ‘abnormal ECG’ and he was asked to consult a cardiologist and a copy of the report was sent to his mobile  phone.

Dr. Singh then consulted with Mr. Saran and his son and told them to visit the hospital at Ambala Cant. at the earliest. “Before this initiative, I would not be able to interpret ECGs with this level of sophistication. The patient would need to visit a cardiologist available two hours away and wait a long time in the OPD for the diagnosis,” said Dr. Singh. For patients who are diagnosed with critical ECGs, an alarm goes off in the tablet to draw the attention of the healthcare worker and a prescription is generated so that patients receive life-saving medicines while the referral to a higher centre is being made.

“We never thought that we would get results within a few minutes of doing the ECG. This tele-ECG service is available in all centres in Yamunagar and is available in even other remote locations in the districts. This  is a very welcome step,”  said Shama Parveen, senior medical officer, Yamunagar CHC.
Primary care matters

Even though PHCs are the first point of contact of medical care for rural patients, they often do not have the necessary equipment or manpower to diagnose and treat heart ailments. A 2024 pre-print that assessed the availability of cardiac care in Vadodara district in Gujarat found only 44.11% of the surveyed PHCs had functional ECGs and employed them where indicated. In most cases patients were simply referred to higher centres for treatment. The time lost due to travel between centres can prove to be fatal for patients.

The impact of Haryana’s initiative has been incredible, said  Kuldeep Singh, former Director General, Health Services (DGHS), Haryana who spearheaded  the partnership. ECGs and early treatment for heart attacks is now available  in rural centres that had earlier not registered a single heart attack due to lack of diagnosis. “We are already witnessing a 20% reduction in deaths in the emergency departments of district hospitals because patients are being stabilised before rushing here,” he said, adding that these are early assessments and more data is still being collected.
After primary care

Once the patient is stabilised with a loading dose, they are sent to higher centres such as district hospitals with Catherisation Labs where angiographies and angioplasties are performed. “Given the geography of Haryana, most patients reach the higher centre within one hour of the diagnosis, saving lives and heart muscles,” said Dr. Singh.

The Haryana government is also in a PPP with private providers to equip and run cath labs in four locations in the State–Panchkula, Gurugram, Faridabad and Ambala Cant. and is planning to soon expand to more locations.

As part of the agreement with the Haryana government, Sunfox Technologies provides equipment, training and on-going support for its tele-ECG system apart from maintaining a live dashboard monitoring cases. “Through the dashboard, we have real-time patient information which has given us rich insights–for example we now know that patients between 30-49 years have a higher incidence of cardiac issues than those over 50 years,” said Rajat Jain, CEO of the startup. Data has also shown that  the incidence of critical ECGs among women in the age group of 30-49 is as much as men and greater than men in the age group of 70+, dispelling the belief that men have a greater risk for heart disease than women. “These kinds of insights are very important for policymakers but were never accessible before,” he said.
Challenges in the process

While the project is picking up steam in Haryana, there are some teething issues – many of the centres have to conduct  repeat ECGs to get accurate ECG readings if they were not conducted properly the first time.  A bump in the road was that the State’s nursing union had issued a diktat stating that nurses should not be conducting the ECGs as the post of ECG technicians has remained vacant in most health centres. The DGHS, however, later issued a letter stating that healthcare workers cannot deny conducting life-saving diagnosis and would face disciplinary action if they failed to do so.  There is also the question of what happens when the partnership between the government and Sunfox Technologies ends: would the pathway to diagnosis and treatment change or would it have improved by then?
Looking ahead

Making ECGs  available at PHCs  is a great start but we need to do much more to improve the public health system as a whole to respond well to non-communicable diseases and their complications, said Chetanya Malik, a doctor who practices in Surguja, a remote district in Chattisgarh for the non-profit Sangwari. In Chhattisgarh, an ECG facility is only available at the district hospital, revealing the vastness of the need and the unevenness of primary care provided within the country. Dr. Malik also noted the need for patients to be given support in finding transport and for referrals to higher centres to be seamless to help solve the problem of cardiac emergencies.

India’s  public health systems have, for decades now, remained focused on infectious diseases and maternal and child health — both still important, but the time has come to also realign the systems to care for  non-communicable diseases. Heart disease alone is estimated to account for nearly 27% of all deaths in India. The need is enormous, and the technology is available. It is time all States implement such programmes, pointed out Dr. Kuldeep Singh.
(Swagata Yadavar is a communications specialist and former independent journalist. She is based in Ahmedabad. swagatayadavar@gmail.com)

(This is the final part of a three-part series on the health system’s response to heart attacks. You can read the first two parts here and here. This series is a project of Nivarana, a digital public health platform and has been supported by Sunfox Technologies)

title: Waymo Self-Driving Taxi Review | Making peace with autonomous driving technology

content.value: On October 27, 2025, a car ran over a cat in San Francisco. Oceans away, I filed a report on the tragic killing of nine-year-old KitKat. Why did news about the death of a cat in California make international headlines? That’s because KitKat was run over by a self-driving Waymo car, owned by Google-parent Alphabet. The company runs a fleet of self-driving electric taxis that are gradually being deployed across cities in the U.S.

While local residents slammed Waymo’s safety standards and erected a monument for KitKat, supporters of self-driving cars pointed out that thousands of animals are run over by human-driven cars every year. Robotaxis, on the other hand, are designed to become safer with every iteration, they claimed.
Almost a year later, I booked a Waymo ride in San Francisco, from my hotel to a nearby metro station — when the roads were empty. And here’s what I discovered.
Cost and Design

Hailing a robotaxi is not too different from ordering an Uber or even an Indian auto. Simply download the Waymo app, set up your profile and payment information, and choose your pick-up point and destination. Riders can decide if they want a car instantly, or if they want to schedule it for later. Waymo ride costs are relatively higher than human-operated taxis.

The Waymo app, while slow to load, was easy and intuitive to use. Apart from arranging rides, it allows users to unlock their self-driving car and start their ride. Users can adjust interior settings or seek customer support via the app, as well as request fewer announcements and shorter walking times to their pick-up point.
The payment process was seamless in spite of using an Indian credit card, and I quickly received an e-receipt. Additionally, Waymo gifted me some credit for my next ride.
Interiors

The Waymo vehicle that pulled up to the curb to take me to my destination was a Jaguar, which was a pleasant surprise. The dark interiors were pristine, comfortable, and scent-free. I had enough space to sit in the back with a large suitcase resting next to me. There was a skylight above, outside of which was mounted the Waymo’s spinning sensor.

There were two main screens within the car: a longer one at the front and a wider one for those sitting at the back. The screens show your journey status, traffic navigation visuals, estimated arrival times, safety announcements, and media settings. After the greetings and safety briefing, the system played soothing, ambient music throughout my ride. Those taking longer rides can sync their Spotify and YouTube lists in order to listen to their preferred media.
The car’s default internal temperature was warm since it was a chilly morning, but riders can adjust this to suit their needs.

The Waymo’s steering wheel moves on its own as the car makes its way along its route, giving you the sense of being chauffeured by an invisible person. There are also brake and accelerator pedals, but these do not visibly move during the journey. Unlike the sleek, minimalistic Tesla Cybercab, the Waymo does retain many of the driving and media buttons in the front seat.
Safety
Needless to say, this should form the heart of any self-driving taxi experience.

Remembering poor KitKat, and having seen multiple videos of Waymo cars running red lights or driving into restricted emergency zones, I was naturally on edge as I booked my car and waited for about two minutes. Though I had entered a preferred pick-up point right outside my hotel, Waymo altered the location and directed me to walk towards the new pick-up point across the road. Why the change? Because my original pick-up point put the car right on a tram line.

Once the Waymo car arrived, I was prompted to unlock it through my phone app. After this, the handles popped out and I was able to open the door. Such a mechanism prevents strangers from taking over or misusing the ride. Once inside and buckled up, a passenger can start the ride via the car’s touchscreen or the app. (The Waymo car is programmed to wait for five minutes before leaving, if the rider does not show up.)

As the Waymo began to gently move, a friendly safety message reminded me to buckle up at all times. I was informed that the cabin could be monitored for safety and security purposes when needed, but that I had the privacy to sing my heart out, if I was so inclined. There were blinking recording panels on the ceiling of the car, both at the front and back.

The ride was on the slower side, but smoothly operated for the most part. The Waymo handled steep, near-vertical roads with confident ease, even when it had to brake on the slopes. There were no rollbacks in these instances. The car also unfailingly braked at every stop sign and complied with all the traffic signals and speed limits, despite the roads being empty at the time. Turnings were fluid and predictable.

The screen tracked the car’s path, as well as other cars, objects, people, and obstructions. Unexpected adjustments were made with caution, and I felt as though I were being chauffeured by a skilled and patient human driver. There were some bumps, though this was largely due to the terrain.

Once at my destination, the car took a couple of extra minutes to find a safe space to pull over, because the sides of the roads were lined with parked cars. In order to exit, riders are directed to pull on the door handle twice. They are given sufficient time to exit the car and collect their things.
My ride, which was a little over 3 kilometres long, took 14 minutes to complete and cost me $23.55. Waymo informed me that I had saved 486 grams of Co2 by riding with them.
Conclusion

Though U.S. regulators and San Francisco locals are still divided on autonomous driving technology, a short Waymo ride opened my eyes to the heavy mental load that a robotaxi removes. One has no need to worry about swapped license plate numbers, aggressive or inebriated drivers, sudden fee and route changes, or unfair/discriminatory ride cancellations. Instead of faking a loud safety call to one’s family during a late night or early morning drive, riders can sit back and truly relax within the comfortable robotaxi cabin.

There are still flaws to be addressed, of course. Users have flagged concerns about miscreants potentially blocking cars, while the NHTSA regulator warned about self-driving cars barging into restricted zones and obstructing first responders. It remains to be seen how Waymo handles the safety issues that arise with longer drives, after its coverage area grows to encompass suburban and rural roadways across America.
But ultimately, Waymo is a game changer for short, inner-city rides where accessibility and women’s safety are priorities.
So, if you find yourself in a city where Waymo is live, take the plunge and experience how an ordinary taxi ride becomes the serene highlight of your day.
This is an independent, non-sponsored review of the Waymo self-driving taxi.

title: Indian non-profits lag on digital maturity, AI adoption: report

content.value: Non-profits lag on technological maturity in India, a new report based on a survey of 500 organisations in the sector said. Even as white collar organisations employing college-educated workers experiment heavily with AI and integrate it into their workflows, non-profits did not score even 50% on digital maturity, even as they showed some interest in using large language models (LLMs) to help with reports and marketing, Delhi-based Digital for Nonprofits (D4NP) said in its State of Nonprofits Digitization Report 2026.

In any industry, D4NP founder and former Google executive Abhinav Chetan said, “nonprofits are always the last, no matter which technological trend you pick … They’re still experimenting. They’re still at level one, by the way — they’re only using it for conversations. They’re not really using it for complicated workflows.”

While AI systems have made it far easier for organisations to do routine work faster, Mr. Chetan said that many were lagging behind on even the earlier digitisation wave. One example the report cited was most organisations not taking advantage of monthly $10,000 ad grants. That came out to millions of dollars of free advertising money simply lying unused.
Also Read | India leads global adoption of AI agents, with 32% of AI users emerging as ‘Frontier Professionals’: Microsoft

Of the twenty signals, only one organisation — Child Rights and You (CRY) — was on the right side of digital maturity. Mr. Chetan attributed CRY’s adoption of these tools to the corporate background of its staff. The digital maturity “percolates” due to this factor, Mr. Chetan said.

This doesn’t mean that organisations are not using AI tools at all. Quite the opposite, the report says, pointing out that the majority of Indian startups, six in ten, use at least one AI tool every day, and 85% use more than one AI tool. But on governance and taking advantage of emerging capabilities, most organisations did not score well.

Only roughly one in four nonprofits had any safeguards for AI tools’ handling of sensitive personal data, and only one in four use online analytics tools (which, incidentally, have become easier to use with LLMs).

But the report marked a “median shift” to more adoption versus the previous year, when D4NP ran this survey last year, Mr. Chetan said. He added, “I wish they could even use it for coding — bring up a quick landing page, or create a dashboard… But that’s my sense for next year.”

title: Illegal riverbed mining inviting catastrophe: Assam tribal students’ body

content.value: GUWAHATI

The All Dimasa Students’ Union (ADSU) has flagged “unscientific, illegal and excessive” riverbed mining in Dima Hasao district in Assam, warning that unchecked extraction was threatening severe bank erosion, threatening key transport corridors and drying up drinking water sources for rural communities.

In a complaint letter to the district’s Chief Conservator of Forests on Friday (September 25, 2026), the ADSU highlighted unregulated commercial extraction of sand, gravel, stone and boulders, driven by the rampant use of heavy mechanised excavators inside active river channels, across the Diyung, Mahur, Langting and Jatinga rivers.
The union said these activities were affecting local ecosystems, infrastructure, and indigenous communities in the district.

The ADSU pointed to severe bank erosion and structural hazards, warning that mechanised dredging and unscientific riverbed scooping were destabilising riverbanks and accelerating soil erosion during the monsoon season. It said this was endangering critical lifelines, including National Highway 27 and railway lines, while triggering recurrent landslides near habitations.

The union further warned of extensive aquatic habitat destruction, with excessive siltation and riverbed disturbance decimating local biodiversity, including native and endangered fish species, by destroying breeding grounds and disrupting natural hydrology.

“Indiscriminate deep mining breaches the natural water table, drastically lowering groundwater levels and drying up vital gravity-fed drinking water streams across rural settlements,” the ADSU said, raising concerns about water security.
Livelihoods affected

The letter, signed by ADSU general secretary Suraj Naiding and president Arujit Kemprai, highlighted the impact of such activities on tribal livelihoods. It noted that rural and indigenous communities, dependent on these riparian systems for traditional fishing, agriculture and household water, were facing immediate socio-economic distress.

The ADSU underlined that Dima Hasao, an ecologically fragile hill region protected under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, was witness to extraction activity in contravention of the Assam Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 2013, the Supreme Court’s mandatory guidelines in Deepak Kumar versus State of Haryana (2012), and standing directions of the National Green Tribunal prohibiting heavy mechanised in-stream extraction without approved district survey reports and valid environmental clearances.

The ADU called for immediate cessation of illegal mining, including a cease-and-desist order against all non-compliant extraction sites and the impounding of unauthorised heavy machinery operating in river channels.

The union also demanded a joint ground inspection and audit, urging the formation of a task force comprising the Forest Department, Revenue and Forest officials of the Dima Hasao Autonomous Council, the district civil administration, ecological experts and local student representatives.

It called for strict penal action against illegal operators and quarry owners operating without approved mining plans, valid leases or environmental clearances from the State-Level Environment Impact Assessment Authority, under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
Additionally, the ADSU sought scientific demarcation of no-mining ecological zones, covering critical river bends, bridge buffers, erosion-prone areas and other ecologically sensitive stretches.

title: Why does male contraception still lag so far behind?

content.value: World Contraception Day on September 26 offers an opportunity to look closely at a part of family planning that receives very little attention:  contraception for men. The key question here is why the range of methods available to men and women  remains so different.

Women today have options including  oral pills, injectables, implants, intrauterine devices and permanent sterilisation, though access and affordability to safe and reliable contraception in our country continues to remain a major challenge. For men, the practical choices are still largely limited to condoms for reversible contraception and vasectomy for permanent contraception. Male and female reproduction are governed by the same broad hormonal axis, yet the biology, anatomy and mechanics of preventing conception create very different problems. Understanding those differences helps explain why a male equivalent of the pill has remained elusive.

title: Why is everything linked to inflammation now?

content.value: A recent episode of the Oprah Winfrey Podcast revealed a stunning new hypothesis in cancer research. It had nothing to do with artificial intelligence (A.I.) or a new drug’s mechanism. Instead, it was about chronic inflammation.

Winfrey’s guest was Siddhartha Mukherjee, cancer researcher, oncologist and author of the Pulitzer-winning book The Emperor of All Maladies. Partway through their conversation, when she asked about the future of cancer treatment, he said, “There are thousands of dormant cancer cells sitting in your body. Then something happens — I call it the sleeping beauty kiss — that wakes them up. We are realising that that one something is chronic inflammation... It really switches around how we think about cancer... If we could test that one particular kind of inflammation, we would have a bio-marker for future cancers that could even be preventive.”

In the longevity era, inflammation is one of the most studied biological phenomena. And increasingly, scientists are discovering evidence that chronic low-level inflammation, or extended activity of immune cells when there’s no immediate threat, is often the cause of disorders, from diabetes and cancer to autoimmune diseases and neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s.

Just last week, new research published in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology showed that chronic inflammation increases the risk of heart attack and stroke by 43%. Scientists from MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences and Imperial College London found that inflammation caused silent structural damage to the heart (thickened walls, smaller chambers and poorer filling) years before symptoms appeared.

Is it any wonder then that inflammation is on everybody’s minds these days? No matter where you look, someone is telling you how to reduce it: from self-help guides to influencers on Instagram breaking down inflammatory foods, inflammation belly, and inflammation face in under three minutes.

Turmeric is hyped as a miracle cure, others swear by elimination diets. Then there’s parasite detoxes, ice baths, celery juice resets and monotrophic cleanses (where you eat only one food item). The more scientists link inflammation to diseases, the more the wellness industry cashes in by marketing anti-inflammatory products. But take them with a dollop of salt. Often, the advice is fed to us by A.I.-generated doctors, healers and wellness influencers.
Acute and chronic: not the same thing

For most of history, doctors and the public focused on what they could see and feel: red, puffy skin around a wound, pain, fever. “I remember reading an article a few years back about how people with stressful jobs have inflammation, which could lead to illnesses as they age. And I recall closing my eyes and doing a mental body check and noting that ‘no, nothing was swollen or achy, so I’m not inflamed’. I was naive and uninformed,” says Kajal S. (name changed), a media professional in her 40s, explaining how she didn’t know the difference between acute and chronic inflammation.

One evening, a couple of years later, the knuckles in her left hand swelled up, and within a few days she was handed a diagnosis of palindromic rheumatism, a rare type of inflammatory arthritis characterised by sudden, recurring flare-ups and severe joint pain. Her doctor talked her through how consistent stress, bad sleep patterns, and gut issues — and the chronic inflammation it caused (that is devoid of swelling or aches) — played the lead role in her condition.

So, what’s the difference between acute and chronic inflammation? The former occurs when the body rallies to defend itself against invading microbes or to heal damaged tissue. Capillaries dilate and grow more porous, enabling white blood cells to flood the damaged site. The region swells, which can put pressure on surrounding nerves, causing pain. Chronic inflammation, however, is often silent and occurs when the immune system is over-stimulated all the time. As researchers are discovering, factors such as poor diet, air pollution, lack of sleep and stress can have a more significant impact on it than previously understood.

“In modern life, inflammation has five faces: ultra-processed food, sleep debt, a disturbed gut, a sedentary body, and the one I speak of most — the red mind or a state of constant stimulation.”Arpit BansalOncology surgeon and chief scientific chair at the Longevity Summit India held last month in Mumbai
Arpit Bansal

Over time, in many cases, our immunity can also get so active that it starts attacking our own cells, which is what autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriasis, vasculitis, Hashimoto’s disease and others are. Inflammation can also fuel chronic diseases (without autoimmunity), like Alzheimer’s and endometriosis.

“Persistent inflammation can contribute to changes in blood vessels and metabolism and is involved in several chronic diseases. The brain is also connected to these processes,” says Dr. Vinaya Bhandari, consultant neurology and neuromuscular disorder specialist from Mumbai’s Jaslok Hospital and Research Centre. “Inflammatory signals from the body can interact with the brain and its blood vessels... and continual activation is increasingly recognised as one component of neurological conditions, including neurodegenerative diseases [Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s].”
Less inflammation doesn’t mean “healthier”

It is easy to see why inflammation is such a perfect social media concept: it is invisible, frightening, scientifically legitimate, associated with many diseases, simple to attach to symptoms, as well as food and products. (Ironically, emerging research shows higher levels of inflammation associated with using social media over face-to-face interaction.)

But detecting chronic inflammation isn’t as easy as going to your physician and asking how your immune system is doing. While tests such as C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) can help identify markers of inflammation, for some people such tests just come back negative.

To complicate things further, not all inflammation have dire results. “Often, a person doesn’t know they have chronic low-grade inflammation because it is not always behind heart disease or endometriosis, or cancer,” says Dr. Suganya Venkat, a Coimbatore-based gynaecologist. “Chronic inflammation can manifest as brain fog or fatigue or lethargy that just won’t go away.”
Gynaecologist Dr. Suganya Venkat
Fringe wellness to mainstream culture

Somewhere between a turmeric shot, a cold plunge and a bowl of berries, inflammation has stopped being an immune response. It has become an explanation for why we are tired, puffy, anxious, ageing, gaining weight, breaking out and not feeling okay. Just the month of September has seen hundreds of guides on how to lower your inflammation naturally or how to reset your circadian rhythm to improve inflammation. And forums such as Reddit, with their believers, sceptics and the longevity crowd, are bandying around new terms such as ‘inflammaging’ (to describe the low-grade inflammation that occurs with ageing).

But the future of inflammation is not on the world wide web. It is in labs and clinics around the world where scientists are tracking inflammation in patients over time, trying to understand what normal looks like and when it can become dangerous.

The cancer-chronic inflammation link is something Indian oncologists have begun to consider. “Chronic inflammation can create a biological environment that promotes malignant transformation,” explains Dr. Aditya Vidushi, medical oncologist at Faridabad’s M|O|C Cancer Care & Research Centre. “A clear example is H. pylori, a stomach bacterium that triggers long-term irritation, a major driver of gastric cancer. Obesity-related low-grade inflammation is linked to higher risks of colorectal, breast, pancreatic, and liver cancers.”

And the body of science is building. Senthilkumar Rajagopal, associate professor at REVA University in Bengaluru, who has led several research papers on inflammation, says, “South Asian populations may have a distinctive susceptibility to chronic low-grade inflammation arising from the interaction of genes, visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, environmental exposures and lifestyle factors.” The central insight emerging from his work is that targeting molecular interfaces between neuron signalling and inflammatory pathways may offer new strategies.
Senthilkumar Rajagopal, associate professor at REVA University
Maintaining the balance

Experts agree that combining medicine and better lifestyle habits can best prevent flare-ups. But what they prescribe can vary widely, and occasionally be controversial. U.S.-based Mark Hyman, considered the pioneer of Functional Medicine, emphasises in his books that inflammation is the common pathway for all chronic diseases. His recommended solution is an anti-inflammatory diet: omitting sugar, caffeine, beans, dairy, gluten, and processed foods, as well as taking a variety of supplements, including probiotics, fish oil, Vitamins C and D, and curcumin, a key molecule in turmeric. Meanwhile, in his book The End of Illness, American oncologist David Agus prescribes, among other things, not wearing high heels because they inflame the feet and that inflammation could possibly affect vital organs.

The healing journey of Goa-based graphic designer Antima Nahar, 48, diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) when she was 35, has taken her to doctors, nutritionists and Ayurvedic retreats. Nahar got the transformative diagnosis after a fall during a monsoon trek on the outskirts of Mumbai. Her doctors told her she would live with pain if she did not take steroids and painkillers all her life. “It started with my toes and fingers, and then became a sharp, pounding pain that kept shifting through different joints in my body. At one point, I couldn’t squeeze a toothpaste tube, couldn’t open jars or bottles, couldn’t hold a phone for long,” Nahar says.
Goa-based graphic designer Antima Nahar

After years of naturopathic and Ayurvedic treatments, she found a balance with lowered doses of allopathic treatment combined with naturopathy and lifestyle modifications. “The last decade has been about knowing my body. Flare-ups can be because of food, weather changes, dancing, anything. I started recording everything, thinking through everything I did.” Nahar also began making illustrations about her RA journey and is now writing a graphic novel about self-discovery through pain.

Interestingly, chronic inflammatory conditions often manifest differently in men and women. Several studies in the past decade reveal that nearly 70% of all autoimmune disease patients in India are women. In men, it can manifest more as heart disease. Indian men face a cardiovascular death rate (349 per 100,000) that is significantly higher than that of men in Western nations, according to the National Noncommunicable Disease Monitoring Survey (NNMS).

Kochi resident Jai Krishnan Sambasivan, 62, says he wouldn’t be able to function well if it were not for steroids. At 42, he was running his own business in Alappuzha, Kerala, when he developed a high fever that lasted months without a diagnosis. Admitted in hospital for over a month, he says he “fit into the category of patients who was clinically well [all tests came back negative], but not well”. What finally led to a diagnosis of vasculitis were two high inflammatory markers: hs-CRP and ESR.
Jai Krishnan Sambasivan just moths before his diagnosis

Vasculitis is an autoimmune disease that inflames blood vessels, often leading to blockage of capillaries and eventually causing cardiac failure. He has managed to control the disease with Prednesol, a steroid drug, and lifestyle modifications. “But what keeps me alive is not medicine, it is breath control,” he believes. “I can say I have mastered it. I have learnt to be fearless.”
What you eat matters

Food plays a major role in managing/ preventing inflammation. According to Delhi-based nutritionist Shonali Sabherwal, a seasonal, pesticide-free, freshly-cooked plant diet is most effective in reducing chronic inflammation. “You need to question staples: the atta that you are using, is it a hybrid variety? Do we know what we are really stocking in our kitchens?”

Sabherwal’s approach, commonly used around the world for conditions such as allergies, autoimmune diseases and other chronic conditions, aligns with Ayurvedic prescriptions for excess agni (fire/ inflammation in the body). Dr. Nitin Kochar, a Mumbai-based Ayurvedic practitioner who specialises in cancer and inflammation, says that “depending on the specific dosha [vata, pitta or kapha, the Ayurvedic way of categorising the human body’s biochemistry], I prescribe fasting, specific plant foods and spices like ginger, cumin, giloy to weaken the fire”.
How do you treat it?

One of the frustrations of treating inflammation is that treatments are so imprecise. Dr. Shreevidya, medical director–preventive health, Apollo Hospitals, says chronic inflammation is usually identified not because someone felt it, but because it surfaced during a preventive health assessment. “Two drivers deserve more attention. One is chronic hidden infection, especially gum disease [untreated periodontitis keeps the whole system inflamed]. The other is air pollution. Long-term exposure to fine particulate matter is consistently associated with higher inflammation,” she says.
Dr. Shreevidya, medical director – preventive health, Apollo Hospitals

Dr. Divya Gopal, additional director of internal medicine at Mumbai’s Sir H.N. Reliance Foundation Hospital, says people should start with lifestyle changes. “Pain relievers like ibuprofen and naproxen reduce inflammation, but taking them long-term brings risks,” says Gopal. “For serious cases, I prescribe newer medications that block inflammation pathways.”

As research into inflammation intensifies, new methods are being discovered. Earlier this year, researchers at University College London uncovered a key mechanism that can help the body switch off inflammation and prevent harmful immune cells from building up. Elsewhere, several clinical studies have shown that, independent of weight loss and diabetes, GLP-1 receptor agonists such as Ozempic and Mounjaro can significantly reduce systemic inflammation markers such as CRP and TNF-alpha. There’s also talk about non-invasive continuous inflammation monitors, much like glucose monitors.

Science may be on the threshold of cures for several diseases that inflammation drives, but it is important to remember the nuance of it all: inflammation is part of our maintenance and repair system. Without inflammation, we can’t heal. The challenge is to master the balance between the healing short spells and the stubborn, prolonged simmer that has profound implications for our health.
The Mumbai-based writer and journalist is behind @the_slow_fix on Instagram.
With inputs from Surya Praphulla Kumar

title: U.S. FDA approves AbbVie's drug for Parkinson's disease

content.value: The United States Food and Drug ​Administration has approved AbbVie's treatment for Parkinson's ‌disease in adults, the health regulator's ​website showed on Friday, September 25, 2026.
The ⁠drug tavapadon, which AbbVie gained access to through its $8.7 billion acquisition of Cerevel Therapeutics ‌in 2023, comes as a once-a-day pill.
It will be sold ‌under the brand name Juvmo, ‌according ⁠to the FDA's website.

Parkinson's is ⁠a long-term brain condition that gradually damages movement control, often causing tremors, stiffness and balance issues. ​More than ‌11 million people live with the disease worldwide, according to AbbVie.
Juvmo works by mimicking dopamine, a vital brain ‌chemical that naturally decreases in people ​with Parkinson's.

The regulator's nod was based on data from ⁠AbbVie's late-stage trial program which showed the drug improved symptoms in patients with ‌the disease. Common side effects reported in the trials included nausea, dizziness and headache.
AbbVie did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on the drug's launch and ‌pricing.
Citi analysts had previously said the launch ​was expected in the third quarter of 2026, but that uptake ⁠was likely to be gradual as negotiations ⁠progressed on the drug's Medicare coverage.
AbbVie continued to target more ‌than $5 billion in combined Parkinson's disease sales, Citi added.

title: Webinar on developments in diagnosis, treatment of heart disease to be organised

content.value: The Hindu, in association with Kauvery Hospital, will conduct a webinar at 11.30 a.m. on Monday (September 28, 2026) on the prevention, detection, and treatment of heart disease.

The webinar, held to mark World Heart Day on September 29 and titled ‘Don’t Miss a Beat: Prevent, Detect, and Treat Heart Disease’, will bring together specialists in different areas of cardiac care to examine how developments in diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation are changing the management of heart disease. The session is held as part of The Hindu’s Wellness Series.

The panel will feature Ajith Pillai, HOD, interventional cardiologist, Kauvery Hospital, Radial Road; Arunkumar Krishnaswamy, senior consultant and cardiothoracic surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Alwarpet; Mahadevan V., senior consultant, interventional cardiology and diabetology, Kauvery Hospital, Vadapalani; and Javid Raja, consultant, Paediatric Cardiac Surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Heartcity, Tiruchi.

The panellists will discuss the role of minimally invasive valve procedures, newer approaches to coronary artery bypass surgery, and minimally invasive robotic cardiac surgery, besides touching on the importance of prevention and cardiac rehabilitation in maintaining long-term heart health. The webinar will also focus on congenital heart disease in children, emphasising the need for early detection and appropriate treatment.
The session will be moderated by Meenakshy S., Principal Correspondent, The Hindu.
To register, please visit https://newsth.live/THKAHBE or scan the QR code below.

title: Focus should be on preventive health screening: Prathap C. Reddy

content.value: Ahead of World Heart Day on September 29, Prathap C. Reddy, founder and chairman, Apollo Hospitals, has urged people not to think they are healthy simply because they exercise, but to continue exercising, consult a medical professional, and undergo preventive health screening from the age of 25. A doctor can help determine if an individual is truly healthy and identify any risk factors or underlying health concerns, he said on Friday.

“Earlier, we recommended preventive health checks from the age of 30 to 60. Now, we are asking people aged 25 and above to get screened. Get yourself completely screened once in your lifetime. A person should know if he/she is free from diseases and is healthy or is predisposed to any of the diseases,” he said.
‘A serious problem’

Dr. Reddy pointed out that non-communicable diseases were among the most serious problems India was facing. These include heart attacks, strokes, cancers, and diabetes, with obesity and mental illness also adding to the list, he said.

Heart attacks are preventable, he said, adding, “It gives you enough time and warning. It is important to detect early and eliminate the risk factors.” With heart attacks occurring at younger ages, he said, apart from genetic factors, smoking, stress, inactivity, lack of diet restrictions, hypertension, diabetes, and family history of heart attacks were among the risk factors for young people.

“We can handle diseases, particularly heart diseases. We perform a large number of heart surgeries with better outcomes. We do minimally invasive cardiac surgeries as well as robotic cardiac surgeries,” Dr. Reddy said, adding that in terms of skills, healthcare professionals — doctors, nurses and paramedics — had proven that they could give excellent outcomes. “Cardiac treatments are improving every day, with more private hospitals providing care and the governments activating their own programmes,” he said.

Dr. Reddy stressed the need to prioritise women’s health. “Women take care of the health and wellbeing of their family. The incidence of heart attacks in women is no less. We are seeing only 25% of women coming for our preventive health checks and this must increase,” he said, urging families to focus on the health of women. “Prevention is best. Everybody should make health a priority. Then we will see a healthy and happy nation,” he added.

title: WHO says Congo Ebola outbreak spreads to two new health zones

content.value: The World Health Organization said on Friday, September 25, 2026 that the Ebola ‌outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic ​Republic of the Congo has spread to ⁠two additional health zones, bringing the total number affected to 63 across seven provinces.
The newly affected zones are Bulu in Sud Ubangi ‌province and Dungu in Haut-Uele province, which borders South Sudan.
As of September 23, Congo had reported ‌7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths, according to the ‌WHO.

WHO ⁠Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said conflict and population ⁠displacement were making it more difficult for health workers to reach affected communities and trace people who may have been exposed to the virus.

"It's ​very difficult to see ‌Ebola in isolation because even our response in Ebola is affected by the conflict because there is displacement and there is access problem to some areas," Tedros said. He said ‌restricted access could leave contacts untraced, while displacement and ​crowding increased transmission risks.
Tedros said cases were declining overall and that contact tracing, safe burials ⁠and community engagement had improved, although transmission remained uneven across affected areas.

The lack of approved vaccines and treatments for the Bundibugyo ‌strain was also complicating the response and could make people reluctant to seek care at treatment centers, Tedros said, adding the WHO was working to accelerate clinical trials of vaccines and treatments.

Turning to the risk of future global health emergencies, Tedros said countries needed to strengthen pandemic preparedness. “Ebola ‌will not be a pandemic, but there could be a respiratory pathogen ​that can become a pandemic," he said. "Before that hits, we need to prepare."
The World Health ⁠Assembly adopted the Pandemic Agreement in May 2025 to strengthen global ⁠prevention, preparedness and response to future pandemics.

"We continue to see significant mis- and disinformation about the WHO ‌Pandemic Agreement, with false claims. It's a power grab that cedes sovereignty to WHO," Tedros said. "This is completely untrue."

title: Dengue, influenza in circulation; Chennai hospitals see steady rise in fever cases

content.value: Dengue and influenza viruses are currently in circulation, with a number of hospitals in the city reporting a steady flow of patients with fever, though doctors say the numbers remain in line with the seasonal trend.

“Currently, both flu and dengue viruses are in circulation. Flu spreads from person to person, while dengue is a vector-borne infection. We need to deal with both the infections carefully. If a person has fever, they should look out for respiratory symptoms such as cold, cough, and throat pain. These are the primary symptoms of Influenza-Like Illness (ILI). If there is a high-grade fever with no respiratory symptoms but body pain and headache, it is a sign of dengue,” a senior government doctor said.
Hidden cases

Epidemiologically, if one case of dengue is notified in a particular area or village, it means there are hidden cases, he said, adding: “There is no need to test everyone, and persons with typical symptoms can be treated appropriately based on a physician consultation. Laboratory tests can be initiated if doctors prescribe.”

He said that in the case of flu, it is mostly self-limiting, but utmost care should be taken for elderly and pregnant women. “ILI can lead to Severe Acute Respiratory Infection and people could land in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome. Early treatment is important for flu-like symptoms. For dengue, a basic blood test — Complete Blood Count — will give us clues, especially a drop in the platelet count. So, with two viruses in circulation, which happens naturally during this season, people should be prepared and alert,” he said. However, there are no official institution-wise figures on fever outpatients or admissions. Authorities of at least two government hospitals in Chennai said the number of fever cases were not rampant and admissions for fever had not increased. In another hospital, senior doctors said all beds in the fever ward were full, and that the patients were recovering.
Seasonal trend

S. Chandrasekar, Professor and Head, Department of Medicine and Critical Care Services, Government Stanley Medical College Hospital, said that at present, the situation was not alarming and the rise in fever cases was in line with the expected seasonal trend typically observed from September to November.

“A mild variant of flu is also in circulation. Dengue cases slowly peak after rainfall in mid-November and usually settle by February-end every year. There is a small excess of cases this year. Many persons, especially adolescents/teenagers, are being referred late, and with complications such as capillary leak syndrome on the fifth or sixth day of illness. We are closely watching the situation. It is important to know the warning symptoms of dengue,” he said.

At Kanchi Kamakoti CHILDS Trust Hospital, medical director Janani Sankar said they were seeing a lot of dengue and influenza A cases as well as a few Respiratory Syncytial Virus infections. “The cases are quite rampant. Our beds are full. We are seeing children with dengue, respiratory infections, wheezing, and bronchiolitis. Some children with dengue are requiring admissions for 24 to 48 hours, but none with complications,” she said.

Dr. Sankar said parents should ensure there are no water collections in and around their homes. As dengue virus is transmitted by a day-biting mosquito, schools must ensure that they take mosquito control measures. “If a child is dull after a fever subsides, they should seek medical help. The warning signs of dengue are abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, drowsiness, and refusal to take feeds,” she said.

title: Health Ministry orders crackdown on nicotine pouches, citing health risks, letter shows

content.value: The Union Health Ministry has ordered States to crack down ‌on the sale of nicotine pouches, which it considers a major health ​risk, saying globally popular brands are being widely sold illegally in ⁠the country, a letter from the Ministry shows.

Nicotine pouches have emerged as one of Big Tobacco's most important bets on a future beyond cigarettes, offering rapid growth, attractive margins and, for now, ‌lighter regulation than many rival smoking alternatives.
In India, where tobacco kills 13.5 lakh people a year, the government has banned e-cigarettes but approved certain nicotine ‌replacements like patches and chewing gums.

Nicotine pouches — small packets placed under the ‌lip ⁠that contain nicotine but no tobacco — remain illegal and unapproved, with a government ⁠source saying they are often smuggled into India for sale online and through local tobacco stores.

A federal study in June called them "a largely unregulated public health concern", with wide consumption among people aged 18 to ​40 of brands such as Philip ‌Morris' Zyn and Swedish Smokeless Solutions' White Fox.

There is increased "availability of oral nicotine pouches through online and offline channels in the country ... Nicotine exposure is of particular concern among children," the Health Ministry wrote in a letter to all States on September ‌19, seen by Reuters.
“Initiate appropriate enforcement action in accordance with the law, in ​the interest of public health and protection of children," it added.
The directive cited provisions of the drug law that allow for the search and ⁠seizure of such products and the prosecution of those selling them.
The Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Philip Morris and Swedish Smokeless did not immediately respond to requests ‌for comment.
Philip Morris on its website says the company has zero tolerance towards illegal trade, while Swedish Smokeless urges users to only buy original products from authorised outlets.

While the World Health Organization has said governments need to introduce more safeguards to protect people, especially youth, from nicotine pouch addiction, some agencies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration say smokers who switch completely to alternatives such as pouches, vapes and heated tobacco ‌products may reduce their health risks.
No new approvals
In April, an investigation found that Mumbai international ​airport's duty-free shops run by billionaire Gautam Adani's business group breached the law by selling nicotine pouches.

Adani has denied wrongdoing, and the Bombay High Court ⁠this week rejected the company's arguments that duty-free shops are immune from domestic laws. It also ⁠told the Adani Group it was free to make representations before the government to make a case for the pouches.

However, the government believes "nicotine pouches are addictive, pose ‌independent health risks and have not been established as effective smoking-cessation aids," according to minutes of the main federal drug panel's meeting published on September 16.
The Drugs Technical ​Advisory Board "recommended that no new nicotine formulation be approved henceforth in public interest," it added.

title: Researchers document first human deaths by Caspian cobra in India

content.value: Researchers have documented the first confirmed snakebite envenomation and subsequent human deaths in India caused by the venomous Caspian cobra (Naja oxiana), which have never previously been reported in the country, according to a case report published in Epidemiology International, a peer-reviewed journal.

The study titled ‘First Report of Deadly Bites by Caspian Cobra (Naja oxiana) From India’ by Bharti O.K., Menon J.C., Phull A., Joy S., Sharma V. and Malhotra A. details two fatalities and two survivals from bites by the species, also called the Central Asian cobra, in Himachal Pradesh’s Chamba’s Pir Panjal mountain range.

“Envenomation and subsequent deaths from the Caspian Cobra (Naja oxiana) have never previously been reported from India. While collecting data for the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) project on snakebites, we came across two deaths due to the bite of N. oxiana,” said Omesh Kumar Bharti of Himachal Pradesh’s Directorate of Health Services, who led the study.

“Deaths due to N. oxiana have never been previously reported from India. Naja oxiana is primarily found in Central Asia, with high human mortality resulting from envenoming. This species has been reported from Pakistan and Kashmir and was recorded in 2019 from Tissa block of Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh. Naja oxiana has been shown to have rapidly expanded its range from Iran towards the northeast and it has been observed to be slowly expanding its range in Chamba towards lower elevations as reported by local rescuers,” noted the study.

The first death occurred in July 2020 in Ullansa village, when a 40-year-old man was bitten twice on the leg while spraying an apple orchard. He was taken to a nearby faith healer. However, his condition continued to worsen and on the third day after the bite, he was taken to the Civil Hospital Bharmour, where he was seen by the doctor and was found to lack a detectable pulse. A second victim, a 62-year-old man from Bhanjraru village, was bitten in July 2021 while walking to work and collapsed within half an hour. He died before reaching Civil Hospital Tissa; a post-mortem attributed the death to the venom’s neurotoxic effects, the study said.

Snakebite envenoming (SBE) remains a major cause of preventable mortality in rural India. The big four species, namely the spectacled cobra (Naja naja), Russell’s viper (Daboia russelii), common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) and saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus), are responsible for the majority of snakebite envenomation and deaths in the country. The commercially available anti-snake venom (ASV) correspondingly covers these species only, it said. The study also noted that the available anti-snake venom (ASV), designed to counter the ‘big four’ species responsible for most snakebite deaths nationally, does not effectively neutralise the venom components of N. oxiana.

The researchers said that there is a need to create greater community awareness about the danger of this species of snake in affected areas and educate them about ways to reduce the risk of being bitten.

title: Biosphere 2, an experiment like no other

content.value: The dream of heading out to space and colonising distant celestial bodies isn’t one that is unique to the time we live in. It is one that humans have aspired for long and continue to strive towards, despite the problems plaguing the only known planet that supports life as we know it: Earth.

Even as we probe the habitability of celestial bodies, near and far, there have also been another set of experimenters, scientists, and researchers here on Earth that have concentrated on gearing up for that mission, whenever that might be. One of the more popular such experiments came in the form of Biosphere 2.

If you were to look up the word “biosphere” in a dictionary, then you will likely learn that it is “a part of a planet’s environment where life exists.” Given that Earth is the only place we know that supports life, the biosphere can also be defined as “the part of the Earth’s environment where life exists.”

With Earth being Biosphere 1, a group of people got together to build Biosphere 2 — a structure that was to serve as a tiny Earth capsule on Earth. This Earth-based laboratory was built to test the ability of human beings to live in outer space in isolation. It was envisioned as a 100-year project, providing for long-term investigation of processes that fundamentally underline our experience here on Earth.
Whose idea was it anyway?

A group of people got together in San Francisco in 1967 to build a community known as the “Synergists”. From building a ship of their own to sailing around the world to living in particular environmental conditions, the Synergists carried out a number of projects that they believed were sustainable both economically and ecologically.

During one such project where members were involved in organic farming, carpentry and performing arts on a New Mexico ranch, the group hit upon the idea for Biosphere 2. Believed to be conceived by American engineer and polymath John Allen, the idea turned into a reality once billionaire businessman Edward Bass decided to pump money into the project.
Design and reality

The site for building Biosphere 2 was in the Sonoran Desert in Oracle, Arizona, U.S. Built at a cost of $150 million (over $440 million today), the construction of Biosphere 2 began in 1984 and was completed in the early 1990s. One of the largest buildings to be almost completely cut off from the atmosphere, Biosphere 2 sprawls across a three-acre area.

The structure looks like a cross between a multi-level greenhouse and a collection of glass pyramids, towers, minarets, and domes. Inside it resided over 3,500 species of plants and animals in five miniature biomes. The biomes included a tropical rainforest with a 25-foot waterfall, an ocean with its own living coral reef, a mangrove-filled marsh and wetland, a savannah, and a fogged desert.

On September 26, 1991, eight people — including some who were involved from the ideation stage — stepped into Biosphere 2. The four women and four men were dressed in dark-blue spacesuits as they bade goodbyes to the gathered friends, family and members of media crews. One of them, Jane Poynter, declared that “The future is here!” before stepping into the ecological laboratory that was hermetically sealed.
“The future is here!”Jane Poynter, one of the first eight Biospherians

The eight “Biospherians” had means to communicate with the outside world in the form of email, telephone, and fax, but that’s as far as things got. There was no physical contact from the outside world, and that wasn’t the only challenge that they faced.
Perception and aftermath

If we were to ever construct colonies in outer space, then there’s the need for those building it and living there to be self-sufficient. As the Biospherians were exploring exactly that, they grew their own crops and ate them; recycled all the air, water, and waste; and took care of their surroundings.

Despite the difficulties that they faced, the first batch of Biospherians stepped outside their sealed enclosure two years later in 1993. The next crew of seven stepped into Biosphere 2 on March 6, 1994, but their stay was terminated months later the same year owing to financial and executive decisions made outside in Biosphere 1.

While there’s no denying that the first crew had help from outside and weren’t entirely transparent with their communication, somewhere along the line the experiment turned into something else for those outside. The problem of enforced social-distancing, both mentally and physically, is better understood now owing to the COVID-19 pandemic. Three decades before that, however, people outside understood little of how things might be. Both the broader public, and a section of the media covering it, became more interested in the storylines and fault lines of the individuals involved, more than what they were trying to achieve.
The property was leased out to Columbia University in 1994, and they converted it into a research facility. It was subsequently leased and eventually gifted to the University of Arizona in 2011.

title: Private spacecraft falls back to Earth after failing to rescue aging NASA telescope

content.value: The robotic spacecraft that failed to rescue an aging NASA telescope plunged back to Earth on Friday (September 25, 2026) less than three months after launching on the bold mission.

Katalyst Space Technologies announced the demise of its three-armed spacecraft named Link. It reentered the atmosphere overnight, bringing the $30 million, NASA-sponsored salvage effort of the Swift Observatory to a close.
Swift is expected to follow in early November as its orbit steadily sinks.
“While we'll be sad to see Swift's mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way,” NASA's Shawn Domagal-Goldman said in a statement.
It provided valuable practice for future satellite-rescue missions and pushed teams to rush against the clock like never before, Domagal-Goldman added.

Thrown together in under a year, Link was supposed to capture the 22-year-old Swift and then boost it to a higher, longer-lasting orbit so it could keep observing some of the biggest explosions in the universe. The sun's intense flare-ups had put the telescope on a downward spiral faster than engineers anticipated.

To buy time, NASA suspended observations early this year and repositioned Swift to minimise the atmosphere's downward drag. Otherwise, the telescope would have come down before help could arrive, according to managers.

Link launched on July 3, but quickly ran into electronic problems that took out two of the three reaction wheels needed to turn the spacecraft. Then a bad valve sent the satellite into a fast spin that disrupted communication. Engineers regained control, but Link didn't have enough fuel left to carry out its job and the rescue effort was called off in August.

Katalyst used the few weeks remaining to practice moving Link's robot arms, each about 3 feet in length with a handlike gripper on the end. Flight controllers even managed to guide the spacecraft to within 12 kilometres to 15 kilometres of Swift, close enough to snap pictures.
“We knew from the beginning that this was an ambitious mission on an aggressive timeline,” Katalyst CEO Ghonhee Lee said in a statement.
Mr. Lee said the company will carry all the lessons learned to its future satellite-recovery endeavours. “This is a foundation we can build on," he added.
Swift is back to scanning the universe in the month or so that it has left.

Launched in 2004, the $364 million observatory is designed to pivot quickly — as its name suggests — to capture gamma ray bursts, exploding stars and other fast-breaking cosmic action. That ability allows Swift to serve as a lookout or first responder for other telescopes that can follow its lead. NASA is scrambling to see how it now will fill that gap.

title: Narrowed posture: On Karnataka and the Kasturirangan Report

content.value: The Kasturirangan Report bears a pro-development attitude that allows human occupation and a range of economic activity across the Western Ghats, yet the Karnataka Assembly unanimously repudiated its recommendations. A grievance concerned the accuracy of the remote-sensing and satellite data from 2012 that the Report uses to distinguish natural from human-dominated landscapes. Another concern was its recommendation that an entire revenue village be placed within an ‘ecologically sensitive area’ (ESA) if at least 20% of its area is sensitive. This could bring farmland and human settlements within the ESA even when sensitive areas occupy only a fraction of the village. Following the Centre’s directive to States in 2013-14 to begin ground-truthing the Report’s recommendations, Karnataka faced bipartisan opposition centered on concerns about livelihoods, with vested interests, including stakeholders of activities both the Gadgil and the Kasturirangan Reports restrict/ban such as mining, allegedly fanning fears of displacement. The State thus elected to resist the ESA framework. Although the Assembly’s resolution proposes returning to the unfinished task of producing an alternative map, the government’s posture also faces a wider challenge.

The Centre’s interim directions in 2013 preserve some protection for the ecosystems that the State stewards, but for the government and the businesses within potential ESAs, the delay may prolong uncertainty over what forms of planned development will ultimately be permitted. Broadly, particular States confront the economic and political consequences of local resistance and foregone development while the country as a whole will capture much of the national benefit of conserving the Ghats, so States have an incentive to negotiate the ESAs’ extent down. However, as of mid-2026, Gujarat was reportedly close to an agreement with the Centre, Tamil Nadu had no substantive disagreement, Kerala wanted to reduce its already ground-truthed 9,993 sq. km to 8,805 sq. km, and Maharashtra and Goa wanted 378 and 21 villages omitted, respectively. These instances of progress (such as they are), the Ghats’ continuity across six States, and the Centre’s 2024 decision to allow ESAs in the region to be notified State by State increase pressure on Karnataka without legally binding it to its neighbours’ choices. Specifically, Karnataka’s ability to continue rejecting the framework as a whole becomes harder to sustain if it does not also produce an equally considered alternative. Karnataka needs to reconcile the apprehensions of its farmers and workers with the responsibilities accruing to the State with the largest share (by area) of the proposed ESAs.

title: Photography exhibition by Induchoodan Foundation showcases the birds of Keralam

content.value: Surrounded by large portraits of birds and sounds of their trills, squawks and hoots, the Durbar Hall art gallery suddenly feels like a tropical forest. An exhibition of bird photographs is underway and it opens a window to the fascinating diversity of birdlife in Keralam. A soundtrack of avian symphonies adds to the effect of the photographs captured from various parts of the State.

Organised by the Induchoodan Foundation, a bird lovers’ fraternity, the show, Parannuyarunna Malayalam, is a tribute to the life and work of KK Neelkantan, an English professor, who was also a keen naturalist and ornithologist. His seminal work Keralthile Pakshikal (Birds of Kerala) published by the Kerala Sahitya Akademi in 1958, is widely considered a pioneering work on Keralam’s bird life. Enriched by his own illustrations, the book, containing detailed descriptions of the birds, is also celebrated for its literary quality.

Founded in his birth centenary year (2024) with writer Paul Zacharia as the chairman, the Induchoodan Foundation is a collective of bird lovers. The aim of the foundation, formed in honour of Neelakantan, is to share the visionary’s knowledge and experience with people. In two years, the Induchoodan Foundation has conducted 15 exhibitions of bird photographs across Keralam. This is the third edition of the exhibition in Kochi.

The pictures on show have been taken by the members of the foundation, who hail from diverse backgrounds. “We have students, professionals and retired people amongst us,” says M Ramachandran, the curator, whose photographs are also part of the show. “The photographs are of birds captured across various places within Keralam.” The idea is to get younger people involved too, “so we usually invite schools and colleges to visit the show,” Ramachandran adds.

Over 50 photographs by 26 photographers are on display across three halls of the gallery. Each photograph is accompanied by a description of the bird as it is given in Neelakantan’s book. Naturalist, filmmaker, author and wildlife photographer Suresh Elamon, who was a disciple of Neelakantan and has written a biography of his titled Pakshikalum oru Manushyanum, recalls the first time Neelakantan and he spotted the the Crab-plover from the Perumathura beach in Thiruvananthapuram. “It was a new addition to his book and I distinctly remember how happy he was that day,” adds Suresh, who has a photograph of the same species that he clicked in Kozhikode, years later. The white bird with heavy black bills, specially designed to catch and eat crabs, is rather endearingly called ‘njandunni’ (crabeater) in Malayalam.

Each photograph on display offers something new to the viewer, a nugget of information, a story or a new perspective. “This is the Banasura Laughing Thrush,” says retired Airforce personnel Dijumon Komanthakkal from Thrissur. An avid bird photographer, he says the Banasura laughing thrush is an endangered song bird, not easy to spot. “Its population is largely confined to the Kodagu region and is the official district bird of Wayanad. Birdwatching and bird photography are serious hobbies, it involves hours of waiting in anticipation of a single sighting, it demands patience,” he adds. Dijumon’s photographs of the Malayan Night Heron and the Oriental Pratincole are also part of the show.
The exhibition is on at Durbar Hall Art Gallery till September 27.

title: Regenagri to be implemented in south Indian tea estates

content.value: As many as 50 to 60 tea gardens in the country, including 10 in south India, are part of the Regenagri programme.

A collaboration of Solidaridad Network Asia Limited, the International Cooperative Alliance, and WWF-India, Regenagri is an international regenerative agriculture programme run by the UK-based Regenagri Community Interest Company.

Shatadru Chattopadhyay, Managing Director of Solidaridad Asia, told The Hindu recently that the Regenagri was launched for the tea estates in December 2024 in association with the Indian Tea Association. It has now tied up with the United Planters Association of Southern India to implement the programme for tea gardens in the south. Erratic rainfalls, poor soil health, and rising temperatures are challenges for the tea sector.

The programme usually runs for three years where the growers are supported to transition to holistic farming techniques that increase soil organic matter, encourage biodiversity, sequester carbon dioxide, and improve water and energy management.

Regenagri is implemented for cotton in Maharashtra. Mr. Chattopadhyay pointed out that cotton requires more fertilizer than any other crop, most of the growers are small-scale and cultivate on rainfed lands. Hence, they find it difficult to convert to organic farming.

Under the Regenagri initiative, the land is certified. Traceability, decarbonisation, and compliances are important. Farmers under the programme found the yield increasing 10%-20%. The farmers are encouraged to form farmer producer organisations through which they source the inputs in bulk. This helps them reduce the cost of production.

Talks are going on with international textile brands to purchase goods made of cotton from the Regenagri certified lands and the carbon credits that were received this year based on last year’s audits are now distributed to farmers. This is another income for the farmers, he pointed out.

title: US government seeks to join Elon Musk in challenge against EU's fine on X

content.value: The ⁠US government said on Thursday it had formally sought to join a legal challenge filed by billionaire Elon Musk to dismiss a ‌fine of €120 million ($136.51 million) by the European Union against his social media platform X.
EU tech regulators ‌fined X late last year for breaching online content ‌rules, ⁠the first sanction under a landmark legislation that ⁠has drawn criticism from Washington.
The US Department of Justice said it had filed an application with the EU’s General Court in support of ​X’s effort to annul the ‌case.
The EU sanction against X followed a two-year-long investigation under the bloc’s Digital Services Act (DSA), which requires online platforms to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content.

“The ‌European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority ​to reach American companies not present or operating within its jurisdiction,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of ⁠the US Justice Department’s civil division said.

Europe’s crackdown on Big Tech to ensure smaller rivals can compete and consumers have ‌more choice has been criticised by the administration of US President Donald Trump, which alleges it singles out American companies.

The European Commission, the EU’s executive, has said its laws do not target any nationality and that it is merely defending its digital and democratic standards, which it ‌says serve as the benchmark for the rest of the world.

Musk, who ​has financially backed candidates from Trump’s Republican Party in elections and supported Trump himself in the last ⁠election, has said the EU’s tech regulations stall technological progress.

Since ⁠Musk’s purchase of X, then known as Twitter, in 2022, rights advocates and experts have been widely ‌critical of the platform over what they say is increased hate speech, misinformation and nonconsensual sexually explicit content.

title: How monetising UPI hurts electronics retailers

content.value: Unified Payments Interface (UPI) was championed as a free, indigenous technological innovation designed to democratise digital payments and accelerate the nation’s formal economy. But a sudden pivot toward monetisation creates severe structural, financial, and operational challenges for small, independent shopkeepers and large, organised retail chains. The recent introduction of a 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on UPI transactions marks a major shift in India’s digital payment ecosystem, sparking profound concern across the mobile retail sector.

Electronics retailers operate in a high-volume, low-margin business where profit margins are thin, often strictly capped by original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) through fixed brand pricing structures and intense online competition. In such a tightly constrained ecosystem, a 0.4% transaction fee represents a significant, direct extraction from a retailer’s profit.

title: OpenAI to preview GPT-6 Cyber within days: Report

content.value: OpenAI is set to preview a cybersecurity-focused ​AI model, GPT-6 Cyber, within days ‌and launch a new product designed ​to help customers deploy ⁠it more securely and automatically, Fortune reported on Thursday (September 25, 2026), citing multiple sources familiar with the ‌plans.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request ‌for comment outside regular business hours.
OpenAI ⁠Chief Executive Sam Altman and ⁠rival Anthropic’s CEO earlier this month joined industry leaders in calling for a slower pace ​of AI development ‌and stronger safety measures.
Cybersecurity is emerging as one of AI’s fastest-growing markets, as tech firms develop tools ‌to combat threats and contain rogue ​AI agents.

OpenAI has warned its flagship Astra model ⁠from the GPT-6 lineup can at times try to evade human oversight, ‌while Australia said on Thursday an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June.

Fortune said GPT-6 Cyber, OpenAI’s fourth cybersecurity-focused model released this year, could be unveiled at ‌the company’s DevDay event in San ​Francisco on Tuesday, along with plans to ship a dozen or ⁠more other products.
A limited group of ⁠customers in OpenAI’s application-only Daybreak Red cybersecurity program already has access ‌to GPT-6 Cyber for alpha testing, the report said.

title: Western Ghats ESA: Keralam submits recommendations to Centre, seeks limiting area to 8,590 sq km

content.value: Keralam has urged the Centre to limit the Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA) in its Western Ghats region to forest areas covering 8,590.69 sq km.

M.G. Rajamanickam, Special Secretary, Environment and Climate Change, formally placed the State’s recommendations and suggestions before the Centre on Thursday (September 24, 2026) on behalf of the Keralam government, Minister for Electricity and Environment Sunny Joseph said in Thiruvananthapuram on Friday (September 25).
The deadline for submitting the recommendations ends on Friday.

Mr. Joseph said the Congress-led UDF government also intends to get a resolution seeking the restriction of ESA to forest areas passed in the State Legislative Assembly when it convenes next. “Our stand is that populated areas, farmlands and plantations should be excluded in their entirety and the ESA limited to forest regions,” Mr. Joseph said.

The State government has sought resetting the ESA from 9,993.7 sq km to 8,590.69 sq km and the number of villages from 131 and 98. The excluded villages include 23 in Idukki district, four in Kottayam, two in Thiruvananthapuram and one each in Wayanad and Palakkad.
Final notification sought

If needed, Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan will lead a delegation to New Delhi to press the State’s case in this regard, said the Minister, adding that Keralam is seeking a final notification from the Centre as the multiple notifications issued from 2014 to July 2026 have all been drafts.

Mr. Joseph described the State government’s recommendations as capable of resolving the ESA-related issues. The government had submitted its recommendations after examining the suggestions and objections raised by stakeholders, including farmer organisations, elected representatives, individuals and local bodies, he said.
‘Unique’ case

Keralam’s case was “unique” given its small size but dense population and large forest cover (29.15% of total area), he said. The State has urged the Centre to limit the ESA to forests as the addition of another law or condition to existing stringent laws protecting the forest and environment and  paddy lands and wetlands could adversely affect the State’s development, agriculture and the everyday life of the people, the Minister added.

In 2013, the K. Kasturirangan Committee recommended fixing the ESA 13,108 sq km covering 123 villages in their entirety in the State. This had sparked widespread protests. Following a study by the Oommen V. Oommen committee, the Ministry of Environment and Forests had issued a draft notification which reduced the area to 9,993.7 sq km. Of this, 9,107 sq km was deemed forest area and 886.7 sq km, non-forest area. Although the number of villages had subsequently increased to 131 due to bifurcation, the total area did not charge.

Although Keralam subsequently sought limiting the area to 8,590.69 sq km by excluding populated areas, farm lands and plantations, the seventh draft published by the Ministry on July 27, 2026, did not accept this change.

title: How much of India’s shift to ‘alternative fuels’ is electric vehicles?

content.value: August 2026 marked a notable milestone in India’s journey towards a shift from fossil-fuel run vehicles to Electric Vehicles (EVs), as the data from the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations’ (FADA) showed that it was a period of a “historic fuel crossover”.

In the passenger vehicles category that mainly includes cars, FA-DA data showed that, for the first time, the share of new vehicles in the alternative fuels category (41.95%) overtook the share of petrol vehicles (40.85%). FADA’S statement said that alternative fuels included “CNG, hybrid and electric combined”.
