Without doubt, India has made considerable progress in moving away from fossil fuels and adapting EVs. As the chart below shows, petrol and diesel still dominate the market by a huge margin, accounting for 83.5% of all the roughly 82 lakh vehicles registered from January to March this year. But this is a sharp 11.5 percentage points drop from the same period in 2021, when petrol and diesel accounted for over 95% of all the 57 lakh vehicles registered then.
Increase in ‘alternative fuels’
The sale of EVs has seen a sharp increase, accounting for 10.6% of total registrations, as this chart shows.

However, a granular analysis of sub-categories under the alternative fuels based on data accessed from the Vahan portal showed that this was driven more by EV adoption in the two-wheeler and three-wheeler categories. When it came to cars, the growth under the alternative fuels is more pronounced in vehicles that use CNG and LPG, which are fossil fuels with significantly lower emissions, than EVs.
Two-wheelers gaining pace

The two-wheeler segment which accounts for over 70% of all the new vehicles registered in the country had shown signs that EV adoption is gaining pace. After registering a marginal increase year-on-year, the share of EVs in two-wheelers has made a jump from 6.4% in 2025 to 9.1% in 2026 (till August). See the chart below.

This is also the first time the share of two-wheelers running on petrol has come down to the 90% mark. This jump in the sale of EV two-wheelers has contributed significantly to the overall share of petrol and diesel vehicles, across all categories, coming down well below the 85% mark this year as shown in the earlier chart.
Rapid transition in three-wheelers

If there is one segment that has made a rapid transition away from petrol and diesel, it is the three-wheeler category. They, however, account for only 4% of all the vehicles sold. Of the roughly 9.8 lakh three-wheelers registered till August this year, 60.5% have been EVs.

The share of petrol and diesel in the registration of three-wheelers has halved from nearly 30% in 2021 to less than 15% in 2026. Interestingly, the share of three-wheelers using CNG or LPG has also come down this year.
Cars shift more to CNG / LPG

It is in the cars segment, which accounts for the second biggest share in total registration of vehicles after two-wheel-ers, that the picture is more nuanced than what the shift indicates when “alternative fuels” are clubbed together.

As the chart below shows, a remarkable drop is seen in the share of petrol and diesel cars from 86% in 2021 to 61.6% 2026. However, this decline is because there are more hybrid cars that run on petrol with CNG or LNG than EVs.

There is certainly progress in the sale of EVs, but it is much slower when compared to vehicles using CNG or LPG. The share of hybrid EVs has remained fairly constant since 2023 at around eight per cent. The data indicates the need for further interventions through measures such as the ramping up of charging infrastructure, which can help accelerate the pace of EV adoption among cars as well.

title: Sustainable tourism in Visakhapatnam: Travel beyond the checklist

content.value: Tourism is often measured in arrivals, room nights and destinations covered. A quieter shift is taking place in the way some travellers experience a place: with smaller groups, local participation and closer attention to the ecosystems they enter.

In the Eastern Ghats and along the Visakhapatnam coast, a handful of nature-based initiatives are building experiences around that approach. Their work spans an eco-stay near Araku, guided treks, tidepool walks and scuba diving. Each operates differently, but the common thread is an attempt to make visitors more observant and reduce the pressure that tourism can place on fragile landscapes.
Pravaham: Staying with the landscape

At Pravaham, an eco-stay in Mettavalasa village near Araku, sustainability is built into the property, quite literally.  Founder V Samved says nearly 90% of its construction uses locally available soil, hay, timber and bamboo. Mud, cob and hydrated lime plaster help regulate indoor temperatures naturally, reducing dependence on artificial cooling.

The stay also draws much of its food, workforce and experiences from nearby villages. Guests are encouraged to spend time by the stream, explore local trails and participate in activities such as the Plant a Memory initiative.

“We want guests to experience  the rhythm of slow living,” says Samved. “Our Black Box digital detox programme is one way of doing that. Instead of a packed sightseeing schedule, guests can wade in the stream, sit around a campfire or learn about natural building.”

Waste management, composting, reduced use of single-use plastic and restrained energy consumption form part of the property’s everyday practices. Carpooling and shared logistics are encouraged to reduce transport-related emissions.
EcoHikes: Smaller groups, deeper trails

For Ravi Teja, trek leader at EcoHikes, sustainability is closely tied to the number of people entering a landscape. The group, which has conducted more than 600 treks and taken over 8,000 participants into the Eastern Ghats over  nine years, has reduced its group size from  30 people to around  12.

At camps, EcoHikes uses gas stoves instead of collecting firewood from the hills. Food is home-cooked, often using local ingredients and served on banana or Bauhinia leaves. Packaged food and plastic have been reduced, while participants are expected to carry back whatever they bring in.

Ravi is also wary of the effect of social media on lesser-known landscapes. “One viral reel can bring crowds within weeks,” he says. “Every place has a carrying capacity and once it is crossed, both the landscape and the experience are lost.”

The group has closed  some trails when it felt that publicity could expose them to excessive footfall. It also works with local families, who contribute food, offer guidance  and knowledge of traditional practices.
“Locals have cared for these mountains for generations. We are only visitors,” Ravi says.
East Coast Conservation: Reading the tidepools

Along Visakhapatnam’s coast, the East Coast Conservation Team (ECCT) is using tidepool walks to bring people closer to marine life. Led by Deepu Visweswar and Priyanka Vedula, the team introduces visitors to an ecosystem that appears and disappears with the tides and can contain hundreds of species in a relatively small area.

For Deepu, the value of these walks lies in changing how people look at a familiar beach. “ People may have visited the same beach hundreds of times, but it can become a completely different world,” he says.

Tidepools can function as nursery and feeding grounds, with algae, corals, fishes, crustaceans and other organisms adapted to repeated cycles of exposure and immersion. The team limits groups to eight participants per instructor and briefs visitors not to touch or handle animals.

The conservation argument extends beyond the walk itself. Participants are encouraged to photograph organisms rather than disturb them and upload observations to citizen science platforms such as iNaturalist.
“Tidepool walks are a way of getting people hooked on marine life,” Priyanka says. “Once people become fascinated by it, they begin to care about protecting it.”

She believes marine tourism can also create economic opportunities for coastal communities if carefully managed, while warning against permanent structures and poorly regulated visitor activity in sensitive habitats.
Platypus Escapes: Diving with restraint

At Platypus Escapes, founder Subhash Chandran sees scuba diving as an entry point to understanding the underwater world. The team combines recreational diving with conservation dives and underwater clean-ups, encouraging participants to regard themselves as visitors in a living ecosystem. Years of diving along the Visakhapatnam coast have also exposed him to the extent of marine pollution, with plastic and other discarded material becoming part of the habitat of marine species.

That experience has also found its way into dive training. Participants are encouraged to understand the marine environment they are entering and to take part in ocean clean-up activities, making conservation part of the learning process rather than an activity separate from diving.

“People protect what they experience and understand,” says Subhash. “Seeing plastic waste entangled around marine life or observing a damaged reef underwater creates a completely different connection.”

For him, responsible diving begins with recognising that divers are visitors in another habitat. Good buoyancy control, maintaining distance from marine animals, avoiding contact with corals and other sensitive organisms, and preventing anchor damage are essential. He is also careful about describing scuba tourism as entirely carbon-free, since boats, transport and equipment carry an environmental cost.

“Marine tourism can be designed to have a very low environmental footprint,” he says. “The focus should be on minimising that footprint and ensuring that tourism gives something back to the ecosystem rather than only taking from it.”

title: Keralam’s 24×7 specialty care rollout falters amid political pushback

content.value: The government’s attempts to provide 24×7 specialty care services in general and district hospitals is faltering, with the Health department barely able to run round-the-clock services in Punalur taluk hospital, where the initiative was piloted, despite concerns raised by stakeholders about the acute shortage of human resources in Health Services.

Health officials said that the idea had been to redeploy doctors with PG qualification, working in the periphery hospitals as assistant surgeons, at Punalur. However, this proposal has reportedly been met with stiff resistance from the local political leadership as well as the people.

Many PG doctors who had been pulled from institutions in Yeroor, Neendakara, Thevalakkara, Mayyanad, Kundara, Pathanapuram, Nedungolam, could not be retained at Punalur because of political interventions at the local level, who demanded their return.

It was last month that the Health Minister made the announcement that in the first phase, 24x7 services specialty services will be provided in General Medicine, General Surgery, Orthopaedics, Anaesthesia, Paediatrics, and Gynaecology.

The Kerala Government Medical College Officers’ Association (KGMOA) had pointed out that there are 799 vacancies of doctors in the Health Service — of which, 300 vacancies are in the specialty cadre — making it impractical that round-the-clock service provision can be made possible through just working arrangements, without post creation.

The government had, however, maintained that they had studied the patient load in various institutions and that judicious redeployment of specialist doctors from hospitals where patient load was much less, was enough for the time being to provide round-the-clock specialty services in many districts. It was pointed out that even some senior residents from Kollam Government Medical College could be utilised on working arrangement basis to provide specialty services at Punalur.

The government later placated the KGMOA that the plan was to provide specialty services from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., and teleconsultation services from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m. It was also stated that a minimum of nine specialist doctors in each medical specialty will be ensured in all hospitals so that 24x7 specialty services can be run smoothly.
Key challenges

“We could run the scheme if at least six specialist doctors could be made available in every speciality. Even that has not happened and the pressure from local political leadership could not be overcome. As for doctors, none are keen on seeing this initiative work and are unwilling to step out of their comfort zone,” a Health department official said.
At present, Punalur has just two or three PG doctors in each specialty against the nine promised.

In Malappuram, the idea was that the 24x7 specialty services can be introduced at Tirur and Nilambur by redeploying doctors from Manjeri Medical College on a temporary basis but this has not happened reportedly due to non-cooperation from doctors.
KGMOA State president PK Sunil denied that government doctors were resisting the initiative as it would affect the private practice that they are legally allowed to do after work hours.

“Only about 30% of the government doctors have the so-called “lucrative” private practice. The basic issue is that unless the human resource shortage is resolved, this plan will  not work. We are not resisting the initiative but when a specialist is moved from the  periphery hospital, there will be local protest,” he said.

Post creation is not as straightforward as it is being made out, as the Finance department is is no position to approve such proposals. Even during the previous government’s term, the Health department secured only 202 posts out of the 1,520 positions it sought, and that result was achieved after prolonged negotiations.
The Health department has now pushed a proposal to the government for the creation of 1,120 posts of specialist doctors and that of 520 posts of casualty medical officers, sources said.

title: GERD is more than just heartburn: why it’s important to understand the difference

content.value: Heartburn is commonly described as acidity and treated with antacids. But gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is not simply acidity. It occurs when the stomach contents repeatedly move into the oesophagus because the normal anti-reflux barrier does not function effectively.

“GERD is not simply a problem of producing too much acid,” said Vishnu Abishek Raju, senior consultant, medical gastroenterology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. Heartburn, therefore, is a symptom, rather than a diagnosis. Some people living with reflux have visible inflammation of the oesophagus, while others have symptoms without any visible injury.
GERD is common in India. A 2021 analysis of nine Indian studies involving 20,614 people estimated its pooled prevalence at 15.6%.
How reflux occurs
The lower oesophageal sphincter acts as a valve between the oesophagus and stomach. It can undergo brief, inappropriate relaxations, allowing stomach contents to move upwards.

A hiatal hernia can weaken the anti-reflux barrier by allowing part of the stomach to move above the diaphragm. Obesity, particularly excess abdominal fat, increases pressure within the abdomen, while delayed gastric emptying can increase the volume and pressure inside the stomach.
The oesophagus also has protective mechanisms. Saliva helps clear refluxed material, while alkaline mucus helps limit acid-related injury.

“People may have acid reflux within a stipulated period. But if that goes beyond the protective mechanisms of the body, those defensive mechanisms fail and the food pipe can ger damaged, a condition called  oesophagitis,” said Arul Prakash, clinical lead and senior consultant in medical gastroenterology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai.
Why symptoms can be misleading
The amount of reflux does not always correspond to the severity of symptoms.

“Some people have increased sensitivity of the oesophagus, so even normal amounts of reflux can produce significant burning or chest discomfort,” Dr. Abishek Raju said. This includes reflux hypersensitivity and functional heartburn. In reflux hypersensitivity, symptoms are linked to reflux events despite normal overall reflux exposure. In functional heartburn, symptoms occur without evidence that reflux is responsible.
“These are people who may feel a burning sensation with almost anything they eat because the nerves in the food pipe are very sensitive,” Dr. Arul Prakash said.
This is one reason why simply increasing acid-suppressing medicines does not necessarily resolve persistent symptoms.
Establishing the diagnosis
A response to a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) can support a diagnosis of GERD, but it does not prove that reflux is the cause.
When symptoms continue despite appropriately used treatment, doctors may need to investigate other causes, including oesophageal motility disorders and disorders of oesophageal sensitivity.

Endoscopy is particularly important when there are alarm symptoms such as difficulty or pain while swallowing, bleeding, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting or anaemia. It can detect oesophagitis, ulcers, strictures and Barrett’s oesophagus.

A normal endoscopy, however, does not exclude reflux. In such cases, 24-hour pH-impedance monitoring can measure reflux episodes, distinguish acid from non-acid reflux and assess whether symptoms occur in association with reflux.
Manometry assesses pressure and movement within the oesophagus and can identify motility disorders. It is also used in selected patients before anti-reflux procedures.

Chest discomfort should not automatically be attributed to GERD because cardiac pain can have a similar presentation. Even discomfort after a heavy meal cannot by itself establish reflux. In people with cardiovascular risk factors, cardiac causes may need to be assessed first.
Lifestyle measures
Weight loss can reduce reflux symptoms in people who are overweight or obese. Avoiding food for about three hours before lying down can help, particularly with night-time symptoms.

Food triggers vary. Rather than eliminating multiple foods routinely, patients should  identify those that consistently worsen their symptoms. Coffee, spicy and high-fat foods, chocolate, mint and acidic foods can trigger symptoms in some people.
For night-time reflux, raising the head end of the bed and, for some people, sleeping on the left side may help.
Complications and treatment

Persistent GERD can cause erosive oesophagitis, ulcers and strictures. It  can also lead to Barrett’s oesophagus, in which the lining of the lower oesophagus changes. Barrett’s is associated with an increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
New difficulty in swallowing, painful swallowing, unexplained weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools or persistent vomiting require medical evaluation.

For patients with objectively confirmed reflux who remain significantly symptomatic, endoscopic or surgical treatment may be considered in selected cases. Laparoscopic fundoplication is one surgical option, while endoscopic anti-reflux procedures are available for some patients.

title: Deaf adults have distinctly superior peripheral vision, finds new study

content.value: In a remarkable example of the human brain’s adaptability to sensory loss, scientists have found that people with deafness develop superior peripheral vision, which is  vision outside the eyes’ central focus.

Researchers from the Universities of York and Sheffield used MRI scans along with visual stimuli among 16 hearing adults and 16 deaf adults and compared them. They found that the latter group responded to objects and movements even in the far-reaches of their eyesight, granting them an extra advantage in sensing their environment and detecting danger.
How this happens

The brain is rewired, with a redistribution of neural resources: among the deaf, there was a greater neural weightage given to far-peripheral vision in the primary visual cortex (the part of the brain responsible for deconstructing visual input) and the lateral geniculate nucleus (a visual relay centre situated deep within the brain).

“The brain does a really clever thing, in that it doesn’t expand overall visual capacity, but does a type of trade-off that redistributes its existing resources,” Heidi Baseler, co-author from the University of York’s Department of Psychology and the Hull York Medical School, explained in a release.
The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

In people with deafness, this adjustment is particularly important as it enables them to better catch “unexpected events that might happen just out of the central line of sight, that those of able hearing would be aware of more acutely through the sound that they might make,” and therefore could avoid, say, a car collision, for instance, Dr. Baseler said.

Interestingly, the brain does not entirely expand its visual processing capacity, but provides more power to peripheral vision and a little less to the central visual field to people with deafness. This finding could help better understand of how the brain adapts to sensory loss.
The compensation effect
It has, in fact, been a long-held belief that those with a sensory deficit develop a stronger ability with other senses as compensation, also known as the ‘compensation effect’.

And this has been scientifically proven in several instances. For instance, 20 years ago, researchers studied the major sensory differences between the visually impaired and sighted persons, and found that the average pure tone hearing (the quietest sounds a person can hear) threshold of people with blindness was significantly higher than that of sighted ones. The paper was published in the International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics.
This research result could help future designers “incorporate human factors in product design,” particularly with respect to visually disabled users, said the paper.

title: FSSAI proposes draft amendment to ensure only milk-derived products are represented as ‘Paneer’

content.value: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed a draft amendment to the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011, to restrict the manufacture and sale of analogue products as “Paneer” and prevent consumers from being misled about the nature and composition of such products, noted a release issued by the Union Health Ministry on Thursday.

The proposed Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Amendment Regulations, 2026 seek to insert a new clause under Regulation 2.1.1 of the existing regulations, specifically covering “paneer made of constituents not derived from milk”.

Under the proposed amendment, products already licensed or registered under the ‘Analogue in Dairy Context’ category would be required to discontinue the use of the term “Paneer” in their nomenclature, labelling or marketing.

The proposed amendment is aimed at ensuring that the nomenclature and presentation of food products accurately reflect their nature and composition, thereby enabling consumers to make informed choices.

As the notification is a draft regulation, FSSAI has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public. The draft regulations will be taken into consideration after the expiry of 60 days from the date on which copies of the Official Gazette containing the notification are made available to the public.

title: When cancer treatment is no longer working

content.value: The hardest conversation in cancer care rarely begins with the words, “There is nothing more we can do.” It usually begins much earlier. “Should we tell him?” “Can we try one more treatment?” “Will she lose hope if she knows?”

These questions are asked quietly: in hospital corridors, outside intensive care units, or after doctors have left the room. They are spoken in whispers because families are not simply making medical decisions; they are trying to protect someone they love.

As a palliative medicine physician working alongside oncology teams, I have learned that when treatment is no longer working as expected, families often find themselves facing conversations they never imagined having. The challenge is not only accepting that the disease has changed; it is learning how to talk about what comes next.
The conversations we prepare least for

Modern oncology has transformed countless lives. New drugs, targeted therapies, immunotherapy and better supportive care have helped many people live longer than ever before. Yet an important gap remains.

We prepare families remarkably well for chemotherapy schedules, blood tests and scan reports. We prepare them far less for conversations about uncertainty. What happens if the treatment stops helping? How much should the patient know? When should children be told? How do we decide what matters most now?
These questions do not signal that hope has disappeared. They signal that hope is changing.

A young man I recently cared for had advanced blood cancer and was admitted to the ICU with severe pain. Over the next few days, his greatest distress was not only physical. Watching critically ill patients around him, he became convinced that he would be next. When he finally asked, “Am I going to die?” he was not asking for a statistical answer. He was asking whether someone would help him understand what was happening.

Another family kept asking whether there was “one last option.” As our conversation unfolded, it became clear that they were not asking for another medicine. They wanted enough time to gather siblings from different cities, celebrate one more birthday together, and prepare for conversations they had been postponing. Often, the real question is different from the one being asked  aloud.
Weaving honesty and hope

Many families worry that honest conversations will extinguish hope. In reality, compassionate communication does not require choosing between honesty and kindness. Patients frequently sense when their condition is changing, even when nobody says it directly. Silence can sometimes create greater fear than truth because people begin imagining conversations they are not allowed to have.

Good communication means understanding how much information a patient wishes to receive, respecting cultural and family dynamics, and revisiting discussions as situations evolve. It is rarely a single conversation. More often, it is a series of conversations built on trust.

Hope also evolves. Early in illness, hope may mean cure. Later, it may mean attending a daughter’s wedding, spending time at home instead of the hospital, sleeping through the night without pain, or simply being able to share one meaningful conversation with a loved one.
What palliative care adds
One of the biggest misconceptions is that palliative care begins only after treatment ends.

In reality, it works alongside cancer treatment by helping patients manage pain, breathlessness, nausea, anxiety, fatigue and caregiver distress while supporting difficult decision-making. Some of the most meaningful palliative care conversations happen while patients are still receiving active treatment. Instead of asking only, “What is the next treatment?”, we also ask: “What matters most to you?”; “What are you hoping for?” and “What are you worried about?”
These questions often reveal priorities that laboratory values never can.
Here are some conversations families should not delay having with loved ones who have cancer. When facing advanced cancer, especially, these discussions are easier before a crisis occurs.
These conversations are not about giving up. They are about giving families the chance to make decisions with clarity instead of panic.
Care that continues

There is one moment I return to often. A family once told me, after losing someone they loved, “We don’t remember every medicine that was given. We remember that she wasn’t in pain, that we were able to sit together, and that we got to say goodbye.”

Years later, families rarely remember every chemotherapy cycle. They remember whether someone explained what was happening; whether suffering was relieved; whether they felt alone. Perhaps that is the real purpose of these conversations. Not to predict the future; not to remove grief: but to ensure that even when treatment changes, care never does.
(Dr. V. Divya Sai is a palliative medicine specialist at MNJ Institute of Oncology & Regional Cancer Centre, Hyderabad. vdivyasai22@gmail.com)

title: Inputs from ASHAs to shape AI-enabled training platform for cervical cancer screening in Assam

content.value: The field experiences of about 110 Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) will help design an Artificial Intelligence-enabled training platform and a multilingual voice chatbot to strengthen cervical cancer screening and community counselling in rural Assam.

The George Institute for Global Health India and Cachar Cancer Hospital and Research Centre in southern Assam’s Barak Valley will develop digital tools based on these ASHAs’ inputs. They shared their day-to-day challenges with a team of trainers, doctors, programme coordinators, researchers, and technologists at a workshop in Silchar.
The workshop, organised recently, was part of a three-year pilot study on leveraging AI for more effective cervical cancer screening funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research.
The ASHAs discussed the day-to-day challenges they face, the support that would actually help them, and how technology could make their community visits and counselling easier.

During the workshop, the ASHAs reviewed 155 common questions people ask about cervical cancer and screening. They used a simple voting system to identify which questions came up most frequently in the field, raised by women, husbands, family members, and others in their communities.

According to experts who conducted the workshop, the exercise highlighted that the questions ASHAs face most often in the field are not always the same as those considered clinically important. They said these insights will inform the development of a chatbot knowledge base that addresses both priority health information needs and the practical concerns ASHAs encounter during their work.

“This workshop started with a simple principle: technology for ASHAs should be designed with ASHAs. Their experience of explaining screening, responding to concerns, and finding answers in real time will guide the language, content, and functions of this AI platform. We aim to develop clinically validated support that fits their work, rather than adding another digital burden,” Anita Gadgil, principal investigator of the project and senior research fellow at The George Institute for Global Health, said.
Digital tech usage

The workshop also explored the ASHAs’ comfort and confidence with digital technology. Younger and middle-aged ASHAs said they regularly use mobile phones to report, communicate, and access information. ASHAs in the older age groups said they find digital tools and language more challenging but expressed a strong willingness to learn and become more confident about using them.

ASHAs also mapped out their career paths, including training, staying sharp on what they have learned, counselling women on pregnancy or childbirth concerns, walking people through test results, and making the right referrals. Through this process, many ASHAs recognised their knowledge gaps and discussed using tools like flipcharts to brush up when needed.

The ASHAs further highlighted the value of voice-based interactions in the local language, simple-language content, and search functions that reflect how ASHAs naturally ask questions. They also suggested features such as short audio-visual lessons, frequently asked questions, reminders, quizzes, and progress tracking.

Cervical cancer is a major health concern in India, and gaps in awareness and screening continue to get in the way of early detection. ASHAs often bridge that gap, reaching women in their communities, explaining what screening involves, and connecting them to care.

title: How will new NCAHP regulations impact allied and healthcare professionals? | Explained

content.value: To establish a comprehensive framework for registration of allied and healthcare professionals (AHP) in both the State Registers and the Central Register, the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions (NCAHP) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare notified the Registration of Allied and Healthcare Professionals Regulations, 2026 on August 31, 2026, and published it in the Gazette of India on September 15, 2026.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)

Under the new regulations,  all allied and healthcare professionals spanning 57 vocations across 10 broad disciplines, including physiotherapists, dietitians, lab technologists, forensic psychologists, among others, will soon have to register in the State and Central registers to practise in their chosen fields.

Registration certificates, including digital certificates featuring the Unique Identification (UID) number and a secure QR code, will be issued to the professionals by the Commission or the respective State Council. This will facilitate identification and verification of registered professionals and support greater transparency in the delivery of allied and healthcare services. The registration and payment of the fee will be processed on a dedicated online portal developed by the Commission.

“These regulations mark a leap towards streamlining the allied and healthcare workforce. Unless and until the professional gets the UID, he/she will not be able to practise/work. There is a penalty of up to 6 months to two years’ jail term under the NCAHP Act-21 if the professional practices without registration,” Dr. Yagna Unmesh Shukla, chairperson of NCAHP said.

“The regulations also aim to bring uniformity in the registration of allied and healthcare professionals and ensure renewal. With this registration, the actual number of qualified professionals will be available, as well as the difference between qualified and non-qualified professionals, which is also one of the key objectives of the NCAHP Act-21,” she added.
Public access

Highlighting that the registration process is the first of its kind in the history of allied and healthcare professions, Dr. Shukla says that the regulations provide a real-time synchronisation between the State Registers and the Central Register through an integrated online system.

Further, the Central and State Registers will be accessible to the public through the websites of the Commission and the respective State Councils, which will display the prescribed particulars of registered professionals.

Since only persons meeting the prescribed eligibility requirements, including recognised qualifications and the applicable exit examination requirements, will be eligible for regular registration, this will provide an important safeguard for patients and service users by promoting the practice of appropriately qualified professionals.

The public will be able to verify the registration status and relevant details of allied and healthcare professionals through the websites of the Commission and the respective State Councils. Professionals residing in a State or Union Territory where a functional State Council has not yet been established may register directly with the Central Register.

A key feature of the Regulations is the flexibility they give to allied and healthcare professionals to register in one State and practise in another State. “This will mitigate the hassles professionals face when applying for registration in another state. All they now need to do is fill out the form and inform the state in which they reside of the state where they intend to practise, so that this information remains on record. Since each registered professional is provided with a UID number, all their records are documented, facilitating the smooth transfer of registration details from one state to another,” Dr. Shukla said.

Apart from registration certificates, including digital certificates featuring the UID and a secure QR code, registered allied and healthcare professionals will also have access to a Good Standing Certificate. It will help professionals pursue any foreign education or profession or participate in student exchange programmes outside India. “There is a big difference between registration and a Good Standing Certificate. Registration is the licence to practise in India, whereas a Certificate of Good Standing is issued by the State Council when required by various countries for professionals who wish to work or study in those countries,” Dr. Shukla says.
Registration of foreign-qualified professionals

The Regulations establish a pathway for Indian citizens holding foreign qualifications in allied and healthcare. A foreign-qualified allied and healthcare professional will be considered eligible to apply for registration provided his qualification is recognised by the Commission, or he has completed the prescribed credential equivalency evaluation, and has also passed the relevant exit examination, where applicable. “It is important to have an equivalence process of foreign qualified professionals in place for the safety of the patients,” Dr. Shukla adds.

There is also provision for temporary registration for eligible foreign-qualified Indian professionals for specific, time-bound purposes, including postgraduate or specialty education, fellowships, clinical research, observerships, advanced workshops, expert visits, and voluntary community service. Such registration remains subject to the conditions laid down in the Regulations and applicable regulatory guidelines.
Validity period

Under the regulations, the registration will remain valid for five years, renewable upon the fulfilment of Continuing Professional Development (CPD) requirements through approved online and offline modes. This means that professionals must upgrade themselves professionally (15 hours per year) by attending seminars, conferences, workshops, training programmes and faculty development programmes.

“It is important for professionals to update and upgrade themselves in their respective professions. Since the regulations are being implemented for the first time, flexibility in the CPD programme is being permitted. This explains why 50% of these participations in online mode are being considered,” Dr. Shukla said.

Additionally, the Commission is making efforts to introduce provisional registration for professionals currently practising in the allied and healthcare sector who lack the prescribed primary qualifications. Such professionals will be provided with an option to undergo a bridge course to attain eligibility for regular registration. The Commission is making concerted efforts to introduce provisional registration for professionals currently practising in the allied and healthcare sector who lack the prescribed primary qualifications.

“Those who are practising for many years and are not qualified as per the provisions of the Act will be registered under the Provisional Registration Act and will have to undergo a prescribed Bridge course within the given time period to attain eligibility for regular registration,” Dr. Shukla said.
Interim registrations

The Regulations have also introduced provisions for interim registration for students enrolled in recognised institutions who are undertaking internships, clinical training, observerships, or practical coursework required to complete an allied and healthcare qualification. Interim registration must be initiated by the recognised institution and obtained from the concerned State Council. No fee will be charged for interim registration applications, the NCAHP regulations stated.
(Rajlakshmi Ghosh is a journalist with over three decades of experience in media houses and educational institutions)

title: The Quest to be a Science Superpower: Where India’s Research Is and What It Will Take to Get Ahead

content.value: Moving past celebratory headlines of space exploration and vaccine manufacturing, this essential e-book asks the tough questions about what it really takes to convert research into industrial capability, and capability industrial into global influence.

The Hindu Group’s e-book, The Quest to be a Science Superpower: Where India’s Research Is and What It Will Take to Get Ahead acknowledges India’s surge in R&D spending, patent filings, and its vast STEM talent pool. At the same time, it unflinchingly examines the persistent systemic barriers that hold the nation back. By comparing India’s trajectory with established giants like the U.S. and China, as well as the East Asian “tigers,” the authors reveal crucial missing links in India’s ambitions. The book also outlines the rigorous road to Viksit Bharat by 2047, arguing that true superpower status demands moving from being a mere assembly hub to becoming a foundational innovator.

Through expert analyses and commentary informed by experience and skill, the book dissects the ingredients needed to build a robust, interconnected innovation ecosystem. It also explores the gaps in translating laboratory research into commercial development, the heavy administrative burdens stifling world-class breakthroughs, the concerning “brain drain” of top talent, and the dangerous rise of institutionalised pseudoscience.
Read this for a piercing, balanced examination of the nation’s scientific and technological landscape.
WHAT’S INSIDE?
