title: Tesla is beginning Semi electric truck deliveries

content.value: Tesla is beginning deliveries of its Semi ​trucks to a first set of customers this week, executives said at ‌its plant in Sparks, Nevada, almost nine years after ​CEO Elon Musk unveiled the electric big rigs.

The ⁠Semi, designed for long-haul freight, expands the market for Tesla, known for its electric sedans and SUVs, into commercial freight haulers at a time ‌when diesel prices in the US have soared to record highs.
Tesla did not disclose production volume plans ‌or pricing of the trucks at a webcast event late ‌on ⁠Thursday at the plant. It reiterated plans to build ⁠50,000 Semis a year at the Nevada plant.
Musk did not attend the event. In a recorded video message he said: “I’d recommend placing more orders if ​you haven’t already, but the ‌waiting list is already pretty significant.”
Customers, including PepsiCo, DHL and US Foods, were invited on stage, and trucks with their logos were shown parked outside.

The long-range variant, loaded, can drive ‌500 miles with one charge. “That’s 500 real-world miles. Our ​customers have validated it,” said Dan Priestley, Tesla’s director of Semi truck engineering. A standard variant has 325 ⁠miles of range.
The Semi was first unveiled in 2017 and production was expected to start in 2019.

The first truck eventually rolled ‌off the high-volume production line in April and volume production was set to start this year. However, Tesla’s July shareholder letter said that production of Semi would begin in 2026, removing an earlier forecast for volume production this year.
Tesla began limited deliveries to customers including PepsiCo in the US in late 2022. ‌Delays, rising competition and a reversal in EV policies in the US ​have since raised concerns about demand.

Still, Tesla this week received an order for 2,500 Semis from a coalition ⁠of the world’s largest cargo-owning shippers, including Microsoft and PepsiCo, according to ⁠clean transportation nonprofit Catalyst Mobility. That is nearly double the existing US fleet of electric Class 8 trucks, ‌the nonprofit said.
Last month, Swedish freight technology company Einride AB announced a deal to add 500 Semi trucks to its ​fleet.

title: Oracle’s Project Jupiter delay sends ripple through AI financing

content.value: Oracle’s move to protect itself against potential delays at a massive data centre project ‌developed by Blue Owl in New Mexico sent a chill through the trillion-dollar market for AI ​infrastructure financing, according to interviews with bankers and investors.

Oracle issued a force majeure notice in connection with Jupiter, ⁠a data centre campus Blue Owl unit STACK Infrastructure is building to support OpenAI, the latest setback for a sector where lenders and investors are growing more cautious about financing the industry’s breakneck expansion.

Blue Owl said the notice did not alter the parties’ commitment to the ‌project. Even so, the event is reverberating through discussions around other proposed data centre financings, including SB Energy, which is developing a campus to serve OpenAI in Ohio, a person close to its financing said. SB Energy ‌decided this week to delay its IPO.

Companies can use force majeure provisions when events beyond their control make ‌it ⁠difficult to meet their contractual obligations. Lawyers say such provisions are becoming more common in data centre development ⁠agreements, raising concerns among lenders and investors.

“The financing side of the AI buildout is starting to ask much harder questions than the demand side,” said Sean McDevitt, a partner at management consulting firm Arthur D. Little. “The underlying demand still appears very strong, but investors and lenders are increasingly focused on how ​risk is allocated.”

With interest rates in the US ‌rising to levels last seen two decades ago, Wall Street is intensifying its scrutiny of the economics and the politics of deals that just months ago appeared settled — meaning that the participation in a deal of highly rated firms such as Oracle isn’t necessarily enough to soothe anxious investors.

The pullback comes as AI-related capital spending by the six biggest US ‌technology companies is projected to reach around $1 trillion in 2027, according to Moody’s — raising concerns among lenders about ​whether markets can absorb the volume of issuance without wider pricing pressure or tighter terms.

Investors and lenders are studying the Oracle situation as a real-world example of how contractual protections may ⁠be tested and who pays the bill when projects run into delays outside the parties’ control, they said.

The program is being delayed by a year, said the person familiar with Oracle’s notice and the deal. Blue Owl has about $3 billion of equity invested ‌in the project and earns a lower return during construction, with returns increasing once the data centre is completed, the person familiar with the terms said.
Oracle invoked force majeure due to delays securing power to the site, the person familiar with the matter said. Delaying completion pushes back the start of those higher returns for Blue Owl.

As developers race to build AI infrastructure at unprecedented scale, the contracts underpinning those projects are changing quickly, said Rajat Rana, a New York-based partner at law firm Quinn Emanuel.
“These contracts are so rapidly evolving. If you look at a data center contract from January this year and a ‌contract today, it’s massively different,” he said.

At least 45 projects worth $68 billion faced opposition from community groups in the second quarter of 2026, according to research ​firm Data Center Watch, after 75 projects worth about $130 billion were disrupted in the first quarter. Banks are involved in several projects that face community action.
Earlier this year, Blue Owl struggled to ⁠syndicate financing for a $4 billion data centre project in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, anchored by CoreWeave.
“Blue Owl, STACK Infrastructure and Oracle remain fully aligned on ⁠Project Jupiter. This notice does not change the financial commitments to this multiyear project,” the company said.
Oracle stock fell 3.5% on Thursday, after media reports of the notice. Blue Owl closed 3.6% lower.

Data centre developments including Meta’s ‌project in El Paso, Texas, and Related Digital’s planned $16 billion Oracle-focused campus in Saline Township, Michigan, have faced opposition from residents of those areas.
Blackstone’s QTS in July said it had terminated its planned Digital Gateway data centre project in Virginia ​and withdrawn the associated filings after years of planning and regulatory review.

title: China fuels rush to turn AI video into an industry

content.value: When Zhu Zhili was looking for a base to set ​up an artificial intelligence film studio in China two years ago, there was just one clear choice: the southern city of Shenzhen with its vast tech ecosystem.
This ‌year, AI filmmaker Zhu said he has fielded calls from officials in cities and industrial parks across China, ​all with the same pitch: bring your AI film business here.
“I am approached every day by a range of cities, ⁠from major metropolitan areas to smaller localities,” Zhu said, “hoping we can establish either technology or the company there.”
Those appeals reflect a major push by China to embed artificial intelligence into every corner of the economy – including the latest movies showing at cinemas.

Local governments have responded by promising to build tech clusters and offering subsidies to ‌AI filmmakers and startups. That is straight out of a familiar industrial policy playbook, treating AI-generated content the way China built electric vehicles, solar panels and robotics into globally competitive industries.
The result is a fast-emerging industry of AI filmmakers, studios and streaming platforms in ‌China seeking an early lead in production techniques and distribution.

China has created the “best environment” for AI filmmakers with “cheap rent, living allowance and ‌computing ⁠support,” said Zhu, who also heads the AI-Generated Content (AIGC) department at China Wit Media in Shenzhen.
Zhu runs his personal studio in ⁠Shenzhen from a shared workspace with the backing of the city government and Hong Kong Polytechnic University.

While China’s all-out push for AI in film has been welcomed by filmmakers like Zhu, the industry faces growing risks familiar to other sectors showered with state support. As companies step up production of goods like cars and ​consumer products, domestic demand remains constrained, driving down prices in what ‌many see as a race to the bottom.

There are signs that AI video content may already be approaching overcapacity. In the first half of the year, 221,900 new AI shows were launched on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, but only 1,055 drew more than 100 million views, a typical benchmark of success, according to DataEye.
Filmmakers say they are drawn to AI by the low production costs.
In the first ‌half of 2026, the cost of producing AI short dramas plunged from 5,000 yuan ($747) per minute to just a few hundred yuan, ​according to state broadcaster CCTV.

“A normal wedding scene might cost me 60,000 yuan to shoot conventionally,” said Pan Xiaojun, a postgraduate film-directing student based in Hainan, southern China. “But with AI, I can bring the same surreal scene to life ⁠for just 1,400 yuan.”
Pan said subsidies and rent waivers from a local government in Hainan allowed him to push his computing costs down further.
Other cities have also stepped up incentives.
Shanghai in May introduced measures to accelerate AI-powered micro-drama production, offering computing power and cloud-based AI models to cut costs and ‌support overseas distribution.
Beijing has a 260 million yuan fund to support audiovisual technology. Its Huairou district, a hub of China’s film industry, offers producers of short AI dramas vouchers to reduce computing costs.
Shenzhen is also stepping up efforts to attract AI film talent, offering technical support for video production, visual effects and content generation, as well as subsidised rent.
Major Chinese streaming platform iQIYI is “all-in” on AI, CEO Gong Yu said in August. It is offering some creators subsidies for AI content that streams on the platform.

The National Film Administration has granted a public-screening licence to the 90-minute science-fiction epic “Sanxingdui: Future Memories”, the first AI film produced by a major Chinese studio to receive regulatory approval for theatrical release in China.
The film ‌is due to be released this year, producer Bona Film Group said.
While Chinese consumers have been receptive to AI-generated content, there has nonetheless been a backlash.
Chinese actors have raised ​concerns over the use of their likenesses in AI films, fuelling worries about copyright infringement and job losses for voice actors.
Consumers also complain of plagiarism and a lack of originality.

“Some people directly blend other people’s original characters or dance clips into ⁠AI-generated content without any credit. I think that behaviour is completely unacceptable,” said Wen, a 22-year-old AI content fan.
The unexpected box-office success of the crudely animated, conventionally ⁠produced film, “Niu Lai,” was seen by some as a backlash against AI content.
China requires explicit labelling for AIGC but has yet to introduce clear copyright rules for it.
For now, AI film content produced in China is surging, and even going abroad.
Director Cao Yiwen ‌premiered her AI-animated film during the World AI Film Festival in Cannes in April, and said she thought that China was taking the lead in the industry.

“France and the rest of Europe are still watching and waiting to see whether China will introduce clear laws,” ​she said. “We fell behind in the first two industrial revolutions, so perhaps this is the Third Industrial Revolution.”

title: BrainyBotz STEM Challenge 2026: Young innovators to design cooler homes

content.value: What if beating the heat begins not with an air-conditioner, but with an idea? That is the question posed by the BrainyBotz STEM Innovation Challenge 2026. The contest invites children aged eight to 16 to explore practical ways of cooling homes without depending on expensive air-conditioning systems or high-cost equipment. Themed ‘Beat the Heat: Cool Homes for All’, the challenge places everyday heat and its impact on families as  an opportunity for young minds to innovate.

Participants, working in teams of two to four, are expected to investigate why homes become hot, understand the science of heat transfer and develop solutions using locally available materials. The emphasis is on affordability, safety and scalability, with proposed solutions aiming to reduce indoor temperatures by 4–8°C.

The competition is divided into three age groups. Explorers aged eight to 10 will observe, sketch and explain their ideas, while junior inventors aged 11 to 13 will build small prototypes, take temperature readings and document their findings. For those aged 14 to 16, the design engineers category adds physics, local cost comparisons and a presentation with a Q&A.

The challenge follows the complete innovation cycle from research and idea development to prototyping, testing, documentation and presentation. Registrations are open till September 25, with the first-level idea submission due on October 10. The finals and awards are scheduled for November 21, with the final projects to be showcased at Brainybotz’ annual show of AROHA 2026.
Participants can register through BrainyBotz STEM’s website, www.brainybotz.in. For details, contact 9391442996 or email team@brainybotz.in.

title: Google to test AI chip in space

content.value: Google is preparing to launch and test its AI chip in space to understand how to scale AI hardware in orbit as part of Project Suncatcher.
The company said it was getting ready for an early test launch and working toward its next milestone in 2027.

Project Suncatcher, which was announced last year, will enable Google’s experts to test hardware survival, cooling processes, and satellite interconnectivity for machine learning infrastructure in space.
While low-Earth orbit allows access to near-constant sunlight and solar power, solar events and cosmic rays are risk factors.
The mission is slated to take place onboard the upcoming Transporter-18 rideshare mission with SpaceX, that was developed in partnership with Planet.

“Exploring space as a viable location for scalable AI compute won’t happen all at once. It takes methodical engineering, starting with proving our hardware can handle the physical and unpredictable realities of operating in orbit. This first launch is about seeing what works, identifying points of failure, and applying those findings to future missions,” said Google in a blog post.

title: Bats first originated in Europe 65 million years ago, scientists say

content.value: From the largest ever study of bat genome and fossils, scientists deduced that the world’s only flying mammals — that account for one fifth of all living mammals — likely originated in Europe, and spread to every continent except Antarctica. The scientists, in a paper in the journal Nature, pegged the bat’s evolution at 65 million years ago, in the late Palaeocene, “coinciding with increased global temperature and environmental change.”

This discovery countered previously held hypotheses that bats originated in Africa or North America. The study, that involved 137 scientists from 64 countries, working together as part of the “Bat1K” consortium, concluded that the animals spread from Europe first to Africa and then to Asia, the Americas and to Australia.

The researchers also found that the bat’s ability to fly and echolocate (that is, when animals emit calls and then listen to the echoes to navigate and hunt, often in darkness) came about at almost the beginning of the animal’s evolution. For instance, echolocation took place before the diversification of modern bats, revealed the study of a fossil bat.
Rewriting the evolutionary tree

Co-author Sonja Vernes from the University of St. Andrews and Bat1K founder, told The Hindu that bats, being the only mammals that are able to fly, gave them “a huge advantage” when it came to dispersing across the globe. “Even today, we know that some modern bats can migrate thousands of kilometres and live in very diverse climates on every continent, except Antarctica,” said Prof. Vernes.

Scientists took decades to build the enormous dataset, which included 103 species, many rare or from remote places, representing every one of the extant 21 families. They used state-of-the-art DNA sequencing methods to compare genomes, including those of fossil bats. They updated their evolutionary tree, answering much debated questions about how bat groups are related.

Bats, which are hugely under-recognised for their ecological role, and instead seen as harbingers of disease outbreaks among people, are in fact vital in pollinating plants, controlling insect pests and dispersing seeds.
Bat-inspired approaches

No less than 1,500 species of bats exist across the globe today, and present extraordinary evolutionary adaptations. “Several species host a diversity of viruses without overt disease symptoms and show unique immune adaptations,” said the paper adding that some species are exceptionally long-lived compared with other mammals of similar body size.

Prof. Vernes said: “Now that we have this extraordinary genomic resource, we can start searching for the genetic mechanisms that make it possible for bats to live such long lives while resisting disease.” The long-term goal, she told The Hindu, is that “once we know how they do this, we can design bat-inspired approaches that could improve human health.”

title: White House asks OpenAI, Anthropic to hold models from British testers: Report

content.value: The White House has asked ​OpenAI and Anthropic to hold ‌new models from British testers ​until a US ⁠review, Politico reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter ‌and a senior US administration official.
The White House ‌wants to take steps ‌to ⁠make sure US systems are ⁠secure before the models are shared with partners, according to the report.
The ​White House, Anthropic ‌and OpenAI did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

The development comes as ‌the White House weighs cybersecurity ​risks posed by increasingly capable AI models, following a ⁠series of incidents in which AI systems gained unauthorized access ‌to real-world computer systems.
Australian officials disclosed on Wednesday that an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access ‌to files.
OpenAI and Anthropic also warned ​the United Nations Security Council about the risks posed ⁠by increasingly powerful AI systems, urging ⁠governments to work together to manage the technology.

title: Caught in kitchen garden net, rescued tiger cub returned to the wild in Assam

content.value: A tiger cub, rescued from a house in Assam’s Biswanath district on September 17, has been released in the Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve.

The forelimbs of the cub, estimated to be three months old, were found entangled in a kitchen garden net behind the house in Natungaon village. Officials said the cub could have wandered into the village after getting separated from its mother because of strong river currents.
Camera trap installed

A rescue team surveyed the neighbouring riverine islands to locate the mother. It subsequently shifted the cub to the Central Range Office of Kaziranga’s Biswanath Division for veterinary observation. C. Ramesh, Kaziranga’s Field Director, said the team transported the cub to an upstream riverine island based on information and evidence indicating that a mother with cubs was present in the area recently.

Before returning, the team installed a camera trap at the release site to gather evidence of an adult tigress in the area. They moved the cub to a more secure location after a drone survey showed that the rising water levels posed a risk to the carnivore.

“On September 23, we found pugmark evidence about 200 metres from where the cub was released. Camera-trap monitoring will continue over the next few weeks,” Panjit Basumatary of the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) said.

Earlier, a team comprising WTI and Assam Forest Department specialists treated an injured male wild elephant sighted at Kacharigaon Tea Estate in Sonitpur district. The elephant was found to have a spear-related injury on its left foreleg, resulting in severe swelling. The animal also had corneal opacity in its left eye, with suspected partial loss of vision.

The elephant was chemically immobilised, and the pus-filled wounds on its injured left foreleg were cleaned and dressed. The affected left eye was also cleaned and dressed, followed by a subconjunctival injection.

title: New Begonia species described from Arunachal Pradesh

content.value: GUWAHATI
A new species of Begonia, a genus of perennial flowering plants, has been described from Keyi Panyor district of Arunachal Pradesh.

Begonia neelamorum, the newly identified species, features in the latest issue of Taiwania, an international peer-reviewed scientific journal, alongside at least two other new members of the family Begoniaceae. They are Begonia salog from the Philippines and Begonia andariasii from Sulawesi.

Dipankar Borah, a botany teacher at Kaliabor College in central Assam’s Nagaon district, is the lead author of the study on the new species from Arunachal Pradesh. The other authors are Madhusadhan Khanal of Sikkim University, Momang Taram of Jawaharlal Nehru College in Arunachal Pradesh, and Neelam Gap, a member of the All Arunachal Pradesh Students’ Union.
During an expedition, the researchers found the single-leaf, tuberous Begonia growing on steep, moist walls along the Keyi River at about 1,000 metres above mean sea level.

They collected a specimen in May. Morphological examination and comparison with herbarium specimens showed it was closest to Begonia prolifera but differed in several characteristics, including its ovate leaves with double-serrated margins, distinct inflorescence structure, and shorter styles.
Named after a clan

The researchers named the new-to-science Begonia species after the Neelam clan of the Nyishis, the dominant community of Keyi Panyor district. Community members helped the researchers collect the plant during the “challenging” expedition.
Locals call the plant “kobiirhopu baabrai”.
Begonia neelamorum is a small plant measuring about 10-12 cm tall, with a single, sessile, light-green leaf. Its leaves have distinctive double-serrated margins and glandular hairs.
The plant produces white male and female flowers on an inflorescence emerging from the stem apex. It is currently known from one location in the district, within an area of about 3 sq. km.

Begonia neelamorum has become the 54th Begonia species recorded from India’s northeastern region. It has been provisionally assessed as data deficient under the International Union for Conservation of Nature criteria.
Begonia, one of the largest angiosperm genera, has about 2,200 accepted species distributed across tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.

title: Australian PM says OpenAI hacked government health website

content.value: A rogue OpenAI model bypassed safeguards during training and hacked an Australian government website, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said as he admonished the ChatGPT creator over an "obviously unacceptable" breach.
The AI tool sought access to a health statistics portal in June and "didn't accept no for an answer", sidestepping restrictions to breach a section hosting private files, Albanese said.
OpenAI did not raise the alarm with the Australian government until September, when it sent a message to a generic email inbox that is only checked once each day.
Global worries about the power of advanced AI tools are mounting after a string of hacking incidents involving models from both OpenAI and rival developer Anthropic.
"Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident," Albanese told reporters in New York on Wednesday.
"I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred," he said.
"It took until September 10 before there was any notification at all - and the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox."
The AI tool accessed public and non-public files hosted on an old health statistics website.
Albanese said there was "no evidence" that personal information had been accessed and that other government services had not been compromised.
"Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable."
The breach occurred in June as leading artificial intelligence company OpenAI ran training exercises to rate the performance of AI models.
It asked the model to trawl the internet for data showing how much the Australian government spent on medicine, Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher told reporters.
OpenAI said it did not spot the rogue activity until August, when it reviewed what the AI tool had been doing.
The San Francisco-based company did not alert the Australian government until September 10, when it sent an email to a generic government inbox.
"That email address is looked at once a day," Gallagher said.
"We have someone who goes and has a look through. It sometimes gets a number of notifications, sometimes many of them are hoaxes."
Defence Minister Richard Marles said the AI model had "scaled the fence".
"It asked a question, the information was not given and rather than leaving at that point, it scaled the fence."
Australia has launched a rapid review of the incident, which will include the national intelligence agency responsible for cyber security.
OpenAI said it spotted the breach while carrying out an "extensive review" of its AI models.

"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation.
"In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," the company said.
Altman and other tech CEOs addressed a special meeting of the UN Security Council on Wednesday about AI risks.

More than 100 organisations around the world, including OpenAI and Anthropic, signed an open letter last month calling for a global effort to "strengthen cyber defenses" against AI-powered cybersecurity threats.
It came after two OpenAI models escaped from a closed testing environment and broke into the internal systems of Hugging Face, a site that AI developers use to store and share code.
Anthropic recently discovered that its models had gained unauthorised access to three unidentified organisations during testing that was supposed to keep them away from "real-world" systems.
Google's consumer AI model Gemini hacked multiple systems through guessing login credentials, the company said last week.

title: Meta's Muse rekindles fears over winners and losers as personal AI agent emerges

content.value: Meta’s Muse, the first major consumer product ​to emerge under Alexandr Wang since he was hired to head its AI ⁠efforts last year, has split the fortunes of US stocks this week.

Muse, which allows users to delegate tasks such as shopping, travel booking and form-filling to an AI agent, overtook ChatGPT as the top free app on Apple’s ‌App Store and Google Play Store in the US and Canada.
The app recorded 2.8 million downloads within two weeks of its launch, posting an average daily download growth ‌of 55% in the first 10 days, according to market intelligence company Sensor Tower.

Investors worried that ‌Meta’s ⁠scale could turn Muse into a powerful comparison-shopping tool, enabling consumers to more easily ⁠find lower-cost alternatives and weakening the loyalty that often keeps users with incumbent providers.
The development dragged on several sectors this week, while Meta and AI-infrastructure related companies rallied.

“Meta has really found lightning in a bottle here and someone who partners with ​Muse is likely to be a ‌clear beneficiary off the bat to me. As far as net losers, it’s just going to take more time to find out,” said Michael O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading.
Financials stocks were the hardest-hit in the previous session and remained under pressure on Wednesday on fears ‌that the AI agent could prompt users to switch to policies with cheaper prices.

Big banks such ​as JPMorgan and Wells Fargo lost more than 3% each so far this week, while brokerage Charles Schwab was down nearly 5%. Insurers such as Marsh and ⁠Arthur J. Gallagher were down 2.4% and 4.6%, respectively.
Art Hogan, chief market strategist for B. Riley Wealth, however, said those disruption concerns were far-fetched.

“If you’re going to trust the management of your finances to something ‌that Muse found for you, then you were likely not a big payer to anyone in that industry to begin with. There’s a whole lot more that goes in asset management than who’s got the cheapest price,” he said.
Booking companies such as TripAdvisor and Booking Holdings, which rely on subscription models, have lost over 6% this week.
Planet Fitness has tanked 17%, while the New York Times is down 10%.
Other decliners included ride-hailing companies such as Uber and Lyft, and online food marketplace DoorDash .
Meta’s shares have soared nearly 13% this week and are set for their fifth-straight week of advances.

The gains were ​fueled by expectations that the mainstream consumer-focused app could generate additional annual revenue, with Truist Securities estimating it to touch at least $28.5 billion by fiscal 2030.

US-listed shares of Canada’s ⁠Shopify have jumped 11.4% this week, after it said it would use Muse to process checkouts. Payments platform ⁠PayPal has marginally gained after saying it would allow users to discover products and complete purchases through the AI agent.
Also Read : Meta’s AI model hacked another company during testing: Report
Privately held companies, including Stripe and Ticketmaster, also struck similar deals ‌with Meta.
Apps such as Muse could drive AI compute demand, accelerating AI infrastructure buildout and benefiting chip stocks.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has gained 7% since Muse’s launch and is ​set for its biggest two-week run since mid-August, with Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices among top gainers.

title: Meta launches camera-free AI glasses amid privacy pushback, teases Muse Charm product

content.value: Meta unveiled several new wearables powered by its AI models on Wednesday, including an audio-only, camera-free version of its smart glasses, amid global concerns about privacy and the filming of women and girls without their consent.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced the new lineup of glasses at the social media giant's annual Connect conference at its Menlo Park headquarters, where he also touted the company's new personal artificial intelligence assistant, Muse.

"There are almost 2 billion people in the world who wear glasses today... and we think that in the coming years, most of these are going to get upgraded to AI glasses," Zuckerberg told the audience of developers and executives.
Muse will be "the centerpiece of our vision," Zuckerberg said.

The audio-only glasses will ship on October 13 and start at $349. They arrive amid growing questions worldwide about privacy violations from tiny cameras on glasses and other wearables, which critics have dubbed "pervert" glasses.
Smart glasses let wearers take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an AI assistant.
The audio-only versions will complement the release of dozens of new smart glasses models that keep the photo and video filming option.
Building in privacy features such as a recording indicator light is "really important," Meta's vice president of AI product, Vishal Shah, told AFP on Wednesday.
"We wanted people to clearly understand that this was something that was recording, and we've only made that light more explicit over time," Shah said.
"We said a lot about that when the glasses first launched, and I think we probably need to keep repeating that more than we have been more recently because none of that's changed," he added.
With nearly four billion monthly active users across its ecosystem, Meta is betting that wearables like smart glasses can become an easy entry point for people to use its AI software.
Meta launched its first smart glasses in 2021, and last year unveiled "display" glasses that project images onto the lens.
Earlier this year, the company released its own Meta-branded AI glasses, separate from its partnership with eyewear maker EssilorLuxottica, which produces several Ray-Ban and Oakley Meta models.

Meta also announced several new styles of its flagship Meta Ray-Ban glasses. The display version, priced from $799, will soon be available in new markets including Britain, France, Italy, Germany and Canada.
The company will also soon launch mixed reality glasses that are much lighter than its earlier Quest VR headsets.
Called Meta VR Glasses, they are powered by an external battery and memory pack tethered by a cord, allowing the headset itself to be lighter.
Zuckerberg said the glasses weigh about as much as a deck of cards.
They have no external controls, relying instead on hand gestures and voice commands.
The VR Glasses will launch in spring 2027 for $1,299.
Meta has spent billions of dollars to stay competitive in AI but faces pushback on multiple fronts.
The glasses are designed to work with Muse, the company's first agentic app for consumers. It performs tasks on users' behalf like a digital personal assistant.
After connecting personal accounts, for finance, health and shopping, users can ask Muse to sign up for services, book appointments and make calls.
The Muse app became the top free app in the Google Play Store and Apple App Store, overtaking OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and Google's Gemini.
Zuckerberg teased another product on Wednesday, the Muse Charm, that will ship ahead of the holidays this year; Meta did not provide a price.
The "charm" is a small, puck-like device with a display that will allow users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone.

Amazon this week blocked Meta from using AI bots to shop automatically for users, while Instacart, Shopify and Expedia have announced partnerships to integrate their services into Muse. Meta said Walmart, Best Buy, Gap and Sephora are also partnering with the app.
Meta, which earns most of its revenue from ads on Instagram and Facebook, faces mounting child safety and privacy challenges worldwide.

In August, it settled a lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of violating consumer protection and children's online privacy laws, agreeing to pay up to $18 billion and impose restrictions for teenagers.
The company also faces age-based restrictions and bans abroad, as well as thousands of potential personal injury suits in the US.

title: How wealth shapes our view of artificial intelligence

content.value: There’s a common assumption that anxiety about artificial intelligence is universal — that everyone, everywhere, is bracing for the same disruption. But, a new Pew Research Centre Survey of over 42,000 adults across 37 countries, suggests otherwise.

The survey’s data points out that worry about AI tracks closely with wealth. The richer the country, the more its people fear AI will take their jobs, widen inequality, and disrupt daily life. The poorer the country, the less its citizens fear AI as they simply haven’t formed an opinion on it yet.
Per capita income, it turns out, may be the single best predictors of how a population feels about AI.

The researchers split 36 core countries into 18 “high-income” and 18 “middle-income” nations, using World Bank’s classifications built on gross national income per capita. The gap between the two groups shows up in nearly every question that was part of the survey.

A median of 55% of adults in high-income countries said AI will lead to fewer jobs in their country over the next decades. In middle-income countries, that figure drops nearly 20 points lower to 36%. People in poorer countries aren’t necessarily more hopeful; they’re more uncertain.
Roughly a third of the adults in middle-income nations said they simply don’t know how AI will affect jobs, compared with about a fifth in wealthy ones.
The same pattern holds for inequality. A median of 35% of adults in high-income countries believe AI will widen the gap between rich and poor, versus 22% in middle-income countries.
In general, 40% of the respondents in the wealthy nations said they were more concerned than excited about AI’s growing presence in their daily lives, compared with 31% in middle-income nations.
A clear divide

When the researchers plotted individual countries against their GDP per capita, the correlation between GDP per capita and the belief that AI cost jobs was strong. On AI awareness — the share of people who said they’ve heard or read ‘a lot’ about AI — the connection was even stronger.

Respondents in two Asian nations capture this divide. In Singapore, for instance, where GDP per capita is close to $100,000, 53% of its adults said they’ve heard or read ‘a lot’ about AI. In Bangladesh, where GDP per capita is about $2,600, just 4% of its adults reported the same level of awareness.

Loss of jobs fear follows the same pattern as roughly seven in ten or more adults in Australia, South Korea and the US expect AI to shrink the job market over the next two decades. But in Kenya, Nigeria and the Philippines, that expectation is far less common as they are yet to form a strong view on the technology.
Nearly half of Americans said the technology will widen the gap between rich and poor. In India, however, which is classified as a middle-income country, only 13% said the same.
This divergence in attitudes of people in high-income and middle-income economies seems to be a function of the level of awareness of new technologies.
People in advanced economies are far more likely to have encountered AI tools directly that have visibly threatened their job prospects.
In middle-income nations, however, where informal labour and manual work still make up a large share of employment, AI’s impact can feel more abstract.
Pew Research Centre found that in many middle-income countries, it’s the wealthier and more educated people within that country who are most likely to say AI will cost jobs or deepen inequality.

Much of the gap traces back to the same driver: people with less income and less formal education are simply more likely to say they’re unsure of this technology. Uncertainty fills the space where worry would otherwise occupy.
The bottomline is that familiarity with AI predicts concerns about AI, and that is a function of income.
Beyond income

Apart from income, age plays a major role in how respondents perceive AI. Younger adults are dramatically more aware of AI than their elders. In Spain and Greece, the awareness gap between 18-to-34-year-olds and those 50 and older exceeds 50 percentage points.
And in several wealthy nations, that awareness is translating into a distinctive kind of unease with a mix of concern, excitement and a rising tide of job-related anxiety among the young.

In the US, share of adults under 35 who say they’re concerned about AI has jumped from 40% to 55% in the last 18-24 months. In Sweden, there is a starker shift as a year ago older Swedes are more worried about AI than younger ones. But now the two groups have converged with younger adults’ concern rising.

This shows that young people in wealthy countries are the most digitally immersed, AI-literate, and most anxious lot — a combination that upends the idea that youth are optimistic about new technology.
In India, just 13% of adults surveyed said they’ve heard or read ‘a lot’ about AI. This is one of the lowest figures in this survey, trailing far behind high-income countries.

And the belief that AI will cost jobs is comparatively muted too. Among Indians 50 and older, just 20% expect fewer jobs over the next two decades, rising to 30% among those 35 to 49 and 33% among adults under 35 — a meaningful generational gap.
That youngest-oldest pattern on jobs fits the broader global trend of younger adults being warier of AI’s economic disruption.

But India breaks from the pack on general sentiment as it is one of the few countries in the survey where older adults (24%) are more likely than the youngest adults (15%) to say they’re primarily concerned rather than excited about AI in daily life — the opposite of what shows up almost everywhere else.

The implication of this survey is double-edged for citizens and governments. Concern is often what drives demand for regulation and worker protections. That means  the countries best positioned to frame laws around AI’s disruptions may be exactly the ones already feeling the most anxious about it.
Meanwhile, in the middle-income economies, the absence of alarm may reflect not resilience, but simply not having been asked the question loudly enough yet.

title: OpenAI says SEC disclosures undermine xAI’s antitrust lawsuit

content.value: ChatGPT maker OpenAI asked a Texas federal judge to throw out an antitrust lawsuit brought by Elon ​Musk’s AI startup xAI before trial, arguing that disclosures by xAI parent company ‌SpaceX undermine claims that Apple’s partnership with OpenAI shut out ​rivals.
OpenAI on Tuesday asked ⁠US District Judge Mark Pittman in Fort Worth to rule for OpenAI based on the facts so far in the case, which is now set for ‌a trial in January.
Musk’s companies sued Apple and OpenAI last year, alleging Apple violated antitrust law by exclusively ‌integrating ChatGPT into Apple Intelligence features on iPhones and other ‌Apple devices.

Apple and OpenAI have denied any wrongdoing. Apple previously said ⁠its integration deal with OpenAI was not exclusive. X said last week it has settled with Apple, but the terms have not been disclosed.

OpenAI’s new court filing ​argued that deposition testimony and other ‌evidence bolstered its defense, including recent securities disclosures from Musk’s SpaceX, which began publicly trading in June.

SpaceX’s initial public offering registration statement, OpenAI said, is “replete with disclosures diametrically opposed” to xAI’s claims of ‌competitive harm alleged in its lawsuit. The registration “bears no resemblance ​to the doomsaying in this litigation,” it said.
OpenAI denied it wields monopoly power, a necessary element to prove ⁠antitrust violations.

The company also said that by early last year Apple’s “integration of ChatGPT appeared to be off to a slow start,” which ‌was far from signaling a chatbot monopoly among iPhone users. OpenAI said it “cut its forecast for the number of incremental logged-in weekly active users that it expected to obtain as a direct result of the integration.”
By the time Musk sued, OpenAI said, “it was clear that Apple’s integration of ChatGPT was dramatically underperforming.”
Apple, OpenAI and xAI did ‌not immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: Interview | Ornithologist Asad Rahmani on his new book ‘Where Have the Birds Gone?’

content.value: Noted conservationist and ornithologist Asad Rahmani’s latest book, Where Have the Birds Gone? Empty Nests. Quiet Skies. One Question (Indian Pitta, an imprint of Juggernaut Books), is dedicated to lost species: “the mountain quail, pink-headed duck and numerous other species that were exterminated, with an apology from humankind”. This sombre beginning sets the tone of his nuanced book.

Where Have the Birds Gone? illuminates “the scale of the crisis confronting birds today — a crisis unfolding not with a single dramatic blow, but through the steady erosion of safe skies, quiet habitats and the fragile continuity on which avian life depends,” writes the Lucknow-based Rahmani, former director of Bombay Natural History Society and author of 27 books and 150 peer-reviewed scientific papers.

The book begins by focusing on 14 of India’s most threatened birds, including the white-bellied heron, green munia, the Bengal florican and Jerdon’s courser, evaluating the factors that threaten their existence. These include habitat loss and fragmentation, alien species, wind farms, power lines, dams, illegal pet trade, pesticides, poaching, glass buildings, and free-ranging stray dogs, which have become apex predators in many ecosystems, according to the 76-year-old. “In India, dogs are reported to have attacked 80 wild species, including 31 threatened species, four of which are critically endangered,” he writes, throwing in a sobering statistic. “In Ladakh, for instance, free-ranging dogs kill nearly 60 per cent of the chicks of the black-necked crane, a species listed by the IUCN as ‘vulnerable’ to extinction.”

The book is full of more such dispiriting facts.  For example, skylarks have declined by nearly 80% while Indian rollers have seen a 30% decline in 12 years; according to BirdLife International and the IUCN, 1,256 species — about 11.5% of all birds — are currently threatened with extinction, and fewer than 120 great Indian bustards persist, largely confined to two pockets in Rajasthan.

But it isn’t all doom and gloom. “I believe that I am an optimist (you cannot be a conservationist without being one),” he writes, citing success stories like the greater adjutant, painted stork, and spot-billed pelican, before offering conservation solutions rooted in “common sense rather than technological wizardry or cutting-edge science”.

Some of these solutions include expanding protected areas, conservation breeding, undergrounding power lines along major migratory routes and reducing free-ranging dog populations, states Rahmani, who firmly believes this. “If India truly aspires to be a Vishwaguru, a teacher to the world, then leadership must extend beyond economics and geopolitics. It must encompass sustainability, climate stability, environmental protection, equity, human rights and the rights of wildlife,” he says.
Edited excerpts from an interview:

Through birds you explore myriad facets of wildlife, from global biodiversity threats to Earth’s sixth mass extinction and climate change and human-wildlife interaction. What makes birds an effective entry point?

Birds and plants are almost the first things we see as children, which is why we feel connected to them. There are lots of positive stories about birds in our literature and culture, and birds like house sparrows and crows have become accustomed to us. Also, birds are not dangerous: no bird has killed a human being so far.

Another big reason why people like birds is that birdwatching is the second-most common (nature-related) hobby in the world, after gardening. Even if we live in small homes, we put flowers on our balconies as a symbolic gesture because we want to bring nature back into our lives. When we go birding, therefore, we aren’t just looking at birds, but at the whole environment. That’s why we end up getting concerned about other things, too.

One thing that came up in this book was that Project Tiger, while certainly offering conservation benefits, wasn’t enough to save many of our threatened birds because these birds don’t always live in protected areas. Could you tell us more?

Well, I wrote a book on India’s threatened birds in 2012. There, I analysed 156 species of threatened and near-threatened birds and where they are found. We found that 50% are not found in Project Tiger areas, or, even if they are, they don’t breed or spend much time there. For instance, the Sarus crane is found in Project Tiger areas, but it does not breed there because big cats like tigers and leopards can easily swim and eat it.

Of course, many birds have benefited from forest protection, but to say everything is protected by [flagship programmes such as] Project Tiger or Project Snow Leopard is not true. Once we accept this, we can think of other ways to protect them.

You’ve championed the Great Indian bustard for many years. The critically endangered bird nearly became India’s national bird before losing out to the peafowl. Is everything stacked against the bustards?
Everything is against them, starting with habitat change: these birds are long-lived and long-ranging. Even in areas where they are not killed, their population declines as their habitats shrink.

The biggest killer of the bustard, however, is high-tension wires. Bustards are largely terrestrial birds and only fly when disturbed by a predator, which is becoming more common because of free-ranging stray dogs in these areas.

This means that the chances of a bustard hitting a wire have increased tremendously. These birds fly at the level of these wires and have a visual blind spot: they see well to both sides but have narrow frontal vision, so they often miss what is directly in front of them. They don’t necessarily die of electrocution, but get injured and fall to the ground below, where the predator will be eagerly waiting for them.

Given that we live in a country where many underprivileged people, particularly pastoralists, fishers and indigenous people, share spaces with wildlife, how do we protect their homes and livelihoods as well as preserve what is left of our wilderness?

There is no single answer because the situation varies from species to species, culture to culture, area to area, and habitat to habitat. But we certainly have to listen to these people and try to protect these spaces through traditional methods.

Community conservation matters more than ever because population growth and shrinking available land have also reduced tolerance for wildlife. In general, if people are not harmed by an animal, they are more tolerant of it, which makes community conservation for animals like birds and reptiles much easier.
Wildlife, like leopards, for instance, become a bigger problem for understandable reasons: no one wants their child to be killed by an animal.

But India’s beauty is that, despite such a large population in such a small area, we have not lost any large animals. People in this country don’t always support conservation, but they never oppose it.
preeti.zachariah@thehindu.co.in

title: Benedict Cumberbatch interview: Why ‘How to Live on Earth’ left him ‘turbocharged’

content.value: Benedict Cumberbatch is possibly the only person who can get away with using a word like “trepidatious” in conversation. The actor, who captured our collective imagination as Sherlock, and has gone on to comfortably inhabit the MCU, as well as smaller films, used the word when talking about presenting How to Live on Earth.

The Open Planet documentary premiered on YouTube on September 20. Speaking over a video call from London, Benedict says  the question, ‘How to live on Earth?’, fascinated him. “I wanted to find out. I’d worked with Fredi (Devas, director) before on a documentary about the Antarctic, (remember penwing, penling?) which I did the voiceover for in New Zealand during the lockdown in 2020.”

It was when he read the script that Benedict felt “slightly trepidatious because there is really only one presenter of natural history documentaries, Sir David Attenborough. I was keen not to tread on those heels or be lost in trying to be that person.”
Three-pillared approach

How to Live on Earth is a very different flavour and character, the Dr Strange actor says. “It drew me in with its humour, and also the revelations of the three-pillared approach that subtitled the film, which is ‘How to Feed the Future’, ‘How to Value Nature’ and ‘How to be Human’.”

Executive producer Jonnie Hughes says Benedict was the right choice because they wanted to take a different tone with the story. “It needed to reach into people’s hearts and minds. Benedict’s back catalogue is perfect in terms of global reach. He has the air of a storyteller with an intellectual argument.”
Walk the talk

The documentary’s use of experts include  wildlife filmmaker and explorer, Dan O’Neill, climate justice activist, Xiye Bastida, and former White House chef and senior policy advisor on nutrition, Sam Kass, who helped Benedict present with authority.

“They are extraordinary and I felt bolstered for the part that I play. That’s what I like to do in my advocacy. I’m not a policy expert, a scientist or a biologist. I’m not part of an indigenous people with ancestralism. These are experts that I am in awe of, who have lived the talk, who have walked the talk. It’s key to me that I feel what I’m saying is backed up by those in the know.”
A variation of self

From mathematician Alan Turing to the coarse rancher in The Power of the Dog, Benedict has inhabited complex characters. Stepping into the role of guide was a different skin to occupy, the Academy Award-nominated actor says “It’s a variation of myself. I have a natural curiosity about the world and how we ought to be living on it. I’m invested in the idea of doing better, both personally, and as a society.”

The makers and Benedict refined both the voiceover and the piece to camera. “It wasn’t too off the beaten track for my personality. There was a quirk to it, yes, but it wasn’t a forced humour or an over-earnest tub thumping tone.”

Not wanting it to look like a performance, Benedict wished for the narration to be grounded. “There’s a presentational aspect to it. You have to hear and understand what I’m saying, the phrasing has to be weighted in the correct way, and you have to want to look at my face every now and again because I’m in it (smiles). But apart from that, it’s got to come from an authentic place.”
Changed the relationship

Making the film changed Benedict’s relationship with the natural world. “It turbocharged my understanding of it. For example, I know that interacting with Nature is good for mental health and for Nature, and seeing the prisoners interact with the turtles underlined it. I know that if you allow Nature to thrive, it comes back online with its own solutions.”

Seeing the emotion of the tribespeople on the removal of the dams on the Klamath River in southern Oregon and northern California  and the return of the salmon was particularly moving, Benedict says. “Every time I’ve watched that sequence, I’ve cried. The emotion is so transparent and potent, that it reaffirms my hope and belief that we do have enough humanity amongst us to make a difference.”
Lessons lost

We are a part of Nature and not apart from it, Benedict says. “The lesson has been lost, in rapid urbanisation, 200 years of capitalism, the rapid increase of automation, the separation of you and I, Descartes’ I think therefore I am, I could go on and on and on.”

It has become useful, Benedict says to think of ourselves as units in a factory. “It’s all about a drive to productivity and unsustainable growth. We’re now putting the brakes on. What is valuable goes into the bigger picture of who we are as human beings.”
Set the controls

The Earth, Benedict says, is a spaceship. “It’s got a biosphere that supports carbon-based life forms, and the bodies we inhabit are the spacesuits. We don’t really need to go to Mars to prove that we’re already in space. Thank you very much. So let’s make this work.”

A lot of modern inventions, Benedicts allows, have been helpful. “We’re not to deny the advances in medicine, education and communication. It has, however, come at a cost, but we’re clawing our way back.”

“Our civilisation has almost given us permission to detach from Nature,” Jonnie adds. “A lot of people are spiritually connected to Nature, as I know they are in India. This connection has been around much longer than the atomisation and separation from Nature. We’ve got to get back on track and rejoin Nature.”

“There is a reason indigenous peoples have been the spirit of Nature,” says Benedict. “Those messages have been coming across in the last few decades of environmental advocacy. How to cohabit and be a part of Nature, not apart from it, is deep-seated in a humanity that has practised sustainability. It’s no small surprise that some of the lessons that we’re learning now are very old.”

Making How to Live on Earth free to watch was a conscious choice according to Benedict. “It’s a completely democratic, open-source piece of material to inspire, provoke and call people to action. It’s very rare that you’re not worried about box office revenue. The philanthropic support through the Villars Institute Foundation and Silvania has created this amazingly impactful, funny, at times moving, and important bit of storytelling for free.”

The film, Benedict says, could be re-constituted for educators, policy forums, political and social outreach. “That is something a normal cinematic or streamer release with its paywall wouldn’t facilitate. It’s a hugely attractive thing to be a part of and the film is revolutionary in its ambition.”
How to Live on Earth is streaming on YouTube

title: Telangana doctors’ body seeks State-wide safety audit of government hospitals

content.value: The Telangana Junior Doctors Association (TJUDA) has urged the government to conduct a State-wide safety and infrastructure audit of all government healthcare institutions following a series of recent hospital incidents, including a fire at the Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS), Adilabad, which claimed the lives of five infants, and the ceiling collapse at MGM Hospital, Warangal, which injured three patients.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, TJUDA said the incidents had highlighted continuing deficiencies in infrastructure, maintenance, safety systems, funding, transportation and patient-care facilities across government hospitals. “The incidents should serve as a wake-up call for preventive and corrective action across the government healthcare system,” it added.

TJUDA called for a comprehensive audit covering government medical colleges and teaching hospitals, district and area hospitals, community and primary health centres, SNCUs, NICUs, PICUs and ICUs, emergency departments, operation theatres, blood banks and diagnostic facilities. They said that the audit should examine structural safety, electrical and fire-safety systems, medical-gas systems, generators, lifts, HVAC systems, water and sanitation facilities, emergency exits and medical equipment. Critical deficiencies should be risk-classified and rectified within a defined timeframe.

The association also raised concerns over the long-standing infrastructure and maintenance requirements at MGM Hospital and urged the government to expedite the Warangal Super Specialty Hospital and make visible progress towards its operationalisation within one month.

They also sought better hostel infrastructure for postgraduate residents, undergraduate medical students, nursing students and other healthcare trainees. For doctors and other healthcare workers posted in remote areas, the association sought safe residential quarters, security arrangements, lighting and CCTV surveillance.

TJUDA also highlighted the shortage of dedicated vehicles at PHCs, CHCs, government medical colleges and peripheral institutions. It said the lack of vehicles affected field visits, disease surveillance, immunisation, maternal and child health programmes, emergency referrals, sample transportation, health camps and disaster response.

title: Front-of-pack nutrition labelling to be rolled out in single phase, FSSAI tells Supreme Court

content.value: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the country’s food regulator, on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) conveyed to the Supreme Court its proposal to adopt a single-phase approach for the implementation of front-of-pack nutrition labelling (FoPL) on packaged food products indicating sugar, salt and saturated fat levels.
The regulator sought a four-month period for issuing and finalising the draft regulations under the Food Safety and Standards Act (FSS Act), 2006.
Also Read | Supreme Court questions FSSAI on thresholds for ‘high’ sugar, salt, fat warnings

“In this time period, FSSAI will notify the draft amendment regulations which is mandatorily required to be published for a period of 60 days for inviting comments from stakeholders through domestic consultation and the WTO platform. Comments received will be examined, and, subsequently with the approval of Food Authority, the final notification will be forwarded to the Ministry for publication in the official gazette,” the FSSAI affidavit said.

The affidavit was based on a petition filed by a Kerala-based NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi, seeking directions to the Centre to introduce front-of-pack warning labels.
Also Read | SC seeks clear timeline for FSSAI’s food warning label rollout, calls for nutritional literacy in schools

The affidavit said that there would be a voluntary implementation period of 365 days by food business operators (FBOs). “This time period has been provided in order to avoid any commercial hardships to the food business operators as they have pre-packaged material already printed in bulk,” it explained.
The FSSAI said it was proposing a red hexagon with a white square-shaped background FoPL format, drawing similarity, more or less, with the FoPL format adopted by Canada.

Furthermore, where only one nutrient of concern was present, the corresponding nutrient would be indicated in the hexagon. Where two or three nutrients of concern were present, the applicable two or three nutrients would also be indicated within a single hexagon. The arrangement, it said, would provide clear and specific information to consumers.
Editorial | Front and centre: On the front-of-package labelling issue
It said that any food product, including beverages, containing non-caloric sweeteners would sport a warning statement, ‘CONTAINS NON CALORIC SWEETENER’ on the front of the pack.
The court had pulled up the FSSAI for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products indicating sugar, salt and saturated fat levels.

title: HEADS to bridge India’s mental healthcare gap with AI

content.value: To address India’s alarming mental healthcare gap, NIMHANS in collaboration with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur, and the Lokopriya Gopinath Bordoloi Regional Institute of Mental Health (LGBRIMH), Tezpur, will formally launch a collaborative project titled ‘HEADS’ (Human-in-the-loop Evaluation of Assisted Depression Screening) on Thursday.

Funded by the Wellcome Trust, a major international charity foundation, the two-year study aims to build and evaluate AI-assisted approaches for the early identification and screening of depression. The initiative places a strong emphasis on Indian regional languages, specifically Kannada, Assamese, Hindi, Bengali, and English, which have historically remained substantially underrepresented in mental health AI research.
Bridging multilingual gap

Lekhansh Shukla, assistant professor of psychiatry at NIMHANS and principal investigator of the project, said India carries one of the world’s largest depression treatment gaps, where only about one in five individuals affected by depression receives timely, appropriate care.

During the project’s hybrid launch event at NIMHANS, experts will highlight the critical limitation of existing digital health innovations. Most mental health AI tools are built using English-language, urban datasets, rendering them ineffective in diverse, non-English clinical settings, he said.

“In our earlier research, we found that even frontier models cannot understand or translate Indian languages, especially when discussion was about feelings and emotions. HEADS instead builds for Indian languages from day one, developing artificial intelligence that understands clinical conversations in Kannada, Hindi, Bengali, Assamese, and English,” Dr. Shukla told The Hindu.
‘Human-in-the-loop’

A central principle of the project is a strict ‘human-in-the-loop’ framework, ensuring that AI tools serve purely as supportive clinical decision-aids to help clinicians recognise symptoms earlier without ever replacing professional clinical judgment.

In a pioneering effort for Indian mental health research, the study has embedded a 15-member panel of Lived Experience Experts - individuals who have survived depression, anxiety, or substance use disorders - across every phase of the project. This panel has actively shaped the study’s design and informed consent protocols. They will also participate in language-evaluation groups across all targeted Indian languages, audit AI algorithms for hidden bias and stigmatising language, and stress-test systems before deployment, the doctor said.
Two-year evaluation

Over its 24-month duration, the HEADS project will record and analyse approximately 4,500 clinical interviews across healthcare sites at NIMHANS and LGBRIMH. Meanwhile, IIT Kharagpur will lead the core engineering, system development, and AI-safety work to ensure responsible deployment. Senior leadership, investigators, and project team members across all partner institutions attended the hybrid launch, marking a landmark step toward equitable digital mental healthcare in India.

title: Five crore Indian children still lack access to sanitation service in their schools, says UN report

content.value: India had the highest number of children with no sanitation service in schools, with 50 million out of the world total of 244 million as of 2025, according to a new global report. Only Nigeria (34 million), Ethiopia (26 million), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11 million) or Indonesia (8 million) had a comparatively large number of schoolchildren who had no access to sanitation service.

The data from ‘Progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools 2015-2025’ shows the progress as well as the challenges India is facing in meeting the water, sanitation and hygiene goals that are part of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) set for 2030.
14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service

The report can also be seen as a decadal report card on the Swachh Bharat Mission, which was launched in India on October 2, 2014. The report cites the achievement of India which saw a 14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service.
Lack of hygiene service

The WHO/UNICEF report that is part of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) shows that globally, 362 million children still had no hygiene service at their school in 2025. Of these, 20 million were from India.

It is not just lack of access that the WHO report flags about India but also gaps in data. “There is now sufficient data to estimate trends in basic hygiene coverage between 2015 and 2025 for all SDG regions except Central and Southern Asia where there were insufficient recent data to generate estimates for India, and therefore the region, beyond 2024.”
Drinking water
On the brighter side, India is among the 28 out of 62 countries that are on track to achieve universal coverage of basic drinking water in schools by 2030.

As of 2025, there were 258 million children who still had no drinking water service at their school. The number of children from Indian schools made up 12 million of this number or about 1 out 20 children in the world.  The report shows that India has made a big progress in basic drinking water services in 2025 and average rates of change between 2015 and 2025. India, Panama, Syrian Arab Republic, Togo and Tuvalu increased coverage by over 4% per year, “demonstrating that rapid progress is possible”.
However, the report found that while gaps in basic water coverage persists between school levels and between rural and urban areas, this did not apply to India, Cambodia and Fiji.
