title: President’s call puts spotlight on celebrity endorsements of harmful products

content.value: Public health experts have called for tighter regulation of celebrity endorsements of harmful products following President Droupadi Murmu’s appeal to artistes to refrain from promoting substances detrimental to health, made against the backdrop of Maharashtra’s action over a Vimal Elaichi advertisement featuring Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff.

The President, speaking at the 72nd National Film Awards in Gujarat on Tuesday (September 22, 2026), said popular artists, particularly those who influence children and young people, should promote disciplined lifestyles and refrain from endorsing substances harmful to health.

The remarks come as the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) examines whether the Vimal Elaichi campaign amounts to surrogate advertising for Vimal Pan Masala. The FDA has issued show-cause notices to the three actors, alleging that the advertisement creates an association with a pan-masala product whose manufacture, storage, transportation, distribution and sale have been prohibited in Maharashtra.

The issue has also reached the courts. The Delhi High Court on September 14 declined to entertain a challenge to the FDA notices on territorial-jurisdiction grounds and directed the petitioner to approach the appropriate court in Maharashtra. The court did not adjudicate on whether the advertisements amounted to surrogate advertising.

Public health advocates have long raised concerns that celebrity endorsements can give socially acceptable imagery to products associated with tobacco, areca nut and other harmful substances, particularly among younger audiences. Cancer specialists have also warned about the health consequences associated with tobacco and areca-nut consumption.
Also read| Due diligence: On surrogate advertising

The Vimal campaign is not the first instance in which Bollywood celebrities have faced scrutiny over such endorsements. Amitabh Bachchan, Salman Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshay Kumar have, at different times, been associated with advertisements for pan masala or related products. Kumar withdrew from a Vimal campaign in 2022 following criticism.

The renewed debate raises a broader public health question over whether regulations governing advertising are keeping pace with the influence of celebrity endorsements, particularly where advertisements for apparently permissible products may create associations with products that are restricted or harmful.

Speaking to The Hindu, Arun Gupta, convener of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi), said appeals to celebrities needed to be backed by a clear legal framework covering the endorsement and advertising of harmful products, including tobacco and ultra-processed foods.

“I wish appeals were taken seriously and work in India, especially when it comes to endorsement and advertising of harmful products which include ultra-processed food products and tobacco products,” he said.
Mr. Gupta said the government should act on the President’s appeal and enact a clearly worded law to prohibit the marketing of unhealthy products.

“This is the only way to curb the trend. Why I am saying this is because the current legal framework is more of self-regulation and is ineffective even though the government believes it to be working,” he said.

Sandeep Nayak, chairman — Oncology and executive director — Surgical Oncology and Robotic Surgery, KIMS Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the President’s remarks highlighted the public-health consequences of celebrity endorsements of tobacco-linked products.

“As oncologists, we witness daily the catastrophic impact of pan masala, alcohol and tobacco addiction in our clinics. When high-profile icons lend their names to these brands, they inadvertently glamorise carcinogenic products for millions of impressionable youth,” he said.
Dr. Nayak said products such as silver-coated cardamom and flavoured mouth fresheners marketed under tobacco-associated brand names could function as surrogate advertisements.

“Using identical brand titles, logos and colour palettes — whether for pan masala or alcohol extensions —” creates a strong association with the primary brand, he said, calling for tighter regulation of such brand extensions.

Giving an insight into the scale of tobacco use in India, the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) found that 21.4% of Indians aged 15-49 used smokeless tobacco, with the prevalence higher among men (29.6%) than women (12.8%). The latest Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), conducted in 2016-17, estimated that 28.6% of Indians aged 15 years and above — nearly 267 million people — used tobacco. The survey also found that smokeless tobacco was the most prevalent form of tobacco use in the country.

A World Health Organisation study estimated the economic cost of diseases and premature deaths attributable to tobacco at ₹1.77 lakh crore in 2017-18, more than 1% of GDP, while treatment of tobacco-related diseases accounted for 5.3% of total health expenditure. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has estimated that smokeless tobacco and areca-nut use caused more than 120,000 oral-cancer cases globally in 2022, with 88% occurring in South-Central Asia.

title: 'Momnesia' pregnancy forgetfulness linked to brain circuit disruption, study finds

content.value:
It is sometimes called "momnesia," "mommy brain," "pregnancy brain" ​or "baby brain" — the forgetfulness, mental fogginess and cognitive changes that many women may experience during pregnancy. For instance, a woman
might walk into the kitchen ‌and forget why she did, or perhaps misplace her car keys in the bathroom.

Scientists know it ​is a real biological phenomenon, and now have found a possible explanation, identifying a specific brain circuit that ⁠becomes disrupted under the sustained high levels of oestrogen that accompany pregnancy.

They conducted experiments using laboratory mice designed to mimic the sustained elevated oestrogen experienced during pregnancy, finding that this led to temporary memory impairment in the animals without mood changes.

Underlying this in the mice, they found, ‌was how the high oestrogen affected a neuronal pathway between two brain structures — the hypothalamus, which acts as a control center and integrative hub, and the hippocampus, which is central to memory formation.
High oestrogen increased the activity of ‌hypothalamus neurons, which in turn suppressed activity in the hippocampus and impaired memory, they found.

"Momnesia" becomes most evident in ‌late ⁠pregnancy and may continue into the postpartum period but usually dissipates after childbirth. Short-term and long-term memory can ⁠be affected, including spatial, social and verbal memory such as having difficulty remembering names or words, or struggling to recall familiar information.

"It is not serious or medically disabling, although it does affect daily functioning and confidence," said Zheng Sun, a professor of medicine at Baylor College of Medicine specialising in endocrinology and molecular ​biology and one of the leaders of the study ‌published in the journal Science Bulletin.

"Typical examples include forgetting why one entered a room, misplacing an item, losing the thread of a conversation or needing reminders for appointments. It is widespread. About 80% of pregnant women notice those changes, but that figure largely reflects self-report and subjective experience rather than objective testing," Dr. Sun said.
The findings suggest that the phenomenon does ‌not represent a general decline in cognitive ability.

"The important point is that pregnancy does not simply make someone 'less intelligent.' ​The effects appear to be more subtle and specific to certain cognitive tasks," said  Yanlin He, director of the Brain Glycemic and Metabolism Control Laboratory at Louisiana State University's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and another ⁠of the study leaders.
Mouse experiments

The mouse experiments shed light on what is happening in the brain. Oestrogen is a hormone that governs a woman's pregnancy, menstrual cycle and puberty, spurring physical changes that help the body support the fetus, foster fetal development and ‌prepare for childbirth. Its levels increase during pregnancy, peaking in the third trimester.
The researchers found that a protein called "oestrogen receptor alpha" transmits estrogen's signals into cells in the hypothalamus.

This region has abundant brain cells called GABAergic neurons that typically transmit calming signals to other parts of the brain. The study showed that high oestrogen levels over-activate the inhibitory signals by these neurons in the mice, and this directly affected the hippocampus.
The researchers performed memory tests including object and location recognition, finding impairment in mice given high oestrogen levels compared to those that were not.

When the researchers experimentally turned off the hypothalamus-to-hippocampus neuronal pathway, the mice no longer experienced oestrogen-induced memory ‌problems. But experimentally activating the same pathway impaired memory in the mice, even without higher amounts of oestrogen present.

"When we genetically removed estrogen receptors from ​these hypothalamic neurons, estrogen-induced and pregnancy-induced memory problems in mice were also reversed. We suspect that a similar circuit may play a similar role in humans, although you cannot do this type of invasive study directly ⁠in humans," Dr. Sun said.

The researchers complemented the mouse experiments with a study assessing memory performance in 70 women, including some across different stages of ⁠pregnancy and some who were not pregnant, using tests of long-term, short-term and working memory. These tests revealed memory impairments that manifested
during late pregnancy, correlating with high circulating oestrogen levels.

"Importantly, higher circulating estrogen levels were associated with poorer ‌performance on several memory-related measures even after accounting for other potential contributing factors. This provides human evidence consistent with the mechanism we identified in mice," Dr. He said.

"However, we should emphasise that we did not directly manipulate or measure this specific neural ​circuit in pregnant women. Therefore, the human findings support the hypothesis but do not establish the same level of causality as the mouse experiments," Dr. He said.

title: This festive season, what you should know about artificial sweeteners and your health

content.value: The festive season has officially arrived, and Indian kitchens are once again coming alive with preparations of laddus, payasam, halwa, burfis, and other traditional sweets. With the rising awareness about the impact of sugar, however, some ingredients in popular sweets are being changed. Refined sugar is increasingly being replaced with jaggery, while some consumers are also experimenting with artificial sweeteners such as stevia, and of late, monk fruit sweetener.

The intention is understandable: enjoy festive food while reducing sugar use. The science behind these sweeteners however, is more nuanced. Not every alternative to sugar is nutritionally equivalent, and ‘natural’ does not automatically mean low-sugar. The important question is not simply what sweetener is being used, but how much sweetness and sugars a person consumes overall.
Jaggery counts as sugar

Jaggery has long been associated with traditional Indian cooking and is often perceived as a healthier alternative to refined sugar because it undergoes less refining and may retain small amounts of minerals. However, it remains a concentrated source of sugar.

This distinction becomes particularly important during festivals, when sweets are rarely eaten in isolation. A person may have a laddu, a serving of payasam/kheer, sweetened beverages and several savoury foods in the same day, or worse in a single meal.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that free sugars contribute less than 10% of total daily energy intake, with a further reduction to below 5%  providing additional health benefits. For a person consuming around 2,000 calories a day, 5%  is roughly 20 to 25 grams, or 4 to 5 teaspoons of sugar.

Therefore, replacing sugar with jaggery does not make a sweet sugar-free. From a doctor’s perspective, portion size and the total amount of free sugar consumed during the day remain far more important than whether the sweetener is brown or white.
Artificial sweeteners

Across the country, many people are now using  low-calorie or no-calorie sweeteners. These include artificial sweeteners such as sucralose, saccharin and aspartame, as well as naturally derived sweeteners such as steviol glycosides and monk fruit extract.

Monk fruit extract, the newest addition to sweeteners in the mass market, is particularly interesting because its sweetness comes from compounds called mogrosides. Monk fruit extracts can be approximately 100 to 250 times sweeter than sugar, depending on their mogroside content. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has noted  that the use of monk fruit extract is ‘generally recognised as safe’  under its intended conditions of use.

Artificial sweeteners work differently. They provide intense sweetness with little or no calories and are commonly used in products marketed as ‘sugar-free’, ‘light’ or ‘diet’. Approved high-intensity sweeteners are considered safe within their specified conditions of use, and several have established acceptable daily intake levels.

However, a ‘safe’ label does not necessarily mean beneficial. The World Health Organization currently advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners as a strategy for long-term weight control. Its recommendation is conditional and is based on evidence that replacing free sugars with non-sugar sweeteners does not provide a clear long-term benefit for reducing body fat.
This is an important distinction for consumers. A sweetener can be safe to consume and still not be a reason to increase the amount of sweet food in the diet.
A better approach
The biggest misconception is that changing the sweetener automatically changes the nutritional quality of the sweet.

A jaggery laddu is still sweet. A sugar-free dessert can be calorie-dense if it contains large amounts of ghee, nuts, cream or other ingredients. Similarly, replacing sugar with monk fruit does not make an otherwise highly processed dessert a health food.

The more useful approach is for us to look at our  entire festive eating pattern. One traditional sweet enjoyed occasionally is very different from consuming several servings every day throughout the season. The goal is not to find a sweetener that allows unlimited sweetness; it should be to reduce excessive sweets  while retaining the cultural and social pleasure associated with festivals.

So, if a festival sweet is made with sugar, moderation matters. If it is made with jaggery, moderation still matters.  Monk fruit essence or other non-sugar sweeteners do not automatically bestow a license to eat more.

The aim should be not to move from sugar to jaggery or from jaggery to monk fruit. It should be to simply learn to enjoy our favourite sweets alittle less sweet, and a little less often. This also aligns with broader dietary recommendations from the WHO that advise building diets on minimally and unprocessed foods, and restricting free sugars.

There is no need to cut out every single sweet, but do  practice portion control and choose wisely. Instead of five laddus, have one and enjoy it mindfully. Keep the overall diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains and fibre, and let sweets remain a small part of the meal.
(Suparna Mukherjee is a dietician with Narayana Health City, Bengaluru. suparna.mukherjee@narayanahealth.org)

title: Extra 100 grams of ultra-processed foods daily related with 14% higher risk of heart event: study

content.value: Each additional 100 grams consumption of ultra-processed foods daily could be associated with a 14%  increased chance of cardiovascular events, according to a study.

Every 10% increase in weight per energy intake due to ultra processed foods was associated with a 16% greater risk of metabolic syndromes or diabetes, findings published in the journal Family Medicine and Community Health showed.

Researchers, including those from Duke-NUS Medical School in Singapore, analysed data from 51 studies from the Americas, Europe, Asia, and Oceania, involving more than 88 lakh participants -- on average aged 23-77 -- with follow-ups ranging between 2 and 32 years.
Eating a lot of ultra processed foods was associated with higher risks of cardiovascular events (24%),  cancer (12%)  and obesity or overweight (23%).

Consumption of the energy-dense, high-on-sugar and salt products was also related with a higher chance of metabolic syndrome or diabetes (24%),  depression and anxiety (27%),  digestive diseases (31%),  high blood pressure (11%)  and death from any cause (18%).
Ultra processed foods are ready-to-eat or heat-and-serve products that have undergone extensive industrial processing. They are low in dietary fibre, protein, vitamins, and minerals.

“Dose-response analyses demonstrated each additional 100 (grams per day) intake was associated with 11%  higher hypertension risk, 14%  higher cardiovascular events risk, 4%  higher cancer risk, and 3%  higher all-cause mortality; each 10%  increase in weight (per) energy intake was associated with a 16%  higher MetS (or) diabetes risk,” the authors wrote.
Emerging evidence suggests that a combination of multiple additives may exert a ‘cocktail effect’ on human health, they said.

The team added that lab studies have shown that the extensively altered physical composition of ultra processed foods may adversely affect the gut microbiome, and promote inflammation and insulin resistance, among other things.

Several compounds that may form during food processing, such as acrylamide -- a contaminant formed in heat-treated processed foods -- and acrolein, generated during fat heating, have been associated with a higher incidence of cardiovascular disease, they said.

"Given that UPF related chronic diseases often cluster as multimorbidity, reducing consumption of UPFs (ultra processed foods) and replacing them with minimally processed alternatives may be relevant for chronic disease prevention and primary care management," the authors said. PTI

title: All you need to know about: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome

content.value: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome is a seldom-discussed group of conditions that affect the connective tissue of the human body, typically loosening or weakening it. Connective tissue supports and provides flexibility to the skin, tendons, ligaments, bones, blood vessels, and organs.

EDS is generally inherited and is commonly associated with hypermobility, meaning one’s joints can move past their normal range of motion. But hypermobile EDS, or hEDS, which often comes with a higher risk of bruising and injury, is only the most common among the 13 types of EDS, some of which are very rare.
In fact, one of the rare forms of the condition, vascular EDS, can be life-threatening. Here’s all you need to know about Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.
Why does EDS occur?

EDS is caused by certain genetic changes and is generally passed down to children by their parents. These genetic changes affect how one’s body makes and uses collagen, a protein that gives structure and strength to joints, skin, blood vessels, and other tissues.
However, in some people, it can occur randomly due to genetic mutations with no family history of the condition.
What are the different types of EDS and their symptoms?

The most common form of EDS is hEDS. Hypermobile EDS, like some other types of EDS, presents with symptoms such as stretchy, fragile skin, loose and clicky joints that dislocate easily, joint pain, and joint hypermobility. hEDS may also manifest as extreme fatigue, skin that bruises quickly, digestive issues, and poor bladder control, among other symptoms.

Classical EDS, which is another, less common type of EDS, also exhibits similar symptoms, but it mostly affects the skin. A person with this condition might have very stretchy and fragile skin that bruises easily or splits easily, especially around the elbows, on the forehead, and on the knees. Wounds may also take longer to heal, and they may leave obvious scars.

The rarer form, vascular EDS, affects one’s internal organs. This results in fragile blood vessels that can tear easily and cause internal bleeding, which can be life-threatening. This condition poses a serious risk of bowel tearing, womb tearing during pregnancy, and lung collapse, among others. Pregnant women with EDS must, therefore, discuss this condition with their gynaecologist/obstetrician.

Another type of EDS, called kyphoscoliotic EDS (kEDS), which is also rare, affects the curvature of the spine. It might manifest during early childhood and is also characterised by joint hypermobility and loose joints.
How is EDS diagnosed?

Most people with EDS generally show symptoms of hEDS, which is diagnosed through physical and not genetic testing. It is also important to note that joint hypermobility is common, and it need not necessarily be caused by hEDS; it could also be a result of hypermobility spectrum disorder. Consult a general practitioner, who may refer you to a specialist if you exhibit symptoms of hEDS.
Some of the rarer forms of EDS may be diagnosed through genetic testing.
How can EDS be treated?
There is no cure for EDS, but symptoms, especially those of hEDS, can be managed. For some, however, the symptoms can be disabling.

A physiotherapist could help recommend muscle and joint strengthening exercises that could have both short- and long-term benefits. In addition to this, doctors may also recommend pain management and appropriate treatment for bowel-related issues.

Depending on the severity of the condition, persons may have to avoid certain activities, such as weight-lifting or contact sports, that put undue pressure on the joints. However, low-risk activities including swimming and pilates could help individuals stay fit.

title: Why is some music able to make us cry?

content.value: — Radhika S., Mumbai
A good song can make us cry because listening to it simultaneously invokes parts of the brain involved in emotion, memories, expectations, and arousal.

Expectation is particularly notable. As we listen, the brain constantly predicts what will come next, from a melody resolving itself to a voice reaching a particular high note. When the song suddenly fulfils or violates these expectations, the resulting build-up and release of tension can trigger strong physiological reactions, including changes in heart rate and tears.

We also associate music with autobiographical memories. When we repeatedly hear a specific sequence of rhythm, timing, lyrics, etc. the brain stores it alongside whatever else it is encoding then. When you hear the opening notes later, it can trigger the brain to recognise the old sensory pattern and ‘activate’ the larger network of information stored with it.

Sadness can also produce changes grounded in shared physiology, such as softer speech and falling pitch contours, and in cultural conventions like the association of particular harmonies with melancholy.
When other people observe these cues alongside sadness, their brains learn the association. In this way, people can be brought to cry to unfamiliar music, too.

title: Human ancestors moved from climbing trees to walking on the ground 1.8 million years ago

content.value: The Hindu’s weekly Science for All newsletter explains all things Science, without the jargon.
(This article forms a part of the Science for All newsletter that takes the jargon out of science and puts the fun in! Subscribe now!)
When did our ancestors begin walking on two legs? This evolutionary question about our terrestrial bipedalism has piqued paleoanthropologists for years.

Now, a new study gives us the most conclusive evidence of when archaic humans transitioned from regularly climbing trees to habitually walking upright on the ground: and the answer is 1.8 million years ago. “Since the time of Darwin and Huxley, terrestrial bipedalism has been posed as a central tenet of the human ecological niche,” said the research paper published in the journal Science Advances.

Scientists from the University of the Witwatersrand (South Africa) and University of Southern California arrived at this conclusion after studying the internal strength of limb bones from two fossil skeletons: one, the Little Foot (a 3.67-million-year-old Australopithecus individual from Sterkfontein Cave in South Africa) and a 1.8-million-year-old archaic human from Georgia.

Much research has focused on determining the when this locomotor behaviour changed in human evolution, going back to our common ancestor, that is the time when human and chimpanzee lineages diverged 9.3 to 6.5 million years ago.

But this latest study looks at the strength of bone shafts of each species, which reflects the physical demands placed on them and how much time each species spent on trees, rather than just at the skeletal shape of their limbs. The bone strength ratios of arms and legs bone in these fossils was compared to those of modern humans, chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans.
While the Little Foot’s limb proportions were more akin to African arboreal apes, the limb strengths in the Dmanisi Homo specimen were closer to modern humans.

The famed “Lucy,” (the 3.2-million-year-old Australopithecus afarensis found in Ethiopia) for instance, had limb strength proportions between those of modern humans and chimpanzees, “but closer to chimpanzees, indicating increased forelimb weight-bearing loads relative to modern humans.” This means a greater time spent on trees.

It is still a mystery why this shift emerged when it did, but the authors hypothesise that it could be linked to changes in their range, foraging behaviour and other factors that demanded stronger lower limbs for an adaptation to life on the ground. At the same time, it is probable that there was a shift to greater use of the forelimbs for stone-tool manufacture and enhanced (high speed) throwing for hunting, said the paper.

In 2020, another research paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, which studied the shape and structure of fossil leg bones suggested that our human ancestors could have been regularly climbing trees two million years ago.

title: ‘Super El Niño’ projected to cause 15,800 additional heat deaths in India, says report

content.value: India could see an estimated 15,800 additional heat-related deaths, give or take 1,600, between September 2026 and February 2027, as the current ‘Super El Niño’ drives unusually high temperatures, according to a report made public on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) by the Climate Impact Lab. The estimate is relative to average conditions during the corresponding months from 1996-2025.

Globally, the report projects 451,000 additional heat-related deaths during the first six months of the El Niño event, including 239,000 during the September 2026-February 2027 period. It projects 19,300 deaths in Indonesia; 19,400 across the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia; 13,300 in Brazil; and 66,800 across the Sahel, a 5,000-kilometre swathe of about 10 countries across Africa, including Senegal, the Gambia, and northern Nigeria.

“This report allows decision-makers to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives in the coming months,” Michael Greenstone, co-founder, Climate Impact Lab, University of Chicago, said.

The report describes the current event as a ‘Super El Niño’, an informal term generally used for exceptionally strong El Niño conditions. El Niño occurs when waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific become unusually warm, altering atmospheric circulation and shifting rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide. Forecasts earlier this month projected a greater than 90% chance of a very strong El Niño during the northern hemisphere autumn and winter, with eastern equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures already more than 3°C above normal.

Its effects are already being observed in different regions. Indonesia has experienced conditions conducive to wildfires, while parts of Central America have faced drought-related agricultural impacts. “This year’s El Niño is also a ‘postcard from our future’, bringing temperatures climate change is projected to deliver 20 years in the future. In this way, it offers a glimpse at what lies ahead without new investments in adaptation,” an accompanying press statement noted.

In India, the southwest monsoon is entering its withdrawal phase after a season marked by deficient rainfall. The national rainfall deficit stood at about 15% below normal up to September 22, 2026 with larger shortfalls in southern and eastern parts of the country.

The heat is also increasing the demand for electricity, with nearly 40% of India’s coal-fired power plants reporting critically low fuel stocks amid increased power demand associated with hotter than usual weather linked to the El Niño.

The study’s mortality estimate, however, comes with methodological limitations. The Climate Impact Lab says it applies previously estimated temperature-mortality relationships across 24,378 regions to seasonal temperature forecasts, accounting for local climate, vulnerability, and adaptive capacity. The report does not spell out the underlying numerical relationship or coefficients connecting a particular temperature increase to a number of deaths; it says full methodological details will appear in a forthcoming peer-reviewed paper.
Also Read : Explained | Why India is watching the El Niño forecast with bated breath

Previous research has established an association between extreme heat and mortality. A 2024 multi-city study found heatwaves were associated with increased all-cause mortality across 10 Indian cities, while a global study estimated India accounted for about 20.7% of heatwave-related excess deaths during 1990-2019.

Absolute death totals also tend to be higher in more populous countries because more people are exposed, although population alone does not determine the burden — temperature, vulnerability, age structure, and adaptive capacity also matter. The summer heatwave across large parts of Europe killed at least 36,000 this year though the direct effects of an El Niño aren’t registered in the continent as much as in tropical countries.

Earlier this week, 188 Indian scientists and ecologists called for expanded monitoring of the El Niño’s effects on India’s marine, freshwater, and terrestrial ecosystems. “We need to mobilise resources now to design, deploy, and evaluate the preparation and planning tools that will save lives in the years ahead,” the release said.

title: Sustainability must move from awareness to measurable impact: CPCL

content.value: Sustainability must move from awareness to action, and from action to measurable impact. “Let us continue to work together, share knowledge, build meaningful partnerships, and translate our commitments into tangible environmental outcomes,” V Sriram, Chief General Manager, HSE, Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) said while delivering the vote of thanks at The Hindu Sustainability Summit 2026.

Mr. Sriram thanked all the panellists and government officials for their insights during the panel discussion and fireside chats. He thanked V. K. Rajeev, Minister for Environment and Climate Change, Government of Tamil Nadu for being a part of the summit.

He thanked IOCL, BPCL, HPCL, MRPL, and other energy-sector organisations for being part of the summit. He thanked The Hindu for putting the event together. “A special word of appreciation to CommuniTree – our NGO partner – and all the sustainability organisations and volunteers who supported the various initiatives such as the Urban Forest Trail, Art for Awareness, and the Installation Art Event at Mathur during the last 30 days,” he said.

title: Start-ups need support from ideation stage to drive energy transition: panellists

content.value: Start-ups working on sustainability solutions need to be supported from the ideation stage to help innovative ideas translate into viable technologies, panellists said at The Hindu Sustainability Summit 2026 held in Chennai on Wednesday (September 23, 2026).

At a session on ‘Ideas to Impact: Start-ups accelerating the energy transition’, speakers discussed about the current status of start-ups, challenges they face and the support needed to scale their innovations.

Elaborating on the importance of incubation and entrepreneurial activities, Indumathi M. Nambi, Environment and Water Resources Division, Department of Civil Engineering, IIT Madras, said not many incubators supported students at ideation stage and many students too did not register with incubators. This indicated a gap in the existing incubation eco system. There was a need to create pre-incubators that could help students develop and test their ideas.

At IIT Madras, gaps had been identified after the piloting stage and corporates and industries must step in to bridge them.  Highlighting that funding was not an issue for deep tech start-ups, she said a major roadblock was the trust about new ideas.
Doctoral programme
She also suggested introducing a doctoral programme in entrepreneurship to help students demonstrate scaled-up products and receive mentorship support for commercialisation.

Speakers called for greater collaboration between industries, academic institutions and start-ups. They also stressed the need to introduce entrepreneurship as a subject at the school level to help students pursue careers aligning with their interests.

Pravin Dongre, Executive Director, Indian Oil Corporation Limited spoke about IOCL’s journey in encouraging the start-up ecosystem. Various start-ups across the value chain, including those working on clean and green energy and water, had received funding with support extended for 18 to 36 months. Some had reached proof of concept stage and some of them, including projects such as eco toilets and nano fillers for oil pipelines had been commercialised, Mr. Dongre said.

He stressed the need for start-ups to have clarity on long-term development. Incubation mechanisms could benefit both start-ups and industries. More support mechanisms were needed to take innovations from modular solutions to commercial scale, he said.
Speakers also emphasised on the need for collaborations to address critical environmental challenges such as air pollution and water issues.

Pointing out various challenges faced by start-ups, Karthika Gopi, Founder and Chief Executive Officer, Carbelim, said achieving net-zero goals did not have a one-stop solution but required an umbrella of solutions. Testing technologies in real world conditions was often challenging, while protecting intellectual property and achieving commercial scale-up were other hurdles.

Start-ups, particularly deep tech start-ups, needed consortium-based support  as investors had to be patient during gestation period. Start-ups must also explore international support and generate early evidence to validate their technologies, she said.
Such consortium-based support from industries and the government would pull out ideas from the lab and facilitate the emergence of new technologies, she added.
The session was moderated by Sangeetha Kandavel, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu.

The summit is supported by Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) as the Presenting Partner, with NLC India Limited, Larsen & Toubro (L&T), Navin’s, WABAG, Tamil Nadu Newsprint and Papers Limited, Indian Bank, Urbando and State Bank of India as Associate Partners.

The summit’s sustainability-focused partnerships include Thermax as the Sustainable Cooling Partner, Treeni as the Sustainability Intelligence Partner, Chennai Port Authority as the Blue Economy Partner and Tamil Nadu Green Climate Company as the Climate Action Partner.
Mangaldeep is the Fragrance Partner, Puthiya Thalaimurai the TV Partner, The Federal the Digital TV Partner and Communitree the NGO Partner.

title: Mindset shift needed to drive sustainable CSR, say speakers at The Hindu Sustainability Summit

content.value: A change in mindset is needed for corporate social responsibility (CSR) to create a meaningful impact, rather than merely meet compliance requirements, speakers said at a session at The Hindu Sustainability Summit 2026 in Chennai on Wednesday (September 23, 2026).

Addressing the session, titled Responsibility to Impact: Driving sustainable CSR through ESG, Data and Digital Innovation, Rohit Kumar Agrawala, Director (Finance), CPCL, said the environmental, social and governance (ESG) framework has become integral to the ecosystem driving industrial growth and is no longer merely a compliance requirement.

Critical resources cannot be ignored in business management and decision-making, said Mr. Agrawala, who sought to highlight how refinery operations can no longer be viewed in isolation, as the cost of production, competitiveness and CSR are interconnected.

Pointing out that sustainability targets in CPCL are more focused on implementation than intent, he said peer collaboration is also important to scale sustainable solutions and create changes in society.

“We need to move beyond incremental changes and shift from linear to exponential growth in our sustainability efforts,” Mr. Agrawala said and added that CSR metrics should focus not on money spent but on measurable outcomes and impact.
Speakers observed that CSR has evolved from merely counting beneficiaries to understanding their needs and measuring the impact of interventions, driven in part by regulatory requirements.

Geetha Ramamoorthi, founder and principal advisor, Herizon Advisory, said health and education account for a significant share of CSR interventions among the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Other SDGs, including sustainable industries and communities, must be brought to the centre of CSR efforts, she said.

A green innovation fund should be created to help startups develop innovative solutions, while cross-skilling programmes can help micro, small and medium industries (MSMEs) build the capabilities needed for the green transition, said Ms. Ramamoorthi.

She also called for greater awareness of sustainability among the future workforce through the introduction of project-based learning in educational institutions. Creating a wider impact in society requires a shift in mindset along with sustained commitment and collective action, she said.

Noting that ESG data largely remains in the reporting phase, Akshay Kurian, head of consulting and supply chain sustainability at Treeni Sustainability Solutions, said it plays an important role in setting a baseline and tracking progress.

With many companies focusing on renewable energy and reducing emissions, Mr. Kurian said ESG data plays a crucial role in decision-making by helping organisations assess progress made and identify areas for improvement. For instance, tracking attrition levels provides insights into workforce trends.
Pointing out that the capability of MSMEs is faster than that of larger companies in addressing sustainability, he said a mindset shift is important to build their capacity for the green transition.
The session was moderated by Geetha Srimathi, senior reporter, The Hindu.

The summit is supported by Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) as the Presenting Partner, with NLC India Limited, Larsen & Toubro (L&T), Navin’s, WABAG, Tamil Nadu Newsprint and Papers Limited, Indian Bank, Urbando and State Bank of India as Associate Partners.

The summit’s sustainability-focused partnerships include Thermax as the Sustainable Cooling Partner, Treeni as the Sustainability Intelligence Partner, Chennai Port Authority as the Blue Economy Partner and Tamil Nadu Green Climate Company as the Climate Action Partner.
