title: Indian plantation sector urged to become global suppliers

content.value: Technology and institutional finance, which are accessible to small-scale growers too, in the plantation sector are critical for the sector’s growth, said Amit Kumar, Joint Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, on Wednesday (September 23).

Speaking at the annual conference of the United Planters Association of Southern India and presenting the TGLIA:STC awards at Coonoor, he said the future of the sector lies in partnership among all the stakeholders of the sector.
An eco system should be built for inclusive growth of the sector, where every kilogram of plantation produce has better value addition and is globally recognised.

The plantation sector contributes to agriculture output and export earnings, is a means of livelihood to thousands, provides raw material to multiple industries, and supports many downstream industries. Hence, it is an entire economic ecosystem, he said.

In a developed India, the plantation sector should have higher value per hectare, better technology adoption, increased exports, higher income for growers, and higher productivity. Its focus should move from commodities to value-added products.

Research in plantation sector should be connected to the farmer, who in turn should be connected to the processor. The processor should develop brands that target global consumers. “Sustainability should be part of our business model. The plantation sector should be able to produce more with less water and other natural resources,” he added.

At the annual meeting of the Association, Abhishek Poddar, managing director of Matheson Bosanquet Enterprises, has been elected president of The United Planters’ Association of Southern India (UPASI) for 2026-27.

Anil Mathew, executive director (Plantations), A V Thomas Group Companies, has been elected vice-president of UPASI for 2026-27. He has 35 years of experience across a wide range of plantations crops, including tea, coffee, rubber, cardamom and pepper.

title: Refinery sector must balance energy security with net-zero push: industry experts at The Hindu Sustainability Summit

content.value: India's refining and energy sector will have to balance growing energy demand and energy security with the transition towards net-zero emissions, industry leaders said at a panel discussion at the The Hindu Sustainability Summit 2026 in Chennai.

At a discussion on the topic of ‘Fossils to Net Zero: Transforming India’s Refinery and Energy Landscape’, S.G. Venkatesh, Director (Technical), Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL); Nandakumar Velayudhan Pillai, Director (Refinery), Mangalore Refinery & Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL); Santosh K. Singh, Chief Sustainability Officer, Larsen & Toubro; and D. Senthil Kumar, Managing Director, Tamil Nadu Petroproducts Limited, spoke about the challenges facing the sector. The session was moderated by Srinivasan Ramani, Deputy National Editor, The Hindu.

Mr. Venkatesh said achieving net zero for a refinery involved reducing the energy required to produce the same quantity of finished products and progressively shifting to cleaner energy sources and technologies.

He said the CPCL had reduced its energy consumption even as it achieved its highest-ever crude throughput through energy conservation measures, use of cleaner fuels, operational optimisation, and digitalisation. The company had also improved its energy efficiency benchmark and was targeting net-zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 2046.

While Scope 1 covers direct emissions from refinery operations and Scope 2 covers emissions associated with purchased electricity, reducing Scope 3 emissions would depend on the wider transition in sectors that consume refinery products, particularly transport, he said.
No immediate replacement of fossil fuels

“Fossil fuels are not going to go away, at least for the next two decades,” Mr. Singh said, adding that the transition should be viewed as a shift from a high-carbon energy system to a low-carbon one rather than an immediate replacement of fossil fuels.

Mr. Singh said green hydrogen had already moved from the policy stage to implementation, but cost remained a major barrier. Scaling up electrolyser manufacturing, reducing renewable energy costs and creating demand would be crucial to making the fuel commercially viable.
The transition to a green hydrogen economy would also require an ecosystem covering renewable power generation, energy storage, electrolysers, hydrogen storage, transportation and end-use, he said.

Mr. Pillai said the intermittent nature of renewable energy posed a particular challenge for refineries, which require a continuous and stable energy supply. “The refinery process cannot have a variation in its feed flow,” he said, pointing to the need for energy storage and technological improvements in electrolysers.

The panellists also discussed how geopolitical conflicts and disruptions to key shipping routes could affect crude supplies and refining operations, particularly for an import-dependent country such as India. They said such shocks underscored the need for refineries to diversify crude sources and strengthen supply resilience while ensuring uninterrupted energy availability.

On sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), Mr. Pillai said refineries had begun developing projects using used cooking oil as a feedstock. The major challenge was collecting adequate quantities of used cooking oil and meeting sustainability certification requirements. A SAF plant using indigenous technology was expected to be commissioned next year, he said.
Carbon Credit Trading Scheme

Mr. Kumar said the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme would shift energy efficiency from a largely voluntary exercise towards a compliance-driven mechanism for refineries and petrochemical industries. Under the scheme, industries would have prescribed emissions-intensity targets for a specified period, against a baseline determined using identified operating parameters. Companies that improve beyond their targets could trade the additional efficiency achieved through certificates, while those unable to meet their targets would have to procure certificates to bridge the shortfall.

He said similar mechanisms were already in place in other industries under the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, including through the Perform, Achieve and Trade scheme. However, the earlier mechanism had not gained sufficient traction. With the carbon market now being expanded to more industries, including refineries and petrochemicals, trading activity could increase significantly, he said. “The trading activities are expected to be very challenging in the future,” he said, adding that the incentives available to industries that perform better than their targets could create greater scope for investment in energy efficiency.

The panellists also stressed that energy efficiency should precede more expensive decarbonisation technologies. The discussion highlighted the need for a gradual transition that safeguards energy security while accelerating investments in efficiency, renewable energy, green hydrogen and sustainable fuels.

title: CPI(M) urges government to declare Anantapur as drought hit

content.value: The Communist Party of India (Marxist) has demanded that Anantapur district be declared as drought-hit and the 31 mandals be designated as drought mandals.

The party’s district committee, in a press release on Wednesday, announced that protests would be held across the district on September 25 and 26 to highlight farmers’ distress, followed by a dharna in front of the Collector’s office on September 28.
The party functionaries said that the district was reeling under severe drought, with crops withering in fields and drinking water and fodder becoming scarce.

As part of its 12-point charter, the party demanded complete waiver of crop loans, input subsidy of ₹50,000 per acre for farmers whose standing crops were lost, and ₹30,000 per acre for those who could not take up sowing in ayacut and upland areas. It also demanded that the Centre declare drought as a national calamity and announce a special package of ₹20,000 crore for Anantapur.

title: Meta acts against 3.7 million scammers' accounts with Singapore police help

content.value: Meta has disrupted more than 3.7 million scam-linked accounts, pages and other content this year based on information provided by the Singapore police, the company said Wednesday.

The social media giant said the Singapore Police Force (SPF) has been helping Meta's investigators "identify and dismantle entire ecosystems of scammers" through an information-sharing collaboration in place over the past two years.
Between January and June, Meta removed more than 113, 000 entities and pages related to fraud and scams on Facebook and Instagram, company executives said at a media briefing.

In June, Meta said it disrupted more than 33,600 entities and pages linked to scammers who were trying to take advantage of the upcoming school holidays when families are rushing to look at travel websites for good deals.

And in July, Meta took action against more than 3.6 million entities and pages, the big majority of which were "shell pages", or those that have no content and are not in active use, but could still be acquired by scammers for their future activities.
Meta did not provide comparative figures.
As scammers operate across different platforms and in varying countries, Meta alone does not have a full view of the problem.

"Scammers count on the fact that no single organisation sees the full picture. What we have built with the Singapore Police Force changes that," said Daryl Poon, director of law enforcement outreach for the Asia Pacific at Meta.
Information given by the police "helps us identify the threats we might not see on our own," he said.
"Our ability to act at scale means these networks can be dismantled before they reach more people," he said.
The collaboration with SPF is a "model which we want to keep building on here and across the region," he added.

Clara Koh, director of public policy for Southeast Asia, said scammers are now operating at an industrial scale and are using artificial intelligence "to mass produce fake profiles", fabricate imagery and generate offensive malicious code.
Meta "is continuing to invest in building the defenses across our platforms and getting to violating scam content quickly, especially before anyone sees them", she said.

title: Anthropic looks to secure more data centre capacity: Report

content.value: In a bid to secure greater data centre capacity, Anthropic is in early-stage discussions to lease up to 1 gigawatt from Stream Data Centers, according to a report from The Information outlet.
The developer is majority-owned by Apollo Global Management.
The outlet previously reported in June that Anthropic had signed over 12 preliminary agreements to this end, in order to lease U.S. data ​centres with a combined capacity of more than ⁠1 GW.
The Claude-maker was also reportedly looking to obtain financial ​backing from Google, in order to cover the lease payments.
Anthropic has not yet confirmed or denied the report.

title: U.S. expresses concerns over Australia’s planned social media regulations

content.value: The U.S. and Australian governments are at odds over the country’s new draft social media regulations, with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese defending the country’s national interest while the U.S. embassy warned of potential censorship.

The new draft laws place more responsibility on social media companies to protect children from online harms. They would also give users the choice to not have their social media feeds dictated by highly personalised algorithms.
If firms fail in these duties, they could face fines of up to Aus$109 million (USD $78 million).
The U.S. embassy in Canberra published a statement on September 22, warning that a majority of platforms affected would be U.S.-headquartered companies.

It expressed “serious concerns” about Australia’s Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 – Exposure Draft, criticising “forced chronological feeds” and “opt-in recommendation systems.”

“If Australia compels platforms to aggressively filter content in algorithmic feeds to satisfy a government mandate, and such filtering draws in protected speech, the effect on a disfavored speaker or media source’s reach would not be meaningfully different than outright removal.  The U.S. government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship,” warned the statement.
“We ask that Australia withdraw any plans to mandate that platforms algorithmically suppress content based on ambiguous government-defined safety criteria,” it added.
The U.S. government asked for further clarifications about the definition of the harms that social media companies would have to address, and how enforcement actions would affect users worldwide.
Mr. Albanese responded to journalists in New York, highlighting that the policy was not a sudden decision.
“It’s not about giving government control, it’s about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices,” he was quoted as saying by AFP.
Australia in December last year instituted a social media ban for children under 16 years, becoming the world’s first country to do so.
However, experts are divided as to the effectiveness of the ban, which relies on still-experimental age verification methods in order to lock out younger children.
With inputs from AFP

title: Anthropic, OpenEvidence partner to bring medical AI worldwide

content.value: Artificial intelligence startup Anthropic and medical knowledge platform OpenEvidence are collaborating to bring AI-powered clinical ​decision support to physicians in regions without access to the technology, the companies said on ‌Tuesday.
OpenEvidence answers doctors’ questions by drawing on peer-reviewed medical research and ​treatment guidelines. The platform is free to clinicians in the United ⁠States and Europe.

The new initiative is a specialised version available to healthcare providers for free in dozens of low- and middle-income countries where limited access to medical literature, specialist expertise and ‌continuing medical education can impair patient care.

Healthcare systems worldwide are exploring whether generative AI can help address shortages of physicians and specialists. Supporters argue ‌that AI tools can help clinicians quickly navigate vast amounts of medical ‌information, ⁠while critics caution that systems trained primarily on data from high-income countries ⁠may not reflect local practice conditions.
The initiative is being rolled out in about 100 countries, including Uganda, Angola, Sudan, Haiti, and Mongolia, according to a list provided by OpenEvidence.
“Access to medical knowledge ​shouldn’t depend on geography,” OpenEvidence founder ‌Daniel Nadler said.

Reuters reported last week that Anthropic had built a lab to do physical biology work as it pushes its artificial intelligence ambitions into drug science and as fears of AI’s reach grip the public, with some ‌executives and lawmakers calling for a slowdown in development.
Anthropic and OpenEvidence did ​not disclose financial terms of the collaboration.

In August alone, US clinicians consulted OpenEvidence 42 million times, according to Nadler. In 2026, ⁠several hundred million Americans will have been treated by a doctor who used OpenEvidence to help guide care, he said.
Anthropic’s technology will provide back-end support, while OpenEvidence will tailor ‌the system to different regions, taking healthcare infrastructure into account, the companies said.

“The technology itself has advanced so dramatically that the sort of structure needed for (bringing OpenEvidence to low-resource regions) is there, but the market incentives alone would not let it happen without this type of entrepreneurial, philanthropically minded work,” Anthropic president Daniela Amodei said.

Earlier this year, OpenEvidence said it was working with health organisations in Rwanda and ‌Botswana to adapt its tools for settings where disease patterns, diagnostic resources and available treatments differ ​markedly from those in wealthier countries.
“One hundred percent of what we are building for these places is context adaptive,” Nadler said.

Even where medical ⁠facilities don’t have around-the-clock electricity, most physicians do have smartphones, he said, which means access ⁠to quality medical information that a decade ago would only be available at leading institutions like the Mayo Clinic.

Dr. Ahmed Bendary, a cardiologist at ‌Benha University in Egypt, said expanding this access outside the United States and Europe “would be a tremendous leap forward, particularly in regions where institutional subscriptions to ​major medical journals are limited, making evidence-based, point-of-care tools even more vital.”

title: Mongolian herders enlist new tech against harsher, drier climate

content.value: When Mongolian herder Ganchimeg's sheep strayed dangerously near a salty lake this summer, driven by hunger as nearby vegetation was poor, she was in a "total panic".
"If they drank or stepped into it, the whole flock would be destroyed," she told AFP outside her traditional ger, the tent's shape silhouetted on the vast horizon of the Gobi Desert.
But thanks to an app helping herders navigate the risks that climate change is bringing to Mongolia, her husband was able to reach the sheep before they drank the brackish water.
"He immediately rushed over at top speed and intercepted them," said Ganchimeg, a mother of four who, like many Mongolians, goes by just one name.
"If we hadn't used that GPS tracker, we might have lost our entire flock."

Herders are on the frontline of both climate change and desertification impacts. Climate change is bringing extreme weather, including deadly cold snaps and droughts, which compound desertification caused by overgrazing.
Huge and sparsely populated, Mongolia is disproportionately affected by human-driven climate change, threatening the country's nomadic population and livestock.

Bilgudei Gankhulug, the 26-year-old founder of the Hunu app used by Ganchimeg, told AFP he was inspired to help herders after a 2024 "dzud"; an extreme weather event that brought temperatures as low as minus 45C.
"Over eight million livestock died. I saw a lot of herders losing their income, losing their livelihoods in just the span of a few months," said Bilgudei.
Meaning "strong nomad", the name Hunu "embodies our mission of empowering nomadic herders with the help of technology," he said.
The app allows nomads to track their livestock with a solar-charging GPS device attached to one animal per group; sufficient for herds that tend to stick together on the spacious steppe.

It has an artificial intelligence-powered weather feature with updates on the deadly dust storms and blizzards made more common in recent years by climate change, which scientists say is intensifying globally.
The app also compiles useful information on maps showing snow depth, wind direction, soil moisture and drought, assisting nomads in crucial decisions on where to move next.
Mongolia hosted talks on a global desertification treaty, known as COP17, last month.
Countries agreed financing for land restoration and tackling drought resilience, but concerns remain over a massive funding shortfall to the growing problem.
Bilgudei told AFP he hopes to expand Hunu to central Asian countries, and met with pastoralists from Tanzania and Uruguay at COP17 interested too.
"Our problems are pretty similar," he said.

About 80 percent of Mongolia is rangelands, large tracts of unfarmed land covered by native grasses and shrubs, according to Chimeddorj Buyanaa, Mongolia conservation director at the World Wildlife Fund.
"Rangelands are critically important for the local communities and also for the livelihoods of all of the Mongolian people," he told AFP.
Compounding the issue of climate change is rampant overgrazing that also endangers the region's wildlife, including snow leopards and saiga antelope, Chimeddorj said.
Around one in four Mongolians are nomadic herders.
Nearly 82 percent of the country's territory is affected by desertification and land degradation, authorities said in August.
Many herder families have simply decided to pack up and seek new lives in the city.
"Dundgovi Province's population has been declining continuously in recent years," the southern region's governor, Munkhchuluun Samdannyam, told AFP at COP17.
The worsening climate is a major problem for the province and three-fifths of its economy depends on livestock husbandry, Munkhchuluun said, but consequences are felt further afield.
"Dust storms can begin here and travel south to China, Korea, Japan and even as far as the United States," Munkhchuluun said.
"(It) is not only Mongolia's problem.
"It is also a global problem."
Speaking to AFP before heading to milk several camels tethered nearby, 49-year-old herder Bolormaa Erdenee said she was sceptical of forums like COP17.
"I often question whether the true voice of our herders is actually reaching decision-makers or not," she said.
Bolormaa and her husband raise about 400 livestock.
In their usual summer grazing area, she said roads for heavy mining trucks now criss-cross the steppe, kicking up dust and disrupting her animals.
Several nomadic households nearby have already relocated nearly 200 kilometres (125 miles) away in search of greener pastures.
Hunu app founder Bilgudei, whose ancestors were nomadic herders, said traditional migration itself is a form of environmental protection.
Bilgudei told AFP it's important to "learn from the traditions... and combine it with the science and technology".

title: Guwahati school students document 1,517 species in biodiversity survey

content.value: A month-long citizen science initiative involving school students across Assam’s Kamrup Metropolitan district has resulted in the documentation of 1,517 species of flora and fauna.
Guwahati is the headquarters of the 1,528-sq. km Kamrup Metropolitan district, comprising three development blocks and five revenue circles.
Wildlife in and around Guwahati, photographed by school students during a month-long biodiversity survey.

Help Earth, a Guwahati-based biodiversity conservation organisation, conducted a 30-day taxonomic survey in association with the Assam Climate Change Management Society. Students from seven schools participated in the exercise, titled Guwahati Bioblitz 2025. Its results were announced on Tuesday (September 22, 2026).
Wildlife in and around Guwahati, photographed by school students during a month-long biodiversity survey.

“The survey was conceived as an intensive biodiversity documentation (exercise) to encourage students to discover, document, and understand the biological diversity within a largely urban landscape. Students were allowed to explore and observe their surroundings and contribute scientifically useful records,” said Help Earth general secretary Jayaditya Purkayastha.
Wildlife in and around Guwahati, photographed by school students during a month-long biodiversity survey.
According to the data released at a school in Guwahati’s Barsajai area, 48 students logged 5,932 observations and documented 1,517 unique species.
Wildlife in and around Guwahati, photographed by school students during a month-long biodiversity survey.
The final tally comprised 993 plant species, 221 insect species, 117 bird species, 25 mammal species, and 10 reptile species.

The survey introduced the participants to biodiversity awareness, field exploration, digital photography, species identification using iNaturalist app, monitoring, and continued engagement with biodiversity.
Wildlife in and around Guwahati, photographed by school students during a month-long biodiversity survey.

“The initiative was designed not merely as a competition, but as a platform to develop a lasting habit of observation, documentation, and appreciation of nature among young learners. The broader vision presented during the programme was to transform biodiversity assessment from a one-time activity into a continuous learning and monitoring process, with schools functioning as living classrooms,” Mr Purkayastha said.
Wildlife in and around Guwahati, photographed by school students during a month-long biodiversity survey.

“Large-scale biodiversity conservation through student participation can go a long way in promoting ecological literacy and the exploration of urban microhabitats, from school grounds to surrounding areas,” said Amlan Kumar Dey, the principal of Maharishi Vidya Mandir III, where the concluding programme of Bioblitz 2025 was organised.

title: A strong ‘El Nino’ and northeast monsoon: What lies ahead for Tamil Nadu? | Explained

content.value: The story so far: El Nino, meaning ‘the little boy’ in Spanish, has emerged as one of this year’s most widely discussed climate phenomena. The exceptional warming of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Equatorial Pacific Ocean is already influencing weather disruptions worldwide and is also hitting hard on Indian monsoon.

With the Southwest monsoon beginning to retreat and leaving rainfall deficits across parts of India, El Nino is being closely monitored as meteorologists await its impact during the ensuing northeast monsoon in the southern peninsula, including Tamil Nadu.
What is the status of El Nino?

While several weather factors influence the monsoon, El Nino is one of the key climate signals being closely watched this year. Sea surface temperatures across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific are well above average and are continuing to rise. According to models from various countries, including the Australian government’s Bureau of Meteorology, both oceanic and atmospheric indicators are consistent with a strong El Nino.

The widely used Niño 3.4 index, which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, has strengthened considerably to an average of +2.51 degrees Celsius, which is well above the El Nino threshold. (+0.80 degrees Celsius). Some models indicate that it may peak above +3.0 degree Celsius in the coming months.
Why is El Nino being closely watched this year?
El Nino conditions that started developing over the equatorial Pacific have been steadily strengthening throughout the year. It is likely to persist till May or June 2027.
The usual cycle of El Nino occurrence is between two and seven years.

The World Meteorological Organisation has warned that a very strong El Nino can significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns across the world and fuel extreme weather events. However, strong El Nino conditions alone do not determine the severity of impact over various regions. Its effects may vary according to region and seasons and may be altered by other climate drivers like Indian Ocean Dipole and conditions in the Indian and Atlantic Oceans, noted international meteorological agencies.

The significance of El Nino comes against the backdrop of a rapidly warming world. 2024 was the warmest year in record, with the global temperature exceeding 1.5 degree Celsius threshold set by the Paris agreement. 2023 and 2025 were also some of the warmest years.

With the Pacific expected to get warmer and El Nino conditions expected to peak in winter and continue next year, 2026-2027 could surpass previous records. The period between 2023 and 2027 could be the warmest five years historically. 1997 experienced one of the strongest El Nino events earlier. This has turned all eyes on El Nino and its impact over the country and coming seasons, noted Sivananda Damodara Pai, Head, Regional Meteorological Centre, Chennai.
What does El Nino mean for TN?

A strong El Nino is generally considered favourable for a wetter northeast monsoon over the southern Peninsular region. El Nino has the potential to change the tracks, frequency and intensity of cyclones in different ocean basins. It could shift monsoon pattern across the globe. This year, it had brought rainfall deficit during southwest monsoon in India, including Tamil Nadu.

El Nino years are normally associated with fewer weather systems forming over Bay of Bengal, with many of them tending to be less intense. Most systems would have a westwards track towards Tamil Nadu-Andhra Pradesh coasts. However, El Nino may not be the only factor for extreme weather events like prolonged dry period or urban flooding. Rising global temperatures and climate change fueled by urbanisation and changes in land use and land cover could amplify its impact, said Mr.Pai.

Meteorologists cited previous records where several El Nino years have been associated with above-normal rainfall between October and December in Tamil Nadu. Y.E.A. Raj, former deputy director general of meteorology, RMC, said northeast monsoon rainfall was exceptionally good during 1997, 2009, 2015 (when Chennai experienced floods) and 2023  when there was El Nino.

However, 2002 was an exception, as TN recorded poor northeast monsoon rainfall despite being an El Nino year.  Similarly, there were many years like 2005, 2010, 2011 and 2021 that registered above-normal monsoon rainfall, but they were not El Nino years.

A strong El Nino is definitely a favourable factor for a good northeast monsoon, but it is not a necessary condition. In 1982, there was El Nino, both Southwest and northeast monsoons failed over India, he said.

Meteorologists point out that the northeast monsoon is of a volatile nature, and El Nino is not the only weather parameter controlling monsoon. The northeast monsoon performance could vary depending on other oceanic and atmospheric conditions.
Why is upcoming monsoon rainfall important?

The northeast monsoon, active between October and December over Tamil Nadu, provides a major share of the State’s annual rainfall. With the Southwest monsoon likely to end rain deficit, northeast monsoon is crucial to bridge the rainfall shortage and replenish drying-up water resources. While meteorologists have suggested a El Nino and a negative Southern Oscillation Index may favour a wetter northeast monsoon, the India Meteorological Department will release seasonal forecast towards September end.

The Tamil Nadu government has formed an Expert Advisory Committee to monitor and assess the potential impact of a strong El Niño and advise the government on preparedness and mitigation measures. IMD and Tamil Nadu Disaster Risk Reduction Agency are planning to host a northeast monsoon seasonal outlook forum on October 1.

title: Three people killed in as many conflicts with elephants in Assam

content.value: GUWAHATI
Three people were killed in separate incidents of conflict with elephants in north-central Assam’s Sonitpur and central Assam’s Karbi Anglong districts on Tuesday (September 22, 2026).
The two incidents in Sonitpur district were reported from the Dhekiajuli area, about 130 km northeast of Guwahati. The Karbi Anglong incident occurred in a village about 230 km east of Guwahati.
The deceased in Sonitpur district were identified as Rahmat Ali of No. 2 Pirakata village and Ganesh Toppo of Ratanjuli village. The Karbi Anglong victim was identified as Ambika Tokbipi, a woman.
The incidents occurred between 4 a.m. and 7.30 a.m.

Locals said Ali was at home, engaged in household work, when a wild elephant emerged from a nearby forest and damaged his house at around 5.30 a.m. Toppo came across the same elephant in a neighbouring village and died trying to shield his two children.
The two children, aged five and seven years, sustained injuries.

Wildlife officials said six people have been killed in such conflicts in Assam in about a fortnight. Two of the other three were killed in western Assam’s Goalpara district and one in eastern Assam’s Tinsukia district.

Policeman Amzad Ali was killed on September 6 after a wild elephant raided the 17th Assam Police Battalion camp in Goalpara’s Dakurbhita. Umakanta Moran, a 39-year-old farmer, was trampled to death near Digboi in Tinsukia district on September 7. Another person died similarly in Goalpara district on September 14.
Assam’s Forest Minister Jayanta Mallabaruah told the 126-member Assembly in July that about 150 people lose their lives in human-elephant conflicts across the State every year.
According to official data, 1,147 people have been killed in human-elephant conflicts since 2016, with 138 deaths reported in 2025.

A few weeks ago, the government announced a two-pronged strategy to address such conflicts, combining faster compensation for victims’ families with long-term measures to reduce encounters with wild elephants.
The strategy entails providing ₹6 lakh as ex-gratia to the kin of people killed in human-elephant conflicts within 72 hours of the death.

title: Stem cell therapy for autism: What does the Health Ministry’s latest advisory mean?

content.value: The story so far: The Union Health Ministry has said that stem cell therapy for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) cannot be offered as routine or commercial treatment and can be used only as part of a duly approved clinical trial. The advisory, issued on September 16 to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, follows a landmark Supreme Court judgment in January that examined the use of stem cells for autism.
What exactly has the government said?

The Health Ministry has reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions or indications included in the Ministry’s approved list. Autism is not among those indications.

For ASD specifically, the Ministry has said that therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain restricted to duly approved clinical trials, following the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, and other applicable regulatory requirements. It should not be offered as a routine, standard or commercial clinical service.
The advisory is an attempt to ensure enforcement of an existing regulatory framework, particularly after the Supreme Court ruling.
Why is this significant for autism?

Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition. There is currently no established stem cell treatment that has been shown to cure autism or to provide sufficient evidence of benefit to make it a standard treatment.

The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), in its evidence review on stem cell therapy for ASD, examined the available scientific evidence and concluded that it did not support using stem cells in addition to behavioural and supportive therapies. It recommended that stem cell therapy for autism should not be offered as standard or routine therapy and that its therapeutic use should be restricted to approved clinical trials.

This distinction is important —  a treatment being investigated in a clinical trial does not mean that it has been established as an effective treatment. A clinical trial is the mechanism through which safety and efficacy are tested.
What did the Supreme Court say?
The issue came before the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., decided on January 30, 2026.

The petition raised concerns about the commercial promotion and administration of stem cell “therapy” for autism. The court examined the scientific and regulatory position and held that, given the evidence available at present, stem cell therapy for ASD could not be offered by medical practitioners as a clinical service outside an approved and monitored clinical trial or research setting.

The court also said that, until further research establishes stem cell therapy as a sound and relevant medical practice for ASD, offering it as routine clinical treatment would not meet the reasonable standard of care expected of medical practitioners.
The court recognised the difficult situation faced by families of people with autism who may look for experimental treatments when conventional interventions do not produce the hoped-for results.

It therefore also addressed patients who were already undergoing such treatment before the judgment. Rather than abruptly discontinuing treatment, the court directed the Health Ministry to work out a mechanism, in consultation with AIIMS and the National Medical Commission, to provide the best possible solution and facilitate their continuation until they could be redirected to institutions conducting clinical trials.
So is all stem cell therapy prohibited in India?

No, that is not what this latest advisory states. The latest advisory does not say that stem cells can never be used clinically. It draws a distinction between approved standard care and experimental use.

The Ministry’s current approved list covers 18 adult and 14 paediatric indications. These include several blood cancers and blood disorders, as well as conditions such as multiple sclerosis and systemic sclerosis. For these indications, the relevant treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation performed appropriately; the Ministry’s list specifically states that mesenchymal stem-cell transplantation is not recommended for any disease condition.
Autism is not on this list.

The 2017 National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research also make a fundamental distinction between established haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and experimental applications. They state that, apart from approved indications, stem-cell use in humans must be within an approved and monitored clinical trial.
What is the way forward for use of stem cells in children with autism?
The advisory states that this therapy cannot be simply prescribe or administer as a routine therapy/treatment.

If stem cells are being investigated for ASD, the treatment has to be part of a properly designed and approved clinical trial. Such research requires the appropriate regulatory and ethical approvals. Depending on the nature and manipulation of the stem cells, different regulatory requirements apply.

This is the key difference between research and treatment being that a clinic cannot describe an experimental intervention as an established therapy and charge patients for it as ordinary clinical care.
What about clinics already offering it?

The Health Ministry has asked State and District regulatory authorities to ensure compliance and to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.

The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory dated September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It has said that unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement beyond those indications would constitute professional misconduct. State Medical Councils have been asked to examine complaints and take disciplinary action where professional misconduct is established following due process.

There can also be consequences for clinical establishments. The Health Ministry has referred to Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, which provide for cancellation of registration and penalties in applicable jurisdictions.
What should parents understand from this?

The advisory does not mean that research into stem cells and autism has stopped. It means that such research has to remain research until there is convincing evidence that establishes safety and efficacy.
For parents, perhaps the most important distinction is between a clinic saying that stem cells are being studied for autism and saying that stem cells are an established treatment for autism.

The first is a legitimate area of scientific investigation, subject to approvals. The second is not supported by the present evidence or India’s regulatory framework. ICMR’s assessment remains that stem-cell therapy should not be offered as routine treatment for ASD.

The September advisory puts renewed emphasis on enforcing the distinction between an experimental intervention being tested under scientific oversight and a commercial treatment being sold to families as established care.

title: Murmu urges actors against endorsing harmful health products; ‘True star spreads light, not darkness’

content.value: President Droupadi Murmu on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) urged popular film artists not to endorse products harmful to people's health, saying a “true star” spreads light, not darkness, highlighting the impact of words and actions of celebrities on young minds.

Ms. Murmu distributed the 72nd National Film Awards for 2024 in various categories of cinema at Ekta Nagar (Kevadia), near the Statue of Unity, in a glittering ceremony attended by top talents of the film industry.

"When successful artists speak about the benefits of a disciplined lifestyle, millions of children and young people emulate them. I urge popular artists not to endorse products that are harmful to people's health. A true star is the one who spreads light, not darkness," Ms. Murmu said.
The President also called for greater participation of women on juries selecting films for the National Film Awards.
"I would like to see women's participation ensured in every regional jury," she said, noting that many women had received awards at the ceremony.
She said women should also be represented on the juries, noting that "incorporating the female perspective in any field makes it possible to form a holistic human outlook".

She appealed to the film industry to ensure respect and social security for workers, small-scale artists, assistants and others who contribute to the creative economy while struggling to make their mark.

"Please ensure that the workers, small-scale artists, assistants, and those struggling to make their mark, who contribute to this economy, receive both respect and social security," President Murmu added.

Ms. Murmu recalled that at the previous National Film Awards ceremony, she had urged the industry to make respect and sensitivity towards every member of the film crew an integral part of its work culture.
"I hope you are paying heed to these requests," she said.
Describing film artists as key representatives of the creative economy, the President said highly popular artists possessed immense potential to influence citizens, especially the youth.
She also praised the quality of films being produced in the country, saying it strengthened her conviction that Indian films would set world-class benchmarks for quality.

"Learning about the quality films being produced in the country strengthens my conviction that our films will set world-class benchmarks for quality. I wish you all and the film industry a golden future," Ms. Murmu said.

Veteran Kannada actor Anant Nag received the prestigious Dadasaheb Phalke award, the highest honour in cinema. Yami Gautam, Mammootty and Kartik Aaryan were conferred with awards for best actors in male and female categories.
Hindi feature film 'Article 370', directed by Aditya Suhas Jambhale, received the Best Feature Film award.

title: Regulator warns against indiscriminate use of painkillers and antibiotics, cites kidney disease risk

content.value: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cautioned against the indiscriminate, repeated, or prolonged use of painkillers and antibiotics, citing the associated risk of chronic kidney disease and renal impairment.

In a circular dated September 21, 2026, the regulator said non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Drugs Rules, 1945, and are required to be sold and distributed on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner.

The CDSCO said most NSAIDs are included in Schedule H of the Drugs Rules and cannot be sold at retail without a prescription. Most antibiotics are included in Schedule H1 and carry warnings that they should not be taken except in accordance with medical advice and should not be sold without a prescription.

The circular directed stakeholders, including healthcare professionals, pharmacists, retailers, hospitals, and State drug control authorities, to ensure that such medicines are used only when clinically indicated, at the appropriate dose and for the appropriate duration.
‘Don’t self-medicate’

The regulator advised the public not to self-medicate with antibiotics or use them for conditions where they are not clinically indicated, including most uncomplicated viral infections. It also said antibiotics prescribed by a healthcare professional should be taken strictly as advised and should neither be shared nor used from leftover medicines.

People with pre-existing kidney disease or other risk factors for renal impairment have been advised to inform their healthcare professionals before taking NSAIDs. The CDSCO also urged people to seek medical advice if pain, fever, or other symptoms persist or recur instead of repeatedly taking painkillers or antibiotics on their own.
Advise for medical professionals

For healthcare professionals, the regulator recommended considering a patient’s age, comorbidities, other medicines and risk factors before prescribing these drugs. It said the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate duration should be considered when prescribing NSAIDs, particularly for those at increased risk of renal impairment.

Doctors have also been advised to follow antimicrobial stewardship principles while prescribing antibiotics and to avoid unnecessary combination therapy, inappropriate drug selection, incorrect dosing, and unnecessarily prolonged treatment.
Pharmacists and retailers have been directed to strictly comply with statutory requirements governing Schedule H and H1 drugs and not facilitate self-medication.

The CDSCO has also asked hospitals and healthcare institutions to strengthen systems for rational prescribing, prescription review, antimicrobial stewardship, and patient counselling. State and Union Territory drug control authorities have been asked to create awareness about the risks and regulatory requirements.

title: Karnataka launches action plan to cut salt intake by 30% by 2030

content.value: Karnataka on Tuesday (September 22) launched a State action plan aimed at reducing population salt intake by 30% by 2030 and promoting healthier dietary habits as part of efforts to prevent non-communicable diseases (NCDs).

The Karnataka State Multisectoral Action Plan for Salt Reduction and Promotion of Healthy Dietary Habits focuses on reducing salt consumption at three levels — households, food consumed outside the home, and processed and packaged foods. It also seeks to encourage healthier food choices and strengthen dietary counselling through the health system.

The plan proposes measures to reduce the use of discretionary salt, encourage food manufacturers to reduce salt in processed and packaged foods, and promote awareness of healthier diets. It also envisages strengthening research and evidence on potassium-enriched low-sodium salt.

The action plan seeks to align Karnataka’s efforts with India’s commitment to the global target of reducing population salt intake by 30% by 2030, while encouraging progress towards the World Health Organisation (WHO) recommendation of less than five grams of salt per person per day.
TAG meeting

Health Minister U.T. Khader launched the plan at a Technical Advisory Group (TAG) meeting at Vidhana Soudha. Former Health Minister Dinesh Gundu Rao and Rajya Sabha member Mansoor Ali Khan were present.

The TAG was constituted under the chairpersonship of Rajiv Gandhi University of Health Sciences (RGUHS) Vice-Chancellor Bhagavan B.C. to provide technical guidance and support evidence-based action on salt reduction and healthier dietary practices.

The TAG brings together experts and representatives from the State Health department, Sri Jayadeva Institute of Cardiovascular Sciences and Research, NIMHANS, academic and nutrition institutions, and public health organisations including the Institute of Public Health (IPH), Resolve to Save Lives and Vision for Social Development.

The Minister said the plan would build on existing initiatives, including salt-reduction measures under PM POSHAN, dietary counselling through Gruha Arogya and dietary risk-factor counselling under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD).
State steering committee

Mr. Khader called for a State Steering Committee involving multiple departments to ensure coordinated and sustained action on healthier diets. Karnataka has already introduced measures addressing foods high in fat, sugar and salt, providing a basis for strengthening healthier food environments, the government said.
Jayadeva institute director Dinesha B. participated in the technical deliberations and stressed the need for coordinated action to address dietary risk factors.

Jnanesh Kamath, State Joint Director, presented the key priorities, objectives and proposed actions under the State plan. Raghunandan, State Deputy Director - Non-Communicable Diseases (NCD), Amrut Kadam of RGUHS; U.S. Vishal Rao, member of the Consultative Group to the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India; Syed Imran Farooq, Executive Director, and Manika Sharma, Principal Advisor, Food Policy, Resolve to Save Lives; and Amit Karnik, Director, Vision for Social Development, were among those present.

title: Three infants killed in fire accident at Telangana’s RIMS Adilabad hospital SNCU ward; 25 children rescued

content.value: Three infants died after a fire broke out at the Special Newborn Care Unit (SNCU) ward of Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS) in Telangana’s Adilabad district late on Monday (September 21) night. The incident occurred around 11.40 p.m. As many as 25 other infants being treated in the ward were safely rescued and evacuated in time.
According to Adilabad District Medical and Health Officer (DMHO) Sadhana, the fire was caused after an air-conditioner in the reception area of the SNCU burst into flames.

“The SNCU has two flanks, one with 11 beds, and another with 13 beds, while the Kangaroo Mother Care area located opposite the SNCU has four beds. The sections are enclosed and have glass windows. When the fire broke out, smoke accumulated inside the unit. As soon as the fire was noticed, the attendants of patients broke the glass windows and evacuated the babies from the affected areas,” the DMHO said.

The rescued infants were subsequently shifted to nearby private hospitals for further treatment. The two infants who died, aged five and four days respectively, were preterm babies. One of them died immediately after the incident, while the other succumbed four hours later. The third infant, a two-day-old girl who was born prematurely at 28 weeks and weighed 1.1 kg, was in a critical condition and died while being shifted to a nearby hospital, confirmed Director of Medical Education (DME) N. Vani.

Upon receiving information about the fire, a fire tender was rushed to the hospital and the blaze was brought under control. The exact cause of the fire was is yet to be ascertained. The police have registered a case and launched an investigation into the incident.

Adilabad Superintendent of Police (SP) Akhil Mahajan said the incident occurred at around 11.40 p.m., and police teams reached the hospital within three minutes, by 11.43 p.m. “Although Ganesh immersion processions were under way and a large number of police personnel were deployed, our teams were able to reach the spot within three minutes and assist in evacuating the children,” he said.
CM conveys condolences

Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy expressed grief over the incident and conveyed his condolences to the families of the infants. He stated that the death of infants was extremely tragic. The Chief Minister directed officials to ensure better medical treatment for the children undergoing treatment at the hospital and to continuously monitor their health condition.

Mr. Reddy ordered an inquiry into the incident and directed officials to submit a report on the causes of the fire. He further instructed authorities to strengthen fire and other safety measures in hospitals across the State to prevent similar incidents in the future.
Govt. support
Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha, who inspected the fire incident site, expressed grief over the deaths and conveyed his condolences to the bereaved families.

The Minister also reviewed the rescue and relief measures undertaken following the incident and the arrangements made to safely shift the infants undergoing treatment in the SNCU to other wards. He also sought updates from doctors on the condition of the infants and other children receiving treatment and directed them to provide the best possible medical care while closely monitoring their health. The Minister later met the families of the affected children and assured them of the government’s support.
“The condition of other children who were in the ward at the time of the incident was stable and none have developed any complications,” said a note from the Minister’s office.
He was accompanied by Adilabad MLA Payal Shanker and Principal Secretary, Health, Medical and Family Welfare, Dr. Christina Z. Chongthu.

A preliminary inquiry indicated that an electrical short circuit in an air-conditioning unit may have triggered the fire, causing plastic components to burn and filling the SNCU with thick smoke, the Minister said. A detailed enquiry by an expert committee would ascertain the exact cause and identify any lapses in safety standards, he added.
The Minister said RIMS staff, district officials, Fire and Police personnel acted swiftly to disconnect the power supply, evacuate the infants and provide emergency medical care.

He said a 150-bed Mother and Child Health (M&CH) Building would be established at RIMS, taking its bed strength from 800 to 950. Plans were also under way to develop the institute into a super-speciality hospital, besides setting up Hematology and Emergency Trauma Care wings.

The Minister said steps were being taken to increase postgraduate medical seats in Paediatrics, Gynaecology, Radiology and other departments and strengthen the out-patient and in-patient services at RIMS.

title: Comprehensive occupational safety and health framework for unorganised labourers in T.N. still in the works

content.value: Over the past five years, at least three meetings involving all stakeholders were convened to address the occupational safety and health concerns faced by workers in the unorganised sector. However, despite these consultations and a plan for a dedicated policy or guidelines, a comprehensive framework to ensure their health and safety is still pending in Tamil Nadu, with health officials noting that a number of recommendations remained on paper.

With Tamil Nadu witnessing a steady increase in the migrant worker population across various sectors, the need for a comprehensive occupational safety and health (OSH) framework has become increasingly important.
What exists

On its part, the Directorate of Medical and Rural Health Services had created the Occupational, Social and Environmental Health Wing for screening, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation and compensation of the unorganised sector workers including micro, small and medium enterprises and inter-State migrant workers nearly a decade ago. Based on its proposal, the Health department constituted State and district-level inter department co-ordination committees and 21 disease and speciality-specific expert (technical) committees. The wing was later made into the State Nodal Centre for Occupational Health and Safety of Unorganised Workers (SNC-OSH).

Health officials said that the State Planning Commission had convened meetings on OSH of unorganised sector workers during which various aspects were discussed. A wider stakeholder consultation with trade union representatives, employers, NGOs and unorganised workers was suggested. Based on the recommendations of these meetings, the need to formulate a policy was also planned but no headway was made.
Key focus areas

Among the key focus areas was the health of the unorganised sector workers. Officials had raised the need for the inclusion of basic occupational health services and universal health coverage as per World Health Organization/International Labour Organization standards and mandatory health screening on job entry and regular check ups for all unorganised labourers. Maintenance of log book/health profile for all workers including inter-State migrants employed for over 30 years to track long-term illnesses like silicosis, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, noise-induced hearing loss, contact dermatitis and occupational cancers to ensure health coverage was also put forward.

One of the key action points was that all departments must provide inputs to outline OSH guidelines for unorganised sector labourers. Industrial and economic units should be required to maintain log books, ensure mandatory health screening/check ups for workers. The need to integrate OSH components into all National Health Mission programmes was another key point.

Apart from these, the need for Tamil Nadu to notify 107 diseases/hazards under OSH for unorganised workers [ILO and WHO have notified 107 diseases/hazards under occupational safety and health administration], sensitisation of workers on NCD management and conducting medical camps for NCD screening were among the other discussion points.
Independent OSH cell

A source privy to these meetings said that a series of discussions were held and one of the proposals was to have a slightly independent OSH cell. “It should have a broader perspective and a larger compass to operate on. This is an important area but least attended to. New industries are coming up and new problems will crop up. It is better to have a Standard Operating Procedure in the beginning to protect workers’ health,” he said.

title: Enveloping patients with safety standards

content.value: (In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)

With stunning regularity in recent years, headlines in India are swept up by news on spurious drugs being sold, poor quality, or contaminated drugs causing hospitalisations and even deaths, and periodic updates from the cops on fake drug busts. If you thought the periodicity of these complaints might have numbed us to what is happening in the pharma sector in the country, well, you have that wrong.

Last week, the exposé of a thriving network re-labelling and repackaging expired drugs as expensive, imported, life-saving medicines used in cancer treatment and in the ICUs, gave any complacence a big jolt. In a farmhouse near Bidadi, the police found a veritable cottage industry doing the repackaging, with its tentacles spread to over 90 hospitals in the State. Indications were that the fraudulent business had been happening for years, and several private hospitals were involved as well.

Shilpa Elizabeth and Imran Gowhar explain this bust; moreover, they try to make sense of what had been happening in terms of supplying fake drugs to hospitals, and what could have been the impact. Read the long-form article here: A dangerous dose of deception in Karnataka and beyond. Also read The Hindu’s editorial on the subject, here: Antidote to Drugs.

Further expanding the concept of patient safety, in the context of World Patient Safety Day, we did a number ofstories hinging on safety of drugs and monitoring at pharmacies, besides creating hospital checklists. In this article, Athira Elssa Johnson takes on polypharmacy, head on. Why taking multiple medicines needs close monitoring is the question she answers here, in consultation with experts.

Further, Bindu Shajan Perappadan reported that CCTVs have been proposed at medical stores for sale of prescription drugs. This move is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of prescription medicines and providing a mechanism to verify transactions in cases of suspected unauthorised sale. Yohaan Varghese noted that 71% of consumers in Mumbai were rarely asked to produce prescriptions, based on the findings of a survey; and wrote that the Maharashtra FDA acted against 880 drug licensees in three months.

Siddharth Kumar Singh added to the debate,recording what happens in neighbourhood medical stores despite all the rules about what drugs can be sold over the counter in Hyderabad, here.He also wrote on the need for exhaustive hospital checklists to ensure patient safety there.

The question of availability and accessibility to drugs, not just drug quality are relevant in a country like India. Here, we report on a study that attempted to find out how India made expensive diabetes medicines affordable.

Whichever way we look at it, the climate angle of health care is difficult to ignore, particularly with winter approaching. A recent study, linked air pollution to death by suicide and suicidal thoughts. Researchers explained that air pollutants and water polluted with arsenic, lead, lithium or nitrate, have been linked to neurological effects, including chronic inflammation and nerve damage, which can impair brain function and influence mood and stress resilience.
Dhinesh Kallungal wrote that climate change had increased the dengue risk in Keralam; cases may rise by 20% by 2040, as per a study.

title: Genome Analysis Centre to be established in Amaravati, says Health Minister

content.value: A large-scale genome analysis centre will be set up at the proposed Quantum Valley in Amaravati to identify genetic causes associated with rare diseases and support advanced medical research, said Minister of Health, Medical, and Family Welfare Satya Kumar Yadav.

Inaugurating a genome sequencing centre at the NATCO cancer centre at the Government General Hospital in Guntur on Tuesday (September 22, 2026), the Minister said the proposed Quantum Valley centre will expand genetic testing and research, including the collection and analysis of genetic information related to cancer and rare diseases. The Guntur facility is being operated on a pilot basis.

Genetic and biomarker tests would be provided free of charge to breast and lung cancer patients through the genetic testing department established at the Guntur centre. The Minister said tests that can cost up to ₹25,000 in private laboratories would be conducted free of charge at this centre.

Genome sequencing can identify genetic alterations in cancer cells, providing doctors with more information to select medicines and treatment methods suited to individual patients, he stated, while adding that in the future, it may also be possible to identify the risk of hereditary diseases within families at an early stage.

He said the government is also focusing on early cancer detection, as part of which free screening is being conducted for oral, breast, and cervical cancers. Of the targeted population of 4.27 crore people, around 2.65 crore have been screened so far, resulting in the identification of nearly 7,500 new cancer cases, the Minister said.

Four comprehensive cancer centres in Guntur, Visakhapatnam, Kurnool, and Kadapa were developed in the first phase at a cost of ₹311 crore, he said. Advanced facilities, including linear accelerators, brachytherapy and CT simulators, have been introduced. Cancer centres are also being developed in Kakinada and Anantapur under the second phase, he said, adding that another 11 teaching hospitals will be developed as cancer centres.

title: ‘Broad daylight dacoity’, says Supreme Court on overpricing of essential cancer drugs

content.value: Terming it a "broad daylight dacoity" against patients, the Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) expressed shock over the overpricing of essential cancermedicines, noting that one drug carried an MRP of ₹27,000 despite being supplied to retailers for ₹2,700.
"It is very surprising that the authorities who are supposed to take action on this are silent," a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said.
The observations came when the Supreme Court was hearing two petitions that raised drug-related issues, including that of ensuring strict price control over medicines.
The court termed it "absolutely shocking" that the printed MRP of an essential cancer drug was ₹27,000 when the price to retailer (PTR) was ₹2,700.
"The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what it is? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment," the Bench said.
"This is absolute rampage and carnage. This is broad daylight dacoity with patients," it said.
The Bench questioned how the patients could be cheated like this.

One of the petitioners told the Bench that his plea also raised the issue concerning the prescription of generic medicines by registered medical practitioners. He said fixing MRP of medicines was of critical importance.
Additional Solicitor General K.M. Nataraj, appearing for the Centre in one of the pleas, said the government was not treating it as an adversarial litigation.
The Bench observed that price fixation was a major issue.
It posted the matter for further hearing on September 29, 2026.
Price control

One of the petitions sought a direction to authorities to make drug formulations more cost-effective by preventing alleged unethical overpricing of essential medicines by pharma companies and retailers.

It also sought directions to ensure strict price control under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, to prevent violations of the price-fixing mechanism in the drug supply chain and disproportionate profit-making by retailers through unfair trade practices.
The other plea has sought disciplinary action against medical practitioners for not prescribing generic medicines to patients.

title: On umbrellas, springs, and superconductivity

content.value: Well after a few months of a hectic summer, rains are here. The campus is green and nature is once again abundant. With rains, however, has also come a usual game of hide and seek. Every time I take my umbrella out, the rain is nowhere to be seen. But when I forget it, I am greeted by sudden bouts of rain spoiling my ambition to reach my class dry and tidy.

Umbrellas, however, have something amazing about them. You press a button and it automatically opens up, stretches itself, and unfolds into a shade, growing much larger than it was. Like a magical genie.
Have you wondered how an umbrella works? You only applied a small amount of energy to push the button. Where did it get all this energy to open up so big?
As always, we are on the cusp of some beautiful physics.
Spring forth
If you have ever broken up an umbrella, you will have seen a spring inside the main rod. That is  the most crucial piece.

Springs are usually metal wires winded in a spiral, giving it a remarkable mechanical property: it becomes a ‘mechanical battery’. Just like batteries allow us to store electrical energy, springs allow us to store mechanical energy. Once pressed, the springs try to come back to their original size and exert a force on its end.

How much force? That depends on how much you have compressed it. The more you compress, the greater the force. The British physicist Robert Hooke discovered this 350 years ago; the relationship between the compression and the force is today called Hooke’s law.

Incidentally, you must have seen batteries and springs together. Where? Well, everytime you try to fit a battery in the sockets in a remote control. The spring keeps the battery snug and tight, and the fact that it is made of metal allows for electrons to easily flow into a circuit from the battery through the spring.

The strength of springs are often quoted in newtons per millimetre, or N/mm. Here, ‘newton’ is the unit of force and ‘metres’ is the unit of distance. A newton is about the force a medium-sized apple exerts on your hand. You can easily see a millimetre on a regular stationery scale. Now, a usual spring you may have seen in a battery socket faces about 1 N/mm. So when you try to tuck a battery in, that battery compresses the spring and the spring in turn pushes on the battery by about one newton of force, to keep it in its place, so that it doesn’t fall, and keeps the circuit connected.

But that’s just one spring you see. You are in fact surrounded by springs, just that they are hidden. The sofa you sit on while entertaining a guest, the mattress you collapse on after a day of office work, and even your car or your scooter where you spend hours managing rainy-season potholes — all of them have several springs to make sure you are comfortable.

If you have ever paid close attention to our trains or metro rails, you might have noticed large springs under the coaches or hanging on the top. These springs help stabilise the train as it moves over uneven terrain. And they can reach up to strengths of hundreds of N/mm.
Now, even though you may have noticed the spring, the real physics question is why it stores any energy at all. And what type of force does it exert?
Forces in nature

In physics, we think of four fundamental forces. One is the electromagnetic force, which decides how electric charges move and magnets attract. The second is the gravitational force, due to which we don’t fly off and remain stuck to the ground. The two other forces are called strong and weak forces: they work at very small distances, like inside the nucleus of an atom.
The force created by springs doesn’t seem to be any of these four options. So what is it?

Turns out even the spring’s force is secretly an electromagnetic force. Think of any metal, say aluminium. It has billions of aluminium atoms arranged like oranges on fruit carts. These atoms have a massive positively charged nucleus and negatively charged electrons that are very light. Electromagnetism teaches us that positively charged particles repel each other while positives and negatives attract. Now, in a metal, even though the atoms stay in their places, the electrons move around, spending their time near whichever atom they like.

The atoms are like residents in a colony who don’t get along with each other. But then all of them have kids (the electrons), which form a group and love to hangout at all the houses in the neighborhood. And the kids are loved by all and everyone takes care of them. So the kids hold the whole neighborhood together.

But remember: the nucleus of the two atoms still repel each other since they are both positively charged. So the atoms strike a deal. The two nuclei of atoms decide to build homes at some convenient distance where they can tolerate each other even while their electrons can happily move between the houses.

Now, when you try to push any material from one side, the distances between these atoms become squished. The positively charged nuclei come closer than they want to, and since positive charges repel each other, they now push back. This is how the elastic force of any material arises.
Vibrations and sound
Now, while one spring can push back, a lot of them arranged together in a material can do something more: they can vibrate together.

Think of a sofa with many springs beneath. When you jump at one end (of course you need to ignore the possibility of damaging it permanently), you can feel the whole bed vibrating even at the other end. The same thing happens in water when you drop a stone at one point. Water molecules vibrate and push and pull on nearby molecules as well, leading to a ripple.

Even in a solid material like iron or aluminum, when we strike one end, we make small changes to the position of atoms at that point. These atoms push and pull nearby atoms using those elastic forces. These vibrations can move at very high speed throughout the material. They are called sound waves. If a steel plate falls from your hand on the floor, the vibrations and sound you hear moves through the plate at a speed of about 20,000 km/hr and reaches you over air molecules at about 1,000 km/hr.
Sound and superconductivity

It may seem that the vibrations of positively charged atoms and the movement of negatively charged electrons do not bother each other much. And they do not, at least not significantly, when they are at room temperature. This is why metals behave like metals when we see them. But when the temperature drops, atoms and electrons can do funny things. For instance, atoms can conspire to generate attraction between two negatively charged electrons.

Imagine two atoms (neighbours) that move closer together using the spring that connects them, to attract a few kids to their garden for a moment. Now, once one electron (Bunty) moves towards them, another electron (Bubly) notices and also approaches the same neighborhood. Now as they move, another set of neighbours on a different road do the same thing. So Bunty and Bubly will continue following each other and form like a pair even though they did not mean to move together.
This pair of electrons is now called a Cooper pair, named after Leon Cooper, a U.S. physicist who won a Nobel Prize in 1972 for discovering this mechanism.

So what if two electrons start attracting each other? Turns out this formation of Cooper pairs leads to superconductivity. This is an extraordinary phenomenon: where a metal decides to completely change its character and start conducting electric currents without any resistance. Your electricity bills would nosedive if such materials could exist at room temperature.

Most metals become superconductors but at very low temperatures. Aluminum, often used to make your pressure cookers, becomes a superconductor at –271.9 C. Even though scientists discovered superconductivity more than a century ago, even today they don’t understand all aspects of it. It really requires quantum mechanics to understand, and is one of the most active areas of research in quantum condensed matter physics — which is the study of quantum materials around us.
Back to umbrellas
Finally, our most important question: why does an umbrella need that big spring?

The umbrella’s rod consists of multiple cylinders one around the other, and the spring opens them up in succession. When you close an umbrella, you compress the spring and store energy in it — essentially squishing billions of atoms slightly closer together than they want to be. This gets locked by a hook. When you press the umbrella button, the hook releases to let the spring push out again.
Next time, when you open an umbrella and walk in the rain, don’t forget to thank the billions of atoms and their small inter-atomic springs, which are also breathing a sigh of relief.
Adhip Agarwala is an assistant professor of physics at IIT Kanpur.

title: Chemists report ‘milder’ way to swap carbon for nitrogen atoms

content.value: When working with drug candidates, chemists sometimes like to replace a carbon atom in a ring of atoms with a nitrogen atom. This is because the switch can significantly alter the molecule’s properties, including how well it dissolves or how it interacts with biological targets in the body. But achieving it has been quite difficult, requiring chemical reactions with powerful oxidants, say, that can damage other parts of the molecule.

A new study in Science offers a breakthrough: researchers from the University of Chicago have reported a reaction to replace carbon with nitrogen in types of molecules often encountered in medical research and industry, in “mild conditions”.

Chemists had previously banked on a highly reactive intermediate compound called a nitrene to help push a nitrogen atom into a ring. The problem is nitrenes can have different electronic states, one of which — called the triplet state — doesn’t perform the desired reaction. But in the new work, the team set up a series of reactions that actually used the triplet nitrene state, together with blue light and oxygen, to temporarily open the ring, rearrange the atoms’ positions, and close it such that a nitrogen occurred where a carbon had been.

When they tested their technique on a type of indoles that had resisted existing methods, the researchers found the nitrogen-containing version in 73% of the reaction’s yield. After also trying it on other molecules, the team turned to biologically active molecules, which can be quite complex. The team modified one of the cancer-fighting compounds called the Vinca alkaloids to produce a version with nitrogen, which they found had better metabolic properties and less inhibited the hERG potassium channel — which drug-developers monitor for signs of dangerous heart-rhythm problems.

Finally, the team was also able to produce nitrogen-containing versions of two natural compounds: yohimbine, a veterinary drug, and catharanthine, one of the precursors of the chemotherapy drug vinblastine. This is valuable because synthesising them with nitrogen at the outset can change the molecules’ reactivity, putting paid to established synthetic routes.

That said, the method is not universal, as the authors have acknowledged, and includes toxic compounds called aryl azides among the starting materials. Even so, as they wrote in their paper, “The mild reaction conditions and broad skeletal diversity … lend an unexpected degree of generality to this method” and that they “anticipate that this addition to the toolkit for C-to-N transmutation will find promising applications in medicinal chemistry.”

title: India’s vast canal network offers a land-free path to solar power

content.value: As India expands its clean energy capacity, finding land for solar projects is becoming a challenge. This is driving interest in innovative solar solutions that can generate power without needing more land.

The recently approved PM Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY) is a step in this direction, aiming to develop 5,000 MW of floating solar capacity on reservoirs and other inland water bodies across the country.

However, India’s water infrastructure has more to offer: the country’s vast canal network — one of the largest in the world — is another under-explored avenue to generate solar power. Built over existing irrigation and water-supply canals, canal-top photovoltaics (CTPV) provides a unique approach to turn them into clean energy assets.

In CTPV, solar panels are mounted on specialised structures built over canal stretches. Unlike floating solar systems, where panels are installed on floating platforms on water bodies, CTPV systems use elevated structures above the canals.

Systems can be built based on the canal’s width, design, and orientation. The elevated structures may span the canal or can be installed along the canal banks. In all cases, the design must allow unobstructed water flow.
Advantages of CTPV

Similar to floating solar, the biggest advantage of CTPV is that it requires virtually no additional land. With land acquisition for large-scale solar becoming increasingly challenging and expensive, CTPV offers a promising way by using India’s canal infrastructure. For instance, in Punjab, the installation of 20 MW of CTPV systems is estimated to have saved nearly 100 acres of land.

CTPV offers another advantage. With solar panels covering canal stretches, the amount of water lost to evaporation can be reduced. This can be particularly useful in India’s water-stressed regions. The cooling effect of the water beneath the panels could improve panel performance in hot weather.
