A 1-MW CTPV system over the Narmada Canal in Mehsana, Gujarat, commissioned in 2012, reportedly saves close to 9 million litres of water every year while generating 1.6 million units of electricity annually.

While CTPV remains largely a niche application, India has been an early adopter, with its first installation in Mehsana in 2012. Between 2014 and 2017, two 10-MW CTPV systems were commissioned in Vadodara, Gujarat, and 20 MW of CTPV systems were commissioned in Punjab between 2017 and 2018.

In September 2025, the Punjab Energy Development Agency invited ‘expressions of interest’ for 40-MW CTPV projects across Punjab’s canal network, spanning over 10,000 km. Haryana has also initiated efforts to explore CTPV systems over six of its irrigation canals.

CTPV also received policy support in 2014, when the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) launched a pilot-cum-demonstration scheme for grid-connected CTPV and canal bank projects with a target of 50 MW each for CTPV and canal-bank projects. The scheme also included financial assistance of Rs 3 crore and Rs 1.5 crore per MW or 30% of project cost, whichever was lower, for CTPV and canal bank systems, respectively.

An assessment in 2024 (co-authored by CSTEP, where the author works) estimated India’s CTPV and canal bank potential at around 131 GW (for canals up to 30 m wide and vertical bifacial installations for canals over 30 m wide). Considerations such as solar irradiation, canal characteristics, distance from substations, and protected areas were included in the assessment to identify the best-suited canal stretches across India. The five States with the highest potential were Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Punjab.
Potential roadblocks
Despite India’s early progress, deployment has remained limited for more than a decade after the first installation.

High system cost is the primary bottleneck. CTPV systems are more expensive than ground-mounted ones as they require elevated structures to span canal stretches. These structures need to be designed to not disrupt canal operations and be sturdy enough to withstand winds. They also need additional structural steel, foundations, and access provisions for operations and maintenance, all of which add to the overall costs.
Maintenance tasks, including cleaning panels and replacement and repair work, can also prove difficult when the structures are elevated above a working canal.

The linear nature of CTPV systems, which run along the course of canals, can also pose challenges when canals follow irregular paths or change direction. This can increase the cost of producing electricity, especially when electrical substations or transformers are not strategically located.
Renewed policy approach

PM-SSY is expected to revitalise the floating solar segment and drive its adoption across India, signalling growing policy interest in exploring land-neutral solar applications. This focus could extend to other solutions like CTPV, potentially giving the technology greater policy attention and momentum.

However, to overcome the aforementioned structural challenges and scale CTPV deployment, identifying and prioritising suitable canal stretches will be critical. Factors such as land scarcity, nearby electricity demand and grid connectivity, and canal orientation and geometry should be considered while selecting sites to maximise the economic viability of CTPV systems.

CTPV also requires accessible and tailored financing mechanisms, including viability gap funding and low-cost debt, to make it an attractive option for developers. This will help support early projects, allowing developers to build experience and eventually reducing costs through scale and standardisation.

However, the 2014 MNRE scheme on CTPV shows that financial support alone may not suffice to convert pilots into large-scale deployment. A renewed policy approach that includes financial assistance and standardised specifications and guidelines, capacity building of state nodal agencies, irrigation departments, and other concerned agencies, and streamlined process flows is required.

While CTPV may not fully substitute ground-mounted or rooftop solar, they offer an untapped opportunity for India’s renewable energy expansion. Even if a fraction of CTPV’s technical potential is realised, it could significantly boost India’s renewable energy capacity without adding to the pressure on land resources.
Shantanu Roy is the Sector Coordinator for Renewables and Energy Conservation at the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP), a research-based think tank.

title: World Rhino Day focus on India-Bhutan joint conservation

content.value: Twenty years ago, western Assam’s Manas National Park and Tiger Reserve had no one-horned rhinos. A reintroduction programme begun in 2006 helped its number increase to almost 50 today, but it has brought a new conservation challenge — the park’s rhinos going international.

The national park authorities marked World Rhino Day on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) by celebrating the herbivore’s “comeback” and three successive years of zero poaching. Rhino specialists, however, called for a policy shift by making Bhutan a conservation partner.

“According to the 2022 census, Manas has an estimated 48 rhinos, although some died and a few were born during these four years. We have a much better environment today because the local stakeholders want more rhinos, which they say draw more tourists than other animals, including the tiger,” Deba Kumar Dutta, a frontline conservation scientist associated with the rhino translocation programme, said.

“Manas National Park has the capacity to carry more rhinos, but some of the ones thriving today are frequently crossing over to Bhutan. This warrants a joint conservation mechanism between the two countries, he told The Hindu.

The 2,837 sq. km Manas Tiger Reserve, which has the 500 sq. km Manas National Park at its core, adjoins the 1,057 sq. km Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan. The tiger reserve is in the Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC)-administered Bodoland Territorial Region.

Forest officials in Assam agreed that India and Bhutan need to expand their friendly relations for the joint conservation of rhinos, tigers, elephants, and the entire fragile transboundary Manas landscape. They underscored the scope for people-to-people conservation efforts apart from a bilateral approach.

Additional Chief Conservator of Forests and the BTC’s Council Head of the (Forest) Department, Sonali Ghosh, credited Manas’s “rhino comeback story” to the people living on the fringes of the tiger reserve. “A breeding, self-sustaining population of rhinos in Manas is proof that community-led conservation works,” she said after the World Rhino Day celebration in the national park’s Bhuyanpara Range.
Extremism-driven civil unrest and poaching, primarily to trade horns for arms, wiped out Manas’s historic population of about 100 rhinos between the late 1980s and the early 2000s.

An initiative under the Indian Rhino Vision 2020 saw 22 rhinos being moved to Manas from Kaziranga National Park and Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary between 2006 and 2021. The translocation during this period also involved 20 orphaned rhinos released from the Centre for Wildlife and Rehabilitation Centre near Kaziranga.

title: Trump says U.S. will henceforth call AI ‘super intelligence’

content.value: U.S. President ​Donald Trump on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) ‌said U.S. government ​documents ⁠would use “super intelligence” going forward instead of artificial ‌intelligence, and repeated his previous ‌calls about ‌AI ⁠warnings being ⁠a hoax.

“From this point forward, all ​of United ‌States documents, and hopefully the world’s will be changed ‌to use ​the much more accurate term ‘super’ as ⁠opposed to artificial. So it’s ‌super intelligence,” Mr. Trump said in a UN General Assembly speech.
“I’m not going ‌to stifle growth ​of something that will be bigger ⁠than the industrial ⁠revolution,” he said.

title: House crows aid efforts to enhance green cover across arid Rayalaseema, finds study

content.value: At 6 a.m., along the dusty railway station road in Vasudevapuram locality of Penukonda town in Sri Sathya Sai district, 72-year-old Papamma sweeps her courtyard and scatters leftover rice. In no time, a flock of crows descends. For Papamma, it is a daily ritual. For ecologists, however, it is the start of a quiet greening process in Rayalaseema, one of Andhra Pradesh’s driest zones.

Rayalaseema, with 500-600 mm of rainfall, unforgiving summers, and recurring droughts in Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai, Kadapa, Kurnool, Annamayya and Chittoor districts, continues its struggle to retain green cover. Afforestation drives in the region have a survival rate of less than 40% due to water stress, grazing and summer fires.
However, researchers claim that an unlikely ally — the house crow (Corvus splendens) — is significantly helping to reclaim the green cover across the dry landscape.

A study by V.V. Bala Subramanyam, an associate professor in the Department of Zoology at Sri Krishnadevaraya University (SKU) in Anantapur, has documented how crows feed on ripe neem fruits from March to June. The study claims that they eat 30 to 40 fruits in one sitting and disperse the seeds through their droppings across villages, fields, tank bunds and semi-urban roads a kilometre or two away from the parent tree.

“This process, called endozoochory, is silently contributing to natural regeneration. Our team marked droppings around the Penakacherla dam foreshore and the SK University campus in Anantapur, forest fringes in Annamayya district, the Idupulapaya road in Kadapa, Kallur tank bund and Nandikotkur road in Kurnool, Tiruchanur Avenue and Chandragiri roadside in Tirupati. The data shows about a 2% increase in urban greenery in parts of Rayalaseema, not just from plantations but from birds,” he said.

Meanwhile, Ramakrishna (72), a retired railway employee from Dharmavaram town, informed the research team that earlier, only jilledu and thorny shrubs were found on the local tank bund. “But now, neem saplings have started to appear without being planted, thanks to the crows,” he said.

Similar reports have come from Vempalli near Kadapa, Kasapuram and Kadiri temple lands, Penukonda and Gooty Fort hillocks, and the Tadipatri Penna bund. Villagers on the outskirts of Rayadurg said that close to a dozen neem saplings had appeared on a rocky patch, with crows raising their young and roosting there.

Birdwatchers from Kadapa, Pulivendula, Jammalamadugu, Rajampeta and Guntakal observed that not only crows but also bulbuls, mynas, babblers and barbets disperse peepal and banyan seeds. In Dharmavaram, Puttaparthi, Hindupur, Adoni, Nandyal, Proddatur, Atmakur, Allagadda, Madanapalle and Horsley Hills, the same multi-species network has been at work.

However, the population of house crows has reportedly dropped year after year. Shopkeepers on the busy Kapila Theertha road in Tirupati, the Old Bus Stand in Anantapur, B-Camp in Kurnool, Church Street in Chittoor and the Market Yard in Hindupur report flock sizes nearly 50% lower than in 2015. The cutting of age-old trees for road widening, garbage burning and covered garbage bins introduced under cleanliness drives are believed to be among the reasons for their decline.

“Afforestation initiatives in the Nallamala stretches of Nandyal and the Lankamala Wildlife Sanctuary in Kadapa require water, labour, and fencing, but bird-assisted regeneration needs only protection. The selection of spots for this natural way of planting by crows or any other bird species is incredible and foolproof. Individuals and public groups only have to protect old, fruit-bearing native trees on various temple premises and forest ghat roads. These are mother trees, while birds carry the seeds for dispersal,” a forest official in Rajampeta said.

title: Experts call for promotion of premium teas

content.value: China’s production and consumption of tea is thrice the quantity of India and most of it are premium teas, said Hariram Govind of Hindustan Unilever at the UPASI Tea Research Foundation’s centenary conference in Coonoor on Tuesday.

At a panel on “Sustainable Tea: Pathways for Future” moderated by S. Soundararajan, Director, Tea Development, Tea Board, Mr. Govind said that earlier 70% of teas consumed in China were premium teas. Now, it is 90%. Even the young generation are consuming tea, creating a market for the future.
In India, tea consumption’s market penetration is 90% and a person consumes three to four cups a day. So, the focus should be on increasing consumption of premium teas, he said.
Further, when the scale of sustainable and regenerative practices go up, it will become economically viable.

According to Ena Irino, S. Ishimitsu and Co, Japan, commoditisation of tea and climate change are the two main challenges the tea sector faces in promoting sustainable tea. Sustainability is all about balancing social responsibility and economic viability and create value through innovation. In Japan, sustainability is a basic standard for the teas, she said.

Commoditisation is lowering the prices for the producers and they are unable to reinvest and climate change has hit productivity. In a measure to overcome this, production of speciality teas and premium teas should increase.

Marcus Wulf of Schroeder & Hanmann, Germany, said sustainability in tea that started three decades ago has become more about having a certificate on the product packet for the consumers. But, the producers should be able to realise more so that they can get more into sustainable production practices. Countries such as Japan, China, and Korea are producing artisan teas, he pointed out.
Buyers go to countries that offer sustainable tea at lower prices. India should focus on bringing down the prices, he added.

title: Bill Gates pushes for ’smart use’ of AI as his foundation builds more representative language data

content.value: Bill Gates told his foundation's Goalkeepers gathering that “increased generosity” and “the smart use of AI” together could accelerate the fight against inequality, urging the world's richest countries to expand international aid and apply artificial intelligence toward what he considers “lifesaving innovations.”

“We failed to build in the right human values and ways of keeping our moral code controlling what these AIs do,” Gates, the foundation's chair, said during a Monday conversation with political commentator Van Jones at Jazz at Lincoln Center in New York.

The Gates Foundation's annual event, usually hosted the week of the United Nations' high-level meetings, opened with a reminder: 26 of the world's 34 wealthiest nations decreased development aid to poorer countries last year. Meanwhile, the U.N. has warned that progress on its sustainable development goals — lofty targets to reduce poverty, improve health and protect the environment by 2030 — is “slow and uneven.”

The contraction comes at a time when Gates suggested “we have some of the best innovations ever to improve people's lives.” His foundation spent much of its two-hour event elevating educators, farmers and health workers who are using AI to identify students' learning gaps, combat pest infestations and better recall patients' medical records.
The Gates Foundation also touted its new coalition of Anthropic, Google, OpenAI Foundation and dozens of other organisations working to make AI more accessible in underrepresented languages.

The partners — 60 in total, according to Monday's announcement — include frontier AI labs, corporations, philanthropies and others already working to expand the number of languages available in AI tools that the Gates Foundation believes could combat global inequality. The coalition aims to reach more than 3 billion people over five years by better coordinating existing efforts.

It's work that must continue “full speed ahead," according to Gates Foundation CEO Mark Suzman, even as some of the largest AI companies urge their industry to slow down development of advanced models. Governments must regulate the impacts on cybersecurity or children's development, he said, while they extend AI's humanitarian applications to poor communities currently “shut out” from the technology.

“Even if AI was frozen right now — which I don’t expect and I am not calling for — we would want to be building these language sets and making them usable with the tools that we have available right now,” Suzman told The Associated Press.

The collaboration follows last week's Goalkeepers report, where the foundation committed $1 billion toward AI-focused efforts to improve health outcomes, upgrade educational tools and inform small farmers' practices around the world. Unrepresentative language data could lead a model to mistranslate a pregnant Malawi woman saying her “water has broken” into the direct English that she'd “thrown away water," the report warned.

The “original sin” is that many AI tools were trained on language data scraped from the internet, according to Mozilla Data Collective CEO E.M. Lewis-Jong, whose company was incubated by the Mozilla Foundation and is now a subsidiary of the not-for-profit Mozilla.org. The data-sharing platform seeks to help communities upload cultural and linguistic data sets on their own terms rather than have that data taken from the web without their explicit consent.

“The internet is not a representative space,” she said. “Why would you think that you were going to get a culturally diverse and representative system out of something that was predominantly trained on Reddit?”

Details such as the coalition’s governance are still getting hammered out, according to Suzman. A secretariat will track each signatory’s commitments and the Gates Foundation may nudge partners to fill larger gaps when necessary.

Google, a member of the coalition, has been funding an effort to collect more than 150,000 hours of audio across every district in India. Known as Project Vaani, the push underscores the need to gather speech data on dialects within languages, according to Google senior vice president James Manyika. To get there, he said, Google is working with local partners to record speech in the field.

Anthropic, whose CEO published an essay calling for industrywide cooperation on decelerating advancements, was already working with the foundation to speed up vaccine developments and bolster its chatbot’s data set of local crops. Elizabeth Kelly, the head of beneficial deployments at Anthropic, acknowledged the company's products “lag in many African languages in particular."

“We’re acutely aware that we can’t achieve any of the benefits we want to see in terms of improving patient outcomes or improving literacy and numeracy for students across the globe unless we actually get this language piece right," she told AP.

title: Microsoft Xbox plans to cut hundreds of jobs

content.value: Xbox is preparing to cut hundreds of jobs this week while the gaming giant plans to streamline some studios, reported the Information outlet, citing an unnamed source.
Xbox is yet to formally confirm or deny the news report, but the company had previously laid out detailed plans for changing operations and reducing headcount under its new CEO Asha Sharma.

On July 6, the new CEO took to X to announce “the most significant restructure in XBOX history,” with the company planning to reduce its team by approximately 3,200 throughout the 2027 financial year.
Ms. Sharma highlighted the need for a “reset” targeting the company’s content portfolio, platform, and team operations.
She noted that the business was “not healthy,” citing margins that were significantly lower than rival platform and publishing businesses.

“In FY26, over 200 million new players came to XBOX and our games, but our business did not grow with our audience. We need to close that gap by investing in what players value. That will take time, but we expect to return to growth by the end of FY27,” posted Ms. Sharma on X on July 30.
Layoffs at Xbox had been widely predicted by industry analysts, and did not come as a shock to insiders.

title: Alibaba Group unveils new AI chip Zhenwu V900, plans to train new AI model

content.value: The Alibaba Group unveiled its new Zhenwu V900 AI chip this week, pitching it as China’s most powerful, and promising tripled performance when compared to its predecessor.
The Chinese e-commerce and internet giant also committed to training a new AI model with between 5 and 10 trillion parameters, apart from growing its global data centre capacity.
The new Zhenwu V900 AI chip comes from the company’s T-Head semiconductor unit.

The unveiling comes at a time when U.S. technologists are clashing over AI safety standards, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for tech restrictions against China to prevent AI distillation. But Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed for the ability to compete in the Asian country’s market against Chinese chip rivals.

On August 20, Alibaba reported a 75% fall in quarterly net profit. However, CEO Eddie Wu hailed a “strong quarter” for the company, noting the commercialisation of its AI capabilities. There was also a 9% rise in revenue during the quarter.

“Alibaba Cloud’s external revenue growth accelerated to 45%, with AI-related product revenue delivering triple-digit growth for the twelfth consecutive quarter. We recently launched frontier language, coding, video, audio, image and music models, all delivering top-tier performance,” he said in the company’s earnings statement for the June quarter 2026.
With inputs from Reuters

title: China's robot dancers limber up for America's Got Talent final

content.value: Chinese street dancer Wu Yufei has spent most of his 13-year career performing solo, but this year, he found some new partners: a crew of robots with sleek moves.
The 27-year-old Sichuan native, together with his fellow robot performers, has made it to the final of "America's Got Talent" (AGT), a stage he had been hoping to reach for years.
A longstanding science-fiction fan, Wu told AFP from Pasadena, California, that dancing with robots in the group Homies gave him a "very magical feeling".
After months of training with them, his robot dancers now feel like more than just "cold, lifeless machines", he said.
"It almost feels as if there's a kind of team spirit there," Wu told AFP, as he and the dance crew of humanoids, made by Chinese robotics group Unitree, prepared for the AGT final this week.

Robot dancing has become a huge craze in China after Unitree robots performed in a breakout performance at China's annual Spring Festival gala performance, the country's most-watched television extravaganza.
Businesses and event planners across the country have since rushed to hire robots to perform and attract visitors.
Training robots to dance involves capturing intricate human movements, running computer simulations, and then transferring results to the robots, said industry insiders.
For Fang Zhenghua, the art director behind Wu and Unitree's AGT performances, training a robot to dance resembles "creating a soul".
"The impact of AI on dance performances, or the impact of robots on dancing - I was quite against it all at the beginning," he told AFP from Shanghai.
But over time, working with the skilled engineers, who he describes as the "mothers" of the robots, changed his perspective.
Training robots requires input from human dancers and relies heavily on engineers to troubleshoot problems, particularly in real-time during performances.
"It takes a lot of fine-tuning," Liu Zhiquan, commercialisation lead at robotics motion-capture firm BridgeDP, told AFP.
A 30-second dance routine could take days, sometimes weeks, to perfect, he added, and performers need to be willing to compromise.
"If the dancers are not tech-savvy, there will be a lot of re-takes," he said.
Wegers Wei, from Shanghai-based dance studio Limit Crew, said that when he designs routines for robots, he avoids movements that he knows will be difficult for them.

"If we find that some routines don't look good for robots or if they look like the robots are making mistakes, we would change them," said Wei, whose robots won first and second places for street dance at this year's World Humanoid Robot Games.
Robots are good at rotating moves, or what street dancers call power moves, Wei said, as it is "just a matter of adjusting the motor power and the torque of the arms".
However, routines that require body flexibility are extremely difficult for robots, he said.
Another blind spot is musicality.
Robot dancing is mostly scripted playback.
Unlike humans, the machines cannot improvise or "make on-the-spot adjustments" if the music changes suddenly, Wu Yufei added.
While the general public in China mostly sees robot dancing as entertainment, industry insiders see it as a chance to show off robotic designs, capabilities and reliability.
"That's why everyone is keen to perform these kinds of high-skill dances," said Guo Renjie, founder and CEO of robotics engineering company Zeroth.
A recent Morgan Stanley report forecast that China's humanoid robotics market could reach $2 billion in value this year.
Accounting for more than 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments in the first half of 2026 globally, the Chinese industry also faces increasing scrutiny from investors and policymakers.
Many companies are struggling to find commercially viable uses for their humanoids beyond entertainment.
Executives at humanoid robotics companies have publicly acknowledged that the industry is still years away from its own "ChatGPT moment;" the point at which robots become useful to ordinary people.
"I think everyone should give this industry time to reach its full potential," said Zeroth's Guo.
Unitree made a blistering debut on the Shanghai stock market in August, surging 629 percent through the first day's trading.
Its market capitalisation has since fallen by around half from its peak.
Back at the AGT filming studio in Pasadena, Wu pointed to another robot benefit: how quickly his robot crew could learn routines.
"Their knowledge can be replicated extremely quickly," he said.
"Not only does a single robot learn quickly, but they can all learn the same things at the same time, which is quite terrifying."

title: Survey discovers six new species from Periyar Tiger Reserve in Keralam

content.value: Highlighting the rich biodiversity of the Periyar Tiger Reserve (PTR) in Keralam’s Thekkady, a four-day faunal survey recorded six species previously undocumented in the reserve, including one bird, one butterfly, and four odonate species.

According to officials, the newly recorded bird species is the golden-headed cisticola (Cisticola exilis). A total of 174 bird species were documented during the exercise, raising the reserve’s cumulative bird count to 347.

The survey also recorded the common onyx butterfly (Horaga onyx). With 192 butterfly species sighted during the four-day event, the total number of documented butterfly species in the reserve has risen to 284.
Odonate species

Additionally, four odonate species (dragonflies and damselflies) were recorded in the reserve for the first time: the parakeet darner (Gynacantha millardi), fraser’s clubtail (Acrogomphus fraseri), spiny horntail (Burmagomphus chaukulensis), and nilgiri clawtail (Lamelligomphus nilgiriensis). With 68 odonate species documented in total, the consolidated odonate checklist for PTR now stands at 111.
Beyond birds, butterflies, and odonates, the composite assessment documented 15 mammal, 30 spider, 34 ant, and five cicada species.

Kalesh Sadasivan, research associate of the Travancore Nature History Society (TNHS) noted that the golden-headed cisticola is a rare species typically found at higher elevations. He added that the findings reflect the importance of the reserve’s elevational gradient, evergreen forests, grasslands, and ecotonal habitats in supporting diverse wildlife assemblages.

“The healthy ecosystem and unpolluted water bodies in PTR are behind these new records. Surveys have been conducted regularly over the last decade, consistently documenting new additions,” Dr. Sadasivan said.
Necessity of surveys

P.P. Pramod, field director of PTR, stated that adding six new distribution records to an area as intensively studied as Periyar highlights the necessity of systematic biodiversity surveys. “These studies help us understand changes in species distribution and habitat use, strengthening the evidence base for long-term conservation management,” he said.
“The survey covered widely separated camps representing varied elevations, habitats, and levels of accessibility,” said Periyar East division deputy director Midhun Mohan.

Held from September 10 to 13, the survey was a collaborative effort involving 75 delegates from 21 NGOs, academic and research institutions, along with Forest department officials and frontline staff. Participants were organised into 21 teams deployed across 20 active base camps to cover all major ecological zones of the tiger reserve.

title: A.P. Health Minister orders action against doctors and staff for remaining absent from duties

content.value: Minister of Health, Medical, and Family Welfare Satya Kumar Yadav on Monday (September 21, 2026) directed officials to take action against doctors and department staff who have remained absent from their duties for an extended period.

Taking part in a review meeting at the APIIC building in Mangalagiri, the Minister said employees should obtain certification from government doctors for illness and required leave, and that medical certificates and recommendations issued by private doctors will not be accepted.

The Minister issued the instructions when he was informed that shortage of staff caused inordinate delays in disposal of files. According to a release from the department, since the TDP-led NDA government came to power, 4,410 matters were brought to the Minister’s attention, most of which were related to transfers. Out of these, only 40% of the files were disposed of.

The Minister said that in case the delay is caused due to inaction on part of an individual, an explanation should be obtained from them and, if necessary, appropriate disciplinary action should be taken against them. Further, the Minister said a file should not remain pending at any level for more than two days. It was decided during the meeting that a dashboard should be developed to monitor the status of files.

After the Minister was informed that 493 doctors are still unauthorisedly absent from duty, he directed officials to take appropriate action against all of them within a maximum period of three months.
Principal Secretary G. Veerapandian, Joint Secretary Ronanki Gopalakrishna, Drug Control Administration Director General Arun Babu, and others took part in the review meeting.

title: Karnataka to track cancer patients after fake drug bust

content.value: Following the seizure of counterfeit drugs, especially those used to treat cancer, Health Department officials are now tracking patients to check the current status of their health.
Licences of 16 retail and wholesale pharmaceutical firms were cancelled and eight licenses were suspended.

Speaking to The Hindu, U.T. Khader, Minister for Health and Family Welfare, said, “Officials will track records of cancer patients from various private hospitals across the State. We will call them up and check the status of their health. They may have unknowingly bought these counterfeit drugs.”
“We don’t sell fake drugs at government hospitals, hence there is no question of tracking patients to know their status,” he added.

Mr. Khader stated that in order to make it easy for laboratories, doctors, and pharmaceutical firms to differentiate between fake and original drugs, the department has written to the headquarters of Pfizer to release their reference standards.

“When the fake drugs are sent to labs for testing, we need to have the company’s reference standards. It will make the process of drug testing easier for our department. However, the company hasn’t replied to our email so far. Hence, we have written to the Union government to take a note of the increasing number of fake drugs and medicines in the market, measures to identify them, and stop them from being sold in medical shops. State governments have a minor role to play in giving permissions to drug manufacturers and what is brought into the market for selling,” he said.

He added that the investigation of counterfeit drugs is ongoing, while the department is contemplating booking fake drug manufacturers, distributors, pharmaceutical firms, and medical store owners under Section 105 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), according to which if the act is done with the intent to cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death, the punishment is either life imprisonment or imprisonment for five to 10 years and penalty depending on the nature of offence.

An all-India health conclave will be hosted in Bengaluru in the third week of October, said Health Minister U.T. Khader. “Health Ministers from across all the States, FSDA officials from State governments, FSSAI officials and other stakeholders will be part of the conclave. We will not only discuss and debate but take some strong decisions to tackle issues like counterfeit drugs across the country,” he said.

title: Researchers at RGCB in Keralam develop nanopore sensors for early detection of Parkinson’s disease

content.value: Researchers at the BRIC-Rajiv Gandhi Centre for Biotechnology (BRIC-RGCB) here have developed a nanopore-based sensing technology that could pave the way for early detection and monitoring of biomarkers linked to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

A research team led by Mahendran K.R., with contributions from PhD student Varsha Shaji and postdoctoral researcher Neethu Puthumadathil, designed the ‘self-assembling dual-diameter’ nanopore sensors that are capable of detecting such biomarkers with high sensitivity, the RGCB said in a statement.
The research published in Nature Nanotechnology represents a significant advance in nanoscience and biomolecular sensing, the RGCB said.
Indicators of diseases

Biomarkers are indicators of diseases that can be used for early detection. Nanopores are extremely small hollow structures. Detecting biomarkers at an early stage using conventional techniques, however, remains challenging as many of these biomarkers occur at extremely low concentrations.

“In the new approach, the researchers designed short peptides that form pores of varying sizes, providing a versatile platform for sensing biomolecules with different shapes and dimensions. The sensors distinguish disease and non-disease-associated forms of the biomarkers, even when they were present in complex protein mixtures at very low concentrations,” according to the RGCB.

In future, these sensors can be used to develop point-of-care devices that detect biomarkers associated with various diseases, such as cancer, directly from biological fluids, including blood, the institute said.
Major challenge

Early and accurate detection remains a major challenge in managing neurodegenerative diseases, BRIC-RGCB director Beena Pillai said. “The nanopore sensor platform demonstrates how advances in nanotechnology and biotechnology can come together to address a critical unmet need in health care,” she said.

The work was carried out in collaboration with Ulrich Kleinekathöfer’s group at Constructor University, Germany, and Krishnananda Chattopadhyay’s group at CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (CSIR-IICB), Kolkata. The study was supported by grants from the Department of Biotechnology, the Department of Science and Technology, the Indian Council of Medical Research and the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research.

title: Tamil Nadu government hospitals running short of critical medicines for pre-term babies

content.value: Government hospitals across Tamil Nadu are facing a shortage of surfactant medicines, a critical and life-saving medicine for pre-term babies.
The shortage has been persisting for the past few months, and several Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs) at government hospitals have been flagging it up for the Health Department.

Doctors said surfactant medicines are essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies in need of the therapy. They utilised external bovine or porcine surfactants (intratracheal) in pre-term babies. These surfactants were part of the speciality drug rate contract purchases of the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation (TNMSC).

Inquiries with a number of hospitals and doctors revealed that a number of centres were facing short supply of surfactants in the past few months. Official sources confirmed that government hospitals, among them medical college hospitals in Theni, Dharmapuri, Tiruppur, Cuddalore, Tiruvannamalai, Vellore and Karur districts and in Chennai, reported surfactant vial shortage, while some hospitals said they had uninterrupted supply.

A doctor, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the shortage prevailed in the past three to four months owing to a number of factors. “First, we got no allotment. Secondly, some centres miscalculated their requirement, which is based on the average number of pre-term babies delivered, and thirdly, there was higher utilisation. This is a life-saving medicine essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies who are otherwise solid,” he said.

A doctor at another hospital said continuous supply was not assured, and shortage occurred frequently.  “Currently, we are borrowing from other sub-centres which are referring babies to us. It is very difficult for us to manage newborn units without surfactants. Sometimes, we purchase them privately using SNCU funds to save the babies,” another doctor said.

A senior paediatrician said that after 34 weeks of gestation, the foetal lungs are generally mature enough to support exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide after birth. “However, in very pre-term babies, the alveoli, which are the tiny air sacs in the lungs, may not be sufficiently mature to function effectively on their own. Surfactant, a substance produced in the lungs, helps keep the alveoli open. But in babies born very prematurely, not enough surfactant may be produced, making it difficult for them to maintain adequate oxygen levels. Depending on the baby’s condition, doctors may use respiratory support such as CPAP or a mechanical ventilator. Surfactant is delivered directly into the lungs through the endotracheal tube to prevent hyaline membrane disease.”
Lung maturity in a newborn is critical as decreased oxygen could cause hypoxia and conditions such as retinopathy of prematurity and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, he said.

A Health Department source denied that there was any shortage. “There was no procurement delay. Some centres may have miscalculated their requirement, resulting in shortage, or may have utilised more vials. In such circumstances, they have obtained the required supply from neighbouring facilities. A six-month purchase order, worth nearly ₹9 crore, has been issued. Additionally, operational costs are provided<u> </u>for paediatricians to make local purchases whenever required,” he said.

Another official said the TNMSC has issued purchase orders and it will be supplied within two days. Officials said Cuddalore faced shortage and arrangements were made to send supplies from Coimbatore. The situation was being closely monitored, they said.

title: Campaign to reduce the intake of salt

content.value: Salt, as an essential electrolyte, sits at the centre of human well-being, but being most prone to overuse and misuse, the condiment remains at the heart of illness as well. When Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj took salt to the floor of the Assembly, he dragged it willy-nilly into public discourse. He announced plans to launch a multi-pronged mission to reduce salt intake, turning attention to the right quantities and forms that must be consumed. The Minister’s speech made it clear that the government’s plans were not merely about a dietary tweak, but instead, a recalibration of how wellbeing is perceived.

Salt, in the right proportions, facilitates hydration, nerve signalling, muscle function, and digestion and also has a role to play in stress physiology. However, in excess, or in ultra-processed foods, it can have a deleterious impact on health, increasing the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney strain over time. On the other hand, very low salt intake can contribute to hypotension, fatigue, dizziness and brain fog, as well.

The health difference comes from the quantity of salt consumed and the overall diet patterns, undergoing rapid changes in favour of ultra-processed, packaged foods, and fast foods, that tend to be high in salt. The Indian diet itself, with its pickles and spicy curries, lends itself to tilting the salt cellar over a little too often. Surveys by the Indian Council of Medical Research show that in India, men consume an average of 8.9 gms daily, while women consume about 7.1 gms. Urban areas tend to consume higher amounts of salt, averaging around 9.2 gms a day. The WHO, which recommends keeping the intake under 5 gms of salt per day, released a set of guidelines in January 2025, recommending the use of lower-sodium salt substitutes, essentially including potassium chloride, and reducing the percentage of sodium chloride in table salt.

In Tamil Nadu, hypertension is a major public health concern. A 2024 study by Selvavinayagam T.S. et al., published in PLOS 1, showed adult prevalence of hypertension hovering around 33.9%, much above the national average of 28.5%. There is a direct link between consuming excess salt and hypertension — eating too much salt causes the body to retain extra water, which increases blood volume and puts higher pressure on the artery walls, leading to clinical hypertension.
Action plan

The Tamil Nadu government’s plan is appropriately comprehensive. For the first time, a statewide survey using urine samples will scientifically measure salt consumption. Salt will be gradually reduced in government-run kitchens, including the Nutritious Meal Programme, ICDS centres, government hospitals and hostels. The feasibility of introducing a low-sodium salt substitute will be examined.

This will be backed by a state-wide awareness campaign on how to read labels on packages, tasting before adding salt and using natural flavour enhancers. Researchers of a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial reported in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, in 2021, wrote that the replacement of salt with a reduced-sodium, added-potassium salt substitute is an acceptable and effective dietary intervention for lowering systolic blood pressure in persons with hypertension in rural India.

The State also intends to step up its hypertension control activities through its community health outreach programme ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ and other public health care institutions. People diagnosed with hypertension will receive systematic counselling and anti-hypertension drugs. There is evidence that such closely-monitored health interventions succeed. A study published recently in Nature, Archana Ramalingam et al., studying the cascade of care between 2019-20 and 2023-24 in Tamil Nadu, showed that overall, hypertension care in Tamil Nadu improved, with increased use of public health facilities for treatment.

The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the new salt reduction campaign of the Tamil Nadu government. Founder Rajan Ravichandran says: “This is a wonderful surprise; we have been knocking at many doors to bring in awareness of salt reduction in the public health sector. It can be very powerful in changing the way people consume salt. We just have to go back to 2005, when the campaign initiated by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health resulted in a reported 30% reduction of salt in bread in the United Kingdom,” Dr. Rajan adds.

G. Sengottuvelu, senior interventional cardiologist, Apollo Hospitals, explains further: “Excess salt is one of the most important and preventable contributors to high blood pressure, heart attack and stroke.” His argument is that Indians’ preference for salty food is largely an acquired habit, often beginning in childhood, and the palate can adapt when salt is gradually reduced. Cutting down salt is a simple change that can make a major difference to cardiovascular health — less salt today can mean lower blood pressure, fewer heart attacks and fewer strokes tomorrow.
Just a pinch can reduce an Indian’s salt overload
Why India should cut down on its salt intake
The cheapest way to prevent NCDs: reducing salt consumption

Incidentally, the regulator Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s submission of guidelines for ingredient labelling on packaged food has grabbed eyeballs. While experts point to lacunae within the labelling guidelines, it does seem that momentum is growing towards building a society that is aware of the importance of salt and regulating it, and reclaiming the kitchen staple as a transformative touchstone for improved public health. As Tamil Nadu rolls out its programme, hopefully with scientific vigour and cultural sensitivity, other States will do well to watch and emulate.  If it is possible to cut down hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and kidney disease with adjusting the size of a single pinch, then, the question is why not?

title: Experts discuss specific diagnosis and brain modulation in Alzheimer’s care

content.value: “Treatable conditions can masquerade as Alzheimer’s disease, including autoimmune disorders and thyroid inflammation,” said Ennapadam S. Krishnamoorthy, founder and behavioural neurologist and neuropsychiatrist, Buddhi Clinic, stressing the importance of a specific diagnosis in people presenting with cognitive symptoms.

He was speaking at The Hindu Wellness Series webinar on Alzheimer’s dementia and the promise of brain stimulation, held on Sunday by The Hindu in association with Buddhi Clinic, marking World Alzheimer’s Day.

Dr. Krishnamoorthy said a detailed, case-based assessment was important to distinguish Alzheimer’s disease from other conditions that can cause cognitive symptoms and may be treatable. He also stressed the need to tailor care to the individual, noting that some medications may offer limited benefits or cause harm in certain patients. He said non-pharmacological interventions also had an important role in dementia care.

Vivek Misra, senior consultant – Neuromodulation and Clinical Neurosciences, Buddhi Clinic, discussed the potential of non-invasive brain stimulation as part of dementia care. The technique uses external stimulation to modulate activity in specific areas of the brain. “It does not require sedation or seizure induction and can be done in an outpatient setting,” Mr. Misra said.

He said brain stimulation should not be viewed as a standalone treatment, but as one component of a broader, precision-based approach to dementia care, with interventions tailored to the individual’s clinical profile and needs.
The session was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu.
The webinar can be viewed here:  https://newsth.live/THBCAY

title: Dengue cases in Tamil Nadu decline for third consecutive year as per government data

content.value: Dengue cases in Tamil Nadu have declined for the third consecutive year, according to data from the State Health and Family Welfare Department. The State recorded 17,049 cases up to September 19, 2026, compared with 25,585 cases in 2025, 46,971 in 2024, and 56,863 in 2023.

The number of reported dengue cases fell by 17% between 2023 and 2024, followed by a 46% decline in 2025. The 2026 figure, however, covers only the period up to September 19 and cannot be compared with the full-year figures of previous years.
The data indicate a sustained decline in reported dengue cases, although the figures for 2026 could change over the remaining months.
The State reported nine dengue-related deaths up to September 19, 2026, as compared with 12 in 2025, 13 in 2024 and 12 in 2023.

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection that can cause high fever, body pain and, in some cases, severe disease. Warning signs such as persistent abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding and extreme weakness require prompt medical attention.
The year-on-year decline in reported cases and deaths provides an overview of the State’s dengue burden, but the data do not establish the reasons for the decline.
Continued surveillance and measures to control the Aedes mosquito, which transmits dengue, remain important for prevention.

title: What is scrub typhus | Explained

content.value: The death of an Anna University student at Government Kilpauk Medical College Hospital (KMCH) on Friday (September 18, 2026), due to scrub typhus, has once again brought this bacterial infection to the fore. University authorities have said they have started screening students for scrub typhus as well, along with dengue and leptospirosis
What is scrub typhus?
Scrub typhus is a bacterial infection caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. It is spread by the bite of infected larval mites or chiggers -- it is not a mosquito-borne disease.

Scrub typhus is a major public health burden in South and Southeast Asia. A 2021 systematic review noted that scrub typhus, a common acute febrile illness, is “a grossly under-recognised public health problem in India.” It stated that the proportion of scrub typhus among acute undifferentiated febrile illness (AUFI) studies was 25.3%, and community seroprevalence was 34.2%. The review also noted that the disease causes severe morbidity and accounts for a large number of deaths, with its bueden “underappreciated.”

A 2025 multi-centre study of 587 children with acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) from Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu revealed that scrub typhus is now the most common infectious cause of AES in southern India.
What are the symptoms?

Symptoms usually begin within 10 days of infection. The United States Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists symptoms of scrub typhus as: fever and chills, headache, body aches and muscle pain, a dark, scab-like region at the site of the chigger bite (also known as eschar), mental changes ranging from confusion to coma, enlarged lymph nodes and a rash.

Timely treatment is critical. If left untreated, severe illness from scrub typhus infection can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), shock, meningitis and kidney failure, which can be fatal, notes a research paper, Incidence of Scrub Typhus in Rural South India published in The New England Journal of Medicine last year.
In India, there is a high mortality of scrub typhus, primarily due to late diagnosis and treatment.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
Since the symptoms of scrub typhus are common to those of several other diseases, diagnosis is often delayed. A blood test (IgM ELISA or PCR) can help confirm the diagnosis.

Scrub typhus should be treated with the antibiotics doxycycline or azithromycin. If the treatment is begun in time, it is effective. Results of a trial carried out in seven centres in India, published in 2023, in which patients were randomly assigned to receive a combination therapy of doxycycline and azithromycin, showed faster resolution of complications compared with two other arms where patients were given monotherapy with either doxycycline or azithromycin. The frequencies of respiratory, renal, hepatic, and central nervous system complications were lower in the combination-therapy group than in either of the monotherapy groups.
How can it be prevented?
There is no vaccine as yet for scrub typhus. The infection is not contagious.
Chiggers live in areas with lots of grass, thick vegetation, agricultural fields, plant litter and bare soil across rural areas of Asia, and usually feed on small mammals such as rats and shrews.

Keeping oneself safe from bites through protective clothing, covered footwear and the use of insect repellent may help. Ensuring surroundings are clean and well maintained can also go some way towards reducing mite habitats.

“Early diagnosis and prompt treatment can significantly reduce complications and mortality. Establishing good surveillance and instituting appropriate control measures are urgently needed,” the 2021 review notes.

title: Why students with disabilities face a digital and remedial learning gap

content.value: India’s higher education policy framework increasingly talks about inclusion. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act) places obligations on educational institutions to promote inclusive education, while the University Grants Commission (UGC) has, over the years, developed guidelines and institutional mechanisms intended to ensure that students with disabilities (SwD) can participate in higher education on an equal basis.

Despite these measures, the dearth of remedial support makes them vulnerable to academic exclusion and widens existing educational inequalities. Limited digital access further restricts their access to online learning resources, digital libraries, academic databases, and other educational platforms, hindering participation in technology-enabled learning and limiting their ability to make full use of academic opportunities.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)

Most recently, the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities listed the Accessibility Guidelines and Standards for Higher Education Institutions and Universities, issued by the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education, on June 25, 2024. The UGC describes these guidelines as part of its effort to ensure equal participation and inclusion of persons with disabilities in higher education.

Importantly, the UGC states that every higher educational institution (HEI) is expected to develop an effective accessibility mechanism extending from the admission process through the completion of the course. The Commission issued fresh directions to universities to furnish a report along with statistical information in respect of students admitted, teaching and non-teaching recruitment, as well as fellowships/scholarships provided to PwD students through the Universities Activity Monitoring Portal (UAMP) by September 30, 2026. It calls for the need to form an Internal Committee comprising teachers, staff, students and parents to take care of the day-to-day needs of persons with disabilities.
Join THEdge LinkedIn group

Yet institutional attention to disability often becomes focused on admission, reservation, and physical infrastructure. The more difficult question of what happens to the student after admission receives considerably less attention.

“The national statistical architecture measures how many students with disabilities enter higher education but does not adequately measure what happens to them after they enter colleges and universities,” disability rights activist and Professor at University College of Medical Sciences, Delhi, Dr. Satendra Singh told The Hindu.

Students with disabilities may enter higher education with varying levels of exposure to accessible learning environments. Some may require additional academic assistance, remedial classes, note-taking support, assistive technologies, or additional time and flexibility to engage with coursework. A student who misses classes because of disability-related issues may not have access to a structured academic mechanism to navigate the backlogs. The result is a form of exclusion that is not visible in institutional statistics.
Supportive system needed

The RPwD Act itself points to Section 16, which requires not merely admission without discrimination, but reasonable accommodation, necessary support, and monitoring of participation, academic progress, and completion. The UGC’s own accessibility framework similarly speaks of an accessible mechanism covering the student journey from admission to completion. But the lack of adequate remedial support has a direct bearing on how students with disability perform academically.
“Majority of the HEIs do not have a rights-based understanding of reasonable accommodation. They are still stuck with ramps, braille and talking books,” Dr. Singh said.

Pointing to the 2023–24 AISHE data, he said, “Of the 4.50 crore students enrolled in HEIs, the reported 54,080 students with benchmark disabilities (SwBD) represent approximately 0.12% of total higher-education enrolment. This is about 12 SwBD per 10,000 students. The AISHE reporting does not provide a detailed disability-type categorisation. This is a significant data gap because ‘SwBD’ is an extremely heterogeneous category. A student who is blind, a deaf student who uses Indian Sign Language (ISL), a student with dyslexia, an autistic student, and a student with psychosocial disability can have completely different accessibility and academic-support requirements.”

Dr. Sanjay Kant Prasad, Director of the National Centre for Disability Studies at IGNOU and former Deputy Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, echoes his views. He said, “Higher education must recognise that the 21 categories of disabilities identified under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act have diverse and often distinct educational needs. While some disabilities may require limited remedial support, students with blindness, low vision, hearing impairment, deafness, cerebral palsy, autism and learning disabilities, among others, may require specific forms of academic and assistive support.”

He stresses that inclusive education does not mean eliminating specialised support. Rather, it is about creating an accessible environment in which the same educational curriculum can be accessed by students with different needs.

“In higher education, teachers may not require specialised training for every disability, but they should at least be oriented to disability-related needs and know how to make classrooms, teaching methods and learning materials accessible. This could include tactile materials and Braille for students with visual impairments, appropriate seating and mobility support, hearing aids or visual aids for students with hearing impairments, and the use of assistive and digital technologies such as text-to-speech software,” Dr. Prasad said.

Citing IGNOU’s efforts to provide study material at students’ doorsteps, counselling through teleconferencing and facilities for submitting assignments using computers, while following government and UGC guidelines, Dr. Prasad feels students’ ability to remain in education depends on broader social and economic support, not just classroom accommodations. Housing, awareness of available services and support from disability organisations are important factors.

Progress has been made over the past several decades from exclusion towards inclusion, but implementation remains uneven, and continued awareness, teacher training, and institutional support are needed to navigate the barriers.

In schools, the structures for remediation are more readily available than in higher institutions. The multi-tiered systems of support are a comprehensive framework that help provide individualised support to students.

Under this tiered system, the first level of support is the universal support that is offered to all students to help them learn better; the second level is classroom-based strategies and only the third level involves intensive care such as remediation.

“Often, students who reach higher education come equipped with an understanding of their own needs, have developed learning strategies, and carry an arsenal of tools that have been offered to them since school. Therefore, not every SwD requires remediation; some might require accommodations and modifications. Here is where inclusive EdTech, digital access, and online learning resources come in handy,” Dr. Rajeshwari Muthukumaran, Assistant Professor at the Centre for Neurodiversity Research and Innovation at Christ (Deemed-to-be University), said. She runs a support group aimed at fostering a sense of belonging and building a community on campus with students with disabilities, and neurodiverse students.
Although SwD might already come with their specific digital tools/modified equipment, they may still need guidance and access to software and tech tools often used in their domain.

Significant resource gaps persist, including the availability of Braille-translated materials and books in accessible typefaces. These constraints make it more challenging to design and implement tailored remediation programmes.

Additionally, institutional resource limitations, including a shortage of faculty with both subject expertise and training in developing accessible curricula, pedagogical practices, and assessment methods, as well as limited spaces and opportunities for one-on-one student-faculty support, further compound the problem.

Drawing from experience, Dr. Muthukumaran said, “I have met students who often enter higher education with a mix of hope, anxiety, and anticipation, and are seeking a supportive and approachable guide/mentor/peer who can offer them a safe and understanding space and serve as a support system. While guiding them in classrooms, I often end up recommending students to mental health professionals/supportive online communities where they can exchange ideas and converse with individuals with similar experiences to help them deal with campus life overall.”

Evidently, more colleges have now started looking into strategies, establishing specialised cells and centres that further look into research and student support. “While there is a long way to go, this scattered chatter needs to grow louder, unanimously, to shape future education and move towards evidence-based inclusive practices,” Dr. Muthukumaran added.
The digital divide

Considering that higher education has become increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure, learning management systems (LMS), university portals, digital libraries, online journals, e-books, recorded lectures, online assignments, examination portals, email systems, and virtual classrooms are now integral to campus life. For many learners, this digital environment offers greater convenience, flexibility, and access to educational resources. But for students with disabilities, digital technologies can be either powerful enablers or, when accessibility is inadequate, can become significant barriers to participation and academic success.

A university website that cannot be navigated effectively with assistive technology can make admission and administrative processes more cumbersome. A PDF that is simply a scanned image may not be usable for a blind student. An online learning platform without appropriate keyboard navigation, captions, transcripts, or alternative texts can prevent students from participating on equal terms.

Digital exclusion can widen the educational divide even when the physical campus is accessible. This is particularly important because UGC’s own framework requires online programmes to meet accessibility standards for learners with disability. If education is delivered digitally, its accessibility must be inclusive.

The lack of adequate data makes it difficult to assess the enormity of students’ plight. “There is no AISHE, NAAC or NIRF indicator reporting the percentage of students with disabilities in higher education who have access to accessible LMS platforms, screen-reader-compatible material, captions, Indian Sign Language interpretation or accessible e-books,” Dr. Singh said.

Without such indicators, institutions may be able to report enrolment and infrastructure without demonstrating whether students with disabilities can actually access, participate in, and benefit from digital learning on an equal basis. The absence of systematic data also makes it difficult to identify gaps, assess institutional performance, or hold institutions accountable for meeting accessibility requirements.

“We need a stricter implementation protocol for higher education institutions as there is mostly a lack of awareness and enforceable rules that institutions should follow,” says Deepa Palaniappan, Disability Inclusion practitioner, highlighting the need for more discussions, training, and handholding, as well as forming national task forces and committees to track effective inclusion of students with disabilities in higher education institutions across the country.
Reality check

For Delhi University (DU) alumnus and disability rights activist Ashutosh Singhal (24), the challenges of being an undergraduate and later postgraduate student of Political Science were harrowing. ‘’I use a regular, mainstream computer with a screen reader that reads out the text and other information displayed on the screen. This means that questions appearing on the computer can be read aloud to me, enabling me to access and answer them independently,” Ashutosh said, who suffers from late-onset visual impairment (retinitis pigmentosa), a condition in which the vision can gradually deteriorate.
Beating the odds, he managed to use a computer to write his Political Science BA and MA exams in Hindi, which was the first instance of its kind.

“Initially, they gave me a computer that crashed. The computer instructor apparently knew that there were problems with the computer but did not inform me beforehand. A substitute computer was eventually provided, but by then considerable examination time had been lost. I was told that I would receive additional time to compensate for the lost time, but this was not implemented adequately. Since the examination authorities had to collect and pack the answer scripts at a fixed time, I was under pressure to finish and submit my answers immediately,” he added. Ashutosh was also made to sit in a computer lab during the exam where the constant noise made it difficult to detect the sounds of the screen reader, disrupting his flow of thoughts.

Ashutosh’s experience made him realise that the biggest difficulty for students with disabilities is often not the technology itself which is already available. It is about getting institutions to recognise and implement accessibility provisions consistently.

A student may have to repeatedly explain their requirements, submit applications, approach different departments, contact outside organisations, and persuade officials to make arrangements that should ideally be part of a standard accessible examination system. “For me, the computer and screen reader made it possible to access examinations independently. But the institutional process surrounding the technology created many obstacles. Accessible examination systems should be implemented proactively rather than requiring students with disabilities to repeatedly request, justify, and negotiate for accommodations each time they have an examination,” he added.
(Rajlakshmi Ghosh is a journalist with over three decades of experience in media houses and educational institutions)

title: AI experts warn against ‘apocalyptic’ rhetoric on risks

content.value: Several experts on a United Nations artificial intelligence committee have warned against the apocalyptic rhetoric used by some professionals in the sector regarding AI risks.

“As scientists, it’s very important to invest in the science, to really understand what we know (from) what we don’t know, and investing in fear is not that helpful,” said Joelle Barral, an executive at Google DeepMind and a member of the International Scientific Panel on AI, an independent body.

Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, who previously worked at OpenAI, said in early September that AI developers believed the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. A research engineer who left Google DeepMind in July made similar comments, saying it might already be “too late to avoid” humanity’s eradication by AI.

“We have to change the way we talk about AI risk because for a very long time, it’s either existential and everything is going to die and the killer robots are coming, or it doesn’t really matter,” Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa, an investigative reporter, said at the same event, held in New York on September 21 on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The International Scientific Panel on AI was created in 2025, with its members selected in February 2026. Its mandate is to advance the scientific understanding of AI and inform UN deliberations. Yoshua Bengio, considered one of the fathers of AI and a co-chair of the panel, said it was important to distinguish between what scientists actually know about AI risks and what can only be “plausibly extrapolated” from that evidence.

title: The science of Gaganyaan parachutes | Explained

content.value: Any spacecraft entering the earth’s atmosphere will rely primarily on atmospheric drag to reduce a significant portion of its velocity as it aerobrakes.
Towards the terminal phase, to gently touchdown on land or in sea, additional decelerating systems like parachutes have to be activated to further reduce its velocity to acceptable limits.
The parachute used for crewed space vehicles demands extraordinary engineering with multi-staging, redundancy, high-performance materials and high-pressure packing for reducing the storage space.
How are parachutes deployed?

Generally, the parachute system contains three types of chutes: pilot, drogue, and main. The pilot chute is a mini-parachute deployed to pull out larger diameter drogue or main chutes. The drogue chute is deployed early in the descent to stabilise the module and first reduce the velocity. The main chute has a wider canopy and is used in the final phase to reduce the velocity enough to achieve gentle soft-landing conditions.

The blunt shape of the crew module creates a turbulent wake in its rear side and the parachute has to be ejected through this wake. The ejection mechanism should ensure that the energy imparted to the parachute is sufficient enough to cross the wake in the shortest time and deploy the parachute in the far-wake region behind the module. Some of the conventional deployment methods used are as follows:

Generally, the parachute deployment takes place when the module has reduced its speed to sub-sonic condition (lower than the speed of sound. At supersonic speeds, standard canopies get shredded due to shockwave interaction and intense dynamic pressure.
What is the purpose of multi-staging in parachute deployment?

The Gaganyaan crew module returning from orbit would be having a high velocity of about 170 m/s ( faster than a Formula 1 car) when it is in the lower atmosphere. If the full-sized main parachute is directly deployed, it would generate very high opening shock levels which will either lead to shredding of parachute canopy fabric or subject the crew to unacceptably high deceleration levels.

The solution is to go for multi-stage release of parachutes wherein the diameter of the chute will be increased in successive stages for reducing the deceleration and dynamic pressure to acceptable levels.
Why do we need reefing in a parachute?

If a large Main parachute opened fully all at once at high speed, the instantaneous large force would destroy the canopy fabric and exert lethal  deceleration forces on the crew. To prevent this, the parachute canopy mouth is allowed to open only in steps. The process is analogous to gradually opening an umbrella in strong winds. If you pop it open all at once, the wind will likely snap the umbrella.

For the parachute, a strong cord is taken through the skirt around the canopy and the length of the cord decides what percentage area of the parachute canopy should open in the first step. Attached to the cord is a reefing line cutter - a small rugged tube containing a tiny blade and a chemical timer. Once a few seconds have passed and the speed is safe, the cutter fires and the cord is cut, allowing the entire canopy to bloom fully.
How are parachutes tested?

There are different platforms used for the testing of parachutes. The RTRS (Rail Track Rocket Sled) is a ground facility where a sled will be accelerated along rails by firing small solid motors and the parachutes will be deployed from the sled at appropriate velocity. The TBRL (Terminal Ballistic Research Lab) in Chandigarh has a state-of-the-art RTRS facility. Other modes of testing include dropping the test article from a Helicopter or aircraft or using small rocket-powered Test vehicles to take the crew module to the appropriate altitude and  releasing from there.

After the splash down in the sea or upon soft-landing on land, if the parachute is not detached immediately, the wind acting on the canopy could drag the module on land or capsize it in sea and this might cause injuries to the astronauts. Hence the parachute is released by activating pyro cutters or mechanical quick-release devices that will release the strap connecting the parachute to the module.
What materials are used in aerospace parachutes?

Material selection for parachutes is controlled by conditions like high tensile strength, thermal resistance and low mass. Modern aerospace parachutes use advanced synthetic polymers engineered to meet specific design conditions.

Kevlar is used in high-load suspension lines, risers, and structural reinforcement tapes due to its exceptional tensile strength and heat resistance.Nomex finds application in heat-exposed areas to withstand hot mortar gas discharge and aerothermal heating.

Nylon is widely used for canopy broadcloths because of its elasticity, which helps absorb initial dynamic shock loads during inflation. It is highly compressible, so it can be packed into a relatively small volume.
What parachutes are in the Gaganyaan crew module?

In crewed missions, recovery systems utilise redundant clusters of pilot, drogue, and main parachutes. The Gaganyaan crew module has two drogue chutes deployed by mortars and three main chutes deployed by mortar-ejected pilot chutes.

If one main parachute suffers a major anomaly, the remaining two independent chains are fully capable of ensuring a safe touchdown. ADRDE in Agra, which is a laboratory under the Defence Research & Development Organisation, is the developing agency.

Unnikrishnan Nair S. is former director, VSSC and IIST; Founding Director, HSFC; and an expert in launch vehicle systems, orbital re-entry and human spaceflight technologies. Currently Dr Sarabhai Professor at VSSC

title: Anthropic considers releasing new AI model ahead of IPO, sources say

content.value: Anthropic is considering rolling out a new AI model to counter OpenAI’s momentum since its launch of GPT-6 Astra, according ‌to three sources, ahead of an expected IPO and after its CEO called for an industrywide slowdown.

The timing of ​a potential launch aimed at addressing competitive pressure from a direct rival follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call on the global ⁠AI community to slow down the pace of releasing new capabilities to address safety concerns, the sources said.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a 3,800-word essay on September 12.
The essay, which painted a bleak picture of swarms of AI agents taking over the internet ‌and outpacing human control, drew support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, released this month, has gained traction among businesses, prompting concerns among some investors who told Reuters they are re-evaluating Anthropic’s position as the leading provider of ‌enterprise AI tools.
Anthropic is evaluating the safety of its next model as part of its deliberations over a release, one of the ‌people ⁠familiar with the matter said.

Some of the discussions involve how to balance investment in releasing new models with efforts to ⁠strengthen the company’s profitability as rising interest rates make investors more focused on the timing of expected profits, said people familiar with the company’s thinking.

The debate over spending highlights the increasing pressure on the firms at the center of the AI boom to produce sustainable cash flows sooner, thanks both to rising rates and tough competition from open-source AI providers, especially in ​China.
Anthropic declined to comment for this story.
The potential launch ‌would test how Anthropic can defend its enterprise market position against OpenAI while maintaining the safety-first identity that has distinguished it from competitors.

OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on September 3, touting gains in computer use, software engineering, cybersecurity and professional work. The model has received a strong response from enterprise users and developers, prompting potential Anthropic IPO investors to scrutinise whether OpenAI could begin taking share from Anthropic, ‌which has been viewed for months as the leader in enterprise AI.
Astra accounted for about 13% of enterprise AI spending tracked by ​corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about 8% for Anthropic’s Claude Fable, according to the latest data.

Astra has also pulled ahead on OpenRouter, a widely used platform that routes developer traffic across AI models. OpenRouter said its users spent ⁠more on OpenAI models than on Anthropic models last week, the first time OpenAI has led on that measure in more than two and a half years.

Some existing investors and those who expect to invest in both Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs said they do not believe Astra poses ‌a significant threat to Anthropic, given the size of its lead in the market for enterprise AI tools and the amount of time it takes to unseat incumbent vendors to large companies.

Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate topped $65 billion by the end of July, up from about $9 billion at the end of 2025. It is also projecting a 2028 revenue of roughly $190 billion to $200 billion, Reuters previously reported. OpenAI’s annualized revenue run rate passed $40 billion in July.

Investors also expect leadership among Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and other major AI developers to shift repeatedly as companies release new generations of models, making any advantage potentially short-lived.

A potentially bigger challenge for Anthropic and other leading AI providers is the rise of open-source and open-weight models, which can ‌lower token costs and allow companies to build more of their own AI infrastructure rather than rely on providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI, investors said.

The shift could put ​pressure on the economics of the AI industry as companies have more options to develop and run models outside the leading commercial providers, broadening the competitive threat beyond the race between Anthropic and OpenAI.

Meta Platforms has been among Anthropic’s largest customers, ⁠but is looking to reduce its use of Anthropic’s models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, people familiar with the matter said. Meta did not ⁠immediately respond to a request for comment.

OpenAI, meanwhile, has taken some pressure off the race to public markets. Its CEO, Altman, confirmed on Saturday that the company would not go public in 2026, saying concerns around AI safety made this an ill-advised time for ‌a listing.
