But, with a young child who climbed every tree she saw and roamed for hours with her dog, I did come to integrate the truth that humans, too, have a right to this wildlife, that we too are a part of this delicate ecosystem and as much a part of Nature as the elephant. The difference being, the elephants were responsible for the forest that the farm was in, and I was literally beholden to them.
Bona fide ecosystem engineers

Elephants move in matrilineal tribes following migratory routes believed to be thousands of years old. Passed down through generations, matriarchs lead the herd through hundreds of kilometres through the country, following the seasons and remembering where to find water. Migration is necessary because they require enormous amounts of food, but the whole time they are walking on these routes, they are creating highly biodiverse forests. Seeds swallowed with fruit are carried across long distances and deposited through dung, helping new plants grow away from the parent tree, supporting genetic diversity through movement.

In the summer, their large bodies move through thick vegetation, acting as natural pruning agents, bringing in sunlight and air, even creating grasslands for other animals. They are considered keystone species that support other wildlife and are bona fide ecosystem engineers.

Imagine knowing all that and stopping elephants from entering your ‘regenerative organic farm’. Things like fences and property papers, even money, feel meaningless in the intensity of eye contact with a wild elephant; you simply make way.
‘Owning’ the planet

I have always been a firm believer in the Natural Commons, that every human being has the nature-given right to air, water, forests and wildlife simply by being born on this planet. In reality, most of these have now been packaged and sold to the rich in their most pristine form. But land and a space to live must surely be a part of these commons as well.

The first human communities understood this, and land was shared within the tribe. Plato, the first Western philosopher to write on private land ownership, was vehemently against it. He argued it would lead to corruption and greed, and proposed communal property for the ruling class in his ideal republic. Eventually, obviously, capitalism won, and private property, defined as property owned by commercial entities, emerged with the great European trading companies of the 17th century — the beginning of colonialism.

Luckily, there are still intellectuals who ruminate on this concept of ‘owning’ a part of this planet, especially in today’s post-capitalist, degraded landscape. In his groundbreaking book Sacred Economics, American activist Charles Eisenstein circumscribes the private right to “use and abuse” private property by proposing a penalty on socially and environmentally harmful activities. It separates, as much as possible, the “enjoyment” (i.e. the fruits) of ownership from the fruits of the labour and creativity added to the thing owned. Permaculture also integrates community-based land stewardship with ecological design to create and maintain natural commons, where land is held in trust for shared ecological and community benefit rather than private ownership.

So, how does one think about the land they own? Putting a fence on a man-made boundary doesn’t separate it from the rest of the planet. I suppose it is a lot like having a child. You are the protector, guardian, and steward of the child — but you could never claim to own them. It feels like that is the part that we have forgotten, that the land can never be really yours.
A series written through the lens of someone who works the land. Let’s make thinking about the ecology feel like Second Nature.

title: Pain that persists after healing needs specialised care, say experts

content.value: Months after a fractured wrist had healed, a 42-year-old homemaker from Mysuru was still unable to cook or even tolerate the touch of clothing on her hand. Despite repeated investigations confirming that the fracture had healed, she continued to have severe burning pain, swelling, stiffness and changes in skin colour.

She was eventually referred to pain specialists and diagnosed with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), in which the nervous system continues to generate pain long after the original injury has healed. With specialised pain management, she gradually regained function and independence.
Pain specialists say such cases highlight the need to recognise chronic pain as a condition that may require specialised care.

At Victoria Hospital, attached to the Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI), more than 1,200 patients have undergone specialised pain-relieving procedures since its pain clinic was established in June 2023. The clinic, run by the Department of Anaesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, has also provided outpatient consultation to over 4,000 patients.
Public awareness campaign

As September is observed as Pain Awareness month, the Karnataka Chapter of the Indian Society for Study of Pain (ISSP) has launched a public awareness campaign urging people not to accept chronic pain as an unavoidable part of life, but to seek specialised care when it persists beyond the normal healing period.

“Our team led by our head of the department Nethra S.S. has performed over 1,200 advanced pain intervention procedures and has seen over 4,000 patients in the outpatient department,” said Satish Kumar M.N., associate professor, Department of Anaesthesia and Pain Medicine, BMCRI, and treasurer of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.

The clinical team, comprising associate professor Nethra H.N., assistant professor Harshavardhan H.S., Satish Kumar and Dr. Nethra, treats patients with cancer pain, neuropathic pain, musculoskeletal disorders, spine-related pain, knee and shoulder pain, trigeminal neuralgia and other chronic pain conditions.
Besides image-guided nerve blocks and joint injections, the clinic performs advanced procedures such as radiofrequency ablation, which interrupts pain signals from affected nerves.
Dr. Kumar said the acquisition of a radiofrequency ablation machine had enabled the BMCRI to offer procedures that were previously available largely in corporate hospitals.
Pain is more than a symptom

Sadasivan S. Iyer, consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, and vice-president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP, said a common misconception was that patients should simply learn to live with chronic pain.

“Many patients are told to simply live with pain because investigations do not reveal an obvious cause. But persistent pain can itself be a medical condition requiring specialised evaluation and treatment,” he said.

While acute pain serves as the body’s warning signal after an injury or illness, pain lasting beyond three months can become a condition in itself, he said. The nervous system can continue to transmit pain signals even after tissues have healed. Therefore, normal scans do not necessarily mean that the pain is imaginary, while abnormalities on imaging do not always explain the severity of symptoms.
Beyond painkillers

Pain medicine is not limited to prescribing stronger painkillers. Depending on the condition, treatment may include medication optimisation, physical rehabilitation, psychological support, lifestyle modification and minimally invasive, image-guided procedures such as nerve blocks, epidural injections and radiofrequency ablation.

“The goal is not simply to reduce a patient’s pain score. It is to help them sleep better, return to work, perform daily activities and regain independence. Pain relief is ultimately about restoring quality of life,” said Murali T.S., consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Apollo Hospitals, Bengaluru, and president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
When should patients seek help?

According to the ISSP, millions of Indians live with persistent back and neck pain, sciatica, diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, cancer pain and pain that continues after surgery.

Specialists advise people to seek evaluation if pain lasts for more than three months, repeatedly returns, interferes with sleep or daily activities, persists despite treatment of the original illness, or is accompanied by burning, shooting or electric shock-like sensations.

title: Preparing for egg retrieval? What to eat in the weeks before the procedure

content.value: An egg retrieval is the culmination of several weeks of ovarian stimulation, as multiple follicles develop under the influence of fertility medicines, with the ovaries undergoing significant changes in response to hormonal stimulation.

The quality and number of eggs ultimately retrieved are influenced by several factors, including age, ovarian reserve, genetics and the underlying cause of infertility. A woman’s diet cannot alter these fundamentals, nor can any particular food guarantee better eggs or a successful IVF outcome. Nutrition can, however, influence the metabolic and physiological environment in which the body responds to treatment. For this reason, what a woman eats in the weeks preceding egg retrieval should be viewed as part of overall preparation rather than as a means of ‘boosting’ fertility.
Biology behind the preparation

Egg development is a prolonged process. Although the final stages of follicular growth occur during the IVF stimulation cycle, the oocytes have been undergoing maturation over a much longer period. This means that nutrition in the weeks before retrieval is unlikely to produce a dramatic change in egg quality on its own, but maintaining good nutritional status can support general metabolic health during a demanding treatment cycle.

During ovarian stimulation, the body is also adapting to changing hormone levels, increased follicular activity and, in some women, symptoms such as bloating, constipation, fatigue or changes in appetite. A balanced diet can help maintain energy levels and provide the protein, fibre, vitamins, minerals and healthy fats required for normal physiological function.

Among dietary patterns studied in relation to IVF outcomes, the Mediterranean-style diet has received some of the most consistent attention. A 2023 evidence-based review published in Frontiers in Nutrition, covering multiple IVF nutritional interventions, concluded that a Mediterranean-style dietary approach is the most consistently supported pattern for women undergoing ovarian stimulation. This diet is rich in vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean protein, with limited processed foods and refined carbohydrates.
What to eat more of

Protein is the macronutrient that most women underestimate in the lead-up to retrieval. Both animal and plant sources such as eggs, fish, lentils, chickpeas and dairy support follicle development and give the body the building blocks it needs during stimulation. Aim to include a source of protein in every meal.

Healthy fats, particularly omega-3 fatty acids, carry documented benefits for IVF outcomes. A review published in Reproductive BioMedicine Online found that supplementation with omega-3 free fatty acids may lead to improvements in both clinical and embryological IVF outcomes. Practical sources in an Indian context include fish such as salmon, sardines, and mackerel, as well as walnuts, flaxseeds, and chia seeds.

Folate belongs in this conversation for two reasons: it supports healthy cell division, and many women undergoing IVF are not getting enough of it through food alone. Dark leafy vegetables such as spinach, methi and palak are among the richest dietary sources. Iron from leafy greens, lentils, and lean meat supports the blood supply that developing follicles depend on.

Antioxidants such as vitamins C and E, selenium, zinc help protect developing eggs from oxidative stress, which increases during stimulation as the ovaries work at higher capacity. Berries, bell peppers, nuts, and seeds are practical sources worth building into daily meals.

Hydration matters more during stimulation than at other times. As follicles grow, the risk of bloating and fluid retention increases. Consistent water intake of at least two to three litres a day supports the body through this phase and helps manage stimulation-related discomfort.
What to limit

There is no single food that will undo an IVF cycle, but some patterns are worth avoiding in the weeks before retrieval. Highly processed foods, refined carbohydrates, and excessive added sugar affect blood sugar stability and create an inflammatory environment that does not serve follicle development. Alcohol should be avoided during stimulation. Excess caffeine, more than one to two cups of coffee a day, is worth reducing, as higher intakes have been associated with poorer IVF outcomes in some studies.
What patients should know

There is no fertility diet that guarantees better egg quality or a successful cycle, and any approach that promises otherwise is worth approaching with scepticism. What a balanced, nutrient-dense diet does is support your body through a physically demanding process the same way good nutrition supports any period of heightened physical demand.

The specifics of what your body needs during your particular stimulation protocol are best discussed with your fertility specialist, who can account for your individual clinical picture, any nutrient deficiencies identified through blood work, and whether supplementation is appropriate in your case.
(Dr. Shivika Gupta is a fertility specialist at Birla Fertility and IVF, Gurgaon Sec- 51. shivika.gupta@birlafertility.com)

title: Diet-exercise combo most effective for lasting weight loss: ICMR-NIN

content.value: Combining healthy dietary practices with regular physical activity is the most effective non-drug strategy for achieving sustained weight loss and improving key metabolic health indicators among adults with overweight or obesity, according to a major review by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) here.

The findings, published in the international journal Obesity Pillars, are based on an umbrella review that analysed evidence from 112 systematic reviews and meta-analyses covering 2,332 randomised controlled trials and more than 5.07 lakh participant observations across over 50 countries.

The review, led by ICMR-NIN scientists Mahesh Kumar Mummadi and Samarasimha Reddy, compared the impact of dietary interventions, physical activity, lifestyle changes and combined approaches on weight management and cardiometabolic health.

Researchers found that all major non-pharmacological interventions produced statistically significant, though generally modest, reductions in body weight and Body Mass Index (BMI). However, the combination of diet and physical activity delivered the most sustained results, with participants losing an average of 3.68 kg beyond 12 months compared with control groups.

Low-calorie diets were found to be the most effective for short-term weight loss, resulting in an average reduction of 2.64 kg within the first three months. Physical activity alone led to smaller reductions in body weight, but its benefits increased over longer follow-up periods.

Lifestyle interventions such as behavioural counselling, goal-setting, self-monitoring and health education also showed positive outcomes, with their effectiveness improving over time. Beyond weight loss, the study highlighted significant improvements in metabolic health. The combination of diet and physical activity produced the greatest benefits in blood sugar control, reducing fasting blood glucose levels and insulin resistance after 12 months.

Physical activity emerged as the most effective strategy for lowering blood pressure, reducing systolic blood pressure by about 6.1 mmHg between six and 12 months. Intermittent fasting showed the largest short-term reduction in diastolic blood pressure and supported weight loss for up to a year, although these benefits were not sustained beyond 12 months.

ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the importance of an integrated approach to tackling obesity. “Healthy dietary practices, regular physical activity and behavioural support each have a role, but their combination can provide broader and more sustained benefits. This is particularly relevant for India, where scalable and sustainable approaches are needed to address the growing burden of overweight, obesity and related non-communicable diseases,” she said.

Mr.Mummadi noted that although the review drew evidence from more than 50 countries, most studies originated from high-income and upper-middle-income nations. India and other lower-middle-income countries remained under-represented, highlighting the need for more locally relevant research, said a press release on Saturday.

title: Himalaya approaching tipping point, report says

content.value: The Himalaya are approaching a tipping point ​as glaciers melt faster than a decade ago, threatening ‌water security as the region approaches “peak water“ ​by mid-century, according to a study ⁠released this month.

The findings come after the collapse of a Himalayan glacier in late August along the Nepal-Tibet border, ‌which caused cascading landslides and flash floods in the valleys below. At least 1,300 people ‌have been confirmed dead and more ‌than ⁠5,300 are missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet ⁠region.
As glaciers retreat, they are leaving behind unstable glacial lakes held back by little more than loose rock and ice, above ​valleys where millions ‌of people live, the study found.

Peak water is the point in time when river flows stop rising and ​start declining. It is expected to have profound implications for water security. As the Himalaya underpin more ⁠than 20% of India’s GDP, the region makes up ⁠a key piece of the country’s national economic infrastructure, upon which hundreds of millions of ‌people depend.

The study was produced by Systemiq, a sustainability advisory firm, together with the Integrated Mountain Initiative, the International Centre ‌for Integrated Mountain Development, and India’s G.B. Pant ​National Institute of Himalayan Environment.

Himalayan glacier mass loss had accelerated in recent decades, while ⁠only 21 glaciers were currently monitored on the ground out of an estimated 40,000 glaciers across the ‌Hindu Kush-Himalaya region, a vast mountain system spanning eight countries from Afghanistan to Myanmar, the study found.
Though making up around 18% of India’s land, the Himalayan region accounted for roughly ​35% of the country’s natural disasters.

title: Trump dismisses new AI guardrails, says there is a ’SICK conspiracy’ against AI and data centers

content.value: U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday (September 14, 2026) that he would be a sufficient guardrail against rogue artificial intelligence, claiming that any efforts to limit the technology was part of a “SICK conspiracy.”

Mr. Trump was pushing back against calls by tech leaders such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk to have greater government oversight of AI. Their goal is to ensure the technology is developed in ways that promote safety, address legal liability, feed economic growth, advance science and preserve national security.

The president maintained that his presence in the Oval Office should assuage any fears about AI, which has become a source of controversy after a series of hacks in recent months that showed AI agents could be working to deceive humans.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Mr. Trump posted on social media.

Mr. Trump specifically said that the administration has already stopped the AI company Anthropic “from doing bad, or potentially bad” things. Anthropic has endured an uncomfortable relationship with the Trump administration, with the Pentagon trying to label the company’s models a security risk and a temporary ban of one of its more advanced models.

Mr. Amodei published a 3,800-word essay on Saturday (September 12, 2026) that called for slower development of AI. Microsoft on Monday (September 14, 2026) published its own code of conduct to ensure that humans control AI. The actions come after a series of warnings by AI experts about the technologies’ capabilities and the July 2026 cyberattack by OpenAI models on the AI company Hugging Face.
But the president has opposed such efforts to constrain AI and claims that doing so could cause China to eclipse America on AI.
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” Mr. Trump said.

The president has long resisted efforts for greater government oversight of AI, embracing his philosophy going back to 2016 of “I alone can fix it.” He returned to the White House last year by revoking a Biden administration executive order on AI oversight and only providing a fuller order of his own more than 16 months later this past June.

The prospect of slower AI buildout led stocks to slip in Monday (September 14, 2026) morning trading, as demand for advanced computer chips and construction materials for data centres could fall. But Mr. Trump’s frustration comes as AI has also emerged as a political liability ahead of November’s midterm elections, with many voters opposing the construction of additional data centres and expressing worries that AI could lead to job losses and undermine the education of children.

Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor, Democratic congressman and White House chief of staff, said on Saturday (September 12, 2026) that the Anthropic CEO’s essay was “an admission that we’re driving down a dark, winding road on wet pavement with the headlights off. And where’s President Trump? Looks like he nodded off again. It’s time to turn the lights on, put both hands on the wheel, and regain control before it’s too late.”
But the administration has repeatedly sought to minimise the risks being highlighted by AI companies.
Vice-President J.D. Vance told reporters Monday (September 14, 2026) morning about AI, “I don’t think Americans should be scared of anything.”

Mr. Vance, speaking as he prepared to fly to Kansas for a midterm election campaign event, said that the Trump administration is concerned about AI but wants to make sure it is regulating the technology smartly, warning that the U.S. is in an AI arms race against China.

“Personally, I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them. It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse,” Mr. Vance said. “So, I think we just have to be careful about this.”

title: Telangana wants its next generation of doctors trained in robotic surgery, plans six-month training for PG students

content.value: Telangana is exploring a proposal to make six months of robotic surgery training mandatory for postgraduate medical students, as the State looks to build a trained workforce to expand advanced robotic procedures across its government hospitals.

Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha said the government would approach the National Medical Commission (NMC) for permission to introduce the dedicated training period as part of the three-year postgraduate programme.

Speaking at the ‘State Level Multi-Specialty Robotic Surgery Workshop’ at the Marri Chenna Reddy Telangana Institute of Medical Sciences (MCR TIMS), Sanathnagar in Hyderabad, the Minister said training would be central to Telangana’s plans to expand robotic surgery, whether through a hub-and-spoke model or dedicated robotic surgery facilities at the district level.
The proposal comes as Telangana is already attempting to build a statewide pool of surgeons trained in robotic procedures.

MCR TIMS Director Dr A. Narendra Kumar said surgeons from 35 medical colleges and 47 hospitals, excluding speciality hospitals, are being trained in robotic surgery at two government institutions, Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) and MNJ Cancer Institute.
Also read: Adyar Cancer Institute enables wider access to robotic cancer surgeries
“The idea is to ensure that robotic surgery does not remain concentrated in a handful of premier institutions in Hyderabad,” he added.

Robotic surgery expert Dr. Sudhir Srivastava said such a model could allow specialist expertise to reach patients without requiring them to travel to major cities. He pointed to the financial and emotional burden faced by families from rural and smaller communities when they have to leave their homes to access specialised treatment.

Former NIMS Director Dr N. Bheerappa said NIMS had recently completed nearly 1,000 robotic surgeries and that the government was bearing the cost of such procedures for eligible patients through the Rajiv Aarogyasri health scheme.

Director of Medical Education (DME) Dr N. Vani said government medical colleges had a dual responsibility of providing patient care while training the next generation of doctors. Introducing young surgeons to newer technologies, she said, could have a multiplier effect across the government healthcare system.
She also stressed that young surgeons should not rely solely on the technology, but must combine it with clinical judgement, human touch and compassion.

Experts at the workshop also cautioned that expanding robotic surgery is about considerably more than installing machines. Government Medical College Nagpur Dean Dr. Raj Gajbhiye said robotic surgery was no longer merely a technology available at a few high-end private institutions.

For government hospitals, however, he said “the real objective should be equitable access to advanced surgical technology. “Success of robotics is not about purchasing a robot,” Dr. Gajbhiye said, pointing instead to the need for appropriate infrastructure, trained faculty, structured protocols, multidisciplinary teamwork and institutional support.

title: Unqualified practitioners found treating patients, prescribing allopathic medicines in Hyderabad

content.value: Several Hyderabad clinics came under the Telangana Medical Council’s (TGMC) scanner on Sunday, September 13, after people without required medical qualifications or statutory registrations were found practising allopathy, prescribing medicines and treating patients during surprise inspections.

The inspections were carried out by TGMC members Dr. G. Srinivas, Dr. V. Naresh Kumar and Dr. K.U.N. Vishnu. At Shifa Clinic in Golconda, M. Shabbir Hussain with a BUMS qualification, was allegedly providing allopathic treatment to both paediatric and adult patients without required registration.

At Health Care Clinic in Rajendranagar, two persons including Farooq, who stated that he had completed Intermediate, and Gazala, with a BUMS qualification, were found treating patients without the requisite medical qualifications.

At Sai Ganesh First Aid Centre, Ch. Narayana, and at Mother First Aid Centre, Dileep, were also providing medical services without the requisite qualifications. At Sai Clinic, Rajasekhar was allegedly practising medicine in the name of B. V. Ramanath without the required registrations.

The council also flagged the medical credentials and surgical practice of a doctor at Shreya Hospital in Serilingampally. Dr P. Sharath Babu, with an MBBS degree, was presenting himself as an MS Orthopaedic and performing orthopaedic procedures, including joint replacement surgeries.  At Bhaskar Clinic, Bhaskar with a BA degree was operating a clinic in the name of Dr. Anita and providing medical services. Further investigation is underway.

title: Tribal children’s deaths in Balaghat: CJP’s Dipke mocks Madhya Pradesh government with resignation letter

content.value: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Sunday (September 13, 2026) resorted to satire to target the Mohan Yadav government over the deaths of tribal children in Balaghat district and posted a tongue-in-cheek letter on X about his "resignation" as "Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh".

The letter, addressed to MP Governor Mangubhai Patel and dated August 13, has Mr. Dipke stating that he was resigning as "my conscience does not allow me to continue occupying this chair after the deaths of more than 30 tribal children in Balaghat".
He also thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi for giving him the "opportunity to serve the people of MP", an opportunity he said he had "clearly failed" to make the most of.
The satirical letter took aim at the government's handling of the Balaghat deaths, particularly the compensation announced for the victims’ families.
Mr. Dipke also questioned if compensation of "₹24 lakh" was adequate had these been the children of ministers or MLAs.
As per Balaghat additional collector DP Burman, kin of 24 deceased kids have been given ₹4 lakh each, while the process is on to give aid to the others.
In the letter, Mr. Dipke said the deaths of innocent children "demand accountability at the highest level".
The post then widens its sweep, taking potshots at the government's claims on tap-water supply, education and tribal welfare.
Mr. Dipke pointed out that some tribal families in Balaghat still depend on river water and alleged schools in several villages are in a condition worse than animal shelters.

He also cited government data on tribal households without electricity, crimes against Scheduled Tribes and malnutrition among children to underline what he called the failures of successive BJP governments in the State.

Concluding his mock resignation letter, Mr. Dipke said he had "failed the tribals of not just Balaghat but the entire State" and, after the loss of so many innocent children, did not believe he had "the moral right to continue in this office".
The post came a day after Mr. Dipke's visit to disease-affected villages in Balaghat, where his interaction with families was disrupted by a confrontation with a group of social media influencers.

Earlier this week, the Jabalpur Bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court sought a response from the State government over the deaths of more than 30 children allegedly due to infectious diseases in Balaghat district.

A Division Bench of Acting Chief Justice Vivek Rusia and Justice Pradeep Mittal issued notices to the State Health Department, Women and Child Development Department, Balaghat Collector and others while hearing a public interest litigation.
The PIL alleged inadequate treatment for children and claimed that around 400 children were being treated at a hospital with a capacity of 50 beds.
It also alleged that yellow-coloured water was coming from handpumps in the affected areas and that children and women had not received nutritious food on time for several months.

title: Health Wrap Episode 50 discusses healthy ageing, longevity and racquet sports

content.value: The 50th episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu explores longevity, healthspan and factors that influence health as people age.

Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, speaks to Navin Gnanasekaran, longevity physician and head of Radiology, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, about healthy ageing and the distinction between lifespan and healthspan.

India’s population is ageing. According to the United Nations Population Fund’s India Ageing Report 2023, the share of people aged 60 and above is projected to increase from 10.5% in 2022 to 20.8% by 2050. The episode discusses what this demographic change means for maintaining health and functional ability in later life.

The conversation covers racquet sports as a key form of physical activity, along with nutrition, sleep, muscle strength, stress, metabolism, inflammation and cognition. It also examines the importance of establishing sustainable health habits.

Physical activity is a key part of the discussion. The World Health Organisation recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week for adults, along with muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days. For older adults, the guidelines also recommend activities that improve balance and help prevent falls.
Racquet sports are discussed as one form of physical activity. Dr. Gnanasekaran looks at how they can combine exercise with social interaction and cognitive engagement.
The episode also discusses whether longevity advice needs to account for Indian lifestyles and health needs, including food habits, physical activity and other aspects of daily life.

The discussion focuses on the practical aspects of maintaining health and physical function as people live longer, and on the difference between simply extending lifespan and maintaining health during those additional years.
The episode can also be viewed here at The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap .

title: Spotted hyena daughters inherit rank, resources, and a taste for power

content.value: Among people, it is common knowledge that privilege is often inherited. But according to new findings, hyenas also inherit resources and status, and not just their forebears’ genes, from their parents.
The findings were published recently in Science Advances — and they challenge the traditional evolutionary theories that assume males always face greater reproductive competition.
In the animal kingdom, the males are generally considered to be the dominant sex. They are stronger and more competitive. But spotted hyenas buck this trend.

Scientists at the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research (Leibniz-IZW) in Berlin and the Institute of Evolutionary Science of Montpellier have found that in spotted hyenas, females dominate males not because they are bigger or stronger but because they have larger networks of social alliances.
The study also showed that female hyenas face more competition shaped by the inheritance of social rank across generations.
Alpha females

Marta Mosna, the lead author of the study and a researcher at Leibniz-IZW and the Ngorongoro Hyena Project, observed during her field visit in Africa that “male hyenas do not compete so much with each other”. Instead, they were found spending their time following the alpha female, the highest-ranking female hyenas, around.
“The males follow them wherever the female goes,” Ms. Mosna said. “They are staying close to her, spending a lot of time watching her, trying to connect with her, and trying to be friends with her.”
On the other hand, the competition is more fierce among the females.
“This is not really what you would expect for the classical sex role that Darwin-Bateman predicts,” she said.

The Darwin-Bateman hypothesis proposes that reproductive inequality is greater among males. That is, between males and females, the males can father more offspring than females and this is why they compete more among themselves for access to mates. In mammals, the females also invest more in each reproductive event than males do — since they bear the physiological costs of pregnancy and lactation — they are more selective about mating. These predictions, formalised as the Darwin-Bateman paradigm, have been confirmed across many mammalian species.

However, among spotted hyenas, the researchers found the females killing off the cubs of other females, despite all living in a matrilineal society in which the individuals were related to each other.

These and other observations supported the researchers’ conclusion that the daughters of ‘elite’ families could build powerful family lineages over time — thus also challenging one of evolutionary biology’s classic paradigms.
Clues in Lemala

For their study, the researchers studied hyenas belonging to eight resident clans in the Ngorongoro Crater in Tanzania. Their work spanned 29 years of data, eight generations, and 2,743 wild spotted hyenas.

The team used faecal samples to track paternity. These samples contained epithelial-rich mucus. “We need DNA information, which we normally take from the mucus around the faeces,” Dr. Mosna said. “We need to look at the males and wait for him to defecate. And then, when he leaves, be sure that this was his poop to do paternity analysis.”

“It is not always easy,” she continued. “Sometimes they even defecate in the water, and then it is gone, or sometimes after they eat it is a bit too liquid — it is not very pleasant to put your hand on. It can also be a bit challenging, but fortunately, our field assistants are very well trained and very good with it.”

For one clan that the team called ‘Lemala’, the researchers pieced together a 30-year genealogical tree and found that almost all the living members had descended from a single founding female lineage.

This led them to investigate how such extreme reproductive inequality could arise, which in turn led to the idea of the social inheritance of rank: since a female’s social position is passed to her daughters, it could give that lineage an advantage increasing across generations.
When nepotism pays

The youngest daughter born to an alpha female inherits her mother’s social status and also benefits from better access to food, allies, and breeding opportunities. Over generations, these benefits accumulate, allowing a few privileged female lineages to produce more descendants.

“Inheriting the privilege … means that you have better access to food and nutrition. They grow faster and survive longer. They also have a better position in the social network, which is also very important for hyenas,” Ms. Mosna said.

“This research teaches us that nothing is fixed. Sex roles are not fixed, like how a male or a female should behave; how our society should behave is not fixed by genetics. Only social processes can actually change society in a meaningful way.”

“This is a terrific paper that breaks a lot of new ground and serves as a powerful testament to the value of long-term field studies,” Kay E. Holekamp, a Michigan State University distinguished professor who was not involved in it, said.
Beyond hyenas

The researchers are now exploring whether similar patterns of socially inherited reproductive inequality occur in other animal species. They have said they also want to investigate whether female hyenas invest differently in sons and daughters depending on their social rank. High-ranking females may invest more in daughters to pass on their privileged position while lower-ranking females may favour sons, so they can leave the clan and reproduce elsewhere, Ms. Mosna said.

“This study has broad implications for how we understand animal societies: social structures can transmit advantages across generations and thereby shape competition, inequality, and evolutionary outcomes,” Amiyaal Ilany of Tel Aviv University said.

“It also shows why inheritance should not be viewed as purely genetic. Socially inherited rank, relationships, and access to resources can have lasting effects on fitness and on the composition of future generations.”
Kavi Bharathi R. is a science writer based at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru.

title: Luna 2: touched by humans, touches the moon

content.value: Picture this. You are standing on a rotating sphere that is revolving around another bigger sphere. You are then required to shoot an arrow at another smaller sphere, which is revolving around the sphere on which you are standing and is also rotating at its own pace. Given that both your platform and your target are moving, even the best of archers might find hitting the target a tad bit difficult.

And yet, we do this regularly these days, so much so that we don’t always pay a lot of attention to it when it happens. Some of you would have figured that the rotating sphere in which you are standing is the Earth, the bigger sphere is the sun and the smaller one, our moon. We’ve not only landed humans on the moon, but have also reached other planets and their moons in the solar system with our crafts, some of which have even entered interstellar space.

This wasn’t the case even three-fourths of a century ago, when humanity was still coming to terms with the damages inflicted during World War II. The scientific and technical advances made then, and in the decades that followed, ensured a steady growth in our space exploration. In fact, the Cold War between the Soviet Union and the U.S. was central to many of the firsts that were achieved in that period, including getting an object touched by humans to strike the surface of the moon. That first was achieved by Luna 2 on September 14, 1959.
Not all successful

Luna 2 was the Soviet Union’s second mission to the moon that achieved some degree of success. There were at least three failures in 1958 in their attempts to reach the moon, owing to different problems with their R-7 rocket. Their first success came on January 2, 1959, when their first Cosmic Rocket (retroactively renamed Luna 1 in 1963) became the first object to escape the Earth’s gravitational pull by achieving speeds greater than the escape velocity. Nearly 34 hours after launch, however, Luna 1’s probe missed the moon by a distance of about 6,500 km. That’s akin to trying to reach Mumbai, only to find yourself in Tokyo, Japan instead.

After another failed launch in June 1959, the Soviets had their second Cosmic Rocket (later renamed Luna 2) ready in September the same year. If the scientists and researchers of the time were just getting on top of the technology that helped them achieve these distant targets, tracking was also a work in progress.

Without a way for others to track their craft, they didn’t possess the means to convince the world if Luna 2 achieved its target, even if it did get to the moon. Speaking about this in a 2010 BBC video clip, Boris Chertok, one of Luna 2’s engineers, mentions that their “bright idea” concerned England’s Jodrell Bank, one of “the best in the world” when it came to directional antenna.
Solving the problem of tracking

Jodrell Bank was indeed the only place in the world back then that could track a probe so far out in space. The Soviets sent a coded message to them. “To our astonishment, I found on the telex machine the long message from Moscow giving complete details…” said Sir Bernard Lovell, Director of the Jodrell Bank Observatory at the time, in the BBC video. “This, of course, was a clear indication that we were meant to do something about it. We sprang into action,” he added.
“To our astonishment, I found on the telex machine the long message from Moscow giving complete details… We sprang into action.”Sir Bernard Lovell, Director of the Jodrell Bank Observatory in 1959

Launched on September 12, Luna 2 achieved escape velocity and was placed on an intercept course with the moon. Almost identical to Luna 1, Luna 2 also did something that its predecessor had done — at a distance of about 1,56,000 km, the upper stage released a kilogram of sodium gas, creating a cloud that ground-based astronomers in the Soviet Union were able to photograph.

About 35 hours from the time of the launch, Luna 2 crashed into the lunar surface, thereby becoming the first spacecraft from Earth to make contact with another celestial body. Given that the technology to slow down the rocket and achieve soft landing was yet to be invented, Luna 2 had no other option but to crash-land on the moon.
Guided by booster third stage

As Luna 2 also lacked a propulsion system, it was left to the third stage of its SS-6 booster rocket to guide it. The two separated only shortly before Luna 2’s impact. The place of impact on the moon was between Mare Imbrium and Mare Serenitatis. Twelve years later, American astronauts would land just 250 km away during the Apollo 15 mission.

In case you are wondering, the third stage of the booster rocket also hit the moon about half an hour after Luna 2. Nobody, however, celebrates it as the second object touched by humans to hit the moon.

The scientific instruments on Luna 2 were able to detect no magnetic fields or radiation belts around the moon. It carried Soviet emblems in two metallic spheres and these were deposited on the lunar surface. Engraved with the Soviet coat of arms, they also carried the date “1959 September” on them.
Media frenzy that followed

“There was, of course, an uproar from the press because it was realised that the Russians had achieved a remarkable degree of technological expertise in doing this,” Lovell recalled in 2010, a little over half a century after his team had confirmed that they had received signals up to the time the rocket hit the moon. Nowhere was it more prominent than in the Soviet Union and the U.S., the Cold War rivals.

“Attention, Moscow speaking,” an announcer for the Moscow radio shouted at 35 minutes past midnight, when a programme of classical music was ongoing. “Today, the 14th of September, at 00:02:24, Moscow time, the second Soviet cosmic rocket reached the surface of the moon. It is the first time in history that a cosmic flight has been made from the earth to another celestial body.”

“Attention, Moscow speaking. Today, the 14th of September, at 00:02:24, Moscow time, the second Soviet cosmic rocket reached the surface of the moon. It is the first time in history that a cosmic flight has been made from the earth to another celestial body”An announcer for the Moscow radio

Once the announcer had read the bulletin from TASS, the official press agency of the Soviet Union, he followed it up by making the same announcement two more times, given the gravity of the situation. A scientific worker then came on, explaining the importance of preventing microorganisms from Earth reaching and contaminating the moon, and the measures that had been put in place to achieve the same. Once he was through, the classical music programme resumed.
Americans fear Soviets getting ahead

Given that 2 minutes and 24 seconds after midnight in Moscow was 5:02:24 P.M. Sunday evening in New York, both the news and its timing got the American reporters scrambling before their deadlines. It made the front pages of their issues on September 14, with obvious comparisons with their own failed attempts. “The time of impact was only 84 seconds later than Soviet scientists had predicted,” stated The New York Times in a front page report that also mentioned that “Soviet propaganda seized upon the event as being of special significance to the forthcoming Eisenhower-Khrushchev talks.”

In India, The Hindu carried a front page headline that read “RUSSIAN ROCKET LANDS ON MOON” on September 15. In addition to talking about the science behind the mission — the signals received and the steps to prevent contamination among other things — there were secondary reports that also carried reactions and praise from scientists in the U.K.

Asked for his comment, then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru said that “It is great news, no doubt,” before jokingly adding, “In old astrology, the moon used to affect all human destiny. Now, obviously, things are reversed. The poor moon is being pursued.” Decades later, we still continue to pursue the moon and the knowledge that it can unlock.

title: Health officials sound caution as soaring temperature triggers fresh wave of fever cases in Ernakulam

content.value: Health officials have sounded caution and warned against self-medication in the wake of a renewed spate of fever cases, including influenza, in the district, triggered by soaring temperatures over the past few weeks.
According to the medical community, the flu season is not yet over, while intense heat followed by heavy rain and the festive season may have created conditions conducive to the spread of diseases.

The district continues to report the highest number of influenza cases in the State, while dengue and leptospirosis cases also persist. Medical professionals have urged people to remain vigilant and seek medical attention if symptoms persist.

A total of 533 influenza cases were reported from Ernakulam till September 11, while the State recorded around 1,222 cases during the month. The district also reported 28 confirmed and four suspected cases of leptospirosis, along with 307 suspected and 128 confirmed dengue cases. Three deaths due to leptospirosis have also been reported in the district.

Rajany Jose, Professor of community medicine and coordinator of the Prevention of Epidemic and Infectious Diseases (PEID) cell at the Government Medical Hospital, Ernakulam, stressed the need for caution, especially among young children and the elderly, given the continued spread of viruses. “With viruses still in circulation, much caution is required. The rapidly fluctuating temperature is not helping either. The general expectation that cases would decline once the rain stopped has been belied,” said Dr. Rajany.

Rajeev Jayadevan, convenor of research cell, IMA, Kerala State, emphasised that infection rates would not drop simply because the rain is over. “The changing climate and the recent festive season may have exacerbated the spread of infectious diseases, especially respiratory viruses. Hot weather is going to affect the very young and the elderly the most, and they must be kept hydrated,” he said.

The changing climate may have contributed to increased viral activity, noted Arun N.M., an internal medicine consultant. He urged those with infections to avoid public places. “Following basic hygiene measures, such as wearing a mask when infected and avoiding crowded places, can help prevent the spread of diseases,” he said.

title: Archibald V. Hill and Otto Meyerhof’s Nobel-winning work on muscle metabolism

content.value: Archibald V. Hill and Otto Meyerhof studied how muscles use chemical energy to contract and recover. Hill measured the heat produced by working muscles, while Meyerhof traced the relationship between oxygen consumption and lactic acid metabolism. Their work earned them the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

The prize was divided equally. Hill was recognised “for his discovery relating to the production of heat in the muscle”, while Meyerhof was recognised “for his discovery of the fixed relationship between the consumption of oxygen and the metabolism of lactic acid in the muscle”. The prize was awarded for 1922 but presented in 1923 because the Nobel Committee had initially decided that no 1922 nomination met the required criteria.
Measuring muscle heat

Hill approached muscle physiology as a problem in physics as well as biology. Working largely with frog muscles, he developed precise methods for measuring the very small amounts of heat generated during contraction.

The changes were tiny. In one experiment described in his Nobel lecture, a single contraction of a frog’s sartorius muscle at 20°C raised its temperature by no more than about 0.003°C. Hill used sensitive instruments and carefully controlled contractions to separate heat produced during activity from heat generated during recovery.

His measurements showed that heat production did not end when the muscle stopped contracting. A second phase, which Hill called recovery heat, continued after contraction and depended on oxygen. When oxygen was removed, this recovery heat was abolished.
This was important because it showed that the energy changes associated with muscle contraction and recovery occurred in distinct phases rather than as one continuous process.
Meyerhof traces the chemistry

Meyerhof investigated the chemical side of the same problem. In experiments on frog muscle, he measured heat production and oxygen consumption and followed the conversion of carbohydrates into lactic acid.

He showed that during muscle activity, lactic acid was formed from carbohydrate. During recovery, some of the lactic acid was oxidised while the remainder was converted back into carbohydrate. These observations helped establish the relationship between oxygen use and lactic acid metabolism for which he received the Nobel Prize.

Meyerhof’s work went further. Between 1918 and 1922, he provided evidence that glycogen was converted into lactic acid when oxygen was absent. He also found that only a fraction of the lactic acid produced during anaerobic muscle activity was subsequently oxidised in the presence of oxygen, with much of the remainder being reconverted to glycogen.
Two sides of muscle metabolism

Hill and Meyerhof were investigating different aspects of the same physiological problem. Hill measured the physical consequences of muscle activity -- heat, work and energy expenditure. Meyerhof examined the associated chemical reactions.

Their findings connected the physical and chemical sides of muscle metabolism. Hill’s measurements of recovery heat could be explained by Meyerhof’s observations on lactic acid and oxygen consumption. Hill himself acknowledged that Meyerhof’s biochemical work helped complete the picture that physical measurements alone could not provide.
A link to modern metabolism
Meyerhof’s research contributed to the emerging understanding of glycolysis, the pathway through which cells break down glucose and other sugars to obtain energy.

His observations also led to what became known as the Pasteur-Meyerhof effect: respiration can suppress the breakdown of carbohydrates through glycolysis. His work provided early evidence that energy transformations in living cells could involve cyclical processes, an idea that became important in the development of modern intermediary metabolism.

The terminology and biochemical models have since changed substantially. Muscle metabolism is now understood to involve multiple pathways and energy carriers, including ATP, rather than being explained simply through lactic acid.
An interesting part of Meyerhof’s scientific career is that he did not remain committed to every interpretation that emerged from his early work.

The discovery of creatine phosphate in 1926 led him to question the idea that lactic acid itself was directly responsible for supplying the energy required for muscle contraction. He subsequently revised aspects of the model that had become associated with his work.
The Nobel recognition
Hill and Meyerhof delivered their Nobel lectures on December 12, 1923. Hill’s lecture was titled The Mechanism of Muscular Contraction, while Meyerhof’s was titled Energy Conversions in Muscle.
Their work established quantitative approaches to studying muscle metabolism, bringing together measurements of heat, mechanical work, oxygen consumption and chemical changes.

More than a century later, the details of muscle energy metabolism are understood in far greater molecular detail. But Hill’s measurements of heat and energy and Meyerhof’s work on oxygen, glycogen and lactic acid were important steps in establishing muscle as a system whose mechanical activity could be linked to measurable chemical and thermodynamic processes.

title: Assam CM highlights ‘big comeback’ of ‘small hog’

content.value: GUWAHATI
The population of the endangered pygmy hog (Porcula salvania), once thought to be extinct, has increased from six individuals in 1996 to 194 through a captive breeding programme in Assam.

Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma described the recovery of the endangered grassland health indicator species, found nowhere else in India, as a “big comeback” for a “small hog” through decades of dedicated conservation efforts.
Standing about 25 cm tall and weighing up to 9.7 kg, the pygmy hog is the world’s smallest and rarest wild pig.
“The goal is to increase their number to 300 by 2040 so that the species can thrive on its own,” the Chief Minister said on Saturday (September 12, 2026).
British naturalist Gerald Durrell and his trust initiated the pygmy hog conservation in 1971. It led to the Pygmy Hog Conservation Programme (PHCP).

The Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust of the United Kingdom, the Assam Forest Department, the Wild Pig Specialist Group of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change are the PHCP collaborators.
Assam-based biodiversity conservation organisation Aaranyak and Ecosystems India are implementing the programme.

The conservation programme began after conservationists captured six pygmy hogs from the Bansbari range of Manas National Park in 1996 and brought them to a captive breeding facility on the southern edge of Guwahati.

Conservationists began reintroducing the pygmy hogs to the wild in 2008. The mammals are now found in the Sonai-Rupai Wildlife Sanctuary, Bornadi Wildlife Sanctuary, Orang National Park, and Manas National Park.

title: Third extension of former Assam PCCF challenged; Gauhati High Court issues notice

content.value: The Gauhati High Court has issued notice to the Assam government on a petition challenging the third extension granted to a former Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (PCCF) as Special Chief Secretary (Forests) after his retirement in February 2024.
Chief Justice Ashutosh Kumar and Justice Arun Dev Choudhury issued the notice on Friday (September 11, 2026).

Eastern Assam-based conservationist Rohit Choudhury filed the petition, arguing that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change had found lapses when M.K. Yadava was Assam’s PCCF. The petitioner said the lapses included diversion of forest land for non-forest use without the Central government’s approval, for which the State government was asked to proceed against him under Sections 3A and 3B of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980.

“This Public Interest Litigation is directed against the post-retirement engagement of respondent No. 3 (Mr. Yadava), a retired Indian Forest Service officer of the Assam-Meghalaya cadre, as Special Chief Secretary (Forest) in the Department of Environment and Forest with full financial and administrative powers,” the court notice said.

It said Mr. Yadava’s post-retirement engagement was “notwithstanding the fact that the Office Memorandum of 2018 allows contractual engagement of retired Government officers only in rare and exceptional circumstances”.
Underlining the “requirement of assessment of satisfactory performance for any continuation or re-engagement”, the court sought a response to the petition by October 15.
Advocates Abir Phukan and P. Sharma represented the petitioner.

title: Melanoma in India: why the messaging needs to change to catch it early

content.value: Thousands of patients in India are diagnosed with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, each year. While melanoma is far less common here than in Western populations, it is far from rare and the way it presents in our patient population makes it uniquely difficult to detect early. Too many patients come to us when the disease is already advanced, precisely at a time when treatment options have never been more powerful or more personalised. This contrast between available therapies and the stage at which patients are diagnosed defines one of the most pressing challenges in melanoma care in India today.
Why melanoma gets missed

The warning signs most people associate with skin cancer come from research developed for fairer-skinned populations, where melanoma tends to appear on sun-exposed areas as an irregular or darkening mole. That picture does not reflect what clinicians see in India.

Melanoma here, most commonly presents on the soles of the feet or beneath the nails, sites that are rarely examined and even more rarely associated with cancer. This condition is called acral lentiginous melanoma, a subtype that accounts for 35 to 60%  of cases in dark-skinned individuals. Such lesions are frequently mistaken for bruises, fungal infections, or diabetic ulcers, and by the time a biopsy is taken, the disease has often progressed.

Mucosal melanomas, a rare  type of cancer that starts in the mucous membranes, are highly aggressive with a very low chance of recovery and produce few early warning signs. Most are diagnosed only after spread has occurred.
Any pigmented lesion that changes or persists, wherever it appears on the body, deserves investigation rather than reassurance.
A decade of transformation
When I began my oncology career, managing advanced melanoma meant offering patients limited and rarely durable options. That has fortunately changed significantly.

The foundational shift came from James Allison and Tasuku Honjo, whose discoveries on CTLA-4 and PD-1 earned them the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their research established the principle of immune-checkpoint blockade: rather than attacking a tumour directly, we can sometimes release the biological brakes that stop the patient’s own immune system from doing so. The results can be extraordinary. Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was diagnosed at 91 with melanoma that had spread to his liver and brain. Surgical resection of liver disease, stereotactic radiation for the brain, and immunotherapy with the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab produced a durable remission, and he lived to 100.

Precision medicine has reshaped the approach in parallel. Some melanomas carry specific mutations, particularly in the BRAF pathway, that can be directly targeted with molecularly designed therapies. This is where next-generation sequencing, or NGS, becomes critical. In simple terms, it reads the genetic blueprint of a patient’s tumour and identifies the alterations that should guide treatment, turning what was once a single clinical decision into a detailed, individualised process.

The melanoma story is not over; it is only becoming more exciting. TIL therapy takes tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, expands them in the laboratory, and reinfuses them in far greater numbers, a step toward truly personalised cellular treatment. In August 2026, intismeran, a personalised mRNA vaccine built from the patient’s own tumour sequence, was combined with pembrolizumab in high-risk melanoma patients after surgery. The results were striking: a significant reduction in recurrence compared with pembrolizumab alone, making it the first positive late-stage trial of a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine, though survival data remain pending.
What still needs to change

All of these advances deliver their best results when treatment begins early. The more sophisticated our therapies become, the more clearly we see that they work best before the disease has spread. In India, awareness and referral gaps continue to push diagnosis toward advanced stages.

Recalibrating public health messaging to reflect how melanoma actually presents in Indian patients is a start. Faster pathways from primary care to specialist centres matter equally. More fundamentally, India needs a national melanoma registry, stronger epidemiological and genomic data, more clinical trials in Indian patients, and deeper international collaboration. The advances of the past decade are genuinely extraordinary. Whether they reach the patients who need them comes down to one thing: a diagnosis early enough to act on.
(Prof. Jyoti Bajpai is director – medical precision immuno-oncology, Apollo Hospitals, Mumbai & Western Zone. drjyoti_ba@apollohospitals.com)

title: Why is NCPCR investigating Meta, Instagram?

content.value: The story so far: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned Meta officials for a hearing on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) as a part of an inquiry on child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) on Instagram. An investigation by British public broadcaster BBC threw up many ads that linked out to CSEAM on other platforms. The IT Ministry has also summoned the company on the issue.
What did the BBC investigation show?

In July, BBC reported that the organisation saw dozens of ads promoting CSEAM on Instagram with a test account. CSEAM is banned around the world, and attracts strict criminal penalties. Meta said in a statement, “Before these cases were brought to our attention, our enforcement systems had already identified and disabled several of the violating ads and the accounts behind them.”

The company said that it automatically removes millions of CSAM posting accounts each year, but that “no system is perfect and that determined criminals will continue to try to exploit our platform”. This month, the Tech Transparency Project reported that it found hundreds of CSAM ads on Facebook and Instagram, including some that were served to India.
Why are CSEAM ads appearing on Instagram?

While social media platforms prohibit CSEAM, automatic moderation systems, that use some AI to detect unlawful media, are not able to catch all violative submissions. The Tech Transparency Project, a US-based nonprofit, said that what Meta was doing was not enough even within the scope of what it could. The nonprofit said that even in cases where Meta was taking down CSEAM, it was tagging the ads as adult sexual content, and so “may be undercounting instances of child sexual abuse”.

While the firm revised this information for ads reported by TTP, “did not fix the flow of child exploitation content in its advertising system,” and continued to show CSEAM ads to certain audiences, the nonprofit said. One of the ads appeared to feature an unidentified “underaged European royal,” TTP said.
Amusing or addictive? The algorithms powering our social feeds

Many such ads were placed by “resellers” for ad spots on Meta’s platforms based in China, who account for billions of dollars of ad revenue. TTP pointed to a Reuters report that indicated that ads going through this channel were subject to a more relaxed enforcement regime, where the platform earned $18 billion in 2024. This channel is intended for Chinese firms who want to advertise to overseas customers.

Even with a human reporting CSEAM posts, action was not guaranteed, TTP found. “With 57% (73) of the CSAM ads reported to Meta, the company sent back a message that said, “We’ve taken a look and found that this ad doesn’t go against our Advertising Standards”,”, TTP said.
What was NCPCR’s reaction to the report?

NCPCR issued a notice on July 3, the same day the BBC report came out, demanding an explanation from the company. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) also sought an explanation from the company.

Shortly after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s July 23 video message to Indian youth was briefly removed from Facebook due to an “error,” MeitY summoned Meta’s global public affairs director Joel Kaplan to demand an explanation on that removal. In that meeting, the BBC reporting was also discussed. The summoning came as the government sent a massive volume of takedown notices for Instagram posts on the Jantar Mantar protests, and footage from the protests and the ensuing police crackdown went viral.

Meta provided written responses to both MeitY and NCPCR. The latter declined a Right to Information request by The Hindu for a copy of the company’s response, arguing that providing this information would impede its investigation.
After the written response, Meta officials were summoned by NCPCR this month. Neither side provided a description of the meeting.
What powers does NCPCR have to conduct an inquiry like this?

Like the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the NCPCR’s founding law, the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, gives the body the powers of a civil court under the Criminal Procedure Code (replaced recently by the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita Bill, 2023).
As such, it has the statutory power to demand explanations on issues of child safety from private organisations and can demand reports from law enforcement.

NCPCR’s remit includes “matters relating to children in need of special care and protection including children in distress,marginalized and disadvantaged children, children in conflict with law, juveniles, children without family and children of prisoners and recommend appropriate remedial measures,” and to “[i]nquire into complaints [relating to] non implementation of laws providing for protection and development of children,” the commission said.
NCPCR has in the past issued notices to firms like Netflix in response to the show Bombay Begums, and to Bourn Vita maker Mondelez over sugar content in their malt powder.

title: Social media opening doors to child marriages?

content.value: Last year, the District Child Welfare Committee in Chennai dealt with a case where a 15-year-old girl from Nepal had married a 28-year-old man working in Chennai, the two having met on Instagram. With the help of friends, they got married in Chennai.

A month into the marriage, the girl was traced after she made a call to her sister in Nepal. The girl’s family lodged a complaint with the police following which India Child Protection, a civil society organisation working in the area of child protection, intervened to rescue the girl.
Social media and online dating are increasingly exposing vulnerable girls to greater risk of child marriage.

“With advancement in digital communication, the modus operandi in child marriage is changing, making more children vulnerable,” says Bhuwan Ribhu, a child rights activist and founder of Just Rights for Children.

Bhuwan Ribhu says trafficking is a borderless crime, and it requires a borderless response. Online methods of enticement or grooming for marriage, sexual abuse and trafficking have become possible irrespective of distance and geography.

In a study taken by NGO Save the Children, they observed that girls in India faced greater online risk of child marriage and trafficking during the pandemic. The agency continues to work with children and teachers to raise awareness about staying safe online.

According to the National Family Health Survey (2019-21), the national average in India for child marriage is 23%. The prevalence rate in India for child marriage has fallen by 10 per cent. The Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat campaign launched by the Central Government in November 2024 promises to make India child marriage-free by 2030 and is seeing various state governments running different initiatives.
A dedicated CMPO needed
Natharsha Malim H, state coordinator - Tamil Nadu, India Child Protection, says while Tamil Nadu has been making steady progress in reporting and stopping child marriages, gaps continue to exist.

Tamil Nadu, he says, does not have Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (CMPOs) that are appointed to prevent marriages, gather evidence, raise awareness and report data. The District Social Welfare Officer (DSWO) is notified as the Child Marriage Prohibition Officer of the concerned district.
“This is an additional role that the DSWO takes up. We have been asking for a dedicated person to be appointed as many other states have done based on a Supreme Court recommendation,” says Malim.

For example, in Karnataka, the Department of Women and Child Welfare has included pre-university (PU) college principals as child marriage prohibition officers, whose responsibility is to prevent any girl child studying in their college from marrying before 18 years.

Dedicated officials tasked with curbing this practice is particularly required in places such as Salem, Dindigul, Namakal and Cuddalore which has reported maximum cases of child marriages, says Malim. Grama panchayats have to be empowered in these districts to curb child marriage
A rule book for intervention
Malim notes that State Governments have to draw up a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for elimination of child marriages.
“The Supreme Court came out with a landmark judgement on child marriages in October 2024, but Tamil Nadu is yet to come out with an SOP,” he says.
Panchayats that make an earnest effort to stop child marriage should be rewarded; and the bravery of young girls that resist coercion by family into child marriage should also be acknowledged.
Bhuwan Ribhu cites the example of a study done by India Child Protection in 2025, wherein cases in Assam dropped by 84 percent following a continuous crackdown by law-enforcement authorities.
Although Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 has been in existence for decades, enforcement leaves a lot to be desired.

“With amendments to the law and judgments by the Supreme Court, we have been able to see much impact on the ground, along with greater awareness,” says Ribhu, adding, “awareness needs to be supplemented with the enforcement of policies, accountability of institutions, and the use of technology for monitoring.”
Residents association in Chennai hails UN declaration

On September 4, 2026, when the United Nations General Assembly declared November 27 as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, a residents group in Anna Nagar celebrated the announcement.

Residents of Kambar Colony displayed awareness banners and charts to celebrate November 27 declared as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage by the United Nations General Assembly.

A small number of residents, close to 150, of Kambar Colony in Anna Nagar gathered at the park in the neighbourhood to watch the live proceedings of the United Nations General Assembly on the designation of November 27 as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage.

The programme was organised by the ICWO Tamil Nadu and Kambar Colony Welfare Association. The designation is a significant global commitment to strengthening awareness, prevention and action against child, early and forced marriage. This is a victory for children and civil society organisation that have been fighting to end child marriage.
Awareness banners and charts were displayed, and the gathering concluded with an oath-taking ceremony to strengthen the community’s commitment to end child marriage.
ICWO is a partner agency with Just Rights with Children in Chennai, working with educational institutions and communities on rights concerning children.

A.J. Hariharan, founder secretary, ICWO, says reporting is the key to preventing child marriage. He notes: “we work closely with schools and colleges to help eradicate child marriage. All what we ask them is report any cases of child marriage to the helpline number or a teacher.”
ChildLine Helpline 1098 can also be dialled to report a case.

title: Nadda highlights need for a resilient healthcare system

content.value: A resilient healthcare system does not just mean an increased number of beds; it must have critical-care capacity, oxygen and medical-gas systems, isolation facilities, trained manpower, laboratory capacity and the ability to detect outbreaks early, while maintaining routine health services, says Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare J.P. Nadda.

Inaugurating 10 Critical Care Blocks (CCBs) and 12 Integrated Public Health Laboratories (IPHLs), costing ₹250 crore, in Andhra Pradesh in the presence of Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and Minister for Health, Medical and Family Welfare Satya Kumar Yadav from Vijayawada on September 12 (Saturday), Mr. Nadda said the facilities mark an important step towards strengthening public health preparedness and health-security architecture in the State.
Earlier, they visited the newly established Critical Care Block and Integrated Public Health Laboratories at the old Government General Hospital in Vijayawada and formally opened the facilities.

Addressing the gathering, Mr. Nadda said the CCBs and Integrated Public Health Laboratories (IPHLs) represent two essential dimensions of a resilient health system. “The capacity to save life when a patient is critically ill, and the capacity to detect and respond to disease threats before they become major public health emergencies,” he said.

Under Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM), the Union government had sanctioned 24 CCBs, with an investment of around ₹606 crore, and 26 IPHLs for the State, the Minister said.

The Centre approved ₹1,271.80 crore for the five-year scheme period under four key components, including Critical Care Blocks, Integrated Public Health Laboratories, Urban Ayushman Arogya Mandirs and Rural Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, Mr. Nadda said.
Later, Mr. Nadda praised Andhra Pradesh’s Sanjeevani programme for taking healthcare to people’s doorstep and facilitating testing for 41 health parameters.

According to official information, the projects have added 500 critical-care beds and include advanced operation theatres, ultrasound facilities and specialised services in cardiology, nephrology, neurology and neurosurgery.

The newly opened 10 Critical Care Blocks are located at GMC Kadapa, ACSR GMC Nellore, GMC Srikakulam, AMC Visakhapatnam, GMC Ongole, District Hospital Anakapalli, GMC Rajamahendravaram, KMC Kurnool, District Hospital Hindupur and SMC Vijayawada. The 12 Integrated Public Health Laboratories are located at Area Hospital Seethampeta, Area Hospital Guntakal, Area Hospital Palamaner, Area Hospital Aganampudi, Area Hospital Nandigama, Area Hospital Chirala, Area Hospital Araku, Area Hospital Narasaraopeta, Area Hospital Banaganapalli, Area Hospital Anaparthy, Area Hospital Tuni and Area Hospital Gudur.

title: NMC revises MBBS seat matrix amid continuing approvals and appeals

content.value: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has revised the MBBS seat matrix for the 2026-27 academic year, while cautioning medical colleges and counselling authorities against admitting students beyond the intake capacity formally approved by the regulator.

In a public notice issued earlier this month, the NMC said the updated matrix incorporated permissions granted for the establishment of new medical colleges and increases in the annual intake of existing colleges following decisions by its Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), its first appeal committee and the second appeal committee under the Union Health Ministry.
Not final

The regulator has also made it clear that the latest matrix is not necessarily final. It said the seat matrix would remain subject to revision based on subsequent decisions of the appeal committees or other competent authorities, with any changes to be uploaded on the NMC website and taken into account by the Central and State counselling committees.

The latest matrix lists 1,40,214 MBBS seats across 836 medical colleges, including 63,971 seats in 391 government colleges and 76,243 seats in 445 private colleges. It follows an earlier matrix listing 1,27,028 renewed seats. The latest update includes 13,186 additional seats, of which 10,400 are in private medical colleges and 2,786 in government institutions.

The NMC’s latest warning comes against the backdrop of continuing approvals, appeals and changes in sanctioned intake. It has specifically directed counselling committees not to permit admissions against seats in excess of those approved and notified by MARB.

“Under no circumstances” should any medical college or institution admit students beyond its approved annual intake, the regulator said, warning that such admissions would constitute non-compliance with the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and the regulations framed under it and could attract regulatory and penal action.
Report any discrepancy
The NMC has also asked counselling committees to refer any discrepancy between the seats being offered by a college and those appearing in the approved matrix to MARB for clarification.

The notice has a further caveat for private medical colleges that have received permission either to establish a new MBBS college or increase their annual intake but have not yet furnished the required electronic bank guarantee.
