The farmers of the Cauvery Delta are seriously prejudiced, as the Kuruvai season is almost over and Mettur could not be open for irrigation for want of adequate storage and cultivation of the samba crop and has been severely affected, which is causing great anxiety amongst the farming community in the Cauvery Delta as they are not getting the due share even on a pro-rata basis in the current water year,” Tamil Nadu submitted, in the affidavit filed by advocate B. Karunakaran.
A Bench headed by Justice Vikram Nath is scheduled to hear the Cauvery case on August 31.

The previous hearing on August 24 had witnessed the top court advising Tamil Nadu to voice its concern about the release of the “proportionate” quantity of Cauvery water due from Karnataka before the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC) and the CWMA, in meetings scheduled during the week.
‘Raised concerns to CWRC’

Tamil Nadu said that its member, in a CWRC meeting held on August 24, had raised the State’s entitlement to receive around 28 TMC. The member had asked the CWRC to facilitate the release of around 22,000 cusecs (1.9 TMC per day) for 15 days, starting from August 24.

The State had also submitted before the CWRC that Karnataka had already drawn over 20 TMC from its canals for irrigation and also through anicut channels and lift irrigation systems, while Tamil Nadu had till date not been able to open the Mettur reservoir for irrigation.

“However, CWRC directed Karnataka to ensure releases from its reservoirs so that the flows at the rate of 9,000 cusecs are realised at Billigundulu with effect from August 25 till September 8,” Tamil Nadu said.
It said that CWRC had fixed 9,000 cusecs for the next 15 days with effect from August 25, without considering the accumulated backlog of 17.415 TMC as of August 23.
‘Backlog must be released’
Tamil Nadu said it had raised its grievance before the CWMA, at its meeting the very next day on August 25, about the “gross inadequacy” of the CWRC order for release of Cauvery water.

The State informed the top court that it had urged the CWMA to direct Karnataka to ensure the release of 1.9 TMC per day from August 24 to September 7 to ensure that the backlog in terms of the pro-rata formula is also released by Karnataka.

“However, CWMA, without considering the purport of the scheme framed under Section 6A of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956, which mandates pro-rata releases in the distress years, scrupulously failed to take any steps to direct Karnataka to make good the same. CWMA mechanically affirmed the recommendation of CWRC and directed Karnataka to ensure only 9,000 cusecs per day from August 25 to September 8,” the Tamil Nadu affidavit said.

title: New study captures Sun’s early warning signs before solar flares

content.value: In a new study, scientists have found small, short-lived brightenings in the Sun’s atmosphere that appear in the hours before a major solar flare erupts and cluster around the very spot where the flare later occurs.

The study was carried out by researchers from the Manipal Centre for Natural Sciences and Manipal Academy of Higher Education, along with scientists from the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), the Department of Space, and other academicians.
It used simultaneous ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray observations from three payloads onboard the Aditya-L1 mission.

The Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT) payload observed the Sun in 11 near-ultraviolet (NUV) filters, revealing different layers from the upper photosphere to the chromosphere, according to ISRO.

“NUV wavelengths are largely inaccessible from the ground because Earth’s atmosphere absorbs most ultraviolet radiation. Complementing SUIT are two X-ray instruments, the Solar Low Energy X-ray Spectrometer (SoLEXS) and the High Energy L1 Orbiting X-ray Spectrometer (HEL1OS), which measure the X-ray emission produced by energetic processes in the solar corona. Combining these data, scientists study how activity in the lower solar atmosphere is linked to energy release in the corona during the build-up to a flare,” ISRO stated.

Analysing several solar flare events in the Mg II h filter of SUIT, the team found numerous small, short-lived brightening ‘transient events’, occurring in active regions before the onset of major flares.

“Some of these also showed corresponding X-ray signatures, indicating that they involve the release of magnetic energy. These pre-flare transient events clustered around the location where the major flare later occurred. The results suggest that repeated small-scale energy release may progressively destabilise the magnetic field in an active region, eventually leading to a large solar flare,” ISRO said.

The findings provide valuable insights into the physical processes that trigger solar flares and move scientists a step closer towards reliable flare forecasting, which will ultimately contribute to better space weather prediction; help protect satellites, astronauts, and communication systems; and other critical technologies.

title: STS-8: Launching and landing at night, with an Indian connection

content.value: There’s nearly half a world between India and the U.S., geographically speaking. You knew that, didn’t you? That means that our time-zones are kind of yin-yang, with most Americans sleeping when we go about our daily duties, and vice versa. If you know folks who work along with American counterparts on a daily basis and see them scheduling their calls, or if you’ve ever tried to wish a friend or a relative residing in the U.S. on their birthday, you might have experienced this first hand.

Funnily enough, the first night time launch and landing of a NASA mission was necessitated because of this yin-yang connection between the two nations. This was because the primary payload of the STS-8 mission was a satellite to be deployed for India and tracking requirements led to the unusual choice of timings. The final orbital location chosen for INSAT-1B dictated a night time launch and landing for the Challenger, a first in the Shuttle programme.
Four turns five

When NASA first announced the crew for STS-8 in April 1982, it was to be a four-member crew comprising Commander Richard H. Truly, a veteran who had flown aboard the STS-2 mission and three others – Pilot Daniel C. Brandenstein and Mission Specialists Dale A. Gardner and Guion S. Bluford – who were first time flyers. The four-man crew for a three-day mission in July 1983 eventually turned into a five-man crew for a six-day mission in August-September 1983.
Also read: Ride rides into the space

As one among every three astronauts on early space shuttle missions had experienced space motion sickness, it was decided in December 1982 to assign physician-astronaut Dr. William E. Thornton to conduct in-flight studies and medical investigations to better understand the phenomenon.
Record turnaround time

Following the end of the STS-7 mission and the Challenger’s return to Earth in California on June 24, 1983, it arrived at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida five days later. With time of the essence, the technicians worked doubly fast to ensure what was then a record turnaround time. The orbiter was refurbished, mated with its twin Solid Rocket Boosters and External Tank and the stack was rolled out to Launch Complex 39A, all before August 2. As if all this wasn’t enough, the stack had to ride out Hurricane Barry, which made its landfall just south of KSC, while it was on the pad.

It all proved worth it as the successful launch of STS-8 took place on the night of August 30, making it just the second night launch among American human spaceflights, following Apollo 17 in 1972. The moment the shuttle cleared the launch tower, the flight’s control shifted from KSC to NASA’s Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston.
First African-American in space

The successful launch also meant that a number of records had already been set. This was because Bluford was the first-ever African-American to fly in space and 54-year-old Thornton became the oldest person in space up until then.

In his recollection of the mission for a oral history with the JSC History Office, Bluford mentions that he fumbled around in zero-G for some time “like all the other astronauts before me”. “However, it was a great feeling, and I knew right away that I was going to enjoy this experience,“ he added.
“I also felt very privileged to have been a role model for many youngsters, including African-Americans kids, who aspired to be scientists, engineers and astronauts in this country.”Guion S. Bluford

Speaking in 2004 for the oral history project, Bluford, who was also part of a number of other missions, also recalled what he felt was his most significant accomplishment as an astronaut. “I also felt very privileged to have been a role model for many youngsters, including African-Americans kids, who aspired to be scientists, engineers and astronauts in this country.

Once in orbit around Earth, the crew members got on their respective tasks. This meant that Dr. Thornton took the first measurements for the space motion sickness studies, something that continued for the rest of the mission.
Bluford deploys INSAT-1B

It was Bluford who was tasked with deploying the INSAT-1B satellite, and he carried it out successfully on August 31, the astronauts’ first full day in space. In the days that followed, the astronauts ticked off the other items on their mission objective, including holding an in-flight press conference and speaking with the then U.S. President Ronald W. Reagan, who congratulated them on their success.

The first night landing in the shuttle’s history took place on September 5. Following 98 orbits around the Earth, the crew fired the engines of Challenger to return to Earth and landed at Edwards Air Force Base in California. The historic mission had lasted six days, one hour, and nine minutes.

The INSAT-1B, the primary payload of the STS-8 mission, was an Indian communications satellite that was part of the Indian National Satellite System. Launched on August 30 and deployed the very next day, it initially seemed like the INSAT-1B was about to suffer the same fate as INSAT-1A. Launched in April 1982, INSAT-1A had to be abandoned in September the same year following a series of failures.

The Hindu, in its editorial titled “The challenge of space” on September 3, 1983, stated that “INSAT 1-B is at once a concrete demonstration of the practical applications of space technology to everyday life and a test of the nation’s scientific and technological capability on the ground to manage and put to full use the opportunities now opened up.” This might have seemed like premature celebration had things not panned out the way it did.
Fully operational by October

This was because the INSAT-1B, built by Ford Aerospace for the Indian Space Research Organisation, failed to deploy its solar array for starters. It was only in mid-September that Ford and the Indian controllers turned the tide, successfully deploying the solar array and stationing it at 74°E in place of INSAT-1A.
Also read: Aryabhata, India’s first satellite

In the days, months, and years that went by, INSAT-1B did turn out to be the “concrete demonstration” that The Hindu envisioned it to be, as it notched up a number of firsts. The first photographs and TV pictures from the satellite were beamed back in September and full operational capacity was achieved by October.
Dedicated to the nation

In February 1984, then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi dedicated INSAT to the nation. She stated that any investment on space science was essential for the future development of the country. “It is not a costly showpiece,” she said.

The 90-minute ceremony was broadcast live to the entire nation, thanks to INSAT-1B. “The country is proud of you all”, she said, congratulating the space scientists, engineers, and everyone involved for the successful operation of the INSAT system.

Built for a seven-year tenure, INSAT-1B outlasted that duration, performing its tasks with aplomb. Its 4,375 two-way voice or equivalent circuits remained in use as long as it remained operational, and it returned around 36,000 Earth images during that time. It was moved in 1992, before eventually being decommissioned in August 1993, nearly 10 years after its launch.
Not the only link

While INSAT-1B being SMS-8’s primary payload was the major link between the mission and India, it wasn’t the only one. The other one was introduced to highlight this existing Indian link, making it a nested link of sorts. Sounds convoluted? Here’s the clarification.

During each of STS-8’s six days in orbit, Mission Control played a recording to awaken the crew, with each of the selections carrying a certain significance. On September 4, which was Flight Day 6 and the astronauts’s final full day in orbit, Mission Control chose “Tala Sawari”. This instrumental composition performed by Indian sitar virtuoso Ravi Shankar was released in 1967 as part of the album “West Meets East, Volume 2” and was chosen as a way to honour the release of the INSAT-1B satellite.
“Thank you for that thoroughly enlightening cultural experience.”Daniel C. Brandenstein

The recording featured Shankar on sitar and Alla Rakha on tabla and the work neatly emphasised improvisation with a structured rhythmic cycle, the Hindustani classical musical style. At the end of it, Brandenstein acknowledged what they’d just heard by saying “Thank you for that thoroughly enlightening cultural experience.”

title: Science Snapshots: August 30, 2026

content.value: Famous supergiant star Betelgeuse may not be alone

Using the Very Large Telescope, astronomers have found strong evidence that Betelgeuse, the famous red supergiant star, has a close companion, now called Betelgeuse B. It seems to be a young star around 2.6-3.1-times as heavy as our sun. And it could explain why Betelgeuse’s brightness changes in a six-year cycle: that is likely caused by the companion periodically blocking some of Betelgeuse’s light. The team is awaiting a second observation to confirm the data.
Children more exposed to extreme humid heat than elderly

Researchers found that children aged 0-9 are currently exposed to roughly thrice as many additional heat stress days as adults in their 60s, meaning they are disproportionately more exposed to extreme humid heat. The root of the disparity is the vast majority of the world’s children living in tropical, low-latitude areas where heat is increasing most intensely. These findings are critical because children are physically more vulnerable to heat and face potential lifelong health risks.
Microclimate under solar panels leads to ‘inferior greening’

By analysing data from 2,344 counties China between 2014 and 2023, researchers found policies promoting large-scale solar farms also supported ‘inferior greening’: while solar installations increased the amount of green on the ground, the new growth was often dense and lacked the variety of natural habitats that supports many bird species. The study found these consequences were also most pronounced in wealthy, non-desert regions, so its authors recommended clustering large solar projects in desert areas.

title: What is the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope?

content.value: NASA is preparing to launch its next flagship space observatory — one scientists plan to use to investigate some of the universe’s biggest mysteries, including dark energy and dark matter, while also testing gravity at vast scales and hunting ​for planets beyond our solar system.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is a roughly $4 billion project. At the time of writing, it was planned for a Sunday launch from the NASA Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The observatory will be lofted into orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.

The telescope is named after the late Nancy Grace Roman, NASA’s first chief astronomer. It is a follow-on to the Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, and the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, and has capabilities that can expand on the knowledge gained by those pioneering observatories, both of which also still operate.
The telescope’s main survey will take more than ​a year, per Roman’s senior project scientist Julie McEnery.

“The survey will contain over two billion galaxies and enable us to study how the structures in our universe — the stars, the galaxies, the clusters of galaxies — grew and evolved. We’ll ​also measure how our universe has expanded over time,” she said.
After launch and separation from the rocket, the telescope will travel towards a location called Lagrange point 2, about 1.6 million km from the earth. Webb also resides at this location.
U.S. ​President Donald Trump tried during both his first and second terms to reduce or eliminate funding for Roman but Congress preserved it.

title: Dharashiv MP pushes for crop loss survey and compensation for farmers in Marathwada region

content.value: Government of Maharashtra should survey crops that may have dried up due to inadequate rainfall said Dharashiv MP from Shiv Sena Omprakash Raje Nimbalkar. He demanded compensation and financial aid for the eligible farmers in the Marathwada region.

Mr. Nimbalkar sent a letter to Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde. In the letter, he said that there has been almost no rainfall in the region of Marathwada for the past 45 days. “The soybean crop has dried due to lack of water. Farmers have faced a financial loss due to this and are in trouble. The situation is serious, and surveys should be conducted through the revenue and agriculture departments to ascertain the losses. The farmers who have faced losses and are eligible should be given financial assistance,” he added.
The Marathwada region has faced a rainfall deficit since June 1. The region has so far received 381 mm (77%) average rainfall in all eight districts against the expected 498.8 mm.

The rainfall deficit in Dharashiv Lok Sabha constituency stood at 25.3%. Dharashiv district has received rainfall of 301.5 mm against the average expected rainfall of 403.5 mm, according to a revenue department report.

title: U.S. officials revise claims that government agencies were hacked by Chinese, now say they were targets

content.value: U.S. officials are correcting earlier statements that several government agencies ⁠were hacked by Chinese hackers, now saying that the organisations were among the hackers’ targets.

In a newly edited statement, the Department of Justice said on Friday that the U.S. Senate, the Federal Reserve, ‌NASA and others were “among the targets of QTFY,” a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group that officials identified on Wednesday during an internet domain seizure operation. A previous version of ‌the statement said the government agencies had been among the hackers’ victims.

A note ‌left ⁠at the bottom of the newly edited statement said that “Edits have been ⁠made to ensure this press release accurately reflects the government’s allegations in the affidavit in support of the domain seizures.”

The DOJ said on Friday it made a correction to the press release because the August 26 ​release “described all agencies as victims whereas ‌the government’s affidavit made clear that all were targeted but only some were compromised.”

The distinction matters because it narrows the scope of confirmed breaches in what the DOJ described as a years-long Chinese cyber-espionage campaign against U.S. government agencies, defense contractors and ‌other sensitive targets.

According to the FBI affidavit released ​alongside the original statement, since at least 2018 the hackers “targeted” U.S. federal networks including those of NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy, the ⁠Department of Justice, the Department of Health and Human Services, the National Institutes of Health, and the U.S. Senate.
A footnote in the affidavit said that the FBI investigated the targeting of ‌NASA and found that the attempted breach of NASA was unsuccessful due to the agency’s patching of targeted software.

The affidavit alleges that in September 2024, the hackers carried out “computer intrusions” at three “DOE National Laboratories, NIH, an HHS agency, and a U.S. security device manufacturer,” and referred to the entities as “victims.”

A separate joint cybersecurity advisory issued by the FBI, National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command’s Cyber National Mission Force published on Wednesday listed ‌successful data thefts from unnamed defense contractors, financial institutions and universities in May 2024, and unsuccessful attempts to access ​networks of the U.S. Senate and a U.S. hospital in March 2026.
Messages seeking clarification from the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency ⁠were not immediately returned on Friday.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request ⁠for comment on Friday.

In response to Wednesday’s announcement, an embassy spokesperson said the U.S. uses cybersecurity to “smear or discredit China” and that China “opposes the ‌U.S. overstretching the concept of national security and using it as a pretext to impose discriminatory restrictions on Chinese companies and will firmly safeguard the legitimate rights and ​interests of Chinese companies.”

title: OpenAI to end partnership with SpaceX's Cursor

content.value: OpenAI ​said on ‌Friday that it ​plans ⁠to end its agreement providing ‌AI models ‌to ‌Cursor, ⁠the coding-tool company ⁠now owned by Elon ​Musk’s ‌SpaceX.
OpenAI said it was not confident ‌that ​SpaceX would use ⁠its technology “within our terms of ‌service.”
SpaceX did not immediately respond to ‌a Reuters ​request for comment outside regular ⁠business hours.

title: Google rolls out Gemini AI feature to help readers analyse their e-books

content.value: Google has rolled out a new AI feature known as Expert Intelligence that allows readers to use AI in order to get personalised insights from the e-books they bought through Google Play Books.

To make use of the feature, readers can upload eligible e-books into a Gemini Notebook. Following this, they can use AI to ask questions, understand the book, generate infographics, create audio overviews, generate quizzes, or even make action plans by uploading their own notes and ideas.

Google cited the hypothetical example of a manager brainstorming strategies in line with a management book, a woman uploading journal entries in order to benefit from the information provided in an e-book about menopause, or a family creating a meal plan inspired by a food culture book.
Expert Intelligence would allow them to apply lessons from their respective books to their own lives.

However, company-based restrictions mean that readers must buy the books they want to analyse with AI from Google Play Books. While the AI Notebook can be shared with others, they too must buy the book in order to engage with the content fully.

More readers are using AI in order to summarise or analyse the books they are reading, but these features rarely exist on one platform. Readers may need to “jailbreak” copyright protections to allow external AI tools to view their e-books. Others opt to run pirated copies through AI systems for ease. A clunkier method involves copying and pasting sections of books into AI chatbots to ask for highly specific and personalised assistance.
Google highlighted that it had developed the Expert Intelligence feature in collaboration with authors and publishers, to both help readers and encourage sales.

“Expert Intelligence launches today with more than 100,000 books from major publishers, including Bloomsbury, De Gruyter Brill, Johns Hopkins University Press, Macmillan Publishers, O’Reilly Media, and Penguin Random House. We’ve also collaborated closely with more than 15 bestselling authors — including Steven Pinker, Michael Pollan, and Jennifer Wallace — to curate special Featured Notebooks that supplement their books with additional sources and engaging artifacts that let readers dive deeper into the author’s work,” stated the company in a blog post.

title: Trump government mulls deal to give away part of Yosemite park to a private developer

content.value: President Donald Trump's administration is considering giving a section of the renowned Yosemite National Park to a private developer, a lawyer for the company confirmed to AFP on Friday (August 28, 2026).

The National Park Service has been holding talks with Nevada-based Kingsbarn Realty Capital to build an access road from an 83-acre private property just outside the park to Yosemite's entrance, in exchange for land elsewhere, lawyer Lanny Davis said.

The news was first reported by the outlet NOTUS and caused an uproar among conservationists and opposition Democrats, who have fiercely objected to moves by the administration to roll back protections of public lands — including pushing to reinstate road building and logging in national forests.

But Mr. Davis, who described himself as a lifelong "progressive Democrat," framed the road as a green move on the grounds that it would shorten trips to and from the currently undeveloped property, cutting emissions compared to the current circuitous route.

"Without a direct access route, every trip from the Hazel Green area requires a significantly longer drive — twice as long, at a minimum — on unpaved forest roads and thus more air pollution," Mr. Davis said. "The new access road would be safer for drivers and generate substantially less vehicle emissions."

He also stressed that the land exchange proposal — which would involve supplying Yosemite National Park with a parcel of land elsewhere — "is expressly provided for under federal law and will not reduce the land area of the park."
The Interior Department earlier said negotiations had taken place but rejected the idea, reported by NOTUS, that there had been political pressure to reach a predetermined outcome.

"Any land exchange or access proposal involving National Park Service lands would be subject to all applicable federal laws, regulations and Departmental policies, including required environmental review and public notification processes," the agency said, adding: "No final decisions have been made."

Kingsbarn CEO Jeff Pori has business connections to people close to the President, NOTUS reported, and federal election commission records show he has made donations to the Republican National Committee and Trump-aligned fundraising committees.
'Backroom deal'
The National Parks Conservation Association, an advocacy organisation, called the move an unlawful "attack."

"The Trump administration's attempts to dismantle America's conservation legacy are now taking aim at Yosemite with this secretive, backroom deal," said Mark Rose, the group's senior Sierra Nevada program manager.
The Yosemite NPS Employees Union said it was "appalled" by the ceding of public lands to private interests, calling the proposed trade "antithetical to what we stand for" as stewards of the park.
There was a previous proposal to develop a road through Yosemite when the 83-acre parcel outside the park had a different owner.

That plan was rejected under the administrations Republican George W. Bush and Democrats Barack Obama and Joe Biden, NOTUS said. Former owner Lewis Geyser sued and lost, first in a lower court in 2007 then at appeal in 2012.

First protected in 1864, Yosemite National Park in California's Sierra Nevada mountains is internationally acclaimed for its spectacular granite cliffs, glaciers, waterfalls, sequoia trees and wildlife.
Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California, a fierce critic of Trump, said in a statement: "Yosemite is one of California's natural wonders, and must be protected from further development.

"The courts struck this project down once, but this administration appears hellbent on moving forward in the face of opposition from the public, Congress and the courts. But the only thing the administration cares about is whether there is money involved. We will fight this again."

title: Garbage dumping in Bengaluru’s lakes turns fatal for Indian darters

content.value: Renuka Selvamani, a birder and bird photographer, has noticed a strange phenomenon at her regular haunt, Doddanekundi Lake. “I am seeing more cases of birds in distress,” she says, pointing out that the culprit is trash dumped by humans. The Oriental or Indian darter (Anhinga melanogaster), also known as the snakebird, a tropical water bird with a long, slender neck and a sharp, spear-like beak that it uses to impale fish, seems to be afflicted more than others, Renuka says.

“The darters are very sensitive because of their beaks, which get entangled in waste, such as the net used to pack  onions,” explains Renuka, who  works as a data scientist with the Expedia Group. She adds that when this happens, they cannot hunt or feed themselves, and end up  starving to death. “I  have seen three birds whose beaks have been tied like this,” she says.

And this is not  happening only at Doddanekundi Lake. According to Jayanthi Kallam, the Executive Director of the Avian and Reptile Rehabilitation Centre (ARRC) in Horamavu, there is a surge in the number of darters in distress reported from at least 10  lakes in the city. She points out that there have been sightings at lakes like Doddanekundi, Jakkur, Yelahanka, Rachenahalli, Hesarghatta, Sampengahalli, Lalbagh and Chelkere, among others.

While the issue itself is not a new one — the darters’ pointed beaks, adapted to spear fish, have always been vulnerable to the large quantities of garbage regularly dumped in the city’s water bodies — the number of birds in distress that have been spotted has gone up considerably this year, says Jayanthi. “We would get a couple of birds every year. But this year we are seeing a sudden surge in the numbers,” she says, adding that ARRC now sees at least one case every week. “Also, a lot of bird watching groups and lake groups are reporting more and more sightings.”

Certain types of garbage seem to be causing most of the danger, says Jayanthi: plastic wrappers or bags, discarded fishing nets and puja items. “People who discard puja cloth don’t even realise the dangers of it, but these tiny pieces of cloth, bright in colour, end up attracting the birds,” she says. Their beaks get tangled in these bits of cloth, and they can’t remove them. “Unlike some birds, like raptors, for instance, who can lift their legs and clean their beak, darters are not built like that. They will wiggle and shake their head, but it is very difficult for them to get something out once it is stuck.”

Additionally, since they are flighted birds, rescuing them also becomes difficult. “We have a team dedicated to this…use a motorised boat, drone tracking and binoculars. But because these are flighted birds, if you intervene too soon, they simply go away.” While they have rescued some birds, they would be in an extremely weak and emaciated condition by the time they are rescued, says Jayanthi.

Some birdwatchers are now planning a poster campaign to raise awareness about the issue. “I am still in talks with local nature groups and trying to figure out permissions,” says Praveen, an avid birder from the city.  As someone who has seen several dead birds and spoken to other birders who have also noticed this trend, he believes it is important to educate people about the pressing issue. “We are trying to set up awareness posters highlighting the problem, possible cause and solution,” he says

title: For vultures near Dehradun, 2.4 km separates survival from electrocution

content.value: Poisoning, veterinary non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), food scarcity, and habitat loss continue to remain survival challenges for vultures in India.

A decade-old study, published in the latest issue of the Journal of Threatened Taxa, suggests that relocating a livestock carcass dump 2.4 km away from high-tension power infrastructure near Uttarakhand’s Dehradun may have saved these large scavengers from another existential threat—electrocution.

The authors of the study are Javed Anver, Yash Vardhan Singh Sengar, Bikash Ghimire, Vonchano Ngullie, Hemam Rama Nanda, Tashi P. Dorji, Ankit Sharma, Akshay Jain, Sas Biswas, Arun Kumar, and M. Muzahed.

Vultures are among the most threatened birds globally, having undergone severe population declines across Asia and Africa due to multiple anthropogenic pressures. According to the study, electrocution from power infrastructure has been the most underreported threat.

The study documented electrocution mortality of vultures in the Sudhauwala region of Dehradun, based on 34 surveys conducted between May 2011 and February 2014. The study recorded 743 individual vultures belonging to five species.

“During the study period, 46 vulture carcasses attributable to electrocution were documented in proximity to high-tension power transmission structures. The highest proportion of mortality relative to observations was recorded for the Himalayan griffon (Gyps himalayensis), followed by the Eurasian griffon (Gyps fulvus), and the cinereous vulture (Aegypius monachus),” the study said.
Lower mortality

“Although surveys were conducted on a non-systematic basis, the number of mortality events observed suggests that electrocution may represent a significant localised threat, particularly for long-lived scavengers such as vultures,” it said.

Based on these observations, local authorities relocated the carcass dumping site about 2.4 km away from the high-risk electricity infrastructure in April 2015. Subsequent observations indicated continued use of the new site by vultures, with no mortality events recorded during limited post-relocation monitoring.
Other raptor species, including the black kite (Milvus migrans) and crested serpent eagle (Spilornis cheela), were also recorded at the relocated site.

“Our findings indicated that relocating carcass dumping sites away from hazardous power infrastructure can be a practical conservation measure for reducing electrocution risk and could potentially be applied in other affected areas,” Mr. Anver of the Dehradun-based Wildlife Institute of India told The Hindu.
Although no studies were conducted after 2015, the carcass dumping site relocation demonstrated the potential of this approach as a practical measure to mitigate vulture mortality.

title: How non-government colleges are dominating India’s AYUSH education boom

content.value: As the Centre pushes to widen the role of AYUSH in India’s healthcare system — including through greater coverage, rural outreach and integration with mainstream health services — the country’s AYUSH medical education infrastructure has expanded rapidly. But government data suggests the expansion has been driven largely by non-government institutions.
Of the 541 Ayurveda colleges in April 2024, 467 were non-government — nearly 86% of the total. In Homoeopathy, 236 of 277 colleges, or about 85%, were non-government.

The pattern was similar in other systems. Of the 58 Unani colleges, only 16 were government-run; just three of 17 Siddha colleges and 15 of 71 Yoga and Naturopathy colleges were government institutions. The data clearly indicate that non-government institutions have become an important source of undergraduate medical education in AYUSH.
How has AYUSH education developed in India?

India’s push to expand AYUSH is not merely a recent revival of traditional medicine but an effort to integrate Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Yoga, Naturopathy, and Homoeopathy into the formal healthcare system.

Ayurveda has roots going back thousands of years, while Siddha developed in southern India and Unani became established in the subcontinent through centuries of interaction with the Islamic world. Yoga and Naturopathy developed along different trajectories, while Homoeopathy arrived from Europe in the 19th century and subsequently acquired a substantial following in India. The modern Indian state has therefore treated AYUSH not merely as folk medicine but as a collection of systems requiring institutions, education, regulation and research.

The institutional journey gathered pace after Independence, with the Government gradually creating structures for education, research and regulation. The decisive change came in November 2014, when AYUSH became a full-fledged Union ministry. Sowa Rigpa, the traditional Tibetan medical system, was subsequently added to the group.

Since 2014, the Government has sought to move AYUSH from the margins of the health system towards greater institutional recognition. Its agenda includes education, research, standardisation of medicines, hospitals and dispensaries, medicinal plants and the integration of AYUSH services into public healthcare. The expansion of medical education is now one of the clearest signs of this growth.
What is the current state of non-government involvement in India?
The number of AYUSH colleges rose from 789 in 2021 to 971 in 2024, while total admission capacity increased from 63,477 to 79,593. The permitted-seat capacity rose even faster, from 50,711 to 72,490.

But the most striking feature is who is providing this education. In Ayurveda, 467 of 541 colleges in April 2024 were non-government institutions. In Homoeopathy, the corresponding figure was 236 of 277.

There is also evidence of strong demand, particularly for Ayurveda. In 2024-25, 39,952 of 40,136 permitted Ayurveda undergraduate seats were filled. Across Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy, 60,890 students were admitted against 63,073 permitted seats. The expansion is consequently producing not just colleges but a growing pipeline of practitioners.

Yet this growth brings a new responsibility. More colleges and graduates do not automatically mean better healthcare. The quality of education, clinical training, regulation and employment will matter enormously — as will the way AYUSH practitioners interact with modern medical services.

The Government’s stated ambition is not necessarily to replace modern medicine, but to make AYUSH part of a broader healthcare system. That makes evidence, patient safety, proper referral and clearly defined professional roles crucial.
How is the AYUSH story moving?
The AYUSH story has moved through three broad stages — preservation of traditional systems, institutional recognition and now large-scale expansion.
“The next challenge is to ensure that this expansion produces competent professionals and useful healthcare rather than simply more seats and degrees,” said an official from AYUSH.

title: FSSAI proposes front-of-pack red pictorial warnings for foods high in fat, sugar, salt

content.value: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday (August 28, 2026) submitted in the Supreme Court a proposal to provide information relating to added sugar, fat and salt in pictorial form on the front-of-pack (FOP) of food products, in line with international regulations.

“The proposal is intended to provide a simple, prominent and easily comprehensible warning to consumers regarding food products which are high in specified nutrients of concern,” an FSSAI affidavit filed in the Supreme Court said.

The affidavit proposes an FOP warning label in red hexagonal shape for food products which are high in any two or more “nutrients of concern” such as added saturated fat, added sugar and salt, based on thresholds specified under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024.

The warning label would read ‘High Fat’, ‘High Sugar’, ‘High Salt’ or ‘Highly Sweetened Beverage’ and be displayed in a font one point larger than that used in the nutrition information table on the back of the pack to help customers readily identify at-risk foods.

The FSSAI said single-ingredient food products and those which are “inherently rich in fat, sugar or salt, like ghee, edible oil, jaggery, honey” are proposed to be exempted from FOP warning requirement.
Phased implementation
The affidavit said the FOP labelling mechanism is intended to be implemented in phases to “facilitate consumer acceptability and provide industry adequate time for reformulation”.
Phase I would cover products high in two or more specified nutrients and specified sweetened beverages. Phase II would extend the warning mechanism to products high in any one of these nutrients.

The affidavit in the Supreme Court came in a petition filed by NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi. Mr. Dvivedi said the NGO would file a comprehensive rejoinder to the FSSAI’s compliance affidavit in the apex court after inviting public comments.

The compliance affidavit by the food regulator follows scathing comments on August 13 from a Bench headed by Justice J.B. Pardiwala on the state’s obligations to protect public health. The court had observed that not only developed but even developing countries were adopting international standards of packaging food products.
Bringing awareness

“A positive step in that direction would further accelerate our country’s endeavour to be fully developed, by bringing awareness to the public in general of the ill-effects, emanating even from indigenous foods, despite our conviction that indigenous foods coming from diverse cultures in this country were never intended to be packaged,” the court had recorded in its August 13 order.
The court had noted that the Economic Survey has already suggested FOP labelling, and the Union government would not have any impediments in implementing the changes.
“We are doing this in public interest. Keep it in mind,” Justice Pardiwala had addressed the government on August 13.

title: Campus on edge: ongoing stir at IIT Delhi places spotlight on student suicides, mental health

content.value: Unprecedented scenes have unfolded at one of India’s most prestigious engineering institutions — the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Delhi — over the past week, following the death by suicide of an MSc student.
Classes have been largely called off, and students have been holding a sit-in where the student died last week. Never has the institute witnessed agitation and student mobilisation at this scale.

“Every death is followed by a copy-paste e-mail from the administration, following which the campus is almost immediately expected to go back to normal, even as memorials are held for those who died on the campus,” said a student who wished to remain anonymous.
On the boil

This “pent-up frustration”, the student added, blew up when students who had seen the 31-year-old’s body were called for classes soon after in the Lecture Hall Complex, the very spot where the death had occured. A comment from an administrative official that the student was “beyond repair” further angered the students.

The administration responded by setting up an external probe committee, which was reconstituted following objections from the protesters, and providing financial assistance to the family, though the amount has not been specified. The institute is yet to comment on allegations over the “insensitive remarks” following the student’s death.

On Thursday, IIT Delhi said the academic load had been lightened significantly since 2025, with lower credit loads in the first semester, smaller classes to minimise stress, fewer weekend exams and flexible credit distribution.

To this, an IIT-D student, who wished to stay anonymous, said, “The academic pressure is intense. Families don’t understand why we can’t give them time. Many of us have to pull all-nighters and function on one or two hours of sleep.”
Mental health support

On the institute’s assertion that students’ well-being is supported by a 24x7 team of counsellors and psychiatrists, fully reimbursed external care and a swift emergency protocol, students said counselling is inaccessible or ineffective. “There has been no monthly roster of counsellors in the past year,” said another student. In addition, the student said that parents are involved in such cases, raising privacy concerns.
A source at the institute countered this, saying the counselling centre is accessible and only minutes away from the hostels.

title: Greenland to present report on forced contraceptions

content.value: A Greenlandic commission is to present a highly anticipated report Friday to determine whether Denmark's forced contraception of thousands of the Arctic island's indigenous Inuit constituted a "genocide".
The forced contraception campaign between the 1960s and 1990 is one of the darkest chapters in Greenland's history with its former colonial master, Denmark.
Once the conclusions are presented, Greenland's government will decide how to move forward.
"For us, it's about trying to understand our history," Naaja Nathanielsen, a member of parliament representing Greenland in Denmark's parliament, told AFP.
"Others may feel that we should simply keep quiet about this and try to be conciliatory, because of the United States' aggressiveness toward Greenland."

Nathanielsen announced the creation of the commission, tasked with shedding light on the legal implications of the campaign, in August 2024 when she was Greenland's minister of justice and gender equality.

During the 1960s to 1990, more than 4,000 Greenlandic women were forced to wear a contraceptive coil -- or intrauterine device (IUD) -- in the vast majority of cases without their consent or that of their parents if they were minors.
Greenland, a Danish colony for three centuries and now an autonomous territory, still has a complicated relationship with Copenhagen.
Despite many thorny issues between them, both Copenhagen and Nuuk have presented a united front rejecting US President Donald Trump's threats to take over Greenland.
He has repeatedly accused Denmark of treating Greenland badly.
"Everything that is happening between Denmark and Greenland now is scrutinised," said historian Astrid Andersen, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS).
"There's this pressure on the relationship so of course, when we start talking about genocide, that increases the pressure.
"But everyone in Greenland has been very clear that this tragic case should not be used to legitimise other political purposes internationally."
The commission's four appointed experts were unable to agree on which approach to take and ended up writing two reports, submitted nearly six months behind schedule.
Not just about history
One of the victims, Henriette Berthelsen, told AFP the conclusions, regardless of what is decided, were skewed from the start since no Greenlandic Inuit were appointed as experts.
"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life, and my right to self-determination," she said.
"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."
The campaign affected girls as young as 12, some of whom were never able to have children afterwards.
Nuuk and Copenhagen are also shedding light on several other painful chapters from the past, including children adopted without parental consent or torn from their families.

On Thursday, the Danish parliament agreed that women affected by the forced contraception campaign can claim compensation from Copenhagen, an initiative pushed by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen who presented Denmark's official apology last year.
Beyond imagination
Media coverage of the case has revived trauma that had been buried for decades.

"I realised everything it had cost me -- all those hospitalisations, those surgeries, the schooling I missed and, above all, those pains I had never associated with that damn IUD," said Kirstine Najarak Berthelsen.
"It was buried so deeply in my subconscious... Everything that happened to people is beyond imagination if you haven't experienced it yourself," she added.
By the late 1970s, one in two Greenlandic women of childbearing age -- at least 4,070 women -- had been fitted with an IUD, according to an investigation presented in September 2025.
The scandal came to light when one of the victims spoke out in the media about the trauma she experienced.
A podcast series in 2022 then revealed the full extent of the campaign.
Henriette Berthelsen has called for a "Truth and Reconciliation" commission to be established. The Danish government is considering the idea.
According to the 68-year-old psychologist, that would make it possible to "acknowledge what happened".
"I believe that only then will we be able to begin to heal and move forward -- not as adversaries, but as human beings and as peoples equal in dignity."

title: Congo begins Ebola vaccinations to fight country's worst outbreak on record, health minister says

content.value: Congo on Thursday began vaccinating people against Ebola as health authorities work to slow the country's deadliest outbreak of the disease on record.
The vaccination campaign was officially launched in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo province, in the country's east, Health Minister Roger Kamba said.
Health workers and other people working on the front lines of the Ebola response are among the first to receive the vaccine.
“We have decided to use the Ervebo vaccine to protect first those who are on the front line, therefore our health care providers, but also people who have been in contact with patients,” Kamba said.
The outbreak has so far affected six provinces in Congo, including Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Bas-Uele.
As of Tuesday, the country had recorded 5,713 confirmed cases, including 2,744 deaths, according to government figures. The overall death rate among confirmed cases was about 48%.

The outbreak in eastern Congo is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers' strike and intense population movements. The World Health Organization has said it remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
More than 50,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine have been received, according to Congo's state news agency.
The World Health Organisation said last week that 70,000 doses of Ervebo had been approved for use in Congo.

About 50,000 doses are intended for frontline and health workers, while another 20,000 will be used in a clinical trial to study whether the vaccine protects against Bundibugyo Ebola, the agency said.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo type of Ebola virus. Ervebo, however, is approved to protect against a different type, known as Zaire ebolavirus. There is currently no approved vaccine specifically for Bundibugyo Ebola.

The vaccine is being used under a compassionate-use program, which allows a medical product to be used in a serious disease situation even though it has not been specifically approved for that particular use.

Health authorities said Ervebo could offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus because the two viruses are related. But whether the vaccine can actually prevent illness in people infected with Bundibugyo Ebola is still being studied.
Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC's director for research, clinical trials and innovation, said data will be collected during the vaccination campaign to measure how well the vaccine works.
The campaign is expected to cover 14 health zones in Tshopo, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele provinces.
Kamba strongly encouraged health workers to get vaccinated, saying the vaccine could protect them from the disease and help prevent them from carrying the virus into their communities.

title: JNCASR scientists develop smartphone-based diagnostic system for detection of Alzheimer’s disease

content.value: Scientists at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR) have developed a low-cost, user-friendly point-of-care diagnostic system for the detection of Alzheimer’s.
The system uses a smartphone-enabled platform employing a fluorescence-responsive tiny molecule to help in the detection of the Alzheimer’s biomarker amyloid-β (Aβ).
Alzheimer’s is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by memory loss, cognitive decline, and behavioural impairment.

Central to its pathology is the misfolding and aggregation of amyloid-β (Aβ), which self-assembles into fibrils and deposits as extracellular plaques that trigger neurotoxic cascades leading to synaptic dysfunction and neurodegeneration.

The National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer’s Association framework identifies Aβ, tau, and neurodegeneration as core biomarkers for definitive Alzheimer’s diagnosis across the brain, cerebrospinal fluid, and blood.
Early bio marker
According to the Department of Science and Technology, Aβ pathology is an early Alzheimer’s disease-specific biomarker, making Aβ a more reliable diagnostic indicator.

“Although positron emission tomography and magnetic resonance imaging provide valuable diagnostic information, their high cost, need for specialised infrastructure, technical expertise, and limited accessibility restrict widespread use. Blood-based assays targeting Aβ and tau have emerged as promising alternatives, but are expensive and complex. These limitations highlight the need for simple, sensitive, and scalable diagnostic platforms capable of the early and accurate detection of Aβ for diagnosis,” it said.

The scientists have developed a smart fluorescence lifetime-responsive probe that enables highly selective, sensitive, and differential detection of Aβ fibrils (Aβf) through turn-on fluorescence and distinct lifetime signatures.

“Upon interaction with Aβ, the tiny molecule called TZ-48 undergoes changes in fluorescence intensity, which are captured and quantified using a dedicated smartphone application. This enables rapid and user-friendly detection, with potential applications in the screening and staging of the disease,” the department said.
Robust detection

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy has emerged as a powerful sensing modality because fluorescence lifetime is largely independent of probe concentration and photobleaching, enabling the robust detection of biomarkers and enhancing diagnostic precision.

A team of scientists comprising Krithi K. Bhagavath, Madhu Ramesh, Yogendra Kumar, Sabyasachi Mandal, Hiriyakkanavar Ila, and Thimmaiah Govindaraju developed ADxFluor, a smartphone-integrated platform that leverages the fluorescence response of TZ-48 for rapid, unbiased quantification of serum Aβ load.

The system combines dual-mode brain imaging, biofluid detection, and smartphone-based quantification of Aβ in biofluids, establishing it, along with ADxFluor, a smartphone-integrated platform, as a foundation for next-generation smart diagnostics for Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Do mRNA tumour vaccines herald a new revolution in cancer treatment?

content.value: Not long ago, a diagnosis of advanced cancer left doctors with little more than symptom control and hope. Over the course of a few of decades, however, that picture changed dramatically. Chemotherapy delivered the first meaningful survival gains, though at a steep cost in side effects, a cost later softened by a new generation of supportive drugs that made treatment safer and more tolerable. The mapping of the human genome then opened up an era of precision medicine, as whole-genome sequencing revealed mutations that could be directly targeted. Survival improved again, but a cure remained elusive: tumours kept finding new, resistant mutations to evade each targeted drug. It took a deeper understanding of the immune system to breach the next frontier: immunotherapy taught the body’s own defences to attack cancers once thought untreatable.

Now, a new contender has emerged that could rewrite the story once more: personalized mRNA tumour vaccines. Recent trial results suggest that the next chapter of the cancer treatment story may already be unfolding.
Evolution of treatment

Cancer treatment has advanced in successive waves. In the 1970s and 80s, chemotherapy became the cornerstone of oncology, improving outcomes across the board and curing diseases such as Hodgkin’s lymphoma and testicular cancer. The sequencing of the human genome and subsequent advances in molecular biology then enabled targeted therapies aimed at specific genetic abnormalities — HER2 in breast cancer, EGFR mutations in lung cancer, and many others.

The most dramatic transformation of the past two decades, however, came with immunotherapy. Checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab (drugs that block certain proteins on T-cells of the immune system, helping to attack cancer cells) changed the outlook for metastatic melanoma, a disease that had previously carried a dismal prognosis. What began in melanoma soon spread to lung, kidney, bladder, liver and head-and-neck cancers, reshaping treatment paradigms worldwide.

Immunotherapy has greatly impacted the management of blood cancers as well. Once primarily managed by chemotherapy, cancers like multiple myeloma and lymphoma, have entered the immunotherapy era through CAR-T cell therapy and bispecific antibodies (lab-made proteins that can attach to two different targets), producing outcomes unimaginable just a decade ago.
Today, personalised mRNA vaccines are poised to build on that foundation.
The melanoma breakthrough

The recent excitement around mRNA vaccines stems from the Phase III INTerpath-001 trial, which evaluated intismeran autogene (mRNA-4157/V940), a personalised mRNA vaccine. The study enrolled roughly 1,100 patients with high-risk melanoma who had undergone complete surgical removal of visible disease. They received either immunotherapy through pembrolizumab alone, or pembrolizumab combined with an individualised vaccine designed, using artificial intelligence, from the genetic profile of each patient’s own tumour. This vaccine essentially trained the patients’ immune systems to recognise and destroy unique mutations (neoantigens) on their tumour cells

The results were striking: the combination significantly improved both recurrence-free and distant metastasis-free survival compared with pembrolizumab alone. Earlier studies of the same strategy had already shown roughly a 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death, and a 59% reduction in the risk of distant metastasis or death, compelling evidence that a personalised vaccine can amplify the effect of existing immunotherapy.
For the first time, a personalised neoantigen-based mRNA therapy has succeeded in a large, randomized Phase III trial, validating a concept researcher have pursued for years.
How does it work?

Unlike traditional vaccines, which prevent infection, these are therapeutic vaccines, developed after a disease has been diagnosed, to help trigger the body’s immune system. Once a tumour is sequenced, sophisticated algorithms pick out the mutations unique to that patient’s cancer (neoantigens), providing the necessary information for production of customised mRNA constructs encoding these tumour-specific neoantigens. When injected, these mRNA constructs train the patient’s immune system, particularly the T cells, to recognise and destroy cancer cells carrying those exact mutations. In effect, every patient receives a vaccine made exclusively for their own cancer.

Cancer is increasingly understood as an ecosystem, shaped by interactions between tumour cells, the immune system and the surrounding microenvironment. Immunotherapy works by altering that ecosystem, changing the ‘immune soil’ in which cancer grows. Personalised mRNA vaccines may be the next step: directing the immune response with even greater precision.
Following on, from immunotherapy

The current moment resembles the early days of immunotherapy. When checkpoint inhibitors first showed unprecedented benefit in melanoma, many assumed the impact would stay confined to a handful of cancers. Instead, immunotherapy became a universal oncology platform, transforming treatment across tumour types.

mRNA vaccines appear to be following a similar trajectory. Melanoma, with its high mutational burden and strong response to immune-based approaches, served as the ideal proving ground. Researchers are now studying personalised vaccine strategies in lung, gastrointestinal, genitourinary and several other cancers.

If these trials succeed, the implications could be enormous. Future treatment may routinely involve genomic sequencing after surgery, followed by the rapid design of a patient-specific vaccine given alongside immunotherapy — aiming to wipe out microscopic residual disease before it can return. This is the essence of personalised cancer treatment.
The path ahead

Further automation of neoantigen discovery through AI and manufacturing techniques refined during the COVID-19 pandemic have demonstrated the capacity to generate sophisticated mRNA therapies at scale. Together, these advances are moving personalised cancer vaccines from concept to clinical reality.
Oncology has moved from supportive care to chemotherapy, from chemotherapy to targeted therapy, and from targeted therapy to immunotherapy. Personalised mRNA vaccines may mark the next great leap.

The battle against cancer is far from over. But history offers an encouraging precedent: melanoma announced the arrival of immunotherapy, and it may now be announcing the arrival of another revolutionary treatment platform. If the promise of mRNA tumour vaccines holds across multiple cancers, future generations may look back on this moment as the beginning of the next major transformation in cancer care.
(Dr. Harish P. is a consultant in medical oncology at Manipal Hospital Yelahanka. harish.p1@manipalhospitals.com)

title: Sandhya Devanathan exits Meta after a decade; to join OpenAI as VP South East Asia, Australia

content.value: Meta's Vice President and Head for India and South East Asia, Sandhya Devanathan, is leaving the social media giant after more than a decade and is all set to join OpenAI as Vice President for South East Asia and Australia.

In this newly-created role, Devanathan will be OpenAI’s most senior leader in South East Asia and Australia, with responsibility for its performance across consumer growth, enterprise adoption and partnerships, regulatory engagement and operations.

The Meta veteran penned an emotional post on LinkedIn, announcing her departure from the social media giant and said she is looking forward to her "next exciting chapter". She, however, did not divulge her next move.

OpenAI confirmed that Devanathan will join as Vice President for Southeast Asia and Australia. She will be based in Singapore and report to Kiran Mani, OpenAI's Managing Director for Asia Pacific, the ChatGPT-maker confirmed.
Devanathan's joining date at OpenAI could not be immediately ascertained.
Notably, the appointment comes as OpenAI expands its presence across Asia Pacific amid growing adoption of its AI tools among consumers, enterprises and developers.

Over the past two years, OpenAI has opened local offices in Singapore, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney and Delhi, and expanded its regional leadership team with the recent appointment of Kiran Mani as Managing Director for APAC.

In June this year, the Sam Altman-led company announced the appointment of Prabhjeet Singh as Managing Director for India, among its top-priority markets and one where the company has been stepping up investments and expanding its footprint.

In fact, OpenAI has been moving its India strategy to top gear through partnerships with enterprises and developers, while strengthening engagement with policymakers. The company opened its first office in New Delhi in November 2025.
Altman himself has repeatedly described India as one of OpenAI's key markets and has praised the country's rapid AI uptake and commitment to investing across the tech stack.

Devanathan brings more than 25 years of experience across the technology and financial services sectors. She joined Meta in 2016 and held several leadership roles across the region, including leading its Asia Pacific gaming business and helping expand the company's presence in Singapore and Vietnam.
In the LinkedIn post, Devanathan described the decision to leave after more than a decade as "bittersweet" and said she would take a short break before beginning her "next exciting chapter".

Looking back at her tenure, she highlighted Meta's work with businesses, startups and creators across the region, including government citizen services on WhatsApp in India and helping small businesses establish storefronts on its apps in Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand.
"I joined Meta when we had just about 300 employees in Singapore," she recounted and reflected on how the landscape looked "so different" in 2016, with everyone talking about digital transformation.

"And we were right in the midst of it - helping startups, companies, creators and the ecosystem grow across the region while delivering great experiences for hundreds of millions of our users," she wrote.
Devanathan said she was "incredibly proud" of what her teams had built and thanked colleagues, businesses, ecosystem partners, non-profits and creators she had worked with during her time at Meta.

"Over the years, I’ve had the privilege of working across sectors like ecommerce and gaming in APAC, and leading talented teams across India and Southeast Asia. Throughout this journey, I’ve been fueled by the belief that our work brings meaningful connections to people and businesses worldwide," she further said.
Describing the day as "emotional", Devanathan said the teams she worked with were nothing short of exceptional and made this an incredible ride.

"I shared with my teams today that I am extraordinarily proud of how they've shown up every day, doing the best work they can in an industry that is rapidly evolving. I’m proud of the work we’ve done together - be the millions of people using government citizen services on WA (WhatsApp) in India or the millions of small businesses in Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand who opened their storefronts on our apps or helping startups become unicorns in Singapore, Malaysia and Philippines...the stories are many and I am incredibly proud of everything we’ve built together," she said.

title: Why the monsoon is one of the best times to explore India’s forests

content.value: The first signs of the monsoon are not always found in the sky. They may hang from the tapered end of a half-built baya-weaver’s nest, pulse from the blue vocal sacs of a breeding Indian bullfrog or appear overnight on a rain-darkened log.

The monsoon is not a biological starting gun, nor does every creature suddenly emerge with the first shower. Species respond differently to rainfall, temperature, humidity, food availability and changes in water levels. Some begin breeding, others change plumage, call more frequently or gather around seasonal food sources. Fungi that have persisted out of sight within soil or wood may produce visible mushrooms. Animals present throughout the year can become easier to observe because the season changes their behaviour.

title: Climate change is denuding Indian languages

content.value: There is a word in the Nicobarese language that translates into “a calm sea”. Tamra, today, is however only used by the islands’ elders and is at risk of fading away from their language forever.
As seasons go awry, species go extinct, and livelihoods change, words and phrases in several Indian languages are at the precipice of vanishing altogether, according to a new analysis.
From Marwari to Maithili, Tulu to Tamil, there are words — evocative, nuanced, onomatopoeic, with much exactitude — that describe everything from wild birds and morphing skies to livelihoods.

Oos ki nami means “dew moisture” in Bundeli in Madhya Pradesh. Raunkha refers to the festive atmosphere during collective sowing in Haryanvi. There is even a term to describe “twilight on wetlands” in Assamese, beelor godhuli. In Khasi, spoken in Meghalaya, shyllien connotes the “pre-monsoon fragrance”.

The new analysis, by the ‘Losing Words, Losing Worlds’ initiative, found that as the environment changes, nearly a hundred words and terms tied to seasons, species, soils, tides, and the skies appear to be fading or have already been lost from 22 languages across India. The findings were drew on a survey of around 100 people conducted by Marisha Karwa, a journalist-turned-climate communicator, and 101Reporters, a pan-India network of grassroots reporters, during October and November 2025.

As weather patterns change, so does the way dew forms and the mahua flowers, and with that “entire systems of knowledge and ways of relating to the natural world” stand to be wiped out, the report read. “That which we cannot name, we cannot understand — or manage, or act on.”

The survey also revealed that everyone from farmers and fishers to forest-dependent people in 15 States believed that with the loss of vernacular words, ecological literacy is vanishing. The mainstream climate narrative in India is largely in English or has been transliterated from the English into local languages, Ms. Karwa said, adding that climate communication excludes a majority of India’s multilingual people.
Monsoon in a tree bark

Terms such as patar bhonra, which denotes the seasonal movement of wild bees in a local language in Chhattisgarh, capture “connections between atmospheric signals, biological behaviour, agricultural and fishing timing and cultural practice,” Ms. Karwa wrote.

Hyper-local and multi-sensory terms or words also integrate biological, atmospheric, and social signals. In Odisha's forests, an elderly person told the reporters that they “could smell the monsoon arrival from tree bark”.

In Bihar, terms linked to the monsoon, such as jeth ke baadal – May clouds, signalling the sowing of rice sowing – “have been abandoned as their ecological referents have disappeared, including the bird species that served as monsoon indicators”.

Likewise, in Maharashtra, the shenvti hawa, the southern breeze that signals pomfret movement, “has become so unreliable that elderly fishermen have abandoned sea-based forecasting altogether, replacing it with phone messages from fish traders in Mumbai,” per the report.

Meanwhile, language is also adapting to climate change. Farmers, fishers, and forest communities described newly emerging environmental phenomena, like bina nishaan to connote unannounced rains; garmi ke baad seedha sardi, an abrupt heat to cold alluding to a vanished autumn; and bhaga jhadu, vanished rains. Conversely, the report noted that in Tamil Nadu, the purattasi mazhai – the September–October rains, critical for samba paddy and crab larval cycles – has failed in four of the last six years.

The vividly illustrated book The Lost Words by Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris, first published in 2017, is an ode to lost words in Britain. As its authors wrote: “Once upon a time, words began to vanish from the language of children… the words were those that children used to name the natural world around them.”

The authors had expressed hope that the book would conjure “lost words” such as “adder”, that conveyed “the echo of a snake or self-escape or a left-behind ghost; and “ivy,” which the authors describe as “a real high flyer/ Via a bark and stone I scale tree and spire/ You can call me ground cover; I say sky-wire.”
‘Interconnected challenge’

Mahesh Rangarajan, professor of environmental studies and history at Ashoka University, told The Hindu that while the new report is “preliminary”, it is still a “landmark” that reflects a complex set of responses to increasingly unpredictable weather patterns. Cultivators must now search for a term for the late onset of winter, or summer extremes, or changes in temperature that affect water bodies.
“Activities like sowing and harvesting, gathering flowers and cutting grass, are all changing and in unexpected ways,” he said, adding that the survey now shows the “way forward”.

Today, almost everyone is losing words: monsoon droughts, cloudbursts in flatlands and ‘false rains’ are experienced but “neither local languages nor English have precise words for them,” the survey reported noted.
Ms. Karwa said she hopes to collaborate with institutions, the government, and partners on the ground, along with committed funders keen to address climate as “an interconnected challenge”.
“The survey must be an annual affair at a deeper, pan-India scale, document native language environmental lexicon from people, folk tales, media and archival research,” she told The Hindu.

title: SRMIST, The Hindu to organise webinar on technology integration in medical profession

content.value: SRM Institute of Science and Technology, in association with The Hindu, will organise a webinar on ‘The Future Doctor: Balancing Clinical Experience with Technology’ as part of the Future Career Conversations series on Saturday (August 29, 2026).

The session will explore how the medical profession is evolving with the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence, robotics, and digital health, and how future doctors can adapt to these advancements while continuing to uphold clinical excellence and patient-centred care. The discussion will examine how medical professionals can effectively leverage tools such as AI-assisted diagnostics to treatment planning, telemedicine, and digital consultations, while addressing the ethical challenges associated with technology-driven healthcare.

The panel will also deliberate on the evolving debate between specialisation and general practice, as well as the need for reforms in medical education while offering insights into the skills, adaptability, and multi-disciplinary approach required to succeed in the medicine of tomorrow.

The panel will consist of R. Jayanthi, Dean, SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre; Vivek Narayanan, Dean (Dental), SRM Kattankulathur Dental College and Hospital; Ritubhan Gautam, Head – Global Health, Deep Tek.ai, and K. Ganapathy, Honorary Distinguished Professor, IIM Jammu, Distinguished Professor, Tamil Nadu Dr. MGR Medical University, and Emeritus Professor, National Academy of Medical Sciences.
The session will be held at 4.30 p.m. on August 29 and will be moderated by Geetha Srimathi S., Senior Reporter, The Hindu. Registration can be made on https://newsth.live/THSRMFE.
