Author -- Jess Fiedorowicz, head and chief of mental health at The Ottawa Hospital and professor at the University of Ottawa, said medications for the mental health disorder can come with varied side effects.
"A tool that incorporates patient preferences and promotes shared decision-making can help find treatments that are a better fit," Dr Fiedorowicz said.
Results from the review have also been used to update guidelines, including those of the International Society for Bipolar Disorders (ISBD), for the management of bipolar disorder.

The study is the first living umbrella review to include all treatment strategies assessed across any age group and phase of bipolar disorder from the largest and best meta-analyses available to date, the researchers said.
The review can be adapted rapidly as new evidence emerges and serves as a foundation for continuously improving care, which is why it is called a "living review", they said.
"Living reviews like this one are game-changers when it comes to updating international treatment guidelines," author Samuele Cortese, research professor at the University of Southampton, UK, said.
"Rather than taking a week to get an answer, experts can consult the website in real time during meetings for the latest evidence," Dr Cortese said.
The authors wrote, "The EBI-BD tool can help clinicians make evidence-based, personalised treatment decisions for bipolar disorder."

title: Definium says LSD-based pill reduces anxiety in late-stage study

content.value: Definium Therapeutics said on Wednesday its LSD-based ​experimental pill significantly reduced anxiety symptoms in a late-stage study, meeting ‌the trial's main goal and sending the drug developer's ​shares up more than 20% premarket.
The 214-patient trial ⁠tested a single 100-microgram dose of DT120, a fast-dissolving tablet of lysergide, the chemical name for LSD, in adults with generalized anxiety disorder, ‌or GAD.
Patients on the drug had an 11.6-point drop on a standard anxiety rating scale at ‌week 12, compared with a 6.2-point drop for those ‌on ⁠a placebo.
The placebo-adjusted difference of 5.4 points ⁠was statistically significant and clinically meaningful, the company said.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Brian Abrahams said the data exceeded Wall Street's expectations and the efficacy seen with other ​therapies for the disease.
The ‌benefit emerged as early as two days after dosing and lasted throughout the 12-week study.
The drug belongs to a class of compounds known as psychedelic medicines.
Regulatory and investor ‌enthusiasm for psychedelic-based therapies has helped Definium shares more ​than triple so far this year.

In April, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing ⁠federal agencies to speed up access to research and treatments based on psychedelic drugs for serious mental health conditions.

GAD is characterised ‌by persistent and excessive worry that can interfere with daily life. It affects about 26 million U.S. adults and is commonly treated with antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicines and psychotherapy.
No new drug has been approved for the condition in nearly two decades, according to Brian Barnett, a Cleveland Clinic psychiatrist who ‌worked on the study.

Unlike most anxiety medicines, which are typically taken regularly, ​DT120 is designed to be administered as a single dose during a monitored dosing session. It ⁠works by acting on brain receptors involved in mood and perception.
Most ⁠side effects were mild to moderate and temporary,occurring mainly on the day of dosing, with no ‌increase in suicidal thoughts.
The trial is Definium's second late-stage success for DT120, following a positive readout in a depression ​study in June.

title: Women with endometriosis at 46% higher risk of diabetes, study suggests

content.value: A new study has found that women with endometriosis may have a 46% higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes, compared to women without the condition in which the tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside.
Endometriosis causes severe pelvic pain, painful periods and fertility challenges.

Researchers, led by those at the George Mason University in the US, followed nearly three million women in the Utah Population Database between 1996 and 2021, including nearly 100,000 diagnosed with endometriosis.
"Endometriosis was associated with a 46% higher risk of type 2 diabetes compared with no endometriosis," the authors wrote.
The team found that diabetes risk varied across different forms of endometriosis, suggesting the condition may have broader long-term health implications than previously recognised.

Chronic inflammation in endometriosis could be contributing to the development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, even as more studies will be important for clarifying biological pathways underlying the observations, according to findings published in the journal Diabetologia.

"Previous studies largely evaluated endometriosis as a single condition and generally reported little or no overall association with type 2 diabetes," lead author Fuzak Nunziato, from George Mason University's college of public health, said.
"Our findings add to a growing understanding that endometriosis may affect more than reproductive health alone," Nunziato said.

The association between endometriosis and a higher diabetes risk was strongest among premenopausal women and women without obesity -- groups not traditionally considered at the highest risk for type 2 diabetes, the researchers said.

Further, certain forms of endometriosis were found to have a much stronger association with diabetes, compared to others. The link was greatest among women with extra-pelvic endometriosis, meaning the disease is found outside the pelvis.

The findings, if confirmed by future research, could help clinicians identify women with endometriosis potentially at a higher risk for type 2 diabetes and who could benefit from an earlier screening or prevention efforts, the researchers said.

title: Making transparency the foundation of trust in medicine

content.value: India marked Doctors’ Day on July 1, but the occasion demands that we continue to look beyond well-deserved expressions of gratitude and reflect on the structural foundations that sustain public confidence in health care. Trust in medicine is frequently thought of as a sacred, isolated bond between patient and doctor. In reality, that trust is forged much earlier — within the institutions that regulate care, the systems that deliver it, and the transparency that connects them.

The limitations of this system are readily observable. This writer tried the simple exercise of verifying a doctor’s credentials on the Tamil Nadu Medical Council (TNMC) website. What should have been a straightforward search turned out to be unexpectedly challenging. The system required specific details, such as the doctor’s exact registration number, which are not easily available to the public. Whether something obvious was missed or the website was simply not designed with the public — or even a colleague concerned — in mind, the experience pointed to a larger question: how much does institutional transparency shape public faith in medicine?
How institutions build trust

In many western countries, public trust is maintained through highly accessible regulatory frameworks. For example, the United Kingdom’s General Medical Council hosts a publicly searchable register where anyone can quickly verify a doctor’s qualifications, registration status, and any history of regulatory restrictions. Similarly, the provincial Colleges of Physicians and Surgeons in Canada require minimal identifying information to view a physician’s professional profile. These organisations explicitly signal that professional standards are being ensured through peer review, continuing education, and clear processes for handling complaints. This transparency does more than just share data. It reassures people that medical practice is open to independent scrutiny, creating a safe environment where individual doctor–patient relationships can thrive.

India’s clinical landscape is evolving admirably, with a workforce that is known for its excellent clinical acumen despite working under considerable constraints. While the National Medical Commission has taken steps to improve medical education and professional standards in recent years, public-facing regulatory transparency remains uneven. State Medical Councils, including the TNMC, hold digital registers, but the ease with which a regular patient can navigate them varies. As India continues its digital transformation, making these regulatory portals genuinely user-friendly is a low-hanging opportunity to reinforce public trust at its foundation.
Beyond individual blame

Between regulatory bodies and individual consultation rooms lie the systems of care — hospitals, clinics, and their organisational processes. These daily workflows heavily influence patient satisfaction, shaping perceptions of fairness long before a clinical outcome is reached.

System transparency requires clear communication about medical costs, operational processes, and pathways to register a grievance. Crucially, it also means having an internal culture of medical auditing. Rather than placing blame entirely on individuals when things go wrong, modern health-care systems — following World Health Organization guidelines — are moving toward analysing the systemic design flaws that allow mistakes to occur in the first place.

This approach requires a formal culture of “Open Disclosure”. In advanced medical jurisdictions, being honest when things go wrong is a professional requirement, not an option. It involves a structured, honest conversation with the patient or their family, acknowledging the incident, explaining how it occurred, and detailing the steps being taken to prevent recurrence.

Formalising open disclosure in India, right from the ground level of clinical care, would be transformative. When hospitals support their doctors to be transparent about clinical uncertainties or complications, they reduce the emotional burden on the practitioner and prevent potential friction with families. A lack of clear information breeds suspicion. When processes are opaque or difficult to navigate, public dissatisfaction builds rapidly — even if the actual clinical care delivered was appropriate. Much of this friction arises not from malice, but from a mismatch between patients’ expectations and their actual experience.

India has seen a worrying rise in violence against health-care workers. The Indian Medical Association reports that over 75% of doctors have faced some form of workplace violence. While the root causes are multifactorial, deep-seated systemic mistrust is often the spark that escalates conflict. In these high-stress settings, transparency is a protective shield, not an administrative burden. A system that is completely honest about limitations and constraints within clinical care makes it less likely that individual frontline doctors will become the sole targets of a family’s anger and resentment.

At the ground level, the doctor–patient relationship remains the ultimate test of the profession — a space where high-stakes decisions are made in moments of profound human vulnerability. Here, transparency transitions from policy into a purely human interaction.

Modern patients increasingly expect clarity regarding who is treating them and why specific clinical decisions are chosen. This means explaining a diagnosis in plain language, detailing the rationale behind investigations, discussing therapeutic alternatives, and being transparent about costs and complications. Providing proactive, periodic updates on a patient’s progress — or lack thereof — is often the single most effective way to ease a family’s distress.

This shift toward shared decision-making recognises that transparency in treatment is about relationships, not just data. However, if transparency is to be a core part of modern medicine, it must be integrated into medical training. This cannot be taught in a lecture hall alone; it must be actively modelled by senior doctors during everyday clinical practice and teaching. By embedding this culture of communication early, we prepare the next generation of physicians to navigate increasing public expectations.

In my experience, the majority of conflicts in health care do not arise from the medical decisions themselves, but from how those decisions were communicated and understood. When patients feel genuinely heard and informed, the bond is strengthened. When communication is poor, even appropriate care may be perceived as inadequate.
A final reflection

Doctors need safe, respectful, and dignified environments in which to work. Patients require reassurance that the care they receive is both ethical and competent. These are not competing demands; they are mutually reinforcing traits.

Trust in medicine is built collectively by what our institutions make visible, how our clinical care systems function, and how doctors and patients talk to one another. When transparency runs through all three layers, it stops being an abstract ethical principle and becomes part of everyday practice.

Doctors’ Day has passed, words of appreciation are important. But the days after also invite a structural look at our systems. At a time when the medical profession is practising under unprecedented strain, enhancing transparency in regulatory frameworks, clinical corridors, and individual consultation rooms is the most meaningful way to protect the integrity of the profession. Trust is not an entitlement to be claimed; it is a professional pact that must be continuously renewed through transparency.

Dr. Vincent Arockiasamy, FRCPC, is Clinical Assistant Professor of Paediatrics, and former Director, Student Assessment, Undergraduate Medical Education, University of British Columbia, Canada, and is also involved in medical professional regulation

title: PfA@30: Taking the animal kingdom under their wing

content.value: Prosthetics for peacocks, electro acupuncture for snakes and implants for the de-feathered may seem far-fetched, but are all in a day’s work for the good folk at Bengaluru’s People For Animals Wildlife Hospital (PfA).

PfA has been working behind the scenes in Bengaluru for the past 30 years, quietly rescuing, rehabilitating and releasing, furred and feathered friends in need of medical attention. Col. Navaz Shariff (retd), PfA’s general manager and chief wildlife veterinarian, talks about their rescue of a seven-month-old leopard cub hit by a bike.

With experience comes practical knowledge that may not always be found in the guidebooks. Though the cub sustained a head injury, it was not fatal and he soon recovered under PfA’s care. Protocol dictates rescued leopard cubs have to be handed to the Bannerghatta Biological Park.

“But, we had seen the mother and her cubs in that area before so we tried to reunite them. After consulting with the chief wildlife warden we recorded the cub’s sounds and spread his urine in areas frequented by the mother. Though we played the cub’s soundbites over loudspeaker in those areas, she didn’t show up. But since the cub was healthy we released him into the forest and soon found out he was back with his mother and sibling.”

Over the years, PfA has developed an aquatic rescue team with a motorised boat; with a four-wheeler equipped with medical supplies and a vet assigned to duty daily, the team is ready to take up rescue operations on all manner of terrain.
Another feather in their hat

Navaz patiently explains the science of imping or feather implantation. “Birds caught in manja or plastic webbing flap their wings frantically, making their situation worse and they lose a lot of feathers in the struggle.”

“We put up boards in Kannada and English around Vijaynagar with boxes attached below, telling passersby to deposit feathers they find. Volunteers bring these to us on a weekly basis; we vacuum clean and store them. Today, we have the feathers of around 32 species including common ones such as peahens and peacocks, owls and parakeets,” he says, adding this might be the only feather bank in the country.
“We make a receptacle for the donor feather and using surgical glue we implant it. Each operation takes about two to three hours, and is quite painstaking,” he continues.

The team surgically implants the primary, secondary, and tail feathers. After a series of test flights, the bird can be released into the wild. Over time, as the bird regains its strength and new, healthy feathers appear, the implanted ones shed naturally.

Paralysis is another issue plaguing a few birds, especially peacocks. “They perch on live wires and are severely shocked by high voltage currents, losing the use of their limbs as a result,” says Navaz. “We used 3D printing to create prosthetic limbs and fit them on these birds. They adapt to them in a few weeks.”

Sadly, these birds cannot be released into the wild but have enough mobility to fend for themselves. Navaz who believes this procedure too, could be the first of its kind in India, says these birds need to be adopted as they require regular monitoring. The team used the same technique to fit a pony in Mysore with a prosthetic limb.

News of the success of this procedure has spread and Navaz says a lady from Romania has requested a prostheticlimb for her calf. “She has sent us the dimensions and we are creating an adjustable limb, keeping in mind future growth of the animal.”
Unfortunately, though the team sees a lot of macaques suffering from gangrene and the loss of limbs due to electrocution, the process has been unsuccessful in monkeys.
Slither hither

PfA has rescued as many as 8,000 spectacled cobras that were displaced due to rampant urbanisation. Needless to say, the ancedotes abound. Navaz talks about a snake that was badly injured when caught in a JCB. “Its injuries were extensive and needed surgery to the aesophagus and trachea. We called him Scarface.”

Caring for Scarface and others of his kind got the team thinking about their survival once they were back in the wild. “I have written to the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests for permission to attach transmitters to these snakes so we can follow up on their healing. We are waiting to hear back from them.”

Snakes usually suffer from broken spines when they are attacked and these take around 45 days or more to set, says Navaz. Conventional methods to restore sensation included UV lights and hot water baths. “Now, to speed  up the process. we use advanced physio laser and electro acupuncture.”
Navaz was encouraged to use electro acupuncture after seeing favourable results in dogs showing 35-40% speedy recovery; today PfA extensively uses this techinique to treat snakes and monkeys.
Action satisfaction

PfA conducts awareness programs and workshops in schools and residential associations to bring about ecological awareness and educate people on how to deal with snakes and other wildlife that may stray into their homes.

As a non-profit, PfA relies on contributions and over the years has built a state-of-the-art operation theatre complete with ultrasonograph, digital X-ray and ventilator. The staff comprises around 30 people with eight rescuers, two rescue coordinators and four veterinarian rehabilitators, among others.
Since the planet never sleeps, the team works long hours, “starting at about 8.30 in the morning and going up to 11.30 at the night on most days.”

PfA has been recognised by the Central Zoo Authority of India as one of the rare conservation centres in the country; they also won the Best Wildlife Conservation Organization at the Wildlife Tourism Conclave and Awards India in 2024, and Green NGO of the Year by Olive Crown Awards in 2022, among a host of other accolades.
More details on www.pfawildlifehospital.org

title: Instagram changes its wordmark logo after over a decade

content.value: Meta introduced a refreshed Instagram wordmark logo on Thursday (August 13, 2026)

The change was announced by Instagram head Adam Mosseri on both Instagram and Threads, where he described the new logo as “sharper and more modern” while still referencing the original and maintaining simplicity, as per TechCrunch.
The new wordmark keeps the familiar script style, with redrawn letterforms.
The last time Instagram updated its design was 2016, when the company moved away from the classic brown camera with the rainbow stripe to the colorful pink gradient that remains the icon today.

“The wordmark at the top of the app hasn’t changed in 10 years, so it was time for a refresh,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri wrote in a post on the platform. “Cleaner and more modern, with references to the original and the simplicity and craft that’s always made it Instagram.”
Some liked it, while many found it disappointing.
Many joked that the logo now looks like it reads “Instagzam” because of the shape of the font used for the “r.”

title: Meta AI glasses spark backlash across borders

content.value: Meta’s AI glasses are sparking backlash both in India and overseas, months after their release, with people complaining of privacy violations and harassment.

The initial rollout of the AI glasses, made in collaboration with companies such as Ray-Ban, involved full-page newspaper ads in India, video commercials, and partnerships with social media influencers. In the U.S., for example, socialite Kylie Jenner teamed up with the company to promote the Meta Starfire Kylie Edition.
However, celebrities and public figures have faced flak in recent weeks over their collaboration with Meta.

Users who visit the official Ray-Ban | Meta account on Instagram can also see dozens of angry or disgusted comments left by users who criticise the technology or slam the influencers who endorse these smart glasses.

Many who are against Meta’s AI smart glasses have taken to calling them “pervert glasses” or “creep glasses,” in an effort to negatively rebrand them. Others accuse the AI glasses wearers of being sexual perverts secretly recording others, in an effort to shame wearers into leaving the devices at home.

One anti-Meta ad campaign in London that went viral online featured a standing poster with the disgraced financier and late child sex abuser Jeffrey Epstein wearing the smart glasses, while the slogan stated: “Glasses for people who don’t do consent”.
Community organisation

Community-led and grassroots efforts in India to trigger legislation against AI glasses and smart glasses are still in the rudimentary stages and lack widespread support. Standardised rules governing the use of Meta AI glasses near sensitive areas, military sites, or in medical or childcare settings have not yet been confirmed and enforced.
This has led to confusion and distress for people who are unsure about whether they can get the authorities involved when they see someone recording them with their glasses.
There are also very few expert guidelines surrounding the use of Meta AI glasses by children, though some schools have started banning the devices due to privacy, safety, and cheating concerns.
Online and offline normalisation

Instagram now adds a label to many of the posts of users who film and upload content with their Meta Ray-Ban AI glasses. This kind of content ranges from hands-free cooking videos and travel vlogs to time-consuming pranks and even sexual harassment, by approaching women to flirt with them.

One seemingly innocent “joy-baiting” prank involves the Meta AI glasses-wearer approaching a person or a group of people without warning and then threatening to report them to the police — for looking too good. The prankster then records the relieved laughter of the people around. Compilations of these videos are easy to find on Instagram, but it is not clear whether the subject of the prank consented to being filmed and having their clip uploaded online. In the process of these “feel good” pranks, the glasses-wearer also records family members, including minor children, to upload them online for views.
Other pranksters try to trick retail employees or tease customer service agents in order to film their candid reactions at their workplace and make content out of their surprised expressions.

One such Instagram Reel in India recorded with the Meta Ray-Ban AI glasses, for example, showed a prankster asking an at-home massage therapist to rub his body with food ingredients. The massage therapist’s employer’s name is clearly visible. The reluctant therapist is filmed being pressured by the smart glasses-wearer, even as he expresses his discomfort. The influencer had thousands of followers.

Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed that Meta would take down video content that involved harassing people or recording them without their knowledge. However, this policy is still not widely enforced.
Meta’s defence

The social media giant has pointed to its recent efforts to make people more aware of when smart glasses-wearers are recording them, using a small shutter sound for the wearer as well as an upgraded blinking LED that indicates camera use.

“It’s there so people around you know when you are taking a photo or video you could save to your gallery and share with others. While mobile phones and action cameras don’t have this on their cameras, ours have had them since day one,” noted Meta in a blog post last month.
If the white light is blocked by the user, it is designed to disable the active camera. This feature begins with Meta’s second generation of glasses.
“We also take legal action against people or businesses that sell services designed for tampering with the capture LED — both on and off our own platforms,” the company added.

title: Meta says it has taken down 756,000 Australian teen accounts as ban enforcement looms

content.value: Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said on Thursday it had taken ​down more than 750,000 accounts it suspected were held by Australians ⁠aged under 16 since a world-first ban on teen accounts, and promised more action in the face of possible regulatory intervention.

The company said it had deactivated 462,000 suspect Instagram accounts and 294,000 ‌suspect Facebook accounts from just before the Australian social media ban went live in December to June, up from 331,000 Instagram accounts and 173,000 Facebook ‌accounts it said it had removed by January. The world’s largest social media ‌company ⁠has said it wants to comply with a law it and ⁠other platforms have vocally opposed, just as Australia’s internet regulator considers an enforcement lawsuit against platforms, including some that Meta owns, that it says have failed to take sufficient steps to comply with the law.

No other ​platforms have released compliance data ‌that matches the date range given by Meta, but Australian government figures and multiple independent studies have shown more than eight in 10 under-16s were still on social media in the ban’s first three months.

The Australian government proposed the landmark law, ‌which came into force on December 10, on concerns about social media’s impact ​on the physical and mental health of children and young teens. With other countries around the world considering similar age-restrictions, Australia has accused the ⁠platforms of intentionally setting the ban up to fail, and has introduced a law to double the maximum penalty for non-compliance to A$99 million ($69.75 million) and give the regulator ‌greater document discovery powers.

Representatives of Meta, TikTok, YouTube owner Google and Snap’s Snapchat are scheduled to give evidence in a parliamentary inquiry about the changes on Friday, as are regulatory and government officials.
“Enforcement is ongoing, and these numbers will continue to grow,” Meta said in a statement.
“We share the Australian Government’s goal of ensuring young people have safe, age-appropriate experiences online, and we are meeting our obligations under ‌the law,” the company added.

A 2025 Australian trial of age assurance technology found products on the ​market could effectively support a ban. Most large platforms, including Meta’s, rolled out photo-based age estimation software, although they say they typically first subject users ⁠to age inference, or assuming a person’s age based on their online activity.

Meta said ⁠it was using AI to analyse user profiles for “contextual clues that an account may belong to someone under 16, such as birthday celebrations or ‌mentions of school grades” and to analyse reports about suspected underage accounts. The company added that it had removed the option for a person to make more ​attempts to set up an account if their previous account was deleted.

title: Faith healing poses challenge to authorities as outbreak kills seven tribal children in Madhya Pradesh

content.value: Seven children have lost their lives and about 100 have fallen ill in some villages of the tribal community in Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district in about 45 days, due to an outbreak of monsoon related diseases while suffering skin infections, officials said, even as they flagged lack of accessibility in remote areas and the community’s reliance on ritualistic healing.

According to officials, about five villages of the Baiga tribe have reported 100 cases of malaria, typhoid, viral infections and skin infections among children aged between one and 13 years since June, showing symptoms like high fever, stomach infection, and rashes and spots on their bodies.
The villages are Bondari, Adori, Machhurda, Korka and Kundekasa in Baihar tehsil, about 85 kilometres from the district hospital.
Additional Collector, Balaghat, Abhishek Saraf told The Hindu that 24 children are currently under treatment at district and civil hospitals while 76 children have recovered so far.

Officials say that the administration came to know about the problem after three children had already died, which prompted authorities to launch measures in the remotely located villages. The first death occurred on June 26 in Bondari village.

The authorities have also collected blood samples from patients and sent them to ICMR-National Institute of Research in Bacterial Infections, Kolkata, and the ICMR-National Institute of Virology, Pune, to check for the exact cause of the outbreak. Whereas, a team from Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose Medical College, Jabalpur, is also investigating the situation.

Mr. Saraf said that special health camps have been setup in the villages to provide early treatment to children and door-to-door screenings are being conducted to check for new cases by deploying ASHA and ANM workers, and special medical teams for diseases like malaria and typhoid.
“We have deployed a team led by a medical officer for each village who will assess the situation and decide if a patient needs to be admitted to the civil or district hospital,” he said.
Mr. Saraf also said that officials have also been deployed to survey houses to collect water samples and assess hygiene conditions.
“They have also been directed to clean water bodies and ensure clean water in the affected areas,” he said.
The official, however, highlighted the challenges in tracing the affected children and as well as in convincing their families to accept the treatment.

The Baiga community, a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG), is known for its ancient practices and rituals, with members of the group often opting for faith healing over modern medicine. Largely located in forest covered districts of eastern and southern Madhya Pradesh, lack of accessibility and awareness also keeps a large section of the community still cut off from the administration and modern infrastructure. The five villages have houses scattered on different hills in dense forest.

“While remote terrain was one problem in reaching the villages and tracing patients, convincing their families to admit their kids to hospitals was more difficult. Many families officials visited refused medicines too. But we have now connected with their spiritual leaders and are convincing the people with their help,” Mr. Saraf said, adding that the situation was now improving.
Balaghat Chief Medical and Health Officer (CMHO) Paresh Uplap said that various families have refused to go to hospital despite senior officials trying to convince them.

“There are about 15 houses atop a hill in Bondari village. The houses are cut off from the rest of the area and two children from a family died there about two weeks ago. The families did not inform anybody or seek help when they fell ill at night,” he said.

“We have deployed ambulances in some villages so that kids can be immediately shifted to the district hospital if needed. People from the community often reach out to faith healers when someone falls sick and think that they will go to hospital once the condition is a little better,” he said.
He said that multiple meetings have also been held with village heads and local people to convince them to take treatment.
Dr. Uplap also said that ANM and ASHA workers are also conducting surveys in all the hostels and schools in the area.
However, Amaar Singh Dhurve, a resident of Bondari who lost his two children, said that he had approached both doctors and faith healers in the nearby areas when his children fell ill.

“We don’t know any medication so I went everywhere but no vaidya or doctor ever comes here. We have gotten tired of calling. Even the villagers don’t come up here [on the hill]. At one point, all six members of my family were sick but there was nobody to take care of us. So, what could I do. I called faith healers and did jhhaad phoonk [ritualistic healing practice] myself too.
A government official also said that practices of animal sacrifice have also been reported from a village, conducted to get rid of the outbreak.

title: Doctors’ body opposes Speaker’s remarks, seeks NEET exemption and medical reforms

content.value: The Doctors’ Association for Social Equality on Wednesday criticised Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly Speaker J.C.D. Prabhakar’s reported anti-abortion remarks, saying they undermined women’s reproductive rights and urging him to refrain from making such statements.

At a press meet in Chennai, the association opposed the State government’s resolution seeking the nationwide abolition of NEET, saying Tamil Nadu should instead seek a permanent exemption for undergraduate, postgraduate and super-speciality medical seats under its control. It said abolition could benefit private medical colleges and deemed universities and increase the burden on poor and middle-class students.
The association disputed the Health Minister’s arguments on NEET and rural healthcare, noting that over 1,000 NEET-qualified doctors were serving in rural Primary Health Centres.

It said NEET was not the sole reason for the lower representation of disadvantaged students in medical education and sought an expert committee to examine the issue. It also demanded an increase in educational assistance for students admitted under the 7.5% government-school quota.

Other demands included implementing the children’s gold-ring scheme through the Revenue or Social Welfare Department instead of doctors; dropping attempts to appoint IAS officers to senior medical posts; retaining the Deputy Director of Tuberculosis post; implementing reservation in contractual appointments; and withdrawing what it termed retaliatory action against Dr. Perumal Pillai, leader of the Government Doctors’ Legal Battle Committee.

title: What happens when AI begins to design viruses?

content.value: The computer did not create a virus. It did not touch a test tube or handle a living cell. What it did may ultimately be more consequential: it helped decide what the virus’s genome should be.

Researchers at Stanford University and the Arc Institute used artificial intelligence (AI) to design complete genomes of bacteriophages - viruses that infect bacteria. Of 285 AI-generated designs physically synthesised and tested in the laboratory, 16 produced functioning phages. Some were able to overcome bacterial resistance that defeated the original virus. The phrase ‘AI-created viruses’ therefore needs qualification. Humans have been synthesising viral genomes and deliberately modifying viruses for decades. What is new, is not the physical manufacture of a virus. AI has entered the design stage of biology. For medicine, that creates remarkable opportunities. For biosecurity, it raises equally important questions.

title: Why bats do not fall ill from the viruses they spread

content.value: (This article forms a part of the Science for All newsletter that takes the jargon out of science and puts the fun in! Subscribe now!)

The world’s only winged mammals, nocturnal bats, of which there are some 1,500 species globally, have never quite got great press. Superstition has them down as bad omens. And science implicates them as the possible origins of the COVID 19 pandemic that killed seven million people globally, and in the outbreak of several other zoonotic diseases (that is, diseases that hop between animals and humans), including SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) in China, MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus) in Saudi Arabia, Ebola in Africa, and Nipah in India.

So how do these animals, that have catalysed sweeping disease outbreaks among people around the world, not fall sick from the viruses they carry and transmit? Now a new paper in Science Advances untangles this conundrum.

Researchers studied the world’s largest family of bats, and found that they, unlike every single mammal in the world, possess two copies of genes that produce antibodies (proteins that help the immune system fend infections), and not just one.

“We’ve never seen anything like this in a mammal before,” said Hannah Frank, associate professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at Tulane University author of the study, in a release. This completely changes our understanding of mammalian immune systems "and raises exciting new questions about why bats have been so evolutionarily successful and how they respond to viruses,” he added.

For the study, the scientists looked at vesper bats, of which there are 500 species across the globe, except Antarctica. They studied the antibodies, which are protective Y-shaped proteins made of two heavy protein chains and two light protein chains. Unlike all other mammals, including humans, vesper bats have two separate heavy-chain gene systems, boosting their antibody diversity, they discovered.

To unravel the evolutionary origins of this duplication, the scientists studied genomes of 34 species of bats, including 26 closely related bats and found that the copy is present in every vespertilionid examined except the pallid bat, Antrozous pallidus.

How bats remain reservoirs of viruses without being infected by them could assist scientists understand immune responses among different species and help prevent disease spillover, said the paper. “It doesn’t fully explain why bats are such effective viral reservoirs, but it reveals a level of immune variety we didn’t know existed and gives us an entirely new direction to explore,” said Dr. Frank

In an older study, also published in Scientific Reports, researchers found that bats and coronaviruses have been evolving together for millions of years: this has produced different strains in different groups of bats around the world, it added. Scientists studied various coronaviruses in 36 bat species from the western Indian Ocean and nearby areas of Africa and found that different groups of bats had their own unique strains of coronavirus.

India is home to 135 species of bats, forming the largest order of mammals in the country, according to State of India’s Bats 2024-2025 published by the Bat Conservation International and Nature Conservation Foundation. Despite the critical role they play in ecosystems, by dispersing seeds, pollinating plants and preying on pest insects, “bats receive an insignificant amount of attention from the country’s research and conservation communities and scant recognition in government policies and programs,” this document said.

title: What is NASA’s Moon Base programme, why it wants India to be part of it? | Explained

content.value: The story so far: At the ninth meeting of the India-U.S. Civil Space Joint Working Group (CSJWG), held in Bengaluru on August 5 and 6, National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) offered a formal invitation to the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to be part of its ambitious Moon Base programme under the Artemis Accords.
What is the Moon Base programme?

NASA is looking to establish an ambitious lunar outpost programme, a first of its kind in the world where humans (astronauts) will make the Moon’s south pole a home from where they will live, work and conduct scientific activities over the next decade and beyond. The U.S. space agency, along with its partners, will execute a series of crewed and uncrewed missions.

On March 24, 2026 the Moon Base programme was announced during NASA’s ‘Ignition’ event. NASA plans a series of transformative initiatives designed to achieve President Donald Trump’s National Space Policy, and advance American leadership in space. The project is expected to cost more than $20 billion.
When and how is NASA planning to execute the Moon Base programme?

At the Ignition event in March, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said, “NASA is committed to achieving the near‑impossible once again, to return to the Moon before the end of President Trump’s term, build a Moon base, establish an enduring presence, and do the other things needed to ensure American leadership in space.”
The U.S. space agency is taking a step-by-step approach to execute this high stake mission. NASA plans to execute this mission in three phases.
The first phase has commenced and will extend till 2029. It will focus on gaining reliable access to the lunar surface and building a deeper understanding of the environment.

Phase two carries on till 2032 as NASA, along with its international partners, will look to extend from what it has learned from the first phase, and deploy the needed infrastructure for further continuing the mission.

Phase three, which is projected to come into effect from 2032, and extend from there on, is the most ambitious and critical phase of the mission as it plans to populate this region of the Moon where astronauts will live and work for an extended period.
Why is NASA planning to establish a lunar outpost in the Moon’s south pole?

The Moon is Earth’s closest celestial neighbour, and has fascinated humankind for long. Many missions, both crewed and uncrewed, have already taken place in the last few decades. However, the Moon Base is the most ambitious programme till date as the Americans, with their partners, look to establish a long-term human presence on the Moon, especially near the south pole, which has a volatile environment with temperatures ranging from -203°C to 54 °C.

NASA is hoping that exploring this hostile frontier in some areas, which never receives sunlight, will provide explorers answers to questions about the origin of the Moon, and the solar system as a whole. It also lays a platform for exploring other planets like Mars and Venus in the future.
Which other countries are planning similar programmes?

Like the US, there is another programme planned by Russia and China to set up a lunar base. The base, known as International Lunar Research Station (ILRS), is being planned to be established in the next decade by Russia’s state space corporation Roscosmos and China National Space Administration.

The ILRS hopes to be a permanent base and a lunar satellite constellation. In the run up to this, China plans to land humans on the Moon by 2030. It has already launched a three-member crew to its orbiting space station earlier this year as part of this programme to send astronauts to the Moon by the end of the decade.

Many countries have already signed up to be members of the ILRS. The space agencies of Russia and China have published a partnership guide .In 2023, a Roscosmos official told The Hindu that Russia is open to India’s participation in the ILRS.
What role can ISRO play in the Moon Base programme?

NASA has invited ISRO to join its Moon Base programme, building on the two countries’ partnership under the Artemis Accords, of which India is a member of since 2023. India became the 27th country to sign the Artemis Accords.

Following the signing of the accord, two Indian astronauts went to the US to train for the Axiom-4 mission to the International Space Station (IIS). Astronaut Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla eventually travelled to the ISS.

The latest invitation by NASA further opens the door for ISRO to gain international exposure on lunar studies considering that India is planning the upcoming Chandrayaan-4 mission, which is meant to collect lunar samples and bring back them back to Earth.
Besides, as part of the Space Vision 2047, India plans to have its own Bharatiya Antariksha Station or the Indian Space Station in orbit by year 2035, and an Indian crewed lunar mission by 2040.

title: Meta AI glasses hit with criminal complaint from German advocacy group

content.value: A German advocacy group ​has filed a criminal complaint against Meta and other companies ⁠selling the technology group’s AI glasses in Germany, arguing the devices violate privacy laws.

Digital rights group HateAid said in a statement on Wednesday that the launch of ‌the devices, the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer in particular, broke German digital privacy laws, in the latest sign of legal scrutiny in ‌a nation where the right to privacy is highly valued.

“There’s no ‌place ⁠to escape from smart glasses. You have to expect at ⁠any moment to be filmed and then exposed on the internet,” said HateAid managing director Josephine Ballon. The organisation reported the management of Meta, units of spectacles maker EssilorLuxottica including ​Ray-Ban, as well as retailers Fielmann, ‌Apollo-Optik, Mister Spex and MediaMarkt to the Frankfurt-based digital crime prosecution unit ZIT.
HateAid said its complaint was based on a federal digital data protection law that prohibits the sale of communication devices designed to film ‌people without them noticing.

ZIT confirmed it received a complaint from ​HateAid invoking that law, saying it would routinely investigate on a preliminary basis whether there are grounds for a deeper ⁠probe. MediaMarktSaturn Retail Group said it was taking the complaint very seriously, adding that its suppliers had contractual obligations for all goods to be compliant with ‌the law.

Mister Spex said it had not been officially notified of a complaint and that it was taking protection of privacy very seriously. The other companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The Federal Network Agency previously issued a statement on smart glasses in late 2023, saying that connected devices for covert audio or video recordings were banned.
The agency, ‌known as BNetzA, told Reuters on Wednesday that it was closely monitoring the smart ​glasses market but was for now not formally investigating any breaches.
“The ownership, import or sale of smart glasses are not banned ... ⁠for as long as the recording function is clearly visible, for instance via ⁠an optical signal,” said a spokesperson.
Broadcaster SWR reported in July that a Hamburg-based state privacy protection agency was taking legal steps ‌against the use of smart glasses.
HateAid said in its statement it had been increasingly registering image-based digital violence, mainly targeting women.
“Smart glasses now allow ​a particularly inconspicuous surveillance technology to be disguised as an everyday object.”

title: Inside the Google executive moves that led to its big AI reshuffle

content.value: Google co-founder Sergey Brin in recent months has urged key AI staff to go all in on the company’s Gemini ​model as parent Alphabet seeks to close the gap with rivals, two people familiar with his remarks told Reuters.

As Anthropic raced ahead with a preview of its powerful Claude Mythos model, Brin addressed hundreds of employees in an April town hall, urging ‌the company’s Google DeepMind AI lab to move faster, said one of the people on condition of anonymity.

Google’s Gemini model briefly overtook competitors last November, but new updates ​from Anthropic and OpenAI once again put it in catch-up mode. By August, Google had delayed the new flagship version of Gemini by two months after internal testing showed its performance continued ⁠to lag behind rivals in areas such as coding, one of the sources and another person familiar with the matter said.

On August 5, the Mountain View, California, tech giant announced a sweeping leadership overhaul of its Google DeepMind AI division in which its chief, Demis Hassabis, stepped aside in favour of his deputy, Koray Kavukcuoglu. Hassabis became chair, with fewer management obligations.

At the same time, the two original technical co-leads of Gemini quit to co-found a startup. While some industry observers have questioned if ‌Google is exiting the model race, interviews with seven people knowledgeable about Gemini’s development efforts show that Alphabet’s commercialisation strategy and reorganisation of ranks last week are tied to its effort to achieve model supremacy.

The changes mark a further erosion of DeepMind’s autonomy, which Google has chipped away at since buying the London-based lab in 2014 in an ongoing push for its AI to power more ‌of its software and make more money. Alphabet’s shakeup included a revelation during an all-hands meeting on August 6 that some teams were moving out of DeepMind and into corporate Google, two sources said. Internal meeting details ‌and ⁠Brin’s remarks have not previously been reported. Other media outlets earlier reported on not-yet-final reorganisations and Brin’s coding push.

Google declined to answer questions from Reuters about Brin’s recent involvement, DeepMind’s structural ⁠changes, and concerns held by staff. Under Hassabis, Google DeepMind pursued a wider range of AI research projects than its rivals while building Gemini models that are essential to corporate commercial interests.
But in past years, Hassabis worked against some efforts that could have meant new revenue for Alphabet or helped it gain better footing in the AI race, a Reuters special report last year showed.

His Google allies previously told Reuters that they rejected the idea that Hassabis gave short shrift to the business or focused too much on long-term science. In 2025, Google ​CEO Sundar Pichai appointed Kavukcuoglu, then DeepMind’s chief technology officer, to an additional senior post as Google’s ‌chief AI architect.

His task was to embed Gemini across the company’s products. Four of the sources told Reuters that in the months that followed, some leaders at DeepMind found their influence diminished while Kavukcuoglu became the central figure shaping Gemini’s direction.
Kavukcuoglu had Brin’s backing, one of them said.
News of the shakeup caused Google’s stock to drop 4% the day of the announcement.

At the unit-wide all-hands meeting on Thursday of last week, Hassabis and Kavukcuoglu sought to assuage concerns by staff — most of whom learned about the change as it became public — about the AI lab’s future.

The Google leaders said ‌day-to-day work at the lab would remain the same, according to three sources with direct knowledge of the meeting. Kavukcuoglu would stay in charge of Gemini, the sources said; he had assumed ​oversight of model development more than a year prior, five sources said.

Hassabis gave a talk about how AI could advance science and alter society, long-term issues that would constitute the focus of his new role as chair, the three sources knowledgeable about the meeting said.

This messaging aside, the all-hands meeting surfaced fresh concerns that DeepMind’s autonomy was being subsumed by Google. Hassabis ⁠and Kavukcuoglu told staff that several nontechnical teams were being moved out of DeepMind and into the corporate reporting structure, two of the sources said.

For an organisation that had once encouraged employees to pursue ancillary projects, the message to reclaim model supremacy was also clear. Executives including Pichai have said in recent months that Google considers itself to be at the frontier in certain areas like video generation, and remained committed to catching up in other areas despite setbacks.

Senior ‌leaders in the cloud division, meanwhile, expect Kavukcuoglu’s appointment to alleviate tensions with DeepMind over allocation of Google’s constrained supply of AI chips, known as Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), another source said.
The Google shakeup comes as Brin has worked to fire up staff, something he also did after OpenAI’s ChatGPT launch in 2022 jolted Google.

Although he no longer holds an executive title, the 52-year-old Brin has been informally influencing model training efforts. For several months now, he has been remarking to key staff that they need to catch up to the frontier, according to one of the sources knowledgeable about his efforts.

Brin has used the implicit power he holds as Google’s co-founder to push resource allocation toward specific areas, such as recursive self-improvement, the point at which the technology can improve without human intervention, this source said.
Google declined to make Brin available for an interview.

Hassabis, meanwhile, decreased his involvement in managing Gemini and passed off that responsibility to his deputies shortly after originally getting the AI model off the ground in 2023, two of the sources said.

Though Google caught up to the frontier last November with the release of Gemini 3, ‌it quickly fell behind again. Four sources characterised its laggard status as a result of lingering structural challenges that made it fall behind in the first place.

Constraints in computing capacity, for instance, and disagreements between Gemini’s many project leaders led to fewer resources for areas that ​would prove critical, such as coding, two of the sources said. Google’s bureaucratic nature also caused it to release models at a slower pace than nimbler rivals, the four sources said.

Google declined to comment on these claims, but Pichai told Wall Street analysts last month that the company would continue to scale up its infrastructure to alleviate constraints around TPUs that it ⁠needed for model training, as well as consumer and enterprise products.
Against this backdrop, Kavukcuoglu has been consolidating power. He moved from London to Mountain View last year for the chief AI architect promotion, reporting to ⁠Pichai.

Some London-based leaders found their influence on Gemini’s technical direction had diminished in the wake of Hassabis decreasing his involvement in Gemini and Kavukcuoglu moving to Google’s headquarters, according to a source with direct knowledge.

Kavukcuoglu began building a reputation within other parts of Google as well, as someone more attuned to commercialisation. Even before his relocation, Kavukcuoglu rather than Hassabis was the primary point of contact between DeepMind and ‌Google Cloud, the company’s main AI revenue engine, according to a source with direct knowledge.
He now will have final say on major decisions for DeepMind, a Google spokesperson told Reuters last week.

Some of the highest-profile leaders other than Kavukcuoglu, including Gemini’s original technical co-leads Jeff Dean and Oriol Vinyals, left as part of last week’s shakeup. Staff reporting to some of these leaders had held a rare degree of agency to conduct ​research not directly related to training Gemini, three sources said.

In the wake of their departures, Google did not immediately share plans for the fate of those teams or those projects, making some anxious that the lab’s bulwark against commercial interests would further erode.

title: NGT petitioned against illegal riverbed mining near Kaziranga

content.value: GUWAHATI Seven years after the Supreme Court ordered a complete ban on mining and related activities along its southern boundary, Assam’s Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve faces a threat from renewed riverbed excavation within its proposed Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ).

Mohajon Kro, a resident of Diphu in Karbi Anglong district, petitioned the National Green Tribunal (NGT) and the Ministry of Environment, Forest, and Climate Change on August 5, alleging large-scale and mechanised sand mining in the Deihori River. He said that excavators, earthmovers, and dumpers are being used to extract sand from the river channel, causing ecological damage to the river and affecting the Scheduled Tribe population dependent on it.

The hilly Karbi Anglong, governed by a tribal council, forms Kaziranga’s southern boundary. The hills become a refuge for rhinos, tigers, deer, and other animals whenever the national park is flooded during the monsoon months.

Seeking an immediate halt to mechanised mining, pending an investigation into alleged violations of environmental norms, Mr. Kro said the local authorities failed to enforce the regulatory safeguards governing sand mining and monitor the extraction activities in Deihori.

“The Deihori River is not merely a source of sand but a living ecosystem that sustains biodiversity, fisheries, groundwater recharge, livestock, and daily domestic needs of the local tribal population. For generations, the indigenous communities have depended upon this river for drinking, bathing, washing, irrigation, fishing, and various cultural and traditional practices,” he wrote to the NGT.

Mr. Kro said sand extraction was being carried out against the principles laid down under India’s sustainable sand-mining framework, which seeks to prevent indiscriminate removal of riverbed material and protect river morphology and aquatic ecosystems. He claimed that the use of heavy machinery destabilised Deihori’s riverbed, altered the waterway’s natural morphology, and damaged fish breeding grounds.

He alleged that the excavation and continuous movement of machinery increased sediment disturbance and water turbidity, affecting the quality of water used by nearby communities. He also raised concerns over the possibility of contamination from diesel, lubricants, grease, and hydraulic fluids associated with heavy machinery operating within or near the river.

Mr. Kro named Songja Terang as the lease or permit holder for the Deihori River sand and gravel mahal (quarry lease area) issued under an order of the Divisional Forest Officer, Karbi Anglong East Division.

He urged the NGT to order an immediate stay on all mechanised sand mining activities in the Deihori River; prohibit the entry and operation of excavators, earthmovers, heavy machinery, and dumpers within the active river channel; and direct an urgent spot inspection by a joint committee for submission of a factual report to the tribunal within a time-bound period.
The Karbi Anglong district authorities are yet to verify the allegations.

A Golaghat district-based conservationist said that the Deihori riverbed mining, along with illegal stone quarrying and hill-cutting in Karbi Anglong, could spell doom for Kaziranga National Park. Many rivers and streams flow into the key wildlife habitat from the Karbi Anglong hills.
The administrative headquarters of the national park is in Golaghat district’s Bokakhat town.

“It appears that the Supreme Court’s April 2019 order has had no impact. If such quarrying and mining continue, Kaziranga could be in for a disaster more severe than what Sivasagar and Charaideo districts further east experienced due to stone and coal mining along the Assam-Nagaland border,” the conservationist said, declining to be quoted.

title: Over 2,950 dogs sterilised to save Black-necked Cranes and wildlife in Ladakh

content.value: Over 2,950 free-ranging dogs (FRDs) were sterilised with the aim of saving Black-necked Cranes (BNC) and boosting wildlife tourism-based livelihoods in Ladakh under the initiative of Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) along with the Indian Army, the Animal Husbandry Department, and the Department of Forest, Ecology and Environment.

The initiative started in 2022 to conserve BNC chicks, after the wildlife expert noticed that FRDs have been killing them in the Alpine Wetlands of Ladakh and preventing BNCs from settling down in one place for nesting.

BNC, globally listed as “vulnerable”, is a cultural symbol and state Bird of Ladakh, but fewer than 100 survive in India, while the estimated world population is roughly 11,000–12,000 individuals, most of which occur on the Tibetan Plateau. They are distributed across four range countries—India, Nepal, Bhutan, and China.

According to BNHS authorities, 110–130 individuals are recorded annually, including 20–25 breeding pairs, depending on the year. The main breeding sites include the Changthang Cold Desert Wildlife Sanctuary, the wetlands of Hanle, Tso Kar, Nyoma, and nearby marshes, with an extended population in the Suru Valley. “During the annual population monitoring conducted in early June 2026, a total of 19 pairs of BNC were recorded across the wetlands of Ladakh,” said Kishor Rithe, Director of BNHS.

However, BNHS scientist Dr Muhammad Raza, working in Ladakh, informed that the actual number of pairs is expected to be slightly higher, saying, “Due to logistical challenges and limited accessibility, several sites could not be surveyed. BNHS is taking necessary measures to get a clear picture of the breeding population of BNC in Ladakh.”
Efforts under the initiative

BNC has been facing threats across its breeding habitats due to increased human use of areas surrounding wetlands, expansion of linear infrastructure, habitat degradation, FRDs, and the impacts of climate change.

To address disturbance to nesting birds at the hands of FRDs, BNHS led the initiative, which also includes efforts to reduce the availability of anthropogenic food subsidies. A pilot waste-management project has been initiated at selected Indian Army outposts to improve the handling and disposal of food and kitchen waste, thereby limiting access to food resources that sustain FRD populations.

“By integrating waste management with sterilisation efforts, the programme seeks to provide a long-term and sustainable approach to reducing dog-related threats in ecologically sensitive wetland landscapes,” said a BHNS authority.
Additionally, capacity-building and awareness programmes have been launched, and 1,000 armed forces personnel have been trained in biodiversity conservation and wildlife management.

title: LGBTQIA+ face widespread harassment in Arunachal, finds survey

content.value: A new survey in Arunachal Pradesh has documented recurring experiences of widespread harassment of members of the LGBTQIA+ community in the State.
Also read | On India’s rainbow trail | Queer-focused walks are finding an audience in the country

According to the Itanagar-based HimKai Research Institute (HRI), the pestering or provocation has led to identity concealment, discrimination-related distress, and low confidence in institutional protection among the LGBTQIA+ respondents in the State.
LGBTQIA+ expands to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer or Questioning, Intersex, and Asexual.

The HRI conducted the anonymous online survey between June 2 and August 2. It received 62 submissions, one of which was excluded during geographic eligibility and data-quality screening because the self-reported home district could not be mapped in Arunachal Pradesh.

“Among the 61 respondents included in the analysis, 49.2% said they hid their gender identity or sexual orientation most of the time or always because of fear of discrimination or violence. Half of valid respondents said they felt accepted within their family rarely or never, while 44.3% said they felt safe in their local community rarely or never,” the HRI report said.

“Experiences of harassment and discrimination were reported across several settings. Some 91.8% of respondents reported verbal harassment at least rarely, while 52.5% reported physical threats or violence at least rarely. Among valid responses, 85.0% reported discrimination in school or college at least rarely, and 63.2% reported workplace discrimination,” it said.

The survey also found that 72.9% of valid respondents felt compelled to change their behaviour or appearance sometimes or more often to retain work or education. A further 57.9% said their identity affected access to employment or income opportunities at least rarely.
Religious, cultural exclusion

“Mental wellbeing emerged as a significant concern. Among valid responses, 76.7% reported experiencing stress, anxiety or emotional distress related to discrimination sometimes or more often, including 48.3% who experienced it most of the time or always. Access to mental-health or peer support was uneven: 41.0% said such support was available most of the time or always, while 36.1% said it was available rarely or never,” the report said.

The findings also point to a gap between awareness of rights and confidence in institutions. While 56.7% of valid respondents agreed that they were aware of their legal rights, 63.3% disagreed that laws and policies adequately protect LGBTQIA+ persons, and 66.7% disagreed that police and authorities respond sensitively to LGBTQIA+ issues.

Religion, culture and social belonging received particularly cautious assessments. Some 72.1% did not agree that religion or faith practices are accepting of LGBTQIA+ persons. More than half disagreed that their identity is compatible with their cultural or tribal background or that local traditions allow space for diverse identities, with 51.7% of valid respondents disagreeing that they feel a sense of belonging in society.

Healthcare emerged as a comparatively more positive area. Among valid respondents, 56.7% said that they felt comfortable accessing healthcare most of the time or always, and 75.0% said healthcare providers treated them with respect most of the time or always.
“Friends were the most frequently reported source of support, mentioned by 37 respondents, followed by LGBTQIA+ networks, mentioned by 12.

Six respondents mentioned. Awareness and sensitisation were the most common single priority identified for improving LGBTQIA+ lives in Arunachal Pradesh, followed by legal protection,” the report said.
HRI director Ranju Dodum said the study was intended to begin building locally grounded evidence on experiences that are often discussed without adequate data.

“LGBTQIA+ experiences in Arunachal Pradesh cannot simply be assumed from national conversations. Family, community, tribal identity, religion, education and employment all shape how people experience acceptance and safety here. This is a baseline study and its numbers must be read with methodological caution, but they point to questions that deserve deeper research and serious public discussion,” he said.

The report recommends sustained sensitisation programmes in schools, colleges, workplaces, healthcare institutions, police and public administration; confidential mechanisms for reporting discrimination; stronger mental-health and peer-support systems; safe community spaces; more inclusive education and workplace practices; and locally grounded engagement with families, community institutions and faith leaders.
The survey sample was predominantly young, with 90.2% of respondents between 18 and 35 years.

title: Rising obesity among Indian women underscores need for preconception interventions

content.value: Nearly one in three Indian women aged 15-49 years is now overweight or obese, up from one in four women five years ago, according to data released by the Central government. The latest National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6) found that 30.7% of women aged 15-49 years were overweight or obese in 2023-24, compared with 24% in NFHS-5 (2019-21). Among men in the same age group, the proportion rose from 22.9% to 27.3%.

Speaking of the rising incidence of lifestyle-related disorders on fertility and pregnancy, which is prompting greater attention to health before conception, doctors and health practitioners are now increasingly focusing on the period before pregnancy, arguing that identifying and addressing health risks in both prospective parents could improve reproductive and pregnancy outcomes.

“The concept is not new to Ayurveda. The traditional system has described garbhadana samskara, a pre-conception regimen aimed at preparing prospective parents physically and mentally before conception. The approach is now being offered as a structured programme at the SDM College of Ayurveda and Hospital in Udupi, Karnataka, which has been providing pre-conception counselling and care to couples from different parts of south India,’’ Mamatha K.V., principal and senior obstetrician at the institution, said.

Describing this approach as the “conscious preparation for conception”, Dr. Mamatha said that the process involves assessment of the health of both partners, along with advice on diet, lifestyle, and other factors that may influence reproductive health. Pre-conception consultations can provide an opportunity to identify risks, review medicines, address nutritional deficiencies and encourage healthier lifestyles before pregnancy.

In Ayurveda, conception is described through four factors — ritu, the appropriate fertile period; kshetra, a healthy reproductive tract; beeja, the healthy sperm and ovum; and ambu, adequate nourishment. “Interventions are tailored around these factors, with dietary and lifestyle changes and, where considered appropriate, traditional therapies,’’ Shreyashri Suvarna, a physician at the hospital, said, adding that traditional interventions need to be individualised and clinically supervised.

title: How Tamil Nadu invested in sustained awareness and building trust to shape its organ donation programme

content.value: From seven deceased donor organ donations in its first year, to 266 in a single year, Tamil Nadu has come a long way in 17 years. Behind the rise is a gradual shift in public perception, shaped by sustained awareness efforts, measures to build confidence, and trust and improvements in the State’s transplant infrastructure and systems.

The numbers tell a compelling story of how far the State has come with regard to organ donation and transplantation. Since 2008, the highest number of deceased organ donors was recorded in 2024, when Tamil Nadu had 268 donors. In 2025, there were 266 donors - 211 men and 55 women. A total of 1,476 organs were utilised - 856 major organs and 620 minor organs and tissues that year, according to the Transplant Authority of Tamil Nadu’s data.
On World Organ Donation Day, which falls on August 13, experts revisit the milestones, the lessons learnt and the road ahead.
How it worked

J. Amalorpavanathan, founder-member secretary, Transplant Authority of Tamil Nadu, said, “When we started in 2008, the concept of brain death was scarcely understood among healthcare professionals. A few coordinated brain death certifications were happening sporadically, with MOHAN Foundation [an NGO] coordinating around two to three such cases a year in a few city hospitals. The State government had decided to start the Cadaver Transplant Programme (CTP), and the groundwork began in April. We went on to issue 10 government orders. It was in September that year that the parents of 15-year-old Hithendran (who had sustained severe injuries in a road accident and was declared brain dead) decided to donate his organs. The CTP was launched in October 2008, and Hithendran’s case helped organ donation pick up in the State.”

Recalling his visits to all districts, he said that initially, there was reluctance among doctors. “But whenever I interacted with the general public,  I found a sense of receptiveness. In fact, though they had questions and sought clarifications, I found the least resistance among them.  We slowly convinced healthcare professionals to certify brain death. We had seven donations in the first year, and crossed 180 in a year in eight years. Though the number of organ donations dipped during the COVID-19 pandemic, it picked up again thereafter,” he pointed out.
Families coming forward

Sunil Shroff, managing trustee of MOHAN Foundation, said there had been a tremendous improvement in awareness levels over the years. “Earlier, we found it hard to obtain consent for organ donation. Now, many families are coming forward to donate. In States such as Tamil Nadu and Telangana, where awareness is relatively high, I think that 10 to 15% of families come forward to donate. This is a paradigm shift,” he observed.

About 72% of deceased organ donations in the country happens in five States - Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka. Southern states, he said, have done well in terms of creating awareness on organ donations.

Compared with other States, awareness about organ donation was far higher in Tamil Nadu. Unpublished data from a major transplant centre showed that the acceptance rate was 70 to 75% after the first counselling and increased by another 10% following the second counselling, a senior doctor noted.

“According to me, awareness creation can be approached in two ways. One is to organise awareness campaigns and sessions and encourage people to take pledges. In T.N.’s experience, we found that news about successful donations, honour walks for donors and giving due recognition to donors were more effective awareness tools. Since October 2023 (the former DMK government issued an order to accord State honours to the mortal remains of deceased donors in September 2023), more than 800 such State honours have been accorded. News about successful donations and the utilisation of donated organs has proved to be a more effective way of creating awareness,” Dr. Shroff explained.
What’s needed now

Dr. Amalorpavanathan said that the involvement of people and healthcare professionals along with government support has helped improve organ donation in the State. “Successive governments did their best to take the programme forward. We have well developed infrastructure and doctors who are willing to go the extra mile,” he said.

However, this brings in another perspective. “We have an unacceptable number of brain deaths due to the high number of road traffic accidents. We need to reduce accidents and make roads safe. Developed countries have moved towards Donation after Circulatory Death (DCD), and we should also explore this possibility. In living donor organ transplants, we should promote swap transplants in a big way,” he noted.

At a recent press conference on a heart transplant in a young patient with Dilated Cardiomyopathy, Rajeev Thilak Chellasamy, heart transplant surgeon at SIMS Hospital, Chennai, elaborated on DCD. He noted that India has a long waiting list for  transplants, and has traditionally relied on donations following brain death, while DCD was not ethically approved in the country. In DCD, the practice of which has been around for nearly 10 to 15 years, the heart is connected to a perfusion system. DCD numbers have increased in North America. If considered, it is a viable opportunity to increase the pool of donor hearts. The number of people dying while on the waiting list has increased and this needs to be addressed, he said.

Dr. Shroff called for establishing green corridors in hospitals for seamless integration of organ donation processes so that there are no missed opportunities. Similarly, every hospital should have nodal officers in place, he said.

title: Meta meets its own 'tobacco' moment as jury selection kicks off trial

content.value: U.S. jury selection kicked off on Wednesday in a California courtroom where Instagram and Facebook owner Meta will defend itself against allegations of harming children in a new trial which experts describe as social media's big tobacco moment.

Federal Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers and lawyers for both sides probed prospective jurors about their views of social media and Meta, asking if they personally had social media accounts, whether their kids use social media, and if they think social media is responsible for mental health, among other questions.
Some said they believed that social media plays a role in mental health, with one person comparing the serotonin boost that some people feel from "doomscrolling" to using cocaine.
Eight people were picked Wednesday afternoon to serve on the jury. They will play an advisory role in the trial, with the judge making the final decision.
A coalition of states sued Meta in 2023 for allegedly designing addictive features for kids in its apps and violating state laws.
Four states were selected to represent their claims: California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey.
Top prosecutors from those states now aim to prove in federal court that Meta deliberately made Facebook and Instagram addictive for children.

Meta "strongly disagrees with these allegations" and is "confident the evidence will show our longstanding commitment to supporting young people," a spokesperson told AFP, adding that the company has "listened to parents, worked with experts and law enforcement."
Although it's not the first lawsuit that seeks to hold a social media company accountable for its impact on mental health and safety, it could become one of the most consequential.
"It really feels like tobacco in the 1990s," Vincent Joralemon, a director at Berkeley's Life Sciences Law and Policy Center, told AFP.

While such cases about social media harms revolve around the intersection of technology and addiction, the legal argument in this case against Meta centres on its business practices, similar to when the federal government sued tobacco companies around three decades ago, Joralemon said.

By the early 1990s, decades of research showed that tobacco use caused health problems such as cancer, and eventually additional investigations revealed how the industry deliberately downplayed, and even concealed, the harmful impacts of its products.

Dozens of US states sued four major tobacco companies, and by 1998, won a landmark settlement agreement which included financial penalties and changes to how products were marketed, particularly to children whom the industry targeted with advertisements featuring cartoon characters, the most famous of which was known as "Joe Camel."
Meta was convicted on similar grounds in separate trials held in Los Angeles and New Mexico, with combined damages that approach $1 billion.

In Oakland, the states are demanding a long list of changes to Meta's apps, in addition to financial penalties as high as $1.4 trillion, close to Meta's entire market value, which hovers around $1.5 trillion.
Despite the eye-popping number, money isn't Meta's biggest problem, if it were to lose the case.
"The huge issue here is reputational harm" and being forced to make major changes, Joralemon said.
"Putting a CEO on the witness stand can be quite damning," as well, he said.
Meta founder and chief Mark Zuckerberg is among the star witnesses expected to testify.
The case could be "the beginning of a broader reckoning" for Meta, Nora Freeman Engstrom told AFP via email. She is a law professor and associate dean at Stanford.
It will be important to see the "gap" between what Meta knew privately and what it disclosed publicly, Engstrom said.
