None of this requires reinventing India’s cancer infrastructure. It requires layering a gender lens onto what already exists: in how programmes are designed, how data is collected, and how care is delivered. Cancer outcomes in India won’t meaningfully improve through more hospitals alone; they’ll improve when the system finally accounts for the very different ways men and women experience the disease, and are able to access and negotiate care.
(Dr. Jyoti Wadhwa is principal lead, medical & precision oncology, Apollo Athenaa Women Cancer Centre, New Delhi. drjyotiwadhwa@apollohospitals.com)

title: TB cases, mortality rate dipped significantly between 2015 and 2024: Nadda

content.value: Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda on Tuesday (August 4, 2026) said India has made significant progress in tuberculosis control, with incidence rate declining by 21% between 2015 and 2024, while over 2.29 crore diabetes cases have been reported under the national non-communicable disease programme over the past three years.

Responding to a query in the Rajya Sabha, Mr. Nadda said public health and hospitals are State subjects and the Centre provides technical and financial support to States and Union territories under the National Health Mission (NHM).
Parliament Monsoon Session: Follow LIVE updates on August 4, 2026

He said tuberculosis (TB) case notification has increased over the past three years, helping bridge the gap in "missing" cases. According to the Ni-kshay portal, 25.52 lakh TB cases were notified in 2023, 26.18 lakh in 2024 and 26.37 lakh in 2025.

Citing the World Health Organisation's Global TB Report 2025, the Minister said India’s TB incidence rate fell from 237 per lakh population in 2015 to 187 per lakh in 2024, a 21% decline, compared to the global decline of 12% over the same period.
The TB mortality rate also declined by 25%, from 28 per lakh population in 2015 to 21 per lakh in 2024, while treatment coverage increased from 53% to 92%, he said.
Mr. Nadda said the government has implemented two phases of the 100-day TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, launched in December 2024 and March 2026, and expanded the campaign to all districts.

The initiative focuses on screening high-risk populations, early diagnosis through chest X-rays and nucleic acid amplification tests, timely treatment, nutritional support and preventive therapy for vulnerable groups.

Further, the Minister said the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD) provides screening, diagnosis and treatment for diabetes and common cancers, including oral, breast and cervical cancer.

Population-based screening for people aged 30 years and above is being carried out through Ayushman Bharat-Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, while 770 district NCD clinics and 6,410 community health centre NCD clinics have been strengthened to provide diabetes care, he said.

The government has also established 524 functional day care cancer centres for decentralised chemotherapy services and approved 19 state cancer institutes and 20 tertiary care cancer centres under a central assistance scheme, he stated.

According to the NP-NCD portal, between 2023-24 and 2025-26, 2.29 crore diabetes cases, 1.53 lakh oral cancer cases, 24,969 breast cancer cases and 37,948 cervical cancer cases were reported under the programme.
Mr. Nadda said expenditure under the National TB Elimination Programme and the non-communicable disease control programme stood at ₹6,763.85 crore in 2025-26.

He further said reductions in customs duty and GST on certain high-cost cancer drugs, along with the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana and AMRIT pharmacies, have improved access to affordable cancer medicines, reducing patients' out-of-pocket expenses.

title: Hexavalent vaccine could improve India’s immunisation programme: Study

content.value: Introducing the hexavalent (six-in-one) vaccine into India’s Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) could improve the efficiency of the country’s childhood immunisation programme, according to a study conducted by the Union Health Ministry along with the George Institute for Global Health India, the Gates Foundation, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and John Snow India Private Limited.

A hexavalent (six-in-one) vaccine is a combination vaccine that protects infants against diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (whooping cough), Hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and polio in a single injection. It reduces the number of injections children need, eases the workload of frontline health workers, lowers cold-chain requirements, and saves caregivers’ time.

According to a release issued by the group, almost 26 million Indian babies are vaccinated annually as part of the nation’s immunisation programme. At present, children receive multiple vaccines during immunisation visits, increasing the number of injections they receive, placing additional demands on caregivers’ time, and adding to the workload of healthcare providers.

Researchers found that the price of the hexavalent vaccine remains the single largest determinant of overall programme costs. Based on trends in vaccine procurement in India, the study estimates that a 50% reduction in the vaccine price would enable operational and system-level savings to outweigh the additional vaccine acquisition costs under the primary immunisation schedule.
The research shows that introducing the hexavalent vaccine could deliver several benefits, including fewer injections for infants, making vaccination more convenient for children and caregivers.

The study assessed two implementation scenarios: replacing the current pentavalent and fractional IPV doses with the hexavalent vaccine during the primary immunisation schedule, and replacing both the primary schedule and the DTP booster dose with the hexavalent booster. Costs were assessed from both government and household perspectives, including vaccine procurement, syringes, cold-chain logistics, healthcare worker time, and caregiver time.

The findings were published in the peer-reviewed international journal *Human Vaccines & Immunotherapeutics*. Previous stakeholder research cited by the authors found that caregivers generally preferred fewer injectable vaccines during each visit.

Susmita Chatterjee, Program Head, Health Economics, the George Institute for Global Health India, said, “Combination vaccines have long been recognised for simplifying immunisation programmes while improving convenience for families and health systems. Our study demonstrates that although the hexavalent vaccine carries a higher upfront procurement cost, it also generates important efficiencies by reducing injections, easing pressure on frontline health workers, lowering cold-chain requirements and saving caregivers’ time. These findings provide important economic evidence that can inform future policy discussions on strengthening India’s immunisation programme.”

title: Eating right, from infancy onwards

content.value: (In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Zubeda Hamid writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)

Open any social media page and look for posts on motherhood and you’ll be deluged with narratives about how glorious, rewarding and fulfilling it is. And while all of that may be true, what is also true is that mothers in our country often do not get even a fraction of the support they need to safeguard the health of both newborns, and their own.
This week, as the globe observes World Breastfeeding Week from August 1 to 7, we’re going to give you a lowdown on women’s health, along with four other important developments and more.
Why breastfeeding, and what’s happening in India?

Globally, medical advice for newborns is the same: exclusive breastfeeding for six months is ideal, not just to support a baby’s growth but to also ensure protective immunity. Just how does it do that? Do read Smruthi Prabhu’s article that explains how breastmilk, which contains a perfect blend of nutrients in proper balance, ‘programmes’ an infant’s health by shaping their gut microbial composition.

And how is India doing when it comes to exclusive breastfeeding? Not so well, as this story by Sonali Mishra and Karan Babbar details: the percentage of exclusively breastfeed infants dropped from 63.7% in the National Family Health Survey-5 to 55.8% in NFHS-6. What is urgently needed, is better support services for mothers to be able to breastfeed, starting from the time of delivery at the hospital, to the home and at workplaces. The spike in C-section deliveries -- linked with delayed breastfeeding initiation -- may also have contributed, and needs to be looked into, the authors say.
And finally, do watch Ramya Kannan explain how a human milk bank works, who can donate breast milk, who receives it, and why does it matter for vulnerable newborns.
The battle against junk food

This week saw the Karnataka government issuing an advisory prohibiting the sale, distribution, advertisement and promotion of foods high in fat, sugar and salt (HFSS), in schools and colleges and within a 50-metre radius of educational institutions. The Maharashtra government has issued a similar directive.

Why was this considered necessary? As Afshan Yasmeenexplains, the government hopes to reduce children’s easy access to unhealthy foods during school hours, amid growing concerns over children’s diets.

Frequent consumption of HFSS foods displaces healthier foods from the diet and increases the risk of obesity, diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular diseases later in life. And this is not a unverified concern: Athira Elssa Johnsondecodes a study that found prediabetes and obesity among adolescents in Chennai rose sharply over 17 years between 2006 and 2023.
Our edit this week points to another important factor: the necessity to start taxing foods high in fat, sugar, and salt.
An update on infectious diseases

They never really go away do they? Kerala has had it especially bad: all major hospitals in Kochi, have been running at full capacity for the past several weeks, with a surge in admissions for fever and influenza cases. And at the same time, the case fatality rate of leptospirosis has been spiralling with 49 deaths (30 confirmed and 19 probable) just in July. Why is this happening? C. Mayaexplains that Kerala’s unique monsoon-heavy environment makes it a hotspot, while late diagnosis contributes to lethality.

Bindu Shajan Perappadan, meanwhile, reports on a study that finds India may be entering a more perilous phase in its dengue epidemic, with multiple strains of the virus now circulating simultaneously across much of the country.
In Gujarat, Abhinay Deshpande reports that 22 children have died due to Chandipura virus infection this monsoon season, with seven others currently undergoing treatment

And internationally, the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has become the fastest-growing such outbreak in history, killing more than 1,500 people. Abhinaya K.writes on why it is so hard to contain.
The drug menace
A new study that looked at over 6,000 teenagers from across 108 schools in India has found that over a fifth might be at moderate-to-high risk of substance use.

The government is aware: PM Modi has launched the Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp Abhiyan (Drug-Free Youth for Developed India Pledge Campaign) as Devesh K. Pandeyexplains, and Abhinay Lakshman reports that higher educational institutions, starting with IITs and IIMs this year, have begun suggesting that incoming students submit a voluntary urine test for drugs along with their admission paperwork.
Social media effects

A lot has been said about what social media does to young people’s brains and emotions. This week, igniting the debate about whether bans really work, Australia has defended its ban on social media for children under 16, even as the country’s internet regulator found that more than eight in ten Australian teenagers were still using social media three ‌months after the restrictions took effect.

But in a closer look at what the effects of social media could be, Sahana Venugopal explores the multiple suicides and violent deaths that have been linked to an OpenAI’s model that is now no longer available: GPT-4o. She also asks if social media is encouraging dangerous home births, following the death of a 32-year-old woman in T.N. after a medically unassisted birth at home.
And more
Dr. Melissa Sathyan says persistent itching without a cause is a symptom you must not ignore
Dr. Sameeta Mercy Prabhu notes that delays or problems with gross motor skills beyond a particular age may point to neurological issues
Here’s why women in Bihar reach menopause in their thirties
Misconceptions about women’s reproductive health are busted here
And Dr. Jaydev Panchawagh stresses the need for awareness about surgical treatment available for hemifacial spasm
There is much more on offer too, do head to our health page and subscribe to the health newsletter here.

title: ICAR develops indigenous vaccine for African swine fever

content.value: The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) has developed India’s first indigenous African swine fever (ASF) vaccine for pigs. The ASF, caused by the African swine fever virus, is considered as one of the most devastating trans-boundary animal diseases affecting domestic and wild pigs worldwide. The ICAR termed the development as a “major leap” in animal health.

Director General of ICAR M.L. Jat said the breakthrough marks the dawn of a new era in veterinary science. “It reflects India’s growing scientific capability to develop world-class animal health solutions and paves the way for a new generation of indigenously developed vaccines and innovative technologies that will strengthen livestock health, enhance disease preparedness, and support the nation’s food and biosecurity,” he said.

Scientists at ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (ICAR-NIHSAD), Bhopal, have developed the vaccine using a novel attenuated “ASFV Genotype II virus”. “The vaccine has successfully undergone comprehensive laboratory evaluation, including sterility, purity, safety, genetic stability, immunogenicity, protective efficacy and virulence reversion studies,” the Union Agriculture Ministry said in a statement.
Helps pig farming sector

The vaccine is recommended for healthy pigs above eight weeks of age and is administered as a 1 millilitre (ml) intramuscular injection, followed by a booster dose 14 days after the primary vaccination. “The indigenous vaccine is expected to substantially reduce pig mortality, minimise economic losses and improve the livelihoods of pig farmers across the country. By providing an effective preventive tool against one of the world’s most destructive livestock diseases, it will significantly strengthen India’s animal health security and support the sustainable growth of the pig farming sector,” the Ministry said.

The ASF’s mortality rates may approach 100% and the disease has caused “severe socio-economic losses” to the global pig farming sector. “Since its first detection in India in 2020, ASF has spread to several States and Union Territories, resulting in massive pig mortality, disruption of pig production, restrictions on animal movement and trade, and significant livelihood losses for smallholder pig farmers, particularly in the Northeastern region,” the Ministry said in the release.

The Ministry said in the absence of an effective treatment or a commercially approved vaccine in India, disease control has largely relied on rapid diagnosis, culling of infected animals and strict biosecurity measures. “The economic impact of ASF outbreaks in India has been significant. During the initial outbreaks in Assam in 2020 and 2021, pig mortality and culling resulted in estimated losses of approximately ₹276 crore. In Mizoram, ASF outbreaks have reportedly affected more than 11,382 households up to 2025, resulting in an estimated financial loss of approximately ₹982 crore,” the Ministry said.

title: Three common medicines classified as carcinogenic by IARC; experts urge patients not to stop treatment | Explained

content.value: The story so far: Three widely prescribed medicines used to treat high blood pressure, life-threatening fungal infections and organ transplant rejection have been classified as “carcinogenic to humans” (Group 1) by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the World Health Organisation’s specialised cancer research agency.

The three drugs — hydrochlorothiazide, voriconazole and tacrolimus — feature on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and are prescribed to millions of people worldwide. Hydrochlorothiazide is commonly used to treat hypertension, voriconazole is an antifungal medicine used to manage serious invasive fungal infections, while tacrolimus is an immunosuppressant that prevents rejection of transplanted organs.

title: Clinical study finds family conflict outweighs academic stress in students’ mental health struggles

content.value: While examinations, marks and academic competition have been considered the primary drivers of stress experienced by students, a new study suggests “family conflict” as a more common reason for students seeking psychological support than academic stress.

A clinical study by Cadabams Hospitals — a priviate hospital which draws on over 58,000 student touchpoints across 3,569 documented counselling sessions conducted by Cadabams psychologists embedded across schools and colleges in Bengaluru — observed that emotional struggles of many young people may begin well beyond the classroom.
Self-harm concerns highest among PU students

In the study, while anxiety accounted for nearly one in three counselling concerns (29%), family conflict (14%) ranked ahead of academic stress (10%), followed by relationship distress (8%) and loneliness (7%).
Students aged 16 to 18 years studying in Pre-University colleges recorded the highest proportion of self-harm concerns among all educational groups assessed.
Mental health concerns of student differed significantly across educational streams.

Engineering students most commonly sought help for relationship distress and ADHD-related concerns, while recording the highest rates of self-referrals. Medical students struggled with the combined burden of academics and clinical responsibilities. Management and architecture students frequently presented with loneliness, homesickness and career uncertainty, while law students recorded the highest density of high-risk mental health cases.
‘Must create safe environments’

Commenting on the findings, Neha Cadabam, Senior Psychologist and Executive Director, Cadabams Hospitals, said, “One of the biggest challenges is that many students continue to suffer silently due to lack of conducive environment for discussing what they are experiencing at home. If we truly want to improve student mental health, we need to move beyond conversations around examinations and create emotionally safe environments where young people feel heard without fear of judgement.”
The study was conducted across more than 20 educational institutions, with nearly 92% of all student touchpoints from Bengaluru.

title: Dr Muthulakshmi Reddy:The doctor who brought reforms

content.value: In 1886, a young girl was born to S. Narayanaswami Iyer, the Principal of Maharaja’s College, and Chandrammal in the Pudukkottai princely state of Tamil Nadu. At a time when women were forced to live in a world of social limitations, the young girl went on to break barriers in medicine and state administration. This is the story of Dr Muthulakshmi Reddy, one of the most brilliant social reformers in India’s history.
Growing up

Muthulakshmi pursued education with determination and became the first female student to be admitted to Maharaja’s College in Pudukottai. It was not an easy win by any means. Not just the principal but also the students and their parents did not want a woman studying in the men’s college. It was the Maharaja of Pudukottai who admitted her and gave her a scholarship. Even then, as the only woman on campus, she had to go through a trial period of three months. After passing from there with flying colours, Muthulakshmi wanted to pursue a bigger dream — medicine.

In 1907, Muthulakshmi became the first woman to be admitted to Madras Medical College, and she completed her studies with a gold medal. She then went on to become a House Surgeon in the Government Hospital for Women and Children in Madras (both these institutes are in present-day Chennai). She was the first woman house surgeon at the Government Maternity and Ophthalmic Hospital, breaking barriers for generations of women in the medical field. This was just the start of her journey in empowering women through the knowledge and experience she had gained.
Into public life

Dr Muthulakshmi’s medical career did not just give her experience in the field but also helped her understand multiple social issues, especially ones faced by women. This helped her work towards reforms to make societal changes.

Her life in the public sphere properly began when she became the first woman legislator, first woman deputy president of the Legislative Council and the first woman in the Madras Corporation. She used her authority to bring in multiple rights for women, including property rights, laws against child marriage and children’s protection. With personal experience in hand, she also campaigned against the devadasi system, which was trapping multiple girls at a very young age.

With equality and justice as her main principles, Muthulakshmi also advocated for a better educational and healthcare system — especially for women through fee exemptions, scholarships and building hostels. She also created better sanitation facilities, improving the quality of life in many economically backward neighbourhoods.
Legacy left behind

Today in Adyar, Chennai, two institutions stand tall as a testimony to Muthulakshmi’s dedication towards making a better future — Avvai Home and Orphanage, an institution created to shelter, protect, and educate girls and women and Adyar Cancer Institute.

In 1956, Dr Muthulakshmi was awarded the Padma Bhushan not just for pioneering in multiple fields but also for bringing such brilliant reforms while interconnecting multiple fields she was passionate about. Even after her death in 1968, her legacy speaks loudly through the community and reforms she brought in to make education, health, freedom, and respect an everyday reality in society.

title: Three common medicines classified as carcinogenic by WHO cancer agency

content.value: Three widely-prescribed medicines used to treat high blood pressure, fungal infections, and organ transplant rejection have been classified as “carcinogenic to humans” (Group 1) by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the World Health Organisation’s (WHO) cancer research agency. Experts stressed that the classification is a hazard identification and should not prompt patients to discontinue treatment without consulting their doctors.

The three medicines — hydrochlorothiazide (hypertension), voriconazole (fungal infections), and tacrolimus (an immunosuppressant preventing transplant rejection) — are on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, prescribed to millions worldwide.
The assessment, published as Volume 137 of the IARC Monographs, expands on conclusions first released in The Lancet Oncology in November 2024. The 22-member panel included Indian scientist G.B. Jena.
Possible DNA damage

There is sufficient evidence that hydrochlorothiazide causes squamous cell skin carcinoma and lip cancer, IARC said. Studies from Denmark and the United States found higher rates of non-melanoma skin cancers among long-term users, attributed to phototoxicity — the drug heightens skin sensitivity to UV radiation, raising the risk of DNA damage after sun exposure.

Voriconazole was similarly linked to squamous cell skin carcinoma in transplant recipients on prolonged therapy, through the same phototoxic mechanism. Tacrolimus was linked to non-Hodgkin lymphoma and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, with limited evidence for leukaemia and skin carcinoma. Unlike the others, its risk stems from immunosuppression, weakening the body’s ability to clear abnormal cells.
IARC Monographs identify whether an agent can cause cancer under certain circumstances, but do not assess real-world risk at prescribed doses.
Indian situation
In India, hydrochlorothiazide is a common first-line hypertension therapy, voriconazole is routinely used in immunocompromised patients, and tacrolimus underpins post-transplant care.

Kabir Sardana is the Director, Professor and Head of the Department (HOD), Department of Dermatology, at Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Medical Sciences and Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital said: “The IARC classification is highly relevant, particularly in India.”

“Hydrochlorothiazide has long been recognised as carrying a risk, especially in rural areas, the Northeast, hilly and coastal regions, and among outdoor workers such as farmers who are exposed to high levels of ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Voriconazole is another concern, not only because of its known association with skin cancer risk, but also because it is frequently prescribed without labelled indications, including for fungal skin infections caused by Trichophyton indotineae. Doctors welcome measures to curb such inappropriate use. We cannot ignore these warnings in a country where irrational prescribing, over-the-counter availability, and poor adherence to ethical prescribing and dispensing practices remain significant challenges,” he noted.

Doctors recommend that patients on hydrochlorothiazide or voriconazole should continue sun-protection measures — sunscreen, limiting UV exposure, periodic skin checks. Transplant patients on tacrolimus are already routinely monitored for skin cancers and lymphoproliferative disorders.

Experts add that patients should not stop or alter medication without medical advice, since these drugs treat serious, often life-threatening, conditions. The priority is informed prescribing and monitoring, not a shift away from treatments whose benefits remain established, they said.

title: Hold tight! How two hurricanes forced a lizard to change its grip

content.value: Picture a lizard the length of your finger clinging to a tree branch. The cause of its desperation is a 265 km/hr wind tearing through the air, threatening to peel it off like a loose sticker.
Just this happened twice in two weeks to a population of small brown anoles in the Turks and Caicos Islands in September 2017. So since then, these lizards have evolved to cling harder.
Two visitors

Four days before Hurricane Irma made landfall, a team of scientists from Princeton and Harvard Universities had wrapped up a routine survey of the Turks and Caicos anole (Anolis scriptus) on two islands, Pine Cay and Water Cay.

They studied the limbs, toes, and toepads, collected tissue samples, and went home. They had no idea a hurricane was coming, leave alone two. Hurricane Irma arrived on September 8 with sustained winds of 265 km/hr. Maria followed on September 22 at 200 km/hr.
Between them, the storms flattened vegetation and, by the look of it, a great many lizards.
Nagging detail

Six weeks later, the team returned to the same two islands and found something peculiar about the lizards that were around. Compared to before the storm, the anoles had longer forelimbs, shorter hind legs, shorter toes on those hind legs, and larger front and back toepads.

They reported these changes in Nature in 2018, describing them as the handiwork of evolution. But one detail from that survey nagged at the researchers: the fourth hind toe, the longest one, had actually become shorter. If longer toes mean better grip, why would evolution shorten one?
The answer has finally arrived, in a new study in Current Biology.
Checking with a cousin

When the researchers again went to Pine Cay and Water Cay, they found five genes on the two islands had become more frequent after the storms — independently. All five genes are known to be involved in muscle and skeletal development.
One in particular, hs6st1, seemed to be responsible for the shorter fourth toe in the surviving Turks and Caicos anoles.

Of course, finding a gene sitting next to a trait is not the same as proving it causes the trait. So the team turned to a lizard better suited to lab work, a cousin called the brown anole (Anolis sagrei). Using CRISPR, they knocked out hs6st1 in brown anole embryos, and they were born with shorter fourth toes, thinner toe cartilage, and, in one unlucky individual, a toe that never developed.
Evolution on steroids

Next, the team built a wind tunnel, placed brown anoles on a wooden dowel, and subjected them to winds of 118 km/hr. When they watched the footage, they found the lizards holding on with their front legs twice as long as with their back legs, on average.
But among all the hind-leg measurements, lizards with a shorter first toe bone clung on much longer than those with a longer one.

Thus, two hurricanes 14 days apart had managed to rewire a wild population’s genome and skeleton in a way that could still be detected in its descendants a year on — a point in favour of evolutionary biology on steroids.

The paper itself ended on a more sober note: extreme weather events are forecast to grow more frequent and severe, and researchers would do well to be mindful of the effects on wild populations, sometimes within a single generation.
D.P. Kasbekar is a retired scientist.

title: ‘Ghost particles’ signature can track where spent nuclear fuel goes

content.value: In the high-stakes world of preventing governments from secretly developing atom bombs, the ability of inspectors to check what happens inside a reactor core — without stepping foot inside the highly radioactive structure — is a holy grail.
For many decades, International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors have used cameras and close inspections to ensure operators are not diverting spent nuclear fuel for illicit uses.

A new study in Physical Review Letters by researchers of the ‘Double Chooz’ Collaboration in France has reported a breakthrough in this domain. The team has reported the first measurement of the signature of particles emitted by spent nuclear fuel, which a detector can detect even from a distance.
Remotely verify

These particles are called neutrinos. They are subatomic particles and are very, very light. They interact so weakly with matter that around 100 billion neutrinos pass through each one of your fingers every second and your body doesn’t even notice.

The nuclear fuel inside a reactor produces antimatter neutrinos in similarly staggering quantities. But while scientists have studied these emissions from active reactors for six decades, the low-intensity stream of neutrinos that persists after a reactor has shut down has remained elusive. This stream is produced by isotopes such as Pr-144 and Rh-106, which continue to decay in the partially burnt fuel within the core and in nearby spent fuel cooling pools for a long time.

Using a detector located 400 m from the Chooz B nuclear power plant in France, the Double Chooz team analysed 2.5 weeks of data. In this window, when both of the plant’s reactor cores were simultaneously offline, the detector recorded around 106 neutrino candidate events.
The researchers used statistical methods to confirm the signal was not a fluke. The data showed that 56% of the signal originated from the reactor cores and 44% came from the cooling pools.

The ability to measure the residual flux allows monitors to remotely verify the spent fuel inventory. If a rogue state clandestinely removes fuel assemblies from a cooling pool to extract plutonium — a key ingredient of nuclear weapons — the neutrino glow from that pool would diminish.
Future detectors

Soviet scientists pioneered this way of using neutrinos in 1978. Now, the Double Chooz team has become the first to describe the energy levels of the neutrinos emitted by spent fuel at high precision. The unique pattern of these energy levels is the signature.

Scientists have also worked out a way to use neutrino detectors to estimate the plutonium content in a reactor core in real-time. This information can be used to check if operators are swapping fuel out prematurely — a common tactic to harvest weapons-grade plutonium.

In a 2019 study in Nature Communications, researchers in the U.S. also reasoned that compact and portable detectors of the future could help authorities discover small, undeclared facilities used to produce fissile materials. However, building such machines is still a significant challenge. Current detectors are large and stationary because they need to filter out cosmic rays, which are constantly streaming in from space.
One of the Double Chooz detectors itself weighed over 500 tonnes, with 300 tonnes of shielding alone.

title: How can parents safely support children’s phone usage?

content.value: Though parents want to give their child a phone-free childhood, this is no longer a reality for many families. Children’s school teachers, instructors, friends, and even key contacts are increasingly reliant on smartphones to keep in touch, provide help, and deliver education.
To accommodate these scenarios, parents can instead set reasonable limits and provide children with safer ways to access social media platforms and/or reduce their screen time.
Here are some strategies to help you understand what works for your family.
Ages 2 - 6 | A “dumb” phone

Since medical experts have repeatedly warned parents not to let babies and toddlers be exposed to screens, a “dumb” phone can be a safer way to introduce the technology to children and teach them basic digital safety. A screen-less phone can be used to teach children to type in their home phone numbers, dial emergency services, and communicate their need for help.

These interactions can be included in fun pretend-play routines or role-playing games, in order to teach children about using technology, without risking an addiction to screens. Child-friendly digital cameras also allow young users to grow familiar with tech without being exposed to algorithmic feeds or short-form videos.
Ages 6 and up | On-device parental controls

Most smartphones have dedicated Parental Controls or Digital Well-Being settings that allow adults to set usage limits for children, as well as remove access to certain apps/websites that are not age-appropriate. Adults can also set up schedules to make sure the device cannot be used during school hours or after bedtime.  Parents and caretakers can further review the child’s app usage statistics via these settings, in order to make sure there is no excessive screentime.

As the child matures, parents can also allow certain apps or websites to be used for longer while other social media apps are locked down, so that the child can use the phone as a study tool without being distracted.

On-device controls make it easy to turn off all notifications such as ads or promotions from individual apps, all at once. These controls further stop children from downloading potentially harmful content or making in-app purchases without the adult’s knowledge, by requiring the adult to enter a PIN number or password to authorise such activities.
All Ages | Google Family Link App

Similar to the phone’s Parental Controls or Digital Well-Being settings, Google’s Family Link app allows a group of people (both children and adults) to securely sync their Google accounts and their devices, so that the responsible adult can remotely review and control the supervised children’s phone usage and screen time.

For example, a supervising parent can use the Google Family Link app to set up a system where they allow their 15-year-old supervised child to use their phone for up to 2 hours a day. This older child is allowed to download a few streaming apps, and they have special permission to use WhatsApp for an extra 1.5 hours every day, in order to video call their other parent who is working overseas. The child is also allowed to play games on the phone until their 10 PM bedtime, after which it is automatically locked.

On the other hand, the supervising parent can set up vastly different controls for their 7-year-old child via the Google Family Link app, by allowing them only 30 minutes of phone time each day. The younger child cannot download any apps at all unless the parent approves each request through their own app. All access to messaging and gaming apps have been cut on this profile, and safe search filters are always on. After 30 minutes of use, the device is locked for the day. The device also stays locked between 8 PM and 7 AM, while the child sleeps, and remains locked during their school hours.

Through their own Google Family Link app, the parent can track the locations of their children’s devices to see where they are, as well as check their phone battery levels. They can change permissions to give the children more/less time on specific apps, as per their daily needs. AI use by the children can also be regulated via the app. The Google Family Link app does not allow supervising members to view others’ private content and messages remotely.
However, some users have complained about slow and glitchy updates, as well as cross-platform weaknesses.
Gmail for children
A parent, who does not want their children to excessively depend on instant messaging apps such as Instagram DMs or WhatsApp, can set up their child with a Google account instead.
Google offers options for parents to set up accounts for their children, and adjust their cybersecurity settings to manage how they log into other services.

With a controlled email ID, children are better protected from ads and media that are aimed at adults. An email account also encourages parents to teach children to draft, edit, and send longer messages, helping them perfect professional communication from a younger age.

Gmail enables thoughtful communication while posing less of an addiction risk than a social media app with a constant stream of videos to watch. YouTube usage can also be appropriately moderated via the Google account.
Social media accounts for children

As Meta faces legal flak world-over due to allegations that its apps lead to addiction and mental health struggles in young users, the social media company has been working to make its apps more child-friendly.

For example, Instagram Teen Accounts require parental permission to change the built-in protections, apart from restricting who can contact these teen users and what kind of material is suggested to them.

Adult Facebook users can find the option of setting up a protected Messenger Kids account for their children. A parental dashboard allows them to configure settings, as well as control the features that they use, and their contacts list.

In March this year, WhatsApp announced the rollout of parent-managed accounts for child users and pre-teens. This will allow parents to review message requests from unknown contacts, as well as change account privacy settings.
However, many users have complained that these parent-managed accounts are not available across all regions yet.

title: Private colleges account for 54% of 1.36 lakh MBBS seats in India

content.value: Private medical colleges continue to account for a majority of the MBBS seats offered in India, with 73,643 private college seats (54%) compared with 63,296 government-run college seats (46%), according to the National Medical Commission’s 2026-27 seat matrix released recently for the academic year 2026-27.
Of the 9,911 MBBS seats added for the 2026-27 academic year, 7,800 seats (79%) have come up in private medical colleges, while 2,111 seats (21%) have been added in government colleges.

“This marks the first time that such a large majority of India’s undergraduate medical seats are in the private sector. This shifting to having more private MBBS seats is a trend that has been showing up over the past few years,’’ former national president of the Indian Medical Association Ravi S. Wankhedkar said. While the number of MBBS seats has expanded, the affordability of medical education has now emerged as a pressing concern, he added.
72,627 applications received for MBBS, BDS courses

Government medical colleges in India typically charge ₹5,000 to ₹1 lakh per year, with the total MBBS tuition cost ranging from about ₹25,000 to ₹5 lakh for the entire five-and-a-half-year course. In some States, including Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Delhi, tuition cost is well below ₹1 lakh for the full course, while in a few other States, it is higher. Hostel and other charges are levied additionally.

MBBS fees in private medical colleges in India vary widely, ranging from ₹3 lakh-₹12 lakh per year for government quota seats to ₹12-₹30 lakh per year for management quota and deemed university seats. The total cost of completing the five-and-a-half-year MBBS course, including hostel and other expenses, can range from ₹25 lakh to over ₹1.5 crore in private colleges, depending on the college and the quota.

India now has 1,36,939 MBBS seats across 823 medical colleges, the highest ever, and according to the Union Health Ministry, this is a significant step towards addressing the country’s shortage of doctors.
India witnessed an expansion in undergraduate medical education over the past decade, with MBBS seats increasing from 51,348 in 2014-15 to 1,36,939 in 2026-27.

Over the past five years, the overall number of MBBS seats has grown steadily, but until recently, government medical colleges retained a slight majority. The balance, however, narrowed every year as private colleges expanded rapidly.

India’s MBBS seat distribution has steadily shifted towards the private sector. Government colleges accounted for about 52% of seats in 2022-23, but the gap narrowed to near parity by 2024-25. Private colleges overtook government institutions in 2025-26 and now account for 53.8% of all 1,36,939 MBBS seats, according to the National Medical Commission.

title: Apple seeks preliminary injunction against OpenAI in trade secrets case

content.value: Apple on Monday asked a U.S. judge for a preliminary injunction barring two former employees ​and OpenAI from accessing, acquiring, using or disclosing alleged confidential information as ‌it moves ahead with its trade secrets case.

Apple ​last month sued OpenAI and the two ⁠former employees, both now working for OpenAI, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT-owner’s foray into consumer hardware, a ‌dramatic escalation of already simmering tension between the two companies.

The iPhone maker also filed a ‌concurrent motion on Monday seeking expedited discovery, including production ‌of ⁠documents relating to the defendants’ alleged access of ⁠Apple’s proprietary and trade secret information.

It asked the judge to order the two former Apple employees named in the lawsuit, Chang Liu and ​Tang Yew Tan, to ‌sit for depositions, along with OpenAI employee Yu-Ting Peng and an unnamed OpenAI employee who previously worked at Apple.
Liu is a former Apple senior system electrical ‌engineer while Tan is Apple’s former vice president of ​product design for iPhone and Apple Watch.
Apple also sought depositions from corporate representatives of OpenAI and ⁠io Products, which is OpenAI’s commercial arm and is listed as a defendant in the lawsuit.

“Apple will be ‌irreparably harmed absent a preliminary injunction,” it said in a filing. “Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction is both based on false information and completely unnecessary because we do not have, nor want, any of their trade secrets,” OpenAI said in a blogpost late on Monday.

Apple’s lawsuit, ‌filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of ​California, comes after OpenAI successfully fended off a legal challenge from Elon Musk’s xAI. The lawsuit sets ⁠up a battle over the control of future AI devices ⁠that may not use traditional apps or operating systems — devices which, if successful, would direct consumer ‌attention away from Apple’s best-selling iPhone. Analysts believe OpenAI is working on a phone or other device of ​its own.

title: Apple launches new legal challenge to UK attempt to access encrypted user data: Report

content.value: Apple has launched a new legal challenge against the ​British government’s latest attempt to create a so-called backdoor to ‌access encrypted customer data, the Financial Times reported ​on Monday.

The report said Apple last ⁠month lodged a legal complaint at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal — Britain’s independent judicial body — over the Interior Ministry’s demand that Apple allow ‌it access to encrypted cloud backups of data belonging to British users.

Britain dropped last ‌year a previous mandate for such a backdoor that ‌would ⁠have allowed access to British and ⁠U.S. customers’ data following months of negotiations with the U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.
However, British authorities subsequently issued a new “technical capability notice” ​to Apple that did ‌not apply to U.S. users, the FT report said.
A British government spokesperson said it would not comment on legal proceedings or operational matters, including confirming or denying ‌the existence of individual notices.

“The UK supports ​strong encryption and robust privacy protections, but it is also vital that law enforcement can access ⁠communications when necessary and proportionate to protect the public from terrorism, serious crime, and child sexual abuse,” the ‌spokesperson said.
Apple confirmed the filing but declined to comment further. The company has previously said it has never built a backdoor or master key to any of its products or services and never would.

“This is a hugely important case that will have ‌far-reaching implications for the public’s privacy rights well into the future,” Ruth Ehrlich, ​director of external relations at human rights advocacy group Liberty, which has previously been involved in ⁠the legal case, said in a statement.

“Opening a backdoor ⁠to all of that information carries a wide range of risks to our personal data. ‌It is critical that the government listens to the many concerns and commits to protecting our privacy ​rights.”

title: Meta, Anthropic, Google, OpenAI to meet Trump officials about AI safety testing

content.value: Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have been invited to meet White ​House officials on Tuesday to discuss voluntary government safety testing for the most advanced ⁠U.S. AI models, according to three sources familiar with the matter and news reports.

Anthropic and OpenAI disclosed in recent days that their AI tools breached the systems of other companies, stirring concerns among U.S. lawmakers about ‌whether increasingly capable AI models could be used to conduct or facilitate cyberattacks.

A White House official said on Monday the Trump administration has finalised the details of ‌voluntary cybersecurity tests to measure the hacking capabilities of the most advanced American AI models, ‌and ⁠is planning to discuss them with the AI industry. The official did not ⁠indicate who would attend the discussions.
Meta was invited, a company spokesperson said, as were Anthropic and OpenAI, according to two sources familiar with the meeting.

The White House did not provide details about the tests, including how results would be reported, ​the metrics used and whether any of it ‌would be made public. A group of 15 Republican state attorneys general on Monday asked OpenAI to preserve all potentially relevant documents related to its disclosure that its AI system escaped containment and hacked AI company Hugging Face.

Citing a Reuters report that the rogue agent in ‌one case left notes for how future versions of itself could escape internal ​guardrails, they wrote that the company may have violated state consumer protection laws.
OpenAI said in a statement it takes the letter from the attorneys general seriously ⁠and will share a technical report about the Hugging Face attack after it completes a review.

The U.S. House of Representatives’ cybersecurity committee on Monday asked OpenAI’s Sam Altman to brief them on the ‌attack on Hugging Face. Altman visited the White House last week to discuss details of the voluntary tests and the company’s upcoming AI products, the company said in a statement.

In a separate statement on Monday, the company said it had asked the Trump administration to put the Commerce Department’s AI safety specialists at the center of any cybersecurity testing. The company pointed to China, whose government has a more centralised strategy on AI compared with the U.S.
The Information, a tech publication, ‌reported on Monday that the Trump administration invited representatives from Google.

A Google spokesperson declined to comment. U.S. President Donald Trumpdirected ​his team in June to write a series of tests to assess the hacking capabilities of the most advanced American AI systems. The Trump administration has had ⁠a rocky relationship with Anthropic.

The company earlier this year refused to allow the U.S. military to use ⁠its AI models for domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons systems, and the government retaliated by putting it on a national security blacklist.

Anthropic said last week that some ‌of its AI models hacked into the systems of three companies during cybersecurity tests. That disclosure followed rival OpenAI’s report that one of its AI agents escaped a testing environment ​and hacked into the systems of the AI company Hugging Face.

title: Apple briefly removed Telegram from App Store after sexual abuse content violated guidelines

content.value: ​Apple said on ‌Monday it briefly removed ​the Telegram ⁠messaging app from its App Store after ‌a review found content that ‌violated its ‌guidelines “prohibiting child ⁠sexual abuse ⁠material.”
The company said it restored the app ​after “the developer promptly ‌removed the content and banned the user who ‌posted it.”
Telegram said ​on X: “Reports of my ⁠demise are greatly exaggerated.”
An Apple spokesperson did ‌not respond to a request for further comment on the guidelines violation. Telegram ‌also did not respond ​to a request for comment.

title: Amazon enters $3 trillion club as AI, cloud growth power rally

content.value: Amazon’s market value topped $3 trillion for the first time ​on Monday, helped by a sharp rally following strong ‌earnings and signs that the AI ​boom is driving fresh demand for ⁠its cloud-computing services, the company’s main profit engine.
Its shares were last up 5.5% at $286.20, hitting a record high ‌and taking their yearly gains to over 23%.

The Seattle-based e-commerce and ‌cloud computing giant’s stock surged 15% on ‌Friday ⁠after it delivered its strongest cloud growth ⁠in more than four years and raised its annual capital spending forecast.

Amazon and Microsoft are the only two ​of the “Magnificent Seven” companies, ‌out of the six that have reported so far, whose AI spending has paid off in investors’ eyes. Tesla, Alphabet and Meta ‌were punished as their massive spending ​plans hit free cash flow last quarter.

Along with other tech giants on ⁠Wall Street, Amazon has been pouring billions to build out its AI infrastructure. It disclosed a ‌new investment in Anthropic in April, which follows Amazon’s announcement earlier this year that it would invest up to $50 billion in OpenAI.

It took just over two years for the company, founded by Jeff Bezos back in ‌1994, to add another trillion dollars to its market ​value after hitting a $2 trillion valuation for the first time in June 2024.

Apple, ⁠Microsoft, Alphabet and Nvidia are the other companies that ⁠have recorded a market value of $3 trillion in the past. Nvidia is currently ‌the world’s biggest company with a market capitalisation close to $5 trillion.

title: ‘Donors got mixer grinders, cash’: blood banks in Bengal under scanner over ‘illegal’ sale to other States

content.value: At least six blood banks in West Bengal are under investigation for allegedly selling blood to individuals and private blood banks outside the State in what Health Department officials have described as an inter-State, multi-crore racket.

The sale of blood is prohibited under the National Blood Policy, which was introduced in 2002. Officials said raids have been conducted at blood banks in Kolkata, Howrah, East Burdwan, West Burdwan, Nadia, and North Dinajpur districts over the past two weeks and large quantities of plasma were found to have been sold to entities in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat, among other States.

Officials said around 11 blood banks have been barred from organising donation drives until the investigation is over. However, they are still permitted to collect blood from donors at their centres. The restrictions came into effect on August 1. Popular medical facilities and pathology labs like Ashok Laboratory, Life Care, Kothari Medical, Health Point Hospital, and several others are on the list.
The racket, worth crores, kept the health department in the dark by selling blood illegally, health department officials said.

Last week, Health Minister Sharadwat Mukherjee told reporters that officials found that people who donated blood at a camp in South 24 Parganas were offered gifts. “You can give food, flowers, a badge or a certificate to a donor, but you cannot give gifts. We recorded instances of donors getting fans, mixer grinders, clocks and money,” said Dr. Mukherjee.

title: 22 children die of Chandipura virus in Gujarat this monsoon

content.value: Twenty-two children have died due to Chandipura virus (CHPV) infection in Gujarat this monsoon season, with seven others currently undergoing treatment, State Health Minister Praful Panseriya said on Monday (August 3, 2026).

The State has reported 184 suspected cases of the virus so far, of which 35 have tested positive, while the results of 11 samples are awaited, the Minister said. All the affected patients are below 15 years of age.
Children admitted to civil hospitals in Gandhinagar, Himmatnagar, Patan, Rajkot and Bhavnagar are receiving specialised treatment, he said, adding that doctors are closely monitoring their condition.
Mr. Panseriya said the cases have been reported from different parts of the State and are not concentrated in any particular village.
To contain the spread of the virus, health teams are carrying out pesticide spraying in areas with animal husbandry activity to control sandflies, which transmit the virus.

The Health Department has instructed all government and private paediatric hospitals to immediately admit children showing symptoms of the infection to intensive care units with oxygen and ventilator support to prevent complications such as multiple organ failure.

Chandipura encephalitis is a viral disease that causes inflammation of the brain and is spread mainly by sandflies and other insects. The virus was first identified in 1965 in Chandipura village in Maharashtra’s Nagpur district.

title: Hospitals in Kerala’s Ernakulam face full capacity with spike in influenza, fever cases

content.value: With the rising number of infectious diseases such as influenza, viral fever, H1N1, and leptospirosis in Ernakulam district of Kerala, hospitals are struggling to cope with the increasing patient load. All major hospitals in Kochi city, including private and government hospitals, have been running at full capacity for the past several weeks and are reporting a surge in inpatient admissions for fever and influenza cases.
Anoop Joseph, superintendent of the Government Medical College, Ernakulam, says that a spike in the number of patients being admitted for influenza and viral fever has been observed.

“There is no denying that there has been an influx of patients, but this is as per our expectation. The months of June and July generally witness a spike in these cases, and we are avoiding any floor cases (accommodating/treating patients on the hospital floor) and ensuring beds for all,” said Dr. Joseph.

The superintendent added that they have not had to start a fever ward yet, indicating that despite the surge in diseases, the situation has been manageable. Dr. Joseph, however, added that, as opposed to earlier years, the severity of the disease has increased this time.
“Patients are getting severely affected and taking a longer time to recover. This could be because of a change in the virus variant,” he added.
Several patients who fell sick after contracting influenza or viral fever complain that they are struggling to get rooms in hospitals due to high occupancy.

Meera Suresh, a native of Kakkanad, Ernakulam, who sought treatment at a private hospital along with her family after contracting influenza, said she had to get discharged at her own risk after they could not get a private room. Devaki Bhaagi, an actor, said she had to wait past midnight in the hospital casualty, hoping they would get a private room for better treatment for her daughter, who was down with viral fever.
“We eventually had to leave for home. We reached out to multiple hospitals, but none had any availability. We eventually got a room the next day, late at night,” said Ms. Bhaagi.

Spokespersons at private hospitals opine that the season has seen a spike in influenza and fever cases and that, with more people opting for private rooms instead of wards, hospitals are struggling to accommodate everyone.
A spokesperson for a private hospital on the outskirts of the city said that the majority of patients being admitted to the hospital were infected with influenza and viral fever.

“We are running at full capacity, and most people want to get admitted to private rooms, which creates a strain. Since we have regular surgeries as well as accident and trauma cases, we have been running at full capacity for some time now,” said the spokesperson.
The same sentiment was echoed by a spokesperson for a premium hospital in the city, who said that the hospital has been seeing several referrals and high-risk cases of fever and influenza.
“All our beds are occupied, and we are trying to accommodate as many referrals as we can,” the spokesperson added.
Curbing spread of disease

According to the medical fraternity, proper cough etiquette and personal hygiene measures need to be followed to avoid the spread of diseases and the subsequent patient load in hospitals during the monsoon months.

Dr. G. Sathyajith Nair, paediatrician and secretary of the Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP), Cochin Branch, said that this is the peak influenza season and that cough etiquette and personal hygiene need to be followed.
“Avoid going to crowded places without masks and stay home if you are sick to prevent the spread of the infection,” said Dr. Nair.

title: Breastfeeding awareness walkathon held in Chennai

content.value: A breastfeeding awareness walkathon was held at Besant Nagar Beach in Chennai on Saturday, ahead of World Breastfeeding Week, bringing together healthcare professionals, medical students, nurses and volunteers to promote the importance of breastfeeding and donor human milk.

Organised by the Neonatology Association of Tamil Nadu in association with the Rotary Club of Chennai Kilpauk, the event highlighted exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life, continued breastfeeding with appropriate complementary feeding, and the role of human milk banks in improving outcomes for sick and preterm newborns.

The organisers said sustained support from families, healthcare providers, workplaces, communities and policymakers is essential to help mothers breastfeed successfully and improve maternal and child health.

title: Study links prolonged heat exposure during pregnancy to adverse birth outcomes

content.value: A nationwide analysis of data from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS) quantifies the link between prolonged exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy and adverse birth outcomes in India. It was associated with a measurable increase in the risk of low birthweight, preterm birth and stillbirths among the mothers, and was tied to the trimester during which exposure occurred.

The paper ‘Effect of extreme heat stress on adverse pregnancy outcomes in India’, analysed 209,266 births recorded between 2015 and 2020, and matched each birth to local heat conditions during the pregnancy. It used nationally representative NFHS-5 data (2019–21) linked to high-resolution heat exposure estimates (India Heat Index) for 2015–20 across 707 districts. It uses ‘consecutive sweltering days’ instead of average temperature.

The researchers, Vineetha Vincent et al, showed that trimester-specific windows: heat extremes during the first trimester were most linked to preterm birth, the second trimester to low birth weight, and the third trimester showed a higher risk for stillbirth.
The risks were also higher among mothers with low Body Mass Index (<18.5), with lower education levels, and from poorer wealth groups, the study concluded.
It also found that urban residents showed slightly higher low birth weight rates than their rural counterparts.
Climate zones

The study also found associations between climatic zones, heat exposure, and pregnancy outcomes — mountainous zones showed stronger associations, while humid subtropical and arid zones also showed significant low birth weight occurrences. This is presented as the first population-scale evidence from India tying prolonged extreme heat stress (not just temperature) to adverse pregnancy outcomes, using a heat index that incorporates humidity, wind, and radiation.

The authors say research evidence already shows the potential biological effects of high ambient temperature: increased maternal core body temperature raises foetal core temperature, leading to birth defects, and dehydration decreases uterine blood flow and foetal growth, and due to reduced blood flow, there is a heightened chance of uterine contractions and an increased risk of preterm birth. Low and middle income countries experience higher birth rates and therefore, a larger absolute number of adverse birth outcomes.

The study was led by researchers at the University of Queensland – IIT Delhi Academy of Research, in association with the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi (Centre for Atmospheric Sciences and School of Public Policy) and the University of Queensland’s School of Public Health, Brisbane, University of New South Wales, Sydney; the University of Exeter, U.K.; and Korea University, Seoul.
Strategies for future

With extreme conditions expected to increase due to global warming, India should prepare to address the heat challenges with more adequate adaptation planning, the authors say. It is crucial to raise awareness of the risks of heat exposure for pregnant women from marginalised populations, particularly those with lower education and in rural areas, they urge.

title: Preference for private healthcare higher in rural Kozhikode, says study

content.value: A study conducted in rural areas of Kozhikode district has found that 174 people per a population of 1,000 (17.4%) required outpatient (OP) medical treatment within a recall period of 15 days and 19 people per a population of 1,000 required (1.9%) inpatient (IP) medical treatment within a recall period of a year for their various illnesses.

It also revealed that the utilisation of private healthcare facilities was higher for both OP and IP care. Out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) was higher in private facilities compared with public facilities for both OP and IP services. A substantial proportion of households were covered under government health insurance schemes. The OOPE, however, remained considerable among both insured and uninsured households.

The study titled ‘Morbidity and out-of-pocket expenditure among rural households of Kozhikode district, Kerala’ was published in Healthline Journal, a peer-reviewed publication of the Indian Association of Social and Preventive Medicine, on July 23, 2026. It was conducted by T. Jayakrishnan, Head of the Department of Community Medicine, P. Sruthi Krishna, Assistant Professor, Community Medicine, and Anjali Lakshman and Ahana Salim junior resident doctors, at KMCT Medical College, Mukkom, Kozhikode.

The community-based cross sectional study was conducted among 700 households and a sample size of 2,371 in a select grama panchayat in the district. Of the total population, 413 illnesses requiring OP treatment were reported over a period of 15 days, corresponding to a rate of 174 per 1,000 population. Most frequently reported cause of OP morbidities were infectious diseases (76.9%) which included viral fever, respiratory tract infections, mumps, chickenpox, and viral hepatitis. Accidents and injuries constituted 7.6%.

As many as 83.1% sought care from any health facilities, while 16.9% managed themselves through self-medication. A total of 53.4% sought care from private facilities, while 46.6% approached public facilities. The median expenditure OOPE for OP care was ₹145 and ₹700 in public and private facilities, respectively. In public facilities, cost of medicines (₹500) accounted for the highest share and in private facilities, it was for investigations (₹1,150).

Over a one-year period, 44 incidents requiring IP treatment were reported with an incident rate of 19 per 1,000 population. Of this, 77% were admitted in private facilities and only 23% were in public facilities. The cause of hospitalisation in 43.1% of the cases were non-communicable diseases and 34.4% were infectious diseases. The median expenditure OOPE for IP care was ₹600 and ₹5,050 in public and private facilities, respectively. In public facilities, cost of medicines accounted for the highest expenditure.

Out of 663 households, 494 were enrolled in any form of health insurance schemes while 25.4% had no such coverage. The most commonly availed scheme was Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, covering 60.3% of the population. The participants who were covered under health insurance schemes, including those belonging to BPL families, had an OOPE of ₹2,625 for IP care, compared to ₹4,250 among those who did not have it. Although the OOPE was relatively lower for the insured belonging to the BPL category, they still incurred substantial expenditure, indicating that they also suffer high financial burden and are not fully protected.

The OOPE for IP care in the private sector was ₹5,050, which was less than that of previous studies, possibly because patients were admitted for minor illnesses or discharged within a day to comply with insurance claim requirements.

The authors of the study said that the preference for private OP care was a sign of increased privatisation in healthcare which may be driven by many causes like increasing health aspirations, reduced waiting times, perceived better quality of care and greater flexibility in service delivery. The lower hospitalisation rate seen in the present study may not reflect a true reduction in morbidity but could be attributed to reduced affordability, where individuals delayed or avoided hospital admission due to financial constraints.

title: Karnataka’s advisory banning junk food near schools: What it means and why it matters  | Explained

content.value: The Karnataka government’s advisory prohibiting the sale, distribution, advertisement and promotion of foods high in fat, sugar and salt (HFSS), commonly referred to as junk food, in schools and colleges and within a 50-metre radius of educational institutions has brought children’s nutrition and preventive healthcare into sharp focus. The advisory, issued by the State’s Food Safety and Drug Administration (FDA), seeks to create healthier food environments for students at a time when childhood obesity and lifestyle-related illnesses are on the rise.

The measure goes beyond regulating school canteens. By extending restrictions to vendors operating immediately outside school gates, the government hopes to reduce children’s easy access to unhealthy foods during school hours. While similar provisions already exist under the Food Safety and Standards (Safe Food and Balanced Diets for Children in School) Regulations, 2020, the advisory places renewed emphasis on implementation and enforcement.
Also Read | Supreme Court asks FSSAI to consider warning labels for packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat
Why has Karnataka taken this step?

The advisory comes amid growing concern over changing food habits among children and adolescents. The Food Safety Department has said inspections at educational institutions found widespread availability of processed snacks, sugary beverages and foods made using refined carbohydrates. Such foods are often energy-dense but nutritionally poor, containing excessive amounts of salt, sugar and unhealthy fats while providing limited vitamins, minerals and fibre.

Rebecca Kuriyan Raj, Professor and Head of the Division of Nutrition at St. John’s Research Institute and Head of Clinical Nutrition Service at St. John’s Medical College Hospital, described the advisory as a timely and much-needed public health intervention. She said schools play a critical role in shaping lifelong eating habits because children spend a significant part of their day there. “Easy access to junk food promotes frequent consumption of energy-dense, nutrient-poor foods over healthier meals,” she said, asserting that schools should foster supportive, health-promoting food environments.

N. Karthik Nagesh, Programme Director, Pediatric Centre of Excellence at Aster CMI Hospital, said children spend a large part of their day in school and the food available around educational institutions directly influences their eating habits. Restricting junk food near schools creates a healthier environment while sending a strong message to children and parents that nutrition is a priority, he said.
Editorial | Front and centre: On the front-of-package labelling issue
What are HFSS foods?

HFSS refers to foods that are high in fat, sugar and salt. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) uses the term to identify foods containing excessive levels of nutrients associated with obesity and non-communicable diseases.

These include packaged chips, sugary soft drinks, chocolates, candies, instant noodles with high sodium content, deep-fried snacks, burgers, pizzas made with processed ingredients, sweetened breakfast cereals and bakery products high in sugar and saturated fat. Not every packaged food falls under the HFSS category; classification depends on its nutritional composition and the limits prescribed under food safety regulations.
Also Read | FSSAI says nutritional information must be highlighted with bigger fonts and bold letters
Why are children particularly vulnerable?

Doctors say childhood is the period during which lifelong eating habits are established. Frequent consumption of HFSS foods displaces healthier foods from the diet and increases the risk of obesity, diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular diseases later in life. India also continues to face a dual burden of undernutrition and rising overweight and obesity among school-going children.

Dr. Raj said India was increasingly witnessing what she described as an “intra-individual double burden of malnutrition”, where even children who appear thin or have normal body weight may carry excess body fat and metabolic abnormalities. “This hidden malnutrition heightens their risk of Type-2 diabetes, hypertension and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease later in life,” she said.

She pointed out that HFSS foods are rich in unhealthy fats, added sugar and salt but poor in protein, fibre, vitamins and other essential nutrients. Regular consumption encourages children to prefer processed snacks over fruits, vegetables and whole grains, creating dietary habits that often continue into adulthood.

Dr. Nagesh said regular intake of foods high in fat, sugar and salt increases the long-term risk of diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease. It can also affect children’s concentration, energy levels and overall growth. “Healthy eating habits start in childhood, and schools play a major role in shaping these habits,” he said.
Comment | Maintaining India’s progress in food safety standards
Is this the first restriction on junk food in schools?

No. The advisory builds on the Food Safety and Standards (Safe Food and Balanced Diets for Children in School) Regulations, 2020, framed by the FSSAI. The regulations require schools to promote balanced diets, discourage HFSS foods and ensure food served on campuses meets nutritional standards.

Karnataka’s latest advisory strengthens implementation by extending restrictions beyond school campuses to a 50-metre radius, recognising that students often purchase snacks from vendors located just outside school gates.
Also Read | Overfed and undernourished in Delhi
What foods are being encouraged?

The government has advised schools to promote balanced diets centred on fresh and locally available foods such as whole grains, millets, pulses, fruits, vegetables, milk and other nutritious traditional foods. Freshly prepared snacks such as idli, upma, avalakki, sprouts and boiled groundnuts are among healthier alternatives that nutritionists recommend.

Dr. Raj said implementation should focus not merely on banning unhealthy foods but on creating a healthier food ecosystem around schools. She suggested that vendors near school gates be encouraged to gradually shift to selling seasonal fruits, tender coconut water, roasted gram, peanuts, sprouts, sweet corn, buttermilk and homemade snacks.

She proposed recognising vendors who consistently sell nutritious and affordable food through incentives such as easier licensing, lower fees, certificates signboards, or a shout-out at school events and on social media, helping these vendors attract more customers.

Schools could also modify popular foods by replacing refined flour with whole wheat or millets, reducing sugar and salt, and offering healthier beverages such as lemon water, lassi and tender coconut water. Parents could be involved through healthy lunchbox guidance and menu suggestions.
Also Read | Bengaluru study finds children in urban slums suffering from ‘moderate child food poverty’ despite government nutrition programmes
How will the advisory be enforced?

Responsibility for implementation has been shared among schools, food business operators and the Food Safety Department. School managements are expected to ensure compliance within their campuses, educate students about healthy eating and display notices prohibiting HFSS foods. Food vendors near schools must comply with food safety regulations, while Food Safety Officers have been directed to conduct inspections and initiate action against violations under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

Dr. Nagesh said the success of the advisory would depend on effective implementation. Authorities should clearly define what constitutes junk or HFSS food to avoid confusion among schools and vendors, undertake regular inspections and ensure that healthy alternatives are both available and affordable. Nutrition education involving parents, teachers and school management should accompany enforcement so that children learn to read food labels and make informed food choices.

Public health doctor and researcher Sylvia Karpagam welcomed the government’s decision to regulate junk food around schools but argued that implementation should distinguish between healthy and unhealthy fats rather than creating a blanket perception against oils. “Healthy fats are important, especially for children. The concern is with unhealthy fats such as refined seed oils and trans fats,” she said.

She also argued that the government’s broader nutrition policy should come under scrutiny. According to Dr. Karpagam, if the State is serious about improving child nutrition, it should also examine the nutritional quality of food served under government-supported meal programmes. She questioned the use of defatted soya chunks in meals supplied by centralised organisations, arguing that such products are highly processed after oil extraction and therefore should also be assessed from a nutrition perspective.
Comment | End the free rein of junk food advertising in India
Will banning junk food alone improve children’s health?

Nutrition experts caution that restricting access to unhealthy food is only one part of improving children’s diets. Eating habits are influenced by families, affordability, food availability, advertising, school meals and broader public policies. Long-term improvements require nutrition education, greater parental awareness, regular physical activity and responsible food marketing.

Dr. Raj said restricting HFSS foods near schools was “a great start”, but lasting change would require schools, parents, vendors, health authorities and communities to work together. Alongside restrictions, healthy, affordable and appealing food should be made readily available, while children should be encouraged to remain physically active and reduce screen time.

Dr. Karpagam argued that improving children’s nutrition would also require changes in school meal policies. She called for greater use of fresh, minimally processed foods, school-based meals that include eggs, and a review of dietary restrictions that, in her view, reduce the nutritional quality and acceptability of meals. Referring to the exclusion of ingredients such as onion and garlic in some institutional meals, she said children may consume less food if they find it unpalatable, affecting both calorie and nutrient intake. She also criticised the continued reliance on what she described as “caste-based organisations” for centralised meal preparation, saying nutrition policy should prioritise children’s dietary needs.

Echoing the need for sustained implementation, Dr. Nagesh said the advisory should not be viewed merely as a restriction but as an investment in the health of the next generation. If implemented consistently, alongside nutrition education and healthier food choices, it could help reduce childhood obesity and enable children to grow into healthier adults.

title: If you go on a trip to the moon, who will look after your health?

content.value: What seemed impossible barely 60 years ago -- getting humans to the moon -- has not just turned into reality, it has transformed our understanding of the cosmos, with decades of research and missions into space bringing to us new, exciting and unthought-of information about our universe. And so, it is quite possible that over the next few decades, a visit to the moon for many -- like a visit to a neighbouring State -- might not be in the realm of fantasy.  The United States space agency, NASA, in fact, has plans for human presence on the moon from 2032 onwards. But this raises a crucial question: what will healthcare look like on the moon?
The lunar surroundings

The moon is not designed for human life.  Extreme environmental hazards include no atmosphere, meaning a base would face direct solar and cosmic radiation and micro meteoroid impacts. Gravity would be 1/6<sup>th</sup> of that on earth. Radiation, dust and temperature swings -- on the moon it can range from  121°C to -246 C would affect human health.
